money-school.fl-biz-1.q2.e: False. Profit measures performance over a period, while cash is whether money is in the account today.

money-school.fl-biz-1.q3.p: A cafe sells each coffee for $4 with $1 of variable cost, and has $3,000 of fixed costs a month. How many coffees must it sell to break even?
money-school.fl-biz-1.q3.h: Gross profit per coffee must cover the fixed costs.
money-school.fl-biz-1.q3.e: Each coffee contributes $3, and $3,000 divided by $3 is 1,000 coffees.

money-school.fl-biz-1.q4.t: Bad timing: it can be paid in September but owe bills in July
money-school.fl-biz-1.q4.p: How can a business with good margins still fail?
money-school.fl-biz-1.q4.e: A business can be profitable on paper yet run out of cash if money arrives later than it must go out.

money-school.fl-biz-2.q1.p: Which statement is a snapshot of one instant, showing what a business owns and owes?
money-school.fl-biz-2.q1.h: The lesson compares it to a photograph.
money-school.fl-biz-2.q1.e: The balance sheet shows assets against liabilities and owner's equity at a single point in time.

money-school.fl-biz-2.q2.t: It touches at least two accounts so the books balance
money-school.fl-biz-2.q2.p: What does double-entry bookkeeping require of every transaction?
money-school.fl-biz-2.q2.e: Every transaction touches at least two accounts, so disagreement between the sides signals an error.

money-school.fl-biz-2.q3.p: A business has revenue of $10,000, cost of goods of $4,000 and expenses of $3,000. What is its profit on the income statement?
money-school.fl-biz-2.q3.h: Revenue minus cost of goods minus expenses.

money-school.fl-biz-2.q4.t: It makes books unreliable and taxes painful, and can risk liability protection
money-school.fl-biz-2.q4.p: Why does the lesson say you should never mix personal and business money?
money-school.fl-biz-2.q4.h: Think about the books and the legal structure.
money-school.fl-biz-2.q4.e: Commingled funds make books unreliable and can put the limited-liability protection of a company at risk.

money-school.fl-biz-3.q1.t: Total sales and marketing spend divided by customers gained
money-school.fl-biz-3.q1.p: How is customer acquisition cost calculated in the lesson?
money-school.fl-biz-3.q1.h: It is spend per customer won.
money-school.fl-biz-3.q1.e: Acquisition cost is total sales and marketing spend divided by the number of customers gained.

money-school.fl-biz-3.q2.p: What does equity cost a business owner, as described in the lesson?
money-school.fl-biz-3.q2.e: Equity costs ownership permanently, including a share of everything the business later becomes, whereas debt costs interest.

money-school.fl-biz-3.q3.p: A business spends $3,000 on marketing and gains 50 customers. Each customer has a lifetime value of $180. What is the lifetime value to acquisition cost ratio?
money-school.fl-biz-3.q3.e: Acquisition cost is $60 per customer, and $180 divided by $60 gives a 3 to 1 ratio, which the lesson cites as a common target.

money-school.fl-biz-3.q4.t: Each new customer loses money, so growth makes the problem larger, faster
money-school.fl-biz-3.q4.p: Why can growth make a business worse if lifetime value does not exceed acquisition cost?
money-school.fl-biz-3.q4.h: Think about what happens when every customer loses money.
money-school.fl-biz-3.q4.e: If each customer costs more to win than they return, adding more customers scales the loss.

econ-school.ec-scar-1.q1.t: Wants exceeding the means available to satisfy them
econ-school.ec-scar-1.q1.p: What is scarcity, as the lesson defines it?
econ-school.ec-scar-1.q1.h: It is a permanent background condition, not a market event.
econ-school.ec-scar-1.q1.e: Scarcity is the condition in which wants exceed available means, and it applies to every society, including the wealthy.

econ-school.ec-scar-1.q2.p: A billionaire does not face scarcity, because scarcity only affects the poor.
econ-school.ec-scar-1.q2.h: Think about the hours in a day.
econ-school.ec-scar-1.q2.e: The lesson says a billionaire still faces scarcity because a day contains twenty-four hours and attention cannot be bought without limit.

econ-school.ec-scar-1.q3.t: The $50 he could have earned mowing lawns
econ-school.ec-scar-1.q3.p: Dev has a free Saturday afternoon. He could mow lawns for $50, volunteer at a shelter, or watch a game. He chooses the game, and mowing was his next-best option. What is the opportunity cost of watching the game?
econ-school.ec-scar-1.q3.h: Opportunity cost is the best alternative given up.
econ-school.ec-scar-1.q3.e: Opportunity cost is the best alternative not taken, which here is mowing lawns for $50.

econ-school.ec-scar-1.q4.t: Whatever else those resources would have produced
econ-school.ec-scar-1.q4.p: The lesson says money is only a way of keeping score. What does this imply about the real cost of a government building a hospital?
econ-school.ec-scar-1.q4.h: The real cost is the road not taken.
econ-school.ec-scar-1.q4.e: Because resources are scarce, the true cost of the hospital is the best other use of those resources.

econ-school.ec-scar-2.q1.t: They should not influence the decision at all
econ-school.ec-scar-2.q1.p: What does the lesson say about sunk costs when making a new decision?
econ-school.ec-scar-2.q1.h: No future choice can undo them.
econ-school.ec-scar-2.q1.e: Sunk costs are already spent and unrecoverable, so they should not affect the next decision.

econ-school.ec-scar-2.q2.t: As long as the additional benefit of one more exceeds the additional cost of one more
econ-school.ec-scar-2.q2.p: According to the marginal rule, when should you keep doing something?
econ-school.ec-scar-2.q2.h: The rule compares one more unit, not the total.
econ-school.ec-scar-2.q2.e: The rule is to continue while the marginal benefit exceeds the marginal cost and to stop when they meet.

econ-school.ec-scar-2.q3.t: Leave, because the ticket money is gone either way and only the next ninety minutes are at stake
econ-school.ec-scar-2.q3.p: You paid for a film ticket and after thirty minutes you are bored. You have a better use for the next ninety minutes. What does marginal thinking suggest?
econ-school.ec-scar-2.q3.h: The ticket money is gone whichever you pick.
econ-school.ec-scar-2.q3.e: The ticket cost is sunk, so the only live question is how best to spend the remaining time.

econ-school.ec-scar-2.q4.t: Price reflects the value of one more unit, and water is abundant while diamonds are scarce
econ-school.ec-scar-2.q4.p: How does marginal thinking explain why water is cheap while diamonds are dear?
econ-school.ec-scar-2.q4.h: Nobody chooses between all the water and all the diamonds.
econ-school.ec-scar-2.q4.e: Price reflects the value of one more unit in actual circumstances: an extra litre of water is worth little, an extra diamond much.

econ-school.ec-mkt-1.q1.t: The price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied
econ-school.ec-mkt-1.q1.p: What is equilibrium in a market?
econ-school.ec-mkt-1.q1.h: It is where the two curves cross.
econ-school.ec-mkt-1.q1.e: Equilibrium is the price at which the quantity buyers want equals the quantity sellers want to supply.

econ-school.ec-mkt-1.q2.p: Which of these shifts the whole demand curve rather than moving along it?
econ-school.ec-mkt-1.q2.h: The good's own price only moves you along the curve.
econ-school.ec-mkt-1.q2.e: Incomes, tastes, related prices and similar factors shift the entire demand curve, while the good's own price moves you along it.

econ-school.ec-mkt-1.q3.t: The supply curve shifted and quantity demanded rose along the demand curve
econ-school.ec-mkt-1.q3.p: A new technology cuts the cost of making bicycles, the price falls, and more bicycles are bought. What happened in the model?
econ-school.ec-mkt-1.q3.h: Separate a shift of a curve from a movement along one.
econ-school.ec-mkt-1.q3.e: Technology shifts supply, and the lower price moves buyers along the unchanged demand curve, raising quantity demanded.

econ-school.ec-mkt-1.q4.t: No one is in charge: buyers and sellers each respond to prices and the outcome emerges
econ-school.ec-mkt-1.q4.p: What makes the supply and demand model powerful according to the lesson?
econ-school.ec-mkt-1.q4.h: Nobody decides how many loaves a city needs.
econ-school.ec-mkt-1.q4.e: Coordination emerges as sellers and buyers observe prices, though the lesson notes it can fail through market power, missing information or third-party costs.

econ-school.ec-mkt-2.q1.p: Which of these is NOT one of the three jobs a price does, according to the lesson?
econ-school.ec-mkt-2.q1.h: The three are about information, behaviour and allocation.
econ-school.ec-mkt-2.q1.e: The lesson says price signals, incentivises and rations; it does not guarantee fairness, since willingness to pay is not the same as need.

econ-school.ec-mkt-2.q2.p: Economists broadly agree that a binding price cap reduces supply and increases demand, producing a shortage.
econ-school.ec-mkt-2.q2.h: The lesson says the mechanism is broadly agreed even if the policy judgement is not.
econ-school.ec-mkt-2.q2.e: A cap suppresses the signal and the incentive, so less is supplied, more is demanded, and the shortage is rationed some other way.

econ-school.ec-mkt-2.q3.t: The cap suppressed the price signal and incentive, so the shortage was rationed by other means
econ-school.ec-mkt-2.q3.p: A city caps rents below the market level. A year later there are long waiting lists and under-the-table payments. Which explanation fits the lesson?
econ-school.ec-mkt-2.q3.h: Look at what a suppressed price stops doing.
econ-school.ec-mkt-2.q3.e: The cap held the price down, reducing supply and increasing demand, so queues, waiting lists and black markets did the rationing.

econ-school.ec-mkt-2.q4.t: Whether the distributional gain is worth the efficiency loss, which is partly a question of values
econ-school.ec-mkt-2.q4.p: Where does the lesson say the genuine disagreement among economists lies on price controls?
econ-school.ec-mkt-2.q4.h: The mechanism is agreed; the weighing is not.
econ-school.ec-mkt-2.q4.e: Economists agree on the mechanism but disagree in good faith about when the distributional gain is worth the efficiency loss, which depends on values.

econ-school.ec-macro-1.q1.t: The market value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a period
econ-school.ec-macro-1.q1.p: How does the lesson define gross domestic product?
econ-school.ec-macro-1.q1.h: Pay attention to the words final, produced within, and market value.
econ-school.ec-macro-1.q1.e: GDP is the market value of final goods and services produced within a country in a period.

econ-school.ec-macro-1.q2.t: To avoid counting the same output twice, such as flour and then bread
econ-school.ec-macro-1.q2.p: Why does GDP count only final goods and services?
econ-school.ec-macro-1.q2.h: Flour in bread is the lesson's example.
econ-school.ec-macro-1.q2.e: Excluding intermediate goods prevents double counting, for example the flour in bread.

econ-school.ec-macro-1.q3.t: It rises through rebuilding, even though wellbeing fell
econ-school.ec-macro-1.q3.p: A hurricane destroys many homes and rebuilding spending surges. What does the lesson say happens to GDP?
econ-school.ec-macro-1.q3.h: GDP counts spending on harm repair as production.
econ-school.ec-macro-1.q3.e: GDP counts rebuilding as production, which shows why it is a poor measure of wellbeing on its own.

econ-school.ec-macro-1.q4.t: GDP omits unpaid work, so growth can appear when work simply moves from home to market
econ-school.ec-macro-1.q4.p: Parents who cared for their children at home start paying for daycare, and measured GDP rises. What limitation does this illustrate?
econ-school.ec-macro-1.q4.h: Think about what GDP leaves out entirely.
econ-school.ec-macro-1.q4.e: GDP misses unpaid work such as care, so a country can seem to grow when work shifts from home to market.

econ-school.ec-macro-2.q1.p: What does core inflation leave out?
econ-school.ec-macro-2.q1.e: Core inflation strips out food and energy because their volatility can obscure the underlying trend.

econ-school.ec-macro-2.q2.t: A basket of goods a typical household buys
econ-school.ec-macro-2.q2.p: Inflation is measured by tracking the cost over time of what?
econ-school.ec-macro-2.q2.h: The index is published monthly and free.
econ-school.ec-macro-2.q2.e: The consumer price index tracks the cost of a basket of goods a typical household buys.

econ-school.ec-macro-2.q3.p: A supply disruption makes energy and shipping more expensive, and prices across the economy rise as firms pass on the costs. Which mechanism is this?
econ-school.ec-macro-2.q3.e: Cost-push inflation arises when production costs such as energy, wages or supply disruption rise and prices follow.

econ-school.ec-macro-2.q4.t: It erodes savings and favours borrowers, since debts are repaid in cheaper money
econ-school.ec-macro-2.q4.p: Why does the lesson say inflation redistributes without anyone deciding to?
econ-school.ec-macro-2.q4.h: Think about who owes and who is owed.
econ-school.ec-macro-2.q4.e: Inflation erodes savings and fixed incomes and favours borrowers over lenders because debts are repaid in cheaper money.

econ-school.ec-macro-3.q1.p: Which condition for being counted as unemployed does the lesson say surprises people most?
econ-school.ec-macro-3.q1.h: Those who give up searching drop out of the count.
econ-school.ec-macro-3.q1.e: To be counted you must be without work, available and actively looking, and the last condition is the one that surprises people.

econ-school.ec-macro-3.q2.p: Which kind of unemployment is a mismatch between skills or locations and available work?
econ-school.ec-macro-3.q2.h: It responds to training and mobility.
econ-school.ec-macro-3.q2.e: Structural unemployment is a mismatch between skills or locations and available work, and it responds to training and mobility.

econ-school.ec-macro-3.q3.t: It can fall, because he leaves the labour force and is no longer counted
econ-school.ec-macro-3.q3.p: A worker gives up searching after a year without success. What happens to the headline unemployment rate?
econ-school.ec-macro-3.q3.h: He is no longer actively looking.
econ-school.ec-macro-3.q3.e: Discouraged workers leave the labour force and stop being counted as unemployed, so the rate can fall while the situation worsens.

econ-school.ec-macro-3.q4.t: More people are working or looking in the first case, whereas in the second the rate may fall because people left the labour force
econ-school.ec-macro-3.q4.p: Why is a falling unemployment rate with rising participation a different story from a falling rate with falling participation?
econ-school.ec-macro-3.q4.h: Ask who is no longer counted in the second case.
econ-school.ec-macro-3.q4.e: The lesson says the headline must be read with participation: a falling rate with falling participation can reflect people leaving the labour force.

econ-school.ec-money-1.q1.p: Which of these is NOT one of the three jobs of money in the lesson?
econ-school.ec-money-1.q1.h: The three are exchange, comparing values, and carrying value forward.
econ-school.ec-money-1.q1.e: Money is a medium of exchange, a unit of account and a store of value.

econ-school.ec-money-1.q2.p: Modern money is fiat, meaning it is backed by a commodity such as gold.
econ-school.ec-money-1.q2.h: Fiat money has no intrinsic worth.
econ-school.ec-money-1.q2.e: Fiat money is not backed by a commodity; it works because it is generally accepted.

econ-school.ec-money-1.q3.p: A baker wants shoes, but the shoemaker does not want bread. Which problem of barter is this?
econ-school.ec-money-1.q3.h: You must find someone who has what you want and wants what you have.
econ-school.ec-money-1.q3.e: Barter requires a double coincidence of wants, which money removes by serving as a medium of exchange.

econ-school.ec-money-1.q4.t: The loan and a matching deposit come into existence together, creating money
econ-school.ec-money-1.q4.p: According to the lesson, what happens when a bank makes a loan?
econ-school.ec-money-1.q4.h: Most modern money is bank deposits.
econ-school.ec-money-1.q4.e: The lesson says most money is deposits and is created when banks lend, with the loan and deposit appearing together.

econ-school.ec-money-2.q1.p: What is a central bank's main lever, according to the lesson?
econ-school.ec-money-2.q1.h: It is a price of borrowing.
econ-school.ec-money-2.q1.e: The main lever is a short-term policy interest rate.

econ-school.ec-money-2.q2.t: The action that cools inflation also cools employment
econ-school.ec-money-2.q2.p: What trade-off sits at the centre of monetary policy?
econ-school.ec-money-2.q2.h: Raising the rate slows hiring too.
econ-school.ec-money-2.q2.e: The same action that eases inflation also slows hiring, so the central bank balances rather than solves.

econ-school.ec-money-2.q3.t: Dearer borrowing, less spending, slower demand, easing prices and slower hiring
econ-school.ec-money-2.q3.p: A central bank raises its policy rate. Which sequence does the lesson describe?
econ-school.ec-money-2.q3.h: Follow the chain one step at a time.
econ-school.ec-money-2.q3.e: A higher rate makes borrowing dearer, cutting financed spending and demand, which eases price pressure and slows hiring.

econ-school.ec-money-2.q4.t: Because expectations matter: if people expect high inflation they behave in ways that produce it
econ-school.ec-money-2.q4.p: Why do central banks talk so much and treat credibility as an asset?
econ-school.ec-money-2.q4.h: Think about how beliefs feed into behaviour.
econ-school.ec-money-2.q4.e: Policy works with long lags and expectations matter, so credibility helps anchor behaviour that affects inflation.

econ-school.ec-data-1.q1.p: Police spending and crime move together. The possibility that crime raises police spending, rather than the reverse, is called what?
econ-school.ec-data-1.q1.h: The causal arrow points the other way.
econ-school.ec-data-1.q1.e: In reverse causation B causes A rather than A causing B.

econ-school.ec-data-1.q2.t: A third factor that causes both of the things being compared
econ-school.ec-data-1.q2.h: It is the usual culprit in the lesson.
econ-school.ec-data-1.q2.e: A confounder is a third factor C that causes both A and B, creating a misleading link between them.

econ-school.ec-data-1.q3.t: Hot weather is a confounder driving both
econ-school.ec-data-1.q3.p: Ice cream sales and drownings both rise in summer. What is the most likely explanation?
econ-school.ec-data-1.q3.e: Hot weather raises both swimming and ice cream sales, so the shared cause explains the correlation.

econ-school.ec-data-1.q4.p: A study cannot say how it estimated what would have happened otherwise. According to the lesson, what is its headline finding?
econ-school.ec-data-1.q4.h: Causal claims depend on the counterfactual.
econ-school.ec-data-1.q4.e: Without an estimate of the counterfactual, the study can show only a correlation, however it is presented.

econ-school.ec-data-2.q1.p: Which set of series makes up the lesson's core panel for a dashboard?
econ-school.ec-data-2.q1.h: GDP, inflation, unemployment and the policy rate are among them.
econ-school.ec-data-2.q1.e: The core panel covers output, prices, labour and money, with distribution as an optional addition.

econ-school.ec-data-2.q2.p: Published economic data is never revised after its first release.
econ-school.ec-data-2.q2.h: The lesson tells you to state your uncertainty.
econ-school.ec-data-2.q2.e: The lesson notes that data is revised, sometimes substantially, so forecasts need an error band.

econ-school.ec-data-2.q3.t: Identify it as a tension, say what each series does not show, and commit to a reading
econ-school.ec-data-2.q3.p: Your dashboard shows unemployment falling while participation also falls. What should you do?
econ-school.ec-data-2.q3.h: The lesson says there is almost always a tension to name.
econ-school.ec-data-2.q3.e: The lesson says a dashboard must put series in context, say what they do not tell you, and name the tension between them.

econ-school.ec-data-2.q4.t: Without labelled axes and cited sources, the reader cannot check it
econ-school.ec-data-2.q4.p: Why does the lesson say an unlabelled chart is an assertion?
econ-school.ec-data-2.q4.h: Think about what a reader can verify.
econ-school.ec-data-2.q4.e: Labelling axes and citing sources lets readers verify the claim, otherwise the chart is just something to take on trust.

econ-school.ec-sys-1.q1.p: On what do living standards depend in the long run, according to the lesson?
econ-school.ec-sys-1.q1.h: Everything else is distribution of a total.
econ-school.ec-sys-1.q1.e: The lesson says long-run living standards depend on productivity, and everything else is the distribution of what productivity sets.

econ-school.ec-sys-1.q2.p: Which channel does the lesson call the largest contributor to productivity over long periods?
econ-school.ec-sys-1.q2.e: Technology, meaning better methods, is the largest contributor over long periods.

econ-school.ec-sys-1.q3.p: An economy growing at 2 percent a year doubles living standards in about thirty-five years. About how long does one growing at 1 percent take?
econ-school.ec-sys-1.q3.h: Halving the growth rate roughly doubles the time.
econ-school.ec-sys-1.q3.e: The lesson says doubling takes about thirty-five years at 2 percent and about seventy at 1 percent.

econ-school.ec-sys-1.q4.t: Which institutions matter most, in what order, and whether they can be transplanted
econ-school.ec-sys-1.q4.p: What does the lesson say is genuinely contested about institutions and growth?
econ-school.ec-sys-1.q4.h: Economics knows more about correlates than about how to produce growth on demand.
econ-school.ec-sys-1.q4.e: The lesson says institutions matter but which ones, in what order, and whether they can be transplanted remain open questions.

econ-school.ec-sys-2.q1.p: What is the term for costs or benefits that fall on third parties?
econ-school.ec-sys-2.q1.e: Externalities are costs or benefits falling on third parties, such as pollution or vaccination effects.

econ-school.ec-sys-2.q2.p: Which two features define a public good in the lesson?
econ-school.ec-sys-2.q2.h: No one can be charged, and one person's use does not use it up.
econ-school.ec-sys-2.q2.e: Public goods are non-excludable and non-rival, so private actors will not fund them because no one can be charged.

econ-school.ec-sys-2.q3.p: A regulator mostly staffed by former executives starts making rules that protect the industry rather than the public. Which government failure is this?
econ-school.ec-sys-2.q3.h: The regulated industry ends up steering the regulator.
econ-school.ec-sys-2.q3.e: The lesson names capture: regulators can be captured by the industries they oversee.

econ-school.ec-sys-2.q4.t: What is the specific failure, what is the proposed remedy, what is that remedy's own failure mode, and is the improvement worth it
econ-school.ec-sys-2.q4.p: What does the lesson say is the honest question about markets and governments?
econ-school.ec-sys-2.q4.h: It is never an abstract choice between market and state.
econ-school.ec-sys-2.q4.e: The lesson says the comparison of a specific failure, its remedy and the remedy's own failure mode is real economics and does not resolve into a slogan.

real-estate-school.re-prop-1.q1.t: A bundle of rights that can be separated and sold on their own
real-estate-school.re-prop-1.q1.p: How do lawyers describe what it means to own land?
real-estate-school.re-prop-1.q1.h: The lesson uses the image of sticks.
real-estate-school.re-prop-1.q1.e: Ownership is a bundle of rights such as possession, use, exclusion and transfer, each of which can be separated.

real-estate-school.re-prop-1.q2.t: Government power to tax and to regulate land use
real-estate-school.re-prop-1.q2.p: Which two limits does the lesson say sit above the whole bundle of rights?
real-estate-school.re-prop-1.q2.h: Zoning and building codes are examples of one of them.
real-estate-school.re-prop-1.q2.e: Government retains the power to tax land and to regulate what may be done on it.

real-estate-school.re-prop-1.q3.t: Rights in the bundle can be separated and held by different parties
real-estate-school.re-prop-1.q3.p: A mining company holds the mineral rights under a house, and the homeowner holds everything above. What does this show?
real-estate-school.re-prop-1.q3.h: Think about sticks held by different people.
real-estate-school.re-prop-1.q3.e: The lesson uses this example of separate sticks in the bundle held by different holders.

real-estate-school.re-prop-1.q4.t: Everything later in the ladder is a calculation performed on those parcel facts
real-estate-school.re-prop-1.q4.p: Why does the lesson say reading a parcel record comes before negotiating or financing?
real-estate-school.re-prop-1.q4.h: Consider what later calculations depend on.
real-estate-school.re-prop-1.q4.e: Title, size, assessment, zoning and recorded claims are the facts on which every later calculation is built.

real-estate-school.re-prop-2.q1.t: The large transaction costs of buying and selling
real-estate-school.re-prop-2.q1.p: Which cost drives the rule that ownership beats renting only over a long enough holding period?
real-estate-school.re-prop-2.q1.h: They typically take several percent of the price each way.
real-estate-school.re-prop-2.q1.e: Round-trip transaction costs mean a short holding period often loses more than it gains.

real-estate-school.re-prop-2.q2.p: True or false: The lesson says renting is simply throwing money away.
real-estate-school.re-prop-2.q2.h: The lesson calls that received advice wrong.
real-estate-school.re-prop-2.q2.e: False. Renting buys shelter, mobility and a known cost; it is a different cost structure, not wasted money.

real-estate-school.re-prop-2.q3.p: A buyer puts $20,000 down on a $200,000 property (10%). If the property value rises 10%, roughly what gain does that represent on the money the buyer put in, ignoring costs?
real-estate-school.re-prop-2.q3.h: Compare the $ gain in value to the deposit.
real-estate-school.re-prop-2.q3.e: A 10% rise is $20,000, equal to the $20,000 deposit, so the gain on the buyer's own money is 100%.

real-estate-school.re-prop-2.q4.t: Leverage magnifies losses as well as gains, and the debt stays even if value falls
real-estate-school.re-prop-2.q4.p: What does the lesson mean when it says leverage is "never the free accelerator it is sold as"?
real-estate-school.re-prop-2.q4.h: A ten-percent fall with a ten-percent deposit.
real-estate-school.re-prop-2.q4.e: A ten-percent fall can wipe out a ten-percent deposit entirely while the debt remains unchanged.

real-estate-school.re-agency-1.q1.t: Loyalty, confidentiality, disclosure, obedience within the law and accounting for money held
real-estate-school.re-agency-1.q1.p: Which set lists duties the lesson says an agent owes?
real-estate-school.re-agency-1.q1.h: Agency is a legal relationship with duties attached.
real-estate-school.re-agency-1.q1.e: The lesson names loyalty, confidentiality, disclosure, lawful obedience and accounting as an agent's duties.

real-estate-school.re-agency-1.q2.t: One agent or firm representing both sides of a transaction
real-estate-school.re-agency-1.q2.h: It dilutes duties that would otherwise be undivided.
real-estate-school.re-agency-1.q2.e: Dual agency is when one agent or firm represents both buyer and seller, which is permitted in some places and banned in others.

real-estate-school.re-agency-1.q3.t: The agent owes loyalty to the seller, so this may lawfully be passed on
real-estate-school.re-agency-1.q3.p: At an open house a buyer tells the seller's agent, "I could go up to $350,000 if I really love it." What does the lesson imply?
real-estate-school.re-agency-1.q3.h: Ask to whom the duties run.
real-estate-school.re-agency-1.q3.e: A seller's agent owes duties to the seller, so information a buyer volunteers about budget can lawfully be shared.

real-estate-school.re-agency-1.q4.t: It costs nothing and changes what you can safely say
real-estate-school.re-agency-1.q4.p: Why does the lesson recommend asking "who do you represent?" before discussing your finances?
real-estate-school.re-agency-1.q4.h: Think about risk versus cost of asking.
real-estate-school.re-agency-1.q4.e: Knowing whom the agent serves tells you what information is safe to share, and asking is free.

real-estate-school.re-agency-2.q1.p: Which two forms did US regulators standardise for mortgage disclosure?
real-estate-school.re-agency-2.q1.h: One comes after application and one before closing.
real-estate-school.re-agency-2.q1.e: The Loan Estimate and the Closing Disclosure were standardised so borrowers could compare offers.

real-estate-school.re-agency-2.q2.p: How long before closing does the Closing Disclosure arrive, according to the lesson?
real-estate-school.re-agency-2.q2.h: It is a short window to compare against the Estimate.
real-estate-school.re-agency-2.q2.e: The lesson says it arrives three days before closing so you can compare it with the Loan Estimate and ask questions.

real-estate-school.re-agency-2.q3.p: Lender A offers a lower interest rate than Lender B but charges much higher fees. Which number does the lesson say folds fees into the rate so you can compare fairly?
real-estate-school.re-agency-2.q3.h: It appears on page three of the Loan Estimate.
real-estate-school.re-agency-2.q3.e: The annual percentage rate folds fees into the rate, so a low rate with high fees stops looking cheap.

real-estate-school.re-agency-2.q4.t: To show where negotiation is possible
real-estate-school.re-agency-2.q4.p: Why does page two split closing costs into services you can shop for and those you cannot?
real-estate-school.re-agency-2.q4.h: The distinction exists for the borrower's benefit.
real-estate-school.re-agency-2.q4.e: The lesson says this split tells you exactly where negotiation is possible.

real-estate-school.re-agency-3.q1.p: Which of these is a protected class listed in the lesson's description of the Fair Housing Act?
real-estate-school.re-agency-3.q1.e: The Act covers race, colour, religion, sex, national origin, familial status and disability.

real-estate-school.re-agency-3.q2.t: Grading neighbourhoods by racial composition and withholding mortgage insurance from those marked hazardous
real-estate-school.re-agency-3.q2.p: What is redlining, as described in the lesson?
real-estate-school.re-agency-3.q2.h: It was federal policy for decades.
real-estate-school.re-agency-3.q2.e: Redlining graded neighbourhoods by racial makeup and withheld mortgage insurance from those it marked as hazardous.

real-estate-school.re-agency-3.q3.p: An agent shows a family only homes in one part of town and avoids showing them homes elsewhere. Which practice from the lesson is this?
real-estate-school.re-agency-3.q3.h: It involves directing buyers toward certain neighbourhoods.
real-estate-school.re-agency-3.q3.e: Showing buyers only certain neighbourhoods is steering, one of the modern forms of violation the lesson lists.

real-estate-school.re-agency-3.q4.t: It lets you apply criteria identically and demonstrate that you did
real-estate-school.re-agency-3.q4.p: Why does the lesson recommend writing criteria down in advance?
real-estate-school.re-agency-3.q4.e: Written criteria help ensure identical application and provide evidence of it.

real-estate-school.re-val-1.q1.t: A property is worth roughly what similar properties recently sold for, adjusted for differences
real-estate-school.re-val-1.q1.p: What is the basic reasoning of the sales comparison approach?
real-estate-school.re-val-1.q1.e: The approach compares to similar recent sales and adjusts for differences.

real-estate-school.re-val-1.q2.p: True or false: Asking prices of listed properties count as evidence as strong as closed sales.
real-estate-school.re-val-1.q2.h: The lesson says asking prices are opinions.
real-estate-school.re-val-1.q2.e: False. Asking prices are opinions; closed sales are evidence.

real-estate-school.re-val-1.q3.p: A comparable sold for $300,000 and has an extra bathroom the subject lacks, which the market values at $10,000. What is the adjusted comparable price?
real-estate-school.re-val-1.q3.h: Adjust the comparable, not the subject.
real-estate-school.re-val-1.q3.e: You subtract $10,000 from the comparable to estimate its price without the bathroom, giving $290,000.

real-estate-school.re-val-1.q4.t: Because several adjusted comparables give several numbers and the appraiser reconciles them with written reasoning
real-estate-school.re-val-1.q4.p: Why does the lesson call valuation a supportable opinion rather than a calculation?
real-estate-school.re-val-1.q4.e: The final value requires weighing comparables, and the defensible opinion is the one whose reasoning is written down.

real-estate-school.re-val-2.q1.p: How is net operating income (NOI) turned into a value in the income approach?
real-estate-school.re-val-2.q1.e: Value is NOI divided by a capitalisation rate drawn from comparable sales.

real-estate-school.re-val-2.q2.p: Which item is NOT an operating expense when calculating NOI?
real-estate-school.re-val-2.q2.h: The lesson says it is about financing, not operating the property.
real-estate-school.re-val-2.q2.e: The lesson notes that mortgage payments and depreciation are not operating expenses.

real-estate-school.re-val-2.q3.p: A building has an NOI of $60,000 and the market cap rate is 6%. What is its value by the income approach?
real-estate-school.re-val-2.q3.h: Divide NOI by the cap rate as a decimal.

real-estate-school.re-val-2.q4.p: The lesson says valuing the same NOI at 6% rather than 5% gives about what change in value?
real-estate-school.re-val-2.q4.e: At 5% the multiple is 20 and at 6% it is about 16.7, roughly 17% lower, showing how sensitive value is to the cap rate.

real-estate-school.re-fin-1.q1.p: Which line item does the lesson say beginners almost always omit from a pro forma?
real-estate-school.re-fin-1.q1.h: Roofs and boilers fail on a schedule.
real-estate-school.re-fin-1.q1.e: A capital replacement reserve is commonly omitted, and a pro forma without one is simply wrong.

real-estate-school.re-fin-1.q2.p: What is NOI minus debt service called in the lesson?
real-estate-school.re-fin-1.q2.h: It is the money that reaches an owner.
real-estate-school.re-fin-1.q2.e: NOI minus debt service is cash flow before tax.

real-estate-school.re-fin-1.q3.p: A property has gross potential rent of $120,000, vacancy and credit loss of 5%, and operating expenses of $45,000. What is the NOI?
real-estate-school.re-fin-1.q3.h: Compute effective gross income first, then subtract expenses.
real-estate-school.re-fin-1.q3.e: Vacancy is $6,000, so effective gross income is $114,000, and minus $45,000 expenses leaves $69,000.

real-estate-school.re-fin-1.q4.t: Because every assumption is a guess, and testing reveals which one the deal actually depends on
real-estate-school.re-fin-1.q4.p: Why does the lesson say to test assumptions like rent growth and exit cap rate?
real-estate-school.re-fin-1.q4.h: The lesson contrasts analysis with wishful thinking.
real-estate-school.re-fin-1.q4.e: Sensitivity testing shows whether a deal is fragile and which assumption you are betting on.

real-estate-school.re-fin-2.q1.p: How is the capitalisation rate calculated?
real-estate-school.re-fin-2.q1.e: The cap rate is NOI divided by price, the property's unlevered yield.

real-estate-school.re-fin-2.q2.p: Which of the three measures accounts for timing and for the eventual sale?
real-estate-school.re-fin-2.q2.h: It is the discount rate at which all cash flows net to zero.
real-estate-school.re-fin-2.q2.e: IRR is the only one of the three that accounts for timing and the sale.

real-estate-school.re-fin-2.q3.p: A property has NOI of $100,000 and annual debt service of $80,000. What is the DSCR?
real-estate-school.re-fin-2.q3.h: Divide NOI by annual debt service.

real-estate-school.re-fin-2.q4.t: When you borrow at a rate above the property's unlevered yield
real-estate-school.re-fin-2.q4.p: When does leverage destroy return even though the property performs as expected?
real-estate-school.re-fin-2.q4.h: Positive leverage is the opposite case.
real-estate-school.re-fin-2.q4.e: Borrowing above the unlevered yield makes leverage negative and reduces return on equity.

real-estate-school.re-fin-3.q1.t: They distribute the large majority of taxable income to shareholders
real-estate-school.re-fin-3.q1.p: Why are REITs typically held for income?
real-estate-school.re-fin-3.q1.h: It is a requirement of the structure.
real-estate-school.re-fin-3.q1.e: REITs are required to distribute most of their taxable income, which is why investors hold them for income.

real-estate-school.re-fin-3.q2.p: In a CMBS structure, which tranches absorb losses first?
real-estate-school.re-fin-3.q2.h: They earn more because they take more risk.
real-estate-school.re-fin-3.q2.e: Junior tranches earn more and absorb losses first; senior tranches are paid first and absorb losses last.

real-estate-school.re-fin-3.q3.p: In a private deal, a waterfall pays limited partners a preferred return first, then returns capital, then splits remaining cash with the sponsor taking a disproportionate share. What is that extra share called?
real-estate-school.re-fin-3.q3.h: It rewards performance above a hurdle.
real-estate-school.re-fin-3.q3.e: The sponsor's disproportionate share above the hurdle is called the promote.

real-estate-school.re-fin-3.q4.t: The underlying loans were more correlated than the models assumed
real-estate-school.re-fin-3.q4.p: What lesson about model risk does the 2008 crisis illustrate in the text?
real-estate-school.re-fin-3.q4.h: Think about the assumption of independence between loans.
real-estate-school.re-fin-3.q4.e: The lesson says correlation between the underlying loans proved far higher than the models assumed.

real-estate-school.re-dev-1.q1.t: The share of the parcel that may sit under building
real-estate-school.re-dev-1.q1.e: Lot coverage caps the share of the parcel that may be covered by building.

real-estate-school.re-dev-1.q2.p: True or false: The lesson says Terra raises explicit blockers when it cannot be certain, rather than guessing.
real-estate-school.re-dev-1.q2.h: It cites missing dimensions and overlay districts.
real-estate-school.re-dev-1.q2.e: True. Missing dimensions, overlays, historic designations and planned developments produce blockers instead of a confident wrong answer.

real-estate-school.re-dev-1.q3.p: A parcel is 5,000 square feet and the zone has a floor area ratio of 2.0. How much floor area is permitted?
real-estate-school.re-dev-1.q3.e: 5,000 times 2.0 is 10,000 square feet of permitted floor area.

real-estate-school.re-dev-1.q4.t: Because someone will build on it
real-estate-school.re-dev-1.q4.p: Why is a zoning analysis that quietly assumes away what it does not know called worse than none?
real-estate-school.re-dev-1.q4.h: Think about how people use the result.
real-estate-school.re-dev-1.q4.e: The lesson says false confidence is dangerous because decisions and construction may rely on it.

real-estate-school.re-dev-2.q1.t: The most that could rationally be paid for the land given what can be built
real-estate-school.re-dev-2.q1.p: What does the residual land value method calculate?
real-estate-school.re-dev-2.q1.h: It runs backwards from the end value.
real-estate-school.re-dev-2.q1.e: It starts from gross development value and subtracts costs and profit to find the maximum land price.

real-estate-school.re-dev-2.q2.p: How does the lesson treat the developer's required profit?
real-estate-school.re-dev-2.q2.h: It is subtracted before finding the land value.
real-estate-school.re-dev-2.q2.e: The lesson treats required profit as a cost, not a residue.

real-estate-school.re-dev-2.q3.p: A scheme will be worth $5,000,000 when finished. Construction with contingency is $3,000,000, fees $300,000, finance $400,000 and required profit $700,000. What is the residual land value?
real-estate-school.re-dev-2.q3.h: Subtract all costs and profit from the end value.
real-estate-school.re-dev-2.q3.e: Costs and profit total $4,400,000 ($3,000,000 + $300,000 + $400,000 + $700,000), leaving $600,000 of residual land value.

real-estate-school.re-dev-2.q4.t: Land value is derived from what can be built, so allowing more increases the residual
real-estate-school.re-dev-2.q4.p: Why does the lesson say upzoning increases land value directly?
real-estate-school.re-dev-2.q4.h: Land value is not intrinsic in this method.
real-estate-school.re-dev-2.q4.e: Because land value is whatever remains after the scheme pays for itself, allowing a bigger scheme raises it.

real-estate-school.re-mkt-1.q1.p: Which indicator does the lesson call a genuine leading indicator of supply?
real-estate-school.re-mkt-1.q1.e: Because construction takes time, permits indicate what is coming.

real-estate-school.re-mkt-1.q2.t: The rate at which available space is taken up
real-estate-school.re-mkt-1.q2.h: It shows how quickly the market clears.
real-estate-school.re-mkt-1.q2.e: Absorption is the rate at which available space is taken up.

real-estate-school.re-mkt-1.q3.t: Households rather than people occupy dwellings
real-estate-school.re-mkt-1.q3.p: Why does the lesson say household formation matters more than raw population for housing demand?
real-estate-school.re-mkt-1.q3.h: Think about who occupies a dwelling.
real-estate-school.re-mkt-1.q3.e: Dwellings are occupied by households, so household formation drives demand more directly.

real-estate-school.re-mkt-1.q4.t: National headlines hide local patterns that matter for a specific decision
real-estate-school.re-mkt-1.q4.p: Why compare a submarket against its metro rather than a national average?
real-estate-school.re-mkt-1.q4.e: The lesson says national figures are close to useless for one building and that local comparisons reveal different propositions.

real-estate-school.re-mkt-2.q1.p: According to the lesson, which policy item most directly changes the income stream of a rental property?
real-estate-school.re-mkt-2.q1.e: The lesson says rent regulation changes the income stream directly.

real-estate-school.re-mkt-2.q2.t: Reduces net income and therefore value
real-estate-school.re-mkt-2.q2.p: What does the lesson say property tax does to value?
real-estate-school.re-mkt-2.q2.e: Property tax is a recurring cost that reduces net income and therefore value.

real-estate-school.re-mkt-2.q3.t: Using the seller's $2,000 as the tax expense
real-estate-school.re-mkt-2.q3.p: A seller pays $2,000 a year in property tax because assessments lag badly. After sale the building is reassessed so the new owner will pay $5,000. What underwriting mistake should an analyst avoid?
real-estate-school.re-mkt-2.q3.h: Which tax figure will the new owner actually pay?
real-estate-school.re-mkt-2.q3.e: The lesson warns that the tax a new buyer pays can differ sharply from the seller's, so using the old figure understates costs.

real-estate-school.re-mkt-2.q4.t: Treat it as an input with its own risk profile and test proposed changes
real-estate-school.re-mkt-2.q4.p: What does the lesson say is the professional habit regarding policy?
real-estate-school.re-mkt-2.q4.e: The lesson compares this to sensitivity testing applied to the political layer.

film-school.fs-found-1.q1.p: Which early filmmaker discovered the substitution splice, letting film show things that never happened?
film-school.fs-found-1.q1.h: He began as a stage magician.
film-school.fs-found-1.q1.e: Georges Melies, a stage magician, stopped the camera, changed the scene and restarted, which let film show impossible events.

film-school.fs-found-1.q2.p: You have footage of a thief climbing a fence and footage of a guard in an office across town. You cut between them as if simultaneous. Which early film pioneered this idea?
film-school.fs-found-1.q2.e: Porter cut between two lines of action in different places at the same time in The Great Train Robbery, and audiences followed it.

film-school.fs-found-1.q3.t: It proved the audience will assemble a coherent world from well-chosen fragments
film-school.fs-found-1.q3.p: Why does the lesson call Porter's discovery more radical than Melies's?
film-school.fs-found-1.q3.h: Think about what the audience is doing with the pieces.
film-school.fs-found-1.q3.e: Cross-cutting showed that viewers build a coherent world from fragments, which underlies every later editing technique.

film-school.fs-found-2.q1.p: Which shot size isolates a face and makes interiority the subject?
film-school.fs-found-2.q1.e: The close-up isolates the face, which is why cinema can show psychology in a way the stage cannot.

film-school.fs-found-2.q2.p: A scene needs the audience to feel that a character is dwarfed and just passing through a vast desert. Which shot size best does that?
film-school.fs-found-2.q2.h: The landscape should become the subject.
film-school.fs-found-2.q2.e: An extreme wide shot makes the landscape the subject and the character contingent and small within it.

film-school.fs-found-2.q3.p: Which answer to "why this size?" is a directing answer rather than a logistics answer?
film-school.fs-found-2.q3.h: Look for an answer about the audience's feeling.
film-school.fs-found-2.q3.e: A directing answer is about the audience's feeling; the others are about logistics or convenience.

film-school.fs-found-3.q1.t: Keep all cameras on one side of the line between two characters
film-school.fs-found-3.q1.p: What does the 180-degree rule tell you to do?
film-school.fs-found-3.q1.h: It involves an imaginary line between characters.
film-school.fs-found-3.q1.e: Staying on one side of the line keeps screen direction consistent so the geography does not collapse.

film-school.fs-found-3.q2.p: You cut between two shots of the same actor taken only about 10 degrees apart and it looks like a glitch. Which guideline explains this?
film-school.fs-found-3.q2.h: Think about how different the angle must be.
film-school.fs-found-3.q2.e: Cuts between angles less than roughly 30 degrees apart on the same subject read as a jump rather than a new view.

film-school.fs-found-3.q3.t: They deliberately refuse the smoothing contract of continuity
film-school.fs-found-3.q3.p: According to the lesson, why are Godard's jump cuts in Breathless NOT simply incompetence?
film-school.fs-found-3.q3.h: Conventions can be broken on purpose.
film-school.fs-found-3.q3.e: The lesson says continuity is a set of conventions; knowing them lets a filmmaker refuse them deliberately, as Godard did.

film-school.fs-found-4.q1.t: The total content of the frame: set, props, costume, light and staging
film-school.fs-found-4.q1.e: Mise-en-scene covers everything inside the frame, including set, props, costume, light and the placement of bodies.

film-school.fs-found-4.q2.p: True or false: a character who has been seated standing and crossing to the window mid-conversation can show a shift in power without any dialogue.
film-school.fs-found-4.q2.e: Changing the geometry of the scene is read by the audience as a change in the balance of power.

film-school.fs-found-4.q3.t: Someone else's choice, usually the location's
film-school.fs-found-4.q3.p: The lesson says that failing to make a mise-en-scene choice produces what?
film-school.fs-found-4.q3.e: Not choosing does not give neutrality; it hands the decision to whatever the location or others supply.

film-school.fs-found-5.q1.t: Sound that exists inside the story's world
film-school.fs-found-5.q1.h: A radio playing in the car is an example.
film-school.fs-found-5.q1.e: Diegetic sound exists within the story world, such as a radio in a car, unlike the score underneath it.

film-school.fs-found-5.q2.p: You have one day and one improvement to make before screening a rough film. Following the lesson, what should you improve?
film-school.fs-found-5.q2.e: Viewers read poor picture as a style and poor audio as incompetence, so sound gives the biggest gain.

film-school.fs-found-5.q3.t: They were scored live, and a different accompanist made it a different film
film-school.fs-found-5.q3.p: Why does the lesson say silent films prove the power of sound?
film-school.fs-found-5.q3.e: Silent films were never silent; with the images unchanged, a different live score gave a different experience.

film-school.fs-found-6.q1.p: Which two things can move in a shot?
film-school.fs-found-6.q1.e: The lesson states that only the subject and the camera can move, and expression comes from their relationship.

film-school.fs-found-6.q2.t: Hold still and let the world do the work
film-school.fs-found-6.q2.p: You are filming a physical-comedy stunt and want to prove it was real. What should the camera do?
film-school.fs-found-6.q2.e: Holding the camera shows the stunt was real; cutting inside the gag would destroy that proof.

film-school.fs-found-6.q3.t: To compress planes so layered motion stays legible
film-school.fs-found-6.q3.p: Why did Kurosawa use long lenses and multiple cameras when staging action in depth?
film-school.fs-found-6.q3.e: Long lenses compress the planes, so foreground, middle and background motion read as layered rather than chaotic.

film-school.fs-found-7.q1.t: A set of promises to the audience
film-school.fs-found-7.q1.p: According to the lesson, a genre is best described as what?
film-school.fs-found-7.q1.h: The lesson calls it an agreement.
film-school.fs-found-7.q1.e: Genre is a contract: it loads expectations about events, tone and ending before conscious thought.

film-school.fs-found-7.q2.t: Choose deliberately one promise to break
film-school.fs-found-7.q2.p: You are making a thriller and want it to feel fresh. What does the lesson recommend?
film-school.fs-found-7.q2.e: Breaking one promise on purpose feels fresh; breaking all causes incoherence and breaking none repeats what the audience has seen.

film-school.fs-found-7.q3.t: Real stakes sit under the banter, creating friction between registers
film-school.fs-found-7.q3.p: In His Girl Friday, which genre rule does the lesson say is broken, and with what effect?
film-school.fs-found-7.q3.e: The film lets the newspaper plot carry real stakes beneath the banter, and the clash of registers gives it charge.

film-school.fs-found-8.q1.t: Watch normally first, then return to key moments to find what produced the feeling
film-school.fs-found-8.q1.h: The first pass is for being affected.
film-school.fs-found-8.q1.e: On pass one you let the film work on you; on pass two you investigate the cause of each noted feeling.

film-school.fs-found-8.q2.t: Something earlier in the film that set it up
film-school.fs-found-8.q2.p: On a second pass you find a moment moved you, but the shot at that moment seems ordinary. What does the lesson suggest the cause probably is?
film-school.fs-found-8.q2.e: The lesson says the cause is usually not where the feeling is; often it was set up much earlier.

film-school.fs-found-8.q3.t: They are chosen as the one thing the character would have registered
film-school.fs-found-8.q3.p: Why do small details like a hand on a bannister read as poetry rather than clutter?
film-school.fs-found-8.q3.h: A detail is a claim about attention.
film-school.fs-found-8.q3.e: Selection makes a detail a claim about someone's attention, so it carries meaning instead of decoration.

film-school.fs-write-1.q1.p: Which of these is a subject rather than a premise?
film-school.fs-write-1.q1.h: A premise has a specific person and pressure.
film-school.fs-write-1.q1.e: The lesson says "a film about grief" is a subject with no engine; a premise has a specific person, situation and pressure.

film-school.fs-write-1.q2.p: Your logline says "or everything changes." Which part of the logline formula needs fixing?
film-school.fs-write-1.q2.h: It is vague about the cost of failure.
film-school.fs-write-1.q2.e: A vague stakes clause means you have not decided what failure costs.

film-school.fs-write-1.q3.t: Will he stop being the kind of man who needs it?
film-school.fs-write-1.q3.p: Which story question can fill a whole film rather than just an hour?
film-school.fs-write-1.q3.h: It is not the plot question.
film-school.fs-write-1.q3.e: The lesson says a question beyond the plot, about who the protagonist is, carries a full film.

film-school.fs-write-2.q1.t: Make the protagonist unable to go back
film-school.fs-write-2.q1.p: What is the first plot point supposed to do?
film-school.fs-write-2.q1.e: The first plot point is the moment the protagonist cannot return to their former life.

film-school.fs-write-2.q2.t: A real midpoint that flips the terms of the pursuit
film-school.fs-write-2.q2.p: Your Act Two feels like the first half repeated. What is probably missing?
film-school.fs-write-2.q2.e: Without a midpoint that flips the pursuit, Act Two becomes a first half followed by a repeat.

film-school.fs-write-2.q3.t: Attention drops sharply once the dramatic question is answered
film-school.fs-write-2.q3.p: Why does the lesson say the resolution after the climax must be brief?
film-school.fs-write-2.q3.e: After the climax answers the dramatic question, each extra minute is spent from a shrinking store of attention.

film-school.fs-write-3.q1.h: The schedule is built from it.
film-school.fs-write-3.q1.e: A slugline gives interior or exterior, location and time of day.

film-school.fs-write-3.q2.p: Which action line follows the lesson's rule about what the camera can record?
film-school.fs-write-3.q2.e: Action lines describe only what the camera can record; stopping buttering toast externalises the realisation.

film-school.fs-write-3.q3.t: Readers with many scripts use anything to shrink the pile
film-school.fs-write-3.q3.p: Why does the lesson say clean format is a competence signal?
film-school.fs-write-3.q3.h: Think about a reader with sixty scripts.
film-school.fs-write-3.q3.e: A reader with sixty scripts will use any excuse to reduce the pile, so sloppy format works against you.

film-school.fs-write-4.q1.p: What defines a scene according to the lesson?
film-school.fs-write-4.q1.h: Something is different at the bottom than at the top.
film-school.fs-write-4.q1.e: A scene is a unit of change: something true at the top is different by the bottom.

film-school.fs-write-4.q2.t: Treat it as a scene that does not exist yet and rework or cut it
film-school.fs-write-4.q2.p: An index card shows the same state at the top and bottom of a scene, though the dialogue is excellent. What should you do?
film-school.fs-write-4.q2.h: Matching top and bottom states are a warning.
film-school.fs-write-4.q2.e: If the two states match, no change occurs, so the scene is not functioning no matter how good the dialogue is.

film-school.fs-write-4.q3.t: So the audience completes the turn and tension is not released
film-school.fs-write-4.q3.p: Why does the lesson say to leave a scene one line before the turn is fully articulated?
film-school.fs-write-4.q3.e: Cutting out just before the turn lets the audience finish it and keeps the tension the scene built.

film-school.fs-write-5.q1.t: The meaning beneath what characters literally say
film-school.fs-write-5.q1.h: People rarely say what they want.
film-school.fs-write-5.q1.e: Subtext is the real meaning underneath, which is the ordinary condition of human conversation.

film-school.fs-write-5.q2.t: Write it with everyone speaking plainly, then rewrite as a conversation about something adjacent
film-school.fs-write-5.q2.p: You want subtext in a confrontation. What mechanical method does the lesson give?
film-school.fs-write-5.q2.e: The plain version reveals what the scene is about; the rewrite about something else is the actual scene.

film-school.fs-write-5.q3.p: You cover the character names and can't tell who speaks. What does that diagnose?
film-school.fs-write-5.q3.e: The lesson calls this the character-specificity test: failing it means you have written one voice with several names.

film-school.fs-write-6.q1.p: In the lesson's terms, what is a character's "want"?
film-school.fs-write-6.q1.e: The want is external, conscious and pursued; it generates plot, while the need generates meaning.

film-school.fs-write-6.q2.t: A lie that makes the sensible solution unavailable
film-school.fs-write-6.q2.p: Your protagonist would solve the film by minute twenty by simply being sensible. What is missing?
film-school.fs-write-6.q2.h: The wound produces a false rule.
film-school.fs-write-6.q2.e: The lie, extracted from a wound, explains why the character cannot take the sensible route.

film-school.fs-write-6.q3.t: Want and need collide, so having one means giving up the other
film-school.fs-write-6.q3.p: What makes the strongest ending according to the lesson?
film-school.fs-write-6.q3.e: The strongest climax forces a choice between keeping the lie to get the want or giving up the want to get the need.

film-school.fs-write-7.q1.t: Examining scene cards for missing state change, repeated beats and a missing midpoint
film-school.fs-write-7.q1.p: What is a structural pass in a rewrite?
film-school.fs-write-7.q1.h: It is done on index cards or a wall.
film-school.fs-write-7.q1.e: The structural pass looks across the whole script for scenes without change, repeated beats and absent midpoint.

film-school.fs-write-7.q2.t: Read it aloud, ideally with other people reading
film-school.fs-write-7.q2.p: During the dialogue pass, which is the best method?
film-school.fs-write-7.q2.e: Hearing it aloud exposes unspeakable, over-explained or repeated lines within seconds.

film-school.fs-write-7.q3.t: Take the diagnosis and discard the prescription
film-school.fs-write-7.q3.p: Someone tells you a scene is boring. According to the lesson, how should you treat the note?
film-school.fs-write-7.q3.h: Right about the symptom, wrong about the cause.
film-school.fs-write-7.q3.e: Notes are usually right about the symptom but wrong about the cause, so use the diagnosis and find your own fix.

film-school.fs-write-8.q1.t: Two instances set a pattern and the third breaks it
film-school.fs-write-8.q1.p: What is the rule of three?
film-school.fs-write-8.q1.h: Fewer than two gives no pattern.
film-school.fs-write-8.q1.e: Two instances establish a pattern and the third breaks it.

film-school.fs-write-8.q2.t: A cut introduces the possibility of a trick, which would kill the gag
film-school.fs-write-8.q2.p: You are staging a Keaton-style visual gag. Why should the camera not cut inside it?
film-school.fs-write-8.q2.e: A cut raises doubt that a trick was used, and the gag works because the physical logic was real.

film-school.fs-write-8.q3.t: The audience builds an expectation and the payoff violates it from an unseen angle
film-school.fs-write-8.q3.p: What does the lesson mean by saying the laugh is "the sound of a model being corrected"?
film-school.fs-write-8.q3.e: A joke builds an expectation the audience commits to, and the payoff corrects it from an angle the expectation hid.

film-school.fs-dir-1.q1.t: Arbitration of hundreds of questions consistently
film-school.fs-dir-1.q1.p: According to the lesson, what is the working account of a director's job?
film-school.fs-dir-1.q1.e: Directing is answering a stream of questions in a consistent way so the film feels like one object.

film-school.fs-dir-1.q2.t: A claim about the film, such as "loyalty to family is a kind of cowardice"
film-school.fs-dir-1.q2.p: It is mid-shoot and you must make quick decisions. Which one-sentence form helps most?
film-school.fs-dir-1.q2.e: A thematic claim lets you test whether any option supports or dilutes it.

film-school.fs-dir-1.q3.t: Prepared ones improvise from priority, under-prepared from panic
film-school.fs-dir-1.q3.p: What does the lesson say is the difference between prepared and under-prepared directors when plans collapse?
film-school.fs-dir-1.q3.e: Thorough preparation tells you what you are protecting, so you can drop the plan without losing the scene.

film-school.fs-dir-2.q1.t: The set of shots that lets a scene be cut
film-school.fs-dir-2.q1.e: Coverage is the set of shots that lets the scene be assembled in the edit.

film-school.fs-dir-2.q2.t: Mark which shots are the scene and which are insurance, and cut insurance
film-school.fs-dir-2.q2.p: You are running out of time on set. How does the lesson say to protect the scene?
film-school.fs-dir-2.q2.e: Marking the list in advance lets you drop the insurance instead of accidentally dropping the scene.

film-school.fs-dir-2.q3.t: It stacks the deck so the audience feels bias without noticing
film-school.fs-dir-2.q3.p: A director gives one character clean singles and the other only over-the-shoulder shots. What does the lesson say this does?
film-school.fs-dir-2.q3.e: Breaking symmetry stacks the deck, and the audience feels the imbalance without knowing why.

film-school.fs-dir-3.q1.p: What does negative space around a figure typically read as?
film-school.fs-dir-3.q1.h: Tightening it reads as the opposite.
film-school.fs-dir-3.q1.e: The lesson says negative space around a figure reads as isolation, while tightening it reads as pressure.

film-school.fs-dir-3.q2.p: You want the audience to feel a character is trapped inside a system. Which compositional strategy suits that?
film-school.fs-dir-3.q2.e: One-point perspective produces a feeling of imposed order, institutional and slightly wrong.

film-school.fs-dir-3.q3.t: In a composed frame the arrangement itself says something
film-school.fs-dir-3.q3.p: What separates a composed frame from an acceptable one?
film-school.fs-dir-3.q3.e: An acceptable frame just shows the subject; a composed frame's arrangement carries meaning.

film-school.fs-dir-4.q1.t: Parallax occurs as the relationship changes
film-school.fs-dir-4.q1.p: What happens to the relationship between foreground and background during a dolly move?
film-school.fs-dir-4.q1.e: A dolly travels through space, so foreground and background shift relative to each other, producing parallax.

film-school.fs-dir-4.q2.p: You want a gliding, dreamlike observation that belongs to nobody. Which support fits best?
film-school.fs-dir-4.q2.h: It removes the body but keeps the travel.
film-school.fs-dir-4.q2.e: A Steadicam removes the operator's body while keeping travel, giving a gliding observation.

film-school.fs-dir-4.q3.t: It changes perspective without changing subject scale
film-school.fs-dir-4.q3.p: Why does the dolly zoom produce a sensation with no real-world equivalent?
film-school.fs-dir-4.q3.h: Track and zoom in opposite directions.
film-school.fs-dir-4.q3.e: The subject stays the same size while the background expands or collapses, which is not something the eye experiences.

film-school.fs-dir-5.q1.t: Get him to apologise before he leaves the room
film-school.fs-dir-5.q1.p: Which of these is a playable note rather than a result note?
film-school.fs-dir-5.q1.h: Look for a verb directed at the other person.
film-school.fs-dir-5.q1.e: Actions are verbs directed at another person, giving the actor something to do instead of manufacturing an emotion.

film-school.fs-dir-5.q2.t: You have already decided to leave tonight
film-school.fs-dir-5.q2.p: You want to change a performance without adjectives. Which note gives the actor information?
film-school.fs-dir-5.q2.e: Giving the actor a fact their character knows changes behaviour more than adjectives do.

film-school.fs-dir-5.q3.t: If failure feels expensive, actors play safe and give only competence
film-school.fs-dir-5.q3.p: Why does the lesson stress never giving a note through someone else or in front of the crew?
film-school.fs-dir-5.q3.e: Actors must feel failure is safe, otherwise they will play safe and you will get mere competence.

film-school.fs-dir-6.q1.t: Early takes are the actor's ideas, and real behaviour emerges after they are exhausted
film-school.fs-dir-6.q1.p: What is the second theory of the take described in the lesson?
film-school.fs-dir-6.q1.h: It explains very high take counts.
film-school.fs-dir-6.q1.e: The second theory holds that early takes are ideas about the scene and true behaviour appears once those are worn away.

film-school.fs-dir-6.q2.p: You are on take thirty with no changes in your notes between takes. According to the lesson, what is this?
film-school.fs-dir-6.q2.e: Repetition without adjustment is just fatigue; high take counts only work when notes change between takes.

film-school.fs-dir-6.q3.t: You have stopped watching technique and started believing the person
film-school.fs-dir-6.q3.p: What practical test tells you that you have the take?
film-school.fs-dir-6.q3.e: The lesson says that when you stop watching the technique and believe the person, print it and move on.

film-school.fs-dir-7.q1.t: Where everyone is, what they want and what winning would be
film-school.fs-dir-7.q1.p: What must the audience always know in an action sequence?
film-school.fs-dir-7.q1.e: Action is a comprehension problem before a spectacle problem; the audience needs the geography and the stakes.

film-school.fs-dir-7.q2.t: Fewer, longer, wider shots demanding more of the performers
film-school.fs-dir-7.q2.p: You shot a fight from twelve angles and cut every eight frames, but it feels confused. What does the lesson suggest instead?
film-school.fs-dir-7.q2.e: Energy comes from clarity and real performer competence, which wide, longer shots capture.

film-school.fs-dir-7.q3.t: Cutting introduces doubt about whether the action really happened
film-school.fs-dir-7.q3.p: Why does the lesson say a wide shot is also "the evidence"?
film-school.fs-dir-7.q3.e: Holding wide proves the body did the thing; cutting raises doubt that it was real.

film-school.fs-dir-8.q1.t: The film's attitude toward its own material
film-school.fs-dir-8.q1.e: Tone is the film's attitude toward its material, including seriousness and distance.

film-school.fs-dir-8.q2.p: You need your costume designer to act on the tone. Which instruction travels best, according to the lesson?
film-school.fs-dir-8.q2.e: The lesson says a list of what the film is not is more actionable than positive descriptions.

film-school.fs-dir-8.q3.t: The sense that the film did not know it was changing
film-school.fs-dir-8.q3.p: What actually breaks a film that moves between comedy and horror?
film-school.fs-dir-8.q3.e: Tonal range is acceptable; what breaks a film is an unprepared shift where the underlying attitude does not hold.

film-school.fs-cine-1.q1.p: What is the side effect of changing aperture?
film-school.fs-cine-1.q1.e: Aperture controls light and has depth of field as its side effect.

film-school.fs-cine-1.q2.p: You shoot at 24 fps and want standard cinematic motion blur. Roughly what shutter speed should you use?
film-school.fs-cine-1.q2.e: The 180-degree shutter convention puts the shutter near double the frame rate, so about 1/48 at 24 fps.

film-school.fs-cine-1.q3.t: Use ND filtration or light control rather than compromising the look
film-school.fs-cine-1.q3.p: The scene is too bright for the depth of field you want. What does the lesson recommend?
film-school.fs-cine-1.q3.e: The professional habit is to decide the look first and solve exposure with light and ND, not by compromising the look.

film-school.fs-cine-2.q1.p: What does a long lens (85mm and up) do to the planes in a scene?
film-school.fs-cine-2.q1.h: Think about running and getting nowhere.
film-school.fs-cine-2.q1.e: Long lenses stack planes together, which is why the running-but-getting-nowhere shot is long.

film-school.fs-cine-2.q2.t: A wide lens close to the face
film-school.fs-cine-2.q2.p: You want a character's face to look unsettling and slightly distorted. Which choice fits best?
film-school.fs-cine-2.q2.h: Noses grow and ears fall away.
film-school.fs-cine-2.q2.e: A face close to a wide lens is distorted, reading as unsettling, comic or aggressive.

film-school.fs-cine-2.q3.t: It can be shot wide from six inches or long from twenty feet, giving entirely different shots
film-school.fs-cine-2.q3.p: The lesson says framing and perspective are separable. What does this mean for a close-up?
film-school.fs-cine-2.q3.e: The same frame size can arise from different lens and distance combinations, which produce different perspectives.

film-school.fs-cine-3.q1.t: How deep the shadow side goes
film-school.fs-cine-3.q1.p: What does the fill light control?
film-school.fs-cine-3.q1.e: Fill sits opposite the key and controls how deep the shadow side goes.

film-school.fs-cine-3.q2.p: You want noir-style low-key lighting. What should you do with the fill?
film-school.fs-cine-3.q2.e: Low-key lighting uses a high key-to-fill ratio, with little or no fill and deep shadow.

film-school.fs-cine-3.q3.t: The size of the source relative to the subject
film-school.fs-cine-3.q3.p: What determines whether light is hard or soft?
film-school.fs-cine-3.q3.e: The lesson says the size of the source relative to the subject determines hardness, not wattage.

film-school.fs-cine-4.q1.t: Putting something black on the shadow side to absorb bounce
film-school.fs-cine-4.q1.h: It deepens contrast without a new source.
film-school.fs-cine-4.q1.e: Negative fill absorbs bounce on the shadow side, deepening contrast without adding a light.

film-school.fs-cine-4.q2.t: Move into open shade and use the sky as the source
film-school.fs-cine-4.q2.p: You are shooting midday in harsh sun with nothing but a reflector. What does the lesson suggest?
film-school.fs-cine-4.q2.e: Open shade lets the sky act as a large soft source instead of harsh midday sun.

film-school.fs-cine-4.q3.t: Screen night is high-contrast light with visible sources and deep shadow
film-school.fs-cine-4.q3.p: Why do motivated pools of light read as night better than an evenly dim image?
film-school.fs-cine-4.q3.e: The lesson says screen night is high-contrast with visible sources and clean shadows, not general dimness.

film-school.fs-cine-5.q1.p: About what colour temperature is daylight in kelvin?
film-school.fs-cine-5.q1.e: Daylight sits near 5600K while tungsten sits around 3200K.

film-school.fs-cine-5.q2.t: Balance for tungsten and let the window go blue
film-school.fs-cine-5.q2.p: You want a warm interior against a cold blue outside window. What white balance choice does this?
film-school.fs-cine-5.q2.e: Balancing for tungsten renders interior lamps neutral and the daylight window blue.

film-school.fs-cine-5.q3.t: An accent colour means something whenever it appears
film-school.fs-cine-5.q3.p: Why does restriction make a colour palette read?
film-school.fs-cine-5.q3.e: In a limited palette, the accent colour carries meaning each time it appears.

film-school.fs-cine-6.q1.p: What does handheld camera reintroduce into the image?
film-school.fs-cine-6.q1.e: Handheld brings an operator's body in, reading as immediacy and witness.

film-school.fs-cine-6.q2.p: You have almost no budget and no dolly. Which tool does the lesson call underrated?
film-school.fs-cine-6.q2.h: It costs nothing and looks composed.
film-school.fs-cine-6.q2.e: Locked-off shots cost nothing, look composed and force you to solve the scene through staging.

film-school.fs-cine-6.q3.t: Its movement belongs to nobody, so it lacks a body's perspective
film-school.fs-cine-6.q3.p: Why can a gimbal or Steadicam be a problem when a scene needs a point of view?
film-school.fs-cine-6.q3.e: Gimbal movement is smooth and floating but unattributed, which is wrong when you need a character's point of view.

film-school.fs-cine-7.q1.t: A shared set of reference images and stills that form the visual vocabulary
film-school.fs-cine-7.q1.e: A look book of images and stills is the vocabulary a director and DP use together for months.

film-school.fs-cine-7.q2.t: This shot should feel like she's being observed
film-school.fs-cine-7.q2.p: Which director note respects the DP's role?
film-school.fs-cine-7.q2.h: A brief, not a technical order.
film-school.fs-cine-7.q2.e: Describing the feeling is a brief; specifying technical details treats the DP as an operator.

film-school.fs-cine-7.q3.t: It makes the film feel posed
film-school.fs-cine-7.q3.p: Why is designing shots first and then fitting the actors into them a problem?
film-school.fs-cine-7.q3.e: The lesson says blocking first then designing coverage avoids films that feel posed.

film-school.fs-edit-1.q1.p: Which is NOT one of the three decisions an editor makes on every cut?
film-school.fs-edit-1.q1.h: Think about shot, timing and duration.
film-school.fs-edit-1.q1.e: The three decisions are what comes next, when to leave and how long to stay; colour grading is separate.

film-school.fs-edit-1.q2.p: The audience seems ahead of you and starts noticing the film instead of watching it. What probably happened?
film-school.fs-edit-1.q2.h: They finished with the image before you left it.
film-school.fs-edit-1.q2.e: Cutting late lets the audience get ahead of the film, and they begin to notice the film itself.

film-school.fs-edit-1.q3.t: It is hard to watch your own material as though you did not make it
film-school.fs-edit-1.q3.p: Why does the lesson say directors should not cut alone?
film-school.fs-edit-1.q3.e: An editor can see what actually works, while a director tends to defend the film they intended.

film-school.fs-edit-2.q1.p: According to Walter Murch's Rule of Six, which element ranks highest?
film-school.fs-edit-2.q1.e: Emotion ranks first and carries about half the weight of the six.

film-school.fs-edit-2.q2.t: Take the performance and fix or hide what you can
film-school.fs-edit-2.q2.p: The only take with the right performance has a prop continuity error. What does the lesson say to do?
film-school.fs-edit-2.q2.e: A cut that breaks continuity but holds emotion will play, so the performance wins.

film-school.fs-edit-2.q3.t: A cut perfect in those but dead emotionally will fail while one that breaks them but holds emotion plays
film-school.fs-edit-2.q3.p: Why does the lesson call the last two items of the Rule of Six least important?
film-school.fs-edit-2.q3.e: Screen direction and spatial continuity matter less than emotion and story, though continuity errors still accumulate costs.

film-school.fs-edit-3.q1.t: Meaning arises from juxtaposition of shots
film-school.fs-edit-3.q1.p: What does the Kuleshov effect demonstrate?
film-school.fs-edit-3.q1.e: The same neutral face read differently depending on the shot beside it, so meaning is built by juxtaposition.

film-school.fs-edit-3.q2.t: Juxtaposition that implies a claim neither shot makes alone
film-school.fs-edit-3.q2.p: You cut from a character saying "trust me" to a locked door. What technique is at work?
film-school.fs-edit-3.q2.e: Placing two shots together creates an implied meaning that neither shot contains, as in montage.

film-school.fs-edit-3.q3.t: It uses cutting by conflict to force an intellectual act, while continuity hides the cut
film-school.fs-edit-3.q3.p: How does Eisenstein's montage differ from continuity editing?
film-school.fs-edit-3.q3.e: Eisenstein used conflicting graphics, directions and rhythms to make the viewer think, while continuity smooths the cut.

film-school.fs-edit-4.q1.t: The rate at which they receive new information
film-school.fs-edit-4.q1.p: What do audiences experience as pace, according to the lesson?
film-school.fs-edit-4.q1.e: Pace is felt as the rate of new information, not the rate of cutting.

film-school.fs-edit-4.q2.p: A scene feels slow so you cut it faster, and it feels slower. What is the likely cause?
film-school.fs-edit-4.q2.e: Speeding up cuts does not help if the scene fails to reveal anything new.

film-school.fs-edit-4.q3.t: It works only when the audience already cares about the outcome
film-school.fs-edit-4.q3.p: Why does the lesson say expanding screen time belongs to climaxes?
film-school.fs-edit-4.q3.e: Holding a two-second action across many cuts only works if viewers already care how it ends.

film-school.fs-edit-5.q1.t: A beat earlier than feels comfortable
film-school.fs-edit-5.q1.p: Where does comedy payoff usually want to land in the edit?
film-school.fs-edit-5.q1.h: Do not let the audience get there first.
film-school.fs-edit-5.q1.e: The payoff usually works a beat earlier than feels comfortable because delay lets the audience get ahead.

film-school.fs-edit-5.q2.t: Left room after the payoff for the laugh to play
film-school.fs-edit-5.q2.p: After a big joke the next line is lost under the laughter. What should you have done?
film-school.fs-edit-5.q2.e: You must leave room for the laugh, which is why comedies are re-cut after screening with real audiences.

film-school.fs-edit-5.q3.t: You can no longer be surprised by your own material
film-school.fs-edit-5.q3.p: Why does the lesson say not to trust your own laughter after the fifth pass?
film-school.fs-edit-5.q3.h: Surprise is what is being measured.
film-school.fs-edit-5.q3.e: After many passes you cannot be surprised, which is exactly the faculty comedy relies on.

film-school.fs-edit-6.q1.t: The point where the cut is frozen so downstream departments can work
film-school.fs-edit-6.q1.h: Sound, VFX and grading depend on it.
film-school.fs-edit-6.q1.e: Picture lock freezes the cut so sound, music, VFX and grading can build on specific frame counts.

film-school.fs-edit-6.q2.t: That is normal; its purpose is to see the whole shape
film-school.fs-edit-6.q2.p: Your assembly is far too long and disheartening. What stage guidance applies?
film-school.fs-edit-6.q2.e: The assembly is always too long; its only purpose is to let you see the whole shape at once.

film-school.fs-edit-6.q3.t: The scene is broken even if it seems clear to you
film-school.fs-edit-6.q3.p: Four viewers who have not read the script are confused at the same point. What does the lesson conclude?
film-school.fs-edit-6.q3.e: Shared confusion shows the scene is broken regardless of how clear it is to the filmmaker.

film-school.fs-edit-7.q1.t: A character looking, what they see, then their reaction
film-school.fs-edit-7.q1.e: The chain of a look, the thing seen and a reaction makes the audience attribute the middle shot to the character.

film-school.fs-edit-7.q2.t: Claims this is what the character noticed, revealing their state
film-school.fs-edit-7.q2.p: You cut to a dripping tap while a character waits for news. What does this do?
film-school.fs-edit-7.q2.e: Cutting to a detail claims it is what the character registered, hinting at their anxiety.

film-school.fs-edit-7.q3.t: It lets the audience feel the character's experience of time, if they care enough
film-school.fs-edit-7.q3.p: Why can holding a shot past its informational use convey dread or boredom?
film-school.fs-edit-7.q3.e: A long hold puts the viewer into the character's experience of time, but only works when the audience already cares.

film-school.fs-sound-1.q1.p: Which of these is NOT one of the four soundtrack elements named in the lesson?
film-school.fs-sound-1.q1.e: The four layers are dialogue, ambience, effects including foley, and music.

film-school.fs-sound-1.q2.p: Cuts between takes produce small audible jumps in your edit. What layer fixes the continuity?
film-school.fs-sound-1.q2.e: A continuous ambient bed hides discontinuity and makes fragments feel like one space.

film-school.fs-sound-1.q3.t: The audience's relationship to what they heard changes retroactively
film-school.fs-sound-1.q3.p: What happens when a piece of music is revealed to be a record playing in the next room?
film-school.fs-sound-1.q3.e: Crossing the diegetic line changes how the audience understands the scene after the fact.

film-school.fs-sound-2.q1.p: What is the single most important variable for production audio quality?
