art-movements-modern.l13.q1.t: The movement of Black Americans from the rural South to northern cities
art-movements-modern.l13.q1.h: It brought many people to Harlem.
art-movements-modern.l13.q1.e: Hundreds of thousands left the South seeking work and safety, shaping Harlem's cultural life.

art-movements-modern.l13.q2.p: Alain Locke edited the 1925 anthology The New Negro.
art-movements-modern.l13.q2.e: The anthology argued that Black artists should draw on their own heritage and experience.

art-movements-modern.l13.q3.p: Which artist made the 60-panel Migration Series in 1940 and 1941?
art-movements-modern.l13.q3.h: A younger artist who studied in Harlem.
art-movements-modern.l13.q3.e: Lawrence told the story of the Great Migration in bold flat colour.

art-movements-modern.l13.q4.p: Which sculptor made "Lift Every Voice and Sing" for the 1939 World's Fair?
art-movements-modern.l13.q4.h: She also taught and organized other artists.
art-movements-modern.l13.q4.e: Savage's plaster work was destroyed after the fair because it could not be cast in bronze.

art-movements-modern.l13.q5.p: Scholars continue to debate how much patrons and white audiences shaped the Harlem Renaissance.
art-movements-modern.l13.q5.h: Consider who funded and bought the work.
art-movements-modern.l13.q5.e: The influence of patrons and audiences is a live debate about the movement.

art-movements-modern.l14.q1.p: Who commissioned many early Mexican murals from the early 1920s?
art-movements-modern.l14.q1.h: A government official aimed at reaching people who could not read.
art-movements-modern.l14.q1.e: Vasconcelos commissioned murals so public images could reach everyone.

art-movements-modern.l14.q2.p: Diego Rivera, Orozco and Siqueiros were known as los tres grandes.
art-movements-modern.l14.q2.e: These three were the leading muralists.

art-movements-modern.l14.q3.t: It was destroyed in 1934 after controversy over a Lenin portrait
art-movements-modern.l14.q3.p: What happened to Rivera's Rockefeller Center mural?
art-movements-modern.l14.q3.h: A political image caused a dispute.
art-movements-modern.l14.q3.e: The mural was removed and destroyed in 1934.

art-movements-modern.l14.q4.p: Which Mexican muralist ran a New York workshop in 1936 where Jackson Pollock worked?
art-movements-modern.l14.q4.h: He used spray guns and car paint.
art-movements-modern.l14.q4.e: Siqueiros experimented with industrial materials in his workshop.

art-movements-modern.l14.q5.p: Critics note a tension in muralism: it idealized Indigenous heritage for a state story while many Indigenous people stayed poor.
art-movements-modern.l14.q5.h: Think about who paid and who benefited.
art-movements-modern.l14.q5.e: The gap between imagery and conditions is a common criticism.

art-movements-modern.l15.q1.p: Which painter began pouring and dripping paint onto canvases on the floor in 1947?
art-movements-modern.l15.q1.e: Pollock's poured method became the best-known form of action painting.

art-movements-modern.l15.q2.p: Mark Rothko is known for colour field painting with soft, glowing rectangles.
art-movements-modern.l15.q2.h: He wanted viewers to respond emotionally up close.
art-movements-modern.l15.q2.e: Rothko's hovering rectangles are a major example of colour field painting.

art-movements-modern.l15.q3.p: Who coined the term "action painting" in 1952?
art-movements-modern.l15.q3.h: A critic who saw the canvas as an arena.
art-movements-modern.l15.q3.e: Rosenberg's essay described the canvas as a place for an event.

art-movements-modern.l15.q4.t: Soaked thinned paint into unprimed canvas
art-movements-modern.l15.q4.p: What did Helen Frankenthaler do in Mountains and Sea (1952)?
art-movements-modern.l15.q4.h: A technique that influenced colour field painters.
art-movements-modern.l15.q4.e: The soak-stain technique was widely influential.

art-movements-modern.l15.q5.p: Historians have documented that the CIA secretly funded the Congress for Cultural Freedom, though how far this shaped Abstract Expressionism is debated.
art-movements-modern.l15.q5.e: The funding is documented; the degree of its influence on the art is argued.

art-movements-modern.l16.q1.p: Which artist showed 32 Campbell's Soup Cans canvases at the Ferus Gallery in 1962?
art-movements-modern.l16.q1.e: Warhol's 32 canvases matched the flavours then sold.

art-movements-modern.l16.q2.p: Roy Lichtenstein enlarged comic-strip frames using Ben-Day dots.
art-movements-modern.l16.q2.e: Ben-Day dots and flat colour imitate printed comics.

art-movements-modern.l16.q3.p: Which group in Britain discussed advertising and science fiction, and included Richard Hamilton?
art-movements-modern.l16.q3.h: Its name suggests freedom from institutions.
art-movements-modern.l16.q3.e: The Independent Group helped lay the ground for Pop in Britain.

art-movements-modern.l16.q4.t: Whether it celebrates, criticizes or simply reports consumer culture
art-movements-modern.l16.q4.p: What question does Pop Art leave open?
art-movements-modern.l16.q4.e: The ambiguity is part of Pop's interest and debate.

art-movements-modern.l16.q5.p: Pop Art helped blur the line between "high" and "low" art.
art-movements-modern.l16.q5.h: Think of comics and soup cans in galleries.
art-movements-modern.l16.q5.e: By using ads, comics and celebrity images, Pop challenged that boundary.

art-movements-modern.l17.q1.h: He made boxes in repeated rows.
art-movements-modern.l17.q1.e: Judd argued for real objects occupying real space.

art-movements-modern.l17.q2.p: Dan Flavin made works from commercially bought fluorescent light tubes.
art-movements-modern.l17.q2.e: Flavin used standard fluorescent tubes, beginning in 1963.

art-movements-modern.l17.q3.t: Its theatricality, the way it depends on the viewer's presence
art-movements-modern.l17.q3.p: What did Michael Fried criticize in Minimalism in his 1967 essay?
art-movements-modern.l17.q3.h: He saw the work as needing an audience's movement.
art-movements-modern.l17.q3.e: Fried called this theatricality; Minimalists welcomed the experience of the viewer.

art-movements-modern.l17.q4.t: Newspapers mocked it as a pile of bricks after the Tate bought it
art-movements-modern.l17.q4.p: Why did Carl Andre's Equivalent VIII become controversial in 1976?
art-movements-modern.l17.q4.e: The purchase triggered a press debate over what counts as art.

art-movements-modern.l17.q5.p: Industrial fabrication in Minimalism challenged the idea that the artist's own hand is essential.
art-movements-modern.l17.q5.h: Think about who actually made the boxes.
art-movements-modern.l17.q5.e: Fabricated work questioned the myth of the artist's touch.

art-movements-modern.l18.q1.t: A machine that makes the art
art-movements-modern.l18.q1.p: What does Sol LeWitt say the idea becomes in conceptual art?
art-movements-modern.l18.q1.h: It is in the 1967 essay quoted in the lesson.
art-movements-modern.l18.q1.e: LeWitt wrote that the idea becomes a machine that makes the art.

art-movements-modern.l18.q2.p: Kosuth's One and Three Chairs includes a real chair, a photograph and a dictionary definition.
art-movements-modern.l18.q2.e: The work asks which version is the artwork and what representation means.

art-movements-modern.l18.q3.t: A certificate or instructions and the right to realize the work
art-movements-modern.l18.q3.p: What does a collector often buy when purchasing a conceptual work?
art-movements-modern.l18.q3.e: Often the purchase is documentation and permission to realize the piece.

art-movements-modern.l18.q4.t: The Dematerialization of Art by Lippard and Chandler
art-movements-modern.l18.q4.p: Which 1968 essay described the trend as dematerialization?
art-movements-modern.l18.q4.h: The title uses a word meaning 'removing matter'.
art-movements-modern.l18.q4.e: Lucy Lippard and John Chandler wrote the essay.

art-movements-modern.l18.q5.p: Even when others carry out LeWitt's wall drawings from his instructions, the instructions are still counted as his work.
art-movements-modern.l18.q5.e: The instructions are his work, even when assistants carry them out.

art-movements-modern.l19.q1.t: Create the perception of vibration or movement with patterns
art-movements-modern.l19.q1.p: What does Op Art try to do?
art-movements-modern.l19.q1.h: The movement is not physically there.
art-movements-modern.l19.q1.e: Op artists use contrast and repeated patterns to create optical effects.

art-movements-modern.l19.q2.p: Bridget Riley painted waving black and white lines in works such as Current.
art-movements-modern.l19.q2.e: Current (1964) is a well-known Op work.

art-movements-modern.l19.q3.p: Which 1965 MoMA exhibition brought Op Art to wide attention?
art-movements-modern.l19.q3.e: The Responsive Eye was organized by William Seitz.

art-movements-modern.l19.q4.p: Which artist's mobiles, begun in the 1930s, balance in the air and respond to drafts?
art-movements-modern.l19.q4.e: Calder's mobiles are a classic form of kinetic art.

art-movements-modern.l19.q5.p: Op Art changed the question from what a picture shows to what happens to the viewer while looking.
art-movements-modern.l19.q5.e: The artwork is partly completed inside the viewer's perception.

art-movements-modern.l20.q1.t: The Great Salt Lake in Utah
art-movements-modern.l20.q1.p: Where is Robert Smithson's Spiral Jetty?
art-movements-modern.l20.q1.h: A very salty lake in the American West.

art-movements-modern.l20.q2.p: The Lightning Field by Walter De Maria is in New Mexico.
art-movements-modern.l20.q2.e: It was completed in 1977 and is visited overnight.

art-movements-modern.l20.q3.t: By removing hundreds of thousands of tons of rock from a mesa edge
art-movements-modern.l20.q3.p: How was Michael Heizer's Double Negative made?
art-movements-modern.l20.q3.e: It is two huge cuts in the edge of a mesa in Nevada.

art-movements-modern.l20.q4.t: Many sites are sacred or home to Indigenous communities and were treated as empty
art-movements-modern.l20.q4.p: Which ethical question does land art raise?
art-movements-modern.l20.q4.h: Think about who lived in those places.
art-movements-modern.l20.q4.e: Artists from outside often treated inhabited or sacred places as blank.

art-movements-modern.l20.q5.p: Christo and Jeanne-Claude funded their projects themselves.
art-movements-modern.l20.q5.h: The lesson mentions how they paid.
art-movements-modern.l20.q5.e: They financed the projects through the sale of their own work rather than public funds.

art-movements-modern.l21.q1.p: Which artist coined the word Happening and staged "18 Happenings in 6 Parts" in 1959?
art-movements-modern.l21.q1.e: Kaprow's 1959 event gave the term wide use.

art-movements-modern.l21.q2.p: In Cut Piece, audience members cut pieces from Yoko Ono's clothing.
art-movements-modern.l21.q2.e: The piece raised questions of consent, gender and power.

art-movements-modern.l21.q3.t: 72 objects the audience could use on her
art-movements-modern.l21.q3.p: In Rhythm 0 (1974), what did Marina Abramovic provide, by her account?
art-movements-modern.l21.q3.e: The performance showed how some audience members escalated their actions.

art-movements-modern.l21.q4.t: Performance is live and disappears, so photos and film shape how it is remembered
art-movements-modern.l21.q4.p: Why does documentation matter in performance art?
art-movements-modern.l21.q4.e: The document is not the event, but it often is what survives.

art-movements-modern.l21.q5.p: Reperformance raises the question of whether a work can exist without its original moment.
art-movements-modern.l21.q5.e: Museums and artists debate whether a restaged performance is the same work.

art-movements-modern.l22.q1.p: Who published "Why Have There Been No Great Women Artists?" in 1971?
art-movements-modern.l22.q1.e: Nochlin argued that institutions, not lack of talent, explained the gap.

art-movements-modern.l22.q2.p: The Dinner Party has 39 place settings.
art-movements-modern.l22.q2.e: It honours 39 mythical and historical women, with 999 more names on the floor.

art-movements-modern.l22.q3.p: Which group began wearing gorilla masks in 1985 to publicize poor representation in museums?
art-movements-modern.l22.q3.e: They posted statistics on women and artists of colour in major museums.

art-movements-modern.l22.q4.t: That daily maintenance and care work deserved attention as art
art-movements-modern.l22.q4.p: What did Mierle Laderman Ukeles propose in her 1969 manifesto?
art-movements-modern.l22.q4.e: She argued maintenance work deserved attention as art.

art-movements-modern.l22.q5.p: Critics have argued that The Dinner Party treats women's identity as biological and centres white women.
art-movements-modern.l22.q5.h: Consider both the imagery and the list of names.
art-movements-modern.l22.q5.e: These are criticisms often raised about the piece.

art-movements-modern.l23.q1.p: How did Photorealist painters usually begin?
art-movements-modern.l23.q1.e: They projected or gridded photographs and painted them.

art-movements-modern.l23.q2.p: Chuck Close painted enormous faces from head-shot photographs.
art-movements-modern.l23.q2.e: His portraits are far larger than life.

art-movements-modern.l23.q3.t: Storefronts full of reflections in glass
art-movements-modern.l23.q3.p: What subject did Richard Estes paint in New York?
art-movements-modern.l23.q3.h: A subject where the camera flattens space.
art-movements-modern.l23.q3.e: Estes made reflective city surfaces his specialty.

art-movements-modern.l23.q4.t: How photographs flatten, edit and glamorize the world
art-movements-modern.l23.q4.p: What do supporters say Photorealism reveals?
art-movements-modern.l23.q4.h: They answer the charge of copying.
art-movements-modern.l23.q4.e: The slow labour of painting changes our attention to the photographic image.

art-movements-modern.l23.q5.p: Gerhard Richter's blurred photo paintings are a deliberate contrast to photorealist sharpness.
art-movements-modern.l23.q5.h: The lesson mentions him in passing.
art-movements-modern.l23.q5.e: Richter blurred images on purpose, unlike the Photorealists' sharp surface.

art-movements-modern.l24.q1.t: Large, rough, emotional painting with figures
art-movements-modern.l24.q1.e: It was a return to bold figurative painting.

art-movements-modern.l24.q2.p: Jean-Michel Basquiat began as a graffiti writer.
art-movements-modern.l24.q2.e: He moved from street writing to dense gallery paintings.

art-movements-modern.l24.q3.p: What is appropriation in postmodern art?
art-movements-modern.l24.q3.e: Artists reused images to question originality and authorship.

art-movements-modern.l24.q4.t: How stereotypes of women are constructed
art-movements-modern.l24.q4.p: What do Cindy Sherman's Untitled Film Stills explore?
art-movements-modern.l24.q4.h: She poses as imagined movie women.
art-movements-modern.l24.q4.e: The photographs show constructed female stereotypes from old films.

art-movements-modern.l24.q5.p: Scholars agree on exactly when Postmodernism began.
art-movements-modern.l24.q5.h: The term is described as slippery.
art-movements-modern.l24.q5.e: Scholars disagree about its start and its definition.

art-movements-modern.l25.q1.p: Which city is usually credited as the origin of modern graffiti in the late 1960s?
art-movements-modern.l25.q1.e: Philadelphia is where modern tagging is usually traced.

art-movements-modern.l25.q2.p: Graffiti done without permission is illegal in most places.
art-movements-modern.l25.q2.h: Think about authorities calling it vandalism.
art-movements-modern.l25.q2.e: Even when it is valued as art, unpermitted painting is usually a crime.

art-movements-modern.l25.q3.t: It was partly shredded by a device in its frame after it sold
art-movements-modern.l25.q3.p: What happened to Banksy's Girl with Balloon at Sotheby's in 2018?
art-movements-modern.l25.q3.h: The sale price was about 1.04 million pounds.
art-movements-modern.l25.q3.e: The piece partly shredded as the sale was completed.

art-movements-modern.l25.q4.p: Which artist drew in chalk on unused black ad panels in New York subway stations?
art-movements-modern.l25.q4.e: Haring's subway drawings were done in the early 1980s.

art-movements-modern.l25.q5.p: A key open question about street art is who decides what is a crime and what is culture.
art-movements-modern.l25.q5.e: Permission, ownership and context change how the same marks are judged.

art-movements-modern.l26.q1.p: Which Korean-born artist is often called a founder of video art?
art-movements-modern.l26.q1.e: Paik exhibited altered TVs in 1963 and later made TV Buddha.

art-movements-modern.l26.q2.p: An NFT is a blockchain record that points to a file.
art-movements-modern.l26.q2.h: It is not the file itself.
art-movements-modern.l26.q2.e: That is how the lesson defines a non-fungible token.

art-movements-modern.l26.q3.p: How much did Beeple's Everydays: The First 5000 Days sell for at Christie's in 2021?
art-movements-modern.l26.q3.e: The sale was about 69.3 million dollars.

art-movements-modern.l26.q4.p: Which program did Harold Cohen develop to make drawings?
art-movements-modern.l26.q4.e: AARON was an early drawing program.

art-movements-modern.l26.q5.p: Questions about authorship and training data in generative AI art are being argued in courts and studios.
art-movements-modern.l26.q5.e: Authorship and copyright for AI-made images remain contested.

art-movements-modern.l27.q1.t: A large international art exhibition held periodically
art-movements-modern.l27.q1.h: The word suggests every two years.
art-movements-modern.l27.q1.e: Biennials such as Venice and Gwangju gather artists from many places.

art-movements-modern.l27.q2.e: He was the first non-European artistic director of Documenta.

art-movements-modern.l27.q3.t: About 100 million hand-painted porcelain sunflower seeds
art-movements-modern.l27.q3.p: What was Ai Weiwei's 2010 Turbine Hall work at Tate Modern?
art-movements-modern.l27.q3.e: The seeds reflected on mass production and individual labour.

art-movements-modern.l27.q4.p: Which artist makes wall-hangings from flattened bottle caps and wire?
art-movements-modern.l27.q4.h: Born in Ghana, based in Nigeria.
art-movements-modern.l27.q4.e: El Anatsui's shimmering works use recycled bottle materials.

art-movements-modern.l27.q5.p: The term global art can hide unequal power, because wealthy institutions still decide whose work travels.
art-movements-modern.l27.q5.e: The word can describe exchange but also mask who controls it.

art-movements-modern.l28.q1.p: Which market involves galleries selling new work directly from artists?
art-movements-modern.l28.q1.e: The primary market is first sale, usually through galleries.

art-movements-modern.l28.q2.e: Christie's dates from 1766 and Sotheby's from 1744.

art-movements-modern.l28.q3.t: It reached 450.3 million dollars including fees, a record auction price at the time
art-movements-modern.l28.q3.p: What was notable about Salvator Mundi's sale in November 2017?
art-movements-modern.l28.q3.h: Its attribution is disputed by some scholars.
art-movements-modern.l28.q3.e: The price was a record, while the attribution to Leonardo is debated.

art-movements-modern.l28.q4.t: A non-binding framework for fair solutions on Nazi-confiscated art
art-movements-modern.l28.q4.p: What are the Washington Principles of 1998?
art-movements-modern.l28.q4.e: Dozens of countries endorsed them as a non-binding framework.

art-movements-modern.l28.q5.p: A high price proves that a work is good.
art-movements-modern.l28.q5.e: Price reflects many factors, such as reputation and scarcity, not quality alone.

audio-engineering.l01.q1.p: Sound can travel through a perfect vacuum, such as empty space.
audio-engineering.l01.q1.h: Think about what the disturbance needs in order to travel.
audio-engineering.l01.q1.e: Sound is a pressure disturbance in a medium, so it needs air, water or a solid to travel.

audio-engineering.l01.q2.e: Frequency is the number of cycles per second, measured in hertz.

audio-engineering.l01.q3.p: Taking the speed of sound as 343 m/s, what is the wavelength of a 500 Hz tone?
audio-engineering.l01.q3.h: Wavelength equals speed divided by frequency.

audio-engineering.l01.q4.t: A pressure disturbance passed from one patch of air to the next
audio-engineering.l01.q4.p: When you clap, what actually travels from your hands to a listener across the room?
audio-engineering.l01.q4.h: Think about what the air molecules do individually.
audio-engineering.l01.q4.e: Air molecules only wobble around their positions; the pressure disturbance is what travels.

audio-engineering.l01.q5.p: If the speed of sound stays the same, doubling a tones frequency doubles its wavelength.
audio-engineering.l01.q5.h: Wavelength equals speed divided by frequency.
audio-engineering.l01.q5.e: Doubling the frequency halves the wavelength because the speed is fixed.

audio-engineering.l02.q1.p: A level of 0 dB SPL means there is no sound at all.
audio-engineering.l02.q1.h: Zero in a logarithmic scale is a reference point.
audio-engineering.l02.q1.e: 0 dB SPL is the reference pressure, close to the threshold of hearing, not silence.

audio-engineering.l02.q2.p: Roughly how many dB does doubling a voltage or sound pressure add?
audio-engineering.l02.q2.h: The formula uses 20 times a logarithm of the ratio.

audio-engineering.l02.q3.p: A sound pressure increases by a factor of 10. By how many dB does the level rise?
audio-engineering.l02.q3.h: Use 20 times the base-10 logarithm of the ratio.

audio-engineering.l02.q4.p: Using the NIOSH guideline of 85 dBA for 8 hours with time halving for every 3 dB increase, how long is the recommended limit at 91 dBA?
audio-engineering.l02.q4.h: Count how many 3 dB steps lie between 85 and 91.
audio-engineering.l02.q4.e: 91 is two 3 dB steps above 85, so 8 hours is halved twice, giving 2 hours.

audio-engineering.l02.q5.t: Hearing sensitivity to bass and treble changes with listening level
audio-engineering.l02.q5.p: Why do engineers often check a mix at several different volumes?
audio-engineering.l02.q5.h: Think about how the ear responds at quiet levels.
audio-engineering.l02.q5.e: The ear is less sensitive to low and very high frequencies at low levels, so balance seems to change with volume.

audio-engineering.l03.q1.p: Doubling a frequency raises the pitch by one octave.
audio-engineering.l03.q1.e: An octave corresponds to a frequency ratio of 2:1.

audio-engineering.l03.q2.p: A note has a fundamental of 110 Hz. What is its third harmonic?
audio-engineering.l03.q2.h: The fundamental counts as the first harmonic.
audio-engineering.l03.q2.e: Harmonics are whole-number multiples, and 3 x 110 = 330 Hz.

audio-engineering.l03.q3.p: Two identical sine waves are summed with a 180 degree phase offset. What is the result?
audio-engineering.l03.q3.e: Opposite peaks and troughs cancel completely for identical waves.

audio-engineering.l03.q4.t: Their harmonic content and envelopes differ
audio-engineering.l03.q4.p: A violin and a flute play the same note at the same loudness yet sound different. What mainly explains this?
audio-engineering.l03.q4.h: The note and loudness are the same.
audio-engineering.l03.q4.e: Timbre comes from the balance of harmonics and how the sound starts and decays.

audio-engineering.l03.q5.t: The fundamental plus only odd harmonics
audio-engineering.l03.q5.p: Which description fits a square wave?
audio-engineering.l03.q5.h: Compare it with the sawtooth described in the lesson.
audio-engineering.l03.q5.e: A square wave consists of the fundamental and odd harmonics only.

audio-engineering.l04.q1.p: What is the highest frequency that can be captured at a 48 kHz sample rate?
audio-engineering.l04.q1.h: It is half the sample rate.
audio-engineering.l04.q1.e: The Nyquist frequency is half the sample rate, so 24 kHz.

audio-engineering.l04.q2.p: A 30 kHz tone can be captured accurately at a 44.1 kHz sample rate.
audio-engineering.l04.q2.h: Compare 30 kHz with half of 44.1 kHz.
audio-engineering.l04.q2.e: 30 kHz is above the 22.05 kHz Nyquist limit, so it would alias.

audio-engineering.l04.q3.p: A 30 kHz tone is sampled at 44.1 kHz with no anti-aliasing filter. At what frequency does the alias appear?
audio-engineering.l04.q3.h: Subtract the tone frequency from the sample rate.

audio-engineering.l04.q4.t: Removes content above the Nyquist frequency before sampling
audio-engineering.l04.q4.p: What does an anti-aliasing filter do?
audio-engineering.l04.q4.h: It acts before the converter measures the signal.
audio-engineering.l04.q4.e: It prevents frequencies above the limit from being misread as lower ones.

audio-engineering.l04.q5.p: When digital audio is properly converted back to analog, the output is a smooth wave rather than visible stair steps.
audio-engineering.l04.q5.h: Consider what reconstruction does with band-limited samples.
audio-engineering.l04.q5.e: Proper reconstruction yields the smooth band-limited waveform, not a staircase.

audio-engineering.l05.q1.p: Each additional bit of depth adds roughly 6 dB of theoretical dynamic range.
audio-engineering.l05.q1.h: Recall the 6.02 dB per bit figure.
audio-engineering.l05.q1.e: Each bit doubles the number of levels, which is about 6.02 dB.

audio-engineering.l05.q2.p: What is the bit rate of uncompressed stereo audio at 48 kHz and 24 bits?
audio-engineering.l05.q2.h: Multiply sample rate, bit depth and channels.

audio-engineering.l05.q3.p: About how large is one minute of mono 48 kHz, 16-bit audio?
audio-engineering.l05.q3.h: Bytes per second equals rate times bits divided by 8.
audio-engineering.l05.q3.e: 48,000 x 16 / 8 = 96,000 bytes per second, which is 5,760,000 bytes in 60 seconds.

audio-engineering.l05.q4.p: Dither should be applied at every processing stage in a project.
audio-engineering.l05.q4.h: Think about when the bit depth is actually reduced.
audio-engineering.l05.q4.e: Dither belongs at the final bit-depth reduction, applied once.

audio-engineering.l05.q5.t: To turn quantization distortion into steady low-level noise
audio-engineering.l05.q5.p: What is the main purpose of dither?
audio-engineering.l05.q5.h: It is added before reducing the bit depth.
audio-engineering.l05.q5.e: Dither randomizes rounding errors so they sound like gentle hiss instead of distortion.

audio-engineering.l06.q1.p: Condenser microphones normally require power for their circuitry.
audio-engineering.l06.q1.e: Condensers need phantom power or a battery; dynamics do not.

audio-engineering.l06.q2.p: What is the nominal voltage of standard phantom power?
audio-engineering.l06.q2.h: It is sent over the XLR cable.

audio-engineering.l06.q3.p: Which type is the usual first choice for close-miking a loud guitar amplifier?
audio-engineering.l06.q3.h: Think of rugged microphones that tolerate high levels.
audio-engineering.l06.q3.e: Dynamic microphones handle very loud sources and need no power.

audio-engineering.l06.q4.t: Check the manufacturer guidance, because phantom power can harm some models
audio-engineering.l06.q4.p: Before connecting an unfamiliar ribbon microphone with phantom power on, what should you do?
audio-engineering.l06.q4.e: Some ribbon designs can be damaged by phantom power, so follow the manufacturer.

audio-engineering.l06.q5.p: Which design converts sound to voltage by moving a coil in a magnetic field?
audio-engineering.l06.q5.e: A dynamic microphone moves a diaphragm-attached coil in a magnetic field.

audio-engineering.l07.q1.p: Where is a cardioid microphone least sensitive?
audio-engineering.l07.q1.h: Think of the heart shape pointing forward.
audio-engineering.l07.q1.e: A cardioid has its null at the rear.

audio-engineering.l07.q2.p: An omnidirectional microphone responds equally to sound from all directions.
audio-engineering.l07.q2.e: Omni means equal sensitivity in every direction.

audio-engineering.l07.q3.p: At which angle is a figure-8 microphone least sensitive?
audio-engineering.l07.q3.h: It picks up front and back equally.
audio-engineering.l07.q3.e: A figure-8 has nulls at the sides.

audio-engineering.l07.q4.t: Choose a tighter pattern and aim its null toward the hi-hat
audio-engineering.l07.q4.p: A loud hi-hat leaks into a tom microphone. Which approach best reduces this bleed?
audio-engineering.l07.q4.e: Aiming a null at the unwanted source reduces how much of it is picked up.

audio-engineering.l07.q5.p: Which kind of pattern does not show the proximity effect?
audio-engineering.l07.q5.h: The effect belongs to directional designs.
audio-engineering.l07.q5.e: Pressure-type omni microphones lack the proximity bass boost.

audio-engineering.l08.q1.p: In an open space, how does the sound pressure level change when the distance from a point source doubles?
audio-engineering.l08.q1.e: Doubling distance gives about 6 dB less sound pressure level in free field.

audio-engineering.l08.q2.p: The proximity effect increases low frequencies as a directional microphone moves very close to a source.
audio-engineering.l08.q2.e: Directional microphones boost bass at close range.

audio-engineering.l08.q3.p: Two microphones are each 20 cm from their sources. By the 3:1 rule, how far apart should the microphones be at minimum?
audio-engineering.l08.q3.h: Multiply the source distance by three.
audio-engineering.l08.q3.e: The microphones should be at least 3 x 20 cm = 60 cm apart.

audio-engineering.l08.q4.p: Which stereo arrangement uses two capsules at the same point?
audio-engineering.l08.q4.h: The name means occupying one point.
audio-engineering.l08.q4.e: X/Y puts the capsules together so there is no time-of-arrival difference between them.

audio-engineering.l08.q5.p: Two microphones are on one source and the summed sound is thin and hollow. What is the most likely cause?
audio-engineering.l08.q5.h: Think about delayed copies adding together.
audio-engineering.l08.q5.e: Delayed copies of the same sound summing produce comb filtering.

audio-engineering.l09.q1.h: The preamp raises one to reach the other.
audio-engineering.l09.q1.e: A preamp raises tiny microphone-level signals up to line level.

audio-engineering.l09.q2.p: Balanced connections reject noise by cancelling interference that appears equally on both conductors.
audio-engineering.l09.q2.e: Common-mode rejection cancels noise that is identical on both conductors.

audio-engineering.l09.q3.p: Professional nominal line level of +4 dBu corresponds to about how many volts RMS?
audio-engineering.l09.q3.h: It is a little over one volt.

audio-engineering.l09.q4.t: Converts a high-impedance signal to a low-impedance balanced one
audio-engineering.l09.q4.p: What does a DI box do for an electric bass plugged into it?
audio-engineering.l09.q4.h: It matches instrument signals to microphone inputs.
audio-engineering.l09.q4.e: A DI box converts the signal for long balanced cable runs and mic inputs.

audio-engineering.l09.q5.t: Trace the signal stage by stage from the source forward
audio-engineering.l09.q5.p: No sound reaches the speakers. Which is the most sensible approach?
audio-engineering.l09.q5.h: Use the chain order from the lesson.
audio-engineering.l09.q5.e: Checking each stage in order isolates the fault efficiently.

audio-engineering.l10.q1.p: In a fixed-point digital system, signal above 0 dBFS cannot be represented and is clipped.
audio-engineering.l10.q1.e: 0 dBFS is the largest representable value, and anything beyond it clips.

audio-engineering.l10.q2.p: A vocal peaks at -18 dBFS and you add 9 dB of gain. Where do the peaks now sit?

audio-engineering.l10.q3.t: The noise floor is already very low, and extra level only risks clipping
audio-engineering.l10.q3.p: Why is it unnecessary to record 24-bit audio with peaks right at 0 dBFS?
audio-engineering.l10.q3.h: Think about the noise floor of 24-bit audio.
audio-engineering.l10.q3.e: 24-bit recording has so much range that high levels add risk with little benefit.

audio-engineering.l10.q4.p: Turning down the channel fader after recording removes clipping distortion that is already in the file.
audio-engineering.l10.q4.h: Consider what the file already contains.
audio-engineering.l10.q4.e: Clipping is baked into the recording; lowering the level does not restore the flattened peaks.

audio-engineering.l10.q5.p: Why does the master bus meter rise as more tracks are added?
audio-engineering.l10.q5.e: Levels add when signals are summed, so leave headroom on the master.

audio-engineering.l11.q1.p: Soundproofing and acoustic treatment are two names for the same thing.
audio-engineering.l11.q1.h: One stops sound crossing walls; the other shapes sound inside a room.
audio-engineering.l11.q1.e: Treatment shapes reflections inside the room, while soundproofing blocks transmission through the structure.

audio-engineering.l11.q2.p: Using the speed of sound as 343 m/s, what is the lowest axial mode frequency between walls 5 m apart?
audio-engineering.l11.q2.h: Divide the speed of sound by twice the distance.

audio-engineering.l11.q3.p: Where are bass traps most commonly placed?
audio-engineering.l11.q3.h: Low-frequency pressure builds up where surfaces meet.
audio-engineering.l11.q3.e: Corners collect low-frequency energy, so thick absorbers there are most effective.

audio-engineering.l11.q4.t: No single system or room is perfectly neutral, so checking shows how the mix translates
audio-engineering.l11.q4.p: Why do engineers check a mix on several playback systems?
audio-engineering.l11.q4.e: Comparing systems reveals problems that one room can hide.

audio-engineering.l11.q5.t: Absorbs high frequencies but does little for bass
audio-engineering.l11.q5.p: Thin acoustic foam on a wall mainly does what?
audio-engineering.l11.q5.h: Consider how thick low-frequency absorbers need to be.
audio-engineering.l11.q5.e: Thin foam is effective on highs only; bass needs thick absorbers.

audio-engineering.l12.q1.p: What is the delay from a 128-sample buffer at 48,000 Hz?
audio-engineering.l12.q1.h: Divide samples by the sample rate.

audio-engineering.l12.q2.p: Increasing the buffer size lowers latency.
audio-engineering.l12.q2.h: More samples per block means a longer wait.
audio-engineering.l12.q2.e: A larger buffer increases latency while reducing processor load.

audio-engineering.l12.q3.t: Giving performers a custom headphone balance
audio-engineering.l12.q3.p: What is a cue mix for?
audio-engineering.l12.q3.h: It is separate from the control-room mix.
audio-engineering.l12.q3.e: A cue mix lets players hear what they need in their headphones.

audio-engineering.l12.q4.t: Three copies, on two kinds of storage, with one off-site
audio-engineering.l12.q4.p: The 3-2-1 backup guideline calls for what?
audio-engineering.l12.q4.h: The numbers are copies, media and location.
audio-engineering.l12.q4.e: It is three copies, two media types and one off-site copy.

audio-engineering.l12.q5.t: Changing it later needs conversion and can complicate mixed-rate material
audio-engineering.l12.q5.p: Why decide the sample rate before starting to record?
audio-engineering.l12.q5.h: Think about what happens when files are converted.
audio-engineering.l12.q5.e: Settling on a rate early avoids later conversion and mismatched files.

audio-engineering.l13.q1.p: Non-destructive editing rewrites the original audio file each time you make a cut.
audio-engineering.l13.q1.e: Non-destructive editing leaves the original file untouched.

audio-engineering.l13.q2.t: To smooth the join between two clips and avoid clicks
audio-engineering.l13.q2.p: What is the purpose of a crossfade?
audio-engineering.l13.q2.e: A crossfade fades one clip out as another fades in.

audio-engineering.l13.q3.t: Assembling the best sections of several takes into one performance
audio-engineering.l13.q3.h: The word is short for compiling.
audio-engineering.l13.q3.e: Comping builds a composite from the best parts of takes.

audio-engineering.l13.q4.t: It evens out levels so the compressor reacts more consistently
audio-engineering.l13.q4.p: Why use clip gain before a compressor?
audio-engineering.l13.q4.h: Think about a single very loud word.
audio-engineering.l13.q4.e: Leveling clips beforehand gives the compressor a steadier input.

audio-engineering.l13.q5.t: A sudden discontinuity in the waveform at the cut
audio-engineering.l13.q5.p: An audible click appears at an edit point. What is the most likely cause?
audio-engineering.l13.q5.h: Think about a jump in the signal.
audio-engineering.l13.q5.e: A cut that makes the waveform leap instantly produces a click.

audio-engineering.l14.q1.p: In the United States, what is the frequency of mains power?
audio-engineering.l14.q1.h: It matches the mains power frequency.
audio-engineering.l14.q1.e: U.S. mains power is 60 Hz; audible hum appears at 60 Hz and its harmonics, often strongest at 120 Hz.

audio-engineering.l14.q2.p: Removing the grounding pin from a power cord is a safe way to cure hum.
audio-engineering.l14.q2.h: Consider what that pin protects against.
audio-engineering.l14.q2.e: The ground pin protects against electric shock and must never be defeated.

audio-engineering.l14.q3.p: A signal at -10 dBFS has noise at -70 dBFS. What is the signal-to-noise ratio?
audio-engineering.l14.q3.h: Find the difference between the two levels.

audio-engineering.l14.q4.t: More than one path to ground between connected devices
audio-engineering.l14.q4.h: The word loop gives a clue.
audio-engineering.l14.q4.e: Multiple ground paths allow current to circulate and create hum.

audio-engineering.l14.q5.p: What should you do if audio and power cables must meet?
audio-engineering.l14.q5.h: Think about how much cable runs alongside the other.
audio-engineering.l14.q5.e: Crossing at right angles minimizes induced noise.

audio-engineering.l15.q1.p: Converting an MP3 to FLAC restores the information lost in the MP3 encoding.
audio-engineering.l15.q1.e: Lossless conversion preserves the MP3 as it is; the discarded data stays lost.

audio-engineering.l15.q2.p: Which of these is a lossless compressed format?
audio-engineering.l15.q2.h: Think of the formats that decode bit for bit.
audio-engineering.l15.q2.e: FLAC is lossless; the others are lossy.

audio-engineering.l15.q3.p: How many bytes is 60 seconds of audio at 128 kbps?
audio-engineering.l15.q3.h: Bits per second times seconds, divided by 8.

audio-engineering.l15.q4.t: Archive in lossless and make lossy copies only for delivery
audio-engineering.l15.q4.e: Keeping masters lossless preserves quality; lossy is a final delivery step.

audio-engineering.l15.q5.t: Each pass discards more information and adds artifacts
audio-engineering.l15.q5.p: Why does repeated lossy re-encoding degrade audio?
audio-engineering.l15.q5.h: Each encode makes decisions about what to remove.
audio-engineering.l15.q5.e: Lossy encoders discard data every time they are run.

audio-engineering.l16.q1.p: A mono track panned hard left plays only from the left speaker.
audio-engineering.l16.q1.e: Hard panning sends the signal to one side only.

audio-engineering.l16.q2.t: Low frequencies carry much energy, and centring shares it between both speakers
audio-engineering.l16.q2.p: Why are kick drum and bass usually kept in the centre?
audio-engineering.l16.q2.e: Centring low-frequency parts distributes the energy evenly across both speakers.

audio-engineering.l16.q3.t: Keep perceived loudness steady as a track moves across the field
audio-engineering.l16.q3.p: What is the purpose of a pan law of -3 dB at the centre?
audio-engineering.l16.q3.h: Consider what changes when a track is in both speakers.
audio-engineering.l16.q3.e: The centre cut compensates for the extra acoustic power when both speakers play the signal.

audio-engineering.l16.q4.t: A rough balance using only faders
audio-engineering.l16.q4.p: What is a common first step in building a mix?
audio-engineering.l16.q4.e: A static balance sets the foundation before processing.

audio-engineering.l16.q5.t: It reveals phase cancellation and balance problems
audio-engineering.l16.q5.p: Why check a mix in mono?
audio-engineering.l16.q5.e: Parts that cancel when summed will shrink or vanish in mono.

audio-engineering.l17.q1.p: What does a high-pass filter do?
audio-engineering.l17.q1.e: A high-pass filter attenuates low frequencies below the cutoff.

audio-engineering.l17.q2.p: Raising the Q of a bell filter makes its affected band narrower.
audio-engineering.l17.q2.e: Higher Q gives a narrower bandwidth.

audio-engineering.l17.q3.t: One sound obscuring another that occupies a similar frequency range
audio-engineering.l17.q3.e: Masking occurs when a sound hides another in the same range.

audio-engineering.l17.q4.t: A louder version tends to sound better, which can bias judgment
audio-engineering.l17.q4.p: Why match levels when comparing EQ on and off?
audio-engineering.l17.q4.e: Louder generally sounds better, so unmatched comparisons mislead.

audio-engineering.l17.q5.t: Slightly cut the guitar where the vocal lives
audio-engineering.l17.q5.p: A guitar and a vocal mask each other in the midrange. Which move best helps?
audio-engineering.l17.q5.e: Carving a small cut from one part leaves room for the other.

audio-engineering.l18.q1.p: At a 4:1 ratio, an input 4 dB over the threshold comes out 1 dB over the threshold.
audio-engineering.l18.q1.h: Divide the overshoot by the ratio.
audio-engineering.l18.q1.e: A 4:1 ratio reduces the overshoot to one quarter.

audio-engineering.l18.q2.p: With threshold -20 dB, ratio 4:1 and an input peak of -8 dB, what is the output peak?
audio-engineering.l18.q2.h: The overshoot is 12 dB; divide it by the ratio.
audio-engineering.l18.q2.e: 12 / 4 = 3 dB over the threshold, which is -17 dB.

audio-engineering.l18.q3.p: With threshold -10 dB, ratio 2:1 and an input of -2 dB, how much gain reduction occurs?
audio-engineering.l18.q3.h: The input is 8 dB over; the output is 4 dB over.
audio-engineering.l18.q3.e: The signal drops from 8 dB over to 4 dB over, so the gain reduction is 4 dB.

audio-engineering.l18.q4.t: Lets more of the initial transient through
audio-engineering.l18.q4.p: What does a slower attack setting typically do to a drum hit?
audio-engineering.l18.q4.h: Think of the compressor reacting late.
audio-engineering.l18.q4.e: A slower attack lets the first part of a transient pass before compression engages.

audio-engineering.l18.q5.p: What can a very fast release cause on bass-heavy material?
audio-engineering.l18.q5.e: Very quick recovery makes the level visibly and audibly jump.

audio-engineering.l19.q1.t: The time for the reverb tail to fall by 60 dB
audio-engineering.l19.q1.e: RT60 is the decay time to a 60 dB reduction.

audio-engineering.l19.q2.p: At 100 BPM, how long is a quarter-note delay?

audio-engineering.l19.q3.p: At 120 BPM, how long is a dotted-eighth-note delay?
audio-engineering.l19.q3.h: An eighth is 250 ms; multiply by 1.5.

audio-engineering.l19.q4.p: Pre-delay lets the dry sound arrive before the reverb begins.
audio-engineering.l19.q4.h: It is a gap before the effect.
audio-engineering.l19.q4.e: Pre-delay is a short wait before the reverb starts.

audio-engineering.l19.q5.t: It shares one space across tracks and saves processing
audio-engineering.l19.q5.p: Why use an auxiliary send for reverb rather than inserting one on every track?
audio-engineering.l19.q5.e: Auxiliary sends give a consistent space and use less CPU.

audio-engineering.l20.q1.p: Automation records movements of controls over time.
audio-engineering.l20.q1.e: Automation stores control changes and replays them.

audio-engineering.l20.q2.t: A group of related tracks mixed down into one file
audio-engineering.l20.q2.h: Drums, vocals or music might each have one.
audio-engineering.l20.q2.e: Stems are submixes of related tracks.

audio-engineering.l20.q3.t: Controls the levels of assigned channels without summing their audio
audio-engineering.l20.q3.p: What does a VCA fader do?
audio-engineering.l20.q3.h: It is a control, not an audio path.
audio-engineering.l20.q3.e: A VCA moves group levels without routing their audio.

audio-engineering.l20.q4.t: To glue the kit together as one sound
audio-engineering.l20.q4.p: What is the purpose of gentle compression on a drum bus?
audio-engineering.l20.q4.h: It processes the sum of the drums.
audio-engineering.l20.q4.e: Bus compression can unify separate drum tracks.

audio-engineering.l20.q5.t: The control returns to its previous automated value
audio-engineering.l20.q5.p: In Touch automation mode, what happens when you let go of the control?
audio-engineering.l20.q5.e: Touch writes only while held; Latch continues at the last value.

audio-engineering.l21.q1.p: One loudness unit (LU) equals how many dB?
audio-engineering.l21.q1.h: The units are designed to match.
audio-engineering.l21.q1.e: A 1 dB change shifts the reading by 1 LU.

audio-engineering.l21.q2.p: LUFS simply reports the highest sample peak in a file.
audio-engineering.l21.q2.h: LUFS is about perceived loudness over time.
audio-engineering.l21.q2.e: LUFS is a weighted, gated average loudness, not a peak value.

audio-engineering.l21.q3.p: A master at -8 LUFS plays on a service that normalizes to -14 LUFS. How much is it turned down?
audio-engineering.l21.q3.e: -14 minus -8 is -6, so playback is lowered by 6 dB.

audio-engineering.l21.q4.t: Inter-sample peaks that can clip after conversion or encoding
audio-engineering.l21.q4.p: What is true peak measurement meant to catch?
audio-engineering.l21.q4.e: True peak estimates levels between samples that can overshoot.

audio-engineering.l21.q5.t: Loud masters are turned down, so only the lost dynamics remain
audio-engineering.l21.q5.p: Why does the loudness war matter less on normalizing platforms?
audio-engineering.l21.q5.h: Think about what normalization does to loud files.
audio-engineering.l21.q5.e: Extra loudness is removed by normalization while the dynamics lost in making it stay lost.

audio-engineering.l22.q1.p: Mastering can fully fix any problem in a mix.
audio-engineering.l22.q1.h: Consider a vocal that is buried.
audio-engineering.l22.q1.e: Large mix problems are best solved by revising the mix.

audio-engineering.l22.q2.p: What is the Red Book audio CD format?
audio-engineering.l22.q2.e: Audio CDs use 44.1 kHz and 16 bits.

audio-engineering.l22.q3.h: It is a code for recordings.
audio-engineering.l22.q3.e: ISRC stands for International Standard Recording Code.

audio-engineering.l22.q4.t: Leave headroom and avoid heavy master-bus limiting
audio-engineering.l22.q4.p: What is common advice for a mix sent to mastering?
audio-engineering.l22.q4.h: The mastering engineer needs room to work.
audio-engineering.l22.q4.e: Headroom and no heavy limiting give the engineer flexibility.

audio-engineering.l22.q5.t: So listeners need not keep adjusting the volume or tone between songs
audio-engineering.l22.q5.p: Why does an album master aim for consistency between tracks?
audio-engineering.l22.q5.e: Consistent level and tone create a smooth listening experience across the album.

audio-engineering.l23.q1.p: How many channels does a 5.1 format have?
audio-engineering.l23.q1.e: Five full-range channels plus one LFE channel make six.

audio-engineering.l23.q2.p: The .1 in 5.1 refers to a low-frequency effects channel.
audio-engineering.l23.q2.h: It is not a full-range speaker.

audio-engineering.l23.q3.t: Content common to both left and right channels
audio-engineering.l23.q3.p: In mid-side processing, what does the mid signal contain?
audio-engineering.l23.q3.e: Mid is the sum (or average) of left and right.

audio-engineering.l23.q4.t: Sounds carry position metadata and are rendered for the playback system
audio-engineering.l23.q4.p: What defines object-based audio such as Dolby Atmos?
audio-engineering.l23.q4.h: A renderer decides the speaker feeds.
audio-engineering.l23.q4.e: Position metadata lets the renderer adapt sounds to the available speakers.

audio-engineering.l23.q5.t: Head-related cues such as timing, level and filtering differences between the ears
audio-engineering.l23.q5.p: Binaural audio for headphones relies on what?
audio-engineering.l23.q5.h: It imitates how ears locate sound.
audio-engineering.l23.q5.e: HRTFs reproduce the directional cues the head and ears create.

audio-engineering.l24.q1.p: A delay speaker sits 17.15 m from the mains. With sound at 343 m/s, what delay aligns it?

audio-engineering.l24.q2.p: Feedback occurs when sound from a loudspeaker re-enters a microphone and is amplified in a loop.
audio-engineering.l24.q2.e: This acoustic loop builds into a ring when its gain reaches one or more.

audio-engineering.l24.q3.p: Where should a cardioid microphone aim its null relative to a monitor wedge?
audio-engineering.l24.q3.h: Use the rear of the pattern.
audio-engineering.l24.q3.e: Placing the wedge in the rear null reduces pickup of the wedge.

audio-engineering.l24.q4.h: It is where the audience mix is made.

audio-engineering.l24.q5.t: Lower the gain or level of the ringing channel
audio-engineering.l24.q5.p: A channel begins to ring with feedback. What is a sensible first action?
audio-engineering.l24.q5.h: Loop gain must drop below one.
audio-engineering.l24.q5.e: Reducing gain lowers the loop gain and stops the ring.

audio-engineering.l25.q1.t: Filling gaps with the sound of the location with no one speaking
audio-engineering.l25.q1.p: What is room tone used for?
audio-engineering.l25.q1.h: It is a recording of silence in place.
audio-engineering.l25.q1.e: Room tone keeps backgrounds consistent between edits.

audio-engineering.l25.q2.p: Foley is performed live, in sync with picture, on a specialised stage.
audio-engineering.l25.q2.h: Think of footsteps recorded while watching.
audio-engineering.l25.q2.e: Foley artists perform sounds while watching the picture.

audio-engineering.l25.q3.p: About how long does one frame last at 24 frames per second?

audio-engineering.l25.q4.t: Re-recording dialogue in a studio while watching the picture
audio-engineering.l25.q4.e: ADR replaces production dialogue with studio recordings.

audio-engineering.l25.q5.p: Playing a recording at half speed by resampling lowers its pitch by one octave and doubles its duration.
audio-engineering.l25.q5.h: Half the frequency is an octave down.
audio-engineering.l25.q5.e: Half speed halves the frequency, one octave, and doubles the length.

audio-engineering.l26.q1.p: Every jurisdiction allows recording any conversation without the consent of the people involved.
audio-engineering.l26.q1.e: Some places require all parties to consent, so check local rules.

audio-engineering.l26.q2.t: The sound recording and the underlying musical composition
audio-engineering.l26.q2.p: A recorded song in the United States typically involves which two copyrights?
audio-engineering.l26.q2.h: One is the performance fixed in sound, the other is the song.
audio-engineering.l26.q2.e: The recording and the composition are separate works with separate owners.

audio-engineering.l26.q3.t: In writing, before the work begins
audio-engineering.l26.q3.p: When is the best time to agree on credits and ownership?
audio-engineering.l26.q3.e: Written agreements made up front avoid disputes.

audio-engineering.l26.q4.t: Limiting exposure to loud sound and using hearing protection
audio-engineering.l26.q4.p: Which habit best protects your ability to work for decades?
audio-engineering.l26.q4.e: Protecting hearing keeps a career possible.

audio-engineering.l26.q5.t: Permission from the rights holders unless a legal exception applies
audio-engineering.l26.q5.p: Using a sample of another artist recording in your track generally requires what?
audio-engineering.l26.q5.h: Think about who owns the recording.
audio-engineering.l26.q5.e: Samples generally need clearance; exceptions are narrow and vary by country.

botany-forest.l01.q1.p: Who is credited with turning plants into a subject of scientific study around 300 BCE?
botany-forest.l01.q1.h: He was a student of Aristotle.
botany-forest.l01.q1.e: Theophrastus described about 500 plants and asked how they are built and why they grow where they do, which founded botany.

botany-forest.l01.q2.t: The compartments he saw in a slice of cork
botany-forest.l01.q2.p: What did Robert Hooke name "cells" in 1665?
botany-forest.l01.q2.h: He used a microscope on a bark tissue.
botany-forest.l01.q2.e: Hooke saw box-like compartments in cork and named them after the rooms of a monastery.

botany-forest.l01.q3.p: A student studies a leaf under a microscope and sees a dense, regular pattern of small compartments, each with a dark central structure. Which structure was named by Robert Brown in 1831?
botany-forest.l01.q3.h: It is the dark structure in the middle of each living cell.
botany-forest.l01.q3.e: Brown named the nucleus as a structure consistently present in living cells.

botany-forest.l01.q4.t: Cork is dead tissue, so only the cell walls remained
botany-forest.l01.q4.p: Hooke saw only empty box-like compartments in cork. What best explains this?
botany-forest.l01.q4.h: Think about what is left of bark that has died.
botany-forest.l01.q4.e: Cork is dead bark, so the living contents were gone and he saw only walls. The word he chose for empty rooms became the name for the unit of life.

botany-forest.l02.q1.p: Which tissue carries water and minerals upward from the roots?
botany-forest.l02.q1.e: Xylem moves water and dissolved minerals up the plant, while phloem moves sugar.

botany-forest.l02.q2.h: Think about where the food is made and where it is needed.
botany-forest.l02.q2.e: Phloem distributes the sugar produced in leaves to roots, growing tips and fruit.

botany-forest.l02.q3.p: A gardener puts a cut celery stalk in water dyed red and sees red lines climb the stalk. Which tissue is showing the dye moving?
botany-forest.l02.q3.h: The dye travels with the water.
botany-forest.l02.q3.e: Dyed water rises through xylem vessels, which is why the stalk shows coloured streaks.

botany-forest.l02.q4.t: Water cannot be pulled much above about 120 metres through the trunk
botany-forest.l02.q4.p: Why does a coast redwood drink fog through its needles at the top?
botany-forest.l02.q4.h: Think about the limit on how high a water column can be lifted.
botany-forest.l02.q4.e: Past roughly 120 metres the water column breaks, so the top of a very tall redwood relies on fog condensing on its needles.

botany-forest.l03.q1.p: Which two raw materials do plants use in photosynthesis?
botany-forest.l03.q1.h: One is a gas in the air and one is taken up by roots.
botany-forest.l03.q1.e: Photosynthesis combines carbon dioxide from the air with water, using light energy.

botany-forest.l03.q2.p: What gas do green plants release in sunlight?
botany-forest.l03.q2.h: It is the gas animals breathe in.
botany-forest.l03.q2.e: Oxygen is released as a product of photosynthesis, as Ingenhousz observed.

botany-forest.l03.q3.t: It stops releasing oxygen and consumes it instead
botany-forest.l03.q3.p: A plant is kept in total darkness for two weeks. Based on what Ingenhousz found, what happens to its oxygen release?
botany-forest.l03.q3.h: Light is required for the process.
botany-forest.l03.q3.e: In darkness green parts consume oxygen rather than release it, because photosynthesis needs light.

botany-forest.l03.q4.p: A tree grows from a small seed to a huge trunk. What is the main source of the carbon in its wood?
botany-forest.l03.q4.e: The carbon in sugar and wood comes mostly from atmospheric CO2 fixed during photosynthesis, which overturned the old idea that plants eat soil.

botany-forest.l04.q1.t: The path carbon dioxide takes on its way to sugar
botany-forest.l04.q1.p: What did Calvin, Benson and Bassham trace with radioactive carbon-14?
botany-forest.l04.q1.h: They followed a labelled carbon atom.
botany-forest.l04.q1.e: Their work revealed the Calvin-Benson cycle, the steps by which CO2 is fixed into sugar.

botany-forest.l04.q2.p: Where in a plant cell does photosynthesis take place?
botany-forest.l04.q2.e: Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll and carry out photosynthesis.

botany-forest.l04.q3.t: Chloroplasts descend from free-living bacteria absorbed by an ancestral cell
botany-forest.l04.q3.p: Which statement correctly describes Margulis's endosymbiotic theory?
botany-forest.l04.q3.h: Think about a partnership between cells.
botany-forest.l04.q3.e: Margulis argued that chloroplasts and mitochondria descend from captured bacteria, and chloroplasts still carry their own DNA.

botany-forest.l04.q4.t: It still contains its own DNA
botany-forest.l04.q4.p: What is the best evidence in a chloroplast today that it once lived independently?
botany-forest.l04.q4.h: Which feature would an independent organism have?
botany-forest.l04.q4.e: Having its own bacterial-type DNA is a survivor of its free-living past, which is why the theory is accepted.

botany-forest.l05.q1.p: What does each tier of branches (whorl) on a Scots pine represent?
botany-forest.l05.q1.e: Each whorl marks a year of growth, so the pine records its own age in its branches.

botany-forest.l05.q2.p: True or false: a date palm has bark, annual rings and many branches like an oak.
botany-forest.l05.q2.h: Think about what a palm trunk is made of.
botany-forest.l05.q2.e: A palm has no bark, rings or branches. Its trunk is a bundle of fibres and it grows from a single point at the crown.

botany-forest.l05.q3.p: One oak grows alone in an open field and another grows in a dense forest. Which shape would you expect for the forest tree?
botany-forest.l05.q3.h: It must race its neighbours toward the light.
botany-forest.l05.q3.e: In a dense forest the same species grows tall and narrow, while the wide open crown belongs to a tree that grew without competition.

botany-forest.l05.q4.t: It has no growth rings, so radiocarbon dating is needed
botany-forest.l05.q4.p: Why can you not count growth rings to find the age of a baobab?
botany-forest.l05.q4.h: Think about the soft, fibrous wood.
botany-forest.l05.q4.e: Baobab wood is soft and fibrous and lacks countable rings, so scientists use radiocarbon to date it.

botany-forest.l06.q1.p: What is the main resource that a forest's layers compete for?
botany-forest.l06.q1.h: The tallest crowns get it first.
botany-forest.l06.q1.e: Layers arise because plants compete for light, with canopy trees intercepting most of it.

botany-forest.l06.q2.p: Which tree is the tallest flowering plant on Earth?
botany-forest.l06.q2.h: It comes from Tasmania and Victoria.
botany-forest.l06.q2.e: Mountain ash, 70 to 100 metres tall, is the tallest flowering plant. The coast redwood is taller but is a conifer.

botany-forest.l06.q3.t: The seeds germinated together on bare, lit ground after one fire
botany-forest.l06.q3.p: A forest of mountain ash trees is all about the same age. What best explains that?
botany-forest.l06.q3.h: Think about what mountain ash seedlings need to start.
botany-forest.l06.q3.e: The seed needs bare ash and full light, so a stand usually germinates together after a single fire.

botany-forest.l06.q4.t: It will fail to establish because it cannot regenerate in its own shade
botany-forest.l06.q4.p: A seedling of a mountain ash is growing under the shade of its parent trees. What is most likely to happen?
botany-forest.l06.q4.h: Remember what the seed needs in order to germinate.
botany-forest.l06.q4.e: Mountain ash cannot regenerate in shade. It depends on disturbance such as fire to open the ground and let light in.

botany-forest.l07.q1.t: A species that arrives first on open or burnt ground
botany-forest.l07.q1.h: Think of who arrives first at a new site.
botany-forest.l07.q1.e: Pioneers such as paper birch colonise bare ground early, grow fast and shelter slower trees that follow.

botany-forest.l07.q2.t: Its thick bark contains almost no resin
botany-forest.l07.q2.p: Why does a coast redwood survive fires that kill nearby plants?
botany-forest.l07.q2.h: The answer is in the bark.
botany-forest.l07.q2.e: The cinnamon-coloured bark is about a foot thick and nearly resin-free, so it resists burning.

botany-forest.l07.q3.p: A burnt hillside is bare. Which tree is most likely to be found there first?
botany-forest.l07.q3.h: It is the pioneer in the examples.
botany-forest.l07.q3.e: Birch colonises open burnt ground quickly; slower trees like maple come later in succession.

botany-forest.l07.q4.t: It shelters slower-growing trees that eventually replace it
botany-forest.l07.q4.p: What is the role of a short-lived pioneer such as birch in the sequence of forest change?
botany-forest.l07.q4.h: It dies young, but not for nothing.
botany-forest.l07.q4.e: Pioneers grow fast and die young, and in doing so shelter the slower trees that will form the later forest.

botany-forest.l08.q1.p: Which kingdom do mushrooms and the threads in a mycorrhiza belong to?
botany-forest.l08.q1.h: The wing calls it a separate kingdom.
botany-forest.l08.q1.e: Fungi are a separate kingdom, not plants, although they are tied to trees through mycorrhizal links.

botany-forest.l08.q2.t: That a lichen is a partnership between a fungus and an alga
botany-forest.l08.q2.p: What did Beatrix Potter argue about lichens?
botany-forest.l08.q2.h: It is a partnership of two organisms.
botany-forest.l08.q2.e: Potter argued for the then-contested view that lichens are a fungus and an alga living together.

botany-forest.l08.q3.p: In a mycorrhizal partnership, what does the tree typically supply to the fungus?
botany-forest.l08.q3.e: The tree pays the fungus in sugar made by photosynthesis, while the fungus extends the root's reach into the soil.

botany-forest.l08.q4.t: Trees are connected below ground and resources pass between them
botany-forest.l08.q4.p: Simard's work showed carbon moving between birch and fir. Which conclusion is best supported?
botany-forest.l08.q4.h: Be careful not to claim more than the evidence supports.
botany-forest.l08.q4.e: Isotope tracing showed carbon transfer through shared fungal networks. How much transfer happens and why is still debated.

botany-forest.l09.q1.p: What did Grew and Malpighi argue in 1682 about flowers?
botany-forest.l09.q1.h: It was controversial at the time.
botany-forest.l09.q1.e: They argued that flowers are the plant's reproductive organs, which made classification by flower structure possible.

botany-forest.l09.q2.t: The movement of pollen to the female part of a flower
botany-forest.l09.q2.h: Think of bats, bees and wind.
botany-forest.l09.q2.e: Pollen is carried by wind or animals to the female part of a flower so that seeds can form.

botany-forest.l09.q3.p: A mature oak drops 4,000 acorns in a good year and only 1 becomes a tree. What fraction of acorns becomes a tree?
botany-forest.l09.q3.h: Divide the one tree by the number of acorns.
botany-forest.l09.q3.e: 1 tree out of 4,000 acorns is a fraction of 1/4,000, which shows how few seeds survive.

botany-forest.l09.q4.t: Angiosperms enclose their seeds in fruit, while pines carry seeds in cones
botany-forest.l09.q4.p: Which statement distinguishes gymnosperms such as pines from angiosperms such as cherries?
botany-forest.l09.q4.h: Think about what protects the seed.
botany-forest.l09.q4.e: Pines are an older lineage that bears seeds in cones, while flowering plants form seeds inside fruit.

botany-forest.l10.q1.p: What plant did Mendel use for his experiments on inheritance?
botany-forest.l10.q1.h: It grows quickly and has clear contrasting traits.
botany-forest.l10.q1.e: Mendel counted about 28,000 pea plants to discover the rules of inheritance.

botany-forest.l10.q2.p: How long was Mendel's work ignored before being rediscovered?
botany-forest.l10.q2.h: He published in 1866; the rediscovery was in 1900.
botany-forest.l10.q2.e: 1900 minus 1866 is 34 years, after which three botanists independently rediscovered his laws.

botany-forest.l10.q3.p: Mendel counted about 28,000 pea plants over eight years. On average, about how many plants was that per year?
botany-forest.l10.q3.h: Divide the total by the number of years.
botany-forest.l10.q3.e: 28,000 divided by 8 is 3,500 plants per year.

botany-forest.l10.q4.t: Traits pass on in discrete units rather than blending
botany-forest.l10.q4.p: Which finding best summarises the importance of Mendel's pea counts?
botany-forest.l10.q4.h: Consider what happens to a trait across generations.
botany-forest.l10.q4.e: Mendel's counts showed that traits are inherited as distinct units, which is the foundation of genetics.

botany-forest.l11.q1.t: It can grow into a new willow that is identical to the parent
botany-forest.l11.q1.p: What happens when a willow branch is pushed into wet ground?
botany-forest.l11.q1.e: Willow cuttings root easily, producing a genetically identical new tree.

botany-forest.l11.q2.t: It backs up the world's crop seed collections
botany-forest.l11.q2.p: What does the Svalbard Global Seed Vault do?
botany-forest.l11.q2.h: It is a safeguard against loss.
botany-forest.l11.q2.e: The vault stores backup copies of crop seed collections inside a mountain in Norway.

botany-forest.l11.q3.t: All of the trees are at risk, because they are genetically identical
botany-forest.l11.q3.p: A city plants a long avenue of Lombardy poplars, all cloned from one tree. A disease arrives that one poplar cannot resist. What is the likely outcome?
botany-forest.l11.q3.h: Think about what cloning does to variation.
botany-forest.l11.q3.e: Clones share the same weaknesses, so a single canker can take out an entire avenue.

botany-forest.l11.q4.t: It tells breeders where to look for genes that can protect a harvest
botany-forest.l11.q4.p: Why does Vavilov's idea of crop centres of origin matter for farming today?
botany-forest.l11.q4.e: Regions where a crop originated still hold wild relatives with diverse genes, which can be used to protect harvests from disease and change.

botany-forest.l12.q1.t: A trunk that stores tens of thousands of litres of water
botany-forest.l12.q1.p: Which feature helps a baobab survive dry seasons?
botany-forest.l12.q1.e: The baobab's soft, fibrous trunk stores large amounts of water and swells and shrinks with the seasons.

botany-forest.l12.q2.t: Needles have a small surface area and waxy skin that reduce water loss
botany-forest.l12.q2.p: Why do conifers such as pine have needles rather than broad leaves?
botany-forest.l12.q2.h: It is an answer to cold and drought.
botany-forest.l12.q2.e: Needles reduce water loss and do not have to be rebuilt each spring.

botany-forest.l12.q3.t: It presents only its edge to the strong overhead sun
botany-forest.l12.q3.p: A eucalyptus leaf hangs vertically. How does this reduce heat stress at midday?
botany-forest.l12.q3.h: Think about which part of the leaf faces the sun.
botany-forest.l12.q3.e: A vertical leaf points its edge toward the midday sun, which reduces heating and water loss.

botany-forest.l12.q4.t: It reflects sunlight and prevents the trunk overheating and cracking
botany-forest.l12.q4.p: A paper birch growing on open, burnt ground has white bark while a shaded forest tree has darker bark. Which advantage best explains the white bark?
botany-forest.l12.q4.e: On open ground the reflective outer layer keeps the trunk from overheating and cracking on bright winter days.

botany-forest.l13.q1.t: By releasing spores from capsules on its fronds
botany-forest.l13.q1.p: How does a fern spread to new places?
botany-forest.l13.q1.h: Look at the underside of a frond.
botany-forest.l13.q1.e: Ferns have no flowers or seeds. They release spores from the brown capsules on the underside of their fronds.

botany-forest.l13.q2.t: A young fern frond curled into a tight spiral
botany-forest.l13.q2.h: It is a shape you see in violin scrolls.
botany-forest.l13.q2.e: Young fronds uncurl from a spiral, the most compact way to store something long.

botany-forest.l13.q3.t: A tiny, separate, heart-shaped organism that makes egg and sperm
botany-forest.l13.q3.p: A spore from a fern lands on damp soil and grows. What does it produce first?
botany-forest.l13.q3.h: It is not another fern right away.
botany-forest.l13.q3.e: The spore grows into a small heart-shaped organism, which produces eggs and sperm. That is the other half of the fern life cycle.

botany-forest.l13.q4.t: A seed is a packaged embryo with a food supply, while a spore is a single cell
botany-forest.l13.q4.p: Why is a seed considered a more elaborate way to start a plant than a spore?
botany-forest.l13.q4.e: A seed carries an embryo and stored food, while a spore is a single cell without that provision.

botany-forest.l14.q1.p: Which of these plant groups appeared most recently?
botany-forest.l14.q1.e: Flowering plants are the youngest lineage, coming after mosses, ferns and conifers.

botany-forest.l14.q2.t: It has no close relatives and is the last survivor of an ancient order
botany-forest.l14.q2.p: What makes the ginkgo a "living fossil"?
botany-forest.l14.q2.h: Think about who its relatives are.
botany-forest.l14.q2.e: The ginkgo is the last of an order that was widespread when dinosaurs lived.

botany-forest.l14.q3.p: A leaf has fan-shaped blades with veins that fork in two and never rejoin. Which tree is it most likely from?
botany-forest.l14.q3.e: Ginkgo leaves have this ancient forking vein pattern.

botany-forest.l14.q4.t: It was cultivated in temple grounds for around a thousand years
botany-forest.l14.q4.p: How did the ginkgo survive after its wild populations declined?
botany-forest.l14.q4.e: Wild populations are endangered, and cultivation in Chinese temple grounds kept the species alive.

color-theory.l01.q1.p: The color you see depends on the light source, the surface and your eyes and brain, not on the object alone.
color-theory.l01.q1.h: Remember the apple under green light.
color-theory.l01.q1.e: Color is an experience produced by light, surface and viewer working together.

color-theory.l01.q2.p: Roughly what range of wavelengths makes up visible light?
color-theory.l01.q2.h: It is a small slice of a much larger spectrum.
color-theory.l01.q2.e: Visible light covers roughly 400 to 700 nanometres, from violet to red.

color-theory.l01.q3.t: It reflects mostly long wavelengths, and green light has few of them to reflect
color-theory.l01.q3.p: A red apple looks almost black under pure green light. What is the best explanation?
color-theory.l01.q3.h: Think about what the surface sends back.
color-theory.l01.q3.e: A red surface reflects mainly long wavelengths, so under green light little light returns to the eye.

color-theory.l01.q4.p: Which cells in the retina work in dim light but do not distinguish colors?
color-theory.l01.q4.h: One of the two receptor types is for dim light.
color-theory.l01.q4.e: Rods handle low light and do not tell colors apart; cones are responsible for color vision.

color-theory.l01.q5.p: Newton used a prism to show that white light can be separated into a spectrum of colors.
color-theory.l01.q5.h: Think about what a prism does to sunlight.
color-theory.l01.q5.e: Newton’s prism experiments showed that white light is a mixture that can be spread into a spectrum.

color-theory.l02.q1.p: Which set gives the additive primaries?
color-theory.l02.q1.h: Think of the lights inside a screen.
color-theory.l02.q1.e: Screens add red, green and blue light.

color-theory.l02.q2.p: Mixing red light and green light together produces yellow light.
color-theory.l02.q2.e: In additive mixing, red and green light together look yellow.

color-theory.l02.q3.t: Real inks overlap into a muddy dark brown rather than a true black
color-theory.l02.q3.p: Why do printers add a separate black ink to cyan, magenta and yellow?
color-theory.l02.q3.e: Because real inks are imperfect, mixing all three gives a muddy dark brown, so black is added.

color-theory.l02.q4.p: In subtractive mixing, what does a layer of pigment do to the light?
color-theory.l02.q4.h: The word subtractive is the clue.
color-theory.l02.q4.e: Pigments absorb some wavelengths, leaving less light to reflect.

color-theory.l02.q5.p: A red spotlight and a green spotlight overlap on a white wall. What do you see where they overlap?
color-theory.l02.q5.h: The spotlights are light, not paint.
color-theory.l02.q5.e: Overlapping red and green light adds up to yellow; paint would give a brown.

color-theory.l03.q1.t: How light or dark a color is
color-theory.l03.q1.e: Value is lightness or darkness, separate from hue.

color-theory.l03.q2.p: Saturation describes how vivid or pure a color is.
color-theory.l03.q2.h: Compare a bright red with a dusty red.
color-theory.l03.q2.e: Saturation, or chroma, is vividness; low saturation is closer to gray.

color-theory.l03.q3.p: A painter adds white to a blue paint. What is the result called?
color-theory.l03.q3.h: There are three names: white, black, gray.
color-theory.l03.q3.e: A tint is a color with white added.

color-theory.l03.q4.p: Two shapes look identical when a picture is converted to grayscale. What does that tell you?
color-theory.l03.q4.e: Grayscale keeps only lightness, so the shapes have similar value.

color-theory.l03.q5.p: Which trio names the properties in the Munsell system?
color-theory.l03.q5.h: It was devised by an American artist in the early 1900s.
color-theory.l03.q5.e: Munsell described colors with hue, value and chroma.

color-theory.l04.q1.p: Which wheel uses red, yellow and blue as primaries?
color-theory.l04.q1.h: It is the one taught in many art classes.
color-theory.l04.q1.e: The traditional painter’s wheel is built on red, yellow and blue.

color-theory.l04.q2.p: On the RGB wheel, which color is opposite red?
color-theory.l04.q2.h: Red light plus its opposite makes white.
color-theory.l04.q2.e: On the RGB wheel the opposite of red is cyan.

color-theory.l04.q3.p: The RYB, RGB and CMY wheels agree on which colors are primaries.
color-theory.l04.q3.h: Compare the three sets of primaries.
color-theory.l04.q3.e: Each wheel has different primaries, so complements and primaries depend on the wheel.

color-theory.l04.q4.t: Those inks can mix a wider range of colors
color-theory.l04.q4.p: Why does printing use cyan, magenta and yellow rather than red, yellow and blue?
color-theory.l04.q4.h: Think about how much each set can produce.
color-theory.l04.q4.e: Cyan, magenta and yellow can mix a wider range than traditional red, yellow and blue pigments.

color-theory.l04.q5.p: A color wheel is a model, useful for a purpose, not a law of nature.
color-theory.l04.q5.e: Each wheel is a simplified model chosen to suit a medium and a purpose.

color-theory.l05.q1.p: Which pair is complementary on the traditional painter’s wheel?
color-theory.l05.q1.e: Blue and orange are opposite on the RYB wheel.

color-theory.l05.q2.t: Hues that sit next to each other on the wheel

color-theory.l05.q3.p: Strong complementary colors used in equal amounts can look harsh or seem to vibrate.
color-theory.l05.q3.e: Equal amounts of saturated complements can feel harsh where they meet.

color-theory.l05.q4.t: A near-complementary accent that draws attention
color-theory.l05.q4.p: A designer uses a calm green room with one coral cushion. What is the cushion’s role?
color-theory.l05.q4.h: Coral sits near the opposite of green.
color-theory.l05.q4.e: The coral is close to green’s complement and works as an accent.

color-theory.l05.q5.t: Mix complementary paints in unequal amounts
color-theory.l05.q5.p: How do painters often make a muted natural neutral without black?
color-theory.l05.q5.e: Mixing complements dulls them toward a neutral gray or brown.

color-theory.l06.q1.p: How many hues are in a triadic scheme?
color-theory.l06.q1.e: A triadic scheme uses three evenly spaced hues.

color-theory.l06.q2.t: The two hues on either side of orange
color-theory.l06.q2.p: A split-complementary scheme for blue uses blue plus which hues?
color-theory.l06.q2.h: Split means the complement is divided.
color-theory.l06.q2.e: It uses the two neighbors of the complement instead of the complement itself.

color-theory.l06.q3.p: A tetradic scheme uses two complementary pairs.
color-theory.l06.q3.e: A tetradic or rectangular scheme uses two complementary pairs, giving four hues.

color-theory.l06.q4.t: Let one hue dominate and use the others in support
color-theory.l06.q4.p: What is a common way to keep a triadic scheme from feeling unbalanced?
color-theory.l06.q4.e: One dominant hue with supporting hues gives balance.

color-theory.l06.q5.p: A color scheme tells you the exact value and saturation to use.
color-theory.l06.q5.e: Schemes describe hue relationships; value and saturation are separate choices.

color-theory.l07.q1.p: Which group is usually called warm?
color-theory.l07.q1.e: Reds, oranges and yellows are called warm.

color-theory.l07.q2.p: Whether a color seems warm or cool can depend on the colors beside it.
color-theory.l07.q2.e: A single color can look warm beside one neighbor and cool beside another.

color-theory.l07.q3.t: Light at a higher kelvin value
color-theory.l07.q3.p: In photography, which light is cooler-looking?
color-theory.l07.q3.h: The kelvin scale runs opposite to common words.
color-theory.l07.q3.e: Higher kelvin values give bluer, cooler-looking light.

color-theory.l07.q4.p: Why does a crimson red feel cooler than an orange-red?
color-theory.l07.q4.h: Think about which direction each leans.
color-theory.l07.q4.e: Red leaning toward blue looks cooler than red leaning toward orange.

color-theory.l07.q5.t: Warm lit areas with cooler shadows
color-theory.l07.q5.p: A painter shows sunlight on a wall. Which combination is a common choice?
color-theory.l07.q5.h: Think about how sunlit scenes appear.
color-theory.l07.q5.e: Warm lights paired with cooler shadows look natural and lively.

color-theory.l08.q1.t: The one on black looks lighter
color-theory.l08.q1.p: Two identical gray squares are placed on a white and on a black background. What happens?
color-theory.l08.q1.h: Perception shifts away from the surroundings.
color-theory.l08.q1.e: Simultaneous contrast makes the gray look lighter against black.

color-theory.l08.q2.p: Simultaneous contrast changes how a color looks without changing the color itself.
color-theory.l08.q2.e: Only the surroundings changed; the perception shifted.

color-theory.l08.q3.p: A gray patch surrounded by saturated red tends to look slightly what?
color-theory.l08.q3.h: Think of the complement of red.
color-theory.l08.q3.e: The patch shifts toward the complement, a slight green or blue-green.

color-theory.l08.q4.p: Staring at a red shape and then seeing a pale blue-green ghost on a white wall is called what?
color-theory.l08.q4.e: An afterimage occurs over time, unlike simultaneous contrast which occurs across space.

color-theory.l08.q5.t: Judge a color in context, not in isolation
color-theory.l08.q5.p: What practical lesson does simultaneous contrast give a designer?
color-theory.l08.q5.e: Colors should be checked in the setting where they will be seen.

color-theory.l09.q1.p: Who published The Principles of Harmony and Contrast of Colours in 1839?
color-theory.l09.q1.h: He was a French chemist at the Gobelins works.
color-theory.l09.q1.e: Chevreul, a French chemist, published it in 1839.

color-theory.l09.q2.p: Chevreul’s law of simultaneous contrast says that colors seen side by side appear to shift away from each other.
color-theory.l09.q2.h: Think about neighbors influencing each other.
color-theory.l09.q2.e: Adjacent colors appear to change in tone and hue relative to each other.

color-theory.l09.q3.t: Complaints that dyed tapestries looked dull
color-theory.l09.q3.p: According to standard accounts, what practical problem led Chevreul to study contrast?
color-theory.l09.q3.h: He worked in a dye workshop.
color-theory.l09.q3.e: He investigated complaints about the dyes at the Gobelins tapestry works.
