color-theory.l09.q4.p: Which painter is often linked with Chevreul’s ideas through the use of small dots of separate color?
color-theory.l09.q4.e: Seurat’s dot technique is often connected to color theorists including Chevreul.

color-theory.l09.q5.p: Chevreul’s work was aimed only at fine artists and never at dyers or manufacturers.
color-theory.l09.q5.e: His work was practical, aimed at dyers, weavers and manufacturers, as well as artists.

color-theory.l10.q1.p: Which teacher wrote Interaction of Color, published in 1963?
color-theory.l10.q1.e: Albers wrote Interaction of Color, published by Yale University Press.

color-theory.l10.q2.p: Albers believed color is highly relative and is seen through its relationships to other colors.
color-theory.l10.q2.e: Albers called color the most relative medium in art.

color-theory.l10.q3.p: Which of these is one of Itten’s seven contrasts?
color-theory.l10.q3.h: One concerns the amount of each color.
color-theory.l10.q3.e: Extension, meaning the relative amounts of colors, is among Itten’s seven contrasts.

color-theory.l10.q4.p: Where did Johannes Itten teach the preliminary course?
color-theory.l10.q4.e: Itten taught the preliminary course at the Bauhaus from 1919.

color-theory.l10.q5.t: Itten offers a framework of named contrasts; Albers emphasises experiments with paper
color-theory.l10.q5.p: How do the two teaching approaches differ in emphasis?
color-theory.l10.q5.e: Itten gave a vocabulary of contrasts; Albers taught through hands-on experiments.

color-theory.l11.q1.p: Research on color psychology finds large, universal effects that are identical for everyone.
color-theory.l11.q1.h: Remember the hedge in the lesson.
color-theory.l11.q1.e: Effects tend to be small, context dependent and variable between people.

color-theory.l11.q2.t: Many are learned from culture and vary by context
color-theory.l11.q2.p: Which statement about color meanings is most accurate?
color-theory.l11.q2.e: Many associations are cultural and depend on setting.

color-theory.l11.q3.t: They have traditionally reversed this, with red for gains
color-theory.l11.q3.p: In U.S. stock charts green usually shows gains. What does the lesson say about several East Asian markets?
color-theory.l11.q3.e: Some East Asian markets traditionally use red for rises and green for falls.

color-theory.l11.q4.t: Languages tend to add basic color terms in a similar order
color-theory.l11.q4.p: What did Berlin and Kay argue in 1969?
color-theory.l11.q4.e: They proposed a common pattern of basic color-term development, a view later debated.

color-theory.l11.q5.t: Check the audience, setting and competing associations
color-theory.l11.q5.p: What is a sound approach for a designer to color meaning?
color-theory.l11.q5.e: Meaning varies, so the audience and context should be checked.

color-theory.l12.q1.p: What is the maximum contrast ratio, black on white, in WCAG?
color-theory.l12.q1.h: It is the top of the scale.

color-theory.l12.q2.p: Under WCAG 2.x level AA, what ratio is generally expected for ordinary body text?
color-theory.l12.q2.h: It is lower than the AAA target of 7:1.
color-theory.l12.q2.e: Level AA asks for 4.5:1 for ordinary text.

color-theory.l12.q3.p: Meeting a contrast ratio guarantees that text is readable for every person.
color-theory.l12.q3.h: Remember the limits of the formula.
color-theory.l12.q3.e: The numbers are useful benchmarks, but they do not guarantee readability for all.

color-theory.l12.q4.t: Some people cannot tell red from green
color-theory.l12.q4.p: Why should a red-green status indicator also use labels or icons?
color-theory.l12.q4.e: Information should not depend on color alone.

color-theory.l12.q5.t: The relative luminance of two colors
color-theory.l12.q5.p: What does the WCAG contrast ratio compare?
color-theory.l12.q5.e: The ratio is calculated from relative luminance.

color-theory.l13.q1.p: What does the K in CMYK stand for?
color-theory.l13.q1.e: K stands for key, which is the black ink.

color-theory.l13.q2.p: A screen makes color by emitting light, while a printed page reflects ambient light through ink.
color-theory.l13.q2.e: Screens emit red, green and blue light; paper reflects light through inks.

color-theory.l13.q3.t: The range of colors a device can reproduce
color-theory.l13.q3.e: Gamut is the range of colors a device or process can reproduce.

color-theory.l13.q4.t: A single premixed ink applied on its own
color-theory.l13.q4.e: A spot color is a premixed ink, such as those specified using Pantone.

color-theory.l13.q5.t: It lies outside the CMYK gamut
color-theory.l13.q5.p: An electric-blue logo looks duller when converted to CMYK. What is the likeliest reason?
color-theory.l13.q5.e: Some vivid screen colors are outside what CMYK inks can reproduce.

color-theory.l14.q1.p: Which color space is the usual default for the web?
color-theory.l14.q1.h: Software assumes it when no profile is attached.
color-theory.l14.q1.e: sRGB is the common default for web and ordinary displays.

color-theory.l14.q2.p: Display P3 covers a wider range of saturated colors than sRGB.
color-theory.l14.q2.e: Display P3 has a noticeably larger gamut than sRGB.

color-theory.l14.q3.t: How to interpret the numbers in an image
color-theory.l14.q3.p: What does a color profile tell software?
color-theory.l14.q3.e: A profile defines what the color numbers mean.

color-theory.l14.q4.p: Which standard is used for high-definition television, with a gamut close to sRGB?
color-theory.l14.q4.h: The wider one is for ultra high-definition and HDR.
color-theory.l14.q4.e: Rec. 709 is the HDTV standard; Rec. 2020 is wider.

color-theory.l14.q5.t: They may assume sRGB and misread the numbers
color-theory.l14.q5.p: A photo edited in Display P3 and shared without a profile may look flat on some devices. Why?
color-theory.l14.q5.e: Without a profile, software may assume sRGB and interpret the numbers differently.

color-theory.l15.q1.p: Natural ultramarine was made from which stone?
color-theory.l15.q1.h: It was mined in what is now Afghanistan.
color-theory.l15.q1.e: Natural ultramarine came from lapis lazuli.

color-theory.l15.q2.p: Tyrian purple was a dye from sea snails and was very expensive.
color-theory.l15.q2.e: Many snails were needed for a small amount of dye, making it costly.

color-theory.l15.q3.p: Who produced the first synthetic aniline dye, mauveine, in 1856?
color-theory.l15.q3.h: He was a young English chemist.
color-theory.l15.q3.e: Perkin discovered mauveine while trying to make a medicine.

color-theory.l15.q4.p: Which pigment is among the earliest known synthetic pigments of the ancient world?
color-theory.l15.q4.e: Egyptian blue, made by heating sand, copper and a flux, dates to ancient Egypt.

color-theory.l15.q5.p: What did John Goffe Rand’s collapsible metal tube make easier?
color-theory.l15.q5.e: The paint tube made paint portable, helping painting outdoors.

color-theory.l16.q1.p: What does a strong value structure help a painting do?
color-theory.l16.q1.e: A good value structure holds the image together without color.

color-theory.l16.q2.t: Yellow ochre, vermilion, ivory black and white
color-theory.l16.q2.p: Which paints make up the Zorn palette?
color-theory.l16.q2.e: The Zorn palette uses yellow ochre, vermilion, ivory black and white.

color-theory.l16.q3.p: Atmospheric perspective paints distant objects lighter and bluer to suggest air.
color-theory.l16.q3.e: Distant objects are often painted lighter and bluer to suggest depth.

color-theory.l16.q4.p: What is often noted about the sun and sky in Monet’s Impression, Sunrise?
color-theory.l16.q4.e: The orange sun and blue-gray sky are close in value, so the sun nearly vanishes in black and white.

color-theory.l16.q5.t: Every mix shares the same ingredients
color-theory.l16.q5.p: Why does a limited palette tend to produce harmony?
color-theory.l16.q5.e: Mixes drawn from the same few paints tend to belong together.

color-theory.l17.q1.t: Adjusting brightness, contrast and color after shooting
color-theory.l17.q1.e: Grading shapes the image after it has been filmed.

color-theory.l17.q2.p: What do the lift, gamma and gain controls adjust?
color-theory.l17.q2.e: They adjust the shadows, midtones and highlights.

color-theory.l17.q3.p: A LUT is a stored set of color conversions that can be applied to footage.
color-theory.l17.q3.e: A LUT maps input colors to output colors and can apply a look.

color-theory.l17.q4.t: The eye is easily fooled by room lighting and fatigue
color-theory.l17.q4.p: Why do colorists rely on scopes?
color-theory.l17.q4.e: Scopes give objective measures of brightness and color.

color-theory.l17.q5.t: The colors are near opposites, so faces stand out
color-theory.l17.q5.p: Why does pairing orange skin tones with teal backgrounds work?
color-theory.l17.q5.e: Orange and teal sit near opposite sides of the wheel, producing strong contrast.

color-theory.l18.q1.p: In interface design, what is the main job of neutral colors?
color-theory.l18.q1.h: They cover most of the screen.
color-theory.l18.q1.e: Neutrals make up most of the surface and carry text.

color-theory.l18.q2.p: The 60-30-10 idea is a rule of thumb, not a law.
color-theory.l18.q2.h: It is a guide for balance.
color-theory.l18.q2.e: It suggests a balance of dominant, secondary and accent colors but is not binding.

color-theory.l18.q3.t: Named color values reused across a product
color-theory.l18.q3.e: Tokens let a change be made once and apply everywhere.

color-theory.l18.q4.t: Color alone should not convey state
color-theory.l18.q4.p: Why should an error field use an icon or message as well as red?
color-theory.l18.q4.e: Information should not rely on color alone.

color-theory.l18.q5.t: Soften highly saturated colors and recheck contrast
color-theory.l18.q5.p: What is a common adjustment when moving a design to dark mode?
color-theory.l18.q5.e: Dark mode is not a simple inversion; colors and contrast need rechecking.

color-theory.l19.q1.p: What kind of mixing do overlapping colored stage lights use?
color-theory.l19.q1.e: Stage lights add together as light.

color-theory.l19.q2.p: A colored gel can only remove light, never add it.
color-theory.l19.q2.e: A gel absorbs wavelengths it does not pass, so it works subtractively.

color-theory.l19.q3.p: A red dress under blue light will look what?
color-theory.l19.q3.e: A red surface reflects little blue light, so it looks dark.

color-theory.l19.q4.t: Surfaces change appearance under colored light
color-theory.l19.q4.p: Why do designers test costumes and sets under working light?
color-theory.l19.q4.e: What the audience sees depends on how light meets each surface.

color-theory.l19.q5.t: The actor stands out from the cool background
color-theory.l19.q5.p: A night scene uses blue wash plus a warm pool on an actor with a lantern. What is the effect?
color-theory.l19.q5.e: Warm light against a cool background makes the actor stand out.

color-theory.l20.q1.p: What is a sensible first step in building a palette?

color-theory.l20.q2.p: A palette of only vivid colors with no neutrals is often tiring to look at.
color-theory.l20.q2.e: Neutrals give the eye rest and let bright colors stand out.

color-theory.l20.q3.t: So shapes and text can separate
color-theory.l20.q3.p: Why include a range of lights and darks in a palette?
color-theory.l20.q3.e: A range of values lets elements separate and read clearly.

color-theory.l20.q4.t: A photograph or painting sampled for swatches
color-theory.l20.q4.p: What is a common source for palette inspiration?
color-theory.l20.q4.e: Many people sample colors from a photo or artwork they like.

color-theory.l20.q5.t: Test in context and record named values
color-theory.l20.q5.p: What is the final step recommended after choosing colors?
color-theory.l20.q5.e: Palettes should be tested in real conditions and documented.

comic-history.l01.q1.t: A single framed picture on a page
comic-history.l01.q1.p: What is a panel in a comic?
comic-history.l01.q1.h: It is the basic unit of the page.
comic-history.l01.q1.e: A panel is one framed image; a page is built from panels.

comic-history.l01.q2.t: One panel filling the whole page
comic-history.l01.q2.p: What does a splash layout contain?
comic-history.l01.q2.h: The name suggests one big image.
comic-history.l01.q2.e: The Splash layout in the studio is a single panel at 100 percent width and height.

comic-history.l01.q3.p: In the studio presets, how is the 6 · Grid arranged?
comic-history.l01.q3.e: 6 · Grid divides the page into two columns and three rows.

comic-history.l01.q4.t: Panel count and size change the rhythm and emphasis of a page
comic-history.l01.q4.p: Why does choosing a layout affect storytelling?
comic-history.l01.q4.h: Think about a big panel versus many small ones.
comic-history.l01.q4.e: A tight grid feels steady while a large panel gives weight, so layout shapes pacing and emphasis.

comic-history.l02.q1.p: What is the gutter in a comic page?
comic-history.l02.q1.h: It is the empty space around panels.
comic-history.l02.q1.e: The gutter is the space separating panels, where the reader connects images.

comic-history.l02.q2.p: In the ComicPanelBuilder, what is the default panelGutter value?
comic-history.l02.q2.h: It is a small number between the slider ends.
comic-history.l02.q2.e: The builder uses page.panelGutter ?? 6 as the default.

comic-history.l02.q3.p: What range does the gutter slider in the panel builder cover?
comic-history.l02.q3.e: The slider has min 0 and max 20.

comic-history.l02.q4.t: Slows the reader and gives each image room
comic-history.l02.q4.p: What does a wide gutter usually do to the feel of a page?
comic-history.l02.q4.e: More space between panels slows the tempo; narrow gutters feel quicker.

comic-history.l03.q1.p: Which balloon type is used for what a character thinks but does not say?
comic-history.l03.q1.e: A thought balloon shows unspoken thoughts.

comic-history.l03.q2.p: What does SFX stand for in comics?
comic-history.l03.q2.h: It is the lettering for noises like POW.
comic-history.l03.q2.e: SFX means sound effects, drawn as lettering in the picture.

comic-history.l03.q3.p: In the panel builder, which bubble type uses a dark box with white text for narrator voice?
comic-history.l03.q3.h: It is not spoken by a character.
comic-history.l03.q3.e: The narration type is labelled Caption and appears as a dark box with white text.

comic-history.l03.q4.t: They guide the eye in reading order and should not cover key art
comic-history.l03.q4.p: Why do creators arrange balloons carefully on a page?
comic-history.l03.q4.h: Think about where readers look next.
comic-history.l03.q4.e: Balloon placement leads the reader through the page and should avoid hiding faces or action.

comic-history.l04.q1.p: In which direction do traditional manga pages read?
comic-history.l04.q1.h: They open from the Western back cover.
comic-history.l04.q1.e: Manga traditionally reads from right to left.

comic-history.l04.q2.t: Left to right, top to bottom
comic-history.l04.q2.p: How do Western comics normally read?
comic-history.l04.q2.e: Western comics follow left-to-right, top-to-bottom order.

comic-history.l04.q3.p: In the ComicReader in right-to-left mode, what does the left arrow key do?
comic-history.l04.q3.e: In RTL mode the keys swap meaning, so left goes forward.

comic-history.l04.q4.t: Rightmost panels first, then top to bottom
comic-history.l04.q4.p: How does the panel builder order panels for manga?
comic-history.l04.q4.e: For manga it sorts so larger x comes first, then smaller y, matching right-to-left reading.

comic-history.l05.q1.p: What does a single large panel usually do to the reading pace?
comic-history.l05.q1.e: A big panel gives an image room and slows the reader down.

comic-history.l05.q2.p: Which preset layout puts one image across the page with small insets on top?
comic-history.l05.q2.e: Inset Reveal places two small insets over a full-page panel.

comic-history.l05.q3.p: Which layout category does Webtoon · Reveal belong to?
comic-history.l05.q3.h: It is a vertical scroll format.
comic-history.l05.q3.e: The data lists Webtoon · Reveal in the webtoon category.

comic-history.l05.q4.t: Space on the page works like time in the story
comic-history.l05.q4.p: What principle sits behind pacing in panel layouts?
comic-history.l05.q4.h: Room for an image equals duration.
comic-history.l05.q4.e: Giving an image more room makes the reader linger; small panels speed up the narrative.

comic-history.l06.q1.p: Which event does the museum say launched the comic book?
comic-history.l06.q1.e: The museum timeline says Action Comics #1 in 1938 introduced Superman and the comic book was born.

comic-history.l06.q2.p: Which of these is a newspaper strip named by the museum?
comic-history.l06.q2.h: It is from the 1890s to 1930s era.
comic-history.l06.q2.e: Yellow Kid, Little Nemo and Krazy Kat are named as early newspaper strips.

comic-history.l06.q3.p: Which creator is described as master of the clear line style?
comic-history.l06.q3.e: The museum credits Herge, the Tintin creator, with the clear line style.

comic-history.l06.q4.t: They reached daily readers and built a mass audience for sequential pictures
comic-history.l06.q4.p: Why did newspaper strips matter to the history of comics?
comic-history.l06.q4.e: Newspapers reached huge daily audiences, which created the mass readership for comics.

comic-history.l07.q1.p: Which era does the museum date from 1938 to 1956?
comic-history.l07.q1.e: The Golden Age runs 1938 to 1956 in the museum timeline.

comic-history.l07.q2.p: Who is called the King of Comics in the museum?
comic-history.l07.q2.e: The museum calls Jack Kirby the King of Comics.

comic-history.l07.q3.t: A science-fueled revival with flawed human heroes
comic-history.l07.q3.p: What is the Silver Age described as in the museum?
comic-history.l07.q3.h: Spider-Man and the X-Men belong here.
comic-history.l07.q3.e: The museum describes it as a science-fueled revival led by Lee, Kirby and Ditko.

comic-history.l07.q4.t: Real relatable humanity: flawed people behind the masks
comic-history.l07.q4.p: What did Stan Lee add to superheroes, per the museum?
comic-history.l07.q4.e: The museum says Lee gave superheroes real, relatable humanity.

comic-history.l08.q1.t: Watchmen and The Dark Knight Returns
comic-history.l08.q1.p: Which two works does the museum say legitimized comics as literature in the Modern Age?
comic-history.l08.q1.e: The museum names Watchmen and The Dark Knight Returns.

comic-history.l08.q2.e: The Sandman is credited to Neil Gaiman in the museum.

comic-history.l08.q3.p: What themes does the museum say grew in the Bronze Age?
comic-history.l08.q3.e: The museum says Bronze Age stories became darker and socially aware, dealing with addiction, race and grief.

comic-history.l08.q4.p: Which comic is credited with a half-century run from 1950 to 2000?
comic-history.l08.q4.e: Peanuts by Charles Schulz ran from 1950 to 2000.

comic-history.l09.q1.p: Which creator is credited with championing the graphic novel as a serious literary form?
comic-history.l09.q1.h: He wrote A Contract with God.
comic-history.l09.q1.e: The museum credits Will Eisner with championing the graphic novel.

comic-history.l09.q2.t: A long-form comic published as a book
comic-history.l09.q2.e: A graphic novel is a long comic story in book form.

comic-history.l09.q3.p: Which pair of works is by Alan Moore?
comic-history.l09.q3.h: One features Guy Fawkes masks in the title lettering.
comic-history.l09.q3.e: Moore wrote Watchmen, V for Vendetta and From Hell.

comic-history.l09.q4.t: European comics, defined by Herge's clear line
comic-history.l09.q4.p: How does the museum describe the term bande dessinee?
comic-history.l09.q4.e: Herge is described as having defined European comics, called bande dessinee.

comic-history.l10.q1.p: Which artist's sketches does the museum cite as early manga?
comic-history.l10.q1.e: The museum timeline mentions Hokusai's sketch manga.

comic-history.l10.q2.e: The museum lists kamishibai street theatre among Japan's early visual story forms.

comic-history.l10.q3.p: What is the museum's title for the earliest manga era in its timeline?
comic-history.l10.q3.e: The first era is titled Roots, running from the Edo period to the 1930s.

comic-history.l10.q4.p: Which term does the museum use alongside manga for Korean comics?
comic-history.l10.q4.e: The museum refers to manga, manhwa and manhua; manhwa is Korean.

comic-history.l11.q1.p: Which creator is called the God of Manga?
comic-history.l11.q1.e: The museum calls Osamu Tezuka the God of Manga.

comic-history.l11.q2.p: Which of these is a Tezuka work in the museum?
comic-history.l11.q2.e: Tezuka's works named include Astro Boy, Black Jack and Phoenix.

comic-history.l11.q3.p: What did Tezuka bring to manga, according to the museum?
comic-history.l11.q3.e: The museum says he invented modern story manga and its cinematic panel language.

comic-history.l11.q4.p: Which panel shape feature in the studio adds dynamic angled cuts in manga layouts?
comic-history.l11.q4.h: The layout data supports a shape option.
comic-history.l11.q4.e: The layout shape field supports rect, diag-left and diag-right for angled manga cuts.

comic-history.l12.q1.p: Which magazine launch does the museum use to mark the Shonen Boom?
comic-history.l12.q1.e: The museum says Weekly Shonen Jump launches in the Shonen Boom period starting 1968.

comic-history.l12.q2.p: Which creator is associated with Dragon Ball?
comic-history.l12.q2.e: Akira Toriyama created Dragon Ball and Dr. Slump.

comic-history.l12.q3.t: Transforming girls' manga into psychologically rich literary work
comic-history.l12.q3.p: What is the Year 24 Group credited with in the museum?
comic-history.l12.q3.e: The museum says the Year 24 Group transformed shojo manga into literary art.

comic-history.l12.q4.t: She is called the queen of the romantic comedy
comic-history.l12.q4.p: Which statement about Rumiko Takahashi matches the museum?
comic-history.l12.q4.e: The museum calls her the queen of the romantic comedy and credits Ranma 1/2 and Inuyasha.

comic-history.l13.q1.e: One Piece is by Eiichiro Oda, per the museum.

comic-history.l13.q2.p: What does the museum say made manga a global language?
comic-history.l13.q2.h: Think of how readers get chapters.
comic-history.l13.q2.e: The Global Era entry credits digital publishing and simultaneous translation.

comic-history.l13.q3.p: Which work brought cyberpunk manga and anime to the world?
comic-history.l13.q3.e: The museum says Otomo's Akira brought cyberpunk manga and anime to the world.

comic-history.l13.q4.p: Which of these is named as a title that broke out worldwide in the Global Era?
comic-history.l13.q4.h: It is in the same list as Dragon Ball and Naruto.
comic-history.l13.q4.e: The museum lists Dragon Ball, Sailor Moon, One Piece and Naruto.

comic-history.l14.q1.p: How is a webtoon normally read?
comic-history.l14.q1.e: A webtoon is a vertical-scroll comic.

comic-history.l14.q2.p: How many rows does the Webtoon · 5 layout have?
comic-history.l14.q2.h: The number is in the name.

comic-history.l14.q3.t: A pause as the reader scrolls before the next image
comic-history.l14.q3.p: In the Webtoon · Reveal layout, what do the gaps between strips create?
comic-history.l14.q3.h: Think of scrolling through empty space.
comic-history.l14.q3.e: The gaps act like long gutters, delaying the reveal of the next image.

comic-history.l14.q4.t: Panels are stacked in rows, so the order is simply top to bottom
comic-history.l14.q4.p: Which statement about reading order in webtoon layouts is correct?
comic-history.l14.q4.e: Webtoon layouts stack panels vertically, so the reader moves from top to bottom.

design-movements.l01.q1.p: The Crystal Palace of 1851 was built mostly from iron and glass.
design-movements.l01.q1.h: Think of the materials named in the lesson.
design-movements.l01.q1.e: Joseph Paxton designed the Great Exhibition building as an iron and glass structure assembled from standard parts.

design-movements.l01.q2.t: That cheap imitation ornament and treating workers like machine parts cost beauty and honest work
design-movements.l01.q2.p: What worry did many Victorian critics have about machine-made goods?
design-movements.l01.q2.h: Consider what machines could copy cheaply.
design-movements.l01.q2.e: Critics such as Pugin and Ruskin objected to imitation decoration and to labour that treated people like machine parts.

design-movements.l01.q3.p: Which writer praised the visible, imperfect work of medieval craftspeople in The Stones of Venice?
design-movements.l01.q3.e: Ruskin admired medieval stonecutters and criticised dehumanising factory labour.

design-movements.l01.q4.p: The Thonet No. 14 chair is offered in the lesson as a sign that industry and good design could coexist.
design-movements.l01.q4.h: It was simple and sold in large numbers.
design-movements.l01.q4.e: Its bent-wood construction was cheap and widely sold, suggesting well-designed mass production was possible.

design-movements.l01.q5.t: respect the flat surface it covers rather than imitate nature realistically
design-movements.l01.q5.p: Owen Jones argued in The Grammar of Ornament that decoration should
design-movements.l01.q5.h: It concerns the relation between pattern and surface.
design-movements.l01.q5.e: Jones argued for flat, stylised pattern suited to the surface it decorates.

design-movements.l02.q1.p: Who was the central figure of the British Arts and Crafts movement?
design-movements.l02.q1.e: William Morris designed, wrote and campaigned for well-made, useful and beautiful things.

design-movements.l02.q2.p: Arts and Crafts designers favoured visible joinery and natural materials such as oak.
design-movements.l02.q2.h: Honesty of construction was a value.
design-movements.l02.q2.e: Exposed construction and natural materials are typical features of the movement.

design-movements.l02.q3.t: A press founded by Morris in 1891 to print beautiful books
design-movements.l02.q3.h: It connects Morris to the book arts.
design-movements.l02.q3.e: Morris founded the Kelmscott Press in 1891 to produce finely made books.

design-movements.l02.q4.p: Which American house, completed 1908 to 1909, is an example of Arts and Crafts design?
design-movements.l02.q4.e: The Greene brothers designed the Gamble House with exposed timber joinery.

design-movements.l02.q5.p: Morris acknowledged that his handmade products were often bought by the wealthy rather than by ordinary workers.
design-movements.l02.q5.e: The irony that costly handwork served wealthy buyers is one of the movement's well-known tensions.

design-movements.l03.q1.t: Flowing, curving lines taken from plants
design-movements.l03.q1.p: Which feature best identifies Art Nouveau?
design-movements.l03.q1.e: The whiplash curve inspired by plant forms is its signature.

design-movements.l03.q2.p: Art Nouveau architects used industrial materials such as iron and glass.
design-movements.l03.q2.e: Unlike some Arts and Crafts designers, Art Nouveau embraced iron and glass.

design-movements.l03.q3.p: What was the German name for Art Nouveau?
design-movements.l03.q3.h: It comes from a Munich magazine.
design-movements.l03.q3.e: Jugendstil took its name from the magazine Jugend, founded in 1896.

design-movements.l03.q4.p: Which designer created entrances to the Paris Metro in cast iron and glass?
design-movements.l03.q4.e: Hector Guimard designed the Metro entrances beginning around 1900.

design-movements.l03.q5.p: In Catalonia, Art Nouveau appeared under which name, seen in Gaudi's Casa Batlló?
design-movements.l03.q5.e: The Catalan variant is called Modernisme.

design-movements.l04.q1.p: Who was the first president of the Vienna Secession?
design-movements.l04.q1.e: Klimt led the group when it formed in 1897.

design-movements.l04.q2.p: The Wiener Werkstatte designed objects ranging from furniture to jewellery.
design-movements.l04.q2.h: It aimed at a total work of art.
design-movements.l04.q2.e: The workshop made furniture, silver, jewellery, textiles and more.

design-movements.l04.q3.p: Which two people founded the Wiener Werkstatte in 1903?
design-movements.l04.q3.h: One was an architect, the other a designer and artist.
design-movements.l04.q3.e: Hoffmann and Moser founded it, with financial backing from Fritz Waerndorfer.

design-movements.l04.q4.t: Applied ornament was wasteful and outdated for modern life
design-movements.l04.q4.p: What position did Adolf Loos take in Ornament and Crime?
design-movements.l04.q4.e: Loos argued against applied ornament, an approach that influenced later modernism.

design-movements.l04.q5.p: The Palais Stoclet is in Vienna.
design-movements.l04.q5.h: Check the city in the lesson.
design-movements.l04.q5.e: The Palais Stoclet is in Brussels, designed by Hoffmann.

design-movements.l05.q1.t: It wanted to improve mass-produced goods rather than reject the machine
design-movements.l05.q1.p: How did the Deutscher Werkbund differ from Morris's approach?
design-movements.l05.q1.e: The Werkbund sought good design in industrial production.

design-movements.l05.q2.p: The Werkbund was founded in Munich in 1907.
design-movements.l05.q2.h: It is the same year Behrens joined AEG.
design-movements.l05.q2.e: The group was founded in 1907 by architects, designers and manufacturers.

design-movements.l05.q3.p: Which designer became artistic consultant to AEG in 1907?
design-movements.l05.q3.e: Behrens designed AEG's buildings, products and graphics in a unified identity.

design-movements.l05.q4.t: Standardised types versus individual artistic creativity
design-movements.l05.q4.p: What was debated at the Werkbund in 1914?
design-movements.l05.q4.h: Muthesius and van de Velde disagreed.
design-movements.l05.q4.e: Muthesius favoured standardisation, while van de Velde defended artistic individuality.

design-movements.l05.q5.p: Which building by Gropius and Adolf Meyer, from 1911, features a largely glass corner?
design-movements.l05.q5.h: It was a factory in Alfeld.
design-movements.l05.q5.e: The Fagus Factory is an early modern landmark by Gropius and Meyer.

design-movements.l06.q1.h: He was an architect and the first director.
design-movements.l06.q1.e: Gropius founded the school in Weimar in April 1919.

design-movements.l06.q2.p: Every Bauhaus student began with the preliminary course (Vorkurs).
design-movements.l06.q2.h: It introduced materials, colour and form.
design-movements.l06.q2.e: The Vorkurs was the foundation of Bauhaus teaching.

design-movements.l06.q3.p: Which teacher first ran the preliminary course?
design-movements.l06.q3.h: His approach was expressive and spiritual.
design-movements.l06.q3.e: Itten ran it first; Moholy-Nagy and Albers later shaped it.

design-movements.l06.q4.t: A shift toward design for industry
design-movements.l06.q4.p: What did the 1923 exhibition slogan signal?
design-movements.l06.q4.h: Look at the words "Art and Technology".
design-movements.l06.q4.e: The slogan indicated a move from craft expressionism toward industrial design.

design-movements.l06.q5.p: The Bauhaus left Weimar partly because regional politics cut its funding.
design-movements.l06.q5.e: After right-wing parties gained power in Thuringia, funding was reduced and the school left in 1925.

design-movements.l07.q1.p: Gropius designed the Bauhaus building in Dessau.
design-movements.l07.q1.e: Gropius designed the Dessau school and the masters' houses.

design-movements.l07.q2.p: Who designed tubular steel furniture, including the chair now called the Wassily chair?
design-movements.l07.q2.h: He worked in the Dessau years.
design-movements.l07.q2.e: Breuer designed the chair around 1925 to 1926.

design-movements.l07.q3.p: Who directed the Bauhaus from 1930 until its closure as a Berlin school?
design-movements.l07.q3.e: Mies took over in 1930 and moved the school to Berlin.

design-movements.l07.q4.p: In what year did the faculty vote to dissolve the Bauhaus under Nazi pressure?
design-movements.l07.q4.h: It was after a police search in April.
design-movements.l07.q4.e: The school dissolved itself in July 1933.

design-movements.l07.q5.p: The Bauhaus lasted about fourteen years.

design-movements.l08.q1.t: Starting design education with basic elements like line, shape and colour
design-movements.l08.q1.p: Which idea was central to Bauhaus teaching?
design-movements.l08.q1.e: Foundation teaching on basic elements remains the Bauhaus's most lasting method.

design-movements.l08.q2.p: Where did Moholy-Nagy found the New Bauhaus in 1937?
design-movements.l08.q2.h: It later became the Institute of Design.
design-movements.l08.q2.e: He founded it in Chicago, and it became the Institute of Design.

design-movements.l08.q3.p: After 1933, Bauhaus teachers took their ideas to schools in the United States.
design-movements.l08.q3.h: Albers, Gropius, Breuer and Mies all moved.
design-movements.l08.q3.e: Exile spread Bauhaus methods through Chicago, Harvard, Yale and elsewhere.

design-movements.l08.q4.p: Which school, founded in 1953, continued some Bauhaus approaches in Germany?
design-movements.l08.q4.h: It is a German design school.
design-movements.l08.q4.e: The Ulm School of Design continued aspects of Bauhaus teaching.

design-movements.l08.q5.p: All Bauhaus products were cheap and widely mass-produced.
design-movements.l08.q5.h: Consider the debate in the lesson.
design-movements.l08.q5.e: Many Bauhaus designs were costly to make, so the dream of cheap mass production was only partly met.

design-movements.l09.q1.t: Red, yellow and blue with black, white and grey
design-movements.l09.q1.p: Which colours are central to De Stijl?
design-movements.l09.q1.e: De Stijl used primary colours plus black, white and grey.

design-movements.l09.q2.p: Who designed the Red and Blue Chair?
design-movements.l09.q2.h: He also designed the Schroder House.
design-movements.l09.q2.e: Rietveld designed the chair around 1917 to 1918.

design-movements.l09.q3.p: Constructivism emerged in Russia after the 1917 revolution.
design-movements.l09.q3.h: The movement wanted art to serve society.
design-movements.l09.q3.e: Its artists designed posters, textiles and buildings for social use.

design-movements.l09.q4.t: A model for a spiralling iron tower that was never built
design-movements.l09.q4.p: What is Tatlin's Monument to the Third International?
design-movements.l09.q4.h: It was a design for a tower.
design-movements.l09.q4.e: Tatlin made a model in 1919 to 1920; the full tower was not built.

design-movements.l09.q5.t: De Stijl sought calm universal balance, Constructivism favoured dynamic diagonals and social use
design-movements.l09.q5.p: How does the lesson contrast De Stijl and Constructivism?
design-movements.l09.q5.e: De Stijl aimed at harmony; Constructivism used dynamic form for social and political purposes.

design-movements.l10.q1.t: A 1925 exhibition in Paris of decorative and industrial arts
design-movements.l10.q1.p: Where did the name Art Deco come from?
design-movements.l10.q1.h: The exposition had a long French title.
design-movements.l10.q1.e: The name was shortened later from the 1925 Paris Exposition internationale des arts decoratifs et industriels modernes.

design-movements.l10.q2.p: The 1925 exposition required exhibits to be modern rather than copies of historical styles.

design-movements.l10.q3.p: Which is a typical Art Deco motif?
design-movements.l10.q3.e: Geometric patterns and stepped forms are hallmarks of Deco.

design-movements.l10.q4.p: Who made luxurious glass for perfume bottles and vases?
design-movements.l10.q4.e: Lalique produced glass perfume bottles, vases and car mascots.

design-movements.l10.q5.p: Le Corbusier's pavilion at the 1925 exposition was richly ornamented in the Deco manner.
design-movements.l10.q5.h: It represented a different modern vision.
design-movements.l10.q5.e: The Pavillon de l'Esprit Nouveau was plain and unornamented.

design-movements.l11.q1.p: Which New York building completed in 1930 has a stainless steel sunburst spire?
design-movements.l11.q1.e: The Chrysler Building, by William Van Alen, was completed in 1930.

design-movements.l11.q2.p: The Chrysler Building was the tallest building in the world for a short time.
design-movements.l11.q2.h: The Empire State Building soon overtook it.
design-movements.l11.q2.e: It held the record briefly until the Empire State Building in 1931.

design-movements.l11.q3.p: Which New Zealand city was rebuilt largely in Art Deco after an earthquake in 1931?
design-movements.l11.q3.e: Napier's rebuilding after the 1931 earthquake produced a Deco town centre.

design-movements.l11.q4.p: Which ocean liner entering service in 1935 was known for lavish interiors?
design-movements.l11.q4.e: The French liner Normandie was a Deco showpiece.

design-movements.l11.q5.p: Who designed the Park Hotel in Shanghai (1934)?
design-movements.l11.q5.e: Hudec designed the hotel, an example of Deco beyond Europe and America.

design-movements.l12.q1.t: The teardrop shape that reduces air resistance
design-movements.l12.q1.e: Smooth curves borrowed from aerodynamic forms inspired the style.

design-movements.l12.q2.p: Streamlining was only applied to vehicles.
design-movements.l12.q2.e: Designers also streamlined stationary objects, which critics noted was symbolic.

design-movements.l12.q3.p: Which designer's Futurama exhibit appeared at the 1939 New York World's Fair?
design-movements.l12.q3.e: Bel Geddes designed Futurama, imagining a future of highways.

design-movements.l12.q4.p: The Douglas DC-3 is described as a practical streamlined aircraft.
design-movements.l12.q4.e: The DC-3 used real aerodynamic thinking.

design-movements.l12.q5.t: The shape symbolised speed but did not serve any real aerodynamic need
design-movements.l12.q5.p: What criticism did some people make of streamlined staplers?
design-movements.l12.q5.e: Streamlining of static objects was symbolic rather than functional.

design-movements.l13.q1.t: The Museum of Modern Art in New York
design-movements.l13.q1.p: Where was the 1932 exhibition that named the International Style held?
design-movements.l13.q1.h: It is a New York museum.
design-movements.l13.q1.e: MoMA staged the show, organised by Hitchcock and Johnson.

design-movements.l13.q2.t: Pilotis lifting the building on columns
design-movements.l13.q2.p: Which is one of Le Corbusier's five points of a new architecture?
design-movements.l13.q2.e: Pilotis were one of his five points of 1927.

design-movements.l13.q3.p: The Seagram Building in New York was designed with Mies van der Rohe's involvement.
design-movements.l13.q3.h: Philip Johnson also worked on it.
design-movements.l13.q3.e: Mies designed it, with Philip Johnson, completed in 1958.

design-movements.l13.q4.p: Which principle did Hitchcock and Johnson list?
design-movements.l13.q4.e: They stressed volume, regularity and absence of applied ornament.

design-movements.l13.q5.t: Modernist planning damaged lively city streets
design-movements.l13.q5.p: What did Jane Jacobs argue in 1961?
design-movements.l13.q5.e: She argued that large-scale modernist planning harmed street life.

design-movements.l14.q1.t: A grid, sans-serif type and white space
design-movements.l14.q1.p: Which features are typical of Swiss Style?
design-movements.l14.q1.e: The grid, sans-serif type and white space define the look.

design-movements.l14.q2.p: Text in Swiss Style is often set flush left and ragged right.
design-movements.l14.q2.h: It is an asymmetric layout habit.

design-movements.l14.q3.p: Who designed the typeface Helvetica, originally Neue Haas Grotesk?
design-movements.l14.q3.h: It came from the Haas foundry in 1957.
design-movements.l14.q3.e: Miedinger and Hoffmann created it in 1957; renamed Helvetica in 1960.

design-movements.l14.q4.p: Which designer wrote Grid Systems in Graphic Design?
design-movements.l14.q4.h: He also made the 1955 Tonhalle poster.

design-movements.l14.q5.p: Which designer in Basel began loosening the strict grid?
design-movements.l14.q5.e: Weingart pushed the rules and influenced postmodern graphic design.

design-movements.l15.q1.p: Which material did Charles and Ray Eames mould into curved chairs?
design-movements.l15.q1.h: They first used it for leg splints.
design-movements.l15.q1.e: Their moulded plywood experiments began with wartime splints.

design-movements.l15.q2.p: The Eames Lounge Chair and Ottoman was made for Herman Miller in 1956.
design-movements.l15.q2.h: It is an icon of the period.

design-movements.l15.q3.p: Which program commissioned modern houses starting in 1945?
design-movements.l15.q3.e: Arts and Architecture magazine started it in 1945.

design-movements.l15.q4.p: Which designer made the Diamond chair from welded steel rod?
design-movements.l15.q4.h: It was made for Knoll in 1952.

design-movements.l15.q5.p: The label "mid-century modern" was popularized by a book published in 1984, decades after the style itself.
design-movements.l15.q5.e: The label became popular later; a 1984 book helped establish it.

design-movements.l16.q1.p: Which Finnish designer bent laminated wood for the Paimio chair?
design-movements.l16.q1.e: Aalto designed the Paimio chair in 1931 to 1932.

design-movements.l16.q2.p: Which Danish designer created the Egg and Swan chairs for the SAS Royal Hotel?
design-movements.l16.q2.h: He also made the Ant chair.
design-movements.l16.q2.e: Jacobsen designed them for the hotel in 1958.

design-movements.l16.q3.p: Scandinavian design often kept warmth through natural wood and soft shapes.
design-movements.l16.q3.h: It differed from some colder modernism.
design-movements.l16.q3.e: Natural woods and craft values define the style.

design-movements.l16.q4.p: Which touring exhibition boosted the Nordic design image in North America?
design-movements.l16.q4.e: Design in Scandinavia travelled North America in those years.

design-movements.l16.q5.p: Which company was founded in 1943 by Ingvar Kamprad?

design-movements.l17.q1.p: What does the French phrase beton brut mean?
design-movements.l17.q1.e: Brutalism is named from "raw concrete", not from brutality.

design-movements.l17.q2.p: Which Le Corbusier building of 1952 is associated with the name?
design-movements.l17.q2.e: The Marseille block shows its formwork marks.

design-movements.l17.q3.p: Brutalist buildings often reveal how they are made and how they work.
design-movements.l17.q3.e: Showing structure and materials is typical.

design-movements.l17.q4.p: Which London complex was designed by Chamberlin, Powell and Bon?
design-movements.l17.q4.e: The Barbican was built from the 1960s and completed in 1982.

design-movements.l17.q5.p: Public opinion about Brutalism has stayed unchanged since the 1960s.
design-movements.l17.q5.e: Opinion has shifted, with many buildings now protected while others are still disliked.

design-movements.l18.q1.p: Which phrase answered "less is more" in Venturi's 1966 book?

design-movements.l18.q2.p: Who led the Memphis group in Milan?
design-movements.l18.q2.e: Sottsass gathered the designers in December 1980.

design-movements.l18.q3.p: Memphis furniture often used bright, clashing colours.
design-movements.l18.q3.e: Bold colour and pattern are signatures.

design-movements.l18.q4.t: The AT&T Building in New York
design-movements.l18.q4.p: Which postmodern building has a broken-top pediment?
design-movements.l18.q4.e: AT&T, completed in 1984, has the broken pediment.

design-movements.l18.q5.p: Who designed the 9093 kettle with a bird whistle for Alessi?

design-movements.l19.q1.h: It concerns objects made by ordinary craftspeople.
design-movements.l19.q1.e: Mingei refers to the art of the people.

design-movements.l19.q2.p: Yanagi Soetsu helped coin the term mingei in the mid-1920s.
design-movements.l19.q2.h: Hamada and Kawai worked with him.
design-movements.l19.q2.e: He did so with Hamada Shoji and Kawai Kanjiro.

design-movements.l19.q3.t: Cities that could grow and change like organisms
design-movements.l19.q3.e: They proposed replaceable capsules attached to permanent cores.

design-movements.l19.q4.p: Which Metabolist building from 1972 put capsules into practice?

design-movements.l19.q5.p: Who designed the Butterfly stool in 1954?
design-movements.l19.q5.h: He was the son of Yanagi Soetsu.
design-movements.l19.q5.e: Sori Yanagi designed it from two plywood pieces.

design-movements.l20.q1.p: Who coined the term Afrofuturism in a 1993 essay?
design-movements.l20.q1.h: The essay was titled "Black to the Future".
design-movements.l20.q1.e: Dery used the term, though the practice is older.

design-movements.l20.q2.p: Ruth E. Carter won an Academy Award for costume design for Black Panther.
design-movements.l20.q2.e: She won the award for costume design.

design-movements.l20.q3.p: Which architect built the Gando Primary School using local clay bricks?
design-movements.l20.q3.e: Kere built it in 2001 and won the Pritzker Prize in 2022.

design-movements.l20.q4.p: Which designer is associated with tropical modernism in Sri Lanka?

design-movements.l20.q5.t: Climate, materials and community shape good design
design-movements.l20.q5.p: What common thread links the global designers in the lesson?

design-movements.l21.q1.p: Who wrote Design for the Real World in 1971?
design-movements.l21.q1.h: He argued designers had social and ecological responsibility.

design-movements.l21.q2.p: Sustainable design considers a product's whole life, including repair and disposal.

design-movements.l21.q3.t: Reuse materials rather than throw them away
design-movements.l21.q3.p: What does the circular economy aim to do?

design-movements.l21.q4.p: Which standard reduces heating needs through insulation and airtightness?

design-movements.l21.q5.p: Engineered timber such as cross-laminated timber can store carbon and allow tall wooden buildings.
design-movements.l21.q5.e: The Norwegian tower of 2019 was for a time the tallest timber building.

design-movements.l22.q1.p: Which movement is recognised by red, yellow and blue lines on white?
design-movements.l22.q1.e: Primary colours with black and white are De Stijl's mark.

design-movements.l22.q2.p: Which movement is recognised by raw concrete masses?

design-movements.l22.q3.p: Postmodernism brought decoration and historical reference back after the International Style.
design-movements.l22.q3.e: Postmodern designers reintroduced ornament and wit.

design-movements.l22.q4.p: Which argument asks whether design should be worldwide or tied to place?
design-movements.l22.q4.e: It contrasts universal modernism with local approaches.

design-movements.l22.q5.p: Which clue best points to Art Deco?
design-movements.l22.q5.e: Symmetry, geometry and luxury are Deco hallmarks.

entertainment-finance.l01.q1.p: In most entertainment projects, the costs arrive before the income does.
entertainment-finance.l01.q1.h: Think about when a film crew is paid compared with when tickets are sold.
entertainment-finance.l01.q1.e: Projects typically spend money up front while revenue arrives later and is uncertain, which is why financing is needed.

entertainment-finance.l01.q2.p: A film has a $2,000,000 budget. Equity gives $800,000, presales $600,000 and a tax incentive $300,000. How much must a loan supply to fully fund it?
entertainment-finance.l01.q2.h: Add the three known sources and subtract from the budget.

entertainment-finance.l01.q3.t: So that no single source carries all of the risk
entertainment-finance.l01.q3.p: Why do producers usually combine several funding sources?
entertainment-finance.l01.q3.h: Think about what happens if one source falls through.
entertainment-finance.l01.q3.e: Mixing sources spreads risk, though it does not remove it.

entertainment-finance.l01.q4.p: A tax incentive that arrives late can leave a project short of cash even if the budget looks fully funded on paper.
entertainment-finance.l01.q4.h: Consider the difference between having money promised and having it in the bank.
entertainment-finance.l01.q4.e: Timing matters: promised money that has not arrived cannot pay today's bills.

entertainment-finance.l01.q5.t: A schedule of how the budget will be paid for, from several sources
entertainment-finance.l01.q5.p: Which description best fits a financing plan?
entertainment-finance.l01.q5.h: It answers the question where the money comes from.
entertainment-finance.l01.q5.e: A financing plan assembles sources of funds to cover the budget; it does not promise profit.

entertainment-finance.l02.q1.t: Borrowed money that must be repaid, usually with interest
entertainment-finance.l02.q1.h: Think about who expects to get the money back no matter what.
entertainment-finance.l02.q1.e: Debt is a loan: the lender expects principal and interest back whether or not the project succeeds.

entertainment-finance.l02.q2.p: A producer borrows $400,000 at 10% simple interest for one year. How much is owed at the end?
entertainment-finance.l02.q2.e: 400,000 x 0.10 = 40,000 of interest, so 440,000 is owed.

entertainment-finance.l02.q3.p: An investor puts in $400,000 for 40% of net profit. The project earns net profit of $1,000,000. What does the investor receive as their profit share?

entertainment-finance.l02.q4.p: If a project earns nothing, an equity investor is still owed their money back with interest.
entertainment-finance.l02.q4.h: Equity is repaid only from profits.
entertainment-finance.l02.q4.e: Equity investors are paid only if there is something to share; interest-bearing repayment is the feature of debt.

entertainment-finance.l02.q5.t: They are repaid first when money comes in
entertainment-finance.l02.q5.p: Why are lenders described as senior to equity investors?
entertainment-finance.l02.q5.h: Seniority relates to order of payment.
entertainment-finance.l02.q5.e: Senior debt is paid ahead of equity, which sits lower in the order and absorbs losses first.

entertainment-finance.l03.q1.t: A contract to pay for distribution rights before the film is made
entertainment-finance.l03.q1.e: In a presale a distributor agrees in advance to pay a fee for rights in a territory.

entertainment-finance.l03.q2.p: A producer signs three presales of $300,000 each, with 10% paid on signing. How much is paid on signing across all three?
entertainment-finance.l03.q2.e: Total is 900,000; 10% of that is 90,000 (30,000 per deal).

entertainment-finance.l03.q3.p: A late or non-conforming delivery can delay or reduce the balance paid under a presale.
entertainment-finance.l03.q3.h: Think about the conditions attached to delivery.
entertainment-finance.l03.q3.e: Distributors usually pay the balance only when the film meets the agreed delivery requirements.

entertainment-finance.l03.q4.p: A 25% incentive applies to $1,200,000 of qualifying spending. What is the incentive?
entertainment-finance.l03.q4.h: Multiply the qualifying spend by the rate.

entertainment-finance.l03.q5.t: Because the incentive often arrives after costs are audited, leaving a timing gap
entertainment-finance.l03.q5.p: Why might a producer borrow against an expected tax incentive?
entertainment-finance.l03.q5.h: Think about when the incentive money actually arrives.
entertainment-finance.l03.q5.e: Incentives frequently arrive after cost audits, so producers may borrow to cover the wait.

entertainment-finance.l04.q1.p: Which loan covers money that is promised but has not arrived yet?
entertainment-finance.l04.q1.h: The name suggests crossing a timing gap.
entertainment-finance.l04.q1.e: A bridge loan covers timing, such as waiting for an incentive; a gap loan covers a shortfall.

entertainment-finance.l04.q2.p: A $5,000,000 film has $2,000,000 in presales, $1,500,000 equity and $1,000,000 incentive. What is the gap?
entertainment-finance.l04.q2.h: Subtract all known sources from the budget.

entertainment-finance.l04.q3.p: A bridge lender lends 80% of a $1,000,000 incentive at 12% annual interest for half a year. How much interest accrues?
entertainment-finance.l04.q3.h: Principal is 800,000; apply the rate for half a year.

entertainment-finance.l04.q4.p: A completion bond guarantees that a film will be profitable.
entertainment-finance.l04.q4.h: Consider what a bond covers: finishing, not success.
entertainment-finance.l04.q4.e: A bond is a guarantee of completion and delivery, not of quality or profit.

entertainment-finance.l04.q5.p: At an illustrative 2% fee, what would a completion bond cost on a $5,000,000 budget?

entertainment-finance.l05.q1.p: A grant is generally money given without an expectation of repayment.
entertainment-finance.l05.q1.e: Grants support work that meets stated aims and are usually not repaid, though they come with conditions.

entertainment-finance.l05.q2.p: A crowdfunding campaign raises $50,000 and fees total 8%. How much does the creator receive before fulfillment costs?
entertainment-finance.l05.q2.h: Subtract the fee from the amount raised.

entertainment-finance.l05.q3.t: Funding several projects together so one hit can offset losses
entertainment-finance.l05.q3.p: What is the main idea of slate financing?
entertainment-finance.l05.q3.e: Slates pool money across projects to reduce reliance on any single one.

entertainment-finance.l05.q4.p: An investor funds four films totaling $8,000,000 that return $12,000,000 in all. What is the overall percentage gain?
entertainment-finance.l05.q4.h: Gain divided by the amount invested.

entertainment-finance.l05.q5.p: Slate financing removes the risk that the whole slate underperforms.
entertainment-finance.l05.q5.h: Diversification spreads risk but does not erase it.
entertainment-finance.l05.q5.e: If all the projects do poorly, the slate loses; pooling reduces single-project risk only.

entertainment-finance.l06.q1.p: A forecast is an updated estimate of final cost made during the project.
entertainment-finance.l06.q1.h: Contrast it with a plan set before spending begins.
entertainment-finance.l06.q1.e: A budget is the plan; a forecast re-estimates where costs will end up.

entertainment-finance.l06.q2.p: A film has $900,000 of base costs budgeted. $300,000 has been spent and $650,000 is expected to be spent. What is the variance?
entertainment-finance.l06.q2.h: Add actual and estimate to complete, then compare with the budget.

entertainment-finance.l06.q3.p: With a $100,000 contingency and a $50,000 overage absorbed, how much contingency remains?
entertainment-finance.l06.q3.h: Subtract the overage from the reserve.

entertainment-finance.l06.q4.t: A reserve in the budget for unexpected costs
entertainment-finance.l06.q4.e: Contingency is a budgeted reserve for unforeseen costs.

entertainment-finance.l06.q5.p: The estimate to complete plus actual costs to date gives the forecast total.
entertainment-finance.l06.q5.h: It combines what has been spent and what is expected.
entertainment-finance.l06.q5.e: Actuals plus estimate to complete equals the estimate at completion, the forecast total.

entertainment-finance.l07.q1.t: The movement of money in and out over time
entertainment-finance.l07.q1.h: Think of a stream through time.
entertainment-finance.l07.q1.e: Cash flow tracks money coming in and going out period by period.

entertainment-finance.l07.q2.p: A production has $400,000 and spends $250,000 per month with no income. What is the balance after month one?

entertainment-finance.l07.q3.p: Continuing that production with no income, what is the balance after month two?
entertainment-finance.l07.q3.h: Subtract another month from the month-one balance.

entertainment-finance.l07.q4.p: A project can be profitable overall and still run out of cash partway through.
entertainment-finance.l07.q4.e: Timing mismatches cause cash shortfalls even when lifetime profit is positive.

entertainment-finance.l07.q5.t: Updating the cash forecast often and arranging a credit facility early
entertainment-finance.l07.q5.p: Which habit best reduces the risk of a cash crunch?
entertainment-finance.l07.q5.e: Frequent forecasts and early financing arrangements give time to solve timing gaps.

entertainment-finance.l08.q1.t: The contractual order in which revenue is paid out
entertainment-finance.l08.q1.p: What is a waterfall in entertainment finance?
entertainment-finance.l08.q1.h: Each tier fills before the next.
entertainment-finance.l08.q1.e: A waterfall lists who is paid first, second and so on as revenue arrives.

entertainment-finance.l08.q2.p: In the lesson example, $1,500,000 arrives. After a 20% distribution fee, how much remains?

entertainment-finance.l08.q3.p: After a fee of 300,000, expenses of 100,000 and loan repayment of 330,000, then equity recoupment of 600,000 from $1,500,000, how much profit remains to split?

entertainment-finance.l08.q4.p: If the remaining $170,000 is split 50/50, how much does each side receive?

entertainment-finance.l08.q5.p: Being earlier in the waterfall generally means being paid sooner and with more certainty.
entertainment-finance.l08.q5.h: Think about who gets first claim on revenue.
entertainment-finance.l08.q5.e: Earlier tiers are filled first, so they are protected when revenue falls short.

entertainment-finance.l09.q1.t: Money coming in, before most deductions
entertainment-finance.l09.q1.p: Which phrase best describes gross receipts?
entertainment-finance.l09.q1.h: Gross is the big top-line number.
entertainment-finance.l09.q1.e: Gross receipts are revenue before deductions defined for net profit.

entertainment-finance.l09.q2.p: The word net has the same meaning in every contract.
entertainment-finance.l09.q2.e: Net profit is whatever the agreement defines, which can include many deductions.

entertainment-finance.l09.q3.p: A film grosses $10,000,000. Deductions are a 25% distribution fee, $3,000,000 expenses, $4,000,000 production cost and $500,000 interest. What is net profit?
entertainment-finance.l09.q3.h: Add all deductions and subtract from gross.

entertainment-finance.l09.q4.p: In that same example, what would 5% of gross have paid?
entertainment-finance.l09.q4.e: 0.05 x 10,000,000 = 500,000, while 5% of net profit of 0 is nothing.

entertainment-finance.l09.q5.p: At $12,000,000 gross with the same costs (fee now 25% of gross), net profit is $1,500,000. What do 5 points of net pay?

entertainment-finance.l10.q1.p: Residuals are payments for reuse of a work, set by agreements such as guild contracts.
entertainment-finance.l10.q1.h: Think about reruns and other releases.
entertainment-finance.l10.q1.e: Residuals compensate covered members when work is reused, under formulas in the contract.

entertainment-finance.l10.q2.t: Minimum pay, conditions and certain reuse payments for guild members
entertainment-finance.l10.q2.p: What does a collective bargaining agreement set?
entertainment-finance.l10.q2.h: It is negotiated between a guild and employers.
entertainment-finance.l10.q2.e: CBAs set minimums, working conditions, credits and reuse payments.

entertainment-finance.l10.q3.p: With a hypothetical rate, a residual pool is 2% of $3,000,000. What is the pool?
entertainment-finance.l10.q3.h: Multiply the revenue by the rate.

entertainment-finance.l10.q4.p: Actor A earned $30,000 and Actor B $10,000. The $60,000 pool is shared in proportion to original pay. What does A receive?
entertainment-finance.l10.q4.h: A earned three quarters of the combined pay.

entertainment-finance.l10.q5.p: Pension and health contributions are real costs that belong in a budget alongside weekly pay.
entertainment-finance.l10.q5.h: Guild contracts add more than the weekly rate.
entertainment-finance.l10.q5.e: Fringes calculated on pay are required costs and must be budgeted.

entertainment-finance.l11.q1.t: Money paid up front and later deducted from royalties earned
entertainment-finance.l11.q1.p: What is an advance in a record deal?
entertainment-finance.l11.q1.h: It is repaid out of future earnings.
entertainment-finance.l11.q1.e: An advance is a prepayment recouped from the artist's royalties.

entertainment-finance.l11.q2.p: An artist has a $150,000 advance and a 20% royalty on $1,000,000 of net receipts. What is paid after recoupment?
entertainment-finance.l11.q2.h: Compute royalties, then subtract the advance.

entertainment-finance.l11.q3.p: With net receipts of only $600,000 at 20%, how much remains unrecouped on a $150,000 advance?

entertainment-finance.l11.q4.p: Cross-collateralization lets a shortfall on one record be recouped from earnings on another.
entertainment-finance.l11.q4.e: Under cross-collateralization, unrecouped amounts can be recovered from other earnings.

entertainment-finance.l11.q5.t: They extend the time before royalties are actually paid
entertainment-finance.l11.q5.p: Why might recoupable extras like video costs hurt an artist?
entertainment-finance.l11.q5.h: Think about what must be earned back before payments start.
entertainment-finance.l11.q5.e: More recoupable costs mean more to earn back before the artist receives money.

entertainment-finance.l12.q1.p: Which right does music publishing mainly handle?
entertainment-finance.l12.q1.e: Publishing deals with the composition; masters are the recordings.

entertainment-finance.l12.q2.p: The writer's share is commonly about half of performance income and is paid directly to the writer.
entertainment-finance.l12.q2.h: Think about the two halves of the pie.
entertainment-finance.l12.q2.e: Performing rights organizations typically pay the writer's half directly.

entertainment-finance.l12.q3.p: In an administration deal, who usually keeps ownership of the copyright?
entertainment-finance.l12.q3.h: The administrator collects for a fee.
entertainment-finance.l12.q3.e: Administration deals let the writer keep ownership while paying a fee for collection services.

entertainment-finance.l12.q4.p: A song earns $200,000 total. The writer self-publishes with a 15% administration fee on the publisher's $100,000 share. What does the writer receive in all?
entertainment-finance.l12.q4.h: Writer share plus publisher share minus the fee.

entertainment-finance.l12.q5.t: Ownership or part-ownership of the copyright in return for an advance and promotion
entertainment-finance.l12.q5.p: What does a traditional publishing deal typically give the publisher?
entertainment-finance.l12.q5.e: Traditional deals trade copyright interest for an advance and active promotion.

entertainment-finance.l13.q1.p: What does a profit and loss statement show?
entertainment-finance.l13.q1.e: A P&L lists revenue and expenses and ends with profit.

entertainment-finance.l13.q2.p: A tour plays 20 shows to 1,500 people each at $50. What is gross ticket sales?

entertainment-finance.l13.q3.p: The artist side receives $1,200,000, with costs of $600,000, a 10% agent and a 15% manager on the $1,200,000. What is net to the artist?

entertainment-finance.l13.q4.p: Because tour costs are largely fixed, selling fewer tickets can shrink profit quickly.
entertainment-finance.l13.q4.h: Consider costs that do not shrink with attendance.
entertainment-finance.l13.q4.e: Fixed costs remain while revenue falls, so profit drops sharply.

entertainment-finance.l13.q5.p: The artist's $300,000 net on $1,200,000 of artist income is what margin?

entertainment-finance.l14.q1.t: A written accounting of the night's revenue, expenses and payments
entertainment-finance.l14.q1.p: What is a settlement in live events?
entertainment-finance.l14.q1.e: Settlement is the post-show accounting that decides who is paid what.

entertainment-finance.l14.q2.p: A show sells 2,000 tickets at $60. What is gross?

entertainment-finance.l14.q3.p: Gross $120,000, expenses $50,000, artist gets 85% of net versus a $50,000 guarantee. What does the artist receive?
entertainment-finance.l14.q3.h: Compare the percentage of net with the guarantee.

entertainment-finance.l14.q4.p: Using that same night, what does the promoter keep after paying the artist?

entertainment-finance.l14.q5.p: If a show sells poorly, a guarantee can mean the promoter loses money while the artist is still paid.
entertainment-finance.l14.q5.h: Consider which side carries the downside.
entertainment-finance.l14.q5.e: A guarantee shifts risk to the promoter, who must pay it regardless of sales.

entertainment-finance.l15.q1.t: A payment made after the developer delivers an agreed build
entertainment-finance.l15.q1.p: What is a milestone payment in game development?
entertainment-finance.l15.q1.e: Milestones tie publisher payments to delivered work.

entertainment-finance.l15.q2.p: A game earns $10,000,000 and a 30% platform fee applies. How much remains?

entertainment-finance.l15.q3.p: With $7,000,000 remaining, a $5,000,000 advance recouped first, and the rest split 50/50, what does the developer receive?
entertainment-finance.l15.q3.h: Recoup first, then split what is left.

entertainment-finance.l15.q4.p: A 30% platform fee has long been a common headline figure, though rates and rules vary and change.
entertainment-finance.l15.q4.h: Consider that fees differ by program.
entertainment-finance.l15.q4.e: The figure is common but not universal, and programs differ.

entertainment-finance.l15.q5.t: They earn and spend continuously after launch
entertainment-finance.l15.q5.p: What makes live-service games different financially?
entertainment-finance.l15.q5.e: Live-service games rely on ongoing content and revenue, so forecasting is continuous.

entertainment-finance.l16.q1.t: A collection of rights that keep earning, like songs or films
entertainment-finance.l16.q1.p: What is a catalog in this context?
entertainment-finance.l16.q1.h: Think of rights producing ongoing income.
entertainment-finance.l16.q1.e: Catalogs are bundles of rights that generate income over time.

entertainment-finance.l16.q2.p: A catalog earned $100,000, $120,000 and $140,000 in three years. What is the average?

entertainment-finance.l16.q3.p: At an illustrative multiple of 12 on $120,000, what is the value?

entertainment-finance.l16.q4.p: At an 8% discount rate, what is $108,000 received in a year worth today?

entertainment-finance.l16.q5.p: A valuation multiple is a fixed rule that applies to every catalog.
entertainment-finance.l16.q5.e: Multiples vary with stability, growth, genre, rights and market conditions.

entertainment-finance.l17.q1.t: An independent check of the payer's relevant records
entertainment-finance.l17.q1.p: What does a contract audit right allow?
entertainment-finance.l17.q1.e: An audit clause lets the payee examine records that support the statements.

entertainment-finance.l17.q2.p: Audit rights often have time limits after each statement, so deadlines matter.
entertainment-finance.l17.q2.h: Consider how long you have to check.
entertainment-finance.l17.q2.e: Contracts typically set a window, after which statements may become binding.

entertainment-finance.l17.q3.p: An audit shows receipts were $900,000, not $800,000, with a 20% rate. What is the underpayment?
entertainment-finance.l17.q3.h: The unreported amount times the rate.

entertainment-finance.l17.q4.p: If that audit cost $15,000 and recovered $20,000, what is the net benefit?

entertainment-finance.l17.q5.t: When the potential recovery is large compared with its cost
entertainment-finance.l17.q5.p: When is an audit most worthwhile?
entertainment-finance.l17.q5.e: Audits make sense when likely recovery outweighs cost, and they also deter errors.

entertainment-finance.l18.q1.t: The amount you bear before the insurer pays
entertainment-finance.l18.q1.h: It is your share of a loss.
entertainment-finance.l18.q1.e: The deductible is what the insured bears first.

entertainment-finance.l18.q2.p: A covered loss is $80,000 with a $10,000 deductible. What does the insurer pay?

entertainment-finance.l18.q3.p: Production insurance typically protects against an audience not showing up.
entertainment-finance.l18.q3.e: Insurance covers specified perils; commercial failure is a business risk it does not cover.

entertainment-finance.l18.q4.p: Which coverage protects against claims such as infringement or defamation in a finished work?
entertainment-finance.l18.q4.h: The name refers to mistakes in the content.
entertainment-finance.l18.q4.e: Errors and omissions insurance addresses claims arising from the content itself.

entertainment-finance.l18.q5.p: Which approach to a risk lowers its likelihood rather than transferring it?
entertainment-finance.l18.q5.e: Reducing a risk means preventing it; insurance transfers cost afterward.

entertainment-finance.l19.q1.p: Which entity type is taxed itself on profits and again on dividends?
entertainment-finance.l19.q1.e: A C corporation pays tax on profits and shareholders pay tax on dividends.

entertainment-finance.l19.q2.p: A pass-through entity reports profit on the owners' own tax returns.
entertainment-finance.l19.q2.e: Pass-through taxation means business income is taxed at the owner level.

entertainment-finance.l19.q3.p: A C corporation earns $100,000 and pays 21% tax. What remains?

entertainment-finance.l19.q4.p: Paying the remaining $79,000 as a dividend taxed at an assumed 15%, what does the shareholder keep?
entertainment-finance.l19.q4.h: Compute tax on the dividend and subtract.

entertainment-finance.l19.q5.t: Tax rules are detailed, change, and depend on your situation
entertainment-finance.l19.q5.e: Rules vary and change, so personalized professional advice matters.

entertainment-finance.l20.q1.t: Tax deducted by the payer before paying the recipient
entertainment-finance.l20.q1.h: The payer holds back part of the payment.
entertainment-finance.l20.q1.e: Payers may be required to deduct tax and send it to the tax authority.

entertainment-finance.l20.q2.p: A $100,000 royalty faces 15% withholding. How much does the artist receive?

entertainment-finance.l20.q3.p: A foreign tax credit can help offset home-country tax by what was paid abroad, within limits.
entertainment-finance.l20.q3.h: The name suggests credit for tax paid elsewhere.
entertainment-finance.l20.q3.e: Many systems allow a credit to reduce double taxation, though limits and paperwork apply.

entertainment-finance.l20.q4.p: A contract is for 1,000,000 euros. At 1.10 dollars per euro, what is it worth in dollars?

entertainment-finance.l20.q5.p: If the rate falls to 1.00, how much value in dollars is lost on that 1,000,000 euro payment?

entertainment-finance.l21.q1.t: Similar past projects that show what the market has paid
entertainment-finance.l21.q1.e: Comps are similar projects used to support expectations.

entertainment-finance.l21.q2.p: An investor puts in $1,000,000. Scenarios: 50% chance of $500,000, 30% of $1,200,000, 20% of $3,000,000. What is the expected return?
entertainment-finance.l21.q2.h: Weight each outcome by its probability.

entertainment-finance.l21.q3.p: A good pitch should guarantee investors a profit.
entertainment-finance.l21.q3.e: Guaranteeing returns is a warning sign; honest ranges are appropriate.

entertainment-finance.l21.q4.t: Offers of shares may be regulated as securities
entertainment-finance.l21.q4.p: Why involve a lawyer before soliciting investors?
entertainment-finance.l21.q4.e: Securities rules can apply, with limits on who may invest and what must be disclosed.

entertainment-finance.l21.q5.p: Scenario probabilities in a pitch are judgments, and should be presented as such.
entertainment-finance.l21.q5.h: Consider whether anyone can know them for sure.
entertainment-finance.l21.q5.e: Probabilities are estimates and should be labeled honestly.

entertainment-finance.l22.q1.t: Mostly not, though some clauses like confidentiality may be
entertainment-finance.l22.q1.p: Is a term sheet usually binding?
entertainment-finance.l22.q1.e: Most terms are non-binding, but clauses like exclusivity can bind.

entertainment-finance.l22.q2.p: An investor puts in $200,000 at an $800,000 pre-money valuation. What is the post-money value?

entertainment-finance.l22.q3.p: What percentage does that investor own?

entertainment-finance.l22.q4.p: A later investor puts in $500,000 at $1,500,000 pre-money. What does the first investor's 20% become?
entertainment-finance.l22.q4.h: Existing owners hold 75% after the new round.
entertainment-finance.l22.q4.e: Post-money is 2,000,000, new investor owns 25%, and 20% x 0.75 = 15%.

entertainment-finance.l22.q5.p: Pressure to sign a term sheet quickly is a reason to slow down and review.
entertainment-finance.l22.q5.e: Careful review, including by a lawyer, protects against unfavorable terms.

entertainment-finance.l23.q1.p: Which is a common red flag?
entertainment-finance.l23.q1.h: Think about promises nobody can keep.
entertainment-finance.l23.q1.e: Guaranteed or very high returns are classic warning signs.

entertainment-finance.l23.q2.p: A producer offers 40% of profits to each of three investors. What total is promised?

entertainment-finance.l23.q3.p: A Ponzi-style scheme pays earlier investors using money from later investors.
entertainment-finance.l23.q3.h: Consider the source of the payments.
entertainment-finance.l23.q3.e: That is the defining feature, and it collapses when new money stops.

entertainment-finance.l23.q4.t: Contact the other party using details you found yourself
entertainment-finance.l23.q4.p: How should you confirm a claimed distribution deal?
entertainment-finance.l23.q4.e: Independent verification avoids relying on the claimant's own contacts.

entertainment-finance.l23.q5.p: A promise of 30% in six months is roughly what annual rate if simple?
entertainment-finance.l23.q5.e: 30% x 2 = 60%, far above what most legitimate investments reliably earn.

entertainment-finance.l24.q1.t: A personal interest that could affect duties to others
entertainment-finance.l24.q1.p: What is a conflict of interest?
entertainment-finance.l24.q1.e: It arises when someone's own interest may affect their duty to others.

entertainment-finance.l24.q2.p: A company charges its own $500,000 film a 10% overhead fee. How much is that?
entertainment-finance.l24.q2.h: Multiply the budget by the rate.

entertainment-finance.l24.q3.p: A related-party fee that is clearly agreed and disclosed can be acceptable.
entertainment-finance.l24.q3.e: Disclosure and agreement are what distinguish acceptable fees from hidden ones.

entertainment-finance.l24.q4.t: Clearer contracts, reasonable caps and transparent reporting
entertainment-finance.l24.q4.p: Which response to the net-profit debate does the lesson favor?
entertainment-finance.l24.q4.e: The lesson suggests clarity and transparency address concerns without presuming bad faith.

entertainment-finance.l24.q5.p: Ethical practice means following the intent of agreements, not only the letter.
entertainment-finance.l24.q5.e: Trust depends on honoring what parties reasonably expected, beyond technical compliance.

film-business.l01.q1.p: Which stage of a film's life covers editing, sound, music, color and creation of delivery materials?
film-business.l01.q1.h: Think of what happens after the shoot ends.
film-business.l01.q1.e: Post-production follows production and turns raw footage into a finished, deliverable film.

film-business.l01.q2.p: A producer spends $20,000 on an option and a rewrite, then a $2,000,000 shoot follows. What share of the $2,020,000 total is the development spend, to the nearest whole percent?
film-business.l01.q2.e: 20,000 divided by 2,020,000 is about 0.0099, or roughly 1 percent. Development is cheap but is the first money at risk.

film-business.l01.q3.p: A producer finishes a film and then discovers the script was never legally optioned. At which stage should this have been fixed, ideally?
film-business.l01.q3.h: Rights are secured before the money and the shoot.
film-business.l01.q3.e: Securing rights is a development task. Finding the gap after production is far more costly.

film-business.l01.q4.t: Production is when costs are largest and fastest, so risk is highest
film-business.l01.q4.p: Why do financiers often want insurance and a completion guarantee before production begins?
film-business.l01.q4.h: Where is spending concentrated in time?
film-business.l01.q4.e: Production is where most cost is incurred quickly, so financiers want protection against overruns and accidents.

film-business.l01.q5.p: A film that is finished has finished earning: exploitation ends when the first release ends.
film-business.l01.q5.h: Think about how long a film can sell across formats and territories.
film-business.l01.q5.e: False. Exploitation is a long tail across windows, formats and territories that can last for years.

film-business.l02.q1.t: The documented sequence of rights transfers from the original author to the producer
film-business.l02.q1.p: What is a chain of title?
film-business.l02.q1.h: It is about ownership, traced through paper.
film-business.l02.q1.e: Chain of title is the documented trail proving who owns the rights, from the author to the producer.

film-business.l02.q2.t: The freelancer, since the magazine did not acquire them
film-business.l02.q2.p: You option a magazine article. The magazine only bought first-publication rights from the freelancer. Who can grant you film rights?
film-business.l02.q2.h: Who still holds the film rights?
film-business.l02.q2.e: The magazine could only grant what it owned. The film rights remained with the freelancer, so the chain runs through the freelancer.

film-business.l02.q3.t: A break in the chain of title that can stall a sale or complicate E&O coverage
film-business.l02.q3.p: A co-writer never signed an agreement vesting rights in the production company. What is the most likely effect?
film-business.l02.q3.h: Buyers and insurers examine every link.
film-business.l02.q3.e: A missing signature creates a gap in the chain. Distributors and E&O insurers examine the chain, and a gap can delay a deal or coverage.

film-business.l02.q4.t: It makes the public record match who actually owns the rights
film-business.l02.q4.p: Why does recording assignment documents with the US Copyright Office help a production?
film-business.l02.q4.h: Think public record versus private paperwork.
film-business.l02.q4.e: Recordation gives public notice of ownership transfers and liens, supporting buyers and lenders who check the record. It does not replace the underlying contracts.

film-business.l02.q5.t: A claim from someone who says they own part of the story
film-business.l02.q5.p: Which delivery risk is a chain-of-title gap MOST directly linked to?
film-business.l02.q5.h: Which risk concerns who owns the story?
film-business.l02.q5.e: A chain gap exposes the film to an ownership claim, which is the kind of risk E&O insurers and distributors screen for.

film-business.l03.q1.t: The exclusive right, for a set period, to buy underlying rights
film-business.l03.q1.p: What does an option agreement give a producer?
film-business.l03.q1.h: It is a right to buy, not the purchase itself.
film-business.l03.q1.e: An option is an exclusive, time-limited right to purchase rights at a stated price. If it is not exercised the rights revert.

film-business.l03.q2.p: A one-year option costs $10,000, a six-month extension costs $5,000, and the purchase price is $100,000 with option payments applicable. You exercise after using the extension. What do you owe at exercise?
film-business.l03.q2.h: Subtract everything already paid from the purchase price.
film-business.l03.q2.e: Applicable payments total $10,000 plus $5,000, or $15,000. $100,000 minus $15,000 leaves $85,000 due.

film-business.l03.q3.p: Using the same terms, you let the option and extension lapse without exercising. What is your total outlay and what do you own?
film-business.l03.q3.e: You paid $10,000 plus $5,000, or $15,000, and because you did not exercise, the rights revert to the owner.
