film-business.l03.q4.t: They are mainly a consent and release agreement, not a standalone property right
film-business.l03.q4.p: Which statement about life rights is most accurate?
film-business.l03.q4.e: A life rights agreement chiefly provides consent, cooperation and waiver of certain claims. It does not remove all risk.

film-business.l03.q5.t: A written agreement signed by both sides stating it is a work made for hire
film-business.l03.q5.p: Which is required for a specially commissioned contribution to be a work made for hire as part of a motion picture under US copyright law?
film-business.l03.q5.h: The statute asks for a writing.
film-business.l03.q5.e: A commissioned work in a listed category, including as part of a motion picture, is made for hire only if both parties sign a written agreement to that effect. Producers often add a backup assignment.

film-business.l04.q1.t: The creative and commercial elements, such as director and cast, attached to make a project financeable
film-business.l04.q1.p: What is a package in film development?
film-business.l04.q1.h: Think of what a financier wants to see attached.
film-business.l04.q1.e: A package is the set of elements, like script, director and cast, that makes a project attractive to financiers and buyers.

film-business.l04.q2.p: A studio spent $200,000 on a script. A new buyer repays costs plus a 10 percent premium to take it out of turnaround. What does the studio receive?
film-business.l04.q2.e: 200,000 times 1.10 is $220,000: the costs plus a $20,000 premium.

film-business.l04.q3.t: The attachment is weak until it becomes a firm or pay-or-play agreement
film-business.l04.q3.p: A lead actor is attached on a handshake, with no pay-or-play offer. A lender asks how solid the package is. What is the best summary?
film-business.l04.q3.h: What does a lender rely on?
film-business.l04.q3.e: An informal attachment can fall away. Firm deals or pay-or-play offers give real weight to a package.

film-business.l04.q4.t: Reclaim a dropped project by finding a new buyer who reimburses the original company
film-business.l04.q4.p: What does turnaround allow a producer to do?
film-business.l04.q4.h: Think of a project leaving one home for another.
film-business.l04.q4.e: In turnaround, a new buyer repays the original company's costs, sometimes plus a premium, so the project can move on.

film-business.l04.q5.p: A first-look arrangement obliges a producer to bring projects to a particular company first.
film-business.l04.q5.h: The name describes the order of approach.
film-business.l04.q5.e: True. In a first-look deal the producer offers projects to that company before going elsewhere, though the details vary.

film-business.l05.q1.p: Which of these is typically an above-the-line cost?
film-business.l05.q1.h: Above the line means creative and deal-driven costs.
film-business.l05.q1.e: Principal creative talent, such as director and leads, falls above the line. Equipment, catering and permits are below the line.

film-business.l05.q2.p: A budget before contingency is $900,000 and contingency is 10 percent. What is the total?
film-business.l05.q2.e: 10 percent of $900,000 is $90,000, so the total is $990,000.

film-business.l05.q3.p: With a $90,000 contingency, a $40,000 reshoot and a $25,000 equipment loss occur. How much contingency remains?

film-business.l05.q4.t: Later weeks still face risk but the reserve to absorb it is gone
film-business.l05.q4.p: Why is spending most of the contingency early in the shoot a warning sign?
film-business.l05.q4.h: Contingency covers surprises throughout the shoot.
film-business.l05.q4.e: Risk continues through the shoot, so an early drain leaves little protection for later surprises.

film-business.l05.q5.t: So actual spend can be tracked line by line against the budget in cost reports
film-business.l05.q5.p: Why are budgets numbered into accounts and sub-accounts?
film-business.l05.q5.e: Account structure lets the production compare actuals with budget by line, which is how overruns are caught early.

film-business.l06.q1.p: In the worked budget, what are the above-the-line costs?
film-business.l06.q1.h: Add story/script, producers, director and cast.

film-business.l06.q2.p: In the worked budget, below-the-line production costs are crew $200,000, equipment $80,000, locations $60,000, art and wardrobe $50,000, and transport and catering $60,000. What is the sum?
film-business.l06.q2.e: 200 plus 80 is 280; plus 60 is 340; plus 50 is 390; plus 60 is $450,000.

film-business.l06.q3.p: Below-the-line production is $450,000 of a $900,000 pre-contingency subtotal. What fraction is that?
film-business.l06.q3.e: 450 divided by 900 is 0.5, one half of the subtotal.

film-business.l06.q4.t: Post is probably under-planned relative to the work
film-business.l06.q4.p: A budget shows $20,000 for post-production on a $900,000 film with a lot of effects shots. What does that most suggest?
film-business.l06.q4.h: Compare it with the 22 percent in the example.
film-business.l06.q4.e: The example allocates about 22 percent to post and music. A tiny allocation for a heavy post workload suggests under-planning.

film-business.l06.q5.t: Marketing, festival fees and loan interest
film-business.l06.q5.p: Which costs are commonly OUTSIDE a production budget but still must be planned?
film-business.l06.q5.h: Think about what happens after the film is made.
film-business.l06.q5.e: The budget covers the cost to make the film. Marketing, festival fees and finance costs often sit outside and need separate planning.

film-business.l07.q1.p: How is scene length conventionally measured in a script breakdown?
film-business.l07.q1.h: A page is divided into small fractions.
film-business.l07.q1.e: Scene length is measured in eighths of a page.

film-business.l07.q2.p: A 90-page script is shot at 5 pages per day. How many shooting days?
film-business.l07.q2.h: Divide pages by pages per day.

film-business.l07.q3.p: A 90-page script is shot at 4 pages per day. How many days, rounded up to a whole day?
film-business.l07.q3.e: 90 divided by 4 is 22.5, which rounds up to 23 days.

film-business.l07.q4.t: To reduce company moves and use cast and locations efficiently
film-business.l07.q4.p: Why do productions group scenes by location rather than shoot in story order?
film-business.l07.q4.h: Think of what moving a crew costs.
film-business.l07.q4.e: Grouping by location limits company moves and actor days, saving time and money.

film-business.l07.q5.p: A scene of one and three-eighths pages is expressed how in eighths?
film-business.l07.q5.e: 1 page is 8 eighths, plus 3 eighths is 11 eighths.

film-business.l08.q1.t: A license of rights in a territory sold before the film exists
film-business.l08.q1.h: The buyer commits before the film is finished.
film-business.l08.q1.e: A pre-sale licenses a territory in advance, with payment on delivery, and can support a loan.

film-business.l08.q2.p: A film is funded by $400,000 of pre-sales, $300,000 of gap debt and $300,000 of equity. What share of the total is equity?
film-business.l08.q2.e: Total is $1,000,000 and equity is $300,000, so 30 percent.

film-business.l08.q3.p: For a $2,000,000 budget with $500,000 of grants and $300,000 from crowdfunding, how much remains to raise?

film-business.l08.q4.t: It is repaid after debt, so it absorbs shortfalls first
film-business.l08.q4.p: Why is equity usually the riskiest layer?
film-business.l08.q4.h: Who is first in line when money comes back?
film-business.l08.q4.e: Equity sits behind lenders in the repayment order, so losses hit it first, which is why it asks for upside.

film-business.l08.q5.p: A completion bond is a source of money that fills a funding gap in the budget.
film-business.l08.q5.h: It guarantees delivery rather than adding a budget line.
film-business.l08.q5.e: False. A completion bond guarantees the film will be finished; it is not a funding source for the original budget.

film-business.l09.q1.t: The layers of financing and their order of repayment
film-business.l09.q1.p: What does a capital stack show?
film-business.l09.q1.e: A capital stack lists funding layers and the priority in which they are repaid.

film-business.l09.q2.p: A stack has a $1,000,000 tax-credit loan, $1,500,000 pre-sales, $1,000,000 gap loan and $1,500,000 equity. What is the budget?

film-business.l09.q3.p: Equity invested is $1,500,000 and it recoups at 120 percent before profit share. How much must it receive first?

film-business.l09.q4.t: They cover part of the budget with lower-risk money, lowering risk for the remainder
film-business.l09.q4.p: Why do pre-sales and incentives make equity easier to raise?
film-business.l09.q4.h: Consider how the stack changes risk.
film-business.l09.q4.e: Contracted or secured layers reduce uncertainty, making the whole financing more credible to equity investors.

film-business.l09.q5.t: $500,000, provided by the completion guarantor within its terms
film-business.l09.q5.p: A $5,000,000 film goes 10 percent over budget. How much extra money is needed, and who typically covers it if there is a completion bond?
film-business.l09.q5.e: 10 percent of $5,000,000 is $500,000. A completion guarantor is committed to fund overruns within the bond terms.

film-business.l10.q1.t: A company formed to make and own one film
film-business.l10.q1.p: What is a single-purpose entity in film?
film-business.l10.q1.e: An SPE, often an LLC, is set up for one project so contracts, assets and liability are contained.

film-business.l10.q2.p: An investor puts $100,000 into an LLC with $1,000,000 of total equity. What percentage of the equity does the investor hold?

film-business.l10.q3.p: The operating agreement gives the investor pool 50 percent of net profit. This 10 percent equity holder shares in the pool pro rata. What share of overall net profit do they receive?
film-business.l10.q3.h: Take 10 percent of the 50 percent pool.
film-business.l10.q3.e: 10 percent of 50 percent is 5 percent of net profit.

film-business.l10.q4.t: Mixing the company's funds with personal funds
film-business.l10.q4.p: Which practice can undermine an LLC's liability protection?
film-business.l10.q4.e: Commingling funds and ignoring formalities can lead a court to disregard the shield.

film-business.l10.q5.t: They can take security in a clearly defined asset without claims from other projects
film-business.l10.q5.p: Why do lenders prefer to lend to a single-purpose film entity?
film-business.l10.q5.h: Think about a clean pool of assets.
film-business.l10.q5.e: A dedicated entity gives lenders a clear asset and revenue stream to secure against.

film-business.l11.q1.p: Which insurance covers claims that a finished film infringes copyright or defames someone?
film-business.l11.q1.h: It protects the finished work after release.
film-business.l11.q1.e: E&O covers claims such as copyright infringement, defamation and privacy arising from the finished film.

film-business.l11.q2.p: A completion bond fee is 3 percent of a $5,000,000 budget. What is the fee?

film-business.l11.q3.p: At a 5 percent fee, what does the bond cost on the same $5,000,000 budget?

film-business.l11.q4.p: A crew member damages a rented house during the shoot. Which cover is most directly relevant?
film-business.l11.q4.e: General liability addresses third-party property damage and bodily injury arising from operations.

film-business.l11.q5.p: Insurers and guarantors generally accept any claim regardless of policy exclusions.
film-business.l11.q5.h: Think about what exclusions are for.
film-business.l11.q5.e: False. Policies and bonds contain exclusions and conditions, so reading them carefully matters.

film-business.l12.q1.h: The A stands for artists and the S for screen actors.
film-business.l12.q1.e: SAG-AFTRA represents actors, stunt performers and other on-camera and voice performers.

film-business.l12.q2.p: A production needs a camera operator, a gaffer and a grip. Which organization represents many such crafts?
film-business.l12.q2.e: IATSE represents many below-the-line crafts through its local unions.

film-business.l12.q3.p: A production wants a unit production manager and assistant directors to work under a guild contract. Which guild typically covers those roles?
film-business.l12.q3.h: They are part of the directing team.
film-business.l12.q3.e: The DGA represents directors and also members of the directing team such as UPMs, ADs and stage managers.

film-business.l12.q4.t: The production agrees to follow that guild's collective bargaining terms
film-business.l12.q4.p: What does becoming a signatory to a guild agreement mean?
film-business.l12.q4.e: A signatory signs the guild's agreement and must follow its minimums, benefits and procedures.

film-business.l12.q5.t: They change with each negotiated contract, so current figures must come from the union
film-business.l12.q5.p: Why does this course avoid quoting guild rates?
film-business.l12.q5.h: Think about how contracts are renewed.
film-business.l12.q5.e: Minimums and terms are renegotiated, so always consult the current agreement.

film-business.l13.q1.t: Synchronization license and master use license
film-business.l13.q1.p: Which two licenses does using a commercial recording of a song in a film require?
film-business.l13.q1.h: One covers the composition, the other the recording.
film-business.l13.q1.e: Sync covers the musical composition; master use covers the specific sound recording.

film-business.l13.q2.t: A sync license from the composition owner
film-business.l13.q2.p: You hire a band to record a cover of a famous song. What do you still need?
film-business.l13.q2.h: You own the new recording, not the song.
film-business.l13.q2.e: The composition still needs a sync license. The master for your new recording belongs to your production.

film-business.l13.q3.t: You cannot lawfully use the song
film-business.l13.q3.p: The label agrees to master use but the publisher refuses sync. What follows?
film-business.l13.q3.e: Both licenses are required. Without sync you cannot use the composition.

film-business.l13.q4.t: To avoid disputes and ensure rights vest in the production
film-business.l13.q4.p: Why are signed documents needed BEFORE the work is done?
film-business.l13.q4.h: Think about leverage after the fact.
film-business.l13.q4.e: Prior agreements settle rights, pay and credit before there is leverage or conflict.

film-business.l13.q5.p: Which signed document best addresses an unpaid extra whose face appears clearly in the film?
film-business.l13.q5.h: It is about use of a person's image.
film-business.l13.q5.e: An appearance release grants permission to use a recognizable person's image.

film-business.l14.q1.t: Registration (or refusal) with the Copyright Office
film-business.l14.q1.p: What is a prerequisite to filing a federal copyright infringement suit for a US work?
film-business.l14.q1.h: It is a filing with a government office.
film-business.l14.q1.e: For a US work, registration or refusal is required before suing for infringement.

film-business.l14.q2.t: Yes, registration was within three months of publication
film-business.l14.q2.p: Film first published March 1; infringement begins April 15; registration April 20. Are statutory damages and attorney's fees available?
film-business.l14.q2.e: Registration within three months after first publication preserves those remedies even if infringement began earlier.

film-business.l14.q3.p: Film first published January 10; infringement begins June 1; registration July 1. Are statutory damages and fees available for that infringement?
film-business.l14.q3.e: Registration came after the infringement began and more than three months after publication, so those remedies are unavailable.

film-business.l14.q4.t: They assess the risk of claims about title and clearance
film-business.l14.q4.p: Why do E&O insurers want clearance procedures and a title report?
film-business.l14.q4.e: Underwriters use clearance work to judge claims risk before issuing coverage.

film-business.l14.q5.t: It gives public notice of ownership and liens
film-business.l14.q5.p: Why record a security interest or assignment with the Copyright Office?
film-business.l14.q5.e: Recordation provides public notice, which lenders and buyers rely on.

film-business.l15.q1.p: What does SVOD stand for in streaming?
film-business.l15.q1.e: SVOD is subscription video on demand: a fee for access to a catalogue.

film-business.l15.q2.p: A streamer licenses your film for a flat fee of $800,000. The film is watched by many viewers. What do you earn from the license?
film-business.l15.q2.e: A flat-fee license pays the agreed amount regardless of views.

film-business.l15.q3.p: A filmmaker rents a cinema and keeps all ticket income, paying the venue a flat rental. What is this called?
film-business.l15.q3.h: The filmmaker takes the cinema's four walls.
film-business.l15.q3.e: Four-walling lets the filmmaker keep the ticket income while carrying the marketing risk.

film-business.l15.q4.t: To give each channel a period of exclusivity
film-business.l15.q4.p: Why does the release window order exist?
film-business.l15.q4.e: Windows protect the value of each channel by sequencing availability, though lengths vary and have shortened.

film-business.l15.q5.p: Festivals are mainly a direct revenue source for most films.
film-business.l15.q5.e: False. They are mainly showcases that generate attention and sales leads.

film-business.l16.q1.t: A neutral third party collects revenue and pays parties in agreed order
film-business.l16.q1.p: What is a collection account management agreement used for?
film-business.l16.q1.h: It's about the flow of money.
film-business.l16.q1.e: A CAMA has a neutral manager collect revenue and disburse it per the waterfall.

film-business.l16.q2.p: Gross receipts are $10,000,000. A 15 percent sales commission is deducted, then $1,500,000 of expenses. What remains?

film-business.l16.q3.p: With $5,000,000 left, equity recoups $3,600,000, deferments are $400,000, and the remainder is split 50/50. What does the producer pool receive?
film-business.l16.q3.h: Find net profit first, then halve it.

film-business.l16.q4.p: Gross is $6,000,000 with the same fee structure and a $2,000,000 loan. What is left for equity after commission, expenses and the loan?
film-business.l16.q4.e: Commission is 900,000, leaving 5,100,000; minus 1,500,000 is 3,600,000; minus 2,000,000 leaves $1,600,000 for equity, less than the $3,600,000 it is owed.

film-business.l16.q5.t: Fees, expenses, debt and recoupment come ahead of profit
film-business.l16.q5.p: Why can a film with large gross receipts show no net profit?
film-business.l16.q5.h: Look at the order of the waterfall.
film-business.l16.q5.e: Net profit is what remains after every priority claim, so it is last in line and can be zero.

film-business.l17.q1.t: The film has not screened publicly before, which some festivals require
film-business.l17.q1.e: Premiere status means the film has not been shown publicly, which can affect festival eligibility.

film-business.l17.q2.p: You submit to 20 festivals at $75 each. Six grant waivers. What do you pay?
film-business.l17.q2.h: Count the festivals you still pay for.

film-business.l17.q3.p: How much do the six waivers save compared with paying for all 20 at $75?

film-business.l17.q4.p: A small local screening takes place before the film applies to a major festival requiring a premiere. What is the risk?
film-business.l17.q4.h: Think about the rule of first public showing.
film-business.l17.q4.e: An early public screening can forfeit premiere status where it is required.

film-business.l17.q5.t: Define the goal, such as a sale, awards or audience, then pick festivals
film-business.l17.q5.p: Which is the best first step in planning a festival run?
film-business.l17.q5.e: Goal-setting guides which festivals, budgets and materials make sense.

film-business.l18.q1.t: A fixed advance a buyer pays for rights in a territory
film-business.l18.q1.h: It is paid regardless of performance.
film-business.l18.q1.e: An MG is an advance the distributor pays regardless of performance.

film-business.l18.q2.p: MGs are Germany $400,000, UK $250,000, France $300,000, Japan $150,000. What is the total?

film-business.l18.q3.p: A 15 percent commission applies to $1,100,000. What does the producer have left before expenses?

film-business.l18.q4.t: To show the film to buyers, negotiate licenses and secure deals
film-business.l18.q4.p: What is the role of a sales agent at a market?
film-business.l18.q4.h: They represent the film to buyers.
film-business.l18.q4.e: Sales agents present the film at markets and negotiate territory licenses.

film-business.l18.q5.t: Buyers' payments often depend on receiving all required materials
film-business.l18.q5.p: Why does late or incomplete delivery matter?
film-business.l18.q5.h: Think of the MG payment schedule.
film-business.l18.q5.e: Payment is tied to delivery, so missing items delay or reduce income.

film-business.l19.q1.t: An entertainment attorney, accountant, insurer or guild
film-business.l19.q1.p: According to this course, tools such as Plajah's production suite can organize work but do not replace what?
film-business.l19.q1.e: Tools organize the work but do not replace professional legal and financial advice.

film-business.l19.q2.p: A shoot of 18 days is complete. The clearance list shows 2 unsigned music cues out of 12 total. How many are signed?

film-business.l19.q3.p: A festival deadline is in 6 weeks, which is 42 days. Counsel needs 10 days to clear the cues and 3 weeks for delivery items. How many days remain after both, assuming they run one after the other?
film-business.l19.q3.e: 10 plus 21 is 31 days, and 42 minus 31 is 11 days remaining.

film-business.l19.q4.t: Check each call sheet, clearance and budget revision against the checklist and bring gaps to counsel
film-business.l19.q4.p: Which approach best uses a production tool alongside this course?
film-business.l19.q4.h: Tools surface problems; professionals fix them.
film-business.l19.q4.e: Tools make missing items visible so professionals can resolve them.

film-business.l19.q5.p: Using a production management tool means you no longer need signed contracts with cast and crew.
film-business.l19.q5.h: Think about who creates legal rights.
film-business.l19.q5.e: False. Signed agreements remain essential; a tool only helps track them.

film-directing.l01.q1.p: A director is mainly responsible for the creative interpretation of the script and for guiding the people who bring it to the screen.
film-directing.l01.q1.h: Think about the one person who keeps everyone's work pointed the same way.
film-directing.l01.q1.e: The director interprets the story and guides actors and departments so their work fits together.

film-directing.l01.q2.t: Handling money, hiring and business decisions
film-directing.l01.q2.p: Which task usually belongs to a producer rather than to the director?
film-directing.l01.q2.h: One of these is about budgets and logistics.
film-directing.l01.q2.e: Producers typically manage finance, schedules and hiring, while directors lead the creative side.

film-directing.l01.q3.p: A director always has complete control over the finished film.
film-directing.l01.q3.e: Budgets, studios, financiers and contracts limit a director's control, and final say varies from film to film.

film-directing.l01.q4.t: Deciding what the film should look and feel like
film-directing.l01.q4.p: A director asks the cinematographer for quiet, simple, steady frames because the story is restrained. Which part of the job is this?
film-directing.l01.q4.h: It is about interpretation, not operating equipment.
film-directing.l01.q4.e: Choosing the look and feel with the cinematographer is part of the director's creative interpretation.

film-directing.l01.q5.t: Different directorial choices about tone and how to tell the story
film-directing.l01.q5.p: Two films on the same set of events end up feeling very different. What most likely explains this?
film-directing.l01.q5.h: What does a director decide beyond the plot?
film-directing.l01.q5.e: Interpretation, tone and the choices made with collaborators can make the same material feel different.

film-directing.l02.q1.p: In which stage does the director often discover what the film really is, because the story can be reshaped?
film-directing.l02.q1.h: It happens after the footage is recorded.
film-directing.l02.q1.e: In the edit the footage is assembled and the shape of the story can change.

film-directing.l02.q2.p: Pre-production is the stage where planning happens, such as casting, location visits and shot lists.
film-directing.l02.q2.h: It comes before the cameras roll.
film-directing.l02.q2.e: Pre-production is the planning stage, when problems are cheapest to solve.

film-directing.l02.q3.p: Who runs the schedule on set day to day, so the director can focus on creative decisions?
film-directing.l02.q3.h: This person calls for quiet and keeps time.
film-directing.l02.q3.e: The first assistant director manages the set schedule and crew movement.

film-directing.l02.q4.t: Mistakes are cheaper to fix before expensive shooting days
film-directing.l02.q4.p: Why is planning in pre-production said to be so valuable?
film-directing.l02.q4.h: Think about the cost of a shoot day.
film-directing.l02.q4.e: Every hour on set is expensive, so solving problems earlier saves money and time.

film-directing.l02.q5.p: Because the stages overlap, some films need extra shooting, called pickups, after principal photography has ended.
film-directing.l02.q5.h: Do the stages always happen in a strict sequence?
film-directing.l02.q5.e: Stages overlap in practice, and extra shoots called pickups sometimes happen later.

film-directing.l03.q1.t: Plot is what happens; theme is what the events add up to
film-directing.l03.q1.p: What is the difference between plot and theme?
film-directing.l03.q1.h: One is about events, the other about meaning.
film-directing.l03.q1.e: Plot is the sequence of events, while theme is the underlying idea they suggest.

film-directing.l03.q2.p: Subtext means the meaning that lies beneath the words characters actually say.
film-directing.l03.q2.h: Think of an argument about dishes that is really about something else.
film-directing.l03.q2.e: Subtext is the unspoken meaning beneath the dialogue.

film-directing.l03.q3.t: Checking that the scene has a change and understanding its beats
film-directing.l03.q3.p: A director reading a scene asks what each character wants, what stops them, and how things are different at the end. What is this method for?
film-directing.l03.q3.h: It tests whether anything happens in a scene.
film-directing.l03.q3.e: A scene where nothing changes is a warning sign, and the questions reveal beats and change.

film-directing.l03.q4.p: The three-act structure is an unbreakable law that every good film must follow.
film-directing.l03.q4.h: The lesson calls it a useful model.
film-directing.l03.q4.e: It is one useful model; many good films do not follow it.

film-directing.l03.q5.t: Pauses and small physical business that carry the unspoken feeling
film-directing.l03.q5.p: A script says two characters only talk about the weather, but the real beat is her fear of losing her father. What should the director plan for?
film-directing.l03.q5.h: Dialogue is not the only way to show feeling.
film-directing.l03.q5.e: Subtext can be carried by performance, pauses and physical action.

film-directing.l04.q1.t: The overall mood or attitude of a film
film-directing.l04.q1.e: Tone is the general mood or attitude, such as tense, tender or wry.

film-directing.l04.q2.p: A reference image or film clip is meant to be discussed with the team, not copied exactly.
film-directing.l04.q2.h: References help people see what you mean.
film-directing.l04.q2.e: Directors use references to talk about light, colour and framing, not to copy.

film-directing.l04.q3.t: The house should feel too large for the family, so we often frame them small in wide, still shots
film-directing.l04.q3.p: Which statement of vision is the most useful to a crew?
film-directing.l04.q3.h: Look for a statement that tells people what to do.
film-directing.l04.q3.e: A specific idea guides concrete decisions; vague words say little.

film-directing.l04.q4.p: A comedy can turn serious without feeling jarring if the film prepares the audience for the shift.
film-directing.l04.q4.h: Consider whether tone may ever change on purpose.
film-directing.l04.q4.e: Tone can shift deliberately, provided the film prepares the audience.

film-directing.l04.q5.t: Slow camera moves and sparse sound
film-directing.l04.q5.p: A director wants a ghost story where fear comes from stillness. Which pair of choices fits that vision?
film-directing.l04.q5.h: Match choices to the stated idea of stillness.
film-directing.l04.q5.e: Slow moves and sparse sound support fear that grows from stillness.

film-directing.l05.q1.p: Casting is mostly about finding actors who can bring the emotional truth of the character, not only the right appearance.
film-directing.l05.q1.h: Ability to play the life of the character matters.
film-directing.l05.q1.e: Appearance counts, but the emotional truth an actor brings matters more.

film-directing.l05.q2.t: A second meeting where the best candidates read again
film-directing.l05.q2.e: Callbacks let the director see the strongest candidates again, often trying different directions.

film-directing.l05.q3.t: Whether two actors work well together on screen
film-directing.l05.q3.p: What does a chemistry read help a director test?
film-directing.l05.q3.h: Think about two actors at once.
film-directing.l05.q3.e: A chemistry read pairs possible actors to see their connection.

film-directing.l05.q4.p: How an actor responds to direction in an audition can be useful information for a director.
film-directing.l05.q4.h: A director will work with this person on many takes.
film-directing.l05.q4.e: An actor who adjusts quickly to direction is valuable on set.

film-directing.l05.q5.p: Besides performance, which of these can legitimately affect casting decisions?
film-directing.l05.q5.e: Availability, budget and funding considerations are real practical factors in casting.

film-directing.l06.q1.t: The cast reading the whole script aloud together
film-directing.l06.q1.h: It involves hearing the script rather than filming it.
film-directing.l06.q1.e: A table read lets everyone hear the story as a whole and notice weak dialogue.

film-directing.l06.q2.p: Rehearsal is time for exploring the script before the cost and pressure of filming.
film-directing.l06.q2.h: Compare it with a shoot day.
film-directing.l06.q2.e: Rehearsal lets director and actors explore away from the camera.

film-directing.l06.q3.t: It can keep performances fresh and spontaneous
film-directing.l06.q3.p: Which is a reason some directors prefer light rehearsal?
film-directing.l06.q3.h: Think of a performance becoming stale.
film-directing.l06.q3.e: Too much rehearsal may dull spontaneity, though heavy rehearsal also has benefits.

film-directing.l06.q4.p: The lesson presents heavy rehearsal as always better than light rehearsal.
film-directing.l06.q4.h: It describes this as a real debate.
film-directing.l06.q4.e: Good directors choose according to the film, the actors and the schedule.

film-directing.l06.q5.t: Consider using that movement in the blocking
film-directing.l06.q5.p: In rehearsal the actors keep drifting toward the window. What is a sensible director response?
film-directing.l06.q5.h: Natural impulses can be useful information.
film-directing.l06.q5.e: Watching where actors naturally move can shape blocking that feels real.

film-directing.l07.q1.t: Planning where actors stand and move in relation to each other and the camera
film-directing.l07.q1.e: Blocking is the planned positions and movements of actors.

film-directing.l07.q2.p: Blocking can tell the story physically, such as showing who has power through who stands and who sits.
film-directing.l07.q2.e: Position and movement suggest power, closeness or tension.

film-directing.l07.q3.t: A piece of tape on the floor showing where an actor should stop
film-directing.l07.q3.p: What is a mark in film work?
film-directing.l07.q3.h: It helps keep actors in focus and in frame.
film-directing.l07.q3.e: Marks help actors stop in the right spot for focus, light and framing.

film-directing.l07.q4.t: Each move has a reason rooted in the character's wants
film-directing.l07.q4.p: What does it mean for blocking to be motivated?
film-directing.l07.q4.h: Think of why a character would cross the room.
film-directing.l07.q4.e: Motivated moves come from what the character wants, not from random movement.

film-directing.l07.q5.p: Blocking only has to work for the room, and the camera position does not matter.
film-directing.l07.q5.e: Blocking must also work for the camera so the shot can be framed and lit.

film-directing.l08.q1.t: Try to get her to stop talking
film-directing.l08.q1.p: Which instruction is an action direction rather than a result direction?
film-directing.l08.q1.h: Which one gives the actor something to do?
film-directing.l08.q1.e: Action directions give a doable aim; result directions ask for an outcome to display.

film-directing.l08.q2.p: Many modern acting approaches descend from the work of Konstantin Stanislavski, who stressed what a character wants and tries to do.
film-directing.l08.q2.e: Stanislavski's emphasis on wants and actions influenced many later approaches.

film-directing.l08.q3.t: Speak privately and give one clear adjustment
film-directing.l08.q3.p: After a take, which approach to giving feedback does the lesson suggest?
film-directing.l08.q3.e: Private, brief and specific notes are easier for an actor to use.

film-directing.l08.q4.p: An actor can usually play a feeling such as sad directly, which is why result directions work best.
film-directing.l08.q4.h: Consider trying to show an emotion on command.
film-directing.l08.q4.e: Trying to show an emotion often looks forced; actions lead to more natural behaviour.

film-directing.l08.q5.t: You are afraid that if you say it, he will leave
film-directing.l08.q5.p: An actor keeps delivering a line with obvious warmth. Which direction would most likely change it in a useful way?
film-directing.l08.q5.h: Pick the one that gives the character a situation and motive.
film-directing.l08.q5.e: A specific, playable motive changes the performance more than a general request.

film-directing.l09.q1.t: The camera is near enough to see tiny movements
film-directing.l09.q1.p: Why might a close-up call for a smaller performance than a wide shot?
film-directing.l09.q1.h: Think about how near the lens is.
film-directing.l09.q1.e: A close camera catches small expressions, so less physical energy is needed.

film-directing.l09.q2.p: A script supervisor keeps notes on details such as dialogue and prop positions for continuity.
film-directing.l09.q2.h: Scenes are shot in pieces and out of order.
film-directing.l09.q2.e: The script supervisor tracks continuity so shots can be joined.

film-directing.l09.q3.t: The glass should be in the right hand too
film-directing.l09.q3.p: An actor holds a glass in the right hand in the wide shot. What should happen in the close-up?
film-directing.l09.q3.h: The editor must be able to join the shots.
film-directing.l09.q3.e: Matching actions across angles allows the editor to cut smoothly.

film-directing.l09.q4.p: Repeating a scene many times can wear down spontaneity, so a director watches for the point where performance stops improving.
film-directing.l09.q4.e: Some performances peak early, and directors decide when to move on or try something new.

film-directing.l09.q5.t: Take a short break, then try holding the tears back for a quieter option
film-directing.l09.q5.p: A director sees an actress crying on every take and starting to look tired. What helpful step is described?
film-directing.l09.q5.h: Offer variation and care for the actor.
film-directing.l09.q5.e: A break and a different approach gives the editor options and protects the actor.

film-directing.l10.q1.p: Which shot size typically shows a person from about the waist up?
film-directing.l10.q1.h: Between a full shot and a close-up.
film-directing.l10.q1.e: A medium shot is roughly waist up.

film-directing.l10.q2.p: A low-angle shot looks up at a subject and can make it seem imposing.
film-directing.l10.q2.h: Where is the camera relative to the subject?
film-directing.l10.q2.e: Low angles tend to make subjects look powerful, though context matters.

film-directing.l10.q3.t: A camera tilted so the horizon is slanted
film-directing.l10.q3.h: It is often used to suggest unease.
film-directing.l10.q3.e: A Dutch angle tilts the horizon, often to create uneasy feelings.

film-directing.l10.q4.p: A low angle always makes a character look heroic, whatever the film.
film-directing.l10.q4.e: The lesson says these effects are tendencies; a low angle can feel comic or heroic depending on context.

film-directing.l10.q5.t: Moves the audience from the room to her feelings
film-directing.l10.q5.p: A director cuts from a wide, slightly high shot of a nervous student to a close-up of her face. What does the change of shot size do?
film-directing.l10.q5.h: Consider what each size is good at showing.
film-directing.l10.q5.e: Wide shots show surroundings and close-ups bring us into feelings.

film-directing.l11.q1.p: Which movement turns the camera left or right from a fixed position?
film-directing.l11.q1.e: A pan swings the camera horizontally without moving its position.

film-directing.l11.q2.t: A dolly moves the camera itself, while a zoom changes the lens focal length
film-directing.l11.q2.p: What is the main difference between a dolly move and a zoom?
film-directing.l11.q2.h: One changes position; the other changes the lens.
film-directing.l11.q2.e: Zooming alters focal length, whereas a dolly physically moves the camera.

film-directing.l11.q3.p: A camera move should have a reason in the story, such as following a character or revealing information.
film-directing.l11.q3.h: The lesson uses the word motivated.
film-directing.l11.q3.e: Motivated movement serves the story; movement for its own sake can feel like showing off.

film-directing.l11.q4.p: The dolly zoom is closely associated with which film?
film-directing.l11.q4.h: Think of a famous 1950s thriller about heights and obsession.
film-directing.l11.q4.e: The dolly zoom is closely associated with Hitchcock's Vertigo.

film-directing.l11.q5.p: A Steadicam is a stabilising rig worn by the operator that allows smooth moves while walking.
film-directing.l11.q5.e: Steadicam steadies the camera so a walking operator can produce smooth shots.

film-directing.l12.q1.p: What does a shorter focal length generally give?
film-directing.l12.q1.e: Shorter focal lengths show more of the scene.

film-directing.l12.q2.p: Telephoto lenses tend to compress space, making background objects look nearer to the subject.
film-directing.l12.q2.e: Long focal lengths seem to flatten depth.

film-directing.l12.q3.t: How much of the image is in focus
film-directing.l12.q3.e: Shallow depth of field keeps only part of the image sharp, while deep depth of field keeps most of it sharp.

film-directing.l12.q4.t: It isolates the subject and guides attention
film-directing.l12.q4.p: Why might a director choose shallow depth of field for a close-up?
film-directing.l12.q4.e: A shallow depth of field blurs distractions and directs attention to the subject.

film-directing.l12.q5.p: The exact millimetre ranges for wide, normal and telephoto lenses depend on the size of the camera sensor or film frame.
film-directing.l12.q5.h: The lesson calls ranges guides, not fixed rules.
film-directing.l12.q5.e: Because sensor size changes the field of view, millimetre ranges are only guides.

film-directing.l13.q1.t: A wider view capturing the whole scene from start to end
film-directing.l13.q1.e: A master covers the scene's action, often with all the characters in frame.

film-directing.l13.q2.p: Coverage means shooting a scene from different angles and sizes so the editor has options.
film-directing.l13.q2.h: It is about giving the editor choices.
film-directing.l13.q2.e: Coverage gives flexibility when assembling the scene.

film-directing.l13.q3.t: A shot of a detail or element away from the main action
film-directing.l13.q3.h: Think of an insert of a clock or a letter.
film-directing.l13.q3.e: A cutaway shows something else and can help an editor trim or join takes.

film-directing.l13.q4.t: It takes time, and time is money
film-directing.l13.q4.p: What is a trade-off of heavy coverage?
film-directing.l13.q4.e: Heavy coverage gives flexibility but uses limited shooting time.

film-directing.l13.q5.p: Good coverage is designed in advance around what the scene needs the audience to see.
film-directing.l13.q5.h: The lesson says it is not random.
film-directing.l13.q5.e: Directors decide where the audience should look and what must be seen.

film-directing.l14.q1.t: The audience's sense of who is where on screen
film-directing.l14.q1.p: What does the 180-degree rule help protect?
film-directing.l14.q1.h: It concerns left and right positions.
film-directing.l14.q1.e: Keeping the camera on one side of the axis preserves screen positions.

film-directing.l14.q2.p: The axis of action is an imaginary line between two characters.
film-directing.l14.q2.h: The rule is built around this line.
film-directing.l14.q2.e: The axis runs between the characters, and the camera stays on one side.

film-directing.l14.q3.t: It should usually move left to right as well
film-directing.l14.q3.p: A car moves left to right in one shot. What does the rule suggest for the next shot of the car?
film-directing.l14.q3.e: Reversing direction can make viewers think the car turned around.

film-directing.l14.q4.t: Moving the camera across it within a shot
film-directing.l14.q4.p: Which approach can help a director smoothly cross the line?
film-directing.l14.q4.e: Showing the camera move across the line, or using a neutral shot, helps avoid confusion.

film-directing.l14.q5.p: Filmmakers are never permitted to break the 180-degree rule.
film-directing.l14.q5.e: Some filmmakers break it on purpose for disorientation or other effects.

film-directing.l15.q1.t: An ordered list of shots needed for each scene
film-directing.l15.q1.h: It helps the first AD estimate time.
film-directing.l15.q1.e: A shot list sets out the shots planned for each scene.

film-directing.l15.q2.p: A storyboard is a sequence of drawings showing how shots will look.
film-directing.l15.q2.e: Storyboards depict planned shots, especially for complex sequences.

film-directing.l15.q3.t: Action, stunts and complex camera moves
film-directing.l15.q3.p: Which type of scene benefits most from detailed storyboards?
film-directing.l15.q3.h: Many departments must agree on exactly what is filmed.
film-directing.l15.q3.e: Storyboards help coordinate many departments on complex sequences.

film-directing.l15.q4.t: A rough moving version of a storyboard with timing
film-directing.l15.q4.h: It adds time to the drawings.
film-directing.l15.q4.e: An animatic lets pacing be judged before filming.

film-directing.l15.q5.p: Every successful director must storyboard every shot.
film-directing.l15.q5.e: Some directors plan meticulously and others respond to the day, and neither guarantees success.

film-directing.l16.q1.t: Everything arranged in front of the camera
film-directing.l16.q1.h: It is a French term meaning placing on stage.
film-directing.l16.q1.e: It includes sets, props, costume, lighting, actor positions and composition.

film-directing.l16.q2.p: The rule of thirds places key elements along the lines of a three by three grid dividing the frame.
film-directing.l16.q2.e: The rule of thirds is a familiar composition tool.

film-directing.l16.q3.t: Colour meaning depends on the story and culture
film-directing.l16.q3.p: Why do directors build their own colour scheme instead of assuming a colour has one fixed meaning?
film-directing.l16.q3.e: A consistent scheme within the film matters more than assumed universal meanings.

film-directing.l16.q4.p: High-contrast lighting with strong shadows tends to feel dramatic or tense.
film-directing.l16.q4.h: Compare it with soft, even light.

film-directing.l16.q5.p: A film shows cluttered, dim rooms at home and bright, empty offices elsewhere to show family pressure. What does this illustrate?
film-directing.l16.q5.h: It is about design and lighting meaning something.
film-directing.l16.q5.e: Set design and lighting can express a story's pressures without dialogue.

film-directing.l17.q1.t: A cut made in the middle of a movement to hide the join
film-directing.l17.q1.p: What is a match on action?
film-directing.l17.q1.h: Think of a hand opening a door.
film-directing.l17.q1.e: Cutting during a movement makes the join feel smooth.

film-directing.l17.q2.p: Continuity editing aims to make cuts smooth so the audience follows the story without noticing the joins.
film-directing.l17.q2.e: Consistent props, light and action support smooth cutting.

film-directing.l17.q3.t: Placing shots together creates meaning neither has alone
film-directing.l17.q3.p: What is the core idea of montage theory as discussed in the lesson?
film-directing.l17.q3.e: Eisenstein and others explored how shot order creates ideas.

film-directing.l17.q4.p: A jump cut deliberately skips time within a single angle and calls attention to itself.
film-directing.l17.q4.h: It is the opposite of an invisible cut.
film-directing.l17.q4.e: Jump cuts break smooth continuity on purpose.

film-directing.l17.q5.p: Which film is given in the lesson as a famous montage example studied in film courses?
film-directing.l17.q5.h: Think of a silent-era Soviet film.
film-directing.l17.q5.e: Battleship Potemkin is a widely studied example of montage.

film-directing.l18.q1.t: Music that comes from within the story world
film-directing.l18.q1.h: A radio a character turns on is one example.
film-directing.l18.q1.e: Diegetic sound is heard by the characters in the story.

film-directing.l18.q2.p: ADR means re-recording dialogue after the shoot when production sound is not usable.
film-directing.l18.q2.e: Automated dialogue replacement is used to re-record lines.

film-directing.l18.q3.t: Performing sound effects in a studio while watching the picture
film-directing.l18.q3.p: What are Foley artists known for?
film-directing.l18.q3.h: They perform sounds such as footsteps.
film-directing.l18.q3.e: Foley artists create many specific sounds after the shoot.

film-directing.l18.q4.t: A minute of silence in a location, used to fill gaps
film-directing.l18.q4.p: What is room tone and why is it recorded?
film-directing.l18.q4.h: Editors need background sound for gaps.
film-directing.l18.q4.e: Room tone gives editors consistent ambience to smooth edits.

film-directing.l18.q5.p: A common beginner mistake is to use music to tell the audience how to feel when the scene already does so.
film-directing.l18.q5.e: Music can underline emotion, but overuse can duplicate what the scene already shows.

film-directing.l19.q1.p: Who is primarily responsible for the image, including lighting and camera choices?
film-directing.l19.q1.h: It is also called the cinematographer.
film-directing.l19.q1.e: The DP leads the lighting and camera crews to create the look.

film-directing.l19.q2.p: The production designer leads the art department and creates the physical world of the film.
film-directing.l19.q2.e: Production designers shape sets, locations and props, working with costume and DP.

film-directing.l19.q3.t: So the director can see whether scenes work while there is still time to fix them
film-directing.l19.q3.p: Why does an editor often cut during the shoot?
film-directing.l19.q3.h: Think about what can still be re-shot.
film-directing.l19.q3.e: Early cutting reveals problems while the production is still shooting.

film-directing.l19.q4.p: Good collaboration generally means explaining goals and trusting specialists instead of dictating every detail.
film-directing.l19.q4.h: Directors still decide firmly when needed.
film-directing.l19.q4.e: Clarity and trust help departments do their best work.

film-directing.l19.q5.t: The DP and designer propose light and furniture that balance cold and human
film-directing.l19.q5.p: A director says a hospital scene should be cold but not sterile. How is this best handled?
film-directing.l19.q5.h: Departments translate a feeling into choices.
film-directing.l19.q5.e: Light and set choices combine to realise the described feeling.

film-directing.l20.q1.t: A document listing the next day's scenes, locations and call times
film-directing.l20.q1.e: Call sheets tell the cast and crew where and when to be.

film-directing.l20.q2.p: Scenes are often shot out of story order to group them by location, cast and equipment.
film-directing.l20.q2.e: Shooting out of order saves time and money.

film-directing.l20.q3.t: No shot is worth a person's safety, and anyone can raise a concern
film-directing.l20.q3.p: Which statement best reflects the lesson on safety?
film-directing.l20.q3.h: It is shared across the production.
film-directing.l20.q3.e: Safety is a shared responsibility with qualified specialists and procedures.

film-directing.l20.q4.p: Props that look like weapons should be handled by trained professionals under strict rules.
film-directing.l20.q4.e: Weapons and weapon-like props call for specialists and agreed procedures.

film-directing.l20.q5.t: Meet the stunt coordinator and first AD, plan it, and walk through it with cast and crew
film-directing.l20.q5.p: Before shooting a car skid on wet pavement, what should the director do?
film-directing.l20.q5.e: Stunts require planning and briefing before cameras roll.

film-directing.l21.q1.p: Which kind of film has a subject that is real people and events?
film-directing.l21.q1.h: It is the form that records reality.
film-directing.l21.q1.e: Documentaries deal with real subjects, though they are still shaped by choices.

film-directing.l21.q2.p: Documentary directors face ethical questions about consent, fairness and representation.
film-directing.l21.q2.e: These questions are central in documentary work.

film-directing.l21.q3.t: Parts of it were staged, showing how long the line between recording and constructing has been debated
film-directing.l21.q3.p: Why is Nanook of the North (1922) often discussed in documentary courses?
film-directing.l21.q3.h: It concerns how real a documentary is.
film-directing.l21.q3.e: It illustrates the long debate on staging in documentary.

film-directing.l21.q4.p: In animation, planning is intense because nothing exists until it is made.
film-directing.l21.q4.e: Animation needs thorough planning since each frame is created.

film-directing.l21.q5.t: Small scale keeps the story focused and the shoot short
film-directing.l21.q5.p: Why might a director choose one location and two actors for a ten-minute short?
film-directing.l21.q5.e: Shorts often have small budgets, so tightly scoped stories work well.

film-directing.l22.q1.p: Which film by Alfred Hitchcock keeps us largely in one apartment?
film-directing.l22.q1.h: Think of a thriller about watching from a window.
film-directing.l22.q1.e: Rear Window is set largely in one apartment.

film-directing.l22.q2.p: Akira Kurosawa directed Rashomon (1950) and Seven Samurai (1954).
film-directing.l22.q2.e: These two films are among Kurosawa's best-known works.

film-directing.l22.q3.t: Low, mostly static camera positions and domestic stories
film-directing.l22.q3.p: Yasujiro Ozu is known for which style?
film-directing.l22.q3.e: Ozu's quiet style used low, mostly still camera positions.

film-directing.l22.q4.p: Barry Lyndon (1975) is famous for scenes lit largely by what?
film-directing.l22.q4.h: Think of an eighteenth-century period drama.
film-directing.l22.q4.e: Barry Lyndon is known for candlelit scenes shot with very fast lenses.

film-directing.l22.q5.p: The lesson says all these directors worked in exactly the same way.
film-directing.l22.q5.h: The point is variety of method.
film-directing.l22.q5.e: Methods follow temperament and the story, and differ widely.

film-directing.l23.q1.t: The point where the cut is final so other departments can finish
film-directing.l23.q1.h: Sound and effects work depends on it.
film-directing.l23.q1.e: After picture lock, sound, music, effects and colour are finalised.

film-directing.l23.q2.p: Who has final cut is set by contract and often is not the director.
film-directing.l23.q2.e: Final cut varies; many films give it to a studio or producer.

film-directing.l23.q3.t: Look for the problem behind the suggestion
film-directing.l23.q3.p: What should a director do with notes like cut the middle?
film-directing.l23.q3.h: Vague notes often point to a deeper issue.
film-directing.l23.q3.e: The real issue may be pacing, confusion or repetition.

film-directing.l23.q4.p: A test screening shows a film to a sample audience whose reactions are recorded.
film-directing.l23.q4.h: It is used to gather feedback.
film-directing.l23.q4.e: Test screenings give directors and studios audience response.

film-directing.l23.q5.t: Move a scene of her vulnerability earlier
film-directing.l23.q5.p: After a test screening, a character feels unlikeable because of one cruel scene. Which fix is described?
film-directing.l23.q5.h: Context can change how a scene lands.
film-directing.l23.q5.e: Re-ordering scenes can change how audiences read a character.

film-directing.l24.q1.t: An event where films are screened for audiences, critics and buyers
film-directing.l24.q1.e: Festivals showcase films and can lead to distribution deals.

film-directing.l24.q2.p: Festivals may have submission fees and premiere requirements, so filmmakers should check the rules.
film-directing.l24.q2.e: Each festival sets its own fees and premiere requirements.

film-directing.l24.q3.t: Making shorts and building a reel
film-directing.l24.q3.p: Which is a common early route to a directing career?
film-directing.l24.q3.e: Shorts and small projects build experience and a body of work.

film-directing.l24.q4.p: The lesson says there is only one required route into directing, which is film school.
film-directing.l24.q4.e: Some learn through film school, others by experience or by moving up from other jobs.

film-directing.l24.q5.t: Read the contract carefully and seek advice from an entertainment lawyer
film-directing.l24.q5.p: Before signing a distribution deal, what should a filmmaker do?
film-directing.l24.q5.e: Distribution terms vary, so careful review and advice are sensible.

film-genres.l01.q1.p: A genre is a family of films that share recognizable conventions, such as settings, character types and story shapes.
film-genres.l01.q1.h: Think about why audiences know what to expect.
film-genres.l01.q1.e: Shared conventions are exactly what let viewers recognize and anticipate a genre.

film-genres.l01.q2.t: The American West after the Civil War
film-genres.l01.q2.p: Which setting is most typical of the Western?
film-genres.l01.q2.h: Think of horses, saloons and railroads.
film-genres.l01.q2.e: Westerns are set mostly in the American West in the decades after the Civil War.

film-genres.l01.q3.p: Which tension is described as running underneath many Westerns?
film-genres.l01.q3.h: It concerns the frontier and the towns being built on it.
film-genres.l01.q3.e: The wilderness-versus-civilization tension recurs throughout the genre.

film-genres.l01.q4.p: Which film directed by John Ford used Monument Valley and sent strangers across dangerous territory?
film-genres.l01.q4.h: It has a vehicle in its title.
film-genres.l01.q4.e: Ford directed Stagecoach in 1939 and helped make Monument Valley a signature of the genre.

film-genres.l01.q5.p: The lesson says classic Westerns usually told the story fairly from the Native American point of view.
film-genres.l01.q5.h: Consider the genre's flaw described in the lesson.
film-genres.l01.q5.e: Classic Westerns often reduced Native Americans to stereotypes or villains and told history from the settlers' side.

film-genres.l02.q1.p: What does the French term film noir mean?
film-genres.l02.q1.h: Noir is the French word for a color.
film-genres.l02.q1.e: Film noir literally means black film.

film-genres.l02.q2.p: Filmmakers of the 1940s generally called their own work film noir at the time.
film-genres.l02.q2.h: Who applied the label, and when?
film-genres.l02.q2.e: French critics applied the label after the fact, which is why noir is still debated as a genre, style or mood.

film-genres.l02.q3.p: Which visual feature is typical of film noir?
film-genres.l02.q3.h: Think of window blinds at night.
film-genres.l02.q3.e: Noir uses low-key lighting that throws hard, striped shadows.

film-genres.l02.q4.p: Which two influences are named as roots of noir?
film-genres.l02.q4.h: One is a film movement, the other a type of crime writing.
film-genres.l02.q4.e: Noir drew on German Expressionist filmmakers who moved to Hollywood and on writers like Hammett, Chandler and Cain.

film-genres.l02.q5.t: It shows from the start that the plan will go wrong
film-genres.l02.q5.p: In Double Indemnity, how does the narration affect the audience's experience?
film-genres.l02.q5.e: The voice-over lets us know from the beginning that the scheme ends badly, building doom rather than a whodunit.

film-genres.l03.q1.p: Horror aims to provoke fear, dread or disgust.
film-genres.l03.q1.e: Provoking fear, dread or disgust is the core purpose of the genre.

film-genres.l03.q2.p: Which film is a German silent vampire classic directed by F. W. Murnau?
film-genres.l03.q2.h: It is the oldest title in the list.
film-genres.l03.q2.e: Nosferatu was released in 1922 and directed by F. W. Murnau.

film-genres.l03.q3.t: It killed its apparent heroine early in the film
film-genres.l03.q3.h: Think about who the audience expects to survive.
film-genres.l03.q3.e: Psycho shocked viewers by killing the apparent main character early.

film-genres.l03.q4.p: Which term did the scholar Carol Clover introduce for the last survivor of many slashers?
film-genres.l03.q4.h: It describes a person, not an action.
film-genres.l03.q4.e: Clover introduced the term final girl in a 1987 article.

film-genres.l03.q5.p: The lesson says any single horror film can be read in only one way, as a mirror of one anxiety.
film-genres.l03.q5.h: Look at the careful wording of the first paragraph.
film-genres.l03.q5.e: The lesson says many theorists see horror as a mirror, but a single film can be read several ways.

film-genres.l04.q1.p: What question is the heart of science fiction?
film-genres.l04.q1.h: It asks us to imagine a change.
film-genres.l04.q1.e: Science fiction asks "what if?" and follows the answer.

film-genres.l04.q2.p: Who made A Trip to the Moon (1902)?
film-genres.l04.q2.h: He was a French pioneer of trick photography.
film-genres.l04.q2.e: Melies made the 1902 film using painted sets and trick photography.

film-genres.l04.q3.t: He arrived to warn humanity against nuclear war
film-genres.l04.q3.p: What was unusual about the alien visitor in The Day the Earth Stood Still (1951)?
film-genres.l04.q3.e: Unlike many 1950s invasion films, this alien delivers a warning about nuclear weapons.

film-genres.l04.q4.t: Science fiction presents wonders as possible through science; fantasy relies on magic
film-genres.l04.q4.p: How does the lesson usually distinguish science fiction from fantasy?
film-genres.l04.q4.h: Think about how the wonders are explained.
film-genres.l04.q4.e: The usual distinction is whether the wonder is explained by science or by magic.

film-genres.l04.q5.p: The lesson says the best science fiction only predicts future events accurately.
film-genres.l04.q5.h: What does the genre really examine?
film-genres.l04.q5.e: It says science fiction uses imagined settings to examine real questions rather than simply predict.

film-genres.l05.q1.t: Music acts as the language of feeling when talk is not enough
film-genres.l05.q1.p: Why do characters in musicals break into song, according to the lesson?
film-genres.l05.q1.e: The lesson says that when an emotion is too big for talk, characters sing.

film-genres.l05.q2.p: Sound film made the film musical possible.
film-genres.l05.q2.e: The Jazz Singer (1927) and the early sound era launched the genre.

film-genres.l05.q3.p: Which film, co-directed by Gene Kelly and Stanley Donen, is set during the move from silent to sound?
film-genres.l05.q3.h: It has weather in its title.
film-genres.l05.q3.e: Singin' in the Rain is set during that transition and is often named among the greatest musicals.

film-genres.l05.q4.t: One where songs advance the plot instead of pausing it
film-genres.l05.q4.h: The word integrated means joined together.
film-genres.l05.q4.e: In an integrated musical, as pioneered by Oklahoma! on Broadway, songs drive the story.

film-genres.l05.q5.p: Who staged the spectacular dance numbers of 42nd Street (1933)?
film-genres.l05.q5.h: He is associated with backstage musicals.
film-genres.l05.q5.e: Busby Berkeley staged the dance numbers of early-1930s backstage musicals.

film-genres.l06.q1.p: Which feature best describes screwball comedy dialogue?
film-genres.l06.q1.e: Screwball is known for fast, overlapping talk.

film-genres.l06.q2.p: Screwball comedy flourished in the 1930s and early 1940s, during the Great Depression.
film-genres.l06.q2.h: Check the decade given in the lesson.
film-genres.l06.q2.e: The genre peaked in the Depression era.

film-genres.l06.q3.p: Who starred in It Happened One Night (1934)?
film-genres.l06.q3.h: One star plays a runaway heiress.
film-genres.l06.q3.e: Colbert and Gable starred; the Hepburn and Grant pairing is Bringing Up Baby.

film-genres.l06.q4.t: Filmmakers used wit and innuendo instead of showing much physical romance
film-genres.l06.q4.p: Why did the Production Code, enforced from 1934, matter to screwball comedy?
film-genres.l06.q4.h: Consider what could not be shown.
film-genres.l06.q4.e: With limited physical romance allowed, sparring talk and innuendo stood in for desire.

film-genres.l06.q5.p: Which of these is a typical convention of romantic comedy mentioned in the lesson?
film-genres.l06.q5.h: It describes how the couple first encounters each other.
film-genres.l06.q5.e: The meet-cute, obstacles, misunderstanding and reunion are common conventions.

film-genres.l07.q1.t: Nineteenth-century stage shows combining drama with music
film-genres.l07.q1.p: Where does the word melodrama come from?
film-genres.l07.q1.e: It comes from stage shows that combined drama with music.

film-genres.l07.q2.p: Film scholars treat melodrama only as an insult for overdone emotion.
film-genres.l07.q2.h: The lesson says it is also a serious mode.
film-genres.l07.q2.e: Scholars regard melodrama as a serious mode with a long history.

film-genres.l07.q3.p: Which director is the key name for Hollywood melodrama in the 1950s?
film-genres.l07.q3.h: He directed All That Heaven Allows.
film-genres.l07.q3.e: Sirk is the central figure, with films like All That Heaven Allows and Imitation of Life.

film-genres.l07.q4.t: Class, gossip and conformity around a widow's love for a younger gardener
film-genres.l07.q4.p: What is All That Heaven Allows (1955) chiefly about?
film-genres.l07.q4.h: Consider the widow and her disapproving friends.
film-genres.l07.q4.e: The film explores class, gossip and conformity.

film-genres.l07.q5.p: Which later filmmaker paid tribute to Sirk with Far from Heaven (2002)?
film-genres.l07.q5.h: The title echoes the earlier film.
film-genres.l07.q5.e: Todd Haynes made Far from Heaven in the tradition of Sirk.

film-genres.l08.q1.p: A film about a war is also a message about that war.
film-genres.l08.q1.h: The lesson calls the genre politically charged.
film-genres.l08.q1.e: War films are political because they frame the war, its enemies and its costs.

film-genres.l08.q2.p: All Quiet on the Western Front (1930) is based on a novel by whom?
film-genres.l08.q2.h: The director is a different person.
film-genres.l08.q2.e: Remarque wrote the novel; Lewis Milestone directed the film.

film-genres.l08.q3.p: What did Frank Capra's Why We Fight series show about World War II film?
film-genres.l08.q3.h: It was made for the U.S. military.
film-genres.l08.q3.e: It is an example of wartime propaganda.

film-genres.l08.q4.t: Military leaders who sacrifice their own men
film-genres.l08.q4.p: What is the film Paths of Glory (1957) known for condemning?
film-genres.l08.q4.e: It condemns leaders who sacrifice their soldiers.

film-genres.l08.q5.t: Exciting action can make combat look thrilling even in an anti-war film
film-genres.l08.q5.p: Which argument does the lesson raise about anti-war films?
film-genres.l08.q5.h: Think about what action does to audiences.
film-genres.l08.q5.e: The debate is whether thrilling combat undermines an anti-war message.

film-genres.l09.q1.p: Which story shape defines the classic gangster film?
film-genres.l09.q1.e: The rise-and-fall arc is the template.

film-genres.l09.q2.p: Little Caesar (1931) stars Edward G. Robinson as a hood who becomes a boss and then falls.
film-genres.l09.q2.e: Robinson plays the rising and falling gangster.

film-genres.l09.q3.p: Why did the gangster film's endings usually punish crime in the 1930s?
film-genres.l09.q3.e: The Code required crime not to pay.

film-genres.l09.q4.t: A film in which a team plans and carries out a robbery
film-genres.l09.q4.e: Heist films center on planning and carrying out a robbery.

film-genres.l09.q5.p: Which film was remade by Martin Scorsese as The Departed (2006)?
film-genres.l09.q5.e: The Departed is a remake of Infernal Affairs.

film-genres.l10.q1.t: It usually stays in a recognizable world with ordinary people in danger
film-genres.l10.q1.p: How is a thriller different from horror, according to the lesson?
film-genres.l10.q1.e: Thrillers usually stay in a recognizable world.

film-genres.l10.q2.t: The audience knows or fears something the characters do not
film-genres.l10.q2.p: In Hitchcock's description, what is suspense?
film-genres.l10.q2.e: Suspense depends on what the audience knows ahead of the characters.

film-genres.l10.q3.p: Rear Window (1954) limits us to what a confined photographer can see.
film-genres.l10.q3.e: The story is tied to his limited view, which raises unease.

film-genres.l10.q4.p: Which film is given as an example of a political thriller?
film-genres.l10.q4.e: All the President's Men is cited as a political thriller.

film-genres.l10.q5.t: Thrillers can mix comedy and class commentary
film-genres.l10.q5.p: What does Parasite (2019) show, according to the lesson?
film-genres.l10.q5.e: It illustrates blending thriller, comedy and social commentary.

film-genres.l11.q1.t: A journey in which a hero is tested and changes
film-genres.l11.q1.h: Think of heroes traveling toward a goal.
film-genres.l11.q1.e: A quest is a journey of testing and change.

film-genres.l11.q2.p: The Adventures of Robin Hood (1938) set the standard for what?
film-genres.l11.q2.h: Think of Errol Flynn and swords.
film-genres.l11.q2.e: The Technicolor film set the swashbuckling standard.

film-genres.l11.q3.p: Raiders of the Lost Ark (1981) deliberately recalled earlier cliffhanger serials.

film-genres.l11.q4.p: Who created the stop-motion creatures in Jason and the Argonauts (1963)?
film-genres.l11.q4.h: His name is linked to mythical creatures.
film-genres.l11.q4.e: Harryhausen's stop-motion work brought myth alive.

film-genres.l11.q5.t: They often presented non-Western peoples as exotic backdrops from an imperial viewpoint
film-genres.l11.q5.p: Which critique do critics make of classic adventure films?
film-genres.l11.q5.h: Think about who the hero is and who the backdrop is.
film-genres.l11.q5.e: Critics note imperial perspectives and exoticism.

film-genres.l12.q1.p: Animation is a method of making films, not a single genre.
film-genres.l12.q1.h: Think about technique versus story type.

film-genres.l12.q2.p: Which film was the first feature entirely computer-animated?
film-genres.l12.q2.e: Toy Story is named as the first fully computer-animated feature.

film-genres.l12.q4.t: Simple black and white drawings can tell a memoir
film-genres.l12.q4.p: What did Persepolis (2007) show about animation?
film-genres.l12.q4.h: It tells a story about Iran.
film-genres.l12.q4.e: It used simple drawings for a memoir.

film-genres.l12.q5.e: Spirited Away is a Studio Ghibli film.

film-genres.l13.q1.p: Who used the word documentary and described it as the creative treatment of actuality?
film-genres.l13.q1.h: He was a Scottish filmmaker in the 1920s.
film-genres.l13.q1.e: Grierson described documentary as the creative treatment of actuality.

film-genres.l13.q2.p: Flaherty staged parts of Nanook of the North (1922).
film-genres.l13.q2.h: The lesson says it is well known.
film-genres.l13.q2.e: Flaherty staged parts and asked participants to use older methods.

film-genres.l13.q3.p: Which mode in Bill Nichols's scheme has a voice explaining the subject?
film-genres.l13.q3.e: The expository mode relies on explanation.

film-genres.l13.q4.p: What did Triumph of the Will (1935) illustrate?
film-genres.l13.q4.h: Consider who it was made for.
film-genres.l13.q4.e: It was made for the Nazi party.

film-genres.l13.q5.p: What technique did The Thin Blue Line (1988) use to question a conviction?

film-genres.l14.q1.t: A clear setup with a surprising payoff
film-genres.l14.q1.h: Think of how jokes are built.
film-genres.l14.q1.e: A gag is a setup and a payoff.

film-genres.l14.q2.p: In which year did Chaplin debut his Little Tramp character?
film-genres.l14.q2.h: It was early in the silent era.

film-genres.l14.q3.p: Buster Keaton was known for a stone face and precisely designed stunts.

film-genres.l14.q4.p: Which film features Harold Lloyd hanging from a clock?

film-genres.l14.q5.t: The economics, so some adapted and others did not
film-genres.l14.q5.p: What did sound change for silent comedians?
film-genres.l14.q5.e: The lesson says sound changed the economics.

film-genres.l15.q1.t: Control of production, distribution and theaters
film-genres.l15.q1.p: What is vertical integration in the studio system?
film-genres.l15.q1.e: The studios controlled production, distribution and many theaters.

film-genres.l15.q2.p: Which studio was known for gritty gangster films?
film-genres.l15.q2.e: Warner Bros. was known for gangster films and social dramas.

film-genres.l15.q3.p: Genre helped studios plan because a proven formula reduced risk.
film-genres.l15.q3.h: Think about why studios liked formulas.
film-genres.l15.q3.e: Formula plus a familiar star reduced risk.

film-genres.l15.q4.p: What did United States v. Paramount Pictures (1948) lead to?
film-genres.l15.q4.e: It led studios to separate theaters from production.

film-genres.l15.q5.p: Who enforced the Production Code strongly from 1934?

film-genres.l16.q1.p: Where did Italian neorealist films often shoot?

film-genres.l16.q2.p: Neorealism mostly rejected genre in favor of everyday realism.
film-genres.l16.q2.e: The lesson contrasts this with the New Wave.

film-genres.l16.q3.p: What was the magazine of the young French critics?
film-genres.l16.q3.e: The critics wrote for Cahiers du Cinema.

film-genres.l16.q4.t: It borrowed the shape of an American gangster film and broke it up with jump cuts
film-genres.l16.q4.e: Godard used and fragmented the gangster film.

film-genres.l16.q5.t: The director as an author, or auteur
film-genres.l16.q5.p: What idea did the critics promote?

film-genres.l17.q1.t: A period drama, often set in the age of the samurai

film-genres.l17.q3.p: Yojimbo (1961) was reworked by Sergio Leone as A Fistful of Dollars (1964).
film-genres.l17.q3.h: This is an example of genre exchange.

film-genres.l17.q4.p: Which film launched the kaiju genre?

film-genres.l17.q5.p: How is Ozu's camera often placed?
film-genres.l17.q5.e: Ozu often placed the camera low and still.

film-genres.l18.q1.t: The Hindi-language industry based in Mumbai
film-genres.l18.q1.p: What does the term Bollywood usually refer to?
film-genres.l18.q1.h: It is one part of a larger picture.

film-genres.l18.q2.t: A mix of romance, action, comedy, melodrama and music
film-genres.l18.q2.p: What is masala in Hindi cinema?
film-genres.l18.q2.h: It is named for a spice mixture.

film-genres.l18.q3.p: Songs in Hindi films are usually sung by playback singers.

film-genres.l18.q4.p: Which film began the Apu trilogy?

film-genres.l18.q5.t: It blends Western conventions with Indian masala
film-genres.l18.q5.p: Why is Sholay called a curry Western?

film-genres.l19.q1.t: Stories of chivalrous swordfighters in a legendary China

film-genres.l19.q2.p: Which star appeared in Enter the Dragon (1973)?

film-genres.l19.q3.p: Jackie Chan fused kung fu with comic stunts.

film-genres.l19.q4.t: Stylish gunfights with loyal, tragic gangsters
film-genres.l19.q4.e: It is associated with Woo and Tsui Hark.

film-genres.l19.q5.p: Who choreographed action for The Matrix (1999)?

film-genres.l20.q2.p: Which film is commonly traced as the start of the Nollywood boom?
film-genres.l20.q2.e: Living in Bondage is commonly cited.

film-genres.l20.q3.p: Ousmane Sembene is often called the father of African cinema.
film-genres.l20.q3.e: He directed Black Girl in 1966 and is widely given this title, though it is a label rather than an official one.

film-genres.l20.q4.t: They shot quickly on video and sold copies directly
film-genres.l20.q4.p: How did Nollywood producers sell films?

film-genres.l20.q5.t: A film festival in Ouagadougou, Burkina Faso

film-genres.l21.q1.p: Which decades are called Mexico's golden age in the lesson?

film-genres.l21.q2.p: Who led Brazil's Cinema Novo and wrote about an aesthetic of hunger?
film-genres.l21.q2.e: Glauber Rocha led the Brazilian Cinema Novo movement and wrote the 1965 manifesto An Aesthetic of Hunger.

film-genres.l21.q3.p: Third Cinema was argued to sit outside both Hollywood and elite art cinema.
film-genres.l21.q3.e: Fernando Solanas and Octavio Getino argued in their manifesto for filmmaking outside both Hollywood and elite art cinema.

film-genres.l21.q4.p: Which film was directed by Tomas Gutierrez Alea?

film-genres.l21.q5.p: Which film won the Academy Award for foreign-language film for Argentina?

film-genres.l22.q1.p: What replaced the Production Code in 1968?
film-genres.l22.q1.e: The MPAA ratings system replaced the Production Code in 1968.

film-genres.l22.q2.t: Revision: keep the shape but question the values
film-genres.l22.q2.p: What was the typical New Hollywood move toward genres?
film-genres.l22.q2.h: Think of McCabe and Mrs. Miller.
film-genres.l22.q2.e: New Hollywood filmmakers often revised existing genres, such as the Western and the crime film, rather than discarding them.

film-genres.l22.q3.p: Jaws (1975) opened in hundreds of theaters with heavy television advertising.
film-genres.l22.q3.e: Jaws opened in 1975 on hundreds of screens with heavy television advertising, and is often cited as a model for the summer blockbuster.

film-genres.l22.q4.t: One easily explained in a sentence and marketable worldwide

film-genres.l22.q5.p: Which film began the Marvel Cinematic Universe?
film-genres.l22.q5.e: Iron Man (2008) began the Marvel Cinematic Universe.

film-genres.l23.q1.t: Who pays, who distributes, or the attitude of the work
film-genres.l23.q1.p: Which of these can independent mean?

film-genres.l23.q2.p: Which film won the top prize at Cannes in 1989 and helped launch a boom?

film-genres.l23.q3.h: It is a category, not a genre.
film-genres.l23.q3.e: The lesson says it is not a genre.

film-genres.l23.q4.t: Major studios created their own specialty divisions
film-genres.l23.q4.p: Why did the independent category blur?

film-genres.l23.q5.e: A24 was founded in 2012 and became known for distributing independent films.

film-genres.l24.q1.t: Delivery over the internet to a screen of the viewer's choosing

film-genres.l24.q2.p: Which film became the first non-English-language Best Picture winner?
film-genres.l24.q2.e: Parasite, directed by Bong Joon-ho, won Best Picture at the 2020 Academy Awards, the first non-English-language film to do so.

film-genres.l24.q3.p: Recommendation systems can create very narrow categories compared with traditional genre labels.
film-genres.l24.q3.e: Streaming recommendation systems can sort films into very narrow categories, far narrower than traditional genre labels.

film-genres.l24.q4.t: Whether a streamed film should compete for the same awards as theatrical releases
film-genres.l24.q4.p: What did Roma (2018) prompt debate about?
film-genres.l24.q4.e: Roma, a Netflix release, prompted debate about whether streaming films should compete for major theatrical awards.

film-genres.l24.q5.p: Which series, created by Hwang Dong-hyuk, became a global hit?
film-genres.l24.q5.e: Squid Game, a 2021 series created by Hwang Dong-hyuk, became a global hit.

film-history.l01.q1.p: In which country did German Expressionist cinema develop?
film-history.l01.q1.h: The name of the movement gives it away.
film-history.l01.q1.e: German Expressionism came out of Weimar Germany between 1919 and 1931.

film-history.l01.q2.p: Which of these is a key German Expressionist film?
film-history.l01.q2.h: Think of painted, angular sets and psychological horror.
film-history.l01.q2.e: The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari is a key Expressionist film, alongside Metropolis, Nosferatu and M.

film-history.l01.q3.p: A designer wants a street scene whose bent, painted walls show a character's unstable mind. Which movement's approach is this?
film-history.l01.q3.h: Which movement used non-naturalistic design on purpose?
film-history.l01.q3.e: Expressionism used painted, angular, non-naturalistic sets to turn the screen into a map of the psyche.

film-history.l01.q4.t: Expressionism used distorted, designed sets; Neorealism used real locations
film-history.l01.q4.p: How does Expressionism differ most from Neorealism in its treatment of settings?
film-history.l01.q4.h: Compare "painted" with "natural light and location shooting".
film-history.l01.q4.e: Expressionism built non-naturalistic sets and heavy shadow, while Neorealism went into real streets with natural light.

film-history.l02.q1.p: Which technique keeps both foreground and background sharp in the same shot?
film-history.l02.q1.h: It relates to what part of the image is in focus.
film-history.l02.q1.e: Welles used deep-focus photography so that foreground and background are equally sharp.

film-history.l02.q2.p: Orson Welles made Citizen Kane when he was about 25 years old.
film-history.l02.q2.h: Check his tagline in the museum.
film-history.l02.q2.e: The museum describes him as the 25-year-old who reinvented film grammar on his first picture.

film-history.l02.q3.t: Low angles and sets with visible ceilings
film-history.l02.q3.p: A director wants a scene where power feels physical and oppressive. Which Welles-style choices would help?
film-history.l02.q3.h: Think about camera height and what is above the actors.
film-history.l02.q3.e: Welles used low angles and ceilinged sets to make power physical and oppressive.

film-history.l02.q4.t: It lets the audience see that one person can never be fully known
film-history.l02.q4.p: Why does a multi-narrator structure built around an unanswerable question suit a film about a powerful man?
film-history.l02.q4.h: Think about many people describing the same person.
