history-arab-world.l09.q4.e: The institution is linked with al-Mamun.

history-arab-world.l09.q5.p: Scholars only preserved translated works and never extended them.
history-arab-world.l09.q5.h: The lesson says they criticised and corrected them.
history-arab-world.l09.q5.e: Scholars criticised, corrected and extended the works.

history-arab-world.l10.q1.p: Which scholar's book title gave us the word algebra?
history-arab-world.l10.q1.h: One of his book titles contained the word al-jabr.
history-arab-world.l10.q1.e: The word al-jabr in his book title gave us algebra.

history-arab-world.l10.q2.p: The astrolabe could be used to tell time and measure the height of stars.
history-arab-world.l10.q2.h: It was a common astronomical instrument.
history-arab-world.l10.q2.e: The astrolabe served several practical functions.

history-arab-world.l10.q3.p: What did Ibn al-Haytham emphasise in his Book of Optics?
history-arab-world.l10.q3.e: He stressed experimental testing of ideas on light.

history-arab-world.l10.q4.t: The direction of Mecca for prayer
history-arab-world.l10.q4.e: The qibla is the direction Muslims face when praying.

history-arab-world.l10.q5.p: All the scholars discussed in this lesson were Arabs by descent.
history-arab-world.l10.q5.h: Some were Persian, Turkic or Central Asian.
history-arab-world.l10.q5.e: Many wrote in Arabic but were from other backgrounds.

history-arab-world.l11.q1.h: They treated patients and trained students.
history-arab-world.l11.q1.e: Bimaristans were hospitals in cities such as Baghdad and Cairo.

history-arab-world.l11.q2.p: Which work by Ibn Sina was used as a textbook in European universities?
history-arab-world.l11.q2.h: It was an encyclopedia of medicine.
history-arab-world.l11.q2.e: The Canon of Medicine was translated into Latin.

history-arab-world.l11.q3.e: Al-Razi wrote a famous work on the two diseases.

history-arab-world.l11.q4.p: Which thinker wrote The Incoherence of the Philosophers?
history-arab-world.l11.q4.h: Ibn Rushd later replied to it.

history-arab-world.l11.q5.p: Ibn Rushd wrote commentaries on Aristotle and lived in al-Andalus.
history-arab-world.l11.q5.h: He was a judge from Cordoba.
history-arab-world.l11.q5.e: His commentaries later influenced Latin scholars.

history-arab-world.l12.q1.e: The qasida was a long ode with a set structure.

history-arab-world.l12.q2.p: Who wrote lively essays on animals, misers and eloquence?
history-arab-world.l12.q2.e: Al-Jahiz was a major prose writer.

history-arab-world.l12.q3.p: The Thousand and One Nights was gathered over centuries from Indian, Persian and Arabic sources.
history-arab-world.l12.q3.h: It was not written by a single person.

history-arab-world.l12.q4.t: It helped protect and standardise the language of the Quran
history-arab-world.l12.q4.p: Why was grammar important in early Islamic society?
history-arab-world.l12.q4.e: Scholars such as Sibawayh systematised Arabic grammar.

history-arab-world.l12.q5.p: Antoine Galland's French translation in the early 1700s helped bring the Nights to Europe.
history-arab-world.l12.q5.e: Galland's translation added tales and popularised the work.

history-arab-world.l13.q1.p: Which art became central in Quran manuscripts and mosques?
history-arab-world.l13.q1.h: It is the art of beautiful writing.
history-arab-world.l13.q1.e: Calligraphy and geometric ornament developed as major arts.

history-arab-world.l13.q2.p: The oud is an ancestor of the European lute.
history-arab-world.l13.q2.h: The word lute comes from its name.
history-arab-world.l13.q2.e: The English lute derives from al-ud.

history-arab-world.l13.q3.e: Muqarnas are stacked niches used in vaults and domes.

history-arab-world.l13.q4.p: Which palace in Granada is known for elaborate plasterwork and water gardens?
history-arab-world.l13.q4.h: It was built mainly under the Nasrids.
history-arab-world.l13.q4.e: The Alhambra is the Nasrid palace-city.

history-arab-world.l13.q5.p: There was no figurative painting at all in any Islamic-world book.
history-arab-world.l13.q5.e: Illustrated secular books existed, such as al-Wasiti's maqamat.

history-arab-world.l14.q1.p: Which city did the Fatimids found next to Fustat?

history-arab-world.l14.q2.p: The Fatimids were an Ismaili Shia dynasty.
history-arab-world.l14.q2.h: They claimed descent from Fatima and Ali.
history-arab-world.l14.q2.e: The Fatimids were Ismailis who claimed the caliphate.

history-arab-world.l14.q3.p: Who ended the Fatimid caliphate in 1171?
history-arab-world.l14.q3.e: Saladin returned Egypt to Sunni rule.

history-arab-world.l14.q4.t: Three rival rulers claiming the title of caliph
history-arab-world.l14.q4.p: What did the tenth century see in the Muslim world?
history-arab-world.l14.q4.e: Abbasids, Fatimids and Umayyads each claimed the title.

history-arab-world.l14.q5.p: The Cairo Geniza documents reveal a thriving Mediterranean trade network.
history-arab-world.l14.q5.h: They were the papers of Jewish merchants.
history-arab-world.l14.q5.e: They show commerce across the Mediterranean and Indian Ocean.

history-arab-world.l15.q1.p: Who led the Muslim army that crossed into Iberia in 711?
history-arab-world.l15.q1.h: The place name Gibraltar comes from his name.
history-arab-world.l15.q1.e: Tariq ibn Ziyad led the crossing.

history-arab-world.l15.q2.p: Abd al-Rahman III declared himself caliph at Cordoba in 929.
history-arab-world.l15.q2.h: This was a high point of Cordoba.
history-arab-world.l15.q2.e: He declared the Cordoba caliphate in 929.

history-arab-world.l15.q3.t: Coexistence involved cooperation and also tension
history-arab-world.l15.q3.p: Why do historians debate the word convivencia?
history-arab-world.l15.q3.h: Think of both cooperation and conflict.
history-arab-world.l15.q3.e: It captures cooperation but can understate conflict.

history-arab-world.l15.q4.p: Which kingdom was the last Muslim state in Iberia, falling in 1492?
history-arab-world.l15.q4.e: Granada fell to Castile and Aragon.

history-arab-world.l15.q5.p: The caliphate of Cordoba broke into small kingdoms called taifas around 1031.
history-arab-world.l15.q5.e: The fragmentation was a key turning point.

history-arab-world.l16.q1.p: Which pope called for the expedition that became the First Crusade?
history-arab-world.l16.q1.e: Pope Urban II launched the call in 1095.

history-arab-world.l16.q2.p: Which commander defeated the Crusaders at Hattin in 1187?
history-arab-world.l16.q2.e: Saladin won at Hattin and then retook Jerusalem.

history-arab-world.l16.q3.p: The Fourth Crusade sacked the Christian city of Constantinople in 1204.
history-arab-world.l16.q3.h: Alliances did not follow neat religious lines.
history-arab-world.l16.q3.e: The sack of Constantinople shows the complexity.

history-arab-world.l16.q4.p: Arabic writers called the Europeans Franks.
history-arab-world.l16.q4.h: The term came from a European people.
history-arab-world.l16.q4.e: They used the term Franks, ifranj in Arabic.

history-arab-world.l16.q5.p: Which Mamluk victory in 1291 ended the Crusader presence on the mainland?
history-arab-world.l16.q5.h: It was the last major stronghold.

history-arab-world.l17.q1.p: Who led the Mongol army that took Baghdad in 1258?
history-arab-world.l17.q1.h: He was a grandson of Genghis Khan.

history-arab-world.l17.q2.p: The Abbasid caliph al-Mustasim was killed when Baghdad fell.
history-arab-world.l17.q2.h: This event marks the end of the Abbasid caliphate in Baghdad.

history-arab-world.l17.q3.p: Where did a Mamluk army defeat a Mongol force in 1260?
history-arab-world.l17.q3.e: Ain Jalut halted Mongol advance westwards.

history-arab-world.l17.q4.p: Which Mongol ruler converted to Islam around 1295?

history-arab-world.l17.q5.p: Modern historians agree on the exact death tolls medieval sources gave.
history-arab-world.l17.q5.h: The lesson says they debate the numbers.

history-arab-world.l18.q1.p: What does the word mamluk mean?
history-arab-world.l18.q1.e: Mamluks were bought, trained and freed soldiers.

history-arab-world.l18.q2.p: Which Mamluk sultan campaigned against both Mongols and Crusaders and ruled 1260-1277?
history-arab-world.l18.q2.e: Baybars was a major early sultan.

history-arab-world.l18.q3.p: The Mamluk sultanate ruled Egypt and Syria until the Ottoman conquest of 1516-1517.

history-arab-world.l18.q4.p: What concept did Ibn Khaldun use to explain the rise and fall of dynasties?
history-arab-world.l18.q4.e: Asabiyya is central to the Muqaddimah.

history-arab-world.l18.q5.p: The Black Death struck Egypt and Syria in 1347-1349 with serious economic effects.
history-arab-world.l18.q5.h: It affected much of the world.
history-arab-world.l18.q5.e: It killed a large share of the population.

history-arab-world.l19.q1.p: Which city did Mehmed II conquer in 1453?

history-arab-world.l19.q2.p: Which sultan conquered Syria and Egypt in 1516-1517?
history-arab-world.l19.q2.e: Selim I took the Mamluk lands.

history-arab-world.l19.q3.p: Timur defeated Sultan Bayezid I at Ankara in 1402.
history-arab-world.l19.q3.h: The state nearly collapsed but recovered.

history-arab-world.l19.q4.p: Under Ottoman rule, Arabic was no longer used for religion and scholarship.
history-arab-world.l19.q4.e: Arabic remained central to religion and scholarship.

history-arab-world.l19.q5.p: Which part of the Arab world stayed outside Ottoman rule?
history-arab-world.l19.q5.h: It lay in the far west.

history-arab-world.l20.q1.t: A system of taking Christian boys for state service
history-arab-world.l20.q1.h: It was a source of suffering for families.
history-arab-world.l20.q1.e: Boys were taken, converted and trained.

history-arab-world.l20.q2.p: Distant Arab provinces had considerable local autonomy in practice.
history-arab-world.l20.q2.h: Think of Egypt and Mount Lebanon.

history-arab-world.l20.q3.t: Nineteenth-century reforms aimed at modernising the empire
history-arab-world.l20.q3.e: The reforms aimed to modernise army, law and taxation.

history-arab-world.l20.q4.t: Places to discuss news and poetry
history-arab-world.l20.q4.p: What did coffeehouses in Ottoman cities serve as?

history-arab-world.l20.q5.p: Historians debate how formal the millet system was in the early centuries.
history-arab-world.l20.q5.h: The lesson says this is debated.
history-arab-world.l20.q5.e: The term describes religious community self-rule.

history-arab-world.l21.q1.p: Which religion did Shah Ismail make official in Iran after 1501?
history-arab-world.l21.q1.h: It is the major branch in Iran today.
history-arab-world.l21.q1.e: Twelver Shia Islam was declared the state religion.

history-arab-world.l21.q3.p: Which battle in 1514 saw the Ottomans defeat the Safavids?

history-arab-world.l21.q4.p: Which Safavid ruler moved the capital to Isfahan?
history-arab-world.l21.q4.e: Shah Abbas I built magnificent Isfahan.

history-arab-world.l21.q5.p: The Treaty of Zuhab in 1639 settled a border roughly close to the later Iran-Iraq border.
history-arab-world.l21.q5.h: The empires had long fought over Iraq.
history-arab-world.l21.q5.e: The treaty fixed a lasting frontier.

history-arab-world.l22.q2.p: Which Egyptian governor ruled from 1805 to 1848 and built a modern army?

history-arab-world.l22.q3.h: It cut the journey between Europe and Asia.
history-arab-world.l22.q3.e: It was opened under French direction.

history-arab-world.l22.q4.p: In what year did Britain occupy Egypt?

history-arab-world.l22.q5.p: Abd al-Qadir led a long resistance to the French in Algeria.
history-arab-world.l22.q5.e: He led a resistance for years.

history-arab-world.l23.q1.p: Which secret 1916 agreement divided the region into spheres of influence?
history-arab-world.l23.q1.h: It was between Britain and France.

history-arab-world.l23.q2.p: The Balfour Declaration of 1917 stated Britain favoured a national home for the Jewish people in Palestine.
history-arab-world.l23.q2.h: It also said rights of others should not be harmed.
history-arab-world.l23.q2.e: It addressed Palestine with that qualification.

history-arab-world.l23.q3.t: Sharif Husayn of Mecca and his sons
history-arab-world.l23.q3.p: Who led the Arab Revolt of 1916?
history-arab-world.l23.q3.h: Faisal and Abdullah were his sons.

history-arab-world.l23.q4.p: Where did French forces defeat Faisal in 1920?

history-arab-world.l23.q5.p: The mandates were assigned by the League of Nations system, with Britain and France in charge.
history-arab-world.l23.q5.h: Many Arabs saw it as colonial rule.
history-arab-world.l23.q5.e: Mandates gave Britain Iraq and Palestine and France Syria and Lebanon.

history-arab-world.l24.q1.t: A cultural revival in the nineteenth century
history-arab-world.l24.q1.e: The Nahda revived classical Arabic and ideas.

history-arab-world.l24.q2.p: Saudi Arabia was named a kingdom in 1932.
history-arab-world.l24.q2.e: Abd al-Aziz Ibn Saud unified it.

history-arab-world.l24.q3.p: Which union of Egypt and Syria collapsed in 1961?
history-arab-world.l24.q3.e: It showed unity was hard to maintain.

history-arab-world.l24.q4.p: Which country fought a war of independence from France from 1954 to 1962?

history-arab-world.l24.q5.p: Turkey became a republic in 1923 under Ataturk.
history-arab-world.l24.q5.h: The sultanate was abolished the year before.
history-arab-world.l24.q5.e: The Ottoman sultanate was abolished in 1922 and the republic was proclaimed in 1923.

history-arab-world.l25.q1.t: A Jewish state and an Arab state in Palestine
history-arab-world.l25.q1.p: What did the 1947 UN partition plan propose?
history-arab-world.l25.q1.h: Jewish leaders accepted and Arab leaders rejected it.

history-arab-world.l25.q2.p: Palestinians call the events of 1948 the Nakba, or catastrophe.
history-arab-world.l25.q2.e: This is their term for it.

history-arab-world.l25.q3.t: West Bank, Gaza, Sinai, East Jerusalem and the Golan Heights
history-arab-world.l25.q3.p: Which territories did Israel take in 1967?
history-arab-world.l25.q3.e: Israel took these areas in the Six-Day War.

history-arab-world.l25.q4.p: Which event made Egypt the first Arab state to make peace with Israel?
history-arab-world.l25.q4.e: Egypt and Israel made peace in 1979.

history-arab-world.l25.q5.p: Historians fully agree on why people fled in 1948.

history-arab-world.l26.q1.p: What did Nasser do in July 1956?
history-arab-world.l26.q1.h: It led to the Suez Crisis.

history-arab-world.l26.q2.p: Britain and France withdrew under US and Soviet pressure after the 1956 attack.
history-arab-world.l26.q2.h: They had acted in secret with Israel.
history-arab-world.l26.q2.e: Political pressure forced them to withdraw.

history-arab-world.l26.q3.p: Which organisation did five oil-producing countries form in 1960?

history-arab-world.l26.q4.p: What did Arab producers do in 1973?
history-arab-world.l26.q4.h: It caused prices to rise sharply.
history-arab-world.l26.q4.e: The embargo led to an oil shock.

history-arab-world.l26.q5.p: Oil was found in Saudi Arabia in 1938.

history-arab-world.l27.q1.p: Who led the creation of the Islamic Republic of Iran after 1979?

history-arab-world.l27.q2.h: A coalition expelled Iraqi forces in 1991.
history-arab-world.l27.q2.e: The invasion led to the Gulf War.

history-arab-world.l27.q4.p: Which agreement of 1989 helped end the Lebanese civil war?

history-arab-world.l27.q5.p: Investigators found the weapons of mass destruction cited for the 2003 invasion.
history-arab-world.l27.q5.h: The lesson says they did not.

history-arab-world.l28.q1.p: In which country did the Arab Spring begin in December 2010?

history-arab-world.l28.q2.e: He stepped down after mass protests.

history-arab-world.l28.q3.p: Which country is described as making the most progress toward democracy?
history-arab-world.l28.q3.h: Think of which transition made the most lasting progress.
history-arab-world.l28.q3.e: Tunisia progressed most, with later setbacks.

history-arab-world.l28.q4.p: Which of these is named as a contemporary challenge?
history-arab-world.l28.q4.e: These are among challenges named in the lesson.

history-arab-world.l28.q5.p: The Arab Spring led to the same outcome in every country.

history-asia.l01.q1.t: The Yellow River and the Yangtze
history-asia.l01.q1.p: Which pair of rivers helped create large farming societies in early China?
history-asia.l01.q1.h: Both flow through what is now China.
history-asia.l01.q1.e: The Yellow River and Yangtze deposited fertile soil and supported dense farming populations in China.

history-asia.l01.q2.p: Monsoon winds bring heavy seasonal rain to much of South and Southeast Asia.
history-asia.l01.q2.h: Think about what monsoons are known for.
history-asia.l01.q2.e: Monsoons are seasonal wind patterns that bring the main rains to South and Southeast Asia and shape the farming calendar.

history-asia.l01.q3.t: The north was drier and suited to millet, while the wetter south suited rice
history-asia.l01.q3.p: In early China, why did the north and south often farm different crops?
history-asia.l01.q3.e: Climate differed between north and south, so millet was common in the drier north and rice in the wetter south.

history-asia.l01.q4.p: The script used in the Indus cities has been fully deciphered by scholars.
history-asia.l01.q4.h: Recall what the lesson said about some ancient writing.
history-asia.l01.q4.e: The Indus script remains undeciphered, so scholars rely heavily on archaeology to understand those cities.

history-asia.l01.q5.t: They combine written records with archaeology, art and scientific methods
history-asia.l01.q5.p: Which statement best describes how historians reconstruct Asia's past?
history-asia.l01.q5.h: One kind of evidence is rarely enough.
history-asia.l01.q5.e: Different kinds of evidence check and fill in for each other, which matters most where writing is missing or undeciphered.

history-asia.l02.q1.p: Which of these was a major city of the Indus Valley civilization?
history-asia.l02.q1.h: It is one of two cities named in the lesson.
history-asia.l02.q1.e: Harappa and Mohenjo-daro were two of the largest Indus cities.

history-asia.l02.q2.p: Many Indus homes had drains connected to covered channels along the streets.
history-asia.l02.q2.h: The cities were known for urban planning.
history-asia.l02.q2.e: Archaeology shows covered drainage systems in many Indus cities.

history-asia.l02.q3.t: Long-distance trade or contact between the regions
history-asia.l02.q3.p: What do Indus seals found in Mesopotamia suggest?
history-asia.l02.q3.h: Consider why an object would travel far from where it was made.
history-asia.l02.q3.e: Seals of Indus type found far away suggest trade and contact across long distances.

history-asia.l02.q4.p: Scholars agree that a single invasion destroyed the Indus cities.
history-asia.l02.q4.h: The lesson says the old idea is no longer widely supported.
history-asia.l02.q4.e: Most scholars now favor gradual or multiple causes such as changing rivers and rainfall, not a single invasion.

history-asia.l02.q5.t: The script is undeciphered and no clear royal palaces or tombs have been identified
history-asia.l02.q5.p: Why is it hard to say how Indus society was governed?
history-asia.l02.q5.h: Think about what evidence is missing.
history-asia.l02.q5.e: Without readable texts or obvious palaces and royal tombs, the question of authority rests on interpretation.

history-asia.l03.q1.t: Animal bones and shells inscribed with questions to ancestors and spirits
history-asia.l03.q1.e: Shang kings had questions carved on bones and shells that were heated and cracked, and these inscriptions are the earliest large body of readable Chinese writing.

history-asia.l03.q2.p: The Mandate of Heaven held that a ruler could lose the right to rule by governing badly.
history-asia.l03.q2.e: The Zhou idea tied legitimacy to just rule, which let later writers explain a dynasty's fall as loss of the mandate.

history-asia.l03.q3.p: Which dynasty developed the Mandate of Heaven to justify its rule?
history-asia.l03.q3.e: The Zhou used the Mandate of Heaven to justify defeating the Shang.

history-asia.l03.q4.p: The Warring States period was peaceful but produced no new philosophies.
history-asia.l03.q4.h: Recall both the wars and the ideas of this age.
history-asia.l03.q4.e: It was a time of constant war, yet also of intense debate among thinkers such as Confucius and later schools.

history-asia.l03.q5.t: They gave a moral justification for replacing the Shang and a standard for judging later rulers
history-asia.l03.q5.p: Why were the Zhou rulers' claims about Heaven politically useful?
history-asia.l03.q5.h: Think about conquest needing an explanation.
history-asia.l03.q5.e: The mandate justified conquest and also offered an explanation for later dynastic change.

history-asia.l04.q1.t: Standardized writing, weights, measures and coinage
history-asia.l04.q1.p: What did Qin Shi Huang do after unifying China in 221 BCE?
history-asia.l04.q1.e: The Qin standardized key systems to bind the newly unified state.

history-asia.l04.q2.p: The Silk Road was a single road traveled from end to end by one merchant.
history-asia.l04.q2.e: Goods usually passed through many middlemen over a network of routes.

history-asia.l04.q3.p: Which dynasty followed the Qin and lasted until 220 CE?
history-asia.l04.q3.h: It was founded by Liu Bang.
history-asia.l04.q3.e: The Han dynasty began in 202 BCE and ended in 220 CE, with a short interruption.

history-asia.l04.q4.p: Legalism stressed strict laws and harsh punishments.
history-asia.l04.q4.h: This was the Qin government's guiding school.
history-asia.l04.q4.e: Legalism, the Qin philosophy of government, relied on strict laws and punishments.

history-asia.l04.q5.t: Tradition credits Cai Lun in 105 CE, but earlier paper has been found by archaeologists
history-asia.l04.q5.p: Why do scholars say paper's origin should be described carefully?
history-asia.l04.q5.h: Tradition and archaeology do not match exactly.
history-asia.l04.q5.e: Archaeology found older paper than Cai Lun's date, so tradition's credit to him is better treated as improvement or promotion of an existing technology.

history-asia.l05.q1.p: What was the capital of the Maurya Empire?
history-asia.l05.q1.h: It was near the modern city of Patna.

history-asia.l05.q2.p: Ashoka's edicts were carved on rocks and pillars for the public to see.
history-asia.l05.q2.h: Think about where the lesson says they are found.
history-asia.l05.q2.e: The edicts were inscribed on rock surfaces and stone pillars across the empire.

history-asia.l05.q3.p: According to Ashoka's own inscriptions, which event led him toward dhamma?
history-asia.l05.q3.h: He expressed remorse about a war.
history-asia.l05.q3.e: His inscriptions describe remorse after the bloody conquest of Kalinga.

history-asia.l05.q4.p: Scholars all agree on exactly who wrote the Arthashastra and when.
history-asia.l05.q4.h: The lesson says its authorship is debated.
history-asia.l05.q4.e: Its authorship and date are debated, and it may have been compiled over time.

history-asia.l05.q5.t: They are public statements by the ruler and so may present him favorably
history-asia.l05.q5.p: Why should a historian read Ashoka's edicts with some caution?
history-asia.l05.q5.h: Who produced the edicts, and why?
history-asia.l05.q5.e: A ruler's own inscriptions are valuable primary sources but also served to shape his public image.

history-asia.l06.q1.p: Which numeral system with a zero took shape in India?
history-asia.l06.q1.h: It became the numerals used widely today.
history-asia.l06.q1.e: The decimal place-value system with zero developed in India and spread through later translators.

history-asia.l06.q2.p: Nalanda was a major center of learning in the Gupta era.
history-asia.l06.q2.h: It was a monastic university in Bihar.
history-asia.l06.q2.e: Nalanda grew into a famous center of Buddhist and other learning.

history-asia.l06.q3.t: It is a label added later and may overlook other regions and problems
history-asia.l06.q3.p: Why do historians treat the phrase "golden age" with care?
history-asia.l06.q3.h: Think about who coined the label and when.
history-asia.l06.q3.e: The term is a later judgement, and other regions and eras were also creative.

history-asia.l06.q4.p: Faxian was a Chinese monk who left an account of travel in India around 400 CE.
history-asia.l06.q4.h: He is a foreign visitor named in the lesson.
history-asia.l06.q4.e: Faxian's account is an important outside source for India in this period.

history-asia.l06.q5.t: As useful evidence of what a visitor saw and understood, checked against other sources
history-asia.l06.q5.p: How should a historian use Faxian's account?
history-asia.l06.q5.h: Every source has a point of view.
history-asia.l06.q5.e: Visitor accounts are valuable but limited, and should be compared with inscriptions, art and other texts.

history-asia.l07.q1.h: The Buddha lived in South Asia.
history-asia.l07.q1.e: Buddhism began with Siddhartha Gautama in northeastern India.

history-asia.l07.q2.p: Hinduism has a single founder and one centralized organization.
history-asia.l07.q2.h: The lesson describes it as many related traditions.
history-asia.l07.q2.e: Hinduism is a name for diverse traditions without one founder or one governing body.

history-asia.l07.q3.t: The Silk Road through Central Asia
history-asia.l07.q3.p: Which route carried Mahayana Buddhism into China?
history-asia.l07.q3.e: Mahayana Buddhism moved along Silk Road routes through Central Asia into China.

history-asia.l07.q4.p: Angkor Wat was originally built as a Hindu temple.
history-asia.l07.q4.e: It was built in the twelfth century as a Hindu temple to Vishnu and later became a Buddhist site.

history-asia.l07.q5.t: Local rulers selectively adapted Indian ideas to their own purposes
history-asia.l07.q5.p: What does Southeast Asia's adoption of Indian religion and Sanskrit titles show?
history-asia.l07.q5.h: Consider who chose to adopt what.
history-asia.l07.q5.e: Evidence suggests local elites invited and adapted Indian culture, not simply that it was imposed.

history-asia.l08.q1.p: Which dynasty had its capital at Chang'an?
history-asia.l08.q1.e: Chang'an was the Tang capital and a major cosmopolitan city.

history-asia.l08.q2.p: Wu Zetian is the only woman to have ruled China as emperor in her own right.
history-asia.l08.q2.h: She ruled in the Tang era.
history-asia.l08.q2.e: Wu Zetian ruled from 690 to 705 CE and is the only woman to hold the title in her own right.

history-asia.l08.q3.t: The Jurchen conquered the north and the dynasty continued in the south
history-asia.l08.q3.p: What happened to the Song dynasty in 1127?
history-asia.l08.q3.e: After the Jurchen took the northern capital Kaifeng, the Song continued from Hangzhou.

history-asia.l08.q4.p: Song China made use of paper money.
history-asia.l08.q4.e: Paper money was issued in Song China, in the Sichuan region.

history-asia.l08.q5.t: Success still favored families who could afford a son's education
history-asia.l08.q5.p: Why is it incomplete to say the examination system was simply open to all talent?
history-asia.l08.q5.h: Think about who could afford to prepare.
history-asia.l08.q5.e: Although the system rewarded learning, it favored those with resources, so merit and wealth were entangled.

history-asia.l09.q1.p: Who was proclaimed Chinggis Khan in 1206?
history-asia.l09.q1.e: Temujin was proclaimed Chinggis Khan by a council of Mongol leaders in 1206.

history-asia.l09.q2.p: The Mongol conquest of the Southern Song was completed in 1279 under Kublai Khan.
history-asia.l09.q2.e: Kublai Khan completed the conquest of the Southern Song in 1279.

history-asia.l09.q3.t: A relay system of riders and stations for messages and officials
history-asia.l09.q3.h: It supported communication across the empire.
history-asia.l09.q3.e: The yam moved messages and officials quickly across Mongol lands.

history-asia.l09.q4.p: The Mongol invasions of Japan in 1274 and 1281 succeeded.

history-asia.l09.q5.t: Conquered peoples and Mongol-sponsored writers described the same events very differently
history-asia.l09.q5.p: Why should historians read Mongol-era sources carefully?
history-asia.l09.q5.h: Whose point of view does each source reflect?
history-asia.l09.q5.e: Accounts by the conquered emphasize suffering, while Mongol-sponsored texts stress order, so both need critical reading.

history-asia.l10.q1.p: Who founded the Ming dynasty in 1368?
history-asia.l10.q1.h: He is known as the Hongwu emperor.
history-asia.l10.q1.e: Zhu Yuanzhang, of peasant origin, founded the Ming.

history-asia.l10.q2.p: Zheng He's voyages were intended mainly to found colonies.
history-asia.l10.q2.e: They aimed to show Ming prestige and gain tribute and recognition, not to found colonies.

history-asia.l10.q3.p: Which Ming emperor moved the main capital to Beijing?
history-asia.l10.q3.h: He also sponsored the treasure voyages.
history-asia.l10.q3.e: The Yongle emperor moved the capital to Beijing and sponsored Zheng He.

history-asia.l10.q4.p: Historians agree on a single reason the treasure voyages ended.
history-asia.l10.q4.h: The lesson uses the word debate.
history-asia.l10.q4.e: Reasons such as cost and frontier defense are debated, with no single agreed explanation.

history-asia.l10.q5.t: Silver flowed in from Japan and the Americas, commercialising the economy but tying it to overseas events
history-asia.l10.q5.p: How did silver shape the Ming economy?
history-asia.l10.q5.e: Silver imports supported commercial growth but made China vulnerable to shifts in supply.

history-asia.l11.q1.p: Which people founded the Qing dynasty?
history-asia.l11.q1.e: The Manchus founded the Qing after taking Beijing in 1644.

history-asia.l11.q2.p: The Qing ended the examination system when they took power.
history-asia.l11.q2.e: The Qing kept the examination system and Confucian forms of government.

history-asia.l11.q3.t: Rules from the late 1750s channeling foreign trade through Guangzhou
history-asia.l11.q3.e: It restricted foreign trade to Guangzhou under Qing supervision.

history-asia.l11.q4.p: Under the Qing, the empire expanded into Mongolia, Tibet and Xinjiang.
history-asia.l11.q4.h: The empire reached its greatest size.
history-asia.l11.q4.e: Expansion into these regions roughly doubled the empire's size.

history-asia.l11.q5.t: Britain saw limits on trade as a barrier, while the Qing saw control as a security measure
history-asia.l11.q5.p: Why did the Canton System cause friction with Britain?
history-asia.l11.q5.h: Each side read the same rules differently.
history-asia.l11.q5.e: The same restrictions meant different things to each side, which fed later conflict.

history-asia.l12.q1.p: Who founded the Mughal empire in 1526?
history-asia.l12.q1.h: He won the Battle of Panipat.
history-asia.l12.q1.e: Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat and founded the Mughal empire.

history-asia.l12.q2.p: The Taj Mahal was built as a tomb for Mumtaz Mahal.
history-asia.l12.q2.h: It was commissioned by Shah Jahan.
history-asia.l12.q2.e: Shah Jahan had it built, from around 1632 to 1653, as a tomb for his wife.

history-asia.l12.q3.p: What did Akbar's sulh-i kul policy promote?
history-asia.l12.q3.h: Its name means peace with all.
history-asia.l12.q3.e: The policy of sulh-i kul promoted tolerance among different faiths.

history-asia.l12.q4.p: Historians agree on a single explanation of Aurangzeb's policies.
history-asia.l12.q4.e: Some stress religious intolerance, others political and fiscal reasons.

history-asia.l12.q5.p: Which event in 1739 showed Mughal weakness?
history-asia.l12.q5.h: A Persian ruler attacked the capital.
history-asia.l12.q5.e: Nader Shah's sack of Delhi in 1739 showed the empire's declining power.

history-asia.l13.q1.p: What was the capital of Japan in the Heian period?
history-asia.l13.q1.h: The period is named for it.
history-asia.l13.q1.e: Emperor Kanmu moved the capital to Heian-kyo, now Kyoto, in 794.

history-asia.l13.q2.p: The Fujiwara family held power partly by serving as regents.
history-asia.l13.q2.h: They also married into the imperial family.
history-asia.l13.q2.e: The Fujiwara dominated the court through marriage ties and regencies.

history-asia.l13.q3.t: Syllabic scripts that let Japanese be written directly
history-asia.l13.q3.h: It helped literature in the Japanese language.
history-asia.l13.q3.e: Kana scripts allowed writing in Japanese without relying only on Chinese characters.

history-asia.l13.q4.p: The Tale of Genji was written by Murasaki Shikibu in the early eleventh century.
history-asia.l13.q4.h: The author was a court woman.
history-asia.l13.q4.e: It is traditionally and widely attributed to her and dated to the early eleventh century.

history-asia.l13.q5.t: They mostly describe the aristocratic elite, not farmers and provincial warriors
history-asia.l13.q5.p: Why do Heian court writings give an incomplete picture of Japanese society?
history-asia.l13.q5.h: Ask who is missing from the sources.
history-asia.l13.q5.e: Surviving literary texts reflect the court's elite, so other groups must be studied through other evidence.

history-asia.l14.q1.p: What title did Minamoto no Yoritomo receive in 1192?
history-asia.l14.q1.e: Yoritomo was named shogun in 1192 and governed from Kamakura.

history-asia.l14.q2.p: In the shogunate system the emperor remained in Kyoto while the shogun held real power.
history-asia.l14.q2.e: The emperor stayed as a figure of prestige while shoguns held political and military power.

history-asia.l14.q3.t: Defense was costly and there was no conquered land to reward warriors
history-asia.l14.q3.p: Why did the Mongol invasions weaken the Kamakura shogunate?
history-asia.l14.q3.e: Warriors who had fought in the defense received little reward, which damaged loyalty to the shogunate.

history-asia.l14.q4.p: The idea of bushido as a fixed ancient code is partly a later development.
history-asia.l14.q4.h: Recall the caution about this term.
history-asia.l14.q4.e: Much of the romantic bushido ideal developed in later centuries, so it should not be projected backward uncritically.

history-asia.l14.q5.t: A long age of warfare among regional lords called daimyo
history-asia.l14.q5.e: From the late fifteenth century, daimyo fought for territory until reunification in the later sixteenth century.

history-asia.l15.q1.p: Where was the Tokugawa government based?
history-asia.l15.q1.e: The Tokugawa shoguns governed from Edo, now Tokyo.

history-asia.l15.q2.p: Under sankin-kotai, daimyo had to spend alternating periods in Edo.
history-asia.l15.q2.h: This helped the shogunate control the lords.
history-asia.l15.q2.e: The system required alternate-year residence and family hostages in Edo.

history-asia.l15.q3.t: Foreign contact was restricted but not entirely cut off
history-asia.l15.q3.h: Recall Nagasaki, Tsushima and the Ryukyu Kingdom.
history-asia.l15.q3.e: Japan limited foreign trade but kept channels with the Dutch, Chinese, Koreans, Ryukyu and Ainu.

history-asia.l15.q4.p: Merchants were officially ranked at the top of Tokugawa society.
history-asia.l15.q4.h: They were officially ranked last of the four groups.
history-asia.l15.q4.e: Merchants ranked lowest officially, though many became wealthy.

history-asia.l15.q5.p: What arrived in 1853 that pressured Japan to open its ports?
history-asia.l15.q5.e: Perry's ships demanded open ports and exposed the shogunate's weakness.

history-asia.l16.q1.p: Which Korean kingdom, allied with Tang China, unified most of the peninsula in 668?
history-asia.l16.q1.e: Silla allied with the Tang to defeat Goguryeo and control most of the peninsula.

history-asia.l16.q2.p: The name Korea comes from Goryeo.
history-asia.l16.q2.e: The word Korea derives from the name of the Goryeo dynasty.

history-asia.l16.q3.e: Hangul was created under King Sejong and designed to be easy to learn.

history-asia.l16.q4.p: The Jikji, printed in 1377, is the oldest surviving book printed with movable metal type.
history-asia.l16.q4.h: It is a Goryeo Buddhist text.
history-asia.l16.q4.e: The Jikji is the oldest surviving book known to be printed this way.

history-asia.l16.q5.t: Japan invaded Korea and was resisted with Ming help and naval victories
history-asia.l16.q5.p: What happened during the Imjin War of 1592 to 1598?
history-asia.l16.q5.e: Hideyoshi's invasions were resisted by Korean forces, Admiral Yi Sun-sin's navy and Ming China.

history-asia.l17.q1.p: What were the barays at Angkor?
history-asia.l17.q1.e: Barays were large reservoirs used to store water.

history-asia.l17.q2.p: Angkor Wat was built as a Hindu temple dedicated to Vishnu.
history-asia.l17.q2.h: It dates from the twelfth century.
history-asia.l17.q2.e: It was built under Suryavarman II as a temple to Vishnu.

history-asia.l17.q3.t: Control of sea trade routes through the straits
history-asia.l17.q3.p: What was the main basis of Srivijaya's power?
history-asia.l17.q3.h: Think about ships moving between India and China.
history-asia.l17.q3.e: It was a maritime network that profited from shipping and trade.

history-asia.l17.q4.p: Scholars agree on a single cause for Angkor's decline.
history-asia.l17.q4.h: The lesson lists several debated causes.
history-asia.l17.q4.e: War, climate and changing trade are among causes debated, with no single agreed answer.

history-asia.l17.q5.t: Sea-based power left fewer large monuments
history-asia.l17.q5.p: Why is Srivijaya harder for historians to trace than Angkor?
history-asia.l17.q5.h: Compare what each power left behind.
history-asia.l17.q5.e: A maritime network leaves less monumental evidence than a temple city does.

history-asia.l18.q1.p: How long was Vietnam under Chinese rule before the tenth century?
history-asia.l18.q1.e: Chinese rule lasted roughly a thousand years until the tenth century.

history-asia.l18.q2.p: Ayutthaya was founded in 1351 and became a major trading capital.
history-asia.l18.q2.h: It was the capital of Siam for centuries.
history-asia.l18.q2.e: Ayutthaya, founded in 1351, grew into a rich trading capital until 1767.

history-asia.l18.q3.p: What battle in 938 is seen as the start of lasting Vietnamese independence?
history-asia.l18.q3.e: Ngo Quyen's victory at the Bach Dang River in 938 is generally seen as the turning point.

history-asia.l18.q4.p: Majapahit was a Hindu-Buddhist kingdom based on Java.
history-asia.l18.q4.e: Majapahit was centered in eastern Java and combined Hindu and Buddhist traditions.

history-asia.l18.q5.t: It may show the court's claims rather than real control
history-asia.l18.q5.p: Why should the Nagarakretagama's list of regions be used carefully?
history-asia.l18.q5.h: A court wrote about its own power.
history-asia.l18.q5.e: A court poem may exaggerate the reach of its ruler, so its claims need checking against other evidence.

history-asia.l19.q1.p: Who reached Calicut in 1498 by sailing around Africa?

history-asia.l19.q2.p: Early European powers in Asia often built fortified ports rather than ruling large territories.
history-asia.l19.q2.e: The Portuguese relied on fortified ports and trade networks.

history-asia.l19.q3.t: The Dutch United East India Company
history-asia.l19.q3.e: The VOC was a Dutch trading company that built a base at Batavia.

history-asia.l19.q4.p: Siam became a European colony in the nineteenth century.
history-asia.l19.q4.e: Siam avoided colonization, though it lost some territory.

history-asia.l19.q5.t: The Company began collecting revenue and ruling large regions
history-asia.l19.q5.p: What change followed the East India Company's victory at Plassey in 1757?
history-asia.l19.q5.h: It shifted from trading to governing.
history-asia.l19.q5.e: After Plassey, the Company moved from being mainly a trader to ruling territory.

history-asia.l20.q1.p: What did British merchants smuggle into China from India?
history-asia.l20.q1.e: Opium from British-ruled India was smuggled into China.

history-asia.l20.q2.p: Lin Zexu destroyed opium held by foreign merchants at Guangzhou in 1839.
history-asia.l20.q2.e: Lin Zexu confiscated and destroyed a large quantity of opium.

history-asia.l20.q3.p: Which territory did China cede to Britain in the Treaty of Nanjing?
history-asia.l20.q3.h: It remained British for over a century.
history-asia.l20.q3.e: The 1842 treaty ceded Hong Kong Island and opened five ports.

history-asia.l20.q4.p: Extraterritoriality meant foreigners in China were tried by their own consuls.
history-asia.l20.q4.h: It was one of the privileges granted.
history-asia.l20.q4.e: Extraterritoriality placed foreigners outside Chinese courts.

history-asia.l20.q5.t: They were forced on China after military defeat and gave foreigners special privileges
history-asia.l20.q5.p: Why did Chinese people call the treaties "unequal"?
history-asia.l20.q5.h: Think about how the terms were obtained.
history-asia.l20.q5.e: The terms were imposed after war and gave one side privileges not given in return.

history-asia.l21.q1.h: He believed he was the younger brother of Jesus.
history-asia.l21.q1.e: Hong Xiuquan founded the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom.

history-asia.l21.q2.p: The Taiping captured Nanjing in 1853 and made it their capital.
history-asia.l21.q2.e: They took Nanjing in 1853 and ruled from there until 1864.

history-asia.l21.q3.p: Which official led a regional army that helped defeat the Taiping?
history-asia.l21.q3.h: He was loyal to the Qing.
history-asia.l21.q3.e: Zeng Guofan led regional armies that helped retake Nanjing.

history-asia.l21.q4.p: Estimates of Taiping deaths are precise and agreed on.
history-asia.l21.q4.h: The lesson says records are poor.
history-asia.l21.q4.e: Records are poor, so estimates vary widely, from around twenty million upward.

history-asia.l21.q5.t: The imperial system, when Puyi abdicated
history-asia.l21.q5.h: The revolution began at Wuchang in 1911.
history-asia.l21.q5.e: Puyi's abdication ended over two thousand years of imperial rule.

history-asia.l22.q1.t: The return of direct rule in the emperor's name and the end of the shogunate
history-asia.l22.q1.p: What was the Meiji Restoration of 1868?
history-asia.l22.q1.e: In 1868 the shogunate was overthrown and government restored in the Meiji emperor's name.

history-asia.l22.q2.p: The Meiji government introduced conscription of commoners in 1873.
history-asia.l22.q2.h: It ended the samurai monopoly on arms.
history-asia.l22.q2.e: A conscript army replaced the old samurai class as the basis of the military.

history-asia.l22.q3.p: What did Japan gain from the Sino-Japanese War of 1894 to 1895?

history-asia.l22.q4.p: The Meiji Constitution of 1889 gave all power to an elected Diet and none to the emperor.
history-asia.l22.q4.h: The emperor and military kept great authority.
history-asia.l22.q4.e: It created an elected lower house but left great authority with the emperor and military.

history-asia.l22.q5.t: Rapid change that benefited some groups and harmed others, and led toward imperial expansion
history-asia.l22.q5.p: How is Meiji modernization best described?
history-asia.l22.q5.e: Modernization strengthened the state but caused hardship, and Japan's empire harmed subject peoples such as Koreans.

history-asia.l23.q1.t: The Crown took direct control of India from the East India Company
history-asia.l23.q1.e: After the 1857 uprising Parliament ended Company rule, beginning the Raj.

history-asia.l23.q2.p: The Indian National Congress was founded in 1885.
history-asia.l23.q2.h: It started as a reform-seeking body.
history-asia.l23.q2.e: Congress was founded in 1885 and later became the leading nationalist party.

history-asia.l23.q3.t: Different groups interpret its causes and meaning differently
history-asia.l23.q3.p: Why do historians describe the 1857 uprising with different names?
history-asia.l23.q3.e: British sources called it a mutiny, while many Indians call it a first war of independence.

history-asia.l23.q4.p: Historians agree that British rule affected the Indian economy in exactly one way.
history-asia.l23.q4.h: The lesson says effects are debated.
history-asia.l23.q4.e: Economic effects are debated, with arguments about drain of wealth, trade, and industry.

history-asia.l23.q5.t: A real technological change that was also built to serve imperial and commercial interests
history-asia.l23.q5.p: What does the example of the railway show?
history-asia.l23.q5.h: Consider who the railways were built for.
history-asia.l23.q5.e: Infrastructure had real benefits but its design reflected colonial priorities.

history-asia.l24.q1.p: What did Gandhi's Salt March of 1930 protest?
history-asia.l24.q1.h: It was a march to the sea.
history-asia.l24.q1.e: The march challenged the British salt monopoly through nonviolent action.

history-asia.l24.q2.p: India and Pakistan became independent in August 1947.
history-asia.l24.q2.e: Pakistan became independent on 14 August and India on 15 August 1947.

history-asia.l24.q3.p: Who led the Muslim League in the 1940s?
history-asia.l24.q3.h: He is associated with the demand for Pakistan.
history-asia.l24.q3.e: Jinnah led the League in demanding separate Muslim-majority states.

history-asia.l24.q4.p: Exact numbers of Partition deaths are known with certainty.
history-asia.l24.q4.e: Estimates range from several hundred thousand to about two million.

history-asia.l24.q5.t: It split provinces like Punjab and Bengal and left millions on the wrong side of the line
history-asia.l24.q5.p: Why was the Radcliffe boundary so painful for ordinary people?
history-asia.l24.q5.e: Borders drawn quickly through mixed communities caused mass migration and violence.

history-asia.l25.q1.p: What did Japan set up in Manchuria in 1932?
history-asia.l25.q1.h: The state was controlled by Japan.
history-asia.l25.q1.e: Japan created Manchukuo as a puppet state after seizing Manchuria.

history-asia.l25.q2.p: Atomic bombs were dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945.
history-asia.l25.q2.e: Hiroshima was bombed on 6 August and Nagasaki on 9 August 1945.

history-asia.l25.q3.t: The events are firmly documented, though the number of dead is debated
history-asia.l25.q3.p: Which statement about the Nanjing atrocities is accurate?
history-asia.l25.q3.e: Historians agree the massacre occurred, while estimates of the death toll vary.

history-asia.l25.q4.p: Japan's occupation of Southeast Asia was uniformly welcomed.
history-asia.l25.q4.h: Many people came to resent it.
history-asia.l25.q4.e: Some initially welcomed Japan's challenge to colonial rule, but the occupation was often harsh and resented.

history-asia.l25.q5.t: Memory and responsibility remain contested, with different national experiences
history-asia.l25.q5.p: Why do different countries' school histories of the war sometimes differ?
history-asia.l25.q5.e: Differences in national experience and politics keep the memory of the war contested.

history-asia.l26.q1.p: When was the People's Republic of China proclaimed?
history-asia.l26.q1.h: Mao proclaimed it after the civil war.
history-asia.l26.q1.e: Mao proclaimed the PRC on 1 October 1949.

history-asia.l26.q2.p: Chiang Kai-shek's government withdrew to Taiwan after the communist victory.
history-asia.l26.q2.e: Chiang's Nationalist government moved to Taiwan in 1949.

history-asia.l26.q3.t: A retreat by communist forces in 1934 to 1935
history-asia.l26.q3.h: Mao emerged as leader during it.
history-asia.l26.q3.e: The Long March was a communist retreat during which Mao rose to leadership.

history-asia.l26.q4.p: Scholars agree on the exact number of deaths in the Great Leap Forward famine.
history-asia.l26.q4.e: Estimates range from around fifteen million to over forty million.

history-asia.l26.q5.t: Economic reforms opening China to markets and foreign trade
history-asia.l26.q5.p: What did Deng Xiaoping begin in 1978?
history-asia.l26.q5.e: Deng's reforms started China's market-oriented growth.

history-asia.l27.q1.p: Near which line was Korea divided after 1945?
history-asia.l27.q1.h: It is a line of latitude.
history-asia.l27.q1.e: Korea was divided near the 38th parallel by Soviet and US occupation zones.

history-asia.l27.q2.p: The Korean War ended with a formal peace treaty in 1953.
history-asia.l27.q2.e: An armistice was signed on 27 July 1953, but no peace treaty has been concluded.

history-asia.l27.q3.t: China entered the war and pushed UN forces back
history-asia.l27.q3.e: China entered the war and forced UN forces to retreat.

history-asia.l27.q4.p: North Korean forces invaded the south on 25 June 1950.
history-asia.l27.q4.h: That is the date the war began.
history-asia.l27.q4.e: The war began with the North Korean invasion on 25 June 1950.

history-asia.l27.q5.t: It began between two Korean governments and then drew in foreign powers
history-asia.l27.q5.p: Why do historians call the Korean War both a civil war and an international war?
history-asia.l27.q5.h: Consider who fought first and who joined.
history-asia.l27.q5.e: It began as a conflict between rival Korean governments and then involved the US, UN allies, China and the USSR.

history-asia.l28.q1.p: Who declared Vietnamese independence on 2 September 1945?
history-asia.l28.q1.e: Ho Chi Minh declared independence in Hanoi.

history-asia.l28.q2.p: The French were defeated at Dien Bien Phu in 1954.
history-asia.l28.q2.h: This ended the First Indochina War.
history-asia.l28.q2.e: The Vietnamese victory at Dien Bien Phu led to the Geneva settlement.

history-asia.l28.q3.t: Divided Vietnam temporarily at the 17th parallel
history-asia.l28.q3.p: What did the Geneva settlement of 1954 do?
history-asia.l28.q3.h: The division was meant to be temporary.
history-asia.l28.q3.e: Vietnam was divided at the 17th parallel pending elections that were never held.

history-asia.l28.q4.p: The Tet Offensive of 1968 was a clear military victory for the communist forces.
history-asia.l28.q4.h: Recall its costs and its political effect.
history-asia.l28.q4.e: It was militarily costly for them but politically shook US confidence.

history-asia.l28.q5.e: Saigon fell on 30 April 1975, and the country was reunified the following year.

history-asia.l29.q1.p: Which country declared independence on 17 August 1945 and fought the Dutch until 1949?
history-asia.l29.q1.e: Indonesia declared independence in 1945, and the Dutch recognised it in 1949.

history-asia.l29.q2.p: The Bandung Conference of 1955 brought together Asian and African countries.
history-asia.l29.q2.e: Leaders of 29 countries met to promote cooperation and oppose colonialism.

history-asia.l29.q3.t: A communist insurgency fought from 1948 to 1960 in British Malaya
history-asia.l29.q3.h: It happened as Britain prepared to leave.
history-asia.l29.q3.e: It was an insurgency fought while Britain prepared Malaya for independence.

history-asia.l29.q4.p: All Asian colonies became independent in the same way.
history-asia.l29.q4.h: Think of the Philippines versus Indonesia.
history-asia.l29.q4.e: Some were handed over by negotiation and others won independence through war.

history-asia.l29.q5.t: Japan's conquests showed colonial powers could be defeated and Europe was weakened
history-asia.l29.q5.p: Why did the Second World War help decolonisation?
history-asia.l29.q5.h: Consider the effect on European prestige.
history-asia.l29.q5.e: Wartime defeats and exhaustion weakened colonial authority, and nationalists pressed their claims.

history-asia.l30.q1.t: South Korea, Taiwan, Hong Kong and Singapore
history-asia.l30.q1.p: Which group of economies is often called the Four Tigers?
history-asia.l30.q1.e: The Four Tigers are South Korea, Taiwan, Hong Kong and Singapore.

history-asia.l30.q2.p: Shenzhen was one of China's special economic zones begun around 1980.
history-asia.l30.q2.e: Shenzhen became a leading special economic zone after 1980.

history-asia.l30.q3.t: They were hit by a financial crisis
history-asia.l30.q3.p: What happened to the Thai, Indonesian and South Korean economies in 1997?
history-asia.l30.q3.e: The 1997 Asian financial crisis exposed weaknesses in financial oversight.

history-asia.l30.q4.p: Economists agree that state guidance alone explains the Tigers' growth.
history-asia.l30.q4.h: The lesson says economists debate it.
history-asia.l30.q4.e: Economists debate the relative roles of state direction and open markets.

history-asia.l30.q5.t: Hundreds of millions escaped extreme poverty, while inequality and pollution also rose
history-asia.l30.q5.p: Which statement fairly balances China's growth since 1978?
history-asia.l30.q5.e: The reforms lifted many from poverty but also created new inequalities and environmental problems.

history-asia.l31.q1.p: Which two countries have the largest populations in Asia?
history-asia.l31.q1.e: China and India are the two most populous countries.

history-asia.l31.q2.h: It is a Southeast Asian group.
history-asia.l31.q2.e: ASEAN was founded in 1967 by five countries and has since grown.

history-asia.l31.q3.p: What arrangement was used when Hong Kong returned to China in 1997?
history-asia.l31.q3.e: Hong Kong returned under the "one country, two systems" framework, whose meaning has been debated.

history-asia.l31.q4.p: Asian countries all share the same political system.
history-asia.l31.q4.e: Political systems range from democracies to one-party states.

history-asia.l31.q5.t: Events change quickly, so recent facts may be out of date
history-asia.l31.q5.p: Why does the lesson advise checking current details?
history-asia.l31.q5.h: Think about how fast news moves.
history-asia.l31.q5.e: Contemporary facts shift, so historians and readers must verify recent information.

history-asia.l32.q1.t: A source from the time being studied
history-asia.l32.q1.h: It is close to the events.
history-asia.l32.q1.e: Primary sources, such as inscriptions, letters and treaties, come from the period studied.

history-asia.l32.q2.p: "The Silk Road" is a nineteenth-century name for a network of many routes.
history-asia.l32.q2.e: The label was coined in the nineteenth century and covers a web of routes, not a single road.

history-asia.l32.q3.t: European portrayals of the East were often shaped by, and served, colonial power
history-asia.l32.q3.p: What did Edward Said argue in Orientalism (1978)?
history-asia.l32.q3.h: He examined outsiders' images of the East.
history-asia.l32.q3.e: Said argued that Western images of the East often reflected and supported colonial power; his argument has been debated and refined since.

history-asia.l32.q4.p: National histories written inside a country are always completely neutral.
history-asia.l32.q4.e: Such histories can serve goals like pride or unity and may omit painful or minority perspectives.

history-asia.l32.q5.t: Compare accounts from different sides and note what each selects and how it frames causes
history-asia.l32.q5.p: What is a good method for studying a disputed event such as the Opium Wars?
history-asia.l32.q5.e: Comparing sources from several viewpoints gives a fuller and more reliable picture.

history-europe.l01.q1.p: Linear B, the script of the Mycenaean palaces, turned out to record an early form of Greek.
history-europe.l01.q1.h: Think about what Michael Ventris showed in 1952.
history-europe.l01.q1.e: Ventris demonstrated that Linear B writes Greek, proving the language was written in the second millennium BCE.

history-europe.l01.q2.p: Which Bronze Age civilisation is centred on palace sites such as Knossos on Crete?
history-europe.l01.q2.h: The name comes from a legendary king of Crete.
history-europe.l01.q2.e: Knossos was the best-known palace centre of the Minoans on Crete.

history-europe.l01.q3.t: Administrative accounts such as inventories of goods and workers
history-europe.l01.q3.p: What do most surviving Linear B tablets contain?
history-europe.l01.q3.h: Think about what palace bureaucrats needed to record.
history-europe.l01.q3.e: The tablets are mostly records of goods, livestock and workers, showing palace-run economies.

history-europe.l01.q4.t: They were composed long after the Mycenaean age
history-europe.l01.q4.p: Why is it risky to treat Homer's epics as a direct record of Mycenaean society?
history-europe.l01.q4.h: Consider the gap in time between the palaces and the poems.
history-europe.l01.q4.e: The epics took shape centuries after the Bronze Age collapse, so they blend memory, later customs and invention.

history-europe.l01.q5.t: Several causes, such as drought, earthquakes, conflict and disrupted trade, are debated rather than one proven cause
history-europe.l01.q5.p: Which statement best reflects the scholarly view of the Late Bronze Age collapse around 1200 BCE?
history-europe.l01.q5.h: The lesson says historians argue over how much weight each cause deserves.
history-europe.l01.q5.e: The evidence is patchy and scholars debate the mix of causes.

history-europe.l02.q1.p: In classical Athens, women and enslaved people could vote in the assembly.
history-europe.l02.q1.e: Citizenship was limited to adult men born to Athenian citizens; women, enslaved people and foreign residents were excluded.

history-europe.l02.q2.p: Who won the Peloponnesian War, fought from 431 to 404 BCE?
history-europe.l02.q2.h: Think about which city was defeated after a long conflict.
history-europe.l02.q2.e: Athens was defeated by Sparta and its allies in 404 BCE.

history-europe.l02.q3.t: A city-state with its surrounding land
history-europe.l02.q3.p: What does the word polis refer to?
history-europe.l02.q3.h: It is the basic unit of Greek political life.
history-europe.l02.q3.e: A polis was a city-state, and hundreds existed with their own laws.

history-europe.l02.q4.p: Which battle in 480 BCE helped the Greeks defeat the Persian fleet?
history-europe.l02.q4.h: It was a naval victory, a decade after Marathon.
history-europe.l02.q4.e: The Greek fleet won at Salamis in 480 BCE, which was followed by victory at Plataea in 479 BCE.

history-europe.l02.q5.p: Alexander the Great's empire stayed unified under a single ruler for centuries after his death in 323 BCE.
history-europe.l02.q5.h: Think about what his generals did.
history-europe.l02.q5.e: His generals divided the realm into separate Hellenistic kingdoms.

history-europe.l03.q1.p: Roman consuls were elected for a single year, and two served at the same time.
history-europe.l03.q1.h: The system was designed so that no one man ruled alone.
history-europe.l03.q1.e: Two consuls held office for one year, sharing power.

history-europe.l03.q2.p: Which general crossed the Alps with an army to attack Rome during the Second Punic War?
history-europe.l03.q2.e: Hannibal of Carthage crossed the Alps and won at Cannae in 216 BCE.

history-europe.l03.q3.t: Protecting ordinary citizens from the actions of aristocratic magistrates
history-europe.l03.q3.p: What was the main job of the tribunes of the plebs?
history-europe.l03.q3.h: The office arose from conflict between plebeians and patricians.
history-europe.l03.q3.e: Tribunes were created to defend plebeians against the power of aristocratic officials.

history-europe.l03.q4.t: Armies became loyal to ambitious generals, and wealth and land became concentrated
history-europe.l03.q4.p: Why did Roman success in conquest strain the Republic, according to the lesson?
history-europe.l03.q4.h: Think about whom soldiers were loyal to.
history-europe.l03.q4.e: Conquest enriched a few, displaced small farmers, and made generals more powerful than the institutions meant to control them.

history-europe.l03.q5.p: The date 509 BCE for the founding of the Republic is a traditional date, not a certain one.
history-europe.l03.q5.h: The lesson says the date comes from Roman tradition.
history-europe.l03.q5.e: Roman accounts of the expulsion of the kings were written much later, so the exact date is traditional.

history-europe.l04.q1.p: Julius Caesar was assassinated by a group of senators in 44 BCE.
history-europe.l04.q1.h: It happened on the Ides of March.
history-europe.l04.q1.e: A group of senators killed Caesar on 15 March 44 BCE.

history-europe.l04.q2.p: Which title did the Senate give to Octavian in 27 BCE?
history-europe.l04.q2.h: It became the name by which he is best known.
history-europe.l04.q2.e: Octavian received the title Augustus in 27 BCE, marking the start of the principate.

history-europe.l04.q3.t: A period of relative stability inside the empire, roughly 27 BCE to 180 CE
history-europe.l04.q3.p: What does the term Pax Romana describe?
history-europe.l04.q3.h: The lesson says it does not mean peace for everyone.
history-europe.l04.q3.e: The Pax Romana was a long period of relative internal stability, although Rome still conquered, fought and used slavery.

history-europe.l04.q4.t: Extended citizenship to nearly all free inhabitants of the empire
history-europe.l04.q4.p: What did the emperor Caracalla do in 212 CE?
history-europe.l04.q4.h: It widened who counted as a Roman.
history-europe.l04.q4.e: Caracalla's edict gave citizenship to almost all free people in the empire.

history-europe.l04.q5.t: Whether he restored the Republic or ended it while keeping its forms
history-europe.l04.q5.p: Which statement best captures the historical debate about Augustus?
history-europe.l04.q5.h: The question concerns what his system really was.
history-europe.l04.q5.e: He kept republican offices but held real power, so historians argue about how to describe the system.

history-europe.l05.q1.p: The Edict of Milan in 313 CE granted toleration to Christians in the Roman Empire.
history-europe.l05.q1.e: The Edict of Milan ended official persecution and granted toleration to Christians.

history-europe.l05.q2.p: Which general removed the last western emperor, Romulus Augustulus, in 476?
history-europe.l05.q2.h: He is the one traditionally credited with ending the western empire.
history-europe.l05.q2.e: Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus in 476, the conventional end date of the western empire.

history-europe.l05.q3.p: Which city did Constantine dedicate as a new eastern capital in 330?
history-europe.l05.q3.e: Constantinople was dedicated in 330 and later became the capital of the eastern empire.

history-europe.l05.q4.t: The Visigoth leader Alaric sacked the city of Rome
history-europe.l05.q4.h: It shocked people across the empire.
history-europe.l05.q4.e: Alaric's sack of Rome in 410 was a psychological blow to the Roman world.

history-europe.l05.q5.t: As a gradual transformation influenced by several pressures
history-europe.l05.q5.p: How do many modern historians prefer to describe the end of Roman rule in the west?
history-europe.l05.q5.h: The lesson contrasts Gibbon's view with newer views.
history-europe.l05.q5.e: Many historians stress gradual change shaped by military pressure, civil wars and economic problems.

history-europe.l06.q1.p: The people of the eastern Roman Empire usually called themselves Romans.
history-europe.l06.q1.e: The term Byzantine was applied by later writers; the people considered themselves Romans.

history-europe.l06.q2.p: Which emperor oversaw the compilation of the Corpus Juris Civilis and the building of Hagia Sophia?
history-europe.l06.q2.e: Justinian had Roman law gathered and organised and built Hagia Sophia, completed in 537.

history-europe.l06.q3.p: What was the dispute known as iconoclasm about?
history-europe.l06.q3.h: The word refers to breaking images.
history-europe.l06.q3.e: Iconoclasm was a conflict over religious images, ending with their restoration in 843.

history-europe.l06.q4.p: In which year did the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II capture Constantinople?
history-europe.l06.q4.h: It marks the end of the Byzantine Empire.
history-europe.l06.q4.e: The fall of Constantinople in 1453 ended the Byzantine Empire.

history-europe.l06.q5.p: The Fourth Crusade sacked the Christian city of Constantinople in 1204.
history-europe.l06.q5.h: A crusade turned on a Christian capital.
history-europe.l06.q5.e: In 1204, Crusaders sacked Constantinople, which weakened the empire and deepened the split between eastern and western churches.

history-europe.l07.q1.p: Charlemagne was crowned emperor by Pope Leo III on Christmas Day in the year 800.
history-europe.l07.q1.e: Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne in Rome on 25 December 800.

history-europe.l07.q2.h: Their kingdom became the core of later France.
history-europe.l07.q2.e: Clovis was a Frankish king who converted to Catholic Christianity around 500.

history-europe.l07.q3.t: They copied manuscripts, ran schools and farms, and kept literacy alive
history-europe.l07.q3.p: Why were monasteries important in the early Middle Ages?
history-europe.l07.q3.h: Think about who could read and write in this period.
history-europe.l07.q3.e: Monks preserved texts and learning when literacy was rare.

history-europe.l07.q4.t: Divided Charlemagne's empire among his grandsons
history-europe.l07.q4.p: What did the Treaty of Verdun in 843 do?
history-europe.l07.q4.h: It concerned the empire after Charlemagne.
history-europe.l07.q4.e: The treaty divided the Carolingian empire into western, eastern and middle parts.

history-europe.l07.q5.h: Recall his campaign against the Saxons.
history-europe.l07.q5.e: His wars, including the campaign against the Saxons, were brutal.

history-europe.l08.q1.p: The invading army that crossed into Iberia in 711 was led by Tariq ibn Ziyad.
history-europe.l08.q1.h: Look at the start of the lesson.
history-europe.l08.q1.e: Tariq ibn Ziyad led the force that defeated the Visigothic king Roderic.

history-europe.l08.q2.p: Which city became the capital of the Umayyad emirate and later caliphate in Iberia?
history-europe.l08.q2.h: It had a great mosque and large libraries.
history-europe.l08.q2.e: Abd al-Rahman I made Córdoba the centre of the Umayyad emirate in 756.

history-europe.l08.q3.t: A period of coexistence among Muslims, Christians and Jews, a term historians debate
history-europe.l08.q3.e: Some historians use the term for coexistence, while others stress persecution and inequality.

history-europe.l08.q4.t: Granada, the last Muslim state, fell
history-europe.l08.q4.h: It is also the year of Columbus's first voyage.
history-europe.l08.q4.e: Granada fell in 1492, ending Muslim political rule in the peninsula.

history-europe.l08.q5.t: It frames the process as retaking land that was seen as rightfully Christian
history-europe.l08.q5.p: Why is the word Reconquista described as reflecting a Christian viewpoint?
history-europe.l08.q5.h: Think about who named the process and why.
history-europe.l08.q5.e: The term presents the northern kingdoms' expansion as recovery of lost land, a perspective not shared by all.

history-europe.l09.q1.p: Archaeology at L'Anse aux Meadows shows that Norse people reached North America around the year 1000.
history-europe.l09.q1.e: L'Anse aux Meadows is a Norse site that confirms contact centuries before Columbus.

history-europe.l09.q2.p: Which monastery raid in 793 is traditionally taken as the start of the Viking Age?
history-europe.l09.q2.h: It is on an island off northeast England.
history-europe.l09.q2.e: The raid on Lindisfarne shocked contemporaries.

history-europe.l09.q3.t: Descendants of Vikings granted land in northern France
history-europe.l09.q3.e: Rollo's group received land around 911 and their descendants became the Normans.

history-europe.l09.q4.t: They were written down long after the events, by Christians looking back
history-europe.l09.q4.p: Why should historians be cautious when using the Icelandic sagas as evidence?
history-europe.l09.q4.h: Consider when they were written compared with the events.
history-europe.l09.q4.e: The sagas date mostly from the thirteenth century and reflect later perspectives.

history-europe.l09.q5.t: Raiders, but also traders, settlers and mercenaries
history-europe.l09.q5.p: Which description of Vikings best matches the lesson?
history-europe.l09.q5.h: The lesson says they did more than raid.
history-europe.l09.q5.e: Vikings raided and enslaved people but also traded, settled and fought as mercenaries.

history-europe.l10.q1.p: Most medieval Europeans were peasants, many of them serfs.
history-europe.l10.q1.h: Think about how most people made a living.
history-europe.l10.q1.e: The great majority worked the land, and many were serfs obliged to a lord.

history-europe.l10.q2.t: Land held from a lord in return for service and loyalty
history-europe.l10.q2.h: It was the basis of the lord and vassal bond.
history-europe.l10.q2.e: A fief was land granted by a superior in exchange for military service and loyalty.

history-europe.l10.q3.t: Whether kings or popes had the right to appoint bishops
history-europe.l10.q3.p: What was the Investiture Controversy about?
history-europe.l10.q3.h: It involved Gregory VII and Henry IV.
history-europe.l10.q3.e: Rulers and popes quarrelled over the appointment of bishops, and the Concordat of Worms in 1122 largely settled it.

history-europe.l10.q4.p: Some historians argue that the neat pyramid of king, lords and vassals oversimplifies how medieval society worked.
history-europe.l10.q4.h: The lesson says to treat the term with care.
history-europe.l10.q4.e: Practices varied widely, so feudalism is better seen as a convenient label than a single system.

history-europe.l10.q5.t: A survey of landholding in England after the Norman conquest
history-europe.l10.q5.p: What was the Domesday Book, compiled in 1086?
history-europe.l10.q5.h: It followed the Battle of Hastings.
history-europe.l10.q5.e: William's officials surveyed England's land and its holders, showing how the Normans organised land and loyalty.

history-europe.l11.q1.p: The First Crusade captured Jerusalem in 1099.
history-europe.l11.q1.h: It was the main goal of the campaign.
history-europe.l11.q1.e: Crusaders took Jerusalem in July 1099 and massacred many of its inhabitants.

history-europe.l11.q2.p: Who preached at the Council of Clermont in 1095, calling for an armed pilgrimage?
history-europe.l11.q2.h: He was the head of the western Church.
history-europe.l11.q2.e: Pope Urban II launched the First Crusade after the Byzantine emperor asked for help.

history-europe.l11.q3.p: Which Muslim leader retook Jerusalem in 1187?
history-europe.l11.q3.h: He had united Egypt and Syria.

history-europe.l11.q4.t: It sacked the Christian city of Constantinople in 1204
history-europe.l11.q4.p: What was unusual about the Fourth Crusade?
history-europe.l11.q4.h: Think about whose city was attacked.
history-europe.l11.q4.e: The Fourth Crusade turned on Constantinople, deepening divisions between eastern and western Christians.

history-europe.l11.q5.t: They were mixed, including religious devotion, hopes of land and wealth, and loyalty to lords
history-europe.l11.q5.p: Which statement fits the lesson's description of crusader motives?
history-europe.l11.q5.h: The lesson says historians debate the mix.
history-europe.l11.q5.e: Historians continue to debate how far religion, economics and politics drove the crusades.

history-europe.l12.q1.p: The Black Death is linked by ancient DNA evidence to the bacterium Yersinia pestis.
history-europe.l12.q1.e: Ancient DNA from victims confirmed the bacterium as the cause.

history-europe.l12.q2.p: Roughly how much of Europe's population do many historians think was lost?
history-europe.l12.q2.h: The lesson calls the figure uncertain because records are patchy.
history-europe.l12.q2.e: Mortality varied by place, but many estimates are around a third or more of the population.

history-europe.l12.q3.t: Labour became scarce because so many workers had died
history-europe.l12.q3.p: Why did wages tend to rise after the Black Death?
history-europe.l12.q3.h: Think of supply and demand for workers.
history-europe.l12.q3.e: With fewer workers, labour was in demand, and some lords struggled to keep serfs on the land.

history-europe.l12.q4.p: What false accusation led to massacres of Jewish communities in 1348 and 1349?
history-europe.l12.q4.e: Rumours about well poisoning led to massacres, even though Jewish communities also suffered from plague.

history-europe.l12.q5.p: The Statute of Labourers of 1351 was an English attempt to hold wages down.
history-europe.l12.q5.h: The government reacted to labour shortages.
history-europe.l12.q5.e: The statute tried to freeze wages, and tensions over such measures contributed to the Peasants' Revolt of 1381.

history-europe.l13.q1.p: Magna Carta was sealed by King John in 1215.
history-europe.l13.q1.e: A group of barons forced John to seal it in 1215.

history-europe.l13.q2.p: Which war lasted from 1337 to 1453 between the English and French crowns?
history-europe.l13.q2.h: The name gives a clue about duration.
history-europe.l13.q2.e: The conflict, with pauses, lasted 116 years.

history-europe.l13.q3.t: That the king was himself subject to law
history-europe.l13.q3.p: What idea does Magna Carta set down that became important later?
history-europe.l13.q3.h: It was a deal between the king and his barons.
history-europe.l13.q3.e: Although practical in aim, it expressed the idea that rulers must obey the law.

history-europe.l13.q4.t: Helped relieve the siege of Orléans
history-europe.l13.q4.p: What did Joan of Arc do in 1429?
history-europe.l13.q4.h: She was a young peasant woman.
history-europe.l13.q4.e: She helped relieve Orléans in 1429, and she was burned after a trial in 1431.

history-europe.l13.q5.t: As bodies for clergy, nobles and townspeople, not democracies
history-europe.l13.q5.p: How should the late medieval representative assemblies be described?
history-europe.l13.q5.e: They gave elites a voice in taxation but did not include ordinary peasants.

history-europe.l14.q1.p: The Renaissance began in Italian city-states such as Florence.
history-europe.l14.q1.e: The movement started in Italy in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries.

history-europe.l14.q2.p: Who developed a European printing system using movable metal type around 1450 in Mainz?
history-europe.l14.q2.e: Gutenberg is credited with developing the European system of movable metal type.

history-europe.l14.q3.t: Woodblock printing and early movable type existed there already
history-europe.l14.q3.p: What does the lesson say about printing in East Asia?
history-europe.l14.q3.h: Gutenberg's was a European invention, not the first anywhere.
history-europe.l14.q3.e: East Asia had woodblock printing and early movable type before Gutenberg.

history-europe.l14.q4.t: A scholar who studied classical texts and stressed education and human potential
history-europe.l14.q4.p: What is a humanist, in this lesson's sense?
history-europe.l14.q4.e: Humanists revived Latin and Greek learning while mostly remaining religious.

history-europe.l14.q5.p: Historians agree that the Renaissance was a sudden break with a uniformly dark Middle Ages.
history-europe.l14.q5.h: The lesson calls this an exaggeration.
history-europe.l14.q5.e: Many ideas and techniques developed earlier, and scholars still debate how sharply the Renaissance differs from the period before.

history-europe.l15.q1.p: Martin Luther's Ninety-Five Theses criticised the sale of indulgences.
history-europe.l15.q1.h: Think about what started the Reformation in 1517.
history-europe.l15.q1.e: The theses attacked indulgences and circulated widely thanks to printing.

history-europe.l15.q2.p: Which English king broke with Rome in the 1530s and became head of the English church?
history-europe.l15.q2.h: The Act of Supremacy was passed in 1534.
history-europe.l15.q2.e: Henry VIII made himself head of the English church, partly because the pope would not annul his marriage.

history-europe.l15.q3.t: German rulers to choose Lutheranism or Catholicism for their territories
history-europe.l15.q3.p: What did the Peace of Augsburg of 1555 allow?
history-europe.l15.q3.h: It was a compromise within the Holy Roman Empire.
history-europe.l15.q3.e: It let rulers decide between the two faiths for their lands.

history-europe.l15.q4.t: It carried reformers' ideas quickly across Germany and beyond
history-europe.l15.q4.p: How did printing affect the Reformation?
history-europe.l15.q4.h: Think about the speed of spreading ideas.
history-europe.l15.q4.e: Printed pamphlets and Bibles spread reform ideas widely.

history-europe.l15.q5.p: Historians are certain that Luther nailed the Ninety-Five Theses to a church door.
history-europe.l15.q5.h: The lesson says whether he did is debated.
history-europe.l15.q5.e: The story is traditional, but historians debate it; what is certain is that the theses circulated.

history-europe.l16.q1.p: The Edict of Nantes of 1598 gave Huguenots limited rights in France.
history-europe.l16.q1.h: Henry IV issued it to end the French Wars of Religion.
history-europe.l16.q1.e: It granted limited toleration and was revoked by Louis XIV in 1685.

history-europe.l16.q2.t: Protestant nobles in Prague threw royal officials from a window
history-europe.l16.q2.p: Which event in 1618 began the Thirty Years' War?
history-europe.l16.q2.e: The Defenestration of Prague began a conflict that spread across Europe.

history-europe.l16.q3.p: Which treaty ended the Thirty Years' War in 1648?
history-europe.l16.q3.h: It is named for a region in Germany.
history-europe.l16.q3.e: The Peace of Westphalia ended the war and added Calvinism to the permitted faiths.

history-europe.l16.q4.t: It is often seen as an early step toward a system of sovereign states, though historians question how much it created that system
history-europe.l16.q4.p: Which statement about the Peace of Westphalia is most accurate?
history-europe.l16.q4.h: The lesson hedges how much it invented sovereignty.
history-europe.l16.q4.e: Historians now question the idea that Westphalia alone created the modern state system.

history-europe.l16.q5.p: The Dutch Republic that emerged from rebellion against Spain tolerated more religious diversity than most states of the time.
history-europe.l16.q5.h: Calvinism was favoured, but other groups were present.
history-europe.l16.q5.e: Calvinism was favoured, yet the Republic was more tolerant than many contemporaries.

history-europe.l17.q1.p: Vasco da Gama reached India by sea in 1498.
history-europe.l17.q1.e: Da Gama's voyage opened a sea route from Europe to India.

history-europe.l17.q2.t: The transfer of plants, animals and diseases between the hemispheres
history-europe.l17.q2.h: It involved potatoes, horses and more.
history-europe.l17.q2.e: Species and diseases crossed the Atlantic in both directions after 1492.

history-europe.l17.q3.t: Divided newly claimed lands outside Europe between Spain and Portugal
history-europe.l17.q3.p: What did the Treaty of Tordesillas of 1494 do?
history-europe.l17.q3.h: It ignored the people who lived in those lands.
history-europe.l17.q3.e: Spain and Portugal divided claims without regard to local inhabitants.

history-europe.l17.q4.p: Which factor killed the largest number of Indigenous people in the Americas after contact?
history-europe.l17.q4.h: Indigenous people had little immunity to these illnesses.
history-europe.l17.q4.e: Epidemics, alongside forced labour and violence, devastated Indigenous populations.

history-europe.l17.q5.t: Well over ten million Africans were shipped across the Atlantic, and the profits shaped European ports and banks
history-europe.l17.q5.p: Which summary of the Atlantic slave trade best fits the lesson?
history-europe.l17.q5.h: The lesson gives a minimum scale.
history-europe.l17.q5.e: The trade lasted centuries, with huge human cost and large economic effects in Europe.

history-europe.l18.q1.p: Copernicus proposed in 1543 that the Earth and other planets orbit the Sun.
history-europe.l18.q1.h: It is called the heliocentric model.
history-europe.l18.q1.e: His book set out a Sun-centred model of the planets.

history-europe.l18.q2.p: Which scientist published the Principia in 1687 setting out laws of motion and universal gravitation?
