lab-architecture.l14.q2.p: A cantilever has a tip point load P and length L. What is its maximum moment?
lab-architecture.l14.q2.h: It occurs at the fixed support.
lab-architecture.l14.q2.e: Maximum moment is PL, at the fixed end.

lab-architecture.l14.q3.p: A simply supported beam spans 4 m with a uniform load of 8 kN/m. What is the maximum moment (wL squared over 8)?

lab-architecture.l14.q4.p: If the span of a uniformly loaded simply supported beam doubles, what happens to the maximum moment?
lab-architecture.l14.q4.h: The span is squared in the formula.
lab-architecture.l14.q4.e: Because M = wL squared over 8, doubling L multiplies the moment by four.

lab-astronomy.l01.q1.p: Who published a Sun-centred model of the solar system in 1543?
lab-astronomy.l01.q1.e: Copernicus placed the Sun, not the Earth, at the centre.

lab-astronomy.l01.q2.p: What did Galileo discover orbiting Jupiter in 1610?
lab-astronomy.l01.q2.h: They showed that not everything orbits the Earth.
lab-astronomy.l01.q2.e: The four large moons of Jupiter were evidence that some bodies orbit something other than Earth.

lab-astronomy.l01.q3.t: They were the most precise naked-eye positions available, which allowed Kepler to detect elliptical orbits
lab-astronomy.l01.q3.p: Why were Tycho Brahe's observations so important for Kepler?
lab-astronomy.l01.q3.h: Think about accuracy and quantity of data.
lab-astronomy.l01.q3.e: Tycho's accurate long-term data on Mars let Kepler show that circles did not fit but ellipses did.

lab-astronomy.l01.q4.t: It showed Venus orbits the Sun, which is incompatible with a simple Earth-centred arrangement
lab-astronomy.l01.q4.p: Galileo observed the phases of Venus. Why did this support a Sun-centred model?
lab-astronomy.l01.q4.h: Phases depend on the geometry of Sun, planet and observer.
lab-astronomy.l01.q4.e: Venus shows a full set of phases, consistent with orbiting the Sun rather than circling the Earth.

lab-astronomy.l02.q1.t: Ellipses with the Sun at one focus
lab-astronomy.l02.q1.p: What shape are planetary orbits according to Kepler's first law?
lab-astronomy.l02.q1.e: Each planet moves along an ellipse with the Sun at one focus.

lab-astronomy.l02.q2.t: When it is closest to the Sun
lab-astronomy.l02.q2.p: According to Kepler's second law, when does a planet move fastest?
lab-astronomy.l02.q2.e: A shorter radius sweeps a given area with a longer arc, so the planet moves faster near the Sun.

lab-astronomy.l02.q3.p: An object orbits the Sun with a semi-major axis of 9 AU. Using T squared = a cubed (years and AU), what is its period?
lab-astronomy.l02.q3.h: Cube 9 first, then take the square root.
lab-astronomy.l02.q3.e: 9 cubed is 729, and the square root of 729 is 27, so T = 27 years.

lab-astronomy.l02.q4.t: The period and orbit size of a moon depend on the planet's mass
lab-astronomy.l02.q4.p: Why can Kepler's third law be used to measure the mass of a planet?
lab-astronomy.l02.q4.h: Look at the central mass M in the full formula.
lab-astronomy.l02.q4.e: In T squared = 4 pi squared a cubed / (G M), the central mass M can be found from a moon's measured T and a.

lab-astronomy.l03.q1.p: How does gravitational force change if the distance between two masses is doubled?
lab-astronomy.l03.q1.e: F is proportional to 1 / r squared, and 2 squared is 4, so the force falls to one quarter.

lab-astronomy.l03.q2.p: About what speed is the escape velocity from Earth's surface?
lab-astronomy.l03.q2.h: A bit over ten kilometres per second.
lab-astronomy.l03.q2.e: Escape velocity from Earth's surface is about 11.2 km/s.

lab-astronomy.l03.q3.p: A spacecraft moves from a distance of 1 unit to 3 units from a planet's centre. By what factor does the gravitational force on it change?
lab-astronomy.l03.q3.h: Square the factor by which the distance changed.
lab-astronomy.l03.q3.e: 3 squared is 9, so the force drops to one ninth.

lab-astronomy.l03.q4.t: They and the station are in continuous free fall around Earth
lab-astronomy.l03.q4.p: Astronauts on the International Space Station float. What is the best explanation?
lab-astronomy.l03.q4.h: Gravity there is still strong, nearly as strong as on the surface.
lab-astronomy.l03.q4.e: Orbiting is falling while moving sideways fast enough to keep missing the Earth, so everything falls together and feels weightless.

lab-astronomy.l04.q1.t: A gas that absorbs light at that specific wavelength
lab-astronomy.l04.q1.p: What does a dark absorption line in a star's spectrum indicate?
lab-astronomy.l04.q1.h: Each element has a pattern of lines.
lab-astronomy.l04.q1.e: Atoms absorb specific wavelengths, so lines reveal what elements are present.

lab-astronomy.l04.q2.p: Which spectral type is the hottest in the sequence O, B, A, F, G, K, M?
lab-astronomy.l04.q2.h: The sequence runs from hottest to coolest.
lab-astronomy.l04.q2.e: The Harvard sequence is ordered by temperature, with O stars hottest and M stars coolest.

lab-astronomy.l04.q3.p: Star X peaks in the blue part of the spectrum, and star Y peaks in the red. Which is hotter?
lab-astronomy.l04.q3.h: Wien's law: peak wavelength shifts inversely with temperature.
lab-astronomy.l04.q3.e: A shorter peak wavelength means a higher temperature, so the blue star is hotter.

lab-astronomy.l04.q4.t: Stars are mostly hydrogen and helium; spectral line differences mainly reflect temperature
lab-astronomy.l04.q4.p: Before Cecilia Payne, many astronomers thought stars were made of the same stuff as Earth. What did she show?
lab-astronomy.l04.q4.h: She applied ionization theory to spectra.
lab-astronomy.l04.q4.e: After accounting for ionization, hydrogen and helium turn out to dominate stars.

lab-astronomy.l05.q1.t: The total energy a star radiates each second
lab-astronomy.l05.q1.h: It is a measure of true power, not apparent brightness.
lab-astronomy.l05.q1.e: Luminosity is the total power output of a star, independent of how far away it is.

lab-astronomy.l05.q2.p: Where do most stars lie on the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram?
lab-astronomy.l05.q2.e: Most stars are fusing hydrogen in their cores and lie along the main sequence.

lab-astronomy.l05.q3.p: Star B has the same radius as star A but twice the surface temperature. How many times more luminous is B?
lab-astronomy.l05.q3.h: Luminosity goes as the fourth power of temperature.

lab-astronomy.l05.q4.t: Its radius is so large that its surface area more than makes up for the lower temperature
lab-astronomy.l05.q4.p: A red giant is cooler than the Sun but much more luminous. How is that possible?
lab-astronomy.l05.q4.h: Luminosity depends on R squared as well as on T to the fourth.
lab-astronomy.l05.q4.e: A vast surface area can outweigh a lower temperature, so a cool giant can radiate a great deal of energy.

lab-astronomy.l06.q1.t: Hydrogen fusion into helium in its core
lab-astronomy.l06.q1.p: What process powers a main-sequence star?
lab-astronomy.l06.q1.e: Main-sequence stars fuse hydrogen into helium, balancing gravity with outward pressure.

lab-astronomy.l06.q2.p: Which property of a star mostly determines its life story?
lab-astronomy.l06.q2.e: Mass sets a star's temperature, lifetime and final fate.

lab-astronomy.l06.q3.p: What is the most likely final state of a star like the Sun?
lab-astronomy.l06.q3.h: It is below about eight solar masses.
lab-astronomy.l06.q3.e: A Sun-like star swells into a red giant, sheds its envelope and leaves a white dwarf.

lab-astronomy.l06.q4.t: They burn their fuel much faster because of higher core pressure and temperature
lab-astronomy.l06.q4.p: Massive stars have far more fuel than small stars, yet they live much shorter lives. Why?
lab-astronomy.l06.q4.e: Fusion rates rise steeply with mass, so massive stars use up their fuel far more quickly.

lab-astronomy.l07.q1.p: What is the approximate value of the Chandrasekhar limit?
lab-astronomy.l07.q1.h: A little more than the Sun's mass.
lab-astronomy.l07.q1.e: A white dwarf above about 1.44 solar masses cannot support itself.

lab-astronomy.l07.q2.h: Repeating radio pulses in chart recordings.
lab-astronomy.l07.q2.e: Jocelyn Bell Burnell spotted the precise pulses that turned out to come from spinning neutron stars.

lab-astronomy.l07.q3.t: It will explode as a Type Ia supernova
lab-astronomy.l07.q3.p: A white dwarf of 1.2 solar masses is slowly gaining mass from a companion. What will happen when it nears 1.44 solar masses?
lab-astronomy.l07.q3.e: Reaching the Chandrasekhar limit triggers a runaway collapse and explosion, a Type Ia supernova.

lab-astronomy.l07.q4.t: They are triggered at nearly the same mass, so their peak brightness is similar
lab-astronomy.l07.q4.p: Why are Type Ia supernovae useful as standard candles?
lab-astronomy.l07.q4.e: Because the exploding white dwarf is always near 1.44 solar masses, the explosions have similar true luminosities.

lab-astronomy.l08.q1.t: The boundary beyond which nothing, not even light, can escape
lab-astronomy.l08.q1.p: What is the event horizon of a black hole?
lab-astronomy.l08.q1.e: Within the event horizon the escape velocity exceeds the speed of light.

lab-astronomy.l08.q2.t: The shadow of the black hole in galaxy M87
lab-astronomy.l08.q2.p: What did the Event Horizon Telescope image in 2019?
lab-astronomy.l08.q2.h: A supermassive black hole in a nearby galaxy.
lab-astronomy.l08.q2.e: The first direct image of a black hole's shadow was of the supermassive black hole in M87.

lab-astronomy.l08.q3.p: The Schwarzschild radius is about 3 km per solar mass. About what is it for a 10 solar-mass black hole?
lab-astronomy.l08.q3.h: The radius is proportional to mass.
lab-astronomy.l08.q3.e: r = 2 G M / c squared scales linearly with M, so 10 times 3 km gives about 30 km.

lab-astronomy.l08.q4.t: It would continue unchanged, since gravity at a distance depends only on mass
lab-astronomy.l08.q4.p: If the Sun were suddenly replaced by a black hole of the same mass, what would happen to Earth's orbit?
lab-astronomy.l08.q4.h: Gravity depends on mass and distance.
lab-astronomy.l08.q4.e: Far from the horizon, a black hole attracts exactly as any object of the same mass would, so Earth would stay in orbit (though in darkness).

lab-astronomy.l09.q1.p: What causes the apparent shift of a nearby star against distant stars over a year?
lab-astronomy.l09.q1.h: Viewing from two sides of an orbit.
lab-astronomy.l09.q1.e: Parallax is the change in viewing angle as Earth moves around the Sun.

lab-astronomy.l09.q2.p: Which spacecraft measured precise parallaxes for nearly two billion stars?
lab-astronomy.l09.q2.e: ESA's Gaia mission mapped positions and distances for nearly two billion stars.

lab-astronomy.l09.q3.p: A star has a parallax of 0.25 arcseconds. How far away is it?
lab-astronomy.l09.q3.e: 1 divided by 0.25 is 4, so the star is 4 parsecs away.

lab-astronomy.l09.q4.t: The angles for distant stars become too small to measure accurately
lab-astronomy.l09.q4.p: Why does parallax work only for relatively nearby stars?
lab-astronomy.l09.q4.h: Consider d = 1 / p for large d.
lab-astronomy.l09.q4.e: The larger the distance, the smaller the parallax angle, and eventually it falls below what can be measured.

lab-astronomy.l10.q1.t: Their pulsation period is related to their true luminosity
lab-astronomy.l10.q1.p: What did Henrietta Leavitt discover about Cepheid variable stars?
lab-astronomy.l10.q1.e: The period-luminosity relation lets astronomers find a Cepheid's true brightness from its period.

lab-astronomy.l10.q2.p: What is the correct order of rungs on the distance ladder, from nearest to farthest?
lab-astronomy.l10.q2.e: Parallax calibrates Cepheids, which calibrate Type Ia supernovae.

lab-astronomy.l10.q3.p: A star has m - M = 5. Using m - M = 5 log10(d) - 5, what is its distance?
lab-astronomy.l10.q3.h: Add 5 to both sides, divide by 5, then undo the logarithm.
lab-astronomy.l10.q3.e: 5 = 5 log10(d) - 5 gives log10(d) = 2, so d = 100 parsecs.

lab-astronomy.l10.q4.t: Each rung is calibrated by the one below it, so errors carry upward
lab-astronomy.l10.q4.p: Why is an error in the parallax measurements a problem for distances to far galaxies?
lab-astronomy.l10.q4.h: Think about how the ladder is built.
lab-astronomy.l10.q4.e: Cepheids are calibrated with parallax and supernovae with Cepheids, so any mistake propagates.

lab-astronomy.l11.q1.t: Its light has been stretched to longer wavelengths, as the galaxy recedes
lab-astronomy.l11.q1.p: What does a redshift in a galaxy's spectrum indicate?
lab-astronomy.l11.q1.e: Redshift means the observed wavelength is longer than emitted, indicating recession or cosmic expansion.

lab-astronomy.l11.q2.t: Recession speed is proportional to distance
lab-astronomy.l11.q2.e: More distant galaxies recede faster, in direct proportion.

lab-astronomy.l11.q3.p: With H0 = 70 km/s per megaparsec, how fast does a galaxy 200 megaparsecs away recede?

lab-astronomy.l11.q4.t: Expansion has no special centre; every observer sees the same pattern
lab-astronomy.l11.q4.p: Astronomers in a distant galaxy would also see other galaxies receding. What does this suggest?
lab-astronomy.l11.q4.h: Think of dots on an inflating balloon.
lab-astronomy.l11.q4.e: With uniform expansion, every location sees distant objects recede in proportion to distance.

lab-astronomy.l12.q1.p: About how old was the universe when the cosmic microwave background light was released?
lab-astronomy.l12.q1.e: At about 380 000 years, electrons and nuclei combined and light could travel freely.

lab-astronomy.l12.q2.p: Who detected the cosmic microwave background in 1965?
lab-astronomy.l12.q2.h: A hiss in a radio antenna.
lab-astronomy.l12.q2.e: Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson found an unexplained microwave signal and won the 1978 Nobel Prize.

lab-astronomy.l12.q3.t: Expansion of the universe has stretched its wavelengths
lab-astronomy.l12.q3.p: Why is the CMB found in the microwave range today rather than visible light?
lab-astronomy.l12.q3.e: The light released at 380 000 years has been stretched by cosmic expansion to a temperature of about 2.7 K.

lab-astronomy.l12.q4.t: They mark slightly denser regions that later grew into galaxies
lab-astronomy.l12.q4.p: Why are the tiny ripples in the CMB temperature important?
lab-astronomy.l12.q4.e: Small density variations in the early universe seeded the structure we see, and their pattern reveals the universe's composition and geometry.

lab-astronomy.l13.q1.p: Whose measurements of galaxy rotation curves provided strong evidence for dark matter?
lab-astronomy.l13.q1.h: Stars far from the centre orbit too fast.
lab-astronomy.l13.q1.e: Vera Rubin showed stars in spiral galaxies orbit faster than visible matter alone can explain.

lab-astronomy.l13.q2.t: Drive the accelerating expansion of the universe
lab-astronomy.l13.q2.p: What is dark energy thought to do?
lab-astronomy.l13.q2.h: Distant supernovae showed something unexpected about expansion.
lab-astronomy.l13.q2.e: Observations of distant supernovae show expansion is accelerating, attributed to dark energy.

lab-astronomy.l13.q3.p: Dark matter and dark energy together make up about what fraction of the universe's contents?
lab-astronomy.l13.q3.h: Ordinary matter is the small remainder.
lab-astronomy.l13.q3.e: Ordinary matter is only about 5 percent; the rest is dark matter and dark energy.

lab-astronomy.l13.q4.t: Most of the mass is in a component that does not interact like ordinary gas
lab-astronomy.l13.q4.p: In the Bullet Cluster, the gravitational mass is displaced from the visible gas. What does this indicate?
lab-astronomy.l13.q4.h: Where is the mass compared with the visible gas?
lab-astronomy.l13.q4.e: After a collision, gas slows down but dark matter passes through, so the mass map separates from the visible gas, supporting an unseen mass component.

lab-biology.l01.q1.p: Who first used the word cell, describing the pores of cork?
lab-biology.l01.q1.e: Robert Hooke named cells after seeing the box-like structure of cork under a microscope.

lab-biology.l01.q2.t: Every cell comes from a pre-existing cell
lab-biology.l01.q2.p: What does the principle omnis cellula e cellula mean?
lab-biology.l01.q2.h: It was added by Virchow in 1855.
lab-biology.l01.q2.e: Virchow established that cells arise only from the division of other cells.

lab-biology.l01.q3.p: A newly discovered organism is found living in a deep-sea vent. According to cell theory, what should it be made of?
lab-biology.l01.q3.h: Cell theory covers all living things.
lab-biology.l01.q3.e: Cell theory states all living things are composed of one or more cells.

lab-biology.l01.q4.t: It says new cells only arise from existing cells, not from non-living matter
lab-biology.l01.q4.p: Why does the principle that every cell comes from a pre-existing cell argue against spontaneous generation?
lab-biology.l01.q4.h: Think about the source of new cells.
lab-biology.l01.q4.e: If cells only arise by division of existing cells, they do not appear spontaneously from non-living matter.

lab-biology.l02.q1.p: In DNA, which base pairs with adenine (A)?
lab-biology.l02.q1.h: It is a base found in DNA but not RNA.
lab-biology.l02.q1.e: A pairs with T and G pairs with C.

lab-biology.l02.q2.p: What did the Meselson-Stahl experiment show?
lab-biology.l02.q2.h: Each daughter helix keeps something from the parent.
lab-biology.l02.q2.e: Each new double helix contains one old strand and one new strand.

lab-biology.l02.q3.p: One strand of DNA has the sequence ATGC. What is the sequence of the complementary strand?
lab-biology.l02.q3.h: Pair each base: A with T, G with C.
lab-biology.l02.q3.e: A pairs with T, T with A, G with C and C with G, giving TACG.

lab-biology.l02.q4.t: Because each strand can serve as a template for the other through base pairing
lab-biology.l02.q4.p: Why does the double-helix structure suggest a way to copy genetic information?
lab-biology.l02.q4.e: Because bases pair specifically, each strand specifies its partner and can be used as a template.

lab-biology.l03.q1.p: What is the direction of information flow described by the central dogma?
lab-biology.l03.q1.e: Information flows from DNA to RNA to protein.

lab-biology.l03.q2.p: How many bases make up one codon?
lab-biology.l03.q2.h: There are 64 codons from four bases.
lab-biology.l03.q2.e: A codon is a group of three bases that specifies one amino acid or a stop signal.

lab-biology.l03.q3.p: A stretch of mRNA is 9 bases long and is read codon by codon. How many amino acids does it specify?
lab-biology.l03.q3.e: 9 bases divided into codons of 3 gives 3 amino acids.

lab-biology.l03.q4.t: All life shares a common ancestor
lab-biology.l03.q4.p: What does the near-universality of the genetic code suggest?
lab-biology.l03.q4.h: The same code is used by bacteria and humans.
lab-biology.l03.q4.e: A shared code across life is strong evidence for a single common ancestor.

lab-biology.l04.q1.p: Which organism did Mendel use for his famous experiments?
lab-biology.l04.q1.h: He worked in a monastery garden.

lab-biology.l04.q2.t: The two copies of a gene separate into different gametes
lab-biology.l04.q2.p: What does Mendel's law of segregation say?
lab-biology.l04.q2.e: The paired factors separate cleanly when gametes form.

lab-biology.l04.q3.p: Two heterozygous parents (Aa x Aa) produce 400 offspring. About how many are expected to be homozygous recessive (aa)?
lab-biology.l04.q3.h: One quarter of offspring are aa.
lab-biology.l04.q3.e: The cross gives 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa, so about 1/4 of 400 = 100 are aa.

lab-biology.l04.q4.t: It linked Mendel's factors to the behaviour of chromosomes in meiosis
lab-biology.l04.q4.p: Why did the Sutton-Boveri chromosome theory matter for Mendel's work?
lab-biology.l04.q4.h: It gave the abstract factors a physical home.
lab-biology.l04.q4.e: It showed Mendelian factors are carried on chromosomes, which separate during meiosis.

lab-biology.l05.q1.p: Which is NOT one of the three ingredients of natural selection?
lab-biology.l05.q1.e: Natural selection needs variation, heritability and differential reproduction, not deliberate acquisition of traits.

lab-biology.l05.q2.t: Beak size shifting within a generation when drought changed available seeds
lab-biology.l05.q2.p: What did the Grants observe in Galapagos finches?
lab-biology.l05.q2.h: Seed types changed during a drought.
lab-biology.l05.q2.e: They measured beak size changing in response to drought-driven changes in seeds.

lab-biology.l05.q3.p: A bacterial population meets an antibiotic and a few resistant cells survive and reproduce. What is the likely outcome over generations?
lab-biology.l05.q3.h: Think about who leaves more descendants.
lab-biology.l05.q3.e: Resistant bacteria leave more descendants, so the trait increases in frequency.

lab-biology.l05.q4.p: Why is it wrong to say natural selection is just random chance?
lab-biology.l05.q4.h: Distinguish the source of variation from the filter.
lab-biology.l05.q4.e: Mutation supplies random variation, but which variants survive and reproduce is non-random.

lab-biology.l06.q1.p: In the Hardy-Weinberg equation p^2 + 2pq + q^2 = 1, what does 2pq represent?
lab-biology.l06.q1.h: It is the middle term, with two ways to get one of each allele.
lab-biology.l06.q1.e: 2pq is the frequency of the heterozygous genotype.

lab-biology.l06.q2.t: Random mating in a large population
lab-biology.l06.q2.p: Which of these is an assumption of Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium?
lab-biology.l06.q2.h: The baseline assumes no evolutionary forces.
lab-biology.l06.q2.e: The equilibrium assumes a large, randomly mating population with no selection, mutation, migration or drift.

lab-biology.l06.q3.p: The recessive allele has frequency q = 0.3. What fraction of the population is expected to be homozygous recessive?

lab-biology.l06.q4.p: If 16 percent of a population shows a recessive trait, what proportion are heterozygous carriers, assuming equilibrium?
lab-biology.l06.q4.h: Find q first, then p, then 2pq.

lab-biology.l07.q1.t: The proportion of phenotypic variance due to additive genetic effects
lab-biology.l07.q1.p: What does narrow-sense heritability (h squared) measure?
lab-biology.l07.q1.h: It is a ratio of variances.
lab-biology.l07.q1.e: h squared = V_A / V_P, the share of total variation due to additive genetic variance.

lab-biology.l07.q2.p: In the breeder's equation R = h^2 S, what is R?
lab-biology.l07.q2.h: It is how much the next generation shifts.
lab-biology.l07.q2.e: R is the change in the mean trait value in one generation.

lab-biology.l07.q3.p: Breeders choose parents averaging 10 g above the population mean for a trait with h squared = 0.4. By how much is the offspring mean expected to rise?

lab-biology.l07.q4.t: The trait changes very little in the next generation
lab-biology.l07.q4.p: A trait has heritability near zero. What happens if breeders select only the largest individuals?
lab-biology.l07.q4.e: With h squared near 0, R is near 0 however strong the selection, because differences are not passed on.

lab-biology.l08.q1.p: What is the key requirement for speciation?
lab-biology.l08.q1.h: Two groups must stop exchanging genes.
lab-biology.l08.q1.e: Reproductive isolation splits one lineage into two.

lab-biology.l08.q2.t: Rapid diversification of a lineage into many niches
lab-biology.l08.q2.e: An adaptive radiation is a burst of speciation into many ecological niches.

lab-biology.l08.q3.p: A new river splits a population of squirrels into two groups that evolve separately and eventually cannot interbreed. What is this kind of speciation called?
lab-biology.l08.q3.e: Speciation following geographic separation is allopatric speciation.

lab-biology.l08.q4.t: It shows speciation can begin without a geographic barrier
lab-biology.l08.q4.p: Why is the Rhagoletis apple maggot fly an important example?
lab-biology.l08.q4.h: Hawthorn and apple trees grow in the same place.
lab-biology.l08.q4.e: A host shift is producing incipient species in the same area, so a physical barrier is not required.

lab-biology.l09.q1.t: Maintenance of a stable internal environment through feedback
lab-biology.l09.q1.h: Think of body temperature staying steady.
lab-biology.l09.q1.e: Organisms keep temperature, pH, ions and fuels within narrow ranges using feedback regulation.

lab-biology.l09.q2.t: The rate doubles for each 10 degree rise
lab-biology.l09.q2.p: What does a Q10 of 2 mean?
lab-biology.l09.q2.e: Q10 is the factor by which a rate changes for a 10 degree Celsius rise.

lab-biology.l09.q3.p: According to Kleiber's law, B is proportional to M^(3/4). By what factor does metabolic rate increase when body mass is 16 times larger?
lab-biology.l09.q3.h: 16 to the power 3/4 equals (16 to the 1/4) cubed.
lab-biology.l09.q3.e: The fourth root of 16 is 2, and 2 cubed is 8.

lab-biology.l09.q4.p: Because the exponent in Kleiber's law is less than 1, how does metabolic rate per kilogram compare between a mouse and a whale?
lab-biology.l09.q4.e: B/M is proportional to M^(-1/4), so smaller animals have higher mass-specific metabolic rates.

lab-biology.l10.q1.p: What is Vmax in Michaelis-Menten kinetics?
lab-biology.l10.q1.h: The curve levels off at this value.
lab-biology.l10.q1.e: Vmax is the maximum rate the enzyme can reach when saturated.

lab-biology.l10.q2.t: It is a biological catalyst that speeds up reactions
lab-biology.l10.q2.p: What is the role of an enzyme?

lab-biology.l10.q3.p: An enzyme has Vmax = 100 and Km = 2 (same concentration units). What is the rate when [S] = 2?
lab-biology.l10.q3.e: v = 100 x 2 / (2 + 2) = 50, which is half of Vmax.

lab-biology.l10.q4.t: The enzyme molecules are all occupied, so the system saturates
lab-biology.l10.q4.p: Why does the rate stop increasing at very high substrate concentration?
lab-biology.l10.q4.h: Think of a fixed number of waiters.
lab-biology.l10.q4.e: When nearly all enzyme molecules are busy, more substrate cannot raise the rate above Vmax.

lab-biology.l11.q1.p: What shape is the logistic growth curve?
lab-biology.l11.q1.e: Logistic growth is S-shaped, levelling off at carrying capacity.

lab-biology.l11.q2.t: Predator and prey populations that oscillate
lab-biology.l11.q2.p: What do the Lotka-Volterra equations describe?
lab-biology.l11.q2.e: They model coupled predator-prey cycles in abundance.

lab-biology.l11.q3.p: A population of 100 grows with lambda = 1.5 per generation. How large is it after two generations?

lab-biology.l11.q4.p: In the logistic model, why does growth slow as N approaches K?
lab-biology.l11.q4.h: Look at the term in brackets.
lab-biology.l11.q4.e: As N approaches K, (1 - N/K) approaches zero so dN/dt approaches zero.

lab-biology.l12.q1.t: Returning nutrients from dead material to the soil
lab-biology.l12.q1.p: What is the role of decomposers in an ecosystem?
lab-biology.l12.q1.e: Decomposers break down dead matter and recycle nutrients.

lab-biology.l12.q2.t: Species richness rises with habitat area
lab-biology.l12.q2.p: What does the species-area relationship say?
lab-biology.l12.q2.h: The law is S = c A^z.
lab-biology.l12.q2.e: Species richness rises with habitat area following a power law.

lab-biology.l12.q3.p: With S = c A^z and z = 0.25, by roughly what factor does species richness change if the area is 16 times larger?
lab-biology.l12.q3.e: 16 to the power 0.25 is 2, so richness roughly doubles.

lab-biology.l12.q4.p: Community A has four species at 25 percent each. Community B has four species but one makes up 97 percent. Which has the higher Simpson diversity?
lab-biology.l12.q4.h: Evenness matters as well as richness.
lab-biology.l12.q4.e: D = 1 - sum of p squared is higher when individuals are spread evenly, as in community A.

lab-biology.l13.q1.p: What was CRISPR originally in bacteria?
lab-biology.l13.q1.h: Bacteria store snippets of viral DNA.
lab-biology.l13.q1.e: CRISPR-Cas is a bacterial immune system against viruses.

lab-biology.l13.q2.p: Who showed in 2012 that Cas9 could be programmed to cut chosen DNA sequences?
lab-biology.l13.q2.h: They shared the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
lab-biology.l13.q2.e: Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier reprogrammed the guide RNA.

lab-biology.l13.q3.p: A researcher wants Cas9 to cut a different gene. What should be changed?
lab-biology.l13.q3.h: The RNA tells the enzyme where to cut.
lab-biology.l13.q3.e: Changing the guide RNA to match another sequence redirects Cas9.

lab-biology.l13.q4.t: They give the guide RNA a match to recognise and cut the same virus later
lab-biology.l13.q4.p: Why does the bacterial system store snippets of viral DNA?
lab-biology.l13.q4.h: Think about how a repeat attack is recognised.
lab-biology.l13.q4.e: The stored snippets provide guide RNAs that direct Cas9 to cut matching invading DNA.

lab-biology.l14.q1.p: What did Linnaeus provide for classifying life?
lab-biology.l14.q1.e: Linnaeus introduced binomial names and a nested hierarchy of ranks.

lab-biology.l14.q2.p: Which project produced a draft of the human genome between 2001 and 2003?
lab-biology.l14.q2.h: It is named after what it mapped.
lab-biology.l14.q2.e: The Human Genome Project completed a draft in the early 2000s.

lab-biology.l14.q3.p: Which of the following is a correctly formed binomial scientific name?
lab-biology.l14.q3.h: It has a genus and a species part.
lab-biology.l14.q3.e: A binomial name has two parts, genus then species, as in Homo sapiens.

lab-biology.l14.q4.t: It reconciled Mendelian inheritance with Darwinian selection
lab-biology.l14.q4.p: What problem did the Modern Synthesis solve?
lab-biology.l14.q4.h: Think of Fisher, Haldane and Wright.
lab-biology.l14.q4.e: It fused genetics and natural selection using mathematical population genetics.

lab-chemistry.l01.q1.p: Which theory did Lavoisier overturn when he explained combustion?
lab-chemistry.l01.q1.h: It claimed burning released a mysterious substance.
lab-chemistry.l01.q1.e: Lavoisier showed combustion is a reaction with oxygen, replacing the phlogiston idea.

lab-chemistry.l01.q2.p: What did Boyle's Sceptical Chymist insist an element should be?
lab-chemistry.l01.q2.h: He wanted chemistry to rest on experiment.
lab-chemistry.l01.q2.e: Boyle treated the element as something defined by experiment, separating chemistry from alchemy.

lab-chemistry.l01.q3.p: In a sealed vessel 5 g of substance A reacts completely with 3 g of substance B to form one product. What is the mass of the product?
lab-chemistry.l01.q3.h: Mass is conserved in a closed system.
lab-chemistry.l01.q3.e: Total mass of reactants equals total mass of products: 5 g + 3 g = 8 g.

lab-chemistry.l01.q4.t: Gases such as carbon dioxide and water vapour carried away the missing mass
lab-chemistry.l01.q4.p: A log burns in an open fireplace and the ash weighs much less than the log. Which explanation fits conservation of mass?
lab-chemistry.l01.q4.h: Ask what you would have to collect to account for all the mass.
lab-chemistry.l01.q4.e: The mass left as gases. In a closed system, the total would be unchanged.

lab-chemistry.l02.q1.p: What did Dalton propose about atoms of one element?
lab-chemistry.l02.q1.e: Dalton proposed that each element consists of identical atoms that combine in whole-number ratios.

lab-chemistry.l02.q2.p: What did Rutherford's gold-foil experiment reveal?
lab-chemistry.l02.q2.h: A few alpha particles were scattered strongly.
lab-chemistry.l02.q2.e: Alpha-particle scattering showed that the atom has a tiny dense nucleus at its core.

lab-chemistry.l02.q3.p: Carbon forms two oxides. One has 16 g of oxygen per 12 g of carbon and the other has 32 g. What is the ratio of the oxygen masses?
lab-chemistry.l02.q3.e: The ratio 16 : 32 reduces to 1 : 2, a small whole-number ratio as the law of multiple proportions predicts.

lab-chemistry.l02.q4.t: Most of an atom is empty space with its mass concentrated in a small centre
lab-chemistry.l02.q4.p: In the gold-foil experiment most alpha particles passed straight through but a few were deflected strongly. What does this imply?
lab-chemistry.l02.q4.h: Why would only a few particles be turned back?
lab-chemistry.l02.q4.e: Most particles met nothing, while the rare strong deflections came from a tiny, dense, positively charged core.

lab-chemistry.l03.q1.t: He left gaps and predicted undiscovered elements
lab-chemistry.l03.q1.p: What did Mendeleev do that made his periodic table so powerful?
lab-chemistry.l03.q1.e: His predictions for gallium, scandium and germanium were later confirmed.

lab-chemistry.l03.q2.p: What did Moseley show elements are ordered by?
lab-chemistry.l03.q2.h: It is the number of protons.
lab-chemistry.l03.q2.e: X-ray spectra showed the true ordering principle is atomic number.

lab-chemistry.l03.q3.p: An atom has 17 protons. What is its atomic number?
lab-chemistry.l03.q3.e: The atomic number equals the number of protons, so it is 17.

lab-chemistry.l03.q4.t: They were found with the properties Mendeleev predicted for the gaps
lab-chemistry.l03.q4.p: Why did the discovery of gallium, scandium and germanium strengthen belief in the periodic law?
lab-chemistry.l03.q4.e: Successful predictions of unseen elements are strong evidence that the pattern reflects a real law.

lab-chemistry.l04.q1.t: They are transferred from one atom to another
lab-chemistry.l04.q1.p: In an ionic bond, what happens to electrons?
lab-chemistry.l04.q1.e: Ionic bonds form when electrons are transferred, giving oppositely charged ions.

lab-chemistry.l04.q2.h: He wrote The Nature of the Chemical Bond.
lab-chemistry.l04.q2.e: Linus Pauling introduced electronegativity to predict bond polarity.

lab-chemistry.l04.q3.p: What type of bonding explains why a copper wire conducts electricity?
lab-chemistry.l04.q3.h: The electrons are not tied to single atoms.
lab-chemistry.l04.q3.e: In metallic bonds electrons are pooled across the lattice and can move.

lab-chemistry.l04.q4.p: Oxygen attracts bonding electrons more strongly than hydrogen. What does this make the O-H bond?
lab-chemistry.l04.q4.e: A difference in electronegativity pulls electrons toward oxygen, giving a polar bond.

lab-chemistry.l05.q1.p: About how many particles are in one mole?
lab-chemistry.l05.q1.e: One mole contains Avogadro's number of particles, about 6.02 x 10^23.

lab-chemistry.l05.q2.p: Which equation relates amount of substance to mass?
lab-chemistry.l05.q2.h: Think about grams divided by grams per mole.
lab-chemistry.l05.q2.e: n = m / M, with mass in grams and molar mass in g/mol.

lab-chemistry.l05.q3.p: The molar mass of water is 18 g/mol. How many moles are in 36 g of water?

lab-chemistry.l05.q4.p: A mole of iron and a mole of sulfur have different masses. What do they have in common?
lab-chemistry.l05.q4.h: Think of a dozen eggs and a dozen bricks.
lab-chemistry.l05.q4.e: A mole is a fixed number of particles, whereas the mass depends on the molar mass of the element.

lab-chemistry.l06.q1.t: The mole ratios in which substances react
lab-chemistry.l06.q1.p: What do the coefficients in a balanced chemical equation give?
lab-chemistry.l06.q1.h: They tell you how much of each is involved.
lab-chemistry.l06.q1.e: Balanced coefficients fix the exact mole ratios of reactants and products.

lab-chemistry.l06.q2.p: Stoichiometry relies on the conservation of atoms and mass.
lab-chemistry.l06.q2.h: Think about why an equation must be balanced.
lab-chemistry.l06.q2.e: Because atoms are conserved, the equation must balance and the ratios are fixed.

lab-chemistry.l06.q3.p: In 2 H2 + O2 gives 2 H2O, how many moles of oxygen are needed to burn 4 mol of hydrogen?
lab-chemistry.l06.q3.h: The ratio of H2 to O2 is 2 to 1.
lab-chemistry.l06.q3.e: The ratio is 2 : 1, so 4 mol of H2 needs 2 mol of O2.

lab-chemistry.l06.q4.p: When 12 g of carbon burns completely with 32 g of oxygen in a closed container, what mass of carbon dioxide forms?
lab-chemistry.l06.q4.e: The total mass is conserved, so the product has a mass of 12 g + 32 g = 44 g.

lab-chemistry.l07.q1.t: Pressure and volume are inversely proportional
lab-chemistry.l07.q1.p: What does Boyle's law say, at constant temperature?
lab-chemistry.l07.q1.h: Squeezing a gas raises its pressure.
lab-chemistry.l07.q1.e: For a fixed amount of gas at constant temperature, P V is constant.

lab-chemistry.l07.q2.p: In which units must temperature be expressed in P V = n R T?
lab-chemistry.l07.q2.h: It must be an absolute scale.
lab-chemistry.l07.q2.e: The law uses absolute temperature, in kelvin.

lab-chemistry.l07.q3.p: A gas at 2 atm and 6 L is compressed to 3 L at constant temperature. What is its new pressure?
lab-chemistry.l07.q3.e: P2 = (2 atm x 6 L) / 3 L = 4 atm.

lab-chemistry.l07.q4.t: The same amount of gas in a smaller volume has higher pressure
lab-chemistry.l07.q4.p: Why does a sealed syringe get harder to push as you compress the air?
lab-chemistry.l07.q4.h: Think about the relation between pressure and volume.
lab-chemistry.l07.q4.e: By Boyle's law, reducing the volume at constant temperature raises the pressure.

lab-chemistry.l08.q1.p: What does a negative delta G indicate for a reaction?
lab-chemistry.l08.q1.h: It is the criterion Gibbs defined.
lab-chemistry.l08.q1.e: A reaction is spontaneous when the change in Gibbs free energy is negative.

lab-chemistry.l08.q2.e: Exothermic reactions release heat to the surroundings.

lab-chemistry.l08.q3.p: A reaction has delta H = +30 kJ/mol and delta S = 0.2 kJ/(mol K) at 300 K. What is delta G?
lab-chemistry.l08.q3.h: Compute T delta S first and keep the units consistent.
lab-chemistry.l08.q3.e: T delta S = 300 x 0.2 = 60 kJ/mol, so delta G = 30 - 60 = -30 kJ/mol.

lab-chemistry.l08.q4.t: The entropy increase can outweigh the energy cost, making delta G negative
lab-chemistry.l08.q4.p: Ice melts in a warm room even though melting absorbs heat. Why is this consistent with delta G = delta H - T delta S?
lab-chemistry.l08.q4.h: Look at the second term in the equation.
lab-chemistry.l08.q4.e: The disordered liquid has higher entropy, so T delta S can exceed delta H.

lab-chemistry.l09.q1.e: Kinetics deals with reaction rates and mechanisms.

lab-chemistry.l09.q2.t: The energy barrier that must be overcome for reaction
lab-chemistry.l09.q2.e: Ea is the minimum energy needed for colliding molecules to react.

lab-chemistry.l09.q3.p: A first-order reaction has rate = k [A], with k = 0.1 per second and [A] = 0.5 mol/L. What is the rate?

lab-chemistry.l09.q4.t: The rate constant k increases as temperature rises
lab-chemistry.l09.q4.p: Food spoils faster in a warm kitchen than in a refrigerator. What does the Arrhenius equation say?
lab-chemistry.l09.q4.h: Look at how T appears in the exponent.
lab-chemistry.l09.q4.e: In k = A e^(-Ea / RT), a larger T makes the exponent less negative, so k is larger.

lab-chemistry.l10.q1.t: The forward and reverse rates are equal
lab-chemistry.l10.q1.p: What is true at chemical equilibrium?
lab-chemistry.l10.q1.e: Molecules keep reacting, but forward and reverse rates match, so concentrations are constant.

lab-chemistry.l10.q2.t: A system at equilibrium shifts so as to oppose an imposed change
lab-chemistry.l10.q2.p: What does Le Chatelier's principle say?
lab-chemistry.l10.q2.h: It is about the response to a disturbance.
lab-chemistry.l10.q2.e: When a stress is applied, the equilibrium shifts to counteract it.

lab-chemistry.l10.q3.p: For 2A converting to B, K = [B] / [A]^2. At equilibrium [B] = 1.0 mol/L and [A] = 0.5 mol/L. What is K?

lab-chemistry.l10.q4.t: The reaction goes from four gas molecules to two, so pressure shifts it toward fewer molecules
lab-chemistry.l10.q4.p: In N2 + 3 H2 reversing to 2 NH3, why does high pressure favour ammonia?
lab-chemistry.l10.q4.h: Count the gas molecules on each side.
lab-chemistry.l10.q4.e: Raising pressure shifts equilibrium toward the side with fewer moles of gas, and the Haber process exploits this.

lab-chemistry.l11.q1.p: In the Bronsted-Lowry theory, what is an acid?
lab-chemistry.l11.q1.h: It donates something to the base.
lab-chemistry.l11.q1.e: Bronsted and Lowry defined acids as proton donors and bases as proton acceptors.

lab-chemistry.l11.q2.p: Who introduced the pH scale in 1909?
lab-chemistry.l11.q2.h: A Danish chemist working in brewing research.
lab-chemistry.l11.q2.e: Soren Sorensen gave acidity a logarithmic, measurable definition.

lab-chemistry.l11.q3.p: A solution has [H+] = 1 x 10^-4 mol/L. What is its pH?

lab-chemistry.l11.q4.p: How does the hydrogen-ion concentration at pH 3 compare with that at pH 5?
lab-chemistry.l11.q4.h: Each pH unit is a factor of ten.
lab-chemistry.l11.q4.e: Two pH units lower means 10 x 10 = 100 times more H+.

lab-chemistry.l12.q1.p: What is transferred in a redox reaction?
lab-chemistry.l12.q1.e: Redox reactions involve the transfer of electrons.

lab-chemistry.l12.q2.p: What does it mean for a species to be oxidised?
lab-chemistry.l12.q2.h: Zinc becoming Zn2+ is an example.
lab-chemistry.l12.q2.e: Oxidation is the loss of electrons and reduction is the gain.

lab-chemistry.l12.q3.p: A cell has a cell potential of +1.10 V. What is the sign of delta G for its reaction, from delta G = -n F E?
lab-chemistry.l12.q3.h: Note the minus sign in front of nFE.
lab-chemistry.l12.q3.e: With a positive E, delta G is negative, so the reaction is spontaneous.

lab-chemistry.l12.q4.t: Zinc is oxidised and copper ions are reduced
lab-chemistry.l12.q4.p: Zinc metal is placed in copper(II) solution and copper metal forms. Which statement is correct?
lab-chemistry.l12.q4.e: Zn loses electrons to become Zn2+ and Cu2+ gains them to become Cu.

lab-chemistry.l13.q1.t: That an organic compound could be made from inorganic materials
lab-chemistry.l13.q1.p: What did Wohler show by synthesising urea?
lab-chemistry.l13.q1.h: It challenged the idea that living things are special.
lab-chemistry.l13.q1.e: The synthesis undermined vitalism and united organic and inorganic chemistry.

lab-chemistry.l13.q2.p: How many bonds does a carbon atom typically form, according to Kekule?
lab-chemistry.l13.q2.e: Carbon is tetravalent and can link into chains and rings.

lab-chemistry.l13.q3.p: Nylon is built from small units joined end to end by covalent bonds into very long molecules. What is such a material called?
lab-chemistry.l13.q3.h: Carothers founded the science of these materials.
lab-chemistry.l13.q3.e: Polymers are long chains of repeating units, and Carothers invented nylon and neoprene.

lab-chemistry.l13.q4.t: It showed that molecules of life obey the same chemistry as other matter
lab-chemistry.l13.q4.p: Why did the synthesis of urea matter for how chemists viewed living matter?
lab-chemistry.l13.q4.e: Making an organic compound from inorganic starting materials showed no special vital force is required.

lab-chemistry.l14.q1.p: What does the Beer-Lambert law relate absorbance to?
lab-chemistry.l14.q1.e: Absorbance is proportional to concentration and to the path length of the light.

lab-chemistry.l14.q2.p: Which structures did Dorothy Hodgkin determine by X-ray crystallography?
lab-chemistry.l14.q2.h: They are important medicines and vitamins.
lab-chemistry.l14.q2.e: Hodgkin revealed the 3-D structures of penicillin, vitamin B12 and insulin.

lab-chemistry.l14.q3.p: With epsilon = 100 L/(mol cm), path length 1 cm and concentration 0.005 mol/L, what is the absorbance?

lab-chemistry.l14.q4.p: A chemist doubles the path length through a sample without changing its concentration. What happens to the absorbance?
lab-chemistry.l14.q4.h: The law is linear in path length.
lab-chemistry.l14.q4.e: Absorbance is proportional to path length, so doubling l doubles A.

lab-combat.l01.q1.p: In what year was Egyptian tahtib inscribed on UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list?
lab-combat.l01.q1.h: It is in the lesson's final paragraph.
lab-combat.l01.q1.e: Tahtib was inscribed in 2016; taekkyeon followed in 2011, the capoeira circle in 2014, and pencak silat in 2019 for other arts.

lab-combat.l01.q2.p: The Medinet Habu temple reliefs, showing refereed stick matches, date to about when?
lab-combat.l01.q2.h: They were carved in the era of Ramesses III.
lab-combat.l01.q2.e: Medinet Habu dates to about 1180 BCE; the Beni Hasan tombs are earlier, around 2000 BCE.

lab-combat.l01.q3.p: Two men with long bamboo staves trade controlled strikes to mizmar and drum at a village wedding in Upper Egypt. Which art is this?
lab-combat.l01.q3.e: Stick play set to mizmar and drum at festivals and weddings is tahtib.

lab-combat.l01.q4.t: They show sequential pairs in holds and counters, like a very early instruction record
lab-combat.l01.q4.p: Why do the Beni Hasan tomb murals matter to historians of martial arts?
lab-combat.l01.q4.h: Think about what a sequence of figures can teach.
lab-combat.l01.q4.e: The hundreds of painted wrestlers in sequences work like a frame-by-frame manual, though this does not prove a single origin for all arts.

lab-combat.l02.q1.h: It is one of the two sticks.
lab-combat.l02.q1.e: The induku is the striking stick; the ubhoko is the longer defensive staff, and the ihawu is the shield.

lab-combat.l02.q2.p: Who refereed traditional Nguni stick bouts?
lab-combat.l02.q2.e: Bouts were refereed by an induna.

lab-combat.l02.q3.p: At a wedding, warriors from the bride's and groom's households spar with sticks and shields, and the strongest is called the Bull. Which tradition?
lab-combat.l02.q3.e: That wedding custom and the title Inkunzi belong to Nguni stick fighting.

lab-combat.l02.q4.t: It was mainly a rite of passage tied to family and community
lab-combat.l02.q4.p: What does the practice of a boy cutting his own stick at sixteen suggest about the tradition?
lab-combat.l02.q4.h: Think about who goes with him to the forest.
lab-combat.l02.q4.e: Cutting one's own stick with a father marks passage into manhood, showing the art was social and ceremonial as well as martial.

lab-combat.l03.q1.p: In which country is laamb the national spectacle?

lab-combat.l03.q2.p: What name is given to the 20,000-seat arena that anchors professional laamb since 2018?
lab-combat.l03.q2.e: The Arene Nationale at Pikine opened in 2018.

lab-combat.l03.q3.p: In the professional avec frappe code, what is unusual about laamb compared with most wrestling?
lab-combat.l03.q3.h: The French phrase means with striking.
lab-combat.l03.q3.e: Avec frappe permits bare-fist punches, so live striking mixes with wrestling.

lab-combat.l03.q4.t: That ritual and spirituality are built into the sport
lab-combat.l03.q4.p: What do marabout blessings, gris-gris and the bakk praise-dance show about laamb?
lab-combat.l03.q4.h: Think of how much of the event is ceremony.
lab-combat.l03.q4.e: Laamb stages ritual more completely than any other African combat art, blending spirituality with athletics.

lab-combat.l04.q1.p: Along which river did engolo develop?
lab-combat.l04.q1.e: Engolo comes from the Cunene River region of Angola.

lab-combat.l04.q2.p: Which Angolan artist reconnected capoeira to engolo in the 1950s?
lab-combat.l04.q2.h: He was a painter who did fieldwork in Angola.
lab-combat.l04.q2.e: Albano Neves e Sousa recognised engolo in Bahia's capoeira.

lab-combat.l04.q3.p: A circle game where players throw kicks from handstands and evade rather than block is closest to which art?
lab-combat.l04.q3.h: The lesson called it the inverted art.
lab-combat.l04.q3.e: Handstand kicks and evasion are core engolo features.

lab-combat.l04.q4.t: It has a clear chain of place, people and technique from Cunene to Ndongo to Bahia
lab-combat.l04.q4.p: Why is the engolo-to-capoeira story considered unusually well documented?
lab-combat.l04.q4.h: Think of the arc named in the lesson.
lab-combat.l04.q4.e: Technique continuity, historical movement of people and scholarship such as Desch-Obi's give a clear origin-to-diaspora arc.

lab-combat.l05.q1.p: Which year's Penal Code criminalised capoeiragem in Brazil?

lab-combat.l05.q2.h: He won legal standing for an academy in the 1930s.
lab-combat.l05.q2.e: Mestre Bimba created Capoeira Regional in 1930s Bahia.

lab-combat.l05.q3.p: A player rocks in a constant base step to keep moving and set up kicks and escapes. What is the step called?
lab-combat.l05.q3.h: It is the rocking base step.
lab-combat.l05.q3.e: The ginga is the foundational rocking step of capoeira.

lab-combat.l05.q4.t: It sets the pace, can slow a heated game, and signals when players enter or leave
lab-combat.l05.q4.p: Why is the music (berimbau and songs) part of capoeira's etiquette as well as its atmosphere?
lab-combat.l05.q4.e: The berimbau and songs govern the tempo and tone of play, which helps keep games controlled and respectful.

lab-combat.l06.q1.e: Shaolin was founded in 495 CE; 728 is the date of the stele, and the temple was burned in 1928.

lab-combat.l06.q2.p: Which weapon is Shaolin's historic signature?
lab-combat.l06.q2.h: Ming-era monks were famous for it.
lab-combat.l06.q2.e: Shaolin staff fighting won empire-wide renown in the Ming dynasty.

lab-combat.l06.q3.t: The attribution is a later legend, not documented history
lab-combat.l06.q3.p: Which statement about Bodhidharma is most accurate?
lab-combat.l06.q3.e: Attribution of Shaolin's arts to Bodhidharma is a later legend; Cheng Zongyou wrote the staff manual.

lab-combat.l06.q4.t: Training is moving meditation within Buddhist discipline
lab-combat.l06.q4.p: What does the saying chan wu he yi suggest about Shaolin training?
lab-combat.l06.q4.e: Chan and martial arts are one frames practice as meditation bounded by monastic precepts.

lab-combat.l07.q1.p: In which Indian state did kalaripayattu develop?

lab-combat.l07.q2.t: A sunken earthen training arena that is also a shrine
lab-combat.l07.q2.h: It is both school and shrine.
lab-combat.l07.q2.e: The kalari is the sunken earthen arena used for training.

lab-combat.l07.q3.p: A student enters a training hall right foot first, touches the earth and the guru's feet and salutes a seven-tiered platform. Which art?
lab-combat.l07.q3.e: This entrance ritual is kalaripayattu etiquette.

lab-combat.l07.q4.t: It builds skill and control progressively before more dangerous weapons are used
lab-combat.l07.q4.p: Why do kalaripayattu students use wooden weapons before metal ones?
lab-combat.l07.q4.e: Training progresses from body conditioning and footwork to wooden arms and then metal, a gradual, safety-minded sequence.

lab-combat.l08.q1.e: Kano Jigoro founded judo and the Kodokan in 1882.

lab-combat.l08.q2.e: Seiryoku zen'yo is maximum efficient use of energy; jita kyoei is mutual welfare and benefit.

lab-combat.l08.q3.p: A judoka breaks a partner's balance before applying a throw using leverage. Which principle is this?
lab-combat.l08.q3.e: Kuzushi is breaking the opponent's balance, the premise of judo throws.

lab-combat.l08.q4.t: They reflect Kano's educational aim of respect and safe training with partners
lab-combat.l08.q4.p: Why do judo dojos emphasise bowing and learning to fall?
lab-combat.l08.q4.e: Etiquette and safe practice express judo's ethic of mutual welfare and its origin as educational training.

lab-combat.l09.q1.p: Where did karate develop before spreading to Tokyo?
lab-combat.l09.q1.e: Karate developed in Okinawa, drawing on local te and Chinese quanfa.

lab-combat.l09.q2.p: Who demonstrated karate in Tokyo in 1922 and founded Shotokan?
lab-combat.l09.q2.e: Gichin Funakoshi demonstrated in Tokyo in 1922 and founded Shotokan.

lab-combat.l09.q3.p: A student performs a solo set of prearranged movements and later studies the applications behind it. Which two terms fit?
lab-combat.l09.q3.h: One is a form, the other its analysis.
lab-combat.l09.q3.e: Kata are solo forms and bunkai is the analysis of their applications.

lab-combat.l09.q4.t: That the art stresses restraint and courtesy
lab-combat.l09.q4.p: What does the idea that there is no first attack in karate show about its moral frame?
lab-combat.l09.q4.e: Funakoshi's teaching that karate begins and ends with courtesy frames technique within restraint.

lab-combat.l10.q1.t: It uses fists, elbows, knees and shins
lab-combat.l10.q1.p: Why is muay thai called the art of eight limbs?
lab-combat.l10.q1.e: Eight limbs refers to two fists, two elbows, two knees and two shins.

lab-combat.l10.q2.t: A ritual dance of homage before a bout
lab-combat.l10.q2.p: What is the wai khru ram muay?
lab-combat.l10.q2.h: It is performed to oboe and drums.
lab-combat.l10.q2.e: The wai khru ram muay is the kneeling, danced homage to teachers.

lab-combat.l10.q3.p: A fighter wears a blessed headband and armbands and performs a dance to oboe and drum music before the bout. Which art?
lab-combat.l10.q3.e: The mongkhon headband, pra jiad armbands and sarama music mark muay thai.

lab-combat.l10.q4.t: It is national legend rather than verifiable record
lab-combat.l10.q4.p: Why does the lesson say the Nai Khanomtom story should be treated carefully?
lab-combat.l10.q4.e: Nai Khanomtom's 1774 victories are celebrated as legend, not documented history.

lab-combat.l11.q1.p: When did pankration enter the Olympic Games?
lab-combat.l11.q1.h: It is in the timeline of ancient events.
lab-combat.l11.q1.e: Pankration joined the Olympic programme in 648 BCE.

lab-combat.l11.q2.p: Which two actions were barred at Olympia?
lab-combat.l11.q2.e: Only biting and eye-gouging were banned.

lab-combat.l11.q3.p: How did a pankratiast signal submission?
lab-combat.l11.q3.e: Submission was signalled with a single raised finger.

lab-combat.l11.q4.t: They are the main technical record that survives
lab-combat.l11.q4.p: Why are painted prize amphorae so important to historians of pankration?
lab-combat.l11.q4.e: Vase iconography is the principal technical record of the fights.

lab-combat.l12.q1.p: Glima is the national sport of which country?
lab-combat.l12.q1.e: Glima is Iceland's national wrestling, with the Islandsglima for the Grettir's Belt.

lab-combat.l12.q2.p: What are the named tricks in glima called?
lab-combat.l12.q2.e: The named tricks of glima are the brogd.

lab-combat.l12.q3.p: Wrestlers grip each other's harness at hip and thigh and circle clockwise. Which art?
lab-combat.l12.q3.e: The fixed harness grip and circling step (stigandi) are glima.

lab-combat.l12.q4.t: Sportsmanlike honour, including upright posture and fair play
lab-combat.l12.q4.p: What does the code of drengskapur add to glima?
lab-combat.l12.q4.e: Drengskapur is sportsmanlike honour, shaping etiquette and fair conduct.

lab-combat.l13.q1.p: What is the name of Fiore dei Liberi's treatise?
lab-combat.l13.q1.e: Fiore wrote the Fior di Battaglia around 1404.

lab-combat.l13.q2.t: Niccolo III d'Este, Marquis of Ferrara
lab-combat.l13.q2.p: For whom did Fiore compose his Fior di Battaglia?
lab-combat.l13.q2.e: Fiore wrote it for Niccolo III d'Este.

lab-combat.l13.q3.p: A fight book teaches wrestling first, then dagger, sword, poleaxe and spear. Which system?
lab-combat.l13.q3.e: Armizare builds from abrazare (wrestling) to weapons.

lab-combat.l13.q4.t: They are reconstructing techniques from old texts and prioritise safety
lab-combat.l13.q4.p: Why do modern HEMA groups wear protective gear while reconstructing plays from the manuscripts?
lab-combat.l13.q4.h: Think about what modern practitioners must manage.
lab-combat.l13.q4.e: Modern reconstruction is carried out with protective equipment and safety rules, even though the sources are historical.

lab-combat.l14.q1.p: Who published boxing's first rules in 1743?
lab-combat.l14.q1.e: Jack Broughton published the first rules in 1743.

lab-combat.l14.q2.p: Which rules of 1867 introduced gloves and timed rounds?
lab-combat.l14.q2.e: The Queensberry rules of 1867 brought gloves and timed rounds.

lab-combat.l14.q3.p: A fighter in the 1790s is celebrated for a scientific, defensive style that transformed technique. Who is he?
lab-combat.l14.q3.e: Daniel Mendoza's scientific defence revolutionised boxing technique.

lab-combat.l14.q4.p: Broughton's rules and mufflers show that boxing's rules developed partly in response to injury and danger.
lab-combat.l14.q4.h: Recall what happened before his rules were written.
lab-combat.l14.q4.e: After an opponent died, Broughton wrote the first code and invented mufflers, an early step toward safer boxing.

lab-cs.l01.q1.p: Which pair of properties is essential for an algorithm?
lab-cs.l01.q1.h: The definition needs it to end and to be precise.
lab-cs.l01.q1.e: An algorithm is a finite, unambiguous sequence of steps that terminates with the correct answer.

lab-cs.l01.q2.t: The greatest common divisor of two numbers
lab-cs.l01.q2.e: Euclid's method, from around 300 BC, finds the greatest common divisor using repeated division with remainder.

lab-cs.l01.q3.p: Using Euclid's algorithm, what is the GCD of 48 and 18?
lab-cs.l01.q3.h: 48 mod 18, then 18 mod that remainder, and so on.
lab-cs.l01.q3.e: 48 mod 18 = 12; 18 mod 12 = 6; 12 mod 6 = 0, so the GCD is 6.

lab-cs.l01.q4.t: No, it must terminate on every valid input with the right answer
lab-cs.l01.q4.p: A procedure is precise at every step but, for some valid inputs, never stops. Is it an algorithm in the usual sense?
lab-cs.l01.q4.e: An algorithm must be finite, so a procedure that fails to halt on valid inputs does not qualify.

lab-cs.l02.q1.t: A tape, a read/write head and a finite rule table
lab-cs.l02.q1.p: Which set of components defines a Turing machine?
lab-cs.l02.q1.e: A Turing machine has an unbounded tape, a head that reads and writes symbols, and a finite table of rules.

lab-cs.l02.q2.t: Anything effectively computable by rote can be computed by a Turing machine
lab-cs.l02.q2.h: Several different formal models turned out to be equivalent.
lab-cs.l02.q2.e: Lambda calculus, recursive functions and Turing machines define the same class of computable functions, matching the intuitive notion of effective computation.

lab-cs.l02.q3.p: A machine starts at the left end of the tape 1011, flips each bit (0 to 1, 1 to 0), moving right until it reaches a blank. What is on the tape when it halts?
lab-cs.l02.q3.e: Flipping 1,0,1,1 gives 0,1,0,0, so the tape reads 0100.

lab-cs.l02.q4.t: Because other formal models of computation turned out to be equivalent in power
lab-cs.l02.q4.p: Why is the Turing machine's extreme simplicity not a limitation as a model of computation?
lab-cs.l02.q4.h: Consider the equivalence results of the 1930s.
lab-cs.l02.q4.e: Lambda calculus and other models define the same computable functions, so the simple machine loses no generality.

lab-cs.l03.q1.t: Whether an arbitrary program will eventually stop on a given input
lab-cs.l03.q1.p: What does the halting problem ask?
lab-cs.l03.q1.h: It is about stopping versus running forever.
lab-cs.l03.q1.e: The halting problem asks for a general method to decide, for any program and input, whether the program eventually halts.

lab-cs.l03.q2.p: Who proved the halting problem undecidable, and when?
lab-cs.l03.q2.h: It was in his paper On Computable Numbers.
lab-cs.l03.q2.e: Alan Turing proved this in 1936 in On Computable Numbers.

lab-cs.l03.q3.t: Doubt it: no program can solve the halting problem for all programs and inputs
lab-cs.l03.q3.p: A company advertises a tool that can examine any program and always correctly report whether it will loop forever. What is the best response?
lab-cs.l03.q3.h: The result applies to all programs in general.
lab-cs.l03.q3.e: Turing's theorem shows no general halting-decider exists, so such a claim cannot be fully true.

lab-cs.l03.q4.t: There is no single algorithm that correctly decides halting for every program, though many specific programs can be analysed
lab-cs.l03.q4.p: Which statement correctly describes what undecidability of the halting problem implies?
lab-cs.l03.q4.h: The result is about a universal method, not every individual case.
lab-cs.l03.q4.e: The theorem rules out one method that works on all programs; specific programs, such as ones without loops, can still be shown to halt.

lab-cs.l04.q1.t: Instructions and data share one addressable memory
lab-cs.l04.q1.p: What is the central idea of the stored-program (von Neumann) architecture?
lab-cs.l04.q1.e: Von Neumann's 1945 report placed program and data in a single addressable memory.

lab-cs.l04.q2.t: First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC
lab-cs.l04.q2.p: Which document of 1945 described the stored-program design?
lab-cs.l04.q2.e: Von Neumann's First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC set out the stored-program architecture.

lab-cs.l04.q3.p: In which order does the processor repeat its basic cycle?
lab-cs.l04.q3.h: You must get the instruction before you can interpret it.
lab-cs.l04.q3.e: The cycle is fetch the instruction, decode it, execute it, then repeat.

lab-cs.l04.q4.t: Programs that read or produce other programs, such as compilers
lab-cs.l04.q4.p: Because code and data share memory, which important kind of software becomes possible?
lab-cs.l04.q4.h: If a program is just data, what else can handle it?
lab-cs.l04.q4.e: A program stored as data can be created or transformed by another program, which is exactly what a compiler does.

lab-cs.l05.q1.t: An upper bound on how cost grows with input size
lab-cs.l05.q1.e: Big-O bounds growth of running time or space as the input size increases.

lab-cs.l05.q2.p: An algorithm takes 3n^2 + 5n + 2 steps. Its growth is
lab-cs.l05.q2.h: Keep only the dominant term and drop constants.
lab-cs.l05.q2.e: For large n the n^2 term dominates, so the cost is O(n^2).

lab-cs.l05.q3.p: An O(n^2) algorithm takes 1 second for 1,000 items. Roughly how long for 2,000 items?
lab-cs.l05.q3.h: Doubling n squares the factor of two.
lab-cs.l05.q3.e: Cost scales with n^2, and (2n)^2 = 4n^2, so about 4 seconds.

lab-cs.l05.q4.t: B is faster for n below 100, and A is faster for n above 100
lab-cs.l05.q4.p: Algorithm A takes 100n steps and algorithm B takes n^2 steps. Which statement is correct?
lab-cs.l05.q4.e: They are equal at n = 100; below that n^2 is smaller, above that 100n is smaller.

lab-cs.l06.q1.t: To stop the recursion by answering the smallest instance directly
lab-cs.l06.q1.p: What is the purpose of a base case in a recursive function?
lab-cs.l06.q1.e: The base case ends the descent; without it, the function calls itself forever.

lab-cs.l06.q2.t: Solve running-time recurrences of divide-and-conquer algorithms
lab-cs.l06.q2.p: The Master Theorem is used to
lab-cs.l06.q2.h: Think of T(n) = a T(n/b) + f(n).
lab-cs.l06.q2.e: It solves recurrences of the form T(n) = a T(n/b) + f(n).

lab-cs.l06.q3.p: A recursive search halves the number of items each call and stops at 1 item. Starting with 1,024 items, how many halvings are needed?
lab-cs.l06.q3.h: How many times must you divide 1,024 by 2 to reach 1?

lab-cs.l06.q4.p: For mergesort, a = 2 subproblems, each of size n/2, with f(n) proportional to n to merge. What running time does the Master Theorem give?
lab-cs.l06.q4.h: Compare f(n) with n raised to log base 2 of 2.
lab-cs.l06.q4.e: Here n^(log2 2) = n, which matches f(n), giving O(n log n).

lab-cs.l07.q1.p: What is the worst-case lower bound for comparison-based sorting of n items?
lab-cs.l07.q1.e: Any comparison sort needs on the order of n log n comparisons in the worst case.

lab-cs.l07.q2.p: How many possible orderings (permutations) do n distinct items have?
lab-cs.l07.q2.h: Choose the first item in n ways, then n-1, and so on.
lab-cs.l07.q2.e: There are n! orderings, and the sorting algorithm must be able to output the right one for each.

lab-cs.l07.q3.p: Three distinct items have 6 possible orderings. What is the minimum number of comparisons that guarantees sorting them in the worst case?
lab-cs.l07.q3.h: k comparisons distinguish at most 2^k outcomes.
lab-cs.l07.q3.e: Two comparisons give at most 4 outcomes, which is less than 6, but three give 8, which is enough.

lab-cs.l07.q4.t: Each distinct input ordering needs its own distinct result, and there are n! of them
lab-cs.l07.q4.p: Why must the decision tree of a correct comparison sort have at least n! leaves?
lab-cs.l07.q4.h: Think about what different inputs require of the output.
lab-cs.l07.q4.e: Different input orderings need different rearrangements, so the tree needs a separate leaf for each of the n! possibilities.

lab-cs.l08.q1.t: Can be solved in polynomial time
lab-cs.l08.q1.p: The class P contains problems that
lab-cs.l08.q1.e: P is the class of problems solvable in polynomial time.

lab-cs.l08.q2.t: Can be checked in polynomial time
lab-cs.l08.q2.p: The class NP contains problems whose solutions
lab-cs.l08.q2.e: NP means a proposed solution can be verified in polynomial time.

lab-cs.l08.q3.p: A problem has the property that any proposed answer can be checked quickly, but no one knows a fast way to find an answer. Which class is it certainly in?
lab-cs.l08.q3.h: Look at what is quick: checking.
lab-cs.l08.q3.e: Quickly checkable solutions are exactly the definition of NP.

lab-cs.l08.q4.t: Every problem in NP could be solved in polynomial time
lab-cs.l08.q4.p: Stephen Cook proved SAT is NP-complete. What would a fast (polynomial-time) algorithm for SAT imply?
lab-cs.l08.q4.h: NP-complete means every NP problem reduces to it.
lab-cs.l08.q4.e: Since every NP problem can be translated into SAT efficiently, a fast SAT solver would solve all of NP quickly.

lab-cs.l09.q1.p: What is the entropy of a fair coin flip?

lab-cs.l09.q2.t: The number of positions where they differ
lab-cs.l09.q2.p: Hamming distance between two equal-length words is
lab-cs.l09.q2.e: It counts the positions at which the two words differ.

lab-cs.l09.q3.p: What is the Hamming distance between 10110 and 11100?
lab-cs.l09.q3.h: Compare the two words position by position.
lab-cs.l09.q3.e: The words differ at positions 2 and 4 (0 vs 1, and 1 vs 0), so the distance is 2.

lab-cs.l09.q4.t: More compressible, since its entropy is lower
lab-cs.l09.q4.p: A coin lands heads 99 percent of the time. Compared with a fair coin, its output should be
lab-cs.l09.q4.e: A biased source has lower entropy, so lossless compression can shrink its output further.

lab-cs.l10.q1.p: Who published the first public-key key-exchange idea in 1976?
lab-cs.l10.q1.e: Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman introduced public-key cryptography in 1976.

lab-cs.l10.q2.p: RSA's security is based on the difficulty of
lab-cs.l10.q2.h: It is easy to multiply primes but hard to undo.
lab-cs.l10.q2.e: RSA relies on the believed difficulty of factoring the product of two large primes.

lab-cs.l10.q3.t: Public-key key exchange such as Diffie-Hellman
lab-cs.l10.q3.p: Two people who have never met want to agree on a secret over an open channel that an eavesdropper can read. Which technique solves this?
lab-cs.l10.q3.h: The need is to establish a secret without prior sharing.
lab-cs.l10.q3.e: Diffie-Hellman key exchange lets them derive a shared secret even though everything exchanged is public.

lab-cs.l10.q4.t: Because its security rests on the hardness of a problem, not on keeping the method secret
lab-cs.l10.q4.p: RSA's algorithm is public, yet it is still considered secure. Why?
lab-cs.l10.q4.h: What exactly must an attacker solve?
lab-cs.l10.q4.e: Modern cryptography relies on computational hardness: breaking the scheme requires solving a problem with no known efficient algorithm.

lab-cs.l11.q1.t: The serial fraction of the work
lab-cs.l11.q1.p: Amdahl's law shows that parallel speed-up is limited by
lab-cs.l11.q1.e: The part of the task that must run serially sets a hard cap on overall speed-up.

lab-cs.l11.q2.p: Moore's observation says transistor density roughly
lab-cs.l11.q2.e: The empirical trend is a doubling roughly every two years.

lab-cs.l11.q3.p: A job is 80 percent parallelisable and runs on 4 processors. What is the Amdahl speed-up?

lab-cs.l11.q4.p: If 90 percent of a task is parallelisable, what is the maximum possible speed-up however many processors you add?
lab-cs.l11.q4.h: Let n become very large and see what remains.
lab-cs.l11.q4.e: As n grows, p/n tends to zero, leaving S = 1 / (1 - 0.9) = 10.

lab-cs.l12.q1.t: Moves parameters a small step opposite the gradient to reduce the loss
lab-cs.l12.q1.e: Gradient descent updates parameters in the direction that most decreases the loss.

lab-cs.l12.q2.t: Fitting the training data while generalising to unseen examples
lab-cs.l12.q2.p: The central tension in machine learning is
lab-cs.l12.q2.h: A model that memorises the training set can fail elsewhere.
lab-cs.l12.q2.e: A useful model must perform well on new examples, not just the data it trained on.

lab-cs.l12.q3.p: A parameter is 5, the learning rate is 0.1 and the gradient of the loss is 4. What is the parameter after one gradient-descent step?

lab-cs.l12.q4.t: Steps overshoot the minimum and the loss may oscillate or diverge
lab-cs.l12.q4.p: What typically goes wrong if the learning rate is set far too large?
lab-cs.l12.q4.h: Imagine overshooting a valley again and again.
lab-cs.l12.q4.e: Overly large steps jump past the minimum, so training can bounce around or diverge.

lab-cs.l13.q1.p: The sigmoid activation maps any real input to
lab-cs.l13.q1.e: The sigmoid squashes values smoothly into the interval (0, 1).

lab-cs.l13.q2.t: Passes positive values unchanged and sets negative values to zero
lab-cs.l13.q2.p: What does the ReLU activation do?

lab-cs.l13.q3.p: A classifier's four output scores are all equal. After softmax, what probability does each class get?
lab-cs.l13.q3.e: Equal scores give equal probabilities that sum to 1, so each is 1/4 = 0.25.

lab-cs.l13.q4.t: Without them, stacked layers collapse into a single linear function
lab-cs.l13.q4.p: Why are nonlinear activation functions essential in a multi-layer network?
lab-cs.l13.q4.h: Compose two linear functions: what do you get?
lab-cs.l13.q4.e: Composing linear layers yields another linear function, so nonlinearity is what lets depth add expressive power.

lab-data.l01.q1.p: What range of values can a probability take?
lab-data.l01.q1.h: Impossible and certain are the endpoints.

lab-data.l01.q2.p: What did the Pascal and Fermat correspondence of the 1650s concern?
lab-data.l01.q2.h: Early probability grew from gambling questions.
lab-data.l01.q2.e: Probability theory began with their letters on problems of games of chance.

lab-data.l01.q3.p: A fair six-sided die is rolled once. What is the probability of getting an odd number?
lab-data.l01.q3.e: Three of six equally likely faces are odd, so the probability is 3/6 = 1/2.

lab-data.l01.q4.t: In about 30 of 100 similar situations it would rain
lab-data.l01.q4.p: A forecast says there is a 30 percent chance of rain. What is the best interpretation?
lab-data.l01.q4.e: Probability describes long-run frequency across similar situations, not the duration or area of rain.

lab-data.l02.q1.p: Which two parameters summarise a normal distribution?
lab-data.l02.q1.e: The normal distribution is determined by its mean mu and standard deviation sigma.

lab-data.l02.q2.p: About what percentage of values in a normal distribution lie within one standard deviation of the mean?
lab-data.l02.q2.e: Roughly 68 percent lie within one standard deviation, 95 percent within two and 99.7 percent within three.

lab-data.l02.q3.p: Test scores are roughly normal with mean 100 and standard deviation 15. About what proportion of scores lie between 85 and 115?
lab-data.l02.q3.h: Express 85 and 115 as distances from the mean.
lab-data.l02.q3.e: 85 and 115 are exactly one standard deviation below and above the mean, so about 68 percent fall in that range.

lab-data.l02.q4.t: Counts, bounded values and heavy-tailed quantities follow other distributions
lab-data.l02.q4.p: Why is it risky to assume all data are normally distributed?
lab-data.l02.q4.h: Think of incomes or event counts.
lab-data.l02.q4.e: Real data can be counts, bounded or heavy-tailed, and assuming normality when it does not hold can mislead an analysis.

lab-data.l03.q1.p: What does the central limit theorem say about the mean of many independent draws?
lab-data.l03.q1.h: Standardised means look like a bell curve.
lab-data.l03.q1.e: The standardised sample mean converges to a standard normal as n grows, regardless of the source distribution.

lab-data.l03.q2.p: What is the standard error of the sample mean?
lab-data.l03.q2.h: It shrinks as n grows, but not linearly.
lab-data.l03.q2.e: The standard deviation of a sample mean is sigma divided by the square root of n.

lab-data.l03.q3.p: Individual measurements have sigma = 20. What is the standard error of the mean of n = 100 measurements?

lab-data.l03.q4.p: A researcher wants to halve the standard error of a mean. By what factor must the sample size increase?
lab-data.l03.q4.h: Standard error depends on the square root of n.
lab-data.l03.q4.e: Because SE is proportional to 1 / sqrt(n), halving it requires sqrt(n) to double, so n must be four times larger.

lab-data.l04.q1.t: The probability of a hypothesis before seeing the new evidence
lab-data.l04.q1.p: In Bayes' theorem, what is the prior?
lab-data.l04.q1.e: The prior P(A) is your belief before the new evidence arrives.

lab-data.l04.q2.t: Ignoring how common the condition is to begin with
lab-data.l04.q2.p: Which concept is usually the cause of the base-rate fallacy?
lab-data.l04.q2.h: Think about rare diseases and accurate tests.
lab-data.l04.q2.e: The base-rate fallacy happens when people ignore the prior probability (how common something is).

lab-data.l04.q3.p: A disease affects 1 percent of people. A test finds 90 percent of sick people and wrongly flags 10 percent of healthy people. Of 1000 people, about what fraction of positive results are from sick people?
lab-data.l04.q3.h: Count true positives: 9. Count false positives: 99.
lab-data.l04.q3.e: 9 true positives out of 9 + 99 = 108 positives is about 8 percent.

lab-data.l04.q4.t: The evidence favours the first hypothesis over the second
lab-data.l04.q4.p: In the odds form of Bayes' rule, what does a likelihood ratio greater than 1 tell you?
lab-data.l04.q4.h: Posterior odds = likelihood ratio x prior odds.
lab-data.l04.q4.e: A likelihood ratio above 1 raises the odds in favour of the first hypothesis relative to the second.

lab-data.l05.q1.t: The probability of data at least this extreme if the null hypothesis were true
lab-data.l05.q1.h: It assumes the null is true.
lab-data.l05.q1.e: The p-value measures how surprising the data would be under the null hypothesis.

lab-data.l05.q2.p: What is a Type I error?
lab-data.l05.q2.e: A Type I error is a false positive: rejecting a null that is actually true.

lab-data.l05.q3.p: A test gives p = 0.03 and the chosen alpha is 0.05. What is the decision?
lab-data.l05.q3.e: Since 0.03 is below 0.05, the result is significant at that level and the null is rejected.

lab-data.l05.q4.p: A researcher runs 20 independent tests at alpha = 0.05 where no real effects exist. About how many false positives are expected?
lab-data.l05.q4.h: Multiply alpha by the number of tests.
lab-data.l05.q4.e: Expected false positives = 20 x 0.05 = 1, which is why multiple testing needs correction.

lab-data.l06.q1.p: What range can the Pearson correlation coefficient r take?

lab-data.l06.q2.p: Who championed exploratory data analysis and designed the box plot?
lab-data.l06.q2.h: He also coined the word bit.
lab-data.l06.q2.e: John Tukey founded exploratory data analysis and designed the box plot.

lab-data.l06.q3.t: A third factor, such as hot weather, probably drives both
lab-data.l06.q3.p: Ice-cream sales and drowning deaths are strongly positively correlated across months. What is the best conclusion?
lab-data.l06.q3.e: Summer heat increases both swimming and ice-cream buying, so the correlation does not show a causal link between them.

lab-data.l06.q4.p: Two variables have a perfect curved (U-shaped) relationship, yet r is close to 0. Why?
lab-data.l06.q4.h: What kind of pattern does r detect?
lab-data.l06.q4.e: Pearson r captures only straight-line relationships, so a strong nonlinear relationship can give a small r.

lab-data.l07.q1.t: The intercept: the prediction when x is 0
lab-data.l07.q1.p: In y-hat = b0 + b1 x, what does b0 represent?
lab-data.l07.q1.h: It is the value with no predictor contribution.
lab-data.l07.q1.e: The intercept b0 is the predicted response when all predictors equal 0.

lab-data.l07.q2.t: Extreme values tend to be followed by less extreme ones
lab-data.l07.q2.p: What does regression to the mean describe?
lab-data.l07.q2.h: Galton noticed it in parents' and children's heights.
lab-data.l07.q2.e: When values are selected for being extreme, later measurements tend to be closer to the average.

lab-data.l07.q3.p: A model predicts price (thousands) as 50 + 3 x, where x is area in square metres. What is the prediction for 40 square metres?

lab-data.l07.q4.t: The relationship may not hold there, so predictions can be nonsense
lab-data.l07.q4.p: Why is it unwise to use a fitted line far outside the range of its training data?
lab-data.l07.q4.e: A fitted relationship is only supported where there are data; extrapolating can give unrealistic predictions.

lab-data.l08.q1.e: Least squares chooses coefficients that minimise the sum of squared differences between observed and predicted values.

lab-data.l08.q2.p: Which two mathematicians are associated with the method of least squares?
lab-data.l08.q2.h: One of them also gave the normal distribution.
lab-data.l08.q2.e: Gauss and Legendre are credited with the method of least squares.

lab-data.l08.q3.p: Observed values are 2, 4, 6, 8 and predictions are 3, 4, 5, 10. What is the mean squared error?
lab-data.l08.q3.h: Square each error, add them, divide by 4.
lab-data.l08.q3.e: Squared errors are 1, 0, 1, 4, which sum to 6; dividing by 4 observations gives 1.5.

lab-data.l08.q4.t: Squaring gives large errors disproportionate weight
lab-data.l08.q4.p: Why is least squares sensitive to outliers?
lab-data.l08.q4.e: Because errors are squared, a single extreme point contributes a very large amount and can pull the fitted line toward it.

lab-data.l09.q1.p: What range of outputs does the sigmoid function produce?
lab-data.l09.q1.h: This is why it can represent probabilities.
lab-data.l09.q1.e: The sigmoid maps any real number into the interval between 0 and 1.

lab-data.l09.q2.p: What kind of outcome is logistic regression designed for?
lab-data.l09.q2.h: Think of spam versus not spam.
lab-data.l09.q2.e: Logistic regression models the probability of a binary outcome.

lab-data.l09.q3.p: In logistic regression the linear score z equals 0 for a case. What probability does the model give for y = 1?

lab-data.l09.q4.t: It can output values below 0 or above 1
lab-data.l09.q4.p: Why not use an ordinary straight-line regression to predict a probability?
lab-data.l09.q4.h: Think about the allowed range of a probability.
lab-data.l09.q4.e: A linear model is unbounded and can predict impossible probabilities; the sigmoid keeps outputs between 0 and 1.

lab-data.l10.q1.t: Modelling noise in the training data instead of the underlying signal
lab-data.l10.q1.h: Good on training data, poor on new data.
lab-data.l10.q1.e: An overfit model memorises the quirks of its training set and generalises poorly.

lab-data.l10.q2.t: Bias squared, variance and irreducible noise
lab-data.l10.q2.p: Which components make up expected squared error in the bias-variance decomposition?
lab-data.l10.q2.h: Three terms, one of which cannot be removed.
lab-data.l10.q2.e: Expected error = bias squared + variance + irreducible noise.

lab-data.l10.q3.p: A model has a training error of 0.1 and a test error of 2.5. What does this most likely indicate?
lab-data.l10.q3.e: A large gap between very low training error and high test error is the signature of overfitting.

lab-data.l10.q4.t: Its high variance means it fits the noise in each training sample
