lab-data.l10.q4.p: A very flexible model has low bias. Why can it still perform badly on new data?
lab-data.l10.q4.h: Think about how much the fit changes between samples.
lab-data.l10.q4.e: Flexible models can change a lot with each sample (high variance), so low bias alone does not ensure good generalisation.

lab-data.l11.q1.h: It adds lambda times a sum over coefficients.
lab-data.l11.q1.e: Ridge adds a penalty proportional to the sum of squared coefficients, shrinking them.

lab-data.l11.q2.p: Which method uses an L1 penalty and can set some coefficients exactly to zero?
lab-data.l11.q2.e: The lasso uses an L1 penalty, which induces sparsity by zeroing some coefficients.

lab-data.l11.q3.p: In 5-fold cross-validation, what fraction of the data is used for testing in each round?
lab-data.l11.q3.h: Divide the data into 5 equal parts.
lab-data.l11.q3.e: Each fold is one of 5 equal parts, so 1/5 = 20 percent is held out each time.

lab-data.l11.q4.t: Coefficients shrink toward zero, raising bias and lowering variance
lab-data.l11.q4.p: What happens as the ridge strength lambda is increased a lot?
lab-data.l11.q4.h: A bigger penalty means smaller coefficients.
lab-data.l11.q4.e: Stronger regularisation shrinks coefficients, making the model simpler: more bias but less variance.

lab-data.l12.q1.p: In gradient descent, what does the learning rate eta control?
lab-data.l12.q1.e: Eta scales the step taken against the gradient at each update.

lab-data.l12.q2.p: Which direction does gradient descent move the parameters?
lab-data.l12.q2.e: It subtracts the gradient, moving in the direction of steepest decrease of the loss.

lab-data.l12.q3.p: Starting at theta = 5 with learning rate 0.1 and gradient 4, what is the new theta?

lab-data.l12.q4.t: Steps overshoot, so the loss may bounce or diverge
lab-data.l12.q4.p: What is the most likely result of using a learning rate that is far too large?
lab-data.l12.q4.e: Overly large steps can jump past the minimum repeatedly, so training oscillates or diverges.

lab-data.l13.q1.t: The direction of greatest variance in the data
lab-data.l13.q1.p: What does the first principal component represent?
lab-data.l13.q1.e: The first principal component is the direction along which the data vary the most.

lab-data.l13.q2.p: Which methods are nonlinear techniques for visualising high-dimensional data?
lab-data.l13.q2.e: t-SNE and UMAP are nonlinear embeddings that preserve local neighbourhoods.

lab-data.l13.q3.p: The first two principal components explain 70 percent and 20 percent of the variance. How much do the two retain together?
lab-data.l13.q3.h: Principal components are orthogonal, so their variances add.
lab-data.l13.q3.e: The variances of orthogonal components add: 70 + 20 = 90 percent.

lab-data.l13.q4.t: t-SNE preserves local neighbourhoods, not global distances
lab-data.l13.q4.p: Why is it a mistake to read exact distances between far-apart clusters on a t-SNE plot as precise?
lab-data.l13.q4.h: Think about what the method tries to preserve.
lab-data.l13.q4.e: The method preserves local structure, so global distances between clusters are not reliably meaningful.

lab-earth.l01.q1.p: In an undisturbed sequence of sedimentary layers, which layer is the oldest?
lab-earth.l01.q1.h: Think about which layer had to be deposited first.
lab-earth.l01.q1.e: Each layer is deposited on top of those already there, so the lowest layer is oldest. This is the law of superposition.

lab-earth.l01.q2.p: Who first stated the law of superposition and the principle of original horizontality?
lab-earth.l01.q2.e: Nicolas Steno set out these principles in 1669, founding stratigraphy.

lab-earth.l01.q3.t: The fish lived after layer D and before layer B was deposited
lab-earth.l01.q3.p: A cliff shows five undisturbed layers, labelled A (top) to E (bottom). Fossils of a fish species appear in layer C. Which statement is supported?
lab-earth.l01.q3.h: Layers below C are older, layers above are younger.
lab-earth.l01.q3.e: Layer C sits above D, so it formed after D, and below B, so it formed before B.

lab-earth.l01.q4.t: Folding and faulting can tilt or overturn layers so the order is no longer simple
lab-earth.l01.q4.p: Why must a geologist be careful when applying superposition to mountain belts?
lab-earth.l01.q4.h: Think about what collisions do to flat layers.
lab-earth.l01.q4.e: Superposition applies to undisturbed sequences; folding and faulting can flip them, so other clues are needed.

lab-earth.l02.q1.t: The same slow natural processes that operate today shaped Earth over long times
lab-earth.l02.q1.h: The present is a key to the past.
lab-earth.l02.q1.e: Hutton and Lyell argued that ongoing processes like erosion and deposition, acting over deep time, explain the rock record.

lab-earth.l02.q2.t: A gap in the rock record representing a long span of time
lab-earth.l02.q2.p: What does an unconformity such as Siccar Point show?
lab-earth.l02.q2.e: Tilted older strata overlain by flat younger strata record deposition, tilting, erosion and new deposition, which takes vast time.

lab-earth.l02.q3.p: A river cuts down into rock at 2 millimetres per year. About how deep a gorge could it cut in 5 million years, assuming a steady rate?
lab-earth.l02.q3.h: Multiply the rate by the time, then convert millimetres to metres.
lab-earth.l02.q3.e: 2 mm times 5 000 000 years is 10 000 000 mm, which equals 10 000 m. Real rivers slow down, but it shows how small rates add up.

lab-earth.l02.q4.t: It accepts them as natural events governed by the same laws
lab-earth.l02.q4.p: Which statement best describes how uniformitarianism treats sudden events like floods or eruptions?
lab-earth.l02.q4.h: The key word is "same laws", not "same rates".
lab-earth.l02.q4.e: The principle is that natural laws are constant; rare, rapid events are part of the normal behaviour of the planet.

lab-earth.l03.q1.t: The time for half of the parent atoms to decay
lab-earth.l03.q1.h: It is about half of the starting amount.
lab-earth.l03.q1.e: After one half-life half of the original parent atoms remain.

lab-earth.l03.q2.p: About how old is Earth, according to radiometric dating of meteorites and the oldest rocks?
lab-earth.l03.q2.h: Clair Patterson found about 4.55 billion years in 1956.
lab-earth.l03.q2.e: Lead-isotope dating of meteorites and old rocks gives about 4.54 billion years.

lab-earth.l03.q3.p: An isotope has a half-life of 100 million years. A mineral now contains 1/8 of the parent atoms it started with. How old is the mineral?
lab-earth.l03.q3.h: Count how many halvings take you from 1 to 1/8.
lab-earth.l03.q3.e: 1 to 1/2 to 1/4 to 1/8 is three half-lives, so 3 times 100 million equals 300 million years.

lab-earth.l03.q4.t: Their crystals lock in parent atoms when the rock crystallises, starting the clock
lab-earth.l03.q4.p: Why are igneous rocks usually the best candidates for radiometric dating?
lab-earth.l03.q4.h: Think about when the clock starts.
lab-earth.l03.q4.e: A crystallising magma traps parent isotopes but not daughters, so the ratio gives the time since crystallisation. Sedimentary grains date older rocks that were eroded.

lab-earth.l04.q1.p: Which type of rock forms when molten rock cools and crystallises?
lab-earth.l04.q1.h: The word comes from the Latin for fire.
lab-earth.l04.q1.e: Igneous rocks form from cooling magma or lava.

lab-earth.l04.q2.t: A natural inorganic solid with a definite composition and crystal structure
lab-earth.l04.q2.e: Minerals are naturally occurring, inorganic solids with a defined chemistry and ordered crystal structure.

lab-earth.l04.q3.p: Limestone is buried deep and heated and squeezed without fully melting. What does it become?
lab-earth.l04.q3.h: Heat and pressure change an existing rock.
lab-earth.l04.q3.e: Limestone recrystallises to marble, a metamorphic rock.

lab-earth.l04.q4.t: Any rock type can be transformed into another through several possible paths
lab-earth.l04.q4.p: Which statement about the rock cycle is accurate?
lab-earth.l04.q4.h: It is a cycle, not a ladder.
lab-earth.l04.q4.e: Weathering, burial, heat, pressure, melting and uplift can connect any rock type to any other, in no fixed order.

lab-earth.l05.q1.p: At which type of plate boundary is new crust created at mid-ocean ridges?
lab-earth.l05.q1.e: At divergent boundaries plates pull apart and rising magma forms new crust.

lab-earth.l05.q2.p: How fast do tectonic plates typically move?
lab-earth.l05.q2.h: About the speed of fingernail growth.
lab-earth.l05.q2.e: GPS measurements show plates creeping a few centimetres each year.

lab-earth.l05.q3.p: A plate moves at 5 centimetres per year. How far does it travel in 10 million years?
lab-earth.l05.q3.h: 5 cm times 10 000 000, then convert to kilometres (100 000 cm per km).
lab-earth.l05.q3.e: 5 cm times 10 million equals 50 million cm, which is 500 km.

lab-earth.l05.q4.t: Subduction zones ring much of the Pacific, where one plate sinks beneath another
lab-earth.l05.q4.p: Why do the largest earthquakes and volcanic arcs often occur together along the edges of the Pacific Ocean?
lab-earth.l05.q4.h: Think about what happens at convergent boundaries with oceanic plates.
lab-earth.l05.q4.e: Subduction produces great earthquakes and melts that feed volcanic arcs, and many subduction zones line the Pacific.

lab-earth.l06.q1.p: Who proposed continental drift in 1915 and the supercontinent Pangaea?
lab-earth.l06.q1.e: Alfred Wegener argued the continents were once joined as Pangaea.

lab-earth.l06.q2.t: Seafloor spreading: new crust forms at ridges and old crust sinks at trenches
lab-earth.l06.q2.p: What did Harry Hess propose in 1962?
lab-earth.l06.q2.e: Hess provided the mechanism that was missing from continental drift.

lab-earth.l06.q3.t: New crust forms at the ridge and spreads outward, recording magnetic reversals
lab-earth.l06.q3.p: Magnetic stripes on the ocean floor are symmetric on both sides of a ridge. What does this best support?
lab-earth.l06.q3.h: Think about a tape recorder running outward from the ridge.
lab-earth.l06.q3.e: Basalt records the field as it cools; mirror-image stripes show that crust was added at the ridge and moved apart.

lab-earth.l06.q4.t: He could not explain a mechanism that could move continents
lab-earth.l06.q4.p: Why was Wegener's hypothesis rejected by most scientists for decades?
lab-earth.l06.q4.h: The evidence was matching coasts and fossils, but what was missing?
lab-earth.l06.q4.e: The evidence for fit was strong, but without a mechanism the idea was unconvincing. Seafloor spreading later supplied one.

lab-earth.l07.q1.p: Which of these is a place where magma commonly forms?
lab-earth.l07.q1.h: Water released by the sinking plate matters.
lab-earth.l07.q1.e: Magma forms at spreading ridges, above subducting slabs and above hotspots.

lab-earth.l07.q2.p: What kind of volcano is built by runny, gas-poor basaltic lava?
lab-earth.l07.q2.e: Fluid basaltic lava spreads out to form broad, gently sloping shield volcanoes.

lab-earth.l07.q3.t: The Pacific plate moved over a fixed mantle plume
lab-earth.l07.q3.p: The Hawaiian-Emperor chain gets older to the northwest away from Hawaii. What does this indicate?
lab-earth.l07.q3.h: Which one moved, the plate or the source of magma?
lab-earth.l07.q3.e: The plate carries older volcanoes away as it moves over a source that stays roughly in place.

lab-earth.l07.q4.t: Gas cannot escape easily, so pressure builds up
lab-earth.l07.q4.p: Why does sticky, gas-rich magma tend to erupt more explosively than runny magma?
lab-earth.l07.q4.h: Think of a shaken soda bottle.
lab-earth.l07.q4.e: High viscosity traps dissolved gas until pressure builds and releases explosively.

lab-earth.l08.q1.p: Which seismic wave is the fastest and arrives first?
lab-earth.l08.q1.e: P-waves are compressional and travel faster than S-waves and surface waves.

lab-earth.l08.q2.p: Who discovered Earth's solid inner core?
lab-earth.l08.q2.h: A Danish seismologist who analysed waves in 1936.
lab-earth.l08.q2.e: Inge Lehmann found that waves reflecting within the core showed a solid inner core.

lab-earth.l08.q3.p: S-waves are not detected on the far side of Earth after passing through the core. What does this suggest?
lab-earth.l08.q3.h: Shear waves cannot travel through liquids.
lab-earth.l08.q3.e: Because S-waves cannot pass through liquid, their absence indicates a liquid outer core.

lab-earth.l08.q4.t: Wave speed depends on the material, so a jump means the material changes
lab-earth.l08.q4.p: Why does a sudden jump in seismic wave speed at shallow depth indicate a boundary between layers?
lab-earth.l08.q4.h: Speed depends on the properties of what the wave is travelling through.
lab-earth.l08.q4.e: Mohorovicic found that speed changes sharply at a depth where rock composition changes, from crust to mantle.

lab-earth.l09.q1.t: Each whole number represents a tenfold change in wave amplitude
lab-earth.l09.q1.p: Why is the Richter scale described as logarithmic?
lab-earth.l09.q1.e: Each unit on the scale means ten times larger recorded amplitude.

lab-earth.l09.q2.p: Which scale do seismologists now prefer for large earthquakes because it does not saturate?
lab-earth.l09.q2.h: It is tied to the fault slip and energy.
lab-earth.l09.q2.e: Moment magnitude is based on seismic moment and works for the largest quakes.

lab-earth.l09.q3.p: A magnitude 7 earthquake produces waves with how many times the amplitude of a magnitude 5 earthquake?
lab-earth.l09.q3.h: Two units apart, each unit a factor of ten.

lab-earth.l09.q4.p: A region records about 2000 earthquakes of magnitude 3 or greater in a year. Using the Gutenberg-Richter law with b = 1, roughly how many of magnitude 5 or greater would you expect?
lab-earth.l09.q4.h: Each magnitude unit up means about ten times fewer; go up two units.
lab-earth.l09.q4.e: Two units up means 10 times 10 = 100 times fewer, so 2000 divided by 100 equals 20.

lab-earth.l10.q1.t: Differences in water density from temperature and salinity
lab-earth.l10.q1.p: What drives the deep global ocean conveyor (thermohaline circulation)?
lab-earth.l10.q1.e: Cold salty water sinks near the poles and drives a slow overturning circulation.

lab-earth.l10.q2.p: Where is the Coriolis effect zero?
lab-earth.l10.q2.e: The sine of 0 degrees is zero, so the Coriolis parameter vanishes at the equator.

lab-earth.l10.q3.p: Using c = sqrt(g d) with g about 10 m/s squared, how fast does a shallow-water wave travel over ocean 4000 metres deep?
lab-earth.l10.q3.h: Compute g times d first, then take the square root.
lab-earth.l10.q3.e: 10 times 4000 is 40 000, and its square root is 200 m/s, about 720 km/h.

lab-earth.l10.q4.t: Water depth decreases, so the wave slows and its energy is compressed into a taller wave
lab-earth.l10.q4.p: Why does a tsunami grow taller as it approaches a shore?
lab-earth.l10.q4.e: In shallower water the wave slows, so the water piles up and the wave height increases.

lab-earth.l11.q1.t: The fraction of sunlight a surface reflects
lab-earth.l11.q1.e: Albedo is the fraction of incoming sunlight that is reflected back to space.

lab-earth.l11.q2.p: Which of these is a greenhouse gas?
lab-earth.l11.q2.e: Methane, CO2 and water vapour absorb infrared; nitrogen and argon do not.

lab-earth.l11.q3.p: If a planet's albedo increases while the sunlight it receives stays the same, what happens to its equilibrium temperature?
lab-earth.l11.q3.h: More reflection means less absorbed energy.
lab-earth.l11.q3.e: The term (1 - albedo) shrinks, so absorbed energy falls and the equilibrium temperature drops.

lab-earth.l11.q4.t: Greenhouse gases absorb and re-emit outgoing infrared, warming the surface
lab-earth.l11.q4.p: Earth's equilibrium temperature without greenhouse gases is about minus 18 degrees Celsius, but the actual average is about plus 15. Which explanation is best?
lab-earth.l11.q4.e: The natural greenhouse effect raises the surface about 33 degrees above the no-atmosphere value.

lab-earth.l12.q1.t: Atmospheric CO2 measured at Mauna Loa since 1958
lab-earth.l12.q1.p: What does the Keeling Curve show?
lab-earth.l12.q1.h: It was started by Charles Keeling.
lab-earth.l12.q1.e: The Keeling Curve is the continuous Mauna Loa CO2 record, showing a seasonal cycle and a steady rise.

lab-earth.l12.q2.t: Seasonal uptake and release of CO2 by plants and the biosphere
lab-earth.l12.q2.p: What does the yearly sawtooth in the Keeling Curve reflect?
lab-earth.l12.q2.h: Northern forests dominate the land area.
lab-earth.l12.q2.e: Plants absorb CO2 in the growing season and release it in winter, so the biosphere appears to breathe.

lab-earth.l12.q3.p: Using delta F = 5.35 ln(C / C0), how do the forcings compare for a rise from 280 to 560 ppm and a rise from 560 to 1120 ppm?
lab-earth.l12.q3.h: Look at the ratio C / C0 in each case.
lab-earth.l12.q3.e: Each is a doubling, so C / C0 equals 2 both times and the forcing is the same, about 3.7 W per square metre.

lab-earth.l12.q4.t: Plants preferentially take up carbon-12, so carbon from ancient plants is relatively low in carbon-13
lab-earth.l12.q4.p: Why does a falling carbon-13 to carbon-12 ratio in the atmosphere point to fossil fuels as a source of added CO2?
lab-earth.l12.q4.h: Fossil fuels come from long-buried living matter.
lab-earth.l12.q4.e: Photosynthesis favours the lighter isotope, so fossil-derived carbon lowers the atmospheric carbon-13 ratio (the Suess effect).

lab-earth.l13.q1.p: Which three orbital factors make up the Milankovitch cycles?
lab-earth.l13.q1.h: Orbit shape, axial tilt and axial wobble.
lab-earth.l13.q1.e: Variations in orbit shape, axial tilt and precession pace the glacial cycles.

lab-earth.l13.q2.t: About 800 000 years of CO2 and temperature
lab-earth.l13.q2.p: What do the Vostok and EPICA ice cores record?
lab-earth.l13.q2.h: Air bubbles trapped in ancient ice.
lab-earth.l13.q2.e: Trapped air bubbles preserve a record of CO2, and the ice itself records temperature.

lab-earth.l13.q3.t: Orbital cycles are too slow to account for it
lab-earth.l13.q3.p: Orbital cycles operate over tens of thousands of years. What does that imply for the warming seen over the last 100 years?
lab-earth.l13.q3.e: Changes in orbit are far too gradual to explain warming within a century.

lab-earth.l13.q4.t: The orbital change in total yearly sunlight is small, so processes like ice-albedo and CO2 release amplify the effect
lab-earth.l13.q4.p: Why are feedbacks needed to explain ice-age swings from a small orbital change?
lab-earth.l13.q4.h: Think about what happens when ice melts or forms.
lab-earth.l13.q4.e: The orbital nudge changes seasonal sunlight slightly; ice-albedo and CO2 feedbacks magnify it into full glacial cycles.

lab-engineering.l01.q1.t: The sum of forces is zero and the sum of moments is zero
lab-engineering.l01.q1.p: Which pair of conditions must hold for a body to be in static equilibrium?
lab-engineering.l01.q1.h: There are two conditions, one about pushes and one about turning.
lab-engineering.l01.q1.e: Static equilibrium requires both the net force and the net moment to be zero.

lab-engineering.l01.q2.p: What are the usual SI units of a moment?
lab-engineering.l01.q2.h: A moment is a force multiplied by a distance.
lab-engineering.l01.q2.e: A moment is force times perpendicular distance, so it is measured in newton-metres.

lab-engineering.l01.q3.p: A seesaw is balanced on a central pivot. A child weighing 300 N sits 2 m from the pivot. What force at 1.5 m on the other side will balance it?
lab-engineering.l01.q3.h: Set weight times distance equal on both sides.
lab-engineering.l01.q3.e: Moments balance: 300 N x 2 m = 600 N·m, so the other force is 600 / 1.5 = 400 N.

lab-engineering.l01.q4.t: The moments of the two forces do not cancel
lab-engineering.l01.q4.p: Two equal and opposite forces act on a plank at different points along it. The net force is zero, yet the plank rotates. Why?
lab-engineering.l01.q4.h: Think about which of the two equilibrium conditions is violated.
lab-engineering.l01.q4.e: The pair forms a couple: the force condition is met but the net moment is not zero, so the plank spins.

lab-engineering.l02.q1.e: Stress is the internal force carried per unit area, in pascals.

lab-engineering.l02.q2.h: Think of change in length divided by original length.
lab-engineering.l02.q2.e: Strain is deformation divided by original length, so it has no units.

lab-engineering.l02.q3.p: A steel bar has Young's modulus of 200 GPa and is stretched elastically to a strain of 0.001. What is the stress?
lab-engineering.l02.q3.h: Use stress = E x strain and watch the prefixes.

lab-engineering.l02.q4.t: Steel needs much more stress than rubber to reach the same strain
lab-engineering.l02.q4.p: Steel has a much larger Young's modulus than rubber. What does this tell you?
lab-engineering.l02.q4.h: Rearrange sigma = E x epsilon for the same strain.
lab-engineering.l02.q4.e: For equal strain, stress is proportional to E, so the stiffer steel requires far more stress.

lab-engineering.l03.q1.p: In the axial deformation formula delta = PL / AE, what happens to the elongation if the bar length doubles (all else equal)?
lab-engineering.l03.q1.e: Elongation is proportional to length, so doubling L doubles delta.

lab-engineering.l03.q2.p: Which property of a material appears in the axial deformation formula?
lab-engineering.l03.q2.h: It is the stiffness constant of Hooke's law.
lab-engineering.l03.q2.e: The formula uses the elastic modulus E, in pascals, as the stiffness of the bar.

lab-engineering.l03.q3.p: A steel bar (E = 200 GPa) is 2 m long with a cross-sectional area of 500 mm2 (0.0005 m2) and carries an axial load of 10 kN. How much does it stretch?
lab-engineering.l03.q3.h: Convert everything to newtons, metres and pascals before substituting.

lab-engineering.l03.q4.p: A rod carries the same load, but its diameter is doubled while its length and material stay the same. By what factor does its elongation change?
lab-engineering.l03.q4.h: Area depends on the square of the diameter.
lab-engineering.l03.q4.e: Area grows by a factor of 4 when the diameter doubles, so delta falls to one quarter.

lab-engineering.l04.q1.t: At the outermost fibres, farthest from the neutral axis
lab-engineering.l04.q1.p: Where in a beam cross-section is the bending stress greatest?
lab-engineering.l04.q1.h: Look at what c means in the formula.
lab-engineering.l04.q1.e: Stress is proportional to c, the distance from the neutral axis, so it peaks at the outer surface.

lab-engineering.l04.q2.t: The second moment of area of the cross-section
lab-engineering.l04.q2.p: In sigma = Mc / I, what does I represent?
lab-engineering.l04.q2.h: Its unit is m to the fourth power.
lab-engineering.l04.q2.e: I is the second moment of area, a shape property measuring resistance to bending.

lab-engineering.l04.q3.p: A beam section carries a bending moment of 1000 N·m. The farthest fibre is 0.1 m from the neutral axis and I = 5 x 10^-5 m^4. What is the maximum bending stress?
lab-engineering.l04.q3.h: Compute M x c first, then divide by I.

lab-engineering.l04.q4.t: Placing material far from the neutral axis greatly increases I, so the beam resists bending better for its weight
lab-engineering.l04.q4.p: Why are steel beams commonly shaped as I-sections rather than solid squares of the same weight?
lab-engineering.l04.q4.h: Think about where in the section the material does the most work.
lab-engineering.l04.q4.e: Material in the flanges is far from the neutral axis, which raises I efficiently and reduces bending stress for the same weight.

lab-engineering.l05.q1.p: Buckling of a slender column is best described as
lab-engineering.l05.q1.h: Think of pressing the ends of a ruler.
lab-engineering.l05.q1.e: Buckling is a stability failure where the column suddenly bows sideways, usually below the crushing stress.

lab-engineering.l05.q2.p: In Euler's critical load formula P_cr = pi^2 EI / (KL)^2, which change raises the critical load?
lab-engineering.l05.q2.e: P_cr grows with EI and falls with the square of the effective length KL.

lab-engineering.l05.q3.p: A pinned column of length 3 m has a critical load of 40 kN. Another identical column, but 6 m long, has what critical load?
lab-engineering.l05.q3.h: Length appears squared in the denominator.
lab-engineering.l05.q3.e: Doubling L multiplies (KL)^2 by 4, so P_cr falls to 40 / 4 = 10 kN.

lab-engineering.l05.q4.t: Its critical load falls with the square of length, so instability occurs before the crushing stress is reached
lab-engineering.l05.q4.p: Why can a long, thin strut fail at a load far below what would crush the same material in a short block?
lab-engineering.l05.q4.h: Compare which limit is reached first as the member gets longer.
lab-engineering.l05.q4.e: Because P_cr scales as 1/L^2, a slender member reaches its buckling load long before the material is crushed.

lab-engineering.l06.q1.t: The ratio of failure stress to allowable working stress
lab-engineering.l06.q1.p: What does the factor of safety measure?
lab-engineering.l06.q1.h: It is a ratio of two stresses.
lab-engineering.l06.q1.e: FS = ultimate (failure) stress divided by allowable working stress.

lab-engineering.l06.q2.p: A factor of safety of exactly 1 means the part is designed to work at its failure stress, leaving no margin.
lab-engineering.l06.q2.e: FS = 1 means working stress equals failure stress, so there is no reserve for uncertainty.

lab-engineering.l06.q3.p: A steel part fails at an ultimate stress of 400 MPa. If the design uses a factor of safety of 2.5, what is the allowable working stress?
lab-engineering.l06.q3.h: Divide the ultimate stress by the factor of safety.

lab-engineering.l06.q4.t: It adds cost and weight, so the factor must balance risk against practicality
lab-engineering.l06.q4.p: Why do engineers not simply use a very large factor of safety on every design?
lab-engineering.l06.q4.e: A bigger factor means more material, weight and expense, so engineers choose it by weighing uncertainty and consequences of failure.

lab-engineering.l07.q1.p: The first law of thermodynamics is a statement of
lab-engineering.l07.q1.h: Heat and work are both forms of energy transfer.
lab-engineering.l07.q1.e: The first law says energy is conserved: delta U = Q - W.

lab-engineering.l07.q2.t: The system does work on its surroundings, lowering its internal energy
lab-engineering.l07.q2.p: In delta U = Q - W, what does a positive W mean?
lab-engineering.l07.q2.h: W is defined as work done by the system.
lab-engineering.l07.q2.e: With this convention, work done by the system takes energy out, reducing internal energy.

lab-engineering.l07.q3.p: A gas absorbs 500 J of heat and does 200 J of work on a piston. What is the change in its internal energy?
lab-engineering.l07.q3.h: Subtract the work done by the system from the heat added.

lab-engineering.l07.q4.t: Over a full cycle delta U is zero, so work out cannot exceed net heat in
lab-engineering.l07.q4.p: An inventor claims a cyclic engine absorbs 1000 J of heat per cycle and delivers 1200 J of work per cycle. What is wrong?
lab-engineering.l07.q4.h: What is delta U after the engine returns to its starting state?
lab-engineering.l07.q4.e: Over a cycle delta U = 0, so W = Q. Delivering more work than heat absorbed would violate energy conservation.

lab-engineering.l08.q1.t: The temperatures of the hot and cold reservoirs
lab-engineering.l08.q1.p: The Carnot efficiency of a heat engine depends only on
lab-engineering.l08.q1.h: Look at the variables in 1 - Tc/Th.
lab-engineering.l08.q1.e: eta = 1 - T_C / T_H uses only the two reservoir temperatures.

lab-engineering.l08.q2.p: Which temperature scale must be used in the Carnot formula?
lab-engineering.l08.q2.h: The ratio needs a true zero point.
lab-engineering.l08.q2.e: The formula uses ratios of absolute temperatures, so kelvin is required.

lab-engineering.l08.q3.p: An ideal engine takes heat at 600 K and rejects it at 300 K. What is its maximum efficiency?

lab-engineering.l08.q4.t: It is impossible, since the Carnot limit is 50 percent
lab-engineering.l08.q4.p: A manufacturer claims a heat engine running between 600 K and 300 K is 60 percent efficient. What can you conclude?
lab-engineering.l08.q4.h: Compare the claim with the Carnot ceiling.
lab-engineering.l08.q4.e: No engine can beat the Carnot limit, which here is 50 percent, so 60 percent cannot be achieved.

lab-engineering.l09.q1.p: According to Bernoulli's principle, in steady ideal flow along a horizontal streamline, where the fluid speeds up the static pressure
lab-engineering.l09.q1.e: The sum of pressure and kinetic terms is conserved, so faster flow means lower static pressure.

lab-engineering.l09.q2.p: The Reynolds number compares which two quantities?
lab-engineering.l09.q2.h: The formula contains density, speed, length and viscosity.
lab-engineering.l09.q2.e: Re is the ratio of inertial to viscous forces and predicts laminar versus turbulent flow.

lab-engineering.l09.q3.p: Water (density 1000 kg/m3, viscosity 0.001 Pa·s) flows at 2 m/s in a pipe of 0.05 m diameter. What is the Reynolds number?
lab-engineering.l09.q3.h: Multiply density, speed and diameter, then divide by viscosity.

lab-engineering.l09.q4.t: Speed increases and static pressure falls
lab-engineering.l09.q4.p: Water flows through a horizontal pipe that narrows. What happens in the narrow section?
lab-engineering.l09.q4.h: Think of continuity (same flow through a smaller area) together with Bernoulli.
lab-engineering.l09.q4.e: Through a narrower area the water must move faster, and by Bernoulli its static pressure drops.

lab-engineering.l10.q1.e: The voltage across a resistor equals the current through it multiplied by its resistance.

lab-engineering.l10.q2.p: Which expression gives the power dissipated in a resistor in terms of current and resistance?
lab-engineering.l10.q2.h: Combine P = VI with Ohm's law.
lab-engineering.l10.q2.e: Substituting V = IR into P = VI gives P = I^2 R.

lab-engineering.l10.q3.p: A 10 ohm resistor carries a current of 2 A. How much power does it dissipate?

lab-engineering.l10.q4.p: The current through a fixed resistor is doubled. What happens to the heat it produces?
lab-engineering.l10.q4.h: Power depends on the square of current.
lab-engineering.l10.q4.e: Since P = I^2 R, doubling I multiplies the power by 4.

lab-engineering.l11.q1.t: The currents into the node sum to zero (current in equals current out)
lab-engineering.l11.q1.p: Kirchhoff's current law says that at any node
lab-engineering.l11.q1.h: It is a conservation law for charge.
lab-engineering.l11.q1.e: Charge cannot accumulate at a node, so total current in equals total current out.

lab-engineering.l11.q2.p: Kirchhoff's voltage law is a consequence of conservation of
lab-engineering.l11.q2.h: A charge going round a loop returns to its starting potential.
lab-engineering.l11.q2.e: Voltage rises and drops around a closed loop sum to zero because energy is conserved.

lab-engineering.l11.q3.p: At a junction, 5 A and 2 A flow in. One branch carries 4 A out. What current does the other branch carry out?
lab-engineering.l11.q3.h: Total in must equal total out.
lab-engineering.l11.q3.e: Current in is 7 A; 4 A leaves on one branch, leaving 7 - 4 = 3 A on the other.

lab-engineering.l11.q4.t: Around the closed loop, the voltage rise from the source equals the total drop, reflecting conservation of energy
lab-engineering.l11.q4.p: A 12 V source drives two resistors in series. If the first resistor drops 5 V, the second drops 7 V. Why must these drops add to 12 V?
lab-engineering.l11.q4.h: Think about a charge going once around the loop.
lab-engineering.l11.q4.e: KVL: the source raises potential by 12 V and the resistor drops remove the same total, so 5 + 7 = 12.

lab-engineering.l12.q1.p: In a feedback controller, the error is
lab-engineering.l12.q1.h: It is the gap the controller tries to close.
lab-engineering.l12.q1.e: Error is the setpoint minus the measured output, and the controller acts to shrink it.

lab-engineering.l12.q2.p: Which term of a PID controller responds to the accumulated past error?
lab-engineering.l12.q2.h: Accumulating is what an integral does.
lab-engineering.l12.q2.e: The integral term sums error over time, which removes lingering offset.

lab-engineering.l12.q3.p: A proportional controller has Kp = 2 and the measured error is 3 degrees. What is the proportional output?

lab-engineering.l12.q4.t: The controller overcorrects, overshoots the setpoint and then overcorrects the other way
lab-engineering.l12.q4.p: Why can too much feedback gain make a system oscillate?
lab-engineering.l12.q4.h: Picture steering a car with huge steering movements.
lab-engineering.l12.q4.e: Excessive gain (or delay) makes each correction too big, so the loop swings past the target repeatedly or becomes unstable.

lab-engineering.l13.q1.t: A small voltage or current controls a much larger one, enabling switching and amplification
lab-engineering.l13.q1.p: What key capability does a transistor provide?
lab-engineering.l13.q1.e: The control of a larger current by a small input is the basis of amplifiers and digital switches.

lab-engineering.l13.q2.p: Where and when was the first transistor demonstrated?
lab-engineering.l13.q2.e: The point-contact transistor was demonstrated at Bell Labs in 1947.

lab-engineering.l13.q3.p: A channel has a bandwidth of 1 MHz and a signal-to-noise ratio of 3. What is its Shannon capacity?

lab-engineering.l13.q4.t: It is impossible, since no coding can exceed the channel capacity for error-free communication
lab-engineering.l13.q4.p: A vendor claims error-free transmission at 5 Mbit/s over the channel above (capacity 2 Mbit/s). What does Shannon's theorem say?
lab-engineering.l13.q4.e: The Shannon-Hartley capacity is the maximum error-free rate, so 5 Mbit/s cannot be reached.

lab-environment.l01.q1.e: Arthur Tansley introduced the word for a community of organisms together with its physical environment.

lab-environment.l01.q2.t: The thin global zone in which life exists
lab-environment.l01.q2.e: The biosphere is the global sum of living things and the zone they inhabit, linking life with rock, water and air.

lab-environment.l01.q3.t: The effects can spread through the pond's food web and water chemistry
lab-environment.l01.q3.p: Fertiliser runs off a farm into a pond. Which statement best reflects the ecosystem view?
lab-environment.l01.q3.h: Think about how parts of an ecosystem are linked.
lab-environment.l01.q3.e: In an ecosystem, organisms and their physical environment are linked, so a change in one part spreads to others.

lab-environment.l01.q4.t: He treated climate, altitude and life as parts of a single connected web
lab-environment.l01.q4.p: Why was Humboldt's approach to nature considered new?
lab-environment.l01.q4.h: Contrast a catalogue with a system.
lab-environment.l01.q4.e: Humboldt connected vegetation belts to climate and altitude and even noted human influence on climate, a systems view.

lab-environment.l02.q1.t: They break down dead material and return nutrients
lab-environment.l02.q1.p: What is the role of decomposers in an ecosystem?
lab-environment.l02.q1.e: Decomposers recycle nutrients from dead organisms back into the soil and water.

lab-environment.l02.q2.p: Roughly what fraction of energy is lost at each trophic step?
lab-environment.l02.q2.h: Only about a tenth is passed on.
lab-environment.l02.q2.e: Roughly 90 percent is lost, mainly as heat, so only about 10 percent reaches the next level.

lab-environment.l02.q3.p: Producers in a meadow fix 20 000 kJ of energy. Using the 10 percent rule, about how much reaches the secondary consumers (carnivores that eat herbivores)?
lab-environment.l02.q3.e: 20 000 times 0.1 is 2000 for herbivores, and 2000 times 0.1 is 200 kJ for carnivores.

lab-environment.l02.q4.t: Energy is lost at each level, leaving little to support the top
lab-environment.l02.q4.p: Why are there so few top predators compared with herbivores?
lab-environment.l02.q4.e: With most energy lost at each step, the upper levels have too little energy to support many individuals.

lab-environment.l03.q1.t: The maximum population the environment can sustain
lab-environment.l03.q1.h: The limit in the logistic equation.
lab-environment.l03.q1.e: K is the population size that the available resources can support in the long term.

lab-environment.l03.q2.p: An outbreak will grow if the basic reproduction number R0 is...
lab-environment.l03.q2.h: Each case must cause more than one new case.
lab-environment.l03.q2.e: If R0 is above 1, each infection causes more than one new infection on average, so the outbreak grows.

lab-environment.l03.q3.p: Using dN/dt = r N (1 - N/K) with r = 0.2 per year, N = 400 and K = 800, what is the population growth per year?
lab-environment.l03.q3.e: 1 - 400/800 = 0.5, so dN/dt = 0.2 times 400 times 0.5 = 40 individuals per year.

lab-environment.l03.q4.t: Resources become limiting, shrinking the factor (1 - N/K) toward zero
lab-environment.l03.q4.p: Why does logistic growth slow down as N approaches K?
lab-environment.l03.q4.h: Look at what happens to the bracket term.
lab-environment.l03.q4.e: The term (1 - N/K) approaches zero as N approaches K, representing limits on resources.

lab-environment.l04.q1.p: Who first showed in 1856 that carbon dioxide traps heat from sunlight?
lab-environment.l04.q1.e: Eunice Foote showed that a jar of carbon dioxide heated more in sunlight and cooled more slowly.

lab-environment.l04.q2.p: Which pair of numbers describes Earth's average surface temperature with and without the natural greenhouse effect?
lab-environment.l04.q2.e: Earth averages about +15 C, but without greenhouse gases it would be near -18 C.

lab-environment.l04.q3.p: Which gas is NOT a significant greenhouse gas?
lab-environment.l04.q3.h: It makes up most of the atmosphere but does not absorb infrared strongly.
lab-environment.l04.q3.e: Molecular nitrogen does not absorb infrared radiation significantly; the others do.

lab-environment.l04.q4.t: They absorb outgoing infrared and re-emit part of it downward
lab-environment.l04.q4.p: Why do greenhouse gases warm the surface even though they do not add heat from the Sun?
lab-environment.l04.q4.h: Think about what happens to the infrared leaving the surface.
lab-environment.l04.q4.e: They slow the escape of infrared to space, so the surface warms until energy out again equals energy in.

lab-environment.l05.q1.t: The fourth power of absolute temperature
lab-environment.l05.q1.p: According to the Stefan-Boltzmann law, radiated power per area is proportional to what?
lab-environment.l05.q1.h: j = sigma T to the fourth.
lab-environment.l05.q1.e: j = sigma T^4, so doubling absolute temperature gives sixteen times the output.

lab-environment.l05.q2.t: The fraction of incoming sunlight reflected by a surface
lab-environment.l05.q2.h: Fresh snow has a high value.
lab-environment.l05.q2.e: Albedo measures reflectivity, from 0 (absorbs everything) to 1 (reflects everything).

lab-environment.l05.q3.p: A surface's absolute temperature rises from 200 K to 400 K. By what factor does its radiated power per area increase?
lab-environment.l05.q3.h: The temperature doubled; apply the fourth power.

lab-environment.l05.q4.t: Dark open water absorbs more sunlight than reflective ice, so albedo falls
lab-environment.l05.q4.p: Why does melting sea ice amplify warming?
lab-environment.l05.q4.h: Compare what each surface does to sunlight.
lab-environment.l05.q4.e: Replacing bright ice with dark ocean lowers albedo, so more sunlight is absorbed, a positive feedback.

lab-environment.l06.q1.p: Where did Charles Keeling begin measuring atmospheric CO2 in 1958?
lab-environment.l06.q1.h: A high Pacific volcano far from cities.
lab-environment.l06.q1.e: The Mauna Loa record is the continuous measurement known as the Keeling Curve.

lab-environment.l06.q2.p: Which process removes CO2 from the air on a seasonal cycle?
lab-environment.l06.q2.e: Plants take up CO2 during the growing season, causing the seasonal dip in the Keeling Curve.

lab-environment.l06.q3.p: Humans emit 40 units of CO2 in a year and about half stays in the atmosphere. How many units remain airborne?
lab-environment.l06.q3.e: Half of 40 is 20 units, with the rest taken up mostly by the ocean and land.

lab-environment.l06.q4.t: Natural removal processes are far slower than the release of carbon buried for millions of years
lab-environment.l06.q4.p: Why is the rate of emissions, not just the amount, the central problem?
lab-environment.l06.q4.h: Compare timescales of emission and removal.
lab-environment.l06.q4.e: Fossil carbon accumulated over hundreds of millions of years is released in decades, much faster than natural sinks can absorb it.

lab-environment.l07.q1.t: It grows with the logarithm of concentration
lab-environment.l07.q1.p: How does CO2 radiative forcing change with concentration?
lab-environment.l07.q1.e: Because forcing is logarithmic, each doubling adds about the same amount.

lab-environment.l07.q2.p: About how much more water vapour can air hold per degree Celsius of warming?
lab-environment.l07.q2.e: Saturation vapour pressure rises about 7 percent per degree, intensifying heavy rainfall.

lab-environment.l07.q3.p: CO2 rises from 280 ppm to 560 ppm, giving a forcing of about 3.7 W/m2. What further rise gives roughly the same extra forcing?
lab-environment.l07.q3.h: Each doubling gives the same forcing.
lab-environment.l07.q3.e: Going from 560 to 1120 is another doubling, which adds about the same forcing.

lab-environment.l07.q4.t: A brighter Sun would warm both layers, whereas greenhouse gases trap heat below
lab-environment.l07.q4.p: Observations show the lower atmosphere warming while the stratosphere cools. Why does this point to greenhouse gases rather than a brighter Sun?
lab-environment.l07.q4.h: Think about where each cause adds energy.
lab-environment.l07.q4.e: Greenhouse gases trap heat in the lower atmosphere, leaving less to warm the stratosphere, so the pattern differs from solar brightening.

lab-environment.l08.q1.t: Its concentration in water is proportional to its partial pressure
lab-environment.l08.q1.p: What does Henry's law say about dissolved gas?
lab-environment.l08.q1.e: More CO2 in the air leads to more CO2 dissolved in the ocean.

lab-environment.l08.q2.t: Corals and shellfish that build calcium carbonate shells
lab-environment.l08.q2.p: Which marine organisms are most directly threatened by ocean acidification?
lab-environment.l08.q2.e: Lower carbonate availability makes shell and skeleton building harder.

lab-environment.l08.q3.p: Seawater pH falls from 8.1 to 7.1. How does the hydrogen ion concentration change?
lab-environment.l08.q3.e: One pH unit corresponds to a factor of 10 in hydrogen ion concentration.

lab-environment.l08.q4.t: pH is a logarithmic scale, so small changes mean large percentage changes
lab-environment.l08.q4.p: A drop of only 0.1 pH units sounds small. Why does it correspond to a notable increase of about 30 percent in acidity?
lab-environment.l08.q4.e: On a log scale a small shift in pH represents a sizeable proportional change in hydrogen ion concentration.

lab-environment.l09.q1.p: What does the stratospheric ozone layer do?
lab-environment.l09.q1.e: Ozone absorbs most of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet light.

lab-environment.l09.q2.e: The Montreal Protocol (1987) phased out ozone-depleting substances such as CFCs.

lab-environment.l09.q3.p: Which chemicals did Molina and colleagues identify as destroying stratospheric ozone?
lab-environment.l09.q3.h: Used in old refrigerators and aerosols.
lab-environment.l09.q3.e: CFCs release chlorine in the stratosphere, which catalytically destroys ozone.

lab-environment.l09.q4.t: Chlorine acts as a catalyst, destroying many ozone molecules before being removed
lab-environment.l09.q4.p: Why can a small amount of CFC cause large ozone loss?
lab-environment.l09.q4.h: A catalyst is not used up.
lab-environment.l09.q4.e: Because chlorine is regenerated in the reactions, one atom can destroy many ozone molecules.

lab-environment.l10.q1.t: Converting nitrogen gas into forms such as ammonia that organisms can use
lab-environment.l10.q1.h: Certain microbes and lightning do it.
lab-environment.l10.q1.e: Fixation converts atmospheric nitrogen gas into usable compounds.

lab-environment.l10.q2.e: Solar energy evaporates water, which condenses and returns as precipitation.

lab-environment.l10.q3.t: Algal blooms followed by low-oxygen dead zones
lab-environment.l10.q3.p: Which outcome is a typical result of fertiliser runoff into coastal waters?
lab-environment.l10.q3.e: Nutrients feed algal blooms, and when the algae die their decomposition consumes oxygen.

lab-environment.l10.q4.t: The excess flows into waterways and disrupts ecosystems far from the fields
lab-environment.l10.q4.p: Industrial fertiliser has roughly doubled natural nitrogen fixation on land. Why is that an environmental concern?
lab-environment.l10.q4.h: Think about where the nitrogen ends up.
lab-environment.l10.q4.e: Surplus nitrogen leaches into rivers and coasts, driving eutrophication and altering natural cycles.

lab-environment.l11.q1.p: Which of these is one of the three levels of biodiversity?
lab-environment.l11.q1.e: Biodiversity spans genes, species and ecosystems.

lab-environment.l11.q2.p: About how many species did the 2019 IPBES assessment estimate face extinction?
lab-environment.l11.q2.e: IPBES estimated around one million species face extinction, many within decades.

lab-environment.l11.q3.p: Using S = c A^z with z = 0.5, what happens to the number of species if habitat area falls to one quarter?
lab-environment.l11.q3.e: A quarter raised to the power 0.5 is one half, so half the species remain.

lab-environment.l11.q4.t: If one species fails, others can fill its functional role
lab-environment.l11.q4.p: Why do diverse ecosystems tend to be more stable?
lab-environment.l11.q4.e: Species differ in how they respond to stress, so diversity gives redundancy and resilience.

lab-environment.l12.q1.p: Which book by Rachel Carson exposed the effects of synthetic pesticides?
lab-environment.l12.q1.e: Silent Spring described harm from pesticides such as DDT and helped launch modern environmentalism.

lab-environment.l12.q2.p: Who founded the Green Belt Movement?
lab-environment.l12.q2.h: A Nobel Peace laureate from Kenya.
lab-environment.l12.q2.e: Wangari Maathai founded the movement, which planted tens of millions of trees.

lab-environment.l12.q3.p: A pesticide becomes more concentrated at each step up a food chain. What is this process called?
lab-environment.l12.q3.h: Carson explained it to the public.
lab-environment.l12.q3.e: Persistent chemicals build up in organisms, leading to the highest levels in top predators.

lab-environment.l12.q4.t: People are members of an ecological community, with responsibilities to it
lab-environment.l12.q4.p: What was the central idea of Aldo Leopold's land ethic?
lab-environment.l12.q4.e: Leopold reframed conservation as an ethical relationship between people and the land.

lab-environment.l13.q1.p: How many Earth-system processes are in the planetary boundaries framework?
lab-environment.l13.q1.e: The framework identifies nine processes, including climate change, biosphere integrity and nutrient flows.

lab-environment.l13.q2.e: Paul Crutzen proposed the term in 2000 for an epoch shaped by human activity.

lab-environment.l13.q3.p: According to the 2023 assessment by Richardson and colleagues, how many of the nine boundaries had been transgressed?
lab-environment.l13.q3.e: The 2023 update reported that six of the nine boundaries had been transgressed.

lab-environment.l13.q4.t: Beyond it the risk of abrupt, large-scale change rises sharply
lab-environment.l13.q4.p: What does it mean for a boundary to define a "safe operating space"?
lab-environment.l13.q4.h: Think of a zone of increasing risk, not a cliff edge.
lab-environment.l13.q4.e: Boundaries mark where the risk to the stable Holocene-like state increases, not a precise tipping point.

lab-history.l01.q1.t: The invention of farming and the domestication of plants and animals
lab-history.l01.q1.h: It is named for a change in how people got food.
lab-history.l01.q1.e: The Neolithic revolution, around 10,000 BCE, was the shift to farming and domestication, which let people settle in one place.

lab-history.l01.q2.p: Which pair are early permanent settlements?
lab-history.l01.q2.h: Think of very early villages, not later empires.
lab-history.l01.q2.e: Catalhoyuk and Jericho are named as the first permanent settlements of the farming era.

lab-history.l01.q3.t: Permanent villages and the first inequalities of wealth and power
lab-history.l01.q3.p: What was a major effect of farming surpluses?
lab-history.l01.q3.h: A surplus means more food than needed right away.
lab-history.l01.q3.e: Surplus food allowed villages to grow and let some people gain more wealth and power than others.

lab-history.l01.q4.t: Writing had not yet been invented, so there are no written records
lab-history.l01.q4.p: Why do historians rely on objects and art to study prehistory?
lab-history.l01.q4.h: The word itself says what is missing.
lab-history.l01.q4.e: Prehistory is defined as the time before writing, so evidence comes from tools, bones, settlements and art.

lab-history.l02.q1.h: Mesopotamia means the land between rivers.
lab-history.l02.q1.e: Mesopotamia lay between the Tigris and Euphrates in the Fertile Crescent.

lab-history.l02.q2.p: How many laws were inscribed on Hammurabi's stele?
lab-history.l02.q2.h: It is a number a little under 300.
lab-history.l02.q2.e: The Code of Hammurabi is described as 282 laws on a diorite stele.

lab-history.l02.q3.h: Compare the dates, not the fame.
lab-history.l02.q3.e: Hammurabi ruled in the eighteenth century BCE, long before the Greek, Roman and Qin examples.

lab-history.l02.q4.t: People could know the rules, so law did not depend only on a ruler's private word
lab-history.l02.q4.p: Why was displaying written laws publicly significant?
lab-history.l02.q4.h: Think about what changes when a rule is visible.
lab-history.l02.q4.e: Public written law makes rules known and more consistent, which is the lasting importance of the code, whatever its harshness.

lab-history.l03.q1.p: Along which river did Ancient Egypt develop?
lab-history.l03.q1.h: It runs north through the desert.
lab-history.l03.q1.e: Ancient Egypt grew in the Nile Valley.

lab-history.l03.q2.p: Which cities belonged to the Indus Valley Civilisation?
lab-history.l03.q2.h: One of them gave the culture its alternate name.
lab-history.l03.q2.e: Harappa and Mohenjo-daro were major Indus cities, known for grid planning and drainage.

lab-history.l03.q3.p: Grid-planned streets and standardised weights suggest the Indus cities had what?
lab-history.l03.q3.e: Planned cities and standard weights point to organisation, although exactly who organised them is uncertain.

lab-history.l03.q4.t: The Indus script is undeciphered, so we lack their own written explanations
lab-history.l03.q4.p: Why must historians be cautious about Indus beliefs and rulers?
lab-history.l03.q4.h: Consider what kind of evidence is missing.
lab-history.l03.q4.e: Without a deciphered script, knowledge comes mainly from archaeology, so claims about rulers and belief remain tentative.

lab-history.l04.q1.p: Which philosopher tutored Alexander the Great?
lab-history.l04.q1.h: He formalised logic and the syllogism.
lab-history.l04.q1.e: Aristotle (384-322 BCE) tutored Alexander the Great.

lab-history.l04.q2.p: Which of these is a hallmark of Ancient Greece?
lab-history.l04.q2.h: Think of the city of Athens.
lab-history.l04.q2.e: Democracy, philosophy, theatre and the Olympic Games are listed hallmarks of Greece.

lab-history.l04.q3.e: Confucius lived in the sixth and fifth centuries BCE, earlier than Aristotle.

lab-history.l04.q4.t: Its ideas in politics, philosophy and drama became models later societies adapted
lab-history.l04.q4.p: Why is Greek influence on later Western societies so strong?
lab-history.l04.q4.h: Think of ideas rather than armies.
lab-history.l04.q4.e: Greek democracy, reasoned argument and theatre gave later Western societies models to adapt and debate.

lab-history.l05.q1.p: Which empire built the Royal Road and divided its land into satrapies?
lab-history.l05.q1.e: The Achaemenid Persian Empire used satrapies and the Royal Road to govern.

lab-history.l05.q2.p: After which campaign did Ashoka renounce war?
lab-history.l05.q2.h: It is named for a region of India.
lab-history.l05.q2.e: Ashoka turned from war after the Kalinga campaign and embraced Buddhism.

lab-history.l05.q3.t: Through provinces called satrapies linked by the Royal Road
lab-history.l05.q3.p: How did Persia govern a huge, varied empire?
lab-history.l05.q3.h: Think of provinces and a highway.
lab-history.l05.q3.e: Satrapies delegated rule to regional governors while the Royal Road kept the empire connected.

lab-history.l05.q4.t: Both used public moral or religious policy to help hold diverse peoples together
lab-history.l05.q4.p: What do Persian tolerance and Ashoka's edicts share as strategies?
lab-history.l05.q4.h: Look at how each ruler addressed different peoples.
lab-history.l05.q4.e: The sources describe Persian religious tolerance and Ashoka's moral edicts as ways of managing diverse populations, though historians weigh how fully they worked.

lab-history.l06.q1.p: What title did Qin Shi Huang take after 221 BCE?
lab-history.l06.q1.h: He was the first to hold it.
lab-history.l06.q1.e: Qin Shi Huang unified China in 221 BCE and became its First Emperor.

lab-history.l06.q2.p: About how many figures make up the Terracotta Army?
lab-history.l06.q2.e: The Terracotta Army has roughly 8,000 life-size figures.

lab-history.l06.q3.h: Shang is the earliest listed dynasty.
lab-history.l06.q3.e: The Shang began about 1600 BCE, long before Confucius and Qin.

lab-history.l06.q4.t: People in different regions could trade, administer and communicate the same way
lab-history.l06.q4.p: Why would standardising writing and measures help hold an empire together?
lab-history.l06.q4.h: Think about trading across many regions.
lab-history.l06.q4.e: Common standards reduced friction in trade and government across regions, which is why the idea outlasted Qin itself.

lab-history.l07.q1.p: Which calendar did Julius Caesar introduce?
lab-history.l07.q1.e: Caesar reformed the calendar into the Julian system.

lab-history.l07.q2.p: What ended with Cleopatra's death in 30 BCE?
lab-history.l07.q2.h: She was the last active ruler of her dynasty.
lab-history.l07.q2.e: Cleopatra VII was the last active ruler of Ptolemaic Egypt.

lab-history.l07.q3.e: Caesar died in 44 BCE, before the empire proper began in 27 BCE.

lab-history.l07.q4.t: They became shared foundations that later European societies inherited
lab-history.l07.q4.p: Why did Roman law, roads and Latin matter after 476?
lab-history.l07.q4.h: Think of what outlives a government.
lab-history.l07.q4.e: Law, language and engineering survived the Western empire and shaped later European states.

lab-history.l08.q1.p: In what year did the Byzantine Empire end?
lab-history.l08.q1.h: It is the fall of Constantinople.
lab-history.l08.q1.e: The Byzantine Empire lasted from 330 to 1453 CE.

lab-history.l08.q2.p: When was Charlemagne crowned emperor by the Pope?
lab-history.l08.q2.h: It is a round number near the start of the ninth century.
lab-history.l08.q2.e: Charlemagne was crowned in the year 800.

lab-history.l08.q3.h: The text says Rome fell in the West first.
lab-history.l08.q3.e: The West fell in 476, nearly a thousand years before Constantinople fell.

lab-history.l08.q4.t: Classical knowledge survived and reached later scholars, including in Europe
lab-history.l08.q4.p: What was a lasting benefit of Byzantine and Islamic scholarship?
lab-history.l08.q4.h: Think about how the Canon of Medicine travelled.
lab-history.l08.q4.e: Byzantine preservation and Islamic scholarship, such as Ibn Sina's Canon used in Europe, kept knowledge alive and moving.

lab-history.l09.q1.p: What did the Pax Mongolica reopen?
lab-history.l09.q1.h: Think of the great overland route.
lab-history.l09.q1.e: The Pax Mongolica reopened Silk Road trade across Eurasia.

lab-history.l09.q2.p: What is the name of Ibn Battuta's travelogue?
lab-history.l09.q2.h: It is a short Arabic title.
lab-history.l09.q2.e: Ibn Battuta recorded his journeys in the Rihla.

lab-history.l09.q3.e: Ibn Battuta lived 1304-1368, before Zheng He and the later explorers.

lab-history.l09.q4.t: Connections can carry goods and ideas but also disease along the same routes
lab-history.l09.q4.p: What does the link between connected trade and the Black Death suggest?
lab-history.l09.q4.h: Think about what travels with merchants.
lab-history.l09.q4.e: Historians see the same networks that moved goods as part of how the plague spread, though they debate details.

lab-history.l10.q1.p: In which year did Mansa Musa make his famous pilgrimage to Mecca?
lab-history.l10.q1.h: It is in the early fourteenth century.
lab-history.l10.q1.e: Mansa Musa's hajj in 1324 is said to have disrupted Mediterranean gold prices.

lab-history.l10.q2.e: Great Zimbabwe's walls were laid without mortar.

lab-history.l10.q3.p: What was the main source of Mali's wealth?
lab-history.l10.q3.h: Think of what crossed the Sahara.
lab-history.l10.q3.e: Mali's wealth rested on trans-Saharan gold trade.

lab-history.l10.q4.t: A southern African kingdom took part in long-distance trade networks
lab-history.l10.q4.p: What do Great Zimbabwe's Indian Ocean trade links show?
lab-history.l10.q4.h: Think about gold, ivory and ports.
lab-history.l10.q4.e: Gold and ivory trade tied Great Zimbabwe into wider networks that reached the Indian Ocean.

lab-history.l11.q1.p: Who painted the Sistine Chapel ceiling?
lab-history.l11.q1.e: Michelangelo painted the Sistine Chapel ceiling.

lab-history.l11.q2.p: In what year did Luther issue his Ninety-five Theses?
lab-history.l11.q2.h: It is early in the sixteenth century.
lab-history.l11.q2.e: Luther challenged the sale of indulgences in 1517.

lab-history.l11.q3.t: Cheap printed copies let ideas and vernacular scripture spread quickly
lab-history.l11.q3.p: How did the printing press help the Reformation?
lab-history.l11.q3.e: Print allowed Luther's writings and his German Bible to reach many readers.

lab-history.l11.q4.t: Art, observation and science were seen as connected
lab-history.l11.q4.p: Leonardo joined art with anatomy and engineering. What does this show about the Renaissance?
lab-history.l11.q4.e: Leonardo is an archetype of a period that prized observation and linked arts with study of nature.

lab-history.l12.q1.p: In what year did Columbus cross the Atlantic on his first voyage?
lab-history.l12.q1.h: The year rhymes in a famous poem.
lab-history.l12.q1.e: Columbus crossed the Atlantic in 1492 under the Spanish crown.

lab-history.l12.q2.p: Whose expedition completed the first circumnavigation (1519-1522)?
lab-history.l12.q2.e: The expedition begun by Magellan achieved the first circumnavigation, though he died in 1521.

lab-history.l12.q3.e: Zheng He lived 1371-1433, so his fleets crossed the Indian Ocean before Columbus sailed.

lab-history.l12.q4.t: Contact brought exchange but also immense suffering and upheaval
lab-history.l12.q4.p: What does it show that voyages launched both the Columbian Exchange and the Atlantic slave trade?
lab-history.l12.q4.h: Think about who benefited and who suffered.
lab-history.l12.q4.e: The exchange of goods and species went with disease, conquest and slavery, so the consequences were mixed and contested.

lab-history.l13.q1.p: Who led the Haitian Revolution to create the first Black republic?
lab-history.l13.q1.e: Toussaint Louverture led the movement that created Haiti.

lab-history.l13.q2.e: Bolivar is called El Libertador and Bolivia is named for him.

lab-history.l13.q3.e: The American Revolution began in 1776, before the others began.

lab-history.l13.q4.t: Enlightenment ideas of liberty and rights, though results fell short of the ideals for some
lab-history.l13.q4.h: Look at the ideas behind them.
lab-history.l13.q4.e: Enlightenment ideals inspired them, and historians debate how fully the outcomes matched those ideals.

lab-history.l14.q1.p: In what year did the Berlin Wall fall?
lab-history.l14.q1.h: It is near the end of the Cold War.

lab-history.l14.q2.p: How many years was Nelson Mandela imprisoned?
lab-history.l14.q2.e: Mandela endured 27 years of imprisonment for resisting apartheid.

lab-history.l14.q3.h: It happened during the first world war.
lab-history.l14.q3.e: The Russian Revolution of 1917 came before the 1945 events and 1989.

lab-history.l14.q4.t: Both led struggles against systems of imposed rule and inspired people worldwide
lab-history.l14.q4.p: What did Gandhi and Mandela have in common?
lab-history.l14.q4.e: Gandhi opposed British rule in India and Mandela opposed apartheid; both became global symbols of freedom movements.

lab-mathematics.l01.q1.t: A chain of deductions from axioms and definitions that establishes a statement beyond doubt
lab-mathematics.l01.q1.h: It is about deduction, not observation.
lab-mathematics.l01.q1.e: A proof deduces a statement step by step from axioms, definitions and earlier results.

lab-mathematics.l01.q2.p: Which ancient work set the template for axiomatic proof?
lab-mathematics.l01.q2.e: Euclid's Elements organised geometry deductively from a small set of postulates and became the model for proof.

lab-mathematics.l01.q3.t: Writing them as 2a and 2b, so the sum is 2(a + b), which is even
lab-mathematics.l01.q3.p: Which argument actually proves that the sum of any two even numbers is even?
lab-mathematics.l01.q3.h: The argument must cover every pair, not just samples.
lab-mathematics.l01.q3.e: Writing the numbers as 2a and 2b shows the sum is 2(a + b), so it works for every pair at once.

lab-mathematics.l01.q4.t: Because a counterexample could still exist beyond those checked
lab-mathematics.l01.q4.p: Why is checking a million examples not a proof that a statement is always true?
lab-mathematics.l01.q4.h: What could happen with example number a million and one?
lab-mathematics.l01.q4.e: Examples can only support a claim; a proof must exclude every possible counterexample.

lab-mathematics.l02.q1.p: What proof technique does Euclid use to show that the primes are infinite?
lab-mathematics.l02.q1.h: He assumes the opposite at the start.
lab-mathematics.l02.q1.e: Euclid assumes there are finitely many primes and derives a contradiction.

lab-mathematics.l02.q2.p: In Euclid's construction N = p1 x p2 x ... x pn + 1, what remainder does N leave when divided by any listed prime?
lab-mathematics.l02.q2.h: The product part is divisible by every listed prime.
lab-mathematics.l02.q2.e: The product is a multiple of each listed prime, so adding 1 leaves remainder 1.

lab-mathematics.l02.q3.p: For the primes 2, 3 and 5, what is Euclid's number N?

lab-mathematics.l02.q4.t: No, N only needs a prime factor that is not on the list, and 59 and 509 are not
lab-mathematics.l02.q4.p: For the first six primes (2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13) the number N = 30031 equals 59 x 509, so it is not prime. Does this break Euclid's proof?
lab-mathematics.l02.q4.h: What does the proof actually need N to provide?
lab-mathematics.l02.q4.e: The proof needs only that N has some prime factor outside the list, which 59 and 509 are.

lab-mathematics.l03.q1.t: The real numbers cannot be listed, so they form a strictly larger infinity
lab-mathematics.l03.q1.p: What did Cantor's diagonal argument show?
lab-mathematics.l03.q1.h: Any claimed list can be shown to be incomplete.
lab-mathematics.l03.q1.e: The diagonal construction produces a real number missing from any proposed list, so the reals are uncountable.

lab-mathematics.l03.q2.p: Russell's paradox of 1901 exposed a flaw in
lab-mathematics.l03.q2.h: It concerns the set of all sets that do not contain themselves.
lab-mathematics.l03.q2.e: It showed naive set theory was inconsistent, motivating axiomatic set theory such as ZFC.

lab-mathematics.l03.q3.p: A list begins with the sequences 0110, 1010, 1111, 0001 (first four digits). Cantor's diagonal method flips the 1st digit of the first, the 2nd of the second, the 3rd of the third and the 4th of the fourth. What four digits does it produce?
lab-mathematics.l03.q3.h: Read off the diagonal digits, then flip each.
lab-mathematics.l03.q3.e: The diagonal digits are 0, 0, 1, 1; flipping each gives 1, 1, 0, 0, so the new sequence starts 1100 and differs from every listed one.

lab-mathematics.l03.q4.t: It can be neither proved nor disproved from the ZFC axioms
lab-mathematics.l03.q4.p: What does it mean that the continuum hypothesis is independent of ZFC?
lab-mathematics.l03.q4.h: Think of Gödel in 1940 and Cohen in 1963.
lab-mathematics.l03.q4.e: Gödel showed it cannot be disproved and Cohen showed it cannot be proved from ZFC, so the axioms do not decide it.

lab-mathematics.l04.q1.t: Contains true statements it cannot prove
lab-mathematics.l04.q1.p: Gödel's first incompleteness theorem says that a consistent formal system rich enough for arithmetic
lab-mathematics.l04.q1.h: The result is about unprovable truths.
lab-mathematics.l04.q1.e: Any such system has true statements that it cannot prove.

lab-mathematics.l04.q2.t: To put all of mathematics on a complete, consistent formal footing
lab-mathematics.l04.q2.p: What was Hilbert's programme trying to achieve?
lab-mathematics.l04.q2.e: Hilbert hoped to formalise all mathematics in a system proven consistent and complete; Gödel showed this cannot be fully achieved.

lab-mathematics.l04.q3.t: It is impossible for a consistent system rich enough to express arithmetic
lab-mathematics.l04.q3.p: A mathematician announces a consistent set of axioms for arithmetic that proves every true arithmetical statement. What does Gödel's theorem say about this claim?
lab-mathematics.l04.q3.h: Compare the claim with the theorem's conclusion.
lab-mathematics.l04.q3.e: Gödel showed that no consistent, sufficiently rich system can prove all arithmetical truths.

lab-mathematics.l04.q4.t: Proofs within a system remain valid, but no single system captures all mathematical truth
lab-mathematics.l04.q4.p: Which reading of Gödel's theorem is correct?
lab-mathematics.l04.q4.h: The theorem limits systems, not individual correct proofs.
lab-mathematics.l04.q4.e: Gödel did not undermine valid proofs; he showed that every sufficiently strong consistent system is incomplete.

lab-mathematics.l05.q1.p: The prime number theorem states that the number of primes up to x, pi(x), is approximately
lab-mathematics.l05.q1.h: The approximation involves the natural logarithm.
lab-mathematics.l05.q1.e: pi(x) is asymptotic to x / ln x.

lab-mathematics.l05.q2.t: Hadamard and de la Vallee Poussin, 1896
lab-mathematics.l05.q2.p: Who proved the prime number theorem, and when?
lab-mathematics.l05.q2.h: It came after Riemann's zeta function work.
lab-mathematics.l05.q2.e: Hadamard and de la Vallee Poussin independently proved it in 1896.

lab-mathematics.l05.q3.p: Near the number e^10 (about 22,026), roughly what fraction of numbers are prime, using the density 1 / ln x?
lab-mathematics.l05.q3.e: ln(e^10) = 10, so about one number in 10 near that size is prime.

lab-mathematics.l05.q4.t: The density falls slowly enough that x / ln x still grows without bound
lab-mathematics.l05.q4.p: The primes thin out, with density 1 / ln x tending to zero. How does this fit with there being infinitely many primes?
lab-mathematics.l05.q4.h: Does x / ln x stay bounded?
lab-mathematics.l05.q4.e: Because x / ln x grows without bound as x increases, the count of primes keeps rising even as their density falls.

lab-mathematics.l06.q1.t: An infinite product over the prime numbers
lab-mathematics.l06.q1.p: Euler's product formula expresses the zeta function as
lab-mathematics.l06.q1.h: It links the integers to the primes.
lab-mathematics.l06.q1.e: zeta(s) equals the product over all primes p of 1 / (1 - p^(-s)).

lab-mathematics.l06.q2.t: The zeros of the zeta function
lab-mathematics.l06.q2.p: Riemann's 1859 paper On the Number of Primes connected the distribution of primes to
lab-mathematics.l06.q2.h: It uses the zeta function extended to complex numbers.
lab-mathematics.l06.q2.e: Riemann linked prime counting to the zeros of the zeta function, leading to the Riemann hypothesis.

lab-mathematics.l06.q3.p: At s = 2, what is the product of the Euler factors 1 / (1 - p^(-2)) for the primes 2 and 3 only?

lab-mathematics.l06.q4.t: Every integer factors uniquely into primes
lab-mathematics.l06.q4.p: Which fact about the integers is the key reason the Euler product equals the sum for zeta(s)?
lab-mathematics.l06.q4.h: Expand the product and ask where each term 1/n^s comes from.
lab-mathematics.l06.q4.e: Unique prime factorisation means each n appears exactly once when the product of geometric series is expanded.

lab-mathematics.l07.q1.t: The title of Al-Khwarizmi's book containing al-jabr
lab-mathematics.l07.q1.e: The Arabic title of Al-Khwarizmi's book contains al-jabr, which gave algebra its name.

lab-mathematics.l07.q2.p: In the quadratic formula, the expression b^2 - 4ac is called the
lab-mathematics.l07.q2.h: Its sign tells you how many real roots exist.
lab-mathematics.l07.q2.e: The discriminant b^2 - 4ac determines whether the roots are two real, one repeated or complex.

lab-mathematics.l07.q3.p: What are the solutions of x^2 - 5x + 6 = 0?
lab-mathematics.l07.q3.e: x = (5 plus or minus 1) / 2, which is 3 or 2.

lab-mathematics.l07.q4.t: No real roots; the parabola never crosses the x-axis
lab-mathematics.l07.q4.p: The equation x^2 + 2x + 5 = 0 has discriminant -16. What does that imply?
lab-mathematics.l07.q4.h: Can you take the real square root of a negative number?
lab-mathematics.l07.q4.e: A negative discriminant means no real roots, so the graph does not meet the x-axis, and the roots are complex.

lab-mathematics.l08.q1.t: Exactly n complex roots, counted with multiplicity
lab-mathematics.l08.q1.p: The fundamental theorem of algebra says a polynomial of degree n has
lab-mathematics.l08.q1.h: Complex numbers and multiplicity both matter.
lab-mathematics.l08.q1.e: Every non-constant complex polynomial of degree n has exactly n complex roots counted with multiplicity.

lab-mathematics.l08.q2.t: There is no general formula in radicals for the quintic
lab-mathematics.l08.q2.p: What did Abel and Ruffini prove in the 1820s?
lab-mathematics.l08.q2.e: They proved that the general quintic cannot be solved by radicals.

lab-mathematics.l08.q3.p: How many complex roots, counted with multiplicity, does (x - 1)^2 (x + 2)(x^2 + 1) have?
lab-mathematics.l08.q3.h: Find the degree of the polynomial.
lab-mathematics.l08.q3.e: The degree is 2 + 1 + 2 = 5, so there are five roots: 1, 1, -2, i and -i.

lab-mathematics.l08.q4.t: No, a quintic still has five complex roots; there is just no general radical formula for them
lab-mathematics.l08.q4.p: Does the Abel-Ruffini theorem mean that a quintic has no roots?
lab-mathematics.l08.q4.h: Combine it with the fundamental theorem of algebra.
lab-mathematics.l08.q4.e: The fundamental theorem guarantees five complex roots; the Abel-Ruffini theorem only rules out a general formula using radicals.

lab-mathematics.l09.q1.p: Which Euclidean postulate resisted proof for about two thousand years?
lab-mathematics.l09.q1.h: It concerns lines that never meet.
lab-mathematics.l09.q1.e: The fifth (parallel) postulate was long thought provable from the others until non-Euclidean geometries were found.

lab-mathematics.l09.q2.t: He generalised geometry to curved spaces of any dimension
lab-mathematics.l09.q2.p: What did Riemann contribute to geometry?
lab-mathematics.l09.q2.h: Einstein needed his language for general relativity.
lab-mathematics.l09.q2.e: Riemann's generalisation provided the mathematical language of general relativity.

lab-mathematics.l09.q3.p: A dodecahedron has 20 vertices and 12 faces. Using V - E + F = 2, how many edges does it have?

lab-mathematics.l09.q4.t: Consistent geometries exist where the parallel postulate fails, so it cannot be proved from the other postulates
lab-mathematics.l09.q4.p: What did the discovery of non-Euclidean geometries by Gauss, Bolyai and Lobachevsky show?
lab-mathematics.l09.q4.h: Consider what independence of an axiom means.
lab-mathematics.l09.q4.e: Because a consistent geometry can deny the parallel postulate, that postulate is independent of the other four.

lab-mathematics.l10.q1.p: The derivative of a function at a point measures
lab-mathematics.l10.q1.h: It is defined as a limit of difference quotients.
lab-mathematics.l10.q1.e: The derivative is the limit of the average rate of change as the interval shrinks to zero.

lab-mathematics.l10.q2.t: Integration and differentiation are inverse operations
lab-mathematics.l10.q2.p: The fundamental theorem of calculus states that
lab-mathematics.l10.q2.h: The definite integral is computed with an antiderivative.
lab-mathematics.l10.q2.e: The definite integral of f from a to b equals F(b) - F(a), linking integration to differentiation.

lab-mathematics.l10.q3.p: What is the definite integral of x^2 from 0 to 3?
lab-mathematics.l10.q3.h: An antiderivative of x^2 is x^3 / 3.

lab-mathematics.l10.q4.t: It relied on infinitesimals that were treated as both zero and non-zero, lacking rigorous foundation
lab-mathematics.l10.q4.p: Why did Berkeley attack early calculus in The Analyst (1734)?
lab-mathematics.l10.q4.h: He called them ghosts of departed quantities.
lab-mathematics.l10.q4.e: Berkeley criticised the logical looseness of infinitesimals, a challenge answered by Cauchy and Weierstrass with limits.

lab-mathematics.l11.q1.p: What is true about the harmonic series 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/4 + ...?
lab-mathematics.l11.q1.h: Its terms shrink, but think about the grouping argument.
lab-mathematics.l11.q1.e: The harmonic series grows without bound even though its terms tend to zero.

lab-mathematics.l11.q2.p: The sum of the reciprocals of the squares, 1 + 1/4 + 1/9 + ..., equals
lab-mathematics.l11.q2.h: Euler solved the Basel problem in 1735.
lab-mathematics.l11.q2.e: Euler showed the sum is pi^2 / 6, about 1.645.

lab-mathematics.l11.q3.p: In the grouping proof of divergence, the four terms 1/5 + 1/6 + 1/7 + 1/8 add up to
lab-mathematics.l11.q3.e: Each of the four terms is at least 1/8, so the sum is more than 4 x 1/8 = 1/2.

lab-mathematics.l11.q4.t: The terms 1/n^2 shrink fast enough for the total to stay finite, while 1/n shrinks too slowly
lab-mathematics.l11.q4.p: Both 1/n and 1/n^2 have terms that tend to zero, yet only one series converges. What explains the difference?
lab-mathematics.l11.q4.h: Terms tending to zero is necessary but not sufficient.
lab-mathematics.l11.q4.e: Convergence depends on how quickly the terms fall: 1/n^2 falls fast enough to sum to a finite value, while 1/n does not.

lab-mathematics.l12.q1.p: Which five constants appear in Euler's identity e^(i pi) + 1 = 0?
lab-mathematics.l12.q1.e: The identity links e, i, pi, 1 and 0.

lab-mathematics.l12.q2.p: Euler's formula e^(i theta) = cos theta + i sin theta connects the exponential function to
lab-mathematics.l12.q2.e: It expresses a complex exponential in terms of cosine and sine.

lab-mathematics.l12.q3.p: Using Euler's formula, what is e^(i pi / 2)?
lab-mathematics.l12.q3.e: e^(i pi/2) = cos(pi/2) + i sin(pi/2) = 0 + i = i.

lab-mathematics.l12.q4.p: As theta varies over real numbers, where do the points e^(i theta) lie in the complex plane?
lab-mathematics.l12.q4.h: Each point is (cos theta, sin theta).
lab-mathematics.l12.q4.e: The point (cos theta, sin theta) always has distance 1 from the origin, so it lies on the unit circle.

lab-mathematics.l13.q1.p: Which major theorem was the first whose proof required a computer to check thousands of cases?
lab-mathematics.l13.q1.e: The four-colour theorem (1976) was the first major result depending on computer verification.

lab-mathematics.l13.q2.p: Who proved Fermat's Last Theorem, and when?
lab-mathematics.l13.q2.e: Andrew Wiles proved Fermat's Last Theorem in 1994.

lab-mathematics.l13.q3.p: Which of these events happened between Gödel's incompleteness theorems (1931) and the four-colour proof (1976)?
lab-mathematics.l13.q3.e: Turing's 1936 paper falls between 1931 and 1976; Hilbert's problems and Cantor came earlier, Wiles later.

lab-mathematics.l13.q4.t: Whether we can be certain of a result when no human can check every step and we must trust the software too
lab-mathematics.l13.q4.p: What new question do very large computer-assisted proofs raise?
lab-mathematics.l13.q4.h: Think about who or what verifies the argument.
lab-mathematics.l13.q4.e: When a proof is too large to check by hand, certainty also depends on the correctness of the program, prompting work on formal, machine-checkable proof.

lab-networks.l01.q1.t: A small chunk of a message carrying its own address
lab-networks.l01.q1.p: What is a packet in packet switching?
lab-networks.l01.q1.e: Messages are cut into small packets, each addressed and forwarded independently.

lab-networks.l01.q2.p: Who coined the term "packet" for this approach?
lab-networks.l01.q2.h: He built the NPL network in Britain.
lab-networks.l01.q2.e: Donald Davies independently invented packet switching and coined the word packet.

lab-networks.l01.q3.t: Links are used only when someone has data, and are shared among many users
lab-networks.l01.q3.p: Why is packet switching more efficient than circuit switching for bursty computer traffic?
lab-networks.l01.q3.h: Think about idle time in a reserved circuit.
lab-networks.l01.q3.e: Sharing links through statistical multiplexing avoids wasting reserved capacity during idle periods.

lab-networks.l01.q4.t: Packets may queue, be reordered or be dropped
lab-networks.l01.q4.p: What is a drawback that packet switching introduces compared with a reserved circuit?
lab-networks.l01.q4.e: Because packets share links, they can wait in queues, arrive out of order, or be dropped, so higher layers must cope.

lab-networks.l02.q1.h: It is the time to push the bits onto the wire.
lab-networks.l02.q1.e: Transmission delay is packet length in bits divided by link bandwidth in bits per second.

lab-networks.l02.q2.p: Which delay can never be reduced by buying a faster (higher-bandwidth) link?
lab-networks.l02.q2.h: It depends on distance and signal speed.
lab-networks.l02.q2.e: Propagation delay depends on distance and the signal speed in the medium, not on bandwidth.

lab-networks.l02.q3.p: A 12,000-bit packet is sent over a 10 Mbit/s link. What is the transmission delay?
lab-networks.l02.q3.h: Divide 12,000 by 10,000,000 and convert to milliseconds.

lab-networks.l02.q4.t: 10 ms, and it stays the same
lab-networks.l02.q4.p: A link is 2000 km long and signals travel at 2 x 10^8 m/s. What is the propagation delay, and what does upgrading the link from 10 Mbit/s to 1 Gbit/s do to it?
lab-networks.l02.q4.h: Distance over speed does not involve bandwidth.
lab-networks.l02.q4.e: 2,000,000 m / 200,000,000 m/s = 0.01 s = 10 ms, and it is unaffected by bandwidth.

lab-networks.l03.q1.h: Average number equals arrival rate times time in system.
lab-networks.l03.q1.e: Little's Law: the average number in the system equals the arrival rate times the average time spent in it.

lab-networks.l03.q2.p: For a queue to be stable, what must the utilisation rho = lambda / mu satisfy?
lab-networks.l03.q2.h: Arrivals cannot exceed service on average.
