lab-networks.l03.q2.e: If arrivals exceed the service rate on average, the queue grows without bound, so rho must be below 1.

lab-networks.l03.q3.p: A router receives 500 packets per second and each spends 0.02 s there on average. How many packets are in the system on average?

lab-networks.l03.q4.p: With mu = 1000 packets/s, the arrival rate rises from 900 to 990 packets/s. By what factor does the M/M/1 average delay change?
lab-networks.l03.q4.e: W goes from 1/100 = 10 ms to 1/10 = 100 ms, ten times larger, though load rose only 10 percent.

lab-networks.l04.q1.t: The maximum error-free data rate of a noisy channel
lab-networks.l04.q1.p: What does the Shannon-Hartley formula give?
lab-networks.l04.q1.h: It involves bandwidth and signal-to-noise ratio.
lab-networks.l04.q1.e: C = B log2(1 + S/N) is the capacity of a channel with bandwidth B and noise.

lab-networks.l04.q2.p: In the Nyquist formula C = 2B log2(M), what does M stand for?
lab-networks.l04.q2.h: More of these give more bits per symbol.
lab-networks.l04.q2.e: M is the number of distinct signal levels used per symbol.

lab-networks.l04.q3.p: A noiseless channel has B = 3000 Hz and uses M = 4 signal levels. What is the Nyquist maximum rate?

lab-networks.l04.q4.p: A channel has B = 1 MHz and S/N = 255. What is the Shannon capacity?

lab-networks.l05.q1.p: Which protocol provides reliable, ordered delivery of a byte stream?
lab-networks.l05.q1.e: TCP adds reliability, ordering and flow control on top of best-effort IP.

lab-networks.l05.q2.p: On what date did the ARPANET switch to TCP/IP?
lab-networks.l05.q2.h: It is called the flag day.
lab-networks.l05.q2.e: The ARPANET flag day on 1 January 1983 moved the whole network to TCP/IP.

lab-networks.l05.q3.t: Packets may be lost, delayed, duplicated or reordered
lab-networks.l05.q3.p: IP is best-effort. What does that mean for an application using only IP?
lab-networks.l05.q3.e: IP tries to deliver but gives no guarantee of delivery or order, which is why TCP is layered on top.

lab-networks.l05.q4.t: Keep the network core simple and put intelligence at the edges
lab-networks.l05.q4.p: What is the main argument of the end-to-end principle?
lab-networks.l05.q4.h: Think about who benefits from a simple core.
lab-networks.l05.q4.e: A simple core is cheap, scales and supports new applications, while end hosts supply the specific services they need.

lab-networks.l06.q1.p: How many bits are in an IPv4 address?
lab-networks.l06.q1.e: IPv4 addresses are 32 bits long, giving about 4.29 billion addresses.

lab-networks.l06.q2.p: Which layer in the Internet suite includes TCP and UDP?
lab-networks.l06.q2.h: It sits between IP and the application.
lab-networks.l06.q2.e: TCP and UDP are transport-layer protocols.

lab-networks.l06.q3.p: How many usable host addresses are in an IPv4 /24 subnet?
lab-networks.l06.q3.e: 2^8 = 256, minus the network and broadcast addresses, gives 254.

lab-networks.l06.q4.t: 62; a longer prefix leaves fewer host bits
lab-networks.l06.q4.p: How many usable host addresses does a /26 subnet have, and why is it smaller than a /24?
lab-networks.l06.q4.e: 2^(32 - 26) - 2 = 64 - 2 = 62; more bits in the network prefix mean fewer bits for hosts.

lab-networks.l07.q1.p: Which algorithm do link-state protocols such as OSPF run on each router?
lab-networks.l07.q1.e: Link-state routers build a topology map and run Dijkstra's algorithm locally.

lab-networks.l07.q2.p: Which protocol exchanges reachability between autonomous systems on the Internet?
lab-networks.l07.q2.e: BGP is the path-vector protocol that connects the Internet's autonomous systems.

lab-networks.l07.q3.t: Each router forwards to a suitable next hop, and the combined hops form the path
lab-networks.l07.q3.p: A router does not know the full path to a distant destination. How can packets still arrive?
lab-networks.l07.q3.e: Each router only needs the next hop toward the destination, so the path emerges from many local decisions.

lab-networks.l07.q4.t: Operators apply business and policy preferences between networks
lab-networks.l07.q4.p: Why does BGP consider more than shortest distance when choosing routes?
lab-networks.l07.q4.h: Autonomous systems are run by different organisations.
lab-networks.l07.q4.e: Between independently run networks, routes are chosen using policies, such as whom to carry traffic for, not only path length.

lab-networks.l08.q1.t: The positions at which two equal-length words differ
lab-networks.l08.q1.h: Compare two words bit by bit.
lab-networks.l08.q1.e: Hamming distance is the number of bit positions at which two words differ.

lab-networks.l08.q2.p: Which check is standard for detecting frame errors in Ethernet and Wi-Fi?
lab-networks.l08.q2.e: A CRC is a polynomial-division checksum used to detect frame errors.

lab-networks.l08.q3.p: What is the Hamming distance between 10110 and 11100?
lab-networks.l08.q3.e: The words differ in positions 2 and 4, so the distance is 2.

lab-networks.l08.q4.p: A code has minimum Hamming distance 5. How many bit errors per word can it correct?

lab-networks.l09.q1.t: The amount of data that can be in flight on the path
lab-networks.l09.q1.p: What does the bandwidth-delay product represent?
lab-networks.l09.q1.e: BDP = B x RTT is the amount of data needed in flight to keep the link fully used.

lab-networks.l09.q2.p: According to the Mathis model, how does TCP throughput change as the round-trip time doubles (other things equal)?
lab-networks.l09.q2.h: T is inversely proportional to RTT.
lab-networks.l09.q2.e: T is proportional to 1 / RTT, so doubling RTT halves the throughput.

lab-networks.l09.q3.p: A path has bandwidth 100 Mbit/s and RTT of 40 ms. What is the bandwidth-delay product in bytes?
lab-networks.l09.q3.h: Compute bits first, then divide by 8.

lab-networks.l09.q4.p: The packet loss rate rises fourfold. By what factor does Mathis-model throughput change?
lab-networks.l09.q4.e: T is proportional to 1 / sqrt(p), and sqrt(4) = 2, so throughput halves.

lab-networks.l10.q1.h: It describes how the window grows and shrinks.
lab-networks.l10.q1.e: AIMD grows the window gently by additive increase and cuts it by a multiplicative factor on loss.

lab-networks.l10.q2.p: Who published the 1988 congestion-control paper that ended Internet congestion collapse?
lab-networks.l10.q2.e: Van Jacobson's Congestion Avoidance and Control introduced slow start and congestion avoidance.

lab-networks.l10.q3.p: A TCP congestion window is 20 segments when a loss occurs. Using the AIMD rule, what is the window afterwards?
lab-networks.l10.q3.e: On loss, w is halved: 20 / 2 = 10 segments.

lab-networks.l10.q4.t: Halving takes more from larger windows while additive increase gives all the same gain
lab-networks.l10.q4.p: Why does AIMD make competing flows converge toward equal shares of a bottleneck?
lab-networks.l10.q4.h: Compare absolute loss on a big window with the equal increase.
lab-networks.l10.q4.e: A larger window loses more in absolute terms when halved, while all flows add the same amount, so the gap shrinks over time (Chiu and Jain).

lab-networks.l11.q1.e: DNS translates human-readable names to IP addresses.

lab-networks.l11.q2.e: DNS replaced the flat HOSTS.TXT file with a hierarchical, delegated system.

lab-networks.l11.q3.t: Answer from its cache without asking again
lab-networks.l11.q3.p: A resolver has just looked up a name and the answer has a TTL of 300 seconds. What can it do for the next 300 seconds?
lab-networks.l11.q3.e: The TTL tells resolvers how long they may reuse an answer, saving time and load on upstream servers.

lab-networks.l11.q4.t: Each level manages only its own part, and caching reduces load on the top
lab-networks.l11.q4.p: Why does a hierarchical, delegated design scale better than one central list?
lab-networks.l11.q4.h: Who holds the data at each level?
lab-networks.l11.q4.e: Delegation spreads responsibility and storage across many operators, and caching keeps queries away from the root.

lab-networks.l12.q1.p: What does TLS provide for a connection?
lab-networks.l12.q1.h: It is what makes HTTPS secure.
lab-networks.l12.q1.e: TLS provides confidentiality via encryption and authentication of the server.

lab-networks.l12.q2.p: Whose 1976 work on public-key key exchange underpins the TLS handshake?
lab-networks.l12.q2.e: Diffie and Hellman introduced public-key key exchange in 1976.

lab-networks.l12.q3.t: Symmetric encryption is much faster for bulk data
lab-networks.l12.q3.p: Why does TLS use public-key methods only to agree a session key and then switch to symmetric encryption for the data?
lab-networks.l12.q3.h: Consider the cost of encrypting large amounts of data.
lab-networks.l12.q3.e: Public-key operations are slow, so they set up a shared symmetric key which is then used efficiently for the data.

lab-networks.l12.q4.t: You reached the named server over an encrypted connection, but not that the site is honest
lab-networks.l12.q4.p: A site shows a valid certificate and the padlock. What does this prove?
lab-networks.l12.q4.h: Authentication is not the same as trust.
lab-networks.l12.q4.e: A valid certificate authenticates the server's identity and enables encryption; it does not vouch for the site's intentions.

lab-networks.l13.q1.p: Who invented the World Wide Web in 1990?
lab-networks.l13.q1.h: He defined HTTP, HTML and the URL.
lab-networks.l13.q1.e: Tim Berners-Lee built the Web as an application-layer system atop TCP/IP.

lab-networks.l13.q2.p: What problem does the Spanning Tree Protocol solve?
lab-networks.l13.q2.e: Radia Perlman's protocol makes bridged LANs loop-free by blocking redundant links.

lab-networks.l13.q3.p: Metcalfe's Law says network value is roughly proportional to n squared. If the number of users doubles, by roughly what factor does the value rise?
lab-networks.l13.q3.e: Doubling n multiplies n squared by 4.

lab-networks.l13.q4.t: It needed no changes to the network core, since it ran on top of TCP/IP at the edges
lab-networks.l13.q4.p: Why was the Web able to spread so quickly on the existing Internet?
lab-networks.l13.q4.e: Because the Web was just an application on TCP/IP, anyone could deploy servers and browsers without changing the network itself.

lab-neuroscience.l01.q1.t: The nervous system is made of discrete individual cells
lab-neuroscience.l01.q1.p: What does the neuron doctrine state?
lab-neuroscience.l01.q1.h: Think about what Cajal argued against Golgi.
lab-neuroscience.l01.q1.e: The neuron doctrine holds that neurons are separate cells that communicate across gaps, not a continuous network.

lab-neuroscience.l01.q2.h: He was a British neurophysiologist who described the reflex arc.
lab-neuroscience.l01.q2.e: Charles Sherrington named the junction between neurons the synapse in 1897.

lab-neuroscience.l01.q3.p: A neuron's signal is described by the law of dynamic polarisation. Which path does the information follow?
lab-neuroscience.l01.q3.e: Cajal proposed that signals enter at dendrites, are integrated in the soma, and leave via the axon.

lab-neuroscience.l01.q4.t: It stained a few whole neurons completely, letting Cajal see each cell as separate
lab-neuroscience.l01.q4.p: Why was Golgi's silver stain so important for settling the debate, even though Golgi himself held the opposing view?
lab-neuroscience.l01.q4.h: Consider why staining only a few cells is useful.
lab-neuroscience.l01.q4.e: Because it blackened only a small fraction of cells entirely, individual neurons and their boundaries could be seen, and Cajal used it to show they were separate.

lab-neuroscience.l02.q1.p: Roughly what is the resting membrane potential of a typical neuron?
lab-neuroscience.l02.q1.h: The inside is negative relative to the outside.
lab-neuroscience.l02.q1.e: A neuron at rest sits at about -70 mV inside relative to outside.

lab-neuroscience.l02.q2.p: Which ion is the membrane most permeable to at rest?
lab-neuroscience.l02.q2.h: The resting potential sits close to this ion's equilibrium potential.
lab-neuroscience.l02.q2.e: At rest the membrane is far more permeable to potassium than to sodium, so the resting potential is close to the potassium Nernst potential.

lab-neuroscience.l02.q3.t: Toward the sodium equilibrium potential, which is positive
lab-neuroscience.l02.q3.p: If a membrane's permeability to sodium were suddenly increased greatly, in which direction would the membrane potential move?
lab-neuroscience.l02.q3.h: The GHK equation weights each ion by its permeability.
lab-neuroscience.l02.q3.e: The potential moves toward the Nernst potential of whichever ion has the greatest permeability; sodium's equilibrium potential is positive.

lab-neuroscience.l02.q4.t: The ion gradients would slowly run down and the resting potential would decay
lab-neuroscience.l02.q4.p: What would happen to the resting potential over time if the sodium-potassium pump stopped working?
lab-neuroscience.l02.q4.h: The pump keeps the concentration gradients in place.
lab-neuroscience.l02.q4.e: The pump maintains the sodium and potassium gradients that set the resting voltage; without it the gradients dissipate and the stored electrochemical energy is lost.

lab-neuroscience.l03.q1.p: Which channels open first when the membrane depolarises past threshold?
lab-neuroscience.l03.q1.h: Sodium floods in during the rising phase.
lab-neuroscience.l03.q1.e: Voltage-gated sodium channels open first, letting sodium rush in and drive the inside positive.

lab-neuroscience.l03.q2.t: Its size does not depend on the strength of a suprathreshold stimulus
lab-neuroscience.l03.q2.p: What does "all-or-nothing" mean for an action potential?
lab-neuroscience.l03.q2.h: Think about whether a harder push makes a bigger spike.
lab-neuroscience.l03.q2.e: Below threshold nothing fires; above it the spike has the same size regardless of stimulus strength.

lab-neuroscience.l03.q3.p: A potassium channel has conductance g = 2 nS and the membrane is at -70 mV while the potassium reversal potential is -90 mV. Using I = g x (Vm - E), what is the current?
lab-neuroscience.l03.q3.h: Find the driving force first: Vm minus E.
lab-neuroscience.l03.q3.e: Driving force = -70 - (-90) = 20 mV. I = 2 nS x 20 mV = 40 pA (nS times mV gives pA).

lab-neuroscience.l03.q4.t: The spike is actively regenerated by voltage-gated channels at each patch of membrane
lab-neuroscience.l03.q4.p: Why can an action potential travel a long axon without fading, whereas a passive voltage change does not?
lab-neuroscience.l03.q4.h: Regeneration happens all along the membrane.
lab-neuroscience.l03.q4.e: Each membrane patch opens its own voltage-gated channels and regenerates the spike, restoring its full size as it propagates.

lab-neuroscience.l04.q1.t: Entry of calcium through voltage-gated channels
lab-neuroscience.l04.q1.p: What triggers synaptic vesicles to release neurotransmitter at the axon terminal?
lab-neuroscience.l04.q1.h: An ion enters when the spike arrives at the terminal.
lab-neuroscience.l04.q1.e: Calcium entering through voltage-gated calcium channels makes vesicles fuse and release their contents into the cleft.

lab-neuroscience.l04.q2.p: Which experiment gave early proof of chemical transmission?
lab-neuroscience.l04.q2.h: It involved fluid being transferred from one heart to another.
lab-neuroscience.l04.q2.e: Loewi showed that fluid from a stimulated vagus nerve slowed a second heart, proving a chemical messenger.

lab-neuroscience.l04.q3.t: Release happens in whole-vesicle units, not in arbitrary amounts
lab-neuroscience.l04.q3.p: Katz showed that neurotransmitter is released in "quantal" packets. What does this mean for a single vesicle?
lab-neuroscience.l04.q3.e: Release occurs in discrete packets, with one vesicle's contents as the basic unit.

lab-neuroscience.l04.q4.t: The chemical step can be strengthened, weakened or blocked, unlike a continuous fibre
lab-neuroscience.l04.q4.p: Why is the synapse a useful place for the nervous system to regulate and change signals?
lab-neuroscience.l04.q4.h: Think about what a chemical step allows that a wire does not.
lab-neuroscience.l04.q4.e: Because transmission is a controllable chemical step, the strength of a synapse can be adjusted, which underlies learning and the action of many drugs.

lab-neuroscience.l05.q1.p: Which neurotransmitter is the brain's main inhibitory signal?
lab-neuroscience.l05.q1.e: GABA is the main inhibitory transmitter; glutamate is the main excitatory one.

lab-neuroscience.l05.q2.p: Which was the first neurotransmitter identified, by Otto Loewi in 1921?
lab-neuroscience.l05.q2.e: Loewi identified acetylcholine as the substance that slowed the frog heart.

lab-neuroscience.l05.q3.t: The two cells have different receptors for it
lab-neuroscience.l05.q3.p: The same neurotransmitter excites one cell type and inhibits another. What is the most likely explanation?
lab-neuroscience.l05.q3.h: Effect depends on what the transmitter binds to.
lab-neuroscience.l05.q3.e: Whether a transmitter excites or inhibits depends on its receptor, not the molecule itself.

lab-neuroscience.l05.q4.p: A drug blocks the re-uptake of a transmitter so that it stays longer in the cleft. What is the most likely effect on signalling through that transmitter?
lab-neuroscience.l05.q4.h: More time in the cleft means more receptor activation.
lab-neuroscience.l05.q4.e: Longer presence of transmitter in the cleft increases and prolongs receptor activation, which is how many psychiatric drugs work.

lab-neuroscience.l06.q1.p: What is the formula for the membrane time constant?
lab-neuroscience.l06.q1.h: It is a simple product of resistance and capacitance.
lab-neuroscience.l06.q1.e: The time constant is the product of membrane resistance and capacitance.

lab-neuroscience.l06.q2.p: Over one length constant, a passive signal falls to about what fraction of its original size?
lab-neuroscience.l06.q2.h: It is the reciprocal of e, roughly.
lab-neuroscience.l06.q2.e: A passive potential decays to about 37 percent of its amplitude over one length constant.

lab-neuroscience.l06.q3.p: A membrane has Rm = 20,000 ohm cm2 and Cm = 1 microfarad per cm2. What is its time constant?
lab-neuroscience.l06.q3.h: Convert microfarads to farads: multiply by 0.000001.

lab-neuroscience.l06.q4.t: Signals fade over a shorter distance
lab-neuroscience.l06.q4.p: A dendrite's membrane becomes much leakier, lowering membrane resistance. How does this change passive signal spread?
lab-neuroscience.l06.q4.e: Lower membrane resistance reduces the length constant, so more current leaks out and passive signals fade over a shorter distance.

lab-neuroscience.l07.q1.p: Which receptor acts as the coincidence detector for LTP?
lab-neuroscience.l07.q1.h: It opens only with glutamate plus depolarisation.
lab-neuroscience.l07.q1.e: The NMDA receptor opens only when presynaptic release and postsynaptic depolarisation coincide.

lab-neuroscience.l07.q2.p: Who discovered LTP in the rabbit hippocampus in 1973?
lab-neuroscience.l07.q2.h: Two researchers whose names start with B and L.
lab-neuroscience.l07.q2.e: Tim Bliss and Terje Lomo showed that high-frequency stimulation lastingly strengthened synapses.

lab-neuroscience.l07.q3.p: Using the Hebbian rule change in weight = eta x xi x xj, with eta = 0.1, xi = 2 and xj = 3, what is the change in weight?

lab-neuroscience.l07.q4.t: It blocks LTP and also impairs spatial learning
lab-neuroscience.l07.q4.p: Why does blocking NMDA receptors in the Morris water maze experiment support a link between LTP and learning?
lab-neuroscience.l07.q4.h: Think about what changed in behaviour.
lab-neuroscience.l07.q4.e: Blocking NMDA receptors prevents LTP and also impairs spatial memory, tying the cellular mechanism to behaviour.

lab-neuroscience.l08.q1.t: The brain's ability to change its connections with experience
lab-neuroscience.l08.q1.e: Neuroplasticity is the lifelong ability of the brain to strengthen, weaken, prune and form connections with experience.

lab-neuroscience.l08.q2.p: Which group showed enlarged posterior hippocampi after years of navigation work?
lab-neuroscience.l08.q2.h: They had to learn thousands of street routes.
lab-neuroscience.l08.q2.e: Maguire found in 2000 that licensed London cab drivers had an enlarged posterior hippocampus.

lab-neuroscience.l08.q3.t: Permanent rewiring of visual cortex toward the open eye
lab-neuroscience.l08.q3.p: In Hubel and Wiesel's experiments, closing one eye of a kitten during early life led to what?
lab-neuroscience.l08.q3.e: Monocular deprivation in the critical period permanently rewired visual cortex in favour of the open eye.

lab-neuroscience.l08.q4.t: Plasticity is highest early but never fully closes, so both timing and later practice matter
lab-neuroscience.l08.q4.p: Why does a critical period matter for how we think about learning and recovery?
lab-neuroscience.l08.q4.h: Remember what Merzenich and Maguire showed in adults.
lab-neuroscience.l08.q4.e: Plasticity is strongest early, yet adult cortical remapping and hippocampal changes show it persists, so training can help throughout life.

lab-neuroscience.l09.q1.p: Which brain structure was crucial to patient H.M.'s inability to form new memories?
lab-neuroscience.l09.q1.h: It is shaped like a seahorse.
lab-neuroscience.l09.q1.e: H.M. lost medial temporal lobe structures including the hippocampus and could no longer form new lasting declarative memories.

lab-neuroscience.l09.q2.p: Who studied H.M. and distinguished declarative from procedural memory?
lab-neuroscience.l09.q2.h: A founder of neuropsychology working in Montreal.
lab-neuroscience.l09.q2.e: Brenda Milner's studies of H.M. revealed separate memory systems.

lab-neuroscience.l09.q3.t: Skill memory can form without memory of the practice episodes
lab-neuroscience.l09.q3.p: A patient with hippocampal damage gets steadily faster at a mirror-drawing task over several days but says each day that they have never done it before. What does this show?
lab-neuroscience.l09.q3.h: Procedural and declarative memory are separate.
lab-neuroscience.l09.q3.e: Procedural learning can be preserved when declarative memory is lost, which shows they rely on different systems.

lab-neuroscience.l09.q4.t: Removing a region that disrupts one ability but spares others shows how functions are divided
lab-neuroscience.l09.q4.p: Why are lesion case studies like H.M. so informative about brain organisation?
lab-neuroscience.l09.q4.h: Compare what was lost with what remained.
lab-neuroscience.l09.q4.e: Selective loss with sparing of other abilities reveals which structures are needed for which functions.

lab-neuroscience.l10.q1.p: Broca's area is associated with what function?
lab-neuroscience.l10.q1.h: Broca's patient could understand but not speak fluently.
lab-neuroscience.l10.q1.e: Broca localised speech production to the left inferior frontal gyrus.

lab-neuroscience.l10.q2.p: What did Wilder Penfield create by stimulating the cortex of awake patients?
lab-neuroscience.l10.q2.h: It is a distorted map of the body on the cortex.
lab-neuroscience.l10.q2.e: Penfield mapped sensory and motor cortex and produced the homunculus.

lab-neuroscience.l10.q3.p: A patient speaks fluently but produces meaningless sentences and cannot understand what others say. Damage to which area is most consistent?
lab-neuroscience.l10.q3.h: Comprehension, not production, is the main problem.
lab-neuroscience.l10.q3.e: Wernicke's area in the temporal lobe supports language comprehension; damage gives fluent but poorly understood speech.

lab-neuroscience.l10.q4.t: Cortical space reflects the density and importance of sensory or motor control, not body size
lab-neuroscience.l10.q4.p: In the homunculus, hands and lips occupy a large share of the map. What is the best interpretation?
lab-neuroscience.l10.q4.h: Think about how finely we sense and move our fingers and lips.
lab-neuroscience.l10.q4.e: Cortical area is allocated by sensory and motor demand, so finely controlled parts get disproportionate space.

lab-neuroscience.l11.q1.t: Information is carried by how many spikes occur in a time window
lab-neuroscience.l11.q1.e: In rate coding, the number of spikes per time window represents the stimulus.

lab-neuroscience.l11.q2.p: Which distribution is a common first model for cortical spike counts?
lab-neuroscience.l11.q2.e: Many cortical neurons fire with near-Poisson variability, so spike counts follow a Poisson distribution.

lab-neuroscience.l11.q3.p: A neuron fires at a mean rate of 20 Hz. How many spikes do you expect on average in a 0.5 s window?

lab-neuroscience.l11.q4.t: Spike counts vary from trial to trial even for the same stimulus
lab-neuroscience.l11.q4.p: Why is a single-trial spike count not a perfect measure of a stimulus?
lab-neuroscience.l11.q4.e: Cortical spike counts are noisy, so the same stimulus produces different counts; averaging or pooling many neurons or trials is needed.

lab-neuroscience.l12.q1.t: Blood-flow changes linked to neural activity
lab-neuroscience.l12.q1.e: fMRI tracks blood-flow signals that follow neural activity.

lab-neuroscience.l12.q2.p: How many neurons are in the C. elegans connectome?
lab-neuroscience.l12.q2.h: It is a small number, a worm's whole nervous system.
lab-neuroscience.l12.q2.e: The roundworm C. elegans has a 302-neuron connectome; the human brain has roughly 86 billion.

lab-neuroscience.l12.q3.t: Tests of cause and effect for specific neurons
lab-neuroscience.l12.q3.p: Optogenetics lets researchers switch defined neurons on or off with light. What kind of conclusion does it allow beyond fMRI?
lab-neuroscience.l12.q3.h: Controlling a cell is different from watching it.
lab-neuroscience.l12.q3.e: Because researchers actively control specific neurons, they can test whether activity in those cells causes a behaviour.

lab-neuroscience.l12.q4.t: Blood flow rose there during the task, which suggests involvement but does not prove it alone performs the task
lab-neuroscience.l12.q4.p: A scan shows a bright patch in a region during a task. What is the most careful conclusion?
lab-neuroscience.l12.q4.e: fMRI reports blood-flow changes, indirect evidence of activity; it does not by itself show that one region is solely responsible.

lab-physics.l01.q1.p: Which law of motion states that an object keeps its state of rest or steady straight-line motion unless a net force acts on it?
lab-physics.l01.q1.e: Newton's first law defines inertia: without a net force, motion does not change.

lab-physics.l01.q2.p: In Newton's second law, what does the net force on an object equal for constant mass?
lab-physics.l01.q2.h: Force is linked to how quickly velocity changes.
lab-physics.l01.q2.e: F = m a: net force is mass times acceleration.

lab-physics.l01.q3.p: A net force of 30 N acts on a 10 kg cart. What is its acceleration?
lab-physics.l01.q3.h: Rearrange F = m a to find a.
lab-physics.l01.q3.e: a = F / m = 30 N / 10 kg = 3 m/s squared.

lab-physics.l01.q4.t: Without air resistance, all objects fall with the same acceleration
lab-physics.l01.q4.p: On the airless Moon a hammer and a feather dropped together land at the same time. What best explains this?
lab-physics.l01.q4.h: Think about what differs on Earth between a feather and a hammer.
lab-physics.l01.q4.e: With no air, the only force that matters is gravity, and acceleration is independent of mass. On Earth, air resistance slows the feather.

lab-physics.l02.q1.t: It is inversely proportional to the distance squared
lab-physics.l02.q1.p: In the law of universal gravitation, how does the force between two masses depend on the distance between them?
lab-physics.l02.q1.h: The force gets weaker with distance, faster than a simple proportion.
lab-physics.l02.q1.e: F = G m1 m2 / r squared, an inverse-square law.

lab-physics.l02.q2.p: Newton's law of gravitation applies to every pair of masses, not just to planets.
lab-physics.l02.q2.h: The word universal is in the name.
lab-physics.l02.q2.e: Every pair of masses attracts, but the force is only noticeable when at least one mass is huge.

lab-physics.l02.q3.p: The distance between two masses is tripled. By what factor does the gravitational force change?
lab-physics.l02.q3.h: The force depends on the square of the distance.
lab-physics.l02.q3.e: Force scales as 1 / r squared, so tripling r gives 1/9 of the force.

lab-physics.l02.q4.t: They and the station are in continuous free fall around the Earth
lab-physics.l02.q4.p: Astronauts on the space station float. What is the correct explanation?
lab-physics.l02.q4.h: Gravity at that height is still strong.
lab-physics.l02.q4.e: Gravity there is still strong; they float because they are falling around the Earth together with the station.

lab-physics.l03.q1.p: What is the formula for kinetic energy?
lab-physics.l03.q1.e: Kinetic energy is E_k = one half m v squared.

lab-physics.l03.q2.p: According to Emmy Noether, what is every conservation law connected to?
lab-physics.l03.q2.h: Her theorem links two ideas, one of them a conserved quantity.
lab-physics.l03.q2.e: Noether proved that each continuous symmetry corresponds to a conserved quantity.

lab-physics.l03.q3.p: What is the kinetic energy of a 2 kg object moving at 3 m/s?
lab-physics.l03.q3.e: E_k = 0.5 x 2 kg x (3 m/s) squared = 0.5 x 2 x 9 = 9 J.

lab-physics.l03.q4.t: Kinetic energy grows with the square of speed, so doubling speed quadruples it
lab-physics.l03.q4.p: Why does doubling a car speed make crashes much more severe than doubling its mass would?
lab-physics.l03.q4.h: Compare how mass and speed each appear in the formula.
lab-physics.l03.q4.e: Doubling mass doubles E_k, but doubling speed multiplies it by 4.

lab-physics.l04.q1.t: The force points opposite to the displacement
lab-physics.l04.q1.p: What does the minus sign in Hooke's law F = -k x tell us?
lab-physics.l04.q1.h: Think about which way a stretched spring pulls.
lab-physics.l04.q1.e: The force is a restoring force, directed back toward the equilibrium position.

lab-physics.l04.q2.p: For small swings, which two quantities set the period of a simple pendulum?
lab-physics.l04.q2.h: The formula is T = 2 pi times the square root of L / g.
lab-physics.l04.q2.e: T depends only on length L and gravitational acceleration g.

lab-physics.l04.q3.p: A spring with k = 200 N/m is stretched 0.05 m. What is the magnitude of its restoring force?
lab-physics.l04.q3.h: Multiply k by x in metres.

lab-physics.l04.q4.p: A pendulum is made 4 times longer. What happens to its period?
lab-physics.l04.q4.h: The length sits under a square root.
lab-physics.l04.q4.e: T is proportional to the square root of L, and the square root of 4 is 2.

lab-physics.l05.q1.p: What is the relation between wave speed, frequency and wavelength?
lab-physics.l05.q1.h: The speed is a product of two of the quantities.
lab-physics.l05.q1.e: Wave speed equals frequency times wavelength.

lab-physics.l05.q2.p: In what unit is frequency measured?
lab-physics.l05.q2.e: One hertz is one cycle per second.

lab-physics.l05.q3.p: A wave has frequency 50 Hz and wavelength 4 m. What is its speed?

lab-physics.l05.q4.p: A wave travels through the same medium and its frequency is doubled. What happens to its wavelength?
lab-physics.l05.q4.h: The medium sets the speed, which stays fixed.
lab-physics.l05.q4.e: With v fixed, v = f lambda means doubling f halves lambda.

lab-physics.l06.q1.p: The first law of thermodynamics is a statement of which principle?
lab-physics.l06.q1.h: Energy can change form but not be created.
lab-physics.l06.q1.e: delta U = Q - W expresses energy conservation for heat and work.

lab-physics.l06.q2.p: In the ideal gas law P V = n R T, in which units must the temperature be given?
lab-physics.l06.q2.h: It must be an absolute scale.
lab-physics.l06.q2.e: The gas law requires absolute temperature in kelvin.

lab-physics.l06.q3.p: A gas absorbs 500 J of heat and does 200 J of work on its surroundings. What is the change in its internal energy?

lab-physics.l06.q4.t: With volume and amount fixed, pressure is proportional to temperature
lab-physics.l06.q4.p: A sealed rigid can of gas is heated. Why does the pressure rise?
lab-physics.l06.q4.h: Which quantities in P V = n R T are fixed here?
lab-physics.l06.q4.e: V and n are constant, so P is proportional to T.

lab-physics.l07.q1.t: The number of microscopic states consistent with a macrostate
lab-physics.l07.q1.p: What does Boltzmann entropy S = k_B ln Omega count?
lab-physics.l07.q1.e: Omega is the number of microstates, and entropy grows with its logarithm.

lab-physics.l07.q2.p: The second law says the entropy of an isolated system never decreases.
lab-physics.l07.q2.e: In an isolated system, entropy stays constant or increases.

lab-physics.l07.q3.t: From the drink to the ice
lab-physics.l07.q3.p: An ice cube is dropped into a warm drink. In which direction does heat flow spontaneously?
lab-physics.l07.q3.h: Entropy increases when energy spreads out.
lab-physics.l07.q3.e: Heat flows from hot to cold, which increases the total entropy.

lab-physics.l07.q4.t: Broken states have vastly more microstates than the intact glass
lab-physics.l07.q4.p: Why does a dropped glass shatter but never spontaneously reassemble?
lab-physics.l07.q4.e: The disordered, broken states are overwhelmingly more probable. It is a statistical statement, not a violation of energy conservation.

lab-physics.l08.q1.p: According to Coulomb's law, what happens between two like charges?
lab-physics.l08.q1.e: Like charges repel and unlike charges attract.

lab-physics.l08.q2.p: Gauss's law relates the electric flux through a closed surface to what?
lab-physics.l08.q2.h: It is about what is inside the surface.
lab-physics.l08.q2.e: The flux is proportional to the enclosed charge divided by epsilon-zero.

lab-physics.l08.q3.p: One charge is doubled and the distance between the two charges is also doubled. How does the electric force change?
lab-physics.l08.q3.h: Force scales with the charge product and 1 / r squared.
lab-physics.l08.q3.e: The force is multiplied by 2 for the charge and by 1/4 for the distance, which gives 1/2.

lab-physics.l08.q4.t: Electric forces can attract or repel, while gravity only attracts
lab-physics.l08.q4.p: Coulomb and gravity are both inverse-square laws. What is a key difference?
lab-physics.l08.q4.h: Consider the two possible signs of charge.
lab-physics.l08.q4.e: Charge has two signs, so electric forces can go either way, while mass only attracts.

lab-physics.l09.q1.t: A current deflects a compass needle
lab-physics.l09.q1.e: A current-carrying wire moves a compass needle, linking electricity and magnetism.

lab-physics.l09.q2.p: What did Heinrich Hertz detect in 1887?
lab-physics.l09.q2.e: Hertz detected electromagnetic waves at light speed, vindicating Maxwell.

lab-physics.l09.q3.t: No induced current, because the flux is not changing
lab-physics.l09.q3.p: A bar magnet is held perfectly still next to a coil of wire. What current flows in the coil?
lab-physics.l09.q3.h: Faraday's law depends on a change.
lab-physics.l09.q3.e: An EMF is induced only when the magnetic flux changes, such as when the magnet moves.

lab-physics.l09.q4.t: His equations predicted a wave travelling at the speed of light
lab-physics.l09.q4.p: What led Maxwell to conclude that light is an electromagnetic wave?
lab-physics.l09.q4.e: Changing electric and magnetic fields sustain each other as a wave whose computed speed matched that of light.

lab-physics.l10.q1.t: Physics is the same in all inertial frames and light speed is the same for all observers
lab-physics.l10.q1.p: What do the two postulates of special relativity say?
lab-physics.l10.q1.h: One concerns frames, the other concerns light.
lab-physics.l10.q1.e: Equivalent physics in all inertial frames and a constant speed of light are the two postulates.

lab-physics.l10.q2.p: What did the Michelson-Morley experiment find?
lab-physics.l10.q2.h: It tested for a medium for light.
lab-physics.l10.q2.e: It detected no ether wind, consistent with light speed being independent of motion.

lab-physics.l10.q3.p: Using E = m c squared with c about 3 x 10^8 m/s, roughly how much energy corresponds to 1 kg of mass?
lab-physics.l10.q3.e: c squared is 9 x 10^16 m squared per s squared, so E is about 9 x 10^16 J.

lab-physics.l10.q4.t: Their clocks run slow because they move fast
lab-physics.l10.q4.p: Cosmic-ray muons reach the ground even though they decay quickly. How does special relativity explain this?
lab-physics.l10.q4.e: The muons are moving so fast that their internal clocks tick slowly, so they survive long enough to reach the ground.

lab-physics.l11.q1.t: The curvature of spacetime produced by mass and energy
lab-physics.l11.q1.p: In general relativity, what is gravity?
lab-physics.l11.q1.e: Mass and energy curve spacetime, and objects follow the straightest available paths.

lab-physics.l11.q2.t: The bending of starlight around the Sun
lab-physics.l11.q2.p: What did the 1919 Eddington eclipse expedition measure?
lab-physics.l11.q2.h: It was observed during a solar eclipse.
lab-physics.l11.q2.e: Starlight bent by the Sun matched general relativity, not Newton.

lab-physics.l11.q3.p: Astronomers found that Mercury's orbit drifts in a way Newtonian gravity could not explain. Which theory accounts for it exactly?
lab-physics.l11.q3.h: Strong gravity near the Sun is involved.
lab-physics.l11.q3.e: The precession of Mercury's perihelion is predicted by general relativity.

lab-physics.l11.q4.t: It confirmed a prediction made about a century earlier
lab-physics.l11.q4.p: Why was the 2015 LIGO detection of gravitational waves so important?
lab-physics.l11.q4.h: Think about when Einstein made the prediction.
lab-physics.l11.q4.e: Ripples from merging black holes confirmed a century-old prediction of general relativity.

lab-physics.l12.q1.t: Energy is emitted in discrete packets
lab-physics.l12.q1.p: What was Planck's key idea in 1900?
lab-physics.l12.q1.h: It resolved the black-body radiation problem.
lab-physics.l12.q1.e: Quantising energy explained black-body radiation and launched quantum theory.

lab-physics.l12.q2.t: The probability of finding it somewhere
lab-physics.l12.q2.p: What does the square of the wavefunction give?
lab-physics.l12.q2.e: The squared wavefunction gives probabilities rather than definite trajectories.

lab-physics.l12.q3.p: According to the uncertainty principle, what happens to the momentum uncertainty if a particle position is pinned down more precisely?
lab-physics.l12.q3.h: The product of the two has a lower bound.
lab-physics.l12.q3.e: The product delta x times delta p cannot fall below h-bar / 2, so reducing one increases the other.

lab-physics.l12.q4.t: It describes atoms, which underlies lasers and semiconductors
lab-physics.l12.q4.p: Why is quantum mechanics relevant to everyday technology?
lab-physics.l12.q4.h: Think about what is inside a phone.
lab-physics.l12.q4.e: Quantum rules for electrons in atoms and solids make lasers and semiconductor chips possible.

lab-physics.l13.q1.p: What did Young's double-slit experiment show about light?
lab-physics.l13.q1.e: The fringes are the signature of wave interference.

lab-physics.l13.q2.p: What did the Davisson-Germer experiment show?
lab-physics.l13.q2.h: It was done with electrons and a crystal.
lab-physics.l13.q2.e: Electron diffraction confirmed the wave nature of matter.

lab-physics.l13.q3.p: The photoelectric effect shows light ejecting electrons in discrete amounts of energy. Which aspect of light does it reveal?
lab-physics.l13.q3.h: Each photon carries energy h f.
lab-physics.l13.q3.e: It is explained by photons, particle-like quanta of energy h f.

lab-physics.l13.q4.t: Each electron is detected at one spot like a particle, yet the pattern is wave-like
lab-physics.l13.q4.p: Electrons are sent through a double slit one at a time and an interference pattern slowly builds up. Why is this surprising?
lab-physics.l13.q4.h: Each detection is a single dot.
lab-physics.l13.q4.e: Individual detections are particle-like, but the accumulated pattern shows wave interference.

lab-physics.l14.q1.p: Which of the four known forces is NOT described by the Standard Model?
lab-physics.l14.q1.h: It is the one described by general relativity.
lab-physics.l14.q1.e: The Standard Model covers three of the four forces; gravity is excluded.

lab-physics.l14.q2.p: Which particle was observed at the Large Hadron Collider in 2012?
lab-physics.l14.q2.h: It is linked to how particles gain mass.
lab-physics.l14.q2.e: The Higgs boson was observed at CERN in 2012.

lab-physics.l14.q3.p: Edwin Hubble showed that "nebulae" were really other galaxies and that they are receding. What did this provide evidence for?
lab-physics.l14.q3.h: The redshift-distance relation is the clue.
lab-physics.l14.q3.e: The redshift-distance relation was the first evidence that the universe expands.

lab-physics.l14.q4.t: It shows the Standard Model particles make up only a small share of the cosmos
lab-physics.l14.q4.p: Why does the discovery of dark matter and dark energy matter for the Standard Model?
lab-physics.l14.q4.h: Think about what makes up most of the universe.
lab-physics.l14.q4.e: Most of the universe is dark matter and dark energy, which the Standard Model does not account for.

law-admin.l01.q1.t: The action exceeds the authority that Congress granted in the agency's enabling statute
law-admin.l01.q1.p: Under the Administrative Procedure Act, what does it mean for an agency action to be ultra vires?
law-admin.l01.q1.h: Think about where an agency's power comes from.
law-admin.l01.q1.e: Agencies have only the powers Congress delegates, so action beyond the organic statute is ultra vires and will be set aside. A missing notice is a procedural defect, not an excess of statutory power.

law-admin.l01.q2.t: A rule is an agency statement with future effect, while an order is the final disposition of a matter other than rulemaking
law-admin.l01.q2.p: Which of the following is the best description of the APA's basic distinction between a rule and an order?
law-admin.l01.q2.h: One looks forward to a class of cases; the other closes a particular matter.
law-admin.l01.q2.e: The APA defines a rule by its future effect and an order as the final disposition in a matter other than rulemaking, typically adjudication. Binding effect on the public is not what separates them.

law-admin.l01.q3.t: The President is not an agency, so his own actions are not reviewable under the APA
law-admin.l01.q3.p: Under Franklin v. Massachusetts (1992), which statement about the President and the APA is correct?
law-admin.l01.q3.h: Look at who the APA's definition of agency covers.
law-admin.l01.q3.e: Franklin held the President is not an agency for APA purposes, so presidential action is not reviewed under it. Agencies carrying out his directions remain subject to the Act.

law-admin.l01.q4.t: The Bureau has only the powers conferred by its statute, and a general welfare purpose does not authorize a ban beyond the standards-setting authority granted
law-admin.l01.q4.p: Congress creates a Bureau of Home Safety by statute and directs it to set safety standards for household appliances. The Bureau, citing a general interest in consumer welfare, issues a rule banning all sales of gas-fired water heaters, which the statute does not mention. A manufacturer sues. What is the strongest argument for the manufacturer?
law-admin.l01.q4.h: Ask where an agency's authority has to come from.
law-admin.l01.q4.e: An agency may act only within delegated authority, so a ban outside the standards power is ultra vires. Agencies lawfully combine rulemaking and enforcement functions, so the second theory fails.

law-admin.l01.q5.t: The Treasury is an executive department under direct presidential control, while the FTC is an independent agency whose commissioners the President may now remove at will under Trump v. Slaughter (2026)
law-admin.l01.q5.p: The Department of the Treasury, headed by a Secretary the President may remove at will, and the Federal Trade Commission, led by commissioners with for-cause removal protection, both issue rules. Which statement is most accurate about their legal differences?
law-admin.l01.q5.h: Compare who may fire the heads.
law-admin.l01.q5.e: Executive departments are led by officials removable at will, and Trump v. Slaughter (2026) held that the FTC's for-cause protection is unconstitutional, so its commissioners are removable at will as well. Both are subject to the APA, so the exemption claim is wrong.

law-admin.l02.q1.t: Congress must lay down an intelligible principle to which the delegate is directed to conform
law-admin.l02.q1.p: Which test did Chief Justice Taft state in J.W. Hampton, Jr. & Co. v. United States (1928) for evaluating delegations of legislative power?
law-admin.l02.q1.h: The test is about guidance for the delegate.
law-admin.l02.q1.e: Hampton requires an intelligible principle so a court can tell whether the delegate stayed within bounds. Congress is not required to specify every detail.

law-admin.l02.q2.t: Two decisions, both in 1935, involving oil shipments and the National Industrial Recovery Act
law-admin.l02.q2.p: In how many Supreme Court decisions has a federal statute been struck down on nondelegation grounds, and in what year?
law-admin.l02.q2.e: Panama Refining and Schechter, both from 1935, are the only occasions on which the Court invalidated a statute on nondelegation grounds. The Court has since upheld very broad standards.

law-admin.l02.q3.t: A plurality upheld the delegation, with Justice Alito concurring in the judgment while signaling willingness to revisit the doctrine
law-admin.l02.q3.p: What was the result in Gundy v. United States (2019)?
law-admin.l02.q3.h: Count the Justices and read the separate writings.
law-admin.l02.q3.e: Four Justices upheld the statute and Alito supplied the fifth vote on the judgment. Three dissented under Justice Gorsuch's stricter approach, which did not command a majority.

law-admin.l02.q4.t: The challenge fails, because the statute states a policy goal and boundaries that satisfy the intelligible principle test
law-admin.l02.q4.p: Congress enacts a statute authorizing the Secretary of Health to issue regulations that are 'requisite to protect the public from imminent and serious health hazards,' and requires findings supported by evidence and a report to Congress. A trade group argues the statute is an unconstitutional delegation. Under the Court's current doctrine, how is the challenge most likely to come out?
law-admin.l02.q4.h: Compare the statute's guidance to Hampton, Whitman and Consumers' Research.
law-admin.l02.q4.e: A statute with a defined goal, a standard and procedural limits easily satisfies the intelligible principle test. Congress need not approve the regulations, which would trigger Chadha problems anyway.

law-admin.l02.q5.t: Private actors cannot be given regulatory power over competitors without governmental control, as Carter v. Carter Coal suggests
law-admin.l02.q5.p: A statute lets a private trade association of coal producers fix minimum wages and maximum hours that bind competing producers, with no agency review. A competitor challenges it. Which argument is strongest?
law-admin.l02.q5.h: Think about who holds the power, not just how broad the standard is.
law-admin.l02.q5.e: Carter Coal invalidated giving private parties authority over competitors, and the later cases rely on continued governmental control. Naming an association an agency does not cure the lack of public oversight.

law-admin.l03.q1.t: They are nominated by the President and confirmed by the Senate
law-admin.l03.q1.p: Under the Appointments Clause, how are principal officers of the United States appointed?
law-admin.l03.q1.e: Principal officers need nomination by the President and Senate confirmation. Congress may vest appointment of inferior officers in the President, courts or department heads.

law-admin.l03.q2.t: They are officers of the United States, so appointment by agency staff rather than the Commission violated the Appointments Clause
law-admin.l03.q2.p: What did Lucia v. SEC (2018) hold about the SEC's administrative law judges?
law-admin.l03.q2.h: Ask whether they exercise significant authority in a continuing position.
law-admin.l03.q2.e: Lucia held the ALJs are officers because of their significant authority and continuing position, and the defective appointment required a new hearing. They were not held to be principal officers.

law-admin.l03.q3.t: Congress may not insulate a single director who wields substantial executive power from at-will removal by the President
law-admin.l03.q3.p: Which statement best describes Seila Law LLC v. CFPB (2020)?
law-admin.l03.q3.h: Focus on the single director and the Court's remedy.
law-admin.l03.q3.e: Seila Law held the single-director structure unconstitutional and severed the protection. It limited rather than overruled Humphrey's, and the agency continued to exist.

law-admin.l03.q4.t: Whether the Commission exercises executive power through rulemaking and enforcement, because if it does the for-cause limit cannot bind the President
law-admin.l03.q4.p: Congress creates a five-member Commission on Transport Standards, with members serving staggered terms and removable only for neglect of duty. The Commission may issue rules and bring civil enforcement actions in court. The President fires a member who is a political opponent without alleging neglect. The member sues for reinstatement. Which analysis best predicts the legal question the court must decide after Trump v. Slaughter (2026)?
law-admin.l03.q4.h: The modern test asks about the body's powers, not its multimember form.
law-admin.l03.q4.e: Slaughter overruled Humphrey's Executor, so a commission that exercises executive power through rulemaking and enforcement has no valid for-cause protection and its members are removable at will. The APA does not regulate presidential personnel decisions.

law-admin.l03.q5.t: Two layers of for-cause protection impermissibly prevent the President from overseeing the officers who execute the law
law-admin.l03.q5.p: A statute provides that Board members can be removed only for cause by Commissioners, who can themselves be removed only for cause by the President. A regulated company challenges a Board enforcement order, arguing the structure is unconstitutional. Under Free Enterprise Fund v. PCAOB (2010), what is the strongest argument?
law-admin.l03.q5.h: Count the layers of insulation between the President and the officer.
law-admin.l03.q5.e: Free Enterprise Fund held that dual for-cause removal layers were unconstitutional because they stripped the President of oversight. Inferior officers can have limited protection, and combined functions are allowed.

law-admin.l04.q1.t: The Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs
law-admin.l04.q1.p: Which office within the Executive Office of the President reviews significant executive agency rules under Executive Order 12866?
law-admin.l04.q1.h: It sits within the Office of Management and Budget.
law-admin.l04.q1.e: OIRA, part of OMB, conducts centralized review under Executive Order 12866. The GAO is a legislative branch agency and does not conduct presidential review.

law-admin.l04.q2.t: A one-house legislative veto of executive action is unconstitutional because it bypasses bicameralism and presentment
law-admin.l04.q2.p: What was the holding of INS v. Chadha (1983)?
law-admin.l04.q2.h: Think about the two lawmaking requirements in Article I.
law-admin.l04.q2.e: Chadha held the legislative veto was legislative in effect and so required passage by both houses and presentment to the President. A Senate-only vote would suffer the same defect.

law-admin.l04.q3.t: Presidential power is at its maximum when acting with congressional authorization and at its lowest ebb when acting against Congress's will
law-admin.l04.q3.p: Which statement best describes Justice Jackson's concurrence in Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer (1952)?
law-admin.l04.q3.h: He described three categories along a spectrum.
law-admin.l04.q3.e: Jackson's tripartite framework ties presidential power to congressional authorization. The majority held Truman's seizure of the steel mills unauthorized.

law-admin.l04.q4.t: The agency is barred from issuing a substantially similar rule unless Congress later authorizes it by statute
law-admin.l04.q4.p: An agency issues a major rule. Congress passes a joint resolution of disapproval under the Congressional Review Act, and the President signs it. Two years later, the agency, under new leadership, wants to issue a substantially similar rule using the same statute. Which analysis is most accurate?
law-admin.l04.q4.h: The CRA contains a bar on reissuance.
law-admin.l04.q4.e: The CRA provides that a disapproved rule has no effect and that a substantially similar rule may not be reissued without new statutory authorization. OIRA has no power to waive it.

law-admin.l04.q5.t: No, because under Chadha a congressional action with the force of law must pass both houses and be presented to the President
law-admin.l04.q5.p: Following a dispute with an agency, the House alone passes a resolution disapproving a rule and declares it void. The agency continues to enforce the rule. A regulated party asks whether the resolution has legal effect. What is the best answer?
law-admin.l04.q5.h: Which constitutional requirements does a House-only vote fail?
law-admin.l04.q5.e: A House-only resolution lacks bicameralism and presentment, so Chadha makes it ineffective. The power of the purse does not allow a single house to void rules directly.

law-admin.l05.q1.t: Publication of notice of proposed rulemaking and an opportunity for interested persons to submit written comments
law-admin.l05.q1.p: Which of the following is a required step in informal rulemaking under section 553 of the APA?
law-admin.l05.q1.h: Think of the three-step core: notice, participation, statement.
law-admin.l05.q1.e: Section 553 requires notice, an opportunity to comment and a concise statement of basis and purpose. Cross-examination belongs to formal procedures under sections 556 and 557.

law-admin.l05.q2.t: Courts may not impose procedural requirements on agencies beyond those found in the APA, the Constitution or another statute
law-admin.l05.q2.p: What did Vermont Yankee Nuclear Power Corp. v. NRDC (1978) hold about courts and rulemaking procedure?
law-admin.l05.q2.h: The Court was reversing an overreaching lower court.
law-admin.l05.q2.e: Vermont Yankee rejects judge-made procedural add-ons, leaving courts to police the reasoning of the agency instead. The idea that courts can add hearings in safety rules is exactly what was rejected.

law-admin.l05.q3.t: Whether the final rule was a logical outgrowth of the proposal, such that interested parties could have anticipated it
law-admin.l05.q3.p: An agency finalizes a rule that differs from its proposal. Which test will a court apply to decide whether notice was adequate?
law-admin.l05.q3.h: The question is about fair notice of what could change.
law-admin.l05.q3.e: The logical outgrowth test asks whether a reasonable commenter could have foreseen the change. Agencies need not republish every time and are not bound by the majority of comments.

law-admin.l05.q4.t: The inspection requirement was not a logical outgrowth of the proposal, so the notice failed to give fair warning
law-admin.l05.q4.p: The Department of Housing proposes a rule requiring landlords to install smoke detectors in all rental units. After comments, it issues a final rule that also requires annual inspections by licensed contractors, a requirement no one mentioned in the proposal and which was never discussed in the preamble. A landlord association sues. Which argument is strongest?
law-admin.l05.q4.h: Ask whether commenters could have anticipated the change.
law-admin.l05.q4.e: A wholly new, costly requirement that commenters could not have foreseen defeats the logical outgrowth standard. Agencies may modify terms in response to comments, so a flat ban on changes is wrong.

law-admin.l05.q5.t: The rescission is invalid because repealing a legislative rule is itself rulemaking and requires the same procedures as issuing it
law-admin.l05.q5.p: An agency, led by a new administration, withdraws a final rule by posting a notice on its website that the rule is rescinded effective immediately. There was no proposal, comment period or explanation. A public interest group sues. How is the court most likely to rule?
law-admin.l05.q5.h: The APA's definition of rule includes repeal.
law-admin.l05.q5.e: The APA treats the repeal of a rule as rulemaking, so notice and comment applies. An agency has no power to avoid section 553 simply by changing policy.

law-admin.l06.q1.t: Interpretive rules and general statements of policy
law-admin.l06.q1.p: Which of the following is exempt from notice-and-comment rulemaking under section 553(b)?
law-admin.l06.q1.h: The statutory list is short and covers non-binding items.
law-admin.l06.q1.e: Section 553(b)(A) exempts interpretive rules, general statements of policy, and rules of agency organization, procedure or practice. There is no exemption based on penalty size or agency certification.

law-admin.l06.q2.t: An agency need not use notice and comment to adopt a new interpretive rule that departs from an earlier interpretation
law-admin.l06.q2.p: What did Perez v. Mortgage Bankers Association (2015) hold?
law-admin.l06.q2.h: The Court rejected a judge-made rule that added procedure.
law-admin.l06.q2.e: Perez rejected the Paralyzed Veterans doctrine and held that the APA's text exempts interpretive rules regardless of whether they change an earlier reading. The idea that interpretive rules bind like law is the opposite of the holding.

law-admin.l06.q3.t: Whether in substance it creates new binding obligations and the agency treats it as binding when it acts
law-admin.l06.q3.p: Which factor is most relevant when a court decides if a guidance document is really a legislative rule?
law-admin.l06.q3.e: Courts look to the practical effect and the agency's conduct, not to the label. A title of guidance does not control the outcome.

law-admin.l06.q4.t: The good cause exception in section 553(b)(B), supported by a finding and a brief statement of reasons incorporated in the rule
law-admin.l06.q4.p: A federal agency finds that a statutory deadline falls in six days and that its previous rule will expire then, leaving a regulatory gap that would permit unsafe products to be sold. It issues a replacement rule without notice and comment, stating in the rule that notice would be impracticable and the reasons. A trade group sues on procedural grounds. What is the strongest ground for the agency?
law-admin.l06.q4.h: The agency recorded a finding in the rule itself.
law-admin.l06.q4.e: Good cause allows skipping notice when it is impracticable, and the agency documented its reasons. The exemptions for interpretive or procedural rules would not fit a rule that sets safety obligations.

law-admin.l06.q5.t: The statement may be treated as a binding legislative rule because the agency applies it as mandatory, so the lack of notice and comment is a defect
law-admin.l06.q5.p: A federal agency issues a policy statement saying that it will generally not prosecute small firms that self-report violations within 30 days. Staff attorneys routinely bring cases against firms that report on day 31, saying they have no discretion to waive the deadline. A firm sues, arguing the 30-day rule was a legislative rule issued without notice and comment. What is the best analysis?
law-admin.l06.q5.h: Look at how the agency uses the document in practice.
law-admin.l06.q5.e: A policy statement applied without discretion operates as a binding rule, so courts may treat it as a legislative rule. A label alone never makes a policy statement exempt.

law-admin.l07.q1.t: When a statute requires that rules be made on the record after opportunity for an agency hearing
law-admin.l07.q1.p: When must an agency use the formal rulemaking procedures in sections 556 and 557 of the APA?
law-admin.l07.q1.h: The trigger lies in the statute.
law-admin.l07.q1.e: Section 553(c) triggers formal procedure only when a statute requires on-the-record rulemaking. Cost or controversy does not trigger it.

law-admin.l07.q2.t: It held that the words after hearing, without more, do not require on-the-record procedure under sections 556 and 557
law-admin.l07.q2.p: In United States v. Florida East Coast Railway Co. (1973), how did the Court treat a statute that authorized the ICC to set rates after hearing?
law-admin.l07.q2.h: The Court wanted clearer statutory language.
law-admin.l07.q2.e: Florida East Coast read the statute narrowly: after hearing is not enough, and on the record language is needed. Because of that, formal rulemaking is rare.

law-admin.l07.q3.t: An evidentiary hearing with cross-examination and a decision based exclusively on the record
law-admin.l07.q3.p: Which feature distinguishes formal from informal rulemaking?
law-admin.l07.q3.e: Formal rulemaking uses a trial-type hearing and record-only decision. There is no judicial pre-approval or presidential signature requirement.

law-admin.l07.q4.t: The agency, because the statute does not clearly require a hearing on the record, so informal procedures suffice
law-admin.l07.q4.p: A statute directs the Food Agency to set standards of identity for a processed food 'after notice and an opportunity for a public hearing.' A producer demands cross-examination of the agency's scientists before the standard is adopted. The agency proceeds by notice and comment only. Applying the Supreme Court's approach, who prevails?
law-admin.l07.q4.h: Compare the statutory wording to on the record.
law-admin.l07.q4.e: Under Florida East Coast, ambiguous hearing language does not trigger formal procedures. The Constitution does not demand cross-examination for general rules.

law-admin.l07.q5.t: Section 557(d) bars interested persons from making ex parte communications on the merits to decision-makers, and the decision may be set aside
law-admin.l07.q5.p: A Commission engaged in formal adjudication receives a private letter from a competitor of the respondent arguing the merits of the case, and the Commissioner reading it decides the case partly based on it. The respondent objects. What is the best analysis?
law-admin.l07.q5.h: The APA has a specific rule for formal proceedings.
law-admin.l07.q5.e: Section 557(d) prohibits ex parte communications relevant to the merits in formal proceedings. The rule applies to formal adjudication and not primarily to informal rulemaking.

law-admin.l08.q1.t: A legitimate claim of entitlement created by an independent source such as a statute or contract
law-admin.l08.q1.p: Under Board of Regents v. Roth (1972), which is required before a person has a property interest protected by procedural due process?
law-admin.l08.q1.h: Property interests come from outside the Constitution.
law-admin.l08.q1.e: Roth requires a legitimate claim of entitlement drawn from state law or other sources, not just a hope. Years of receipt do not by themselves create an entitlement.

law-admin.l08.q2.t: The private interest, the risk of erroneous deprivation and value of added safeguards, and the government's interest
law-admin.l08.q2.p: Which three factors does Mathews v. Eldridge (1976) use to determine what process is due?
law-admin.l08.q2.h: A balancing test with three interests.
law-admin.l08.q2.e: Mathews balances private interest, risk of error with value of safeguards, and governmental burden. The alternatives list factors that are not part of the test.

law-admin.l08.q3.t: Combining these functions does not by itself violate due process, because adjudicators are presumed honest and impartial
law-admin.l08.q3.p: What did Withrow v. Larkin (1975) hold about an agency that combines investigative and adjudicative functions?
law-admin.l08.q3.h: The Court rejected a structural per se rule.
law-admin.l08.q3.e: Withrow held that structural combination alone is not a due process violation without specific bias. A separation rule applies within a case under the APA, but not as a constitutional absolute.

law-admin.l08.q4.t: It will weigh her interest in uninterrupted subsidy, the chance that a pre-termination hearing would catch errors, and the state's burden, and it may find that a prompt post-termination hearing is enough if she is not at risk of destitution
law-admin.l08.q4.p: A state statute entitles any person who meets certain income criteria to a monthly housing subsidy. The state agency terminates Marisol's subsidy on the basis of a written report that she exceeded the income limit. She disputes the figures. Under existing law the state offers a full hearing within 60 days after termination, with back payment if she wins. She claims she is entitled to a hearing before termination. How is a court applying Mathews most likely to resolve it?
law-admin.l08.q4.h: This is a balancing test and the answer depends on the stakes.
law-admin.l08.q4.e: Mathews is flexible: the weight of the interest and risk of error matter. Goldberg required a pre-termination hearing for subsistence welfare, but Mathews allowed post-termination review where the decision turned on documents.

law-admin.l08.q5.t: The adviser prevails, because the Seventh Amendment requires a jury when the SEC seeks civil penalties for fraud, a claim resembling a common-law action
law-admin.l08.q5.p: The SEC institutes an in-house proceeding before an ALJ seeking civil penalties from a hedge fund adviser for alleged securities fraud. The adviser objects that it is entitled to a jury trial in federal court. Under SEC v. Jarkesy (2024), what is the most likely outcome?
law-admin.l08.q5.h: Consider the legal nature of the claim and the remedy.
law-admin.l08.q5.e: Jarkesy held that the Seventh Amendment applies to SEC fraud penalty claims and the public rights exception did not cover them. The appointment issue was not the ground of the decision.

law-admin.l09.q1.t: No individual hearing was required when a board raised valuations for all property across a large area
law-admin.l09.q1.p: What did Bi-Metallic Investment Co. v. State Board of Equalization (1915) hold?
law-admin.l09.q1.h: Compare it with Londoner v. Denver.
law-admin.l09.q1.e: Bi-Metallic held that a generally applicable decision affecting many people needs no individual hearing, while Londoner required a hearing for individualized assessments. The political process protects against general rules.

law-admin.l09.q2.t: A reviewing court may uphold agency action only on the grounds that the agency itself invoked
law-admin.l09.q2.p: What is the central holding of SEC v. Chenery Corp. (Chenery I, 1943)?
law-admin.l09.q2.h: The reviewing court is limited to the agency's explanation.
law-admin.l09.q2.e: Chenery I holds that courts judge agency action on the agency's own stated reasons. The agency may reconsider on remand and reach the same result on proper grounds.

law-admin.l09.q3.t: The agency, in the exercise of discretion that is reviewed only for abuse
law-admin.l09.q3.p: According to Chenery II (1947), who decides whether to announce a new principle by rulemaking or by adjudication?
law-admin.l09.q3.h: The choice is largely the agency's.
law-admin.l09.q3.e: Chenery II lets the agency choose between rulemaking and adjudication, subject to limits like fair notice. Courts do not select the method for it.

law-admin.l09.q4.t: The agency may announce new standards in adjudication, but imposing a penalty for conduct that earlier guidance approved denies fair notice and imposes unfair retroactive liability
law-admin.l09.q4.p: Under a statute that authorizes the Labor Agency to enforce a ban on unfair practices, the agency announces for the first time in a case against Brightway Corp. that a common scheduling practice is unfair, and imposes a large fine for conduct that occurred before the announcement. Brightway had followed agency guidance that approved the practice. What is Brightway's strongest argument?
law-admin.l09.q4.h: Chenery II permits the method but not unfair surprise.
law-admin.l09.q4.e: Adjudication is a legitimate way to set policy, but fair-notice and reliance principles restrict retroactive penalties. The absolute rule against adjudicative policymaking is not the law.

law-admin.l09.q5.t: The rezoning of many properties needs no individual hearing, but the demolition decision turns on facts peculiar to one owner, so notice and a hearing are required
law-admin.l09.q5.p: A city council passes a measure reclassifying the zoning of every lot on one street and, separately, orders the demolition of one named owner's building after finding it unsafe, without a hearing. The owner of the building sues under due process. Applying Londoner and Bi-Metallic, what is the best analysis?
law-admin.l09.q5.e: Londoner requires process when a decision rests on individualized facts, while Bi-Metallic excuses hearings for general rules. Emergencies can justify summary action in genuine cases, but the facts do not state one.

law-admin.l10.q1.t: The action marks the consummation of the agency's decision-making process, and rights or obligations are determined or legal consequences flow from it
law-admin.l10.q1.p: Under Bennett v. Spear (1997), what are the two conditions for final agency action?
law-admin.l10.q1.h: One concerns the process finishing, the other concerns consequences.
law-admin.l10.q1.e: Bennett's test is consummation of the decision process plus legal consequences. A signature, publication or payment of a penalty is not required.

law-admin.l10.q2.t: The refusal is presumptively unreviewable, though the presumption may be rebutted by statutory guidelines
law-admin.l10.q2.p: What is the effect of Heckler v. Chaney (1985) on challenges to an agency's refusal to bring an enforcement action?
law-admin.l10.q2.h: Consider why enforcement decisions are special.
law-admin.l10.q2.e: Chaney recognizes a presumption of unreviewability that can be rebutted if the statute gives guidelines. Saying it is never reviewable overstates the rule.

law-admin.l10.q3.t: Only in rare circumstances where the statute gives a court no meaningful standard against which to judge the discretion
law-admin.l10.q3.p: Under Citizens to Preserve Overton Park v. Volpe (1971), when is action committed to agency discretion by law under section 701(a)(2)?
law-admin.l10.q3.e: Overton Park limits the exception to cases with no law to apply. Technical expertise alone does not trigger it, as courts review technical decisions regularly.

law-admin.l10.q4.t: Carrier X's denial is reviewable final action, but the refusal to bring enforcement against Carrier Y is presumptively unreviewable under Heckler v. Chaney
law-admin.l10.q4.p: A statute directs the Transportation Agency to issue a safety certificate to any carrier that meets specified standards. Carrier X applies, meets the standards, and receives a one-line denial. A competitor files a complaint with the agency urging it to open an enforcement proceeding against Carrier Y for violating the same standards, and the agency takes no action. Which statement is most accurate?
law-admin.l10.q4.h: Separate denial of a benefit from a refusal to prosecute someone else.
law-admin.l10.q4.e: A licensing denial under defined standards is final and reviewable, while nonenforcement is presumptively unreviewable. Licensing decisions are not generally committed to discretion when there are standards.

law-admin.l10.q5.t: The claim fails, because section 706(1) lets a court compel only discrete agency action that the agency is legally required to take
law-admin.l10.q5.p: A plaintiff asks a court to order an agency to complete an overall land use plan faster and to issue more thorough monitoring of the lands it manages, under section 706(1). The statute describes broad goals but no specific required step. Under Norton v. Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance (2004), what is the likely result?
law-admin.l10.q5.h: The APA does not authorize programmatic supervision.
law-admin.l10.q5.e: Norton limits section 706(1) to discrete, required action, not broad programmatic improvement. The provision is not limited to rules.

law-admin.l11.q1.t: Arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion, or otherwise not in accordance with law
law-admin.l11.q1.p: Which standard applies under section 706(2)(A) to most agency policy decisions and informal rulemaking?
law-admin.l11.q1.h: The statutory text names the standard.
law-admin.l11.q1.e: Section 706(2)(A) supplies the arbitrary and capricious standard. Courts may not substitute their own policy judgment, so the final option is wrong.

law-admin.l11.q2.t: The agency entirely failed to consider an important aspect of the problem
law-admin.l11.q2.p: According to Motor Vehicle Manufacturers Association v. State Farm (1983), which is a ground for finding a rule arbitrary and capricious?
law-admin.l11.q2.h: Recall the list of failures from State Farm.
law-admin.l11.q2.e: State Farm says failing to consider an important aspect of the problem is arbitrary. Cost or change alone is not a ground, as agencies may change policy with reasons.

law-admin.l11.q3.t: It must consider the whole record, including evidence that detracts from the agency's finding
law-admin.l11.q3.p: Under Universal Camera Corp. v. NLRB (1951), how must a court apply the substantial evidence standard?
law-admin.l11.q3.h: The phrase whole record is central.
law-admin.l11.q3.e: Universal Camera requires review of the whole record, including contrary evidence. Courts do not reweigh evidence, and a single supporting item does not end the inquiry.

law-admin.l11.q4.t: The agency failed to display awareness of the change, to consider the evidence and reliance interests, and to respond to significant comments
law-admin.l11.q4.p: An agency rescinds a seven-year-old rule requiring ventilation in warehouses. Its explanation says only that the rule is burdensome. Comments from workers, which the agency's notice does not mention, say injuries dropped sharply after the rule took effect and many employers relied on it in building design. A trade group supports the rescission. A public health group sues. What is the strongest ground for setting aside the rescission?
law-admin.l11.q4.h: Fox and State Farm set the expectations for reasoned change.
law-admin.l11.q4.e: Under Fox, a change in position requires reasoned explanation, including attention to reliance interests and facts underlying the old rule. Agencies need not show the new policy is better, so the proof claim fails.

law-admin.l11.q5.t: The court may set aside the action because the stated explanation was contrived, and the APA requires a genuine rationale that explains the agency's decision
law-admin.l11.q5.p: In its rulemaking record, an agency says it is adding a question to a federal survey to help enforce a civil rights statute. Internal documents in the record, produced in discovery, show that the stated reason was not the real reason and that the question was pursued for other purposes. A state sues. Under Department of Commerce v. New York (2019), what is the best analysis?
law-admin.l11.q5.h: A reasoned explanation must also be real.
law-admin.l11.q5.e: The Court held the stated reason was pretextual and could not sustain the decision. Chenery I points the other way, since a court cannot substitute its own rationale.

law-admin.l12.q1.t: An injury in fact that is concrete and particularized, fairly traceable to the defendant, and redressable by a favorable decision
law-admin.l12.q1.p: Which of the following is a required element of Article III standing as stated in Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife (1992)?
law-admin.l12.q1.h: There are three elements: injury, causation, redress.
law-admin.l12.q1.e: Lujan requires injury in fact, traceability and redressability. A generalized grievance shared by everyone is not particularized.

law-admin.l12.q2.t: The states lacked standing, because a litigant generally has no judicially cognizable interest in the prosecution or non-prosecution of another
law-admin.l12.q2.p: In United States v. Texas (2023), what did the Supreme Court hold about states challenging federal immigration enforcement priorities?
law-admin.l12.q2.e: The Court emphasized the longstanding principle that private parties cannot compel prosecution of others, and rejected the states' claim. Special solicitude did not salvage standing.

law-admin.l12.q3.t: A bare statutory violation is not enough, and a plaintiff must show a concrete harm with a close relationship to a traditionally recognized injury
law-admin.l12.q3.p: What does TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez (2021) hold about statutory violations and standing?
law-admin.l12.q3.h: Congress cannot create standing by labeling a violation an injury.
law-admin.l12.q3.e: TransUnion requires a concrete harm even when a statute gives a cause of action. Class members whose files were never shared lacked standing.

law-admin.l12.q4.t: The association likely lacks standing, because the injury depends on speculative downstream events and the statute shields the members from being compelled
law-admin.l12.q4.p: A national association of physicians who say they object to a particular medical procedure sues to challenge a federal agency's approval of a drug used in that procedure. None of its members prescribes the drug. The members claim they might someday be asked to treat a patient who suffers complications. A federal conscience statute protects them from being required to assist. Which analysis is most consistent with FDA v. Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine (2024)?
law-admin.l12.q4.h: Trace the chain of events between the approval and the members.
law-admin.l12.q4.e: The Court found no sufficiently direct, non-speculative injury and noted conscience protections. Germane purpose is only one part of associational standing, not a substitute for injury.

law-admin.l12.q5.t: Its commercial interest may fall outside the zone of interests that a consumer safety statute protects, which is the only real obstacle, though that APA test is lenient
law-admin.l12.q5.p: A small manufacturer sues to challenge an agency rule that lets foreign competitors import goods more easily. It alleges that its sales will drop, supported by an affidavit with specific sales projections. The statute authorizing the rule aims to protect domestic consumer safety and says nothing of domestic producers. Which is the strongest argument against the manufacturer's APA claim, even if a weak one?
law-admin.l12.q5.h: Separate the constitutional question from the statutory one.
law-admin.l12.q5.e: Economic injury is a classic injury in fact, so the real question is the zone of interests, which is lenient. The APA supplies the cause of action to those within the zone.

law-admin.l13.q1.t: The fitness of the issues for judicial decision and the hardship to the parties of withholding court consideration
law-admin.l13.q1.p: What two considerations make up the ripeness test from Abbott Laboratories v. Gardner (1967)?
law-admin.l13.q1.h: One looks at the legal question, the other at the burden of waiting.
law-admin.l13.q1.e: Abbott pairs fitness and hardship. The other pairs are not factors of the test.

law-admin.l13.q2.t: A party in an agency enforcement proceeding may bring a structural constitutional challenge in district court rather than waiting for appellate review after the agency decides
law-admin.l13.q2.p: What did Axon Enterprise, Inc. v. FTC (2023) hold?
law-admin.l13.q2.h: The harm is being subjected to an unconstitutional proceeding.
