law-conlaw.l01.q4.h: Distinguish the open question from the settled one.
law-conlaw.l01.q4.e: The debate concerns how far the oath and the Court's interpretations bind other officials. Where the Supreme Court has ruled, Cooper treats the ruling as binding; where it has not, departmentalists say officials may use their own judgment. Both views accept judicial review exists.

law-conlaw.l01.q5.t: Congress has broad control over federal jurisdiction under the Exceptions Clause, but a court would likely examine whether the measure is a bar on constitutional enforcement that violates other provisions
law-conlaw.l01.q5.p: Congress passes a law removing the Supreme Court's appellate jurisdiction over every case in which a person challenges a federal statute on First Amendment grounds. Which analysis best reflects the current understanding?
law-conlaw.l01.q5.h: Congress has power over jurisdiction, but not unlimited power.
law-conlaw.l01.q5.e: Article III lets Congress make exceptions to the Court's appellate jurisdiction, which is wide, but scholars debate its limits where the exclusion would deny any forum or aim at particular outcomes. The question is unsettled.

law-conlaw.l02.q1.t: When the President acts contrary to the express or implied will of Congress
law-conlaw.l02.q1.p: In Justice Jackson's concurrence in Youngstown, when is presidential power at its lowest ebb?
law-conlaw.l02.q1.e: In the third zone, where the President acts against Congress, he can rely only on his own constitutional powers minus any power of Congress over the matter.

law-conlaw.l02.q2.t: It is unconstitutional because it has legislative effect without passage by both houses and presentment to the President
law-conlaw.l02.q2.p: What did INS v. Chadha hold about the one-house legislative veto?
law-conlaw.l02.q2.e: Chadha held that a one-house veto altered legal rights and was legislative action requiring both houses and presentment.

law-conlaw.l02.q3.t: Under the intelligible principle test, a delegation is valid if Congress gives the agency a standard to guide its discretion, so the statute is likely valid
law-conlaw.l02.q3.p: Congress passes a statute telling an agency to set air-quality standards that are "requisite to protect the public health," with findings and procedures. A challenger says Congress unconstitutionally delegated legislative power. How would the Court most likely analyze the claim under current doctrine?
law-conlaw.l02.q3.h: Think of the standard from Mistretta.
law-conlaw.l02.q3.e: The Court has applied the intelligible principle test and has upheld broad delegations; whether it will tighten the test is debated, though recent cases have upheld delegations.

law-conlaw.l02.q4.t: The for-cause removal limit on a single head of an agency with substantial executive power violates the separation of powers, because it limits the President's control of executive power
law-conlaw.l02.q4.p: A statute creates an agency headed by a single director with a five-year term and removable by the President only for inefficiency, neglect of duty or malfeasance. The agency has significant executive authority over private parties. The director is sued to invalidate an enforcement action. What is the strongest argument for the challenger under Seila Law?
law-conlaw.l02.q4.e: Seila Law limited Humphrey's Executor and held that a single director with significant power cannot be insulated by for-cause removal. Seila Law did not overrule Humphrey's; that came later, in Trump v. Slaughter (2026), and neither case holds that every limit on every officer is invalid.

law-conlaw.l02.q5.t: The agency must point to clear congressional authorization, and ambiguity in a general statute will likely be read against the claim of such power
law-conlaw.l02.q5.p: An agency claims a statute from decades ago, written in general terms, authorizes it to impose a nationwide program that would reshape a large portion of the economy and affect millions of people. Congress never mentioned such authority. Under the major questions doctrine, how is the claim most likely treated?
law-conlaw.l02.q5.h: Think West Virginia v. EPA and Loper Bright.
law-conlaw.l02.q5.e: The major questions doctrine requires clear authorization for powers of vast economic and political significance, and Loper Bright rejected Chevron deference in general, so ambiguity does not favor the agency.

law-conlaw.l03.q1.p: Which case upheld federal regulation of wheat grown for personal consumption because of its aggregate effect on interstate commerce?
law-conlaw.l03.q1.e: Wickard held that the aggregate effect of home-grown wheat on the national market allowed regulation under the Commerce Clause.

law-conlaw.l03.q2.t: Possessing a gun in a school zone was not economic activity and the statute had no jurisdictional element tying it to interstate commerce
law-conlaw.l03.q2.p: Why did the Court strike down the Gun-Free School Zones Act in United States v. Lopez?
law-conlaw.l03.q2.h: Economic activity and a jurisdictional hook.
law-conlaw.l03.q2.e: Lopez held that the statute regulated noneconomic activity without a jurisdictional element and was outside the substantial effects category.

law-conlaw.l03.q3.t: Congress may regulate the channels of interstate commerce, so a ban on shipping those goods is likely valid regardless of how the goods were made
law-conlaw.l03.q3.p: Congress bans the interstate shipment of goods made by a factory that employs workers for more than a statutory number of hours per week. A manufacturer argues that production is local and outside the commerce power. Which statement best describes the doctrine now?
law-conlaw.l03.q3.h: Which category of Commerce power is involved?
law-conlaw.l03.q3.e: The modern Court recognizes the power to regulate the channels of interstate commerce, and the older production-commerce distinction was abandoned after 1937.

law-conlaw.l03.q4.t: The Commerce Clause regulates existing activity and does not allow Congress to compel individuals to enter commerce by purchasing a product
law-conlaw.l03.q4.p: Congress passes a law requiring every adult to purchase a specific product from a private company, justified under the Commerce Clause as a means to regulate the market in related goods. Which is the strongest argument against the law under NFIB v. Sebelius?
law-conlaw.l03.q4.e: A majority in NFIB held that the Commerce Clause does not authorize compelling people to engage in commerce. The same mandate was sustained under the taxing power by Chief Justice Roberts.

law-conlaw.l03.q5.t: The federal law is valid as applied, because Congress could rationally conclude that intrastate cultivation affects the interstate market in a comprehensive scheme
law-conlaw.l03.q5.p: A state resident grows and uses marijuana at home under a state medical program, and none of it enters commerce. Federal agents seize the plants under the Controlled Substances Act. Under Gonzales v. Raich, what is the most likely result of a Commerce Clause challenge?
law-conlaw.l03.q5.h: Compare Lopez and Morrison with a broader regulatory scheme.
law-conlaw.l03.q5.e: Raich upheld application of the Controlled Substances Act because homegrown marijuana is part of an economic class of activity that Congress can regulate as part of a comprehensive scheme.

law-conlaw.l04.q1.t: It was a valid exercise of the taxing power because it functioned as a tax collected by the IRS
law-conlaw.l04.q1.p: What did the Court hold in NFIB v. Sebelius about the individual mandate's payment under the taxing power?
law-conlaw.l04.q1.e: The Chief Justice held that the payment could be read as a tax, though the Commerce Clause did not authorize the mandate itself.

law-conlaw.l04.q2.t: Congress may not command state legislatures or executive officers to enact or administer a federal regulatory program
law-conlaw.l04.q2.h: New York v. United States and Printz.
law-conlaw.l04.q2.e: Anticommandeering protects states from being conscripted into federal service. The second option describes limits on conditional spending, the third McCulloch, and the fourth the dormant Commerce Clause.

law-conlaw.l04.q3.t: The condition is valid because it is related to highway safety, is unambiguous, and the financial incentive is not so large as to be coercive
law-conlaw.l04.q3.p: Congress threatens to withhold a small percentage of highway funds from states that do not adopt a minimum drinking age of 21. A state claims the condition is unconstitutional. Under South Dakota v. Dole, what is the likely result?
law-conlaw.l04.q3.h: Five conditions on the spending power.
law-conlaw.l04.q3.e: Dole upheld the condition as related to the federal interest in safe interstate travel, with modest financial pressure. The Twenty-first Amendment does not bar conditional spending.

law-conlaw.l04.q4.t: The statute is invalid because it directs the states how to legislate and so commandeers state legislatures
law-conlaw.l04.q4.p: Congress enacts a statute prohibiting any state from authorizing or licensing a certain category of private gambling, and the state has an existing licensing program. Under Murphy v. NCAA, what is the most likely result?
law-conlaw.l04.q4.h: Compare a command to states with regulation of private actors.
law-conlaw.l04.q4.e: Murphy held that a federal law prohibiting states from authorizing sports betting regulated the states, not private parties, and so violated the anticommandeering rule. Preemption must regulate private conduct.

law-conlaw.l04.q5.t: The statute likely survives because it regulates the state as a market participant in the same way as private actors and does not require the state to enact or enforce federal law
law-conlaw.l04.q5.p: Congress passes a statute that makes it illegal for any person, including state agencies, to sell personal information from motor vehicle records. A state challenges the statute as commandeering. Under Reno v. Condon, what is the best analysis?
law-conlaw.l04.q5.h: Generally applicable laws are different from commands to states.
law-conlaw.l04.q5.e: Reno v. Condon upheld a law that regulated both state and private actors in the resale of data, with no requirement that the state legislate or enforce federal rules.

law-conlaw.l05.q1.t: Whether the state law discriminates against interstate commerce in its text, purpose or effect
law-conlaw.l05.q1.p: What is the first question a court asks in a dormant Commerce Clause challenge?
law-conlaw.l05.q1.e: Discriminatory laws are virtually per se invalid; neutral laws receive Pike balancing. Congressional authorization can validate a law, but it is not the first question.

law-conlaw.l05.q2.t: Compliance with both federal and state law is impossible, or state law blocks the accomplishment of federal purposes
law-conlaw.l05.q2.e: Conflict preemption includes impossibility and obstacle preemption. Express preemption depends on statutory text, and field preemption on pervasive regulation.

law-conlaw.l05.q3.t: The law is virtually per se invalid because it discriminates on its face, unless the state shows a legitimate purpose that cannot be served by nondiscriminatory means
law-conlaw.l05.q3.p: A state bans the sale of milk that was processed outside the state. Producers from other states sue. What standard applies?
law-conlaw.l05.q3.e: Discrimination on its face triggers the strictest scrutiny in the dormant Commerce Clause, such as in Philadelphia v. New Jersey. Pike balancing applies to evenhanded laws.

law-conlaw.l05.q4.t: Pike balancing applies, and the rule may be invalid if the burden on interstate commerce is clearly excessive in relation to the local benefits
law-conlaw.l05.q4.p: A state adopts a neutral rule requiring all trucks to use a particular type of mudflap, which is different from the rule in neighboring states and forces carriers to change equipment at the border. The rule is claimed to improve safety but evidence of the benefit is thin. Which analysis best fits?
law-conlaw.l05.q4.h: Neutral law with a burden on commerce.
law-conlaw.l05.q4.e: A neutral law with incidental burdens is analyzed under Pike. Courts weigh the burden against the benefit, but in practice challengers often have difficulty prevailing, as National Pork Producers shows.

law-conlaw.l05.q5.t: The policy is likely valid under the market participant doctrine, because the state is acting as a buyer and seller and not as a regulator
law-conlaw.l05.q5.p: A state buys cement for its own highway projects and, by statute, sells only to in-state buyers the cement from a plant it owns. An out-of-state contractor challenges the sales policy under the dormant Commerce Clause. What is the likely result?
law-conlaw.l05.q5.h: The state is not regulating; it is trading.
law-conlaw.l05.q5.e: Under the market participant exception the state may prefer its own residents when it acts as a participant in the market, subject to limits on downstream restrictions.

law-conlaw.l06.q1.t: The doctrine that most provisions of the Bill of Rights apply to the states through the Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause, one at a time
law-conlaw.l06.q1.e: Selective incorporation applies particular rights to states if they are fundamental to the scheme of ordered liberty or deeply rooted in history and tradition.

law-conlaw.l06.q2.p: Which case held that the Second Amendment right to keep and bear arms applies to the states?
law-conlaw.l06.q2.e: McDonald (2010) incorporated the Second Amendment. Heller (2008) addressed the federal enclave of the District of Columbia.

law-conlaw.l06.q3.t: Ramos v. Louisiana, which requires a unanimous jury verdict in serious criminal cases tried in state court
law-conlaw.l06.q3.p: A state convicts a defendant of a serious crime by a 10-to-2 jury vote. Which decision most directly bears on the validity of the verdict?
law-conlaw.l06.q3.e: Ramos held that the Sixth Amendment's unanimity requirement applies to the states through the Fourteenth Amendment. Barron and Slaughter-House stand for older limits.

law-conlaw.l06.q4.t: The Excessive Fines Clause of the Eighth Amendment is incorporated and so limits state and local governments, as Timbs v. Indiana held
law-conlaw.l06.q4.p: A county imposes a very large fine and forfeiture on a person for a minor drug offense. Which argument best uses the incorporation doctrine?
law-conlaw.l06.q4.e: Timbs incorporated the Excessive Fines Clause, so it applies to states and localities. The grand jury clause is not incorporated.

law-conlaw.l06.q5.t: It has been advanced by some justices and scholars, but the Court's incorporation decisions have rested on the Due Process Clause since Slaughter-House narrowed the clause
law-conlaw.l06.q5.p: A justice argues that the original meaning of the Privileges or Immunities Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment, rather than the Due Process Clause, is the proper basis for applying the Bill of Rights to the states. Which is the most accurate description of this view's status?
law-conlaw.l06.q5.h: Think about who wrote what in McDonald.
law-conlaw.l06.q5.e: Justice Thomas, concurring in McDonald, urged the Privileges or Immunities route, but the majority used due process. The Slaughter-House Cases narrowed the clause long ago.

law-conlaw.l07.q1.p: Which of these constitutional provisions applies to private conduct and is not limited by the state action requirement?
law-conlaw.l07.q1.e: The Thirteenth Amendment reaches private conduct. The Fourteenth generally requires state action, and the Fifteenth and the First are likewise directed at government.

law-conlaw.l07.q2.t: When it performs a function that has traditionally and exclusively been performed by the government
law-conlaw.l07.q2.p: Under the public function exception, when is a private party treated as a state actor?
law-conlaw.l07.q2.e: The exception is narrow. Funding, licensing and regulation alone are not enough, as in Rendell-Baker and Blum.

law-conlaw.l07.q3.t: The private owner performs a public function by operating the town, so the First Amendment applies to its restrictions
law-conlaw.l07.q3.p: A private nonprofit operates a company-owned town whose streets are open to the public and has the sidewalks function as a town center. It bars a person from distributing religious pamphlets. Under Marsh v. Alabama, what is the best argument for the speaker?
law-conlaw.l07.q3.e: Marsh applied the First Amendment to a company town that functioned like a municipality. The Court has not extended the holding to all private property open to the public.

law-conlaw.l07.q4.t: The nonprofit is not a state actor, because operating a forum for speech is not a function traditionally and exclusively performed by government
law-conlaw.l07.q4.p: A private nonprofit operates public access cable channels under an arrangement with a city and removes two producers after they criticize the nonprofit. The producers sue under the First Amendment. What is the likely outcome under Halleck?
law-conlaw.l07.q4.h: Recent Supreme Court public function case.
law-conlaw.l07.q4.e: Halleck held that merely hosting speech is not a traditional and exclusive government function, and a government designation or regulation does not change that.

law-conlaw.l07.q5.t: Symbiotic relationship or entanglement, as in Burton v. Wilmington Parking Authority, where the government's involvement made it a joint participant in the discrimination
law-conlaw.l07.q5.p: A private restaurant leases space in a city-owned parking garage, and the garage's financial success is tied to the restaurant's rent. The restaurant refuses service to a customer because of race. Which doctrine best supports a claim that the restaurant is a state actor?
law-conlaw.l07.q5.h: Interdependence between state and private actor.
law-conlaw.l07.q5.e: Burton found state action where the state was so entwined with the private business that it was a joint participant. Restaurants are not a traditional exclusive state function.

law-conlaw.l08.q1.p: What standard does a court apply to a law burdening a right it holds to be fundamental under substantive due process?
law-conlaw.l08.q1.e: Fundamental rights receive strict scrutiny. Rational basis applies if no fundamental right is involved. Pike is a dormant Commerce Clause test.

law-conlaw.l08.q2.t: The right must be deeply rooted in the nation's history and tradition and implicit in the concept of ordered liberty, carefully described
law-conlaw.l08.q2.p: What method did Washington v. Glucksberg set for identifying unenumerated fundamental rights?
law-conlaw.l08.q2.e: Glucksberg used the history-and-tradition test with a careful description, and rejected a right to assisted suicide.

law-conlaw.l08.q3.t: Because the Constitution does not confer a right to abortion, state regulation is reviewed deferentially and must be rationally related to a legitimate interest
law-conlaw.l08.q3.p: What does it mean to say that the current federal law on abortion, after Dobbs, is a matter of rational basis review?
law-conlaw.l08.q3.h: State the law as a fact.
law-conlaw.l08.q3.e: Dobbs held that there is no constitutional right to abortion, and that abortion regulations are subject to rational basis review. The undue burden test was overruled with Casey.

law-conlaw.l08.q4.t: Pierce v. Society of Sisters, which held that parents have a liberty interest in directing their children's education
law-conlaw.l08.q4.p: A state law forbids parents from sending their children to any school but a public school. Parents sue. Which line of authority gives the strongest support to the parents' claim?
law-conlaw.l08.q4.e: Pierce (1925) struck down a law requiring public school attendance. Griswold concerned contraception, Lochner economic liberty, and Carolene Products deference to economic regulation.

law-conlaw.l08.q5.t: Obergefell held that states must license and recognize such marriages, has not been overruled, and the Respect for Marriage Act of 2022 adds a statutory requirement of recognition
law-conlaw.l08.q5.p: A challenger argues that same-sex couples have the right to marry under both due process and equal protection. Which statement correctly describes the current law?
law-conlaw.l08.q5.h: Distinguish what was decided from what is argued.
law-conlaw.l08.q5.e: Obergefell remains good law as of this writing. Dobbs did not overrule it, and it relied on both due process and equal protection.

law-conlaw.l09.q1.t: First whether a protected life, liberty or property interest is at stake, then what process is due
law-conlaw.l09.q1.p: What are the two steps of a procedural due process claim?
law-conlaw.l09.q1.e: Courts ask whether there is a deprivation of a protected interest and then apply Mathews to decide what procedure is required.

law-conlaw.l09.q2.t: Independent sources such as state law, statutes, contracts and understandings creating a legitimate claim of entitlement
law-conlaw.l09.q2.p: Where do property interests protected by due process come from, according to Board of Regents v. Roth?
law-conlaw.l09.q2.e: Roth held that property interests arise from independent sources and must be more than a unilateral expectation.

law-conlaw.l09.q3.t: Cleveland Board of Education v. Loudermill, which requires notice and an opportunity to respond before termination of a public employee with a property interest
law-conlaw.l09.q3.p: A public university terminates a tenured professor without notice or hearing. Which authority most directly supports the professor's claim that some process was due before the termination?
law-conlaw.l09.q3.e: Loudermill requires pretermination notice and an opportunity to respond, followed by a fuller hearing. Daniels and Paul limit due process claims.

law-conlaw.l09.q4.t: The state likely prevails, because the decision turns on medical records, the risk of error is modest, and a postdeprivation hearing may suffice
law-conlaw.l09.q4.p: A state terminates a person's disability benefits after reviewing medical records and offers a full hearing only after the termination. The recipient argues a pretermination evidentiary hearing is required. Under the Mathews balancing test, what is the most likely result?
law-conlaw.l09.q4.h: This is the Mathews fact pattern.
law-conlaw.l09.q4.e: Mathews upheld the procedure because the decision was based on documents, the private interest was less dire than in Goldberg, and the government's interest weighed against more process.

law-conlaw.l09.q5.t: The claim fails, because negligence by a state official does not constitute a deprivation under the Due Process Clause
law-conlaw.l09.q5.p: A prison guard negligently leaves a mop on a stair, and an inmate slips and is injured. The inmate sues under the Fourteenth Amendment for deprivation of liberty without due process. What is the most likely result?
law-conlaw.l09.q5.e: Daniels held that mere negligence is not a deprivation within the Due Process Clause. State tort law may supply a remedy.

law-conlaw.l10.q1.t: Intermediate scrutiny, requiring an important interest and a substantial relationship to it
law-conlaw.l10.q1.p: What standard of review applies to classifications based on sex?
law-conlaw.l10.q1.e: Sex classifications receive intermediate scrutiny. In United States v. Virginia the Court spoke of an exceedingly persuasive justification.

law-conlaw.l10.q2.t: Both a discriminatory effect and a discriminatory purpose
law-conlaw.l10.q2.p: What must a plaintiff show to prove that a facially neutral law violates equal protection?
law-conlaw.l10.q2.e: Disparate impact alone is not enough for an equal protection claim, although it can be evidence of purpose under Arlington Heights.

law-conlaw.l10.q3.t: The law is neutral on its face, so the claim fails unless she shows it was adopted because of its adverse effect on women, not just in spite of it
law-conlaw.l10.q3.p: A state law gives a hiring preference in public jobs to veterans, who are overwhelmingly male. A woman challenges the preference as sex discrimination. What is the most likely analysis?
law-conlaw.l10.q3.e: A facially neutral law that has a disparate effect requires discriminatory purpose, defined as acting because of, not merely in spite of, the effect on a group. This follows Washington v. Davis and Personnel Administrator v. Feeney.

law-conlaw.l10.q4.t: Race-based admissions are subject to strict scrutiny, and the interests are not sufficiently measurable, the program uses race as a negative and lacks a logical endpoint
law-conlaw.l10.q4.p: A state university uses race as one factor in admissions to obtain the educational benefits of diversity and says it will review the program every five years. After SFFA v. Harvard, what is the strongest argument against the program?
law-conlaw.l10.q4.e: SFFA applied strict scrutiny and found that the programs lacked measurable objectives, used race negatively and stereotypically, and had no endpoint. The opinion did not bar considering an applicant's own discussion of how race affected his or her life.

law-conlaw.l10.q5.t: By showing that the denial rests on irrational prejudice and bare hostility, which is not a legitimate government interest even under rational basis review
law-conlaw.l10.q5.p: A city denies a zoning permit for a group home for people with intellectual disabilities, citing neighbors' fears. The law applies rational basis review to disability classifications. Under Cleburne, how might the challenger prevail?
law-conlaw.l10.q5.e: Cleburne held disability is not a suspect class but struck the permit requirement as based on irrational fear and prejudice. This line of cases is often called rational basis with bite.

law-conlaw.l11.q1.p: What review applies to a content-based restriction on speech?
law-conlaw.l11.q1.e: Content-based laws are presumptively invalid and survive only if narrowly tailored to a compelling interest.

law-conlaw.l11.q2.t: Brandenburg: the speech must be directed to inciting imminent lawless action and likely to produce it
law-conlaw.l11.q2.p: What test governs advocacy of unlawful conduct under the First Amendment?
law-conlaw.l11.q2.e: Brandenburg replaced the older tests with a demanding rule requiring imminence and likelihood.

law-conlaw.l11.q3.t: The ordinance is content-neutral, so it is reviewed as a time, place and manner rule: significant interest, narrow tailoring, and ample alternatives
law-conlaw.l11.q3.p: A town ordinance bans all signs larger than six square feet in public parks, regardless of message. A resident challenges it. What is the best statement of the standard?
law-conlaw.l11.q3.h: Does the rule depend on the message?
law-conlaw.l11.q3.e: A neutral size limit is analyzed under intermediate scrutiny, which does not require the least restrictive means (Ward). Parks are traditional public forums, so regulation is limited.

law-conlaw.l11.q4.t: The code is content-based on its face because the rules depend on message, so strict scrutiny applies regardless of the town's motive
law-conlaw.l11.q4.p: A town allows temporary directional signs for religious services up to six square feet, but permits signs about political candidates up to twenty square feet, and signs for ideological messages up to twenty. A church challenges the rule. Under Reed v. Gilbert, what is the most accurate analysis?
law-conlaw.l11.q4.h: Look at the face of the law.
law-conlaw.l11.q4.e: Reed held that a law distinguishing signs by their message is content-based, no matter its motive, and must survive strict scrutiny. Not every sign law is invalid.

law-conlaw.l11.q5.t: It is a prior restraint, which bears a heavy presumption of invalidity, and the government has not shown the direct, immediate and irreparable harm needed under the Pentagon Papers decision
law-conlaw.l11.q5.p: A court issues an injunction barring a newspaper from publishing a lawful, truthful story based on a leaked government document that the government says may embarrass officials and harm the national interest in general terms. What is the strongest argument against the injunction?
law-conlaw.l11.q5.h: Think of New York Times Co. v. United States.
law-conlaw.l11.q5.e: Prior restraints are presumptively invalid, and the Pentagon Papers case required a very heavy showing. The Court has not said that no prior restraint can ever be justified.

law-conlaw.l12.q1.t: That the statement was false and made with actual malice, meaning knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard for the truth
law-conlaw.l12.q1.p: What must a public official prove to win a defamation claim under New York Times Co. v. Sullivan?
law-conlaw.l12.q1.e: Sullivan requires actual malice, which is knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard, not ill will.

law-conlaw.l12.q2.t: The speaker must have consciously disregarded a substantial risk that the statements would be viewed as threatening violence
law-conlaw.l12.q2.p: Which standard does Counterman v. Colorado set as the minimum for prosecuting a true threat?
law-conlaw.l12.q2.e: Counterman held that the First Amendment requires proof of subjective mental state, and recklessness suffices.

law-conlaw.l12.q3.t: A substantial interest, that the ban directly advances it, and that the ban is not more extensive than necessary
law-conlaw.l12.q3.p: A state bans truthful advertising of a lawful product on the ground that it will increase consumption. Under Central Hudson, what must the state show?
law-conlaw.l12.q3.e: Central Hudson sets a four-part intermediate scrutiny test for truthful speech about lawful activity.

law-conlaw.l12.q4.t: The rival cannot show actual malice, because failing to investigate, without more, does not show knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard for the truth
law-conlaw.l12.q4.p: A candidate for public office publishes a statement that a rival has been convicted of fraud, which is false. The candidate had a doubt about the claim and did not check it, though the candidate genuinely believed it to be true. The rival is a public figure. What is the strongest defense under Sullivan?
law-conlaw.l12.q4.e: Failure to investigate does not prove reckless disregard without a serious doubt about truth; the standard is subjective. The candidate's belief matters, though doubts alleged may be tested at trial.

law-conlaw.l12.q5.t: The speech is protected, because hate speech as such is not an unprotected category, and the law targets viewpoint
law-conlaw.l12.q5.p: A group publicly advocates, in offensive and hateful terms, a position that many find deeply hurtful, without threatening anyone or inciting imminent violence. A state prosecutes the speakers under a statute against hate speech. How would the Court most likely analyze it?
law-conlaw.l12.q5.h: Matal v. Tam and Snyder v. Phelps.
law-conlaw.l12.q5.e: The Court has held that offensive speech is protected unless it falls within an established category such as true threats or incitement. Fighting words are narrowly confined.

law-conlaw.l13.q1.t: The Court said it had abandoned Lemon and that the Establishment Clause is interpreted by reference to historical practices and understandings
law-conlaw.l13.q1.p: What did Kennedy v. Bremerton School District say about the Lemon test?
law-conlaw.l13.q1.e: Kennedy said that the Court had long ago abandoned Lemon and its endorsement offshoot, and relied on history and tradition.

law-conlaw.l13.q2.p: Which case held that government-sponsored prayer in public schools violates the Establishment Clause?
law-conlaw.l13.q2.h: A 1962 decision about a regents' prayer.
law-conlaw.l13.q2.e: Engel held that official school prayer is unconstitutional. Zelman and Carson concern funding and Greece concerns legislative prayer.

law-conlaw.l13.q3.t: The practice is likely valid as consistent with historical tradition, so long as there is no coercion and no discrimination in selecting speakers
law-conlaw.l13.q3.p: A town council opens its meetings with a prayer given by volunteer local clergy, most of them Christian, but the town has not excluded other faiths and no one is pressured to join. Under Town of Greece v. Galloway, what is the likely result?
law-conlaw.l13.q3.h: Legislative prayer has a long history.
law-conlaw.l13.q3.e: Greece upheld sectarian legislative prayer as part of tradition and noncoercive. Marsh did not require nonsectarian prayers.

law-conlaw.l13.q4.t: The exclusion violates the Free Exercise Clause because it denies a generally available benefit based on the religious character of the school
law-conlaw.l13.q4.p: A state offers a tuition program that pays for private schooling in towns without public high schools, but excludes schools that provide religious instruction. A family wants to use the funds at a religious school. After Carson v. Makin, what is the strongest argument?
law-conlaw.l13.q4.h: Status and use of religion in funding.
law-conlaw.l13.q4.e: Carson held that a state that offers a generally available benefit may not exclude religious schools because of their religious exercise. The Establishment Clause does not require the exclusion.

law-conlaw.l13.q5.t: The prayer is likely unconstitutional because the setting creates subtle coercive pressure on students to participate
law-conlaw.l13.q5.p: A public school principal invites a local clergy member to deliver a prayer at a graduation ceremony; students are expected to stand respectfully. Under Lee v. Weisman, how is this analyzed?
law-conlaw.l13.q5.e: Lee held that clergy-led prayer at a graduation was impermissibly coercive. Greece distinguished school settings from legislative prayer by adult audiences.

law-conlaw.l14.q1.t: They do not violate the Free Exercise Clause even if they incidentally burden religious practice, and no compelling interest is required
law-conlaw.l14.q1.p: What did Employment Division v. Smith hold about neutral laws of general applicability?
law-conlaw.l14.q1.e: Smith held that neutral, generally applicable laws are valid without exemptions. RFRA and many state laws later restored a stricter standard by statute.

law-conlaw.l14.q2.t: Strict scrutiny for any substantial burden on the exercise of religion, even from a rule of general applicability
law-conlaw.l14.q2.p: What does the Religious Freedom Restoration Act of 1993 require of the federal government?
law-conlaw.l14.q2.e: RFRA provides strict scrutiny for substantial burdens by federal action; Boerne held that it cannot apply to the states.

law-conlaw.l14.q3.t: The ordinances are not neutral or generally applicable because they target one faith, so strict scrutiny applies and they likely fail
law-conlaw.l14.q3.p: A city passes ordinances prohibiting ritual animal sacrifice but allows slaughter for food, hunting, pest control and kosher slaughter. The ordinances were passed after a particular church announced its plans. Under Lukumi, what is the likely result?
law-conlaw.l14.q3.h: Object and design of the law.
law-conlaw.l14.q3.e: Lukumi found the ordinances were gerrymandered to target one religion and underinclusive, so they failed strict scrutiny.

law-conlaw.l14.q4.t: The order is not neutral and generally applicable if it treats any comparable secular activity more favorably than religious activity, so strict scrutiny applies
law-conlaw.l14.q4.p: A state's public health order limits attendance at religious services to 25 people but allows gatherings at retail stores and similar businesses to be larger. A church sues. Under Tandon v. Newsom, what is the best analysis?
law-conlaw.l14.q4.e: Tandon said the comparison is based on the risks posed, and the government's asserted interest does not alone decide comparability. If secular activity is treated better, strict scrutiny applies.

law-conlaw.l14.q5.t: The suit is likely barred, because the exception protects a religious school's autonomy in choosing those who carry out its faith
law-conlaw.l14.q5.p: A teacher at a religious school who teaches religion classes and leads prayer sues the school for disability discrimination after being dismissed. Under the ministerial exception, what is the most likely result?
law-conlaw.l14.q5.h: Hosanna-Tabor and Our Lady of Guadalupe.
law-conlaw.l14.q5.e: The exception turns on the employee's function and not title, as Our Lady of Guadalupe held in extending Hosanna-Tabor.

law-conlaw.l15.q1.t: Injury in fact, causation, and redressability
law-conlaw.l15.q1.p: Which set lists the three elements of Article III standing?
law-conlaw.l15.q1.e: Plaintiffs must show concrete injury, traceable to the defendant, and likely redressable. The other lists describe due process, other justiciability doctrines and civil procedure.

law-conlaw.l15.q2.t: A doctrine that withholds from courts issues committed to another branch or lacking judicially manageable standards
law-conlaw.l15.q2.p: What is the political question doctrine?
law-conlaw.l15.q2.e: The doctrine identifies issues for the political branches. Rucho held partisan gerrymandering claims to be nonjusticiable.

law-conlaw.l15.q3.t: The suit is dismissed for lack of standing, because a generalized taxpayer grievance is not an injury in fact
law-conlaw.l15.q3.p: A citizen sues to stop the federal government from spending funds in a way she believes violates the Constitution, claiming only her status as a federal taxpayer. What is the likely result?
law-conlaw.l15.q3.e: Taxpayer status alone is a generalized grievance. The Flast exception for Establishment Clause challenges to congressional spending has been narrowly confined.

law-conlaw.l15.q4.t: The plaintiffs lack a concrete injury, because a bare statutory violation without a harm bearing a close relationship to a traditionally recognized harm does not confer Article III standing
law-conlaw.l15.q4.p: A group sues over a data-sharing practice that violated a federal statute but caused no loss and no risk of harm to the plaintiffs. The statute provides statutory damages for each violation. Under TransUnion, what is the strongest ground for dismissal?
law-conlaw.l15.q4.e: TransUnion held that Congress cannot confer standing by creating a cause of action for violations that lack a concrete harm. The cause of action may exist, but the federal court lacks jurisdiction.

law-conlaw.l15.q5.t: The voluntary cessation exception to mootness, under which a case continues if the defendant could resume the challenged conduct
law-conlaw.l15.q5.p: A challenger sued to stop enforcement of a law and then the law is repealed before the court rules. The legislature says it may re-enact the law if the suit is dismissed. Which doctrine is most useful to the plaintiff?
law-conlaw.l15.q5.e: Voluntary cessation does not moot a case unless it is absolutely clear that the conduct will not recur. A repeal by statute is sometimes treated differently, but a stated intent to re-enact weighs against mootness.

law-conlaw.l16.q1.t: Congruence and proportionality between the injury to be prevented and the means adopted
law-conlaw.l16.q1.p: What standard did City of Boerne v. Flores set for legislation under Section 5 of the Fourteenth Amendment?
law-conlaw.l16.q1.e: Boerne limits Congress to enforcing and not redefining rights, and requires congruence and proportionality.

law-conlaw.l16.q2.t: Jones v. Alfred H. Mayer Co.
law-conlaw.l16.q2.p: Which case held that Congress may reach private racial discrimination in the sale of housing under the Thirteenth Amendment?
law-conlaw.l16.q2.e: Jones held that Congress could rationally determine the badges and incidents of slavery and bar discrimination in property sales.

law-conlaw.l16.q3.t: The coverage formula in the Voting Rights Act was unconstitutional because it was based on outdated data and burdened state sovereignty
law-conlaw.l16.q3.p: What did Shelby County v. Holder hold?
law-conlaw.l16.q3.e: Shelby County struck the formula that determined which jurisdictions needed preclearance. It left Section 2 in force; the Court applied it in Allen v. Milligan (2023) and narrowed vote-dilution claims in Louisiana v. Callais (2026).

law-conlaw.l16.q4.t: The suit is barred because Congress cannot abrogate state sovereign immunity under its Article I powers
law-conlaw.l16.q4.p: A private individual sues a state agency for damages under a federal statute that Congress enacted under the Commerce Clause, and the statute purports to allow suits against states. The state asserts sovereign immunity. Under Seminole Tribe and Alden, what is the likely result?
law-conlaw.l16.q4.e: Seminole Tribe held Congress cannot abrogate under Article I; Alden extended the principle to suits in state courts. Section 5 abrogation requires congruence and proportionality.

law-conlaw.l16.q5.t: A suit against the official in her official capacity for prospective injunctive relief under Ex parte Young
law-conlaw.l16.q5.p: A state official is violating a federal civil rights law by enforcing a policy against a group of residents. The state has sovereign immunity from damages suits. Which route is most likely to give the residents relief?
law-conlaw.l16.q5.e: Ex parte Young permits suits for prospective relief against state officials who violate federal law, even if the state itself cannot be sued for damages.

law-conlaw.l17.q1.t: The principle that courts generally follow their own precedents, which is weaker for constitutional decisions
law-conlaw.l17.q1.e: Stare decisis is a policy of adhering to precedent, and the Court has said it is at its weakest in constitutional cases where only the Court or an amendment can correct a mistake.

law-conlaw.l17.q2.t: If the text covers the conduct, the government must show that the regulation is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation
law-conlaw.l17.q2.p: Which test did New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen adopt for Second Amendment claims?
law-conlaw.l17.q2.e: Bruen rejected the two-step means-end scrutiny used by lower courts and required historical analogues. Rahimi later explained that principles, not twins, are the point.

law-conlaw.l17.q3.t: It states a method as a holding and omits that justices differ about methods and that opinions often combine text, history, precedent and structure
law-conlaw.l17.q3.p: A student summary says, "The Court ruled that originalism is the only legitimate way to read the Constitution." What is the best fair-teaching critique of the summary?
law-conlaw.l17.q3.e: The Court has not declared a single exclusive method. Fair teaching distinguishes holdings from arguments and acknowledges the use of multiple sources.

law-conlaw.l17.q4.t: State the holding neutrally, separate it from reasoning, present the strongest arguments on each side in terms its supporters would use, and anchor the lesson to the case and related precedents
law-conlaw.l17.q4.p: A study guide on Dobbs lists only the arguments of the majority and describes the dissenters' position as a mistake. Which revision best follows a fair-teaching routine?
law-conlaw.l17.q4.e: A fair lesson states the law as a fact, then presents each side at its best and identifies anchors so changes can be tracked. Dissents are part of the legal landscape and often shape later cases.

law-conlaw.l17.q5.t: Courts should look to the principles underlying historical regulations, and need not find a historical twin to the modern law
law-conlaw.l17.q5.p: Rahimi upheld a federal ban on firearm possession by a person subject to a domestic-violence restraining order. What does this case most clearly show about the Bruen test?
law-conlaw.l17.q5.e: Rahimi, decided in 2024, clarified Bruen: the government must show consistency with the principles that underlie the tradition, not a dead ringer. Heller remains the anchor for the individual right.

law-contracts.l01.q1.t: UCC Article 2, because wheat is a movable good
law-contracts.l01.q1.p: Which body of law governs a contract for the sale of 200 bushels of wheat between two businesses?
law-contracts.l01.q1.h: Think about whether the subject matter is movable.
law-contracts.l01.q1.e: Article 2 covers sales of goods, and wheat is goods. The Restatement is only persuasive authority, and Article 9 concerns secured transactions, not sales.

law-contracts.l01.q2.t: It is persuasive authority from the American Law Institute that courts may adopt or reject
law-contracts.l01.q2.p: What is the legal status of the Restatement (Second) of Contracts?
law-contracts.l01.q2.h: Who publishes it, and does that body have lawmaking power?
law-contracts.l01.q2.e: The American Law Institute publishes the Restatements as summaries of the law, and courts treat them as persuasive. Only a legislature can enact a statute such as the UCC.

law-contracts.l01.q3.t: The predominant purpose test applied by a majority of courts
law-contracts.l01.q3.p: A homeowner signs a contract in which a company will supply and install a custom set of kitchen cabinets, with the price split roughly evenly between the cabinets and the labour. Which approach asks whether the contract is mainly for goods or mainly for services?
law-contracts.l01.q3.e: The predominant purpose test decides whether goods or services dominate the transaction. The other rules concern acceptance, offer irrevocability and extrinsic evidence.

law-contracts.l01.q4.t: Greer, because a reasonable person would have understood the offer as serious
law-contracts.l01.q4.p: At a dinner party, Hollis, after several drinks, writes on a napkin "I sell my boat to Greer for 9,000 dollars" and signs it. Greer, who knows Hollis likes to joke, asks if he is serious, Hollis says "Absolutely," and Greer hands over a check. The next day Hollis says he was joking and had no intention to be bound. Who most likely prevails?
law-contracts.l01.q4.h: Is assent measured by private intent or by outward conduct?
law-contracts.l01.q4.e: Contract formation follows the objective theory, so Hollis's outward manifestations control, as in Lucy v. Zehmer. Intoxication makes a contract voidable only if the other party knew or had reason to know of the incapacity, which is not shown here.

law-contracts.l01.q5.t: Classify the contract as predominantly goods and apply Article 2 with common law gap fillers
law-contracts.l01.q5.p: Fenner agrees to sell her used car to Ibarra for 6,000 dollars, and also promises to provide 20 hours of driving instruction because Ibarra has never driven manual. Fenner then refuses to go through with the deal. In analysing Ibarra's claim, which is the best first step?
law-contracts.l01.q5.h: Which element is the main thrust of the deal?
law-contracts.l01.q5.e: The car is the main purpose, so Article 2 applies, with common law supplementing it where the Code is silent. The instruction is incidental, and the Restatement is not controlling law.

law-contracts.l02.q1.t: For the stated time, up to a maximum of three months, even if the writing states a longer period
law-contracts.l02.q1.p: Under the UCC firm offer rule, how long may a merchant's signed written offer to buy or sell goods, which promises to be held open, remain irrevocable without consideration?
law-contracts.l02.q1.e: Section 2-205 caps irrevocability at three months. The other periods are not provided for in the section.

law-contracts.l02.q2.t: An invitation to customers to make offers
law-contracts.l02.q2.p: A store advertises "Coats on sale this weekend, all sizes." Under the general rule, the advertisement is best characterised as which of the following?
law-contracts.l02.q2.h: Is the ad definite about quantity and to whom it is directed?
law-contracts.l02.q2.e: Ordinary advertisements are invitations to negotiate. Only an ad that is clear, definite and explicit and leaves nothing open, as in Lefkowitz, is an offer.

law-contracts.l02.q3.t: Yes, because the promise to hold it open was not supported by consideration
law-contracts.l02.q3.p: On Monday, Tara offers by letter to sell her piano to Cho for 2,000 dollars and says the offer will stay open for ten days. Cho gives Tara nothing for the promise to hold it open. On Wednesday, Tara sells the piano to someone else and tells Cho. Under the common law, was Tara's offer revoked?
law-contracts.l02.q3.h: Think about what turns a promise to keep an offer open into an option.
law-contracts.l02.q3.e: Without consideration, a promise to hold an offer open is not an option and the offer can be revoked at any time before acceptance. No reliance by Cho is stated, and no writing is required for revocation.

law-contracts.l02.q4.t: Lowell should have reasonably expected its quote to induce Kestrel's reliance, making the offer binding under section 87(2)
law-contracts.l02.q4.p: Kestrel Builders, a general contractor, is preparing a bid for a municipal project and receives a written quote from Lowell Electric for the electrical work. Kestrel uses Lowell's figure in its bid, which wins the contract. Before Kestrel accepts, Lowell revokes, saying its figure was too low. Kestrel then has to pay another electrician more. Which is Kestrel's strongest argument that Lowell could not revoke?
law-contracts.l02.q4.h: Think of a doctrine that makes an offer binding without consideration.
law-contracts.l02.q4.e: Section 87(2) makes an offer binding to the extent necessary to avoid injustice when the offeror should reasonably expect substantial reliance before acceptance. The bid was not consideration for the quote, so the option theory fails.

law-contracts.l02.q5.t: The revocation is ineffective because Whitmore is a merchant who gave a signed assurance
law-contracts.l02.q5.p: Whitmore, a merchant, signs a written offer to sell 500 bolts of fabric to Dunne and states, "This price is firm for 90 days." Dunne never pays for this assurance. At day 20, Whitmore tries to revoke. A court is most likely to hold that:
law-contracts.l02.q5.h: Which statute changes the common-law rule for merchants?
law-contracts.l02.q5.e: UCC 2-205 makes a signed merchant's firm offer irrevocable for the stated time up to three months without consideration. Ninety days is within the cap, so it is enforceable.

law-contracts.l03.q1.t: A counteroffer that rejects and terminates the original offer
law-contracts.l03.q1.p: Under the common law mirror image rule, an acceptance that adds a new term to the offer is treated as what?
law-contracts.l03.q1.h: The acceptance must match the offer exactly.
law-contracts.l03.q1.e: The mirror image rule makes a varied acceptance a rejection plus a counteroffer. The other results describe how the UCC, not the common law, handles additional terms.

law-contracts.l03.q2.t: When it is properly dispatched by a reasonable medium
law-contracts.l03.q2.p: When an offer is silent about the method of acceptance, the mailbox rule provides that an acceptance sent by a reasonable means is effective at which moment?
law-contracts.l03.q2.h: The offeror takes the risk of delay.
law-contracts.l03.q2.e: Under the mailbox rule, acceptance takes effect on dispatch. Receipt governs revocations, rejections and option contract acceptances.

law-contracts.l03.q3.t: A contract formed Tuesday, because acceptance is effective on dispatch and revocation only on receipt
law-contracts.l03.q3.p: Rae mails an offer to Sam on Monday. Sam mails an acceptance on Tuesday. Before it arrives, Rae mails a revocation on Wednesday that reaches Sam on Thursday. What is the best analysis?
law-contracts.l03.q3.h: Compare when acceptance and revocation each take effect.
law-contracts.l03.q3.e: Acceptance by mail was effective when dispatched on Tuesday, before the revocation was received, which is when revocation takes effect. The revocation came too late.

law-contracts.l03.q4.t: She was the master of her offer and prescribed delivery in person, so the fax was not the invited mode
law-contracts.l03.q4.p: Orla offers to sell her bakery to Vance and says that the offer may be accepted only by delivering a signed contract to her at her shop by noon Friday. Vance faxes a signed contract to Orla's shop at 11 a.m. Friday and Orla has her staff discard it unread. Orla later refuses to sell. Which is the strongest argument for Orla?
law-contracts.l03.q4.h: Who controls the manner of acceptance?
law-contracts.l03.q4.e: The offeror may specify an exclusive manner of acceptance. Some courts would still accept an equivalent mode if it served the offer's purpose, but Orla's argument is strongest on the prescribed delivery. The silence and mailbox points are not the issue.

law-contracts.l03.q5.t: A contract exists, because the acceptance arrived first and Jonas did not rely on the rejection
law-contracts.l03.q5.p: Piper mails Jonas a rejection of his offer on Monday and mails an acceptance of the same offer on Tuesday. The acceptance arrives Wednesday and the rejection arrives Thursday, and Jonas has not changed position. A court is most likely to hold that:
law-contracts.l03.q5.h: Which communication arrives first, and did the offeror rely?
law-contracts.l03.q5.e: When a rejection is sent first and an acceptance later, the first to arrive generally controls absent detrimental reliance. Here the acceptance arrived first, so a contract exists.

law-contracts.l04.q1.t: It is expressly made conditional on the offeror's assent to the additional terms
law-contracts.l04.q1.p: Under UCC 2-207(1), an acceptance that adds terms does not operate as an acceptance if:
law-contracts.l04.q1.e: The statute states that acceptance is not effective if expressly conditional on assent to the added or different terms. Different forms or terms alone do not prevent acceptance.

law-contracts.l04.q2.p: Under 2-207(2), between merchants, additional terms in an acceptance become part of the contract unless which of the following is true?
law-contracts.l04.q2.e: Additional terms between merchants become part of the contract unless they materially alter it, the offer limits acceptance to its terms, or the offeror objects. The other factors are irrelevant.

law-contracts.l04.q3.t: They cancel each other out and UCC gap fillers supply the term
law-contracts.l04.q3.p: A buyer's purchase order specifies a one-year warranty. The seller's acknowledgment accepts the order and states a ninety-day warranty. Both are merchants, and neither form is expressly conditional. Under the majority knockout rule, what happens to the conflicting warranty terms?
law-contracts.l04.q3.h: Conflicting terms are treated as different, not additional.
law-contracts.l04.q3.e: The knockout rule eliminates conflicting terms and applies default Code provisions. The minority rules let the offer's terms win or ignore the acceptance's, but the fourth option conflicts with 2-207(1).

law-contracts.l04.q4.t: No contract arose from the writings, but the parties' conduct forms one under 2-207(3) on agreed terms plus gap fillers
law-contracts.l04.q4.p: Atlas Corp. sends a purchase order for 500 motors, and Dyno Inc. replies with an acknowledgment that says "Acceptance is expressly conditional on Buyer's assent to the terms below," listing an arbitration clause. Atlas never responds, but Dyno ships and Atlas accepts and pays. A dispute arises. The most likely analysis is:
law-contracts.l04.q4.h: Is the acceptance conditional, and what did the parties do afterwards?
law-contracts.l04.q4.e: The expressly conditional reply is a counteroffer, so there is no contract by writings, but conduct recognising a contract creates one under 2-207(3), with terms on which the writings agree plus gap fillers. Silence does not assent to the arbitration clause.

law-contracts.l04.q5.t: The clause is not part of the contract because the offer limited acceptance to its terms
law-contracts.l04.q5.p: Maple Co., a merchant, sends an offer for 100 chairs and states that acceptance is limited to the terms of the offer. Birch Co., a merchant, replies with "We accept," adding a clause that shortens the period for reporting defects to five days. Maple says nothing. Which statement is best?
law-contracts.l04.q5.e: The offer expressly limited acceptance to its terms, so the additional clause drops out under 2-207(2)(a); a contract still forms under (1). Silence does not turn a proposal into a term where an exception applies.

law-contracts.l05.q1.t: A performance or return promise that is bargained for
law-contracts.l05.q1.p: Which description best fits the requirement of consideration under Restatement (Second) section 71?
law-contracts.l05.q1.h: Focus on the exchange between the parties.
law-contracts.l05.q1.e: Consideration requires a bargained-for performance or promise. Courts do not examine adequacy, a recital is not enough, and moral obligation is generally insufficient alone.

law-contracts.l05.q2.t: Giving up a lawful right was a legal detriment sought in exchange for the promise
law-contracts.l05.q2.p: In Hamer v. Sidway, a nephew gave up drinking and smoking until age 21 in return for his uncle's promise of 5,000 dollars. Why did the court find consideration?
law-contracts.l05.q2.h: Think about detriment rather than benefit.
law-contracts.l05.q2.e: The nephew forbore from doing something he was legally free to do, which is a legal detriment bargained for. The uncle received no tangible benefit, and the case is not about reliance.

law-contracts.l05.q3.t: Unenforceable for lack of consideration, because the work was already done
law-contracts.l05.q3.p: After a neighbour spends a weekend repairing a stranger's fence without being asked, the stranger says, "I'll pay you 500 dollars for that." Later the stranger refuses to pay. Under the general common-law rule, the promise is:
law-contracts.l05.q3.h: When did the act occur relative to the promise?
law-contracts.l05.q3.e: Past consideration is no consideration, so the later promise is gratuitous, as in Mills v. Wyman. Section 86 may help in some cases, but the benefit here was not conferred in circumstances of unjust enrichment as presented.

law-contracts.l05.q4.t: Pell's promise is illusory as written, so there is no consideration unless a court implies a good-faith or best-efforts duty
law-contracts.l05.q4.p: Pell Distributing promises to buy "all the widgets I may want" from Quill Mfg. at 3 dollars each for one year, and Quill promises to supply them. Pell has no obligation to want any widgets and could cancel at will. Quill later claims it need not perform. The best analysis is:
law-contracts.l05.q4.h: Does Pell bind itself to anything?
law-contracts.l05.q4.e: A promise that leaves the promisor free to perform or not is illusory, though courts may imply a good-faith duty, and the UCC 2-306 requirements rule would imply one. Adequacy is distinct from whether any promise exists.

law-contracts.l05.q5.t: The trip was the occasion for a conditional gift, not the price bargained for
law-contracts.l05.q5.p: A grandmother tells her grandson, "If you come to my house on Saturday, I will give you my watch." The grandson goes, but the grandmother refuses to hand over the watch. The grandmother's best argument is:
law-contracts.l05.q5.h: Was the trip sought as the price of the promise?
law-contracts.l05.q5.e: Where the condition is simply the occasion for a gift, there is no bargain. Adequacy of consideration is not tested, and the trip was after, not before, the promise.

law-contracts.l06.q1.t: Needs no new consideration but must satisfy good faith
law-contracts.l06.q1.p: Under UCC 2-209(1), a modification of a contract for the sale of goods:
law-contracts.l06.q1.h: The UCC relaxed the pre-existing duty rule.
law-contracts.l06.q1.e: Section 2-209(1) abolishes the consideration requirement for modifications but keeps good faith. A signed writing may be required if the contract so provides, not in general.

law-contracts.l06.q2.t: Reasonable expected and actual reliance, with injustice avoidable only by enforcement
law-contracts.l06.q2.p: Promissory estoppel under Restatement (Second) section 90 requires which element?
law-contracts.l06.q2.h: This is a substitute for consideration.
law-contracts.l06.q2.e: Section 90 enforces a promise that induces reasonable reliance where injustice can be avoided only by enforcement. It requires no bargain, no writing and no benefit to the promisor.

law-contracts.l06.q3.t: Can recover it, because payment of part of an undisputed debt is not consideration for discharging the whole
law-contracts.l06.q3.p: A debtor owes a creditor exactly 5,000 dollars, an undisputed amount that is due. The creditor promises to accept 4,000 dollars in full satisfaction, and the debtor pays 4,000 dollars. Later the creditor demands the remaining 1,000 dollars. Under the traditional rule, the creditor:
law-contracts.l06.q3.h: Is the debtor giving up anything he was not already obliged to give?
law-contracts.l06.q3.e: The debtor only did what he was bound to do, so there is no consideration for the discharge. Reliance could change the outcome, but mere payment of the lesser sum is not detrimental reliance.

law-contracts.l06.q4.t: The modification is binding because it was fair and equitable in light of unanticipated circumstances
law-contracts.l06.q4.p: Mercer, a contractor, agrees to renovate a restaurant for 50,000 dollars. Midway, an unforeseen surge in the price of steel arises, and the owner, Dahl, signs a note agreeing to pay 55,000 dollars, receiving no further promise from Mercer. Dahl later refuses to pay the extra amount. Which result is most likely in a court following Restatement section 89?
law-contracts.l06.q4.e: Section 89 enforces a modification fair and equitable in view of circumstances not anticipated when the contract was made, even without new consideration. The pre-existing duty rule is the older, stricter approach.

law-contracts.l06.q5.t: Promissory estoppel, because the franchisor should have expected reliance and the baker reasonably relied
law-contracts.l06.q5.p: A franchisor tells a baker that for 18,000 dollars he will receive a franchise, and the baker sells his bakery and moves, relying on that assurance. The franchisor then raises the price and the baker cannot proceed. No contract is signed. The baker's best theory is:
law-contracts.l06.q5.e: Hoffman v. Red Owl found liability on promissory estoppel where negotiations did not produce a full agreement. A bilateral contract theory fails for indefiniteness, and the other doctrines concern different risks.

law-contracts.l07.q1.p: Under UCC 2-201, a contract for the sale of goods is subject to the statute of frauds if the price is at least:
law-contracts.l07.q1.e: Section 2-201 applies to sales of goods for 500 dollars or more. The other numbers are not the statutory threshold.

law-contracts.l07.q2.t: A contract that by its terms cannot be performed in under a year
law-contracts.l07.q2.p: Which of the following contracts is within the one-year provision of the statute of frauds?
law-contracts.l07.q2.e: Only contracts that cannot possibly be performed within a year are covered. A lifetime or indefinite contract could end within a year.

law-contracts.l07.q3.t: Cannot raise the statute of frauds unless it objected in writing within ten days of receipt
law-contracts.l07.q3.p: A merchant buyer sends a signed written confirmation of an oral order for 3,000 dollars of electronics to a merchant seller, who receives it, does not object, and later denies the deal. Under 2-201(2), the seller:
law-contracts.l07.q3.h: The merchant confirmation rule has a time limit.
law-contracts.l07.q3.e: Between merchants, a signed confirmation satisfies the statute against the recipient unless a written objection is made within ten days. The signature of the party to be charged is otherwise needed.

law-contracts.l07.q4.t: Rudd may prevail under the part performance doctrine, despite the lack of a writing
law-contracts.l07.q4.p: Calder orally agrees to sell her farm to Rudd for 900,000 dollars. Rudd, relying on the agreement, takes possession, pays 100,000 dollars, and builds a new barn. Calder then refuses to convey. Rudd sues for specific performance. The most likely outcome is:
law-contracts.l07.q4.h: Possession, payment and improvements together matter.
law-contracts.l07.q4.e: Many courts enforce oral land contracts where the buyer has taken possession and made substantial improvements or payment. The statute makes such a contract unenforceable, not void.

law-contracts.l07.q5.t: Ortiz's promise is a suretyship within the statute, but the main purpose exception could take it outside if his own economic interest was primary
law-contracts.l07.q5.p: Ortiz, the owner of a hardware business, orally promises a supplier, "If my son doesn't pay you for the tools, I will." The son defaults, and the supplier sues Ortiz. Ortiz's main purpose in making the promise was to keep his son employed in the business. Which is the best analysis?
law-contracts.l07.q5.h: Think of the exception for the promisor's own interest.
law-contracts.l07.q5.e: A promise to answer for another's debt is within the statute, but under the main purpose exception it is outside if the surety acted primarily for his own economic benefit. Keeping a son employed is a weak showing of this, which is why the result is uncertain.

law-contracts.l08.q1.t: Voidable at the minor's option, on or within a reasonable time after reaching majority
law-contracts.l08.q1.p: A contract made by a minor is generally:
law-contracts.l08.q1.h: The protected party has a choice.
law-contracts.l08.q1.e: The minor may disaffirm, and the adult is bound unless the minor does. It is not void, and it is not enforceable against the minor if disaffirmed.

law-contracts.l08.q2.t: Necessaries such as food, shelter and medical care
law-contracts.l08.q2.p: For which type of contract may a minor who disaffirms still be liable for the reasonable value of what was received?
law-contracts.l08.q2.e: A minor may be liable in quasi-contract for the reasonable value of necessaries actually furnished. Other categories are generally not subject to that exception.

law-contracts.l08.q3.t: A supplier knows the buyer cannot obtain the parts elsewhere in time and threatens to withhold them unless a modification is signed
law-contracts.l08.q3.p: Which fact pattern best illustrates economic duress making a contract voidable?
law-contracts.l08.q3.h: Look for an improper threat that leaves no reasonable alternative.
law-contracts.l08.q3.e: Under the Austin Instrument approach, a bad-faith threat to breach that leaves the victim without reasonable alternative is duress. Hard bargaining or lawful refusals are not.

law-contracts.l08.q4.t: Undue influence, because of a relationship of trust and suspicious circumstances
law-contracts.l08.q4.p: Edna, 84 and recently widowed, relies heavily on her caretaker Bram for daily needs. Bram, without telling her family, drives her to a lawyer of his choosing, and she signs a deed conveying her house to him for a small sum. Which doctrine gives Edna's estate the strongest claim to avoid it?
law-contracts.l08.q4.e: Undue influence turns on a dominating or confidential relationship plus suspicious circumstances such as secrecy and lack of independent advice. No improper threat appears, so duress does not fit.

law-contracts.l08.q5.t: Disaffirmance may be barred or limited by ratification through use after reaching majority
law-contracts.l08.q5.p: Teague, 17, buys a laptop from a retailer for 1,200 dollars in cash and uses it for a year. Two months after turning 18, Teague, who has continued using it, tells the retailer he wants a full refund. The best analysis is:
law-contracts.l08.q5.h: Conduct after majority can confirm the contract.
law-contracts.l08.q5.e: Continued use for an unreasonable time after turning 18 can ratify the contract. The contract was voidable, not void, and disaffirmance does not ordinarily release the minor from returning what he still has.

law-contracts.l09.q1.t: A material misstatement of fact on which the recipient justifiably relied
law-contracts.l09.q1.p: Which is an element of misrepresentation making a contract voidable?
law-contracts.l09.q1.h: The statement must be about fact and material.
law-contracts.l09.q1.e: A material assertion of fact justifiably relied upon makes a contract voidable. Opinion and puffery do not, and silence is not misrepresentation without a duty.

law-contracts.l09.q2.t: There was no meeting of the minds because each party meant a different ship
law-contracts.l09.q2.p: In Raffles v. Wichelhaus, what was the court's reasoning when there were two ships named Peerless?
law-contracts.l09.q2.e: Each side intended a different ship and neither was at fault, so no contract formed. It was not a fraud case or a unilateral mistake.

law-contracts.l09.q3.t: Fail, because the seller bore the risk of the mistake by agreeing to sell as is
law-contracts.l09.q3.p: Two parties sell a field believing it has no mineral rights worth anything, and it later proves to contain valuable minerals. The seller had expressly agreed to sell all rights "as is" without any warranty. Under Restatement section 152, a mutual mistake claim by the seller would likely:
law-contracts.l09.q3.e: Even a mistake about a basic assumption does not allow avoidance where the adversely affected party bears the risk, as with "as is" sales or conscious ignorance. Value alone is not the central reason.

law-contracts.l09.q4.t: The owner had reason to know of the mistake and enforcement would be unconscionable
law-contracts.l09.q4.p: A general contractor's bid contains a 300,000-dollar arithmetic error, which makes its price far lower than other bids, and the owner, who has seen the other bids, accepts at once without comment. The contractor seeks to rescind. Under the unilateral mistake rules, relief is most likely because:
law-contracts.l09.q4.h: Knowledge of the other side matters.
law-contracts.l09.q4.e: A unilateral mistake permits avoidance if the other party knew or had reason to know of it or enforcement would be unconscionable. Carelessness alone does not bar relief, but the owner's knowledge is the key.

law-contracts.l09.q5.t: May rescind or recover damages because a known latent defect created a duty to disclose
law-contracts.l09.q5.p: A home seller knows the basement floods every spring but does not mention it, and the buyer, who asks only about the roof, does not notice. After closing, the buyer discovers the flooding. Many states would hold that the buyer:
law-contracts.l09.q5.h: Think of duties to speak despite silence.
law-contracts.l09.q5.e: Many jurisdictions impose a duty on sellers to disclose known latent material defects, and active concealment counts as misrepresentation. Silence is not always safe.

law-contracts.l10.q1.t: Refuse to enforce the contract, strike the clause, or limit the clause
law-contracts.l10.q1.p: Under UCC 2-302, if a court finds a clause unconscionable at the time the contract was made, it may:
law-contracts.l10.q1.e: Section 2-302 allows refusal to enforce the contract, enforcement of the remainder without the clause, or limiting its application. It does not authorise wholesale rewriting.

law-contracts.l10.q2.t: The process of bargaining, such as hidden terms and lack of meaningful choice
law-contracts.l10.q2.e: Procedural unconscionability looks at how the contract was formed. Substantive unconscionability concerns the content.

law-contracts.l10.q3.t: Find it overbroad and either narrow it or refuse enforcement depending on local practice
law-contracts.l10.q3.p: A noncompete agreement for a salesperson bars work in the entire country for ten years. In a state that follows the common-law reasonableness approach, a court is most likely to:
law-contracts.l10.q3.h: Reasonableness in scope and duration is key.
law-contracts.l10.q3.e: Noncompetes must protect a legitimate interest and be reasonable in geography and time; courts differ on blue-pencilling. Signing alone does not cure overbreadth.

law-contracts.l10.q4.t: Unconscionability, based on lack of meaningful choice and unreasonably favourable terms
law-contracts.l10.q4.p: Gannet, a low-income consumer, buys a refrigerator on credit from a retailer in a store where all contracts contain the same fine-print clause allowing repossession of every item ever bought until all debts are cleared. The retailer's salesperson did not explain the clause, and Gannet cannot shop elsewhere for credit. Which argument has the best chance of preventing enforcement of the clause?
law-contracts.l10.q4.e: The clause combines procedural elements (fine print, no choice) with a harsh substantive term, matching the unconscionability analysis. Consideration was present, and the other doctrines do not address one-sided terms.

law-contracts.l10.q5.t: Seldon cannot recover on the contract because the statute protects the public and the contract is unenforceable
law-contracts.l10.q5.p: Seldon, who runs an unlicensed home-repair business in a state whose licensing statute is aimed at protecting the public from incompetent contractors, completes a roof repair for Wyatt, who refuses to pay. Most courts would likely hold that:
law-contracts.l10.q5.h: Is the licensing statute protective or merely revenue-raising?
law-contracts.l10.q5.e: Where a statute protects the public, an unlicensed party typically cannot enforce the contract. If the statute were only for revenue, courts usually enforce. Wyatt is in the protected class, so in pari delicto does not apply.

law-contracts.l11.q1.t: Strong but not conclusive evidence that the writing is completely integrated
law-contracts.l11.q1.p: A merger clause in a written contract is best described as:
law-contracts.l11.q1.h: It states that the writing is the entire agreement.
law-contracts.l11.q1.e: A merger clause supports complete integration but courts still examine the circumstances. It does not bar evidence of fraud or other defenses.

law-contracts.l11.q2.t: Evidence of fraud in the inducement of the contract
law-contracts.l11.q2.p: Which of the following is NOT barred by the parol evidence rule?
law-contracts.l11.q2.h: The rule has exceptions for defenses.
law-contracts.l11.q2.e: Fraud, duress, mistake and similar issues are not barred. Prior agreements that contradict a final writing are excluded.

law-contracts.l11.q3.t: Course of performance, course of dealing, usage of trade and consistent additional terms unless the writing is complete
law-contracts.l11.q3.p: Under UCC 2-202, a final written agreement for sale of goods can be supplemented by:
law-contracts.l11.q3.h: The UCC allows explanation and supplementation.
law-contracts.l11.q3.e: Section 2-202 allows explanation by trade and dealing evidence and consistent additional terms unless the writing is complete and exclusive. Contradictory terms stay out.

law-contracts.l11.q4.t: The contextual approach used in Pacific Gas & Electric v. G.W. Thomas Drayage
law-contracts.l11.q4.p: A written contract states that Hollis will deliver "chicken" to a buyer for a price, and a dispute arises over whether the term includes older stewing chickens or only young broilers. The buyer wants to introduce evidence of trade usage supporting the narrower meaning. Which approach lets the court consider this evidence even if the term looks clear?
law-contracts.l11.q4.e: Under the contextual approach, a court provisionally receives extrinsic evidence to test whether language is reasonably susceptible to a proposed meaning. Textualists look at the writing alone.

law-contracts.l11.q5.t: Admissible, because the rule bars only agreements made before or at the time of the writing
law-contracts.l11.q5.p: A fully integrated written contract for the sale of a business states a 500,000-dollar price. The buyer offers to testify that, three weeks after signing, the parties orally agreed to reduce the price to 450,000 dollars. The seller objects under the parol evidence rule. The evidence is likely:
law-contracts.l11.q5.e: The parol evidence rule does not exclude evidence of later modifications, though other doctrines such as consideration or a no-oral-modification clause may matter. Complete integration only bars earlier agreements.

law-contracts.l12.q1.t: The duty it conditions does not arise, and there is no breach
law-contracts.l12.q1.p: What is the effect of the non-occurrence of a condition precedent?
law-contracts.l12.q1.h: A condition is not a promise.
law-contracts.l12.q1.e: Failure of a condition precedent prevents the duty from arising, without liability for breach. A promise breached creates liability.

law-contracts.l12.q2.t: Strictly, unlike promises, which require substantial performance
law-contracts.l12.q2.p: Express conditions are generally required to be satisfied:
law-contracts.l12.q2.e: Express conditions typically need strict compliance, while promises are satisfied by substantial performance. Courts soften this with excuse doctrines.

law-contracts.l12.q3.t: An objective reasonable-person standard of satisfaction, because the work is commercial in nature
law-contracts.l12.q3.p: A contract says an architect must be satisfied with a builder's work before payment is due, and the work is for a commercial building's structure. Which standard likely applies?
law-contracts.l12.q3.e: Satisfaction clauses involving operative fitness or commercial value are judged objectively. Subjective standards apply to taste or personal judgment.

law-contracts.l12.q4.t: The seller prevails because the buyer's bad-faith prevention excuses the condition
law-contracts.l12.q4.p: A buyer signs a contract for a house "subject to the buyer obtaining a mortgage commitment within 30 days." The buyer, who changed his mind, never applies for a loan, and after 30 days says the condition failed. The seller sues. The most likely result is:
law-contracts.l12.q4.h: A party cannot benefit from preventing a condition.
law-contracts.l12.q4.e: Prevention or hindrance of a condition in breach of good faith excuses it. The buyer's strict-condition argument fails because he caused the failure.

law-contracts.l12.q5.t: Excuse the minor deviation to avoid disproportionate forfeiture and award the price less minimal damages
law-contracts.l12.q5.p: A contractor installs a different brand of pipe than specified, but of identical quality, and the specification is not a material part of the exchange. The owner refuses to pay anything, relying on the contract, which states, "Payment is conditioned on strict compliance with all specifications." Applying Restatement section 229 and Jacob & Youngs principles, the court will most likely:
law-contracts.l12.q5.e: Courts may excuse a non-material condition to avoid disproportionate forfeiture, and the contractor recovers the price less the owner's minimal loss. Strict enforcement would give the owner a windfall.

law-contracts.l13.q1.t: Reject the whole, accept the whole, or accept any commercial units and reject the rest
law-contracts.l13.q1.p: Under the UCC perfect tender rule, if goods fail to conform in any respect, a buyer may:
law-contracts.l13.q1.h: It is stricter than substantial performance.
law-contracts.l13.q1.e: Section 2-601 allows rejection of the whole or part if goods fail to conform in any respect. Installment contracts use a different standard.

law-contracts.l13.q2.t: An unequivocal statement or act showing the party will not perform when performance is due
law-contracts.l13.q2.p: Anticipatory repudiation is best described as:
law-contracts.l13.q2.h: It occurs before the performance date.
law-contracts.l13.q2.e: Repudiation is a clear refusal or an act making performance impossible, allowing immediate remedies. Requesting assurance is different.

law-contracts.l13.q3.t: Treat the failure as a repudiation of the contract and pursue its remedies for breach
law-contracts.l13.q3.p: A buyer has reasonable grounds for insecurity about a seller's ability to deliver and demands written adequate assurance. The seller fails to respond within a reasonable time. Under UCC 2-609, the buyer may:
