law-contracts.l13.q3.e: Under 2-609, failure to provide adequate assurance within a reasonable time not exceeding thirty days is a repudiation. The buyer may suspend its own performance in the meantime.

law-contracts.l13.q4.t: The seller may have a reasonable further time to cure because it had reasonable grounds to believe the tender would be acceptable, if it seasonably notifies the buyer
law-contracts.l13.q4.p: A seller delivers goods on the last day, and they fail to conform because of a minor defect. The seller had reasonable grounds to believe the goods would be acceptable, and asks to replace them within a few days. The buyer rejects the delivery and refuses a replacement. Under 2-508(2), the most likely result is:
law-contracts.l13.q4.h: There is a special cure right beyond the deadline.
law-contracts.l13.q4.e: Section 2-508(2) allows a further reasonable time to substitute a conforming tender when the seller reasonably believed the original would be acceptable. 2-508(1) covers cure before the deadline.

law-contracts.l13.q5.t: Entitled to restitution for the value of labour conferred, less the employer's damages from the breach
law-contracts.l13.q5.p: Sloane, a farmhand, agrees to work a full year for 12,000 dollars payable at year's end. After nine months, Sloane quits without justification. Under the Restatement approach exemplified by Britton v. Turner, Sloane is most likely:
law-contracts.l13.q5.h: A breaching party can sometimes recover in restitution.
law-contracts.l13.q5.e: Section 374 allows a party in breach to recover restitution in excess of the injured party's loss. Total forfeiture is disfavoured, though some courts deny recovery for wilful breach.

law-contracts.l14.q1.t: The expectation interest, putting the plaintiff where performance would have left her
law-contracts.l14.q1.p: The primary interest protected by contract damages is:
law-contracts.l14.q1.e: Expectation damages are the default. Reliance and restitution are alternatives, and punitive and emotional damages are generally unavailable.

law-contracts.l14.q2.t: The difference between the cover price and the contract price, plus incidental and consequential damages, less expenses saved as a result of the seller's breach
law-contracts.l14.q2.p: Under UCC 2-712, a buyer who covers after a seller's breach recovers:
law-contracts.l14.q2.e: Section 2-712 awards the cover-contract difference plus incidentals and consequentials, less expenses saved. The other options are not Code measures.

law-contracts.l14.q3.t: Can still recover lost profit on the original sale because it would have made both sales
law-contracts.l14.q3.p: A seller of used cars has unlimited supply and a buyer repudiates a purchase of one car. The seller resells it to another buyer at the same price. Under the lost-volume seller concept, the seller:
law-contracts.l14.q3.h: The resale did not replace the lost sale.
law-contracts.l14.q3.e: A lost-volume seller would have made both sales, so the resale does not offset the loss and the profit is recoverable under 2-708(2) or the common law.

law-contracts.l14.q4.t: Contract price less cost avoided plus salvage value, giving the manufacturer its benefit of the bargain
law-contracts.l14.q4.p: Pike contracts to buy a restaurant's custom-built oven for 30,000 dollars. The manufacturer builds it at a cost of 20,000 dollars, then Pike repudiates. The oven cannot be resold except as scrap for 2,000 dollars. The best measure of the manufacturer's expectation damages is:
law-contracts.l14.q4.h: Expectation is net of costs avoided and the value of resale.
law-contracts.l14.q4.e: The manufacturer should recover the position of performance: price less costs saved and what it recovers on resale. Here that is the profit plus the cost incurred but not recovered. Recovering the full price would overcompensate it.

law-contracts.l14.q5.t: 400,000 dollars, as reliance is reduced by the loss the producer would have suffered anyway
law-contracts.l14.q5.p: A film producer spends 500,000 dollars preparing a film in reliance on a distributor's contract and the distributor breaches. The producer cannot prove expected profits with reasonable certainty, and the distributor shows that the film would have lost 100,000 dollars even if performed. Under the reliance interest, the likely recovery is:
law-contracts.l14.q5.e: Reliance damages are reduced by the loss the plaintiff would have suffered had the contract been performed, which is the effect of the expectation ceiling. Failure to prove profits is why reliance is used.

law-contracts.l15.q1.t: They arise naturally from the breach or the breaching party had reason to know of special circumstances at contracting that made the loss foreseeable
law-contracts.l15.q1.p: Under Hadley v. Baxendale, consequential damages are recoverable only if:
law-contracts.l15.q1.h: Foreseeability at the time of contracting.
law-contracts.l15.q1.e: Hadley limits damages to those that naturally flow from breach or were within the contemplation of the parties given known special circumstances. Intent is not required.

law-contracts.l15.q2.t: A contract for personal services, which courts cannot supervise
law-contracts.l15.q2.p: Courts will generally not order specific performance of:
law-contracts.l15.q2.h: Think of supervision and involuntary servitude.
law-contracts.l15.q2.e: Personal services contracts are not specifically enforced. Land and unique goods are classic situations where specific performance is available.

law-contracts.l15.q3.t: The amount is unreasonably large compared with anticipated or actual loss and the difficulty of proof
law-contracts.l15.q3.p: A liquidated damages clause will be unenforceable as a penalty when:
law-contracts.l15.q3.e: Under section 356 and UCC 2-718(1), unreasonably large liquidated damages are penalties. Difficulty of proof and sophistication support enforcement.

law-contracts.l15.q4.t: The lost sponsorship is not recoverable because it was not foreseeable at contracting, though foreseeable costs are
law-contracts.l15.q4.p: Banner Print agrees to supply invitations for a wedding, knowing only that they are needed by a certain date, and delivers them two weeks late. The customer claims 40,000 dollars lost when the wedding venue cancelled a major sponsorship deal that the printer never knew existed. The best analysis is:
law-contracts.l15.q4.e: Under Hadley, special damages need reason to know of special circumstances. The printer did not know of the sponsorship, so that loss is outside the contemplation, while ordinary losses are recoverable.

law-contracts.l15.q5.t: Reduced by the amount she could have earned through reasonable mitigation
law-contracts.l15.q5.p: A laid-off sales executive claims wrongful termination, and the employer shows that a comparable job at the same pay was available and the executive refused it. The executive's damages are most likely:
law-contracts.l15.q5.h: The plaintiff must make reasonable efforts to avoid loss.
law-contracts.l15.q5.e: Mitigation reduces damages by what could reasonably have been earned in a comparable position. The employer bears the burden to prove it. Emotional distress damages are not generally allowed.

law-contracts.l16.q1.t: Performance will satisfy a money debt owed by the promisee or the promisee intends to give a gift of the performance
law-contracts.l16.q1.p: Under Restatement (Second) section 302, an intended beneficiary is one for whom recognising a right to performance is appropriate to effectuate the parties' intent and:
law-contracts.l16.q1.h: This replaced the creditor and donee labels.
law-contracts.l16.q1.e: Section 302 asks about intent, with a debt satisfaction or gift intent. Naming and payment are not required.

law-contracts.l16.q2.t: Has no right to enforce the contract against the promisor
law-contracts.l16.q2.p: An incidental beneficiary of a contract:
law-contracts.l16.q2.e: Incidental beneficiaries benefit by accident, and have no enforcement rights.

law-contracts.l16.q3.t: Defenses the promisor has against the promisee arising from the contract
law-contracts.l16.q3.p: A third-party beneficiary's rights are subject to which of the following?
law-contracts.l16.q3.h: The beneficiary's rights derive from the contract.
law-contracts.l16.q3.e: The beneficiary stands in the promisee's shoes with respect to contract defenses like fraud or failure of consideration.

law-contracts.l16.q4.t: Can recover as an intended beneficiary because Lyle's promise would discharge a debt that Marsh, the promisee, owes to Nolan
law-contracts.l16.q4.p: Lyle promises Marsh, in return for a loan, to pay a debt Marsh owes to Nolan. Lyle fails to pay and Nolan sues Lyle. Lyle argues Nolan is a stranger to the contract. Under the leading approach, Nolan:
law-contracts.l16.q4.e: Lawrence v. Fox allowed a creditor to sue the promisor who agreed with the debtor to pay the debt. Privacy of contract is overcome by the intended beneficiary doctrine.

law-contracts.l16.q5.t: The change is effective because Pia's rights had not yet vested by notice, assent or reliance
law-contracts.l16.q5.p: Orin agrees to pay an insurer premiums, and the insurer promises to pay 100,000 dollars to Orin's sister Pia on his death. Orin and the insurer later agree to change the beneficiary to a friend, before Pia knows of the policy or relies on it. The best analysis is:
law-contracts.l16.q5.e: Rights vest on reliance, suit or assent; until then the original parties can modify the contract. Pia's status as a donee beneficiary does not by itself prevent modification.

law-contracts.l17.q1.t: A right to receive the obligor's promised performance
law-contracts.l17.q1.e: An assignment transfers rights, and delegation transfers duties. Assignment applies to rights beyond money payment.

law-contracts.l17.q2.t: Remains liable unless the obligee agrees to a novation
law-contracts.l17.q2.p: After a valid delegation of duties, the delegating party:
law-contracts.l17.q2.e: The delegator remains liable absent a novation. The delegate becomes liable on acceptance.

law-contracts.l17.q3.t: Delegation of duties, leaving assignment of rights unaffected
law-contracts.l17.q3.p: A contract provides that "the contract may not be assigned." Under UCC 2-210(3) and the common law, this language is most likely read to bar:
law-contracts.l17.q3.e: A general prohibition on assigning "the contract" is read as barring delegation absent contrary language. Clear language that rights cannot be assigned is needed to bar assignment of rights.

law-contracts.l17.q4.t: The delegation may be ineffective because Zed had a substantial interest in Maya's personal performance
law-contracts.l17.q4.p: Maya is a freelance muralist hired by Zed to paint a mural for 5,000 dollars. Maya delegates the job to a competent painter, Pat, who completes it with a different technique than Maya's. Zed refuses to pay, saying he wanted Maya's distinctive style, which he mentioned in negotiations. The best analysis is:
law-contracts.l17.q4.h: Some duties depend on personal skill.
law-contracts.l17.q4.e: Delegation is not allowed where the obligee has a substantial interest in having the original promisor perform, as with personal artistic services. Pat is a delegate, not an assignee.

law-contracts.l17.q5.t: Hart takes subject to Frame's defenses against Gale arising before notice
law-contracts.l17.q5.p: Frame Co. owes Gale 10,000 dollars under a contract. Gale assigns the right to payment to Hart and notifies Frame. Frame, however, has a valid defense against Gale for Gale's earlier breach. Hart demands payment. Which is correct?
law-contracts.l17.q5.h: An assignee stands in the assignor's shoes.
law-contracts.l17.q5.e: The assignee takes subject to defenses the obligor has against the assignor. After notice, Frame owes the assignee, not Gale.

law-contracts.l18.q1.t: Performance is still possible but the value of the other side's performance has been destroyed
law-contracts.l18.q1.p: Frustration of purpose differs from impracticability in that frustration applies where:
law-contracts.l18.q1.e: In frustration, the principal purpose known to both parties is destroyed. In impracticability, performance itself becomes impracticable.

law-contracts.l18.q2.t: Both parties were excused from performance because the hall's continued existence was assumed
law-contracts.l18.q2.p: In Taylor v. Caldwell, the destruction of a music hall by fire before concerts led to which result?
law-contracts.l18.q2.h: The existence of the hall was a basic assumption.
law-contracts.l18.q2.e: The court excused both sides since the continued existence of the hall was assumed. The case is the origin of the modern impossibility doctrine.

law-contracts.l18.q3.t: Deny relief because a cost increase of this kind is a normal market risk
law-contracts.l18.q3.p: A seller's production costs rise by 20 percent due to a foreseeable market fluctuation. The seller claims impracticability under UCC 2-615. A court will most likely:
law-contracts.l18.q3.h: Cost increases are usually allocated to the seller.
law-contracts.l18.q3.e: Mere increases in cost, even substantial ones, do not excuse performance unless they result from an unforeseen event that makes performance extremely unreasonable. A modest foreseeable increase falls well short.

law-contracts.l18.q4.t: The fireworks were the known shared basis of the rental and their cancellation, without his fault, destroyed its value, a risk he did not assume
law-contracts.l18.q4.p: Warren rents a lakeside cabin for the week of a famous annual fireworks show, saying so to the owner. The show is cancelled by the city because of a storm, but the cabin is available. Warren refuses to pay rent, citing frustration of purpose. Which is Warren's strongest argument?
law-contracts.l18.q4.e: Frustration applies where a supervening event destroys the principal purpose known to both. The weaker the shared purpose, the weaker the claim, but this one is the closest. Impossibility is wrong as the cabin was available.

law-contracts.l18.q5.t: Allocate production fairly and reasonably among customers and notify them
law-contracts.l18.q5.p: A manufacturer contracts to supply 10,000 units to several customers. An unforeseen government embargo prevents it from obtaining enough raw materials to fill more than half its orders. Under UCC 2-615 and 2-616, what must it do?
law-contracts.l18.q5.e: Where a seller's capacity is only partly affected, 2-615(b) requires reasonable allocation and notification. Favouring one customer entirely is not required.

law-crimlaw.l01.q1.t: Due process requires proof beyond a reasonable doubt of every fact necessary to constitute the crime charged
law-crimlaw.l01.q1.p: What did In re Winship (1970) hold?
law-crimlaw.l01.q1.h: The standard of proof for elements.
law-crimlaw.l01.q1.e: Winship made proof beyond a reasonable doubt a constitutional requirement for every element. It did not require disproof of all affirmative defenses, which Patterson later confirmed.

law-crimlaw.l01.q2.t: must be dismissed, because federal courts have no power to create or punish common-law crimes
law-crimlaw.l01.q2.p: A federal prosecutor charges a defendant with a crime that is defined only by older English court decisions and not by any act of Congress. Under United States v. Hudson and Goodwin, the charge
law-crimlaw.l01.q2.e: Hudson and Goodwin held that there are no federal common-law crimes. State recognition of the offense does not make it a federal offense.

law-crimlaw.l01.q3.p: Which doctrine best describes the rule that ambiguity in a penal statute should be resolved in the defendant's favour?
law-crimlaw.l01.q3.e: Lenity resolves genuine ambiguity in favour of the defendant. Void for vagueness invalidates a statute, rather than interpreting it, and ex post facto bars retroactive changes.

law-crimlaw.l01.q4.t: Due process fair warning, as in Bouie v. City of Columbia, against unforeseeable retroactive judicial expansion of a statute
law-crimlaw.l01.q4.p: A state supreme court, in the case of a defendant who was arrested in 2019, announces for the first time that a long-standing trespass statute also covers conduct on public sidewalks, and it applies that new reading to the 2019 conduct. Which constitutional principle is most directly implicated?
law-crimlaw.l01.q4.h: The court changed the law after the conduct.
law-crimlaw.l01.q4.e: Bouie held that an unforeseeable judicial construction applied retroactively violates due process like an ex post facto law. The other provisions address different problems.

law-crimlaw.l01.q5.t: void for vagueness, because it gives no clear notice and invites arbitrary enforcement by officers
law-crimlaw.l01.q5.p: A city ordinance makes it a crime to loiter with no apparent purpose and gives officers discretion to order a person to move along. Walker is arrested for standing on a corner. The strongest constitutional argument is that the ordinance is
law-crimlaw.l01.q5.e: Ordinances giving unguided discretion to police fail for vagueness, as in Papachristou. Loitering is conduct, not a status like addiction, and the ordinance operates only prospectively.

law-crimlaw.l02.q1.p: Under Model Penal Code section 2.01, which of the following is NOT a voluntary act?
law-crimlaw.l02.q1.e: The Code excludes reflexes, convulsions, sleep and hypnosis from voluntary acts. Habitual conduct, though unreflective, is still the product of effort or determination under the Code.

law-crimlaw.l02.q2.t: A parent's relationship to a young child
law-crimlaw.l02.q2.p: Which of these is a recognised source of a legal duty to act that can support liability for an omission?
law-crimlaw.l02.q2.e: Parent-child is a classic status duty. A bystander has no common-law duty to aid a stranger however easy the rescue.

law-crimlaw.l02.q3.t: the defendant was taken to the highway by police and his presence there was not voluntary
law-crimlaw.l02.q3.p: In Martin v. State (Alabama, 1944), the conviction for public drunkenness was reversed because
law-crimlaw.l02.q3.h: He did not choose to be in public.
law-crimlaw.l02.q3.e: Martin turned on the absence of a voluntary act, because the officers carried him into public. It was not a status case and did not rest on mens rea.

law-crimlaw.l02.q4.t: No liability on the first facts absent a statutory duty, but a legal duty from the parent-child relationship supports liability on the second
law-crimlaw.l02.q4.p: Mara, a pharmacist, learns that a customer standing at her counter has collapsed from what looks like an overdose. She does nothing and the customer dies. Elsewhere, Mara's own child, left in her sole care, dies after she neglects to feed him. Which analysis is most accurate?
law-crimlaw.l02.q4.e: There is no general duty to rescue a customer, but the parental duty of care is a recognised legal duty. Professional training alone does not create a duty to strangers.

law-crimlaw.l02.q5.t: Being addicted to narcotics, without proof of any act of use or possession
law-crimlaw.l02.q5.p: Under Robinson v. California and Powell v. Texas, a statute criminalising which of the following would be most clearly unconstitutional?
law-crimlaw.l02.q5.e: Robinson struck down punishment for the status of addiction. Powell upheld punishing public drunkenness, as conduct, and possession and driving offenses involve acts. Grants Pass v. Johnson (2024) later held that enforcing generally applicable camping laws is not cruel and unusual punishment.

law-crimlaw.l03.q1.t: consciously disregards a substantial and unjustifiable risk, in gross deviation from the standard of a law-abiding person
law-crimlaw.l03.q1.p: Under Model Penal Code section 2.02, a person acts recklessly when he
law-crimlaw.l03.q1.e: Recklessness is conscious disregard of a risk. Option two is negligence, three is knowledge and four is purpose.

law-crimlaw.l03.q2.t: not guilty, because her honest mistake negates the specific intent required, even though it was unreasonable
law-crimlaw.l03.q2.p: Taylor takes an umbrella from a stand, honestly but unreasonably believing it is hers. Larceny requires intent to permanently deprive another of his property. Taylor is
law-crimlaw.l03.q2.h: Specific intent offenses and honest mistake.
law-crimlaw.l03.q2.e: For specific intent crimes an honest mistake negates the intent. The reasonableness requirement applies only to general intent crimes at common law.

law-crimlaw.l03.q3.t: A sincere belief that the tax laws do not apply, even if unreasonable, can negate willfulness, but a belief that the laws are unconstitutional cannot
law-crimlaw.l03.q3.p: What did Cheek v. United States (1991) hold about the tax-evasion willfulness requirement?
law-crimlaw.l03.q3.e: Cheek held that a good-faith misunderstanding of the law negates willfulness, even if unreasonable, but disagreement with the law's validity does not.

law-crimlaw.l03.q4.t: must prove he knew the features that make the weapon fall within the statute's regulated category
law-crimlaw.l03.q4.p: A statute punishes anyone who knowingly possesses an unregistered firearm of a type defined by technical features. Sullivan owns a rifle that, unknown to him, has been altered to fire automatically. Under Staples v. United States, the best reading is that the prosecution
law-crimlaw.l03.q4.h: Knowledge of the characteristics that make it a regulated weapon.
law-crimlaw.l03.q4.e: Staples required knowledge of the features that bring the weapon within the statute, avoiding strict liability. It did not require knowledge of the law itself.

law-crimlaw.l03.q5.t: a reasonable person would regard the communication as a threat, without proof of the defendant's own mental state
law-crimlaw.l03.q5.p: Under Elonis v. United States, a federal conviction for transmitting threats may not rest solely on proof that
law-crimlaw.l03.q5.e: Elonis held that the reasonable-person standard alone is insufficient and a mental state is required. The Court did not decide whether recklessness would suffice.

law-crimlaw.l04.q1.t: whether the result would have occurred but for the defendant's conduct
law-crimlaw.l04.q1.p: Actual cause in criminal law is generally tested by asking
law-crimlaw.l04.q1.e: Actual cause is the but-for test. Foreseeability belongs to proximate cause, and a defendant need not be the only cause.

law-crimlaw.l04.q2.t: Yes, because ordinary negligent medical treatment is a foreseeable dependent intervening cause that does not break the chain
law-crimlaw.l04.q2.p: Moore stabs Ames, who receives foreseeable but slightly negligent hospital care and dies. Is Moore's conduct a proximate cause of death?
law-crimlaw.l04.q2.e: Ordinary medical negligence is foreseeable and does not supersede. Only grossly abnormal treatment as the sole cause would.

law-crimlaw.l04.q3.t: is not excused, even though the victim's unusual frailty was unforeseeable
law-crimlaw.l04.q3.p: Under the thin-skull principle in criminal law, a defendant who strikes a victim with unusually fragile health
law-crimlaw.l04.q3.h: Take the victim as you find him.
law-crimlaw.l04.q3.e: The defendant takes the victim as found, so frailty does not break causation, though some courts limit liability for extremely unforeseeable results.

law-crimlaw.l04.q4.t: cannot apply, because the statute requires that the drug be a but-for cause of the death
law-crimlaw.l04.q4.p: Under a federal statute, a penalty is enhanced when death results from the use of a drug distributed by the defendant. The victim died after taking heroin from the defendant together with other drugs, and the evidence shows the heroin was not by itself a but-for cause of death. Under Burrage v. United States, the enhancement
law-crimlaw.l04.q4.e: Burrage held that the death-results language requires but-for causation, so mere contribution fails. The Court did not require the drug to be the sole cause.

law-crimlaw.l04.q5.t: it was a but-for cause and the result was within the risk of which the actor was aware, and not too remote or accidental to bear on his liability
law-crimlaw.l04.q5.p: Under Model Penal Code section 2.03, where the offense requires recklessness as to the result, the defendant's conduct is a sufficient cause of the result if
law-crimlaw.l04.q5.h: The Code ties causation to the required mental state.
law-crimlaw.l04.q5.e: The Code asks whether the result falls within the risk the actor consciously disregarded and is not too remote or accidental. It does not use a free-standing natural consequences test.

law-crimlaw.l05.q1.t: Negligent failure to perceive a risk of death
law-crimlaw.l05.q1.p: Which of the following is NOT one of the traditional common-law states of mind that satisfy malice aforethought?
law-crimlaw.l05.q1.e: Mere negligence does not amount to malice. The classic forms are intent to kill, intent to inflict serious harm, depraved heart and felony murder.

law-crimlaw.l05.q2.t: purposely or knowingly, or recklessly under circumstances manifesting extreme indifference to the value of human life
law-crimlaw.l05.q2.p: Under the Model Penal Code, a killing is murder if it is committed
law-crimlaw.l05.q2.e: Section 210.2 defines murder by purpose, knowledge or extreme-indifference recklessness. The Code does not use premeditation to define degrees and rejects automatic felony murder.

law-crimlaw.l05.q3.t: Firing a gun repeatedly into an occupied house to scare the residents, killing one of them
law-crimlaw.l05.q3.p: Which is the best example of depraved-heart murder?
law-crimlaw.l05.q3.h: Extreme indifference, no intent to kill.
law-crimlaw.l05.q3.e: Firing into an occupied building shows extreme indifference to life without intent to kill. The planned shooting is premeditated intentional murder, and the others show at most ordinary negligence or lesser recklessness.

law-crimlaw.l05.q4.t: second-degree murder, unless evidence shows she reflected beforehand, because the intent to kill can be inferred but premeditation requires reflection beyond the instant
law-crimlaw.l05.q4.p: Dana, furious after an argument, grabs a kitchen knife and stabs her partner once in the chest within seconds, killing him. In a jurisdiction where first-degree murder requires a premeditated and deliberate killing, she is most likely guilty of
law-crimlaw.l05.q4.h: Intent can be inferred; premeditation needs more.
law-crimlaw.l05.q4.e: The weapon and target support intent to kill, giving murder, but first degree needs evidence of premeditation, which courts differ on in how much time is required. Words and a quarrel are generally not adequate provocation.

law-crimlaw.l05.q5.t: To reserve the death penalty for the most serious murders
law-crimlaw.l05.q5.p: Why did Pennsylvania in 1794 divide murder into degrees, a model followed by most states?
law-crimlaw.l05.q5.h: The purpose was to limit capital punishment.
law-crimlaw.l05.q5.e: Degrees were created to confine the death penalty to the worst murders. Malice remained a concept and felony murder was kept as a first-degree theory.

law-crimlaw.l06.q1.t: adequate provocation that would arouse sudden passion in a reasonable person, no time to cool off, and actual heat of passion
law-crimlaw.l06.q1.p: Under the traditional common-law approach, voluntary manslaughter requires
law-crimlaw.l06.q1.e: Voluntary manslaughter involves heat of passion, adequate provocation, no reasonable cooling-off time and no actual cooling off. The others describe other doctrines.

law-crimlaw.l06.q2.t: It drops fixed categories of provocation and the cooling-off rule, and tests reasonableness from the actor's situation as he believes it to be
law-crimlaw.l06.q2.p: How does the Model Penal Code's extreme mental or emotional disturbance doctrine differ from common-law provocation?
law-crimlaw.l06.q2.h: A broader but still partly objective test.
law-crimlaw.l06.q2.e: Section 210.3(1)(b) looks to whether there is a reasonable explanation or excuse from the viewpoint of a person in the actor's situation. It does not require violence and is not limited to family.

law-crimlaw.l06.q3.t: involuntary manslaughter based on recklessness or gross negligence
law-crimlaw.l06.q3.p: A defendant's carelessness with a loaded firearm, which creates a high risk of death but not extreme indifference, kills a friend. The most likely charge is
law-crimlaw.l06.q3.e: Reckless or grossly negligent killing is involuntary manslaughter. Extreme indifference would make it depraved-heart murder, but carelessness short of that is manslaughter.

law-crimlaw.l06.q4.t: Hal's case supports a manslaughter reduction, while Ira's passion has cooled and mere words are inadequate provocation, so murder is likely
law-crimlaw.l06.q4.p: Hal finds his sibling being beaten and, enraged, shoots the attacker moments later. In a second case, Ira learns of an insult from a rival and waits two days before ambushing him. Which is the best analysis?
law-crimlaw.l06.q4.e: Witnessing a serious attack on a close relative is a traditional adequate provocation, but a delay of two days and mere words for Ira defeat the doctrine. It applies to intentional killings.

law-crimlaw.l06.q5.t: violates due process, because heat of passion negates malice, an element the state must prove, unlike the extreme emotional disturbance defense upheld in Patterson
law-crimlaw.l06.q5.p: A state defines murder as a killing with malice aforethought, treats heat of passion on sudden provocation as negating malice, and instructs juries that the defendant must prove heat of passion by a preponderance. Under Mullaney v. Wilbur and Patterson v. New York, the instruction
law-crimlaw.l06.q5.e: Mullaney barred shifting the burden on an element, malice, and Patterson allowed shifting the burden of extreme emotional disturbance because it is not an element in that statute. The line depends on how the offense is defined.

law-crimlaw.l07.q1.t: a death is caused in the commission or attempt of a felony, without proof of intent to kill
law-crimlaw.l07.q1.p: Felony murder holds a person liable for murder when
law-crimlaw.l07.q1.e: Felony murder substitutes the intent to commit the underlying felony for malice. It requires a felony commission or attempt, not just an intent or any unlawful act.

law-crimlaw.l07.q2.t: a felony that is an integral part of the homicide, such as assault with a deadly weapon, cannot be the predicate felony
law-crimlaw.l07.q2.p: The merger doctrine in felony murder means that
law-crimlaw.l07.q2.e: Without merger, every assault resulting in death would be murder. Merger limits the predicate felonies to those independent of the assault.

law-crimlaw.l07.q3.t: a police officer, responding to the robbery, accidentally kills a bystander
law-crimlaw.l07.q3.p: Under the agency rule for felony murder, felons are NOT liable when
law-crimlaw.l07.q3.e: The agency rule imposes liability only for killings by the felons or their co-felons, so killings by police or victims are excluded. Some courts treat death from fright as caused by the felons.

law-crimlaw.l07.q4.t: was a major participant in the felony and acted with reckless indifference to human life
law-crimlaw.l07.q4.p: Under Enmund v. Florida and Tison v. Arizona, a death sentence for felony murder is constitutionally permitted for a person who
law-crimlaw.l07.q4.e: Tison allows execution for major participation combined with reckless indifference, while Enmund bars it for a minor participant who neither killed nor intended killing.

law-crimlaw.l07.q5.t: not guilty of felony murder under the agency rule, but may be guilty under the proximate cause rule
law-crimlaw.l07.q5.p: Two robbers hold up a store; during the robbery, an armed clerk shoots and kills one robber. In a jurisdiction following the agency rule and one following the proximate cause rule, the surviving robber is
law-crimlaw.l07.q5.e: Under the agency rule, a killing by the victim is not attributable to the felons, while the proximate cause rule holds them responsible for deaths that foreseeably result from the felony. Some courts also reject liability when a co-felon is the one killed. Commonwealth v. Redline (Pa. 1958, a co-felon shot by police) and People v. Washington (Cal. 1965, an accomplice shot by the robbery victim) are agency-rule decisions on facts like these.

law-crimlaw.l08.q1.t: the unlawful application of force to the person of another
law-crimlaw.l08.q1.e: Battery is the unlawful application of force. Option two describes assault.

law-crimlaw.l08.q2.t: The use of a deadly weapon or an attempt to cause serious bodily injury
law-crimlaw.l08.q2.p: Which is an aggravating factor that typically converts a simple assault into an aggravated assault?
law-crimlaw.l08.q2.e: Deadly weapons and serious injury aggravate assault. Acquaintance and delayed reporting are not statutory aggravators.

law-crimlaw.l08.q3.t: To avoid converting robbery or rape into kidnapping, since those crimes involve some confinement
law-crimlaw.l08.q3.p: Why do courts generally require that movement in a kidnapping be more than incidental to another crime?
law-crimlaw.l08.q3.e: Incidental movement is part of the other crime. Statutes do not require state-line crossing, and ransom is only one of several purposes.

law-crimlaw.l08.q4.t: The first movement is incidental to robbery and does not support kidnapping, while the second is substantial and increases the risk of harm
law-crimlaw.l08.q4.p: During a robbery, Kim forces a store clerk to walk twenty feet to the register. In another incident, she drives a clerk across town to prevent a report to police. Which is the most likely result under the majority approach?
law-crimlaw.l08.q4.e: Courts commonly decline to treat brief incidental movement as kidnapping, but substantial movement that adds risk or helps avoid detection supports it.

law-crimlaw.l08.q5.t: attempting or purposely, knowingly or recklessly causing bodily injury, and attempting by physical menace to put another in fear of imminent serious injury
law-crimlaw.l08.q5.p: Under the Model Penal Code, simple assault includes
law-crimlaw.l08.q5.h: Bodily injury, not mere offensive touching.
law-crimlaw.l08.q5.e: Section 211.1 requires bodily injury or attempt or physical menace. It drops the common-law offensive-touching battery.

law-crimlaw.l09.q1.p: Which feature of the traditional common-law definition of rape has been eliminated in most modern statutes?
law-crimlaw.l09.q1.e: Most states abolished the marital exemption, the resistance requirement and the female-victim limitation. Lack of consent or force remains central.

law-crimlaw.l09.q2.t: sexual penetration without the affirmative and freely given permission of the victim, with no additional force needed
law-crimlaw.l09.q2.p: In State in the Interest of M.T.S. (N.J., 1992), the court held that the statutory element of force was satisfied by
law-crimlaw.l09.q2.h: Force is inherent in non-consensual penetration.
law-crimlaw.l09.q2.e: M.T.S. read the statute to require no force beyond the act of penetration done without affirmative permission. Resistance is not required.

law-crimlaw.l09.q3.t: A reasonable mistake about the victim's age is generally not a defense because the offense is strict liability as to age
law-crimlaw.l09.q3.p: Which statement about statutory rape and mistake of age is accurate for most states?
law-crimlaw.l09.q3.e: Most states treat statutory rape as strict liability as to age, as Garnett did, though some states allow a defense. Knowledge of age is usually not required.

law-crimlaw.l09.q4.t: It is an offense because a sleeping person cannot consent, and whether his honest mistake is a defense depends on the jurisdiction's mens rea rule
law-crimlaw.l09.q4.p: A defendant has sex with a person who is asleep, honestly believing she was awake and consenting because of ambiguous earlier flirting. Which analysis is most accurate?
law-crimlaw.l09.q4.e: Sleep makes consent impossible, but jurisdictions differ on whether the defendant's mistake about consent must be reasonable, honest or is irrelevant. Resistance is not required.

law-crimlaw.l09.q5.t: bars the death penalty for the rape of an adult and for child rape where the victim did not die
law-crimlaw.l09.q5.p: Under Coker v. Georgia and Kennedy v. Louisiana, the Eighth Amendment
law-crimlaw.l09.q5.e: The cases hold the death penalty disproportionate for rape of an adult and, in Kennedy, for child rape not resulting in death. They do not address murders accompanying rape.

law-crimlaw.l10.q1.p: Which crime involves obtaining title to property by a knowingly false representation of a past or existing fact?
law-crimlaw.l10.q1.e: False pretenses transfers title through a false statement. Larceny by trick obtains only possession and embezzlement involves lawfully held property.

law-crimlaw.l10.q2.t: embezzlement, because she converted property she lawfully possessed
law-crimlaw.l10.q2.p: An employee lawfully holds her employer's cash while making deposits and decides to keep it. At common law, this is most likely
law-crimlaw.l10.q2.e: Embezzlement is conversion by one already in lawful possession. Larceny requires a trespassory taking, which is absent when the property was lawfully entrusted.

law-crimlaw.l10.q3.t: In larceny by trick the owner intends to transfer only possession, and in false pretenses the owner intends to transfer title
law-crimlaw.l10.q3.p: What is the difference between larceny by trick and false pretenses?
law-crimlaw.l10.q3.e: The distinction turns on what the victim meant to give up. Force and fear are elements of robbery, and there is no writing requirement.

law-crimlaw.l10.q4.t: No larceny, because the intent to deprive did not exist at the time of the taking, though a modern theft offense may apply
law-crimlaw.l10.q4.p: Rhea borrows a neighbour's lawnmower with permission, intending to return it. A week later she decides to sell it and does so. Which is the most accurate analysis at common law?
law-crimlaw.l10.q4.h: Concurrence of act and intent at taking.
law-crimlaw.l10.q4.e: Larceny requires intent to steal at the time of the taking. The Model Penal Code's consolidated theft offenses would reach her later disposition.

law-crimlaw.l10.q5.t: not guilty of larceny, because he lacks the intent to steal even if his belief is mistaken or unreasonable
law-crimlaw.l10.q5.p: A defendant takes property from a debtor in an honest belief that the debtor owes him the money and that he is entitled to the property. Under the claim of right defense, he is
law-crimlaw.l10.q5.e: An honest claim of right negates the intent to steal, even if mistaken. Many courts limit it when force is used, but the defense does not depend on reasonableness for the intent element.

law-crimlaw.l11.q1.t: larceny from the person or presence of another by force or threat of force
law-crimlaw.l11.q1.e: Robbery is aggravated larceny with force or fear. Option two is burglary and three is arson.

law-crimlaw.l11.q2.t: They drop the breaking requirement and extend to buildings other than dwellings and to entries by day
law-crimlaw.l11.q2.p: Which change is typical of modern burglary statutes compared with the common-law offense?
law-crimlaw.l11.q2.e: Modern statutes typically eliminate breaking, the dwelling limit and the night requirement. Burglary is complete on entry with the required intent, whether or not any crime is later committed.

law-crimlaw.l11.q3.t: entering a building or occupied structure with the purpose to commit a crime therein, unless the entry was licensed or privileged
law-crimlaw.l11.q3.p: Under the Model Penal Code, burglary is committed by
law-crimlaw.l11.q3.e: Section 221.1 requires entry with purpose to commit a crime, unless licensed or privileged. It does not require breaking, night or a dwelling.

law-crimlaw.l11.q4.t: No, because his entry was licensed and the intent to steal was formed after entering, though he is guilty of larceny
law-crimlaw.l11.q4.p: Ravi enters a friend's house at night through an unlocked door, with the permission of the owner, who invited him to dinner. After dinner, he decides to take a laptop and does so. Is Ravi guilty of burglary under a modern statute?
law-crimlaw.l11.q4.h: Intent at the time of entry.
law-crimlaw.l11.q4.e: Burglary requires an unprivileged entry with intent to commit a crime. Ravi's entry was invited and his intent formed later, so only larceny applies.

law-crimlaw.l11.q5.t: larceny from the person, not robbery, because the taking involved no force or threat against the victim
law-crimlaw.l11.q5.p: At common law, a pickpocket quietly lifts a wallet from a victim's coat pocket, and the victim does not notice until later. The crime committed is
law-crimlaw.l11.q5.h: Force or fear is the extra element.
law-crimlaw.l11.q5.e: Robbery needs force or fear used to take or keep the property, and stealth is not enough, so a pickpocket commits larceny from the person. False pretenses needs a misrepresentation that induces the owner to hand over title, and embezzlement needs lawful possession before the conversion. A sudden snatching with some force is treated differently by different courts, which is why this question uses the stealthy taking.

law-crimlaw.l12.q1.t: A specific intent to commit the target offense
law-crimlaw.l12.q1.p: What mental state is required for attempt?
law-crimlaw.l12.q1.e: Attempt requires intent to commit the target crime. A person cannot be guilty of attempted reckless murder.

law-crimlaw.l12.q2.t: a substantial step in a course of conduct planned to culminate in the crime, strongly corroborating criminal purpose
law-crimlaw.l12.q2.p: The Model Penal Code's test for attempt requires
law-crimlaw.l12.q2.e: Section 5.01(1)(c) uses the substantial step test. The last-act and proximity tests are narrower common-law alternatives.

law-crimlaw.l12.q3.t: guilty of attempted murder, because factual impossibility is not a defense
law-crimlaw.l12.q3.p: A defendant aims a gun at an empty bed he believes holds his sleeping rival, and fires. He is
law-crimlaw.l12.q3.h: Judge on the facts as he believed.
law-crimlaw.l12.q3.e: Factual impossibility is no defense. Under both the common law and the Code he intended a murder and took a substantial step.

law-crimlaw.l12.q4.t: no attempt occurred because the defendants had not come dangerously close to success
law-crimlaw.l12.q4.p: Defendants drive around a neighbourhood armed, hoping to rob a payroll messenger whom they have not yet located. Under a dangerous-proximity test, as in People v. Rizzo, the court would most likely hold that
law-crimlaw.l12.q4.e: Rizzo held that defendants who had not found the intended victim had not come dangerously close. Under the Model Penal Code's substantial step test, the result might differ.

law-crimlaw.l12.q5.t: Under the Model Penal Code, voluntary and complete renunciation is an affirmative defense to attempt, while most common-law courts reject abandonment once the attempt is complete
law-crimlaw.l12.q5.p: A defendant plans to carry out a burglary but, before entering, voluntarily and completely abandons the plan out of conscience. Which statement is most accurate?
law-crimlaw.l12.q5.e: The Code recognises renunciation as a defense if voluntary and complete, not prompted by a change that makes success harder. The common law traditionally does not.

law-crimlaw.l13.q1.t: Intent to agree and intent that the object offense be committed
law-crimlaw.l13.q1.p: What is the key mental state requirement for conspiracy?
law-crimlaw.l13.q1.e: Conspiracy requires both intent to agree and intent that the object offense occur. Knowledge alone is not enough.

law-crimlaw.l13.q2.t: substantive crimes committed by co-conspirators in furtherance of the conspiracy that were reasonably foreseeable
law-crimlaw.l13.q2.p: Under the Pinkerton rule, a conspirator is liable for
law-crimlaw.l13.q2.e: Pinkerton imposes liability for foreseeable crimes in furtherance of the conspiracy. The Model Penal Code rejects it in favour of accomplice liability.

law-crimlaw.l13.q3.t: not guilty of conspiracy because there is no genuine agreement between two persons
law-crimlaw.l13.q3.p: Under the traditional bilateral approach to conspiracy, if one party to the agreement is an undercover agent who feigns agreement, the other party is
law-crimlaw.l13.q3.e: The bilateral approach needs two genuine parties. The Model Penal Code's unilateral approach would convict, and the defendant might alternatively be guilty of solicitation or attempt.

law-crimlaw.l13.q4.t: Parties whose participation is necessary to the offense and whom the legislature did not intend to punish, such as the woman transported under the Mann Act
law-crimlaw.l13.q4.p: Under Gebardi v. United States and Wharton's rule, which defendants cannot be convicted of conspiracy to commit the substantive offense?
law-crimlaw.l13.q4.e: Gebardi held that a person whose participation the statute does not punish cannot conspire to violate it, and Wharton's rule similarly bars conspiracy for offenses requiring two participants. Conspiracy and the completed crime do not merge.

law-crimlaw.l13.q5.t: The general federal conspiracy statute requires an overt act, while the federal drug conspiracy statute does not
law-crimlaw.l13.q5.p: Under 18 U.S.C. section 371 and cases such as United States v. Shabani, which statement is correct?
law-crimlaw.l13.q5.e: Section 371 requires an overt act, while Shabani held that the federal drug conspiracy provision does not.

law-crimlaw.l14.q1.t: acts with the purpose of promoting or facilitating the offense and solicits, aids or agrees to aid in its commission
law-crimlaw.l14.q1.p: Under Model Penal Code section 2.06(3)(a), a person is an accomplice if he
law-crimlaw.l14.q1.e: The Code requires purpose to promote or facilitate plus an act of solicitation or aid. Presence and benefit are not enough.

law-crimlaw.l14.q2.t: the target offense and for other crimes that are the natural and probable consequences of the offense he aided
law-crimlaw.l14.q2.p: The majority common-law rule holds an accomplice liable for
law-crimlaw.l14.q2.e: The majority approach imposes natural-and-probable-consequences liability. The Code rejects it, limiting liability to offenses intended or subject to its mental state rules.

law-crimlaw.l14.q3.t: may be convicted even though the principal was acquitted in a separate trial
law-crimlaw.l14.q3.p: Under Standefer v. United States, an aider and abettor
law-crimlaw.l14.q3.h: Derivative but not dependent on conviction.
law-crimlaw.l14.q3.e: Standefer held that an aider may be convicted despite the principal's acquittal. The accomplice's liability depends on proof of the offense, not on the principal's conviction.

law-crimlaw.l14.q4.t: not an accomplice to the robbery, because he lacked the purpose to facilitate it, though he may be an accomplice to the shoplifting
law-crimlaw.l14.q4.p: A driver takes a friend to a store, knowing only that the friend plans to shoplift. The friend instead robs the clerk at gunpoint. Under the Model Penal Code, the driver is
law-crimlaw.l14.q4.e: The Code limits liability to the offenses he intended to facilitate. Under the natural and probable consequences rule, he might face liability, but an armed robbery is not a natural consequence of shoplifting in many courts' view.

law-crimlaw.l14.q5.t: advance knowledge that a confederate would carry a gun, with enough time to walk away from the crime
law-crimlaw.l14.q5.p: In Rosemond v. United States, the Court held that to be convicted of aiding and abetting the use of a firearm in a drug crime, a defendant must have
law-crimlaw.l14.q5.h: Intent as to the full offense.
law-crimlaw.l14.q5.e: Rosemond held that the aider must intend to facilitate the offense as committed, which requires advance knowledge of the gun and a chance to withdraw. He need not supply the gun or know the legal classification.

law-crimlaw.l15.q1.t: A reasonable belief that unlawful force is imminent and that the force used is necessary and proportionate
law-crimlaw.l15.q1.p: Which element must be present for a self-defense claim?
law-crimlaw.l15.q1.e: Self-defense turns on a reasonable belief in imminent unlawful force and proportionate response. A prior attack is not required and deadly force is allowed against deadly threats.

law-crimlaw.l15.q2.t: need not retreat before using deadly force when he reasonably believes it necessary to protect himself
law-crimlaw.l15.q2.p: Under the majority rule stated in Brown v. United States, a person attacked in a place where he has a right to be
law-crimlaw.l15.q2.e: The majority rule imposes no duty to retreat. The minority rule requires retreat if safe, except in the home under the castle doctrine.

law-crimlaw.l15.q3.t: he withdraws and communicates it, or the victim escalates to deadly force against a nonlethal attack
law-crimlaw.l15.q3.p: An initial aggressor loses the right of self-defense unless
law-crimlaw.l15.q3.e: An aggressor may regain the right by withdrawing and communicating it, or when the victim responds with disproportionate force.

law-crimlaw.l15.q4.t: Self-defense fails because deadly force was disproportionate to a nonlethal threat, so Pat is guilty of a homicide offense
law-crimlaw.l15.q4.p: Pat is punched in the face in a bar by a stranger and responds by pulling a gun and shooting him. The stranger was unarmed and had no apparent intent beyond a fistfight. Which analysis is most likely?
law-crimlaw.l15.q4.e: Deadly force may be used only against a threat of death or serious bodily harm. A retreat rule is irrelevant if the threat did not justify deadly force.

law-crimlaw.l15.q5.t: does not violate due process, because self-defense does not negate an element of the offense as defined
law-crimlaw.l15.q5.p: Under Martin v. Ohio, a state that requires a defendant to prove self-defense by a preponderance of the evidence
law-crimlaw.l15.q5.e: Martin held that placing the burden on the defendant did not violate due process where self-defense is not an element. Most states nonetheless make the prosecution disprove it.

law-crimlaw.l16.q1.t: did not know the nature and quality of his act or did not know it was wrong
law-crimlaw.l16.q1.p: Under the M'Naghten test, a defendant is legally insane if, because of a disease of the mind, he
law-crimlaw.l16.q1.e: M'Naghten is a cognitive test. Option two is irresistible impulse, three is the Model Penal Code volitional prong and four is Durham.

law-crimlaw.l16.q2.t: has a rational and factual understanding of the proceedings and can consult with his lawyer
law-crimlaw.l16.q2.p: Competence to stand trial under Dusky v. United States asks whether the defendant
law-crimlaw.l16.q2.e: Competence concerns the present ability to participate in the trial. Insanity concerns the mental state at the time of the offense.

law-crimlaw.l16.q3.t: Narrowed the federal test to severe mental disease making the defendant unable to appreciate the nature or wrongfulness of his acts, with the burden on the defendant
law-crimlaw.l16.q3.p: After John Hinckley's acquittal, the Insanity Defense Reform Act of 1984 did what?
law-crimlaw.l16.q3.e: The Act narrowed the defense to cognitive incapacity, required severe disease and placed the burden on the defendant by clear and convincing evidence. It did not abolish the defense.

law-crimlaw.l16.q4.t: reject the claim, because due process does not require a state to adopt a particular insanity test including moral incapacity
law-crimlaw.l16.q4.p: Kansas does not allow a moral-incapacity insanity defense and permits evidence of mental illness only to negate mens rea. A defendant argues that this violates due process. Under Kahler v. Kansas, the court should
law-crimlaw.l16.q4.e: Kahler held that states have wide latitude to define insanity and Kansas's mens-rea approach is permissible. It did not require M'Naghten or a volitional test.

law-crimlaw.l16.q5.t: his delusion prevented him from knowing that the act was morally wrong, because he sincerely believed it was justified
law-crimlaw.l16.q5.p: A defendant, in a psychotic delusion, believes his neighbour is a demon who will kill him and kills the neighbour. He knows the neighbour is a human being and knows that killing humans is illegal, but sincerely believes the act is necessary to save his own life. In a jurisdiction that applies M'Naghten and reads "wrong" as morally wrong, the strongest argument for insanity is that
law-crimlaw.l16.q5.e: M'Naghten asks about knowledge of wrongfulness, and courts disagree whether it means legal or moral wrong; where it means moral wrong, a delusion that makes the defendant believe the act is justified can satisfy it, while under a legal-wrong reading this defendant, who knew the killing was illegal, would not qualify. The other options describe different tests, not M'Naghten.

law-crimlaw.l17.q1.t: Duress arises from a threat by another person, while necessity arises from natural or circumstantial pressures
law-crimlaw.l17.q1.e: Duress comes from human threats and necessity from circumstances. Both require the lack of a reasonable alternative.

law-crimlaw.l17.q2.p: Under the common-law rule in most jurisdictions, duress is
law-crimlaw.l17.q2.e: Most jurisdictions deny duress as a defense to murder. The Model Penal Code is broader.

law-crimlaw.l17.q3.t: offer evidence of a bona fide effort to surrender or report to authorities once the claimed threat has lost its coercive force
law-crimlaw.l17.q3.p: In United States v. Bailey, a prisoner who escapes and wishes to raise duress or necessity must
law-crimlaw.l17.q3.e: Bailey required evidence of an effort to return to custody once the threat ended. Prior reporting is not the test.

law-crimlaw.l17.q4.t: may excuse the driving, but is not available for the killing
law-crimlaw.l17.q4.p: A gunman orders a bystander to drive the getaway car under threat of immediate death. In another case, he orders a person to shoot an innocent victim under the same threat. At common law, duress
law-crimlaw.l17.q4.e: Duress can excuse a lesser crime under an imminent deadly threat, but common-law courts do not allow it as a defense to murder. The Code would permit it.

law-crimlaw.l17.q5.t: is unavailable, because Congress determined that marijuana has no accepted medical use, leaving no room for the defense
law-crimlaw.l17.q5.p: Under United States v. Oakland Cannabis Buyers' Cooperative, a medical necessity defense to distribution of marijuana under the federal Controlled Substances Act
law-crimlaw.l17.q5.e: The Court held that the statute left no room for a medical necessity defense because Congress had already weighed the values. State law does not change the federal rule.

law-crimlaw.l18.q1.t: on whether the defendant formed a required specific intent
law-crimlaw.l18.q1.p: Under the majority approach, evidence of voluntary intoxication may be considered
law-crimlaw.l18.q1.e: Voluntary intoxication may negate specific intent, such as intent to permanently deprive. It is not a defense to recklessness under the Code.

law-crimlaw.l18.q2.t: is treated as aware of the risk that he would have perceived if sober
law-crimlaw.l18.q2.p: Under Model Penal Code section 2.08(2), where a crime requires recklessness, a defendant who failed to perceive a risk because of self-induced intoxication
law-crimlaw.l18.q2.e: The Code treats unawareness due to self-induced intoxication as immaterial for recklessness. Involuntary intoxication is treated differently.

law-crimlaw.l18.q3.t: whether the defendant was predisposed to commit the crime before government inducement
law-crimlaw.l18.q3.p: Under the subjective test of entrapment, the key question is
law-crimlaw.l18.q3.e: The subjective test focuses on predisposition, as in Sorrells and Jacobson. Option two is the objective test of the Model Penal Code.

law-crimlaw.l18.q4.t: the government had not proved beyond a reasonable doubt that the defendant was predisposed independent of its inducement, so the conviction was reversed
law-crimlaw.l18.q4.p: In Jacobson v. United States, the government spent over two years sending the defendant mailings that encouraged him to order illegal materials. The Court held that
law-crimlaw.l18.q4.h: Predisposition must be independent of the government's pressure.
law-crimlaw.l18.q4.e: Jacobson held that the prosecution failed to prove predisposition beyond a reasonable doubt, apart from the inducement. Entrapment does not require force.

law-crimlaw.l18.q5.t: unavailable under both tests, because the defendant was predisposed and one request would not induce a law-abiding person
law-crimlaw.l18.q5.p: An undercover officer asks a known dealer once to sell him drugs, and the dealer agrees quickly. Under the subjective and objective tests respectively, entrapment is
law-crimlaw.l18.q5.e: Providing an opportunity to a predisposed person is not entrapment, and a single request would not tempt a law-abiding person. Police initiating contact alone is not enough.

law-crimlaw.l19.q1.p: Which theory of punishment looks backward and holds that punishment is justified because the offender deserves it?
law-crimlaw.l19.q1.e: Retributivism justifies punishment by desert for wrongdoing. The others are forward-looking.

law-crimlaw.l19.q2.t: The certainty of apprehension deters more than the severity of the sentence
law-crimlaw.l19.q2.p: What is the most widely held reading of empirical research on deterrence?
law-crimlaw.l19.q2.e: Research is generally read as showing that certainty matters more than severity, though evidence differs by crime and context.

law-crimlaw.l19.q3.t: prevent crime by physically restraining the offender during the period of confinement
law-crimlaw.l19.q3.p: Incapacitation as a theory of punishment aims to
law-crimlaw.l19.q3.e: Incapacitation prevents offending while the offender is confined. Option two is rehabilitation, three is expressive and four is restorative.

law-crimlaw.l19.q4.t: the retributivist objects that the sentence exceeds desert, while the utilitarian asks whether the severity deters at acceptable cost
law-crimlaw.l19.q4.p: A legislature raises the penalty for a common minor property offense to ten years to deter it. A retributivist and a utilitarian would most likely respond that
law-crimlaw.l19.q4.e: Desert limits punishment for the retributivist, while the utilitarian weighs deterrence benefits against costs. The theories need not agree.

law-crimlaw.l19.q5.t: sufficient but not greater than necessary to serve the purposes of sentencing
law-crimlaw.l19.q5.p: Under 18 U.S.C. section 3553(a), a federal sentence should be
law-crimlaw.l19.q5.e: Section 3553(a) states the parsimony principle, along with factors to consider. It is not a maximum or a minimum rule.

law-crimlaw.l20.q1.t: submitted to a jury and proved beyond a reasonable doubt
law-crimlaw.l20.q1.p: Under Apprendi v. New Jersey, any fact that increases a penalty beyond the statutory maximum, other than a prior conviction, must be
law-crimlaw.l20.q1.e: Apprendi requires jury findings beyond a reasonable doubt for facts increasing the maximum. Prior convictions are the exception, although Erlinger v. United States (2024) holds that the finding that prior offenses occurred on separate occasions for ACCA purposes must be made by a unanimous jury beyond a reasonable doubt.

law-crimlaw.l20.q2.t: Mandatory Guidelines violate the Sixth Amendment, so the remedy was to make them advisory
law-crimlaw.l20.q2.p: What did United States v. Booker hold about the federal Sentencing Guidelines?
law-crimlaw.l20.q2.e: Booker applied Apprendi and made the Guidelines advisory. Courts still must calculate them.

law-crimlaw.l20.q3.t: Miller v. Alabama held that mandatory life without parole for juvenile homicide offenders is unconstitutional
law-crimlaw.l20.q3.p: Which Eighth Amendment holding concerns juvenile offenders?
law-crimlaw.l20.q3.e: Miller barred mandatory life without parole for juveniles. Roper barred the death penalty for juveniles, Graham barred life without parole for nonhomicide and Montgomery made Miller retroactive.

law-crimlaw.l20.q4.t: may not be imposed on the judge's finding alone, because facts that raise a mandatory minimum must be found by a jury beyond a reasonable doubt
law-crimlaw.l20.q4.p: A statute imposes up to ten years for drug possession, with a five-year mandatory minimum if the judge finds, by a preponderance, that the amount exceeded a threshold. Under Alleyne v. United States, the minimum
law-crimlaw.l20.q4.e: Alleyne held that any fact increasing a mandatory minimum is an element for the jury. The below-maximum argument was rejected.

law-crimlaw.l20.q5.t: The death penalty is constitutional in principle under Gregg v. Georgia, subject to categorical limits such as those for juveniles and persons with intellectual disability
law-crimlaw.l20.q5.p: Which of the following is a correct statement of current constitutional law on capital punishment?
law-crimlaw.l20.q5.e: Gregg upheld guided-discretion statutes, with limits from Atkins, Roper, Coker and Kennedy. It is not banned outright and not unlimited.

law-crimlaw.l21.q1.t: directed to inciting imminent lawless action and likely to produce such action
law-crimlaw.l21.q1.p: Under Brandenburg v. Ohio, the government may punish advocacy only if it is
law-crimlaw.l21.q1.e: Brandenburg requires intent to incite imminent lawless action and likelihood of producing it. Offensiveness and criticism are protected.

law-crimlaw.l21.q2.t: that the defendant had some subjective understanding of the threatening nature of his statements, at least recklessness
law-crimlaw.l21.q2.p: In Counterman v. Colorado (2023), the Court held that to convict someone for true threats the state must prove
law-crimlaw.l21.q2.e: Counterman requires at least recklessness. An objective standard alone is not enough, and an intent to carry out the threat is not required.

law-crimlaw.l21.q3.t: a statute criminalising private consensual same-sex sexual conduct between adults is unconstitutional
law-crimlaw.l21.q3.e: Lawrence overruled Bowers and found that the liberty protected by due process covers private consensual conduct. It is a due process holding.

law-crimlaw.l21.q4.t: overbroad and vague, because it reaches a substantial amount of protected speech and leaves enforcement to officers' discretion
law-crimlaw.l21.q4.p: A town makes it a crime to say anything offensive to a police officer. A resident is charged for a rude comment made on a sidewalk. The strongest constitutional challenge is that the ordinance is
law-crimlaw.l21.q4.e: Statutes that sweep in protected speech are overbroad, and unlimited discretion makes them vague. The other provisions do not address the problem.

law-crimlaw.l21.q5.t: criminalising possession of a gun in a school zone, where the activity was not economic and lacked a substantial effect on commerce
law-crimlaw.l21.q5.p: Under United States v. Lopez (1995), Congress exceeded its Commerce Clause power by
law-crimlaw.l21.q5.e: Lopez invalidated the Gun-Free School Zones Act because possession is not economic activity substantially affecting commerce. Regulating channels and interstate shipment remains valid.

law-crimpro.l01.q1.t: A physical intrusion on a protected effect for the purpose of obtaining information
law-crimpro.l01.q1.p: Which test did United States v. Jones (2012) rely on when it held that attaching a GPS device to a car was a search?
law-crimpro.l01.q1.h: Think of the trespass idea that the Court said Katz supplemented rather than replaced.
law-crimpro.l01.q1.e: Jones relied on the property-based test: a physical intrusion on a protected effect to gather information. The privacy test would have been awkward because the car's movements were exposed to the public.

law-crimpro.l01.q2.t: A search, because the porch is curtilage and the implied license to approach does not cover this
law-crimpro.l01.q2.p: Officers bring a trained drug-detection dog onto the enclosed front porch of a suspect's house and the dog alerts at the door. Under the Court's case law, this is most likely:
law-crimpro.l01.q2.h: Consider the difference between a visitor's license and investigative purpose.
law-crimpro.l01.q2.e: Jardines held that using a dog on the porch is a search of curtilage. The Caballes principle for sniffs applies to a lawfully stopped car, not to the home.

law-crimpro.l01.q3.t: Acquiring seven or more days of historical cell-site location records is generally a search requiring a warrant
law-crimpro.l01.q3.p: What did Carpenter v. United States (2018) decide?
law-crimpro.l01.q3.h: The Court stressed that its decision was narrow.
law-crimpro.l01.q3.e: Carpenter held that obtaining extended historical CSLI is a Fourth Amendment search. The Court did not abolish the third-party doctrine, and it left other data collection techniques open.

law-crimpro.l01.q4.t: Granted, because using sense-enhancing technology not in general public use to learn about the home's interior is a search
law-crimpro.l01.q4.p: Without a warrant, an officer stands on a public sidewalk and aims a specialized thermal imager, not available to the general public, at Rowan's house. It reveals heat patterns suggesting grow lamps inside. Rowan moves to suppress the results. The most likely ruling is that the motion is:
law-crimpro.l01.q4.e: Kyllo held that using such a device to explore details of the home is a search, and it rejected a minimum-intimacy requirement. The sidewalk vantage point does not matter, and the trash analogy fails.

law-crimpro.l01.q5.t: Denied, because the teller's private search is not state action and the police may examine what she revealed
law-crimpro.l01.q5.p: A bank teller, acting entirely on her own after noticing suspicious activity, copies a customer's private letters from a safe-deposit box and mails them to the police. The police read them without a warrant. The customer moves to suppress. The most likely outcome is that the motion is:
law-crimpro.l01.q5.h: Ask first whether the person doing the search was acting for the government.
law-crimpro.l01.q5.e: The Fourth Amendment restrains government action; a private search is not covered, and police may repeat what the private party did without exceeding its scope. The third-party answer is wrong because the outcome rests on the absence of state action, not on bank records.

law-crimpro.l02.q1.t: A fair probability that contraband or evidence will be found in the place to be searched
law-crimpro.l02.q1.p: What standard of proof does probable cause represent for a search warrant?
law-crimpro.l02.q1.h: It is lower than a preponderance.
law-crimpro.l02.q1.e: Gates describes probable cause as a fair probability under the totality of the circumstances. A preponderance or higher standard is not required.

law-crimpro.l02.q2.t: The affiant knowingly or recklessly included a false statement that was necessary to probable cause
law-crimpro.l02.q2.p: A defendant claims that the affidavit for a search warrant contained a false statement. To obtain a Franks hearing the defendant must make a substantial preliminary showing that:
law-crimpro.l02.q2.e: Franks requires deliberate or reckless falsity plus materiality. Mere negligence, or an honest report of an informant's false statement, does not qualify.

law-crimpro.l02.q3.t: Admissible, because the warrant was valid when issued and the mistake was objectively reasonable
law-crimpro.l02.q3.p: Officers who executed a valid warrant for Apartment 3A in a building with two apartments on the third floor entered 3B by reasonable mistake and found contraband. The evidence is most likely:
law-crimpro.l02.q3.e: Garrison holds that reasonable mistakes about the place described do not invalidate a warrant valid on its face. The outcome could differ if the officers should have realized the error before entering.

law-crimpro.l02.q4.t: Open to challenge, because the corroboration confirmed only innocent, public details and nothing about criminal activity
law-crimpro.l02.q4.p: A confidential informant, reliable on four prior occasions, tells Detective Voss that Alvarez keeps stolen jewelry in his garage, giving no basis for knowing this. Voss drives by and confirms only that Alvarez has a garage and a car matching the informant's description parked there, details anyone could observe. Voss obtains a warrant. The warrant is most likely:
law-crimpro.l02.q4.h: Under Gates, ask what the corroboration actually corroborates.
law-crimpro.l02.q4.e: The totality test lets strong corroboration of predictive or incriminating details make up for a gap in basis of knowledge, but here nothing incriminating was verified. A track record helps but is not automatically sufficient, and deference is not unlimited.

law-crimpro.l02.q5.t: Denied, because violation of the knock-and-announce rule does not trigger the exclusionary remedy
law-crimpro.l02.q5.p: Police execute a valid search warrant and, in violation of the knock-and-announce rule and without justification, burst in unannounced and seize cocaine named in the warrant. Under current Supreme Court law, the defendant's motion to suppress should be:
law-crimpro.l02.q5.h: Remember that a violation and a remedy are different questions.
law-crimpro.l02.q5.e: Hudson v. Michigan held that suppression is not the remedy for knock-and-announce violations. The rule is part of Fourth Amendment reasonableness (Wilson v. Arkansas), so the last option is wrong.

law-crimpro.l03.q1.t: An arrest warrant and reason to believe the suspect is inside
law-crimpro.l03.q1.p: Under Payton v. New York, police generally need what to enter a suspect's own home to make a routine felony arrest?
law-crimpro.l03.q1.h: The home receives the highest protection.
law-crimpro.l03.q1.e: Payton requires an arrest warrant (with reason to believe the suspect is home) absent exigency or consent. Probable cause alone is enough in a public place.

law-crimpro.l03.q2.t: Impermissible without a warrant or another exception, because phone data poses no physical danger to officers
law-crimpro.l03.q2.p: Officers lawfully arrest Pat for a drug sale and seize his smartphone from his pocket. Without a warrant, an officer scrolls through the phone's photos. Under Riley v. California, this search is:
law-crimpro.l03.q2.h: Consider the two Chimel rationales: officer safety and evidence preservation.
law-crimpro.l03.q2.e: Riley held that the digital contents are not searchable incident to arrest without a warrant. The officers may secure the phone, but the container analogy fails because of the quantity and nature of the data.

law-crimpro.l03.q3.t: Lawful, because the exception reaches the parts of the vehicle and the containers inside it where the items could be found
law-crimpro.l03.q3.p: Officers have probable cause to believe that a parked sedan contains stolen electronics somewhere inside. Without a warrant they open the trunk and a duffel bag. Under the automobile exception this search is:
law-crimpro.l03.q3.h: The scope follows the object of the search.
law-crimpro.l03.q3.e: Ross and Acevedo allow a search of any area and container where the object could be located. The exception is not limited to the passenger compartment.

law-crimpro.l03.q4.t: He was secured and not within reaching distance, and evidence of a suspended license is unlikely to be inside the car
law-crimpro.l03.q4.p: Officers stop a car for speeding and arrest the driver, Quinn, for driving on a suspended license. They handcuff him, put him in a patrol car, and search the passenger compartment, where they find a pistol under the seat. They had no other suspicion. Quinn's best argument for suppression is that:
law-crimpro.l03.q4.h: Apply both prongs of Arizona v. Gant.
law-crimpro.l03.q4.e: Under Gant a vehicle search incident to arrest needs an unsecured arrestee within reach or reasonable belief that evidence of the offense of arrest is inside. Neither applies, and the plain-view point is a distraction.

law-crimpro.l03.q5.t: A routine inventory under standardized procedures is not an investigative search and the policy was not a pretext to find evidence
law-crimpro.l03.q5.p: Police impound a car after the driver is arrested for DUI and, following a written department policy requiring inventory of every impounded vehicle, open a closed backpack and find drugs. The strongest basis for admitting the drugs is that:
law-crimpro.l03.q5.h: The legitimate purpose is not to find crime.
law-crimpro.l03.q5.e: Bertine and Opperman permit inventory searches conducted under standardized criteria. Search incident to arrest would be limited by Gant, and impoundment does not remove all expectation of privacy in containers.

law-crimpro.l04.q1.t: Police need not inform the person of the right to refuse, and voluntariness is judged by the totality of the circumstances
law-crimpro.l04.q1.p: Under Schneckloth v. Bustamonte, which statement about consent searches is correct?
law-crimpro.l04.q1.e: Schneckloth rejected a required warning for consent. Custody is one factor, not an automatic bar.

law-crimpro.l04.q2.t: Admissible against Sam, because Riley's consent as a co-occupant is effective and an absent person's unvoiced objection does not count
law-crimpro.l04.q2.p: Police arrive at an apartment and, without a warrant, ask Riley for permission to search. Riley, who shares it with her roommate Sam, says yes. Sam, who is not present, would have said no. Evidence found in the shared living room is:
law-crimpro.l04.q2.h: Randolph concerns a present, objecting co-occupant.
law-crimpro.l04.q2.e: Common authority supports Riley's consent. Randolph's exception requires a physically present co-tenant who expressly objects.

law-crimpro.l04.q3.t: Valid, because plain view does not require that the discovery be inadvertent
law-crimpro.l04.q3.p: An officer, lawfully inside a suspect's living room under a valid warrant for stolen laptops, sees what he immediately recognizes as a bag of cocaine on a table. He seizes it. Under Horton v. California the seizure is:
law-crimpro.l04.q3.e: Horton held that the officer's anticipation does not matter if the vantage point is lawful and the incriminating nature is immediately apparent.

law-crimpro.l04.q4.t: The police did not create the exigency through an actual or threatened Fourth Amendment violation, so the entry was reasonable
law-crimpro.l04.q4.p: Detectives with probable cause to arrest Cole for drug dealing knock on his apartment door and say only, "Police." They make no demand and no threat. Hearing sounds of items being flushed, they reasonably fear evidence is being destroyed and force the door. They find drugs. They had time to get a warrant before knocking but did not. Which is the strongest argument for the state?
law-crimpro.l04.q4.h: Remember the limit stated in Kentucky v. King.
law-crimpro.l04.q4.e: King holds that police-created exigency is acceptable unless the police engaged or threatened to engage in a Fourth Amendment violation. Probable cause to arrest alone does not authorize home entry under Payton, and the belief must be objectively reasonable.

law-crimpro.l04.q5.t: Moving the stereo was a separate search that needed probable cause, so the seizure is not justified by plain view
law-crimpro.l04.q5.p: Officers lawfully present in a home investigating a burglary notice a stereo they suspect is stolen. To read its serial number they turn it over, confirm that it matches a stolen-goods report, and seize it. They had only a hunch before moving it. Under Arizona v. Hicks the stronger view is that:
law-crimpro.l04.q5.e: Hicks held that moving the equipment exposed new information and thus was a search requiring probable cause. Mere lawful presence is not enough because the incriminating character was not immediately apparent without the extra search.

law-crimpro.l05.q1.t: Specific and articulable facts supporting reasonable suspicion that criminal activity is afoot
law-crimpro.l05.q1.p: What level of justification is required for a brief investigative stop under Terry v. Ohio?
law-crimpro.l05.q1.h: It is a middle tier between a hunch and probable cause.
law-crimpro.l05.q1.e: Terry stops need reasonable suspicion. The armed-and-dangerous belief is the extra requirement for a frisk, not the stop.

law-crimpro.l05.q2.t: Only when he was caught, because a show of authority is a seizure only if the person submits
law-crimpro.l05.q2.p: Officers in a patrol car shout "Stop!" at Ben on the sidewalk. Ben keeps running and drops a bag of drugs, then is caught two blocks later. Under California v. Hodari D., when was Ben seized?
law-crimpro.l05.q2.h: Ask whether Ben submitted to authority.
law-crimpro.l05.q2.e: Hodari D. held that a show of authority without submission is not a seizure, so the dropped bag was not the fruit of a seizure. Torres v. Madrid, which concerns physical force, is different.

law-crimpro.l05.q3.t: Unlawful, because a stop may not be extended beyond the stop's mission without reasonable suspicion
law-crimpro.l05.q3.p: An officer lawfully stops a car for a broken tail light and issues the warning. With no suspicion of drugs, he holds the driver another seven minutes until a canine unit arrives, and the dog alerts. Under Rodriguez v. United States this prolonged stop is:
law-crimpro.l05.q3.h: The key idea is the mission of the stop.
law-crimpro.l05.q3.e: Rodriguez rejected a de minimis exception to extensions for a dog sniff. A sniff is not itself a search, but the extension is the seizure problem.

law-crimpro.l05.q4.t: Granted, because a bare anonymous tip identifying a person without predictive detail does not supply reasonable suspicion
law-crimpro.l05.q4.p: Officers receive an anonymous call that "a man in a plaid shirt at the bus stop has a gun." They find a man matching the description, who is calm and does nothing unusual. They immediately frisk him and find a pistol. The call gave no information about future behavior. The motion to suppress should most likely be:
law-crimpro.l05.q4.e: Under Florida v. J.L., corroborating only the person's readily observable appearance does not show the tipster knew about hidden criminality. There is no firearm exception, and a frisk needs only reasonable suspicion.

law-crimpro.l05.q5.t: Denied, because passengers are seized during the stop and the frisk was supported by reasonable suspicion of armed danger
law-crimpro.l05.q5.p: Deputy Cruz stops Maya's car for following too closely. He sees that Pete, a passenger, is nervous and, based on a reasonable belief that Pete is armed and dangerous, frisks him and finds a pistol. Pete is a felon. Pete moves to suppress, arguing that the stop was only about the driver. The likely outcome is:
law-crimpro.l05.q5.h: Think about Brendlin and Arizona v. Johnson.
law-crimpro.l05.q5.e: Brendlin holds passengers are seized, and Arizona v. Johnson allows a frisk where the officer reasonably suspects armed danger. The nervousness alone would not suffice, but the problem stipulates the reasonable belief.

law-crimpro.l06.q1.t: Suppression of evidence derived from an illegality, unless an exception such as attenuation applies
law-crimpro.l06.q1.p: What does the fruit of the poisonous tree doctrine from Wong Sun v. United States address?
law-crimpro.l06.q1.h: The word fruit signals derivative evidence.
law-crimpro.l06.q1.e: Wong Sun extends exclusion to derivative evidence. The doctrine has exceptions, and inevitable discovery requires more than chance.

law-crimpro.l06.q2.t: Admissible, because isolated negligence in recordkeeping is not sufficiently culpable to justify exclusion
