law-g68.l18.q1.t: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights
law-g68.l18.q1.p: Which document, adopted in 1948, lists basic human rights for all people?
law-g68.l18.q1.h: It was adopted by the UN General Assembly.
law-g68.l18.q1.e: The UDHR was adopted in 1948. The other documents are from other times and purposes.

law-g68.l18.q2.t: The Convention on the Rights of the Child
law-g68.l18.q2.p: Which treaty focuses on the rights of children?
law-g68.l18.q2.e: The Convention on the Rights of the Child, adopted in 1989, focuses on children's rights.

law-g68.l18.q3.t: The United States signed it but has not ratified it
law-g68.l18.q3.p: Which statement about the Convention on the Rights of the Child and the United States is accurate?
law-g68.l18.q3.h: Signing and ratifying are different steps.
law-g68.l18.q3.e: The United States signed but has not ratified the Convention, so it is not binding as a treaty on the United States.

law-g68.l18.q4.t: Its ideas shaped later binding treaties and national laws
law-g68.l18.q4.p: A student says, "The UDHR was a declaration at first, so it has had no influence." What is the best correction?
law-g68.l18.q4.e: The UDHR began as a non-binding declaration, but its ideas influenced later binding treaties and national laws.

law-g68.l19.q1.t: A penalty such as limits on trade or travel
law-g68.l19.q1.p: What is a sanction in international affairs?
law-g68.l19.q1.h: It is a penalty used to pressure a country.
law-g68.l19.q1.e: Sanctions are penalties like trade or travel limits. They are not gifts or ceremonies.

law-g68.l19.q2.t: The countries have agreed to its jurisdiction in some way
law-g68.l19.q2.p: The International Court of Justice can hear a dispute between countries only if what is true?
law-g68.l19.q2.e: The ICJ's jurisdiction depends on the consent of the states. Individuals and news reports cannot start such a case.

law-g68.l19.q3.p: A country breaks a trade agreement and its partners respond with their own restrictions. Which reason for compliance does this show?
law-g68.l19.q3.e: Partners responding in kind shows reciprocity, one of the main reasons countries keep agreements.

law-g68.l19.q4.t: The judgment binds, but enforcement is limited and often political
law-g68.l19.q4.p: The ICJ rules against a country, but the country ignores the judgment. Which statement best describes the situation?
law-g68.l19.q4.h: Binding does not mean easily enforced.
law-g68.l19.q4.e: ICJ judgments bind the parties, but the Court has no police, so enforcement is limited and often political. It does not automatically become law elsewhere.

law-g912.l01.q1.p: Which of these sources of law ranks highest in the United States?
law-g912.l01.q1.h: Everything else must fit beneath it.
law-g912.l01.q1.e: The Constitution is the supreme law. Statutes, regulations, and ordinances must all conform to it.

law-g912.l01.q2.t: Follow earlier decisions on the same legal issue in its own court system
law-g912.l01.q2.p: What does stare decisis tell a court to do?
law-g912.l01.q2.e: Stare decisis means following precedent from the same or a higher court. It does not allow ignoring prior decisions over small factual differences.

law-g912.l01.q3.t: The power to strike down unconstitutional laws
law-g912.l01.q3.p: In Marbury v. Madison (1803), what power did the Supreme Court recognize for itself?
law-g912.l01.q3.h: It is the power to say what the law is.
law-g912.l01.q3.e: Marbury recognized judicial review, the power to hold laws that conflict with the Constitution invalid. Vetoes belong to the President.

law-g912.l01.q4.t: The federal statute controls where the two conflict
law-g912.l01.q4.p: A state enacts a law that conflicts with a valid federal statute passed under Congress's constitutional powers, on the same subject. A business asks which governs. Which analysis is most accurate?
law-g912.l01.q4.e: The Supremacy Clause makes valid federal law override conflicting state law, which is preemption. The state police power does not let a state defeat valid federal law.

law-g912.l02.q1.p: Which Article of the Constitution vests executive power in the President?
law-g912.l02.q1.h: The order follows the three branches.
law-g912.l02.q1.e: Article II vests executive power. Article I is legislative and Article III is judicial.

law-g912.l02.q2.t: Two thirds of the members of each chamber
law-g912.l02.q2.p: What vote in each chamber does Congress need to override a presidential veto?
law-g912.l02.q2.h: It is the same fraction needed for treaty consent in the Senate.
law-g912.l02.q2.e: Veto overrides require two thirds of both chambers. Three fifths is the old cloture figure and three fourths is for ratifying amendments in the states.

law-g912.l02.q3.t: The President lacked authority to seize the mills
law-g912.l02.q3.p: What did the Court hold in Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer (1952)?
law-g912.l02.q3.h: The President's job is to carry out laws, not make them.
law-g912.l02.q3.e: The Court held the seizure unauthorized because neither the Constitution nor a statute granted the power. The Court plainly reviewed the action, and it did not bar all regulation of steel.

law-g912.l02.q4.t: Weakest, since the President acts against Congress
law-g912.l02.q4.p: Congress passes a statute banning the President from sending troops to a specific region. The President orders troops there anyway, and a lawsuit follows. Using Justice Jackson's framework from Youngstown, where does the President's claim fall?
law-g912.l02.q4.h: Compare the action with what Congress has said.
law-g912.l02.q4.e: Jackson's lowest category is presidential action that conflicts with Congress's express will, where the President must rely on exclusive powers alone. Silence would be the middle category.

law-g912.l03.q1.p: Which amendment makes most of the Bill of Rights applicable to the states through due process?
law-g912.l03.q1.h: It was ratified after the Civil War.
law-g912.l03.q1.e: The Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause has been used for selective incorporation. The Tenth reserves powers, and the Fifth originally limited only the federal government.

law-g912.l03.q2.t: The Bill of Rights restricts only the federal government
law-g912.l03.q2.p: What did Barron v. Baltimore (1833) hold?
law-g912.l03.q2.h: This was before the Fourteenth Amendment.
law-g912.l03.q2.e: Barron held that the Bill of Rights did not apply to the states. Both-government application came later through incorporation.

law-g912.l03.q3.t: The evidence is excluded under the exclusionary rule
law-g912.l03.q3.p: A state police officer conducts an unreasonable search and finds evidence. Under Mapp v. Ohio (1961), what is the likely result in the state criminal trial?
law-g912.l03.q3.h: Mapp applied a remedy to the states.
law-g912.l03.q3.e: Mapp applied the exclusionary rule to the states, so evidence from an unreasonable search is generally excluded. Barron-era thinking that states are not bound was superseded by incorporation.

law-g912.l03.q4.t: Heller recognized an individual right to keep a handgun at home
law-g912.l03.q4.p: A city bans all handgun possession in the home, with no exception, and a resident challenges it citing the Second Amendment. Based on Heller (2008) as described in this lesson, what is the strongest argument for the resident?
law-g912.l03.q4.h: Recall what the Court said about the home and self-defense.
law-g912.l03.q4.e: Heller held that the Second Amendment protects an individual right to keep a handgun at home for self-defense. The other options contradict its holding, and it did say some regulations remain valid.

law-g912.l04.q1.p: Which amendment reserves powers not given to the nation to the states or the people?
law-g912.l04.q1.h: It is the last of the rights group about reserved powers.
law-g912.l04.q1.e: The Tenth Amendment is the reserved powers amendment. The others cover searches, criminal procedure, and trial rights.

law-g912.l04.q2.t: Congress could charter a national bank under implied powers, and a state could not tax it
law-g912.l04.q2.p: What was the outcome in McCulloch v. Maryland (1819)?
law-g912.l04.q2.e: The Court upheld the bank under the Necessary and Proper Clause and barred the state tax. The other combinations misstate one or both holdings.

law-g912.l04.q3.t: Carrying a gun near a school was not economic and was too weakly tied to commerce
law-g912.l04.q3.p: Why did the Court in United States v. Lopez (1995) strike down the Gun-Free School Zones Act?
law-g912.l04.q3.e: The Court held the Act exceeded the Commerce Clause power. It did not decide that Congress cannot pass any school-related law.

law-g912.l04.q4.t: The statute is invalid because Congress cannot commandeer states
law-g912.l04.q4.p: Congress passes a statute ordering every state legislature to enact a particular licensing law for private businesses. Under the anti-commandeering principle recognized in Murphy v. NCAA (2018), what is the most likely outcome of a challenge by a state?
law-g912.l04.q4.h: Compare regulating private actors with commanding states.
law-g912.l04.q4.e: Congress may regulate private actors directly but may not commandeer state legislatures. The Supremacy Clause does not itself give Congress a power to order states to legislate.

law-g912.l05.q1.p: Which court generally decides most disputes between private parties over state-law matters?
law-g912.l05.q1.h: Think of courts of general jurisdiction.
law-g912.l05.q1.e: State courts hear most disputes. The Supreme Court and courts of appeals take narrow categories, and the ICJ handles disputes between states.

law-g912.l05.q2.t: Federal question and diversity of citizenship
law-g912.l05.q2.p: What are the two main routes to federal jurisdiction described in this lesson?
law-g912.l05.q2.h: One is about the law, the other about the parties.
law-g912.l05.q2.e: Federal courts hear federal-question cases and diversity cases meeting the amount requirement. The others are not bases for jurisdiction.

law-g912.l05.q3.p: A resident of Ohio sues a Michigan company for $200,000 over a contract in federal court. What does Erie Railroad Co. v. Tompkins (1938) require the federal court to apply?
law-g912.l05.q3.h: Think about which law supplies the rules of decision.
law-g912.l05.q3.e: Erie requires federal courts hearing state-law claims in diversity to apply state substantive law. There is no general federal common law of contracts.

law-g912.l05.q4.t: It lacks jurisdiction: no federal question and no diversity
law-g912.l05.q4.p: A citizen of Texas sues a citizen of Texas in federal court over an unpaid $500,000 loan. The loan is governed only by state law. What is the best description of the court's jurisdiction?
law-g912.l05.q4.e: Diversity requires citizens of different states, and there is no federal question. Parties cannot create subject-matter jurisdiction by agreement.

law-g912.l06.q1.p: What document begins a civil lawsuit?
law-g912.l06.q1.e: A civil case begins with a complaint. An indictment starts a criminal case, and a verdict form is used at the end of trial.

law-g912.l06.q2.t: Whether the law gives a remedy if the complaint's facts are true
law-g912.l06.q2.p: A defendant files a Rule 12(b)(6) motion. What question does the court ask?
law-g912.l06.q2.h: No evidence is weighed at this stage.
law-g912.l06.q2.e: A 12(b)(6) motion tests the legal sufficiency of the complaint, assuming its facts are true. Credibility and jury predictions belong to later stages.

law-g912.l06.q3.t: It is granted when no material fact is genuinely disputed
law-g912.l06.q3.p: Which statement describes summary judgment under Rule 56?
law-g912.l06.q3.h: Think about whether a reasonable jury could find for the other side.
law-g912.l06.q3.e: Summary judgment requires no genuine dispute of material fact. Judges do not weigh credibility at that stage.

law-g912.l06.q4.t: Denied, since a material fact is genuinely disputed
law-g912.l06.q4.p: After discovery, the plaintiff's own deposition and the defendant's records conflict about whether a payment was ever made, and both are supported by sworn testimony. The defendant moves for summary judgment. What is the most likely ruling?
law-g912.l06.q4.e: A real conflict on a material fact means a jury could find either way, so the motion is denied. Documents do not automatically outweigh testimony, and the motion is available to either party.

law-g912.l07.q1.p: What standard generally supports a lawful arrest or a warrant?
law-g912.l07.q1.h: It is a fair probability, not certainty.
law-g912.l07.q1.e: Probable cause supports arrests and warrants. Beyond a reasonable doubt is the trial standard for conviction.

law-g912.l07.q2.t: States must provide counsel to felony defendants who cannot afford a lawyer
law-g912.l07.q2.p: What did Gideon v. Wainwright (1963) hold?
law-g912.l07.q2.h: It extended a Sixth Amendment right to the states.
law-g912.l07.q2.e: Gideon held that indigent felony defendants in state courts are entitled to appointed counsel. Miranda concerns warnings, not Gideon.

law-g912.l07.q3.p: Which describes the situation in which Miranda warnings are required?
law-g912.l07.q3.e: Warnings are required before custodial interrogation. They are not needed for every conversation, and the offense type is irrelevant.

law-g912.l07.q4.t: Admissible, because Miranda requires custody and she was not in custody
law-g912.l07.q4.p: Police stop Lena on the street and ask where she was last night. She is not under arrest and may walk away. She says she was near the store that was robbed. At trial, she argues that the statement must be excluded because she was not given Miranda warnings. What is the best analysis?
law-g912.l07.q4.e: Without custody, Miranda warnings are not required, so the statement is not excluded on that ground. Miranda does not cover every question and is not limited to written statements.

law-g912.l08.q1.p: Which standard of proof is lowest?
law-g912.l08.q1.h: It means more likely than not.
law-g912.l08.q1.e: Preponderance is the lowest and is the usual civil standard. Clear and convincing is in between, and reasonable doubt is the highest.

law-g912.l08.q2.t: Proof beyond a reasonable doubt is required in juvenile delinquency cases, as in adult trials
law-g912.l08.q2.p: What did In re Winship (1970) hold?
law-g912.l08.q2.h: It applied the criminal standard to juvenile cases.
law-g912.l08.q2.e: Winship extended proof beyond a reasonable doubt to delinquency proceedings. The jury question was decided differently in McKeiver.

law-g912.l08.q3.t: Persuasion is about convincing, production is about offering enough evidence
law-g912.l08.q3.p: What is the difference between the burden of persuasion and the burden of production?
law-g912.l08.q3.h: One is about convincing, the other about bringing forward evidence.
law-g912.l08.q3.e: Persuasion concerns convincing the fact finder to the required degree, while production concerns producing enough evidence to put an issue in play. They are different duties and not reserved to judges or juries.

law-g912.l08.q4.t: A preponderance may be met, but conviction needs much more certainty
law-g912.l08.q4.p: A jury in a civil case believes it is about seventy percent likely that a defendant took a ring, and it is a case in which the plaintiff must prove the claim by a preponderance. Separately, the state prosecutes the same defendant for theft. What is the most accurate statement?
law-g912.l08.q4.e: Seventy percent can satisfy a preponderance, but the criminal standard demands much greater certainty. Outcomes can differ because the standards differ.

law-g912.l09.q1.t: Makes a fact of consequence more or less probable
law-g912.l09.q1.p: Under Federal Rule of Evidence 401, evidence is relevant if it does what?
law-g912.l09.q1.e: Evidence is relevant if it makes a fact that matters more or less probable. It does not need to prove the fact conclusively.

law-g912.l09.q2.p: A prosecutor offers the defendant's old, unrelated conviction only to suggest that he is a dishonest person who probably committed the charged theft. What is the most likely objection?
law-g912.l09.q2.e: Evidence of character offered to show conduct on a specific occasion is generally barred under Rule 404(a). The other objections do not fit.

law-g912.l09.q3.t: Its probative value is substantially outweighed by unfair prejudice
law-g912.l09.q3.p: What is the standard under Rule 403 for excluding relevant evidence?
law-g912.l09.q3.h: Probative value is weighed against dangers.
law-g912.l09.q3.e: Rule 403 excludes evidence when probative value is substantially outweighed by unfair prejudice and similar dangers. Merely harming a party is not enough.

law-g912.l09.q4.t: It is relevant to planning and the clerk authenticated it
law-g912.l09.q4.p: In an arson trial, the prosecution calls a hardware store clerk who identifies a receipt as the one she gave the defendant for a gasoline can two days before the fire. The defense objects to the receipt. Which response is strongest?
law-g912.l09.q4.e: The purchase makes planning more probable, and the clerk can authenticate the receipt under Rule 901. The other responses misdescribe the issues.

law-g912.l10.q1.t: To prove the truth of the matter asserted
law-g912.l10.q1.p: Under Rule 801(c), hearsay is an out-of-court statement offered for what purpose?
law-g912.l10.q1.e: Hearsay is a statement offered to prove the truth of what it asserts. Offered for another purpose, such as notice, it may not be hearsay.

law-g912.l10.q2.t: It is defined as not hearsay when offered against that party
law-g912.l10.q2.p: A party offers the opposing party's own earlier statement against that party. How does Rule 801(d)(2) treat it?
law-g912.l10.q2.e: A statement of an opposing party offered against that party is defined as not hearsay. It does not require unavailability or an oath.

law-g912.l10.q3.t: Not hearsay, since it is offered for its effect on the listener
law-g912.l10.q3.p: A witness testifies: "My neighbor told me the stairs were broken." The statement is offered only to show that the witness knew about the danger and walked carefully. What is the best analysis?
law-g912.l10.q3.h: Ask why it is being offered.
law-g912.l10.q3.e: Offered to show notice or state of mind, not the stairs' actual condition, it is not hearsay. Not every out-of-court statement qualifies as hearsay.

law-g912.l10.q4.t: Excluded, because it is testimonial and the defendant never cross-examined
law-g912.l10.q4.p: A bystander makes a formal statement to a police officer describing a stabbing, and then cannot be found for trial. The prosecution offers the statement against the defendant, and the defendant never had a chance to cross-examine the bystander. Under Crawford v. Washington (2004), what is the most likely result?
law-g912.l10.q4.h: The Sixth Amendment may bar it even if a hearsay rule would allow it.
law-g912.l10.q4.e: Crawford bars testimonial statements of absent witnesses unless the witness is unavailable and the defendant had a prior chance to cross-examine. Unavailability alone is not enough.

law-g912.l11.q1.p: Which of these is NOT an element of negligence?
law-g912.l11.q1.e: Negligence requires duty, breach, causation, and damages. Intent to harm is the mark of an intentional tort.

law-g912.l11.q2.t: Actual cause is the but-for link; proximate cause limits liability to foreseeable harm
law-g912.l11.q2.p: What is the difference between actual cause and proximate cause?
law-g912.l11.q2.h: One is factual, the other policy-based.
law-g912.l11.q2.e: Actual cause asks whether the harm would not have occurred but for the conduct. Proximate cause limits liability to foreseeable results, and the two are separate.

law-g912.l11.q3.t: $60,000, the defendant's share of the fault
law-g912.l11.q3.p: In a state that follows pure comparative negligence, a plaintiff who is forty percent at fault for a $100,000 injury will recover about what?
law-g912.l11.q3.e: Under pure comparative negligence, damages are reduced by the plaintiff's share of fault, so the plaintiff recovers sixty percent. Contributory negligence would have barred recovery.

law-g912.l11.q4.t: It owed Rosa no duty, since she was outside the foreseeable zone of danger
law-g912.l11.q4.p: A porter helps a passenger board a moving train and the passenger drops a package that, unknown to anyone, holds fireworks. The explosion topples scales on a distant platform, injuring Rosa. Under the majority view in Palsgraf, what is the strongest argument for the railroad?
law-g912.l11.q4.e: In the majority view the duty extends to foreseeable plaintiffs, and Rosa was not within the zone of danger. Strict liability and assumption of risk do not fit the story.

law-g912.l12.q1.t: UCC Article 2 on sales of goods
law-g912.l12.q1.p: Which body of law governs contracts for the sale of goods?
law-g912.l12.q1.e: UCC Article 2 governs sales of goods. The others cover evidence, crimes, and civil procedure.

law-g912.l12.q2.t: To give the non-breaching party the benefit of the bargain it made
law-g912.l12.q2.p: What is the usual goal of expectation damages?
law-g912.l12.q2.h: Think about what the contract promised.
law-g912.l12.q2.e: Expectation damages aim to put the injured party where full performance would have. Restoring the pre-contract position describes reliance or restitution.

law-g912.l12.q3.t: The carrier could not foresee that a delay would stop the mill
law-g912.l12.q3.p: In Hadley v. Baxendale (1854), why could the mill owner not recover lost profits?
law-g912.l12.q3.h: Foreseeability when the contract was made.
law-g912.l12.q3.e: Consequential losses are recoverable only if foreseeable to the breacher at contracting. Lost profits can be recovered in other cases.

law-g912.l12.q4.t: Max is bound, because assent is judged objectively
law-g912.l12.q4.p: Max, a farm owner, signs a restaurant check saying he sells his farm to Joe for a stated price, and later claims it was only a joke he never intended seriously. Joe reasonably believed it was serious. Under Lucy v. Zehmer (Va. 1954), how is the case likely decided?
law-g912.l12.q4.h: Is intent judged secretly or objectively?
law-g912.l12.q4.e: The objective theory looks at how a reasonable person would read the parties' words and conduct. A private joke is not controlling, though not every writing is a contract.

law-g912.l13.q1.p: In Tinker (1969), students were suspended for wearing what?
law-g912.l13.q1.e: The students wore black armbands. The Court held that the school could not punish the quiet expression absent a forecast of substantial disruption.

law-g912.l13.q2.p: Which case allows schools to control school-sponsored expression like a class newspaper if actions are reasonably related to legitimate educational concerns?
law-g912.l13.q2.h: The case involved a student newspaper.
law-g912.l13.q2.e: Hazelwood established that standard for school-sponsored speech. Tinker covers independent student speech, and Mahanoy concerns off-campus speech.

law-g912.l13.q3.t: The school violated her rights, with its interest weaker off campus
law-g912.l13.q3.p: What did the Court hold in Mahanoy Area School District v. B.L. (2021)?
law-g912.l13.q3.h: The Court did not choose either extreme.
law-g912.l13.q3.e: The Court ruled for the student, saying the school's interest is weaker off campus, but it did not say schools can never act. It also did not exclude social media from the First Amendment.

law-g912.l13.q4.t: Hazelwood, since the paper is school-sponsored
law-g912.l13.q4.p: A principal removes an article from the school newspaper, which is produced in a journalism class, because it discusses a sensitive topic. The students sue. Which framework most likely controls?
law-g912.l13.q4.e: A class-produced newspaper is school-sponsored, so Hazelwood applies. Fraser concerns lewd speech at an assembly, and no facts suggest off-campus speech or compelled salutes.

law-g912.l14.q1.p: What standard did New Jersey v. T.L.O. (1985) adopt for school searches?
law-g912.l14.q1.h: It relaxes the standard for police searches.
law-g912.l14.q1.e: T.L.O. requires reasonable suspicion at the start and reasonable scope. School officials need neither a warrant nor probable cause.

law-g912.l14.q2.t: The suspected items posed little danger and the search was too intrusive
law-g912.l14.q2.p: Why did the Court in Safford v. Redding (2009) find the search unreasonable?
law-g912.l14.q2.h: Compare the intrusion with the suspicion.
law-g912.l14.q2.e: The search was excessively intrusive for the suspected infraction. Schools can sometimes search for drugs, and Miranda is not at issue.

law-g912.l14.q3.t: Notice and a chance to respond
law-g912.l14.q3.p: According to Goss v. Lopez (1975), what must a school provide before a short suspension?
law-g912.l14.q3.e: Goss requires notice and an informal opportunity to respond for suspensions of ten days or less. A jury or federal judge is not needed.

law-g912.l14.q4.t: The policy is upheld, given reduced privacy and an important school interest
law-g912.l14.q4.p: A school adopts a policy of random drug tests for all students in competitive extracurricular activities after finding a rise in drug use. A student in the debate club challenges it. Based on Vernonia and Earls, what is the most likely result?
law-g912.l14.q4.e: Earls upheld testing of students in competitive extracurriculars, building on Vernonia. The Fourth Amendment does apply in schools, but the reasonableness balance favors the school.

law-g912.l15.q1.p: Which case held that juveniles in delinquency proceedings that may lead to commitment have a right to counsel?
law-g912.l15.q1.h: It involved a fifteen-year-old in Arizona.
law-g912.l15.q1.e: Gault recognized the right to counsel and other due process rights. McKeiver rejected a jury right, and Roper and Graham concern sentencing.

law-g912.l15.q2.t: The death penalty is barred for offenders who were under age eighteen at the time of the crime
law-g912.l15.q2.p: What did Roper v. Simmons (2005) hold?
law-g912.l15.q2.h: It is about the Eighth Amendment and the death penalty.
law-g912.l15.q2.e: Roper barred the death penalty for offenders under eighteen. Graham and Miller addressed life without parole.

law-g912.l15.q3.t: Mandatory life without parole for juveniles is unconstitutional
law-g912.l15.q3.p: What did Miller v. Alabama (2012) hold?
law-g912.l15.q3.e: Miller held that mandatory life without parole for juveniles is unconstitutional, because sentencers must be able to consider youth. It did not bar all prison sentences.

law-g912.l15.q4.t: The mandatory sentence violates the Eighth Amendment under Miller
law-g912.l15.q4.p: A state requires that every seventeen-year-old convicted of homicide automatically receive life without parole, with no consideration of age or circumstances. Which argument is strongest for the defendant based on the cases in this lesson?
law-g912.l15.q4.e: Miller bars mandatory life without parole for juveniles. Gideon, Winship, and Roper address different issues.

law-g912.l16.q1.t: A believable story that ties the facts and law to your result
law-g912.l16.q1.p: What is a theory of the case in a mock trial?
law-g912.l16.q1.e: A theory is a simple, believable story tied to the facts and law. A fact list or objection list is not a theory.

law-g912.l16.q2.p: In a typical trial, which side presents its case first in a criminal matter?
law-g912.l16.q2.h: The burden is on the government.
law-g912.l16.q2.e: The prosecution carries the burden and presents first. The judge and jury do not present cases.

law-g912.l16.q3.t: Stay consistent with the statement and add only harmless details
law-g912.l16.q3.p: A witness in a mock trial is asked a question the written statement does not answer. What is the best approach?
law-g912.l16.q3.e: Witnesses must stay consistent with their statements and may add only reasonable, non-contradicting details if the rules allow. Inventing facts is improper.

law-g912.l16.q4.t: The defendant was not there, and the witness could not have identified him reliably
law-g912.l16.q4.p: A defense team has a case where the only evidence linking the defendant is a brief nighttime sighting by one witness. Which theory is most coherent and focused?
law-g912.l16.q4.h: A theory should be simple and fit the evidence.
law-g912.l16.q4.e: A mistaken-identification theory is simple, rests on the packet, and connects to the evidence. Shifting stories and personal attacks undermine credibility.

law-g912.l17.q1.t: A leading question that suggests the answer to the witness
law-g912.l17.q1.p: Which type of question is generally not allowed on direct examination?
law-g912.l17.q1.h: Direct is for the witness's story.
law-g912.l17.q1.e: Leading questions are generally barred on direct under Rule 611(c), with exceptions such as preliminary matters.

law-g912.l17.q2.t: Preview the evidence and the story
law-g912.l17.q2.p: What should an opening statement do?
law-g912.l17.q2.h: It is a preview, not an argument.
law-g912.l17.q2.e: An opening previews the case and the evidence. Argument and personal opinion are generally reserved for closing or barred.

law-g912.l17.q3.t: Lay a foundation by having the witness identify it as a fair and accurate picture
law-g912.l17.q3.p: You want to introduce a photograph through a witness. What should you do first?
law-g912.l17.q3.e: Foundation shows the witness knows the item and that it is accurate. Skipping it invites a sustained objection.

law-g912.l17.q4.t: Leading, fixed by rephrasing as an open question: "What, if anything, did you see?"
law-g912.l17.q4.p: On direct, the attorney asks, "You saw the defendant take the bag, didn't you?" The opposing attorney objects. What is the best ground and the best fix?
law-g912.l17.q4.e: The question suggests its answer, so the ground is leading. Rephrasing it as an open question cures the problem.

law-g912.l18.q1.p: Which kind of question is generally allowed on cross-examination?
law-g912.l18.q1.e: Leading questions are permitted on cross under Rule 611(c). Narrative questions invite the witness to control the story.

law-g912.l18.q2.t: Confronting a witness with an earlier statement that conflicts with testimony
law-g912.l18.q2.p: What is impeachment by prior inconsistent statement?
law-g912.l18.q2.h: It uses the witness's own earlier words.
law-g912.l18.q2.e: Impeachment by prior inconsistent statement shows a conflict between the earlier statement and the testimony, under Rule 613. The other options describe different procedures.

law-g912.l18.q3.t: "Why do you think the driver was speeding?"
law-g912.l18.q3.p: Which question is poor technique on cross-examination?
law-g912.l18.q3.e: A "why" question invites a speech and loses control. The others are short leading questions on specific facts.

law-g912.l18.q4.t: Impeachment by attacking her ability to perceive the event clearly
law-g912.l18.q4.p: A witness testified on direct that she clearly saw the shooter's face. On cross, you establish that it was night, the streetlight was out, she was across a wide street, and the encounter lasted two seconds. Which type of impeachment are you using?
law-g912.l18.q4.h: Focus on lighting, distance and time.
law-g912.l18.q4.e: The questions attack opportunity and ability to perceive. No conviction, bias, or character witness is involved.

law-g912.l19.q1.t: The judge agrees with the objection and the evidence is not allowed
law-g912.l19.q1.p: What does it mean when the judge says "sustained"?
law-g912.l19.q1.e: Sustained means the objection is accepted. Overruled means it is rejected.

law-g912.l19.q2.p: A lawyer asks a witness, "When did you stop stealing from your employer?" The witness has never been shown to have stolen. What is the best objection?
law-g912.l19.q2.h: The question slips in an unproven fact.
law-g912.l19.q2.e: The question assumes the witness stole, which is not in evidence. Hearsay, privilege, and authentication do not fit.

law-g912.l19.q3.p: Which objection fits a lay witness who says, "I am sure the defendant is a violent person at heart"?
law-g912.l19.q3.e: The statement is improper lay opinion and character evidence under Rules 701 and 404. The other objections concern form or documents.

law-g912.l19.q4.t: The attorney should rephrase or identify a valid exception
law-g912.l19.q4.p: On direct, the attorney asks a witness, "What did your sister tell you about the accident?" The answer is offered to prove how the accident happened. The opposing side objects "hearsay." What is the most helpful response?
law-g912.l19.q4.e: Hearsay is a separate barrier from relevance, and being under oath does not change that. The proponent must identify a non-hearsay purpose or exception, or rephrase.

law-g912.l20.q1.t: A lawyer may argue fair inferences drawn from the evidence
law-g912.l20.q1.p: Which statement about closing argument is correct?
law-g912.l20.q1.h: Argument must rest on the record.
law-g912.l20.q1.e: Closing arguments may draw reasonable inferences from the evidence. They may not rely on unproven or excluded facts.

law-g912.l20.q2.p: Which ABA Model Rule concerns a lawyer's duty of candor to the tribunal?
law-g912.l20.q2.h: It is about not making false statements to the court.
law-g912.l20.q2.e: Rule 3.3 is candor toward the tribunal. Rule 1.6 concerns confidentiality, and the others cover competence and supervision.

law-g912.l20.q3.t: To answer the opponent's closing argument, not to add new points
law-g912.l20.q3.p: Why do many mock trial formats allow the party with the burden of proof a rebuttal?
law-g912.l20.q3.e: Rebuttal answers what the opponent said, rather than adding new points. It is not a chance to call new witnesses.

law-g912.l20.q4.t: Improper, as the lawyer asserts private knowledge
law-g912.l20.q4.p: A defense attorney closes: "Ladies and gentlemen, I know for a fact that my client is innocent because he told me privately." What is the best analysis?
law-g912.l20.q4.h: Closings must stay within the record.
law-g912.l20.q4.e: A lawyer may not offer personal knowledge of facts outside the evidence, and the statement is also a confidential client communication. A lawyer may argue that the prosecution failed to prove guilt.

law-g912.l21.q1.p: What degree do most lawyers earn in law school?
law-g912.l21.q1.e: Most U.S. lawyers earn the Juris Doctor. The other degrees are not the standard law school degree.

law-g912.l21.q2.t: They defend people charged with crimes who cannot afford a lawyer
law-g912.l21.q2.h: The name tells you whom they defend.
law-g912.l21.q2.e: Public defenders represent defendants who cannot afford lawyers. Prosecutors represent the government.

law-g912.l21.q3.t: They support lawyers but generally cannot give legal advice
law-g912.l21.q3.p: Which statement about paralegals is accurate?
law-g912.l21.q3.e: Paralegals assist lawyers with research and documents and generally may not practice law. A J.D. and bar passage are required for lawyers, not paralegals.

law-g912.l21.q4.t: No, since many legal careers involve little courtroom work
law-g912.l21.q4.p: A student who likes writing and negotiating but dislikes public speaking asks whether law is a poor fit. Which reply is most accurate?
law-g912.l21.q4.h: Think about the range of legal jobs.
law-g912.l21.q4.e: Many lawyers draft contracts, advise clients, or work in government or business with little courtroom work. The claims that every job needs trials or that lawyers never speak are both overstated.

law-g912.l22.q1.p: Which document lists the traditional sources of international law that the ICJ applies?
law-g912.l22.q1.h: It is the Court's own Statute.
law-g912.l22.q1.e: Article 38 of the ICJ Statute lists treaties, custom, general principles, and subsidiary means. The others concern U.S. law, evidence, and the ICC.

law-g912.l22.q2.t: Members to avoid the threat or use of force against another state's territorial integrity
law-g912.l22.q2.p: What does Article 2(4) of the UN Charter require?
law-g912.l22.q2.h: It is the Charter's rule on force.
law-g912.l22.q2.e: Article 2(4) prohibits the threat or use of force against territorial integrity or political independence. It does not require disarmament or send all disputes to the ICC.

law-g912.l22.q3.t: A peremptory norm of general international law that treaties cannot override
law-g912.l22.q3.p: Which of the following describes a jus cogens norm?
law-g912.l22.q3.e: Jus cogens norms are peremptory rules that cannot be set aside by treaty. A bilateral treaty or recommendation does not have that status.

law-g912.l22.q4.t: Article 51, which recognizes self-defense against an armed attack
law-g912.l22.q4.p: State A is attacked by armed forces of State B and responds with force against the attacking units. The Security Council has not yet acted. Which provision most directly supports State A's claim of lawful force?
law-g912.l22.q4.h: Look for the Charter's self-defense provision.
law-g912.l22.q4.e: Article 51 recognizes self-defense in response to an armed attack. Article 2(4) is the general prohibition, Article 38 lists sources of law, and the Rome Statute creates a criminal court.

law-g912.l23.q1.t: The European Court of Human Rights
law-g912.l23.q1.p: Which court enforces the European Convention on Human Rights?
law-g912.l23.q1.e: The European Court of Human Rights enforces the Convention. The ICJ hears state disputes, and the ICC prosecutes individuals for grave crimes.

law-g912.l23.q2.t: It was not directly enforceable without action by Congress
law-g912.l23.q2.p: What did the Court hold in Medellin v. Texas (2008) about an ICJ judgment?
law-g912.l23.q2.e: The Court held that the ICJ judgment was not directly enforceable in state courts without implementing action. It did not hold that the ICJ has no authority at all.

law-g912.l23.q3.t: The United States has signed it but has not ratified it
law-g912.l23.q3.p: Which statement about the United States and the Convention on the Rights of the Child is accurate?
law-g912.l23.q3.e: The United States signed but has not ratified the Convention. The 1992 ratification relates to the ICCPR.

law-g912.l23.q4.t: The provision is likely not enforceable without implementing legislation
law-g912.l23.q4.p: A treaty ratified by the United States contains a provision that the Senate declared requires implementing legislation. A private person sues in federal court relying directly on that provision, but Congress has passed no implementing statute. What is the most likely result?
law-g912.l23.q4.e: A non-self-executing provision needs implementing legislation before courts can enforce it directly. Treaties are part of the supreme law, but not every provision is self-executing.

law-intl-human-rights.l01.q1.t: On 10 December 1948, by the UN General Assembly
law-intl-human-rights.l01.q1.p: On which date, and by which organ, was the Universal Declaration of Human Rights adopted?
law-intl-human-rights.l01.q1.h: Think of the organ in which all UN members are represented.
law-intl-human-rights.l01.q1.e: The General Assembly adopted the Declaration on 10 December 1948 as resolution 217A (III). The 1945 date belongs to the Charter, and 1966 to the two Covenants.

law-intl-human-rights.l01.q2.t: Assembly resolutions are not treaties, but some of its content may bind as customary law
law-intl-human-rights.l01.q2.p: A lawyer argues that the Universal Declaration binds every state because it was adopted by the General Assembly with no votes against. Which response is most accurate?
law-intl-human-rights.l01.q2.h: Separate the form of the instrument from the sources of the rules it contains.
law-intl-human-rights.l01.q2.e: The resolution is non-binding in form, though provisions such as the ban on torture are binding through custom. It was not a Charter amendment, which requires the Article 108 procedure.

law-intl-human-rights.l01.q3.t: Y is wrong about the Declaration, but the prohibition of torture is binding on X as custom
law-intl-human-rights.l01.q3.p: State X has ratified no human rights treaty. Its police torture a detainee. State Y protests, citing only the Universal Declaration as a treaty obligation. What is the strongest legal position?
law-intl-human-rights.l01.q3.h: The question is which source of law actually supplies the obligation.
law-intl-human-rights.l01.q3.e: The Declaration is not a treaty, but the torture ban is also customary and peremptory, so X is bound. Articles 55 and 56 are general pledges and do not incorporate the Declaration's list.

law-intl-human-rights.l01.q4.t: The Declaration is non-binding, and customary status would have to be proved for that particular right
law-intl-human-rights.l01.q4.p: A court is asked whether the right to paid holidays in the Declaration binds a state that has ratified nothing. Which analysis best fits the doctrine in the lesson?
law-intl-human-rights.l01.q4.h: Is custom shown for the instrument as a whole, or right by right?
law-intl-human-rights.l01.q4.e: Customary status must be shown provision by provision, and the lesson notes it is disputed for many. The Charter lists no rights, and no rule excludes economic rights from custom as such.

law-intl-human-rights.l01.q5.t: It makes promoting respect for rights a UN purpose and obliges members to cooperate, without listing the rights
law-intl-human-rights.l01.q5.p: Which statement correctly describes what the UN Charter itself does on human rights?
law-intl-human-rights.l01.q5.h: Recall what Articles 1(3), 55 and 56 do and do not contain.
law-intl-human-rights.l01.q5.e: The Charter's provisions are general pledges. It neither catalogues rights nor creates an individual complaints court, which is why the Declaration was needed.

law-intl-human-rights.l02.q1.t: To respect and ensure the Covenant rights of all individuals within its territory and subject to its jurisdiction
law-intl-human-rights.l02.q1.p: What does Article 2(1) of the ICCPR require of a state party?
law-intl-human-rights.l02.q1.h: The obligation is immediate and not limited to citizens.
law-intl-human-rights.l02.q1.e: Article 2(1) is an immediate duty to respect and ensure rights for all within jurisdiction. Progressive realisation belongs to the ICESCR.

law-intl-human-rights.l02.q2.t: Article 2(1) of the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights
law-intl-human-rights.l02.q2.p: Which treaty text contains the obligation to take steps, to the maximum of available resources, towards progressive realisation?
law-intl-human-rights.l02.q2.h: Look at the Covenant dealing with work, health and education.
law-intl-human-rights.l02.q2.e: The ICESCR's Article 2(1) contains the progressive-realisation formula. The ICCPR's Article 4 concerns derogation in emergencies.

law-intl-human-rights.l02.q3.t: She has no Committee complaint under either Covenant, and the ICESCR does not bind A as treaty law
law-intl-human-rights.l02.q3.p: State A has signed the ICESCR but not ratified it, and has ratified the ICCPR without the First Optional Protocol. A trade unionist alleges a violation of the right to strike. Which is correct?
law-intl-human-rights.l02.q3.h: Check ratification and the optional complaint procedure for each treaty.
law-intl-human-rights.l02.q3.e: Complaints need acceptance of the protocol, and a signatory is only bound not to defeat the treaty's object and purpose (VCLT Article 18). So the signed-only ICESCR creates no complaint route, and the ICCPR route is closed.

law-intl-human-rights.l02.q4.t: The ICESCR is a binding treaty, and the 1993 Vienna Declaration treats all rights as indivisible and interdependent
law-intl-human-rights.l02.q4.p: A government argues that because the ICCPR and ICESCR are separate treaties, economic and social rights are merely aspirational and civil rights are the only real law. Which reply is strongest?
law-intl-human-rights.l02.q4.h: A treaty duty can be gradual without being optional.
law-intl-human-rights.l02.q4.e: The ICESCR creates binding obligations, some immediate, and Vienna 1993 rejects any ranking. Both Covenants were adopted by the General Assembly on the same day, and the ICCPR has no right to work.

law-intl-human-rights.l02.q5.t: Ratified the ICCPR in 1992 with reservations, and signed but did not ratify the ICESCR
law-intl-human-rights.l02.q5.p: Which pair correctly matches the status of the United States toward the Covenants?
law-intl-human-rights.l02.q5.h: One Covenant is ratified with caveats; the other is not ratified.
law-intl-human-rights.l02.q5.e: The US ratified the ICCPR in 1992 with declarations that it is not self-executing, and has only signed the ICESCR. The other pairings reverse or invent its record.

law-intl-human-rights.l03.q1.t: Independent experts elected by states parties, serving in their personal capacity
law-intl-human-rights.l03.q1.p: Who sits on a UN human rights treaty body such as the Human Rights Committee?
law-intl-human-rights.l03.q1.h: The design is meant to protect independence from governments.
law-intl-human-rights.l03.q1.e: Treaty body members are elected independent experts. The Human Rights Council is the body of state representatives, which is why its work is more political.

law-intl-human-rights.l03.q2.t: A general comment, which is an authoritative interpretation rather than a binding judgment
law-intl-human-rights.l03.q2.p: A committee publishes its interpretation of the right to life in the ICCPR, covering every state party. What is this document called?
law-intl-human-rights.l03.q2.h: It is addressed to all states, not to one state's report.
law-intl-human-rights.l03.q2.e: General comments are thematic interpretations. Concluding observations address one state after its report, and neither is a court judgment.

law-intl-human-rights.l03.q3.t: The communication is inadmissible against B, though B still owes periodic reports and may face the UPR
law-intl-human-rights.l03.q3.p: State B is party to the ICCPR but not its First Optional Protocol. A prisoner, after exhausting local remedies, writes to the Human Rights Committee about ill-treatment. What follows?
law-intl-human-rights.l03.q3.h: Individual complaints depend on separate consent.
law-intl-human-rights.l03.q3.e: Individual communications require acceptance of the First Optional Protocol. The UPR is a peer review of states, not a complaint forum, and individuals cannot go to the ICJ.

law-intl-human-rights.l03.q4.t: The views are not formally binding, yet they carry great weight as the interpretation of the body set up to supervise the treaty
law-intl-human-rights.l03.q4.p: State C rejects a committee's finding, saying the final views are not binding like a court judgment. Which analysis is most accurate?
law-intl-human-rights.l03.q4.h: Recall the position taken in the Diallo case.
law-intl-human-rights.l03.q4.e: The ICJ in Diallo (2010) gave great weight to the Committee's interpretations without calling them binding. The Committee is not a court and does not need Council endorsement.

law-intl-human-rights.l03.q5.t: States review other states' records, so it covers every UN member and is more political
law-intl-human-rights.l03.q5.p: How is the Universal Periodic Review different from treaty body reporting?
law-intl-human-rights.l03.q5.e: The UPR is peer review among governments through the Human Rights Council and applies to all UN members. Expert-led review is what the treaty bodies do.

law-intl-human-rights.l04.q1.t: When it is incompatible with the object and purpose of the treaty
law-intl-human-rights.l04.q1.p: Under VCLT Article 19, when is a reservation impermissible even if the treaty does not prohibit reservations?
law-intl-human-rights.l04.q1.h: Recall the Genocide Convention advisory opinion test.
law-intl-human-rights.l04.q1.e: Article 19(c) bars a reservation incompatible with the treaty's object and purpose. A single objection does not suffice, and the other options are not in the article.

law-intl-human-rights.l04.q2.t: Jus cogens concerns a norm's non-derogable rank; erga omnes concerns whether all states may invoke its breach
law-intl-human-rights.l04.q2.p: What is the difference between jus cogens and erga omnes?
law-intl-human-rights.l04.q2.h: One idea is about hierarchy, the other about standing.
law-intl-human-rights.l04.q2.e: Peremptory status determines that no derogation by treaty is allowed (VCLT Article 53). Erga omnes concerns the legal interest of all states in compliance. The distractor reverses the two.

law-intl-human-rights.l04.q3.t: The reservation is severed as incompatible, and F remains bound by the provision
law-intl-human-rights.l04.q3.p: State F ratifies a human rights treaty with a reservation excluding its detainee-protection article. State G objects, saying the reservation defeats the treaty's object. Following General Comment 24 of the Human Rights Committee, what is the likely result?
law-intl-human-rights.l04.q3.h: Human rights treaties are not reciprocal bargains.
law-intl-human-rights.l04.q3.e: The Committee holds that incompatible reservations are severable, so the reserving state stays bound. The other outcomes follow the classical reciprocal model, which fits human rights treaties poorly.

law-intl-human-rights.l04.q4.t: Obligations erga omnes partes, owed to every party to the treaty, as in Belgium v Senegal
law-intl-human-rights.l04.q4.p: State H, a party to the Convention against Torture, allegedly allows torture. State J, which has no victims of its own, brings a claim before the ICJ. Which doctrine most directly supports J's standing?
law-intl-human-rights.l04.q4.h: The Court has accepted standing without a direct national injury.
law-intl-human-rights.l04.q4.e: In Belgium v Senegal (2012) the Court accepted that each party has a legal interest in compliance. Diplomatic protection and reciprocity require a national or direct injury, which J lacks.

law-intl-human-rights.l04.q5.t: It did not by itself create jurisdiction where the state's reservation excluded the treaty's jurisdictional clause
law-intl-human-rights.l04.q5.p: In Armed Activities (DRC v Rwanda, ICJ, 2006), what did the Court hold about the peremptory status of the prohibition of genocide?
law-intl-human-rights.l04.q5.h: Rank of a norm and consent to jurisdiction are separate matters.
law-intl-human-rights.l04.q5.e: The Court distinguished substantive peremptory status from jurisdiction, which still depends on consent. Peremptory status does not override a valid jurisdictional reservation.

law-intl-human-rights.l05.q1.t: To respect, to protect and to fulfil the right
law-intl-human-rights.l05.q1.p: Which three-part typology describes the duties that apply to every human right?
law-intl-human-rights.l05.q1.h: They run from non-interference to positive action.
law-intl-human-rights.l05.q1.e: The tripartite typology covers non-interference, preventing interference by third parties, and positive measures. The distractors name unrelated state actions.

law-intl-human-rights.l05.q2.t: Guaranteeing that the rights are exercised without discrimination of any prohibited kind
law-intl-human-rights.l05.q2.p: According to General Comment 3 of the CESCR, which obligation under the ICESCR is of immediate effect regardless of available resources?
law-intl-human-rights.l05.q2.h: Some duties do not depend on how wealthy the state is.
law-intl-human-rights.l05.q2.e: Non-discrimination is immediate, and the obligation to take steps is too. Full realisation of health and housing is progressive, and no fixed spending percentage appears in the Covenant.

law-intl-human-rights.l05.q3.t: The cut is presumptively retrogressive, and the state must show that it used maximum available resources and weighed alternatives
law-intl-human-rights.l05.q3.p: A cash-strapped state cuts primary health clinics in poor regions while keeping spending on a new stadium. Which analysis best fits the ICESCR framework?
law-intl-human-rights.l05.q3.h: The Committee reverses the burden when a retreat from a right is shown.
law-intl-human-rights.l05.q3.e: Deliberately retrogressive steps are presumed impermissible unless justified. They are not absolutely barred, and the resource-use burden is on the state, which makes stadium spending relevant.

law-intl-human-rights.l05.q4.t: Government of the Republic of South Africa v Grootboom, decided by the Constitutional Court in 2000
law-intl-human-rights.l05.q4.p: A court reviewing a housing programme finds it makes no provision for people in desperate need, but declines to set an individual minimum-core entitlement. It orders the government to devise a reasonable programme. This most closely matches which decision?
law-intl-human-rights.l05.q4.h: The court used reasonableness review of a state programme.
law-intl-human-rights.l05.q4.e: Grootboom used reasonableness review in the housing context. Airey concerned legal aid and access to court, and the other two do not involve social rights.

law-intl-human-rights.l05.q5.t: Effective access to court for a litigant may require legal aid, and no water-tight division exists between the two groups
law-intl-human-rights.l05.q5.p: What did the ECtHR decide in Airey v Ireland (1979) that is relevant to the divide between civil and social rights?
law-intl-human-rights.l05.q5.h: The Court read a civil right so that it works in practice.
law-intl-human-rights.l05.q5.e: The Court held that access to a court must be effective, which in that case required legal aid. It did not require aid in every dispute, so the last option overstates the ruling.

law-intl-human-rights.l06.q1.t: The prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment
law-intl-human-rights.l06.q1.p: Which right can never be suspended by derogation under both ICCPR Article 4 and ECHR Article 15?
law-intl-human-rights.l06.q1.h: Think of the absolute rights in both lists.
law-intl-human-rights.l06.q1.e: Torture is non-derogable under both regimes. Assembly, liberty and privacy can be derogated from if strictly necessary, subject to the other conditions.

law-intl-human-rights.l06.q2.t: The requirement that the restriction be provided by law that is accessible and precise
law-intl-human-rights.l06.q2.p: A state restricts a newspaper under a vague, unpublished decree to protect an unspecified public interest. Which element of the limitation test most clearly fails?
law-intl-human-rights.l06.q2.h: Consider what makes a rule foreseeable to the person affected.
law-intl-human-rights.l06.q2.e: Limits must have a clear legal basis and a legitimate aim. The proclamation and notification requirements apply to derogation, not to ordinary limitations.

law-intl-human-rights.l06.q3.t: The assembly measure may be valid if strictly required, but the interrogation measure breaches a non-derogable prohibition
law-intl-human-rights.l06.q3.p: After a major attack, State K proclaims an emergency, suspends the right of assembly and authorises coercive interrogation of detainees. Which statement is correct?
law-intl-human-rights.l06.q3.h: Sort the two measures by whether the right affected can be derogated from.
law-intl-human-rights.l06.q3.e: Assembly can be derogated from if the Article 4 conditions are met. Torture and cruel treatment are non-derogable, so an emergency never justifies them.

law-intl-human-rights.l06.q4.t: A public emergency existed, but the measure was disproportionate and discriminatory in applying only to non-nationals
law-intl-human-rights.l06.q4.p: A state indefinitely detains foreign terror suspects without trial but not its own nationals who pose a comparable risk. In A and Others v United Kingdom (2009), what did the Grand Chamber hold about the derogation?
law-intl-human-rights.l06.q4.h: The Court accepted one condition but rejected another.
law-intl-human-rights.l06.q4.e: The Court accepted the emergency but held that detention only of foreigners was not strictly required and discriminated. The Convention applies to everyone within jurisdiction, and discretion is limited.

law-intl-human-rights.l06.q5.t: A derogation requires an officially proclaimed emergency, and the state must notify other parties through the UN Secretary-General
law-intl-human-rights.l06.q5.p: Which statement about Article 4 of the ICCPR is accurate?
law-intl-human-rights.l06.q5.h: Procedure matters as well as substance.
law-intl-human-rights.l06.q5.e: Article 4 requires official proclamation, strict necessity and international notification. Secret or open-ended derogations fail those conditions.

law-intl-human-rights.l07.q1.t: The European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg, a Council of Europe body
law-intl-human-rights.l07.q1.p: Which institution supervises the European Convention on Human Rights?
law-intl-human-rights.l07.q1.h: Do not confuse the Council of Europe with the European Union.
law-intl-human-rights.l07.q1.e: The Strasbourg Court belongs to the Council of Europe. The Luxembourg court interprets EU law, and the ICJ and the OSCE are not Convention organs.

law-intl-human-rights.l07.q2.t: The Convention is a living instrument, read in light of present-day conditions
law-intl-human-rights.l07.q2.p: In Tyrer v United Kingdom (1978), the Court treated birching of a juvenile as degrading punishment despite local acceptance on the Isle of Man. Which principle did it apply?
law-intl-human-rights.l07.q2.h: The Court moves with changing standards rather than freezing 1950 views.
law-intl-human-rights.l07.q2.e: The living-instrument approach lets the Court reflect current European standards. A margin of appreciation did not save the practice, and drafters' intent is not controlling.

law-intl-human-rights.l07.q3.t: The application is inadmissible for failure to exhaust available domestic remedies under Article 35
law-intl-human-rights.l07.q3.p: A national court rejects an applicant's complaint about prison conditions. Without using any remaining domestic appeal, she goes straight to the Strasbourg Court. What is the most likely result?
law-intl-human-rights.l07.q3.h: Admissibility rules require use of national remedies first.
law-intl-human-rights.l07.q3.e: Article 35 requires exhaustion of effective domestic remedies, including a remaining appeal. Article 3 cases are not exempt, and the CJEU is not involved.

law-intl-human-rights.l07.q4.t: It will give the state a relatively wide margin of appreciation, while still supervising proportionality
law-intl-human-rights.l07.q4.p: A state restricts a publication on grounds of public morals, and there is no consensus among European states on the question. Which statement best predicts the Court's approach?
law-intl-human-rights.l07.q4.h: Recall what Handyside said about morals and national authorities.
law-intl-human-rights.l07.q4.e: Where there is no European consensus on morals, the margin is wider, but the Court supervises. It never treats a national decision as unreviewable, and morals are a listed legitimate aim.

law-intl-human-rights.l07.q5.t: It binds the respondent state, with the Committee of Ministers supervising its execution
law-intl-human-rights.l07.q5.p: Under Article 46, what is the legal effect of a Strasbourg judgment finding a violation?
law-intl-human-rights.l07.q5.e: Judgments bind the respondent state, and the Committee of Ministers supervises. The Court cannot annul domestic decisions, and the judgment is formally binding only in the case.

law-intl-human-rights.l08.q1.t: The Inter-American Commission or a state party, and not the individual petitioner directly
law-intl-human-rights.l08.q1.p: In the Inter-American system, who may refer a contentious case to the Inter-American Court of Human Rights?
law-intl-human-rights.l08.q1.h: Individuals go through an intermediate organ first.
law-intl-human-rights.l08.q1.e: Under the American Convention only the Commission and states can refer cases. Unlike in Strasbourg, individuals lack direct access to the Court.

law-intl-human-rights.l08.q2.t: The American Declaration of the Rights and Duties of Man, as a source of OAS Charter obligations
law-intl-human-rights.l08.q2.p: Which legal basis do OAS members that are not parties to the American Convention, such as the United States, face in the Commission's work?
law-intl-human-rights.l08.q2.h: The Declaration dates from 1948 and predates the Convention.
law-intl-human-rights.l08.q2.e: The Commission reviews non-party OAS members under the American Declaration. The Convention binds only its parties, and the Universal Declaration is not a treaty.

law-intl-human-rights.l08.q3.t: The state can be responsible for failing to prevent, investigate and punish, despite no direct proof of attribution
law-intl-human-rights.l08.q3.p: A student disappears after being seized by unidentified men. No one proves state agents did it, but a pattern of disappearances exists and the state never investigated. Under Velasquez Rodriguez v Honduras, what follows?
law-intl-human-rights.l08.q3.h: Article 1(1) means more than refraining from violating rights directly.
law-intl-human-rights.l08.q3.e: The Court imposed a duty of due diligence, and a practice of disappearances plus failure to investigate engaged responsibility. A domestic conviction and a later treaty are not required.

law-intl-human-rights.l08.q4.t: Compare the amnesty with the American Convention as interpreted by the Court, and decline to apply it if incompatible
law-intl-human-rights.l08.q4.p: A national judge is asked to apply an amnesty law shielding officials who committed enforced disappearances. Under conventionality control as developed by the Inter-American Court, what should the judge do?
law-intl-human-rights.l08.q4.h: The doctrine extends review beyond the constitution.
law-intl-human-rights.l08.q4.e: Conventionality control directs judges to review domestic law against the Convention and the Court's case law, as in Almonacid Arellano (2006). The Assembly and the Commission's precautionary measures are not gatekeepers.

law-intl-human-rights.l08.q5.t: Article 21 protects indigenous communal property in land held by customary tenure, even without formal title
law-intl-human-rights.l08.q5.p: What did the Court decide in Mayagna (Sumo) Awas Tingni Community v Nicaragua (2001)?
law-intl-human-rights.l08.q5.h: Think of how customary use relates to title.
law-intl-human-rights.l08.q5.e: The Court held that customary communal possession is protected by the property right and ordered demarcation. It did not recognise a right to statehood, and the other options reverse the holding.

law-intl-human-rights.l09.q1.t: It recognises peoples' rights and imposes duties on individuals, alongside economic and social rights
law-intl-human-rights.l09.q1.p: Which is a distinctive feature of the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights compared with the European Convention?
law-intl-human-rights.l09.q1.h: Think of the word peoples in the title.
law-intl-human-rights.l09.q1.e: The Charter mixes individual and peoples' rights, includes duties, and covers economic and social rights. The other options describe the European model or are false.

law-intl-human-rights.l09.q2.t: In Arusha, Tanzania, and its judgments are binding on the states concerned
law-intl-human-rights.l09.q2.p: Where does the African Court on Human and Peoples' Rights sit, and what effect do its judgments have?
law-intl-human-rights.l09.q2.h: The Commission sits elsewhere and issues recommendations.
law-intl-human-rights.l09.q2.e: The Court is in Arusha and its judgments are binding. Banjul is the seat of the Commission, whose decisions are recommendations, and San Jose hosts the Inter-American Court.

law-intl-human-rights.l09.q3.t: The NGO cannot sue directly, but may use the Commission, which may refer the case if the state is a party to the protocol
law-intl-human-rights.l09.q3.p: An NGO wants to bring a case directly before the African Court against State M. State M ratified the Court's protocol but made no Article 34(6) declaration. Which course is correct?
law-intl-human-rights.l09.q3.h: Direct access depends on a further declaration.
law-intl-human-rights.l09.q3.e: Direct NGO and individual access needs an Article 34(6) declaration. The NGO may use the Commission, which can refer cases, so there is an avenue.

law-intl-human-rights.l09.q4.t: The Endorois decision against Kenya (2009), which found violations of property and development rights
law-intl-human-rights.l09.q4.p: A community is evicted from ancestral lands for a nature reserve and a tourism project. Which Commission decision most closely parallels this situation?
law-intl-human-rights.l09.q4.h: Look for eviction from land around a lake.
law-intl-human-rights.l09.q4.e: The Endorois case concerned eviction from land at Lake Bogoria. SERAC concerned pollution, and the other two are cases from different regional systems.

law-intl-human-rights.l09.q5.t: The Arab Charter on Human Rights of 2004 provides for an expert committee that reviews state reports
law-intl-human-rights.l09.q5.p: Which statement about other regional human rights arrangements is accurate?
law-intl-human-rights.l09.q5.h: Look for the body that the Charter itself sets up.
law-intl-human-rights.l09.q5.e: The Charter's own monitoring body is a committee of experts that examines state reports. The ASEAN Declaration is non-binding, no Asian regional court takes individual petitions, and a later Arab Court statute is not part of the 2004 Charter.

law-intl-human-rights.l10.q1.t: Severe pain or suffering inflicted for a purpose, by or with the acquiescence of a public official
law-intl-human-rights.l10.q1.p: Which element is part of the definition of torture in Article 1 of the Convention against Torture?
law-intl-human-rights.l10.q1.h: Four elements: severity, intent, purpose and official involvement.
law-intl-human-rights.l10.q1.e: Article 1 requires severity, intent, purpose and official involvement, and it excludes pain arising from lawful sanctions. Private, trivial or humiliation-only conduct is not torture in the CAT sense.

law-intl-human-rights.l10.q2.t: Article 2(2) CAT, which says no exceptional circumstances, including war or emergency, justify torture
law-intl-human-rights.l10.q2.p: A state argues that, during an armed insurgency, coercive interrogation of detainees is permitted because the nation's survival is at stake. Which treaty text most directly answers this argument?
law-intl-human-rights.l10.q2.h: The CAT text closes off the emergency defence.
law-intl-human-rights.l10.q2.e: Article 2(2) CAT bars any exceptional-circumstances justification. Article 4 ICCPR lists Article 7 as non-derogable, and the other texts concern refugees and compensation.

law-intl-human-rights.l10.q3.t: Soering v United Kingdom (1989), where the death-row phenomenon risk breached Article 3
law-intl-human-rights.l10.q3.p: State P wants to extradite a murder suspect to a state where he faces capital punishment under conditions of extreme delay and harsh confinement on death row. Which ECtHR case provides the strongest authority against extradition?
law-intl-human-rights.l10.q3.h: The Court has held that a transfer can itself breach the Convention.
law-intl-human-rights.l10.q3.e: Soering held that extradition into a real risk of Article 3 treatment violates the Convention. Tyrer concerns punishment inflicted by the state itself and not transfer, and the other two concern different rights.

law-intl-human-rights.l10.q4.t: Reject the balancing, because the Article 3 prohibition is absolute and the danger posed cannot be weighed against it
law-intl-human-rights.l10.q4.p: State Q argues that a deportee's threat to national security outweighs the risk that he will be tortured abroad, so the balance favours deportation. Under Chahal and Saadi, how should the Strasbourg Court respond?
law-intl-human-rights.l10.q4.h: Consider why this right is described as absolute.
law-intl-human-rights.l10.q4.e: Chahal and Saadi hold that Article 3 allows no weighing of national security against the risk of ill-treatment. The margin of appreciation does not apply to absolute rights in this way.

law-intl-human-rights.l10.q5.t: Senegal breached its duty under the Convention to submit the case to prosecuting authorities
law-intl-human-rights.l10.q5.p: What did the ICJ decide in Belgium v Senegal (2012) about the alleged torturer Hissene Habre?
law-intl-human-rights.l10.q5.h: The treaty duty is to extradite or submit for prosecution.
law-intl-human-rights.l10.q5.e: The Court found that Senegal failed its Article 7 duty to submit the case for prosecution. Territoriality does not excuse the duty, and no one has exclusive jurisdiction.

law-intl-human-rights.l11.q1.t: Race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group, and political opinion
law-intl-human-rights.l11.q1.p: Which list correctly states the grounds of persecution in the 1951 Convention definition of a refugee?
law-intl-human-rights.l11.q1.h: There are five, and gender is not named separately.
law-intl-human-rights.l11.q1.e: The five Convention grounds are race, religion, nationality, particular social group and political opinion. Gender and poverty are not listed, though gender claims may fit the social group ground.

law-intl-human-rights.l11.q2.t: Expelling or returning a refugee to territories where life or freedom would be threatened for a Convention reason
law-intl-human-rights.l11.q2.p: What does Article 33(1) of the Refugee Convention prohibit?
law-intl-human-rights.l11.q2.h: It is the principle of non-refoulement.
law-intl-human-rights.l11.q2.e: Article 33(1) bars return to persecution. It does not bar all detention, though Article 31 limits penalties for illegal entry.

law-intl-human-rights.l11.q3.t: He may fall outside the 1951 definition, but human rights law and complementary protection can still bar his return
law-intl-human-rights.l11.q3.p: A man fleeing a civil war is targeted only as part of general violence, with no Convention ground. In his host state, the ECtHR would find a real risk of inhuman treatment if he is returned. Which analysis is correct?
law-intl-human-rights.l11.q3.h: Distinguish refugee status from protection against return.
law-intl-human-rights.l11.q3.e: The 1951 definition is limited to five grounds, but Article 3 ECHR and the CAT bar return to real risk. Refugee status is declaratory, and war is not a listed ground.

law-intl-human-rights.l11.q4.t: Hirsi Jamaa v Italy (2012), which found Italian jurisdiction, an Article 3 breach and a collective expulsion
law-intl-human-rights.l11.q4.p: Italian vessels intercept migrants on the high seas and return them to Libya without screening for protection needs. Which decision most closely supports a challenge under the European Convention?
law-intl-human-rights.l11.q4.h: The facts were nearly the same as in the hypothetical.
law-intl-human-rights.l11.q4.e: Hirsi found jurisdiction by effective control at sea and found violations of Article 3 and Protocol 4. Sale is the contrasting US ruling, and Chahal did not involve interception at sea.

law-intl-human-rights.l11.q5.t: It is declaratory, so a person is a refugee as soon as the definition is met, even before recognition
law-intl-human-rights.l11.q5.p: Which statement about refugee status is correct?
law-intl-human-rights.l11.q5.h: Recognition confirms a status that already exists.
law-intl-human-rights.l11.q5.e: Status is declaratory under the UNHCR approach. Article 1F excludes war criminals, and Article 31 contemplates irregular entry, so the others are wrong.

law-intl-human-rights.l12.q1.t: As disjunctive: a state owes duties to anyone within its power or effective control, wherever located
law-intl-human-rights.l12.q1.p: How does the Human Rights Committee read the phrase within its territory and subject to its jurisdiction in ICCPR Article 2(1)?
law-intl-human-rights.l12.q1.h: General Comment 31 gives the Committee's reading.
law-intl-human-rights.l12.q1.e: General Comment 31 reads the clause disjunctively, a view the US has contested. The cumulative reading is the traditional literal one, and the Covenant is not limited to citizens.

law-intl-human-rights.l12.q2.t: The complaint about the NATO bombing of Belgrade's broadcaster was inadmissible for lack of jurisdiction
law-intl-human-rights.l12.q2.p: What did the ECtHR decide in Bankovic v Belgium and Others (2001)?
law-intl-human-rights.l12.q2.h: The Court emphasised the territorial character of jurisdiction.
law-intl-human-rights.l12.q2.e: The Grand Chamber held the applicants were not within the respondents' jurisdiction. Later cases, such as Al-Skeini, developed broader models, so Bankovic is now seen as narrow.

law-intl-human-rights.l12.q3.t: Al-Skeini v United Kingdom (2011), based on the state's authority and control through its soldiers
law-intl-human-rights.l12.q3.p: A State R patrol shoots a civilian in a district of a foreign country where R, as occupying power, has assumed policing powers. R refuses to investigate, citing the foreign location. Which authority best supports an obligation to investigate under Article 2 of the European Convention?
law-intl-human-rights.l12.q3.h: Look for the case about Basra and the exercise of public powers.
law-intl-human-rights.l12.q3.e: Al-Skeini found jurisdiction where the UK exercised public powers in Basra, and required an effective investigation. Bankovic is the narrower precedent that Al-Skeini limited.

law-intl-human-rights.l12.q4.t: S may be responsible for aiding or assisting T, given its knowledge of the circumstances (Article 16)
law-intl-human-rights.l12.q4.p: A State S gives intelligence and logistical help to State T, knowing that T will use it to commit unlawful detention. Under the ILC Articles on State Responsibility, what is S's position?
law-intl-human-rights.l12.q4.h: Responsibility can attach to a state's own contribution.
law-intl-human-rights.l12.q4.e: Article 16 imposes responsibility for aid or assistance given with knowledge, to the extent of the contribution. It does not attribute T's conduct to S wholesale.

law-intl-human-rights.l12.q5.t: Conduct of state organs is attributable to the state, even when the officials exceed their authority
law-intl-human-rights.l12.q5.p: Which principle of attribution is stated in the ILC Articles for acts of state officials?
law-intl-human-rights.l12.q5.h: The state cannot disown its officials by pointing to excess of authority.
law-intl-human-rights.l12.q5.e: Articles 4 and 7 attribute organ conduct even if ultra vires, when acting in an official capacity. Prior approval and territoriality are not conditions.

law-intl-human-rights.l13.q1.t: Every human being below eighteen, unless majority is reached earlier under the applicable law
law-intl-human-rights.l13.q1.p: How does Article 1 of the Convention on the Rights of the Child define a child?
law-intl-human-rights.l13.q1.h: The Convention uses a fixed age with an exception.
law-intl-human-rights.l13.q1.e: Article 1 sets eighteen with an exception for earlier majority. The other ages are not the Convention's definition, and it sets no age of criminal responsibility.

law-intl-human-rights.l13.q2.t: Best interests are a primary consideration, which must be assessed and weighed but not always decisive
law-intl-human-rights.l13.q2.p: A court is told that, under Article 3, the child's best interests must always override every other consideration. Which response is accurate?
law-intl-human-rights.l13.q2.h: Note the wording: a primary consideration.
law-intl-human-rights.l13.q2.e: Article 3(1) says a primary consideration, not the sole or paramount one, and it covers all actions concerning children, including legislation.

law-intl-human-rights.l13.q3.t: The sentence breaches Article 37(a) of the CRC, and Roper v Simmons shows the same trend on capital punishment
law-intl-human-rights.l13.q3.p: A 15-year-old is convicted of murder in State V, a party to the CRC. The court proposes life imprisonment without any possibility of release. Which statement best reflects the Convention and the cited US ruling?
law-intl-human-rights.l13.q3.e: Article 37(a) bars life without possibility of release for offences committed under eighteen as well as the death penalty. Roper barred the juvenile death penalty, and Article 12 does not require consent to sentences.

law-intl-human-rights.l13.q4.t: Her views must be given weight according to her maturity, as her evolving capacities reduce parental direction
law-intl-human-rights.l13.q4.p: A 16-year-old wishes to attend a political rally against her parents' wishes. Which reading best fits Articles 5 and 12 of the CRC?
law-intl-human-rights.l13.q4.h: Parental authority is balanced by evolving capacities.
law-intl-human-rights.l13.q4.e: Articles 5 and 12 require due weight to the child's views in accordance with age and maturity. They give neither parents nor child an absolute veto, and the Convention protects children's association and assembly (Article 15).

law-intl-human-rights.l13.q5.t: Eighteen, which is higher than the age of fifteen set in Article 38 of the Convention
law-intl-human-rights.l13.q5.p: What age does the CRC's Optional Protocol on children in armed conflict set for compulsory recruitment and direct participation in hostilities?
law-intl-human-rights.l13.q5.h: The Protocol raised the standard in the Convention itself.
law-intl-human-rights.l13.q5.e: The Protocol requires states to ensure that persons under eighteen do not take a direct part in hostilities and are not compulsorily recruited. Fifteen is the weaker rule in Article 38.

law-intl-human-rights.l14.q1.t: Distinctions with the effect of impairing women's enjoyment of rights, even without any discriminatory purpose
law-intl-human-rights.l14.q1.p: Which concept does Article 1 of CEDAW's definition of discrimination include that goes beyond intentional unequal treatment?
law-intl-human-rights.l14.q1.h: The text says effect or purpose.
law-intl-human-rights.l14.q1.e: Article 1 covers distinctions with the effect or purpose of impairing rights, which is the basis for indirect discrimination. Article 2 also reaches private actors.

law-intl-human-rights.l14.q2.t: A temporary special measure under Article 4, which is not discrimination and must end once equality is reached
law-intl-human-rights.l14.q2.p: A state reserves seats in parliament for women until the proportion of women reaches a defined level. Under CEDAW, how is this measure classified?
law-intl-human-rights.l14.q2.h: Article 4 concerns accelerating de facto equality.
law-intl-human-rights.l14.q2.e: Article 4(1) permits temporary special measures and requires that they cease once their aims are achieved. They are not a reservation, which is a statement about the treaty obligations themselves.

law-intl-human-rights.l14.q3.t: The rule may be indirect discrimination under Article 1, unless the state shows a legitimate and proportionate justification
law-intl-human-rights.l14.q3.p: A state grants pensions only to full-time workers, and most part-time workers are women. A woman complains of discrimination. Which analysis best fits CEDAW?
law-intl-human-rights.l14.q3.h: The definition looks to effects as well as purposes.
law-intl-human-rights.l14.q3.e: CEDAW's effects-based definition reaches neutral rules that disadvantage women, but a justified, proportionate rule may be defensible. Economic life is covered by Articles 11 and 13.

law-intl-human-rights.l14.q4.t: Opuz v Turkey (ECtHR, 2009), which found violations of the right to life and discrimination
law-intl-human-rights.l14.q4.p: A woman suffers repeated domestic violence. Police know of the danger and take no steps, and she is eventually killed. Which authority most directly suggests state responsibility for gender discrimination?
law-intl-human-rights.l14.q4.h: Look for a case on failure to protect from domestic violence.
