law-intl-human-rights.l14.q4.e: Opuz held that passivity of the authorities violated Articles 2 and 3 and amounted to discrimination. Lovelace concerned a different type of sex discrimination, and the others do not involve domestic violence.

law-intl-human-rights.l14.q5.t: They go to the core of the Convention and may be incompatible with its object and purpose under Article 28(2)
law-intl-human-rights.l14.q5.p: Why are reservations to Articles 2 and 16 of CEDAW so controversial?
law-intl-human-rights.l14.q5.h: Think about what the Convention is for.
law-intl-human-rights.l14.q5.e: The Committee regards Articles 2 and 16 as central, so reservations to them risk breaching Article 28(2). The Convention does permit reservations that are compatible with its object and purpose.

law-intl-human-rights.l15.q1.t: Enjoy their culture, practise their religion and use their language
law-intl-human-rights.l15.q1.p: Article 27 of the ICCPR protects the right of persons belonging to minorities to do which of the following, in community with others?
law-intl-human-rights.l15.q1.h: The right is cultural, and it is exercised individually and in community.
law-intl-human-rights.l15.q1.e: Article 27 lists culture, religion and language. It does not grant secession, a veto or land title, and it is framed as an individual right.

law-intl-human-rights.l15.q2.t: Loss of Indian status through marriage, with exclusion from the reserve, violated Article 27
law-intl-human-rights.l15.q2.p: What was the outcome in Lovelace v Canada (Human Rights Committee, 1981)?
law-intl-human-rights.l15.q2.h: A Maliseet woman challenged a status rule that discriminated by sex.
law-intl-human-rights.l15.q2.e: The Committee found that denying her access to her community was an unreasonable restriction. Article 27 protects individuals belonging to minorities, and Canada was a party.

law-intl-human-rights.l15.q3.t: UNDRIP calls for free, prior and informed consent, and the Inter-American Court requires it for major projects
law-intl-human-rights.l15.q3.p: A state grants a mining concession over the customary land of an indigenous people, after only a brief notice in a newspaper. The people had no say in the decision. Which statement best reflects current international standards?
law-intl-human-rights.l15.q3.h: Consultation duties are now in several instruments.
law-intl-human-rights.l15.q3.e: UNDRIP (Articles 19 and 32) and Saramaka require consent or effective participation, and the exact legal force of FPIC is debated. UNDRIP is not a treaty, and Article 3 is understood as internal self-determination.

law-intl-human-rights.l15.q4.t: Limited interference may be compatible with Article 27, but cumulative impact may eventually deny the right
law-intl-human-rights.l15.q4.p: A state quarries a small area of land used for reindeer herding by a minority, with limited effect on herding. Which approach does the Human Rights Committee's Lansman v Finland (1994) reflect?
law-intl-human-rights.l15.q4.h: The Committee asked about the degree of interference.
law-intl-human-rights.l15.q4.e: The Committee accepted that limited quarrying did not deny the herders' right, but warned of cumulative effects. It did not hold that every change violates Article 27.

law-intl-human-rights.l15.q5.t: Four voted against, and all four later endorsed it
law-intl-human-rights.l15.q5.p: How many states voted against the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples in 2007, and what happened afterwards?
law-intl-human-rights.l15.q5.h: Australia, Canada, New Zealand and the United States.
law-intl-human-rights.l15.q5.e: The vote was 144 to 4 with 11 abstentions, and the four later endorsed the Declaration. So it was adopted by recorded vote, not consensus.

law-intl-human-rights.l16.q1.t: The state duty to protect, the corporate responsibility to respect, and access to remedy for victims
law-intl-human-rights.l16.q1.p: What are the three pillars of the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights?
law-intl-human-rights.l16.q1.e: The three pillars come from the Ruggie framework. The alternatives swap the actors or invent duties that are not in the Principles.

law-intl-human-rights.l16.q2.t: They are soft law, setting out a corporate responsibility to respect and not a binding treaty obligation
law-intl-human-rights.l16.q2.p: Which description of the legal status of the Guiding Principles is accurate?
law-intl-human-rights.l16.q2.h: The Principles use the word responsibility for companies.
law-intl-human-rights.l16.q2.e: The Principles were endorsed by the Human Rights Council and are not a treaty. They use responsibility rather than obligation for companies, and they carry no criminal sanctions.

law-intl-human-rights.l16.q3.t: Vedanta Resources v Lungowe (UK Supreme Court, 2019), which accepted a possible parent-company duty of care
law-intl-human-rights.l16.q3.p: Foreign villagers sue the English parent of a mining group over pollution caused by its Zambian subsidiary. The parent argues that England is the wrong forum and that it owes no duty. Which decision most supports letting the claim go forward?
law-intl-human-rights.l16.q3.h: Look for the English parent-company case.
law-intl-human-rights.l16.q3.e: Vedanta accepted that a parent can owe a duty of care and that the English court could hear the claim. Kiobel and Jesner are US decisions that restricted such claims.

law-intl-human-rights.l16.q4.t: Dismissal, because the claim does not touch and concern US territory with sufficient force
law-intl-human-rights.l16.q4.p: A foreign national sues a foreign corporation in a US federal court under the Alien Tort Statute for abuses that all occurred abroad, with only general corporate activity in the United States. What result does the Supreme Court case law make most likely?
law-intl-human-rights.l16.q4.h: Kiobel, Jesner and Nestle all narrowed the statute.
law-intl-human-rights.l16.q4.e: Kiobel's presumption against extraterritoriality, applied in Nestle v Doe, defeats claims where the conduct is abroad. Filartiga concerned an individual defendant, and individuals can be sued.

law-intl-human-rights.l16.q5.t: A legally binding agreement between global brands and trade unions on factory fire and building safety
law-intl-human-rights.l16.q5.p: What did the 2013 Rana Plaza collapse in Bangladesh lead to?
law-intl-human-rights.l16.q5.h: It was a private but enforceable agreement.
law-intl-human-rights.l16.q5.e: The Accord on Fire and Building Safety bound signatory brands and unions. No UN treaty has yet been adopted, and the OECD Guidelines were revised, not repealed.

law-intl-human-rights.l17.q1.t: A state's power to prosecute certain grave crimes without any territorial or nationality link to the case
law-intl-human-rights.l17.q1.h: It dispenses with the usual links to the forum state.
law-intl-human-rights.l17.q1.e: Universal jurisdiction covers the gravest crimes, such as genocide and torture, without any link to the forum. It does not cover minor offences or give the ICJ jurisdiction over all states.

law-intl-human-rights.l17.q2.t: Belgium violated the immunity of the sitting foreign minister by issuing and circulating the warrant
law-intl-human-rights.l17.q2.p: In Arrest Warrant (DRC v Belgium, ICJ, 2002), what did the Court decide?
law-intl-human-rights.l17.q2.h: A serving foreign minister enjoys personal immunity from foreign criminal courts.
law-intl-human-rights.l17.q2.e: The Court held that a sitting foreign minister has immunity from criminal jurisdiction abroad even for war crimes, though immunity is not impunity. Universal jurisdiction does not override it.

law-intl-human-rights.l17.q3.t: Pinochet (No 3), where the Lords held that torture cannot be an official function protected by immunity
law-intl-human-rights.l17.q3.p: A former head of state, now out of office, is arrested abroad for torture ordered while in office, after the date on which the forum state and his own state were both bound by the Convention against Torture. Which authority best supports denying him immunity?
law-intl-human-rights.l17.q3.h: Look at what happened after leaving office, and at the date of the treaty.
law-intl-human-rights.l17.q3.e: Pinochet (No 3) denied a former head of state immunity for torture after the Convention bound the states concerned. Arrest Warrant concerned a serving minister, and the other cases do not concern immunity.

law-intl-human-rights.l17.q4.t: The case is inadmissible under Article 17, because the state is genuinely investigating and is willing and able
law-intl-human-rights.l17.q4.p: A national court in State W is genuinely investigating a case of alleged war crimes by one of its own officers. The ICC Prosecutor wants to take the case. What is the likely result under the Rome Statute?
law-intl-human-rights.l17.q4.e: Complementarity means the Court steps in only where states are unwilling or unable. Article 27 removes immunity, not admissibility rules, and the Council is only one trigger.

law-intl-human-rights.l17.q5.t: It may act where the crime occurred on a state party's territory or the accused is a state party's national
law-intl-human-rights.l17.q5.p: Which of these statements is correct about the Court's jurisdiction under Article 12 of the Rome Statute?
law-intl-human-rights.l17.q5.h: Territorial and nationality bases are the usual ones.
law-intl-human-rights.l17.q5.e: Article 12 uses territory and nationality, subject to Security Council referral or a state's acceptance of jurisdiction. The Council route is only one of the triggers, and the Court is not universal.

law-intl-human-rights.l18.q1.t: All human rights are universal, indivisible, interdependent and interrelated, and states must protect them whatever their systems
law-intl-human-rights.l18.q1.p: What does the 1993 Vienna Declaration say about the universality of human rights?
law-intl-human-rights.l18.q1.h: The Declaration was adopted by consensus and uses four adjectives.
law-intl-human-rights.l18.q1.e: Vienna 1993 affirms universality and indivisibility while saying particularities must be borne in mind. The other options distort or reverse that text.

law-intl-human-rights.l18.q2.t: Cultures are internally diverse and change, so the claim may silence the very persons whose rights are at stake
law-intl-human-rights.l18.q2.p: Which argument is typical of a universalist reply to a state that says its culture justifies a restriction on women's rights?
law-intl-human-rights.l18.q2.h: Consider who speaks for a culture.
law-intl-human-rights.l18.q2.e: A universalist stresses diversity within cultures and the risk that the claim reflects the powerful, not the affected. The Declaration states a universal standard and not relativism.

law-intl-human-rights.l18.q3.t: As a margin of appreciation for qualified rights within a universal framework, which does not extend to absolute rights
law-intl-human-rights.l18.q3.p: A regional court gives a government room to decide how to balance freedom of expression against religious sensitivities because European states disagree on the question, while insisting that torture admits no such room. How is this best analysed?
law-intl-human-rights.l18.q3.e: Margin of appreciation operates for qualified rights and is sometimes called institutional relativism, while absolute rights have no margin. Expression is a derogable right, so Article 15 is not the mechanism.

law-intl-human-rights.l18.q4.t: The Declaration is a non-binding regional document, so it cannot displace treaty obligations that the state has accepted
law-intl-human-rights.l18.q4.p: A government cites the Cairo Declaration on Human Rights in Islam (1990), which makes rights subject to Shariah, to justify limits on freedom of religion. Which analysis is most accurate?
law-intl-human-rights.l18.q4.h: Consider the legal status of regional declarations.
law-intl-human-rights.l18.q4.e: The Cairo Declaration is a non-binding political document, so it cannot excuse a breach of treaty duties the state has accepted. It is not a treaty or peremptory norm, and treaty obligations stand despite it.

law-intl-human-rights.l18.q5.t: Whether a right exists, how broadly it is defined, and who decides how it applies locally are different questions
law-intl-human-rights.l18.q5.p: Which statement best separates questions that the universalism debate should not confuse?
law-intl-human-rights.l18.q5.h: A dispute about application is not always a dispute about existence.
law-intl-human-rights.l18.q5.e: Distinguishing existence, scope and local application lets one accept universality while allowing differences. Ratification counts as evidence but does not alone determine existence, as custom shows.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l01.q1.t: Article 2(4), which obliges members to refrain from force against the territorial integrity or political independence of any state
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l01.q1.p: Which provision of the UN Charter contains the general prohibition on the threat or use of force between states?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l01.q1.h: Think of the Charter provision usually cited as the cornerstone of jus ad bellum.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l01.q1.e: Article 2(4) states the prohibition. Article 51 is the self-defence exception, not the prohibition itself, and Article 39 concerns the Security Council determining threats to the peace.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l01.q2.t: Humanitarian rules bind all parties to an armed conflict in the same way, whatever the legality of the resort to force or the cause they espouse
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l01.q2.p: What does the principle of equal application of international humanitarian law mean?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l01.q2.h: Consider why the law would keep the legality of the war apart from the treatment of victims.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l01.q2.e: IHL protections do not depend on whether a party is the aggressor. Reciprocity of ratification and the international/non-international distinction are different matters.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l01.q3.t: Q must treat him as a prisoner of war, since his status does not depend on the lawfulness of P's resort to force
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l01.q3.p: State P invades State Q in violation of Article 2(4). Q captures a P soldier who wore a uniform and carried arms openly. Which statement is correct?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l01.q3.h: Ask whether status depends on who started the war.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l01.q3.e: Prisoner-of-war status turns on the Geneva criteria, not the aggressor label. Q may not prosecute him for lawful acts of war, and the Conventions do apply to an unlawful invasion.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l01.q4.t: The argument is incomplete because the strike must still satisfy IHL, so the expected civilian harm must not be excessive relative to the concrete military advantage
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l01.q4.p: State R is lawfully acting in self-defence after an armed attack by State S. R's air force strikes a bridge used by S's supply convoys but expects heavy civilian casualties because the bridge is in a crowded market district. R's lawyers argue that the self-defence right resolves the matter. What is the best response?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l01.q4.h: Keep the two bodies of law separate: one decides if force may be used, the other how.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l01.q4.e: A lawful resort to force does not suspend jus in bello. The strike is assessed under distinction, proportionality and precautions. Security Council authorisation is not required for Article 51 action.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l01.q5.t: It treats jus in bello proportionality, which examines expected incidental harm against the advantage of a specific attack, as if it were the jus ad bellum question of whether the whole response was proportionate
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l01.q5.p: A commentator says: "The strike was proportionate because the overall defensive campaign against S was a proportionate response to the armed attack." What is the main flaw in this reasoning?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l01.q5.h: The same word is used in two different legal questions.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l01.q5.e: Ad bellum proportionality concerns the scale of the response to the armed attack; in bello proportionality is attack-by-attack. The other options misstate what each test compares.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l02.q1.t: The third Convention, on the treatment of prisoners of war
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l02.q1.p: Which 1949 Geneva Convention protects prisoners of war?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l02.q1.h: The numbering follows the order of the categories of protected persons.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l02.q1.e: Convention III is the prisoner-of-war Convention. Convention IV deals with civilians, I and II with the wounded and sick on land and at sea.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l02.q2.t: A preambular principle that, where no specific rule applies, civilians and combatants stay under the principles of humanity and the dictates of public conscience
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l02.q2.h: It is a safety net for gaps in treaty law.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l02.q2.e: The clause preserves protection under custom, humanity and public conscience when treaties are silent. The other options describe treaty relativity, reprisals and weapons review.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l02.q3.t: X is bound because the prohibition on attacking civilians reflects customary law that applies whether or not X has ratified the Protocol
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l02.q3.p: State X has not ratified Additional Protocol I. Its forces deliberately attack a civilian market. Which statement best explains X's legal position?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l02.q3.h: A rule can bind through more than one source.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l02.q3.e: The prohibition is customary and applies to non-parties. Reciprocity is not a condition of humanitarian obligations, and Security Council action is not needed.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l02.q4.t: The state objected to the rule consistently while it was forming, and the practice and opinio juris on which the study relies are neither extensive nor uniform
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l02.q4.p: A state official argues that a particular rule listed in the ICRC customary law study does not bind her state. Which argument would be the strongest legally?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l02.q4.h: Custom needs practice plus opinio juris; the study is evidence, not a source.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l02.q4.e: A persistent objector or a showing that practice and opinio juris are lacking would defeat the claim. Treaty rules can reflect custom, and custom can develop after 1949.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l02.q5.t: Assess it under general principles, such as distinction and the ban on unnecessary suffering, with the Martens clause, and look to custom for rules
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l02.q5.p: A newly developed weapon is not mentioned in any treaty. A tribunal must assess whether its use is lawful. Which approach is most consistent with the sources of IHL discussed here?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l02.q5.h: Silence in treaties does not mean a legal vacuum.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l02.q5.e: General principles and the Martens clause apply in treaty gaps. The presumption that silence permits everything is not accepted for humanitarian limits.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l03.q1.t: Common Article 3, found in all four Conventions
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l03.q1.p: Which provision of the Geneva Conventions applies to armed conflicts not of an international character?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l03.q1.h: It is found in all four Conventions and is sometimes called a convention in miniature.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l03.q1.e: Common Article 3 governs non-international armed conflicts; common Article 2 governs international ones including occupation.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l03.q2.t: Protracted armed violence and the involvement of organised armed groups as a party to the fighting, whether against the government or against one another
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l03.q2.p: According to the ICTY Appeals Chamber in Tadic (1995), which pair of elements is used to identify a non-international armed conflict?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l03.q2.e: Tadic stated that a NIAC exists where there is protracted armed violence between governmental authorities and organised armed groups, or between such groups. Declarations, numeric death tolls and foreign fighters are not required.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l03.q3.t: An international armed conflict, because armed force between states generally suffices and no minimum duration or intensity is required
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l03.q3.p: Two states exchange a single artillery barrage across a border, killing several soldiers, and then return to diplomatic talks. How is this most likely classified?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l03.q3.h: Ask what threshold common Article 2 sets for conflicts between states.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l03.q3.e: Common Article 2 covers any armed conflict between states, even without a declaration. The "internal disturbance" category concerns violence within a state.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l03.q4.t: IHL applies as a matter of fact if the intensity and organisation thresholds are met, so common Article 3 binds both H and G regardless of H's label and of any recognition by H
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l03.q4.p: Armed Group G controls a district of State H, has a command structure and fights H's army daily. H describes the situation as "counter-terrorism" and denies that IHL applies. G holds three captured soldiers. Which analysis is most accurate?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l03.q4.h: The test is factual, not a matter of the government's label.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l03.q4.e: Classification is objective. Common Article 3 binds all parties including armed groups. Full prisoner-of-war status belongs to international armed conflicts, so the last option overstates it.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l03.q5.t: Rebel violations are not attributed to F unless F exercised effective control over the specific operations in which they occurred
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l03.q5.p: Foreign State F supplies weapons and training to a rebel group fighting State H, but does not direct specific operations. Under the ICJ's approach in Nicaragua for attributing the group's conduct to F, which is the likely result?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l03.q5.h: Support is not the same as control of specific operations.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l03.q5.e: Nicaragua required effective control of the specific operations for attribution; supply and training alone were not enough. Formal incorporation is a different, narrower route.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l04.q1.t: Any object by nature, location, purpose or use that contributes effectively to military action, whose destruction gives a definite advantage
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l04.q1.p: Under Article 52(2) of Additional Protocol I, which description of a military objective is correct?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l04.q1.h: Two cumulative requirements: contribution and advantage.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l04.q1.e: Article 52(2) requires an effective contribution to military action and a definite military advantage in the circumstances ruling at the time.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l04.q2.t: It is presumed to be a civilian object and must not be attacked on a mere suspicion of military use
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l04.q2.p: If it is doubtful whether a normally civilian object, such as a school, is being used for military action, what does Article 52(3) of Protocol I provide?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l04.q2.h: The presumption protects civilians in cases of uncertainty.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l04.q2.e: Article 52(3) presumes civilian character in case of doubt. The other options reverse or distort the rule.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l04.q3.t: The attack violates distinction because it deliberately targets civilians or a civilian object, so it is never evaluated under proportionality
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l04.q3.p: A commander directs an attack on a building because enemy sympathisers live there, with no military use of the building. Which analysis is correct?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l04.q3.h: Proportionality concerns incidental harm to a lawful target.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l04.q3.e: Deliberate targeting of civilians breaches distinction; proportionality applies only where a lawful military objective is attacked and civilians are incidentally harmed. Warnings do not legalise attacking civilians.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l04.q4.t: The commander breached the duty of feasible precautions, and the expected harm may also be excessive
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l04.q4.p: An ammunition depot adjoins an apartment block. A drone strike with a small precision weapon at 3 a.m. would destroy the depot and is expected to harm few civilians. A larger bomb would be cheaper and would expect heavy civilian casualties. The commander uses the larger bomb. Which is the strongest legal criticism?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l04.q4.e: Article 57 requires feasible precautions in choosing means and methods to minimise civilian harm. Proximity to civilians does not strip a depot of its military objective status.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l04.q5.t: It is judged by what the commander could reasonably have expected on available information, not by hindsight
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l04.q5.p: After an attack on a lawful military target, investigators find that much more civilian harm resulted than the commander had predicted. The commander had reasonably relied on intelligence showing the building was empty. Under the prevailing standard, how should the legality of the attack be assessed?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l04.q5.h: Consider what the commander knew and could have known.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l04.q5.e: Proportionality and precautions are assessed on reasonably available information at the time. Outcome-only and success-only tests are not the accepted standard.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l05.q1.t: The red crystal, which has the same protective legal value as the other two emblems
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l05.q1.p: Which emblem was added to the Red Cross and Red Crescent by the 2005 Additional Protocol III?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l05.q1.h: It is a diamond-shaped, neutral device.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l05.q1.e: Protocol III created the red crystal as an additional emblem with the same status. The other options are not emblems created by that Protocol.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l05.q2.t: The attacker must give a warning with a reasonable time limit, and the warning must go unheeded
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l05.q2.p: Under Article 21 of Geneva Convention I, what must usually happen before a medical unit loses its protection because it is used for acts harmful to the enemy?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l05.q2.e: Article 21 conditions loss of protection on a warning with a reasonable time limit that is not heeded. The other options invent requirements.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l05.q3.t: The argument fails because medical staff may carry light individual weapons for self-defence or to defend the wounded without losing protection
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l05.q3.p: A military hospital staffed by medical personnel who carry light pistols for their own defence is attacked by an adversary who argues that the weapons forfeit its protection. What is the most accurate assessment?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l05.q3.h: Think about what Article 22 says does not count as a harmful act.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l05.q3.e: Article 22 provides that light individual arms for defence do not forfeit protection. Protection is lost by acts harmful to the enemy after warning, so it is not absolute either.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l05.q4.t: The shot is unlawful because an incapacitated person who abstains from hostile acts is hors de combat and may not be made the object of attack
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l05.q4.p: A unit of Army Alpha is retreating. One soldier, wounded and unconscious, lies on the ground. A rifleman from Army Bravo sees him and fires, saying that the man was an enemy combatant and might wake and resume fighting. Which analysis is correct?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l05.q4.e: A person rendered unconscious or incapacitated who abstains from hostile acts is hors de combat and protected; this is also customary. The possibility of recovery does not change the status.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l05.q5.t: The commander must warn, set a reasonable time for the misuse to cease and attack only if ignored, still applying proportionality and precautions for the protected patients inside
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l05.q5.p: A hospital bearing the red cross is used as a firing position by enemy forces. A commander wants to destroy it and asks what the law requires. Which answer is the most accurate?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l05.q5.h: Loss of protection is narrow and conditional.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l05.q5.e: Article 21 requires a warning with a reasonable time limit; the patients remain protected persons so proportionality and precautions still apply. Immediate attack and absolute immunity are both wrong.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l06.q1.t: Name, rank, date of birth and army, regimental, personal or serial number
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l06.q1.p: Under Article 17 of Convention III, what information is a prisoner of war bound to give when questioned?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l06.q1.h: The list is short and does not include military information.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l06.q1.e: Article 17 limits compulsory disclosure to identity details. The other lists add information that cannot be demanded.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l06.q2.t: Without delay after the cessation of active hostilities, and not upon completion of a peace treaty
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l06.q2.p: Under Article 118 of Convention III, when must prisoners of war be released and repatriated?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l06.q2.h: It does not wait for a final political settlement.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l06.q2.e: Article 118 requires release and repatriation without delay after active hostilities cease. A peace treaty is not a precondition.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l06.q3.t: The prosecution is barred because a lawful combatant is immune for acts that comply with IHL, though he may still be tried for war crimes
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l06.q3.p: Soldier S of State A is captured by State B in an international armed conflict. B charges him with murder for killing a B soldier in a lawful attack on a military barracks. What is the most likely result under IHL?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l06.q3.e: Lawful combatants are not punishable for acts that comply with IHL; war crimes remain prosecutable. The other options invent conditions.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l06.q4.t: He keeps prisoner-of-war treatment until a competent tribunal determines his status under Article 5, and in any event retains minimum guarantees such as those in Article 75 of Protocol I
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l06.q4.p: Fighters in civilian dress infiltrate State C's territory in an international armed conflict, carry no arms openly and attack a convoy. One is captured. His status is disputed by his own government, which says he is a soldier. Which is the most accurate procedural statement?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l06.q4.h: Article 5 provides for doubt about status.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l06.q4.e: Where status is doubtful, POW treatment continues until a competent tribunal decides; minimum guarantees apply to everyone in the power of a party. Government claims and the absence of any category are both wrong.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l06.q5.t: The commissions fell short of common Article 3's regularly constituted court requirement, which applied as the conflict was not international
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l06.q5.p: In Hamdan v. Rumsfeld (2006), which conclusion did the US Supreme Court reach about the military commissions created to try a detainee captured in the conflict with al Qaeda?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l06.q5.h: Remember how the Court characterised the conflict.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l06.q5.e: The Court held that common Article 3 applied and that the commissions as structured did not satisfy it. It did not treat the conflict as an international one nor hold that only POWs have rights.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l07.q1.t: Article 42, which treats territory as occupied once it is actually placed under the authority of a hostile army
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l07.q1.p: Which provision of the 1907 Hague Regulations states when territory is considered occupied?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l07.q1.h: Occupation is a matter of effective control.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l07.q1.e: Article 42 provides the test of actual authority. The other articles deal with different subjects.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l07.q2.t: The occupying power deporting or transferring parts of its own civilian population into the territory it occupies
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l07.q2.p: What does Article 49(6) of Convention IV prohibit?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l07.q2.h: It concerns the occupier's own nationals.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l07.q2.e: Article 49(6) bans transfers of the occupier's own civilians into occupied territory. Evacuation for security is allowed under Article 49, and labour and penal rules are covered elsewhere.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l07.q3.t: Article 53 of Convention IV, which bars destruction of property save where military operations make it absolutely necessary
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l07.q3.p: The occupying power in a territory orders the destruction of a bridge it considers dangerous, but not because of any military operation underway. Which provision is most clearly engaged?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l07.q3.e: Article 53 of Convention IV prohibits destruction not absolutely necessary for military operations. The other provisions concern different issues.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l07.q4.t: The code change may violate the duty to respect existing laws unless absolutely prevented, and the resettlement conflicts with Article 49(6)
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l07.q4.p: State X occupies part of State Y. X repeals Y's criminal code and replaces it with a code designed to entrench X's economic interests, and it resettles thousands of its own citizens there. Which assessment is the most accurate?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l07.q4.h: The occupant is an administrator, not a sovereign.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l07.q4.e: Hague Regulations Article 43 and Convention IV Article 64 limit legislative change, and Article 49(6) bars transfers. Occupation law is not limited to property.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l07.q5.t: U may be an occupying power in the district where it substituted its authority for that of the government, and responsible for violations there including failures to prevent looting
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l07.q5.p: State U's forces control a district of State D, replacing local authority, and soldiers loot resources there. U argues it is not an occupying power because it never declared occupation and did not control the whole country. Based on the ICJ's approach in DRC v. Uganda (2005), what is the best response?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l07.q5.h: Occupation is a question of effective control in the area concerned.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l07.q5.e: The Court found Uganda an occupying power in Ituri and responsible for looting, including failures to prevent it. A declaration or control of the whole country is not needed, and resources are not war spoil.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l08.q1.t: Cruel treatment and torture, and the taking of hostages
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l08.q1.p: Which of the following does common Article 3 prohibit at any time and in any place regarding persons taking no active part in hostilities?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l08.q1.h: It protects those hors de combat from violence to life and person.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l08.q1.e: Common Article 3 prohibits cruel treatment, torture and hostage-taking. It encourages special agreements and permits ICRC offers of service.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l08.q2.t: That applying humanitarian rules to an armed group does not give it recognition or legitimacy as a government or alter its status
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l08.q2.p: What does the final sentence of common Article 3 (that application does not affect the legal status of the parties) mean?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l08.q2.h: It was designed to reassure governments.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l08.q2.e: The clause means that applying the rules confers no legitimacy on rebels. It does not create POW status or bar domestic prosecution.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l08.q3.t: He is a detainee entitled to humane treatment and fair trial, but IHL does not give him prisoner-of-war status or combatant immunity, although he may be prosecuted under domestic law for taking up arms
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l08.q3.p: A rebel fighter is captured by government forces in a non-international armed conflict. Which statement is correct?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l08.q3.h: POW status is limited to international armed conflicts.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l08.q3.e: In a NIAC there is no POW status or combatant immunity, but humane treatment and fair trial guarantees apply. Common Article 3 does regulate detainee treatment.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l08.q4.t: Rome Statute Article 8(2)(c), which covers serious common Article 3 violations such as murder and unfair sentencing
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l08.q4.p: An armed group tries a captured soldier in a single hearing before its commander, with no defence counsel, and shoots him that evening. Under which provision is this most clearly a war crime in a non-international armed conflict?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l08.q4.h: Common Article 3 violations are listed separately for non-international conflicts.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l08.q4.e: Article 8(2)(c) covers common Article 3 violations, including murder and unfair sentencing. Article 8(2)(b) is for international conflicts, and Article 7 concerns crimes against humanity.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l08.q5.t: Article 6(5) encourages the broadest amnesty, read as excluding persons suspected of war crimes
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l08.q5.p: A government and a rebel movement end a civil war. The government proposes an amnesty for all who fought, including a commander who ordered the massacre of villagers. Reading Protocol II, Article 6(5), and the ICRC's interpretation, which is the best assessment?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l08.q5.h: The article encourages amnesty but has an important limit.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l08.q5.e: The ICRC reads Article 6(5) as not covering war crimes suspects. The provision encourages rather than requires an amnesty, and it concerns non-international conflicts.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l09.q1.t: To determine whether the employment of a new weapon, means or method would be prohibited by the Protocol or other rules of international law
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l09.q1.p: What does Article 36 of Additional Protocol I require of a state party?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l09.q1.h: It is a legal review requirement.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l09.q1.e: Article 36 requires states to review new weapons, means and methods for legality. It does not require Security Council approval.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l09.q2.t: The Chemical Weapons Convention of 1993, in force from 1997
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l09.q2.p: Which treaty created an organisation (the OPCW) to verify the destruction of a class of weapons and to carry out inspections?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l09.q2.h: The organisation name relates to chemical weapons.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l09.q2.e: The CWC created the OPCW. The BWC lacks a verification body, and the Gas Protocol only bans use.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l09.q3.t: The question is whether the harm exceeds what a legitimate purpose requires, so suffering alone does not make it unlawful
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l09.q3.p: A weapon causes a very painful death to combatants but is also the only means of achieving a legitimate military aim in a particular scenario, and it can be directed at military objectives. Which statement best reflects the rule against superfluous injury or unnecessary suffering?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l09.q3.h: Compare the harm with the military purpose.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l09.q3.e: The rule prohibits harm that is superfluous or unnecessary relative to military purpose, not suffering as such. It concerns combatants, and no Council authorisation is required.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l09.q4.t: N is not bound by the treaty as a non-party, but general rules such as distinction still apply to its mine use
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l09.q4.p: State N has not joined the Ottawa Convention and uses anti-personnel mines. A neighbouring state says N breaches the treaty. What is the most accurate analysis?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l09.q4.h: Treaties bind parties, but other law remains.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l09.q4.e: A non-party is not bound by the Ottawa Convention, but distinction and the indiscriminate-attack rules still apply to mine use. The ban is not universal custom, and other mine rules exist.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l09.q5.t: The Court said any threat or use must comply with IHL and would generally be contrary to its rules, while leaving open an extreme circumstance of self-defence in which the very survival of a state is at stake
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l09.q5.p: A state claims that the ICJ 1996 Advisory Opinion on nuclear weapons proves that all use of nuclear weapons is lawful. Which response is most accurate?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l09.q5.h: The opinion was more qualified than either extreme.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l09.q5.e: The Court found no comprehensive prohibition, said IHL applies and use would generally be contrary to it, and could not conclude on an extreme survival case. The other options misstate it.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l10.q1.t: Using inflatable decoy tanks and camouflage to mislead the enemy about positions
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l10.q1.p: Which of the following is a lawful ruse of war under Article 37 of Additional Protocol I?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l10.q1.h: A lawful ruse does not exploit a protection that the law gives.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l10.q1.e: Decoys and camouflage mislead without abusing legal protection. The other three feign protected status and are perfidy.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l10.q2.t: The ban on starving civilians as a method of warfare and on attacking objects indispensable to survival
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l10.q2.p: A besieging force blocks all food and fuel entering a city with the aim of making civilians so desperate that the defenders will surrender. Which rule is most directly engaged?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l10.q2.e: Article 54 prohibits starving civilians as a method of warfare. Sieges are not unlawful as such, and the other rules are not engaged.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l10.q3.t: Attacks on religious and historic buildings in Timbuktu, Mali, as a war crime
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l10.q3.p: In Prosecutor v. Al Mahdi (ICC, 2016), what was the charged conduct?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l10.q3.h: It concerned mausoleums in West Africa.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l10.q3.e: Al Mahdi pleaded guilty to intentionally directing attacks against religious and historic buildings in Timbuktu. The other options describe different cases or crimes.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l10.q4.t: It is perfidy because feigning civilian status invited the guards to accord protection and the confidence was betrayed, causing death
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l10.q4.p: Soldiers of State A put on civilian clothes, approach a checkpoint of State B as if they were farmers and, when the guards relax and let them near, open fire and kill two guards. Which analysis is correct?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l10.q4.h: Did the soldiers invite confidence that protection would be accorded?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l10.q4.e: Feigning civilian status to kill is perfidy under Article 37. The guards' protection was irrelevant; the abuse of civilian status is the wrong. No warning requirement applies in this way.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l10.q5.t: The damage does not meet the widespread, long-term and severe threshold of Article 55 of Protocol I, because those requirements are cumulative
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l10.q5.p: A commander destroys an oil installation, causing a spill that harms a river for some weeks before it recovers. Which statement about the legal consequences of this damage is correct on the facts given?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l10.q5.h: The treaty threshold is cumulative and high.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l10.q5.e: Temporary damage that heals within weeks does not meet the widespread, long-term and severe test, which is cumulative. A dual-use installation can still be a military objective, and the Rome Statute offence requires damage that is clearly excessive and known to be so.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l11.q1.t: Unless and for such time as they take a direct part in hostilities
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l11.q1.p: Under Article 51(3) of Additional Protocol I, when do civilians lose protection from attack?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l11.q1.h: Loss of protection is temporary and conditional.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l11.q1.e: Article 51(3) provides for loss of protection only for such time as direct participation lasts. Support and residence are not enough.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l11.q2.t: A civilian who sells groceries to soldiers of a party and pays taxes that indirectly fund the war effort
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l11.q2.p: Which of the following would not count as direct participation in hostilities under the ICRC's three-part test?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l11.q2.h: Direct causation in a single step is required.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l11.q2.e: Selling groceries and paying taxes do not directly cause harm. The other acts directly cause harm and have a belligerent nexus.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l11.q3.t: It is a military objective only if it satisfies Article 52(2), and, if so, any attack is still limited by proportionality and precautions
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l11.q3.p: A power station supplies both an army base and a city hospital. Under the treaties, how is it classified?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l11.q3.h: Dual-use is not a treaty category.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l11.q3.e: There is no separate dual-use category; the object is tested under Article 52(2) and the attack is then subject to proportionality and precautions.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l11.q4.t: IHL applies to cyber operations, but whether data loss alone is an attack is debated among states
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l11.q4.p: A state's cyber unit launches malware that corrupts the records of a civilian bank during an armed conflict, with no physical damage or injury. Which statement best describes the current state of the law?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l11.q4.h: Agreement on applicability does not settle the meaning of attack.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l11.q4.e: IHL applies, but the treatment of non-physical effects is disputed. The Tallinn Manual is non-binding academic work, and the economic-support theory is not accepted.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l11.q5.t: The argument fails because IHL applies, the state remains responsible and commanders deploying the system may incur responsibility
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l11.q5.p: A state deploys a weapon that selects and engages targets without further human input. After an erroneous strike on civilians, the state argues that no human decided to fire and so no one is responsible. What is the best response under the prevailing view?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l11.q5.h: Existing law continues to apply to new technology.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l11.q5.e: There is wide agreement that IHL applies and that state and individual responsibility remains. No treaty shifts responsibility to the manufacturer.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l12.q1.t: To ensure respect for the Conventions in all circumstances, in addition to respecting them itself
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l12.q1.p: Which obligation of common Article 1 of the Geneva Conventions requires states to act beyond their own conduct?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l12.q1.e: Common Article 1 obliges states to respect and to ensure respect for the Conventions. The other duties do not appear there.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l12.q2.t: Search for them and prosecute them regardless of nationality, or hand them over to another party with a prima facie case
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l12.q2.p: What does Article 146 of Convention IV require states to do regarding persons alleged to have committed grave breaches?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l12.q2.h: It is an obligation to prosecute or extradite.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l12.q2.e: Article 146 provides for search, prosecution regardless of nationality or handing over. It is not conditional on ICC requests, nationality or amnesty.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l12.q3.t: He had immunity from criminal jurisdiction of other states while in office, though immunity is not the same as impunity
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l12.q3.p: In DRC v. Belgium (Arrest Warrant, ICJ 2002), what did the Court hold about an incumbent foreign minister?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l12.q3.h: The Court distinguished immunity from impunity.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l12.q3.e: The Court held that incumbent foreign ministers enjoy immunity from other states' criminal jurisdiction, noting routes to accountability. It did not extend immunity to all courts or for life.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l12.q4.t: The reprisal is unlawful because reprisals against civilians are prohibited, and the earlier violation does not justify them
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l12.q4.p: State A's forces attack a village of State B's civilians as a reprisal for earlier attacks on A's soldiers by B. A says the action is a lawful belligerent reprisal. Which analysis is the best?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l12.q4.h: Reprisals against certain persons are now prohibited.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l12.q4.e: Reprisals against protected persons and civilians are prohibited by the Conventions and Protocol I. Proportionality and notice do not cure this.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l12.q5.t: Immunity is not impunity: the host's ability to prosecute depends on its law and on whether immunity of former officials covers the acts, which is debated
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l12.q5.p: A retired general accused of ordering war crimes while in office travels abroad as a private citizen. An ICC-style case is not available, and the host state is considering prosecution on a universal jurisdiction basis. Which statement is the most accurate?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l12.q5.h: The status of former officials is contested.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l12.q5.e: The scope of immunity for former officials for official acts is debated, and the host's domestic law matters. Absolute immunity and an automatic duty to arrest are overstatements.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l13.q1.t: Crimes against peace, war crimes and crimes against humanity, each defined in Article 6 of the Charter
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l13.q1.p: Which three categories of crime did the Charter of the International Military Tribunal at Nuremberg give the Tribunal jurisdiction over?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l13.q1.h: Genocide was not in the Charter.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l13.q1.e: The Charter named crimes against peace, war crimes and crimes against humanity. Genocide as a separate crime came with the 1948 Convention.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l13.q2.t: It was not a complete defence, though it could be considered in mitigation of punishment where justice required
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l13.q2.p: What was the Tribunal's position on the defence of superior orders?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l13.q2.h: Think of the Charter provision on orders and mitigation.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l13.q2.e: Superior orders did not free a person from responsibility but could mitigate punishment. The other options misstate the rule.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l13.q3.t: That some defined crimes, such as crimes against peace and crimes against humanity, were not clearly criminal when committed
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l13.q3.p: Which objection to the Nuremberg trials relied on the principle nullum crimen sine lege?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l13.q3.h: The principle concerns the timing of criminalisation.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l13.q3.e: Nullum crimen sine lege objects to punishment for conduct not clearly criminal at the time. The other objections concern sovereignty, penalty or composition.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l13.q4.t: The argument fails because a commander can answer for failing to control subordinates, though modern law requires knowledge and effective control
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l13.q4.p: A defendant in a modern international trial argues that, as in In re Yamashita, he cannot be convicted for subordinates' crimes unless he personally ordered them. What is the best response based on the Yamashita precedent and modern law?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l13.q4.h: Yamashita concerned failure to control troops.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l13.q4.e: Yamashita is a command responsibility precedent, but modern law, such as Article 28, requires knowledge or constructive knowledge and effective control. It does not impose strict liability.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l13.q5.t: It is partly right for Nuremberg, but the link was a jurisdictional limit that later instruments such as the Rome Statute dropped
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l13.q5.p: A commentator says the Nuremberg Charter's requirement that crimes against humanity be linked to other crimes in the Tribunal's jurisdiction shows that the crime was only a form of war crime. Which comment is the most accurate?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l13.q5.h: Later instruments changed the connection requirement.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l13.q5.e: The Nuremberg link was jurisdictional and later dropped; the Rome Statute requires no armed conflict. The other options misdescribe the Charter or later law.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l14.q1.t: It is irrelevant to criminal responsibility
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l14.q1.p: Under Article 27 of the Rome Statute, what is the effect of official capacity such as being a head of state?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l14.q1.h: The Statute applies equally to all persons.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l14.q1.e: Article 27 states that official capacity is irrelevant. Questions about immunity before national courts and cooperation are dealt with separately.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l14.q2.t: That the forces were under his effective control and he failed to take all necessary and reasonable measures to prevent crimes
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l14.q2.p: Which element is required for a military commander to be responsible under Article 28(a) of the Rome Statute?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l14.q2.h: Effective control and failure to act.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l14.q2.e: Article 28(a) requires effective command and control, knowledge or constructive knowledge and failure to take reasonable measures. It does not require a personal order or formal rank.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l14.q3.t: He is not relieved of responsibility on this ground alone, because an order to kill prisoners is manifestly unlawful
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l14.q3.p: A soldier shoots unarmed prisoners after being ordered to do so by his sergeant. Under Article 33 of the Rome Statute, which statement is correct?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l14.q3.h: Consider the three conditions in Article 33.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l14.q3.e: Article 33 requires an obligation to obey, ignorance of unlawfulness and a not manifestly unlawful order. Killing prisoners is manifestly unlawful, and it is a war crime.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l14.q4.t: Whether he took all necessary and reasonable measures must be judged on what he could realistically do
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l14.q4.p: A politician controls a militia from abroad. Evidence shows he knew of its crimes, but he had little practical ability to discipline it from outside the country and did take some measures. The Appeals Chamber in Bemba Gombo (2018) reversed the conviction. What was the central legal lesson?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l14.q4.h: Feasibility of measures was in issue.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l14.q4.e: The Appeals Chamber stressed assessing reasonable measures in light of what was actually possible. It did not hold that absent superiors are exempt, nor that militia leaders fall outside Article 28.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l14.q5.t: Civilian superiors can be liable if they knew or consciously disregarded clear information about crimes within their effective responsibility
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l14.q5.p: An accused argues that as a civilian official he cannot be liable under Article 28(b) because he did not command soldiers. Which response is most accurate?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l14.q5.h: Compare the mental element for civilians and military commanders.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l14.q5.e: Article 28(b) covers civilian superiors, with a higher knowledge threshold (knew or consciously disregarded) and effective responsibility and control. It is not limited to uniformed persons or orders.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l15.q1.t: Intentionally directing attacks against the civilian population as such
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l15.q1.p: Which of the following is a war crime listed in both the international and non-international armed conflict provisions of the Rome Statute?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l15.q1.h: Several listed crimes are specific to international conflicts.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l15.q1.e: Attacks on civilians appear in both lists. The others are tied to occupation, grave breaches or prisoner of war status, which belong to international conflicts.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l15.q2.t: Lubanga Dyilo, in 2012, for child soldier war crimes
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l15.q2.p: What was the first conviction by the ICC, and for what?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l15.q2.h: It concerned child soldiers in the DRC.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l15.q2.e: Lubanga was the first judgment, in 2012, on child soldier war crimes. Bemba was convicted for command responsibility crimes, not genocide, and Al Mahdi concerned cultural property.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l15.q3.t: The conduct must be associated with an armed conflict, and the accused must know the facts establishing it
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l15.q3.p: What does the nexus requirement for a war crime mean?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l15.q3.h: It links the crime to the conflict.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l15.q3.e: War crimes require a nexus to an armed conflict and awareness of the facts establishing it. Plan or policy is a guide in Article 8(1), not a strict element, and no numerical threshold exists.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l15.q4.t: The commander has not committed the crime because it requires knowledge that the attack would cause clearly excessive harm
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l15.q4.p: A commander orders an attack on a legitimate military objective, knowing that it will cause some civilian casualties. He did not expect harm clearly excessive in relation to the anticipated advantage, but a later investigation finds the casualties were heavier than predicted. Which analysis is the best?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l15.q4.h: The Rome Statute adds knowledge and a higher threshold.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l15.q4.e: Article 8(2)(b)(iv) requires that the perpetrator knew the attack would cause clearly excessive harm. Unforeseen outcomes do not meet it, and not every harm is a grave breach.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l15.q5.t: The violence did not reach the Article 8(2)(f) threshold of protracted conflict, so the conduct is not a war crime
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l15.q5.p: An armed group carries out sporadic bombings in a state, with no sustained fighting or organised command, and civilians die. A prosecutor charges war crimes in a non-international armed conflict. What is the strongest defence argument?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l15.q5.e: The threshold of protracted armed conflict with organised groups is a real defence argument. Civilians can commit war crimes, plan or policy is not strictly required, and ratification is not the issue.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l16.q1.t: Genocide requires the intent to destroy a national, ethnical, racial or religious group in whole or in part
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l16.q1.p: Which feature distinguishes genocide from crimes against humanity?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l16.q1.e: The special intent (dolus specialis) to destroy a protected group is the hallmark of genocide. Neither crime requires armed conflict under modern law.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l16.q2.t: A political party whose members are killed because of their political opinions
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l16.q2.p: Which group would not be protected by the definition of genocide in the 1948 Convention?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l16.q2.h: The list is limited to four group types.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l16.q2.e: The Convention protects national, ethnical, racial and religious groups only. Political groups are not covered, though killings of them may be crimes against humanity.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l16.q3.t: The attack on a civilian population, of which his act must form part
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l16.q3.p: Under Article 7 of the Rome Statute, what does the "widespread or systematic attack" requirement apply to?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l16.q3.h: The context is a course of conduct against civilians.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l16.q3.e: The widespread or systematic attack is the contextual element; the individual act need only be part of it, and the accused must know of it. No armed conflict or specific group is required.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l16.q4.t: Crimes against humanity, because the acts form part of a systematic attack against a civilian population, but not genocide since no intent to destroy a protected group is shown
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l16.q4.p: A government campaign kills thousands of civilians suspected of supporting an opposition party, with a systematic policy and open orders. No evidence shows an intent to destroy a national, ethnic, racial or religious group. Which charge best fits?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l16.q4.h: Which element is missing for genocide?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l16.q4.e: The facts show crimes against humanity but not the genocidal intent against a protected group. Political groups are not protected groups, and the crime is not merely domestic.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l16.q5.t: Serbia breached its obligation to prevent genocide and to cooperate with the ICTY, though the Court did not find that it committed genocide or was complicit in it
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l16.q5.p: In Bosnia v. Serbia (ICJ, 2007), which conclusion did the Court reach about Serbia's responsibility in relation to Srebrenica?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l16.q5.h: The Court distinguished prevention from commission.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l16.q5.e: The Court found a breach of the duty to prevent and of the duty to cooperate with the ICTY, but not direct commission or complicity. The other options overstate or understate its findings.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l17.q1.t: By a resolution of the Security Council acting under Chapter VII of the UN Charter
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l17.q1.h: Think of the body with the power to adopt binding measures.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l17.q1.e: The ICTY was established by Security Council Resolution 827 (1993) under Chapter VII. The ICC, by contrast, is a treaty body.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l17.q2.t: That rape can be an act of genocide if committed with intent to destroy a protected group, and a crime against humanity
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l17.q2.p: What did Prosecutor v. Akayesu (ICTR, 1998) decide about sexual violence?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l17.q2.h: It was a landmark for sexual violence.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l17.q2.e: Akayesu held that rape and sexual violence can be acts of genocide and crimes against humanity. The other options misstate the holding.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l17.q3.t: The ICTY had primacy and could request national courts to defer to it, the opposite of ICC complementarity
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l17.q3.p: Which statement best describes the relationship between the ICTY and national courts?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l17.q3.h: Compare ad hoc primacy with ICC complementarity.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l17.q3.e: The ad hoc tribunals had primacy. The ICC works on complementarity, under which national courts have the first opportunity.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l17.q4.t: The argument fails because the Council can create it as a Chapter VII measure to maintain or restore peace
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l17.q4.p: A defendant before an international tribunal argues that the tribunal was not lawfully established because the Security Council has no power to create judicial bodies. Which answer reflects the ICTY Appeals Chamber's reasoning in Tadic (1995)?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l17.q4.h: The Chamber relied on Chapter VII measures.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l17.q4.e: The Appeals Chamber held that the Council acted within Chapter VII powers. Article 29 concerns subsidiary organs generally, not criminal courts expressly.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l17.q5.t: The SCSL was created by agreement between the UN and Sierra Leone, a hybrid court with mixed elements
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l17.q5.p: A scholar says the Special Court for Sierra Leone is the same kind of body as the ICTR. What is the best correction?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l17.q5.h: Hybrid means mixed origin and mixed staffing.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l17.q5.e: The SCSL was a hybrid court created by agreement between the UN and Sierra Leone. It is not a Chapter VII creation like the ICTR, and it was not established under the Rome Statute.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l18.q1.t: Genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and aggression
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l18.q1.p: Which crimes are listed in Article 5 of the Rome Statute?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l18.q1.e: Article 5 lists the four core crimes. The other combinations include crimes not within the Court's jurisdiction.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l18.q2.t: If the crime was on a state party's territory or by its national, or a non-party accepted jurisdiction
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l18.q2.p: Under Article 12 of the Rome Statute, when may the Court exercise jurisdiction following a state party referral or the Prosecutor's own initiative?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l18.q2.e: Article 12 gives jurisdiction on the basis of territory or nationality of a state party, or consent by declaration. It is not universal and does not require both states to be parties.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l18.q3.t: By Security Council referral under Chapter VII, or if the state lodges an Article 12(3) declaration accepting jurisdiction
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l18.q3.p: How can the ICC exercise jurisdiction over crimes committed in a non-party state by its own nationals?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l18.q3.h: Two routes bypass the party-state preconditions.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l18.q3.e: Security Council referral or an Article 12(3) declaration enables jurisdiction. The Assembly cannot extend jurisdiction, and the Prosecutor needs the Article 12 preconditions unless the Council refers.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l18.q4.t: No jurisdiction over a non-party national for aggression under a state referral, but a Council referral would not face this limit
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l18.q4.p: State X, a non-party, invades State Y, a state party, and X's leader orders the invasion. Y refers the situation to the Court. Considering the Kampala amendments, which statement is the most accurate about aggression jurisdiction?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l18.q4.h: The aggression regime is narrower for non-parties.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l18.q4.e: The amendments exclude aggression by nationals of non-parties under state referral or proprio motu routes, but a Council referral is not so limited. The jurisdiction was activated in 2018, and no prior Council determination is required.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l18.q5.t: Authorisation by the Pre-Trial Chamber after the Prosecutor submits a request with supporting material
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l18.q5.p: The Prosecutor wishes to open an investigation on her own initiative into crimes in a state party. What procedural step does Article 15 require?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l18.q5.h: A judicial check applies to proprio motu investigations.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l18.q5.e: Article 15 requires authorisation by a Pre-Trial Chamber. Council approval, state consent and Assembly confirmation are not required.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l19.q1.t: The ICC complements national courts and acts only where states are unwilling or unable to prosecute
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l19.q1.p: What is the principle of complementarity?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l19.q1.e: Complementarity makes national courts primary and the ICC secondary. Primacy was a feature of the ad hoc tribunals.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l19.q2.t: A state with jurisdiction is genuinely investigating or prosecuting the case
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l19.q2.p: Which of the following would make a case inadmissible under Article 17 of the Rome Statute?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l19.q2.h: The test concerns genuine national proceedings.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l19.q2.e: A genuine national investigation or prosecution makes the case inadmissible. Temporal limits concern jurisdiction, and consultation with victims is not an admissibility criterion.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l19.q3.t: The case is inadmissible, as genuine proceedings ending in acquittal satisfy complementarity unless they were a sham
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l19.q3.p: A state holds a trial of a former official for the same conduct under investigation by the ICC. The trial is genuine and ends in acquittal. What follows?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l19.q3.h: The test is genuineness, not the outcome.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l19.q3.e: Article 20 and Article 17 respect genuine proceedings whatever the result. The Court may act only if proceedings were to shield the person or were not independent or impartial.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l19.q4.t: S is unwilling to prosecute, given unjustified delay and lack of independence
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l19.q4.p: State S has a sitting government that for years has repeatedly removed prosecutors from investigating a general accused of mass killings. A year-long investigation file shows no steps taken. What is the best argument that the case is admissible?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l19.q4.h: Look at the indicators in Article 17(2).
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l19.q4.e: Unjustified delay and lack of independence indicate unwillingness. The facts do not show a collapsed system, nor a trial, and complementarity applies to the admissibility of a case whatever the status of the state.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l19.q5.t: No customary rule recognises head-of-state immunity before an international court, so Jordan failed to comply
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l19.q5.p: In the Jordan Referral re Al-Bashir decision (Appeals Chamber, 2019), what did the Court hold?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l19.q5.h: The issue was immunity before an international court.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l19.q5.e: The Appeals Chamber held that there is no such customary immunity before international courts, and that Jordan failed to comply. Sudan's situation had been referred by the Security Council, and Jordan was a state party.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l20.q1.t: The amnesty did not bar prosecution for international crimes before the Court
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l20.q1.p: What did the Special Court for Sierra Leone decide about the Lome Accord amnesty in Kallon and Kamara (2004)?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l20.q1.h: The Court did not accept the amnesty as a bar.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l20.q1.e: The SCSL held that the amnesty did not prevent prosecution for international crimes. The other options misstate the decision.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l20.q2.t: That the caseload and the Council veto produce uneven scrutiny of powerful states
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l20.q2.p: Which is the strongest form of the "selectivity" criticism of the ICC?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l20.q2.h: It concerns who is and is not reached.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l20.q2.e: The selectivity argument concerns uneven reach caused by jurisdictional gaps and the Council's role. The other options do not describe it.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l20.q3.t: The argument fails because jurisdiction turns on the Article 12 preconditions, whatever the critique
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l20.q3.p: A state argues that the ICC lacks legitimacy and therefore has no jurisdiction over events on a state party's territory involving its nationals. Which response is correct as a statement of law?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l20.q3.h: Do not mistake a debate for a rule.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l20.q3.e: Jurisdiction turns on the legal preconditions, such as territory of a state party. Legitimacy debates do not change them, and the Council has not approved every investigation.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l20.q4.t: The amnesty may not bar prosecution before international courts, though it may inform the interests of justice assessment
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l20.q4.p: A peace agreement offers a rebel leader a blanket amnesty for all crimes, including the massacre of civilians. Which assessment best reflects the current position of international criminal law?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l20.q4.h: Amnesties are contested but generally not a bar.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l20.q4.e: International courts have not treated blanket amnesties for grave crimes as a bar, though Article 53 allows the Prosecutor to consider the interests of justice. The Statute does not require respect for amnesties.

law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l20.q5.t: National trials complement but cannot replace the ICC, as they depend on presence, domestic law and will
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l20.q5.p: A government argues that universal jurisdiction trials in foreign courts, such as the 2022 Koblenz verdict, show that the ICC is unnecessary. Which response is strongest?
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l20.q5.h: Consider the practical limits of national prosecutions.
law-intl-humanitarian-criminal.l20.q5.e: National trials depend on presence of the accused, domestic law and political will, so they complement rather than replace international courts. They are not unlawful, and they are not the same as the ICC.

law-intl-public.l01.q1.t: Its main lawmakers are the states bound by it, acting through treaties and custom
law-intl-public.l01.q1.p: Which description best captures how international law is made and applied compared with domestic law?
law-intl-public.l01.q1.h: Think about who writes the rules and whether any central authority stands above states.
law-intl-public.l01.q1.e: The system is horizontal: states make law mainly by treaty and custom. No world legislature exists, and the Security Council does not legislate general rules by majority vote.

law-intl-public.l01.q2.t: States have equal legal status whatever their size or power
law-intl-public.l01.q2.p: Article 2(1) of the UN Charter states sovereign equality. What does that principle mean in law?
law-intl-public.l01.q2.h: The principle concerns legal status, not material power.
law-intl-public.l01.q2.e: Sovereign equality is equality of legal status. Equal influence is not required, and the principle does not exempt small states from rules or grant larger legal rights to powerful ones.

law-intl-public.l01.q3.t: It has international legal personality and the capacity to bring such claims
law-intl-public.l01.q3.p: A UN mediator is killed while on duty and the UN wants to bring a claim against the responsible state. In the Reparation for Injuries opinion (ICJ, 1949), what did the Court conclude about the UN?
law-intl-public.l01.q3.h: The Court reasoned from what the organisation needs to carry out its functions.
law-intl-public.l01.q3.e: The Court held the UN has objective international personality and capacity to claim. It said such personality is not identical to that of a state, so the full-sovereignty option is wrong.

law-intl-public.l01.q4.t: A is bound only if the ban also exists as a customary rule or A has otherwise consented
law-intl-public.l01.q4.p: State A has not ratified a multilateral treaty banning a certain weapon. State B, a party, says A is nonetheless bound because "the treaty binds the whole international community". Which response is most accurate?
law-intl-public.l01.q4.h: Ask whether another source, apart from the treaty, could bind A.
law-intl-public.l01.q4.e: Treaties bind parties only, but the same content may exist as custom binding A. Majority adoption does not bind non-parties, and treaty rules can sometimes generate custom, so the third option is wrong.

law-intl-public.l01.q5.t: Q's effort to justify its conduct in legal terms indicates that it treats international rules as binding
law-intl-public.l01.q5.p: State Q's government argues that international law is "not real law" because no authority compels it to obey. State Q then publishes a legal memorandum defending its border operation as consistent with the UN Charter. What is the best analytic point to make about this?
