law-intl-public.l01.q5.h: Consider what the justification itself reveals about how the state regards the rules.
law-intl-public.l01.q5.e: States habitually justify their conduct by reference to legal rules, which is evidence the rules are treated as binding. A state's own opinion is not conclusive, and international law does not derive its force from domestic law.

law-intl-public.l02.q1.t: Resolutions of the Security Council adopted by a simple majority as general legislation
law-intl-public.l02.q1.p: Which of the following is NOT one of the sources listed in Article 38(1) of the ICJ Statute as something the Court applies?
law-intl-public.l02.q1.h: Three of these appear in the list directly; one is not on it.
law-intl-public.l02.q1.e: Article 38(1) lists conventions, custom and general principles, with judicial decisions and teachings as subsidiary means. Security Council resolutions are not listed as a formal source.

law-intl-public.l02.q2.t: It binds only the parties and only for that particular case
law-intl-public.l02.q2.p: Under Article 59 of the ICJ Statute, what is the legal force of an ICJ decision?
law-intl-public.l02.q2.h: Think of the ICJ as lacking a formal doctrine of binding precedent.
law-intl-public.l02.q2.e: Article 59 limits the binding force of a decision to the parties and the case. It does not create a stare decisis system binding all states.

law-intl-public.l02.q3.t: General principles such as acquiescence and estoppel based on fairness and consistency
law-intl-public.l02.q3.p: In the Temple of Preah Vihear case (ICJ, 1962), the Court relied on Thailand's long acceptance of a map without objection. Which type of source does this reasoning illustrate?
law-intl-public.l02.q3.h: The reasoning concerns the effect of silence and consistency, not a particular treaty text.
law-intl-public.l02.q3.e: Acquiescence and estoppel are general principles of fairness. The Court relied on conduct, not on a convention or a peremptory norm, and not on scholarly writings.

law-intl-public.l02.q4.t: Article 103 of the UN Charter, under which Charter obligations prevail over conflicting obligations under other agreements
law-intl-public.l02.q4.p: State R owes State S obligations under a bilateral trade treaty. The UN Security Council later adopts a binding Chapter VII sanctions decision requiring R to stop all trade with S. R's obligations under the two instruments conflict. Which rule most directly resolves the conflict?
law-intl-public.l02.q4.h: One provision of the Charter creates a hierarchy in favour of its own obligations.
law-intl-public.l02.q4.e: Article 103 gives Charter obligations priority, which extends to binding Security Council decisions. Article 59 concerns the effect of ICJ judgments, and Article 38(2) concerns ex aequo et bono decisions by consent of parties.

law-intl-public.l02.q5.t: Is not binding in itself but may be evidence of opinio juris that contributes to the formation of customary law
law-intl-public.l02.q5.p: A General Assembly resolution on a principle of non-intervention was adopted by consensus and has been repeatedly cited by states as stating the law. An advocate says it is a binding statute. A better analysis is that the resolution:
law-intl-public.l02.q5.h: Distinguish between a source that creates law and evidence that helps identify custom.
law-intl-public.l02.q5.e: General Assembly resolutions are generally recommendations but may be evidence of opinio juris. The Assembly lacks general legislative power, and consensus does not itself create a peremptory norm.

law-intl-public.l03.q1.t: State practice and opinio juris, meaning a belief that the conduct is legally required or permitted
law-intl-public.l03.q1.p: Which two elements are needed to form a rule of customary international law?
law-intl-public.l03.q1.h: One element concerns what states do and the other why they do it.
law-intl-public.l03.q1.e: Custom needs practice and opinio juris. No fixed time period or institutional approval is required, and the Court has said time alone is not decisive.

law-intl-public.l03.q2.t: Germany had not ratified the convention
law-intl-public.l03.q2.p: In North Sea Continental Shelf (ICJ, 1969), why was Germany not bound by the equidistance rule in Article 6 of the 1958 Geneva Convention on the Continental Shelf?
law-intl-public.l03.q2.h: The Court asked two questions: treaty status and custom status.
law-intl-public.l03.q2.e: Germany had signed but not ratified, and the Court found the rule had not become custom. The Court did not hold that treaty rules never generate custom; it set demanding conditions for it.

law-intl-public.l03.q3.t: The rule will not be opposable to that state, unless the rule is a peremptory norm of general international law
law-intl-public.l03.q3.p: A state objects openly and consistently from the earliest stages to an emerging customary rule on baselines. If the rule later crystallises, what is the likely result under the persistent objector doctrine?
law-intl-public.l03.q3.h: Timing and consistency of the objection matter, as does the character of the rule.
law-intl-public.l03.q3.e: A persistent objector may escape a non-peremptory customary rule. One objection does not prevent a custom from forming, and objection is ineffective against jus cogens.

law-intl-public.l03.q4.t: T's courtesy statement shows T lacked opinio juris, so U must still prove that states generally act out of a sense of legal obligation, since conduct done as a courtesy does not create custom
law-intl-public.l03.q4.p: For three decades most coastal states have inspected cargo vessels at a particular distance from shore, citing "customary rights". State T did the same, but its foreign ministry states that it does so solely as a courtesy to neighbours and without any legal obligation. State U, a neighbour, claims a customary rule exists binding T. What is the strongest analysis?
law-intl-public.l03.q4.h: What is the relationship between practice and the belief that the conduct is legally required?
law-intl-public.l03.q4.e: Custom needs opinio juris as well as practice; conduct done out of courtesy lacks it. Time alone is not decisive, and universal practice is not required, only extensive and virtually uniform practice.

law-intl-public.l03.q5.t: Article 53, which makes a treaty void if it conflicts with a peremptory norm of general international law
law-intl-public.l03.q5.p: State V enters a treaty with State W in which the two agree that either may use force against nationals of the other for any reason. A third state argues that the treaty is void on a ground drawn from the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties 1969. Which provision best supports this?
law-intl-public.l03.q5.h: The relevant concept is a norm from which no derogation is permitted.
law-intl-public.l03.q5.e: Article 53 makes a treaty conflicting with jus cogens void; the prohibition on the use of force is widely treated as peremptory. Article 26 is pacta sunt servanda, and Article 62 is a narrow fundamental change of circumstances rule.

law-intl-public.l04.q1.p: Which of the following is one of the Montevideo Convention (1933) criteria for statehood?
law-intl-public.l04.q1.h: Montevideo lists four factual elements; democracy and membership are not among them.
law-intl-public.l04.q1.e: Population, territory, government and capacity to enter relations make up the criteria. Democracy, UN membership and recognition by particular states are not required.

law-intl-public.l04.q2.t: Under the declaratory theory statehood exists once the criteria are met and recognition merely acknowledges it
law-intl-public.l04.q2.p: What distinguishes the declaratory theory of recognition from the constitutive theory?
law-intl-public.l04.q2.h: Ask whether recognition creates statehood or only records it.
law-intl-public.l04.q2.e: The declaratory theory treats recognition as evidence of existing fact. The constitutive theory makes recognition decisive, which creates the problem of an entity being a state for some but not others.

law-intl-public.l04.q3.t: That the declaration did not violate general international law
law-intl-public.l04.q3.p: What did the ICJ conclude in its 2010 advisory opinion on Kosovo's declaration of independence?
law-intl-public.l04.q3.h: The Court answered a narrowly framed question and avoided broader issues.
law-intl-public.l04.q3.e: The Court held that general international law contained no prohibition of declarations of independence. It did not decide that Kosovo was a state or that a right of remedial secession exists.

law-intl-public.l04.q4.t: Three recognitions do not settle statehood: Z must meet the Montevideo criteria and the rules on lawful creation, and no general right of secession exists outside colonial contexts
law-intl-public.l04.q4.p: Province Z has a population of 2 million, clear borders and a capable government, and declares independence from State Y after Y's army is ordered into the province. Y was not oppressing the province, and no armed conflict preceded the declaration. Three states recognise Z. A lawyer for Z says that statehood is now complete. The strongest response is:
law-intl-public.l04.q4.h: Separate the factual criteria, recognition practice and the self-determination background.
law-intl-public.l04.q4.e: Statehood depends on the factual criteria and lawfulness of the process, and recognition is evidence rather than creation under the declaratory approach. Secession is not prohibited, but neither is there a general right to it outside colonial or similar contexts.

law-intl-public.l04.q5.t: The state's identity and treaty obligations continue despite the change of government
law-intl-public.l04.q5.p: After a coup, the military of State K removes the elected government and takes control of the capital. The new regime announces it will not honour K's existing treaty debts. A creditor state argues that K remains bound. Which analysis is most accurate?
law-intl-public.l04.q5.h: Distinguish between the continuity of the state and a change of its government.
law-intl-public.l04.q5.e: A change of government does not alter the state's identity or its obligations. The creditor's recognition of the new regime is not a condition of K's continued statehood.

law-intl-public.l05.q1.p: Which term describes a state's authority to carry out law through arrests, seizures and similar acts?
law-intl-public.l05.q1.h: Three jurisdictions differ by function: making, deciding and carrying out the law.
law-intl-public.l05.q1.e: Enforcement jurisdiction means carrying out the law. Prescriptive means making rules, adjudicative refers to courts hearing cases, and protective is a basis rather than a type of function.

law-intl-public.l05.q2.t: The protective principle, which covers conduct abroad threatening the state's security or essential functions
law-intl-public.l05.q2.p: State D forges the passports of State E in order to pass off its agents abroad. Which basis of jurisdiction most directly supports prosecution in State E of the forgers when they are later found within E?
law-intl-public.l05.q2.h: Ask what interest of the prosecuting state is injured.
law-intl-public.l05.q2.e: Forging a state's passports threatens its essential functions, so the protective principle applies. Passive personality depends on victim nationality and universality is for crimes of universal concern.

law-intl-public.l05.q3.t: A state may exercise jurisdiction over foreign conduct unless a prohibitive rule of international law forbids it
law-intl-public.l05.q3.p: What approach to jurisdiction did the PCIJ adopt in the Lotus case (1927)?
law-intl-public.l05.q3.h: The Court presumed independence, not restriction.
law-intl-public.l05.q3.e: The Court held that restrictions on independence cannot be presumed, so a state may act unless a prohibitive rule exists. The treaty rule on collisions at sea later changed the particular outcome.

law-intl-public.l05.q4.t: The arrest violated Q's sovereignty, because enforcement cannot be exercised on foreign soil without consent, even where R has a basis to prescribe law
law-intl-public.l05.q4.p: A national of State P assaults a national of State R in the territory of State Q. Later, the assailant travels to State R. Officers of State R, acting without Q's consent, arrest the assailant while he is visiting State Q's capital and take him to R for trial. What is the strongest analysis of R's conduct?
law-intl-public.l05.q4.h: Separate the right to make a law apply from the right to carry out arrests abroad.
law-intl-public.l05.q4.e: Even if R has a basis for prescriptive jurisdiction, enforcement on Q's territory without consent violates Q's sovereignty. The other options wrongly merge prescriptive and enforcement jurisdiction.

law-intl-public.l05.q5.t: G may not prosecute: only the flag state or the state of nationality of the person concerned may bring penal proceedings after a collision at sea
law-intl-public.l05.q5.p: Two vessels, one flying the flag of State F and one carrying the flag of State G, collide on the high seas, killing a crew member on the G vessel. State G prosecutes the F captain once the vessel enters a G port. Under Article 97 of the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea 1982, which analysis is most accurate?
law-intl-public.l05.q5.h: A treaty rule altered the specific result of the Lotus case.
law-intl-public.l05.q5.e: Article 97 limits penal proceedings after a collision on the high seas to the flag state or the state of the person's nationality, so G cannot rely on the Lotus outcome. Port presence does not alter the rule, and no Assembly authorisation exists.

law-intl-public.l06.q1.t: It must be an international agreement between states in written form and governed by international law
law-intl-public.l06.q1.p: Under Article 2(1)(a) of the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties 1969, which feature is essential for an instrument to be a treaty?
law-intl-public.l06.q1.h: The Convention disregards the name given to the instrument.
law-intl-public.l06.q1.e: Article 2(1)(a) requires a written international agreement between states governed by international law, whatever its designation. Title, Assembly approval and universal signature are not required.

law-intl-public.l06.q2.t: It must refrain from acts that would defeat the object and purpose of the treaty until it makes its intention clear
law-intl-public.l06.q2.p: A state signs a treaty that requires ratification but has not yet ratified it. Under Article 18 of the VCLT, what is its position?
law-intl-public.l06.q2.h: Signature creates a limited obligation short of full treaty obligations.
law-intl-public.l06.q2.e: Article 18 obliges a signatory to refrain from defeating the treaty's object and purpose pending ratification. Full obligations come only with consent to be bound, so the first option is wrong.

law-intl-public.l06.q3.t: A reserving state remains a party only if the reservation is compatible with the object and purpose of the convention
law-intl-public.l06.q3.p: What did the ICJ hold in the Reservations to the Genocide Convention advisory opinion (1951)?
law-intl-public.l06.q3.h: The Court moved away from the traditional unanimity rule.
law-intl-public.l06.q3.e: The Court looked to compatibility with the convention's object and purpose. It rejected the rule that any single objection blocks the reserving state, and also rejected validity regardless of content.

law-intl-public.l06.q4.t: It is likely impermissible under Article 19(c) as vague and subordinating the treaty to domestic law, so B's objection does not stop it applying between A and B
law-intl-public.l06.q4.p: State A ratifies a multilateral human rights treaty with a reservation excluding "any obligation that conflicts with A's domestic law, as it may exist from time to time." State B objects, stating the reservation defeats the treaty's object and purpose, but does not say it opposes the treaty entering into force between itself and A. Which analysis is most defensible?
law-intl-public.l06.q4.h: Consider how a reservation that defers to national law affects the treaty's purpose.
law-intl-public.l06.q4.e: A blanket reservation referring to domestic law is generally seen as incompatible with object and purpose. Under Article 20 an objection does not prevent entry into force unless the objecting state says so, so the third option is wrong.

law-intl-public.l06.q5.t: Under Article 7 a foreign minister represents the state for treaty-making acts without full powers, so C is likely bound if consent was otherwise expressed
law-intl-public.l06.q5.p: The foreign minister of State C signs a boundary agreement with State D, without producing full powers. C's president later says the minister had no authority and that C is not bound. Which response best reflects the VCLT?
law-intl-public.l06.q5.h: Article 7 gives certain office-holders automatic representative capacity.
law-intl-public.l06.q5.e: Heads of state, heads of government and foreign ministers need not show full powers. Whether the signature expressed consent to be bound depends on the treaty, but lack of full powers is not a defence.

law-intl-public.l07.q1.t: Every treaty in force binds its parties and must be performed by them in good faith
law-intl-public.l07.q1.p: Which rule does Article 26 of the VCLT state?
law-intl-public.l07.q1.h: The Latin maxim is pacta sunt servanda.
law-intl-public.l07.q1.e: Article 26 states pacta sunt servanda. Internal law is no excuse under Article 27, and the other options describe rules that do not exist in the Convention.

law-intl-public.l07.q2.t: The ordinary meaning of the terms in their context and in the light of the treaty's object and purpose
law-intl-public.l07.q2.p: Under the general rule of interpretation in Article 31 of the VCLT, which element comes first in the analysis?
law-intl-public.l07.q2.h: Think text first, and supplementary material second.
law-intl-public.l07.q2.e: Article 31(1) starts with ordinary meaning in context and in light of object and purpose. The travaux are supplementary means under Article 32.

law-intl-public.l07.q3.t: It creates no obligation or right for C without C's consent
law-intl-public.l07.q3.p: State A and State B conclude a treaty. State C is not a party and has not consented to it. What is the effect of the treaty on C under Article 34?
law-intl-public.l07.q3.h: A treaty is a consensual instrument and the consent of the third state matters.
law-intl-public.l07.q3.e: Article 34 says a treaty creates neither obligations nor rights for a third state without its consent. Article 38 preserves binding custom, which is why the last clause matters.

law-intl-public.l07.q4.t: Begin with the ordinary meaning of "vehicles" in context and in light of the treaty's purpose
law-intl-public.l07.q4.p: A treaty between State E and State F obliges both to give "vehicles" free transit over a shared bridge. E bans motorbikes at the bridge, saying the treaty covers only cars and trucks, and cites a negotiating draft that listed "motor vehicles" which was later changed to "vehicles". F says motorbikes are included. Which approach would a tribunal apply?
law-intl-public.l07.q4.h: The structure of Articles 31 and 32 sets the order of analysis.
law-intl-public.l07.q4.e: Text, context and purpose come first, and travaux confirm or resolve ambiguity. The change from "motor vehicles" to "vehicles" would also support a broader reading. Neither a general pro-sovereignty nor contra proferentem rule is in the VCLT.

law-intl-public.l07.q5.t: Hungary's termination was not lawful and the treaty remained in force
law-intl-public.l07.q5.p: Hungary in the Gabcikovo-Nagymaros dispute (ICJ, 1997) suspended and then abandoned works, relying on necessity, and purported to terminate the 1977 treaty. Which conclusion did the Court reach?
law-intl-public.l07.q5.h: The Court applied strict limits on termination but recognised environmental concerns.
law-intl-public.l07.q5.e: The Court held Hungary's termination was ineffective and the treaty continued, while urging good faith negotiation. It did not treat environmental risk as an automatic override or the treaty as void.

law-intl-public.l08.q1.p: Under Article 53 of the VCLT, what is the consequence of a treaty conflicting with a peremptory norm at the time of its conclusion?
law-intl-public.l08.q1.h: Peremptory norms permit no derogation by agreement.
law-intl-public.l08.q1.e: Article 53 makes a conflicting treaty void. It is not merely voidable by one party or suspended.

law-intl-public.l08.q2.t: Only if denunciation was intended or is implied by the treaty's nature, with twelve months' notice
law-intl-public.l08.q2.p: A state wishes to withdraw from a treaty that has no termination or denunciation clause. Under Article 56, when may it withdraw?
law-intl-public.l08.q2.h: The default presumption is that the treaty is not terminable at will.
law-intl-public.l08.q2.e: Article 56 allows denunciation only where intended or implied by the treaty's nature, with twelve months' notice. Neither unrestricted withdrawal nor a Security Council approval rule exists.

law-intl-public.l08.q3.t: Article 62(2) excludes treaties establishing a boundary from the doctrine
law-intl-public.l08.q3.p: Why can the fundamental change of circumstances doctrine in Article 62 not be used by a state seeking to escape a boundary treaty?
law-intl-public.l08.q3.h: The Convention carves out a specific category to protect stability.
law-intl-public.l08.q3.e: Article 62(2)(a) says the doctrine cannot be invoked for treaties establishing a boundary. Boundary treaties are not as a class peremptory norms, and Article 62 is not limited to commerce.

law-intl-public.l08.q4.t: The treaty is void under Article 52 if the threat was a threat of force in violation of the principles of the UN Charter
law-intl-public.l08.q4.p: Under duress from an invasion threat, State A signs a treaty in which it cedes a coastal strip to State B. B had mobilised troops on the border and told A's government it would attack the capital unless the treaty was signed. Years later A says the treaty is void. What is the best analysis?
law-intl-public.l08.q4.h: Distinguish coercion of the state by force from other kinds of pressure.
law-intl-public.l08.q4.e: Article 52 voids a treaty procured by the threat or use of force in violation of the Charter. Representative authority does not cure coercion, and no Security Council ruling is a precondition.

law-intl-public.l08.q5.t: Q may terminate the treaty or suspend its operation in whole or in part
law-intl-public.l08.q5.p: State P and State Q are parties to a bilateral treaty of friendship and trade. P materially breaches by repudiating the treaty without legal basis. Q wants to respond. What does Article 60 of the VCLT permit?
law-intl-public.l08.q5.h: Bilateral treaties allow a direct response to material breach, with an exception for human protection.
law-intl-public.l08.q5.e: Under Article 60(1) a party may terminate or suspend in response to a material breach by the other party in a bilateral treaty, but Article 60(5) excludes humanitarian protections. No court judgment or consent is required.

law-intl-public.l09.q1.t: A party may not invoke its internal law as justification for failure to perform a treaty, subject to the narrow rule in Article 46
law-intl-public.l09.q1.p: What does Article 27 of the VCLT provide about a state's internal law?
law-intl-public.l09.q1.h: International responsibility is not excused by domestic constraints.
law-intl-public.l09.q1.e: Article 27 provides that a party may not invoke internal law to justify non-performance, subject to Article 46 on manifest violations of fundamental rules concerning competence to conclude treaties.

law-intl-public.l09.q2.t: Dualism treats the two as separate systems, so treaties generally need legislation before domestic courts apply them
law-intl-public.l09.q2.p: What distinguishes a dualist from a monist approach to international law?
law-intl-public.l09.q2.h: Think about whether a ratified treaty is directly part of the domestic order.
law-intl-public.l09.q2.e: Dualism holds the systems are separate and requires transformation. The first option reverses the definitions, and the last two are inaccurate generalisations.

law-intl-public.l09.q3.t: The judgment was not directly enforceable as domestic law in state court
law-intl-public.l09.q3.p: In Medellin v. Texas (U.S., 2008), what did the Supreme Court hold concerning the ICJ's Avena judgment?
law-intl-public.l09.q3.h: The Court asked whether the relevant treaty provisions were self-executing.
law-intl-public.l09.q3.e: The Court held that the relevant treaty provisions were not self-executing and that the President's memorandum could not override state procedural rules. It did not hold the ICJ lacked authority.

law-intl-public.l09.q4.t: A non-self-executing treaty will generally not be applied directly by the courts without implementing legislation, although the international obligation remains
law-intl-public.l09.q4.p: The United States ratifies a treaty with the Senate's consent, and the treaty states that parties will "provide" a private right of action but Congress passes no implementing legislation. A litigant sues a state official under the treaty, and the state argues the treaty is non-self-executing. Which analysis is most accurate?
law-intl-public.l09.q4.h: Separate domestic enforceability from international responsibility.
law-intl-public.l09.q4.e: A non-self-executing treaty needs implementing legislation for domestic enforcement, but the international obligation remains, per Article 27 VCLT. Not every treaty is self-executing, as Medellin shows.

law-intl-public.l09.q5.t: The later statute generally prevails domestically under the last-in-time rule
law-intl-public.l09.q5.p: Congress passes a statute inconsistent with an earlier ratified treaty to which the United States is a party. In a domestic case between private parties, which answer best states the usual consequence?
law-intl-public.l09.q5.h: Domestic rank and international obligation can diverge.
law-intl-public.l09.q5.e: Treaties and federal statutes have equal rank, so the later controls domestically, subject to the canon of reading statutes consistently with international law where possible. International responsibility is unaffected, so the first option is wrong.

law-intl-public.l10.q1.t: Conduct attributable to the state under international law, and a breach of an international obligation of that state
law-intl-public.l10.q1.p: According to Article 2 of the ILC Articles on State Responsibility (2001), what are the two elements of an internationally wrongful act?
law-intl-public.l10.q1.h: One element concerns who acted, the other what rule was broken.
law-intl-public.l10.q1.e: Article 2 requires attribution and breach. Injury, a court decision or a constitutional violation is not a general requirement.

law-intl-public.l10.q2.t: The conduct is attributable to the state as the act of a state organ, whatever the organ's position in the state's structure, and no prior approval is needed
law-intl-public.l10.q2.p: A provincial police unit of a federal state beats a detained foreign national in breach of an international obligation, and the federal government says it has no control over provincial police. What is the position under Article 4 of the Articles?
law-intl-public.l10.q2.h: International law looks at the state as a whole, regardless of its internal division of power.
law-intl-public.l10.q2.e: Article 4 attributes the conduct of any state organ, including organs of territorial units. Internal structure is no excuse, and no prior approval is needed.

law-intl-public.l10.q3.t: Albania knew or must have known of the mines in its waters and failed to warn the ships, breaching its duty not to let its territory be used against the rights of others
law-intl-public.l10.q3.p: In the Corfu Channel case (ICJ, 1949), on what ground did the Court hold Albania responsible for damage to British warships from mines?
law-intl-public.l10.q3.h: The Court did not find that Albania laid the mines.
law-intl-public.l10.q3.e: The Court based responsibility on Albania's knowledge and failure to warn, a breach of its duty not to knowingly allow its territory to be used contrary to others' rights. Direct laying by Albania was not established.

law-intl-public.l10.q4.t: The massacre is not attributable to N unless N directed or effectively controlled the specific operation in which the massacre occurred
law-intl-public.l10.q4.p: State N supplies arms and funding to an armed group in State M and gives general strategic advice, but the group chooses its own targets and operates independently. The group commits a massacre in M. Under the effective control test applied by the ICJ in the Nicaragua and Bosnian Genocide cases, what is the most likely result?
law-intl-public.l10.q4.h: The test focuses on control over the specific operations in which violations occurred.
law-intl-public.l10.q4.e: Effective control over the specific operation is needed for attribution; general support is not enough, though it may breach other rules such as non-intervention. Armed groups are not state organs of the territory state merely by operating there.

law-intl-public.l10.q5.t: S may be responsible for breaching its separate obligation to prevent genocide, given its influence, knowledge of the risk and capacity to act
law-intl-public.l10.q5.p: Paramilitaries not controlled by State S commit genocide in a neighbouring region. S had strong influence over them, knew of the serious risk and had the capacity to act, but did nothing. Using the reasoning of the ICJ in Bosnia v. Serbia (2007), what is the best analysis of S's responsibility?
law-intl-public.l10.q5.h: Distinguish responsibility for the acts from responsibility for a failure to prevent.
law-intl-public.l10.q5.e: The Court found Serbia not responsible for committing the genocide because effective control was not shown, but found that it breached its duty to prevent. Influence alone does not satisfy attribution, and formal domestic status is not required.

law-intl-public.l11.q1.p: Under the ILC Articles, which of the following is a form of reparation listed in Article 34?
law-intl-public.l11.q1.e: Article 34 lists restitution, compensation and satisfaction. Retorsion and countermeasures are responses by injured states, not forms of reparation.

law-intl-public.l11.q2.t: To wipe out the consequences of the illegal act and restore the situation that would probably have existed
law-intl-public.l11.q2.p: According to the Chorzow Factory case (PCIJ, 1928), what is the aim of reparation?
law-intl-public.l11.q2.h: The aim is restorative rather than punitive.
law-intl-public.l11.q2.e: The Court said reparation must wipe out the consequences as far as possible and restore the probable situation. It is not punitive and not a fixed penalty.

law-intl-public.l11.q3.t: Expelling the responsible state's ambassador, which is an unfriendly but lawful act
law-intl-public.l11.q3.p: Which of the following would qualify as retorsion rather than a countermeasure?
law-intl-public.l11.q3.h: Retorsion is lawful in itself, while countermeasures would otherwise be unlawful.
law-intl-public.l11.q3.e: Expelling diplomats is lawful though unfriendly, so it is retorsion. The other options would breach a legal obligation, which makes them countermeasures if the conditions are met.

law-intl-public.l11.q4.t: Distress under Article 24, because the crew had no other reasonable way of saving their lives and those of the persons entrusted to their care, which precludes wrongfulness
law-intl-public.l11.q4.p: State A's aircraft, with its crew in grave danger after a storm damaged its engines, enters State B's airspace without permission and lands at a B airport. B protests the violation. Which circumstance precluding wrongfulness is most relevant?
law-intl-public.l11.q4.h: The life of the persons on board is what is at stake.
law-intl-public.l11.q4.e: Distress under Article 24 applies where the author of the act has no other reasonable way of saving lives. Necessity (Article 25) cannot seriously impair another state's essential interest, and no consent or countermeasure is present.

law-intl-public.l11.q5.t: The duties can be a lawful countermeasure if proportionate and reversible, but the threat to bombard the capital is unlawful whatever X's breach
law-intl-public.l11.q5.p: State X violates a trade treaty with State Y. Y, after demanding compliance and notifying X, imposes proportionate duties on X's goods in breach of a separate treaty, to be lifted once X complies. Y also threatens to bombard X's capital if X does not comply. Which analysis is best?
law-intl-public.l11.q5.h: Countermeasures have both procedural and substantive limits, and one limit concerns force.
law-intl-public.l11.q5.e: Countermeasures must be proportionate, reversible and may not involve the threat or use of force. Countermeasures are permitted in principle, and a trade breach is not a use of force.

law-intl-public.l12.q1.t: Acts of sovereign authority, for which the state is immune, and commercial or private acts
law-intl-public.l12.q1.p: What is the distinction between acta jure imperii and acta jure gestionis in the law of state immunity?
law-intl-public.l12.q1.h: The restrictive theory looks at the nature of the act.
law-intl-public.l12.q1.e: Restrictive immunity covers sovereign acts but not commercial acts. Location, rank or legality of the act is not the test.

law-intl-public.l12.q2.t: That a serving foreign minister is immune from foreign criminal jurisdiction, so Belgium's warrant violated the DRC's rights, even for alleged crimes against humanity
law-intl-public.l12.q2.p: What did the ICJ decide in the Arrest Warrant case (DRC v. Belgium, 2002)?
law-intl-public.l12.q2.h: The Court spoke about incumbent holders of high office.
law-intl-public.l12.q2.e: The Court held that a serving foreign minister enjoys full criminal immunity and inviolability. It did not hold that universal jurisdiction is impermissible in general, only that it cannot override this immunity.

law-intl-public.l12.q3.t: Declare the diplomat persona non grata at any time without having to explain its decision
law-intl-public.l12.q3.p: Under the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations 1961, what may a receiving state do when it no longer wishes to accept a diplomat?
law-intl-public.l12.q3.h: The Convention gives the receiving state a political remedy rather than a judicial one.
law-intl-public.l12.q3.e: Article 9 allows the receiving state to declare a diplomat persona non grata at any time without giving reasons. Diplomats do have immunity from criminal jurisdiction under Article 31.

law-intl-public.l12.q4.t: The suit is barred by State G's immunity, because the immunity rules are procedural and do not conflict with the substantive jus cogens prohibitions
law-intl-public.l12.q4.p: Victims of wartime atrocities by State G's armed forces sue State G for damages in the courts of State I, and say that immunity cannot apply to violations of peremptory norms. Using the reasoning of the ICJ in Germany v. Italy (2012), what is the best analysis?
law-intl-public.l12.q4.h: The Court distinguished procedural rules from substantive prohibitions.
law-intl-public.l12.q4.e: The Court held that the law of immunity applied to the armed forces' conduct and did not conflict with jus cogens as procedural. The 2004 Convention is not in force and was not the basis of the ruling.

law-intl-public.l12.q5.t: His personal immunity has ended, so private acts can be prosecuted, while official acts stay covered by functional immunity, subject to the debate over international crimes
law-intl-public.l12.q5.p: A former head of state of State T is visiting State U after leaving office. State U's prosecutors wish to charge him for acts he committed privately before taking office, and for official acts during office. Which analysis is most defensible?
law-intl-public.l12.q5.h: Immunity attaching to the office is different from immunity attaching to official acts.
law-intl-public.l12.q5.e: Immunity ratione personae ends with office, while immunity ratione materiae for official acts can persist, with debate over international crimes. Private acts before office are not covered by either.

law-intl-public.l13.q1.p: Which Article of the UN Charter provides that members must comply with ICJ decisions in cases to which they are parties?
law-intl-public.l13.q1.h: It also allows a party to seek Security Council action if the other fails to comply.
law-intl-public.l13.q1.e: Article 94 contains the undertaking to comply and the route to the Security Council. Article 2(4) concerns force, Article 51 self-defence, and Article 103 the priority of Charter obligations.

law-intl-public.l13.q2.t: States follow common aviation and shipping standards because all benefit from a shared system
law-intl-public.l13.q2.p: Which of the following is the best example of compliance explained by coordination rather than by threat of enforcement?
law-intl-public.l13.q2.h: Think of rules where everyone gains from uniformity.
law-intl-public.l13.q2.e: Technical standards in aviation and shipping work because uniformity benefits all. The other examples involve pressure or sanctions.

law-intl-public.l13.q3.t: The Council may adopt binding decisions on non-military measures such as sanctions
law-intl-public.l13.q3.p: Which statement about Security Council enforcement under Chapter VII is correct?
law-intl-public.l13.q3.e: Chapter VII measures require a determination under Article 39, bind members under Article 25, and are subject to the veto. They do not require unanimity of the Assembly.

law-intl-public.l13.q4.t: The judgment remains legally binding on A, but enforcement through the Council may be blocked by the veto
law-intl-public.l13.q4.p: State A refuses to comply with an ICJ judgment ordering it to return disputed property to State B. B takes the matter to the Security Council under Article 94(2). A's ally, a permanent member, threatens to veto any resolution. Which analysis of the situation is most accurate?
law-intl-public.l13.q4.h: Binding legal status and practical enforcement can diverge.
law-intl-public.l13.q4.e: The judgment stays binding, and the veto can block Council action, a recognised weakness. The Charter does not exclude ICJ matters from the veto, and the judgment does not lapse.

law-intl-public.l13.q5.t: Reciprocity, under which states obey because their own interests are served by mutual observance of the rule
law-intl-public.l13.q5.p: A scholar argues that states mostly comply with the law of diplomatic relations even though no body enforces it, because each state hosts foreign diplomats and sends its own abroad, so breach invites retaliation against its own envoys. Which explanation of compliance is she mainly relying on?
law-intl-public.l13.q5.h: Her point is about mutual exposure to retaliation.
law-intl-public.l13.q5.e: The argument rests on reciprocity: each state's own diplomats are exposed to retaliation. The ICJ lacks compulsory jurisdiction over every state, and the Council does not enforce diplomatic law routinely.

law-intl-public.l14.q1.t: Article 2(4), which bars the threat or use of force against territorial integrity or political independence, or in any other manner inconsistent with UN purposes
law-intl-public.l14.q1.p: Which provision of the UN Charter contains the general prohibition on the threat or use of force between states?
law-intl-public.l14.q1.h: The prohibition appears among the principles in Article 2.
law-intl-public.l14.q1.e: Article 2(4) is the prohibition. Articles 42 and 51 are exceptions or enforcement provisions, and Article 103 concerns priority of obligations.

law-intl-public.l14.q2.t: Mere assistance to rebels in the form of weapons supply or logistical support from another state
law-intl-public.l14.q2.p: According to the ICJ in Nicaragua v. United States (1986), which of the following does NOT by itself amount to an armed attack giving rise to the right of self-defence?
law-intl-public.l14.q2.h: The Court distinguished the gravest forms of force from less grave ones.
law-intl-public.l14.q2.e: The Court held that assistance to rebels such as arms and logistics is not itself an armed attack, though it may be unlawful intervention. Regular forces and armed bands of sufficient gravity do count.

law-intl-public.l14.q3.t: The resolution is adopted because abstention by a permanent member is not treated as a veto under Council practice
law-intl-public.l14.q3.p: The Security Council adopts a Chapter VII resolution with twelve votes in favour, none against, and China abstaining. What is the legal result under Article 27 and Council practice?
law-intl-public.l14.q3.h: Consider how the Council has treated abstentions in practice, a position confirmed by the ICJ in Namibia.
law-intl-public.l14.q3.e: Under practice accepted in the Namibia opinion, abstention does not block adoption. The text requires nine affirmative votes, and no Assembly ratification is needed.

law-intl-public.l14.q4.t: S's response may be lawful self-defence, but T's strike is unlawful because S never requested T's help
law-intl-public.l14.q4.p: State R's forces seize a border village in State S. S, which has not been attacked by anyone else, immediately launches necessary and proportionate counter-operations to recapture the village, and reports its action to the Security Council. State T, an ally of S that has not been asked by S for help, bombs R's capital citing collective self-defence. Using Nicaragua, what is the best analysis?
law-intl-public.l14.q4.h: Collective self-defence has a procedural condition that rests on the victim state.
law-intl-public.l14.q4.e: The Court held that collective self-defence requires the victim's declaration and request. Council authorisation is not required for Article 51, which preserves the right until the Council acts.

law-intl-public.l14.q5.t: V's claim of self-defence is doubtful on the Court's approach, since the attacks were not shown attributable to U, and the Court left wider questions open
law-intl-public.l14.q5.p: Armed rebels operating from State U's territory repeatedly attack State V's border posts. V cannot show that U directed or controlled the rebels, and U's government has not itself attacked V. V's forces enter U to destroy rebel bases. Using the reasoning in DRC v. Uganda (ICJ, 2005), what is the most likely assessment?
law-intl-public.l14.q5.h: Consider what the Court required before accepting a self-defence claim and what it left open.
law-intl-public.l14.q5.e: The Court rejected Uganda's self-defence claim because the attacks were not attributed to the DRC, and expressly left open the wider question. States do not automatically bear responsibility for private groups.

law-intl-public.l15.q1.t: Fifteen members, of which five are permanent
law-intl-public.l15.q1.p: How many members does the UN Security Council have, and how many are permanent?
law-intl-public.l15.q1.h: Five hold the veto and ten are elected.
law-intl-public.l15.q1.e: The Council has fifteen members: five permanent and ten elected for two-year terms. The other figures do not match the Charter.

law-intl-public.l15.q2.t: They are generally recommendations, though internal matters such as the budget are binding
law-intl-public.l15.q2.p: What is the legal effect of most General Assembly resolutions?
law-intl-public.l15.q2.h: The Assembly has no general legislative power, though it has some binding institutional powers.
law-intl-public.l15.q2.e: Assembly resolutions are generally recommendatory, with internal exceptions like the budget. Two-thirds majorities determine adoption on important questions but do not make external resolutions binding.

law-intl-public.l15.q3.t: By decision of the General Assembly on the recommendation of the Security Council
law-intl-public.l15.q3.p: Under Article 4 of the UN Charter, how is a state admitted to membership?
law-intl-public.l15.q3.h: Two principal organs take part, in a set order.
law-intl-public.l15.q3.e: Admission is by the Assembly on the Council's recommendation, so the permanent members can block it. The ICJ and Secretary-General have no such role.

law-intl-public.l15.q4.t: The resolution is not adopted because a negative vote by a permanent member on a non-procedural matter blocks it
law-intl-public.l15.q4.p: A draft Security Council resolution imposing non-military sanctions on State W receives fourteen votes in favour and one vote against, cast by a permanent member. Which statement is most accurate?
law-intl-public.l15.q4.h: Distinguish between procedural matters and all other matters under Article 27.
law-intl-public.l15.q4.e: On non-procedural matters nine votes including the concurring votes of all permanent members are required, so a negative vote is a veto. The Assembly cannot overturn Council decisions, and the abstention duty applies only to Chapter VI disputes in which a member is a party.

law-intl-public.l15.q5.t: Consider the matter and recommend collective measures to members
law-intl-public.l15.q5.p: The Security Council is deadlocked because of a veto when an apparent breach of the peace occurs. The General Assembly meets in an emergency special session under the Uniting for Peace resolution. What may the Assembly lawfully do?
law-intl-public.l15.q5.h: The Assembly may recommend, but its recommendatory character remains.
law-intl-public.l15.q5.e: The Assembly can consider the matter and make recommendations, including on collective measures. It cannot adopt Chapter VII-style binding decisions, abolish the Council or order the ICJ.

law-intl-public.l16.q1.t: Fifteen judges, elected for a term of nine years
law-intl-public.l16.q1.p: How many judges sit on the ICJ, and for what term are they elected?
law-intl-public.l16.q1.h: Election is by the General Assembly and the Security Council voting concurrently.
law-intl-public.l16.q1.e: The Court has fifteen judges with nine-year terms and staggered renewal every three years. The other combinations are incorrect.

law-intl-public.l16.q2.t: The Court lacks jurisdiction unless B consents
law-intl-public.l16.q2.p: State A files a case against State B before the ICJ concerning a boundary. Neither has an optional clause declaration and no treaty between them contains a compromissory clause. B does not appear. What is the likely outcome?
law-intl-public.l16.q2.h: Contentious jurisdiction depends on the consent of the respondent state.
law-intl-public.l16.q2.e: Consent is required. UN membership makes a state party to the Statute but does not itself confer compulsory jurisdiction, and the merits do not decide jurisdiction.

law-intl-public.l16.q3.t: The General Assembly and Security Council, and other organs and agencies the Assembly has authorised
law-intl-public.l16.q3.p: Who may request an advisory opinion from the ICJ?
law-intl-public.l16.q3.h: Article 96 of the Charter limits the right to certain organs.
law-intl-public.l16.q3.e: Article 96 allows the Assembly and Council to request opinions, and authorised organs and agencies on questions arising within their activities. States and private parties cannot.

law-intl-public.l16.q4.t: The judgment binds X, and Y may seek action from the Security Council under Article 94(2)
law-intl-public.l16.q4.p: State X loses an ICJ judgment requiring it to pay compensation to State Y and refuses to pay. Which analysis is most accurate?
law-intl-public.l16.q4.h: Binding force and enforceability are separate questions.
law-intl-public.l16.q4.e: The judgment is binding under Article 59 and Article 94(1), and Article 94(2) provides recourse to the Council, subject to the veto. Judgments are final without appeal under Article 60, and bind only the parties.

law-intl-public.l16.q5.t: M may rely on its own reservation, and on reciprocity N may too
law-intl-public.l16.q5.p: State M has made an optional clause declaration under Article 36(2) excluding disputes concerning its maritime boundaries. State N, which has made a broader declaration, sues M over a maritime boundary. On what principle will the Court most likely decide the case?
law-intl-public.l16.q5.h: Declarations operate on a basis of reciprocity, so each party can invoke the other's limits.
law-intl-public.l16.q5.e: Jurisdiction exists only to the extent the two declarations coincide, and a respondent can invoke its own reservation. The broader declaration does not override the narrower one, and reservations are permitted.

law-intl-public.l17.q1.p: Under UNCLOS, which forum applies by default if the parties to a dispute have not accepted the same procedure under Article 287?
law-intl-public.l17.q1.h: The default is an arbitral procedure, not a standing court.
law-intl-public.l17.q1.e: Annex VII arbitration is the default under Article 287(3) and (5). The Council does not decide such disputes, and the ICJ and ITLOS apply only if chosen.

law-intl-public.l17.q2.t: Complementarity, under which the ICC acts when states are unwilling or unable genuinely to investigate or prosecute
law-intl-public.l17.q2.p: What principle governs the relationship between the International Criminal Court and national courts under the Rome Statute?
law-intl-public.l17.q2.h: The Court is meant to be a court of last resort.
law-intl-public.l17.q2.e: Complementarity means national jurisdiction comes first. The ICC is not an unconditional primary court, can proceed in other ways than Council referral, and does not displace national prosecution of core crimes.

law-intl-public.l17.q3.t: That there was no legal basis for historic rights to resources within the line beyond UNCLOS entitlements
law-intl-public.l17.q3.p: What did the 2016 arbitral tribunal in the South China Sea case (Philippines v. China) conclude about China's nine-dash line claims?
law-intl-public.l17.q3.h: The tribunal proceeded despite China's non-participation.
law-intl-public.l17.q3.e: The tribunal found no legal basis for historic rights beyond UNCLOS entitlements and that features in the Spratlys do not generate an EEZ. China's non-participation did not stop the proceedings under Annex VII.

law-intl-public.l17.q4.t: Q may ask ITLOS for prompt release of the vessel and crew under Article 292 and begin Annex VII arbitration on the merits
law-intl-public.l17.q4.p: State P arrests a vessel flying State Q's flag and detains its crew. Both P and Q are UNCLOS parties, and neither made any Article 287 declaration. Q wants the vessel and crew released at once, and also wants a merits ruling. Which approach is best supported by UNCLOS?
law-intl-public.l17.q4.h: ITLOS has special powers for urgent matters, while the merits follow the default procedure.
law-intl-public.l17.q4.e: Annex VII arbitration is the default for the merits, and ITLOS has special powers on prompt release and provisional measures. The ICJ has no compulsory jurisdiction here, and Part XV does provide procedures.

law-intl-public.l17.q5.t: The ICC may have jurisdiction on the basis of territory, and T's unwillingness genuinely to prosecute would support admissibility
law-intl-public.l17.q5.p: State T is a party to the Rome Statute. A national of non-party State U commits a war crime on T's territory. T declines to prosecute because the suspect is politically connected. Which assessment is most defensible?
law-intl-public.l17.q5.h: Jurisdiction can rest on the place of the crime, and admissibility turns on genuine national proceedings.
law-intl-public.l17.q5.e: The ICC can exercise jurisdiction over crimes on the territory of a state party, and unwillingness to prosecute genuinely supports admissibility. Nationality of the offender is not the only basis, and Council referral is not the only route.

law-intl-public.l18.q1.t: Twelve nautical miles from the baseline, subject to the right of innocent passage for foreign ships
law-intl-public.l18.q1.p: Under UNCLOS, what is the maximum breadth of the territorial sea measured from the baseline?
law-intl-public.l18.q1.h: The Convention fixed one limit for the territorial sea and another for the EEZ.
law-intl-public.l18.q1.e: Article 3 permits a territorial sea up to twelve nautical miles. Twenty-four is the contiguous zone limit and two hundred the EEZ limit.

law-intl-public.l18.q2.t: Sovereign rights over natural resources and jurisdiction over specified matters
law-intl-public.l18.q2.p: What rights does a coastal state have in its exclusive economic zone?
law-intl-public.l18.q2.h: The EEZ is not part of the territorial sea.
law-intl-public.l18.q2.e: The EEZ gives sovereign rights over resources and certain jurisdiction, with navigation and overflight freedoms retained. It is not territorial sovereignty, and it covers more than customs and fisheries.

law-intl-public.l18.q3.t: The principle of the common heritage of mankind
law-intl-public.l18.q3.p: The seabed and subsoil beyond national jurisdiction, known as the Area, are governed by which principle?
law-intl-public.l18.q3.h: Part XI of UNCLOS establishes a distinctive regime.
law-intl-public.l18.q3.e: The Area and its resources are the common heritage of mankind, administered by the Authority. First occupation and equidistance do not apply to the Area.

law-intl-public.l18.q4.t: C's demand is questionable, because Article 17 gives ships of all states innocent passage, which this peaceful transit does not forfeit
law-intl-public.l18.q4.p: A State F warship sails through State C's territorial sea without stopping, uses no force, and conducts no weapons exercises, but it did not notify or seek permission from C. C's coast guard orders it to leave, saying all foreign warships need prior authorisation. Using UNCLOS and Corfu Channel, what is the most defensible analysis?
law-intl-public.l18.q4.h: Article 17 refers to ships of all states, and some states have asserted notification rules.
law-intl-public.l18.q4.e: Article 17 gives all ships innocent passage, and the Court in Corfu Channel supported warship passage through straits; some states require notice or authorisation, which is a recognised controversy. The territorial sea is subject to the right of passage.

law-intl-public.l18.q5.t: The arrest is lawful as hot pursuit under Article 111, because the pursuit began in the EEZ for a violation of C's laws and was uninterrupted
law-intl-public.l18.q5.p: A foreign-flagged fishing vessel is found fishing without a licence 120 nautical miles off State C's coast, in C's EEZ, and flees onto the high seas when ordered to stop. C's patrol vessel pursues it continuously from the EEZ and arrests it 300 nautical miles from the coast. Which analysis is most accurate?
law-intl-public.l18.q5.h: Hot pursuit can begin in the EEZ for violations of laws applicable there.
law-intl-public.l18.q5.e: Article 111 allows continuous pursuit begun in the EEZ for violations of applicable laws. The flag state's exclusivity has an exception, and Council authorisation is not required.

law-intl-public.l19.q1.t: The Trail Smelter arbitration between the United States and Canada
law-intl-public.l19.q1.p: Which arbitration is the classic authority for the customary duty not to allow one's territory to be used to cause serious transboundary harm?
law-intl-public.l19.q1.h: The harm came from fumes drifting across a border in North America.
law-intl-public.l19.q1.e: Trail Smelter held that a state may not permit its territory to be used to cause serious injury in another's territory. Island of Palmas concerned sovereignty over territory.

law-intl-public.l19.q2.t: It is required by general international law where significant transboundary harm is a risk, with content left to national law
law-intl-public.l19.q2.p: What did the ICJ hold in Pulp Mills on the River Uruguay (2010) about environmental impact assessment?
law-intl-public.l19.q2.h: The Court described EIA as part of the duty of due diligence in preventing harm.
law-intl-public.l19.q2.e: The Court found EIA required under general international law for activities risking significant transboundary harm, leaving content to domestic law. It is not limited to treaties or to watercourses.

law-intl-public.l19.q3.t: Through nationally determined contributions prepared by each party
law-intl-public.l19.q3.p: How does the Paris Agreement 2015 primarily seek to reach its temperature goals?
law-intl-public.l19.q3.h: The Agreement shifted away from top-down national targets.
law-intl-public.l19.q3.e: The Agreement relies on NDCs, transparency and the global stocktake. Binding national caps characterised Kyoto for developed countries, and no UN tax or sanctions mechanism exists.

law-intl-public.l19.q4.t: M has breached customary international law, which requires an impact assessment where significant transboundary harm is a risk
law-intl-public.l19.q4.p: State M's government approves a large mine on a river flowing into State N without a transboundary impact assessment and without notifying N, though the mine's discharge may seriously affect N's fisheries. M and N are not parties to any treaty on the river. M says its domestic law does not require an assessment. What is the best analysis?
law-intl-public.l19.q4.h: Consider the prevention principle as stated in Trail Smelter and Pulp Mills.
law-intl-public.l19.q4.e: Prevention and EIA requirements exist as general international law and apply even without a treaty and before harm occurs. The polluter pays principle is a policy principle, not a binding rule fixing compensation.

law-intl-public.l19.q5.t: Treaties that combine clear targets with incentives and assistance can induce broad participation and compliance without central enforcement
law-intl-public.l19.q5.p: A scientist argues that the Montreal Protocol 1987 succeeded partly because of design features such as phase-out schedules, trade restrictions on non-parties and a fund for developing countries. Which general conclusion about environmental treaty design does this example best support?
law-intl-public.l19.q5.h: The features listed are incentives and support, not coercion.
law-intl-public.l19.q5.e: The example suggests targets, incentives and assistance can drive compliance without coercive enforcement. Montreal included differentiated arrangements and did not need universal participation at entry into force.

law-intl-public.l20.q1.t: They are not subject to national appropriation by claim of sovereignty, by means of use or occupation, or by any other means
law-intl-public.l20.q1.p: Which principle in Article II of the Outer Space Treaty 1967 applies to the Moon and other celestial bodies?
law-intl-public.l20.q1.e: Article II bars national appropriation by any means. The UN does not own celestial bodies, and there is no mechanism for dividing them.

law-intl-public.l20.q2.t: The appropriate state, which must authorise and continuously supervise the company's activities on a continuing basis
law-intl-public.l20.q2.p: Under Article VI of the Outer Space Treaty, who bears international responsibility for the space activities of a private company?
law-intl-public.l20.q2.h: The treaty channels responsibility through states.
law-intl-public.l20.q2.e: Article VI makes states internationally responsible for national activities, including private ones, and requires authorisation and supervision. The company alone is not the bearer of treaty responsibility.

law-intl-public.l20.q3.t: Absolute liability, with no need to prove fault
law-intl-public.l20.q3.p: Under the Liability Convention 1972, on what basis is a launching state liable for damage caused by its space object to an aircraft in flight?
law-intl-public.l20.q3.h: The Convention distinguishes between damage on Earth or to aircraft and damage elsewhere.
law-intl-public.l20.q3.e: Article II makes the launching state absolutely liable for damage on the surface of the Earth or to aircraft in flight. Fault is required only under Article III for damage elsewhere, such as in orbit.

law-intl-public.l20.q4.t: The question is unsettled: the treaty bans appropriation of the bodies but is silent on resource extraction, and states disagree on whether owning extracted material is appropriation
law-intl-public.l20.q4.p: A privately owned lunar mining company licensed by State A extracts regolith from the Moon and sells it. State B objects, saying that A's licence amounts to national appropriation, contrary to Article II. State A says it claims no sovereignty and only allows its company to own the extracted material. Which characterisation is most accurate?
law-intl-public.l20.q4.h: The treaty text does not address resource extraction directly, and states have taken different positions.
law-intl-public.l20.q4.e: The treaty does not expressly address extraction, and practice and views diverge. The Moon Agreement has few parties and none of the major space powers.

law-intl-public.l20.q5.t: P may claim against S as a launching state, but only on a fault basis because the damage occurred in orbit
law-intl-public.l20.q5.p: A satellite of State P, launched by a private operator from State Q's territory on a rocket procured through State R, is struck in orbit by debris from a State S rocket stage, and S's fault is shown. Which analysis is most defensible under the Liability Convention?
law-intl-public.l20.q5.h: Damage in orbit engages the fault-based provision, and launching states can include states other than the operator's.
law-intl-public.l20.q5.e: Article III imposes liability based on fault for damage in space, and the Convention's definition of launching state includes states that launch, procure a launch or provide the territory or facility. Absolute liability applies only to damage on Earth or to aircraft.

law-intl-trade-business.l01.q1.t: Not applying a tariff on a bound product above the maximum rate listed in its schedule of concessions
law-intl-trade-business.l01.q1.p: Under GATT Article II, what does a tariff binding commit a member to?
law-intl-trade-business.l01.q1.e: A binding is a ceiling: applied rates may be at or below it but not above it. The member may apply a lower rate than the bound one, so the second option is wrong.

law-intl-trade-business.l01.q2.t: Article III, which requires national treatment for imported products once they have entered the market
law-intl-trade-business.l01.q2.p: Which GATT rule most directly addresses an internal tax that falls more heavily on imported goods than on like domestic goods?
law-intl-trade-business.l01.q2.h: The tax applies after the goods are already inside the country.
law-intl-trade-business.l01.q2.e: Article III covers internal taxes and regulations. Article I is about discrimination between foreign sources, so it would not catch a domestic-versus-foreign tax difference.

law-intl-trade-business.l01.q3.t: A breach of Article I, since the lower rate must be extended to like bicycles from all members
law-intl-trade-business.l01.q3.p: Country A applies a 5 percent tariff to bicycles from Country B, a WTO member, and 9 percent to like bicycles from Country C, also a member, with no trade agreement involved. What is the best analysis?
law-intl-trade-business.l01.q3.h: Staying under the bound rate does not settle the question.
law-intl-trade-business.l01.q3.e: Article I requires immediate and unconditional extension of an advantage to all members. Being below the binding is a different issue and does not cure discrimination.

law-intl-trade-business.l01.q4.t: Whether the products are at least directly competitive or substitutable, which brings the second sentence of Article III:2 into play
law-intl-trade-business.l01.q4.p: Country D imposes an excise tax on imported spirits at a rate double the rate on domestic spirits made from different raw materials, which consumers treat as direct substitutes. D argues the products are not like and no Article III breach exists. Which line of reasoning best tests D's position?
law-intl-trade-business.l01.q4.h: Like products is not the only test in Article III:2.
law-intl-trade-business.l01.q4.e: Article III:2 has two sentences: the second reaches directly competitive or substitutable products taxed dissimilarly so as to protect domestic production. The Article II option is wrong because internal taxes fall under Article III even when collected at importation.

law-intl-trade-business.l01.q5.t: Article XI:1 for the quantitative ban and Article I for the discrimination against F's product alongside other members' goods
law-intl-trade-business.l01.q5.p: Country E prohibits imports of a product from Country F, with which it has no FTA, but allows it from all other members, citing a political dispute. F, a member, challenges. Which claim has the strongest basis?
law-intl-trade-business.l01.q5.h: Two separate GATT obligations are engaged by the same measure.
law-intl-trade-business.l01.q5.e: A prohibition is a quantitative restriction under Article XI and selective treatment violates Article I. Article II is wrong because a ban is analysed as a quantitative restriction, not as a tariff.

law-intl-trade-business.l02.q1.t: Mode 3, commercial presence of a foreign supplier in the territory of the member
law-intl-trade-business.l02.q1.p: Under GATS, which mode of supply describes a foreign bank establishing a subsidiary in the host country?
law-intl-trade-business.l02.q1.h: The supplier sets up a physical establishment.
law-intl-trade-business.l02.q1.e: Establishing a branch or subsidiary is commercial presence. Mode 1 is wrong because there the service itself crosses the border while the supplier stays abroad.

law-intl-trade-business.l02.q2.t: Articles XVI and XVII bind a member only in sectors and modes it has scheduled, under the positive list approach
law-intl-trade-business.l02.q2.p: Why can Country X restrict foreign suppliers in a service sector it did not list in its GATS schedule, without breaching market access or national treatment?
law-intl-trade-business.l02.q2.h: Think of how GATS differs from GATT in who is bound.
law-intl-trade-business.l02.q2.e: Market access and national treatment are specific commitments, undertaken only for what is listed. The second option is wrong because Articles XVI and XVII exist but apply only to scheduled sectors.

law-intl-trade-business.l02.q3.t: It lets a country export medicines made under compulsory licence to members lacking manufacturing capacity
law-intl-trade-business.l02.q3.p: What does Article 31bis of TRIPS, in force since 2017, accomplish?
law-intl-trade-business.l02.q3.h: It fixed the domestic-market limit in Article 31(f).
law-intl-trade-business.l02.q3.e: Article 31bis made permanent the 2003 waiver for export under compulsory licence. The pandemic-vaccine option mixes it up with a different, narrower 2022 ministerial decision.

law-intl-trade-business.l02.q4.t: A likely breach of GATS Article XVII or XVI, because the new rule goes beyond the 49 percent limitation M entered in its schedule
law-intl-trade-business.l02.q4.p: Country M has scheduled national treatment for telecommunications Mode 3 with the limitation that foreign ownership cannot exceed 49 percent. It then enacts a rule requiring foreign operators to be wholly domestic-owned. What is the best analysis?
law-intl-trade-business.l02.q4.h: Schedules fix the maximum level of restriction a member may keep.
law-intl-trade-business.l02.q4.e: A member is bound to the terms of its schedule, and a measure more restrictive than the entry breaches the commitment. The tightening option is wrong because commitments cannot be reduced without the modification procedure in Article XXI.

law-intl-trade-business.l02.q5.t: N is likely in breach of Article 27.1 on fields of technology and of the minimum 20-year term in Article 33
law-intl-trade-business.l02.q5.p: Country N, a TRIPS member, grants patents for all inventions except drug products, which it treats as unpatentable, and offers a 10-year term for the rest. Which statement is most accurate?
law-intl-trade-business.l02.q5.h: TRIPS sets minimums, and exclusions are limited to a short list.
law-intl-trade-business.l02.q5.e: Article 27.1 requires patents in all fields of technology, subject to listed exclusions, and Article 33 sets the 20-year minimum term. The free-to-set option is wrong because TRIPS flexibilities do not extend to removing the minimum standards.

law-intl-trade-business.l03.q1.t: A panel is set up at the second request unless all members, including the complainant, agree not to
law-intl-trade-business.l03.q1.p: What does the negative (reverse) consensus rule mean for establishing a WTO panel?
law-intl-trade-business.l03.q1.h: The respondent can no longer block by simply refusing.
law-intl-trade-business.l03.q1.e: Panel establishment is automatic absent consensus against it. The respondent-consent option describes the pre-1995 GATT practice that the DSU abolished.

law-intl-trade-business.l03.q2.t: Adoption waits for the appeal to conclude, and the Appellate Body lacks the quorum of three members needed to hear it
law-intl-trade-business.l03.q2.p: Why can a losing party stop a panel report from becoming binding by appealing it, as of this writing?
law-intl-trade-business.l03.q2.h: Consider why the body cannot sit at all.
law-intl-trade-business.l03.q2.e: Without a quorum of three members the Appellate Body cannot decide, so the report stays unadopted. The budget option is wrong because the cause is the failure to fill vacancies, not funding.

law-intl-trade-business.l03.q3.t: An arrangement among participating members to use DSU Article 25 arbitration as an appeal stage among themselves
law-intl-trade-business.l03.q3.p: What is the Multi-Party Interim Appeal Arbitration Arrangement (MPIA)?
law-intl-trade-business.l03.q3.h: It works through an existing DSU provision, and only for those who join.
law-intl-trade-business.l03.q3.e: The MPIA uses Article 25 arbitration and binds only participants. The reformed-Appellate-Body option is wrong because the Appellate Body itself has not been restored.

law-intl-trade-business.l03.q4.t: G cannot obtain an adopted report, so it cannot rely on the DSU to authorise retaliation unless H withdraws the appeal or agrees to another route
law-intl-trade-business.l03.q4.p: Country G wins a panel report against Country H, a non-MPIA member, on a subsidy dispute. H files a notice of appeal. What is the position of G?
law-intl-trade-business.l03.q4.h: Think of what the appeal does to the adoption step.
law-intl-trade-business.l03.q4.e: The appeal prevents adoption, and without adoption there is no DSU path to retaliation. The immediate-retaliation option is wrong because Article 22 requires authorisation after an adopted report.

law-intl-trade-business.l03.q5.t: Article 23, which requires members to use the DSU and bars unilateral determinations of breach
law-intl-trade-business.l03.q5.p: Country J wants to retaliate against Country K, which it says breached WTO rules, but has no adopted report. J announces higher tariffs on K's goods to offset the injury. Which DSU provision is most directly implicated?
law-intl-trade-business.l03.q5.h: This provision is the guard against self-help.
law-intl-trade-business.l03.q5.e: Article 23 obliges members to seek redress through the DSU rather than determine breach and retaliate on their own. Article 3.7 is only a policy preference, not the prohibition on unilateral action.

law-intl-trade-business.l04.q1.t: It was applied in a way that amounted to unjustifiable discrimination under the chapeau of Article XX
law-intl-trade-business.l04.q1.p: In US - Shrimp (Appellate Body, 1998), why did the United States measure fail despite falling within Article XX(g)?
law-intl-trade-business.l04.q1.h: The first tier was passed; the second was not.
law-intl-trade-business.l04.q1.e: The measure was provisionally justified under (g) but the rigid, unevenly negotiated application failed the chapeau. The resource option is wrong because the Appellate Body treated turtles as exhaustible.

law-intl-trade-business.l04.q2.t: The respondent member that invokes the exception to justify its otherwise inconsistent measure
law-intl-trade-business.l04.q2.p: Who bears the burden of proving that a measure is justified under GATT Article XX?
law-intl-trade-business.l04.q2.e: Article XX operates as an affirmative defence. The complainant carries no burden of disproving it, so the option placing it on the complainant is wrong.

law-intl-trade-business.l04.q3.t: The listed circumstances are subject to objective review by the panel, though the member defines its essential interests in good faith
law-intl-trade-business.l04.q3.p: What did the panel in Russia - Traffic in Transit (2019) decide about GATT Article XXI(b)?
law-intl-trade-business.l04.q3.h: The words it considers did not remove all review.
law-intl-trade-business.l04.q3.e: The panel held that whether the listed circumstances exist is for objective determination, with deference on the interest itself. The wholly-self-judging reading was the one the panel rejected.

law-intl-trade-business.l04.q4.t: The measure may fit paragraph (b) but risks failing the chapeau for unjustifiable discrimination between countries with the same conditions
law-intl-trade-business.l04.q4.p: Country R bans imports of a pesticide to protect farm workers, and the ban is scientifically supported. R permits the same pesticide from two allied countries while denying it from others, without explanation. Under Article XX, what is the likely result?
law-intl-trade-business.l04.q4.h: The two-tier test looks at both the objective and how it is applied.
law-intl-trade-business.l04.q4.e: Paragraph (b) may be satisfied, but selective permission raises the chapeau problem seen in Shrimp. The design-only option is wrong because the chapeau specifically addresses application.

law-intl-trade-business.l04.q5.t: Health risk can be relevant to likeness, as it affects competition and consumer preferences between the fibres
law-intl-trade-business.l04.q5.p: In EC - Asbestos (2001), France banned asbestos and asbestos products. The complainant argued that chrysotile asbestos fibres and substitute fibres were like products, so the ban discriminated. What did the Appellate Body say about how to assess likeness?
law-intl-trade-business.l04.q5.h: The inquiry asks about competitive relationship, not just chemistry.
law-intl-trade-business.l04.q5.e: The Appellate Body found that the carcinogenic risk could bear on whether products are in a competitive relationship, and then accepted the ban under Article XX(b). The physical-properties-only option is wrong because it rejects that reasoning.

law-intl-trade-business.l05.q1.t: Members adopt a common external tariff and a common commercial policy toward non-members
law-intl-trade-business.l05.q1.p: Which feature distinguishes a customs union from a free trade area?
law-intl-trade-business.l05.q1.h: Think about what happens at the outer border.
law-intl-trade-business.l05.q1.e: A customs union has a common external tariff. The second option describes a free trade area, which keeps separate external tariffs and therefore needs rules of origin.

law-intl-trade-business.l05.q2.t: Goods from outside the area entering through the member with the lowest tariff and then circulating to the others
law-intl-trade-business.l05.q2.p: What problem do rules of origin in a free trade area address?
law-intl-trade-business.l05.q2.h: Each member keeps its own tariff on outsiders.
law-intl-trade-business.l05.q2.e: Rules of origin stop trade deflection by limiting preference to goods with a genuine regional connection. The subsidy option concerns a different set of disciplines altogether.

law-intl-trade-business.l05.q3.t: It is available only if the measure was necessary to form the customs union, which the quotas were not
law-intl-trade-business.l05.q3.p: What did the Appellate Body decide in Turkey - Textiles (1999) about the Article XXIV defence?
law-intl-trade-business.l05.q3.h: The defence has two conditions, one about the union and one about the measure.
law-intl-trade-business.l05.q3.e: The union must satisfy Article XXIV and the measure must be necessary for forming it. The any-measure option fails because Turkey could have formed the union without the quotas.

law-intl-trade-business.l05.q4.t: The bicycles will not qualify for preference, and shipping them to Q under the agreement would be a false origin claim
law-intl-trade-business.l05.q4.p: Country P and Country Q form a free trade area. P imports unassembled bicycle parts from a non-member and assembles bicycles, adding 5 percent of the final value, while the area's rule requires a regional value content of 50 percent. Q has a higher external tariff than P. What is the likely outcome?
law-intl-trade-business.l05.q4.h: Compare the value added in the region to the threshold.
law-intl-trade-business.l05.q4.e: With only 5 percent regional value the stated threshold is not met, so no preference applies. The assembly-qualifies option is wrong because origin depends on the agreement's rule, not the mere fact of assembly.

law-intl-trade-business.l05.q5.t: Article XXIV requires that duties on outsiders not on the whole be higher or more restrictive after formation, and the rise breaches the bindings
law-intl-trade-business.l05.q5.p: A customs union of Countries A and B raises its common external tariff on cars from 10 to 25 percent on formation, though its previous bound rates in the members' schedules were 10 percent. Exporters in Country C object. What is the strongest ground?
law-intl-trade-business.l05.q5.h: The test compares the overall incidence of duties before and after.
law-intl-trade-business.l05.q5.e: Article XXIV:5 sets a ceiling on the general incidence of duties and the compensation procedure in XXIV:6 applies if bindings must be raised. The Article I option is wrong because it ignores that ceiling.

law-intl-trade-business.l06.q1.t: The transaction value, meaning the price actually paid or payable when sold for export to the importing country, with specified adjustments
law-intl-trade-business.l06.q1.p: What is the primary method of customs valuation under the WTO Customs Valuation Agreement?
law-intl-trade-business.l06.q1.h: It starts from what the buyer actually paid.
law-intl-trade-business.l06.q1.e: Transaction value is the first method, and the others are fallbacks used only when it cannot be applied. Deductive value is wrong as a primary method because it applies only after earlier methods fail.

law-intl-trade-business.l06.q2.t: The General Rules of Interpretation apply in order, starting with the terms of the headings and any relevant section or chapter notes
law-intl-trade-business.l06.q2.p: Which is a correct description of how goods are classified under the Harmonized System?
law-intl-trade-business.l06.q2.h: There is an order, and it starts with the text of the heading itself.
law-intl-trade-business.l06.q2.e: The rules apply sequentially with the headings and notes first. The second option is wrong because the system is shared, and its six-digit rules bind parties.

law-intl-trade-business.l06.q3.t: Test whether the relationship influenced the price and, if so, use a fallback valuation method instead of transaction value
law-intl-trade-business.l06.q3.p: An importer buys goods from a related supplier at a price the customs authority considers unusually low because of the relationship. What may the authority do?
law-intl-trade-business.l06.q3.h: Relationship alone is not disqualifying, but influence on price is.
