law-prek2.l09.q1.e: The first step is to stop and use calm words, not to grab or hit.

law-prek2.l09.q2.t: Take turns with the red crayon or use a timer
law-prek2.l09.q2.p: Which is a good idea for solving a crayon problem fairly?
law-prek2.l09.q2.h: The idea has to work for both children.
law-prek2.l09.q2.e: A turn or a timer gives both children a fair chance. The others favor one side or remove the choice.

law-prek2.l09.q3.t: Ask a grown-up to listen to both of you
law-prek2.l09.q3.p: You cannot solve a problem with your friend. What can you do?
law-prek2.l09.q3.e: A grown-up can listen to both sides and help you find something fair.

law-prek2.l09.q4.t: Both listen to each side and help find a fair answer
law-prek2.l09.q4.p: How is a grown-up helping two children solve a problem like a judge?
law-prek2.l09.q4.h: Think about what a fair listener does.
law-prek2.l09.q4.e: A fair helper listens to both sides before helping to decide. A judge does this for bigger disagreements.

law-prek2.l10.q1.t: To protect our heads if we fall
law-prek2.l10.q1.p: Why do we wear a helmet on a bike or scooter?
law-prek2.l10.q1.h: Think of what is inside the helmet.
law-prek2.l10.q1.e: A helmet protects your head. Safety rules work before an accident happens.

law-prek2.l10.q2.t: Stop at the curb, look both ways, and cross with a grown-up
law-prek2.l10.q2.p: What should you do before crossing a street?
law-prek2.l10.q2.h: The first step is to stop.
law-prek2.l10.q2.e: Stopping, looking, and crossing with a grown-up keeps you safe near cars.

law-prek2.l10.q3.t: Go outside with your grown-up and stay out
law-prek2.l10.q3.p: You hear a smoke alarm at home. What is the safest choice?
law-prek2.l10.q3.h: Safety comes first, even before toys.
law-prek2.l10.q3.e: When a smoke alarm sounds, go outside right away and stay out. Toys can be replaced.

law-prek2.l10.q4.t: Accidents happen quickly, and the rule helps before anything goes wrong
law-prek2.l10.q4.p: Why follow safety rules even on days when you feel fine?
law-prek2.l10.q4.h: Think of a seat belt that is already buckled.
law-prek2.l10.q4.e: Safety rules work in advance. A seat belt that is already on can protect you in a sudden stop.

law-prek2.l11.q1.p: Which community helper puts out fires and rescues people?
law-prek2.l11.q1.h: This helper wears a big coat and helmet.
law-prek2.l11.q1.e: Firefighters put out fires and rescue people. They also teach fire safety.

law-prek2.l11.q2.t: A police officer or a worker in the store
law-prek2.l11.q2.p: You are lost in a store and cannot find your grown-up. Who is a safe person to ask for help?
law-prek2.l11.q2.h: Look for someone whose job is to help.
law-prek2.l11.q2.e: A police officer or store worker is a good person to ask. Never go off with someone who asks you to come with them.

law-prek2.l11.q3.t: They help people follow safety rules and help people who need it
law-prek2.l11.q3.p: Why are police officers called "rule helpers"?
law-prek2.l11.q3.e: Police officers help people follow safety rules and help people who are in trouble. They follow rules too.

law-prek2.l11.q4.t: In a real emergency, when someone needs help right now
law-prek2.l11.q4.p: When is it right to call 9-1-1 in the United States?
law-prek2.l11.q4.h: Emergency numbers are only for emergencies.
law-prek2.l11.q4.e: Call only in a real emergency. Calling for fun can keep helpers away from someone who really needs them.

law-prek2.l12.q1.t: Listens to everybody and decides what is fair by following the rules
law-prek2.l12.q1.h: A judge is like a referee.
law-prek2.l12.q1.e: A judge listens to both sides, learns the facts, follows the law, and decides fairly.

law-prek2.l12.q2.p: Where does a judge usually work?
law-prek2.l12.q2.h: Courts are special places with rules.
law-prek2.l12.q2.e: Judges work in courts, which are places where disagreements and laws are handled fairly.

law-prek2.l12.q3.t: Neither plays for one team; both know the rules and try to be fair
law-prek2.l12.q3.p: How is a judge like a referee in a game?
law-prek2.l12.q3.h: Think of who a referee plays for.
law-prek2.l12.q3.e: A referee and a judge do not take a side. They know the rules and try to be fair to everyone.

law-prek2.l12.q4.t: Because a fair choice needs all the facts from everyone
law-prek2.l12.q4.p: Why is it important that a judge listens to both sides?
law-prek2.l12.q4.h: A fair choice needs more than one story.
law-prek2.l12.q4.e: If you hear only one side, you can miss important facts. Listening to both helps a judge be fair.

law-prek2.l13.q1.t: Stay calm and get a grown-up right away
law-prek2.l13.q1.p: A friend falls off the slide and is crying. What should you do first?
law-prek2.l13.q1.e: Get a grown-up right away. Do not move a badly hurt child or give food or drink.

law-prek2.l13.q2.t: "Mia fell off the slide and her arm hurts."
law-prek2.l13.q2.p: You tell a grown-up about a hurt friend. Which message is the most helpful?
law-prek2.l13.q2.e: A clear message tells who is hurt and what happened so the grown-up can help quickly.

law-prek2.l13.q3.t: Stay near your friend and say, "A grown-up is coming."
law-prek2.l13.q3.p: While you wait for a grown-up to come, what is a kind thing you can do?
law-prek2.l13.q3.h: Kind words can help your friend feel safer.
law-prek2.l13.q3.e: Staying nearby and speaking kindly helps your friend feel safe while help is on the way.

law-prek2.l13.q4.t: Call 9-1-1 in the United States, say what happened, and stay on the phone
law-prek2.l13.q4.p: A grown-up at home is sick, cannot wake up, and no other grown-up is there. What is the best thing to do if you know how?
law-prek2.l13.q4.h: The helper on the phone will tell you what to do.
law-prek2.l13.q4.e: This is a real emergency. Call the emergency number, say what happened, and follow the helper's directions. Do not give medicine.

law-prek2.l14.q1.t: You. Your body belongs to you.
law-prek2.l14.q1.e: Your body belongs to you. Nobody should hurt you or touch your private parts in ways that make you feel unsafe.

law-prek2.l14.q2.t: A parent, teacher, school counselor or relative who cares about you
law-prek2.l14.q2.p: Who is a trusted grown-up you could tell?
law-prek2.l14.q2.h: Trusted grown-ups care about your safety.
law-prek2.l14.q2.e: A trusted grown-up cares about you and will help you stay safe. A new stranger who asks for secrets is not one.

law-prek2.l14.q3.t: Tell a trusted grown-up, even if you were asked not to
law-prek2.l14.q3.p: Someone asks you to keep a secret that makes you feel yucky and scared. What should you do?
law-prek2.l14.q3.h: Some secrets are not safe to keep.
law-prek2.l14.q3.e: A secret that makes you feel scared or uncomfortable should be told to a trusted grown-up. You will not be in trouble.

law-prek2.l14.q4.t: Keep telling another trusted grown-up until someone helps
law-prek2.l14.q4.p: You told one grown-up that you felt unsafe, but they did not listen. What is the best next step?
law-prek2.l14.q4.e: If the first person does not help, tell another trusted grown-up. It is never your fault, and someone should listen.

law-profresp.l01.q1.t: The state's highest court, acting through its power over admission and discipline
law-profresp.l01.q1.p: Which body has primary authority to adopt and enforce rules of professional conduct for lawyers in a given state?
law-profresp.l01.q1.h: The ABA only proposes model rules.
law-profresp.l01.q1.e: State supreme courts regulate their own bar, and ABA models bind no one until adopted. Legislatures may pass related statutes but the courts typically hold the core power.

law-profresp.l01.q2.t: Black-letter rules with explanatory comments replaced the Canons, Ethical Considerations and Disciplinary Rules
law-profresp.l01.q2.p: How does the 1983 ABA Model Rules format differ from the earlier 1969 Model Code of Professional Responsibility?
law-profresp.l01.q2.h: Think about what replaced the three-tier structure.
law-profresp.l01.q2.e: The Model Rules use numbered rules followed by comments. The Model Code had Canons, aspirational Ethical Considerations and mandatory Disciplinary Rules.

law-profresp.l01.q3.t: It should not by itself create a cause of action, though it may be evidence of the standard of care
law-profresp.l01.q3.p: A lawyer's breach of a Model Rule is most accurately described, in the Scope section of the Rules, as having what effect on civil liability?
law-profresp.l01.q3.h: The Rules are designed for discipline, not tort law.
law-profresp.l01.q3.e: The Scope states the Rules are not designed to be a basis for civil liability, but courts often use them as evidence. Negligence per se is a different doctrine and is generally rejected.

law-profresp.l01.q4.t: The rules of the place where the conduct predominantly occurred, with a safe harbor for reasonable belief in the rules of predominant effect
law-profresp.l01.q4.p: A New York lawyer represents a Texas client in a transaction negotiated and papered in Ohio with no tribunal involved. A disciplinary complaint arises over a conflict. Under Rule 8.5 which standard most likely applies to the lawyer's conduct?
law-profresp.l01.q4.h: There is no tribunal, so the first branch of the choice-of-law rule does not apply.
law-profresp.l01.q4.e: Rule 8.5(b)(2) applies the law of the place of predominant conduct, with a safe harbor. The home state keeps disciplinary authority but does not necessarily supply the standard, and there is no national binding code.

law-profresp.l01.q5.t: They are independent: each has its own standard, decision-maker and remedy, so outcomes can differ
law-profresp.l01.q5.p: Attorney Reed misses a limitations deadline. The client suffers a loss, sues for malpractice and also files a grievance. A judge also considers disqualifying Reed in a related pending matter. Which statement correctly describes how these mechanisms relate?
law-profresp.l01.q5.e: Discipline protects the public and profession, malpractice compensates the client and disqualification protects the process. A discipline finding is not automatically binding as malpractice, and none is a precondition for the others.

law-profresp.l02.q1.t: The client, after consulting with the lawyer
law-profresp.l02.q1.p: Under Rule 1.2, who ordinarily decides whether a criminal defendant will plead guilty?
law-profresp.l02.q1.h: It is a decision about objectives, not tactics.
law-profresp.l02.q1.e: Plea, jury waiver and whether to testify belong to the client. The lawyer advises. Strategy and tactics are generally for the lawyer after consultation.

law-profresp.l02.q2.t: The stranger reasonably relied on legal advice that the lawyer chose to give, so a relationship may be implied by conduct
law-profresp.l02.q2.p: A lawyer meets a stranger at a party who describes a possible injury claim. The lawyer says, "I doubt there's a case," and the stranger drops the matter and misses the limitations period. What is the strongest argument that the lawyer owes a duty?
law-profresp.l02.q2.e: A relationship can arise by conduct where the person reasonably relies on advice. Nothing in this fact pattern involves a writing or payment, and neither is required.

law-profresp.l02.q3.t: Settle the lawsuit for an amount the lawyer thinks is too low
law-profresp.l02.q3.p: Which instruction by a client should a lawyer follow because it concerns the objectives of the representation, even if the lawyer considers it unwise?
law-profresp.l02.q3.h: Which of these is the client's decision rather than the lawyer's?
law-profresp.l02.q3.e: Whether to settle is the client's decision. The other options are tactical or administrative and are normally the lawyer's after consultation.

law-profresp.l02.q4.t: Maintain a normal relationship, assess capacity himself, and follow Martha's instructions unless there is a reasonable belief of incapacity with risk of substantial harm
law-profresp.l02.q4.p: A lawyer represents Martha, 84, who is mildly forgetful but clearly explains that she wants to give her house to a longtime neighbor rather than her son. Her son tells the lawyer that Martha is "confused" and demands that the lawyer refuse. What should the lawyer do under Rule 1.14?
law-profresp.l02.q4.h: Diminished capacity is not the same as incapacity.
law-profresp.l02.q4.e: Rule 1.14 requires treating the client as normally as possible and acting protectively only upon the stated reasonable belief. A forgetful client who articulates a clear decision keeps autonomy, and the son is not the client.

law-profresp.l02.q5.t: The lawyer is disqualified unless both give informed consent, or the lawyer limited exposure to the information and the firm timely screens
law-profresp.l02.q5.p: A lawyer interviews Kim about a possible suit against Delta Co., then decides not to take the case. Later Delta Co. asks the same lawyer to defend it in the same dispute. Kim had told the lawyer information that could be significantly harmful to her. What is the most likely result under Rule 1.18?
law-profresp.l02.q5.h: Prospective clients get protections even without a retainer.
law-profresp.l02.q5.e: Rule 1.18 bars representation adverse in the same matter where significantly harmful information was received, with limited cures. The absence of a formal relationship does not remove the duty.

law-profresp.l03.q1.t: Agreement by a person after the lawyer has communicated adequate information about the material risks and reasonably available alternatives
law-profresp.l03.q1.p: Which description fits "informed consent" in the Model Rules?
law-profresp.l03.q1.h: Think of the explanation, not the paperwork.
law-profresp.l03.q1.e: Rule 1.0(e) defines informed consent through adequate information about risks and alternatives. A signature or silence by itself is not enough.

law-profresp.l03.q2.t: The lawyer has likely violated Rule 1.4 because the client decides whether to settle and must be told of the offer
law-profresp.l03.q2.p: A lawyer receives a settlement offer on Monday and does not mention it to the client because the lawyer thinks the amount is too low. What is the likely consequence?
law-profresp.l03.q2.e: The client decides whether to settle, so offers should generally be conveyed promptly. A reasonable-client test or a written request is not the standard.

law-profresp.l03.q3.t: She likely violated competence and certification duties and risks sanctions, because the lawyer remains responsible for verifying output
law-profresp.l03.q3.p: A lawyer files a brief with several case citations generated by an AI tool. She did not read the cases. Opposing counsel shows that three do not exist. Which analysis is the most accurate?
law-profresp.l03.q3.e: Lawyers are responsible for what they sign, and comment 8 to Rule 1.1 covers technology. Custom and vendor reliance do not excuse unverified filings.

law-profresp.l03.q4.t: A reasonable probability that the result of the trial would have been different, measured against a strong presumption of reasonable performance
law-profresp.l03.q4.p: A criminal defendant claims ineffective assistance because counsel failed to investigate a witness. Which element must the defendant prove under Strickland that a civil malpractice plaintiff would not describe the same way?
law-profresp.l03.q4.h: Compare prejudice with the case within a case.
law-profresp.l03.q4.e: Strickland requires deficient performance and a reasonable probability of a different outcome, with a strong presumption of competence. Malpractice requires breach, causation and damages, typically by showing the underlying case would have won.

law-profresp.l03.q5.t: Prepare a plan, such as designating another competent lawyer to review files and notify clients
law-profresp.l03.q5.p: According to the Comments to Rule 1.3, what should a sole practitioner do about the risk of his own death or disability?
law-profresp.l03.q5.e: The comment encourages planning, for example designating a lawyer to take over. Retaining files or assuming the duty ends does not protect clients.

law-profresp.l04.q1.t: A contingent fee for representing a defendant in a criminal case
law-profresp.l04.q1.p: Which fee arrangement is prohibited by Model Rule 1.5(d)?
law-profresp.l04.q1.e: Contingent fees are barred in criminal defense and in domestic relations matters contingent on securing a divorce or the amount of support. Personal injury contingencies are standard.

law-profresp.l04.q2.t: In the lawyer's client trust account until it is earned
law-profresp.l04.q2.p: A client pays a lawyer 10,000 dollars as an advance for work not yet done. Where should the money be held?
law-profresp.l04.q2.h: The money belongs to the client until earned.
law-profresp.l04.q2.e: Unearned advance fees are client property and go in trust, though some states allow flat-fee exceptions. Using other accounts risks commingling or conversion.

law-profresp.l04.q3.t: Conversion of client funds, ordinarily treated more severely than commingling even when the client is eventually repaid
law-profresp.l04.q3.p: A lawyer receives a 3,000 dollar settlement check for a client and deposits it into the firm's operating account to cover rent, intending to repay when the next fee arrives. The client is paid two months late. What is the most accurate characterization?
law-profresp.l04.q3.h: Compare mixing funds with using them.
law-profresp.l04.q3.e: Using client money for the lawyer's own purposes is conversion, usually met with severe sanctions. Late repayment does not cure it, and fee-dispute processes do not cover it.

law-profresp.l04.q4.t: The first lawyer can recover the reasonable value of services in quantum meruit, usually payable when the contingency occurs
law-profresp.l04.q4.p: Fiona signs a contingent-fee agreement and later fires her lawyer without cause. The lawyer had worked extensively. Fiona then settles with new counsel. What is the most likely rule on the first lawyer's compensation?
law-profresp.l04.q4.e: The usual rule lets the discharged lawyer recover the value of services, often payable only if the contingency occurs. Full-contract recovery would chill the client's right to discharge.

law-profresp.l04.q5.t: The division must be proportional to services performed or each lawyer must assume joint responsibility, and the client must agree in writing
law-profresp.l04.q5.p: Lawyer A refers a client to Lawyer B in another firm and wants to receive a third of the fee while doing no further work or assuming responsibility. Under Rule 1.5(e), which condition is missing?
law-profresp.l04.q5.e: Rule 1.5(e) allows division between firms only if proportional or with joint responsibility, with written client agreement and a reasonable total fee. Pure referral fees do not satisfy it.

law-profresp.l05.q1.t: Broader, covering all information relating to the representation regardless of source
law-profresp.l05.q1.p: Compared with attorney-client privilege, the ethical duty of confidentiality in Rule 1.6 is
law-profresp.l05.q1.h: One is an evidence rule and the other an ethics duty.
law-profresp.l05.q1.e: Confidentiality reaches all information relating to the representation, even public or third-party information. Privilege is a narrower evidentiary protection.

law-profresp.l05.q2.t: May reveal information to the extent reasonably necessary to prevent reasonably certain death or substantial bodily harm
law-profresp.l05.q2.p: A client tells his lawyer he plans to burn a building next week with people inside. Under Model Rule 1.6(b)(1), the lawyer
law-profresp.l05.q2.e: The Model Rule permits disclosure to prevent reasonably certain death or serious bodily harm. Some states make disclosure mandatory. Waiting until after the fire or a court order is not required.

law-profresp.l05.q3.t: Lawyer may disclose to the extent reasonably necessary to rectify the financial injury resulting from the fraud in which her services were used
law-profresp.l05.q3.p: Lawyer drafts a loan application for her client Orla. After closing, Lawyer learns Orla inflated her income, and the lender has already lost money. Lawyer's services were used in the fraud. In a state following the Model Rules, what is the best description of Lawyer's options?
law-profresp.l05.q3.e: Rule 1.6(b)(3) permits disclosure to prevent, mitigate or rectify financial harm from a crime or fraud in which the lawyer's services were used. It is permissive and limited to what is reasonably necessary.

law-profresp.l05.q4.t: Disclose only what is reasonably necessary to respond to the allegations, preferably under a protective order
law-profresp.l05.q4.p: A client sues her former lawyer for malpractice, alleging that he mishandled her divorce. To defend himself, the lawyer wants to reveal communications from the representation. Which approach is consistent with Rule 1.6(b)(5)?
law-profresp.l05.q4.h: The exception is limited to what is necessary.
law-profresp.l05.q4.e: The self-defense exception is narrow and tailored. It does not authorize a full data dump or public disclosure, and does not require waiver.

law-profresp.l05.q5.t: Reasonable efforts to prevent inadvertent or unauthorized disclosure of, or access to, client information
law-profresp.l05.q5.p: What does Rule 1.6(c) require regarding technology?
law-profresp.l05.q5.e: The duty is reasonable efforts, scaled to sensitivity and risk. It is not a guarantee, and no fixed retention period appears in the Rule.

law-profresp.l06.q1.t: A confidential communication made to obtain legal advice
law-profresp.l06.q1.p: Which is generally protected by attorney-client privilege?
law-profresp.l06.q1.e: The privilege protects confidential communications for legal advice. It does not shield underlying facts or pre-existing documents merely because they were later shown to a lawyer.

law-profresp.l06.q2.t: The cousin's presence likely destroys confidentiality, so the communication may not be privileged
law-profresp.l06.q2.p: A client brings her cousin, who has no role in the case, to a meeting with her lawyer to give emotional support. What is the likely effect on privilege for what is said?
law-profresp.l06.q2.h: Was the third person necessary to the communication?
law-profresp.l06.q2.e: A third party who is not necessary to the consultation generally breaks confidentiality. Family status alone does not make someone an agent.

law-profresp.l06.q3.t: The crime-fraud exception may apply because the client sought advice to further a fraud, even though the lawyer was innocent
law-profresp.l06.q3.p: A corporation consults counsel about drafting a deceptive prospectus, intending to sell securities to unsuspecting buyers. Counsel does not know the plan and drafts the document in good faith. In later litigation the buyers seek the communications. What is the best analysis?
law-profresp.l06.q3.h: Whose purpose matters for the exception?
law-profresp.l06.q3.e: The exception turns on the client's purpose, not the lawyer's knowledge. The client holds the privilege, and work product is not absolute.

law-profresp.l06.q4.t: No waiver, because the disclosure was inadvertent and the holder took reasonable steps to prevent and rectify it
law-profresp.l06.q4.p: Before trial, a litigant produces a privileged memo by mistake in a federal case. The litigant took reasonable steps to prevent such mistakes and asked for the memo back promptly after noticing. Under Federal Rule of Evidence 502(b), what is the likely result?
law-profresp.l06.q4.h: Rule 502 sets a three-part test for inadvertence.
law-profresp.l06.q4.e: Rule 502(b) protects inadvertent disclosure when the holder took reasonable steps to prevent it and promptly to rectify it. Subject-matter waiver is for intentional disclosures.

law-profresp.l06.q5.t: Protects materials prepared in anticipation of litigation and may be overcome by a showing of substantial need
law-profresp.l06.q5.p: Work product protection under Hickman v. Taylor and Rule 26(b)(3) differs from privilege in that it
law-profresp.l06.q5.h: Think about documents prepared for a lawsuit.
law-profresp.l06.q5.e: Work product covers materials prepared in anticipation of litigation, with a substantial-need override for fact work product, and opinion work product receives stronger protection.

law-profresp.l07.q1.t: The organization itself, acting through authorized constituents
law-profresp.l07.q1.p: When a lawyer is hired by a corporation, who is the client under Rule 1.13?
law-profresp.l07.q1.h: The entity is an independent client.
law-profresp.l07.q1.e: Rule 1.13(a) says the lawyer represents the organization. Officers, directors and shareholders are not clients unless separately represented.

law-profresp.l07.q2.t: The control group test, limiting privilege to top management
law-profresp.l07.q2.p: In Upjohn Co. v. United States, the Supreme Court rejected which test for corporate privilege?
law-profresp.l07.q2.h: The Court wanted a broader approach.
law-profresp.l07.q2.e: The Court rejected the control group test and held that communications by lower-level employees to counsel to enable legal advice can be privileged. The privilege belongs to the company.

law-profresp.l07.q3.t: The manager may claim an implied relationship, creating a conflict and risks to the company's privilege control
law-profresp.l07.q3.p: In an internal investigation, a company lawyer interviews a manager, who later says he thought the lawyer was his personal counsel and tells the lawyer a confidential plan. The lawyer gave no warning. What is the most likely consequence?
law-profresp.l07.q3.h: Rule 1.13(f) calls for explaining who the client is.
law-profresp.l07.q3.e: Failure to explain whom the lawyer represents can create claims of an implied relationship. Not automatic disbarment, and the privilege generally remains the company's if properly structured.

law-profresp.l07.q4.t: Refer the matter to higher authority, including the board or audit committee if warranted
law-profresp.l07.q4.p: A company lawyer learns that the CFO is falsifying revenue figures to meet a covenant. The harm to the company would be substantial. The CEO supports the CFO. The lawyer has already raised the issue. Under Rule 1.13, what is the next step?
law-profresp.l07.q4.h: The duty is to report up the ladder.
law-profresp.l07.q4.e: Rule 1.13(b) directs the lawyer to refer the matter to higher authority, up to the highest authority that can act. Reporting out is a later and limited option.

law-profresp.l07.q5.t: They require attorneys appearing before the SEC for an issuer to report evidence of a material violation up the ladder within the issuer
law-profresp.l07.q5.p: Which statement about the Sarbanes-Oxley implementing rules in 17 C.F.R. Part 205 is accurate?
law-profresp.l07.q5.e: Part 205 calls for up-the-ladder reporting to the chief legal officer or CEO and, if needed, the audit committee or board. It does not abolish privilege.

law-profresp.l08.q1.p: Under Rule 4.4(b), what must a lawyer do on realizing that a document was sent to her inadvertently?
law-profresp.l08.q1.e: Rule 4.4(b) requires prompt notice to the sender. Whether to stop reading or return the document is governed by other law and rules.

law-profresp.l08.q2.t: Rule 1.8(b), which bars using information relating to the representation to the client's disadvantage without informed consent
law-profresp.l08.q2.p: A lawyer learns from a client's file that a local parcel will be rezoned for development and buys adjoining land before the news is public. Which rule is most directly violated?
law-profresp.l08.q2.h: Think about exploitation of confidential information.
law-profresp.l08.q2.e: Using client information for personal advantage, particularly to the client's disadvantage, violates Rule 1.8(b). The other rules deal with fees, tribunals and unlicensed practice.

law-profresp.l08.q3.t: The firm likely must act to stop the breach, assess the harm and notify affected current clients, consistent with duties of competence, communication and confidentiality
law-profresp.l08.q3.p: A law firm's server is breached and attackers access files of several current clients. The firm does nothing for a week. Which analysis best fits current ABA guidance?
law-profresp.l08.q3.e: ABA Opinion 483 says lawyers must monitor, stop and remedy breaches and notify clients whose confidential information is affected. Silence is inconsistent with Rules 1.1, 1.4 and 1.6(c).

law-profresp.l08.q4.t: As a likely violation, because Rule 1.6(b)(5) permits only what is reasonably necessary and a public rebuttal rarely qualifies
law-profresp.l08.q4.p: A client posts a one-star review claiming the lawyer ignored her case. The lawyer responds online with details of the legal matter, to show the review is unfair. How would many state bars view this?
law-profresp.l08.q4.e: Self-defense disclosures must be reasonably necessary, and bars have disciplined lawyers for detailed online responses. Posting a review does not waive confidentiality.

law-profresp.l08.q5.t: The misappropriation theory, based on deceptive breach of a duty to the source of the information
law-profresp.l08.q5.p: In United States v. O'Hagan, the Supreme Court upheld liability for a lawyer who traded on confidential information about a client's planned tender offer. Which theory supported liability?
law-profresp.l08.q5.h: The trader owed no duty to the target's shareholders.
law-profresp.l08.q5.e: O'Hagan approved the misappropriation theory: deception of the source of the information supports liability. The classical theory requires a duty to those trading counterparties.

law-profresp.l09.q1.t: there is a significant risk of material limitation from duties to others or the lawyer's own interests
law-profresp.l09.q1.p: A concurrent conflict of interest under Model Rule 1.7(a) exists when a representation is directly adverse to another current client or when
law-profresp.l09.q1.h: The second category concerns limits on the lawyer's independent judgment.
law-profresp.l09.q1.e: Rule 1.7(a)(2) covers material limitation. Previous work for an adversary falls under Rule 1.9, and shared office space or inability to pay is not itself a conflict.

law-profresp.l09.q2.t: Suing a company the firm represents in tax matters on behalf of an unrelated plaintiff in a wage dispute
law-profresp.l09.q2.p: Which representation involves direct adversity to a current client even though the matters are unrelated?
law-profresp.l09.q2.h: Direct adversity does not depend on relatedness.
law-profresp.l09.q2.e: Suing a current client is directly adverse even when matters are unrelated. Parallel representation of aligned clients and positional differences are not direct adversity by themselves.

law-profresp.l09.q3.t: Under the hot potato doctrine, Alpha is still treated as a current client, so the firm is likely disqualified from Beth's case
law-profresp.l09.q3.p: A firm represents Alpha Co. in a patent matter and takes a case for Beth suing Alpha Co. over an unrelated workplace injury. When Alpha objects, the firm promptly drops Alpha as a client and keeps Beth. How will courts most likely treat this?
law-profresp.l09.q3.h: Dropping a client to avoid a conflict does not work.
law-profresp.l09.q3.e: Most courts apply the hot potato doctrine to prevent firms from converting a current client into a former one. Rule 1.9 does not govern because Alpha is treated as current.

law-profresp.l09.q4.t: The lawyer may proceed if she reasonably believes she can represent both diligently and each gives informed consent confirmed in writing
law-profresp.l09.q4.p: Two co-owners of a business want one lawyer to represent both in a lawsuit brought against them by a customer, where their stories align. Which is the best conclusion under Rule 1.7(b)?
law-profresp.l09.q4.h: Think about the four conditions for consentability.
law-profresp.l09.q4.e: Joint representation of aligned co-defendants is often consentable under Rule 1.7(b). It is not forbidden in every civil case, and each client must consent.

law-profresp.l09.q5.t: Representing both the plaintiff and the defendant in the same pending litigation against one another
law-profresp.l09.q5.p: Which of the following is a nonconsentable conflict under Rule 1.7(b)(3)?
law-profresp.l09.q5.h: Same litigation, one client against another.
law-profresp.l09.q5.e: Rule 1.7(b)(3) bars representation involving assertion of a claim by one client against another in the same litigation, regardless of consent. The others may be consentable with informed consent.

law-profresp.l10.q1.t: The former client's informed consent, confirmed in writing
law-profresp.l10.q1.p: Under Rule 1.9(a), whose consent is required for a lawyer to represent a new client against a former client in a substantially related matter?
law-profresp.l10.q1.h: The protected person is the one whose confidences were learned.
law-profresp.l10.q1.e: Rule 1.9(a) protects the former client, who must give informed consent confirmed in writing. The new client's consent is not the relevant one.

law-profresp.l10.q2.t: To isolate the lawyer from the matter and fee so that the conflict is not imputed to the firm
law-profresp.l10.q2.p: What is the point of a screen for a lateral lawyer under Rule 1.10(a)(2)?
law-profresp.l10.q2.e: A screen separates the lawyer from the matter and fees, with notice to the former client. It does not require disclosure of confidences and is not a payment arrangement.

law-profresp.l10.q3.t: It is probably not substantially related, because general knowledge of a client's practices is usually insufficient, but Rule 1.9(c) still bars using confidential information
law-profresp.l10.q3.p: Dana defended Marlow Inc. in a wage case, learned its confidential litigation strategy for handling employee claims, and moves to a firm representing a new employee suing Marlow in an unrelated wage matter with different facts. What is the best assessment?
law-profresp.l10.q3.h: Compare playbook knowledge with matter-specific confidences.
law-profresp.l10.q3.e: General knowledge of a client's approach rarely makes matters substantially related, but the duty not to use confidences continues. The test does not depend on appearing in court or on identical facts.

law-profresp.l10.q4.t: Timely screening of the lawyer, no fee share for her, and written notice to the government agency so it can ascertain compliance
law-profresp.l10.q4.p: A former government lawyer who personally and substantially handled an investigation of Vega Corp. joins a private firm that is retained by a whistleblower against Vega Corp. in the same matter. Which route can allow the firm to proceed under Rule 1.11?
law-profresp.l10.q4.h: Rule 1.11 uses screening and notice to the agency.
law-profresp.l10.q4.e: A former government lawyer is personally barred absent agency consent, but the firm can avoid imputation by screening and notice. The key consent is the agency's, not the private parties'.

law-profresp.l10.q5.t: Requiring the former client to reveal the very confidences it wished to protect in order to prove disqualification
law-profresp.l10.q5.p: In T.C. Theatre Corp. v. Warner Bros., the court's approach to the substantial relationship test avoided which problem?
law-profresp.l10.q5.h: Proving the confidence would require revealing it.
law-profresp.l10.q5.e: The test looks to whether confidences could have been shared, rather than demanding proof of what was said. The other options are not part of the doctrine.

law-profresp.l11.q1.t: the lawyer is related to the client
law-profresp.l11.q1.p: Under Rule 1.8(c), a lawyer may not prepare an instrument giving the lawyer a substantial gift from a client unless
law-profresp.l11.q1.h: The rule carves out one relationship.
law-profresp.l11.q1.e: Rule 1.8(c) excepts lawyers related to the client. Consent alone does not cure a lawyer-drafted substantial gift.

law-profresp.l11.q2.t: Written advice that the client may seek independent counsel, with a reasonable chance to do so, and the client's signed informed consent
law-profresp.l11.q2.p: A lawyer wants to take a 10 percent equity stake in a client's start-up in place of fees. Which step is required under Rule 1.8(a)?
law-profresp.l11.q2.e: Rule 1.8(a) calls for fair terms, written disclosure, advice to seek independent counsel, and informed consent signed by the client. Prior bar or court approval is not required.

law-profresp.l11.q3.t: The lawyer may not accept the settlement for the objecting client without that client's informed consent in a signed writing
law-profresp.l11.q3.p: Three plaintiffs agree to a lump-sum settlement of their combined claims, in which the lawyer has allocated shares. Two clients agree, and the third objects but is outvoted by the others. What is the correct analysis?
law-profresp.l11.q3.e: Aggregate settlements require each client's informed consent in a signed writing. Majority rule and lawyer discretion do not apply, and later court approval is not a substitute.

law-profresp.l11.q4.t: Rule 1.8(f) allows third-party payment only if there is no interference with independent judgment, so the lawyer must follow the client's decisions on settlement
law-profresp.l11.q4.p: A client's employer pays the lawyer's fee and tells the lawyer to push for a settlement the client opposes, saying that otherwise payments stop. Which rule analysis fits best?
law-profresp.l11.q4.h: Who is the client when someone else pays?
law-profresp.l11.q4.e: Third-party payment is allowed only with consent, independence and confidentiality. The client, not the payer, decides on settlement. A blanket bar does not exist.

law-profresp.l11.q5.t: The relationship violates the rule because it did not exist when the representation began, and client consent is not a defense
law-profresp.l11.q5.p: A client, in a family law matter, begins a sexual relationship with her lawyer after the representation starts, and the two had no prior relationship. Which statement is most accurate under Rule 1.8(j)?
law-profresp.l11.q5.h: The exception covers only pre-existing relationships.
law-profresp.l11.q5.e: Rule 1.8(j) bars sexual relations with a current client unless a consensual relationship preceded the representation. Consent or disclosure is not a defense.

law-profresp.l12.q1.t: Automatic reversal without a showing of prejudice
law-profresp.l12.q1.p: In Holloway v. Arkansas, what remedy applied when a trial court forced joint representation over a timely conflict objection?
law-profresp.l12.q1.h: The Court said the harm is difficult to measure.
law-profresp.l12.q1.e: Holloway treats the denial of separate counsel after a timely objection as reversible without proof of prejudice. Cuyler later covered cases lacking objection.

law-profresp.l12.q2.t: Trial courts may refuse a waiver where there is an actual conflict or serious potential for one, even if all defendants consent
law-profresp.l12.q2.p: What did Wheat v. United States hold about waivers of conflicts in joint representation of codefendants?
law-profresp.l12.q2.h: The court has its own interest in the integrity of proceedings.
law-profresp.l12.q2.e: Wheat gives trial courts substantial latitude to refuse waivers. Choice of counsel is not absolute, and refusal occurs before trial, not after conviction.

law-profresp.l12.q3.t: An actual conflict that adversely affected counsel's performance, after which prejudice is presumed
law-profresp.l12.q3.p: Without any objection at trial, Pat and Quinn are represented by one lawyer. On appeal, Pat shows that the lawyer did not offer a plausible defense that would have helped Pat but harmed Quinn. Under Cuyler v. Sullivan, what must Pat show?
law-profresp.l12.q3.h: No objection means the Holloway rule does not apply.
law-profresp.l12.q3.e: Cuyler requires an actual conflict adversely affecting performance, then presumes prejudice. Joint representation alone is not enough, and a judge's refusal after objection is the Holloway situation.

law-profresp.l12.q4.t: Where the testimony relates to the nature and value of legal services rendered in the case
law-profresp.l12.q4.p: Under Rule 3.7, in which situation may a lawyer who is likely to be a necessary witness still act as trial advocate?
law-profresp.l12.q4.e: The listed exceptions are uncontested issues, nature and value of legal services, and substantial hardship. Opposing consent or a colleague's examination are not on the list.

law-profresp.l12.q5.t: The lawyer should have addressed information sharing at the outset, and may need to withdraw if the secret materially limits the lawyer's duties to the other spouse
law-profresp.l12.q5.p: Two spouses jointly retain a lawyer for estate planning. One spouse privately tells the lawyer about an affair and asks that the lawyer not share it with the other, who is making a will based on assumptions about the marriage. What is the sound approach?
law-profresp.l12.q5.h: Joint clients usually cannot keep secrets from each other.
law-profresp.l12.q5.e: Joint representation requires a clear understanding on sharing. When a secret materially limits representation, withdrawal may be necessary, and automatic secrecy or disclosure is not the rule.

law-profresp.l13.q1.t: Directly adverse legal authority in the controlling jurisdiction known to the lawyer
law-profresp.l13.q1.p: Under Rule 3.3(a)(2), which authority must a lawyer disclose to the tribunal if opposing counsel has not?
law-profresp.l13.q1.e: Rule 3.3(a)(2) requires disclosure of directly adverse controlling authority. Persuasive authority and adverse facts need not be volunteered.

law-profresp.l13.q2.t: The lawyer did not violate the Sixth Amendment, because the right to counsel does not include assistance in presenting perjured testimony
law-profresp.l13.q2.p: In Nix v. Whiteside, what did the Supreme Court hold about a lawyer who threatened to withdraw and reveal if the client committed perjury?
law-profresp.l13.q2.e: Nix held that counsel's refusal to assist perjury was not deficient and caused no prejudice. The right to testify does not include a right to testify falsely.

law-profresp.l13.q3.t: Take reasonable remedial measures, including disclosure to the tribunal if necessary, even though the information is otherwise confidential
law-profresp.l13.q3.p: In a civil trial, a lawyer's own witness testifies that a delivery was made on June 1. The lawyer learns from documents that it was made on June 20 and that the witness knows it. The witness will not correct the testimony. What should the lawyer do under Rule 3.3?
law-profresp.l13.q3.e: Rule 3.3(c) overrides Rule 1.6 and requires remedial measures, up to disclosure. Silent withdrawal or waiting for the other side does not meet the duty.

law-profresp.l13.q4.t: She may not refuse to offer the criminal defendant's testimony based only on a reasonable belief that it is false, because the refusal standard is knowledge
law-profresp.l13.q4.p: A criminal defense lawyer strongly suspects, but does not know, that her client's planned alibi testimony is false. Under Rule 3.3(a)(3), what is the lawyer's position?
law-profresp.l13.q4.h: The text carves out the criminal defendant.
law-profresp.l13.q4.e: The reasonable-belief refusal power does not extend to a criminal defendant's testimony. Only knowledge of falsity triggers the duty. Suspicion alone is not enough to disclose.

law-profresp.l13.q5.t: To inform the tribunal of all material facts known to the lawyer that will enable an informed decision, whether or not adverse
law-profresp.l13.q5.p: Under Rule 3.3(d), what is required of a lawyer in an ex parte proceeding?
law-profresp.l13.q5.h: No one else is there to correct the record.
law-profresp.l13.q5.e: In ex parte matters the lawyer must disclose material facts even if adverse. The rule does not require refusing to proceed or favoring the client.

law-profresp.l14.q1.t: A party served with a sanctions motion may withdraw or correct the challenged filing within 21 days to avoid sanctions
law-profresp.l14.q1.p: What does the 21-day safe harbor in Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 11(c)(2) permit?
law-profresp.l14.q1.h: It gives time to fix a challenged filing.
law-profresp.l14.q1.e: The safe harbor allows withdrawal or correction after service of the motion. It is not a delay on sanctions by the court on its own initiative.

law-profresp.l14.q2.t: Rule 4.2, which bars communication about the matter with a represented organization's constituent who supervises or regularly consults with its lawyer
law-profresp.l14.q2.p: A plaintiff's lawyer calls a defendant's supervisor who regularly consults with the company's lawyer about the dispute, without the company lawyer's consent. Which rule is implicated?
law-profresp.l14.q2.h: Think about who counts as represented for an organization.
law-profresp.l14.q2.e: Rule 4.2 reaches constituents who supervise or regularly consult with counsel. Rule 4.3 concerns unrepresented persons, and 3.5 and 3.6 concern judges and publicity.

law-profresp.l14.q3.t: It is likely improper, because paying a fact witness for testimony is prohibited, though reasonable expenses and lost time may be reimbursed
law-profresp.l14.q3.p: A lawyer pays a fact witness 5,000 dollars "for time" so that the witness will be willing to testify for the client. Which analysis is most accurate under Rule 3.4?
law-profresp.l14.q3.e: Rule 3.4 bars inducing testimony with payment contingent on content; reasonable expenses and lost time are allowed. The lawyer cannot make payment depend on a witness being willing to testify.

law-profresp.l14.q4.t: Rule 3.6 and Rule 3.8(f), which limit extrajudicial statements likely to materially prejudice the proceeding or heighten condemnation of the accused
law-profresp.l14.q4.p: After a high-profile arrest, a prosecutor holds a press conference describing the defendant's alleged confession and calling him "a monster." Which rule is most clearly implicated?
law-profresp.l14.q4.h: Think about statements outside the courtroom.
law-profresp.l14.q4.e: Rule 3.6 and 3.8(f) govern extrajudicial statements, with 3.8(f) specifically addressing prosecutors. The other rules address different problems.

law-profresp.l14.q5.t: a substantial-likelihood-of-material-prejudice standard for lawyer speech is constitutional, but Nevada's safe-harbor language was unconstitutionally vague as applied
law-profresp.l14.q5.p: In Gentile v. State Bar of Nevada, the Supreme Court held that
law-profresp.l14.q5.h: The Court split the analysis into two parts.
law-profresp.l14.q5.e: The Court accepted the standard but found the safe-harbor wording misleading as applied, so discipline could not stand. It did not hold speech absolutely protected or categorically bannable.

law-profresp.l15.q1.t: moral, economic, social and political factors that may be relevant to the client's situation
law-profresp.l15.q1.p: Under Rule 2.1, a lawyer advising a client may refer to
law-profresp.l15.q1.h: The rule invites candor beyond narrow law.
law-profresp.l15.q1.e: Rule 2.1 allows lawyers to refer to nonlegal factors. The other options misstate the rule.

law-profresp.l15.q2.t: ordinarily not treated as a statement of material fact, because it concerns a party's intentions about acceptable settlement terms
law-profresp.l15.q2.p: During negotiation, a lawyer states that her client "will not accept less than 800,000 dollars," when the client would in fact accept 600,000. Under the Comments to Rule 4.1, this statement is
law-profresp.l15.q2.h: Conventional negotiating posture is handled specially.
law-profresp.l15.q2.e: The comment excludes estimates of price or value and statements of a party's intentions about settlement from material facts. A fabricated fact such as a competing offer would be different.

law-profresp.l15.q3.t: She may not assist, but may discuss the legal consequences of the proposed conduct with the client
law-profresp.l15.q3.p: A lawyer asked to design a structure for a client says she can set up a series of shell companies so that regulators will not see the client's true ownership, in order to hide proceeds of a scheme that she knows is fraudulent. Which statement is correct under Rule 1.2(d)?
law-profresp.l15.q3.h: Explaining consequences is allowed, assisting is not.
law-profresp.l15.q3.e: Rule 1.2(d) bars assisting known fraud but permits discussing consequences. Disclaiming benefit, warning of risk or a second lawyer's approval does not change that.

law-profresp.l15.q4.t: The lawyer may face discipline and civil liability, since third parties rely on an evaluation that must be honest and based on adequate inquiry
law-profresp.l15.q4.p: A lawyer gives a third-party lender an opinion letter stating that a borrower is validly organized and the loan is enforceable, without reviewing organizational documents, because the client says it is fine. The opinion is false. What is the likely analysis?
law-profresp.l15.q4.h: Third parties relying on the opinion matter.
law-profresp.l15.q4.e: Rule 2.3 and related rules require honest evaluations based on adequate inquiry. Third parties can sue in some circumstances, and client assurance alone is not adequate.

law-profresp.l15.q5.t: Federal law still prohibits the conduct while many states have changed their rules to permit advice on state-legal conduct, and others have not
law-profresp.l15.q5.p: As of this writing, why does the jurisdiction matter for a lawyer asked to advise a client on a state-licensed cannabis business?
law-profresp.l15.q5.h: Federal and state law diverge here.
law-profresp.l15.q5.e: Because of the federal-state divide, state rules vary on whether lawyers may assist with state-lawful conduct. The Model Rules do not settle the matter nationwide.

law-profresp.l16.q1.t: all evidence or information known to the prosecutor that tends to negate guilt or mitigate the offense, unless a protective order relieves the duty
law-profresp.l16.q1.p: Under Rule 3.8(d), a prosecutor must timely disclose to the defense
law-profresp.l16.q1.h: The ethics rule is broader than the constitutional one.
law-profresp.l16.q1.e: Rule 3.8(d) is not limited by materiality or by a request. The constitutional standard in Brady is narrower.

law-profresp.l16.q2.t: Prosecutors have absolute immunity from civil damages under section 1983 for conduct intimately associated with the judicial phase of the criminal process
law-profresp.l16.q2.p: Which holding is correct about Imbler v. Pachtman?
law-profresp.l16.q2.e: Imbler gives absolute immunity for advocacy functions. Buckley later limited it for investigative acts. Immunity does not depend on conviction.

law-profresp.l16.q3.t: The government is responsible for favorable evidence known to police acting on its behalf, and the question is whether its cumulative effect is material
law-profresp.l16.q3.p: A prosecutor, before trial, learns that a police detective has a memo showing a key witness first identified someone else. The prosecutor never sees the memo and does not ask the detective. After conviction, the defense discovers the memo. Under Kyles v. Whitley, which analysis is the best?
law-profresp.l16.q3.e: Kyles imposes a duty to learn of favorable evidence known to those acting on the government's behalf, and materiality is assessed cumulatively. Good faith is irrelevant under Brady.

law-profresp.l16.q4.t: The charging decision is constitutional, because the threat is an accepted part of plea bargaining when probable cause supports the charge
law-profresp.l16.q4.p: After arrest, a prosecutor tells a defendant who has refused to plead guilty to a charge carrying two years that he will add a charge carrying life if the defendant goes to trial, and then does so when he refuses. Under Bordenkircher v. Hayes, what is the most likely result?
law-profresp.l16.q4.e: Bordenkircher upheld the practice where the prosecutor had probable cause and the defendant was free to accept or refuse. It is not vindictive per se.

law-profresp.l16.q5.t: A district attorney's office is not liable under section 1983 for a single Brady violation absent proof of deliberate indifference in training
law-profresp.l16.q5.p: What did Connick v. Thompson hold?
law-profresp.l16.q5.e: The Court said a single violation does not show the deliberate indifference needed for failure-to-train liability. It did not impose strict liability or abolish absolute immunity.

law-profresp.l17.q1.t: there is a rational connection between the applicant's past conduct and present fitness to practice law
law-profresp.l17.q1.p: Schware v. Board of Bar Examiners held that a state may deny bar admission on grounds of character only if
law-profresp.l17.q1.h: It is a due process case.
law-profresp.l17.q1.e: Schware required a rational connection between conduct and fitness. Arrests or associations alone do not suffice.

law-profresp.l17.q2.t: When the lawyer knows of a violation that raises a substantial question about the other lawyer's honesty, trustworthiness or fitness, unless the information is protected by Rule 1.6
law-profresp.l17.q2.p: Under Rule 8.3(a), when must a lawyer report another lawyer's violation?
law-profresp.l17.q2.h: The trigger is knowledge and seriousness.
law-profresp.l17.q2.e: Rule 8.3 requires reporting of known serious violations, subject to confidentiality. Minor suspected violations do not trigger it.

law-profresp.l17.q3.t: The knowing nondisclosure, which implicates Rule 8.1 and honesty, more than the old arrest itself
law-profresp.l17.q3.p: An applicant to the bar lists no arrests, although he was arrested for disorderly conduct ten years ago as a teenager and the charge was dismissed. The board discovers this. Which issue is likely the most serious?
law-profresp.l17.q3.e: Concealment of a material fact can be a more serious fitness problem than the underlying minor event. Questions on forms vary by state, so the question as phrased matters.

law-profresp.l17.q4.t: Due process was likely violated because the lawyer is entitled to fair notice of the charges before the proceedings, in a process that is quasi-criminal in nature
law-profresp.l17.q4.p: A state disciplinary agency charges a lawyer based on a ground that was not stated in the original notice, and the hearing proceeds on that ground. Under In re Ruffalo, what is the best analysis?
law-profresp.l17.q4.e: Ruffalo held that disbarment proceedings are adversary proceedings of a quasi-criminal nature, requiring due process including notice. Amending charges without notice violates it.

law-profresp.l17.q5.t: A mandatory bar may not use compelled dues for political or ideological activity unrelated to regulating the profession or improving legal services
law-profresp.l17.q5.p: What did Keller v. State Bar of California hold about integrated bars?
law-profresp.l17.q5.h: The case limited the use of dues.
law-profresp.l17.q5.e: Keller held that compelled dues may fund regulation and improvement of legal services but not unrelated political activity over members' objection. It did not end mandatory bars.

law-profresp.l18.q1.t: share legal fees with a nonlawyer, subject to narrow exceptions
law-profresp.l18.q1.p: Under Rule 5.4, a lawyer generally may not
law-profresp.l18.q1.e: Fee sharing with nonlawyers is generally prohibited. Hiring paralegals, renting space or advertising are not barred by Rule 5.4.

law-profresp.l18.q2.t: It held that a blanket ban on lawyer advertising of routine services violated the First Amendment, while allowing regulation of misleading ads
law-profresp.l18.q2.p: Which statement about Bates v. State Bar of Arizona is correct?
law-profresp.l18.q2.h: This is the starting point of modern lawyer advertising.
law-profresp.l18.q2.e: Bates struck a blanket ban but preserved regulation of deception. In-person solicitation was addressed in Ohralik.

law-profresp.l18.q3.t: The associate is bound by the Rules, and the supervisor's order is no defense where the violation is clear rather than an arguable question of duty
law-profresp.l18.q3.p: A senior partner tells an associate to file a motion that she knows asserts a fact the associate has seen disproven. The associate files it, saying she was following orders. Under Rule 5.2, how should this be analyzed?
law-profresp.l18.q3.e: A subordinate is not liable for following a supervisor's reasonable resolution of an arguable question, but not for clear violations.

law-profresp.l18.q4.t: The waiting period is likely valid under Went For It, though a categorical ban on targeted truthful mail would be invalid under Shapero
law-profresp.l18.q4.p: A lawyer mails letters to people who were just injured in a train derailment, offering representation. Under Shapero and Went For It, what is the most likely outcome of a challenge to a state rule imposing a 30-day waiting period on such letters?
law-profresp.l18.q4.e: Shapero barred a total ban on targeted truthful mail, while Went For It, 5-4, upheld a 30-day ban on direct mail to accident victims. Mail is not treated as identical to in-person contact.

law-profresp.l18.q5.t: an agreement restricting a lawyer's right to practice after leaving a firm, except for retirement benefits
law-profresp.l18.q5.p: Which of the following does Model Rule 5.6 prohibit?
law-profresp.l18.q5.e: Rule 5.6 protects client choice by barring restrictions on practice. The other arrangements are governed by different rules.

law-profresp.l19.q1.p: Which case held that indigent defendants in state felony prosecutions have a right to appointed counsel?
law-profresp.l19.q1.h: The 1963 case is the best known.
law-profresp.l19.q1.e: Gideon established the right in state felony cases. Powell was a capital case in 1932, and Lassiter and Turner concern civil proceedings.

law-profresp.l19.q2.t: A misdemeanor defendant who receives a sentence of actual imprisonment
law-profresp.l19.q2.p: Under Argersinger and Scott, which defendant has a Sixth Amendment right to appointed counsel?
law-profresp.l19.q2.h: The line is drawn at actual imprisonment.
law-profresp.l19.q2.e: Counsel is required where imprisonment is actually imposed. A fine-only sentence does not trigger the right.

law-profresp.l19.q3.t: Due process does not automatically require counsel, if the state provides substitute safeguards such as notice and an opportunity to show inability to pay
law-profresp.l19.q3.p: A father faces jail for civil contempt for failing to pay child support. The mother is unrepresented and the state has simple procedures. He asks for appointed counsel. What does Turner v. Rogers suggest?
law-profresp.l19.q3.h: The Court looked at circumstances, including the other side's counsel.
law-profresp.l19.q3.e: Turner held no automatic right to counsel where the opposing party is unrepresented and procedures are safeguarded. The Sixth Amendment does not govern civil contempt, and some process is required.

law-profresp.l19.q4.t: The restriction was invalid because it distorted the function of the courts by prohibiting arguments to the judiciary
law-profresp.l19.q4.p: A legal aid group funded by the Legal Services Corporation wants to challenge the validity of a state welfare law on behalf of a client. In Legal Services Corp. v. Velazquez, what did the Court hold about a federal restriction barring such challenges?
law-profresp.l19.q4.h: The Court focused on the role of lawyers and courts.
law-profresp.l19.q4.e: Velazquez struck the restriction as an impermissible limit on the advocacy that courts expect. It rejected an unlimited government-funding rationale.

law-profresp.l19.q5.t: aspire to render at least 50 hours of pro bono publico legal services per year, primarily to people of limited means
law-profresp.l19.q5.p: Rule 6.1 says that every lawyer should
law-profresp.l19.q5.e: Rule 6.1 is aspirational and not a basis for discipline in the Model Rules, though a few jurisdictions require reporting.

law-profresp.l20.q1.t: a lawyer is not morally judged for the client's lawful goals or cause by virtue of representing the client
law-profresp.l20.q1.p: In the standard conception of the lawyer's role, the principle of neutrality means that
law-profresp.l20.q1.h: It concerns accountability for the client's aims.
law-profresp.l20.q1.e: Neutrality separates the lawyer from the client's ends. It does not mean impartiality between the parties.

law-profresp.l20.q2.p: Which thinker defended the lawyer as a "special-purpose friend" who respects client autonomy in using the law?
law-profresp.l20.q2.h: The article is "The Lawyer as Friend."
law-profresp.l20.q2.e: Fried advanced the friend analogy. Simon and Luban were critics of the standard conception, and Wasserstrom analyzed role-differentiated morality.

law-profresp.l20.q3.t: The standard conception says raise the defense, while a contextual approach like Simon's asks whether doing so serves legal merit and justice
law-profresp.l20.q3.p: A lawyer defends a developer who may lawfully use a statute-of-limitations defense against a tenant's valid claim. The lawyer thinks the claim is morally strong. Which pairing of view and conclusion is correct?
law-profresp.l20.q3.h: One view treats role as a license, the other as contextual.
law-profresp.l20.q3.e: The standard conception endorses partisan use of legal defenses. Simon's contextual view asks whether doing so promotes justice. Neither requires disclosure to the opponent.

law-profresp.l20.q4.t: defending a criminal accused against the power of the state than in many civil settings between unequal parties or affecting third parties
law-profresp.l20.q4.p: Luban argues that adversary advocacy is more easily defended when
law-profresp.l20.q4.e: Luban treats criminal defense as the strongest case for partisan advocacy. Civil settings with unequal parties or third-party harm are weaker.

law-profresp.l20.q5.t: the limits of zealous advocacy, including cross-examining a truthful witness and handling client perjury
law-profresp.l20.q5.p: Freedman's "three hardest questions" are meant to test
law-profresp.l20.q5.e: The questions concern cross-examining truthful witnesses, putting on perjury, and advising clients about law that may encourage lies. They do not concern conflicts or fees.

law-profresp.l21.q1.t: a public citizen having special responsibility for the quality of justice
law-profresp.l21.q1.p: The Preamble to the Model Rules describes a lawyer as a representative of clients, an officer of the legal system and
law-profresp.l21.q1.e: The Preamble names the public citizen role. The lawyer is not an agent of the state or an employee of the court.

law-profresp.l21.q2.t: a litigant's chief executive spent very large sums on the election of a justice who then heard the litigant's case, creating a serious risk of actual bias
law-profresp.l21.q2.p: In Caperton v. A.T. Massey Coal Co., the Supreme Court held that due process required recusal when
law-profresp.l21.q2.e: Caperton applies to extreme facts presenting serious risk of actual bias. It does not require recusal for ordinary contributions or the fact of election.

law-profresp.l21.q3.t: The blog post likely violates the rule as a statement made with reckless disregard for the truth, while the brief is protected criticism based on the record
law-profresp.l21.q3.p: A lawyer, losing a motion, writes in a public blog that the judge "is on the take" with no factual basis. Another lawyer writes a brief arguing the same judge showed bias, citing specific rulings and transcript pages. Which analysis fits Rule 8.2(a) best?
law-profresp.l21.q3.h: The rule targets falsity or recklessness.
law-profresp.l21.q3.e: Rule 8.2(a) punishes knowingly false or reckless statements about judges. Honest criticism tied to the record is protected.

law-profresp.l21.q4.t: The ban is likely upheld, as it serves the compelling interest in public confidence in judicial integrity and is narrowly tailored
law-profresp.l21.q4.p: A state bans judicial candidates from personally soliciting campaign contributions but allows committees to do so. A candidate challenges the ban under the First Amendment. Based on Williams-Yulee v. Florida Bar, what is the most likely result?
law-profresp.l21.q4.e: Williams-Yulee, 5-4, upheld a ban on personal solicitation under strict scrutiny. Allowing committees did not defeat the claim of narrow tailoring.

law-profresp.l21.q5.p: Which rule requires a lawyer to withdraw when a physical or mental condition materially impairs the ability to represent a client?
law-profresp.l21.q5.h: It is in the rule on declining and terminating representation.
law-profresp.l21.q5.e: Rule 1.16(a)(2) requires withdrawal in that situation. Rule 1.14 concerns clients, 5.1 supervision and 8.3 reporting.

law-property.l01.q1.t: Pursuit alone, even with a good chance of success, gives no property right; actual capture, mortal wounding or trapping is required
law-property.l01.q1.p: In Pierson v. Post, what did the court hold about a hunter who is pursuing a wild fox with hounds?
law-property.l01.q1.h: Think about what the majority wanted: a bright-line rule.
law-property.l01.q1.e: The court required actual possession, defined to include capture, mortal wounding or trapping. Pursuit that gives only a hope of capture is not enough, which is why the chase did not protect Post.

law-property.l01.q2.t: Ownership is a collection of separable rights such as possession, use, exclusion and transfer, which can be held and transferred separately by different people
law-property.l01.q2.p: Which description best captures the bundle-of-rights picture of property?
law-property.l01.q2.h: Think of a landlord, a tenant and a lender with respect to one building.
law-property.l01.q2.e: The metaphor treats ownership as divisible: a landlord, tenant, easement holder and lender may each hold different sticks. It is not a single indivisible power or a mere privilege.

law-property.l01.q3.t: Ames, because courts may give effect to a reasonable, established trade custom even though it differs from the ordinary rule of actual capture
law-property.l01.q3.p: Whalers in a port have a long-standing custom that the first person to strike and kill a whale owns it even if it sinks and later washes ashore. Ames kills a whale with a lance, and it sinks. Bell, a stranger who knows nothing of the custom, finds the carcass on the beach and sells the oil. Who has the stronger claim?
law-property.l01.q3.e: In Ghen v. Rich the court enforced the whalers' custom in favor of the killer. Bell's argument fails because the custom is a reasonable trade rule that does not depend on the later finder's knowledge.

law-property.l01.q4.t: Orr loses on a first-possession theory because location and marking are like pursuit and do not amount to actual control; Dunn, as landowner, may have a claim against Pike for trespass
law-property.l01.q4.p: Orr and Pike both want a rare orchid growing wild on unfarmed land owned by Dunn. Orr spends a week locating it, marks it with tape, and tells Pike he plans to dig it up the next morning. That night Pike digs it up and leaves with it, while Dunn is away. Orr sues Pike for the orchid. Which analysis is most consistent with the first-possession logic of Pierson v. Post?
law-property.l01.q4.h: Ask who actually possessed the plant, and whose land it was.
law-property.l01.q4.e: Under Pierson, intention and pursuit do not create ownership; actual control does. Pike, who took it, may still be liable to Dunn for trespass. Orr's announced plan, even with labor, is not possession.

law-property.l01.q5.t: The driller owns the oil produced from the well on Lot A, so Lot B's owner has no claim for the drained oil absent a regulatory scheme or other violation
law-property.l01.q5.p: A well driller on Lot A pumps oil from a reservoir that extends under Lot B and drains Lot B's owner of some oil. No statute or regulation applies, and the driller did not trespass underground at the wellbore. Under the traditional rule of capture, what is the outcome of a claim by Lot B's owner?
law-property.l01.q5.h: Think of the fox: who actually captured it?
law-property.l01.q5.e: The rule of capture awards the oil to the one who reduces it to possession through a well on his own land. Modern correlative-rights and spacing regulation limits it, but absent such rules, Lot B's owner has no claim.

law-property.l02.q1.t: Possession without the true owner's permission, judged objectively, regardless of the possessor's state of mind
law-property.l02.q1.p: Under the majority view, what does the hostility element of adverse possession require?
law-property.l02.q1.e: The majority treats hostility as lack of permission. A good-faith mistake and a knowing trespass can both qualify, although a minority of states require good faith or a claim of right.

law-property.l02.q2.t: When the statutory period has run, the owner's right to recover is barred and the possessor's title is recognized, usually confirmed by a quiet title judgment
law-property.l02.q2.p: Which statement about the effect of adverse possession is correct?
law-property.l02.q2.h: It operates like a statute of limitations.
law-property.l02.q2.e: The statute bars the owner's ejectment action and the possessor's title ripens. The owner need not consent and no payment is required in the traditional rule.

law-property.l02.q3.t: Rosa, because her use was actual, open, exclusive and continuous for the period and, being without permission, was hostile despite her good-faith mistake
law-property.l02.q3.p: For eleven years Rosa mowed and planted a garden on a strip that she mistakenly believed to be hers; the strip belonged to Quinn, who knew of the use and never objected. The statutory period is ten years. In a state following the majority view on hostility, who owns the strip?
law-property.l02.q3.h: The majority test for hostility is objective.
law-property.l02.q3.e: Under the majority view the possessor's state of mind is irrelevant. Knowledge and failure to object is not permission; the owner must grant it. Mere silence does not defeat hostility.

law-property.l02.q4.t: Tacking is allowed because Gil and Ines are in privity through the voluntary transfer of the land Gil occupied, so the periods combine to eleven years
law-property.l02.q4.p: Gil adversely possessed part of Hart's land for six years. Gil then sold his house and the disputed strip to Ines, who occupied for another five years; the statutory period is ten years. Gil's deed to Ines described only the house lot, not the strip. Ines sues to quiet title in the strip. Which argument is strongest for Ines?
law-property.l02.q4.e: Courts permit tacking where successive possessors are in privity, and a transfer of the occupied land satisfies it even when the deed omits the strip, as Howard v. Kunto held. The periods combine to eleven years.

law-property.l02.q5.t: Title to the life estate only, since the clock does not run against the remainderman until the remainder becomes possessory on Farmer's death
law-property.l02.q5.p: Farmer holds a life estate in Greenacre, with a remainder to Niece. Neighbor enters and adversely possesses the whole of Greenacre for the full statutory period, which expires in the year Farmer is still alive. What does Neighbor most likely acquire?
law-property.l02.q5.h: When may the holder of a future interest sue?
law-property.l02.q5.e: The limitation period does not run against Niece until her interest is possessory. Neighbor can acquire only what the life tenant could have lost, which is the life estate, measured by Farmer's life.

law-property.l03.q1.p: Which set lists the three elements generally required for a valid inter vivos gift?
law-property.l03.q1.e: A gift requires present donative intent, delivery, and acceptance, which is presumed for beneficial gifts. Consideration is not needed.

law-property.l03.q2.t: The gift is revoked by operation of law and the donor may reclaim the property
law-property.l03.q2.p: What happened to the gift in a gift causa mortis if the donor recovers from the illness that prompted it?
law-property.l03.q2.h: It is conditioned on imminent death.
law-property.l03.q2.e: A causa mortis gift is made in contemplation of imminent death and is revocable. If the donor survives the peril, it fails.

law-property.l03.q3.t: The nephew prevails because the letter showed present intent to give a remainder in the painting, which passed without physical delivery, subject to Farah's life interest
law-property.l03.q3.p: Farah hands her nephew a sealed envelope containing a letter that says, "I give you my painting now, but I will keep it hanging in my home as long as I live." Farah keeps the painting until she dies. The nephew claims it from her estate. What is the likely result?
law-property.l03.q3.e: Gruen v. Gruen treated such a letter as a present gift of a remainder, with delivery satisfied by the letter. The retained life interest did not make it testamentary because the donor expressed present intent.

law-property.l03.q4.t: The bracelet is mislaid, not lost, so the owner of the premises is the custodian for the true owner and keeps it against the finder
law-property.l03.q4.p: Dev finds a gold bracelet in the public area of a store, behind a display, apparently placed there and then forgotten. He hands it to the manager and later asks that, if nobody claims it, it be given to him. The store refuses. In most states, what is the strongest argument for the store?
law-property.l03.q4.h: Consider how the item came to be placed.
law-property.l03.q4.e: Mislaid property is intentionally placed and forgotten, and the premises owner is the likely custodian for the owner. The rule depends on classification; if the bracelet were lost, Dev would likely prevail against the store.

law-property.l03.q5.t: The finder has title good against everyone except the true owner, so he may recover the value of the stones from the jeweler
law-property.l03.q5.p: A boy finds a jewel on the street and takes it to a jeweler for appraisal; the jeweler's apprentice removes the stones and returns the empty setting. No true owner appears. Under Armory v. Delamirie, what is the best statement of the finder's rights?
law-property.l03.q5.h: A finder is superior to everyone but the owner.
law-property.l03.q5.e: The case held that the finder's possession gave him title adequate to sue the goldsmith. The true owner would prevail, but a wrongdoer cannot defend by pointing to a stranger.

law-property.l04.q1.t: "To the School Board so long as the land is used for a school"
law-property.l04.q1.p: Which language most likely creates a fee simple determinable?
law-property.l04.q1.h: Durational words end the estate automatically.
law-property.l04.q1.e: So long as is durational language, and the estate ends automatically with a possibility of reverter in the grantor. The second is a condition subsequent, the fourth an executory limitation.

law-property.l04.q2.t: The possibility of reverter takes effect automatically when the event occurs; the right of entry requires the holder to act to terminate the estate by asserting the right
law-property.l04.q2.p: What is the main difference between a possibility of reverter and a right of entry?
law-property.l04.q2.h: One is automatic, one is not.
law-property.l04.q2.e: A determinable fee ends automatically leaving a possibility of reverter; a fee subject to condition subsequent continues until the holder of the right of entry acts. Neither is generally subject to the common law RAP.

law-property.l04.q3.t: It holds an executory interest, and its interest becomes possessory automatically on the event, cutting short Library's estate
law-property.l04.q3.p: O conveys Blackacre "to Library, but if alcohol is ever served on the premises, then to the Garden Society." Library serves wine at a fundraiser. What interest does Garden Society hold, and what happens?
law-property.l04.q3.h: The gift over goes to a third party, not the grantor.
law-property.l04.q3.e: When an estate is cut short in favor of a third party, the third party's interest is an executory interest. Possibility of reverter and right of entry belong only to the grantor.

law-property.l04.q4.t: Brin can seek relief for permissive waste for the neglect and unpaid taxes, since the life tenant must pay carrying charges up to the income from the property
law-property.l04.q4.p: O conveys "to Alma for life." Alma, a life tenant, stops paying the property taxes, though the land produces rent income that exceeds the tax bill, and neglects the roof. Brin holds a vested remainder. Which claim by Brin is most likely to succeed?
law-property.l04.q4.h: Think about what a life tenant owes the future interest holder.
law-property.l04.q4.e: A life tenant who allows the property to deteriorate or does not pay taxes within the income commits permissive waste. Brin may sue for relief during the life estate to protect the value of the remainder.

law-property.l04.q5.t: Dara holds a fee simple subject to a condition subsequent; the estate did not end automatically, and O's right of entry requires O to act
law-property.l04.q5.p: O conveys "to Dara and her heirs, but if the land is ever used for a tavern, O may re-enter and retake the estate." Years later Dara opens a tavern, and O does nothing for several years while Dara continues. How should the interests be classified?
law-property.l04.q5.h: Look at the words but if and may re-enter.
law-property.l04.q5.e: But if with a power to re-enter is a condition subsequent. The estate continues until O exercises the power; the words and her heirs are words of limitation creating the fee simple.

law-property.l05.q1.p: What does a grantor hold after conveying "to A for life" with no further disposition?
law-property.l05.q1.h: The fee comes back to the grantor.
law-property.l05.q1.e: The grantor carves a shorter estate from a larger one and keeps the rest, which is a reversion. It is not an interest in a transferee and does not require a condition.

law-property.l05.q2.t: It is created in an unascertained person or is subject to a condition precedent
law-property.l05.q2.h: Who is to take, and on what condition?
law-property.l05.q2.e: A remainder is contingent if the taker is unascertained or if a condition precedent must be satisfied. It is not contingent merely because it is a remainder after a life estate.

law-property.l05.q3.t: A has a life estate, B has a contingent remainder, and O has a reversion
law-property.l05.q3.p: O conveys "to A for life, then to B if B survives A." Immediately after the conveyance, who holds which interests?
law-property.l05.q3.e: B's remainder depends on surviving A, so it is a contingent remainder. Because it may fail, O keeps a reversion. A shifting or springing executory interest would require cutting short another estate.

law-property.l05.q4.t: A vested remainder subject to open: Ben holds a vested interest that will be shared with after-born children of A
law-property.l05.q4.p: O conveys "to A for life, then to A's children." At the time of the conveyance A has one child, Ben, and may have more. Which classification is best for the children's interest, and what is the effect of Ben's birth?
law-property.l05.q4.h: At least one member of the class is ascertained.
law-property.l05.q4.e: When at least one class member exists and others may be added, the remainder is vested subject to open. The unborn members do not make it contingent, and the interest is not an executory interest because it takes only on the natural end of A's estate.

law-property.l05.q5.t: A springing executory interest, with O holding a reversion during the gap
law-property.l05.q5.p: O conveys "to A for life, then to B and her heirs one year after A's death." No one is given the land during the gap. After the conveyance, which interest does B hold?
law-property.l05.q5.h: Is there a gap between the end of the life estate and B's possession?
