law-property.l05.q5.e: A remainder must take immediately on the natural end of the prior estate. A gap means the interest cuts short the grantor's retained fee, so it is a springing executory interest.

law-property.l06.q1.t: No interest is good unless it must vest, if at all, not later than twenty-one years after some life in being at the creation of the interest
law-property.l06.q1.p: Which formulation states the classic common law Rule Against Perpetuities?
law-property.l06.q1.h: Lives in being plus twenty-one years.
law-property.l06.q1.e: This is the Gray formulation. The ninety-year period belongs to the Uniform Statutory Rule's wait-and-see alternative, and the rule concerns vesting, not possession.

law-property.l06.q2.t: A reversion retained by the grantor
law-property.l06.q2.p: Which of these interests is NOT subject to the common law Rule Against Perpetuities?
law-property.l06.q2.h: Interests retained by the transferor are exempt at common law.
law-property.l06.q2.e: Reversions, possibilities of reverter and rights of entry are generally exempt. The other three can vest too late.

law-property.l06.q3.t: It judges validity by what actually happens over a statutory period, not by what might happen at creation
law-property.l06.q3.p: What approach does a wait-and-see statute take?
law-property.l06.q3.e: Wait-and-see looks at actual events during the period; for example, the Uniform Statutory Rule allows ninety years. It does not abolish duration limits, but it prevents interests from failing on remote possibilities.

law-property.l06.q4.t: The gift to Sam's children who are living at the widow's death, because Sam could marry someone not yet born and the widow may outlive all lives in being by more than twenty-one years
law-property.l06.q4.p: O conveys land "to my son Sam for life, then to Sam's widow for her life, then to Sam's children who are then living." Under the traditional common law rule, which interest is most vulnerable?
law-property.l06.q4.e: At creation Sam's eventual spouse is not a life in being if Sam marries a person not yet born, and her life may extend beyond all lives in being plus twenty-one years. The gift to the children is therefore void under the what-might-happen test.

law-property.l06.q5.t: It is void, because A could have another child after the conveyance, and that child could have a child who reaches 25 more than 21 years after all lives in being are gone
law-property.l06.q5.p: O conveys land "to A for life, then to such of A's grandchildren as reach age 25." At O's death A has two children and no grandchildren, and A is alive. Under the traditional rule applied at creation, what is the best analysis of the grandchildren's interest?
law-property.l06.q5.h: Can A have an after-born child?
law-property.l06.q5.e: A's unborn child is not a life in being. That child's children could reach twenty-five too late, so the class gift cannot be guaranteed to vest in time. Wait-and-see or reform could save it.

law-property.l07.q1.p: What is the key feature that distinguishes a joint tenancy from a tenancy in common?
law-property.l07.q1.h: What happens when one owner dies?
law-property.l07.q1.e: Joint tenants have survivorship, so the survivors take the deceased's interest. Tenants in common may leave their shares by will. Both can generally seek partition.

law-property.l07.q2.t: The unities of time and title as to the conveyed interest
law-property.l07.q2.p: Which of the four unities is destroyed when a joint tenant conveys her interest to a stranger?
law-property.l07.q2.h: The buyer acquires at a different time and by a different instrument.
law-property.l07.q2.e: The stranger takes at a different time and by a different deed, so that share is held as a tenancy in common. The remaining joint tenants stay joint between themselves.

law-property.l07.q3.t: C owns two-thirds and D owns one-third, as tenants in common
law-property.l07.q3.p: A, B and C hold as joint tenants. A conveys her interest to D. Later B dies, leaving everything to his spouse by will. Who owns Blackacre?
law-property.l07.q3.e: A's conveyance severed as to her third only, so D is a tenant in common of that third. B and C remained joint tenants, so B's death gives B's third to C, who holds two-thirds. The will does not affect joint tenancy property.

law-property.l07.q4.t: Lena cannot recover rent from Kai for mere occupancy absent ouster, but can claim a share of the rent that Mia collected from the stranger
law-property.l07.q4.p: Two siblings, Kai and Lena, own a house as tenants in common. Kai lives in it and refuses to let Lena move in but does not change the locks. Lena sues Kai for half the fair rental value. Another cotenant, Mia, has rented the garage to a stranger and collected rent. What is the most likely result in the majority view?
law-property.l07.q4.e: A cotenant in possession owes no rent absent ouster, but rents collected from third parties must be shared after expenses. Merely refusing to let a cotenant in, without exclusion, does not amount to ouster.

law-property.l07.q5.t: The creditor generally cannot reach the entireties property while both spouses are alive, because neither spouse can convey or encumber it alone
law-property.l07.q5.p: Husband and Wife hold land as tenants by the entirety in a state that recognizes it. Husband alone borrows money, and his creditor obtains a judgment against him only. Which statement is most accurate?
law-property.l07.q5.e: The entireties form protects against the separate creditors of one spouse in states that retain it. Its protection ends on divorce, but the creditor cannot reach it while the marriage continues and both are alive.

law-property.l08.q1.p: Which leasehold estate ends automatically at a fixed date without notice?
law-property.l08.q1.h: It has a stated end date.
law-property.l08.q1.e: A term of years has a definite beginning and end and ends without notice. The periodic tenancy renews and the others depend on either party or on the tenant's wrongful holding.

law-property.l08.q2.t: Claim constructive eviction and possibly damages for breach of the implied warranty of habitability
law-property.l08.q2.p: In most states, what is the tenant's remedy when a landlord leaves the heat out for months in winter and the tenant moves out after a reasonable period?
law-property.l08.q2.h: Substantial interference plus leaving within a reasonable time.
law-property.l08.q2.e: Constructive eviction requires a substantial interference attributable to the landlord, notice, and vacating within a reasonable time. The warranty of habitability also supports damages or rent relief.

law-property.l08.q3.t: The landlord can recover only the rent less what could reasonably have been obtained by reletting, because the landlord must mitigate
law-property.l08.q3.p: Tess leases an apartment for two years. After a year she leaves and moves away without notice, and the landlord makes no effort to relet. The jurisdiction follows the majority modern rule. What is the likely outcome of the landlord's suit for the remaining rent?
law-property.l08.q3.e: In the modern majority, a landlord must make reasonable efforts to relet. Some states, treating a lease as a conveyance, still let the landlord leave the unit vacant and sue.

law-property.l08.q4.t: The landlord loses against Subtenant because a sublease creates privity of neither estate nor contract between landlord and subtenant, so the landlord must sue Lessee
law-property.l08.q4.p: Lessee leases a store to Subtenant for the last six months of Lessee's five-year term, which still has two years to run. Subtenant stops paying rent. The landlord sues Subtenant directly for rent. What is the most likely result?
law-property.l08.q4.h: Compare an assignment with a sublease.
law-property.l08.q4.e: Lessee kept a reversion by subleasing for less than the entire remaining term, so this is a sublease. The sublessee owes rent to Lessee, and the landlord looks to Lessee.

law-property.l08.q5.t: The eviction is retaliatory and barred by statute or case law in most states, which gives the tenant a defense even though notice would otherwise suffice
law-property.l08.q5.p: A tenant complains to the city housing inspector about severe code violations in her apartment. Two weeks later the landlord serves a notice to quit for no stated reason. Month-to-month tenancies are normally terminable by notice. Which argument is strongest for the tenant?
law-property.l08.q5.h: Think about public policy and protected complaints.
law-property.l08.q5.e: Retaliatory eviction doctrines protect tenants who report violations. The landlord's usual power to end a periodic tenancy does not extend to retaliation.

law-property.l09.q1.t: An appurtenant easement benefits the owner of a particular parcel and passes with it; an easement in gross benefits a person regardless of land ownership
law-property.l09.q1.p: What is the difference between an easement appurtenant and an easement in gross?
law-property.l09.q1.e: An appurtenant easement attaches to the dominant estate and runs with it. An easement in gross serves a person or entity, like a utility, without a dominant parcel.

law-property.l09.q2.t: Permission given orally to a neighbor to park a car on a lot, revocable at will
law-property.l09.q2.p: Which of the following is a license and not an easement?
law-property.l09.q2.h: Which one is personal and revocable?
law-property.l09.q2.e: A license is permission, revocable at will and not an interest in land. The others are easements by express grant, prescription, and necessity.

law-property.l09.q3.t: Easement implied from prior use, because the use was apparent, continuous and reasonably necessary when the lots were divided
law-property.l09.q3.p: Orla owns two lots. For years a visible gravel driveway across Lot 1 has been the only convenient access to Lot 2. She sells Lot 2 to Pim; the deed says nothing about the driveway. Orla later blocks it. What is Pim's best theory?
law-property.l09.q3.h: Look at use before the severance.
law-property.l09.q3.e: Apparent, continuous and reasonably necessary use before the split supports an implied easement. Pim's own use has not run the period, and necessity requires strict necessity, which is less clear when other access might exist.

law-property.l09.q4.t: The easement by necessity ended when the necessity ended, so the landowner may block the path
law-property.l09.q4.p: A landowner conveys the back half of his land to Quinn, which has no road access, and keeps the front. Years later a new public road is built along the back boundary of Quinn's lot, giving direct access. The landowner then blocks the old path across the front lot. What is the best result?
law-property.l09.q4.h: Necessity is the basis of the right.
law-property.l09.q4.e: An easement by necessity lasts only as long as the necessity. Once Quinn has other access, the easement ends. Nonuse alone is not abandonment, but here the basis disappeared.

law-property.l09.q5.t: The owner of B may enjoin the use to serve Parcel C, since an easement appurtenant to one parcel cannot be used for the benefit of other land
law-property.l09.q5.p: Parcel A holds an express appurtenant easement to cross Parcel B to reach a road. The owner of Parcel A purchases adjoining Parcel C, which has no easement, and begins using the crossing to serve a shopping center on both parcels, tripling the traffic. Parcel B's owner sues. What is the most likely result?
law-property.l09.q5.h: Scope limits the use to the dominant parcel.
law-property.l09.q5.e: The holder may not extend the easement to non-dominant land. A court may enjoin the excess use, but it will not usually terminate the easement itself.

law-property.l10.q1.t: A real covenant is enforced by a damages judgment; an equitable servitude is enforced by an injunction against the burdened owner
law-property.l10.q1.p: What is the usual remedy for breach of a real covenant, as compared with an equitable servitude?
law-property.l10.q1.e: Covenants at law yield damages, while servitudes were developed in equity and are enforced by injunction.

law-property.l10.q2.p: Which element is required for a covenant to run at law but NOT for an equitable servitude?
law-property.l10.q2.h: Equity dispensed with a particular relationship requirement.
law-property.l10.q2.e: Real covenants require horizontal and vertical privity, while equitable servitudes need not. Intent, touch and concern, and a writing apply to both.

law-property.l10.q3.t: Implied reciprocal servitude based on a common scheme of development
law-property.l10.q3.p: A subdivider sells thirty lots, each with a deed that restricts the land to residential use. The subdivider sells the last lot by a deed with no restriction. The buyer of the last lot has notice from the neighborhood's uniform plan. When the buyer plans a gas station, which doctrine do the neighbors invoke?
law-property.l10.q3.e: Where a developer follows a general plan, lots sold without restriction may be burdened by an implied reciprocal servitude if the buyer had notice. The other options do not describe a restriction on use.

law-property.l10.q4.t: It should refuse enforcement, because judicial enforcement of a racially restrictive covenant is state action that violates the Equal Protection Clause under Shelley v. Kraemer
law-property.l10.q4.p: A restrictive covenant bars the owners of Lots in a subdivision from selling to members of a named racial group. A seller wishes to sell to a buyer in that group, and a neighbor sues in state court to enforce the covenant. How should the court rule, and why?
law-property.l10.q4.h: The state's judicial enforcement is the key.
law-property.l10.q4.e: Shelley v. Kraemer held that judicial enforcement is state action and violates equal protection. The covenant's private origin does not matter, and the holding is not limited to injunctions.

law-property.l10.q5.t: The restriction is presumed valid and enforced unless it is arbitrary, violates public policy, or burdens a fundamental constitutional right
law-property.l10.q5.p: A condominium declaration recorded before any unit was sold bans all pets. An owner, who bought later, keeps a cat and argues the ban is unreasonable as applied to a quiet indoor cat. The jurisdiction follows the approach of Nahrstedt v. Lakeside Village. What is the likely result?
law-property.l10.q5.e: Under the Nahrstedt approach, restrictions in a recorded declaration are presumptively valid, and the challenger bears the burden. They bind subsequent buyers with notice.

law-property.l11.q1.t: A substantial and unreasonable interference with the private use and enjoyment of the plaintiff's land
law-property.l11.q1.p: What is the usual standard for a private nuisance?
law-property.l11.q1.e: Private nuisance requires an interference that is both substantial and unreasonable. A physical intrusion is trespass; zoning violation is evidence but not the test.

law-property.l11.q2.t: An injunction conditioned on the defendant's failure to pay permanent damages to the neighbors for the loss in value of their land
law-property.l11.q2.p: In Boomer v. Atlantic Cement Co., what remedy did the court select?
law-property.l11.q2.h: Damages in lieu of closing the plant.
law-property.l11.q2.e: The court allowed the plant to continue if it paid permanent damages, treating the neighbors' entitlement as protected by a liability rule.

law-property.l11.q3.t: The feedlot was enjoined, but the developer who brought residents to the area had to indemnify the feedlot for relocation costs
law-property.l11.q3.p: A feedlot has operated for years in a rural area. A developer builds a retirement community nearby, and the residents sue to stop the odors. In Spur Industries v. Del E. Webb, what was the approach to coming to the nuisance?
law-property.l11.q3.h: The court protected the public but compensated the first user.
law-property.l11.q3.e: Spur held the feedlot a nuisance to the residents but required the developer to pay the cost of moving because the developer came to the nuisance.

law-property.l11.q4.t: Cho loses, because the interference is judged by the standard of a normal person in the community and not by the plaintiff's particular sensitivity
law-property.l11.q4.p: Homeowner Cho has an unusually sensitive condition and can sleep only in absolute silence. A neighbor plays an ordinary, moderate-volume radio during normal evening hours, which a normal person would not find disturbing. Cho sues for private nuisance. What is the most likely result?
law-property.l11.q4.h: Substantial means to a normal person.
law-property.l11.q4.e: The substantial-interference element is objective. Hypersensitivity does not make ordinary conduct a nuisance, and the neighbor's priority is not the point.

law-property.l11.q5.t: The neighbor loses, because there is no common law right to light and air across another's land, and the addition is not a nuisance merely because it casts shade
law-property.l11.q5.p: A hotel adds a tall wing that casts shade on a neighbor's swimming deck for much of the day, and the neighbor sues to enjoin it, claiming a right to sunlight. No statute or easement applies. What is the most likely outcome under the traditional American rule?
law-property.l11.q5.e: The traditional rule gives no right to light and air without an express easement. A few courts, as in Prah v. Maretti, may recognize a nuisance claim for unreasonable blocking of sunlight, but that is a minority position.

law-property.l12.q1.t: The buyer, who is treated as the equitable owner
law-property.l12.q1.p: Under the doctrine of equitable conversion, who bears the risk of loss between contract and closing in the majority view?
law-property.l12.q1.h: The buyer is the equitable owner.
law-property.l12.q1.e: In the majority rule the buyer bears the risk and must still pay, absent contrary agreement. A minority rule and some statutes put it on the seller until closing.

law-property.l12.q2.t: Title free from reasonable doubt as to its validity, such that a reasonable buyer would accept it
law-property.l12.q2.p: What does the implied covenant of marketable title require at closing?
law-property.l12.q2.e: Marketable title is title a reasonable buyer would accept, free from reasonable doubt. It need not be perfect, and disclosed easements may be accepted by the contract.

law-property.l12.q3.t: Bree must pay the price, though she may recover under any insurance she bought on the property
law-property.l12.q3.p: Bree signs a contract to buy a house from Sol. Both are silent about risk of loss. Before closing, a flood destroys the house through no fault of either party. The jurisdiction follows the majority rule. What is the most likely result?
law-property.l12.q3.e: The buyer bears the risk of loss in the majority rule. Her right to insurance proceeds is a consequence of her equitable ownership. A contract term or statute could change this.

law-property.l12.q4.t: Fraudulent misrepresentation or active concealment, which is an exception to caveat emptor that survives the merger of the contract into the deed
law-property.l12.q4.p: Seller tells Buyer that the basement is dry, knowing it floods every spring and having hidden the stains with paint. Buyer inspects, closes, and finds the flooding. The contract was silent on condition, and the home is old, not new. What is Buyer's best claim?
law-property.l12.q4.e: Active concealment and misrepresentation fall outside caveat emptor and are not barred by merger. The implied warranty applies mainly to new homes from builders, and marketable title concerns title, not physical condition.

law-property.l12.q5.t: The statute of frauds requires a signed writing with the essential terms, not notarization, so the contract is enforceable and Buyer may seek specific performance
law-property.l12.q5.p: Buyer and Seller sign a written contract, with a signed memo of the price and a legal description, for land. Before closing Seller refuses to proceed and claims the contract is unenforceable because it was not notarized. Buyer sues. What is the best response?
law-property.l12.q5.h: What the statute of frauds requires.
law-property.l12.q5.e: The statute requires a writing signed by the party to be charged with the parties, description, and price. Notarization and recording are not requirements, and specific performance is the traditional remedy for land.

law-property.l13.q1.p: Which deed covenant is a future covenant that runs with the land?
law-property.l13.q1.h: Future covenants are breached on eviction.
law-property.l13.q1.e: The future covenants (quiet enjoyment, warranty, further assurances) run to successors. The other three are present covenants breached, if at all, at delivery.

law-property.l13.q2.p: Which deed makes no covenants about title?
law-property.l13.q2.h: It transfers only whatever interest the grantor has.
law-property.l13.q2.e: A quitclaim conveys any interest the grantor holds without warranty. A special warranty deed covers only the grantor's own period of ownership.

law-property.l13.q3.t: Natural monuments, then artificial monuments, then courses and distances, then area
law-property.l13.q3.p: Which is the usual hierarchy when a land description is internally inconsistent?
law-property.l13.q3.h: A river is more reliable than a measurement.
law-property.l13.q3.e: Courts prefer physical features that are hard to mistake over measured distances and total area, which are more likely to contain errors.

law-property.l13.q4.t: The deed fails for lack of present delivery because Grantor retained control and a testamentary transfer needed will formalities
law-property.l13.q4.p: Grantor handed a deed to a friend with instructions to give it to Grantee when Grantor dies, and kept the right to call it back at any time. Grantor died, and the friend delivered the deed to Grantee. A competing devisee under Grantor's will challenges the deed. What is the most likely result?
law-property.l13.q4.h: The question is whether the grantor gave up control.
law-property.l13.q4.e: Where the grantor reserves the power to recall the deed there is no present delivery, and an attempted transfer at death is testamentary and must meet the requirements for wills. If the grantor had irrevocably parted with control, the result would differ.

law-property.l13.q5.t: Estoppel by deed, which gives Tess title automatically when Sam later acquires the interest he warranted
law-property.l13.q5.p: Sam deeds Blackacre to Tess by a general warranty deed, though Sam owns nothing. A year later Sam inherits Blackacre from his aunt. Tess then sues to establish title in Blackacre. What doctrine best supports Tess?
law-property.l13.q5.h: A grantor cannot deny what he warranted.
law-property.l13.q5.e: Under estoppel by deed, after-acquired title passes to a grantee under a deed with warranties. Merger and conversion address other situations, and one year is not adverse possession.

law-property.l14.q1.p: Which type of recording act protects a subsequent bona fide purchaser who takes without notice, regardless of whether the purchaser records first?
law-property.l14.q1.e: A notice statute protects a subsequent BFP without notice. A race-notice statute also requires first recording, and a pure race statute looks only at recording order.

law-property.l14.q2.t: A person who takes from a BFP gets the BFP's protection even if she has notice of the prior interest
law-property.l14.q2.p: What is the main effect of the shelter rule?
law-property.l14.q2.e: The shelter rule preserves the value of the BFP's ability to resell. Otherwise a BFP could not sell to a buyer who knew of the old interest.

law-property.l14.q3.t: C, because C takes the protection of B, who was a BFP without notice, under the shelter rule
law-property.l14.q3.p: O conveys to A, who does not record. O conveys to B, who pays value and has no notice of A, and B does not record. B then conveys to C, who has actual notice of A, and C records. The state is a notice jurisdiction. Who prevails between A and C?
law-property.l14.q3.h: Does C take from a BFP?
law-property.l14.q3.e: B was a BFP without notice, and C steps into B's shoes under the shelter rule. Recording order is irrelevant in a pure notice state, and C's notice does not defeat protection derived from B.

law-property.l14.q4.t: B prevails, because B was a bona fide purchaser without notice who recorded first, satisfying both parts of a race-notice statute
law-property.l14.q4.p: O conveys to A for value. A does not record. O then conveys to B, who pays value, knows nothing of A, and records immediately. The state is a race-notice state. Later A sues B. What is the outcome, and what is the best explanation?
law-property.l14.q4.h: Both notice and recording order matter.
law-property.l14.q4.e: A race-notice statute protects a subsequent BFP who takes without notice and records first. B satisfied both. Recording promptly is not evidence of notice.

law-property.l14.q5.t: O prevails, because a forged deed is void and conveys nothing, and recording acts do not turn void deeds into valid ones
law-property.l14.q5.p: Forger signs O's name on a deed to Ana, who pays full value in good faith and records. O later learns of it. Ana relies on the recording act against O. What is the likely result?
law-property.l14.q5.h: Void is different from voidable or unrecorded.
law-property.l14.q5.e: Recording acts protect against competing unrecorded conveyances from the same owner. A forged deed is void and a BFP takes nothing from it, though title insurance may protect Ana.

law-property.l15.q1.t: Comprehensive zoning that separates land uses is a valid exercise of the police power unless clearly arbitrary and unreasonable
law-property.l15.q1.p: What did Village of Euclid v. Ambler Realty Co. hold?
law-property.l15.q1.e: Euclid upheld comprehensive zoning under the police power with deferential review. It did not find that diminution of value is automatically a taking.

law-property.l15.q2.t: A lawful use that predates a new zoning restriction and is generally allowed to continue
law-property.l15.q2.e: A nonconforming use is lawful when begun and protected from the later restriction, subject to limits on expansion and amortization.

law-property.l15.q3.t: An area variance based on unnecessary hardship from unique features of the property
law-property.l15.q3.p: A landowner seeks a variance to build a house closer to the street than the setback rule allows. The lot is oddly shaped and the only compliant footprint would be unusable. The hardship was not caused by the owner. Which variance standard best fits this request?
law-property.l15.q3.e: A setback is a dimensional standard, so this is an area variance justified by hardship from unique property features and not self-created. Use variances face a tougher standard.

law-property.l15.q4.t: Moore v. City of East Cleveland, which struck down an ordinance that narrowly defined family and intruded on extended family living arrangements
law-property.l15.q4.p: A city ordinance defines family to include only parents and their children, so that a grandmother cannot live with two grandsons who are cousins. Owner is cited. Which precedent best supports Owner's constitutional challenge?
law-property.l15.q4.e: Moore invalidated a narrow definition that barred a grandmother from living with grandsons who were cousins. Belle Terre upheld a limit on unrelated residents and distinguishes the family-based claim.

law-property.l15.q5.t: A developing municipality must provide a realistic opportunity for its fair share of the regional need for low- and moderate-income housing
law-property.l15.q5.p: A suburban town bans all multifamily housing and requires a minimum lot size that makes new homes unaffordable to low-income families. A civil rights group sues under the state constitution in a state that follows Mount Laurel. What is the strongest argument?
law-property.l15.q5.e: Mount Laurel held that developing municipalities must make realistic provision for their fair share of regional housing needs. It does not require every project, and many states have not adopted it.

law-property.l16.q1.t: Taking property under a comprehensive economic development plan can satisfy the public use requirement
law-property.l16.q1.p: What did Kelo v. City of New London decide?
law-property.l16.q1.h: Five to four, deferential to local planning.
law-property.l16.q1.e: Kelo upheld the taking under an economic development plan and noted that states may impose stricter limits, as many did afterward.

law-property.l16.q2.t: The Penn Central factors: economic impact, interference with investment-backed expectations, and character of the action
law-property.l16.q2.p: Which test governs most regulatory takings claims that fall short of a total wipeout or physical occupation?
law-property.l16.q2.h: Three factors from the Grand Central case.
law-property.l16.q2.e: Penn Central supplies the default ad hoc test. Lucas applies to total deprivation, and Nollan/Dolan apply to exactions.

law-property.l16.q3.t: It is a per se taking, however small the space, because it is a permanent physical occupation of the owner's property authorized by law
law-property.l16.q3.p: A city requires every owner of a rental building to allow the installation of a small permanent device on the roof for a public utility, with no payment. Under Loretto, what is the result?
law-property.l16.q3.e: Loretto held that a permanent physical occupation is a taking regardless of the public interest or size. The Penn Central balancing is not used.

law-property.l16.q4.t: The Nollan/Dolan nexus and proportionality requirements apply to legislatively imposed conditions as well as administrative ones, including a fee demanded as a permit condition
law-property.l16.q4.p: A county conditions a building permit for a larger home on the owner's paying a large fee for roadway improvements. The fee is set by a general schedule adopted by the legislature, not by case-by-case negotiation, and bears no relationship to the traffic the home will generate. After Sheetz, which argument is strongest for the owner?
law-property.l16.q4.h: Does the legislative source of the condition exempt it?
law-property.l16.q4.e: Sheetz held that the legislative origin of an exaction does not exempt it from Nollan and Dolan; whether the fee meets the standard is for remand. Knick removed any state-litigation requirement.

law-property.l16.q5.t: The owner states a takings claim for the surplus beyond the tax debt, because the government may not keep proceeds above what is owed
law-property.l16.q5.p: A county forecloses on a home for $15,000 in unpaid taxes, sells it for $200,000 under a statute allowing it to keep all proceeds, and the former owner sues. What does Tyler v. Hennepin County indicate about the claim?
law-property.l16.q5.h: Who is entitled to the surplus?
law-property.l16.q5.e: Tyler held that a county may take what the tax debt requires but not the surplus value, which remains the owner's property. The full proceeds are not due, because the debt is real.

law-property.l17.q1.t: Facts in a telephone directory are not copyrightable, because copyright requires originality and rejects sweat of the brow
law-property.l17.q1.p: What did Feist Publications v. Rural Telephone Service decide?
law-property.l17.q1.e: Feist held that copyright requires originality, which the white pages lacked. Effort alone does not create protection for facts.

law-property.l17.q2.t: Indefinitely, as long as it is used in commerce and not abandoned, with periodic maintenance filings
law-property.l17.q2.p: How long can a trademark last?
law-property.l17.q2.e: Trademark rights depend on continued use and are not limited to a fixed term. The other durations belong to patent and copyright.

law-property.l17.q3.t: Protection requires reasonable measures to keep the information secret, and the lack of any measures weakens the claim
law-property.l17.q3.p: A rival learns the secret formula of a beverage because an employee of the maker leaves a copy in a public cafe, which the owner had taken no steps to protect. Which statement about trade secret law is most accurate?
law-property.l17.q3.h: What must the owner have done?
law-property.l17.q3.e: Trade secrets require reasonable efforts to maintain secrecy. Independent discovery and lawful reverse engineering are permitted, and protection ends if secrecy is lost.

law-property.l17.q4.t: Breach of fiduciary duty or lack of informed consent, because the physician failed to disclose a research and economic interest
law-property.l17.q4.p: A patient's cells, taken during treatment, are used without his knowledge to create a valuable cell line. Under Moore v. Regents of the University of California, which claim is most likely to succeed?
law-property.l17.q4.e: Moore refused a conversion claim over the cells but allowed claims based on failure to disclose research and economic interests. The other theories misapply IP categories.

law-property.l17.q5.t: No infringement, because copyright protects expression and not ideas or general themes
law-property.l17.q5.p: A novelist publishes a story about a boy who attends a school for magic. A second author writes a new story with different characters, plot and text, which also features a boy at a school for magic. Under copyright law, what is the most likely result of an infringement suit?
law-property.l17.q5.e: Copyright does not protect ideas, premises or themes. It protects the particular expression, such as the text, characters and plot details, so copying paragraphs would differ.

law-torts.l01.q1.t: Acts desiring the contact or knowing with substantial certainty that contact will result
law-torts.l01.q1.p: In tort law, a defendant has the intent required for battery if the defendant:
law-torts.l01.q1.h: Intent is about the contact, not the motive.
law-torts.l01.q1.e: Intent means desire for the consequence or substantial certainty of it. Motive, malice and a purpose to injure are not required, and carelessness is negligence, not intent.

law-torts.l01.q2.t: A reasonable apprehension of imminent harmful or offensive contact
law-torts.l01.q2.p: Which of the following is required for civil assault?
law-torts.l01.q2.h: Assault concerns the victim's mental state, not contact.
law-torts.l01.q2.e: Assault protects against apprehension of imminent contact, and no touching is needed. Threats of future harm are not imminent, and injury is not an element.

law-torts.l01.q3.t: Not liable for false imprisonment because of the shopkeeper's privilege exercised reasonably
law-torts.l01.q3.p: A store detains a customer in a back office for 30 minutes after a security guard reasonably believes the customer concealed an item. The customer had not stolen anything. In most states, the store is most likely:
law-torts.l01.q3.h: Think of a privilege tied to reasonable belief.
law-torts.l01.q3.e: Most states give merchants a privilege to detain on reasonable grounds for a reasonable time and in a reasonable manner, even if the suspect is innocent. Actual theft is not required.

law-torts.l01.q4.t: Olsen is liable to Quill for battery and to Pruitt for assault under transferred intent
law-torts.l01.q4.p: Olsen, intending to frighten his neighbour Pruitt by throwing a rock near him, instead hits Quill, a bystander Olsen did not see, breaking her arm. Pruitt saw the rock coming and was frightened. Which statement is most accurate?
law-torts.l01.q4.h: Transferred intent works among the classic five intentional torts.
law-torts.l01.q4.e: Intent to commit assault against Pruitt transfers to the battery against Quill, and Pruitt has an assault claim from his own apprehension. Negligence need not be used, since transferred intent applies between these torts.

law-torts.l01.q5.t: Vance intended the contact, so he is liable for all resulting harm, even if unforeseeable in extent
law-torts.l01.q5.p: Vance, a college student, playfully taps the shoulder of Wells, who has an undiagnosed fragile bone condition, and Wells suffers a fracture. Wells sues for battery. Which is the strongest argument for Wells?
law-torts.l01.q5.e: Under Vosburg, the intent need only be to make the contact, and the defendant takes the victim as he finds him. Foreseeability of the extent of harm is not required for intentional torts.

law-torts.l02.q1.t: Extreme and outrageous conduct beyond all bounds of decency
law-torts.l02.q1.p: Which standard must conduct satisfy to support a claim for intentional infliction of emotional distress?
law-torts.l02.q1.h: Courts set a very high bar.
law-torts.l02.q1.e: IIED requires conduct so extreme and outrageous it is atrocious in a civilised community. Insults and annoyances fall short, and the violation of a statute is not required.

law-torts.l02.q2.t: A false statement of fact made with actual malice
law-torts.l02.q2.p: In Hustler Magazine v. Falwell, the Supreme Court held that a public figure could not recover for IIED based on a parody advertisement unless he showed:
law-torts.l02.q2.h: The First Amendment limits the tort.
law-torts.l02.q2.e: The Court required a false statement of fact made with actual malice, the same standard as in defamation cases. Offensiveness and commercial motive are not enough.

law-torts.l02.q3.t: At most nominal trespass to chattels, since there was no serious interference or impairment
law-torts.l02.q3.p: Rowan borrows a neighbour's power drill without asking, uses it for ten minutes, and returns it undamaged the same day. Which is the most accurate classification of the neighbour's claim?
law-torts.l02.q3.h: Consider the extent and duration of the interference.
law-torts.l02.q3.e: A brief use that does not damage the chattel or dispossess the owner for a substantial time is not conversion. Many courts require impairment even for trespass to chattels.

law-torts.l02.q4.t: Sable is liable for conversion, since good faith is no defense to exercising dominion over another's chattel
law-torts.l02.q4.p: Sable purchases a used bicycle from a seller in good faith, not knowing it was stolen from Tennant, and Sable later sells it to a third party. Tennant sues Sable. Which is the best analysis?
law-torts.l02.q4.h: The intent needed is to exercise control, not to wrong the owner.
law-torts.l02.q4.e: Conversion requires intent to exercise dominion, not wrongful purpose, so innocent purchasers who resell are liable for the value. The other choices wrongly import knowledge or damage requirements.

law-torts.l02.q5.t: The rancher prevails and recovers at least nominal damages, because the hiker intended to enter the land
law-torts.l02.q5.p: A hiker walks onto a rancher's unfenced land, believing in good faith that it is public land, and picnics for an hour without causing damage. The rancher sues for trespass. The most likely outcome is:
law-torts.l02.q5.e: Trespass requires only intent to enter, so a mistake about ownership is no defense, and nominal damages are available without harm. Posting is not required for the tort.

law-torts.l03.q1.t: Reasonable non-deadly force, but never deadly force solely to protect property
law-torts.l03.q1.p: Under the majority view, a landowner may use which of the following to protect property from a trespasser?
law-torts.l03.q1.e: Reasonable non-deadly force is allowed after a request to leave, but deadly force to protect property alone is not, as in Katko. Mechanical devices are treated like deadly force.

law-torts.l03.q2.t: Not liable for trespass but liable for actual damage caused
law-torts.l03.q2.p: A defendant who enters another's land under private necessity to avoid a serious harm is:
law-torts.l03.q2.e: Private necessity excuses the entry but does not excuse the harm done, so the actor pays for damage. Public necessity, by contrast, usually carries no liability.

law-torts.l03.q3.t: Liable for battery, because the patient's consent did not extend to the unrelated procedure
law-torts.l03.q3.p: A patient consents to a minor knee procedure, and while she is under anaesthesia the surgeon, without any emergency, also performs an unrelated procedure that he thinks would help. The surgeon is most likely:
law-torts.l03.q3.e: Consent is effective only within its scope, and a procedure beyond it absent emergency is a battery. Good motives do not matter, and unconsciousness does not create consent.

law-torts.l03.q4.t: Danner may be protected if her belief in the need for force was reasonable, but the force used may be excessive for a non-deadly threat
law-torts.l03.q4.p: Danner, who is walking home, is confronted by Esch, who raises a fist and says, "I'm going to hit you." Danner, who reasonably believes that she is about to be attacked, strikes Esch with a heavy flashlight, causing a serious wound. Esch was actually only gesturing in a joke. Which is the best analysis of Danner's liability?
law-torts.l03.q4.h: Reasonable belief matters, and so does proportion.
law-torts.l03.q4.e: Self-defense turns on reasonable belief, even if mistaken, but force must be proportionate to the apparent threat. Striking with a heavy object in response to a threatened punch may be excessive.

law-torts.l03.q5.t: No liability for the trespass, but the tenant must pay for the shrubs and the gate under private necessity
law-torts.l03.q5.p: A tenant is caught in a sudden fire and, to escape, smashes a neighbour's locked gate and runs across his garden, destroying shrubs. The neighbour sues for trespass and damage. Which result is most likely?
law-torts.l03.q5.h: Private necessity excuses entry but not harm.
law-torts.l03.q5.e: Private necessity is a privilege to enter but a duty to compensate for damage caused. Complete immunity would apply only to public necessity.

law-torts.l04.q1.t: No legal duty to rescue the stranger
law-torts.l04.q1.p: Under the majority rule, a person who sees a stranger in danger, with no special relationship and no role in creating the danger, has:
law-torts.l04.q1.h: The common law does not impose a general duty to act.
law-torts.l04.q1.e: There is traditionally no affirmative duty to rescue absent a special relationship or a creation of peril. Some statutes require reporting, but not rescue.

law-torts.l04.q2.t: Duty runs only to foreseeable plaintiffs within the zone of danger
law-torts.l04.q2.p: In Palsgraf v. Long Island Railroad Co., Judge Cardozo's majority opinion held that:
law-torts.l04.q2.h: Think about the relationship between the plaintiff and the risk.
law-torts.l04.q2.e: Cardozo limited duty to foreseeable plaintiffs and found Mrs. Palsgraf was not one. Andrews's dissent took the opposite view of duty.

law-torts.l04.q3.t: Make reasonable inspection and repair or warn of dangerous conditions
law-torts.l04.q3.p: A shop owner who invites customers to enter owes them, under the traditional status categories, a duty to:
law-torts.l04.q3.h: Invitees receive the highest level of care.
law-torts.l04.q3.e: Invitees are owed reasonable inspection and repair or warning. Licensees are owed warnings of known concealed dangers, and trespassers only protection against wilful harm.

law-torts.l04.q4.t: The club owes the guest a duty because of the special relationship, but the diver has no duty absent a relationship
law-torts.l04.q4.p: A lifeguard employed by a private pool club stops watching the pool to chat. A guest drowns in the pool, and a diver nearby who did not know the guest chooses not to act. The guest's estate sues the club and the diver. Which is the best analysis?
law-torts.l04.q4.h: Special relationships create duties to act.
law-torts.l04.q4.e: The club's possessor-invitee relationship and its voluntary assumption of lifeguard services give rise to a duty. The diver is a stranger with no duty to rescue.

law-torts.l04.q5.t: Fail, because she was not present at the scene and did not contemporaneously perceive the injury-causing event
law-torts.l04.q5.p: Roth is driving when she sees a friend's son, Tad, in a car crash that injures him. Tad's mother, Uma, is at home four miles away and learns of it by phone, suffering severe distress with physical symptoms. In a jurisdiction following Thing v. La Chusa, Uma's claim for negligent infliction of emotional distress would most likely:
law-torts.l04.q5.h: The bystander test has several requirements.
law-torts.l04.q5.e: Under Thing, a bystander must be closely related, present at the scene and aware of the injury-producing event. Uma was neither present nor contemporaneously aware.

law-torts.l05.q1.t: Less than the probability of harm multiplied by the magnitude of loss
law-torts.l05.q1.p: In the Hand formula, a defendant is negligent if the burden of precaution is:
law-torts.l05.q1.e: Under Carroll Towing, failure to take a precaution that costs less than the expected loss is negligent. The other formulations are not Hand's.

law-torts.l05.q2.t: By the standard of a reasonable child of like age, intelligence and experience
law-torts.l05.q2.p: How are children generally judged in negligence cases that do not involve adult activities?
law-torts.l05.q2.e: Children receive an adjusted standard, but when engaged in adult activities such as driving, they are held to the adult standard.

law-torts.l05.q3.t: Compliance with custom is evidence of due care, but not conclusive, as a whole industry may be negligent
law-torts.l05.q3.p: A trucking industry has for decades not installed an inexpensive safety device, and a driver without one causes a crash that the device would have prevented. The industry custom is relevant, but:
law-torts.l05.q3.h: Custom is evidence, not a rule of law.
law-torts.l05.q3.e: Custom informs but does not set the standard of care, as an entire industry may lag in adopting available precautions. It is neither conclusive nor irrelevant.

law-torts.l05.q4.t: That the oil was present long enough that a reasonable inspection would have found it
law-torts.l05.q4.p: Zeller, a shopper, slips on a puddle of oil in a store aisle and is injured. The store's records show the aisle was last inspected four hours earlier, and an oil bottle leaked from a shelf at an unknown time. No employee knew of the oil. Which element is Zeller most likely to need to prove for breach?
law-torts.l05.q4.e: When a defendant did not create the hazard, the plaintiff must show actual or constructive notice, meaning it existed long enough to be discovered by reasonable inspection. Intent is not required.

law-torts.l05.q5.t: Apply the reasonable person standard without adjustment for the mental disability
law-torts.l05.q5.p: Parr, who has a severe cognitive disability, drives a car negligently and injures a pedestrian. The pedestrian sues, and Parr argues that he should be judged by the standard of a reasonable person with his cognitive disability. Under the majority rule, the court will most likely:
law-torts.l05.q5.h: Physical and mental disabilities are treated differently.
law-torts.l05.q5.e: Courts adjust the standard for physical disabilities but generally not for mental ones, to protect victims and encourage supervision. Sudden unforeseeable incapacity may be an exception.

law-torts.l06.q1.t: The event is of a kind that ordinarily does not occur without negligence
law-torts.l06.q1.p: Which of the following is a typical element of res ipsa loquitur?
law-torts.l06.q1.h: The doctrine draws an inference from the type of accident.
law-torts.l06.q1.e: The first element is that the event usually signals negligence. Statutory violation is a separate negligence per se doctrine.

law-torts.l06.q2.t: The harm be of the type the statute was designed to prevent
law-torts.l06.q2.p: Negligence per se requires that the plaintiff be within the class the statute was meant to protect and that:
law-torts.l06.q2.h: Think about the purpose of the statute.
law-torts.l06.q2.e: The harm must be of the type the statute was designed to prevent, and the violation must have caused it. Intent and a private right of action are not required.

law-torts.l06.q3.t: May reach the jury, which can but need not infer negligence
law-torts.l06.q3.p: In most states, the effect of res ipsa loquitur is that the plaintiff:
law-torts.l06.q3.h: It is a permissible inference in the majority.
law-torts.l06.q3.e: The majority treats res ipsa as a permissible inference that gets the plaintiff past a directed verdict, while a minority use a presumption. It does not compel a verdict.

law-torts.l06.q4.t: Established if the worker is within the protected class, a fall is the type of harm prevented, and the low railing caused it
law-torts.l06.q4.p: A state statute requires that stairwell railings in apartment buildings be at least 36 inches high to prevent falls. A landlord installs 30-inch railings. A delivery worker, who is not a tenant, leans on the railing and falls over it. In the delivery worker's case, negligence per se is most likely:
law-torts.l06.q4.h: Class of persons, type of harm and causation.
law-torts.l06.q4.e: The statute plausibly protects persons using the stairs, not only tenants, and a fall is the danger it targets. Knowledge of the violation is not required.

law-torts.l06.q5.t: Allowed to use res ipsa loquitur against all defendants, who must then explain their roles
law-torts.l06.q5.p: A patient is unconscious during a hospital operation and wakes with a nerve injury in the arm that was not part of the operation. She sues the surgeon, the anaesthetist and the nurses who had control of her during the operation, and does not know which of them caused it. Under Ybarra v. Spangard, she is most likely:
law-torts.l06.q5.h: The control requirement was relaxed in medical cases.
law-torts.l06.q5.e: Ybarra allowed the doctrine against multiple defendants responsible for an unconscious patient. A strict single-control rule would leave her without a remedy.

law-torts.l07.q1.t: The injury would not have occurred without the negligent conduct
law-torts.l07.q1.p: Under the but-for test, a defendant's negligence is an actual cause of an injury if:
law-torts.l07.q1.h: Ask whether the harm would have happened anyway.
law-torts.l07.q1.e: But-for causation asks whether the harm would have occurred absent the conduct. Foreseeability and closeness belong to proximate cause.

law-torts.l07.q2.t: Two independent sufficient causes combine to produce the harm
law-torts.l07.q2.p: The substantial factor test is typically used where:
law-torts.l07.q2.e: Where each of two causes would alone have been sufficient, but-for fails, and courts ask if each was a substantial factor. The other situations raise different issues.

law-torts.l07.q3.t: Both defendants were negligent, and the plaintiff could not identify which caused the injury
law-torts.l07.q3.p: In Summers v. Tice, two hunters negligently fired toward the plaintiff, and one bullet hit him. The court shifted to each defendant the burden to prove that he did not cause the harm because:
law-torts.l07.q3.e: Alternative liability applies when all potential tortfeasors acted negligently and are before the court, so the plaintiff cannot be left without remedy. It does not rest on concert or strict liability.

law-torts.l07.q4.t: Lose, because it cannot show it was more likely than not that timely diagnosis would have saved the patient
law-torts.l07.q4.p: A hospital negligently delays diagnosing a patient's cancer, and the patient, who had a 30 percent chance of survival if diagnosed on time, dies. The patient's estate sues. In a jurisdiction that rejects loss of chance and requires but-for causation by a preponderance, the estate will most likely:
law-torts.l07.q4.h: A 30 percent chance is below the threshold.
law-torts.l07.q4.e: Without loss of chance, plaintiff must prove survival was more likely than not. A 30 percent chance fails. States that accept loss of chance would allow proportional recovery.

law-torts.l07.q5.t: Each defendant may be liable for a share of damages matching its market share, unless it proves it did not make the pills
law-torts.l07.q5.p: Three manufacturers sold an identical, fungible drug, and the plaintiff cannot identify which one made the pills her mother took. Her state follows Sindell v. Abbott Laboratories. She sues manufacturers that together held a substantial share of the market. Which result is most likely?
law-torts.l07.q5.e: Sindell adopted several liability proportional to market share when the product is fungible and a substantial share of the market is before the court. Many states do not follow it, but the question assumes this one does.

law-torts.l08.q1.t: Harm of a kind that was reasonably foreseeable
law-torts.l08.q1.p: Under the Wagon Mound (No. 1) approach, a negligent defendant is liable for:
law-torts.l08.q1.h: The test is foreseeability of the type of harm.
law-torts.l08.q1.e: Wagon Mound rejected the directness test in favour of foreseeability of the kind of harm. The defendant's actual foresight is not the standard.

law-torts.l08.q2.t: For the full extent of the injury, even if the plaintiff was unusually susceptible
law-torts.l08.q2.p: The eggshell plaintiff rule provides that a defendant who causes a foreseeable type of injury is liable:
law-torts.l08.q2.e: The defendant takes the plaintiff as found, so unforeseen extent of harm is recoverable. Knowledge of the susceptibility is not required.

law-torts.l08.q3.t: Still liable, because medical negligence is a foreseeable intervening cause
law-torts.l08.q3.p: A driver negligently injures a pedestrian, who is taken to a hospital where a nurse negligently administers the wrong drug and worsens the injury. As to the added harm, the driver is most likely:
law-torts.l08.q3.h: Foreseeable intervening forces do not break the chain.
law-torts.l08.q3.e: Negligent medical treatment is a foreseeable consequence of causing serious injury, so it is not superseding. The nurse and hospital may share liability.

law-torts.l08.q4.t: The assault was the very risk that made leaving the door unlocked negligent, so it does not supersede
law-torts.l08.q4.p: A landlord negligently leaves the lobby door of an apartment building unlocked in a neighbourhood with frequent break-ins. A stranger enters and assaults a tenant. The tenant sues the landlord. The landlord argues that the criminal act of the assailant is a superseding cause. The best response is:
law-torts.l08.q4.e: When the risk that made the conduct negligent includes third-party crime, the crime is within the scope of risk and not superseding. Intentional acts are not always superseding, nor is the landlord strictly liable.

law-torts.l08.q5.t: Kemp is not liable, because the earthquake was an unforeseeable extraordinary event that was not within the risk of speeding
law-torts.l08.q5.p: A speeding driver, Kemp, loses control and hits a utility pole. Ten minutes later, during an unusual earthquake, the pole falls and injures a bystander who had been standing nearby because of the accident. The bystander sues Kemp. Which result is most likely?
law-torts.l08.q5.h: Scope of risk and extraordinary natural events.
law-torts.l08.q5.e: The harm came from an extraordinary event unrelated to the risk of speeding, so the earthquake is likely a superseding cause. But-for cause alone does not establish proximate cause.

law-torts.l09.q1.t: May not reduce damages by benefits the plaintiff received from independent sources
law-torts.l09.q1.p: Under the collateral source rule, a defendant generally:
law-torts.l09.q1.h: The plaintiff's insurance does not help the tortfeasor.
law-torts.l09.q1.e: The rule bars offsetting payments from sources like health insurance, though some states have modified it by statute.

law-torts.l09.q2.t: Proof of actual harm to the plaintiff
law-torts.l09.q2.p: Negligence differs from many intentional torts in that it requires:
law-torts.l09.q2.h: Nominal damages are not available for negligence.
law-torts.l09.q2.e: A negligence plaintiff must show actual damage, whereas some intentional torts allow nominal damages without harm.

law-torts.l09.q3.t: Cannot recover, because its loss is purely economic and derivative of damage to other property
law-torts.l09.q3.p: A negligent driver collides with a bridge support, closing a bridge for a week. A restaurant near the bridge, which suffers no physical harm, loses 15,000 dollars in revenue from fewer customers. Under the economic loss rule in most jurisdictions, the restaurant:
law-torts.l09.q3.e: Pure economic loss without personal injury or property damage is generally not recoverable in negligence. Foreseeability alone does not overcome the rule.

law-torts.l09.q4.t: The deduction is denied under the collateral source rule
law-torts.l09.q4.p: A plaintiff is injured in a car accident caused by a defendant's negligence, and her employer continues to pay her salary for six months under a sick leave policy. At trial, the defendant seeks to deduct the salary from her lost wages award. The most likely ruling is:
law-torts.l09.q4.e: Sick pay is a collateral source, and a defendant generally cannot reduce damages by it. The plaintiff is deemed to have earned the benefit independently.

law-torts.l09.q5.t: That she was present, perceived the injury event contemporaneously and is closely related to the victim
law-torts.l09.q5.p: Paulson, a mother, is present when her young son is struck by a negligently driven delivery van, and she sees it happen. She develops severe anxiety requiring treatment but has no physical injury. Her state follows the modern bystander approach. Which element is most important to her claim?
law-torts.l09.q5.h: This is the Dillon and Thing line of cases.
law-torts.l09.q5.e: The bystander approach requires closeness of relationship, presence and contemporaneous perception. The zone of danger rule is a different, narrower approach.

law-torts.l10.q1.p: In a jurisdiction applying pure comparative negligence, a plaintiff who is 80 percent at fault with damages of 100,000 dollars may recover:
law-torts.l10.q1.e: Under pure comparative fault, recovery is reduced by the plaintiff's percentage, leaving 20 percent. A bar would apply only in a modified system.

law-torts.l10.q2.t: A small number of jurisdictions, including Maryland and Virginia
law-torts.l10.q2.p: Contributory negligence as a complete bar to recovery survives today in:
law-torts.l10.q2.h: Only a handful of states remain.
law-torts.l10.q2.e: A few states, including Alabama, Maryland, North Carolina, Virginia and D.C., still use it. Nearly all others adopted comparative fault.

law-torts.l10.q3.t: Fail, because the stadium owes no duty to protect against an inherent risk of the game
law-torts.l10.q3.p: A spectator at a baseball game is struck by a foul ball in the seating area that was not protected by netting. The state recognises primary assumption of risk. The spectator's claim against the stadium will most likely:
law-torts.l10.q3.h: The risk is inherent in the activity.
law-torts.l10.q3.e: Primary assumption of risk negates duty for inherent risks, and it applies even in comparative jurisdictions. Waivers are a separate express assumption doctrine.

law-torts.l10.q4.t: 80,000 dollars in total, all of which may be collected from X if Y cannot pay
law-torts.l10.q4.p: In a state following joint and several liability with a pure comparative fault system, a jury finds the plaintiff 20 percent at fault, defendant X 50 percent at fault and defendant Y 30 percent at fault, with damages of 100,000 dollars. Y is insolvent. The plaintiff may collect:
law-torts.l10.q4.h: Joint and several liability allows full collection from any liable defendant.
law-torts.l10.q4.e: The plaintiff's damages are reduced to 80,000, and under joint and several liability X is liable for all of it, with a contribution claim against Y. Under several liability the answer would be only 50,000.

law-torts.l10.q5.t: Be unenforceable as to the gym's reckless conduct, even if enforceable for ordinary negligence
law-torts.l10.q5.p: A rock climber signs a release stating that she waives all claims against a gym for any injuries, including those from the gym's negligence. She is injured when the gym recklessly fails to inspect a rope that frays. In most jurisdictions, the release will:
law-torts.l10.q5.e: Courts typically enforce releases for ordinary negligence but not for gross negligence or recklessness. Releases are not void in all cases.

law-torts.l11.q1.t: Blasting with dynamite in a populated area
law-torts.l11.q1.p: Which of the following is typically treated as an abnormally dangerous activity?
law-torts.l11.q1.h: High risk that care cannot eliminate and not common usage.
law-torts.l11.q1.e: Blasting in populated areas satisfies the Restatement factors. Driving is common usage and care reduces the risk.

law-torts.l11.q2.t: The owner knew or had reason to know of the animal's dangerous propensity
law-torts.l11.q2.p: Under the traditional rule, the owner of a domestic animal is strictly liable for harm it causes if:
law-torts.l11.q2.e: The owner is liable if aware of a dangerous propensity abnormal to its class, and many states now use dog-bite statutes. Prior training or location is not the test.

law-torts.l11.q3.t: Strict liability for an abnormally dangerous activity
law-torts.l11.q3.p: A chemical storage company keeps large quantities of toxic gas in a tank in a densely populated area, using the best available safety practice. A valve fails unforeseeably and gas harms neighbours. Which theory best supports the neighbours' recovery without proof of carelessness?
law-torts.l11.q3.h: No fault needs to be shown.
law-torts.l11.q3.e: Storing toxic gas in a populated area can be an abnormally dangerous activity, giving strict liability. Negligence and res ipsa depend on fault.

law-torts.l11.q4.t: Available, but reduced if the hiker knowingly and unreasonably encountered the risk
law-torts.l11.q4.p: A quarry blasts rock using ordinary safeguards, and flying fragments strike a passing hiker, who had entered through a fence marked with warning signs. The hiker sues in strict liability. The state follows the Restatement (Second) and recognises comparative fault. The hiker's recovery will most likely be:
law-torts.l11.q4.e: Knowingly and unreasonably encountering the risk can reduce or defeat recovery, while ordinary carelessness cannot. Trespassers' status is handled differently and may affect the duty.

law-torts.l11.q5.t: The harm resulted from the plaintiff's abnormal sensitivity and not from the kind of risk that makes blasting dangerous
law-torts.l11.q5.p: A mink farmer sues a construction company that blasts nearby, alleging that the noise made the minks eat their young, which caused a large loss. The blasting is abnormally dangerous in the area. The company's best argument against strict liability is:
law-torts.l11.q5.h: The risk must be the kind that makes the activity dangerous.
law-torts.l11.q5.e: Strict liability extends to harm from the risks that make the activity abnormally dangerous, such as flying debris, not to an unusual sensitivity. Negligence is not required, and social utility is only a factor.

law-torts.l12.q1.t: The ultimate user, even without a contract with the manufacturer
law-torts.l12.q1.p: In MacPherson v. Buick Motor Co., Cardozo held that a manufacturer of a product likely to be dangerous if defective owes a duty of care to:
law-torts.l12.q1.e: MacPherson removed the privity requirement in negligence for dangerous products. The duty runs to foreseeable users.

law-torts.l12.q2.t: Foreseeable risks could have been reduced by a reasonable alternative design that was not adopted
law-torts.l12.q2.p: Under the Restatement (Third) of Torts: Products Liability, a design defect exists when:
law-torts.l12.q2.h: Risk-utility with a reasonable alternative design.
law-torts.l12.q2.e: The Third Restatement requires a reasonable alternative design for design defect, whereas departure from intended design is a manufacturing defect.

law-torts.l12.q3.t: Strict liability for a manufacturing defect, without proof of negligence
law-torts.l12.q3.p: A can of soup contains a shard of metal that entered during canning, an event that was an aberration in the manufacturer's process. The injured consumer sues the manufacturer. Which is the best theory?
law-torts.l12.q3.h: The product departed from the intended design.
law-torts.l12.q3.e: A departure from the intended design is a manufacturing defect, subject to strict liability. A design theory is for flaws in all units of a line.

law-torts.l12.q4.t: Fail if the warning to the physician was adequate, since the manufacturer's duty is generally satisfied by warning the prescriber
law-torts.l12.q4.p: A prescription drug carries a warning, directed to physicians, of a rare serious side effect, and a patient who suffers it sues the manufacturer for failure to warn, arguing she was not warned directly. Under the learned intermediary doctrine, the claim will most likely:
law-torts.l12.q4.h: The physician stands between manufacturer and patient.
law-torts.l12.q4.e: Under the learned intermediary rule, an adequate warning to the prescribing physician usually discharges the duty. Other doctrines may apply but the claim as framed fails.

law-torts.l12.q5.t: The product was substantially altered after it left the manufacturer's control, so the defect was not present when sold
law-torts.l12.q5.p: A homeowner buys a ladder and modifies it by removing a locking brace, which causes it to collapse during use and injure a guest. The guest sues the manufacturer in strict liability. The manufacturer's best defense is:
law-torts.l12.q5.h: The defect must exist when the product leaves the defendant.
law-torts.l12.q5.e: Strict liability requires that the defect exist when the product left the defendant's control, and a substantial post-sale alteration breaks that link. Privity and care are irrelevant to strict liability.

law-torts.l13.q1.t: That the defendant published a false statement with actual malice
law-torts.l13.q1.p: What must a public official prove to recover for defamation under New York Times Co. v. Sullivan?
law-torts.l13.q1.h: The standard concerns knowledge or reckless disregard.
law-torts.l13.q1.e: Actual malice means knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard for the truth, proved by clear and convincing evidence. Negligence is not enough for officials.

law-torts.l13.q2.t: Impute a serious crime or professional incompetence
law-torts.l13.q2.p: Slander per se, which allows recovery without proof of special damages, traditionally includes statements that:
law-torts.l13.q2.e: The categories are crime, loathsome disease, professional incompetence and, traditionally, unchastity. Opinions and neutral rumours are not within them.

law-torts.l13.q3.t: At least negligence, with the state free to set the standard
law-torts.l13.q3.p: Under Gertz v. Robert Welch, Inc., a private figure suing a media defendant over a statement involving a matter of public concern may recover actual damages upon proof of:
law-torts.l13.q3.e: Gertz allows states to set a standard no lower than negligence for private figures, but actual malice is required for presumed or punitive damages. Strict liability is not allowed.

law-torts.l13.q4.t: Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act, which protects an interactive service provider from treatment as the publisher of third-party content
law-torts.l13.q4.p: An online forum user posts a false statement that a local restaurant owner has been convicted of fraud. The owner sues the forum operator, which merely hosts user posts and took no part in writing or editing the statement. The operator's best defense is:
law-torts.l13.q4.e: Section 230 largely bars treating a host as the publisher of another's content. Opinion is wrong because conviction is a factual claim, and the operator's knowledge is not the test.

law-torts.l13.q5.t: The fair report privilege for an accurate account of official proceedings
law-torts.l13.q5.p: A newspaper accurately reports a statement made by a witness during a court hearing, and the statement is later shown to be false and damaging to the plaintiff. The plaintiff sues the newspaper. Which defense is most likely to succeed?
law-torts.l13.q5.e: A fair and accurate report of an official proceeding is privileged. The witness's absolute privilege does not automatically extend to republishers, and form of publication does not matter here.

law-torts.l14.q1.p: Which privacy tort requires that the plaintiff be placed before the public in a false and highly offensive manner?
law-torts.l14.q1.e: False light involves publicity that misrepresents the plaintiff in a highly offensive way. The other torts do not require falsity.

law-torts.l14.q2.t: No, because the tort is based on the exposure of true private information
law-torts.l14.q2.p: Is truth a defense to a claim for public disclosure of private facts?
law-torts.l14.q2.h: The wrong lies in the exposure.
law-torts.l14.q2.e: The tort concerns true facts, so truth is not a defense. Newsworthiness is the main limit.

law-torts.l14.q3.t: Intrusion upon seclusion, which is complete upon the intrusion without any publication
law-torts.l14.q3.p: A person secretly installs a camera in a rented bedroom and records the tenant. No recording is shown to anyone. The tenant sues. Which claim is most directly available?
law-torts.l14.q3.e: Intrusion is complete upon the offensive intrusion and requires no publication. The other torts depend on publicity or commercial use.

law-torts.l14.q4.t: Fail, because the First Amendment bars liability for truthfully publishing information obtained from public court records
law-torts.l14.q4.p: A local news site lawfully obtains a court record that includes the name of a crime victim and publishes the name truthfully in a report about a trial. The victim sues for public disclosure of private facts. Under Cox Broadcasting Corp. v. Cohn, the claim will most likely:
law-torts.l14.q4.h: Public records and the First Amendment.
law-torts.l14.q4.e: Cox held that states cannot impose liability for truthful publication of information in public court records. Truth not being a defense at common law gives way to the constitutional limit.

law-torts.l14.q5.t: Appropriation of name or likeness, or right of publicity, for commercial advantage
law-torts.l14.q5.p: A clothing company uses a photograph of a well-known athlete, without permission, on a billboard implying that the athlete endorses the brand. The athlete sues. Which claim is the strongest?
law-torts.l14.q5.e: Unauthorised commercial use of likeness is the core of appropriation and the right of publicity. A public photograph is not a private fact and no intrusion is involved.

law-torts.l15.q1.t: A property interest in the land affected
law-torts.l15.q1.p: To bring a private nuisance claim, the plaintiff must have:
law-torts.l15.q1.h: Nuisance protects use and enjoyment of land.
law-torts.l15.q1.e: Private nuisance protects possessory or use interests in land. Physical injury and malice are not required.

law-torts.l15.q2.t: Special injury different in kind from that suffered by the general public
law-torts.l15.q2.p: A private individual suing over a public nuisance generally must show:
law-torts.l15.q2.h: Public officials normally abate public nuisances.
law-torts.l15.q2.e: A private plaintiff must show harm different in kind from the public's. Adjacency and intent are not required.

law-torts.l15.q3.t: Granted an injunction conditioned on payment of permanent damages to the neighbours
law-torts.l15.q3.p: A cement plant emits dust and vibration that harm neighbours, but closing it would destroy a very large investment compared with the harm. In Boomer v. Atlantic Cement Co., the court:
law-torts.l15.q3.e: The court allowed the plant to continue if it paid permanent damages, treating the remedy as a balancing of equities. It did not deny relief or order closure.

law-torts.l15.q4.t: Weigh the gravity of the harm against the utility of the use, judged by a normal person of ordinary sensibilities in the community
law-torts.l15.q4.p: A homeowner runs a hobby workshop with loud machinery from 10 p.m. to 2 a.m. in a quiet residential area. A neighbour who works night shift and sleeps during the day is unaffected, but a neighbour with a newborn is kept awake. A court assessing private nuisance will most likely:
law-torts.l15.q4.e: Nuisance uses a normal person standard and balancing of utility and gravity. Intent is not required, and loud noise is not abnormally dangerous.

law-torts.l15.q5.t: Coming to the nuisance is not a complete defense but is a factor in the balance of reasonableness
law-torts.l15.q5.p: A farmer operates a pig farm, and years later a developer builds a subdivision next to it and the new residents sue for nuisance. The farm uses ordinary practices. Which statement is most accurate under the majority approach?
law-torts.l15.q5.h: The plaintiff's arrival is relevant but not dispositive.
law-torts.l15.q5.e: Most courts treat coming to the nuisance as one factor and not a bar. Right-to-farm statutes in many states add protection for existing farms.

law-torts.l16.q1.t: Scienter, meaning knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard for the truth
law-torts.l16.q1.p: Which of the following is an element of fraudulent misrepresentation?
law-torts.l16.q1.h: Intentional deceit requires a mental state.
law-torts.l16.q1.e: Fraud requires knowing or reckless falsity. A writing and a fiduciary relationship are not required.

law-torts.l16.q2.t: Persons the supplier intended or knew the recipient would intend to benefit from the information
law-torts.l16.q2.p: Negligent misrepresentation under Restatement (Second) section 552 generally limits liability to:
law-torts.l16.q2.h: The class of plaintiffs is limited.
law-torts.l16.q2.e: Section 552 limits liability to a limited group known or intended by the supplier. It is broader than privity but narrower than all foreseeable readers.

law-torts.l16.q3.t: Was not liable in negligence to a lender who relied on it, though fraud remained possible
law-torts.l16.q3.p: In Ultramares Corp. v. Touche, the court held that an accounting firm that negligently certified a balance sheet:
law-torts.l16.q3.e: The court limited negligence liability to near-privity relationships, while leaving room for fraud. It did not impose strict or unlimited liability.

law-torts.l16.q4.t: The buyer prevails, because the statement was a knowing false representation of material fact and reliance was justifiable
law-torts.l16.q4.p: Gaines tells a prospective buyer of his boat that it has never been in an accident, knowing that it was recently damaged in a collision and repaired. The buyer, who has an opportunity to inspect but does not, buys the boat and later discovers the history. The buyer sues in fraud. The most likely outcome is:
law-torts.l16.q4.h: A failure to investigate is rarely a bar to fraud.
law-torts.l16.q4.e: Most courts do not require a plaintiff to investigate a deliberate misstatement of fact. The fraud elements are met, and fiduciary status is not needed.

law-torts.l16.q5.t: Improper means, because the competitor used fraud to induce the breach
law-torts.l16.q5.p: A competitor knows that a supplier has a binding three-year exclusive contract with a bakery. The competitor tells the supplier, falsely, that the bakery is about to go bankrupt, and the supplier stops deliveries to the bakery. The bakery sues the competitor for tortious interference. The strongest element in the bakery's favour is:
law-torts.l16.q5.h: Competition is privileged unless the means are improper.
law-torts.l16.q5.e: Fraud is an improper means, which defeats the competition privilege. Profit motive alone is not improper.

law-torts.l17.q1.p: Under respondeat superior, an employer is vicariously liable for torts committed by an employee:
law-torts.l17.q1.h: The test is the scope of the work.
law-torts.l17.q1.e: Respondeat superior holds employers liable for torts within the scope of employment, regardless of employer fault. Negligent hiring is a separate direct-liability theory.

law-torts.l17.q2.t: The employer's right to control the manner and details of the work
law-torts.l17.q2.p: The primary factor distinguishing an employee from an independent contractor is:
law-torts.l17.q2.e: The right to control details is the central factor, and labels do not control.

law-torts.l17.q3.t: Likely liable, because a minor detour remains within the scope of employment
law-torts.l17.q3.p: A salesperson, on the way to a client meeting, makes a short stop to pick up personal dry cleaning and then negligently collides with a car. Under the usual rule, the employer is:
law-torts.l17.q3.h: A detour is not a frolic.
law-torts.l17.q3.e: Minor deviations from the work are detours within scope, while substantial personal trips are frolics. The going-and-coming rule concerns commuting, not travel between client visits.

law-torts.l17.q4.t: Negligent retention, which does not depend on the employee acting within scope, though the harm must relate to the risk
law-torts.l17.q4.p: A trucking firm hires a driver without checking his record and later learns he has multiple prior convictions for reckless driving. The firm continues to employ him, and while on a personal weekend trip in his own car, he causes a crash. The injured plaintiff sues the firm. Which theory has the best chance?
law-torts.l17.q4.h: Direct liability for the employer's own negligence.
law-torts.l17.q4.e: Negligent retention and hiring are direct claims and need not satisfy scope of employment, though a causal link to the known risk is needed. Respondeat superior fails because the trip was personal.

law-torts.l17.q5.t: Potentially liable under ostensible agency, because the patient reasonably believed the physician was the hospital's agent
law-torts.l17.q5.p: A patient goes to a hospital emergency room and is treated by a physician who is an independent contractor but wears a hospital badge, with signs suggesting the hospital provides the doctors. The physician negligently treats the patient. In many states, the hospital is:
law-torts.l17.q5.h: Reasonable belief induced by the principal.
law-torts.l17.q5.e: Ostensible agency applies where the principal's conduct leads the plaintiff reasonably to rely on an agency appearance. The independent contractor label does not end the inquiry.

law-torts.l18.q1.t: Punish outrageous conduct and deter similar conduct
law-torts.l18.q1.p: The main purpose of punitive damages is to:
law-torts.l18.q1.e: Punitive damages punish and deter and are not compensatory. Attorney fees follow the American rule and are generally not recoverable.

law-torts.l18.q2.t: A tort actionable without proof of harm has been committed but no loss is shown
law-torts.l18.q2.e: Nominal damages vindicate a right where the tort does not require harm and none is proved. The other situations call for different measures.

law-torts.l18.q3.t: The disparity between the harm or potential harm and the punitive award
law-torts.l18.q3.p: Under BMW of North America v. Gore, which of the following is one of the three guideposts for reviewing the constitutionality of a punitive damages award?
law-torts.l18.q3.e: The guideposts are reprehensibility, the ratio to harm and comparison with civil penalties. The defendant's wealth is not a guidepost.

law-torts.l18.q4.t: Reduce the punitive award substantially, since the ratio is extreme and the conduct lacks high reprehensibility
law-torts.l18.q4.p: A jury awards 100,000 dollars in compensatory damages and 10 million dollars in punitive damages against a company whose conduct was negligent but not reckless, and which harmed only the plaintiff. Applying State Farm v. Campbell, a reviewing court is most likely to:
