law-torts.l18.q4.e: State Farm said few awards beyond single-digit multiples satisfy due process, and reprehensibility is the most important guidepost. Wealth alone does not justify it.

law-torts.l18.q5.t: The conduct was reckless toward tenant safety and the ratio is a modest single-digit multiple
law-torts.l18.q5.p: A plaintiff proves that a landlord knowingly rented an apartment with an unrepaired gas leak, and the plaintiff suffered injury. The jury finds actual damages of 50,000 dollars and awards punitive damages of 150,000 dollars. In reviewing the award, which consideration is most helpful to sustaining it?
law-torts.l18.q5.e: Knowing disregard for safety increases reprehensibility, and a 3 to 1 ratio fits within due process guidelines. Ordinary negligence would not support punitives, and wealth alone is not a justification.

lighting-design.l01.q1.p: If a small lamp is moved twice as far from a wall, the light reaching the wall becomes about one quarter as strong.
lighting-design.l01.q1.h: The same light spreads over a larger area.
lighting-design.l01.q1.e: Light spreads over an area that grows with the square of the distance, so doubling the distance gives roughly a quarter of the illuminance.

lighting-design.l01.q2.p: A small lamp gives 400 lux on a table at 1 metre. About how much does it give at 2 metres?
lighting-design.l01.q2.h: Doubling the distance quadruples the area covered.
lighting-design.l01.q2.e: At twice the distance the light covers four times the area, so 400 divided by 4 is about 100 lux.

lighting-design.l01.q3.p: When light strikes a matte black cloth, what mostly happens to it?
lighting-design.l01.q3.h: Think about why black fabric looks dark.
lighting-design.l01.q3.e: A matte black surface absorbs most of the light that lands on it and reflects very little.

lighting-design.l01.q4.t: It becomes four times brighter, or two stops
lighting-design.l01.q4.p: A photographer moves a small lamp from 4 metres to 2 metres away from the subject. By how much does the light on the subject change?
lighting-design.l01.q4.h: Halving the distance does the reverse of doubling it.
lighting-design.l01.q4.e: Halving the distance gives four times the illuminance, and each doubling is one stop, so that is two stops.

lighting-design.l01.q5.p: The inverse square law says that doubling the distance to a small source cuts the light on a surface in half.
lighting-design.l01.q5.h: Check whether the drop is linear or squared.
lighting-design.l01.q5.e: Doubling the distance cuts the light to one quarter, not one half, because the falloff follows the square of the distance.

lighting-design.l02.q1.p: Which of these gives the softest light?
lighting-design.l02.q1.h: Which source acts like one very large glowing panel?
lighting-design.l02.q1.e: Clouds scatter the sunlight so the whole sky acts as a very large source, which makes shadows soft.

lighting-design.l02.q2.p: Moving a softbox closer to a subject makes the light on the subject softer.
lighting-design.l02.q2.h: Closer sources look bigger from the subject.
lighting-design.l02.q2.e: A closer source has a larger apparent size from the subject, so shadow edges become softer.

lighting-design.l02.q3.t: How large the source appears from the subject
lighting-design.l02.q3.p: What mainly decides whether a shadow edge looks crisp or feathered?
lighting-design.l02.q3.h: The key word is apparent size.
lighting-design.l02.q3.e: A small apparent source gives crisp edges and a large apparent source gives gradual ones.

lighting-design.l02.q4.t: The glowing sheet becomes a larger source
lighting-design.l02.q4.p: Why does placing a sheet of diffusion in front of a small lamp soften its light?
lighting-design.l02.q4.h: Think about what the subject now sees in place of the small bulb.
lighting-design.l02.q4.e: The diffusion material scatters the light and becomes a larger glowing surface, which is a larger apparent source.

lighting-design.l02.q5.p: Because the sun is enormously large, it always gives soft light on a clear day.
lighting-design.l02.q5.h: Consider how big the sun looks in the sky.
lighting-design.l02.q5.e: The sun appears as a small disc from Earth, so on a clear day it casts hard shadows.

lighting-design.l03.q1.t: From the side, close to the wall
lighting-design.l03.q1.p: Which light direction is best at revealing the texture of a brick wall?
lighting-design.l03.q1.h: Think about which direction makes each bump cast a shadow.
lighting-design.l03.q1.e: Side light rakes across the surface, so every raised detail casts a shadow and texture appears.

lighting-design.l03.q2.p: Light coming from near the camera tends to make a face look flatter.
lighting-design.l03.q2.h: Shadows hide behind the subject from this angle.
lighting-design.l03.q2.e: Front light fills the shadows the camera can see, which reduces the sense of depth.

lighting-design.l03.q3.t: We are used to being lit from above
lighting-design.l03.q3.p: Why does light from below a face, like a flashlight under the chin, often look eerie?
lighting-design.l03.q3.h: Think about where most natural light comes from.
lighting-design.l03.q3.e: Sun and ceiling lights come from above, so light from below looks unnatural and is often used to unsettle.

lighting-design.l03.q4.t: A bright edge that separates the subject from the background
lighting-design.l03.q4.p: What does a light placed behind the subject and aimed toward the camera most often add?
lighting-design.l03.q4.h: Think about the outline of hair and shoulders.
lighting-design.l03.q4.e: Back light traces a thin bright edge, which helps the subject stand out from what is behind it.

lighting-design.l03.q5.t: A small triangle of light on the cheek on the shadow side
lighting-design.l03.q5.p: Which feature identifies Rembrandt lighting on a portrait?
lighting-design.l03.q5.h: It is named for the way the shadow and cheek meet.
lighting-design.l03.q5.e: Rembrandt lighting comes from a key to the side and above, leaving a small lit triangle on the shadowed cheek.

lighting-design.l04.q1.p: Which colour temperature looks the warmest, most orange?
lighting-design.l04.q1.e: On the Kelvin scale, lower values look warmer and higher values look cooler and bluer.

lighting-design.l04.q2.p: A higher Kelvin value means the light looks warmer and more orange.
lighting-design.l04.q2.h: The scale runs opposite to hot and cold in everyday speech.
lighting-design.l04.q2.e: Higher Kelvin values look cooler and bluer; lower values look warmer.

lighting-design.l04.q3.p: Studio tungsten lights are typically rated at about which colour temperature?
lighting-design.l04.q3.h: It is a warm value, but not as warm as a household bulb.
lighting-design.l04.q3.e: Film and studio tungsten lamps are typically rated at 3200 K, while daylight-balanced sources are around 5600 K.

lighting-design.l04.q4.t: How faithfully it shows colours compared with a reference
lighting-design.l04.q4.p: What does the colour rendering index, CRI, tell you about a light?
lighting-design.l04.q4.h: It is about colour accuracy, not colour warmth.
lighting-design.l04.q4.e: CRI is a scale up to 100 comparing how naturally a source renders a set of test colours.

lighting-design.l04.q5.p: A camera is set for daylight and a tungsten lamp appears in the frame. How does the lamp look?
lighting-design.l04.q5.h: Tungsten is much warmer than the white the camera expects.
lighting-design.l04.q5.e: Relative to a daylight setting, 3200 K tungsten reads as noticeably orange.

lighting-design.l05.q1.p: Which instrument has a lens built from concentric stepped rings?
lighting-design.l05.q1.h: It is named for a French physicist.
lighting-design.l05.q1.e: The Fresnel lens uses stepped rings, a design named for Augustin-Jean Fresnel.

lighting-design.l05.q2.p: An ellipsoidal spotlight can project a pattern, called a gobo, by placing it in the gate.
lighting-design.l05.q2.h: Think about what sits at the focal point of the beam.
lighting-design.l05.q2.e: A gobo slides into the gate of an ellipsoidal and the lens focuses its pattern onto a surface.

lighting-design.l05.q3.p: A designer needs a crisp-edged square pool of light on a stage floor. Which tool is the best choice?
lighting-design.l05.q3.h: Which fixture has shutters in a gate?
lighting-design.l05.q3.e: Shutters in the gate of an ellipsoidal cut the beam to a sharp shape that the lens focuses.

lighting-design.l05.q4.t: By sliding the lamp and reflector toward or away from the lens
lighting-design.l05.q4.p: How is a Fresnel adjusted from a wide flood to a narrow spot?
lighting-design.l05.q4.e: Moving the lamp and reflector unit relative to the lens changes the beam angle.

lighting-design.l05.q5.p: The beam of a Fresnel has a soft edge that blends easily with neighbouring lights.
lighting-design.l05.q5.h: Think about why it works well for washes.
lighting-design.l05.q5.e: The Fresnel beam edge is soft, which is why it is popular for blending washes of light.

lighting-design.l06.q1.t: Turns it into a larger, softer source
lighting-design.l06.q1.p: What does a softbox do to a small lamp inside it?
lighting-design.l06.q1.h: Look at the white panel on the front.
lighting-design.l06.q1.e: The diffusion panel becomes the apparent source, so the light is larger and softer.

lighting-design.l06.q2.p: A practical is a working lamp that is visible in the shot.
lighting-design.l06.q2.h: The name suggests it actually does something.
lighting-design.l06.q2.e: Practicals, such as table lamps or neon signs, are working lights that appear in the frame.

lighting-design.l06.q3.t: More light for the electricity they use and less heat
lighting-design.l06.q3.p: Compared with tungsten lamps, what do LED fixtures typically offer?
lighting-design.l06.q3.e: LED fixtures typically produce more light per watt and run cooler than tungsten lamps.

lighting-design.l06.q4.t: Some LEDs have lower CRI or a colour tint
lighting-design.l06.q4.p: Why is it wise to check an LED fixture specification and test it before filming skin tones?
lighting-design.l06.q4.e: Cheaper LEDs may render colours poorly or have a tint, so testing prevents surprises on skin.

lighting-design.l06.q5.t: The lamp alone is usually too dim to expose the scene
lighting-design.l06.q5.p: Why might a crew add a hidden light near a bedside lamp that appears in the shot?
lighting-design.l06.q5.h: A household bulb is not very strong.
lighting-design.l06.q5.e: A hidden light matching the practical gives enough exposure while the audience still sees a believable source.

lighting-design.l07.q1.t: Adjusts the power to a lamp to change its brightness
lighting-design.l07.q1.h: It deals with gradual change instead of on and off.
lighting-design.l07.q1.e: A dimmer changes the power delivered to a lamp so that it can be brighter or dimmer.

lighting-design.l07.q2.p: A single DMX512 line, called a universe, carries 512 channels of control data.
lighting-design.l07.q2.h: The number is in the name.
lighting-design.l07.q2.e: DMX512 refers to the 512 channels in one universe.

lighting-design.l07.q3.p: On a simple dimmer channel, what does a DMX value of 255 usually mean?
lighting-design.l07.q3.e: Values run from 0 to 255, with 0 off and 255 full for a simple dimmer.

lighting-design.l07.q4.t: Builds, stores and plays back lighting states called cues
lighting-design.l07.q4.p: Which job does a lighting console do?
lighting-design.l07.q4.h: Think about what an operator uses to repeat the show every night.
lighting-design.l07.q4.e: The console builds and stores states and sends data so the show can be repeated exactly.

lighting-design.l07.q5.p: A tungsten lamp becomes warmer in colour as it is dimmed.
lighting-design.l07.q5.h: It looks more orange at low levels.
lighting-design.l07.q5.e: Dimming lowers the filament temperature, which shifts the colour toward warmer orange.

lighting-design.l08.q1.t: Warming daylight-balanced light to match tungsten
lighting-design.l08.q1.p: What is a CTO gel typically used for?
lighting-design.l08.q1.h: The letters stand for colour temperature orange.
lighting-design.l08.q1.e: CTO warms daylight-balanced light so it matches tungsten sources.

lighting-design.l08.q2.p: A gel adds extra light to the fixture it is placed on.
lighting-design.l08.q2.h: Think about what a filter does to the wavelengths it does not pass.
lighting-design.l08.q2.e: Gels work by absorbing, so they always cost some light.

lighting-design.l08.q3.t: It absorbs more of the light
lighting-design.l08.q3.p: Why does a deep saturated gel usually reduce brightness more than a pale one?
lighting-design.l08.q3.e: A saturated colour passes fewer wavelengths and absorbs more of the light.

lighting-design.l08.q4.p: What is a neutral density gel used for?
lighting-design.l08.q4.h: The word neutral is the clue.
lighting-design.l08.q4.e: ND filters reduce intensity evenly without a colour shift.

lighting-design.l08.q5.t: Diffusion in front of the lamp
lighting-design.l08.q5.p: You want to soften harsh light from a small lamp without changing its colour. What is the best addition?
lighting-design.l08.q5.h: Which filter enlarges the apparent source?
lighting-design.l08.q5.e: Diffusion scatters light and creates a larger glowing surface, which softens it.

lighting-design.l09.q1.p: In three-point lighting, which light is the main source?
lighting-design.l09.q1.h: It sets direction and most of the exposure.
lighting-design.l09.q1.e: The key is the main light and establishes direction and exposure.

lighting-design.l09.q2.p: The fill light is generally softer and dimmer than the key.
lighting-design.l09.q2.e: The fill lifts shadows and is usually softer and dimmer than the key.

lighting-design.l09.q3.t: To separate the subject from the background
lighting-design.l09.q3.p: What is the main purpose of the back light?
lighting-design.l09.q3.h: Think of a bright edge around the head.
lighting-design.l09.q3.e: The back light draws a bright edge that separates the subject and adds depth.

lighting-design.l09.q4.p: How can you deepen shadows in a three-point setup?
lighting-design.l09.q4.h: Think about which light fills the shadows.
lighting-design.l09.q4.e: A dimmer fill leaves shadows darker and raises contrast.

lighting-design.l09.q5.p: If the fill light is turned off and nothing else changes, what is the result?
lighting-design.l09.q5.h: Fill is what lifts the shadows.
lighting-design.l09.q5.e: Without fill, the shadow side loses its light and contrast rises.

lighting-design.l10.q1.t: Deepens shadows by absorbing light on the shadow side
lighting-design.l10.q1.e: A black flag absorbs bounced light that would otherwise fill the shadow.

lighting-design.l10.q2.p: A 4:1 lighting ratio is more contrasty than a 2:1 ratio.
lighting-design.l10.q2.h: A bigger ratio means a bigger difference.
lighting-design.l10.q2.e: A higher ratio means a larger difference between the lit and shadow sides.

lighting-design.l10.q3.p: In the common convention, a 4:1 ratio corresponds to how many stops of difference?
lighting-design.l10.q3.e: Four to one is two doublings, so two stops.

lighting-design.l10.q4.t: Bright with low contrast and few deep shadows
lighting-design.l10.q4.e: High-key lighting has low ratios and bright, open tones.

lighting-design.l10.q5.t: To shape or brighten the backdrop so the subject does not vanish into it
lighting-design.l10.q5.p: What is the job of a background light?
lighting-design.l10.q5.h: It lights the area behind the subject.
lighting-design.l10.q5.e: A background light controls how the backdrop looks and helps separation.

lighting-design.l11.q1.t: The light appears to come from a believable source in the scene
lighting-design.l11.q1.h: A light has a reason to be there.
lighting-design.l11.q1.e: Motivated light agrees in direction, quality and colour with a source we believe in.

lighting-design.l11.q2.p: A motivating source must always be visible in the frame.
lighting-design.l11.q2.h: Think about a window just off screen.
lighting-design.l11.q2.e: The source can be implied and off-screen as long as the light looks consistent with it.

lighting-design.l11.q3.t: It is more controllable and can match the direction of the sun
lighting-design.l11.q3.p: Why do crews often place a stronger light outside a window instead of relying on real daylight?
lighting-design.l11.q3.h: Real light changes and may not be strong enough.
lighting-design.l11.q3.e: A fixture outside the window gives constant, adjustable light aimed to match the motivation.

lighting-design.l11.q4.t: A hard light from below on a person in a sunny kitchen
lighting-design.l11.q4.p: Which is the best example of lighting without an apparent motivation?
lighting-design.l11.q4.h: Look for the one with no source that fits.
lighting-design.l11.q4.e: Hard light from below in a sunny kitchen has no source that explains it.

lighting-design.l11.q5.p: Motivated lighting must look plain and cannot be stylised.
lighting-design.l11.q5.e: Designers can push colour and contrast as long as the light stays consistent with its source.

lighting-design.l12.q1.t: A small reflection of the light source in the eyes
lighting-design.l12.q1.h: Look at the eyes in a portrait.
lighting-design.l12.q1.e: Catchlights are reflections of the source in the eyes, and they add life.

lighting-design.l12.q2.p: In butterfly lighting the key sits high and in front, above the lens axis.
lighting-design.l12.q2.h: The nose shadow gives it its name.
lighting-design.l12.q2.e: A high frontal key leaves a butterfly-shaped shadow under the nose.

lighting-design.l12.q3.t: A key above and a reflector or fill below
lighting-design.l12.q3.h: Picture the two halves of a shell.
lighting-design.l12.q3.e: Clamshell frames the face with light from above and below for smooth even light.

lighting-design.l12.q4.t: The side turned away from the camera
lighting-design.l12.q4.p: In short lighting, which side of the face does the key light?
lighting-design.l12.q4.h: Short lighting tends to slim the face.
lighting-design.l12.q4.e: In short lighting the lit side is the one turned away from the camera.

lighting-design.l12.q5.t: A large soft source close to the subject
lighting-design.l12.q5.p: Which source gives smooth skin transitions in a portrait?
lighting-design.l12.q5.e: A large close source is soft and gives gentle gradations on skin.

lighting-design.l13.q1.t: Light bounces off a smooth surface at the same angle it arrived
lighting-design.l13.q1.p: Which rule explains why you see a lamp reflected in a glossy product?
lighting-design.l13.q1.h: It is called the law of reflection.
lighting-design.l13.q1.e: For a smooth surface, the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence.

lighting-design.l13.q2.p: A large soft source can make a smooth gradient highlight on a glossy product.
lighting-design.l13.q2.h: The reflection takes the size of the source.
lighting-design.l13.q2.e: A large source reflects as a broad smooth band, which describes the shape well.

lighting-design.l13.q3.t: Wraps them in diffused light to reduce harsh reflections
lighting-design.l13.q3.p: What does a light tent do for small shiny products?
lighting-design.l13.q3.e: The translucent tent diffuses the light around the product.

lighting-design.l13.q4.t: Light from the side or at a raking angle
lighting-design.l13.q4.p: How do you bring out the texture of a matte fabric product?
lighting-design.l13.q4.e: Raking light makes small surface details cast shadows.

lighting-design.l13.q5.t: Change the angle of the item or source so the reflection leaves the lens view
lighting-design.l13.q5.p: What can you do if a lamp reflection in a glossy item runs straight into the lens?
lighting-design.l13.q5.e: Changing the angle redirects the reflected light away from the lens.

lighting-design.l14.q1.p: What is a risk of overloading a circuit?
lighting-design.l14.q1.e: An overloaded circuit can overheat, which is why designers add up loads first.

lighting-design.l14.q2.p: It is fine to handle a halogen bulb with bare fingers.
lighting-design.l14.q2.h: Skin oils and heat are both an issue.
lighting-design.l14.q2.e: Skin oils can cause a halogen bulb to fail, and the bulb is very hot in use.

lighting-design.l14.q3.p: A 1200 watt lamp runs on 120 volts. About how many amps does it draw?
lighting-design.l14.q3.e: Amps equal watts divided by volts, so 1200 divided by 120 is 10 amps.

lighting-design.l14.q4.t: To catch the fixture if the clamp fails
lighting-design.l14.q4.p: Why is a secondary safety cable used on a hung fixture?
lighting-design.l14.q4.e: A safety cable is a backup that stops the fixture falling if the main support fails.

lighting-design.l14.q5.t: Stabilising it so it does not tip
lighting-design.l14.q5.p: What are sandbags used for on a light stand?
lighting-design.l14.q5.e: Weighting the base keeps the stand stable.

lighting-design.l15.q1.t: By heating a block of lime with an oxygen and hydrogen flame
lighting-design.l15.q1.h: It has lime in its name.
lighting-design.l15.q1.e: A flame fed with oxygen and hydrogen heated lime until it glowed brightly.

lighting-design.l15.q2.p: Gas lighting was used in theatres before electric lighting.
lighting-design.l15.q2.h: Think of the order of the nineteenth century.
lighting-design.l15.q2.e: Gas arrived in the early nineteenth century and electric lighting came later.

lighting-design.l15.q3.p: What was a major hazard of gas and limelight in theatres?
lighting-design.l15.q3.e: Open flames made theatre fires an ongoing problem.

lighting-design.l15.q4.t: Gas lighting, then incandescent electric lighting
lighting-design.l15.q4.h: Think of the long sequence from flame to LED.
lighting-design.l15.q4.e: Gas came before incandescent electric lighting, which came before LEDs.

lighting-design.l15.q5.t: That light should shape the stage as an expressive element
lighting-design.l15.q5.p: What did designers such as Adolphe Appia argue about light on stage?
lighting-design.l15.q5.h: They saw light as more than visibility.
lighting-design.l15.q5.e: Appia and Craig argued that light is an active, expressive part of stage design.

lighting-design.l16.q1.p: What is the first step of a theatre lighting design?
lighting-design.l16.q1.h: It comes long before any lamp is on.
lighting-design.l16.q1.e: Designers begin by reading the script for time, place and mood.

lighting-design.l16.q2.p: A light plot is a scaled drawing showing where each instrument hangs and where it points.
lighting-design.l16.q2.h: It is a drawing of the rig.
lighting-design.l16.q2.e: The plot shows the position, type and aim of each fixture.

lighting-design.l16.q3.t: A stored lighting state and the instruction to change to it
lighting-design.l16.q3.h: Think of what the console plays back.
lighting-design.l16.q3.e: A cue is a stored state with fade times that the operator triggers.

lighting-design.l16.q4.t: To work through the lighting changes without playing every scene
lighting-design.l16.q4.p: What is the purpose of a cue-to-cue rehearsal?
lighting-design.l16.q4.e: A cue-to-cue lets the team refine the timing of lighting changes efficiently.

lighting-design.l16.q5.t: To keep faces modelled and visible
lighting-design.l16.q5.p: Why are acting areas often lit from two directions about 45 degrees to each side?
lighting-design.l16.q5.h: Think of keeping a face visible from all stage positions.
lighting-design.l16.q5.e: Two angled sources model the face and keep it visible, an approach linked to McCandless.

lighting-design.l17.q1.t: It scatters light so beams become visible
lighting-design.l17.q1.p: Why is haze used at concerts?
lighting-design.l17.q1.h: Beams do not show in clear air.
lighting-design.l17.q1.e: Particles in the air scatter light so beams look like shafts.

lighting-design.l17.q2.p: A follow spot is operated by a person who tracks a performer.
lighting-design.l17.q2.e: A follow spot is hand-operated and tracks the performer.

lighting-design.l17.q3.p: What can a moving light do remotely?
lighting-design.l17.q3.e: Moving lights can be controlled for pan, tilt, colour, gobo and other attributes.

lighting-design.l17.q4.t: So lighting stays in sync with the music on every performance
lighting-design.l17.q4.p: Why might cues be triggered by timecode?
lighting-design.l17.q4.e: Timecode makes sure cues land at the same musical moment each night.

lighting-design.l17.q5.t: So the audience and cameras can see the performer
lighting-design.l17.q5.p: Why does even a moody concert design still need face light?
lighting-design.l17.q5.e: Without front or face light, performers appear only as silhouettes.

lighting-design.l18.q1.p: Which three layers do architectural designers commonly use?
lighting-design.l18.q1.h: They concern general, working and highlight light.
lighting-design.l18.q1.e: Ambient, task and accent layers work together in most spaces.

lighting-design.l18.q2.p: Grazing light close to a textured wall emphasises the texture.
lighting-design.l18.q2.e: A fixture aimed along the surface makes every bump cast a shadow.

lighting-design.l18.q3.p: Which layer is a reading lamp?
lighting-design.l18.q3.e: A reading lamp provides stronger light for a specific activity.

lighting-design.l18.q4.t: Discomfort from a bright source in the field of view
lighting-design.l18.q4.e: Glare is the discomfort and reduced visibility caused by an overly bright source in view.

lighting-design.l18.q5.p: Which colour temperature is typical for a cosy living room?
lighting-design.l18.q5.e: Warm white around 2700 K is typical for living rooms and restaurants.

lighting-design.l19.q1.p: Which lighting style tends to feel tense or secretive?
lighting-design.l19.q1.e: Low-key lighting has high contrast and large dark areas, which suits tension.

lighting-design.l19.q2.p: The emotional meanings of colours are the same in every culture.
lighting-design.l19.q2.e: Colour associations vary between cultures, so designers consider the audience.

lighting-design.l19.q3.t: The passing of time or a mood sinking
lighting-design.l19.q3.p: What can a slow fade from bright to dim show?
lighting-design.l19.q3.e: Changes over time can signal a day passing or an emotional shift.

lighting-design.l19.q4.t: Strong contrast of light and dark, as in the work of Caravaggio and Rembrandt
lighting-design.l19.q4.e: Chiaroscuro is the strong use of light against dark, seen in painting and later in film.

lighting-design.l19.q5.p: Which choice would most likely suggest gentleness or calm?
lighting-design.l19.q5.h: Recall what softness tends to signal.
lighting-design.l19.q5.e: Soft, low-contrast light tends to suggest calm, memory and gentleness.

lighting-design.l20.q1.t: Define the story and what the viewer should feel
lighting-design.l20.q1.p: What is the first step in the design method?
lighting-design.l20.q1.e: Technical choices should serve the story, so it is defined first.

lighting-design.l20.q2.p: You should add up the electrical load against the circuits before you wire the lights.
lighting-design.l20.q2.e: Checking the load before wiring helps avoid overloads.

lighting-design.l20.q3.t: A large soft window-like key with gentle fill
lighting-design.l20.q3.p: Which setup best suits a quiet morning in a kitchen?
lighting-design.l20.q3.e: A large soft key with gentle fill gives a calm, low-contrast look.

lighting-design.l20.q4.t: Set the ratio with fill or negative fill
lighting-design.l20.q4.p: After setting the key, what is the sensible next step?
lighting-design.l20.q4.e: The ratio comes next, controlled with fill, bounce or negative fill.

lighting-design.l20.q5.t: The eye adjusts and can be fooled
lighting-design.l20.q5.p: Why test by looking at the camera or monitor?
lighting-design.l20.q5.e: The camera sees what the eye adapts to, so a test view catches issues.

lit-studies-early.l01.q1.p: Close reading asks why a writer chose particular words, not only what happens in the story.
lit-studies-early.l01.q1.e: Close reading attends to the choices a text makes in wording, order and detail.

lit-studies-early.l01.q2.p: Which sequence matches the three-move method in this lesson?
lit-studies-early.l01.q2.e: The method moves from noticing details to asking what they do to forming an evidence-based claim.

lit-studies-early.l01.q3.p: A reader says a poem "feels sad" but points to no words in it. What is missing?
lit-studies-early.l01.q3.e: Close reading ties each claim to specific words or details in the passage.

lit-studies-early.l01.q4.p: In Sonnet 18, the poem begins as a comparison but soon lists the flaws of summer.
lit-studies-early.l01.q4.h: Look at the rough winds and the short season.
lit-studies-early.l01.q4.e: The poem opens by comparing the beloved to summer and then shows summer falling short.

lit-studies-early.l01.q5.t: The repetition builds tension, as shown by the word recurring in each line
lit-studies-early.l01.q5.p: Which is the strongest close-reading statement about a repeated word in a passage?
lit-studies-early.l01.q5.h: Strong claims explain an effect and cite the text.
lit-studies-early.l01.q5.e: A good claim names an effect and points to where the evidence appears.

lit-studies-early.l02.q1.p: A genre is a family of works that share conventions readers expect.
lit-studies-early.l02.q1.h: Think of "contract" between writer and reader.
lit-studies-early.l02.q1.e: Genres are bundles of shared conventions that guide expectations.

lit-studies-early.l02.q2.p: Which genre is described as a long narrative poem about heroes and large events?
lit-studies-early.l02.q2.e: An epic is a long narrative poem, usually in an elevated style, about heroic deeds.

lit-studies-early.l02.q3.t: The book plays against conventions the reader already recognizes
lit-studies-early.l02.q3.p: Why does the joke in Don Quixote about romances work best for a reader who knows romances?
lit-studies-early.l02.q3.e: Parody works by recalling and twisting expected conventions.

lit-studies-early.l02.q4.t: A short poem expressing a speaker's thought or feeling
lit-studies-early.l02.q4.h: It is usually short and personal.
lit-studies-early.l02.q4.e: Lyrics are compressed poems that express a speaker's thought or feeling.

lit-studies-early.l02.q5.p: When a writer breaks a genre convention, it can be a clue that the writer is saying something new.
lit-studies-early.l02.q5.e: Unfollowed conventions stand out and often carry meaning.

lit-studies-early.l03.q1.p: A narrator and the author of a work are always the same person.
lit-studies-early.l03.q1.e: A narrator is a voice created by the author and may differ from the author in knowledge and views.

lit-studies-early.l03.q2.p: In first-person narration, the story is told by
lit-studies-early.l03.q2.e: First-person narration comes from a character telling the story from inside it.

lit-studies-early.l03.q3.t: One whose account may be mistaken, biased or deceptive
lit-studies-early.l03.q3.e: An unreliable narrator forces the reader to read around the account.

lit-studies-early.l03.q4.p: Which structure places a story told by one character inside another story?
lit-studies-early.l03.q4.h: The outer story holds the inner ones.
lit-studies-early.l03.q4.e: A frame narrative nests tales within a surrounding story.

lit-studies-early.l03.q5.p: Chaucer the pilgrim may praise people in a way that invites readers to notice more than he says.
lit-studies-early.l03.q5.h: The narrator is a created figure.
lit-studies-early.l03.q5.e: The gap between his praise and the details is a source of irony.

lit-studies-early.l04.q1.t: People cope with death by making things that outlast them
lit-studies-early.l04.q1.p: Which is a theme rather than only a topic?
lit-studies-early.l04.q1.h: A theme is a full claim.
lit-studies-early.l04.q1.e: A theme states what a work suggests about a topic, in a sentence.

lit-studies-early.l04.q2.p: A motif is an image or idea that recurs in a work.
lit-studies-early.l04.q2.e: A motif is a recurring element that points to what a work cares about.

lit-studies-early.l04.q3.t: A concrete thing that stands for something beyond itself
lit-studies-early.l04.q3.e: A symbol is a concrete object or image that represents a larger idea.

lit-studies-early.l04.q4.p: A good interpretation of a theme should be tested against other passages in the work.
lit-studies-early.l04.q4.e: Interpretations gain strength when multiple passages support them and none contradict them.

lit-studies-early.l04.q5.t: Revise the claim to account for it
lit-studies-early.l04.q5.p: You find a passage that contradicts your theme claim. What should you do?
lit-studies-early.l04.q5.e: Counterevidence should lead to a better, more accurate claim.

lit-studies-early.l05.q1.p: The Epic of Gilgamesh comes from ancient Mesopotamia and was written in cuneiform on clay tablets.
lit-studies-early.l05.q1.h: Think of early writing on clay.
lit-studies-early.l05.q1.e: The poem survives on cuneiform tablets from ancient Mesopotamia.

lit-studies-early.l05.q2.t: The death of his friend Enkidu
lit-studies-early.l05.q2.p: What event drives Gilgamesh to seek eternal life?
lit-studies-early.l05.q2.e: Enkidu's death makes Gilgamesh fear his own mortality.

lit-studies-early.l05.q3.t: He does not gain it and returns to Uruk
lit-studies-early.l05.q3.p: How does the poem end for Gilgamesh's quest for immortality?
lit-studies-early.l05.q3.h: The poem does not reward the quest.
lit-studies-early.l05.q3.e: He fails to win immortality and returns home to the city's walls.

lit-studies-early.l05.q4.p: Because some tablets are broken, every translation of Gilgamesh involves scholarly choices about gaps.
lit-studies-early.l05.q4.e: Missing sections mean translators and editors must reconstruct or leave gaps.

lit-studies-early.l05.q5.t: The walls appear near both the beginning and the end of the poem
lit-studies-early.l05.q5.p: A reader argues that the walls of Uruk suggest lasting human work. Which kind of evidence supports this best?
lit-studies-early.l05.q5.h: Look for repetition in the text.
lit-studies-early.l05.q5.e: A motif that recurs and frames the poem supports a symbolic reading.

lit-studies-early.l06.q1.p: What is the central subject that opens the Iliad?
lit-studies-early.l06.q1.h: It is the poem's first word.
lit-studies-early.l06.q1.e: The poem begins with the wrath of Achilles, not the whole war.

lit-studies-early.l06.q2.p: The Iliad covers the entire ten years of the Trojan War from start to finish.
lit-studies-early.l06.q2.h: It focuses on a single episode.
lit-studies-early.l06.q2.e: The poem centres on a short stretch of the war's tenth year.

lit-studies-early.l06.q3.t: His friend Patroclus has been killed by Hector
lit-studies-early.l06.q3.p: Why does Achilles return to fight?
lit-studies-early.l06.q3.h: It is a loss, not a prize.
lit-studies-early.l06.q3.e: Patroclus's death by Hector sends Achilles back into battle.

lit-studies-early.l06.q4.t: A fixed descriptive phrase used with a character
lit-studies-early.l06.q4.p: What is an epithet like "swift-footed" for Achilles?
lit-studies-early.l06.q4.e: Epithets are fixed phrases that helped oral poets compose and help readers recognize characters.

lit-studies-early.l06.q5.p: The poem ends with Hector's funeral after Priam asks Achilles for his body, which supports reading grief as a key emphasis.
lit-studies-early.l06.q5.e: Ending on mourning rather than victory suggests grief as central.

lit-studies-early.l07.q1.p: Where is Odysseus trying to return?
lit-studies-early.l07.q1.e: Odysseus is trying to reach Ithaca, his wife and his son.

lit-studies-early.l07.q2.p: Odysseus himself tells the story of many of his adventures to the Phaeacians.
lit-studies-early.l07.q2.h: Think of a first-person narrator inside the poem.
lit-studies-early.l07.q2.e: The long flashback is narrated by Odysseus, so readers should ask how he shapes it.

lit-studies-early.l07.q3.t: The old nurse sees his scar
lit-studies-early.l07.q3.p: Which is a recognition scene in the poem?
lit-studies-early.l07.q3.h: Identity is shown by a sign.
lit-studies-early.l07.q3.e: The scar is one of several gradual signs that reveal his identity.

lit-studies-early.l07.q4.p: Which values does the Odyssey stress compared with the Iliad?
lit-studies-early.l07.q4.e: The Odyssey emphasizes cleverness, endurance and return to a household.

lit-studies-early.l07.q5.t: How hosts and guests treat strangers shows their character
lit-studies-early.l07.q5.p: Why can hospitality serve as a moral measure in the poem?
lit-studies-early.l07.q5.e: Characters are judged by how they treat guests and strangers.

lit-studies-early.l08.q1.p: Greek tragedies were performed at religious festivals in honor of Dionysus.
lit-studies-early.l08.q1.e: Tragedy was part of Athenian festivals honoring Dionysus.

lit-studies-early.l08.q2.t: The audience understands more than the speaker does
lit-studies-early.l08.q2.e: Dramatic irony arises when the audience grasps meanings that a character misses.

lit-studies-early.l08.q3.t: He himself is the cause of the trouble in Thebes
lit-studies-early.l08.q3.p: What discovery does Oedipus make in Sophocles' play?
lit-studies-early.l08.q3.h: He investigates, then it turns on him.
lit-studies-early.l08.q3.e: He learns that he unknowingly killed his father and married his mother.

lit-studies-early.l08.q4.t: Both Creon and Antigone appeal to real values
lit-studies-early.l08.q4.p: Why is Antigone not a simple contest of right versus wrong?
lit-studies-early.l08.q4.e: Loyalty and divine duty clash with civic order, each with real weight.

lit-studies-early.l08.q5.p: Because the audience knew the myth already, the interest in a Greek tragedy lay mainly in how it was told.
lit-studies-early.l08.q5.e: With known plots, the dramatist's choices of emphasis and language become the focus.

lit-studies-early.l09.q1.e: Medea was first performed in 431 BCE.

lit-studies-early.l09.q2.p: Euripides often puts women, foreigners or the defeated at the center of his plays.
lit-studies-early.l09.q2.h: Think of Medea and Trojan women.
lit-studies-early.l09.q2.e: Many of his plays center on outsiders and victims.

lit-studies-early.l09.q3.t: It helps them understand her pain even as they recoil from her act
lit-studies-early.l09.q3.p: What does Medea's speech about her position do for the audience?
lit-studies-early.l09.q3.e: The play makes judgment difficult by giving her grievances real force.

lit-studies-early.l09.q4.t: A formal debate between opposing positions
lit-studies-early.l09.q4.p: What is an agon in Greek drama?
lit-studies-early.l09.q4.e: An agon is a structured contest of arguments between characters.

lit-studies-early.l09.q5.p: The Trojan Women celebrates the victors of the war without showing the losses of the defeated.
lit-studies-early.l09.q5.e: The play follows the women who will be enslaved and dwells on loss.

lit-studies-early.l10.q1.h: He lived in the fourth century BCE.

lit-studies-early.l10.q2.p: Which part of tragedy does Aristotle rank first?
lit-studies-early.l10.q2.h: It concerns the arrangement of events.
lit-studies-early.l10.q2.e: He treats plot as the most important part.

lit-studies-early.l10.q3.p: Peripeteia means a reversal, in which events turn to the opposite of what was expected.
lit-studies-early.l10.q3.e: Peripeteia is a reversal; anagnorisis is a recognition.

lit-studies-early.l10.q4.p: Which unity does Aristotle clearly stress?
lit-studies-early.l10.q4.h: The other unities came from later critics.
lit-studies-early.l10.q4.e: Later critics codified time and place; Aristotle stresses unity of action.

lit-studies-early.l10.q5.t: Its terms are debated and many plays do things it does not describe
lit-studies-early.l10.q5.p: Why is it wise to use the Poetics as a lens, not a rulebook?
lit-studies-early.l10.q5.h: Terms like catharsis are interpreted differently.
lit-studies-early.l10.q5.e: Concepts like catharsis and hamartia are disputed, and plays can exceed his categories.

lit-studies-early.l11.q1.p: Virgil's Aeneid tells of a Trojan survivor whose descendants will found Rome.
lit-studies-early.l11.q1.e: Aeneas flees Troy and journeys to Italy.

lit-studies-early.l11.q2.t: Dutiful devotion to family, gods and homeland
lit-studies-early.l11.q2.p: What does "pietas" mean in the poem?
lit-studies-early.l11.q2.e: Pietas describes Aeneas's sense of duty.

lit-studies-early.l11.q3.t: She is abandoned by Aeneas and takes her own life
lit-studies-early.l11.q3.p: What happens to Dido in Book 4?
lit-studies-early.l11.q3.h: The gods command him to leave.
lit-studies-early.l11.q3.e: Aeneas leaves Carthage at the gods' command and Dido kills herself.

lit-studies-early.l11.q4.e: Allusion refers to or echoes earlier texts to create meaning.

lit-studies-early.l11.q5.p: Scholars agree that the Aeneid is only a celebration of Augustus and contains no questioning of empire.
lit-studies-early.l11.q5.e: Many scholars debate whether the poem celebrates, questions, or does both.

lit-studies-early.l12.q1.t: It contains many books of different genres
lit-studies-early.l12.q1.p: Why is the Bible described as a library?
lit-studies-early.l12.q1.e: It includes narrative, law, poetry, prophecy, gospel, letters and more.

lit-studies-early.l12.q2.p: A literary reading of the Bible aims to describe how its texts are built, not to replace religious readings.
lit-studies-early.l12.q2.e: It describes genres and techniques while respecting faith traditions.

lit-studies-early.l12.q3.t: Parallelism, in which a line repeats, extends or contrasts another
lit-studies-early.l12.q3.p: Which feature is common in biblical poetry?
lit-studies-early.l12.q3.e: Parallel lines are a basic feature of Hebrew poetry.

lit-studies-early.l12.q4.t: It is spare and leaves motives for readers to infer
lit-studies-early.l12.q4.p: What is notable about much biblical narrative?
lit-studies-early.l12.q4.e: Narratives often give few details, leaving gaps for readers.

lit-studies-early.l12.q5.p: The King James Version of 1611 influenced English style.
lit-studies-early.l12.q5.e: The KJV shaped English idiom and prose rhythm.

lit-studies-early.l13.q1.p: The Quran is arranged in 114 chapters called surahs.
lit-studies-early.l13.q1.e: The Quran has 114 surahs, made of ayat.

lit-studies-early.l13.q2.p: Why is sound central to the Quran?
lit-studies-early.l13.q2.e: The text is experienced through recitation, so rhythm and sound matter.

lit-studies-early.l13.q3.t: It tells one continuous story, of Yusuf
lit-studies-early.l13.q3.p: How does Surah 12 differ from many other surahs?
lit-studies-early.l13.q3.e: It is a continuous narrative and calls itself the best of stories.

lit-studies-early.l13.q4.t: Roughly by length, with longer ones earlier
lit-studies-early.l13.q4.e: Longer surahs generally come earlier and shorter ones later.

lit-studies-early.l13.q5.p: A translation of the Quran can fully reproduce the Arabic's sound.
lit-studies-early.l13.q5.e: Translations are interpretations and cannot reproduce Arabic sound features.

lit-studies-early.l14.q1.p: Which are the two great Sanskrit epics of India?
lit-studies-early.l14.q1.e: The Mahabharata and the Ramayana are the two great Sanskrit epics.

lit-studies-early.l14.q2.p: The Bhagavad Gita is a dialogue between Arjuna and Krishna set before a battle in the Mahabharata.
lit-studies-early.l14.q2.e: The Gita is a philosophical dialogue within the Mahabharata.

lit-studies-early.l14.q3.p: Who is the Ramayana traditionally attributed to?
lit-studies-early.l14.q3.h: The other name goes with the Mahabharata.
lit-studies-early.l14.q3.e: Tradition attributes the Ramayana to Valmiki and the Mahabharata to Vyasa.

lit-studies-early.l14.q4.t: They grew over long periods, with stories inside stories
lit-studies-early.l14.q4.p: What does a layered, nested structure suggest about these epics?
lit-studies-early.l14.q4.e: Scholars see layers of composition rather than a single author.

lit-studies-early.l14.q5.p: The Mahabharata shows heroes making troubling choices and the costs of war.
lit-studies-early.l14.q5.e: The epic presents conflict between duties and shows the war's consequences.

lit-studies-early.l15.q1.t: A collection of sayings and conversations attributed to Confucius and disciples
lit-studies-early.l15.q1.h: It is made of short scenes.
lit-studies-early.l15.q1.e: It is a compilation of sayings and brief dialogues assembled by followers.

lit-studies-early.l15.q2.p: The Analects is a single continuous argument written by Confucius.
lit-studies-early.l15.q2.e: It is a collection of short passages compiled after his lifetime.

lit-studies-early.l15.q3.e: Ren is translated as humaneness or goodness; li is ritual or proper conduct.

lit-studies-early.l15.q4.t: The best answer depends on the person
lit-studies-early.l15.q4.p: Why might Confucius answer different students differently?
lit-studies-early.l15.q4.e: The text suggests that guidance suits each learner.

lit-studies-early.l15.q5.t: Compare it with other passages and imagine its context
lit-studies-early.l15.q5.p: What is a good strategy for reading a short saying?
lit-studies-early.l15.q5.e: Brief passages gain meaning when read alongside related ones.

lit-studies-early.l16.q1.p: The Tang dynasty is often called a golden age of Chinese poetry.
lit-studies-early.l16.q1.h: Li Bai and Du Fu belong to it.
lit-studies-early.l16.q1.e: The Tang dynasty (618 to 907) produced major poets.

lit-studies-early.l16.q2.p: Which two poets are named in the lesson?
lit-studies-early.l16.q2.h: Both lived in the eighth century.
lit-studies-early.l16.q2.e: Li Bai and Du Fu are two of the best-known Tang poets.

lit-studies-early.l16.q3.p: In "Quiet Night Thought," what feeling does the moonlight image carry?
lit-studies-early.l16.q3.h: The last action is thinking of home.
lit-studies-early.l16.q3.e: The speaker looks up at the moon and then thinks of home.

lit-studies-early.l16.q4.p: In Du Fu's "Spring View," the enduring landscape contrasts with a broken state.
lit-studies-early.l16.q4.e: The contrast sharpens the sense of human loss.

lit-studies-early.l16.q5.t: Much of the music and form of the Chinese is lost
lit-studies-early.l16.q5.p: Why should readers of translations remember that they see only part of the poem?
lit-studies-early.l16.q5.e: The tonal and formal patterns do not carry over into English.

lit-studies-early.l17.q1.p: Who wrote The Tale of Genji?
lit-studies-early.l17.q1.h: A court woman of the Heian period.
lit-studies-early.l17.q1.e: Murasaki Shikibu wrote it in the early eleventh century.

lit-studies-early.l17.q2.p: Characters in Genji often exchange short poems called waka.
lit-studies-early.l17.q2.h: Poetry is woven into the prose.
lit-studies-early.l17.q2.e: Waka exchanges are part of how characters communicate.

lit-studies-early.l17.q3.t: What counts as a novel depends on definition
lit-studies-early.l17.q3.p: Why is calling Genji a "novel" something to handle with care?
lit-studies-early.l17.q3.e: Whether it is a novel depends on how the term is defined.

lit-studies-early.l17.q4.t: Sensitivity to the fleeting beauty of things
lit-studies-early.l17.q4.p: What does mono no aware refer to, according to Motoori Norinaga?
lit-studies-early.l17.q4.e: The phrase names a sensitivity to transience as the work's central quality.

lit-studies-early.l17.q5.p: In Genji, much of the meaning of a scene can lie in social and emotional nuance rather than action.
lit-studies-early.l17.q5.e: Small gestures like the timing of a reply carry meaning.

lit-studies-early.l18.q1.e: The qasida is the classical Arabic ode.

lit-studies-early.l18.q2.p: In One Thousand and One Nights, Shahrazad tells stories to stay alive.
lit-studies-early.l18.q2.e: Her storytelling saves her life night after night.

lit-studies-early.l18.q3.t: Remembering a lost love, a journey, then praise or boast
lit-studies-early.l18.q3.p: Which is a typical movement in a pre-Islamic qasida?
lit-studies-early.l18.q3.e: Many odes open with an abandoned campsite and move through journey to praise.

lit-studies-early.l18.q4.p: Who helped popularize the Nights in Europe with a translation in the early 1700s?
lit-studies-early.l18.q4.e: Galland's French translation spread the tales in Europe.

lit-studies-early.l18.q5.p: Every tale now associated with the Nights, including Aladdin, appears in the earliest Arabic manuscripts.
lit-studies-early.l18.q5.e: Some famous tales, such as Aladdin, are not in the earliest manuscripts.

lit-studies-early.l19.q1.p: In what language was Beowulf written?
lit-studies-early.l19.q1.h: It is the language of early medieval England.

lit-studies-early.l19.q2.p: Beowulf is set in Scandinavia, not England.
lit-studies-early.l19.q2.h: Think of the Geats and Danes.
lit-studies-early.l19.q2.e: The hero is a Geat who helps the Danish king.

lit-studies-early.l19.q3.e: Kennings are compound metaphors for familiar things.

lit-studies-early.l19.q4.p: How does the poem treat heroic glory through its digressions?
lit-studies-early.l19.q4.h: Notice the stories of past feuds.
lit-studies-early.l19.q4.e: References to old stories and feuds create a sense that every hero dies.

lit-studies-early.l19.q5.p: The poem mixes a pre-Christian setting with reflections that seem Christian.
lit-studies-early.l19.q5.e: The setting is pre-Christian but the poet reflects on God and fate.

lit-studies-early.l20.q1.t: Writing in a vernacular Romance language rather than Latin
lit-studies-early.l20.q1.e: The term came from works in vernacular languages like French.

lit-studies-early.l20.q2.p: Typical medieval romances include a journey, trials and a test of the hero.
lit-studies-early.l20.q2.e: A quest with trials is a core pattern.

lit-studies-early.l20.q3.p: Who wrote some of the earliest major Arthurian romances?
lit-studies-early.l20.q3.e: Chretien de Troyes wrote early Arthurian romances.

lit-studies-early.l20.q4.t: A gap between chivalric ideals and human weakness
lit-studies-early.l20.q4.p: What does Gawain's acceptance of a magic girdle reveal in Sir Gawain and the Green Knight?
lit-studies-early.l20.q4.e: The poem uses the test to explore the frailty beneath the ideal.

lit-studies-early.l20.q5.p: Courtly love in romance is a topic about which scholars debate how closely it matched real life.
lit-studies-early.l20.q5.e: Scholars debate how far courtly love reflected real social behavior.

lit-studies-early.l21.q1.p: What are the three parts of the Divine Comedy?
lit-studies-early.l21.q1.e: Dante moves from Hell to Purgatory to Paradise.

lit-studies-early.l21.q2.p: Dante wrote the poem in the Tuscan vernacular rather than in Latin.
lit-studies-early.l21.q2.e: The choice helped establish Italian as a literary language.

lit-studies-early.l21.q3.p: Which rhyme scheme is terza rima?
lit-studies-early.l21.q3.e: Terza rima chains rhymes across three-line stanzas.

lit-studies-early.l21.q4.p: Who guides Dante through Hell and most of Purgatory?
lit-studies-early.l21.q4.e: Virgil guides him until Beatrice takes over.

lit-studies-early.l21.q5.t: The poet arranges the story while the pilgrim is learning inside it
lit-studies-early.l21.q5.p: Why is it important to separate Dante the poet from Dante the pilgrim?
lit-studies-early.l21.q5.e: The pilgrim's reactions are shaped by the poet's design.

lit-studies-early.l22.q1.t: A pilgrimage in which travelers tell stories
lit-studies-early.l22.q1.p: What is the frame of The Canterbury Tales?
lit-studies-early.l22.q1.e: The pilgrims tell tales on the way to Canterbury.

lit-studies-early.l22.q2.p: The Canterbury Tales was left unfinished.
lit-studies-early.l22.q2.h: There are gaps in the plan.
lit-studies-early.l22.q2.e: Chaucer wrote fewer tales than he planned, so the collection is incomplete.

lit-studies-early.l22.q3.e: A fabliau is a short, comic tale, often bawdy.

lit-studies-early.l22.q4.t: The narrator praises people while details suggest their faults
lit-studies-early.l22.q4.p: What creates irony in the General Prologue?
lit-studies-early.l22.q4.e: The gap between praise and the details reveals the pilgrims' flaws.

lit-studies-early.l22.q5.p: Chaucer the pilgrim is a created narrator and not simply the poet speaking.
lit-studies-early.l22.q5.e: He is a constructed persona within the poem.

lit-studies-early.l23.q1.p: How many lines does a sonnet have?

lit-studies-early.l23.q3.p: What is the Shakespearean rhyme scheme?
lit-studies-early.l23.q3.e: Three quatrains and a couplet make the usual pattern.

lit-studies-early.l23.q4.t: Shifts the direction of the poem
lit-studies-early.l23.q4.e: The volta is a turn in argument or mood.

lit-studies-early.l23.q5.t: Lists how the mistress does not match them, yet affirms love
lit-studies-early.l23.q5.p: What does Sonnet 130 do with Petrarchan clichés?
lit-studies-early.l23.q5.e: The poem parodies stock comparisons while declaring the love honest.

lit-studies-early.l24.q1.p: A soliloquy is a speech in which a character alone on stage voices thoughts.
lit-studies-early.l24.q1.e: A soliloquy shares a character's thoughts with the audience.

lit-studies-early.l24.q2.e: Blank verse has a steady rhythm without rhyme.

lit-studies-early.l24.q3.t: A change of mood or status
lit-studies-early.l24.q3.p: What can a shift from verse to prose signal?
lit-studies-early.l24.q3.e: Shakespeare may use prose for lower-status characters or for changes in tone.

lit-studies-early.l24.q4.p: What does the repetition in "Tomorrow, and tomorrow, and tomorrow" enact?
lit-studies-early.l24.q4.e: The repeated word mirrors time creeping on.

lit-studies-early.l24.q5.p: The text of Hamlet settles the reason for Hamlet's delay with a single clear answer.
lit-studies-early.l24.q5.e: The text supports several explanations without choosing one.

lit-studies-early.l25.q1.p: What does Don Quixote mistake for giants?
lit-studies-early.l25.q1.e: He attacks windmills, believing them to be giants.

lit-studies-early.l25.q2.p: Don Quixote was published in two parts, in 1605 and 1615.
lit-studies-early.l25.q2.e: Cervantes published Part 1 in 1605 and Part 2 in 1615.

lit-studies-early.l25.q3.p: What does Sancho Panza represent in contrast to Quixote?
lit-studies-early.l25.q3.e: Sancho's practicality contrasts with Quixote's idealism, though both change.

lit-studies-early.l25.q4.t: Fiction that refers to itself as fiction
lit-studies-early.l25.q4.e: Metafiction draws attention to its own fictional status.

lit-studies-early.l25.q5.p: Calling Don Quixote the first modern novel depends on how the term is defined.
lit-studies-early.l25.q5.e: Scholars debate the label because definitions of the novel differ.

lit-studies-early.l26.q1.p: When was Paradise Lost first published?
lit-studies-early.l26.q1.e: The first edition appeared in 1667 in ten books.

lit-studies-early.l26.q2.p: Milton composed Paradise Lost after he had become blind.
lit-studies-early.l26.q2.e: He was blind and dictated the poem.

lit-studies-early.l26.q3.p: What verse form does Paradise Lost use?
lit-studies-early.l26.q3.e: Milton chose blank verse and rejected rhyme.

lit-studies-early.l26.q4.t: Whether his speeches are attractive or exposed as self-deceiving
lit-studies-early.l26.q4.p: What is the central debate about Satan in the poem?
lit-studies-early.l26.q4.e: Readers disagree on whether the poem makes Satan attractive or exposes him.

lit-studies-early.l26.q5.t: An eloquent voice is not necessarily a reliable one
lit-studies-early.l26.q5.p: What reading skill does Satan's speech teach?
lit-studies-early.l26.q5.e: Persuasive rhetoric must be tested against the whole poem.

lit-studies-early.l27.q1.h: It describes a way of thinking.
lit-studies-early.l27.q1.e: Montaigne's title describes thinking as an attempt.

lit-studies-early.l27.q2.p: Montaigne published his first Essays in 1580.

lit-studies-early.l27.q3.p: Which technique does Richardson's Pamela use?
lit-studies-early.l27.q3.e: The novel is told through letters.

lit-studies-early.l27.q4.p: Which work first appeared in 1719 as a fictional memoir?

lit-studies-early.l27.q5.p: The early novelists experimented with narrative techniques that Jane Austen later built on.
lit-studies-early.l27.q5.e: Austen's technique builds on earlier experiments.

lit-studies-early.l28.q1.t: Writing that uses humor and irony to criticize
lit-studies-early.l28.q1.e: Satire uses irony and exaggeration to expose problems.

lit-studies-early.l28.q2.p: In A Modest Proposal, the speaker's calm voice is the same as Swift's own view.
lit-studies-early.l28.q2.e: The speaker is a persona, and the real target is indifference to poverty.

lit-studies-early.l28.q4.t: That this is the best of all possible worlds

lit-studies-early.l28.q5.t: Identify the speaker and the target
lit-studies-early.l28.q5.p: What is the best first step for reading satire?
lit-studies-early.l28.q5.e: Satire works through a gap between what is said and what is meant.

lit-studies-modern.l01.q1.p: Wordsworth argued that poetry should use the language of ordinary people.
lit-studies-modern.l01.q1.e: The preface to Lyrical Ballads argued for everyday language.

lit-studies-modern.l01.q2.p: Which pair of poets published Lyrical Ballads in 1798?
lit-studies-modern.l01.q2.e: Lyrical Ballads was a joint work by William Wordsworth and Samuel Taylor Coleridge.

lit-studies-modern.l01.q3.t: The beginning of the French Revolution
lit-studies-modern.l01.q3.p: Which event in 1789 formed part of the background to Romanticism?
lit-studies-modern.l01.q3.h: It was a political upheaval in Europe.
lit-studies-modern.l01.q3.e: The French Revolution began in 1789 and shaped Romantic hopes and fears.

lit-studies-modern.l01.q4.t: Memory of the flowers brings him pleasure again
lit-studies-modern.l01.q4.p: In the daffodils poem, what happens at the end when the speaker lies on his couch?
lit-studies-modern.l01.q4.h: The final turn moves from outer scene to inner life.
lit-studies-modern.l01.q4.e: The "inward eye" lets the speaker enjoy the experience again through memory.

lit-studies-modern.l01.q5.t: Good poems begin in strong feeling but are shaped by later reflection
lit-studies-modern.l01.q5.p: Which claim about Wordsworth's view of poetry is most accurate?
lit-studies-modern.l01.q5.h: Recall that he spoke of both overflow and recollection.
lit-studies-modern.l01.q5.e: He paired spontaneous feeling with emotion recollected in tranquillity.

lit-studies-modern.l02.q1.p: Percy Bysshe Shelley wrote the sonnet "Ozymandias."
lit-studies-modern.l02.q1.h: It is about a ruined statue in the desert.

lit-studies-modern.l02.q2.t: Being able to stay in uncertainty without forcing an answer
lit-studies-modern.l02.q2.p: What does negative capability mean in Keats's letter of 1817?
lit-studies-modern.l02.q2.h: It is about doubt and mystery.
lit-studies-modern.l02.q2.e: Keats described the capacity to dwell in uncertainties without reaching irritably after fact and reason.

lit-studies-modern.l02.q3.t: They will never kiss, but will never grow old
lit-studies-modern.l02.q3.p: In "Ode on a Grecian Urn," what is true of the lovers painted on the vase?
lit-studies-modern.l02.q3.h: Consider what is gained and lost by being frozen in art.
lit-studies-modern.l02.q3.e: The poem weighs the permanence of art against the loss of living fulfilment.

lit-studies-modern.l02.q4.t: Broken statue parts and empty desert
lit-studies-modern.l02.q4.p: In "Ozymandias," what remains of the ruler's works?
lit-studies-modern.l02.q4.h: Look at the contrast with the inscription.
lit-studies-modern.l02.q4.e: The inscription boasts of great works, but only a ruined statue stands in the sand.

lit-studies-modern.l02.q5.t: The speaker repeats a story told by a traveller about a sculpture
lit-studies-modern.l02.q5.p: Why is "Ozymandias" a good example of layered narration?
lit-studies-modern.l02.q5.h: Count how many voices stand between you and the statue.
lit-studies-modern.l02.q5.e: The poem reports what a traveller said about the statue, adding layers of telling.

lit-studies-modern.l03.q1.p: In the novel, the creature is called Frankenstein.
lit-studies-modern.l03.q1.e: Frankenstein is the scientist's surname; the creature has no name.

lit-studies-modern.l03.q2.p: Where did Mary Shelley begin Frankenstein in 1816?
lit-studies-modern.l03.q2.h: The ghost-story challenge took place in Switzerland.
lit-studies-modern.l03.q2.e: She began it during a summer stay near Lake Geneva.

lit-studies-modern.l03.q3.t: As nested narratives: Walton, Victor and the creature
lit-studies-modern.l03.q3.e: Walton's letters frame Victor's tale, which in turn contains the creature's account.

lit-studies-modern.l03.q4.t: The scientist resembles the Greek figure who defied the gods to give humans fire
lit-studies-modern.l03.q4.p: What does the subtitle "The Modern Prometheus" suggest?
lit-studies-modern.l03.q4.h: Prometheus is a figure from Greek myth.
lit-studies-modern.l03.q4.e: The subtitle links Victor's ambition to the myth of Prometheus.

lit-studies-modern.l03.q5.p: Readers have debated whether the main fault in the novel is creating the creature or abandoning him.
lit-studies-modern.l03.q5.h: The text supports more than one reading.
lit-studies-modern.l03.q5.e: Critics commonly discuss both the act of creation and Victor's failure of responsibility.

lit-studies-modern.l04.q1.p: Jane Austen's early novels were published anonymously.
lit-studies-modern.l04.q1.h: Think of how women authors often published then.
lit-studies-modern.l04.q1.e: Her early novels appeared without her name.

lit-studies-modern.l04.q2.p: Which of these novels was published in 1813?
lit-studies-modern.l04.q2.h: It begins with a famous remark about a single man.

lit-studies-modern.l04.q3.t: A grand statement that the story quickly undercuts
lit-studies-modern.l04.q3.p: What is irony in Austen's opening of Pride and Prejudice?
lit-studies-modern.l04.q3.h: The tone is not what it seems.
lit-studies-modern.l04.q3.e: The solemn "truth" turns out to describe the families' wishes more than the man's.

lit-studies-modern.l04.q4.t: Narration that slides into a character's viewpoint without quotation marks
lit-studies-modern.l04.q4.h: It blends the narrator's voice and a character's thoughts.
lit-studies-modern.l04.q4.e: The narrator voices a character's thoughts and judgments in the character's own manner without tagging them.

lit-studies-modern.l04.q5.t: It lets readers share Emma's confidence and then see its errors
lit-studies-modern.l04.q5.p: Why can free indirect style be useful in Emma?
lit-studies-modern.l04.q5.h: Think about how we perceive her mistakes.
lit-studies-modern.l04.q5.e: We hear Emma's certainty from inside, which sets up the irony when she is wrong.

lit-studies-modern.l05.q1.p: The Bronte sisters first published under the names Currer, Ellis and Acton Bell.
lit-studies-modern.l05.q1.h: Their real names were Charlotte, Emily and Anne.
lit-studies-modern.l05.q1.e: They used pseudonyms that hid their sex but kept their initials.

lit-studies-modern.l05.q2.e: Emily Bronte published Wuthering Heights in 1847 as Ellis Bell.

lit-studies-modern.l05.q3.t: In the first person by Jane herself
lit-studies-modern.l05.q3.e: Jane narrates, which lets readers follow her moral reasoning.

lit-studies-modern.l05.q4.p: Which narrators chiefly tell Wuthering Heights?
lit-studies-modern.l05.q4.h: One is a visitor and one a housekeeper.
lit-studies-modern.l05.q4.e: The story is nested through Lockwood and the housekeeper Nelly Dean.

lit-studies-modern.l05.q5.t: Imagines the earlier life of Bertha from Jane Eyre
lit-studies-modern.l05.q5.p: What does Jean Rhys's Wide Sargasso Sea (1966) do?
lit-studies-modern.l05.q5.h: It is a response to a Bronte novel.
lit-studies-modern.l05.q5.e: Rhys's novel gives a Caribbean background to the character Bertha.

lit-studies-modern.l06.q1.p: Many of Dickens's novels first appeared in instalments.
lit-studies-modern.l06.q1.h: Think of magazines and monthly parts.
lit-studies-modern.l06.q1.e: Serial publication was central to how his novels reached readers.

lit-studies-modern.l06.q2.p: Which Dickens novel features a boy who asks for more food in a workhouse?
lit-studies-modern.l06.q2.e: Oliver asks for more in Oliver Twist.

lit-studies-modern.l06.q3.t: Chapters often end on hooks to bring readers back
lit-studies-modern.l06.q3.p: How can serial publication shape a novel's structure?
lit-studies-modern.l06.q3.h: Readers had to wait for the next part.
lit-studies-modern.l06.q3.e: Instalment form encourages cliffhangers and branching plots.

lit-studies-modern.l06.q4.t: An education and industry system that values only facts and figures
lit-studies-modern.l06.q4.p: What target does Hard Times (1854) criticise?
lit-studies-modern.l06.q4.h: Look at the novel's title and setting.
lit-studies-modern.l06.q4.e: Dickens attacks a rigid utilitarian approach to schooling and industry.

lit-studies-modern.l06.q5.t: A tiny, polite request is met with horror, revealing the system's cruelty
lit-studies-modern.l06.q5.p: Why does the "more" scene show how an institution works?
lit-studies-modern.l06.q5.h: Compare the size of the request with the reaction.
lit-studies-modern.l06.q5.e: The adults' shock at a small plea exposes the institution's harshness.

lit-studies-modern.l07.q1.p: George Eliot was a pen name used by Mary Ann Evans.
lit-studies-modern.l07.q1.e: Mary Ann Evans wrote as George Eliot.

lit-studies-modern.l07.q2.p: What is the subtitle of Middlemarch?
lit-studies-modern.l07.q2.h: It points to the novel's observational method.
lit-studies-modern.l07.q2.e: Middlemarch carries the subtitle "A Study of Provincial Life."

lit-studies-modern.l07.q3.t: She marries Casaubon expecting to share a great intellectual project
lit-studies-modern.l07.q3.p: What mistake does Dorothea make early in Middlemarch?
lit-studies-modern.l07.q3.e: Her idealism leads her to marry Casaubon, whose work proves stalled.

lit-studies-modern.l07.q4.t: To reflect on and analyse characters' motives and their society
lit-studies-modern.l07.q4.p: What is the role of Eliot's narrator?
lit-studies-modern.l07.q4.h: The voice is learned and comments.
lit-studies-modern.l07.q4.e: Eliot's narrator steps back to analyse and extend sympathy.

lit-studies-modern.l07.q5.t: The world's good depends partly on ordinary, unrecorded lives
lit-studies-modern.l07.q5.p: What idea does Middlemarch's ending stress?
lit-studies-modern.l07.q5.h: It honours those history does not record.
lit-studies-modern.l07.q5.e: The ending suggests small, unremembered acts matter.

lit-studies-modern.l08.q1.p: Serfdom in Russia was abolished in 1861.
lit-studies-modern.l08.q1.h: It was a major mid-century reform.
lit-studies-modern.l08.q1.e: Emancipation of the serfs took place in 1861.

lit-studies-modern.l08.q2.e: Dostoevsky published Crime and Punishment in 1866.

lit-studies-modern.l08.q3.t: That an extraordinary person might break the moral law for a greater purpose
lit-studies-modern.l08.q3.p: What is Raskolnikov's idea in Crime and Punishment?
lit-studies-modern.l08.q3.h: It is a theory he tests with a murder.
lit-studies-modern.l08.q3.e: He persuades himself that extraordinary people may transgress, and the novel tests that idea.

lit-studies-modern.l08.q4.p: Which novel by Tolstoy is set around the Napoleonic invasion of Russia?
lit-studies-modern.l08.q4.h: The title pairs two large themes.
lit-studies-modern.l08.q4.e: Tolstoy's War and Peace is set during the Napoleonic era.

lit-studies-modern.l08.q5.t: Many independent voices argue without one being simply the author's mouthpiece
lit-studies-modern.l08.q5.p: What did Bakhtin mean by calling Dostoevsky polyphonic?
lit-studies-modern.l08.q5.h: Think of a chorus of equal voices.
lit-studies-modern.l08.q5.e: Bakhtin saw Dostoevsky's novels as dialogues among independent viewpoints.

lit-studies-modern.l09.q1.p: Flaubert's Madame Bovary was the subject of a trial in 1857, and he was acquitted.
lit-studies-modern.l09.q1.h: The charge was offending public morals.
lit-studies-modern.l09.q1.e: Flaubert was tried and acquitted in 1857.

lit-studies-modern.l09.q2.t: That it will match the romantic novels she reads
lit-studies-modern.l09.q2.p: What does Emma Bovary expect from life?
lit-studies-modern.l09.q2.e: Emma's romantic reading leads to disappointment with provincial life.

lit-studies-modern.l09.q3.t: A vast series of connected novels called La Comedie humaine
lit-studies-modern.l09.q3.p: What was Honore de Balzac's great project?
lit-studies-modern.l09.q3.e: Balzac planned a large interconnected series called La Comedie humaine.

lit-studies-modern.l09.q4.t: The author and publisher were fined and six poems were suppressed
lit-studies-modern.l09.q4.p: What happened to Baudelaire's Les Fleurs du mal in 1857?
lit-studies-modern.l09.q4.h: Like Flaubert, he faced a court.
lit-studies-modern.l09.q4.e: A court fined them and ordered six poems removed.

lit-studies-modern.l09.q5.t: It prizes suggestion and mood over detailed description
lit-studies-modern.l09.q5.p: How does Symbolism differ from realism?
lit-studies-modern.l09.q5.h: Think about evoking rather than explaining.
lit-studies-modern.l09.q5.e: Symbolists used suggestion and musicality to point beyond the visible.

lit-studies-modern.l10.q1.p: Nathaniel Hawthorne wrote The Scarlet Letter.
lit-studies-modern.l10.q1.e: Hawthorne published The Scarlet Letter in 1850.

lit-studies-modern.l10.q2.p: Which story is narrated by a man who insists he is sane while describing a murder?
lit-studies-modern.l10.q2.e: Poe's "The Tell-Tale Heart" is narrated by a murderer who claims sanity.

lit-studies-modern.l10.q3.t: A single effect, with every detail serving it
lit-studies-modern.l10.q3.p: What did Poe argue a short story should aim for?
lit-studies-modern.l10.q3.e: Poe argued for unity of effect in short fiction.

lit-studies-modern.l10.q4.p: Which historical event is linked to Hawthorne's ancestor John Hathorne?
lit-studies-modern.l10.q4.e: John Hathorne was a judge at the Salem witch trials.

lit-studies-modern.l10.q5.t: It shifts and is left open rather than fixed
lit-studies-modern.l10.q5.p: What happens to the meaning of the scarlet letter over the course of the novel?
lit-studies-modern.l10.q5.e: Hawthorne leaves the symbol ambiguous as Hester's actions change how it is seen.

lit-studies-modern.l11.q1.p: Moby-Dick begins with the sentence "Call me Ishmael."
lit-studies-modern.l11.q1.e: That is the novel's famous opening line.

lit-studies-modern.l11.q2.p: What is the name of Captain Ahab's ship?
lit-studies-modern.l11.q2.h: Melville's own ship had a different name.
lit-studies-modern.l11.q2.e: Ahab commands the Pequod; Melville himself sailed on the Acushnet.

lit-studies-modern.l11.q3.p: What does Bartleby say in response to requests?
lit-studies-modern.l11.q3.e: Bartleby's refrain is "I would prefer not to."

lit-studies-modern.l11.q4.t: It sold poorly and was largely neglected until the 1920s
lit-studies-modern.l11.q4.p: How was Moby-Dick received when first published in 1851?
lit-studies-modern.l11.q4.e: The book was a commercial disappointment and was revived in the twentieth century.

lit-studies-modern.l11.q5.t: Ahab's obsession and the diverse working crew
lit-studies-modern.l11.q5.p: What are the two poles of Moby-Dick described in the lesson?
lit-studies-modern.l11.q5.h: One is a single will and the other a community.
lit-studies-modern.l11.q5.e: The book sets Ahab's monomania against the varied crew of the Pequod.

lit-studies-modern.l12.q1.p: Emily Dickinson published nearly all of her poems during her lifetime.
lit-studies-modern.l12.q1.h: Her sister found the manuscripts after her death.
lit-studies-modern.l12.q1.e: Only a handful were published before she died; most appeared after 1890.

lit-studies-modern.l12.q2.p: What was the title of Whitman's main collection, first published in 1855?
lit-studies-modern.l12.q2.e: Whitman published Leaves of Grass in 1855 and revised it for decades.

lit-studies-modern.l12.q3.t: Short poems with dashes and slant rhyme
lit-studies-modern.l12.q3.p: Which feature is typical of Dickinson's style?
lit-studies-modern.l12.q3.e: Dickinson used dashes, slant rhyme and hymn-like meter.

lit-studies-modern.l12.q4.t: As a courteous driver who stops a carriage for the speaker
lit-studies-modern.l12.q4.p: How is Death presented in "Because I could not stop for Death"?
lit-studies-modern.l12.q4.e: Death is personified as a polite gentleman calling for her.

lit-studies-modern.l12.q5.t: Whitman expands to include a nation; Dickinson condenses to a sharp image
lit-studies-modern.l12.q5.p: Which contrast between the two poets does the lesson draw?
lit-studies-modern.l12.q5.h: One is expansive and the other compressed.
lit-studies-modern.l12.q5.e: Whitman's catalogues and long lines contrast with Dickinson's brevity.

lit-studies-modern.l13.q1.p: Frederick Douglass published his Narrative in 1845.
lit-studies-modern.l13.q1.e: The Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass appeared in 1845.

lit-studies-modern.l13.q2.t: An autobiography by a person who escaped or was freed from slavery
lit-studies-modern.l13.q2.h: It is a form of life writing.
lit-studies-modern.l13.q2.e: Slave narratives are first-person accounts by formerly enslaved people.

lit-studies-modern.l13.q3.t: To vouch for the author's authenticity for sceptical readers
lit-studies-modern.l13.q3.p: Why did many narratives carry prefaces from white abolitionists?
lit-studies-modern.l13.q3.h: Think about doubts the authors faced.
lit-studies-modern.l13.q3.e: Such prefaces aimed to establish credibility with doubting audiences.

lit-studies-modern.l13.q4.t: That literacy is the path to freedom
lit-studies-modern.l13.q4.p: What does Douglass learn from Hugh Auld's objection to his lessons?
lit-studies-modern.l13.q4.h: The master's fear reveals the value of reading.
lit-studies-modern.l13.q4.e: Auld's warning shows Douglass that learning to read undermines slavery.

lit-studies-modern.l13.q5.p: Who wrote Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl (1861) under the name Linda Brent?
lit-studies-modern.l13.q5.h: It describes dangers faced by enslaved women.
lit-studies-modern.l13.q5.e: Harriet Jacobs wrote the book under a pseudonym.

lit-studies-modern.l14.q1.p: Du Bois wrote The Souls of Black Folk in 1903.

lit-studies-modern.l14.q2.t: Seeing oneself through one's own eyes and through a contemptuous society's eyes
lit-studies-modern.l14.q2.h: It is a state of divided self-perception.
lit-studies-modern.l14.q2.e: Du Bois used it for the divided awareness created by racism.

lit-studies-modern.l14.q3.p: Which writer published Their Eyes Were Watching God in 1937?

lit-studies-modern.l14.q4.p: Which book gave the Harlem Renaissance a statement of its spirit in 1925?
lit-studies-modern.l14.q4.h: It was an anthology edited by a philosopher.
lit-studies-modern.l14.q4.e: Locke's anthology The New Negro appeared in 1925.

lit-studies-modern.l14.q5.t: Writers of the era disagreed about how to portray Black life
lit-studies-modern.l14.q5.p: What does the debate over Hurston's use of dialect show?
lit-studies-modern.l14.q5.h: Consider the era's conversation about representation.
lit-studies-modern.l14.q5.e: Contemporaries differed over the portrayal of Black speech and life.

lit-studies-modern.l15.q1.p: Modernist writers often tried to show the flow of a mind's thoughts.
lit-studies-modern.l15.q1.e: Stream of consciousness is a common modernist technique.

lit-studies-modern.l15.q2.p: Which event from 1914 helped shape modernist doubt about the old order?
lit-studies-modern.l15.q2.e: The war shook confidence in earlier certainties.

lit-studies-modern.l15.q3.p: What does Pound's slogan "make it new" encourage?
lit-studies-modern.l15.q3.h: It is a call for innovation.
lit-studies-modern.l15.q3.e: The phrase became a modernist rallying cry for innovation.

lit-studies-modern.l15.q4.t: It may place us inside a character's shifting thoughts
lit-studies-modern.l15.q4.p: How might a modernist narrative differ from a Victorian one?
lit-studies-modern.l15.q4.h: Compare the two descriptions of a morning.
lit-studies-modern.l15.q4.e: Modernists often rendered inner life moment by moment.

lit-studies-modern.l15.q5.t: No single date marks it, but people were beginning to see the world differently
lit-studies-modern.l15.q5.p: What did Woolf mean by her 1924 remark about December 1910?
lit-studies-modern.l15.q5.e: The remark pointed to a shift in perception rather than a literal date.

lit-studies-modern.l16.q1.p: Mrs Dalloway takes place over a single day in London.
lit-studies-modern.l16.q1.e: The novel is set in one day in June 1923.

lit-studies-modern.l16.q2.p: Which sound recurs in Mrs Dalloway to mark clock time?
lit-studies-modern.l16.q2.e: Big Ben's chimes mark public time throughout the novel.

lit-studies-modern.l16.q3.t: That a woman needs money and a room of her own to write fiction
lit-studies-modern.l16.q3.p: What did Woolf argue in A Room of One's Own (1929)?
lit-studies-modern.l16.q3.e: The essay ties women's writing to material independence.

lit-studies-modern.l16.q4.t: A war veteran suffering from shell shock
lit-studies-modern.l16.q4.e: Septimus is a veteran haunted by the war.

lit-studies-modern.l16.q5.p: What press did Virginia and Leonard Woolf found in 1917?
lit-studies-modern.l16.q5.e: They founded the Hogarth Press in 1917.

lit-studies-modern.l17.q1.p: Joyce's Ulysses takes place over a single day in Dublin.

lit-studies-modern.l17.q2.p: Which ancient epic does the structure of Ulysses parallel?
lit-studies-modern.l17.q2.h: The title is the Latin name of a hero.
lit-studies-modern.l17.q2.e: Joyce modelled his episodes on Homer's Odyssey.

lit-studies-modern.l17.q3.t: It reverses the usual picture of spring as joyful
lit-studies-modern.l17.q3.p: What does the opening line of The Waste Land, "April is the cruellest month," do?
lit-studies-modern.l17.q3.h: Spring is usually a hopeful season.
lit-studies-modern.l17.q3.e: The line overturns the conventional image of spring.

lit-studies-modern.l17.q4.p: Who heavily edited an early draft of The Waste Land?
lit-studies-modern.l17.q4.h: He was a fellow modernist poet.
lit-studies-modern.l17.q4.e: Pound edited it closely before publication.

lit-studies-modern.l17.q5.t: A federal court ruled it was not obscene
lit-studies-modern.l17.q5.p: What happened to Ulysses in the United States in 1933?
lit-studies-modern.l17.q5.e: A federal court allowed the book, ending the ban.

lit-studies-modern.l18.q1.p: Most of Kafka's major novels were published after his death.
lit-studies-modern.l18.q1.h: Max Brod did not burn the papers.
lit-studies-modern.l18.q1.e: The Trial and The Castle appeared in 1925 and 1926.

lit-studies-modern.l18.q2.p: What does the word Kafkaesque describe?
lit-studies-modern.l18.q2.e: The term refers to nightmarish bureaucratic absurdity.

lit-studies-modern.l18.q3.t: He is arrested without being told the charge
lit-studies-modern.l18.q3.p: What happens to Josef K. at the start of The Trial?
lit-studies-modern.l18.q3.e: Officials arrest him but never explain the accusation.

lit-studies-modern.l18.q4.t: The German word suggests unclean vermin, which has no exact English equivalent
lit-studies-modern.l18.q4.p: Why do translators differ over the creature in The Metamorphosis?
lit-studies-modern.l18.q4.e: Translators have rendered the word as insect, bug or vermin.

lit-studies-modern.l18.q5.t: The nature of the transformation was less important than the family's response
lit-studies-modern.l18.q5.p: What did Kafka's request about the cover illustration suggest?
lit-studies-modern.l18.q5.h: He asked the creature not to be shown.
lit-studies-modern.l18.q5.e: Kafka asked that the creature not be depicted, which suggests the response mattered more.

lit-studies-modern.l19.q1.p: The Great Gatsby is narrated by Nick Carraway.
