lit-studies-modern.l19.q1.h: He is a neighbour of Gatsby.
lit-studies-modern.l19.q1.e: Nick tells the story of Gatsby and Daisy.

lit-studies-modern.l19.q2.p: Which writer used the phrase "lost generation" as an epigraph in The Sun Also Rises?
lit-studies-modern.l19.q2.h: He wrote in a spare style.
lit-studies-modern.l19.q2.e: Hemingway used the phrase, attributed to Gertrude Stein.

lit-studies-modern.l19.q3.t: The writer may omit what he knows and the omitted part still gives the story weight
lit-studies-modern.l19.q3.h: It concerns what is left unsaid.
lit-studies-modern.l19.q3.e: Hemingway described leaving things out while keeping their force.

lit-studies-modern.l19.q4.p: Which of these is a Southern Gothic writer from the lesson?
lit-studies-modern.l19.q4.h: She wrote darkly comic stories about faith and grace.
lit-studies-modern.l19.q4.e: O'Connor is a leading Southern Gothic writer.

lit-studies-modern.l19.q5.p: What does Yoknapatawpha County refer to?
lit-studies-modern.l19.q5.e: Faulkner set many works in this invented county.

lit-studies-modern.l20.q1.p: In magical realism, extraordinary events are typically treated as ordinary by the narrator.
lit-studies-modern.l20.q1.e: That calm treatment is a defining feature.

lit-studies-modern.l20.q2.p: Who wrote One Hundred Years of Solitude?

lit-studies-modern.l20.q3.p: What is the invented town in that novel?
lit-studies-modern.l20.q3.h: It is home to the Buendia family.

lit-studies-modern.l20.q4.t: His stories explore ideas such as labyrinths and infinite libraries
lit-studies-modern.l20.q4.p: How is Borges usually distinguished from Garcia Marquez in the lesson?
lit-studies-modern.l20.q4.e: Borges's compact fictions are philosophical rather than social-historical.

lit-studies-modern.l20.q5.t: Express trauma, culture or politics in unusual terms
lit-studies-modern.l20.q5.p: What can the magical element in such fiction do?
lit-studies-modern.l20.q5.h: Ask what it does, not whether it is real.
lit-studies-modern.l20.q5.e: The lesson suggests the magic can convey trauma, culture or politics.

lit-studies-modern.l21.q1.p: Chinua Achebe published Things Fall Apart in 1958.

lit-studies-modern.l21.q2.p: Whose poem supplies the title Things Fall Apart?
lit-studies-modern.l21.q2.e: The title comes from a poem by Yeats.

lit-studies-modern.l21.q3.t: Igbo society as missionaries and colonial officials arrive
lit-studies-modern.l21.q3.p: What is Okonkwo's world in the novel?
lit-studies-modern.l21.q3.h: The setting is late nineteenth-century Nigeria.
lit-studies-modern.l21.q3.e: The novel follows an Igbo wrestler amid colonial arrival.

lit-studies-modern.l21.q4.t: That writers should use African languages
lit-studies-modern.l21.q4.p: What argument did Ngugi wa Thiong'o make in Decolonising the Mind (1986)?
lit-studies-modern.l21.q4.h: He began writing fiction in Gikuyu.
lit-studies-modern.l21.q4.e: Ngugi urged African writers to use African languages.

lit-studies-modern.l21.q5.t: How Western writers represented the East
lit-studies-modern.l21.q5.p: What does Edward Said's Orientalism (1978) study?
lit-studies-modern.l21.q5.h: It is a work of critical theory.
lit-studies-modern.l21.q5.e: Said analysed Western depictions of the East.

lit-studies-modern.l22.q1.p: Indigenous stories belong to particular nations and communities.
lit-studies-modern.l22.q1.h: The lesson says not to treat them as one mythology.
lit-studies-modern.l22.q1.e: Many stories have protocols and belong to specific nations.

lit-studies-modern.l22.q2.p: Who won the 1969 Pulitzer Prize for fiction with House Made of Dawn?
lit-studies-modern.l22.q2.e: Momaday's novel won the Pulitzer in 1969.

lit-studies-modern.l22.q3.t: Through traditional ceremony and reconnecting with the land
lit-studies-modern.l22.q3.p: In Ceremony (1977), how does Tayo begin to heal?
lit-studies-modern.l22.q3.e: Silko ties his recovery to ceremony and land.

lit-studies-modern.l22.q4.p: Who served as United States Poet Laureate from 2019 to 2022?
lit-studies-modern.l22.q4.h: She is a member of the Muscogee Creek Nation.
lit-studies-modern.l22.q4.e: Harjo held the position in those years.

lit-studies-modern.l22.q5.t: Attend to the specific community and place, and do not treat one writer as the voice of all
lit-studies-modern.l22.q5.p: Which approach is recommended when reading Indigenous works?
lit-studies-modern.l22.q5.e: The lesson stresses specificity of nation and place.

lit-studies-modern.l23.q1.p: In A Doll's House, Nora leaves her husband at the end.
lit-studies-modern.l23.q1.h: The sound of a door became famous.
lit-studies-modern.l23.q1.e: Nora walks out, and the play was controversial for it.

lit-studies-modern.l23.q2.e: Chekhov's last play is The Cherry Orchard (1904).

lit-studies-modern.l23.q3.t: What characters feel and mean but do not say
lit-studies-modern.l23.q3.p: What does subtext mean in Chekhov's plays?
lit-studies-modern.l23.q3.h: Meaning lies in what is unspoken.
lit-studies-modern.l23.q3.e: Subtext is the unspoken meaning beneath dialogue.

lit-studies-modern.l23.q4.t: It was the first play by a Black woman produced on Broadway
lit-studies-modern.l23.q4.p: What makes A Raisin in the Sun historically notable?
lit-studies-modern.l23.q4.e: Hansberry's play was the first by a Black woman on Broadway.

lit-studies-modern.l23.q5.t: A play narrated and shaped by a character's recollections
lit-studies-modern.l23.q5.p: What is a memory play, as in The Glass Menagerie?
lit-studies-modern.l23.q5.e: The Glass Menagerie is filtered through Tom's memory.

lit-studies-modern.l24.q1.p: Imagism emphasised direct treatment of the thing and the removal of unnecessary words.
lit-studies-modern.l24.q1.h: Pound's 1913 two-line poem is an example.
lit-studies-modern.l24.q1.e: Imagist principles favoured economy and the single image.

lit-studies-modern.l24.q2.p: Which poet was killed in November 1918, a week before the Armistice?
lit-studies-modern.l24.q2.h: His poems appeared after his death.

lit-studies-modern.l24.q3.p: Which poem by Allen Ginsberg was published by City Lights in 1956?

lit-studies-modern.l24.q4.t: Private pain, family and mental illness
lit-studies-modern.l24.q4.p: What do confessional poets treat as subjects?
lit-studies-modern.l24.q4.e: Confessional poetry makes the personal central.

lit-studies-modern.l24.q5.t: First African American to win the Pulitzer Prize for poetry
lit-studies-modern.l24.q5.p: What distinction did Gwendolyn Brooks earn in 1950?
lit-studies-modern.l24.q5.e: Brooks was the first African American Pulitzer poet.

lit-studies-modern.l25.q1.p: Karel Capek brought the word robot to the public in his play R.U.R. (1920).
lit-studies-modern.l25.q1.e: The play popularized the word, which Capek credited his brother Josef with coining.

lit-studies-modern.l25.q2.p: Which novel by Ursula K. Le Guin uses a planet whose people have no fixed sex?
lit-studies-modern.l25.q2.e: Le Guin used an invented world to question gender.

lit-studies-modern.l25.q3.t: An imagined society shaped by oppressive control
lit-studies-modern.l25.q3.e: Dystopias imagine societies marked by control and fear.

lit-studies-modern.l25.q4.t: Sends a modern Black woman to a Maryland plantation in the past
lit-studies-modern.l25.q4.p: What does Octavia Butler's Kindred (1979) do?
lit-studies-modern.l25.q4.h: It links the genre to history.
lit-studies-modern.l25.q4.e: The novel uses time travel to confront slavery.

lit-studies-modern.l25.q5.t: It changes one feature of society to question our assumptions
lit-studies-modern.l25.q5.p: Why is The Left Hand of Darkness called a thought experiment?
lit-studies-modern.l25.q5.e: The story varies gender to question real assumptions.

lit-studies-modern.l26.q1.p: In Maus, Art Spiegelman depicts Jews as mice and Germans as cats.
lit-studies-modern.l26.q1.h: Animal figures carry the book's design.
lit-studies-modern.l26.q1.e: Spiegelman uses animals to represent groups.

lit-studies-modern.l26.q2.p: What does McCloud call the process of connecting panels in the reader's mind?
lit-studies-modern.l26.q2.e: McCloud's term for connecting separate images is closure.

lit-studies-modern.l26.q3.t: Will Eisner's A Contract with God
lit-studies-modern.l26.q3.p: Whose 1978 book popularised the term graphic novel?
lit-studies-modern.l26.q3.h: He was a pioneering American cartoonist.
lit-studies-modern.l26.q3.e: Eisner's book helped popularise the term.

lit-studies-modern.l26.q4.p: What is the gutter in comics?
lit-studies-modern.l26.q4.e: The gutter is the space between panels.

lit-studies-modern.l26.q5.t: Attend to layout, line, colour and how image relates to caption
lit-studies-modern.l26.q5.p: Which is a good way to read graphic narrative?

lit-studies-modern.l27.q1.p: Translation is a form of interpretation.
lit-studies-modern.l27.q1.h: Choices of wording change the book.
lit-studies-modern.l27.q1.e: Translators make decisions that shape tone and meaning.

lit-studies-modern.l27.q2.p: Which author wrote The Remains of the Day (1989)?
lit-studies-modern.l27.q2.e: Ishiguro wrote it, and Stevens narrates.

lit-studies-modern.l27.q3.p: What is notable about Elena Ferrante?

lit-studies-modern.l27.q4.p: Which translated novel won the 2016 International Booker Prize?
lit-studies-modern.l27.q4.e: Han Kang's book in Deborah Smith's translation won.

lit-studies-modern.l27.q5.t: Prizes shape which books are noticed
lit-studies-modern.l27.q5.p: Why should readers ask what a prize rewards and overlooks?

lit-studies-modern.l28.q1.p: Formalism treats the text as a self-contained object and focuses on structure and language.
lit-studies-modern.l28.q1.h: It is also called New Criticism.

lit-studies-modern.l28.q2.p: Which lens asks how class and economic power shape a text?
lit-studies-modern.l28.q2.e: Marxist criticism foregrounds class and economics.

lit-studies-modern.l28.q3.t: That the reader, not the author, completes a text's meaning
lit-studies-modern.l28.q3.e: Barthes argued meaning arises in reading.

lit-studies-modern.l28.q4.p: Which book discusses Bertha Mason from a feminist perspective?
lit-studies-modern.l28.q4.e: Gilbert and Gubar's book discusses such figures.

lit-studies-modern.l28.q5.t: State a claim, support it from the text, and note what the lens leaves out
lit-studies-modern.l28.q5.p: What is the lesson's advice on using critical lenses?
lit-studies-modern.l28.q5.h: Be specific and aware of limits.
lit-studies-modern.l28.q5.e: Evidence and awareness of limits are the skill.

med-anatomy.l01.q1.t: The L1-L2 level, with the cauda equina below it
med-anatomy.l01.q1.p: At what approximate vertebral level does the adult spinal cord end as the conus medullaris?
med-anatomy.l01.q1.h: The cord is shorter than the canal.
med-anatomy.l01.q1.e: The adult conus lies at about L1-L2; the L4-L5 distractor is where lumbar puncture is done, safely below the conus.

med-anatomy.l01.q2.t: The laminae of the vertebral arch joining at the midline
med-anatomy.l01.q2.p: Which structure fuses to the posterior arch to form the roof of the vertebral foramen on each side?
med-anatomy.l01.q2.h: Think of the arch behind the body.
med-anatomy.l01.q2.e: The pedicles and laminae form the arch; transverse processes do not meet in the midline.

med-anatomy.l01.q3.t: The arachnoid mater, after the dura mater
med-anatomy.l01.q3.p: Which layer is the last one the needle crosses before reaching CSF during lumbar puncture?
med-anatomy.l01.q3.h: CSF lies in the subarachnoid space.
med-anatomy.l01.q3.e: The needle crosses dura then arachnoid to reach the subarachnoid space; the pia lies on the cord and is not crossed.

med-anatomy.l01.q4.t: The traversing L5 root, passing beneath the L4-L5 disc
med-anatomy.l01.q4.p: A 45-year-old man has sudden low back pain radiating down the lateral leg to the dorsum of the foot, with weakness of great toe extension. MRI shows a posterolateral disc herniation at L4-L5. Which nerve root is most likely compressed?
med-anatomy.l01.q4.h: Posterolateral herniation hits the root that is crossing, not exiting.
med-anatomy.l01.q4.e: In the lumbar spine a posterolateral herniation compresses the traversing root, here L5; the exiting L4 root is usually spared except with far-lateral herniations.

med-anatomy.l01.q5.t: The conus medullaris ends lower in infants, around L3
med-anatomy.l01.q5.p: A 6-month-old needs a spinal tap. An experienced clinician chooses a lower interspace than for an adult because of which anatomical fact?
med-anatomy.l01.q5.h: Growth of the column outpaces the cord, and the process continues after birth.
med-anatomy.l01.q5.e: In newborns the conus lies about L3 and ascends to adult level; the dura is not fused to the cord, and a cauda equina exists.

med-anatomy.l02.q1.t: The left spinothalamic tract after crossing near the entry level
med-anatomy.l02.q1.p: Which tract carries pain and temperature sensation from the right leg to the brain?
med-anatomy.l02.q1.h: Fibres cross in the anterior white commissure.
med-anatomy.l02.q1.e: Spinothalamic fibres cross within a few segments of entry; the dorsal column carries touch and vibration and crosses in the medulla.

med-anatomy.l02.q2.t: Vibration and proprioception, carried in the dorsal columns
med-anatomy.l02.q2.p: Occlusion of the anterior spinal artery would most likely spare which function?
med-anatomy.l02.q2.h: The posterior spinal arteries supply the posterior third.
med-anatomy.l02.q2.e: The anterior spinal artery supplies the anterior two thirds, including the motor and pain pathways; the dorsal columns survive.

med-anatomy.l02.q3.t: Muscle atrophy with fasciculations and diminished reflexes
med-anatomy.l02.q3.p: Which finding is characteristic of a lower motor neuron lesion rather than an upper motor neuron lesion?
med-anatomy.l02.q3.h: Think about loss of the final common path.
med-anatomy.l02.q3.e: LMN lesions cause flaccid weakness, atrophy, fasciculations and hyporeflexia; the other options describe UMN signs.

med-anatomy.l02.q4.t: Spinothalamic fibres cross to the opposite side within a few segments of entry
med-anatomy.l02.q4.p: A 28-year-old man is stabbed in the back on the right at T8. He has right leg weakness, loss of vibration and position sense in the right leg, and loss of pain and temperature in the left leg below the umbilicus. What explains the contralateral pain loss?
med-anatomy.l02.q4.e: Brown-Sequard syndrome: the crossed spinothalamic fibres are interrupted on the opposite side; corticospinal fibres cross higher, in the medulla.

med-anatomy.l02.q5.t: The great anterior radicular artery feeding the anterior spinal artery
med-anatomy.l02.q5.p: A 70-year-old man has an elective thoracoabdominal aortic aneurysm repair. On waking he has flaccid paraplegia with loss of pain and temperature below the groin, but vibration sense in the legs is preserved. Which vessel is most likely compromised?
med-anatomy.l02.q5.h: Dorsal columns survive because of their separate supply.
med-anatomy.l02.q5.e: Loss of the radicular contribution infarcts the anterior cord and spares the dorsal columns, supplied by the posterior spinal arteries.

med-anatomy.l03.q1.p: In which order do the structures of the intercostal neurovascular bundle lie from superior to inferior?
med-anatomy.l03.q1.e: The bundle runs in the costal groove in the order vein, artery, nerve from above downwards.

med-anatomy.l03.q2.p: Which nerve provides the motor supply to the diaphragm?
med-anatomy.l03.q2.e: The phrenic nerve supplies the diaphragm; the long thoracic supplies serratus anterior.

med-anatomy.l03.q3.t: It is shorter, wider and more vertical than the left
med-anatomy.l03.q3.p: Why do aspirated foreign bodies enter the right main bronchus more often than the left?
med-anatomy.l03.q3.e: The right main bronchus is shorter, wider and more vertical; the left is longer and passes under the aortic arch.

med-anatomy.l03.q4.t: Just above the upper border of a rib, in the intercostal space
med-anatomy.l03.q4.p: A 22-year-old tall thin man develops sudden right pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea. Breath sounds are absent on the right and the trachea is central with normal blood pressure. Where is the best site to avoid the neurovascular bundle if a needle must be placed?
med-anatomy.l03.q4.h: The bundle hugs the lower rib border.
med-anatomy.l03.q4.e: The bundle lies in the costal groove under the rib above, so insertion is over the rib below; the groove sites are where vessels run.

med-anatomy.l03.q5.t: Phrenic nerve afferents from the diaphragm to C3-C5 sharing dermatomes with the shoulder
med-anatomy.l03.q5.p: A patient with a subphrenic abscess complains of pain at the tip of the right shoulder. Which nerve pathway best explains this?
med-anatomy.l03.q5.h: Embryologic origin of the diaphragm is in the neck.
med-anatomy.l03.q5.e: Central diaphragm sensation travels in the phrenic nerve (C3-C5), referred to the shoulder skin supplied by C3-C4; the other pathways serve different regions.

med-anatomy.l04.q1.p: Which coronary artery typically gives rise to the posterior descending artery in a right-dominant heart?
med-anatomy.l04.q1.h: Dominance is defined by the PDA origin.
med-anatomy.l04.q1.e: In about 80 percent of people the RCA gives the PDA; the circumflex does so in left-dominant hearts.

med-anatomy.l04.q2.t: The mitral valve at the cardiac apex
med-anatomy.l04.q2.p: Which valve is best heard at the left fifth intercostal space in the midclavicular line?
med-anatomy.l04.q2.h: This position is the cardiac apex.
med-anatomy.l04.q2.e: The mitral sounds project to the apex; the tricuspid is at the left lower sternal border.

med-anatomy.l04.q3.t: T4-T5, at the second costal cartilage
med-anatomy.l04.q3.p: At which vertebral level does the sternal angle lie, marking the aortic arch beginning and the carina?
med-anatomy.l04.q3.h: It is a landmark for counting ribs.
med-anatomy.l04.q3.e: The sternal angle is level with T4-T5 and the 2nd costal cartilage; T9 is the xiphisternal joint.

med-anatomy.l04.q4.t: The proximal right coronary artery supplying the AV node
med-anatomy.l04.q4.p: A 58-year-old man has crushing chest pain, bradycardia and ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF with a new first-degree AV block. Which artery is most likely occluded?
med-anatomy.l04.q4.e: RCA occlusion causes an inferior infarct and nodal ischaemia; LAD occlusion causes anterior changes.

med-anatomy.l04.q5.t: Blood in the pericardial cavity limiting ventricular filling
med-anatomy.l04.q5.p: A 30-year-old man is stabbed in the left fifth intercostal space near the sternum. He has hypotension, distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds. Which anatomical consequence explains this picture?
med-anatomy.l04.q5.h: The fibrous pericardium is not distensible quickly.
med-anatomy.l04.q5.e: The non-compliant fibrous pericardium makes a small rapid effusion cause tamponade; a haemothorax would cause dullness and shift, not Beck triad.

med-anatomy.l05.q1.p: Which layer of the spermatic cord is derived from the internal oblique muscle?
med-anatomy.l05.q1.h: Each layer matches an abdominal wall layer.
med-anatomy.l05.q1.e: Cremaster comes from the internal oblique; internal spermatic fascia comes from transversalis fascia.

med-anatomy.l05.q2.p: Which structure forms the anterior wall of the inguinal canal along its whole length?
med-anatomy.l05.q2.h: The superficial ring is a defect in it.
med-anatomy.l05.q2.e: The external oblique aponeurosis forms the anterior wall; transversalis fascia forms the posterior wall.

med-anatomy.l05.q3.p: A hernia emerges medial to the inferior epigastric vessels through Hesselbach triangle. Which type is this?
med-anatomy.l05.q3.h: Note the location relative to the vessels.
med-anatomy.l05.q3.e: Direct hernias pass medial to the epigastric vessels; indirect hernias pass through the deep ring lateral to them.

med-anatomy.l05.q4.t: A patent processus vaginalis through the deep inguinal ring
med-anatomy.l05.q4.p: A 5-year-old boy has an intermittent groin swelling extending into the scrotum that is worse when he cries. At repair, the sac lies within the spermatic cord, lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels. What is the underlying anatomical cause?
med-anatomy.l05.q4.e: Indirect hernias in children arise from a persistent processus vaginalis; a direct hernia involves a weakened posterior wall.

med-anatomy.l05.q5.t: The femoral ring is narrow and bounded by rigid ligamentous structures
med-anatomy.l05.q5.p: A 68-year-old woman has a tender, firm lump just below and lateral to the pubic tubercle with small bowel obstruction. Why is this hernia especially likely to strangulate?
med-anatomy.l05.q5.h: Consider the boundaries of the ring.
med-anatomy.l05.q5.e: The femoral ring is narrow with the lacunar ligament medially, so the contents are easily trapped; inguinal canal hernias have softer boundaries.

med-anatomy.l06.q1.p: Which structure within the hepatoduodenal ligament forms the posterior-most element of the portal triad?
med-anatomy.l06.q1.h: It is the largest and most posterior structure.
med-anatomy.l06.q1.e: The portal vein lies posterior to the bile duct and hepatic artery within the free edge of the lesser omentum.

med-anatomy.l06.q2.h: It fused to the posterior wall during development.
med-anatomy.l06.q2.e: The ascending and descending colon become fixed to the posterior wall; the transverse colon retains a mesentery.

med-anatomy.l06.q3.p: Visceral pain from the appendix is initially perceived in which area?
med-anatomy.l06.q3.h: The appendix is a midgut derivative.
med-anatomy.l06.q3.e: Midgut visceral afferents enter at about T10, so pain is periumbilical; localised right lower quadrant pain comes later from parietal peritoneum.

med-anatomy.l06.q4.p: A 52-year-old man with long-standing epigastric pain presents with sudden severe haematemesis. Imaging shows a deep ulcer in the posterior wall of the first part of the duodenum. Which artery is most likely eroded?
med-anatomy.l06.q4.h: The first part of the duodenum has a close posterior relation.
med-anatomy.l06.q4.e: Posterior duodenal ulcers erode the gastroduodenal artery; a perforated anterior ulcer causes peritonitis.

med-anatomy.l06.q5.t: Ectopic gastric mucosa in a vitelline duct remnant
med-anatomy.l06.q5.p: A 19-year-old has painless rectal bleeding. Technetium scanning shows uptake in the right lower abdomen, and a diverticulum is found on the antimesenteric border of the ileum. What best explains the bleeding?
med-anatomy.l06.q5.e: A Meckel diverticulum may contain ectopic gastric mucosa that ulcerates adjacent ileum; the IMA does not supply the ileum.

med-anatomy.l07.q1.p: At which vertebral level does the superior mesenteric artery arise?
med-anatomy.l07.q1.h: It is between the coeliac and the inferior mesenteric.
med-anatomy.l07.q1.e: The coeliac arises at T12, SMA at L1 and IMA at L3.

med-anatomy.l07.q2.p: Which vein joins the superior mesenteric vein to form the portal vein?
med-anatomy.l07.q2.h: It crosses behind the pancreas body.
med-anatomy.l07.q2.e: The splenic and superior mesenteric veins unite behind the pancreatic neck; the left gastric drains separately.

med-anatomy.l07.q3.t: Left gastric veins with oesophageal veins draining to the azygos
med-anatomy.l07.q3.p: Which portosystemic anastomosis lies at the gastro-oesophageal junction?
med-anatomy.l07.q3.e: Left gastric to oesophageal veins links the portal and azygos systems; the rectal and umbilical sites are separate anastomoses.

med-anatomy.l07.q4.t: Portal hypertension diverting blood through left gastric to azygos veins
med-anatomy.l07.q4.p: A 55-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis vomits a large volume of blood. Endoscopy shows distal oesophageal varices. Which pathway best explains their development?
med-anatomy.l07.q4.e: Raised portal pressure diverts flow through the left gastric-oesophageal anastomosis into the azygos system; IVC compression would not specifically produce varices.

med-anatomy.l07.q5.t: The left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein, which a mass can obstruct
med-anatomy.l07.q5.p: A 24-year-old man has a left varicocele that persists when lying down, with flank pain and haematuria. Which anatomical feature most plausibly explains the left-sided location and warrants imaging?
med-anatomy.l07.q5.e: The left gonadal vein enters the left renal vein, so a renal tumour or thrombus can cause a fixed varicocele; the right drains straight into the IVC.

med-anatomy.l08.q1.p: What is the order of structures at the renal hilum from anterior to posterior?
med-anatomy.l08.q1.e: The renal vein is anterior, then the artery, then the renal pelvis.

med-anatomy.l08.q2.p: Which is the narrowest part of the ureter, where stones often lodge?
med-anatomy.l08.q2.h: It is where the ureter enters the bladder wall.
med-anatomy.l08.q2.e: The VUJ is the narrowest; the pelviureteric junction and pelvic brim are the other classical sites.

med-anatomy.l08.q3.p: Which adrenal vein drains directly into the inferior vena cava?
med-anatomy.l08.q3.h: The left one joins a renal vein.
med-anatomy.l08.q3.e: The right is short and enters the IVC; the left enters the left renal vein.

med-anatomy.l08.q4.t: The ureter passes beneath the uterine artery near the cervix
med-anatomy.l08.q4.p: A 35-year-old woman undergoing hysterectomy has an unexpected hydronephrosis afterwards, and imaging shows the distal left ureter was ligated. Which relationship explains the injury?
med-anatomy.l08.q4.e: The ureter runs under the uterine artery near the cervix and is vulnerable during clamping; the other relationships are not at the site of ligation.

med-anatomy.l08.q5.p: A 62-year-old man has painless jaundice, weight loss and a palpable gallbladder. CT shows a mass in the head of the pancreas. Which structure is compressed to cause jaundice?
med-anatomy.l08.q5.h: The duct runs through or behind the pancreatic head.
med-anatomy.l08.q5.e: The distal common bile duct passes through the pancreatic head; compression causes obstructive jaundice. The cystic duct compression would not cause jaundice.

med-anatomy.l09.q1.p: Which structure is the lowest point of the peritoneal cavity in an upright female?
med-anatomy.l09.q1.e: The rectouterine pouch is the lowest point and can be reached through the posterior fornix; the hepatorenal pouch is the lowest point when supine.

med-anatomy.l09.q2.t: The peripheral zone, palpable on rectal examination
med-anatomy.l09.q2.p: Which prostatic zone is the most common site of adenocarcinoma?
med-anatomy.l09.q2.e: Most prostate cancers arise in the peripheral zone; benign prostatic hyperplasia affects the transition zone.

med-anatomy.l09.q3.p: Which ligament is the main support of the uterine cervix and carries the uterine vessels?
med-anatomy.l09.q3.h: Think of the ligament at the base of the broad ligament.
med-anatomy.l09.q3.e: The cardinal ligament supports the cervix; the round ligament runs to the labium majus and does little to support.

med-anatomy.l09.q4.t: Enlargement of the periurethral transition zone compresses the prostatic urethra
med-anatomy.l09.q4.p: A 68-year-old man has weak urinary stream, nocturia and a smooth enlarged prostate. Which anatomical statement best explains his obstruction?
med-anatomy.l09.q4.h: The enlargement is in the zone around the urethra.
med-anatomy.l09.q4.e: BPH arises in the transition zone around the urethra; the peripheral zone is mainly involved in cancer.

med-anatomy.l09.q5.t: The rectouterine pouch is the most dependent part of the female peritoneal cavity
med-anatomy.l09.q5.p: A 27-year-old woman has lower abdominal pain, fever and a bulging posterior vaginal fornix. Which anatomical fact explains where pus has collected?
med-anatomy.l09.q5.e: Fluid pools in the rectouterine pouch, in contact with the posterior fornix; the vesicouterine pouch is anterior to the uterus.

med-anatomy.l10.q1.p: Which nerve is the principal sensory and motor nerve of the perineum?
med-anatomy.l10.q1.h: It loops around the ischial spine.
med-anatomy.l10.q1.e: The pudendal nerve supplies the perineum; the ilioinguinal supplies skin of the anterior scrotum or labia.

med-anatomy.l10.q2.p: Which feature of the anal canal is the junction of hindgut endoderm and ectoderm?
med-anatomy.l10.q2.h: Venous and lymph drainage change here.
med-anatomy.l10.q2.e: The pectinate line is the embryologic junction; the other structures are nearby but are not the endoderm-ectoderm boundary.

med-anatomy.l10.q3.t: To the superficial inguinal lymph nodes
med-anatomy.l10.q3.p: Where do lymphatics from the anal canal below the pectinate line drain?
med-anatomy.l10.q3.e: Below the line, lymph drains to the superficial inguinal nodes; above it, to internal iliac nodes.

med-anatomy.l10.q4.t: The ischial spine, near where the nerve crosses it
med-anatomy.l10.q4.p: A 32-year-old woman in labour receives a pudendal nerve block. Which landmark should the clinician palpate to place the injection correctly?
med-anatomy.l10.q4.h: The nerve loops around a bony spine.
med-anatomy.l10.q4.e: The pudendal nerve passes around the ischial spine and sacrospinous ligament; the tuberosity is not the site.

med-anatomy.l10.q5.t: The mucosa above the line has visceral innervation without pain-sensitive somatic fibres
med-anatomy.l10.q5.p: A 45-year-old man has bright red painless bleeding at the end of defecation and, on anoscopy, a soft swelling at 7 o'clock above the pectinate line. Why is it painless?
med-anatomy.l10.q5.h: Consider the nerve supply of the endodermal portion.
med-anatomy.l10.q5.e: Above the line, sensation is visceral and poorly localised, so internal haemorrhoids are painless; below the line the somatic inferior rectal nerve gives sharp pain.

med-anatomy.l11.q1.p: Which nerve supplies the quadriceps femoris?
med-anatomy.l11.q1.h: It lies lateral to the femoral artery.
med-anatomy.l11.q1.e: The femoral nerve supplies the quadriceps; the obturator supplies adductors.

med-anatomy.l11.q2.p: What is the order of structures in the femoral triangle from lateral to medial?
med-anatomy.l11.q2.e: The femoral vein is medial to the artery and the nerve is lateral, outside the sheath.

med-anatomy.l11.q3.p: Which artery contributes the majority of the blood supply to the femoral head in adults?
med-anatomy.l11.q3.h: It forms a ring around the neck.
med-anatomy.l11.q3.e: The circumflex femoral arteries, especially the medial, supply the head; the ligamentum teres artery contributes only a little.

med-anatomy.l11.q4.t: Avascular necrosis from interruption of retinacular vessels
med-anatomy.l11.q4.p: A 72-year-old woman falls and has a shortened, externally rotated right leg. Radiographs show a displaced subcapital femoral neck fracture. Which complication is most feared in the head fragment?
med-anatomy.l11.q4.h: Think about the blood supply running up the neck.
med-anatomy.l11.q4.e: Retinacular vessels from the circumflex arteries run along the neck and are torn; the other complications are less typical.

med-anatomy.l11.q5.t: Right gluteus medius, from superior gluteal nerve injury
med-anatomy.l11.q5.p: A 40-year-old man has a gait where the pelvis drops to the left when he stands on his right leg, after a deep injection into the right buttock. Which muscle weakness best explains this?
med-anatomy.l11.q5.h: The abductors stabilise the pelvis on the standing side.
med-anatomy.l11.q5.e: Standing on the affected side, weak abductors fail to hold the pelvis, so it drops on the opposite side; gluteus maximus injury causes difficulty climbing.

med-anatomy.l12.q1.p: Which ligament prevents anterior translation of the tibia on the femur?
med-anatomy.l12.q1.e: The ACL resists anterior tibial translation; the PCL resists posterior translation.

med-anatomy.l12.q2.p: Which ankle ligament is most commonly torn in an inversion sprain?
med-anatomy.l12.q2.h: It is part of the lateral complex and is weakest.
med-anatomy.l12.q2.e: The ATFL is the weakest of the lateral complex and is injured first; the deltoid is medial and stronger.

med-anatomy.l12.q3.p: Which nerve is most vulnerable to injury around the neck of the fibula?
med-anatomy.l12.q3.e: The common fibular nerve winds around the fibular neck; the tibial nerve is deep in the popliteal fossa.

med-anatomy.l12.q4.t: Loss of the restraint to anterior tibial translation on the femur
med-anatomy.l12.q4.p: A 19-year-old footballer lands awkwardly, hears a pop and develops a haemarthrosis. The anterior drawer test is positive. Which statement explains the instability?
med-anatomy.l12.q4.e: A positive anterior drawer reflects ACL rupture and excessive anterior tibial translation; PCL injury gives posterior translation.

med-anatomy.l12.q5.t: Raised pressure within a closed fascial compartment compromising capillary perfusion
med-anatomy.l12.q5.p: A 24-year-old man with a tibial shaft fracture has escalating leg pain unrelieved by analgesia, severe pain with passive toe flexion, and a tense calf, but palpable pedal pulses. What is the best explanation?
med-anatomy.l12.q5.e: Compartment syndrome compromises microvascular perfusion while large-vessel pulses are often present; arterial occlusion would cause a pulseless limb.

med-anatomy.l13.q1.t: Supraspinatus, supplied by the suprascapular nerve
med-anatomy.l13.q1.p: Which rotator cuff muscle initiates abduction of the arm and is most commonly torn?
med-anatomy.l13.q1.e: Supraspinatus starts abduction and is the most frequently torn; infraspinatus is an external rotator.

med-anatomy.l13.q2.t: The long thoracic nerve; the scapula becomes winged
med-anatomy.l13.q2.p: Which nerve supplies serratus anterior, and what is the result of its injury?
med-anatomy.l13.q2.h: The nerve runs on the lateral chest wall.
med-anatomy.l13.q2.e: The long thoracic nerve (C5-C7) supplies serratus anterior; trapezius injury also causes a drooping shoulder but is supplied by CN XI.

med-anatomy.l13.q3.t: At the inferior border of teres major
med-anatomy.l13.q3.p: Where does the axillary artery become the brachial artery?
med-anatomy.l13.q3.e: The axillary artery starts at the first rib and becomes the brachial artery at the lower border of teres major.

med-anatomy.l13.q4.t: The axillary nerve, wrapping the surgical neck of the humerus
med-anatomy.l13.q4.p: A 22-year-old rugby player dislocates his shoulder anteriorly. Afterwards he has weak arm abduction and numbness over the lateral upper arm. Which structure is most likely injured?
med-anatomy.l13.q4.h: The nerve supplies deltoid and the skin over it.
med-anatomy.l13.q4.e: The axillary nerve supplies deltoid and the regimental badge skin; the radial nerve in the groove would cause wrist drop.

med-anatomy.l13.q5.t: Injury to the nerve on the lateral thoracic wall supplying serratus anterior
med-anatomy.l13.q5.p: A 55-year-old woman after axillary node dissection has her medial scapular border lifting off the chest wall when she pushes against a wall. Which injury best explains this?
med-anatomy.l13.q5.h: Pushing against a wall tests protraction.
med-anatomy.l13.q5.e: The long thoracic nerve supplies serratus anterior; trapezius palsy produces a different pattern with shoulder droop.

med-anatomy.l14.q1.t: The anterior rami of C5 to T1
med-anatomy.l14.q1.p: Which spinal nerves form the brachial plexus?
med-anatomy.l14.q1.e: The plexus is formed by the anterior rami of C5-T1; posterior rami supply the back.

med-anatomy.l14.q2.p: Which cord of the brachial plexus gives rise to the axillary and radial nerves?
med-anatomy.l14.q2.e: The axillary and radial nerves are posterior cord branches; the lateral cord gives the musculocutaneous nerve.

med-anatomy.l14.q3.t: The lower trunk or C8-T1 roots
med-anatomy.l14.q3.p: A claw hand with sensory loss on the medial hand and Horner syndrome suggests injury to which part of the plexus?
med-anatomy.l14.q3.e: Klumpke palsy involves C8-T1 and may include sympathetic fibres; the upper trunk lesion gives the waiter's tip position.

med-anatomy.l14.q4.t: Upper trunk traction injury of C5-C6
med-anatomy.l14.q4.p: A newborn delivered after shoulder dystocia holds the right arm adducted, internally rotated and pronated, with an intact grasp. Which injury is most likely?
med-anatomy.l14.q4.e: Erb palsy (C5-C6) causes the waiter's tip posture with preserved hand function; lower trunk injury would cause hand weakness.

med-anatomy.l14.q5.t: Invasion of the lower trunk and the sympathetic chain at the thoracic inlet
med-anatomy.l14.q5.p: A 60-year-old smoker has shoulder pain, hand weakness, ulnar-side numbness, ptosis and miosis on the right. Chest imaging shows an apical lung mass. Which anatomy explains the full picture?
med-anatomy.l14.q5.h: A Pancoast tumour lies at the lung apex.
med-anatomy.l14.q5.e: Apical tumours invade the lower trunk and the sympathetic chain, causing hand weakness and Horner syndrome; the radial nerve is not located there.

med-anatomy.l15.q1.p: Which nerve passes in the radial groove of the humerus?
med-anatomy.l15.q1.h: It accompanies the profunda brachii artery.
med-anatomy.l15.q1.e: The radial nerve lies in the spiral groove; the ulnar nerve passes behind the medial epicondyle.

med-anatomy.l15.q2.t: Wrist drop with preserved elbow extension
med-anatomy.l15.q2.p: Which finding is characteristic of radial nerve injury in the spiral groove?
med-anatomy.l15.q2.h: The triceps branches leave higher up.
med-anatomy.l15.q2.e: The triceps is spared since its branches leave before the groove; ape hand is a median nerve sign.

med-anatomy.l15.q3.p: Which structure lies immediately lateral to the brachial artery in the cubital fossa?
med-anatomy.l15.q3.h: The nerve is medial to the artery.
med-anatomy.l15.q3.e: From lateral to medial: biceps tendon, brachial artery, median nerve.

med-anatomy.l15.q4.t: The anterior interosseous branch of the median nerve
med-anatomy.l15.q4.p: A 7-year-old falls on an outstretched hand and has a displaced supracondylar fracture. He cannot flex the thumb interphalangeal joint or index distal phalanx, but sensation is intact. Which structure is injured?
med-anatomy.l15.q4.e: The anterior interosseous nerve is motor only, supplying flexor pollicis longus and lateral flexor digitorum profundus.

med-anatomy.l15.q5.t: The ulnar nerve, in the groove behind the epicondyle
med-anatomy.l15.q5.p: A 35-year-old man fractures the medial epicondyle of the humerus. Weeks later he has numbness of the little finger and cannot adduct his thumb, so flexes the thumb interphalangeal joint when gripping paper. Which nerve is involved?
med-anatomy.l15.q5.e: Adductor pollicis is supplied by the ulnar nerve, which passes behind the medial epicondyle; the median nerve does not supply the little finger.

med-anatomy.l16.q1.p: Which structure lies within the carpal tunnel along with the flexor tendons?
med-anatomy.l16.q1.h: It is the nerve compressed in the syndrome.
med-anatomy.l16.q1.e: The median nerve is the only nerve in the tunnel; the ulnar nerve and artery pass through Guyon canal.

med-anatomy.l16.q2.p: Which muscle group is supplied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve?
med-anatomy.l16.q2.e: The interossei, medial lumbricals and adductor pollicis are ulnar; thenar muscles are median.

med-anatomy.l16.q3.t: The palmar cutaneous branch arises proximal to the tunnel
med-anatomy.l16.q3.p: Why is thenar skin sensation preserved in carpal tunnel syndrome?
med-anatomy.l16.q3.h: Think where the branch leaves the median nerve.
med-anatomy.l16.q3.e: The palmar cutaneous branch leaves before the retinaculum and passes superficial to it.

med-anatomy.l16.q4.t: Compression of the median nerve beneath the flexor retinaculum
med-anatomy.l16.q4.p: A 38-year-old pregnant woman has night-time numbness of her thumb, index and middle fingers, weak thumb abduction, and a positive Tinel sign at the wrist. What explains her symptoms?
med-anatomy.l16.q4.h: Lateral three and a half digits.
med-anatomy.l16.q4.e: Carpal tunnel syndrome is median nerve compression and is more frequent in pregnancy; Guyon canal involvement affects the little finger.

med-anatomy.l16.q5.t: Its blood supply enters distally and flows retrograde to the proximal pole
med-anatomy.l16.q5.p: A 25-year-old man falls on an outstretched hand and has tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox, with initially normal radiographs. Why is he at risk of nonunion of the injured bone?
med-anatomy.l16.q5.h: The scaphoid is a notorious carpal bone for avascular necrosis.
med-anatomy.l16.q5.e: Retrograde supply makes proximal pole fractures prone to avascular necrosis; the bone does have cartilage and the radial artery crosses its snuffbox region.

med-anatomy.l17.q1.p: Which foramen transmits the middle meningeal artery into the cranial cavity?
med-anatomy.l17.q1.h: It is a small foramen near the foramen ovale.
med-anatomy.l17.q1.e: The middle meningeal artery enters via foramen spinosum; the foramen ovale carries the mandibular nerve.

med-anatomy.l17.q2.t: The abducens nerve and internal carotid artery
med-anatomy.l17.q2.p: Which structure runs within the cavernous sinus itself rather than in its lateral wall?
med-anatomy.l17.q2.h: CN VI hangs in the sinus.
med-anatomy.l17.q2.e: CN VI and the internal carotid lie in the sinus; CN III, IV, V1 and V2 are in the wall.

med-anatomy.l17.q3.t: A bridging vein crossing to a dural sinus
med-anatomy.l17.q3.p: Which vessel is torn in a subdural haematoma?
med-anatomy.l17.q3.e: Subdural bleeding comes from bridging veins; the middle meningeal artery causes epidural bleeding.

med-anatomy.l17.q4.t: The middle meningeal artery beneath the pterion
med-anatomy.l17.q4.p: A 19-year-old is struck on the side of the head with a bat, briefly loses consciousness, then talks normally for an hour before becoming drowsy with a dilated left pupil. CT shows a biconvex collection that stops at a suture. Which vessel is most likely torn?
med-anatomy.l17.q4.e: An epidural haematoma is arterial and limited by sutures; subdural collections cross sutures and are crescentic.

med-anatomy.l17.q5.t: Spread through valveless facial and ophthalmic veins to the cavernous sinus
med-anatomy.l17.q5.p: A 22-year-old squeezes a pustule on the upper lip. Days later he has fever, proptosis, ophthalmoplegia and numbness of the forehead. Which pathway explains this?
med-anatomy.l17.q5.h: Think of the danger triangle of the face.
med-anatomy.l17.q5.e: The valveless venous connections allow retrograde spread to the cavernous sinus, affecting nerves III, IV, V1 and VI; an olfactory path would cause anosmia and meningitis.

med-anatomy.l18.q1.p: Which cranial nerve supplies the lateral rectus muscle?
med-anatomy.l18.q1.e: Abducens (VI) supplies the lateral rectus; trochlear (IV) supplies the superior oblique.

med-anatomy.l18.q2.p: Which feature distinguishes a lower motor neuron facial palsy from an upper motor neuron lesion?
med-anatomy.l18.q2.h: Bilateral cortical input to the upper face.
med-anatomy.l18.q2.e: In LMN lesions the whole face is paralysed; with UMN lesions the forehead is spared via bilateral input.

med-anatomy.l18.q3.p: A patient's tongue deviates to the right on protrusion. Which lesion is most consistent?
med-anatomy.l18.q3.h: The tongue points toward the weak side.
med-anatomy.l18.q3.e: The tongue deviates toward the lesion because the intact genioglossus pushes it out and across.

med-anatomy.l18.q4.t: A posterior communicating artery aneurysm compressing the third nerve
med-anatomy.l18.q4.p: A 60-year-old woman has a sudden severe headache and a left eye that is down and out with ptosis and a dilated pupil. Which cause is most likely given the pupil?
med-anatomy.l18.q4.e: Compressive lesions affect the outer parasympathetic fibres early and dilate the pupil; ischaemic lesions typically spare the pupil.

med-anatomy.l18.q5.t: The recurrent laryngeal nerve near the inferior thyroid artery
med-anatomy.l18.q5.p: A 45-year-old woman undergoes total thyroidectomy and wakes hoarse with a weak, breathy voice. Which nerve was most likely injured?
med-anatomy.l18.q5.h: The nerve runs in the tracheo-oesophageal groove.
med-anatomy.l18.q5.e: The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies most intrinsic laryngeal muscles; external laryngeal injury causes tone loss but is less hoarse.

med-anatomy.l19.q1.p: Which nerve crosses the posterior triangle superficially and is at risk during lymph node biopsy?
med-anatomy.l19.q1.e: The accessory nerve crosses the posterior triangle superficially; the phrenic lies deep on scalenus anterior.

med-anatomy.l19.q2.t: The inferior thyroid artery from the thyrocervical trunk
med-anatomy.l19.q2.p: Which artery supplies the thyroid gland from the subclavian system?
med-anatomy.l19.q2.e: The inferior thyroid artery arises from the thyrocervical trunk; the superior thyroid comes from the external carotid.

med-anatomy.l19.q3.p: Which structure moves upward with tongue protrusion when it is a midline neck mass?
med-anatomy.l19.q3.e: The thyroglossal duct tracks to the foramen caecum, so the cyst elevates; branchial cleft cysts are lateral.

med-anatomy.l19.q4.t: Airway obstruction from bilateral submandibular space infection
med-anatomy.l19.q4.p: A 30-year-old man has fever, dysphagia, trismus and bilateral submandibular swelling elevating the tongue after a molar extraction. What is the main concern?
med-anatomy.l19.q4.e: Ludwig angina can displace the tongue and block the airway; cavernous sinus thrombosis is related to facial veins above the mouth.

med-anatomy.l19.q5.t: Removal or devascularisation of the parathyroid glands on the posterior thyroid surface
med-anatomy.l19.q5.p: A 50-year-old woman after thyroidectomy has perioral tingling and carpopedal spasm two days later. What anatomical explanation is most likely?
med-anatomy.l19.q5.e: Hypocalcaemia follows loss of the parathyroids, which lie behind the thyroid; nerve injuries cause voice changes, not tetany.

med-anatomy.l20.q1.p: Which division of the trigeminal nerve supplies the skin of the lower lip and chin?
med-anatomy.l20.q1.e: V3 supplies the lower lip and chin; the marginal mandibular branch of VII is motor.

med-anatomy.l20.q2.t: The chorda tympani, a branch of the facial nerve
med-anatomy.l20.q2.p: Which nerve carries taste from the anterior two thirds of the tongue?
med-anatomy.l20.q2.h: The lingual nerve carries touch, not taste, of this area.
med-anatomy.l20.q2.e: Chorda tympani joins the lingual nerve to supply taste; the lingual nerve itself carries general sensation.

med-anatomy.l20.q3.p: Which fissure transmits the oculomotor, trochlear, abducens and ophthalmic nerves into the orbit?
med-anatomy.l20.q3.h: Four nerves pass through one gap.
med-anatomy.l20.q3.e: The superior orbital fissure carries III, IV, V1 and VI; the optic canal carries only II and the ophthalmic artery.

med-anatomy.l20.q4.t: A floor fracture entrapping the inferior rectus and injuring the infraorbital nerve
med-anatomy.l20.q4.p: A 17-year-old is punched in the eye and cannot look upward with the left eye, has diplopia and numbness over the left cheek. CT shows fluid in the maxillary sinus. Which injury is most likely?
med-anatomy.l20.q4.e: Blowout fractures of the orbital floor entrap the inferior rectus and injure the infraorbital nerve; the optic canal is not involved.

med-anatomy.l20.q5.t: Injury to the branches of the facial nerve running within the gland
med-anatomy.l20.q5.p: A 55-year-old man has a hard mass in the parotid gland and, after surgery, cannot close his right eye or raise his right eyebrow. What explains this?
med-anatomy.l20.q5.h: The nerve passes through the gland.
med-anatomy.l20.q5.e: The facial nerve branches within the parotid gland supply the orbicularis oculi and frontalis; the other nerves are sensory or do not supply facial muscles.

med-anatomy.l21.q1.p: At which vertebral level does the transpyloric plane lie?
med-anatomy.l21.q1.h: Midway between the suprasternal notch and the pubic symphysis.
med-anatomy.l21.q1.e: The transpyloric plane is at about L1; the supracristal plane is at L4.

med-anatomy.l21.q2.t: The line joining the highest points of the iliac crests
med-anatomy.l21.q2.p: Which landmark marks the vertebral level at which the common iliac arteries and aorta divide, useful for lumbar puncture?
med-anatomy.l21.q2.e: The supracristal plane at L4 is the intercristal line; the scapular angles lie at T7.

med-anatomy.l21.q3.t: The left fifth intercostal space in the midclavicular line
med-anatomy.l21.q3.p: Where is the apex beat normally found in a healthy adult?
med-anatomy.l21.q3.e: The apex beat is in the fifth left intercostal space at the midclavicular line; displacement suggests cardiomegaly.

med-anatomy.l21.q4.t: The left ventricle near the apex
med-anatomy.l21.q4.p: A 28-year-old man is stabbed in the left fifth intercostal space at the midclavicular line and becomes hypotensive. Which structure is most likely penetrated?
med-anatomy.l21.q4.h: Think of the position of the apex.
med-anatomy.l21.q4.e: The left ventricle forms the apex at this location; the right atrium lies to the right of the sternum.

med-anatomy.l21.q5.t: The line crosses about L4, below the conus medullaris at L1-L2
med-anatomy.l21.q5.p: A 32-year-old woman needs a lumbar puncture. The clinician finds the level by palpating the highest points of both iliac crests and inserting just below. Why is this safe?
med-anatomy.l21.q5.h: Compare the level with the cord.
med-anatomy.l21.q5.e: The supracristal plane is at about L4; the cord ends at L1-L2 in adults, so the needle meets only the cauda equina roots.

med-anatomy.l22.q1.p: Which pharyngeal arch is supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve?
med-anatomy.l22.q1.e: The glossopharyngeal nerve supplies the third arch; the second is supplied by the facial nerve.

med-anatomy.l22.q2.t: The septum transversum forms at cervical levels and carries its nerve down
med-anatomy.l22.q2.p: Why does the phrenic nerve arise in the neck although the diaphragm lies in the trunk?
med-anatomy.l22.q2.h: The central tendon has a cervical origin.
med-anatomy.l22.q2.e: The septum transversum originates at cervical levels (C3-C5) and descends, dragging the phrenic nerve.

med-anatomy.l22.q3.t: The ductus arteriosus (the remnant of the sixth arch artery)
med-anatomy.l22.q3.p: Which structure explains why the left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops under the aortic arch?
med-anatomy.l22.q3.h: It is the fetal bypass between the pulmonary trunk and the aorta.
med-anatomy.l22.q3.e: The left nerve hooks under the ligamentum arteriosum, the sixth arch remnant.

med-anatomy.l22.q4.t: Failure of the pleuroperitoneal membrane to close the posterolateral defect, causing pulmonary hypoplasia
med-anatomy.l22.q4.p: A term newborn has respiratory distress, a scaphoid abdomen and bowel sounds in the left chest. Which developmental failure explains the lung findings?
med-anatomy.l22.q4.h: The hernia is posterolateral and often left sided.
med-anatomy.l22.q4.e: A Bochdalek hernia results from incomplete closure of the pleuroperitoneal canal and compresses the developing lung.

med-anatomy.l22.q5.t: The foramen ovale, from incomplete fusion of the septum primum and secundum
med-anatomy.l22.q5.p: A 22-year-old woman has a stroke attributed to a venous clot, and echocardiography with bubble contrast shows bubbles crossing into the left atrium at rest and with Valsalva. What developmental structure is persistent?
med-anatomy.l22.q5.h: A paradoxical embolus crosses the atrial septum.
med-anatomy.l22.q5.e: A patent foramen ovale allows paradoxical embolism; a PDA causes a left-to-right shunt through a different structure.

med-anatomy.l23.q1.p: On a T2-weighted MRI, which tissue appears bright?
med-anatomy.l23.q1.e: On T2 images fluid is bright, making oedema conspicuous; cortical bone and air give little signal.

med-anatomy.l23.q2.p: Which modality is the first choice for rapid assessment of acute intracranial haemorrhage?
med-anatomy.l23.q2.h: Blood is bright and the scan is fast.
med-anatomy.l23.q2.e: Non-contrast CT detects acute blood quickly; plain skull films cannot show brain haemorrhage.

med-anatomy.l23.q3.p: On an axial CT image displayed in the standard convention, where is the patient's right side?
med-anatomy.l23.q3.h: You look from the feet upward.
med-anatomy.l23.q3.e: Axial images are viewed from below, so the patient's right is on the viewer's left.

med-anatomy.l23.q4.t: The right middle lobe, abutting the right heart border
med-anatomy.l23.q4.p: A 67-year-old man with cough has a chest film showing loss of the right heart border while the right hemidiaphragm outline is preserved. Which location of consolidation best explains this?
med-anatomy.l23.q4.e: The middle lobe lies against the right heart border, so consolidation there effaces it; lower lobe disease obscures the diaphragm.

med-anatomy.l23.q5.t: Stones reflect sound and cast acoustic shadows within anechoic bile
med-anatomy.l23.q5.p: A 30-year-old woman has right upper quadrant pain after meals. The best first imaging test to look for gallstones uses which property?
med-anatomy.l23.q5.h: Fluid is black, stones are bright with a shadow.
med-anatomy.l23.q5.e: Ultrasound shows gallstones as echogenic foci with acoustic shadowing in black bile; many stones are not radio-opaque on plain film.

med-biochem-genetics.l01.q1.t: The substrate concentration at which the reaction velocity is half of Vmax, an inverse index of apparent affinity
med-biochem-genetics.l01.q1.p: In the Michaelis-Menten model, what does the Km represent?
med-biochem-genetics.l01.q1.h: Think about the shape of the hyperbola.
med-biochem-genetics.l01.q1.e: Km is the [S] giving half-maximal velocity, so a low Km indicates high apparent affinity. The maximum velocity is Vmax, which scales with enzyme concentration.

med-biochem-genetics.l01.q2.t: Competitive inhibition, which can be overcome by increasing the substrate concentration
med-biochem-genetics.l01.q2.p: A drug raises the apparent Km of an enzyme but leaves Vmax unchanged. Which kind of inhibition does this describe?
med-biochem-genetics.l01.q2.h: Which parameter does a substrate-like molecule change?
med-biochem-genetics.l01.q2.e: A competitive inhibitor competes at the active site, raising apparent Km with no change in Vmax. Noncompetitive inhibition would lower Vmax instead.

med-biochem-genetics.l01.q3.t: They lower the activation energy without altering the equilibrium constant of the reaction they catalyse
med-biochem-genetics.l01.q3.p: Which of the following is true of enzymes as catalysts?
med-biochem-genetics.l01.q3.e: Enzymes speed approach to equilibrium in both directions without changing it. They are not consumed.

med-biochem-genetics.l01.q4.t: A line with a steeper slope that crosses the untreated line on the y-axis, because Vmax is unchanged and apparent Km is higher
med-biochem-genetics.l01.q4.p: A child is brought in after drinking antifreeze containing ethylene glycol and is started on an infusion of fomepizole. On a double-reciprocal plot of alcohol dehydrogenase activity, what would the addition of this competitive inhibitor produce compared with the untreated enzyme?
med-biochem-genetics.l01.q4.h: Where do the lines of a competitive inhibitor meet?
med-biochem-genetics.l01.q4.e: Competitive inhibition keeps 1/Vmax (the y-intercept) fixed and shifts the x-intercept toward zero, so the lines meet on the y-axis. Crossing on the x-axis is the pattern for noncompetitive inhibition.

med-biochem-genetics.l01.q5.t: The inhibitor binds a site distinct from the active site and effectively lowers the quantity of functional enzyme
med-biochem-genetics.l01.q5.p: An experimenter adds an inhibitor to a purified enzyme and observes that Vmax falls to half of the control value while Km is unchanged. Doubling the substrate concentration does not restore activity. Which conclusion best fits these data?
med-biochem-genetics.l01.q5.h: A Km that does not move rules out one mechanism and an uncompetitive pattern.
med-biochem-genetics.l01.q5.e: Reduced Vmax with unchanged Km that is not rescued by substrate is the noncompetitive pattern. A competitive inhibitor would leave Vmax intact at high [S].

med-biochem-genetics.l02.q1.t: Phosphofructokinase-1, activated by AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate and inhibited by ATP and citrate
med-biochem-genetics.l02.q1.p: Which enzyme catalyses the rate-limiting step of glycolysis?
med-biochem-genetics.l02.q1.h: It is the committed step that adds a second phosphate to a hexose.
med-biochem-genetics.l02.q1.e: PFK-1 is the main control point of glycolysis. The other enzymes listed belong to gluconeogenesis.

med-biochem-genetics.l02.q2.t: Biotin, the carrier for carboxylation reactions such as that of pyruvate carboxylase
med-biochem-genetics.l02.q2.p: Which cofactor is NOT required by the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex?
med-biochem-genetics.l02.q2.h: Remember the five cofactors of the complex.
med-biochem-genetics.l02.q2.e: The complex uses TPP, lipoate, CoA, FAD and NAD+. Biotin is used by carboxylases, such as pyruvate carboxylase.

med-biochem-genetics.l02.q3.t: Cyanide, which binds the ferric heme of the terminal oxidase and halts electron transfer to oxygen
med-biochem-genetics.l02.q3.p: Which electron transport chain inhibitor acts at complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase)?
med-biochem-genetics.l02.q3.h: Carbon monoxide acts at the same site.
med-biochem-genetics.l02.q3.e: Cyanide and CO inhibit complex IV. Rotenone acts at I, antimycin A at III and oligomycin at V.

med-biochem-genetics.l02.q4.t: Pyruvate kinase, impairing ATP production in cells that have no mitochondria and rely on glycolysis
med-biochem-genetics.l02.q4.p: A 3-year-old with recurrent haemolytic anaemia has splenomegaly. Red cells show no spherocytes or Heinz bodies, and a screen for G6PD is normal. A defect in which of the following is the most likely underlying cause?
med-biochem-genetics.l02.q4.h: Which pathway is the only ATP source of an erythrocyte?
med-biochem-genetics.l02.q4.e: Without mitochondria, red cells depend on glycolytic ATP; low ATP from pyruvate kinase deficiency causes membrane failure and haemolysis. The TCA cycle enzyme is irrelevant in a cell lacking mitochondria.

med-biochem-genetics.l02.q5.t: Pyruvate dehydrogenase, because deficient thiamine leaves pyruvate unable to enter the cycle and shunted to lactate
med-biochem-genetics.l02.q5.p: A malnourished man with chronic alcohol use is given intravenous glucose and soon develops confusion, ophthalmoplegia, and a serum lactate rise with metabolic acidosis. Impaired activity of which enzyme complex best explains the acidosis?
med-biochem-genetics.l02.q5.h: Glucose loading increases flux into the step that needs vitamin B1.
med-biochem-genetics.l02.q5.e: Thiamine is required by the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase; a glucose load in a deficient patient precipitates lactic acidosis and Wernicke encephalopathy. Biotin deficiency is not the issue here.

med-biochem-genetics.l03.q1.t: Glucose-6-phosphatase, the final enzyme that releases free glucose from the liver and kidney
med-biochem-genetics.l03.q1.p: Which enzyme is deficient in von Gierke disease (glycogen storage disease type I)?
med-biochem-genetics.l03.q1.h: The enzyme is found in the endoplasmic reticulum of liver.
med-biochem-genetics.l03.q1.e: Type I is glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency. Pompe, McArdle and Cori diseases involve the other enzymes.

med-biochem-genetics.l03.q2.t: It lacks glucose-6-phosphatase, so glucose-6-phosphate cannot be converted to free glucose for export
med-biochem-genetics.l03.q2.p: Why is muscle unable to raise blood glucose during fasting?
med-biochem-genetics.l03.q2.h: Think about what the liver has that muscle does not.
med-biochem-genetics.l03.q2.e: Muscle has phosphorylase, debranching enzyme and hexokinase, but lacks glucose-6-phosphatase, the enzyme needed to release free glucose.

med-biochem-genetics.l03.q3.t: Glucagon raises cAMP, activating phosphorylase and inactivating glycogen synthase through phosphorylation
med-biochem-genetics.l03.q3.p: Which statement about the regulation of glycogen metabolism in the liver is correct?
med-biochem-genetics.l03.q3.e: Glucagon activates PKA and the phosphorylase cascade. Insulin favours dephosphorylation, which activates synthase.

med-biochem-genetics.l03.q4.t: Glucose-6-phosphate cannot be converted to free glucose, so both glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis end in the same blocked step
med-biochem-genetics.l03.q4.p: A 9-month-old has hepatomegaly, a fasting seizure, and a distended abdomen with a round face. Labs show glucose 30 mg/dL, elevated lactate, uric acid and triglycerides. Glucagon administered during fasting does not raise glucose. Which of the following best explains the failure of glucagon?
med-biochem-genetics.l03.q4.h: The elevated lactate and uric acid point to a block shared by two pathways.
med-biochem-genetics.l03.q4.e: Raised lactate and urate with fasting hypoglycaemia indicate glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency, a common final step. In type III lactate would be normal.

med-biochem-genetics.l03.q5.t: Muscle glycogen phosphorylase, so glycogen cannot supply glucose to glycolysis during exertion
med-biochem-genetics.l03.q5.p: A 14-year-old develops painful cramps, weakness and dark urine each time he sprints. During an ischaemic forearm exercise test, lactate does not rise, but ammonia does. Fasting glucose is normal. Which enzyme is most likely deficient?
med-biochem-genetics.l03.q5.h: Normal glucose and absent lactate rise point to the muscle itself.
med-biochem-genetics.l03.q5.e: Absent lactate response with myoglobinuria is the pattern of McArdle disease. Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency would cause fasting hypoglycaemia.

med-biochem-genetics.l04.q1.t: Production of NADPH for reductive biosynthesis and the protection of cells from oxidative damage
med-biochem-genetics.l04.q1.p: What is the principal role of the oxidative phase of the pentose phosphate pathway?
med-biochem-genetics.l04.q1.h: Which reduced cofactor is produced by G6PD?
med-biochem-genetics.l04.q1.e: The oxidative phase yields NADPH, used for glutathione reduction and biosynthesis. It does not produce net ATP.

med-biochem-genetics.l04.q2.t: X-linked recessive, with episodic haemolysis and Heinz bodies following oxidant stress
med-biochem-genetics.l04.q2.p: Which of the following is the inheritance pattern and key finding of G6PD deficiency?
med-biochem-genetics.l04.q2.h: Fava beans and certain antimalarials are classic triggers.
med-biochem-genetics.l04.q2.e: G6PD deficiency is X-linked recessive with oxidant-triggered haemolysis and Heinz bodies; the other options do not fit.

med-biochem-genetics.l04.q3.t: Aldolase B, so fructose-1-phosphate accumulates and depletes intracellular phosphate in the liver
med-biochem-genetics.l04.q3.p: Which enzyme is deficient in hereditary fructose intolerance?
med-biochem-genetics.l04.q3.h: Symptoms start when sucrose or fruit is introduced.
med-biochem-genetics.l04.q3.e: Aldolase B deficiency causes toxic fructose-1-phosphate accumulation. Fructokinase deficiency is benign.

med-biochem-genetics.l04.q4.t: Trapped phosphate in fructose-1-phosphate inhibits glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis in the liver
med-biochem-genetics.l04.q4.p: A 7-month-old begins vomiting and becomes lethargic and jaundiced after parents start fruit purees and a formula containing sucrose. Glucose is low and the liver is enlarged. Urine reducing substances are positive. Which mechanism most directly explains the hypoglycaemia?
med-biochem-genetics.l04.q4.h: The onset follows dietary exposure, not fasting alone.
med-biochem-genetics.l04.q4.e: Aldolase B deficiency leads to fructose-1-phosphate accumulation, depleting phosphate and impairing glucose release. Absent galactitol is unrelated.

med-biochem-genetics.l04.q5.t: Galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase deficiency, treated by eliminating galactose from the diet
med-biochem-genetics.l04.q5.p: A 10-day-old breastfed infant has jaundice, hepatomegaly, vomiting, and lens opacities. Sepsis from Escherichia coli is diagnosed. Which pair best describes the defect and the correct management?
med-biochem-genetics.l04.q5.h: Lactose is a disaccharide of glucose and galactose.
med-biochem-genetics.l04.q5.e: Jaundice, cataracts and E. coli sepsis after milk feeds are classic for GALT deficiency; management is a galactose-free diet. The fructose disorders occur after sucrose or fruit exposure.

med-biochem-genetics.l05.q1.t: Carnitine palmitoyltransferase I, the outer-membrane enzyme that is the rate-limiting step of oxidation
med-biochem-genetics.l05.q1.p: Which enzyme controls the entry of long-chain fatty acids into mitochondria and is inhibited by malonyl-CoA?
med-biochem-genetics.l05.q1.e: CPT-I is inhibited by malonyl-CoA so newly made fatty acids are not oxidised at once. Acetyl-CoA carboxylase makes malonyl-CoA but is not the carnitine shuttle.

med-biochem-genetics.l05.q2.t: The liver produces them but cannot use them because it lacks the thiophorase enzyme required for activation
med-biochem-genetics.l05.q2.p: Which statement about ketone bodies is correct?
med-biochem-genetics.l05.q2.h: Which tissue lacks succinyl-CoA:acetoacetate CoA transferase?
med-biochem-genetics.l05.q2.e: Hepatic ketogenesis supplies other tissues; the liver lacks the transferase. Red cells have no mitochondria and the brain can adapt to ketones.

med-biochem-genetics.l05.q3.t: Biotin for propionyl-CoA carboxylase and adenosylcobalamin for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase
med-biochem-genetics.l05.q3.p: Which cofactor pair is required to convert propionyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA?
med-biochem-genetics.l05.q3.h: A carboxylation step is followed by a rearrangement.
med-biochem-genetics.l05.q3.e: Carboxylation needs biotin; the mutase is a vitamin B12 enzyme. The other pairs belong to other reactions.

med-biochem-genetics.l05.q4.t: Failure of beta-oxidation of medium-chain fatty acids, so fat cannot supply energy or ketones while glucose is consumed
med-biochem-genetics.l05.q4.p: An 18-month-old is found lethargic after a diarrhoeal illness with poor intake. Glucose is 28 mg/dL; urine ketones are minimal and urine organic acid analysis shows dicarboxylic acids. Which of the following best explains the metabolic findings?
med-biochem-genetics.l05.q4.h: Fasting hypoglycaemia without ketones means that fat cannot be burned.
med-biochem-genetics.l05.q4.e: Hypoketotic hypoglycaemia with dicarboxylic aciduria indicates MCAD deficiency. Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency would produce abundant lactate and normal-to-high ketones.

med-biochem-genetics.l05.q5.t: Low insulin releases hormone-sensitive lipase, and the fatty acid flux to the liver exceeds the capacity of the TCA cycle, so acetyl-CoA enters ketogenesis
med-biochem-genetics.l05.q5.p: A woman with type 1 diabetes who missed insulin for two days presents with rapid deep breathing and abdominal pain. Which mechanism most directly drives her ketone body production?
med-biochem-genetics.l05.q5.e: Insulin deficiency permits lipolysis and a flood of acetyl-CoA beyond TCA capacity, because oxaloacetate is committed to gluconeogenesis. High insulin would suppress ketogenesis.

med-biochem-genetics.l06.q1.t: ApoC-II, acquired by chylomicrons and VLDL from HDL in the circulation
med-biochem-genetics.l06.q1.p: Which apolipoprotein activates lipoprotein lipase on capillary endothelium?
med-biochem-genetics.l06.q1.h: The letter C is for cofactor.
med-biochem-genetics.l06.q1.e: ApoC-II is the cofactor for lipoprotein lipase. ApoB-48 and ApoB-100 are structural; ApoA-I activates LCAT.

med-biochem-genetics.l06.q2.t: HMG-CoA reductase, which converts HMG-CoA to mevalonate in the endoplasmic reticulum
med-biochem-genetics.l06.q2.p: Which of the following is the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis and the target of statins?
med-biochem-genetics.l06.q2.h: Statins are named for the molecule they structurally resemble.
med-biochem-genetics.l06.q2.e: HMG-CoA reductase is the committed step and statin target; the mitochondrial synthase serves ketogenesis.

med-biochem-genetics.l06.q3.t: Fabry disease, caused by alpha-galactosidase A deficiency with ceramide trihexoside accumulation
med-biochem-genetics.l06.q3.p: Which lysosomal storage disease is X-linked recessive and presents with burning limb pain and angiokeratomas?
med-biochem-genetics.l06.q3.h: Only two commonly tested lysosomal diseases are X-linked.
med-biochem-genetics.l06.q3.e: Fabry disease is X-linked; Hunter syndrome is the other. The remaining options are autosomal recessive.

med-biochem-genetics.l06.q4.t: Hexosaminidase A, which degrades GM2 ganglioside in neuronal lysosomes
med-biochem-genetics.l06.q4.p: A 6-month-old has loss of developmental milestones, an exaggerated startle response and hypotonia. Fundoscopy shows a cherry-red spot at the macula. The liver and spleen are not enlarged. Which enzyme is most likely deficient?
med-biochem-genetics.l06.q4.h: The absence of organomegaly is the discriminating clue.
med-biochem-genetics.l06.q4.e: Cherry-red spot with no hepatosplenomegaly is Tay-Sachs disease. Niemann-Pick disease has the same macular finding but also an enlarged liver and spleen.

med-biochem-genetics.l06.q5.t: Defective LDL receptor function; statins upregulate remaining receptors by lowering intracellular cholesterol
med-biochem-genetics.l06.q5.p: A 25-year-old man has Achilles tendon xanthomas, corneal arcus and an LDL cholesterol more than three times normal. His father had a myocardial infarction at age 42. Which defect best explains his condition, and what is the effect of a statin?
med-biochem-genetics.l06.q5.h: Which receptor delivers LDL into cells?
med-biochem-genetics.l06.q5.e: Familial hypercholesterolaemia is usually an LDL receptor defect with xanthomas and early coronary disease; statins upregulate the receptor via SREBP. Lipase and MTP defects produce triglyceride-dominant disease.

med-biochem-genetics.l07.q1.t: Tyrosine, because it can no longer be made from phenylalanine through hydroxylation in the liver
med-biochem-genetics.l07.q1.p: Which amino acid becomes conditionally essential in phenylketonuria?
med-biochem-genetics.l07.q1.h: Phenylalanine hydroxylase makes the product of that name.
med-biochem-genetics.l07.q1.e: Phenylalanine hydroxylase converts phenylalanine to tyrosine, so tyrosine must then come from the diet. Tryptophan is an essential amino acid with no such origin.

med-biochem-genetics.l07.q2.t: Ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency, in which carbamoyl phosphate spills into pyrimidine synthesis
med-biochem-genetics.l07.q2.p: In which condition are urinary orotic acid levels elevated together with hyperammonaemia?
med-biochem-genetics.l07.q2.h: Which enzyme sits just downstream of carbamoyl phosphate?
med-biochem-genetics.l07.q2.e: OTC deficiency leaves carbamoyl phosphate in excess, which drives orotate production. UMP synthase deficiency raises orotic acid but ammonia is normal.

med-biochem-genetics.l07.q3.t: Alkaptonuria, a deficiency of homogentisate oxidase in the tyrosine degradation pathway
med-biochem-genetics.l07.q3.p: Which of the following conditions causes dark urine on standing and ochronotic pigmentation of cartilage?
med-biochem-genetics.l07.q3.h: Homogentisic acid oxidises to a dark pigment.
med-biochem-genetics.l07.q3.e: Alkaptonuria produces homogentisic acid that darkens in air and deposits in cartilage. The others do not produce dark urine.

med-biochem-genetics.l07.q4.t: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I deficiency, a mitochondrial urea cycle defect
med-biochem-genetics.l07.q4.p: A 5-day-old term infant, healthy at discharge, is brought in with poor feeding, vomiting and lethargy that progress to seizures. Ammonia is markedly elevated, glucose and pH are near normal, and urine orotic acid is undetectable. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
med-biochem-genetics.l07.q4.h: Use the orotic acid result to separate the two proximal urea cycle enzymes.
med-biochem-genetics.l07.q4.e: Hyperammonaemia with low orotic acid points to CPS-I deficiency. OTC deficiency would show high orotic acid.

med-biochem-genetics.l07.q5.t: Cystathionine beta-synthase, which condenses homocysteine with serine to form cystathionine
med-biochem-genetics.l07.q5.p: A tall 12-year-old with long limbs has downward-displaced lenses, a history of a deep venous thrombosis, and intellectual disability. A urine cyanide-nitroprusside test is positive and plasma homocysteine and methionine are elevated. Which enzyme is most likely deficient?
med-biochem-genetics.l07.q5.h: Lens direction and thrombosis help distinguish this from Marfan syndrome.
med-biochem-genetics.l07.q5.e: Homocystinuria features downward lens dislocation, thrombosis and intellectual disability, with high homocysteine. Marfan syndrome lens dislocation is upward and does not cause thrombosis.

med-biochem-genetics.l08.q1.t: Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase, a purine salvage enzyme that uses PRPP
med-biochem-genetics.l08.q1.p: Which enzyme is deficient in Lesch-Nyhan syndrome?
med-biochem-genetics.l08.q1.e: Lesch-Nyhan syndrome is an X-linked HGPRT defect. The other enzymes correspond to different disorders.

med-biochem-genetics.l08.q2.t: It inhibits xanthine oxidase, reducing the conversion of hypoxanthine and xanthine to uric acid
med-biochem-genetics.l08.q2.p: Which statement describes the mechanism of allopurinol in chronic gout?
med-biochem-genetics.l08.q2.h: It acts on the last steps of purine degradation.
med-biochem-genetics.l08.q2.e: Allopurinol blocks xanthine oxidase. Uricosurics act on the tubule, pegloticase makes allantoin, and colchicine targets microtubules.

med-biochem-genetics.l08.q3.t: Methotrexate, which blocks reduction of dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate in dividing cells
med-biochem-genetics.l08.q3.p: Which of the following drugs inhibits dihydrofolate reductase and so interferes with thymidine and purine synthesis?
med-biochem-genetics.l08.q3.h: Folate is recycled by this enzyme.
med-biochem-genetics.l08.q3.e: Methotrexate and trimethoprim inhibit DHFR. 5-FU, hydroxyurea and mycophenolate act on different enzymes.

med-biochem-genetics.l08.q4.t: Uridine, which bypasses the deficient UMP synthase activity and supplies pyrimidine nucleotides
med-biochem-genetics.l08.q4.p: A 3-year-old boy has poor growth, megaloblastic anaemia that does not respond to folate or vitamin B12, and crystals in the urine. Ammonia is normal. Which treatment targets the underlying defect?
med-biochem-genetics.l08.q4.h: The block lies in pyrimidine synthesis, with orotic acid excreted.
med-biochem-genetics.l08.q4.e: Orotic aciduria is UMP synthase deficiency, treated with uridine. Benzoate is for urea cycle defects and ADA is for SCID.

med-biochem-genetics.l08.q5.t: Failure of purine salvage leaves PRPP unused, which stimulates de novo purine synthesis
med-biochem-genetics.l08.q5.p: A 6-year-old boy has dystonia, intellectual disability and a habit of biting his lips and fingers. Serum uric acid is markedly elevated. What best explains the overproduction of uric acid?
med-biochem-genetics.l08.q5.h: Think about what PRPP does at the committed step.
med-biochem-genetics.l08.q5.e: Without HGPRT, PRPP accumulates and drives de novo synthesis, with more purines degraded to uric acid. Pyrimidines do not form uric acid.

med-biochem-genetics.l09.q1.t: GLUT4, whose translocation from intracellular vesicles to the membrane is stimulated by insulin
med-biochem-genetics.l09.q1.p: Which glucose transporter is recruited to the cell membrane in response to insulin in skeletal muscle and adipose tissue?
med-biochem-genetics.l09.q1.h: Exercise also recruits this transporter in muscle.
med-biochem-genetics.l09.q1.e: GLUT4 is the insulin-responsive transporter. GLUT1, 2 and 5 are not insulin-dependent in the same way.

med-biochem-genetics.l09.q2.t: Gluconeogenesis from lactate, glycerol and glucogenic amino acids in the liver
med-biochem-genetics.l09.q2.p: Which process is the main source of blood glucose after liver glycogen has been depleted during a prolonged fast?
med-biochem-genetics.l09.q2.h: Muscle cannot export glucose and fatty acids cannot make net glucose.
med-biochem-genetics.l09.q2.e: After about a day, hepatic gluconeogenesis predominates. Muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase and fatty acids cannot make net glucose.

med-biochem-genetics.l09.q3.t: Epinephrine and glucagon activate hormone-sensitive lipase through cAMP-dependent phosphorylation
med-biochem-genetics.l09.q3.p: Which hormone and enzyme pairing correctly describes the mobilisation of fat from adipose tissue in fasting?
med-biochem-genetics.l09.q3.h: This is a covalent modification triggered by a second messenger.
med-biochem-genetics.l09.q3.e: Catecholamines and glucagon raise cAMP and phosphorylate hormone-sensitive lipase. Insulin inhibits it.

med-biochem-genetics.l09.q4.t: Low insulin, high glucagon, elevated ketone bodies and free fatty acids, and glucose that is low-normal
med-biochem-genetics.l09.q4.p: A healthy volunteer fasts for 72 hours. Compared with the fed state, which pattern is expected?
med-biochem-genetics.l09.q4.h: Fasting suppresses insulin; the brain adapts to alternative fuel.
med-biochem-genetics.l09.q4.e: Fasting lowers insulin and raises glucagon, driving lipolysis and ketogenesis while gluconeogenesis keeps glucose just within range.

med-biochem-genetics.l09.q5.t: Small body muscle mass and limited glycogen stores provide less alanine for gluconeogenesis and less glycogen reserve
med-biochem-genetics.l09.q5.p: A previously well 6-year-old has a seizure after a gastroenteritis illness with 18 hours of fasting. Glucose is 30 mg/dL, ketones are strongly positive, and insulin is suppressed. Lactate and uric acid are normal. Which of the following most likely explains the reduced glucose in a child of this age?
med-biochem-genetics.l09.q5.h: Ketotic hypoglycaemia is a diagnosis of exclusion in young children.
med-biochem-genetics.l09.q5.e: Ketotic hypoglycaemia occurs in small children with limited gluconeogenic substrate and glycogen. Insulinoma would give suppressed ketones, and the ketones here are high.

med-biochem-genetics.l10.q1.t: Aldehyde dehydrogenase, a mitochondrial enzyme that uses NAD+ as the oxidising cofactor
med-biochem-genetics.l10.q1.p: Which enzyme converts acetaldehyde to acetate and is inhibited by disulfiram?
med-biochem-genetics.l10.q1.h: It is the second step in ethanol oxidation.
med-biochem-genetics.l10.q1.e: Disulfiram inhibits ALDH so acetaldehyde accumulates. ADH acts at the first step.

med-biochem-genetics.l10.q2.t: Pyruvate is converted to lactate, reducing its availability for gluconeogenesis
med-biochem-genetics.l10.q2.p: Which change in the liver results from the high NADH/NAD+ ratio produced by ethanol metabolism?
med-biochem-genetics.l10.q2.h: Excess NADH pushes reversible dehydrogenase reactions toward reduced products.
med-biochem-genetics.l10.q2.e: A high NADH level drives lactate dehydrogenase toward lactate and oxaloacetate toward malate, impairing gluconeogenesis.

med-biochem-genetics.l10.q3.t: Prominent ketone body production and an anion-gap acidosis, because insulin is severely lacking
med-biochem-genetics.l10.q3.p: Which finding best distinguishes diabetic ketoacidosis from hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state?
med-biochem-genetics.l10.q3.h: Residual insulin in type 2 diabetes suppresses lipolysis.
med-biochem-genetics.l10.q3.e: Severe insulin deficiency allows lipolysis and ketogenesis, so DKA features an anion-gap acidosis. In HHS, residual insulin suppresses ketone formation.

med-biochem-genetics.l10.q4.t: Excess NADH from ethanol oxidation diverts pyruvate and oxaloacetate away from gluconeogenesis in a patient with depleted glycogen
