med-biochem-genetics.l10.q4.p: A 45-year-old man with chronic alcohol use is found confused after three days of binge drinking and no food. Glucose is 38 mg/dL, lactate is elevated, and there is a high anion gap with positive ketones. Which is the best explanation for the hypoglycaemia?
med-biochem-genetics.l10.q4.h: Both glycogen and the ability to make new glucose matter here.
med-biochem-genetics.l10.q4.e: Ethanol metabolism raises NADH, impairing gluconeogenesis when glycogen is exhausted. Insulin would suppress ketones, which are positive here.

med-biochem-genetics.l10.q5.t: Hypokalaemia, since insulin drives potassium into cells and total body potassium is depleted
med-biochem-genetics.l10.q5.p: A 19-year-old with type 1 diabetes presents with nausea, deep rapid breathing, glucose 520 mg/dL, pH 7.1 and serum potassium 5.6 mEq/L. After insulin therapy begins, which complication is most important to anticipate?
med-biochem-genetics.l10.q5.h: A normal or high potassium may hide a total body deficit.
med-biochem-genetics.l10.q5.e: Insulin shifts potassium into cells; osmotic diuresis has depleted total body potassium despite the initial high serum level, so hypokalaemia can follow.

med-biochem-genetics.l11.q1.t: Niacin, the precursor of NAD+ and NADP+ that can also be made from tryptophan
med-biochem-genetics.l11.q1.p: Which vitamin deficiency causes pellagra, with the triad of dermatitis, diarrhoea and dementia?
med-biochem-genetics.l11.q1.h: Sun-exposed skin develops a Casal necklace.
med-biochem-genetics.l11.q1.e: Pellagra is niacin deficiency. Thiamine deficiency produces beriberi.

med-biochem-genetics.l11.q2.t: Elevated methylmalonic acid and neurologic signs such as dorsal column loss
med-biochem-genetics.l11.q2.p: Which finding distinguishes vitamin B12 deficiency from folate deficiency?
med-biochem-genetics.l11.q2.h: Only one of the two vitamins is needed by methylmalonyl-CoA mutase.
med-biochem-genetics.l11.q2.e: B12 is needed by the mutase, so methylmalonic acid rises and the nervous system is affected. Both deficiencies raise homocysteine.

med-biochem-genetics.l11.q3.t: Pyridoxine, because the drug depletes pyridoxal phosphate by forming a hydrazone
med-biochem-genetics.l11.q3.p: A patient receiving isoniazid for tuberculosis develops numbness and tingling in the feet. Which vitamin supplementation prevents this complication?
med-biochem-genetics.l11.q3.h: The same drug can also produce sideroblastic anaemia.
med-biochem-genetics.l11.q3.e: Isoniazid interferes with pyridoxine function, causing neuropathy that supplementation prevents.

med-biochem-genetics.l11.q4.t: Neurologic damage may progress because folate does not correct the methylmalonyl-CoA mutase deficiency of B12 lack
med-biochem-genetics.l11.q4.p: A 68-year-old woman has fatigue, a glossitis with a smooth red tongue, and paraesthesias in her feet with reduced vibration sense. MCV is 112 fL, and smear shows hypersegmented neutrophils. She is treated with folic acid, and her anaemia improves. Which statement best describes the expected outcome?
med-biochem-genetics.l11.q4.h: Why does the methyl-folate trap matter?
med-biochem-genetics.l11.q4.e: Folate can mask the anaemia of B12 deficiency, but it does not prevent the progressive demyelination caused by the mutase defect. Hence the cause must be identified.

med-biochem-genetics.l11.q5.t: Impaired hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues, which weakens collagen cross-linking
med-biochem-genetics.l11.q5.p: A 70-year-old man living alone has bleeding gums, perifollicular haemorrhages and corkscrew hairs. Prothrombin time, platelet count and bleeding time are normal. Which biochemical defect is most likely?
med-biochem-genetics.l11.q5.h: The coagulation tests are normal, so the problem is in the vessel wall.
med-biochem-genetics.l11.q5.e: Scurvy results from a lack of ascorbate for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases. Vitamin K deficiency would prolong prothrombin time.

med-biochem-genetics.l12.q1.t: Factors II, VII, IX and X, together with proteins C and S
med-biochem-genetics.l12.q1.p: Which clotting factors require vitamin K-dependent gamma-carboxylation?
med-biochem-genetics.l12.q1.h: Warfarin prolongs the prothrombin time by affecting these.
med-biochem-genetics.l12.q1.e: Vitamin K carboxylates factors II, VII, IX, X and proteins C and S. The other combinations are incorrect.

med-biochem-genetics.l12.q2.t: The kidney, by 1-alpha-hydroxylase stimulated by parathyroid hormone
med-biochem-genetics.l12.q2.p: In which organ is 25-hydroxyvitamin D converted to the active hormone calcitriol?
med-biochem-genetics.l12.q2.h: This step is lost in chronic kidney disease.
med-biochem-genetics.l12.q2.e: Renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase makes calcitriol and is stimulated by PTH. The liver makes the 25-hydroxy storage form.

med-biochem-genetics.l12.q3.t: Pitting oedema with a fatty liver, caused by low albumin and reduced lipoprotein export
med-biochem-genetics.l12.q3.p: Which finding is characteristic of kwashiorkor rather than marasmus?
med-biochem-genetics.l12.q3.h: Think about why the abdomen is swollen despite the starvation.
med-biochem-genetics.l12.q3.e: Kwashiorkor is protein deficiency with oedema and steatosis. Marasmus is generalised calorie deficiency with wasting.

med-biochem-genetics.l12.q4.t: Fat malabsorption causes combined deficiency of vitamins A and K, which are absorbed with dietary fat in micelles
med-biochem-genetics.l12.q4.p: A 6-year-old with cystic fibrosis and pancreatic insufficiency who has not taken enzyme supplements develops night blindness and, separately, easy bruising with a prolonged prothrombin time. Which mechanism links these findings?
med-biochem-genetics.l12.q4.h: Which vitamins depend on bile and pancreatic lipase for absorption?
med-biochem-genetics.l12.q4.e: Fat-soluble vitamins need micellar solubilisation, which fails in pancreatic insufficiency. Night blindness reflects A and the long prothrombin time reflects K.

med-biochem-genetics.l12.q5.t: Deficient gamma-carboxylation of factors II, VII, IX and X, because the neonatal gut is not yet colonised and milk contains little vitamin K
med-biochem-genetics.l12.q5.p: A 3-week-old exclusively breastfed infant who did not receive prophylaxis at birth presents with bruising and bleeding from the umbilical stump. Prothrombin time is prolonged, partial thromboplastin time is prolonged, and platelets and fibrinogen are normal. Which of the following is the best explanation?
med-biochem-genetics.l12.q5.h: Normal platelets and fibrinogen narrow the cause to the vitamin-dependent factors.
med-biochem-genetics.l12.q5.e: Newborn vitamin K deficiency bleeding results from poorly carboxylated factors, prolonging both PT and aPTT. Platelet function and fibrinogen are normal.

med-biochem-genetics.l13.q1.t: DNA polymerase I, which uses its 5' to 3' exonuclease activity before synthesising new DNA
med-biochem-genetics.l13.q1.p: Which enzyme removes RNA primers and fills the gap during replication in bacteria?
med-biochem-genetics.l13.q1.h: This enzyme also repairs DNA gaps.
med-biochem-genetics.l13.q1.e: Polymerase I removes primers and fills gaps; polymerase III does the bulk of the synthesis. Primase makes the primers.

med-biochem-genetics.l13.q2.t: It is a reverse transcriptase that uses an intrinsic RNA template to add repeats to chromosome ends
med-biochem-genetics.l13.q2.p: Which statement about telomerase is correct?
med-biochem-genetics.l13.q2.h: It is active in germ cells and most cancers.
med-biochem-genetics.l13.q2.e: Telomerase carries its own RNA template for reverse transcription of TTAGGG repeats. The other options describe different enzymes.

med-biochem-genetics.l13.q3.t: Nucleotide excision repair, which cuts out a short oligonucleotide containing the lesion
med-biochem-genetics.l13.q3.p: Which DNA repair pathway removes UV-induced pyrimidine dimers?
med-biochem-genetics.l13.q3.e: Bulky distorting lesions such as dimers are handled by nucleotide excision repair. Base excision acts on small base changes.

med-biochem-genetics.l13.q4.t: Repair of replication errors by the mismatch repair system, as in Lynch syndrome
med-biochem-genetics.l13.q4.p: A 38-year-old woman has colon cancer. Her father had colon cancer at 45 and her paternal aunt had endometrial cancer at 50. The tumour shows microsatellite instability, and she has no history of numerous polyps. Which process is most likely defective in this family?
med-biochem-genetics.l13.q4.h: Microsatellite instability reflects uncorrected replication slippage.
med-biochem-genetics.l13.q4.e: MSI with early colon and endometrial cancer and no polyposis is Lynch syndrome, a mismatch repair defect. FAP would present with hundreds of polyps.

med-biochem-genetics.l13.q5.t: Recognition of double-strand DNA breaks through the ATM checkpoint kinase
med-biochem-genetics.l13.q5.p: A young boy has unsteady gait, dilated blood vessels on the conjunctiva, and recurrent sinopulmonary infections. Serum alpha-fetoprotein is elevated and he shows sensitivity to ionising radiation. A defect in which process best explains this disorder?
med-biochem-genetics.l13.q5.h: Cerebellar ataxia plus telangiectasias plus immunodeficiency.
med-biochem-genetics.l13.q5.e: Ataxia-telangiectasia results from an ATM defect in the response to double-strand breaks, causing radiation sensitivity. Dimer repair defects produce xeroderma pigmentosum.

med-biochem-genetics.l14.q1.t: RNA polymerase II, which is inhibited by alpha-amanitin from the death cap mushroom
med-biochem-genetics.l14.q1.p: Which RNA polymerase transcribes mRNA in eukaryotes?
med-biochem-genetics.l14.q1.h: The death cap mushroom toxin targets this enzyme.
med-biochem-genetics.l14.q1.e: RNA polymerase II makes mRNA. Polymerase I and III make rRNA and tRNA.

med-biochem-genetics.l14.q2.t: Cleavage downstream of an AAUAAA signal followed by addition of adenines by poly-A polymerase
med-biochem-genetics.l14.q2.p: Which processing event adds a poly-A tail to eukaryotic mRNA?
med-biochem-genetics.l14.q2.h: The tail is added without a template.
med-biochem-genetics.l14.q2.e: The poly-A tail is added after cleavage at the AAUAAA signal, by poly-A polymerase. The cap is at the 5' end.

med-biochem-genetics.l14.q3.t: Anti-Smith antibody, directed against small nuclear ribonucleoproteins
med-biochem-genetics.l14.q3.p: Which autoantibody is highly specific for systemic lupus erythematosus and targets a component of the spliceosome?
med-biochem-genetics.l14.q3.e: Anti-Smith antibodies are specific for SLE. Anti-histone is typical of drug-induced lupus.

med-biochem-genetics.l14.q4.t: Synthesis of mRNA by RNA polymerase II, impairing protein production in hepatocytes
med-biochem-genetics.l14.q4.p: A 25-year-old woman has a family history of severe anaemia and a hepatocellular injury after eating wild mushrooms collected in a forest. Which molecular process is most directly inhibited by the toxin ingested?
med-biochem-genetics.l14.q4.h: Death cap mushroom ingestion causes delayed liver failure.
med-biochem-genetics.l14.q4.e: Alpha-amanitin inhibits RNA polymerase II, blocking mRNA synthesis, and the liver is especially affected. Anaemia in the family history is unrelated.

med-biochem-genetics.l14.q5.t: The abnormal mRNA encodes a nonfunctional beta-globin or is degraded, so little normal beta-globin is made
med-biochem-genetics.l14.q5.p: A patient with beta-thalassaemia is found to have a G-to-A substitution in an intron that creates a new splice acceptor site. The mutant gene produces an mRNA with an additional segment of intron inserted between exons. Which statement best explains the consequence?
med-biochem-genetics.l14.q5.e: A cryptic splice site retains intronic sequence, usually creating a frameshift and nonsense-mediated decay of the mRNA, so beta-globin is reduced. Ribosomes do not splice.

med-biochem-genetics.l15.q1.t: A nonsense mutation, which creates a premature termination codon in the mRNA
med-biochem-genetics.l15.q1.p: A mutation changes a codon so that it specifies a stop signal, producing a truncated protein. What is this mutation called?
med-biochem-genetics.l15.q1.h: Stop codons are UAA, UAG and UGA.
med-biochem-genetics.l15.q1.e: A premature stop codon defines a nonsense mutation. A missense mutation changes an amino acid; a frameshift involves insertion or deletion.

med-biochem-genetics.l15.q2.t: Aminoglycosides, which cause misreading of the mRNA and are ineffective against anaerobes
med-biochem-genetics.l15.q2.p: Which antibiotic class inhibits the 30S ribosomal subunit and requires oxygen-dependent uptake into bacteria?
med-biochem-genetics.l15.q2.e: Aminoglycosides bind the 30S subunit and need oxygen for uptake. The other drugs act on the 50S subunit.

med-biochem-genetics.l15.q3.t: Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase, which charges tRNA and checks that the correct amino acid is attached
med-biochem-genetics.l15.q3.p: Which enzyme is responsible for the accuracy of matching each amino acid to its tRNA?
med-biochem-genetics.l15.q3.h: The ribosome only checks the codon-anticodon match.
med-biochem-genetics.l15.q3.e: Synthetases are the step determining which amino acid goes onto which tRNA. A mischarged tRNA would be accepted by the ribosome.

med-biochem-genetics.l15.q4.t: A missense point mutation, since a different amino acid is substituted without altering the reading frame
med-biochem-genetics.l15.q4.p: A 10-year-old with sickle cell disease is found to have the substitution of valine for glutamate at position 6 of beta-globin, the result of a single base change. Which classification of this mutation is most accurate?
med-biochem-genetics.l15.q4.h: A single base change that substitutes one amino acid.
med-biochem-genetics.l15.q4.e: Sickle cell disease is caused by a missense mutation (GAG to GTG). Frameshifts arise from insertions or deletions, not substitutions.

med-biochem-genetics.l15.q5.t: ADP-ribosylation of elongation factor 2, which halts translocation of the ribosome on mRNA
med-biochem-genetics.l15.q5.p: A 6-year-old with a pharyngeal membrane and a swollen neck from diphtheria is treated. The exotoxin responsible acts on the human host by which mechanism?
med-biochem-genetics.l15.q5.h: Pseudomonas exotoxin A acts in the same way.
med-biochem-genetics.l15.q5.e: Diphtheria toxin ADP-ribosylates eEF-2 and halts translation. Cleavage of 28S rRNA is the action of Shiga toxin.

med-biochem-genetics.l16.q1.t: It binds the repressor and releases it from the operator, allowing transcription
med-biochem-genetics.l16.q1.p: In the lac operon, what does allolactose do?
med-biochem-genetics.l16.q1.e: Allolactose binds the repressor, which then leaves the operator. CAP is regulated by cAMP.

med-biochem-genetics.l16.q2.t: Methylation of cytosine in CpG dinucleotides, together with histone deacetylation
med-biochem-genetics.l16.q2.p: Which epigenetic change is most typically associated with silencing of a gene promoter?
med-biochem-genetics.l16.q2.h: Silenced genes sit in tightly packed chromatin.
med-biochem-genetics.l16.q2.e: DNA methylation and histone deacetylation compact chromatin and silence the gene. Acetylation opens chromatin.

med-biochem-genetics.l16.q3.t: A long non-coding RNA that coats one X chromosome and initiates its silencing in each female cell
med-biochem-genetics.l16.q3.p: What is the role of XIST in X chromosome inactivation?
med-biochem-genetics.l16.q3.e: XIST is a lncRNA expressed from the inactive X. It is not a protein enzyme.

med-biochem-genetics.l16.q4.t: Hypermethylation of CpG sites in the MLH1 promoter, which silences transcription
med-biochem-genetics.l16.q4.p: A colon tumour shows loss of MLH1 protein and microsatellite instability, yet sequencing of the MLH1 gene and germline testing find no mutation. Which mechanism most likely explains the loss of expression?
med-biochem-genetics.l16.q4.h: The sequence is normal but the protein is absent.
med-biochem-genetics.l16.q4.e: Promoter hypermethylation can silence MLH1 without any sequence change. Hypomethylation does not create stop codons.

med-biochem-genetics.l16.q5.t: A mutation in the operator that prevents the repressor from binding, causing constitutive expression
med-biochem-genetics.l16.q5.p: A bacterial strain is found to express the lac operon enzymes even in the absence of lactose, and expression is not increased further by lactose. Which mutation best explains this?
med-biochem-genetics.l16.q5.h: Constitutive expression means that the brake no longer works.
med-biochem-genetics.l16.q5.e: Operator mutation or repressor binding failure leads to constitutive expression. A repressor unable to bind inducer would give permanent repression.

med-biochem-genetics.l17.q1.t: Western blot, in which proteins are transferred to a membrane and detected by antibody
med-biochem-genetics.l17.q1.p: Which technique detects specific proteins in a sample using labelled antibodies after gel electrophoresis?
med-biochem-genetics.l17.q1.e: Western blotting detects proteins. Southern detects DNA and Northern detects RNA.

med-biochem-genetics.l17.q2.t: Annealing, performed at a lower temperature after the DNA strands have been separated
med-biochem-genetics.l17.q2.p: Which step of PCR allows the primers to bind to their complementary sequences?
med-biochem-genetics.l17.q2.h: The temperature is lowered after heating.
med-biochem-genetics.l17.q2.e: Primers anneal when the temperature is lowered. Denaturation separates strands and extension adds nucleotides.

med-biochem-genetics.l17.q3.t: Fluorescence in situ hybridisation using a fluorescent probe against the gene
med-biochem-genetics.l17.q3.p: Which method would best detect a gene amplification such as HER2 in a breast tumour cell?
med-biochem-genetics.l17.q3.h: A probe binds a specific sequence in cells.
med-biochem-genetics.l17.q3.e: FISH detects amplification or deletion of a locus in cells. A karyotype is too coarse and Sanger sequencing detects sequence changes.

med-biochem-genetics.l17.q4.t: Fluorescence in situ hybridisation or microarray for deletion of 22q11.2
med-biochem-genetics.l17.q4.p: A newborn has a cleft palate, a conotruncal heart defect and hypocalcaemia from absent parathyroid tissue. Karyotype shows 46,XY with no visible abnormality. Which test is the most appropriate next step to confirm the suspected diagnosis?
med-biochem-genetics.l17.q4.h: A microdeletion is smaller than a karyotype can resolve.
med-biochem-genetics.l17.q4.e: DiGeorge syndrome results from a 22q11.2 microdeletion detected by FISH or microarray. Karyotype cannot detect it.

med-biochem-genetics.l17.q5.t: A single nucleotide substitution within one gene, or a small intragenic insertion of a few bases
med-biochem-genetics.l17.q5.p: A laboratory reports that a child with developmental delay has a normal karyotype and a chromosomal microarray that finds no copy-number changes. Which type of genetic abnormality could still be present and would NOT be excluded by these two tests?
med-biochem-genetics.l17.q5.h: Neither test reads the base sequence.
med-biochem-genetics.l17.q5.e: Karyotype and microarray detect large structural or copy-number changes but cannot see point mutations or tiny indels, which need sequencing. The other abnormalities would be detected by at least one of the tests.

med-biochem-genetics.l18.q1.t: There is no male-to-male transmission, and affected males are born to carrier mothers
med-biochem-genetics.l18.q1.p: Which feature best distinguishes X-linked recessive inheritance from autosomal dominant inheritance in a pedigree?
med-biochem-genetics.l18.q1.h: Fathers pass their Y chromosome to their sons.
med-biochem-genetics.l18.q1.e: XLR traits are never transmitted from father to son. The vertical pattern of AD inheritance includes male-to-male transmission.

med-biochem-genetics.l18.q2.t: 2/3, because the unaffected outcome excludes only the homozygous-affected possibility
med-biochem-genetics.l18.q2.p: A healthy man has a sister with cystic fibrosis (autosomal recessive). His parents are both unaffected. What is the probability that he is a carrier?
med-biochem-genetics.l18.q2.h: He is known to be unaffected, so the affected quarter is removed.
med-biochem-genetics.l18.q2.e: Among unaffected children of two carriers, 2 of 3 are carriers. Without conditioning the carrier probability would be 1/2.

med-biochem-genetics.l18.q3.t: Penetrance, which is reduced when a mutation carrier remains entirely unaffected
med-biochem-genetics.l18.q3.p: Which term describes the proportion of individuals with a disease-causing genotype who express any phenotype at all?
med-biochem-genetics.l18.q3.h: Skipped generations in an AD pedigree suggest reduced penetrance.
med-biochem-genetics.l18.q3.e: Penetrance is all-or-none expression of the phenotype. Expressivity is the severity among those who express it.

med-biochem-genetics.l18.q4.t: 50 percent, since each son of a carrier mother inherits the mutant X with equal probability
med-biochem-genetics.l18.q4.p: A 4-year-old boy has difficulty climbing stairs, uses his hands to push up from the floor, and has enlarged calves. His mother is healthy and his maternal uncle died of a similar illness in adolescence. What is the risk that this boy's future brother will be affected, assuming the mother is a carrier?
med-biochem-genetics.l18.q4.h: Each son receives one of his mother's two X chromosomes.
med-biochem-genetics.l18.q4.e: A carrier mother has a 1/2 chance of passing the mutated X to each son. The father contributes the Y.

med-biochem-genetics.l18.q5.t: A de novo mutation, whose frequency increases with advancing paternal age
med-biochem-genetics.l18.q5.p: A newborn with short limbs and a large head has achondroplasia. Both parents have normal stature and there is no family history. What is the most likely explanation for the occurrence of an autosomal dominant disease in this family?
med-biochem-genetics.l18.q5.h: Most affected children are born to average-statured parents.
med-biochem-genetics.l18.q5.e: Most achondroplasia is due to a new FGFR3 mutation. The recurrence risk to siblings is low unless germline mosaicism exists.

med-biochem-genetics.l19.q1.t: Affected mothers transmit the trait to all offspring, and affected fathers transmit it to none
med-biochem-genetics.l19.q1.e: Mitochondrial DNA is inherited from the mother. Variable expression reflects heteroplasmy.

med-biochem-genetics.l19.q2.t: Loss of the maternally inherited 15q11-q13 region, affecting UBE3A expression in neurons
med-biochem-genetics.l19.q2.p: Which genetic finding is most associated with Angelman syndrome?
med-biochem-genetics.l19.q2.h: Happy puppet syndrome; the same region as Prader-Willi.
med-biochem-genetics.l19.q2.e: Angelman syndrome arises from loss of the maternal copy; loss of the paternal copy causes Prader-Willi.

med-biochem-genetics.l19.q3.t: Anticipation from expansion of the CAG repeat during transmission
med-biochem-genetics.l19.q3.p: Which phenomenon explains the earlier age of onset and greater severity of Huntington disease in successive generations?
med-biochem-genetics.l19.q3.h: The repeat tends to lengthen during gametogenesis.
med-biochem-genetics.l19.q3.e: Trinucleotide repeat disorders show anticipation as repeats expand. Heteroplasmy applies to mitochondrial DNA.

med-biochem-genetics.l19.q4.t: CGG repeat expansion in FMR1, with a premutation in the grandfather and a full mutation in the boy
med-biochem-genetics.l19.q4.p: A 3-year-old boy has intellectual disability, a long face with prominent ears, and autistic features. His maternal grandfather has a tremor and ataxia that began in his sixties. Which of the following best explains the family's findings?
med-biochem-genetics.l19.q4.h: Premutation carriers may present with tremor and ataxia later in life.
med-biochem-genetics.l19.q4.e: Fragile X: premutation carriers may have FXTAS, and expansion to a full mutation occurs through maternal transmission. Huntington disease would not explain the boy's phenotype.

med-biochem-genetics.l19.q5.t: Maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 15, giving two maternal copies and no paternal contribution
med-biochem-genetics.l19.q5.p: A 6-month-old girl has marked hypotonia and feeding difficulty. Methylation testing shows only the maternal pattern at 15q11-q13, and FISH shows no deletion. Both parents have normal chromosomes. Which mechanism is the most likely cause?
med-biochem-genetics.l19.q5.h: Only the maternal methylation pattern means that no paternal allele is expressed.
med-biochem-genetics.l19.q5.e: Prader-Willi syndrome with normal FISH and only a maternal methylation pattern points to maternal UPD. Paternal UPD would cause Angelman syndrome.

med-biochem-genetics.l20.q1.t: 2pq, since either allele can come from either parent in the two possible orders
med-biochem-genetics.l20.q1.p: In a population in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium with allele frequencies p and q, which expression gives the frequency of heterozygotes?
med-biochem-genetics.l20.q1.h: The binomial expansion has a middle term.
med-biochem-genetics.l20.q1.e: Heterozygotes occur at 2pq. p squared and q squared are the two homozygous classes.

med-biochem-genetics.l20.q2.t: 1 in 50, since q is 1/100 and carriers are approximately 2q
med-biochem-genetics.l20.q2.p: An autosomal recessive disease affects 1 in 10,000 people in a population in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium. Approximately what is the carrier frequency?
med-biochem-genetics.l20.q2.h: Take the square root of the incidence first.
med-biochem-genetics.l20.q2.e: q squared is 1/10,000, so q is 1/100 and 2pq is about 2/100, or 1 in 50. Carriers are far more common than affected people.

med-biochem-genetics.l20.q3.t: The incidence in males equals the allele frequency q, and the incidence in females is q squared
med-biochem-genetics.l20.q3.p: Which statement about an X-linked recessive disease in a population in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium is correct?
med-biochem-genetics.l20.q3.e: Hemizygous males express the disease whenever they carry the allele, so their incidence is q; females need two copies.

med-biochem-genetics.l20.q4.t: Heterozygote advantage, since carriers have relative protection from severe falciparum malaria
med-biochem-genetics.l20.q4.p: In a particular region where malaria is endemic, the frequency of the sickle cell allele remains high despite the severe disease in homozygotes. Which population genetic mechanism best explains the persistence of the allele?
med-biochem-genetics.l20.q4.h: Why would a carrier survive better than non-carriers?
med-biochem-genetics.l20.q4.e: Balanced polymorphism through heterozygote advantage maintains the allele. Inbreeding changes genotype but not allele frequencies.

med-biochem-genetics.l20.q5.t: About 1 in 300, calculated as 2/3 x 1/50 x 1/4
med-biochem-genetics.l20.q5.p: A woman's brother has an autosomal recessive disease with a population incidence of 1 in 10,000. She and her unaffected partner, who has no family history, plan a pregnancy. What is the approximate risk that their child will be affected?
med-biochem-genetics.l20.q5.h: Her carrier risk is 2/3, and his is about twice the square root of the incidence.
med-biochem-genetics.l20.q5.e: Her carrier risk is 2/3 and his is about 2q, or 1/50 (q is 1/100). Then 2/3 x 1/50 x 1/4 is about 1 in 300.

med-biochem-genetics.l21.q1.t: 45,X, with a single X chromosome in each cell and no second sex chromosome
med-biochem-genetics.l21.q1.p: What is the karyotype of Turner syndrome in the most common form?
med-biochem-genetics.l21.q1.e: Turner syndrome is 45,X. 47,XXY is Klinefelter syndrome.

med-biochem-genetics.l21.q2.t: Tall stature with small firm testes, gynaecomastia and elevated FSH and LH
med-biochem-genetics.l21.q2.p: Which finding is most characteristic of Klinefelter syndrome?
med-biochem-genetics.l21.q2.e: 47,XXY causes primary hypogonadism with high FSH and LH. The other options describe Turner, Williams and cri-du-chat syndromes.

med-biochem-genetics.l21.q3.t: Meiotic nondisjunction of chromosome 21, which increases in frequency with maternal age
med-biochem-genetics.l21.q3.p: Which mechanism accounts for the majority of cases of Down syndrome?
med-biochem-genetics.l21.q3.h: About 95 percent of cases arise this way.
med-biochem-genetics.l21.q3.e: Most cases result from meiotic nondisjunction. Translocations account for about 4 percent and mosaicism about 1 percent.

med-biochem-genetics.l21.q4.t: She carries a balanced Robertsonian translocation and has a higher recurrence risk than for ordinary nondisjunction
med-biochem-genetics.l21.q4.p: A 26-year-old woman has had two miscarriages and now has a child with Down syndrome. Her karyotype shows 45 chromosomes with a fusion of the long arms of chromosomes 14 and 21. Which statement about her situation is correct?
med-biochem-genetics.l21.q4.h: A balanced carrier has 45 chromosomes but a normal amount of genetic material.
med-biochem-genetics.l21.q4.e: A balanced Robertsonian carrier has 45 chromosomes with no net loss of essential genes, but may produce gametes with extra 21 material, with raised recurrence risk.

med-biochem-genetics.l21.q5.t: Coarctation of the aorta, associated with 45,X
med-biochem-genetics.l21.q5.p: A 16-year-old girl has short stature and primary amenorrhoea. Examination shows a webbed neck and widely spaced nipples. Blood pressure is higher in the arms than in the legs, and femoral pulses are weak. Which cardiac lesion best explains the blood pressure findings, and with which karyotype is it associated?
med-biochem-genetics.l21.q5.h: Arm-leg blood pressure difference with weak femoral pulses suggests narrowing of the aorta.
med-biochem-genetics.l21.q5.e: Turner syndrome is associated with coarctation and bicuspid aortic valve. AV septal defects accompany Down syndrome.

med-biochem-genetics.l22.q1.t: BCR-ABL, a fusion tyrosine kinase formed by the t(9;22) translocation
med-biochem-genetics.l22.q1.p: Which gene is the target of imatinib in chronic myeloid leukaemia?
med-biochem-genetics.l22.q1.e: Imatinib inhibits the BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase. The other fusions are associated with different malignancies.

med-biochem-genetics.l22.q2.t: Every cell already carries one mutated RB1 allele, so only one further somatic hit is needed
med-biochem-genetics.l22.q2.p: According to Knudson's two-hit hypothesis, why do hereditary retinoblastoma cases tend to be bilateral and earlier in onset than sporadic cases?
med-biochem-genetics.l22.q2.h: A first hit is present in every cell from conception.
med-biochem-genetics.l22.q2.e: Hereditary cases need only one additional somatic hit, so tumours arise earlier and more often in both eyes.

med-biochem-genetics.l22.q3.t: TP53, causing Li-Fraumeni syndrome through loss of cell cycle arrest and apoptosis
med-biochem-genetics.l22.q3.p: Which germline mutation causes a syndrome of sarcomas, early breast cancer, brain tumours and adrenocortical carcinoma?
med-biochem-genetics.l22.q3.e: Li-Fraumeni syndrome is due to TP53. The others cause different cancer syndromes.

med-biochem-genetics.l22.q4.t: The tumour cells cannot repair double-strand breaks by homologous recombination, so blocking base excision repair is lethal
med-biochem-genetics.l22.q4.p: A 34-year-old woman has breast cancer, her mother had ovarian cancer at 52, and her sister had breast cancer at 40. A pathogenic BRCA1 variant is found. Why might a PARP inhibitor be effective for her tumour?
med-biochem-genetics.l22.q4.e: BRCA-deficient cells rely on other repair pathways, and PARP inhibition removes single-strand break repair so lesions become lethal double-strand breaks.

med-biochem-genetics.l22.q5.t: Loss of function of a tumour suppressor gene (WT1) on chromosome 11p, with both alleles inactivated in tumour cells
med-biochem-genetics.l22.q5.p: A 5-year-old boy is found to have bilateral renal Wilms tumours, aniridia and developmental delay. Which statement best describes the genetic basis of his tumours?
med-biochem-genetics.l22.q5.h: The WAGR deletion includes aniridia and a tumour suppressor.
med-biochem-genetics.l22.q5.e: Wilms tumour with aniridia suggests deletion at 11p13 involving WT1, a tumour suppressor. N-MYC amplification occurs in neuroblastoma.

med-biochem-genetics.l23.q1.t: The Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act of 2008, which does not cover life or disability insurance
med-biochem-genetics.l23.q1.p: Which US law prohibits health insurers and employers from discriminating on the basis of genetic information?
med-biochem-genetics.l23.q1.e: GINA protects against genetic discrimination in health insurance and employment, but not in life, disability or long-term care insurance.

med-biochem-genetics.l23.q2.t: Variant of uncertain significance, which should not by itself direct medical management
med-biochem-genetics.l23.q2.p: Which category should be assigned to a sequence variant for which the evidence is insufficient or conflicting?
med-biochem-genetics.l23.q2.h: The ACMG/AMP scheme has five classes.
med-biochem-genetics.l23.q2.e: VUS is the correct class when evidence is inadequate. Reclassification may follow as evidence accumulates.

med-biochem-genetics.l23.q3.t: HLA-B*57:01, an immune gene whose presence predicts a hypersensitivity reaction
med-biochem-genetics.l23.q3.p: A genetic variant in which gene predicts hypersensitivity to abacavir?
med-biochem-genetics.l23.q3.h: This is an immune-mediated reaction, not a metabolic one.
med-biochem-genetics.l23.q3.e: HLA-B*57:01 testing is used before abacavir. The other genes affect drug metabolism.

med-biochem-genetics.l23.q4.t: Explore her reasons, discuss implications and insurance issues, and support her autonomous decision with follow-up
med-biochem-genetics.l23.q4.p: A healthy 28-year-old woman whose father died of Huntington disease requests predictive testing. She is not pregnant and is not planning a pregnancy. Which approach by the genetic counsellor is most appropriate?
med-biochem-genetics.l23.q4.h: There is no cure; consent and psychological readiness are central.
med-biochem-genetics.l23.q4.e: Predictive testing for adult-onset conditions without cure requires pre-test counselling and informed, autonomous decision making. Testing relatives without their consent violates their autonomy.

med-biochem-genetics.l23.q5.t: Offer diagnostic testing by amniocentesis or chorionic villus sampling, because at a low prior risk the positive predictive value of screening is limited
med-biochem-genetics.l23.q5.p: A first-trimester cell-free DNA screen is positive for trisomy 21 in a 24-year-old woman with a low prior risk. Which statement best describes the next step and why?
med-biochem-genetics.l23.q5.h: Screening estimates risk; diagnosis needs fetal or placental cells.
med-biochem-genetics.l23.q5.e: Even highly accurate screening tests have a modest positive predictive value in low prior risk women, so a positive result needs diagnostic confirmation.

med-clin-em.l01.q1.p: In the primary survey of an injured patient, which step follows airway with cervical spine protection?
med-clin-em.l01.q1.e: The order is airway, breathing, circulation, disability, exposure. Breathing follows airway.

med-clin-em.l01.q2.p: Which paralytic is contraindicated in a patient with a crush injury three days ago because of the risk of hyperkalemia?
med-clin-em.l01.q2.h: Depolarizing agent with upregulated receptors in injured muscle.
med-clin-em.l01.q2.e: Succinylcholine can cause lethal potassium release in crush injury, denervation and burns. Non-depolarizing agents such as rocuronium do not.

med-clin-em.l01.q3.t: Early endotracheal intubation before airway edema progresses
med-clin-em.l01.q3.p: A 30-year-old man pulled from a house fire is hoarse, with soot around the nose and mouth, and has facial burns. His oxygen saturation is normal. What is the best next step?
med-clin-em.l01.q3.h: The airway will worsen over hours.
med-clin-em.l01.q3.e: Signs of inhalation injury predict rapid airway edema, so early definitive airway is required even with normal saturation. Observation risks a lost airway.

med-clin-em.l01.q4.p: Intubation fails three times in a 35-year-old man with massive facial trauma, and bag-mask ventilation and a supraglottic device cannot maintain oxygenation. Which action is appropriate?
med-clin-em.l01.q4.e: Failed airway with inability to oxygenate requires a surgical airway through the cricothyroid membrane. Repeated attempts delay rescue.

med-clin-em.l01.q5.p: Which method provides the most reliable confirmation of endotracheal tube placement?
med-clin-em.l01.q5.h: It detects exhaled carbon dioxide continuously.
med-clin-em.l01.q5.e: Waveform capnography is the most reliable confirmation. Auscultation and chest rise are fallible, especially in obese or noisy settings.

med-clin-em.l02.q1.p: Which shock type is characterized by low preload, high systemic vascular resistance and flat neck veins?
med-clin-em.l02.q1.e: Hypovolemic shock reduces preload with compensatory vasoconstriction. Cardiogenic and obstructive shock show distended neck veins.

med-clin-em.l02.q2.t: Hypotension, muffled heart sounds and distended neck veins
med-clin-em.l02.q2.e: Beck triad is hypotension, muffled heart sounds and jugular venous distension. Tracheal deviation describes tension pneumothorax.

med-clin-em.l02.q3.p: A 24-year-old man falls from a height and has hypotension, a heart rate of 52, warm dry skin and flaccid paralysis of the legs. Which shock type is most likely?
med-clin-em.l02.q3.h: Loss of sympathetic tone with unopposed vagal tone.
med-clin-em.l02.q3.e: Spinal cord injury causes neurogenic shock with bradycardia and warm skin. Hemorrhagic shock produces tachycardia and cool clammy skin.

med-clin-em.l02.q4.p: A 62-year-old man has hypotension, cool extremities, distended neck veins, crackles throughout both lungs and ST elevation in the anterior leads. What is the best treatment strategy?
med-clin-em.l02.q4.e: This is cardiogenic shock from myocardial infarction, where revascularization improves survival (SHOCK trial). Large fluid loads worsen pulmonary edema.

med-clin-em.l02.q5.t: Class III, with early blood product transfusion and hemorrhage control
med-clin-em.l02.q5.p: A trauma patient has a heart rate of 128, systolic pressure of 85, confusion and cool skin after an estimated loss of 35 percent of blood volume. Which class of hemorrhage is this and what resuscitation is preferred?
med-clin-em.l02.q5.h: Thirty to forty percent loss with hypotension.
med-clin-em.l02.q5.e: Class III hemorrhage causes hypotension and confusion, and blood products with source control are preferred over large crystalloid volumes. Vasopressors do not replace lost volume.

med-clin-em.l03.q1.p: Which rhythm is shockable in cardiac arrest?
med-clin-em.l03.q1.h: Defibrillation needs a chaotic or rapid ventricular rhythm.
med-clin-em.l03.q1.e: Ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia are shockable. Asystole and PEA are not.

med-clin-em.l03.q2.t: Compression rate of 100 to 120 per minute with full chest recoil
med-clin-em.l03.q2.p: Which is a recommended feature of high-quality adult CPR?
med-clin-em.l03.q2.e: Rate of 100 to 120, depth of about 5 to 6 cm and full recoil are recommended. Interruptions lower coronary perfusion.

med-clin-em.l03.q3.p: A 55-year-old man in pulseless electrical activity arrest has a monitor showing narrow complexes, flat neck veins and a history of a massive gastrointestinal bleed. Which reversible cause is most likely?
med-clin-em.l03.q3.h: Think about volume and the bleeding history.
med-clin-em.l03.q3.e: Hemorrhage with flat neck veins suggests hypovolemia, treated with blood and source control. Tamponade and tension pneumothorax would produce distended veins.

med-clin-em.l03.q4.p: A 70-year-old woman with chronic kidney disease is in cardiac arrest with a wide complex rhythm, and an earlier potassium was 7.4 mEq/L. Which intervention best stabilizes the myocardium?
med-clin-em.l03.q4.h: Antagonize the effect of potassium on the membrane.
med-clin-em.l03.q4.e: Calcium stabilizes the cardiac membrane in hyperkalemia. Lidocaine and atropine do not address the cause.

med-clin-em.l03.q5.t: Pediatric arrest is usually asphyxial rather than primary arrhythmic
med-clin-em.l03.q5.p: A 4-year-old drowned and is found pulseless and apneic. Why is early rescue breathing emphasized in this case?
med-clin-em.l03.q5.h: The cause of arrest differs in children.
med-clin-em.l03.q5.e: Most pediatric arrests are caused by respiratory failure and hypoxia, so ventilation is critical. Compressions and AEDs are still used.

med-clin-em.l04.q1.t: Life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection
med-clin-em.l04.q1.p: According to Sepsis-3, how is sepsis defined?
med-clin-em.l04.q1.h: The definition focuses on organ dysfunction.
med-clin-em.l04.q1.e: Sepsis-3 defines sepsis by infection-related organ dysfunction. SIRS criteria were the older definition, and unresponsive hypotension describes septic shock.

med-clin-em.l04.q2.p: Which vasopressor is first-line in septic shock?
med-clin-em.l04.q2.h: Target a mean arterial pressure of 65.
med-clin-em.l04.q2.e: Norepinephrine is the first-line agent in septic shock. Dopamine causes more arrhythmias, and dobutamine is an inotrope.

med-clin-em.l04.q3.t: Broad-spectrum antibiotics after cultures, source control and norepinephrine
med-clin-em.l04.q3.p: A 68-year-old woman with a urinary catheter has fever, confusion, a blood pressure of 82/48 after two liters of crystalloid, and a lactate of 4.5 mmol/L. Which set of actions is most appropriate?
med-clin-em.l04.q3.h: Septic shock requires prompt antimicrobials and source control.
med-clin-em.l04.q3.e: Persisting hypotension and high lactate define septic shock, needing antibiotics, source control and vasopressor support. Delaying antibiotics for cultures worsens survival.

med-clin-em.l04.q4.p: A patient with septic shock remains hypotensive despite escalating norepinephrine and vasopressin. Which additional therapy is suggested?
med-clin-em.l04.q4.h: Refractory shock may have relative adrenal insufficiency.
med-clin-em.l04.q4.e: Hydrocortisone is suggested for septic shock requiring ongoing vasopressors. Bicarbonate is not routinely recommended for lactic acidosis.

med-clin-em.l04.q5.t: Balanced crystalloid such as lactated Ringer's solution
med-clin-em.l04.q5.p: Which fluid type is generally preferred for initial sepsis resuscitation?
med-clin-em.l04.q5.e: The 2021 guideline suggests balanced crystalloids over saline, and recommends against starches because of kidney injury.

med-clin-em.l05.q1.p: Within what time after arrival should an ECG be obtained for acute chest pain?
med-clin-em.l05.q1.e: The ACC/AHA guideline recommends an ECG within 10 minutes of arrival.

med-clin-em.l05.q2.p: Which medication should be avoided in a patient with inferior STEMI and right ventricular infarction?
med-clin-em.l05.q2.h: The right ventricle is preload dependent.
med-clin-em.l05.q2.e: Nitrates reduce preload and can cause profound hypotension in right ventricular infarction. Aspirin and anticoagulants are still indicated.

med-clin-em.l05.q3.t: Intravenous beta-blocker with rapid blood pressure and heart rate control, plus surgical consultation
med-clin-em.l05.q3.p: A 45-year-old man with Marfan syndrome has sudden tearing chest pain radiating to the back, a blood pressure of 170/100 in the right arm and 130/80 in the left, and a new diastolic murmur. What is the best initial management?
med-clin-em.l05.q3.h: Reduce shear stress, avoid anticoagulation until excluded.
med-clin-em.l05.q3.e: This is likely type A aortic dissection, which requires heart rate and pressure control and emergent surgery. Thrombolytics and heparin could be catastrophic.

med-clin-em.l05.q4.p: A 66-year-old man has dyspnea, a heart rate of 170 with a narrow regular rhythm, and blood pressure of 78/40 with altered mentation. What is the best treatment?
med-clin-em.l05.q4.h: This is an unstable tachycardia with a pulse.
med-clin-em.l05.q4.e: Unstable tachycardia with a pulse needs synchronized cardioversion. Adenosine may be attempted in stable regular narrow tachycardia but should not delay shock.

med-clin-em.l05.q5.p: A man five days after an anterior myocardial infarction develops sudden hypotension, a new harsh holosystolic murmur at the left sternal border and a step-up in oxygen saturation from right atrium to right ventricle. What is the diagnosis?
med-clin-em.l05.q5.e: Septal rupture causes a new holosystolic murmur and oxygen step-up in the right ventricle. Papillary rupture causes acute mitral regurgitation without a step-up.

med-clin-em.l06.q1.p: What is the first-line immediate treatment of anaphylaxis?
med-clin-em.l06.q1.e: Epinephrine is the first-line treatment and reverses airway edema and shock. Antihistamines and steroids are adjuncts.

med-clin-em.l06.q2.p: A patient with a COPD exacerbation has pH 7.28 and PaCO2 of 70 mmHg. Which intervention reduces intubation and mortality?
med-clin-em.l06.q2.e: Noninvasive ventilation improves outcomes in hypercapnic COPD exacerbation. Excess oxygen and sedatives can worsen hypercapnia.

med-clin-em.l06.q3.t: Immediate needle decompression followed by chest tube
med-clin-em.l06.q3.p: A 22-year-old tall thin man develops sudden left chest pain, and then hypotension, distended neck veins, absent left breath sounds and tracheal deviation to the right. What is the best next step?
med-clin-em.l06.q3.h: This is a clinical diagnosis with obstructive shock.
med-clin-em.l06.q3.e: Tension pneumothorax needs immediate decompression without imaging. Delay for radiography risks cardiac arrest.

med-clin-em.l06.q4.t: Systemic thrombolysis or reperfusion therapy with anticoagulation
med-clin-em.l06.q4.p: A hospitalized patient who is recovering from a hip fracture surgery develops sudden dyspnea, tachycardia and pleuritic pain. His blood pressure is 82/50 and oxygen saturation is 86 percent. Which treatment is indicated?
med-clin-em.l06.q4.e: Hypotension with probable pulmonary embolism defines high-risk disease, which warrants reperfusion with anticoagulation. Diuretics would reduce preload.

med-clin-em.l06.q5.p: A 16-year-old with severe asthma has wheezing that suddenly decreases, with lethargy and a PaCO2 of 48 mmHg, which is normal to high for her. What does this indicate?
med-clin-em.l06.q5.h: A hyperventilating asthmatic should have low carbon dioxide.
med-clin-em.l06.q5.e: A normal or rising PaCO2 with fading wheeze and lethargy indicates tiring and impending respiratory failure, which may need intubation.

med-clin-em.l07.q1.p: Which toxidrome includes miosis, salivation, lacrimation, bronchorrhea and bradycardia?
med-clin-em.l07.q1.e: Excess acetylcholine produces miosis, secretions, bronchospasm and bradycardia. Anticholinergic toxicity gives dry skin and mydriasis.

med-clin-em.l07.q2.p: Which substance is poorly adsorbed by activated charcoal?
med-clin-em.l07.q2.h: Think about small ions and alcohols.
med-clin-em.l07.q2.e: Charcoal does not bind lithium, iron, alcohols or caustics well. Aspirin and theophylline are adsorbed.

med-clin-em.l07.q3.p: A 22-year-old is agitated with temperature 39.5 C, dry flushed skin, dilated pupils, a heart rate of 140, urinary retention and decreased bowel sounds. Which agent most likely caused this?
med-clin-em.l07.q3.h: Dry skin differentiates it from sympathomimetics.
med-clin-em.l07.q3.e: Dry flushed skin, urinary retention and decreased bowel sounds suggest anticholinergic toxicity. Cocaine causes diaphoresis, and heroin causes miosis.

med-clin-em.l07.q4.t: Atropine, with pralidoxime for nicotinic effects
med-clin-em.l07.q4.p: A farmer has miosis, drooling, wheezing, diarrhea, bradycardia and muscle fasciculations after spraying a field. Which therapy treats the muscarinic effects?
med-clin-em.l07.q4.e: Atropine blocks muscarinic effects and pralidoxime reactivates cholinesterase, helping nicotinic effects. Physostigmine and neostigmine would add more cholinergic activity.

med-clin-em.l07.q5.p: A patient with unknown ingestion has blurred vision, an anion gap metabolic acidosis and an osmolar gap. Which substance is most likely?
med-clin-em.l07.q5.h: Osmotically active alcohols create a gap.
med-clin-em.l07.q5.e: An osmolar gap with anion gap acidosis points to toxic alcohols such as methanol or ethylene glycol. Salicylates and isoniazid cause acidosis without a gap in osmolality.

med-clin-em.l08.q1.p: Which antidote replenishes glutathione in acetaminophen overdose?
med-clin-em.l08.q1.e: Acetylcysteine restores glutathione and binds NAPQI. Fomepizole treats toxic alcohols.

med-clin-em.l08.q2.p: Which agent is the antidote for dabigatran?
med-clin-em.l08.q2.e: Idarucizumab binds dabigatran. Protamine reverses heparin. Andexanet alfa targeted factor Xa inhibitors but was withdrawn from the U.S. market in December 2025.

med-clin-em.l08.q3.t: Plot a serum level on the nomogram and give acetylcysteine if above the treatment line
med-clin-em.l08.q3.p: A 19-year-old took many acetaminophen tablets six hours ago and has no symptoms. What is the best approach?
med-clin-em.l08.q3.h: Treat based on the level, not symptoms.
med-clin-em.l08.q3.e: Symptoms and enzymes lag, so the nomogram guides treatment after four hours. Waiting for liver injury risks failure.

med-clin-em.l08.q4.t: Digoxin-specific antibody fragments with correction of electrolytes
med-clin-em.l08.q4.p: A 70-year-old on digoxin and furosemide has nausea, yellow-tinged vision, a potassium of 2.9 mEq/L and bidirectional ventricular tachycardia. Which is the best treatment?
med-clin-em.l08.q4.e: Digoxin Fab fragments are the antidote for life-threatening toxicity, with electrolyte repair. Dialysis does not remove digoxin effectively.

med-clin-em.l08.q5.p: A teenager overdosed on a beta-blocker and has bradycardia of 38 and hypotension unresponsive to fluids and atropine. Which antidotal therapy is first-line?
med-clin-em.l08.q5.h: It bypasses the beta receptor to raise cyclic AMP.
med-clin-em.l08.q5.e: Glucagon acts through its own receptor to increase cAMP and heart rate. The other antidotes act on opioid, benzodiazepine and cholinesterase targets.

med-clin-em.l09.q1.p: Which antidote is used for methanol or ethylene glycol poisoning?
med-clin-em.l09.q1.e: Fomepizole inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase, preventing formation of toxic metabolites. The others treat methemoglobinemia, cyanide and iron.

med-clin-em.l09.q2.t: It reads carboxyhemoglobin as if it were oxyhemoglobin
med-clin-em.l09.q2.p: Why is pulse oximetry unreliable in carbon monoxide poisoning?
med-clin-em.l09.q2.e: Carboxyhemoglobin absorbs light similarly to oxyhemoglobin, so saturation appears normal. Co-oximetry is needed.

med-clin-em.l09.q3.t: Intravenous sodium bicarbonate with consideration of hemodialysis
med-clin-em.l09.q3.p: A 35-year-old with tinnitus, vomiting, rapid breathing and a pH of 7.45 with low bicarbonate and a low PaCO2 has a high anion gap. Which treatment is most appropriate?
med-clin-em.l09.q3.e: Salicylate toxicity needs alkalinization and dialysis if severe. Intubating with low ventilation removes the respiratory compensation and can be fatal.

med-clin-em.l09.q4.p: A man rescued from a house fire has coma, severe lactic acidosis, hypotension and a very high central venous oxygen saturation. Which treatment is most appropriate for the toxin that inhibits cytochrome c oxidase?
med-clin-em.l09.q4.e: This is cyanide toxicity from smoke, treated with hydroxocobalamin. Nitrites generate methemoglobin and are hazardous with carbon monoxide.

med-clin-em.l09.q5.p: A teenager overdoses on amitriptyline and develops seizures, a QRS of 140 ms and hypotension. Which pair of drugs is appropriate?
med-clin-em.l09.q5.h: Treat sodium channel blockade and seizures.
med-clin-em.l09.q5.e: Bicarbonate counters sodium channel blockade and benzodiazepines treat seizures. Physostigmine, flumazenil and class IA agents can worsen toxicity.

med-clin-em.l10.q1.t: Core temperature above about 40 C with central nervous system dysfunction
med-clin-em.l10.q1.p: Which feature distinguishes heat stroke from heat exhaustion?
med-clin-em.l10.q1.e: Heat stroke requires severe hyperthermia plus CNS dysfunction. Heat exhaustion has intact mental status.

med-clin-em.l10.q2.p: What is the best cooling method for exertional heat stroke?
med-clin-em.l10.q2.h: The set point is normal, so antipyretics fail.
med-clin-em.l10.q2.e: Cold water immersion cools fastest and improves survival. Antipyretics do not work because the hypothalamus is not the cause.

med-clin-em.l10.q3.t: Continue CPR and rewarm, with extracorporeal rewarming if available
med-clin-em.l10.q3.p: A 70-year-old man found outdoors in winter has a core temperature of 27 C, bradycardia, and a J wave on the ECG, and he is pulseless with ventricular fibrillation. What is the preferred approach?
med-clin-em.l10.q3.h: Nobody is dead until warm and dead.
med-clin-em.l10.q3.e: Severe hypothermic arrest warrants continued resuscitation with rewarming, ideally extracorporeal. Drug and shock efficacy are reduced at low temperatures.

med-clin-em.l10.q4.t: Start with rescue breaths and ventilation, then compressions
med-clin-em.l10.q4.p: A 5-year-old is pulled from a pool, pulseless and apneic. Which resuscitation approach is most appropriate?
med-clin-em.l10.q4.e: Drowning arrest is hypoxic, so ventilation is prioritized. Abdominal thrusts to remove water are not recommended.

med-clin-em.l10.q5.t: Dark urine positive for blood with no red cells and a high creatine kinase
med-clin-em.l10.q5.p: A runner with a temperature of 41 C is confused. Which test finding would suggest rhabdomyolysis as a complication?
med-clin-em.l10.q5.e: Myoglobinuria gives a heme-positive dipstick without red cells, and a very high creatine kinase. The other patterns indicate other disorders.

med-clin-em.l11.q1.p: Which treatment is first-line for the prevention of acute mountain sickness during ascent?
med-clin-em.l11.q1.h: It induces a bicarbonate diuresis and speeds acclimatization.
med-clin-em.l11.q1.e: Acetazolamide with graded ascent prevents acute mountain sickness. Nifedipine is for pulmonary edema.

med-clin-em.l11.q2.t: Keeping the limb at heart level, immobilizing and rapid transport
med-clin-em.l11.q2.p: Which is the recommended first aid after a rattlesnake bite?
med-clin-em.l11.q2.e: Calm, immobilization at heart level and transport are advised. Tourniquets, incision and ice worsen tissue injury.

med-clin-em.l11.q3.t: Immediate descent with oxygen and nifedipine
med-clin-em.l11.q3.p: A hiker at 3,800 m has dyspnea at rest, a wet cough with pink sputum and crackles. What is the best treatment?
med-clin-em.l11.q3.e: High-altitude pulmonary edema is treated with descent, oxygen and nifedipine. Dexamethasone treats cerebral edema.

med-clin-em.l11.q4.t: Aggressive intravenous fluids with monitoring for rhabdomyolysis and compartment syndrome
med-clin-em.l11.q4.p: A worker has a high-voltage electrical contact burn on the hand, dark urine and a markedly raised creatine kinase. Which intervention is a priority?
med-clin-em.l11.q4.e: High-voltage injury causes deep muscle destruction, so fluids protect the kidneys. Skin findings underestimate the injury.

med-clin-em.l11.q5.t: Rabies immune globulin and a vaccine series
med-clin-em.l11.q5.p: A child is bitten by a bat that is not available for testing, and the wound is washed. What is the most appropriate additional management?
med-clin-em.l11.q5.h: Rabies is almost always fatal after symptoms appear.
med-clin-em.l11.q5.e: Bat exposures with unavailable animals warrant postexposure prophylaxis with immune globulin and vaccine. Observation applies to healthy dogs and cats.

med-clin-em.l12.q1.p: What is the first-line drug class for status epilepticus?
med-clin-em.l12.q1.e: A benzodiazepine is first-line in status epilepticus. The others are second-line or later.

med-clin-em.l12.q2.p: Which intervention stabilizes the myocardial membrane in hyperkalemia with ECG changes?
med-clin-em.l12.q2.e: Calcium protects the heart within minutes. Insulin shifts potassium, and binders and diuretics remove it.

med-clin-em.l12.q3.t: Replace potassium and fluids before starting insulin
med-clin-em.l12.q3.p: A patient in diabetic ketoacidosis has a glucose of 520 mg/dL, pH 7.1 and a serum potassium of 2.8 mEq/L. What is the best next step?
med-clin-em.l12.q3.e: Insulin would lower potassium further and risk arrhythmia. Total body potassium is depleted in DKA.

med-clin-em.l12.q4.t: Intravenous thrombolytic and evaluation for thrombectomy
med-clin-em.l12.q4.p: A 65-year-old has sudden right arm weakness and aphasia 90 minutes ago. CT shows no hemorrhage, blood pressure is 170/95 and glucose is normal. What is the best treatment?
med-clin-em.l12.q4.e: He meets criteria for thrombolysis within 4.5 hours with an imaging workup for large vessel occlusion. Aggressive pressure lowering can worsen ischemia.

med-clin-em.l12.q5.t: Lumbar puncture for xanthochromia or CT angiography
med-clin-em.l12.q5.p: A woman had a thunderclap headache 12 hours ago, and a non-contrast head CT obtained just now is normal. Suspicion for subarachnoid hemorrhage remains. What is the most appropriate next step?
med-clin-em.l12.q5.h: Sensitivity of CT falls with time.
med-clin-em.l12.q5.e: A negative CT within six hours of onset is very sensitive, but sensitivity falls afterward, so at 12 hours lumbar puncture or CT angiography should be pursued. Missing subarachnoid hemorrhage carries a high risk of rebleeding.

med-clin-em.l13.q1.p: Which injury is treated in the primary survey with an occlusive dressing taped on three sides?
med-clin-em.l13.q1.e: A three-sided dressing acts as a flutter valve for an open pneumothorax, and a chest tube is placed at a separate site.

med-clin-em.l13.q2.t: At the aortic isthmus distal to the left subclavian artery
med-clin-em.l13.q2.p: Where does traumatic aortic rupture most commonly occur?
med-clin-em.l13.q2.h: Deceleration injury at a fixed point.
med-clin-em.l13.q2.e: The ligamentum arteriosum fixes the isthmus, so deceleration tears the aorta there. A widened mediastinum prompts CT angiography.

med-clin-em.l13.q3.t: Left chest tube with blood transfusion and surgical evaluation
med-clin-em.l13.q3.p: A 28-year-old man stabbed in the left chest has hypotension, absent breath sounds on the left, dullness to percussion and flat neck veins. What is the best next step?
med-clin-em.l13.q3.h: Dullness and flat veins mean blood, not air.
med-clin-em.l13.q3.e: This is massive hemothorax, treated with chest tube and transfusion. Needle decompression is for tension pneumothorax with distended veins.

med-clin-em.l13.q4.t: Balanced transfusion of red cells, plasma and platelets with warming and early hemorrhage control
med-clin-em.l13.q4.p: A trauma patient receiving large volumes of crystalloid is cold, acidotic and oozing from all wounds. Which approach best prevents progression of this problem?
med-clin-em.l13.q4.e: Damage control resuscitation uses balanced products and warming. Crystalloid dilutes clotting factors and worsens the triad.

med-clin-em.l13.q5.p: A patient with multiple rib fractures has paradoxical chest wall movement and an oxygen saturation of 84 percent. What is the main cause of the hypoxemia?
med-clin-em.l13.q5.h: The lung under the segment is injured.
med-clin-em.l13.q5.e: Hypoxemia in flail chest results chiefly from the pulmonary contusion beneath the segment. The paradoxical movement itself contributes less.

med-clin-em.l14.q1.t: A biconvex lens-shaped collection that does not cross suture lines
med-clin-em.l14.q1.p: Which finding on CT or imaging is classic for an epidural hematoma?
med-clin-em.l14.q1.e: Epidural hematomas are biconvex and limited by sutures. Crescent-shaped collections crossing sutures are subdural.

med-clin-em.l14.q2.p: A male trauma patient has blood at the urethral meatus and a high-riding prostate. What should be done before placing a urinary catheter?
med-clin-em.l14.q2.e: Signs of urethral injury require a retrograde urethrogram first. Blind catheterization can convert a partial tear to a complete one.

med-clin-em.l14.q3.p: A 70-year-old man falls and has weakness of the hands greater than the legs and a burning sensation in the arms, with preserved bowel function. Which syndrome is most likely?
med-clin-em.l14.q3.e: Central cord syndrome causes greater arm than leg weakness after cervical hyperextension. Anterior cord syndrome spares only dorsal column functions.

med-clin-em.l14.q4.t: Nonoperative management with observation, with angioembolization if needed
med-clin-em.l14.q4.p: A hemodynamically stable 25-year-old has splenic laceration on CT after a motor vehicle collision with no active extravasation. What is the usual management?
med-clin-em.l14.q4.e: Stable splenic injuries are often managed nonoperatively. Instability or peritonitis requires laparotomy.

med-clin-em.l14.q5.p: A teenager hit in the temple lost consciousness briefly, woke lucid, then became drowsy with a dilated ipsilateral pupil. CT shows a lens-shaped collection. What is the best management?
med-clin-em.l14.q5.e: Epidural hematoma with herniation signs requires urgent evacuation. Lumbar puncture is dangerous with raised pressure.

med-clin-em.l15.q1.p: Using the rule of nines, what percentage of body surface area does one adult leg represent?
med-clin-em.l15.q1.e: Each adult leg is 18 percent, and each arm and the head are 9 percent.

med-clin-em.l15.q2.p: Which fluid is typically used in Parkland-based burn resuscitation?
med-clin-em.l15.q2.e: Lactated Ringer's is the usual fluid and the rate is titrated to urine output.

med-clin-em.l15.q3.t: Displace the uterus to the left or tilt her left
med-clin-em.l15.q3.p: A 36-week pregnant woman in a collision is hypotensive when lying flat, and her heart rate is 120. What is the best simple maneuver?
med-clin-em.l15.q3.e: The gravid uterus compresses the vena cava supine, so left displacement improves venous return. Maternal resuscitation helps the fetus.

med-clin-em.l15.q4.p: A chemical worker has a painful hand burn after hydrofluoric acid exposure and develops arrhythmia. Which treatment is specific?
med-clin-em.l15.q4.e: Hydrofluoric acid causes hypocalcemia and arrhythmia, and calcium gluconate binds fluoride.

med-clin-em.l15.q5.t: Compensated shock with hypotension as a late sign
med-clin-em.l15.q5.p: A 5-year-old has a heart rate of 150 and cool extremities after a fall, but a normal blood pressure. What does this indicate?
med-clin-em.l15.q5.h: Children maintain blood pressure until late.
med-clin-em.l15.q5.e: Children compensate by tachycardia and vasoconstriction, and hypotension appears late.

med-clin-em.l16.q1.p: Which ventilator setting primarily determines oxygenation in addition to FiO2?
med-clin-em.l16.q1.e: PEEP and FiO2 are the main determinants of oxygenation. Rate and tidal volume mainly determine ventilation.

med-clin-em.l16.q2.t: Increased airway resistance such as a mucus plug or bronchospasm
med-clin-em.l16.q2.p: On volume-control ventilation, peak pressure rises but plateau pressure is unchanged. What is the most likely cause?
med-clin-em.l16.q2.e: A rise in peak pressure with a stable plateau indicates resistance problems. A rise in both suggests a compliance problem.

med-clin-em.l16.q3.t: Lower the respiratory rate and lengthen expiratory time
med-clin-em.l16.q3.p: A ventilated patient with severe asthma becomes hypotensive, and the expiratory flow tracing does not return to zero before the next breath. What is the best immediate management?
med-clin-em.l16.q3.e: Air trapping from short expiratory time causes auto-PEEP and low venous return. Raising the rate worsens it.

med-clin-em.l16.q4.t: Disconnect from the ventilator and hand-ventilate while assessing for tube displacement or pneumothorax
med-clin-em.l16.q4.p: A recently intubated patient develops sudden hypoxia and high peak pressure, absent breath sounds on the left and hypotension. What should be done first?
med-clin-em.l16.q4.e: Sudden deterioration needs hand ventilation and a search for displacement, obstruction, pneumothorax and equipment failure.

med-clin-em.l16.q5.t: Based on predicted body weight from height and sex
med-clin-em.l16.q5.p: A 170 cm adult man with ARDS is ventilated. How should tidal volume be selected?
med-clin-em.l16.q5.e: Lung size correlates with height, so predicted body weight is used. Actual weight overestimates lung size in obesity.

med-clin-em.l17.q1.t: About 6 mL per kg of predicted body weight
med-clin-em.l17.q1.p: What tidal volume is used for lung-protective ventilation in ARDS?
med-clin-em.l17.q1.e: The ARDS Network trial showed lower mortality with 6 mL per kg predicted body weight versus 12.

med-clin-em.l17.q2.p: Which intervention reduced mortality in severe ARDS in the PROSEVA trial?
med-clin-em.l17.q2.e: Prone positioning for at least 12 to 16 hours daily lowered mortality in severe ARDS. HFOV did not help.

med-clin-em.l17.q3.t: Severe ARDS requiring lung-protective ventilation, with prone positioning if oxygenation stays poor
med-clin-em.l17.q3.p: A 45-year-old with pancreatitis has bilateral infiltrates, a PaO2/FiO2 of 90 on PEEP of 10, and a normal echocardiogram. Which statement describes her?
med-clin-em.l17.q3.e: A ratio of 100 or below with PEEP defines severe ARDS. A normal echocardiogram argues against cardiogenic edema.

med-clin-em.l17.q4.p: A ventilated septic patient has a glucose of 250 mg/dL. Which glucose target is supported by the evidence?
med-clin-em.l17.q4.e: The NICE-SUGAR trial found more hypoglycemia and mortality with tight control, so a moderate target is used.

med-clin-em.l17.q5.t: Raised BNP with reduced ejection fraction and response to diuresis
med-clin-em.l17.q5.p: Which sign best points to cardiogenic pulmonary edema over ARDS in a patient with bilateral infiltrates?
med-clin-em.l17.q5.e: Elevated BNP, low ejection fraction and response to diuresis suggest cardiac failure. ARDS has a direct or indirect lung insult.

med-clin-em.l18.q1.p: What does the Winter formula predict?
med-clin-em.l18.q1.e: The Winter formula estimates the expected PaCO2 as 1.5 times bicarbonate plus 8, plus or minus 2.

med-clin-em.l18.q2.p: Which vasoactive drug is a beta-1 inotrope with vasodilatory effects, used in cardiogenic shock?
med-clin-em.l18.q2.e: Dobutamine increases contractility and dilates vessels. Phenylephrine and vasopressin are pure vasoconstrictors.

med-clin-em.l18.q3.t: Anion gap metabolic acidosis with concurrent respiratory acidosis
med-clin-em.l18.q3.p: A patient in diabetic ketoacidosis has pH 7.12, bicarbonate 10 mEq/L and PaCO2 32 mmHg. What is the interpretation?
med-clin-em.l18.q3.e: Expected PaCO2 is 1.5 x 10 + 8 = 23 plus or minus 2 (21 to 25), and the measured 32 is clearly higher, indicating inadequate compensation from an additional respiratory acidosis, such as from fatigue.

med-clin-em.l18.q4.p: A patient with severe head injury has coma, absent brainstem reflexes and no respiratory effort during a correctly performed apnea test, after confounders are excluded. What is the status?
med-clin-em.l18.q4.h: The entire brain, including the brainstem.
med-clin-em.l18.q4.e: Coma, absent brainstem reflexes and apnea after excluding confounders establish brain death. Vegetative states preserve brainstem function.

med-clin-em.l18.q5.t: Honor the wishes through the surrogate and provide palliative care
med-clin-em.l18.q5.p: A family asks to withdraw ventilator support from a patient who, before losing capacity, stated she would not want prolonged mechanical ventilation. What is the best approach?
med-clin-em.l18.q5.e: Withdrawing and withholding are ethically equivalent when they reflect patient values, and palliative care continues.

med-clin-fm.l01.q1.t: Quaternary prevention, which guards against overmedicalization
med-clin-fm.l01.q1.p: Which term describes protecting patients from unnecessary or harmful medical interventions?
med-clin-fm.l01.q1.h: It is the fourth level of prevention.
med-clin-fm.l01.q1.e: Quaternary prevention targets overdiagnosis and overtreatment. The other levels address onset, early detection and complications.

med-clin-fm.l01.q2.t: Patients present earlier and with less differentiated symptoms
med-clin-fm.l01.q2.p: Why is the pretest probability of a serious disease lower in primary care than in a referral clinic?
med-clin-fm.l01.q2.h: Think of the filter between community and specialist.
med-clin-fm.l01.q2.e: Primary care sees illness at an early stage, so common benign causes dominate. Referral selects patients with more disease.

med-clin-fm.l01.q3.t: The low prevalence makes the positive predictive value very low
med-clin-fm.l01.q3.p: A 22-year-old woman has a rare condition with a 1 in 10,000 prevalence. A screening test has 95 percent sensitivity and 95 percent specificity. Why would most positive results still be false?
med-clin-fm.l01.q3.h: Think about predictive value and prevalence.
med-clin-fm.l01.q3.e: Positive predictive value depends strongly on prevalence, and in a rare disease false positives outnumber true positives. Sensitivity and specificity do not change with prevalence.

med-clin-fm.l01.q4.t: Describe benefits and harms, ask about his values, and decide together
med-clin-fm.l01.q4.p: A man says he does not want to decide about prostate screening alone, and asks the clinician what to do. Which response best reflects shared decision-making?
med-clin-fm.l01.q4.h: Both information and values are needed.
med-clin-fm.l01.q4.e: Shared decision-making combines evidence with patient values, which is crucial when evidence is balanced. Paternalism in either direction omits one half.

med-clin-fm.l01.q5.t: Urgent evaluation, including MRI, for cauda equina syndrome
med-clin-fm.l01.q5.p: A patient with chronic low back pain reports new urinary retention and numbness around the perineum. What is the most appropriate step?
med-clin-fm.l01.q5.h: Red flags override benign base rates.
med-clin-fm.l01.q5.e: Retention and saddle anesthesia are red flags for cauda equina syndrome and require emergency imaging despite the usual benign course of back pain.

med-clin-fm.l02.q1.t: Lengthens apparent survival without delaying death
med-clin-fm.l02.q1.p: What does lead-time bias do in a screening program?
med-clin-fm.l02.q1.h: Earlier diagnosis starts the clock sooner.
med-clin-fm.l02.q1.e: Lead time adds time between detection and the usual diagnosis without changing the date of death. Length bias favors indolent tumors, and overdiagnosis detects cancers that never matter.

med-clin-fm.l02.q2.t: 45 to 75, with 45 to 49 graded B and 50 to 75 graded A
med-clin-fm.l02.q2.p: At what ages does the 2021 USPSTF recommend colorectal cancer screening as a grade A or B?
med-clin-fm.l02.q2.h: The start age was lowered in 2021.
med-clin-fm.l02.q2.e: The 2021 recommendation begins at 45, with a B for 45 to 49 and an A for 50 to 75. Several test options are available.

med-clin-fm.l02.q3.t: Annual low-dose CT lung cancer screening
med-clin-fm.l02.q3.p: A 52-year-old woman smoked one pack daily for 30 years and quit one year ago. Which recommendation best fits her?
med-clin-fm.l02.q3.h: Count pack-years and years since quitting.
med-clin-fm.l02.q3.e: She is 50 to 80 with at least 20 pack-years and quit within 15 years, so annual low-dose CT is recommended. Chest radiography did not reduce mortality.

med-clin-fm.l02.q4.p: A 26-year-old woman has had normal cytology results. What is the recommended interval according to the 2018 USPSTF?
med-clin-fm.l02.q4.h: HPV testing alone is not used in this age group.
med-clin-fm.l02.q4.e: Women aged 21 to 29 should have cytology every three years. Primary HPV testing is recommended starting at age 30.

med-clin-fm.l02.q5.t: Recommends against routine screening at age 70 and older
med-clin-fm.l02.q5.p: A 72-year-old man asks for a PSA test for prostate cancer screening, and he has a 15-year life expectancy. What is the USPSTF position?
med-clin-fm.l02.q5.e: The 2018 statement gives a D grade for screening at age 70 and older because harms outweigh benefits. The individual decision applies at 55 to 69.

med-clin-fm.l03.q1.t: Ambulatory or home blood pressure monitoring
med-clin-fm.l03.q1.p: Which test is recommended to confirm an elevated office blood pressure before diagnosing hypertension?
med-clin-fm.l03.q1.e: The 2021 USPSTF recommends confirming with out-of-office measurement, which excludes white coat hypertension.

med-clin-fm.l03.q2.t: A statin is recommended for adults 40 to 75 with a risk factor and a risk of 10 percent or more
med-clin-fm.l03.q2.p: A 58-year-old man with diabetes, a 10-year risk of 12 percent and no prior cardiovascular events asks about a statin. What is the USPSTF recommendation?
med-clin-fm.l03.q2.h: Age 40 to 75 plus a risk factor plus the 10 percent threshold.
med-clin-fm.l03.q2.e: The 2022 USPSTF gives a B grade for statins at this risk level. Aspirin is not preferred for primary prevention.

med-clin-fm.l03.q3.p: A 67-year-old man, a former smoker, has no symptoms. Which screening is recommended once?
med-clin-fm.l03.q3.e: One-time abdominal ultrasound is a grade B for men aged 65 to 75 who have ever smoked. Carotid and ECG screening are not recommended in asymptomatic adults.

med-clin-fm.l03.q4.p: A 49-year-old woman with a 10-year cardiovascular risk of 8 percent has borderline risk and prefers to avoid a statin if possible. Which test may help refine the decision?
med-clin-fm.l03.q4.e: Guidelines allow a coronary artery calcium score in borderline-risk patients to guide statin use. A zero score supports deferral.

med-clin-fm.l03.q5.t: Not initiating aspirin for primary prevention at age 60 or older
med-clin-fm.l03.q5.p: A 63-year-old man with no cardiovascular disease asks to start daily aspirin for prevention. What does the 2022 USPSTF recommend?
med-clin-fm.l03.q5.e: The USPSTF recommends against initiating aspirin at 60 or older because bleeding outweighs benefit.

med-clin-fm.l04.q1.t: Measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, which is a live attenuated vaccine
med-clin-fm.l04.q1.p: Which vaccine is contraindicated in pregnancy?
med-clin-fm.l04.q1.e: Live attenuated vaccines such as MMR and varicella are avoided in pregnancy. Inactivated and recombinant vaccines are safe.

med-clin-fm.l04.q2.t: To produce a T-cell-dependent response with immune memory in young children
med-clin-fm.l04.q2.p: Why are polysaccharide vaccines conjugated to a protein carrier?
med-clin-fm.l04.q2.e: Conjugation recruits T-cell help, producing memory and efficacy in infants. Plain polysaccharide responses are T-independent and weak under age two.

med-clin-fm.l04.q3.t: Give age-appropriate catch-up doses, counting any documented doses and using minimum intervals without restarting series
med-clin-fm.l04.q3.p: A 16-year-old has no immunization records and arrives for a sports physical. Which approach is correct?
med-clin-fm.l04.q3.e: Undocumented doses are treated as not given, and series are continued rather than restarted. Serologic testing is not required before vaccination.

med-clin-fm.l04.q4.t: Mild illness with low-grade fever is not a contraindication to vaccination
med-clin-fm.l04.q4.p: A 6-year-old develops a mild cold with a low-grade fever and is due for MMR and DTaP. Which statement is correct?
med-clin-fm.l04.q4.e: Mild illness is not a contraindication, while anaphylaxis to a prior dose or component is. Antibiotics do not interfere with vaccines.

med-clin-fm.l04.q5.t: Yes, two doses are recommended for adults aged 50 and older
med-clin-fm.l04.q5.p: A 62-year-old man with no history of shingles asks whether he should get the recombinant zoster vaccine. What is the recommendation?
med-clin-fm.l04.q5.h: It is a non-live, two-dose series.
med-clin-fm.l04.q5.e: The recombinant vaccine is recommended from age 50, including people who have not had shingles, and it is not a live vaccine.

med-clin-fm.l05.q1.p: Which test is recommended once for all adults aged 18 to 79 according to the 2020 USPSTF?
med-clin-fm.l05.q1.h: Direct-acting antivirals can cure this infection.
med-clin-fm.l05.q1.e: The 2020 USPSTF recommends one-time hepatitis C screening for adults aged 18 to 79. Routine herpes serology is not recommended.

med-clin-fm.l05.q2.t: Sexually active women aged 24 and younger, and older women at increased risk
med-clin-fm.l05.q2.p: Which group does the USPSTF recommend screening for chlamydia and gonorrhea?
med-clin-fm.l05.q2.h: Nucleic acid amplification tests are used.
med-clin-fm.l05.q2.e: The 2021 recommendation targets sexually active young women and older women at risk. Evidence for screening men in general is insufficient.

med-clin-fm.l05.q3.t: Treat latent tuberculosis, such as with four months of rifampin
med-clin-fm.l05.q3.p: A 29-year-old with a positive interferon-gamma release assay has a normal chest radiograph and no symptoms. What is the best management?
med-clin-fm.l05.q3.e: This is latent tuberculosis, and shorter rifamycin-based regimens are preferred. Active disease would need four drugs and evidence of symptoms or radiographic disease.

med-clin-fm.l05.q4.t: HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B surface antigen and rubella immunity
med-clin-fm.l05.q4.p: A pregnant woman is at the first prenatal visit. Which set of infectious screens is routinely recommended?
med-clin-fm.l05.q4.h: The newborn can be protected by early identification.
med-clin-fm.l05.q4.e: Routine prenatal screening includes HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B and rubella immunity, among others. Herpes serology is not routine.

med-clin-fm.l05.q5.p: A 27-year-old woman is planning a pregnancy. Which supplement does the USPSTF recommend daily to prevent neural tube defects?
med-clin-fm.l05.q5.e: The USPSTF recommends folic acid at 0.4 to 0.8 mg daily. High-dose vitamin A is teratogenic.

med-clin-fm.l06.q1.p: Which class of antihypertensive can cause a dry cough because of bradykinin accumulation?
med-clin-fm.l06.q1.e: ACE inhibitors reduce bradykinin breakdown, causing cough and sometimes angioedema. ARBs do not.

med-clin-fm.l06.q2.p: Which is a contraindication to ACE inhibitors and ARBs?
med-clin-fm.l06.q2.e: ACE inhibitors and ARBs cause fetal renal injury and are contraindicated in pregnancy. They are preferred in diabetic kidney disease and heart failure.

med-clin-fm.l06.q3.p: A 28-year-old woman has hypertension, hypokalemia and a low renin. What is the best next test?
med-clin-fm.l06.q3.e: Hypertension with hypokalemia suggests primary aldosteronism, and the aldosterone-to-renin ratio is the screening test. Metanephrines screen for pheochromocytoma.

med-clin-fm.l06.q4.t: A single-pill combination of two first-line classes, with lifestyle changes
med-clin-fm.l06.q4.p: A 55-year-old man with a repeated reading of 152/94 and no comorbid disease needs treatment. Which initial regimen is reasonable?
med-clin-fm.l06.q4.e: The 2025 AHA/ACC guideline prefers a single-pill combination of first-line classes (thiazide-type diuretic, calcium channel blocker, ACE inhibitor or ARB) for stage 2 hypertension. Combining an ACE inhibitor and an ARB is harmful and not recommended.

med-clin-fm.l06.q5.t: Statin therapy, as for all adults with diabetes aged 40 to 75
med-clin-fm.l06.q5.p: A 52-year-old man with diabetes has an LDL of 130 mg/dL and no cardiovascular disease. What does the 2026 ACC/AHA dyslipidemia guideline recommend?
med-clin-fm.l06.q5.e: Adults with diabetes aged 40 to 75 are recommended statin therapy. Fibrates and niacin have not shown outcome benefit on top of statins.

med-clin-fm.l07.q1.t: SGLT2 inhibitors, which reduce glomerular hyperfiltration
