med-epi-biostats.l02.q5.h: Ask what a snapshot can and cannot reveal about sequence.
med-epi-biostats.l02.q5.e: The design cannot show that obesity preceded depression, so reverse causation is plausible. Effect size does not remove confounding or ambiguity about direction.

med-epi-biostats.l03.q1.t: Investigators can deliberately enroll heavily exposed people and then follow them for outcomes
med-epi-biostats.l03.q1.p: Which feature makes a cohort study the preferred observational design for a rare exposure?
med-epi-biostats.l03.q1.h: The design begins with exposure status.
med-epi-biostats.l03.q1.e: Cohorts sample by exposure, so they can enrich for rare exposures. Matching controls and starting with ill participants describe case-control reasoning.

med-epi-biostats.l03.q2.t: Relative risk 3.0 and attributable risk 20 per 1,000
med-epi-biostats.l03.q2.p: In a cohort, 30 of 1,000 exposed participants and 10 of 1,000 unexposed participants develop the disease over five years. What are the relative risk and the attributable risk?
med-epi-biostats.l03.q2.h: Risk ratio is a division; risk difference is a subtraction.
med-epi-biostats.l03.q2.e: RR = 30/10 = 3.0 and the risk difference is 30 - 10 = 20 per 1,000. Reversing the operations gives the other combinations.

med-epi-biostats.l03.q3.t: Healthy worker effect, because people able to work tend to be healthier than the general population
med-epi-biostats.l03.q3.p: A study of foundry workers compares their cancer mortality with that of the general population and finds a lower rate. Which bias most plausibly masks a true occupational hazard?
med-epi-biostats.l03.q3.h: Consider who is able to hold a job in the first place.
med-epi-biostats.l03.q3.e: Employed people are selected for good health, so comparing them with the general population understates harm. Using another group of workers is a better comparison.

med-epi-biostats.l03.q4.t: It is biased toward the null, because the participants most likely to have developed dementia are missing from the exposed group
med-epi-biostats.l03.q4.p: A 10-year prospective cohort compares incident dementia between people with and without midlife hypertension. By year 10, 35% of participants have dropped out, and dropout was higher among hypertensive participants who were already showing cognitive decline. What is the likely effect on the estimated relative risk?
med-epi-biostats.l03.q4.h: Who is leaving, and what was their outcome risk?
med-epi-biostats.l03.q4.e: Differential loss of high-risk exposed people removes cases from the exposed group and pulls the RR toward 1. Loss to follow-up related to both exposure and outcome is a classic source of bias, not just lost precision.

med-epi-biostats.l03.q5.t: It can be completed faster and cheaper, but depends on the quality of past exposure records
med-epi-biostats.l03.q5.p: A retrospective cohort uses 1980s factory payroll and cancer registry records to compare exposed and unexposed workers. Compared with a prospective cohort, which statement is most accurate?
med-epi-biostats.l03.q5.h: The timing of the data collection differs; the logic of the design does not.
med-epi-biostats.l03.q5.e: A historical cohort still classifies exposure before outcome and measures incidence, and the main trade-off is record quality. It is not immune to confounding.

med-epi-biostats.l04.q1.t: It starts with existing cases, so few participants and little follow-up time are needed
med-epi-biostats.l04.q1.p: Why is a case-control study well suited to a rare disease with a long latency period?
med-epi-biostats.l04.q1.h: Sampling is based on outcome, not exposure.
med-epi-biostats.l04.q1.e: Selecting cases directly avoids waiting for rare events to occur. Following exposed groups is cohort logic and randomization belongs to trials.

med-epi-biostats.l04.q2.t: The odds ratio is 2.67, found by cross-multiplying 40 x 80 and dividing by 60 x 20
med-epi-biostats.l04.q2.p: Among 100 cases, 40 were exposed; among 100 controls, 20 were exposed. What is the odds ratio?
med-epi-biostats.l04.q2.h: Use the cross-product of the 2 x 2 table.
med-epi-biostats.l04.q2.e: OR = (40 x 80) / (60 x 20) = 3,200 / 1,200 = 2.67. Dividing proportions (40/20 = 2.0) gives a risk-ratio-like figure that is not the OR.

med-epi-biostats.l04.q3.t: When the disease is rare in the source population, so odds and risk are nearly equal
med-epi-biostats.l04.q3.p: When does the odds ratio from a case-control study approximate the relative risk?
med-epi-biostats.l04.q3.h: Odds and probability converge when the probability is small.
med-epi-biostats.l04.q3.e: With a rare outcome, the odds of disease are close to the risk. Matching and a large control group do not make the OR equal the RR, and equal recall bias does not either.

med-epi-biostats.l04.q4.t: Recall bias, because mothers of affected children search memory harder for explanations
med-epi-biostats.l04.q4.p: A study of a rare brain tumor compares mothers of affected children with mothers of unaffected children about prenatal exposures. Mothers of affected children report more exposures, but medical records show equal exposure rates. Which bias is demonstrated?
med-epi-biostats.l04.q4.h: Records and memory disagree in only one group.
med-epi-biostats.l04.q4.e: Differential reporting of exposure between cases and controls is recall bias, and objective records expose it. Surveillance bias involves unequal detection of the outcome, not unequal reporting of exposure.

med-epi-biostats.l04.q5.t: The odds ratio is biased toward the null, because the controls have higher exposure than the source population
med-epi-biostats.l04.q5.p: An investigator picks hospitalized patients with fractures as controls for a case-control study of alcohol use and liver cancer. Fracture patients drink more than the general population. What is the most likely consequence?
med-epi-biostats.l04.q5.h: Controls should reflect exposure in the population that produced the cases.
med-epi-biostats.l04.q5.e: Controls with unusually high exposure raise the denominator odds and shrink the OR toward 1. Using hospital settings alone does not guarantee validity, because the control illness is related to the exposure.

med-epi-biostats.l05.q1.t: Enrolling clinicians predicting or steering the next assignment, which causes selection bias
med-epi-biostats.l05.q1.p: What does allocation concealment protect against?
med-epi-biostats.l05.q1.h: It operates before assignment, not afterward.
med-epi-biostats.l05.q1.e: Concealment keeps recruiters from knowing the upcoming allocation. Blinding after assignment handles performance and detection bias, and intention-to-treat handles dropped participants.

med-epi-biostats.l05.q2.t: Intention-to-treat, because patients should be analyzed as randomized regardless of treatment received
med-epi-biostats.l05.q2.p: In a surgical trial, 15% of patients randomized to surgery decline it and receive medical therapy, and are analyzed in the medical group. Which analysis principle is violated?
med-epi-biostats.l05.q2.h: Randomization is preserved only by analyzing as assigned.
med-epi-biostats.l05.q2.e: Analyzing by treatment actually received breaks the balance created by randomization. Crossover designs are a separate design in which each person receives both treatments in sequence.

med-epi-biostats.l05.q3.t: Non-adherence dilutes differences toward zero, which hides a true benefit but can make a worse drug look equivalent
med-epi-biostats.l05.q3.p: Why is intention-to-treat analysis considered conservative in a superiority trial but potentially anti-conservative in a non-inferiority trial?
med-epi-biostats.l05.q3.h: Think about what dilution toward no difference does to each claim.
med-epi-biostats.l05.q3.e: Dilution toward no difference works against proving superiority but toward proving non-inferiority. The second option reverses the direction of dilution.

med-epi-biostats.l05.q4.t: The effect estimate may be exaggerated, because trials stopped early for benefit tend to capture random highs
med-epi-biostats.l05.q4.p: A phase III trial of a new anticoagulant is stopped after an interim analysis shows a large reduction in the primary endpoint after only 30 events. Which concern is most appropriate?
med-epi-biostats.l05.q4.h: Consider what a trial that stops at its best moment looks like.
med-epi-biostats.l05.q4.e: Early stopping for benefit tends to overestimate effects, particularly with few events. Interim analyses by a monitoring committee are legitimate, and randomization does not remove random error.

med-epi-biostats.l05.q5.t: Performance and detection bias, because unblinded participants may report symptoms differently by arm
med-epi-biostats.l05.q5.p: A 58-year-old with type 2 diabetes is offered a trial in which participants are told whether they are in a new-device or a standard-care arm, and the primary outcome is self-reported symptom score. Which limitation is greatest?
med-epi-biostats.l05.q5.h: Subjective outcomes are most susceptible to knowledge of assignment.
med-epi-biostats.l05.q5.e: When participants know their arm and the outcome is self-reported, expectation can shift scores. Randomization still balances baseline factors on average.

med-epi-biostats.l06.q1.t: The reciprocal of the absolute risk reduction, rounded up to a whole patient
med-epi-biostats.l06.q1.p: How is the number needed to treat calculated?
med-epi-biostats.l06.q1.h: It converts an absolute difference into a count of patients.
med-epi-biostats.l06.q1.e: NNT = 1 / ARR, rounded up. The relative risk is a ratio rather than a difference and gives no direct count of patients.

med-epi-biostats.l06.q2.t: An NNT of about 25 over the 3 years of the trial
med-epi-biostats.l06.q2.p: In a 3-year trial, 10% of controls and 6% of treated patients have a stroke. What is the NNT?
med-epi-biostats.l06.q2.h: Find the absolute difference in risk first.
med-epi-biostats.l06.q2.e: ARR = 10% - 6% = 4% = 0.04, so NNT = 1 / 0.04 = 25. An answer of 40 would result from using the relative risk reduction, 40%, instead.

med-epi-biostats.l06.q3.t: They are 20 and 200, because the same relative effect gives a tenfold smaller absolute benefit at low baseline risk
med-epi-biostats.l06.q3.p: Drug X reduces the relative risk of an event by 25% in two populations. Population 1 has a baseline risk of 20% and population 2 has a baseline risk of 2%. How do the NNTs compare?
med-epi-biostats.l06.q3.h: Multiply the baseline risk by the relative risk reduction in each group.
med-epi-biostats.l06.q3.e: ARR is 5 points in population 1 (NNT 20) and 0.5 points in population 2 (NNT 200). NNT rises as baseline risk falls, which the second option states backward.

med-epi-biostats.l06.q4.t: The statement overstates the effect, because for a common outcome the RR is 2.0 and the OR exaggerates it
med-epi-biostats.l06.q4.p: Event risk is 40% in exposed patients and 20% in unexposed patients in a cohort. A reviewer reports the odds ratio as 2.67 and states that exposed patients are 2.67 times as likely to have the event. What is the most accurate comment?
med-epi-biostats.l06.q4.h: Compute the relative risk directly from the two risks.
med-epi-biostats.l06.q4.e: RR = 0.40 / 0.20 = 2.0, and OR = (0.4/0.6) / (0.2/0.8) = 2.67. When the outcome is common, the OR lies further from 1 than the RR.

med-epi-biostats.l06.q5.t: The NNT is about 333, because the absolute risk reduction is 0.3 percentage points in that stratum
med-epi-biostats.l06.q5.p: A trial reports that a statin lowers cardiovascular events by 30% relative to placebo in two risk strata. In the high-risk stratum, event rates are 10% on placebo; in the low-risk stratum, 1% on placebo. For a patient in the low-risk stratum, which statement is most defensible?
med-epi-biostats.l06.q5.h: Apply 30% to each stratum's placebo risk before taking the reciprocal.
med-epi-biostats.l06.q5.e: Low-risk ARR = 0.30 x 1% = 0.3 points, so NNT = 1 / 0.003, about 333. In the high-risk stratum ARR is 3 points and NNT about 33, so the two differ tenfold.

med-epi-biostats.l07.q1.t: Healthy-user (volunteer) bias, a form of selection bias that is related to both exposure and outcome
med-epi-biostats.l07.q1.p: Which bias occurs when people who choose a health behavior are healthier in other ways than those who do not?
med-epi-biostats.l07.q1.h: The people who self-select into the exposure differ in other ways.
med-epi-biostats.l07.q1.e: Self-selection of healthier people into a behavior produces healthy-user bias. The Hawthorne effect concerns behavior under observation, not who chooses the behavior.

med-epi-biostats.l07.q2.t: Toward the null value, because non-differential misclassification of a dichotomous exposure weakens associations
med-epi-biostats.l07.q2.p: A cohort study measures a dichotomous exposure with a test that misclassifies 20% of participants equally among those who do and do not develop disease. In which direction is the association expected to be biased?
med-epi-biostats.l07.q2.h: Equal error in both outcome groups blurs the contrast.
med-epi-biostats.l07.q2.e: Non-differential misclassification of a dichotomous exposure tends to bias toward the null. It is a bias and not merely imprecision, because it shifts the expected estimate.

med-epi-biostats.l07.q3.t: Detection (surveillance) bias, because more frequent testing finds more of the disease in users
med-epi-biostats.l07.q3.p: People taking a drug that requires regular blood tests are diagnosed with mild kidney disease more often than non-users. Which explanation involves a bias rather than a true effect?
med-epi-biostats.l07.q3.h: Where you look harder, you find more.
med-epi-biostats.l07.q3.e: Unequal intensity of testing yields unequal detection of disease. Lead-time bias concerns survival from diagnosis, not frequency of diagnosis.

med-epi-biostats.l07.q4.t: Berksonian selection bias, because admission depends on both conditions and distorts the sampled association
med-epi-biostats.l07.q4.p: A hospital-based study compares patients admitted with disease A and disease B and finds that a drug used to treat B appears protective against A. The drug has no effect on A. Which mechanism best explains the finding?
med-epi-biostats.l07.q4.h: Think about who ends up in a hospital sample.
med-epi-biostats.l07.q4.e: When admission depends on either disease, restricting to hospitalized patients creates a spurious association. Random misclassification would weaken, not manufacture, a protective effect.

med-epi-biostats.l07.q5.t: It is probably underestimated, because the missing participants have a higher prevalence than the respondents
med-epi-biostats.l07.q5.p: A survey with a 25% response rate finds that 12% of respondents use a supplement and 3% of respondents have heart disease. Non-responders are older and more likely to have heart disease. What is the best conclusion about the estimate of heart-disease prevalence?
med-epi-biostats.l07.q5.h: Consider how the people you could not reach differ from those you did reach.
med-epi-biostats.l07.q5.e: Differential non-response removes people at higher risk, biasing prevalence downward. Sample size shrinks random error but not this systematic error.

med-epi-biostats.l08.q1.t: It lies on the causal pathway between the exposure and the outcome
med-epi-biostats.l08.q1.p: Which of the following is NOT a requirement for a variable to be a confounder?
med-epi-biostats.l08.q1.h: A confounder is a nuisance, not a mechanism.
med-epi-biostats.l08.q1.e: A variable on the causal pathway is a mediator, and adjusting for it removes part of the true effect. The other three describe the standard criteria.

med-epi-biostats.l08.q2.t: Confounding by smoking, because the stratum-specific estimates agree with each other but differ from the crude
med-epi-biostats.l08.q2.p: The crude RR for an exposure is 3.0. After stratifying by smoking, the RR is 2.0 in smokers and 2.0 in non-smokers. What do these results indicate?
med-epi-biostats.l08.q2.h: Compare crude with adjusted; compare strata with each other.
med-epi-biostats.l08.q2.e: Uniform strata that differ from the crude point to confounding, with an adjusted RR near 2.0. Effect modification requires the strata to differ from each other.

med-epi-biostats.l08.q3.t: Confounding by indication, because the reason for prescribing is related to the outcome
med-epi-biostats.l08.q3.p: A drug appears to raise mortality in an observational study, but doctors prescribed it mainly to patients who were already very ill. Which term describes this problem?
med-epi-biostats.l08.q3.h: The indication for treatment is itself a prognostic factor.
med-epi-biostats.l08.q3.e: Sicker patients receive the drug and also die more often, so severity confounds the association. Collider bias requires conditioning on a common effect, which is not described here.

med-epi-biostats.l08.q4.t: Report the age-specific estimates, because a true difference in effect by age is effect modification and averaging hides it
med-epi-biostats.l08.q4.p: A study of a vaccine finds a relative risk of 0.2 for infection in adults under 50 and 0.9 in adults over 50. An analyst proposes a single pooled age-adjusted estimate of 0.5. What is the best response?
med-epi-biostats.l08.q4.h: Ask whether the effect itself differs across groups.
med-epi-biostats.l08.q4.e: Strongly different stratum-specific effects are effect modification and should be reported separately, since a single number misdescribes both groups. Heterogeneity is a finding, not proof of failed randomization.

med-epi-biostats.l08.q5.t: Overadjustment for a mediator probably removed the pathway through which salt acts, so the model underestimates the total effect
med-epi-biostats.l08.q5.p: An investigator studying whether dietary salt causes stroke adjusts the model for blood pressure measured after salt intake, since salt raises blood pressure. The adjusted salt-stroke association shrinks to near null. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
med-epi-biostats.l08.q5.h: Blood pressure lies between the exposure and the outcome.
med-epi-biostats.l08.q5.e: Blood pressure is a mediator, so adjusting for it removes the effect that operates through it. This is not proof of no effect, and blood pressure was measured here, so residual confounding by it is not the problem.

med-epi-biostats.l09.q1.t: Temporality, because the cause must come before the effect in time
med-epi-biostats.l09.q1.p: Which Bradford Hill viewpoint is strictly required for an association to be causal?
med-epi-biostats.l09.q1.h: Think about what would make a cause impossible regardless of other evidence.
med-epi-biostats.l09.q1.e: Only temporality is indispensable, since an effect cannot precede its cause. Specificity is weak because many exposures cause multiple diseases, and the others are supporting considerations.

med-epi-biostats.l09.q2.t: A component cause within a sufficient cause, which acts together with other factors
med-epi-biostats.l09.q2.p: A risk factor can cause a disease that also occurs in people without the risk factor, and not everyone with it develops the disease. In the language of causal models, the factor is best described as which kind of cause?
med-epi-biostats.l09.q2.h: Neither always required nor always enough.
med-epi-biostats.l09.q2.e: Most chronic disease involves component causes that combine into sufficient causes. A confounder is a different role, defined relative to a particular exposure-outcome pair.

med-epi-biostats.l09.q3.t: Biological gradient, because disease risk increases with the dose of exposure
med-epi-biostats.l09.q3.p: In a cohort study, relative risk of lung cancer rises from 1.0 to 8 to 20 across none, light and heavy smokers. Which Hill viewpoint does this pattern most directly support?
med-epi-biostats.l09.q3.h: The risk changes in step with the amount of exposure.
med-epi-biostats.l09.q3.e: A dose-response relationship is the biological gradient. A cohort study observes exposure and does not assign it, so it is not experimental evidence.

med-epi-biostats.l09.q4.t: A weak association can be causal, and strength is one viewpoint to weigh with consistency, gradient and design quality
med-epi-biostats.l09.q4.p: An investigator argues that, because a weak association (RR 1.2) between an air pollutant and asthma was found in a single study, the association cannot be causal. Which response is most consistent with Hill's original discussion?
med-epi-biostats.l09.q4.h: Hill said his viewpoints are not a rigid checklist.
med-epi-biostats.l09.q4.e: A small effect can be real, particularly for common exposures, and strength is one consideration among several. Hill expressly denied that the viewpoints were indispensable rules, apart from temporality.

med-epi-biostats.l09.q5.t: Persistently higher risk in heavier smokers and falling risk in those who quit, consistent across many studies
med-epi-biostats.l09.q5.p: A 1950s argument suggested that a hidden genotype might cause both smoking and lung cancer. Which line of evidence most directly weakened this alternative explanation?
med-epi-biostats.l09.q5.h: Which evidence would a fixed genotype struggle to explain?
med-epi-biostats.l09.q5.e: A gradient and a risk decline after cessation are hard to explain by a fixed genetic confounder, and convergent results across studies strengthen the case. A single study, or a trend over time alone, does not rule out confounding.

med-epi-biostats.l10.q1.t: The proportion of people without the disease who test negative
med-epi-biostats.l10.q1.h: It is calculated among those who are free of disease.
med-epi-biostats.l10.q1.e: Specificity = TN / (TN + FP), the true negative rate. Sensitivity is the second option, PPV the third and NPV the fourth.

med-epi-biostats.l10.q2.t: Sensitivity 90% and specificity 90%, with 20 false negatives and 80 false positives
med-epi-biostats.l10.q2.p: A test is applied to 200 patients with a disease, of whom 180 test positive, and to 800 patients without the disease, of whom 720 test negative. What are the sensitivity and specificity?
med-epi-biostats.l10.q2.h: Divide within the diseased column and within the healthy column.
med-epi-biostats.l10.q2.e: Sensitivity = 180/200 = 90%, and specificity = 720/800 = 90%. The other options misstate the false positive or false negative counts.

med-epi-biostats.l10.q3.t: The disease is likely ruled out, because few diseased people have a negative result
med-epi-biostats.l10.q3.p: A highly sensitive test is negative in a patient. Which statement follows most directly?
med-epi-biostats.l10.q3.e: High sensitivity means few false negatives, so a negative result argues against disease. Sensitivity does not guarantee that every negative is correct, since prevalence also matters.

med-epi-biostats.l10.q4.t: Spectrum bias, because the study used clear-cut cases and healthy controls instead of ambiguous patients
med-epi-biostats.l10.q4.p: A new troponin assay is evaluated by comparing 50 patients with confirmed myocardial infarction against 50 healthy young volunteers, giving a sensitivity of 98% and specificity of 99%. When used in emergency patients with chest pain, its performance is much lower. Which bias best explains this?
med-epi-biostats.l10.q4.h: Consider the mix of patients in the study compared with practice.
med-epi-biostats.l10.q4.e: Using extremes of the disease spectrum inflates accuracy. Verification bias would require unequal use of the reference standard, which is not described.

med-epi-biostats.l10.q5.t: Sensitivity rises and specificity falls, because more people are classified as positive
med-epi-biostats.l10.q5.p: A 45-year-old woman has a result just above the cutoff on a continuous test. The laboratory lowers the cutoff for a positive result, hoping to catch more cases. What is the expected effect on the test characteristics?
med-epi-biostats.l10.q5.h: A lower threshold for positivity classifies more people as positive.
med-epi-biostats.l10.q5.e: Moving the cutoff trades one error for the other: more true positives and more false positives. The predictive values change too, but so do sensitivity and specificity.

med-epi-biostats.l11.q1.t: It falls, because false positives make up a larger share of all positive results
med-epi-biostats.l11.q1.p: What happens to positive predictive value when a test is applied to a population with lower disease prevalence?
med-epi-biostats.l11.q1.h: Think about the ratio of diseased to healthy people in the denominator.
med-epi-biostats.l11.q1.e: With fewer diseased people, false positives from the large healthy group make up more of the positives. Sensitivity and specificity are fixed, but predictive values are not.

med-epi-biostats.l11.q2.t: About 15%, because 90 true positives fall among 585 positive results
med-epi-biostats.l11.q2.p: A test has 90% sensitivity and 95% specificity, and disease prevalence is 1% in 10,000 people. What is the positive predictive value?
med-epi-biostats.l11.q2.h: Construct the 2 x 2 table from 10,000 people.
med-epi-biostats.l11.q2.e: There are 90 true positives and 495 false positives, so PPV = 90 / 585 = 15.4%. Using sensitivity or specificity answers a different question.

med-epi-biostats.l11.q3.t: An LR+ of 18, calculated as the sensitivity divided by 1 minus the specificity
med-epi-biostats.l11.q3.p: A test has sensitivity 90% and specificity 95%. What is the positive likelihood ratio?
med-epi-biostats.l11.q3.h: Compare the chance of a positive result in diseased and healthy people.
med-epi-biostats.l11.q3.e: LR+ = 0.90 / (1 - 0.95) = 0.90 / 0.05 = 18. The other formulas are not likelihood ratios.

med-epi-biostats.l11.q4.t: About 67%, because pre-test odds of 0.25 multiplied by 8 give odds of 2
med-epi-biostats.l11.q4.p: A 67-year-old man with exertional dyspnea is judged to have a 20% pre-test probability of heart failure. A natriuretic peptide test with LR+ of 8 is positive. What is the approximate post-test probability?
med-epi-biostats.l11.q4.h: Convert to odds before multiplying by the likelihood ratio.
med-epi-biostats.l11.q4.e: Odds = 0.20 / 0.80 = 0.25; times 8 = 2.0; probability = 2 / 3 = 67%. Multiplying the probability itself by the LR is a mistake, and a probability cannot exceed 100%.

med-epi-biostats.l11.q5.t: PPV will be much lower, because the same specificity produces many more false positives per true positive
med-epi-biostats.l11.q5.p: A published study reports a PPV of 80% for a rapid assay in an infectious disease clinic, where 40% of those tested have the disease. A health department plans to use the same assay for community screening, where prevalence is 0.5%. What is the best prediction?
med-epi-biostats.l11.q5.h: Which measure is tied to prevalence, and which is not?
med-epi-biostats.l11.q5.e: PPV falls steeply at low prevalence, so most positives in a community screen would be false. Likelihood ratios are stable, but the PPV they imply changes with the pre-test probability.

med-epi-biostats.l12.q1.t: Discrimination no better than chance, as the curve follows the diagonal
med-epi-biostats.l12.q1.p: What does an area under the ROC curve of 0.5 indicate?
med-epi-biostats.l12.q1.e: AUC 0.5 equals chance, and AUC 1.0 is perfect. The ROC curve itself does not depend on prevalence.

med-epi-biostats.l12.q2.t: Lead-time bias, because survival from diagnosis lengthens without any delay in the date of death
med-epi-biostats.l12.q2.p: A cancer is diagnosed at age 63 without screening, and the patient dies at 65. With screening, it is found at 60 and the patient still dies at 65. Which statement describes this situation?
med-epi-biostats.l12.q2.h: Compare dates of death, not survival from diagnosis.
med-epi-biostats.l12.q2.e: Earlier detection moved the start of the clock but not the end, which is lead-time bias. Length-time bias concerns the type of tumor that screening detects, and overdiagnosis involves disease that would never matter.

med-epi-biostats.l12.q3.t: Disease-specific or all-cause mortality in randomized screened and unscreened groups
med-epi-biostats.l12.q3.p: Which outcome is the most appropriate for judging whether a cancer screening program works?
med-epi-biostats.l12.q3.h: Choose an outcome that lead time and overdiagnosis cannot inflate.
med-epi-biostats.l12.q3.e: Mortality in a randomized comparison avoids lead-time, length-time and overdiagnosis bias. Survival from diagnosis and detection counts are both inflated by those biases.

med-epi-biostats.l12.q4.t: Lead-time bias, length-time bias and overdiagnosis, which inflate survival without reducing deaths
med-epi-biostats.l12.q4.p: A program offers annual screening for a slow-growing malignancy. Screen-detected cancers show 95% five-year survival, compared with 60% for cancers found through symptoms, but population mortality has not changed. Which combination of biases best explains these findings?
med-epi-biostats.l12.q4.h: Better survival with unchanged mortality points to artifacts of timing and tumor type.
med-epi-biostats.l12.q4.e: Earlier detection, preferential finding of indolent tumors and detection of non-lethal lesions raise survival statistics but leave mortality unchanged. The other combinations do not predict that pattern.

med-epi-biostats.l12.q5.t: There is an 85% probability that a randomly chosen diseased patient has a higher marker value than a randomly chosen healthy patient
med-epi-biostats.l12.q5.p: Two biomarkers for early pancreatic disease are compared. Marker X has an AUC of 0.85 and marker Y has an AUC of 0.65 in the same patients. A clinician asks what the AUC of 0.85 means. Which interpretation is correct?
med-epi-biostats.l12.q5.h: AUC is a probability about pairs of patients.
med-epi-biostats.l12.q5.e: AUC is the chance that a random diseased person scores higher than a random healthy person. It is not a predictive value, and sensitivity and specificity vary along the curve.

med-epi-biostats.l13.q1.t: The mean is greater than the median because the long right tail pulls the mean upward
med-epi-biostats.l13.q1.p: In a right-skewed distribution such as hospital length of stay, how are the mean and median related?
med-epi-biostats.l13.q1.h: Which summary measure is pulled by extreme values?
med-epi-biostats.l13.q1.e: Extreme high values pull the mean toward the tail, so mean exceeds median in right skew. In symmetric data all three would coincide.

med-epi-biostats.l13.q2.t: About 100 to 140 mm Hg, which is two SD either side of the mean
med-epi-biostats.l13.q2.p: Systolic blood pressure in a population is approximately normal with mean 120 mm Hg and SD 10 mm Hg. Within roughly what range do 95% of individuals fall?
med-epi-biostats.l13.q2.e: Roughly 95% lie within 1.96 SD, about 100 to 140. One SD covers about 68% and three SD about 99.7%.

med-epi-biostats.l13.q3.t: A standard error of 2, found by dividing 12 by the square root of 36
med-epi-biostats.l13.q3.p: A sample of 36 patients has a standard deviation of 12 mm Hg. What is the standard error of the mean?
med-epi-biostats.l13.q3.h: The SEM scales with the square root of n.
med-epi-biostats.l13.q3.e: SEM = SD / sqrt(n) = 12 / 6 = 2. Dividing by n rather than its square root is a common slip.

med-epi-biostats.l13.q4.t: The mean exceeding the median and the large SD suggest right skew, so median with IQR is more suitable
med-epi-biostats.l13.q4.p: A trial reports baseline serum triglycerides as mean 210 and median 150 mg/dL, with SD 140. A resident states that the data are well described as normal. What is the best critique?
med-epi-biostats.l13.q4.h: Compare the mean with the median and the SD with the mean.
med-epi-biostats.l13.q4.e: A mean well above the median together with an SD that is large relative to the mean signals right skew. A mean greater than the median is right skew, not left.

med-epi-biostats.l13.q5.t: Around the 99th percentile, since values 2.5 SD above the mean are higher than about 99% of the cohort
med-epi-biostats.l13.q5.p: A cardiologist notes that a patient's ejection fraction is 2.5 SD above the cohort mean, which is approximately normal. Approximately where does the patient rank?
med-epi-biostats.l13.q5.e: A z of 2.5 corresponds to about the 99.4th percentile. One SD above the mean is about the 84th percentile, and z-scores do imply rank under normality.

med-epi-biostats.l14.q1.t: The probability of a result at least this extreme if the null hypothesis were true
med-epi-biostats.l14.q1.p: What does a p-value of 0.03 represent?
med-epi-biostats.l14.q1.h: It is conditional on the null hypothesis.
med-epi-biostats.l14.q1.e: The p-value is the chance of data at least as extreme assuming H0 and the model. It does not give the probability that H0 is true or that the effect is important.

med-epi-biostats.l14.q2.t: Power is 80%, the chance of detecting a true effect of the specified size
med-epi-biostats.l14.q2.p: A study has a type II error probability (beta) of 0.20. What is its power, and what does it mean?
med-epi-biostats.l14.q2.h: Power is the complement of beta.
med-epi-biostats.l14.q2.e: Power = 1 - beta = 80%, the chance of detecting a true effect of the assumed size. Rejecting a true null is a type I error, with probability alpha.

med-epi-biostats.l14.q3.t: 0.005 for each test, found by dividing 0.05 by 10
med-epi-biostats.l14.q3.p: A study tests 10 independent outcomes. To keep the family-wise type I error at 0.05 using the Bonferroni method, what significance threshold applies to each test?
med-epi-biostats.l14.q3.h: Divide alpha by the number of tests.
med-epi-biostats.l14.q3.e: Bonferroni uses alpha / k = 0.05 / 10 = 0.005. Using 0.05 for every test would let the overall false positive chance rise to about 40%.

med-epi-biostats.l14.q4.t: The conclusion is unsupported, because a small study may lack power and the result is inconclusive, not proof of no effect
med-epi-biostats.l14.q4.p: A trial of 12 patients per arm finds that a new analgesic lowers pain scores by 1.5 points, p = 0.12. The authors conclude that the drug is ineffective. What is the best evaluation?
med-epi-biostats.l14.q4.h: Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.
med-epi-biostats.l14.q4.e: A non-significant result in a small trial may reflect low power; the confidence interval would show which effect sizes remain plausible. Failing to reject H0 is not proof of no effect.

med-epi-biostats.l14.q5.t: The effect is statistically significant but probably too small to matter clinically
med-epi-biostats.l14.q5.p: A very large trial finds that a drug lowers systolic pressure by 1 mm Hg more than placebo, p < 0.001, with 95% CI 0.6 to 1.4. Which interpretation is best?
med-epi-biostats.l14.q5.h: Separate how certain the effect is from how large it is.
med-epi-biostats.l14.q5.e: With a very large n, trivial differences reach tiny p-values. The interval is narrow and excludes zero, so it is both precise and significant, but small.

med-epi-biostats.l15.q1.t: A hazard ratio with a 95% CI of 0.55 to 0.90, which excludes the null value of 1
med-epi-biostats.l15.q1.p: Which result is statistically significant at the two-sided 0.05 level?
med-epi-biostats.l15.q1.h: Check whether the interval contains the no-effect value.
med-epi-biostats.l15.q1.e: The null for ratios is 1, and an interval that excludes it indicates significance at the matching level. The other three intervals include their null value.

med-epi-biostats.l15.q2.t: About 1.1 to 8.9 mm Hg, using the estimate plus or minus 1.96 standard errors
med-epi-biostats.l15.q2.p: The mean difference in blood pressure between two groups is 5 mm Hg with a standard error of 2. What is the approximate 95% confidence interval?
med-epi-biostats.l15.q2.e: 5 plus or minus 1.96 x 2 = 5 plus or minus 3.92, about 1.1 to 8.9. One SE gives a 68% interval, not 95%.

med-epi-biostats.l15.q3.t: The interval would be about half as wide, because standard error falls with the square root of n
med-epi-biostats.l15.q3.p: A study of 400 patients finds a response rate of 20%, with a 95% CI of about 16% to 24%. What would happen to the width of the interval if the sample were four times larger with the same response rate?
med-epi-biostats.l15.q3.h: Standard error scales with the square root of sample size.
med-epi-biostats.l15.q3.e: Quadrupling n halves the SE and therefore halves the width. The interval would be roughly 18% to 22%.

med-epi-biostats.l15.q4.t: The trial is inconclusive on safety, because the interval is compatible with 40% fewer to a doubling of bleeding events
med-epi-biostats.l15.q4.p: A trial of a new anticoagulant reports a hazard ratio for major bleeding of 1.10 (95% CI 0.60 to 2.00). The sponsor states that the drug is safe. What is the best interpretation?
med-epi-biostats.l15.q4.h: Look at both ends of the interval, not only the point estimate.
med-epi-biostats.l15.q4.e: The interval spans from a substantial reduction to a doubling, so the data cannot exclude meaningful harm. The interval includes 1, so the result is not significant.

med-epi-biostats.l15.q5.t: The range reflects values compatible with the data, and the method captures the true value in about 95% of repeated samples
med-epi-biostats.l15.q5.p: A 95% CI for a relative risk is reported as 1.4 to 2.9. Which statement most accurately describes what the interval means?
med-epi-biostats.l15.q5.h: The 95% describes the long-run behavior of the method.
med-epi-biostats.l15.q5.e: The 95% refers to the procedure over repeated sampling, and the interval is read as the range of compatible values. Patients do not each have a risk ratio, and future studies would vary around their own estimates.

med-epi-biostats.l16.q1.t: One-way analysis of variance, followed by corrected post hoc comparisons
med-epi-biostats.l16.q1.p: Which test is appropriate for comparing the mean of a continuous outcome among three independent groups?
med-epi-biostats.l16.q1.h: Three or more means require a single omnibus test.
med-epi-biostats.l16.q1.e: ANOVA compares three or more means. Multiple unadjusted t-tests would inflate type I error.

med-epi-biostats.l16.q2.p: In a 2 x 2 table of 200 patients, 80 received a drug and 50 improved overall. Under independence, what is the expected number of improved patients among the 80 on the drug?
med-epi-biostats.l16.q2.h: Expected count equals row total times column total over grand total.
med-epi-biostats.l16.q2.e: (80 x 50) / 200 = 20. The overall improvement rate is 25%, and 25% of 80 is 20.

med-epi-biostats.l16.q3.t: Mann-Whitney U test, which compares ranks and does not assume normality
med-epi-biostats.l16.q3.p: Which test is the best choice for comparing a skewed continuous outcome in two small independent groups?
med-epi-biostats.l16.q3.h: Rank-based tests suit skewed data in small groups.
med-epi-biostats.l16.q3.e: The Mann-Whitney test is the nonparametric alternative to the unpaired t-test. The paired t-test is wrong because the groups are independent.

med-epi-biostats.l16.q4.t: The paired test uses within-patient differences, which removes between-person variability and increases power
med-epi-biostats.l16.q4.p: In a study of 25 patients each measured before and after a 12-week program, the investigators apply an unpaired t-test to the two sets of values and find p = 0.09. A statistician re-analyzes with the appropriate test and finds p = 0.01. Why did the result change?
med-epi-biostats.l16.q4.h: Think about what changes when each person serves as their own control.
med-epi-biostats.l16.q4.e: Pairing removes stable person-to-person differences, making the test more sensitive. It does not increase the number of patients. The unpaired test overstates the variability, giving a larger p-value, not a smaller one.

med-epi-biostats.l16.q5.t: The reader is incorrect, because r of 0.6 means steps explain about 36% of the variance, and correlation does not show cause
med-epi-biostats.l16.q5.p: A study reports a Pearson correlation of 0.6 between daily steps and HbA1c reduction. A reader concludes that increased walking causes 60% of the improvement in glycemic control. What is the best response?
med-epi-biostats.l16.q5.h: Square the coefficient to get the variance explained.
med-epi-biostats.l16.q5.e: r-squared = 0.36, so about 36% of the variance is shared, and correlation alone cannot show causation because of confounding or reverse causation.

med-epi-biostats.l17.q1.t: A participant's event has not been observed by the end of their follow-up, so only event-free time is known
med-epi-biostats.l17.q1.p: What does censoring mean in survival analysis?
med-epi-biostats.l17.q1.h: It concerns incomplete observation of time to event.
med-epi-biostats.l17.q1.e: Censored participants contribute event-free time until censoring. Deleting them biases the result, and an event that prevents the outcome describes a competing risk.

med-epi-biostats.l17.q2.p: Ten patients are at risk. One dies at month 2. One other is censored at month 3. Two of the remaining eight die at month 5. What is the Kaplan-Meier survival estimate just after month 5?
med-epi-biostats.l17.q2.h: Multiply the stepwise survival fractions, using the number at risk at each event time.
med-epi-biostats.l17.q2.e: S(2) = 9/10 = 0.90, and at month 5, 6 of 8 survive, so S = 0.90 x 0.75 = 0.675. Dividing by all 10 ignores censoring.

med-epi-biostats.l17.q3.t: At any moment, the instantaneous event rate is 40% lower in the treated group, assuming proportional hazards
med-epi-biostats.l17.q3.p: A Cox model reports a hazard ratio of 0.60 for a treatment versus control. Which interpretation is most accurate?
med-epi-biostats.l17.q3.h: A hazard is a rate among those still at risk.
med-epi-biostats.l17.q3.e: The HR compares instantaneous event rates under the proportional hazards assumption. It does not translate directly into longer survival or into 40% fewer total events.

med-epi-biostats.l17.q4.t: Immortal time bias, because treated patients had to survive until the prescription to be classified as treated
med-epi-biostats.l17.q4.p: A cohort study of statin use in older adults defines the treated group as anyone who filled a statin prescription at any point during follow-up, counting follow-up from the date of entry. Treated patients show remarkably low mortality. Which bias is most likely?
med-epi-biostats.l17.q4.h: Consider the period between entry and the first prescription.
med-epi-biostats.l17.q4.e: Time before first prescription is guaranteed to be event-free for those labelled as treated, producing spurious benefit. Competing risks and lead time are not the main problem here.

med-epi-biostats.l17.q5.t: The single hazard ratio is misleading, because crossing curves violate the proportional hazards assumption
med-epi-biostats.l17.q5.p: In a trial of surgery versus medical therapy, the Kaplan-Meier curves cross at 6 months: surgery has more early deaths and fewer later deaths. A single Cox hazard ratio of 0.85 is reported. What is the best critique?
med-epi-biostats.l17.q5.h: Think about what a constant HR assumes across time.
med-epi-biostats.l17.q5.e: Crossing curves mean the hazard ratio changes direction over time, so a single average HR misdescribes both phases. The log-rank test can compare two groups.

med-epi-biostats.l18.q1.t: It uses explicit, prespecified and reproducible methods to find and appraise all relevant studies
med-epi-biostats.l18.q1.p: What distinguishes a systematic review from a narrative review?
med-epi-biostats.l18.q1.h: The key is the method of selecting evidence, not the statistics.
med-epi-biostats.l18.q1.e: Systematic reviews follow a protocol with a documented search and appraisal. Meta-analysis is optional, and expert opinion alone is narrative.

med-epi-biostats.l18.q2.t: 0.48, because the precise study has four times the weight of the other
med-epi-biostats.l18.q2.p: Study A has effect 0.4 with SE 0.1, and study B has effect 0.8 with SE 0.2. Using inverse-variance weights, what is the pooled effect?
med-epi-biostats.l18.q2.h: Weights are the reciprocals of the variances.
med-epi-biostats.l18.q2.e: Weights are 100 and 25, so the pooled effect = (40 + 20) / 125 = 0.48. A simple average ignores precision, and weights are inversely, not directly, related to SE.

med-epi-biostats.l18.q3.t: I-squared of 60%, indicating substantial heterogeneity between studies
med-epi-biostats.l18.q3.p: A meta-analysis reports a Cochran Q of 20 with 8 degrees of freedom. What is I-squared, and how should it be read?
med-epi-biostats.l18.q3.e: I-squared = (20 - 8) / 20 = 60%, suggesting substantial heterogeneity, which would favor a random-effects model and an exploration of its causes.

med-epi-biostats.l18.q4.t: Publication bias or small-study effects, so the pooled estimate probably overstates the true effect
med-epi-biostats.l18.q4.p: A funnel plot from a meta-analysis of 25 trials of a supplement shows that small trials with negative results are missing, and the pooled effect shrinks when only the largest trials are analyzed. Which explanation is most consistent with this?
med-epi-biostats.l18.q4.h: Which studies are missing from the plot, and why?
med-epi-biostats.l18.q4.e: Asymmetry with missing small negative studies suggests publication bias or small-study effects. Blinded assessment reduces, not creates, detection bias.

med-epi-biostats.l18.q5.t: Pooling cannot reduce confounding, because it combines biased estimates into a more precise but still possibly biased one
med-epi-biostats.l18.q5.p: A 2020 meta-analysis pools 18 observational cohort studies on coffee and cancer and reports a precise relative risk of 0.90 (95% CI 0.88 to 0.92). A trainee says that pooling resolves confounding. What is the best response?
med-epi-biostats.l18.q5.h: A narrow interval describes precision, not freedom from bias.
med-epi-biostats.l18.q5.e: Meta-analysis shrinks random error but does not fix systematic error shared across studies. Observational studies can be pooled, and pooling raises, not lowers, the sample size.

med-epi-biostats.l19.q1.t: A cohort study following patients with the disease over time to record outcomes
med-epi-biostats.l19.q1.p: Which study design best answers a question about the prognosis of a disease?
med-epi-biostats.l19.q1.h: Prognosis concerns what happens over time.
med-epi-biostats.l19.q1.e: Prognosis questions use cohort designs. Diagnostic accuracy needs a reference standard comparison, and treatment questions use trials.

med-epi-biostats.l19.q2.t: The claim of protection from serious events is unsupported, because the least important component drives the composite
med-epi-biostats.l19.q2.p: A trial of an antihypertensive reports a significant 40% relative reduction in a composite of death, stroke and hospitalization for dizziness. All of the benefit comes from hospitalizations for dizziness. What is the best interpretation?
med-epi-biostats.l19.q2.e: A composite driven by a soft component does not show benefit on death or stroke. Composites are acceptable when components are reported separately and importance is considered.

med-epi-biostats.l19.q3.t: Eligibility criteria that excluded patients over 70 and those with significant comorbidity
med-epi-biostats.l19.q3.p: Which feature of a trial most directly limits its applicability to a 79-year-old patient with multiple comorbidities?
med-epi-biostats.l19.q3.h: Ask whether the trial included people like the patient.
med-epi-biostats.l19.q3.e: External validity depends on who was enrolled. Allocation concealment, randomization and ITT affect internal validity, not whether the population resembles the patient.

med-epi-biostats.l19.q4.t: Outcome switching, which raises the chance of a false positive and warrants comparison with the registry
med-epi-biostats.l19.q4.p: A registered trial lists "change in HbA1c at 12 weeks" as its primary outcome, found no difference, and was published with a new primary outcome of "proportion with weight loss over 5%", which was significant. What is the main concern?
med-epi-biostats.l19.q4.h: Compare what was prespecified with what was reported.
med-epi-biostats.l19.q4.e: Replacing a null primary outcome with a positive secondary one inflates false positive findings, and the trial registry reveals it. The other biases are not described.

med-epi-biostats.l19.q5.t: This can be reasonable when benefits clearly outweigh harms, though it should be revisited as better evidence appears
med-epi-biostats.l19.q5.p: A guideline panel gives a strong recommendation for an intervention that reduces mortality from a rapidly fatal condition, although the evidence comes from low-certainty observational data. Which statement is most appropriate?
med-epi-biostats.l19.q5.h: Strength of recommendation and certainty of evidence are separate judgments.
med-epi-biostats.l19.q5.e: Grading systems separate the two, allowing strong recommendations on weak evidence when the balance of harm and benefit is obvious. Observational data are acceptable evidence, especially when no trial is feasible.

med-epi-biostats.l20.q1.t: Retraction, which withdraws a paper whose findings are considered unreliable
med-epi-biostats.l20.q1.p: Which of the following is the most severe route of correcting the published record?
med-epi-biostats.l20.q1.h: One route removes the paper's standing as reliable evidence.
med-epi-biostats.l20.q1.e: Retraction withdraws the paper. Corrections and expressions of concern are lesser steps, and a letter does not alter the paper at all.

med-epi-biostats.l20.q2.t: Healthy-user confounding, because women who chose hormone therapy were healthier in other ways
med-epi-biostats.l20.q2.p: Observational studies suggested that menopausal hormone therapy prevented coronary disease, but the randomized Women's Health Initiative reported no cardiac protection and more coronary events. Which explanation accounts for much of the discrepancy?
med-epi-biostats.l20.q2.h: Who chose to take hormones in the observational studies?
med-epi-biostats.l20.q2.e: Women who used hormone therapy tended to be healthier and wealthier, which confounded observational comparisons. Randomization removes this self-selection.

med-epi-biostats.l20.q3.t: A drug that improves a surrogate marker may still harm the outcomes patients care about
med-epi-biostats.l20.q3.p: In the Cardiac Arrhythmia Suppression Trial, drugs that suppressed ventricular ectopy after myocardial infarction were associated with higher mortality. What general lesson does this teach?
med-epi-biostats.l20.q3.h: The marker improved, and the patients did not.
med-epi-biostats.l20.q3.e: Suppressing ectopy was a plausible surrogate, but it did not translate into survival and mortality increased. Randomized outcome trials are what exposed this.

med-epi-biostats.l20.q4.t: A case series has no comparison group or denominator, so it cannot show that exposure is more common in cases than in others
med-epi-biostats.l20.q4.p: A 1998 case series of 12 children reported a link between MMR vaccination and a new syndrome of autism and bowel disease. Later, most co-authors withdrew the interpretation, a regulator found serious professional misconduct, and the journal retracted the paper. Which statement best captures why a case series of this kind could not support the claim?
med-epi-biostats.l20.q4.h: Think about what comparison the design allows.
med-epi-biostats.l20.q4.e: Without controls or a denominator, a series can generate a hypothesis but cannot test it. Large controlled studies later found no association.

med-epi-biostats.l20.q5.t: Reversal is common when practice rests on weak evidence, so a well-designed sham trial deserves serious weight
med-epi-biostats.l20.q5.p: A 64-year-old patient asks whether an established procedure that has been standard for 20 years should be doubted after a new sham-controlled trial found no benefit. What is the best framing?
med-epi-biostats.l20.q5.h: Weigh the design quality of the new trial and the basis of the old practice.
med-epi-biostats.l20.q5.e: Practices adopted from physiology and observational data are often overturned by controlled trials, and blinded sham comparison controls for placebo effects. A single trial is weighed in context and is not automatically conclusive.

med-ethics-hs.l01.q1.p: Which set correctly names the four principles in the Beauchamp and Childress framework?
med-ethics-hs.l01.q1.h: Two of them are about doing good and avoiding harm.
med-ethics-hs.l01.q1.e: The four principles are autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence and justice. The other sets mix in duties that belong to other lists.

med-ethics-hs.l01.q2.t: Each binds unless it conflicts with a weightier principle in the situation
med-ethics-hs.l01.q2.p: What does it mean to call the principles prima facie?
med-ethics-hs.l01.q2.h: Think of a duty that can be outweighed.
med-ethics-hs.l01.q2.e: Prima facie duties are binding unless outweighed by another. They are not ranked in a fixed order, and they are not mere suggestions.

med-ethics-hs.l01.q3.p: A capable adult declines a treatable infection's antibiotics after a full discussion. Which principle most directly supports respecting the refusal?
med-ethics-hs.l01.q3.h: The patient is the decision-maker for their own body.
med-ethics-hs.l01.q3.e: Respect for the choices of a capable patient is autonomy. Beneficence and non-maleficence would point toward treatment.

med-ethics-hs.l01.q4.t: Justice, because scarce benefits should be distributed by fair criteria that are relevant to need and outcome
med-ethics-hs.l01.q4.p: A hospital must decide how to distribute a limited number of ICU beds during a surge. A committee proposes giving priority by medical need and likelihood of benefit rather than social status. Which principle is the committee mainly applying, and what does it require?
med-ethics-hs.l01.q4.h: The question is about fair distribution of a scarce resource.
med-ethics-hs.l01.q4.e: Allocation by relevant criteria is justice. Non-maleficence does not forbid triage in scarcity, and financial return is not an ethical criterion.

med-ethics-hs.l02.q1.t: an adult of sound mind has a right to decide what is done to his own body
med-ethics-hs.l02.q1.p: In Schloendorff v. Society of New York Hospital (1914), the court recognized that:
med-ethics-hs.l02.q1.h: Judge Cardozo wrote about the right of self-determination.
med-ethics-hs.l02.q1.e: Schloendorff established that surgery without consent is a legal wrong. Entering a hospital does not forfeit that right.

med-ethics-hs.l02.q2.t: The reasonable patient standard, based on risks material to a patient's decision
med-ethics-hs.l02.q2.p: Canterbury v. Spence (D.C. Cir. 1972) is associated with which disclosure standard?
med-ethics-hs.l02.q2.h: The question is whose view of materiality counts.
med-ethics-hs.l02.q2.e: Canterbury looks to what a reasonable patient would want to know. The older approach follows physician custom.

med-ethics-hs.l02.q3.t: It is decision-specific and can be present for one decision but not another
med-ethics-hs.l02.q3.p: Which feature of capacity is most accurate?
med-ethics-hs.l02.q3.h: Capacity depends on the task at hand.
med-ethics-hs.l02.q3.e: Capacity is assessed for a particular decision. Disagreeing with a doctor is not evidence of incapacity.

med-ethics-hs.l02.q4.t: Respect her informed refusal while offering non-blood alternatives and continuing to discuss
med-ethics-hs.l02.q4.p: A 68-year-old woman with a bleeding gastric ulcer is alert, understands that refusing a transfusion may kill her, explains that it conflicts with her religious faith, and has said the same for years. Which is the most ethically and legally appropriate response?
med-ethics-hs.l02.q4.h: She understands, appreciates, reasons and is consistent.
med-ethics-hs.l02.q4.e: A capable adult may refuse treatment, including life-saving treatment. Overriding her would violate autonomy, and illness alone does not show incapacity.

med-ethics-hs.l02.q5.p: An unconscious trauma patient arrives bleeding heavily with no family present. Treatment is begun without a signed form. Which doctrine justifies this?
med-ethics-hs.l02.q5.h: The patient cannot speak and delay would be dangerous.
med-ethics-hs.l02.q5.e: In true emergencies, consent is presumed. Therapeutic privilege concerns withholding information, not emergencies.

med-ethics-hs.l03.q1.t: It encourages honest disclosure, which supports both individual care and public health
med-ethics-hs.l03.q1.p: Which statement best describes the role of confidentiality in medicine?
med-ethics-hs.l03.q1.h: Think about why patients speak candidly.
med-ethics-hs.l03.q1.e: Confidentiality builds the trust needed for candid disclosure. It has recognized exceptions and covers spoken information too.

med-ethics-hs.l03.q2.t: Mandated reporting of suspected child abuse
med-ethics-hs.l03.q2.p: Which is a common legal exception to confidentiality in many places?
med-ethics-hs.l03.q2.h: Think of a situation where the law requires a report.
med-ethics-hs.l03.q2.e: Mandated reporting of suspected abuse is a standard exception. The others are improper disclosures without authorization.

med-ethics-hs.l03.q3.t: use reasonable care to protect the intended victim
med-ethics-hs.l03.q3.p: In Tarasoff v. Regents of the University of California (Cal. 1976), the court held that a therapist who determines a patient is a serious danger to another person must:
med-ethics-hs.l03.q3.h: The duty runs to the potential victim.
med-ethics-hs.l03.q3.e: Tarasoff recognized a duty to use reasonable care to protect the victim. States differ on how they implement it.

med-ethics-hs.l03.q4.t: Provide care, explain confidentiality and its limits, and encourage her to involve a trusted adult
med-ethics-hs.l03.q4.p: A 16-year-old tells a clinic physician she is sexually active and wants contraception and asks that her parents not be told. Local law permits minors to consent to contraception. What is the best approach?
med-ethics-hs.l03.q4.h: Combine legal permission, honesty about limits, and support.
med-ethics-hs.l03.q4.e: When the law allows minor consent, the clinician honors confidentiality and is open about its limits. A promise of absolute secrecy would be wrong if abuse emerges.

med-ethics-hs.l04.q1.t: A diagnosis does not by itself mean a person lacks capacity for a decision
med-ethics-hs.l04.q1.p: Which statement about psychiatric diagnosis and capacity is most accurate?
med-ethics-hs.l04.q1.h: Capacity is assessed one decision at a time.
med-ethics-hs.l04.q1.e: Many people with psychiatric diagnoses retain capacity for most decisions. Capacity is specific to the decision.

med-ethics-hs.l04.q2.t: A mental disorder together with danger to self or others
med-ethics-hs.l04.q2.p: Which of these is a typical legal criterion for involuntary commitment in many US states?
med-ethics-hs.l04.q2.h: The state needs both illness and risk.
med-ethics-hs.l04.q2.e: Typical standards combine a mental disorder with dangerousness or, in some states, grave disability. Disagreeing with a doctor is not enough.

med-ethics-hs.l04.q3.t: A state may not confine a non-dangerous person who can live safely in freedom simply because of mental illness
med-ethics-hs.l04.q3.p: What did the Supreme Court hold in O'Connor v. Donaldson (1975)?
med-ethics-hs.l04.q3.h: The case limited confinement based on diagnosis alone.
med-ethics-hs.l04.q3.e: The Court held that mental illness alone is not sufficient to confine someone who is not dangerous and can live safely. The other options overstate the holding.

med-ethics-hs.l04.q4.t: Autonomy extended across time, since the directive reflects his considered values while well
med-ethics-hs.l04.q4.p: A man with schizophrenia, stable on medication, writes a psychiatric advance directive during remission stating which treatments he accepts in a future relapse. During a later relapse he refuses admission. Which ethical idea best supports giving weight to his directive?
med-ethics-hs.l04.q4.h: The directive speaks for the person when they are unwell.
med-ethics-hs.l04.q4.e: Advance directives extend autonomy across time. Beneficence does not automatically override the patient's prior considered wishes.

med-ethics-hs.l05.q1.t: The voluntary consent of the human subject is absolutely essential
med-ethics-hs.l05.q1.p: What is the first principle of the Nuremberg Code?
med-ethics-hs.l05.q1.h: It begins the Code and concerns the subject's choice.
med-ethics-hs.l05.q1.e: Voluntary consent leads the Code. Social value alone does not justify an experiment, and payment is not one of the principles.

med-ethics-hs.l05.q2.t: The Doctors' Trial held after the Second World War
med-ethics-hs.l05.q2.p: The Nuremberg Code arose from which event?
med-ethics-hs.l05.q2.h: Think of the trials of Nazi physicians.
med-ethics-hs.l05.q2.e: The Code was part of the judgment in the Doctors' Trial at Nuremberg. The other events are unrelated to its origin.

med-ethics-hs.l05.q3.t: It was written by the medical profession and added independent review of research protocols
med-ethics-hs.l05.q3.p: How does the Declaration of Helsinki (1964) differ from the Nuremberg Code?
med-ethics-hs.l05.q3.h: The World Medical Association wrote it.
med-ethics-hs.l05.q3.e: Helsinki is a professional statement that includes independent review. The Nuremberg Code came from a criminal judgment.

med-ethics-hs.l05.q4.t: Benefit to society cannot replace voluntary informed consent of each subject
med-ethics-hs.l05.q4.p: A researcher argues that a dangerous experiment on prisoners is justified because the knowledge gained would save thousands of lives. Under the Nuremberg Code, what is the best response?
med-ethics-hs.l05.q4.h: The first principle is not outweighed by expected benefit.
med-ethics-hs.l05.q4.e: The Code treats voluntary consent as essential, so benefit to others cannot substitute. Permission from officials is not consent from the subjects.

med-ethics-hs.l06.q1.t: Participants were not offered effective treatment and were not told the truth
med-ethics-hs.l06.q1.p: What was the central ethical failure of the Tuskegee study after penicillin became standard for syphilis?
med-ethics-hs.l06.q1.h: The men were deceived and denied known treatment.
med-ethics-hs.l06.q1.e: The men were deceived and withheld from treatment. The study actually continued for forty years.

med-ethics-hs.l06.q2.t: Respect for persons, beneficence and justice
med-ethics-hs.l06.q2.p: Which three principles are named in the Belmont Report (1979)?
med-ethics-hs.l06.q2.h: They underlie IRB review in the United States.
med-ethics-hs.l06.q2.e: Belmont names respect for persons, beneficence and justice. The other lists are invented combinations.

med-ethics-hs.l06.q3.t: Institutional review boards for federally funded research with human subjects
med-ethics-hs.l06.q3.p: What did the National Research Act of 1974 require?
med-ethics-hs.l06.q3.h: It created a system of local oversight.
med-ethics-hs.l06.q3.e: The Act required IRB review and created the commission that wrote Belmont. It did not ban research.

med-ethics-hs.l06.q4.t: Justice, because burdens and benefits should be fairly distributed in selecting subjects
med-ethics-hs.l06.q4.p: A committee reviewing a trial notices that all participants are drawn from one low-income community, while the likely beneficiaries are wealthy patients elsewhere. Which Belmont principle is most directly implicated?
med-ethics-hs.l06.q4.h: Think about who bears risk and who gains.
med-ethics-hs.l06.q4.e: Fair subject selection is justice. Low income does not mean lack of capacity to consent.

med-ethics-hs.l07.q1.t: They were the first human cells to grow continuously in the laboratory
med-ethics-hs.l07.q1.p: What made HeLa cells scientifically significant?
med-ethics-hs.l07.q1.h: Her cells could divide again and again outside the body.
med-ethics-hs.l07.q1.e: HeLa was the first immortal human cell line. Cells had been removed from humans before, and the line was not hybrid with plants.

med-ethics-hs.l07.q2.t: doctors must disclose research and financial interests, but the patient had no property right in the cells
med-ethics-hs.l07.q2.p: In Moore v. Regents of the University of California (1990), the court held that:
med-ethics-hs.l07.q2.h: The ruling was split between disclosure and ownership.
med-ethics-hs.l07.q2.e: Moore recognized a disclosure duty, not a property right. Doctors cannot hide financial interests.

med-ethics-hs.l07.q3.t: Ask what the law required in 1951 and, separately, what respect for persons suggests now
med-ethics-hs.l07.q3.p: Which approach best separates the legal and ethical questions in the Lacks story?
med-ethics-hs.l07.q3.h: Law and ethics are not identical.
med-ethics-hs.l07.q3.e: Legality and ethics can diverge. Distinguishing them lets us judge past conduct fairly and improve present rules.

med-ethics-hs.l07.q4.t: Genetic data can reveal information about donors and relatives, and donors may object to uses they did not expect
med-ethics-hs.l07.q4.p: A biobank wants to reuse stored, identifiable tissue samples for a new genetic study that donors never heard about. Which consideration most strongly favors asking donors again or obtaining broad consent upfront?
med-ethics-hs.l07.q4.h: Think about what genetic results can reveal.
med-ethics-hs.l07.q4.e: Genetic data can be sensitive and affect families, which supports meaningful consent. Courts such as Moore did not recognize a property right in tissue.

med-ethics-hs.l08.q1.t: To review proposed human research for risk, fairness, consent and privacy
med-ethics-hs.l08.q1.p: What is the main purpose of an institutional review board?
med-ethics-hs.l08.q1.h: It acts before the study begins.
med-ethics-hs.l08.q1.e: IRBs review protocols to protect participants. Funding and journal publication are different functions.

med-ethics-hs.l08.q2.t: Genuine uncertainty among experts about which treatment is better
med-ethics-hs.l08.q2.h: It is the ethical justification for randomizing.
med-ethics-hs.l08.q2.e: Equipoise is real expert uncertainty. Equal group sizes are a design matter, not an ethical concept.

med-ethics-hs.l08.q3.t: They may be more easily coerced or less able to protect their own interests
med-ethics-hs.l08.q3.p: Why do extra protections apply to groups such as prisoners and children in research?
med-ethics-hs.l08.q3.e: Vulnerability to coercion or limited ability to protect oneself justifies extra safeguards. Everyone has the right to withdraw.

med-ethics-hs.l08.q4.t: Equipoise is absent, so withholding a known effective therapy exposes the control group to serious harm
med-ethics-hs.l08.q4.p: Researchers want to test a new drug for a serious infection for which an effective antibiotic already exists. They propose giving half the participants only a sugar pill. What is the strongest ethical objection?
med-ethics-hs.l08.q4.h: A good treatment is already known.
med-ethics-hs.l08.q4.e: When effective treatment exists for a serious condition, a placebo-only control usually fails equipoise and risks harm. Placebos are not generally illegal, and consent is possible.

med-ethics-hs.l09.q1.t: Liberty may be limited to prevent harm to others
med-ethics-hs.l09.q1.p: Which idea is most closely associated with the harm principle?
med-ethics-hs.l09.q1.e: The harm principle allows limits to prevent harm to others, not simple paternalism or majority preference.

med-ethics-hs.l09.q2.t: A state law requiring smallpox vaccination or payment of a modest fine
med-ethics-hs.l09.q2.p: What did Jacobson v. Massachusetts (1905) uphold?
med-ethics-hs.l09.q2.h: A Massachusetts local board and a smallpox rule.
med-ethics-hs.l09.q2.e: The Court upheld a vaccination requirement with a small penalty under state police power. It did not authorize forced vaccination.

med-ethics-hs.l09.q3.t: Quarantine separates exposed people who may become ill, and isolation separates people who are sick
med-ethics-hs.l09.q3.p: Which pair correctly distinguishes quarantine from isolation?
med-ethics-hs.l09.q3.e: Quarantine is for people who may have been exposed, and isolation is for those known to be infected.

med-ethics-hs.l09.q4.t: Proportionality, since the burden may be far greater than the expected public health benefit
med-ethics-hs.l09.q4.p: A city proposes closing all parks for six months to slow a mildly contagious illness that is rarely severe. Which ethical criterion most clearly raises concern?
med-ethics-hs.l09.q4.h: Consider burden against benefit and the least restrictive means.
med-ethics-hs.l09.q4.e: A drastic measure for a mild threat may not be proportionate or least restrictive. Equal application alone does not make it justified.

med-ethics-hs.l10.q1.t: Buying or selling human organs for valuable consideration
med-ethics-hs.l10.q1.p: What does the National Organ Transplant Act of 1984 prohibit in the United States?
med-ethics-hs.l10.q1.e: The Act bars the sale of organs. Donation by family members and registering as a donor remain lawful.

med-ethics-hs.l10.q2.t: A person is presumed to be a donor unless they register an objection
med-ethics-hs.l10.q2.p: Which describes an opt-out (presumed consent) system?
med-ethics-hs.l10.q2.e: Opt-out systems presume willingness unless a person objects. The United States uses opt-in.

med-ethics-hs.l10.q3.t: vital organs be taken only from a person who is dead, and procurement not cause death
med-ethics-hs.l10.q3.p: The dead donor rule requires that:
med-ethics-hs.l10.q3.h: It concerns the status of the person from whom organs are taken.
med-ethics-hs.l10.q3.e: The rule prevents procurement from causing death. It says nothing about waiting time or relatives.

med-ethics-hs.l10.q4.t: Medical urgency and expected benefit can conflict, so allocation rules must weigh both fairly
med-ethics-hs.l10.q4.p: Two patients need a liver. One is critically ill and has a high chance of dying within days, with moderate expected benefit from transplant. The other is stable, with a slightly better expected outcome. Which statement best describes the ethical tension?
med-ethics-hs.l10.q4.e: Allocation balances urgency, benefit and fairness, and neither wealth nor private negotiation is an accepted criterion.

med-ethics-hs.l11.q1.t: Somatic changes are not inherited, whereas germline changes can be passed to descendants
med-ethics-hs.l11.q1.p: What is the difference between somatic and germline gene editing?
med-ethics-hs.l11.q1.e: Germline edits alter reproductive cells or embryos and are heritable. Somatic edits affect only the treated person.

med-ethics-hs.l11.q2.t: Discrimination by health insurers and employers based on genetic information
med-ethics-hs.l11.q2.p: What does the Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act of 2008 cover?
med-ethics-hs.l11.q2.e: GINA covers health insurance and employment. It does not cover life, disability or long-term care insurance.

med-ethics-hs.l11.q3.t: the birth of children from gene-edited embryos, with unresolved safety and consent concerns
med-ethics-hs.l11.q3.p: The announcement by He Jiankui in 2018 was widely condemned mainly because it involved:
med-ethics-hs.l11.q3.h: It concerned heritable changes to embryos.
med-ethics-hs.l11.q3.e: The work produced babies from edited embryos, a heritable change, without adequate safety or oversight.

med-ethics-hs.l11.q4.t: That selection may express a devaluing message about the lives of people with the condition
med-ethics-hs.l11.q4.p: A couple who are both carriers of a recessive condition use in vitro fertilization and preimplantation genetic testing to select an unaffected embryo. Which concern would a disability-rights critic most likely raise?
med-ethics-hs.l11.q4.h: The critique is about meaning and social attitudes.
med-ethics-hs.l11.q4.e: The expressive objection is that selection sends a negative message about living with disability. Selection is not editing, and recessive carriers can be tested.

med-ethics-hs.l12.q1.t: The Constitution does not confer a right to abortion, and the matter returns to the states
med-ethics-hs.l12.q1.p: What did Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization (2022) decide?
med-ethics-hs.l12.q1.e: Dobbs overruled Roe and Casey and left regulation to the states. It did not create a federal ban.

med-ethics-hs.l12.q2.t: moral status grows over time, so early and late abortion may be judged differently
med-ethics-hs.l12.q2.p: A gradualist view of the moral status of the fetus holds that:
med-ethics-hs.l12.q2.e: Gradualist views tie moral status to development, such as viability or sentience. They are distinct from conception-based and birth-based views.

med-ethics-hs.l12.q3.t: The current law is a matter of fact that varies by place, whereas the moral arguments remain contested
med-ethics-hs.l12.q3.p: Which statement best separates law from argument in this lesson?
med-ethics-hs.l12.q3.h: One is descriptive and the other is normative.
med-ethics-hs.l12.q3.e: Law describes rules in force, while ethics debates what ought to be. The two can diverge, and law differs by place.

med-ethics-hs.l12.q4.t: It depends mainly on a disagreement over the moral status of the embryo, which leads to different views on discarding or donation
med-ethics-hs.l12.q4.p: A fertility clinic has several frozen embryos that the couple no longer needs. One person says the embryos have the moral status of persons, and another says they are clusters of cells with potential. Which is the most accurate analysis of their disagreement?
med-ethics-hs.l12.q4.h: Find the premise beneath the argument.
med-ethics-hs.l12.q4.e: The root disagreement concerns embryo status. Storage cost and past fertility history do not explain the moral dispute.

med-ethics-hs.l13.q1.t: Removal of a ventilator from a patient in a persistent vegetative state at her guardian's request
med-ethics-hs.l13.q1.p: What did the New Jersey Supreme Court allow in In re Quinlan (1976)?
med-ethics-hs.l13.q1.h: The case concerned a ventilator and a young woman.
med-ethics-hs.l13.q1.e: The court allowed withdrawal of ventilation based on privacy rights. It did not authorize active euthanasia.

med-ethics-hs.l13.q2.t: Clear and convincing evidence of the incompetent patient's wishes
med-ethics-hs.l13.q2.p: What standard did Cruzan v. Director, Missouri Department of Health (1990) permit a state to require?
med-ethics-hs.l13.q2.h: It is a middle evidentiary standard.
med-ethics-hs.l13.q2.e: Cruzan allowed states to require clear and convincing evidence. It did not require a criminal standard or give spouses automatic authority.

med-ethics-hs.l13.q3.t: They are generally seen as morally equivalent when a patient may refuse the treatment
med-ethics-hs.l13.q3.p: Which statement about withholding and withdrawing life-sustaining treatment reflects the mainstream ethical view?
med-ethics-hs.l13.q3.h: The intention and the patient's right to refuse are the same.
med-ethics-hs.l13.q3.e: Most ethicists treat them as equivalent because the underlying right to refuse applies equally. Treating them differently can lead patients to avoid trying treatment.

med-ethics-hs.l13.q4.t: The doctrine of double effect, because the intent is relief of pain and the earlier death is a foreseen side effect
med-ethics-hs.l13.q4.p: A 79-year-old woman with terminal cancer asks her doctor for medicine to relieve intense pain, understanding that high doses may slightly shorten her life. The doctor intends only to relieve suffering. Which doctrine best explains why many ethicists consider this acceptable?
med-ethics-hs.l13.q4.h: Intention and foreseen side effects matter here.
med-ethics-hs.l13.q4.e: Double effect distinguishes intended relief from a foreseen, unintended risk. The dead donor rule concerns organ procurement.

med-ethics-hs.l13.q5.t: there is no constitutional right to assisted suicide, and states may regulate it
med-ethics-hs.l13.q5.p: In Washington v. Glucksberg (1997), the Supreme Court held that:
med-ethics-hs.l13.q5.h: The decision left the matter to state legislatures.
med-ethics-hs.l13.q5.e: Glucksberg found no constitutional right to assisted suicide but left states free to decide. It did not mandate or ban it nationwide.

med-ethics-hs.l14.q1.t: To set fair rules in advance for allocating scarce resources during a crisis
med-ethics-hs.l14.q1.p: What is the purpose of crisis standards of care?
med-ethics-hs.l14.q1.e: These standards guide fair allocation in advance. Wealth and social status are not accepted criteria.

med-ethics-hs.l14.q2.t: First come, first served, because it favors those who can reach the hospital fastest
med-ethics-hs.l14.q2.p: Which criterion do most triage ethicists reject as the sole basis for ranking patients?
med-ethics-hs.l14.q2.h: One criterion rewards luck and access.
med-ethics-hs.l14.q2.e: Pure first-come order rewards access and chance. The other options are commonly accepted features of triage plans.

med-ethics-hs.l14.q3.t: It can rest on stereotypes and may violate disability discrimination law
med-ethics-hs.l14.q3.p: Why might excluding patients with disabilities from ventilators on the basis of assumed quality of life be criticized?
med-ethics-hs.l14.q3.h: Consider the Americans with Disabilities Act.
med-ethics-hs.l14.q3.e: Assumptions about quality of life are not evidence of short-term benefit and can be discriminatory. The other effects are not implied.

med-ethics-hs.l14.q4.t: Priority based on likely benefit and non-abandonment, with decisions separated from the treating team
med-ethics-hs.l14.q4.p: During a surge, a plan allocates the last ventilator to the patient with the best short-term survival odds, assessed by a triage team separate from the bedside clinicians, and offers palliative care to the other patient. Which two ethical features does this plan reflect?
med-ethics-hs.l14.q4.h: Look for benefit, fairness and continued care.
med-ethics-hs.l14.q4.e: The plan uses expected benefit, separates the triage decision and keeps caring for the other patient. The alternatives rely on discredited or arbitrary criteria.

med-ethics-hs.l15.q1.t: The tendency to over-trust the output of an automated system
med-ethics-hs.l15.q1.e: Automation bias is human over-reliance on a machine's answer. It is not a machine attitude or a legal rule.

med-ethics-hs.l15.q2.t: The data may reflect past inequities, and a poorly chosen prediction target can carry that bias
med-ethics-hs.l15.q2.p: Why can an algorithm trained on historical data produce unjust results?
med-ethics-hs.l15.q2.h: Think about what the model learns from.
med-ethics-hs.l15.q2.e: Models learn patterns in data that may encode inequity, as when cost was used as a proxy for need. They are not forbidden from using data.

med-ethics-hs.l15.q3.t: Test it on its own patients and equipment, and keep monitoring it after use begins
med-ethics-hs.l15.q3.p: A model for detecting disease from images performed well at the hospital that built it. What should a new hospital do before relying on it?
med-ethics-hs.l15.q3.e: Local validation and monitoring are needed because patients and equipment differ. Removing human review would be unsafe.

med-ethics-hs.l15.q4.t: The model's target, such as past spending, may be a biased proxy for actual need
med-ethics-hs.l15.q4.p: A hospital deploys an AI tool that flags which patients should receive extra care management. Months later, an audit finds that at the same risk score, patients from one racial group are sicker than patients from another. Which diagnosis of the problem is most consistent with the 2019 Science study discussed in the lesson?
med-ethics-hs.l15.q4.h: What did the model actually predict?
med-ethics-hs.l15.q4.e: A proxy such as spending can understate need for groups with less access to care. Mathematics does not guarantee fairness, and removing health data would defeat the purpose.
