med-ethics-prof.l01.q1.p: Which set correctly lists the four principles of principlism as set out by Beauchamp and Childress?
med-ethics-prof.l01.q1.h: Two of them concern harm and benefit separately.
med-ethics-prof.l01.q1.e: The framework uses respect for autonomy, nonmaleficence, beneficence and justice. Fidelity and veracity are derived rules, and utility and reciprocity are not among the four.

med-ethics-prof.l01.q2.t: It binds unless it conflicts with an equal or stronger duty in the particular circumstances
med-ethics-prof.l01.q2.p: What does it mean to say a principle is prima facie binding?
med-ethics-prof.l01.q2.h: Think of a duty that can be outweighed.
med-ethics-prof.l01.q2.e: A prima facie duty holds unless outweighed by a stronger duty in context. An absolute duty cannot be overridden, which principlism rejects.

med-ethics-prof.l01.q3.t: The duty not to harm is generally more stringent than the duty to provide benefit
med-ethics-prof.l01.q3.p: Why do Beauchamp and Childress treat nonmaleficence and beneficence as separate principles?
med-ethics-prof.l01.q3.h: Compare how strongly each duty binds.
med-ethics-prof.l01.q3.e: Avoiding harm usually carries more weight than conferring benefit, so the principles behave differently. They do not apply to separate professions and can conflict.

med-ethics-prof.l01.q4.t: Autonomy is decisive because capacity and understanding are intact; the team explores her reasons, offers alternatives and respects the refusal
med-ethics-prof.l01.q4.p: A competent 58-year-old Jehovah's Witness with a bleeding gastric ulcer, fully informed that transfusion may be lifesaving, declines blood products and accepts other treatment. Her surgeon strongly believes transfusion is in her interest. Which analysis best reflects principlism?
med-ethics-prof.l01.q4.h: Ask whether the choice is informed and made by someone with capacity.
med-ethics-prof.l01.q4.e: With capacity and understanding, her informed refusal governs, though the team should still explore it. The other options assume a fixed ranking that principlism denies.

med-ethics-prof.l01.q5.t: The framework supplies specification and balancing, requiring explicit reasons for how each principle is weighed in the case
med-ethics-prof.l01.q5.p: A critic says principlism is "a checklist" that gives no way to decide when autonomy conflicts with beneficence. Which response from within the framework is most accurate?
med-ethics-prof.l01.q5.h: The method has two named steps for conflicts.
med-ethics-prof.l01.q5.e: Specification and balancing with defensible reasons is the method. Ranking autonomy first is the unqualified priority principlism rejects, and conflicts are not left arbitrary.

med-ethics-prof.l02.q1.p: Which moral theory is most associated with the idea that persons must never be treated merely as means?
med-ethics-prof.l02.q1.h: It is the formulation tied to Immanuel Kant.
med-ethics-prof.l02.q1.e: Treating persons as ends is Kant's formula. Utilitarianism aggregates welfare, and virtue ethics asks about character.

med-ethics-prof.l02.q2.p: A hospital board evaluates a policy purely by asking which option yields the greatest total improvement in patient outcomes per dollar. Which approach is it using?
med-ethics-prof.l02.q2.h: Focus on outcomes counted in aggregate.
med-ethics-prof.l02.q2.e: Weighing aggregate outcomes is consequentialist. A deontologist would ask what duties and rights constrain the policy.

med-ethics-prof.l02.q3.t: The bad effect is foreseen but not intended as the means of achieving the good effect
med-ethics-prof.l02.q3.p: Which feature is a standard condition of the doctrine of double effect?
med-ethics-prof.l02.q3.h: The distinction is between intending and merely foreseeing.
med-ethics-prof.l02.q3.e: The bad effect may be foreseen but must not be the means to the good. If the good came through the bad, the doctrine would not permit it.

med-ethics-prof.l02.q4.t: Virtue ethics, because it evaluates settled character traits such as compassion and practical wisdom alongside rule following
med-ethics-prof.l02.q4.p: A surgeon who consistently follows consent protocols is nonetheless described by patients as curt and dismissive, and trust in her unit is falling. Which theoretical tradition best explains why compliance with rules does not exhaust what is wrong?
med-ethics-prof.l02.q4.h: Which theory is about the kind of person one is?
med-ethics-prof.l02.q4.e: Virtue ethics asks about character and so can criticise a rule-compliant but uncaring clinician. Utilitarianism does not say rules cannot matter, and legal positivism is not a moral theory of conduct.

med-ethics-prof.l02.q5.t: Rules protecting individuals, such as consent, tend to produce better outcomes overall, so the proposed policy would likely do more harm than good
med-ethics-prof.l02.q5.p: A utilitarian argument claims that a healthy patient should be sacrificed to supply organs to five dying patients. Which reply best reflects a sophisticated consequentialist position?
med-ethics-prof.l02.q5.h: Consider the long-run effects of such a practice on trust and safety.
med-ethics-prof.l02.q5.e: Indirect consequences, such as loss of trust and fear of hospitals, count against the policy. The theory does count lives, and organs are scarce.

med-ethics-prof.l03.q1.p: Which scholar is most closely associated with the development of narrative medicine?
med-ethics-prof.l03.q1.h: The method trains clinicians in close reading and reflective writing.
med-ethics-prof.l03.q1.e: Rita Charon developed narrative medicine. Gilligan is associated with care ethics, Jonsen with casuistry, and Beauchamp with principlism.

med-ethics-prof.l03.q2.t: Moral life is built from relationships of dependence and responsiveness, so attentiveness and responsibility are core moral activities
med-ethics-prof.l03.q2.p: What is the central ethical claim of care ethics about the nature of moral life?
med-ethics-prof.l03.q2.h: It challenges the picture of the patient as an isolated chooser.
med-ethics-prof.l03.q2.e: Care ethics centres relationships and responsiveness. The other options describe deontology, utilitarianism and authority-based ethics.

med-ethics-prof.l03.q3.t: Reasoning from paradigm cases to harder cases by analogy and attention to circumstances
med-ethics-prof.l03.q3.p: Which feature best describes casuistry as developed by Jonsen and Toulmin?
med-ethics-prof.l03.q3.h: Think of how common-law courts reason.
med-ethics-prof.l03.q3.e: Casuistry works by analogy to paradigm cases. Deduction from one supreme principle is a different, theory-driven method.

med-ethics-prof.l03.q4.t: Narrative competence, by attending to the meaning the illness and hospitals have within the patient's life story
med-ethics-prof.l03.q4.p: A 79-year-old man with end-stage lung disease repeatedly declines hospital admission. His clinicians see only non-adherence. Further conversation reveals that he cared for his wife in hospital for months before she died and now equates hospitals with loss of dignity. Which approach most directly brought this crucial information to light?
med-ethics-prof.l03.q4.h: The key finding is something only listening to his story would reveal.
med-ethics-prof.l03.q4.e: Narrative competence recovers the meaning behind his refusal. The other approaches do not look for personal meaning and would treat the refusal as a problem to be managed.

med-ethics-prof.l03.q5.t: Paradigm cases must be justified by broad agreement, and the relevant circumstances of the new case must be argued explicitly, which constrains cherry picking
med-ethics-prof.l03.q5.p: A critic argues that casuistry is unreliable because a reasoner can pick whichever analogous cases support a favoured conclusion. What is the strongest reply available to a casuist?
med-ethics-prof.l03.q5.h: The method needs a way of justifying which cases count.
med-ethics-prof.l03.q5.e: Paradigms rest on broad agreement and the differences must be argued, which limits arbitrary choice. Casuistry does use analogy and does not claim certainty.

med-ethics-prof.l04.q1.t: The phrase does not appear in the Oath; a related idea appears in the Hippocratic Epidemics, and the Latin tag is later
med-ethics-prof.l04.q1.p: The phrase "first do no harm" is often attributed to the Hippocratic Oath. What is the accurate position?
med-ethics-prof.l04.q1.h: Check which text contains the related idea of helping or at least not harming.
med-ethics-prof.l04.q1.e: The Oath does not contain the phrase. The related idea is in Epidemics. The AMA code and Nuremberg are later documents.

med-ethics-prof.l04.q2.t: Respect for persons, beneficence and justice
med-ethics-prof.l04.q2.p: The Belmont Report identified which three principles for research with human subjects?
med-ethics-prof.l04.q2.h: It was commissioned under the National Research Act of 1974.
med-ethics-prof.l04.q2.e: Belmont names respect for persons, beneficence and justice. Autonomy, nonmaleficence and veracity mix principlism with other norms and are not its three.

med-ethics-prof.l04.q3.t: Helsinki recognises independent ethics committee review and surrogate consent for those unable to consent, which Nuremberg did not
med-ethics-prof.l04.q3.p: Which statement correctly distinguishes the Nuremberg Code from the Declaration of Helsinki?
med-ethics-prof.l04.q3.h: One document came from a trial judgment, the other from a medical association.
med-ethics-prof.l04.q3.e: Helsinki added committee review and provision for those unable to consent. The Nuremberg Code is not US law and starts from the absolute need for voluntary consent.

med-ethics-prof.l04.q4.t: Justice, because selection of subjects must be fair and vulnerable groups should not be chosen for convenience while others reap the benefits
med-ethics-prof.l04.q4.p: A research ethics board reviewing a study is asked what a Belmont-based analysis requires. The study would enrol only residents of a low-income institution because they are convenient and easy to monitor, though the findings would benefit the general population. Which Belmont principle is most directly engaged and how?
med-ethics-prof.l04.q4.h: Think about who bears the burden and who receives the benefit.
med-ethics-prof.l04.q4.e: Belmont ties justice to fair selection and warns against burdening convenient or vulnerable groups. Convenience does not imply consent and benefit to others does not settle fairness.

med-ethics-prof.l04.q5.t: It is mistaken: Nuremberg was a judgment-based statement that left gaps on matters such as incapacitated subjects and independent review, which later documents addressed
med-ethics-prof.l04.q5.p: A student states: "The Nuremberg Code settled all later ethical questions in research, so Helsinki and Belmont were unnecessary." Which analysis of this claim is most accurate?
med-ethics-prof.l04.q5.h: Consider what Nuremberg did not cover.
med-ethics-prof.l04.q5.e: Nuremberg left gaps, such as consent for those who cannot give it and review procedures. It is not a treaty and was not repealed by Belmont.

med-ethics-prof.l05.q1.t: Schloendorff v. Society of New York Hospital (1914)
med-ethics-prof.l05.q1.p: In which case did a New York court recognise that an adult of sound mind may decide what is done to his body and that surgery without consent is a battery?
med-ethics-prof.l05.q1.h: It is an early Cardozo opinion.
med-ethics-prof.l05.q1.e: Schloendorff is the early statement of the right to consent. Salgo coined the phrase informed consent, and Canterbury adopted the reasonable-patient standard.

med-ethics-prof.l05.q2.t: The information a reasonable person in the patient's position would consider material to the decision
med-ethics-prof.l05.q2.p: Under the reasonable patient standard of disclosure, what must the physician disclose?
med-ethics-prof.l05.q2.h: The measuring stick is the patient, not the profession.
med-ethics-prof.l05.q2.e: Canterbury adopted a patient-oriented measure of materiality. The customary-practice measure is the professional standard, and a duty to disclose every conceivable risk is not what courts require.

med-ethics-prof.l05.q3.t: That a reasonable person in the plaintiff's position would not have consented if the risk had been disclosed
med-ethics-prof.l05.q3.p: A plaintiff claims a surgeon failed to disclose a material risk that then occurred. What additional element must usually be proved in a negligence-based informed consent claim?
med-ethics-prof.l05.q3.h: The claim needs causation connecting nondisclosure and the decision.
med-ethics-prof.l05.q3.e: Causation requires showing the decision would have been different for a reasonable person. Intent is not required, and the quality of technique is a separate question.

med-ethics-prof.l05.q4.t: A negligence claim for nondisclosure may succeed because the risk was material, it materialised, and a reasonable patient would have declined
med-ethics-prof.l05.q4.p: A 54-year-old woman is told about the benefits of a spinal fusion but not about a 2 percent risk of permanent bladder dysfunction, which a reasonable patient would consider material. The operation is performed skilfully and the complication occurs. She states that she would have chosen physiotherapy instead. In a jurisdiction that follows the Canterbury approach, what is the most likely analysis?
med-ethics-prof.l05.q4.h: Consider whether competence of the operation answers the disclosure question.
med-ethics-prof.l05.q4.e: Nondisclosure of a material risk can be negligent even if surgery is competent, provided causation is shown. Battery is generally reserved for treatment fundamentally different from what was agreed.

med-ethics-prof.l05.q5.t: Consent is implied under the emergency exception because he lacks capacity, delay would endanger life, and a reasonable person would consent
med-ethics-prof.l05.q5.p: An unconscious 30-year-old man with massive traumatic haemorrhage arrives alone, with no identification and no surrogate reachable. Surgery is urgently needed to save his life. Which analysis of consent is most accurate?
med-ethics-prof.l05.q5.h: Think about what the law presumes when delay means death.
med-ethics-prof.l05.q5.e: The emergency exception implies consent for necessary lifesaving care. Therapeutic privilege concerns withholding information from a capable patient, not treating an unconscious one.

med-ethics-prof.l06.q1.t: Understanding, appreciation, reasoning and expressing a choice
med-ethics-prof.l06.q1.p: Which list correctly gives the four abilities commonly assessed in decision-making capacity?
med-ethics-prof.l06.q1.h: One ability is about applying information to oneself.
med-ethics-prof.l06.q1.e: The Appelbaum and Grisso abilities are understanding, appreciation, reasoning and choice. Orientation and intelligence are not the criteria, and agreement is not required.

med-ethics-prof.l06.q2.t: It is specific to a particular decision and time, so a patient may have capacity for one choice but not another
med-ethics-prof.l06.q2.p: Which statement about capacity is correct?
med-ethics-prof.l06.q2.e: Capacity is decision-specific and can fluctuate. It is a clinical judgment, and a court decides legal competence, and refusal alone does not prove incapacity.

med-ethics-prof.l06.q3.t: Appreciation, because he does not recognise that the information applies to his own situation
med-ethics-prof.l06.q3.p: A patient with severe depression says he understands that antidepressants help many people but that they cannot help him because he is beyond saving. Which ability is most clearly impaired?
med-ethics-prof.l06.q3.h: He can state the facts but does not apply them to himself.
med-ethics-prof.l06.q3.e: Failure to apply accurate information to oneself is a failure of appreciation. His ability to state facts shows understanding is intact.

med-ethics-prof.l06.q4.t: Capacity is doubtful for reasoning and voluntariness, so the team should explore her own values and may need surrogate involvement
med-ethics-prof.l06.q4.p: A 72-year-old woman with moderate dementia is recommended an operation for a broken hip. She repeats that surgery will fix the bone, that anaesthesia has risks, and that without it she may not walk again. She says she wants surgery because her son told her to say yes and she does not want to disappoint him, and she cannot say what she would do if he were absent. What is the best assessment?
med-ethics-prof.l06.q4.h: Agreement with the clinician does not prove capacity.
med-ethics-prof.l06.q4.e: Assent that does not reflect her own weighing of options may fail reasoning, so the team should probe further. A dementia diagnosis alone does not remove capacity and family influence is not automatically coercion.

med-ethics-prof.l06.q5.t: The refusal does not itself show incapacity if she understands, appreciates and reasons within her values, so the team should continue to engage with her
med-ethics-prof.l06.q5.p: A competent 40-year-old woman declines chemotherapy recommended by her oncologist because of a belief in the healing power of prayer. She understands the prognosis with and without treatment and has held the belief for decades. Her oncologist thinks she is irrational. Which conclusion is best supported?
med-ethics-prof.l06.q5.h: A bad outcome or an unusual belief is not the test.
med-ethics-prof.l06.q5.e: Capacity turns on her abilities, not on whether the clinician agrees with the decision. The sliding scale demands care in assessment, not a lower bar for overriding refusals.

med-ethics-prof.l07.q1.t: Disclosure to a consulting specialist for the purpose of treating the patient
med-ethics-prof.l07.q1.p: Under the HIPAA Privacy Rule, which use of protected health information generally requires no individual authorisation?
med-ethics-prof.l07.q1.h: Think of the three routine purposes the Rule permits.
med-ethics-prof.l07.q1.e: Treatment, payment and operations are permitted without authorisation. Marketing and employer disclosures generally need written authorisation.

med-ethics-prof.l07.q2.t: A therapist who determines that a patient is a serious danger of violence to another must use reasonable care to protect the intended victim
med-ethics-prof.l07.q2.p: What did the California Supreme Court hold in Tarasoff v. Regents of the University of California (1976)?
med-ethics-prof.l07.q2.h: The duty is tied to an identifiable potential victim and reasonable care.
med-ethics-prof.l07.q2.e: The duty is to take reasonable steps to protect an identifiable victim. Confidentiality is not absolute, and the court did not impose strict liability for all violence.

med-ethics-prof.l07.q3.t: States differ: some impose a mandatory duty to protect, some permit disclosure, and some recognise no such duty
med-ethics-prof.l07.q3.p: Which statement about the response of states to Tarasoff is correct?
med-ethics-prof.l07.q3.h: The answer is a split, not a single rule.
med-ethics-prof.l07.q3.e: States vary in whether the duty is mandatory, permissive or absent. There is no uniform national rule.

med-ethics-prof.l07.q4.t: Because state law allows the minor to consent to this service, her information is protected and the physician should not disclose it without her permission
med-ethics-prof.l07.q4.p: A 16-year-old girl tells her physician she is sexually active and requests contraception, asking that her parents not be told. Her state law permits minors to consent to contraception. Her mother telephones asking for information about the visit. What is the best approach?
med-ethics-prof.l07.q4.h: Who consented to the service determines who controls the information.
med-ethics-prof.l07.q4.e: When the minor lawfully consents to a service, she generally controls related information. HIPAA does cover minors, and parental access is not unconditional.

med-ethics-prof.l07.q5.t: Take reasonable protective steps, such as notifying the coworker and the police, and document the assessment, since HIPAA permits disclosure to avert a serious and imminent threat
med-ethics-prof.l07.q5.p: A patient on a psychiatric ward tells his clinician in confidence that he will "deal with" a named coworker the next day and has described buying a weapon. The clinician assesses the threat as serious and imminent. The state has a permissive disclosure statute. Which course is most defensible?
med-ethics-prof.l07.q5.h: The Rule has an exception for serious and imminent threats.
med-ethics-prof.l07.q5.e: HIPAA allows disclosure to avert a serious and imminent threat and the state statute permits it. It does not require waiting for harm, and family are not the only recipients.

med-ethics-prof.l08.q1.t: A six-step approach to delivering bad news that begins with setting up the conversation and assessing the patient's perception
med-ethics-prof.l08.q1.p: Which description best fits the SPIKES protocol?
med-ethics-prof.l08.q1.e: SPIKES is a communication framework. It is not a legal standard, a capacity tool or a regulation.

med-ethics-prof.l08.q2.t: Withholding information because disclosure would itself seriously harm the patient, a narrow and contested exception
med-ethics-prof.l08.q2.p: What is the best description of therapeutic privilege?
med-ethics-prof.l08.q2.h: It is about the clinician withholding, not the patient waiving.
med-ethics-prof.l08.q2.e: Therapeutic privilege is a narrow exception for withholding harmful information. A patient's own refusal is the right not to know, a different matter.

med-ethics-prof.l08.q3.t: Explore the family's concerns and ask the patient how much information she wants, instead of assuming either way
med-ethics-prof.l08.q3.p: A family asks that an elderly capable patient not be told her cancer diagnosis. What is the most appropriate first response?
med-ethics-prof.l08.q3.h: The patient's own wishes about information are the key.
med-ethics-prof.l08.q3.e: Asking the patient and exploring the family's fears respects both truth and the patient's preferences. Automatic compliance or blunt disclosure ignores one of them.

med-ethics-prof.l08.q4.t: Ask what he understands, share the realistic estimate with its uncertainty, acknowledge his emotions, and plan around his goals
med-ethics-prof.l08.q4.p: A 61-year-old man with metastatic disease says: "Doc, I just want to know whether to plan for my son's wedding in March." Previous clinicians gave only vague reassurance. The physician estimates survival of perhaps a few months. Which approach best balances truthfulness and compassion?
med-ethics-prof.l08.q4.h: Honest information can still be delivered gently and with uncertainty stated.
med-ethics-prof.l08.q4.e: Truthful, paced disclosure with acknowledgement of uncertainty respects autonomy and trust. False reassurance deceives, and false precision overstates what can be known.

med-ethics-prof.l08.q5.t: The right not to know, an aspect of autonomy, provided she understands what information exists and what she is declining
med-ethics-prof.l08.q5.p: A patient tells her geneticist she wants to be tested for a hereditary cancer syndrome but does not want to learn whether she carries a separate variant linked to untreatable late-onset dementia. Which principle is most clearly at stake in respecting her wishes?
med-ethics-prof.l08.q5.h: The choice is hers, not the clinician's.
med-ethics-prof.l08.q5.e: A patient may decline information, an aspect of autonomy. Therapeutic privilege is the clinician's decision to withhold, which is not what happens here.

med-ethics-prof.l09.q1.t: Expressed wishes, then substituted judgment, then best interests
med-ethics-prof.l09.q1.p: In descending order of preference, which sequence of standards should a surrogate decision-maker use?
med-ethics-prof.l09.q1.h: The patient's own words come first.
med-ethics-prof.l09.q1.e: Known wishes take priority, then what the patient would choose, then best interests when nothing is known. The reverse order disregards the patient.

med-ethics-prof.l09.q2.t: A state may require clear and convincing evidence of the patient's wishes before a surrogate may withdraw life-sustaining treatment
med-ethics-prof.l09.q2.p: What did Cruzan v. Director, Missouri Department of Health (1990) hold regarding an incompetent patient's wishes?
med-ethics-prof.l09.q2.h: It concerned the evidentiary standard a state may adopt.
med-ethics-prof.l09.q2.e: Cruzan allowed a high evidentiary standard, though it did not require every state to adopt it. It did not ban withdrawal and does not rest on physician orders.

med-ethics-prof.l09.q3.t: It is a portable medical order signed by a clinician for seriously ill or frail patients, rather than a statement of preferences
med-ethics-prof.l09.q3.p: Which feature distinguishes a POLST form from a living will?
med-ethics-prof.l09.q3.h: One is an order, the other is a statement of wishes.
med-ethics-prof.l09.q3.e: A POLST is a clinician-signed medical order. A durable power of attorney for health care appoints an agent, and a guardianship order comes from a court.

med-ethics-prof.l09.q4.t: Follow the living will as her expressed wish and support the son, who is empowered to speak for her, not to substitute his own preferences
med-ethics-prof.l09.q4.p: A 70-year-old woman with advanced dementia has aspiration pneumonia. Her son, the designated health care agent, says he cannot accept her death and requests intubation. Her living will, signed ten years earlier while competent, states she would refuse mechanical ventilation if she could no longer recognise her family. Which approach is most appropriate?
med-ethics-prof.l09.q4.h: The agent's role is to carry out the patient's wishes, and a clear directive speaks first.
med-ethics-prof.l09.q4.e: A clear directive applies to this situation and the agent should honour it, with support. An agent does not override the patient's own expressed wishes, and directives do not expire automatically.

med-ethics-prof.l09.q5.t: The wife is the legal surrogate, and her account of his wishes supports substituted judgment, with an ethics consultation available if the dispute persists
med-ethics-prof.l09.q5.p: A 55-year-old man in a persistent vegetative state has no directive. His wife and brother disagree. His wife recalls him saying he would never want to be kept alive like that. His brother wants treatment continued. State law ranks a spouse above a sibling. Which analysis is best?
med-ethics-prof.l09.q5.h: The statute ranks the surrogates, and the standard is the patient's own views.
med-ethics-prof.l09.q5.e: The statutory order places the wife first and her report of his values fits substituted judgment. Unresolved disputes go to ethics consultation or court, and the physician does not decide by default.

med-ethics-prof.l10.q1.t: Certification by a physician that the patient would likely die within six months if the illness runs its expected course
med-ethics-prof.l10.q1.p: In the United States, what does the Medicare hospice benefit generally require?
med-ethics-prof.l10.q1.h: There is a prognosis threshold, not an age threshold.
med-ethics-prof.l10.q1.e: Hospice eligibility is a six-month prognosis certification if the disease runs its course. It does not require a patient to be elderly or incompetent.

med-ethics-prof.l10.q2.t: They are morally equivalent when the treatment is not wanted or no longer serves the patient's goals
med-ethics-prof.l10.q2.p: Which statement about withholding versus withdrawing life-sustaining treatment reflects the prevailing ethical and legal view?
med-ethics-prof.l10.q2.h: The disease, not the act of stopping, causes death.
med-ethics-prof.l10.q2.e: The prevailing view treats them as equivalent. Treating withdrawal as killing would discourage trials of treatment that might help.

med-ethics-prof.l10.q3.t: The intention is symptom relief with a proportionate dose, accepting a foreseen risk of hastening death without intending it
med-ethics-prof.l10.q3.p: Which condition is necessary for the doctrine of double effect to justify giving opioids in the dying?
med-ethics-prof.l10.q3.h: Intention and proportionality are the key words.
med-ethics-prof.l10.q3.e: Relief is the aim and the risk is foreseen, not intended. Intending death would be euthanasia, which the doctrine does not justify.

med-ethics-prof.l10.q4.t: Withdrawing an unwanted ventilator is respecting a refusal of treatment, and his underlying disease is the cause of death, with comfort medicines given for symptoms
med-ethics-prof.l10.q4.p: A 77-year-old with end-stage emphysema on a ventilator for three weeks has not weaned. He previously told his family, "No long-term machines." They request withdrawal. The nurse worries that this makes the team responsible for his death. Which reply is most accurate?
med-ethics-prof.l10.q4.h: Ask what actually causes the death and whose decision is being carried out.
med-ethics-prof.l10.q4.e: Withdrawing treatment at a patient's wish is refusal of treatment, not euthanasia. A court order is not generally required and ending a trial of treatment is accepted practice.

med-ethics-prof.l10.q5.t: Sedation aims at relief of suffering, is titrated to symptoms, and death follows from the underlying disease, whereas euthanasia aims at death by administering a lethal agent
med-ethics-prof.l10.q5.p: A 59-year-old with metastatic cancer and severe refractory suffering in the last days of life is given continuous sedation to relieve distress. His family asks whether this is euthanasia. Which analysis best distinguishes the two?
med-ethics-prof.l10.q5.h: Compare intention, proportionality and cause of death.
med-ethics-prof.l10.q5.e: Palliative sedation differs by aim, proportionate dosing and cause of death. Critics argue the line is thinner in practice, but the three-part distinction is the standard one, and sedation does not require a written request for death.

med-ethics-prof.l11.q1.t: The Constitution does not guarantee a right to assistance in suicide, leaving the question to the states
med-ethics-prof.l11.q1.p: What did the Supreme Court hold in Washington v. Glucksberg (1997)?
med-ethics-prof.l11.q1.h: The Court left the issue to democratic decision at state level.
med-ethics-prof.l11.q1.e: Glucksberg found no constitutional right to assisted suicide. The opposite claims reverse the holding, and Vacco rejected the equal protection argument.

med-ethics-prof.l11.q2.t: In euthanasia the clinician administers the lethal agent, whereas in assisted suicide the patient takes a prescribed means
med-ethics-prof.l11.q2.p: Which of the following correctly distinguishes euthanasia from physician-assisted suicide?
med-ethics-prof.l11.q2.h: Ask who performs the final act.
med-ethics-prof.l11.q2.e: The clinician acts in euthanasia and the patient acts in assisted suicide. Euthanasia is not lawful in any US state.

med-ethics-prof.l11.q3.t: An adult with decision-making capacity and a terminal illness with a prognosis of six months or less
med-ethics-prof.l11.q3.p: Which is a typical eligibility feature of US state aid-in-dying statutes?
med-ethics-prof.l11.q3.h: The statutes limit access to capable adults with limited prognosis.
med-ethics-prof.l11.q3.e: The typical statute requires capacity and a six-month prognosis. Family requests and minors are not eligible, and chronic pain alone does not qualify.

med-ethics-prof.l11.q4.t: Examine data on how eligibility and use have changed over time in jurisdictions with the law, and consider whether differences reflect legislative change or the practice itself
med-ethics-prof.l11.q4.p: A legislator argues: "Once a state allows assistance for those with terminal illness, it will inevitably extend to people who are not dying." A researcher responds that the claim is empirical. Which approach best evaluates it?
med-ethics-prof.l11.q4.h: A slippery slope claim predicts something that can be checked.
med-ethics-prof.l11.q4.e: The claim is testable by comparing trends and distinguishing legislative change from practice drift. Inevitability and total irrelevance both overstate the evidence.

med-ethics-prof.l11.q5.t: A state may rationally distinguish refusing treatment from assisted suicide, relying on differences in causation and intention, so the first does not entail the second
med-ethics-prof.l11.q5.p: A hospital ethics committee is asked to evaluate this statement: "Because we allow patients to refuse ventilators, we must also allow physicians to prescribe lethal drugs." Which response best reflects the reasoning used in Vacco v. Quill?
med-ethics-prof.l11.q5.h: The Court accepted that the two acts can be treated differently.
med-ethics-prof.l11.q5.e: Vacco accepted a distinction between refusal and assistance based on causation and intent, and rejected the equal protection argument. Identity of outcome did not erase it.

med-ethics-prof.l12.q1.t: It overruled Roe and Casey, holding that the Constitution does not confer a right to abortion and returning regulation to the states
med-ethics-prof.l12.q1.p: What was the effect of Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization (2022)?
med-ethics-prof.l12.q1.h: It concerned a Mississippi law and the earlier precedents.
med-ethics-prof.l12.q1.e: Dobbs overruled both prior decisions and left regulation to state legislatures. It did not create a national ban.

med-ethics-prof.l12.q2.t: Even if the fetus is a person, a woman is not necessarily obliged to sustain it with her body
med-ethics-prof.l12.q2.p: In the argument associated with Judith Jarvis Thomson, what is the core claim?
med-ethics-prof.l12.q2.h: The argument grants the premise about personhood for the sake of argument.
med-ethics-prof.l12.q2.e: Thomson argues from bodily autonomy while granting fetal personhood. The other options deny personhood, restrict justification or assert the opposing view.

med-ethics-prof.l12.q3.t: Courts have, with few exceptions, held that a competent pregnant patient retains the right to refuse treatment
med-ethics-prof.l12.q3.p: Which statement about maternal-fetal conflict in United States courts is generally accurate?
med-ethics-prof.l12.q3.h: Capacity is not lost by pregnancy.
med-ethics-prof.l12.q3.e: Competent pregnant patients keep the right to refuse. Compelled treatment is rare and criticised by professional bodies.

med-ethics-prof.l12.q4.t: The expressivist objection claims selection expresses a negative judgment of disabled lives, while defenders respond that the choice concerns a particular family's situation and not the worth of persons
med-ethics-prof.l12.q4.p: A couple using preimplantation genetic testing asks for embryos to be screened for a severe, early-onset, fatal condition that runs in the family. A disability-rights advocate argues this expresses disvalue for disabled people. A clinician considers how to reason through this. Which analysis best captures the debate?
med-ethics-prof.l12.q4.h: Both positions are serious and stated in the reasoning.
med-ethics-prof.l12.q4.e: The expressivist objection and the reply are both live positions. Neither is settled by law, and the objection is directed at the practice as well as providers.

med-ethics-prof.l12.q5.t: Avoid imposing personal views, inform the patient honestly of options, and ensure timely referral or transfer according to institutional policy
med-ethics-prof.l12.q5.p: A physician has a conscientious objection to participating in a particular reproductive service. A patient requests it in a state where it is legal. Which response best fits professional guidance in this area?
med-ethics-prof.l12.q5.h: Conscientious objection is balanced against the patient's access to care.
med-ethics-prof.l12.q5.e: Objection is usually accommodated alongside honest information and timely referral. Withholding information or deceiving the patient violates duties owed to her.

med-ethics-prof.l13.q1.t: Researchers observed men who already had syphilis, deceived them about the study, and withheld penicillin after it became standard treatment
med-ethics-prof.l13.q1.p: Which description of the Tuskegee study of untreated syphilis is accurate?
med-ethics-prof.l13.q1.h: Consider what the men were told and what was withheld.
med-ethics-prof.l13.q1.e: The men already had syphilis and were deceived and denied treatment. Infection of healthy men is a common misconception, and full consent was absent.

med-ethics-prof.l13.q2.t: The National Research Act of 1974, which required institutional review boards and created the commission that produced the Belmont Report
med-ethics-prof.l13.q2.p: What was the main US legislative response to the revelations about Tuskegee?
med-ethics-prof.l13.q2.e: The 1974 Act required IRB review for federally funded research and created the Belmont commission. The other laws concern directives, privacy and insurance.

med-ethics-prof.l13.q3.t: It described 22 examples of ethically troubling research conducted at respected American institutions
med-ethics-prof.l13.q3.p: What did Henry Beecher's 1966 article in the New England Journal of Medicine do?
med-ethics-prof.l13.q3.h: It was a catalogue of questionable studies, not a trial judgment.
med-ethics-prof.l13.q3.e: Beecher catalogued problematic studies and increased pressure for oversight. Tuskegee was revealed in 1972 and the Nuremberg Code came from the Doctors' Trial.

med-ethics-prof.l13.q4.t: Her tumour cells were taken in 1951 without her knowledge and became the HeLa line, raising consent and ownership issues, but she was not infected with cancer by researchers
med-ethics-prof.l13.q4.p: A trainee says: "Henrietta Lacks was subjected to an unethical experiment in which doctors infected her with cancer." What is the best correction?
med-ethics-prof.l13.q4.h: Separate the source of her disease from what was done with her cells.
med-ethics-prof.l13.q4.e: Her cervical cancer arose naturally and cells were taken without her knowledge. She did not consent and did not receive payment.

med-ethics-prof.l13.q5.t: Both involved vulnerable populations and consent problems, but at Tuskegee the men already had the disease and were denied treatment, while at Willowbrook children were deliberately infected
med-ethics-prof.l13.q5.p: A teaching exercise compares the Tuskegee study with the Willowbrook hepatitis studies. Which comparison is most accurate?
med-ethics-prof.l13.q5.h: In one study the disease was introduced and in the other it was already present.
med-ethics-prof.l13.q5.e: In Tuskegee men already had syphilis, while Willowbrook deliberately infected children. Neither was a German study, and neither provided full consent.

med-ethics-prof.l14.q1.t: Generating generalisable knowledge, with benefit to participants incidental
med-ethics-prof.l14.q1.p: What is the primary aim of research that distinguishes it from clinical care?
med-ethics-prof.l14.q1.h: Think of what the study is designed to produce.
med-ethics-prof.l14.q1.e: Research aims at generalisable knowledge. Care aims at the patient's own benefit, and research does not guarantee identical treatment.

med-ethics-prof.l14.q2.t: Genuine uncertainty or disagreement in the expert clinical community about which treatment is better
med-ethics-prof.l14.q2.p: Which definition best describes clinical equipoise as proposed by Benjamin Freedman?
med-ethics-prof.l14.q2.h: It is a community standard, not an individual state of mind.
med-ethics-prof.l14.q2.e: Clinical equipoise is honest uncertainty in the expert community. The investigator's belief is theoretical equipoise, and arm size is unrelated.

med-ethics-prof.l14.q3.t: A participant's belief that research procedures are designed for her personal therapeutic benefit
med-ethics-prof.l14.q3.h: It concerns participants confusing a trial with care.
med-ethics-prof.l14.q3.e: Therapeutic misconception is confusing research with individualised treatment. The other options describe different errors.

med-ethics-prof.l14.q4.t: Reject the placebo arm because withholding a proven effective therapy causes serious risk, and require an active comparator
med-ethics-prof.l14.q4.p: A proposed trial would randomise patients with a serious bacterial infection to a new antibiotic or to saline placebo, although an established antibiotic is known to be highly effective and withholding it risks death. How would an IRB most appropriately respond?
med-ethics-prof.l14.q4.h: Ask what a participant in the placebo arm might lose.
med-ethics-prof.l14.q4.e: A placebo is unjustified when it withholds a proven therapy with serious risk. Consent alone cannot justify exposing participants to excessive risk.

med-ethics-prof.l14.q5.t: Stopping for benefit serves participants in the control arm but may overestimate the effect, so pre-specified stopping rules and sufficient events are important
med-ethics-prof.l14.q5.p: An interim analysis of a large cancer trial shows a larger benefit than expected in the treatment arm, and the data monitoring board is deciding whether to stop. Which consideration is most appropriate?
med-ethics-prof.l14.q5.h: Early stopping trades participant welfare against precision.
med-ethics-prof.l14.q5.e: Early stopping may protect participants but tends to inflate effect estimates, so rules and event counts matter. Involving marketing would compromise independence.

med-ethics-prof.l15.q1.t: The purchase and sale of human organs for transplantation
med-ethics-prof.l15.q1.p: What does the National Organ Transplant Act of 1984 prohibit?
med-ethics-prof.l15.q1.e: The Act prohibits buying and selling organs and set up the national network. It does not ban donation or waiting lists.

med-ethics-prof.l15.q2.p: Which distributive approach gives extra weight to benefiting the worst off, which in medicine often means the sickest patients?
med-ethics-prof.l15.q2.h: The name suggests giving priority to someone.
med-ethics-prof.l15.q2.e: Prioritarianism weights benefits to the worst off more heavily. Strict utilitarianism counts benefits equally and libertarianism stresses voluntary exchange.

med-ethics-prof.l15.q3.t: Publicity, relevance, appeals and revision, and enforcement
med-ethics-prof.l15.q3.p: Which set lists the four conditions of accountability for reasonableness as described by Daniels and Sabin?
med-ethics-prof.l15.q3.h: The framework is about legitimate process when people disagree.
med-ethics-prof.l15.q3.e: The conditions are publicity, relevance, revision and appeal, and enforcement. The other lists mix in unrelated concepts.

med-ethics-prof.l15.q4.t: Decide by a fair procedure such as a lottery, since prognosis is equal and wealth or social status is not a legitimate criterion
med-ethics-prof.l15.q4.p: A hospital in a surge has one ventilator and two patients with equal prognosis: a 28-year-old unemployed man and a 28-year-old prominent philanthropist who offers a large donation to the hospital. Which approach best fits mainstream allocation ethics?
med-ethics-prof.l15.q4.h: Equal claims call for a procedure that does not rely on status.
med-ethics-prof.l15.q4.e: With equal clinical claims, a lottery respects equal worth and excludes social status or wealth. Weighing donation or social worth is rejected by mainstream frameworks.

med-ethics-prof.l15.q5.t: The categorical exclusion conflicts with disability-rights law and sound ethics, which require individualised assessment of the likelihood of benefit
med-ethics-prof.l15.q5.p: A crisis standards of care protocol excludes all patients with intellectual disability from ventilators regardless of individual prognosis. A disability-rights group objects. Which analysis is best?
med-ethics-prof.l15.q5.h: Ask whether the criterion measures benefit or a group label.
med-ethics-prof.l15.q5.e: Triage should rest on individualised likelihood of benefit and not group labels, and the ADA prohibits categorical exclusion. The ADA does not require it, and notice does not cure discrimination.

med-ethics-prof.l16.q1.t: The Physician Payments Sunshine Act, part of the Affordable Care Act
med-ethics-prof.l16.q1.p: Which US law requires drug and device manufacturers to report payments to physicians, which are published in a public database?
med-ethics-prof.l16.q1.h: The database is called Open Payments.
med-ethics-prof.l16.q1.e: The Sunshine Act created Open Payments. The Stark Law concerns self-referral, and the other two laws address organs and directives.

med-ethics-prof.l16.q2.t: Knowingly and willingly offering or accepting remuneration to induce referrals of items or services paid for by federal health programmes
med-ethics-prof.l16.q2.p: What does the federal Anti-Kickback Statute criminalise?
med-ethics-prof.l16.q2.h: It concerns payment to induce referrals.
med-ethics-prof.l16.q2.e: The Statute criminalises remuneration intended to induce referrals. It does not ban all ownership or all payments, and disclosure is encouraged.

med-ethics-prof.l16.q3.t: A physician must disclose personal research or economic interests unrelated to the patient's health that may affect professional judgment
med-ethics-prof.l16.q3.p: What did the court hold in Moore v. Regents of the University of California (1990) about the physician's duty?
med-ethics-prof.l16.q3.h: The court recognised a disclosure duty but not a property claim.
med-ethics-prof.l16.q3.e: The court recognised a duty to disclose such interests and rejected the conversion claim. It did not ban research use of excised tissue.

med-ethics-prof.l16.q4.t: Disclosure informs others but leaves the potential influence on her vote intact, so recusal from the decision is the stronger management
med-ethics-prof.l16.q4.p: A cardiologist who receives consulting fees from a stent manufacturer sits on a committee choosing which stent the hospital will buy. She discloses the fees and then votes. A colleague argues disclosure solves the problem. Which response is most accurate?
med-ethics-prof.l16.q4.h: Compare what disclosure changes with what recusal changes.
med-ethics-prof.l16.q4.e: Disclosure does not remove the influence, whereas recusal does. Fees do not automatically make a vote unlawful.

med-ethics-prof.l16.q5.t: Choices of comparator, outcomes, analysis and reporting can favour the sponsor's product even without data fabrication
med-ethics-prof.l16.q5.p: A systematic review finds that industry-sponsored trials more often report favourable conclusions than non-industry trials, even when risk of bias ratings look similar. A reader proposes explanations. Which is most consistent with the evidence on how bias can arise?
med-ethics-prof.l16.q5.h: Bias can enter at design and reporting without any fraud.
med-ethics-prof.l16.q5.e: Design and reporting choices can create favourable results without fraud. Universal falsification and independent-trial unreliability go beyond the evidence.

med-ethics-prof.l17.q1.p: Which term describes a patient safety event that reaches a patient and causes death, permanent harm or severe temporary harm?
med-ethics-prof.l17.q1.h: The harm reached the patient and was severe.
med-ethics-prof.l17.q1.e: A sentinel event is a serious event reaching the patient. A near miss does not reach the patient, and a latent condition is an underlying weakness.

med-ethics-prof.l17.q2.t: A weakness in a safeguard, which can align with others to allow harm to reach a patient
med-ethics-prof.l17.q2.p: In the Swiss cheese model, what does a "hole" in a layer of defence represent?
med-ethics-prof.l17.q2.h: Think about layers of protection and how failures line up.
med-ethics-prof.l17.q2.e: Holes are weaknesses in defences that can align. The model is about systems, not about assigning blame to individuals or patients.

med-ethics-prof.l17.q3.t: Reckless behaviour, conscious disregard of a substantial risk, warrants discipline, while human error warrants support and system repair
med-ethics-prof.l17.q3.p: Under a just culture framework, how should a recklessly unsafe behaviour be treated differently from a simple human error?
med-ethics-prof.l17.q3.h: The framework judges the behaviour, not simply the outcome.
med-ethics-prof.l17.q3.e: Just culture distinguishes by behaviour type. Treating all events identically or by outcome alone discourages reporting.

med-ethics-prof.l17.q4.t: Disclose promptly with the supervising physician, explain what happened, apologise, describe corrective steps and report the event for system review
med-ethics-prof.l17.q4.p: A resident notices after discharge that a patient was given the wrong anticoagulant dose, which led to a minor bleed that resolved without lasting harm. The resident worries that disclosure will invite a lawsuit. Which approach is most consistent with professional guidance?
med-ethics-prof.l17.q4.h: Consider the patient's need to know and the integrity of the record.
med-ethics-prof.l17.q4.e: Professional guidance supports prompt, honest disclosure with reporting. Silence, waiting to be asked, and chart alteration all breach honesty and the last may be fraud.

med-ethics-prof.l17.q5.t: Some institutions report no rise in claims and possibly lower costs, though the evidence is mixed and the effect depends on context
med-ethics-prof.l17.q5.p: A hospital adopts a programme of prompt disclosure of errors, investigation and early offers of compensation. A critic predicts that claims will inevitably rise. Which statement about the evidence is most accurate?
med-ethics-prof.l17.q5.h: Evidence from early adopters is suggestive but limited.
med-ethics-prof.l17.q5.e: Reports are encouraging but mixed and context-dependent. Claims of universal effects overstate the evidence, and apology statutes support disclosure.

med-ethics-prof.l18.q1.p: Which four elements must a plaintiff prove in a medical malpractice claim?
med-ethics-prof.l18.q1.h: They are the elements of any negligence claim.
med-ethics-prof.l18.q1.e: Malpractice is negligence, so duty, breach, causation and damages must be shown. Intent is not required.

med-ethics-prof.l18.q2.t: A surgical instrument is found inside a patient after an abdominal operation
med-ethics-prof.l18.q2.p: In which situation is the doctrine of res ipsa loquitur most likely to allow an inference of negligence without expert testimony?
med-ethics-prof.l18.q2.h: The event must be one that does not ordinarily occur without negligence.
med-ethics-prof.l18.q2.e: A retained instrument ordinarily indicates negligence. Recurrence, known complications and death after high-risk surgery occur without negligence.

med-ethics-prof.l18.q3.t: Recovery when negligence reduced a patient's chance of survival below fifty percent, even if survival was not more likely than not
med-ethics-prof.l18.q3.p: What does a loss-of-chance jurisdiction allow that a jurisdiction following the traditional all-or-nothing rule generally does not?
med-ethics-prof.l18.q3.h: It concerns the probability needed to prove causation.
med-ethics-prof.l18.q3.e: Loss of chance relaxes the more-likely-than-not causation requirement. The other options change duty, damages type or standing instead.

med-ethics-prof.l18.q4.t: The plaintiff loses on causation because earlier diagnosis would not more likely than not have changed the outcome
med-ethics-prof.l18.q4.p: A 62-year-old man with chest pain is told he has indigestion and is sent home. The emergency physician did not order an electrocardiogram, which a reasonably competent emergency physician would have obtained. He returns the next day with a myocardial infarction. An expert testifies that prompt diagnosis would have given him a 35 percent chance of avoiding permanent heart damage. In a jurisdiction following the traditional all-or-nothing rule, what is the most likely result?
med-ethics-prof.l18.q4.h: Breach alone is not enough; consider the probability of a different outcome.
med-ethics-prof.l18.q4.e: All-or-nothing causation requires more than fifty percent likelihood that the outcome would have differed. A duty existed, and res ipsa does not cover missed diagnoses generally.

med-ethics-prof.l18.q5.t: Battery, because the procedure was substantially different from the one to which the patient consented
med-ethics-prof.l18.q5.p: A surgeon performs a hernia repair competently, but the patient had consented only to a repair on the left side and the surgeon, finding no problem there, repaired the right side instead without any emergency or a further discussion. Which claim is most directly supported?
med-ethics-prof.l18.q5.h: Consider the tort for treatment outside the scope of consent.
med-ethics-prof.l18.q5.e: Treatment materially different from that consented to is traditionally battery, which does not require intent to harm. EMTALA concerns emergency screening and not consent to elective surgery.

med-ethics-prof.l19.q1.t: An internal state that reduces functional ability below the species-typical level for a reference class
med-ethics-prof.l19.q1.p: According to Boorse's biostatistical theory, what is disease?
med-ethics-prof.l19.q1.h: The theory is naturalist and statistical.
med-ethics-prof.l19.q1.e: Boorse defines disease as reduced typical functioning relative to a reference class. The social-values definition is normativist, and subjective feeling is illness.

med-ethics-prof.l19.q2.t: Disease is a pathophysiological abnormality as understood by clinicians, while illness is the person's lived experience of being unwell
med-ethics-prof.l19.q2.p: What is the best description of the distinction between disease and illness?
med-ethics-prof.l19.q2.h: One term is the clinician's view and the other is the patient's.
med-ethics-prof.l19.q2.e: Disease is the biomedical abnormality and illness is the experience. Severity and mind-body division are not the distinction.

med-ethics-prof.l19.q3.t: A disorder requires both a failure of a naturally selected mechanism and harm as judged by social values
med-ethics-prof.l19.q3.p: Which feature characterises Wakefield's harmful dysfunction analysis?
med-ethics-prof.l19.q3.h: It is a hybrid account with a factual and an evaluative component.
med-ethics-prof.l19.q3.e: The account joins a factual dysfunction condition and an evaluative harm condition. Statistical rarity or distress alone is not sufficient.

med-ethics-prof.l19.q4.t: The student says the reclassification reflected shifting values about what counts as harmful; the classmate replies that it also reflected evidence that no dysfunction or distress was inherent, so naturalists can explain it too
med-ethics-prof.l19.q4.p: A student argues that the 1973 removal of homosexuality from the American Psychiatric Association's diagnostic manual supports normativism about disease. A classmate objects. Which exchange best reflects the philosophical debate?
med-ethics-prof.l19.q4.h: Both sides can claim the example; look for the reply that does.
med-ethics-prof.l19.q4.e: The example can be read as value-driven or as evidence-driven, which is why it is debated. The other exchanges contain false historical or legal claims.

med-ethics-prof.l19.q5.t: Medicalization and overdiagnosis, because widening a category labels more people who might not have been harmed
med-ethics-prof.l19.q5.p: A pharmaceutical company proposes that mildly elevated but statistically common blood pressure readings in a population be reclassified as a disease needing drug treatment. Which concern is most directly raised by the discussion of definitions?
med-ethics-prof.l19.q5.h: A wider definition changes how many people are labelled.
med-ethics-prof.l19.q5.e: Broadened thresholds risk overdiagnosis and medicalization. Statistical normality does not guarantee absence of disease, and normativism does not forbid treating common conditions.

med-ethics-prof.l20.q1.t: Temporality, because the cause must precede the effect
med-ethics-prof.l20.q1.p: Which of the Bradford Hill considerations is the only one generally regarded as essential for causation?
med-ethics-prof.l20.q1.h: It concerns the order of events in time.
med-ethics-prof.l20.q1.e: Temporality is necessary. Specificity, analogy and strength are supportive viewpoints that are neither necessary nor sufficient.

med-ethics-prof.l20.q2.t: They assume a single necessary organism, which does not fit diseases with carriers, multiple causes or organisms that cannot be cultured
med-ethics-prof.l20.q2.p: Why do Koch's postulates fail for many chronic and multifactorial diseases?
med-ethics-prof.l20.q2.h: Think about carriers and multiple contributing causes.
med-ethics-prof.l20.q2.e: The postulates assume a single organism that causes disease. Carriers and multiple causes break that assumption, and they were designed for infections.

med-ethics-prof.l20.q3.t: A factor associated with both the exposure and the outcome, not on the causal path, that can create a spurious association
med-ethics-prof.l20.q3.h: It distorts the apparent link between exposure and outcome.
med-ethics-prof.l20.q3.e: A confounder is associated with both exposure and outcome and not a mediator. A factor on the path is a mediator.

med-ethics-prof.l20.q4.t: Smoking confounds the association, and adjusting for it should remove the apparent effect of carrying matches
med-ethics-prof.l20.q4.p: An observational study finds that people who carry matches have higher rates of lung cancer than those who do not. Smoking explains both match carrying and lung cancer. Which statement best describes this situation?
med-ethics-prof.l20.q4.h: Identify the factor that is associated with both match carrying and cancer.
med-ethics-prof.l20.q4.e: Smoking is a common cause of both, so it confounds. A mediator lies on the path, and observational studies can detect real causes when confounding is handled.

med-ethics-prof.l20.q5.t: Population relative risk can suggest that an exposure more likely than not caused a case when it exceeds two, but this is a rough heuristic that cannot prove cause in the individual
med-ethics-prof.l20.q5.p: A court must decide whether a chemical exposure caused a specific plaintiff's cancer. An epidemiological study shows that exposure doubled the relative risk in the population. Which statement best reflects the problem of moving from population to individual causation?
med-ethics-prof.l20.q5.h: Consider what a population risk can and cannot say about one person.
med-ethics-prof.l20.q5.e: A relative risk above two is sometimes used as a heuristic, but it cannot establish individual cause with certainty. Population data are used, and tumours rarely reveal their cause.

med-ethics-prof.l21.q1.t: The conscientious, explicit and judicious use of current best evidence in decisions about individual patients, integrated with clinical expertise and patient values
med-ethics-prof.l21.q1.p: How did Sackett and colleagues define evidence-based medicine in 1996?
med-ethics-prof.l21.q1.e: The definition combines evidence, expertise and patient values. It does not replace judgment with trials and does not rank expert opinion highest.

med-ethics-prof.l21.q2.t: It balances known and unknown confounders between groups on average so that differences can be attributed to the intervention
med-ethics-prof.l21.q2.p: What is the main rationale for randomisation in a clinical trial?
med-ethics-prof.l21.q2.h: Randomisation addresses factors the investigators did not measure.
med-ethics-prof.l21.q2.e: Randomisation balances confounders on average, including unmeasured ones. It does not guarantee benefit, and it is separate from blinding.

med-ethics-prof.l21.q3.t: An effect on the surrogate may not reliably predict an effect on the outcome that matters to patients, and some treatments improve surrogates while causing harm
med-ethics-prof.l21.q3.p: Why is a surrogate endpoint potentially misleading?
med-ethics-prof.l21.q3.h: The CAST trial illustrates the risk.
med-ethics-prof.l21.q3.e: Surrogate effects do not always translate to clinical benefit, as in CAST. They are used in humans and are permitted when validated.

med-ethics-prof.l21.q4.t: The patient differs from the trial population in age and comorbidity, so the average effect may not apply and harms such as falls may weigh more heavily
med-ethics-prof.l21.q4.p: A trial of a new antihypertensive enrolled adults aged 45 to 65 with no other illnesses, and showed fewer strokes. A geriatrician considers it for an 86-year-old with advanced kidney disease and frequent falls. Which concern best illustrates the problem of external validity?
med-ethics-prof.l21.q4.h: Ask how similar the patient is to those who were studied.
med-ethics-prof.l21.q4.e: External validity concerns whether results extend to dissimilar patients. Randomisation supports internal validity, and strokes are patient-important outcomes.

med-ethics-prof.l21.q5.t: The chance that she has the disease is still low, because false positives from the large unaffected group outnumber true positives
med-ethics-prof.l21.q5.p: A screening test for a rare disease that affects 1 in 1,000 people has sensitivity of 95 percent and specificity of 95 percent. A patient with no symptoms tests positive. Which conclusion is correct?
med-ethics-prof.l21.q5.h: Consider how many unaffected people there are for each affected person.
med-ethics-prof.l21.q5.e: With low prevalence, false positives greatly outnumber true positives, so the positive predictive value is low, under about 2 percent here. Sensitivity and false-positive rate are not the probability of disease given a positive.

med-ethics-young.l01.q1.t: Make him a card and tell him something funny
med-ethics-young.l01.q1.p: Sam is home with a tummy ache. Which is a caring thing a friend can do?
med-ethics-young.l01.q1.h: Think about what would make Sam feel cared for.
med-ethics-young.l01.q1.e: A card and a kind story show you are paying attention to him. Telling someone to stop being sick does not help, because they cannot choose that.

med-ethics-young.l01.q2.t: Making sure children never have any fun
med-ethics-young.l01.q2.p: What is the job of doctors and nurses?
med-ethics-young.l01.q2.h: Think about what happens at a hospital.
med-ethics-young.l01.q2.e: Doctors and nurses care for people and try to help them get well. Riding a bike is not their job.

med-ethics-young.l01.q3.t: Tell a grown-up right away so they can help
med-ethics-young.l01.q3.p: You see a classmate fall on the playground and cry a lot. What is the best thing to do?
med-ethics-young.l01.q3.h: Who is able to help if someone is hurt?
med-ethics-young.l01.q3.e: Getting a grown-up quickly is a caring act. Laughing or ignoring hurts feelings and does not get help.

med-ethics-young.l01.q4.t: what the other person needs right now
med-ethics-young.l01.q4.p: Caring for others means paying attention to...
med-ethics-young.l01.q4.h: Caring is about the other person.
med-ethics-young.l01.q4.e: Caring starts with noticing what the person needs. Doing only what you want ignores them.

med-ethics-young.l02.q1.t: Because the doctor cannot see inside you and needs true answers
med-ethics-young.l02.q1.p: Why does the doctor ask you questions?
med-ethics-young.l02.q1.h: The doctor cannot see what you feel.
med-ethics-young.l02.q1.e: True answers tell the doctor what is wrong. A doctor is not trying to catch you in trouble.

med-ethics-young.l02.q2.t: "I don't know," which is an honest answer
med-ethics-young.l02.q2.p: If you do not know the answer to a question, what can you say?
med-ethics-young.l02.q2.e: Saying you do not know is truthful. Making something up could send the doctor in the wrong direction.

med-ethics-young.l02.q3.t: That he ate lots of sweets, because it helps the doctor
med-ethics-young.l02.q3.p: Leo ate too many sweets and now has a sore tummy. What should he tell the doctor?
med-ethics-young.l02.q3.h: The doctor is there to help, not scold.
med-ethics-young.l02.q3.e: The truth about the sweets gives the doctor a clue. Hiding it could make it harder to help him.

med-ethics-young.l02.q4.t: honest, so you know what to expect
med-ethics-young.l02.q4.p: A good doctor who says "This shot will pinch for a moment" is being...
med-ethics-young.l02.q4.e: Telling you what will happen is honest and helps you trust the doctor. A secret would be more scary.

med-ethics-young.l03.q1.t: A parent or caregiver, with advice from the doctor
med-ethics-young.l03.q1.p: Who usually makes health choices for a young child?
med-ethics-young.l03.q1.h: Grown-ups who love you help with big choices.
med-ethics-young.l03.q1.e: Caregivers and doctors work as a team, and the child is included. A stranger has no role.

med-ethics-young.l03.q2.t: Say no, get away if you can, and tell a trusted grown-up
med-ethics-young.l03.q2.p: What should you do if someone touches you in a way that feels unsafe?
med-ethics-young.l03.q2.h: It is never your fault, and you can tell.
med-ethics-young.l03.q2.e: Telling a trusted grown-up is the safe thing. Keeping it secret does not keep you safe.

med-ethics-young.l03.q3.t: It includes you and tells you what is going to happen
med-ethics-young.l03.q3.p: A doctor says, "I'm going to listen to your heart. Is that okay?" Why is that kind?
med-ethics-young.l03.q3.h: The doctor is asking you, not only telling you.
med-ethics-young.l03.q3.e: Asking and explaining treats you as part of the team. It has nothing to do with money or ending the visit.

med-ethics-young.l03.q4.t: You get to make more of them yourself
med-ethics-young.l03.q4.p: As you grow older, what happens with choices about your own body?
med-ethics-young.l03.q4.h: Think about how kids grow up.
med-ethics-young.l03.q4.e: Over time you take on more responsibility for your own health choices. They stay important.

med-ethics-young.l04.q1.t: Feeling scared and still doing the hard thing, or asking for help
med-ethics-young.l04.q1.h: Brave and scared can happen together.
med-ethics-young.l04.q1.e: Brave people feel fear too. Being brave means acting anyway or asking for support.

med-ethics-young.l04.q2.t: Take slow deep breaths and hold a grown-up's hand
med-ethics-young.l04.q2.p: Which is a way to feel calmer before a shot?
med-ethics-young.l04.q2.e: Slow breathing and a comforting hand help your body relax. Holding your breath makes things tenser.

med-ethics-young.l04.q3.t: How to help Ava feel more comfortable
med-ethics-young.l04.q3.p: Ava says "I'm scared" at the clinic. What does that tell the nurse?
med-ethics-young.l04.q3.h: Sharing a feeling helps people help you.
med-ethics-young.l04.q3.e: Saying you are scared lets the nurse comfort you. It does not mean you are weak or must stop.

med-ethics-young.l04.q4.t: So there are fewer surprises and you feel safer
med-ethics-young.l04.q4.p: Why might a nurse tell you what will happen step by step?
med-ethics-young.l04.q4.e: Knowing what is coming helps many kids feel less afraid. It is also fine to ask questions.

med-ethics-young.l05.q1.t: Saying yes freely after you understand what will happen
med-ethics-young.l05.q1.h: Think about a free and informed yes.
med-ethics-young.l05.q1.e: Consent is a free yes given after understanding. Silence out of fear or agreeing without an explanation is not real consent.

med-ethics-young.l05.q2.t: The child agrees and is included, though a parent usually has the legal say
med-ethics-young.l05.q2.p: What is assent, when a child is at the doctor?
med-ethics-young.l05.q2.h: It is about including the child.
med-ethics-young.l05.q2.e: Assent means a child is included and agrees where possible, while a parent or guardian usually gives legal consent.

med-ethics-young.l05.q3.t: Offer a high five or a wave instead
med-ethics-young.l05.q3.p: A relative wants a hug, but you do not feel like one. What is a respectful option?
med-ethics-young.l05.q3.h: You can say no to touch and still be polite.
med-ethics-young.l05.q3.e: You may choose how to greet people and still be kind. Forcing yourself to hug does not respect your own choice.

med-ethics-young.l05.q4.t: A grown-up responsible for the child, with the doctor making it as comfortable as possible
med-ethics-young.l05.q4.p: Some health care, like a needed shot, still happens even if a child is scared. Who decides?
med-ethics-young.l05.q4.h: Think about who is responsible for a young child.
med-ethics-young.l05.q4.e: A responsible adult decides and the care team tries to ease the fear. Children are included but do not hold the final legal say.

med-ethics-young.l06.q1.t: It is yours, and it should be shared only with people who need to know
med-ethics-young.l06.q1.p: Whose information is your health information?
med-ethics-young.l06.q1.e: Health information is private. It is shared only with people who need it to help you.

med-ethics-young.l06.q2.t: A secret that makes you feel unsafe or scared
med-ethics-young.l06.q2.p: Which secret should you ALWAYS tell a trusted grown-up?
med-ethics-young.l06.q2.h: One kind of secret is never okay to keep.
med-ethics-young.l06.q2.e: Secrets that make you feel unsafe must be told. Surprise parties and gifts are happy secrets that end soon.

med-ethics-young.l06.q3.t: They trust that the information will not be spread around
med-ethics-young.l06.q3.p: Why do people tell doctors the truth more easily when records stay private?
med-ethics-young.l06.q3.e: Privacy builds trust, and trust leads to honest answers. Spreading information around would destroy that trust.

med-ethics-young.l06.q4.t: Ask if they want to talk about it, and keep it private unless they say otherwise
med-ethics-young.l06.q4.p: A classmate tells you they had to visit the hospital. What is the best thing to do?
med-ethics-young.l06.q4.h: Before you share news, ask whose it is.
med-ethics-young.l06.q4.e: The news is the classmate's to share. Telling others or joking about it could embarrass them.

med-ethics-young.l07.q1.t: Each person who needs care should be able to get it, no matter who they are
med-ethics-young.l07.q1.p: What does fairness in health care mean?
med-ethics-young.l07.q1.h: Care should not depend on who you are.
med-ethics-young.l07.q1.e: Fairness means everyone who needs care should have a chance to get it. Money, looks or place of birth should not decide.

med-ethics-young.l07.q2.t: To help patients and doctors understand each other when they speak different languages
med-ethics-young.l07.q2.p: Why do some hospitals use interpreters?
med-ethics-young.l07.q2.h: Think about talking to someone who speaks another language.
med-ethics-young.l07.q2.e: Interpreters make care fairer by helping everyone understand. They are not there to choose who is seen first.

med-ethics-young.l07.q3.t: Give each child the help that fits what they need
med-ethics-young.l07.q3.p: One child has a cold and another has a broken leg. Which is the fair way to help?
med-ethics-young.l07.q3.e: Fairness means matching help to need. Giving the same thing to both would leave one child without proper care.

med-ethics-young.l07.q4.t: By how urgently each person needs it for their health
med-ethics-young.l07.q4.p: When a hospital has only one bed left, how should doctors choose who gets it?
med-ethics-young.l07.q4.h: Health need is the fair reason.
med-ethics-young.l07.q4.e: Health need is a fair reason. Looks, loudness or popularity say nothing about who needs the care most.

med-ethics-young.l08.q1.t: Not teasing or staring, and being kind to people who are not the same as you
med-ethics-young.l08.q1.p: What does it mean to respect differences?
med-ethics-young.l08.q1.h: Respect and sameness are not the same.
med-ethics-young.l08.q1.e: Respect means kindness and politeness toward differences. Staying away or asking loud questions is unkind.

med-ethics-young.l08.q2.t: Let them do it in peace and ask if they would like any help
med-ethics-young.l08.q2.p: Which is a kind way to help a classmate who needs to check their blood sugar?
med-ethics-young.l08.q2.h: Being helpful can also mean giving space.
med-ethics-young.l08.q2.e: Giving space while offering help respects the classmate. Telling everyone or teasing would be unkind.

med-ethics-young.l08.q3.t: To give care that fits what matters to you and your family
med-ethics-young.l08.q3.p: A doctor asks about your family's customs. Why might the doctor do that?
med-ethics-young.l08.q3.h: Care works better when it fits the person.
med-ethics-young.l08.q3.e: Knowing your family's customs helps the doctor fit the care to you. It is not about ranking families.

med-ethics-young.l08.q4.t: only one small part of who they are
med-ethics-young.l08.q4.h: People are more than a diagnosis.
med-ethics-young.l08.q4.e: Everyone is a whole person with many parts, and a health condition is just one of them.

med-ethics-young.l09.q1.t: They must complete training and pass exams before treating patients
med-ethics-young.l09.q1.p: Why must doctors and nurses be licensed?
med-ethics-young.l09.q1.h: A license is a promise about training.
med-ethics-young.l09.q1.e: Licensing shows a clinician has been trained and tested. It does not remove safety rules.

med-ethics-young.l09.q2.t: To ask whether a study is safe, fair and clearly explained to participants
med-ethics-young.l09.q2.p: What is the job of a research review board?
med-ethics-young.l09.q2.h: It is a group that checks studies before they begin.
med-ethics-young.l09.q2.e: Review boards check safety, fairness and consent. Volunteers are always free to leave.

med-ethics-young.l09.q3.t: So companies cannot sell something dangerous and call it a cure
med-ethics-young.l09.q3.p: Why are medicines checked by government agencies before they are sold?
med-ethics-young.l09.q3.e: Review protects people from unsafe or false products. It cannot guarantee a result for every person.

med-ethics-young.l09.q4.t: They can feel annoying, but they protect people when something goes wrong
med-ethics-young.l09.q4.p: The lesson compares medical rules to seat belts. What is the point of the comparison?
med-ethics-young.l09.q4.h: Think about why people buckle up.
med-ethics-young.l09.q4.e: Both protect people from harm. The lesson also says rules are not perfect and can be debated.

med-ethics-young.l10.q1.t: A treatment with no active medicine, used to compare with a real one
med-ethics-young.l10.q1.p: In a clinical trial, what is a placebo?
med-ethics-young.l10.q1.h: It looks like a treatment but has no active ingredient.
med-ethics-young.l10.q1.e: A placebo is a stand-in with no active drug, which shows how much improvement comes from hope or time.

med-ethics-young.l10.q2.t: Using chance to decide who goes into which group so the groups are alike
med-ethics-young.l10.q2.p: What is randomization in a clinical trial?
med-ethics-young.l10.q2.e: Random assignment makes groups similar. Letting volunteers or researchers pick could tilt the results.

med-ethics-young.l10.q3.t: Colds often get better on their own, so the tea may not have done anything
med-ethics-young.l10.q3.p: Your friend drank tea and her cold went away, so she says the tea cures colds. What is the main problem with that claim?
med-ethics-young.l10.q3.h: Would she have gotten better anyway?
med-ethics-young.l10.q3.e: Without a comparison, we cannot tell whether the tea or time caused the improvement.

med-ethics-young.l10.q4.t: To check safety first before giving it to larger groups of people
med-ethics-young.l10.q4.p: Why do scientists test new medicines in steps, starting small?
med-ethics-young.l10.q4.e: Small first tests look for safety. Larger tests later check whether it works.

med-ethics-young.l11.q1.t: Making the most money for the hospital
med-ethics-young.l11.q1.p: Which of these is NOT one of the four ideas used to think about medical ethics?
med-ethics-young.l11.q1.h: The four are autonomy, doing good, avoiding harm and justice.
med-ethics-young.l11.q1.e: The four principles do not include profit. They are autonomy, beneficence, avoiding harm and justice.

med-ethics-young.l11.q2.t: A person's right to make choices about their own care
med-ethics-young.l11.q2.e: Autonomy is respect for a person's own informed choices. Doctors advise but patients decide.

med-ethics-young.l11.q3.t: Would the treatment cause suffering that is worse than its benefit?
med-ethics-young.l11.q3.p: In the story, Grandpa is unsure about a strong treatment. Which question is about avoiding harm?
med-ethics-young.l11.q3.h: Harm means pain or damage from the treatment.
med-ethics-young.l11.q3.e: Weighing suffering against benefit is avoiding harm. The other questions are autonomy, doing good and fairness.

med-ethics-young.l11.q4.t: Disagreeing while staying respectful and listening to each other
med-ethics-young.l11.q4.p: Two thoughtful people still disagree about a hard health question. What does the lesson say is okay?
med-ethics-young.l11.q4.e: Careful, respectful disagreement is a normal part of ethics. The four ideas help us ask better questions.

med-ethics-young.l12.q1.t: It grows, and doctors explain things to them directly and ask what they think
med-ethics-young.l12.q1.p: As teens get older, what usually happens with their voice in health care?
med-ethics-young.l12.q1.e: Teens are included more and more. A parent or guardian usually still holds the legal say.

med-ethics-young.l12.q2.t: part of health, and problems can be treated like other health problems
med-ethics-young.l12.q2.p: Which statement about mental health is the most accurate?
med-ethics-young.l12.q2.h: Treat it like any other health issue.
med-ethics-young.l12.q2.e: Mental health is health. Feeling very sad or anxious for a long time is a reason to talk to a trusted adult.

med-ethics-young.l12.q3.t: Tell a trusted adult right away, because safety comes before the secret
med-ethics-young.l12.q3.p: A friend tells you they have thought about hurting themselves and asks you to keep it secret. What should you do?
med-ethics-young.l12.q3.h: This is one secret that is not safe to keep.
med-ethics-young.l12.q3.e: Safety comes first, so you tell a trusted adult. Keeping the secret could leave your friend without help.

med-ethics-young.l12.q4.t: Because they believe someone is in danger and safety comes first
med-ethics-young.l12.q4.p: Why might a doctor break privacy and get other people involved?
med-ethics-young.l12.q4.e: Doctors may share information when a person is in danger. Curiosity or gossip is never a reason.

med-g35.l01.q1.t: The nucleus, which works like the control room of the cell
med-g35.l01.q1.p: Which part of a cell holds the DNA, the instructions for building and running the body?
med-g35.l01.q1.e: The nucleus holds DNA. The membrane is only the outer skin, and mitochondria release energy rather than store instructions.

med-g35.l01.q2.t: They turn food and oxygen into energy that the cell can use
med-g35.l01.q2.p: What do mitochondria do inside a cell?
med-g35.l01.q2.e: Mitochondria release usable energy from food and oxygen. Deciding what enters is the job of the membrane.

med-g35.l01.q3.t: Each kind of cell has a shape that fits the job it does
med-g35.l01.q3.p: Why are nerve cells long and thin, while red blood cells are small round discs?
med-g35.l01.q3.e: A long thin shape helps nerve cells send messages far, and a small disc suits carrying oxygen through narrow tubes. The shapes are not accidents.

med-g35.l01.q4.t: Cells make copies of themselves to fill in the damaged spot
med-g35.l01.q4.p: Your knee is scraped and a few days later new skin has grown. Which cell activity explains this?
med-g35.l01.q4.e: Healing happens because nearby cells divide to make new ones. Cells do not simply turn into a completely different tissue.

med-g35.l02.q1.t: It holds you up and protects soft parts like the brain
med-g35.l02.q1.p: Which of these is a job of the skeleton?
med-g35.l02.q1.e: Bones give support and protection, such as the skull around the brain. Carrying oxygen is the blood's job.

med-g35.l02.q2.t: It can only pull by getting shorter, so it cannot push
med-g35.l02.q2.e: A muscle works by shortening and pulling. That is why joints need pairs of muscles to move in two directions.
