med-g35.l02.q3.t: The arm straightens, because the pair pulls the other way
med-g35.l02.q3.p: When the muscle on the back of your upper arm gets shorter, what happens at the elbow?
med-g35.l02.q3.e: The back muscle pulls the arm straight. The front muscle pulls it to bend, and muscles never push.

med-g35.l02.q4.t: Eating foods with calcium and getting active, weight-bearing play
med-g35.l02.q4.p: A child wants strong bones for the future. Which habit best helps?
med-g35.l02.q4.h: Bones are alive and like to be used.
med-g35.l02.q4.e: Calcium plus activity builds bone. Bones get stronger when they are used, so a lot of resting does the opposite.

med-g35.l03.q1.t: They carry blood away from the heart to the body
med-g35.l03.q1.e: Arteries carry blood away from the heart. Veins return it, and capillaries are the tiny tubes between them.

med-g35.l03.q2.t: Carrying oxygen from the lungs to cells around the body
med-g35.l03.q2.p: What is the main job of red blood cells?
med-g35.l03.q2.e: Red blood cells carry oxygen. White blood cells fight germs and platelets help with clotting.

med-g35.l03.q3.t: Your working muscles need more oxygen, so the heart pumps faster
med-g35.l03.q3.p: After running hard, your pulse is faster. What is the best explanation?
med-g35.l03.q3.e: Active muscles need more oxygen delivered, so the heart speeds up. This is normal and healthy.

med-g35.l03.q4.t: Through the thin walls of the tiny capillaries
med-g35.l03.q4.p: Where do oxygen and food pass out of the blood and into body cells?
med-g35.l03.q4.e: Capillary walls are very thin, which lets things pass through. Artery walls are thick, so little passes through them.

med-g35.l04.q1.p: Which gas do your cells make as waste that you breathe out?
med-g35.l04.q1.h: It is not the gas you need.
med-g35.l04.q1.e: Cells release carbon dioxide as waste. Oxygen is the gas breathed in and used.

med-g35.l04.q2.t: The diaphragm, a dome-shaped muscle under the lungs
med-g35.l04.q2.p: Which muscle does most of the work of moving air in and out?
med-g35.l04.q2.e: The diaphragm moves down to pull air in. The lungs have no muscles of their own.

med-g35.l04.q3.t: It lets oxygen pass into the blood and carbon dioxide pass out
med-g35.l04.q3.p: Why are the walls of the tiny air sacs very thin and wrapped in capillaries?
med-g35.l04.q3.e: Thin walls close to capillaries allow gas swapping. The sacs are made for exchange, not for trapping air.

med-g35.l04.q4.t: Staying away from cigarette smoke and being active often
med-g35.l04.q4.p: Which choice best helps keep your lungs healthy?
med-g35.l04.q4.e: Smoke harms the lungs and exercise strengthens breathing. Holding the breath does not make lungs healthier.

med-g35.l05.q1.t: The small intestine, a long narrow coiled tube
med-g35.l05.q1.p: In which organ does most digestion finish and most nutrients pass into the blood?
med-g35.l05.q1.e: Nutrients move into the blood through the walls of the small intestine. The large intestine mainly takes in water.

med-g35.l05.q2.t: It mixes the food with strong juices into a thick liquid
med-g35.l05.q2.p: What does the stomach do to food?
med-g35.l05.q2.e: The stomach churns food with juices. Chewing happens in the mouth, and water is absorbed later in the large intestine.

med-g35.l05.q3.t: Muscles in the esophagus squeeze in waves and push food along
med-g35.l05.q3.p: Why can a person swallow food and have it reach the stomach even while upside down?
med-g35.l05.q3.e: Waves of muscle squeezing move food along regardless of body position. Gravity helps only when upright.

med-g35.l05.q4.t: They filter waste and extra water out of the blood as urine
med-g35.l05.q4.p: What is the job of the kidneys?
med-g35.l05.q4.e: Kidneys filter blood and make urine. The liver and pancreas are the ones that help with digestion.

med-g35.l06.q1.t: The cerebellum, found at the back of the brain
med-g35.l06.q1.p: Which part of the brain mostly helps with balance and smooth movement?
med-g35.l06.q1.e: The cerebellum coordinates balance and movement. The cerebrum is more about thinking and memory.

med-g35.l06.q2.t: As tiny electrical signals that move very quickly
med-g35.l06.q2.p: How do messages travel along nerve cells?
med-g35.l06.q2.e: Nerve cells carry electrical signals. Blood, air and food are not how nerves send messages.

med-g35.l06.q3.t: A reflex through the spinal cord acts faster than conscious thought
med-g35.l06.q3.p: You touch a hot pan and your hand jerks away before you feel pain. What best explains this?
med-g35.l06.q3.e: Reflexes use short nerve paths through the spinal cord, so they are quick and protective.

med-g35.l06.q4.t: Wearing a helmet when biking and getting enough sleep
med-g35.l06.q4.p: Which habit best protects the brain?
med-g35.l06.q4.h: Think about head injuries and rest.
med-g35.l06.q4.e: Helmets prevent head injuries and sleep helps the brain work well. The skull alone does not prevent all injuries.

med-g35.l07.q1.t: It keeps water in and most germs out as a barrier
med-g35.l07.q1.p: What is one job of skin?
med-g35.l07.q1.e: Skin forms a tough barrier. Pumping blood is the heart's job.

med-g35.l07.q2.t: As sweat dries on the skin it cools you down
med-g35.l07.q2.p: How does sweating help the body?
med-g35.l07.q2.e: Drying sweat takes heat away from the skin, which helps you cool off.

med-g35.l07.q3.t: It warns the brain of danger so you can move away from harm
med-g35.l07.q3.p: Why is pain, though unpleasant, useful?
med-g35.l07.q3.e: Pain signals danger. People who cannot feel pain are often hurt without noticing.

med-g35.l07.q4.t: Use shade, a hat or sunscreen, since any skin can burn
med-g35.l07.q4.p: Two friends have different skin shades. What should both of them do on a very sunny day?
med-g35.l07.q4.h: Melanin helps, but only a bit.
med-g35.l07.q4.e: Melanin gives some protection but no skin shade is completely safe from sun damage.

med-g35.l08.q1.t: The retina at the back of the eye
med-g35.l08.q1.p: Which part of the eye has cells that notice light and color?
med-g35.l08.q1.e: The retina holds the light-sensing cells. The lens only focuses light onto it.

med-g35.l08.q2.t: It shakes, and tiny bones pass the shaking inward
med-g35.l08.q2.p: What happens to the eardrum when sound reaches it?
med-g35.l08.q2.e: Sound makes the eardrum vibrate and three tiny bones carry the vibration to the inner ear.

med-g35.l08.q3.t: Flavor depends on smell and taste working together
med-g35.l08.q3.p: Why does food seem to lack flavor when you have a stuffy nose?
med-g35.l08.q3.e: Much of what we call flavor comes from smell. Blocked smell makes food seem plain even though taste buds still work.

med-g35.l08.q4.t: Loud noise can permanently damage the hair cells of the inner ear
med-g35.l08.q4.p: A child goes to many loud concerts without ear protection. What is the likely risk?
med-g35.l08.q4.e: Hair cells in the inner ear can be damaged by loud noise and do not grow back, which may cause hearing loss.

med-g35.l09.q1.t: The common cold, which spreads in tiny droplets
med-g35.l09.q1.p: Which of these is caused by a virus?
med-g35.l09.q1.h: Colds are not treated with antibiotics.
med-g35.l09.q1.e: Colds and the flu are caused by viruses. Strep throat is the example of a bacterial illness.

med-g35.l09.q2.t: About twenty seconds, scrubbing all over the hands
med-g35.l09.q2.p: How long should you wash your hands with soap and water?
med-g35.l09.q2.h: Think of singing a short song twice.
med-g35.l09.q2.e: Twenty seconds of scrubbing with soap helps remove germs. A quick rinse removes far fewer.

med-g35.l09.q3.t: Colds are caused by viruses, and antibiotics work only on bacteria
med-g35.l09.q3.p: A child has a cold and the family asks for antibiotics. Why would a doctor probably say no?
med-g35.l09.q3.h: Match the medicine to the germ.
med-g35.l09.q3.e: Antibiotics kill bacteria and do nothing against viruses. Needless use can also make bacteria harder to treat.

med-g35.l09.q4.t: Sneezing into your elbow, then washing your hands
med-g35.l09.q4.p: Which action best stops a sneeze from spreading germs to others?
med-g35.l09.q4.e: Using the elbow keeps droplets off the hands that touch other things. Sneezing into bare hands leaves germs on surfaces.

med-g35.l10.q1.t: They stick to a particular germ and mark it for removal
med-g35.l10.q1.h: They are made by white blood cells.
med-g35.l10.q1.e: Antibodies are proteins that target specific germs. Carrying oxygen is done by red blood cells.

med-g35.l10.q2.t: It lets the immune system practice on a harmless piece of a germ
med-g35.l10.q2.p: How does a vaccine help the body?
med-g35.l10.q2.e: Vaccines train the immune memory without causing the full disease. They protect against specific germs, not every germ.

med-g35.l10.q3.t: The immune system remembers the virus and reacts quickly later
med-g35.l10.q3.p: Why do most people catch chicken pox only once?
med-g35.l10.q3.h: The immune system has a memory.
med-g35.l10.q3.e: Memory cells let the body respond fast the second time. A fever helps fight but does not make a permanent barrier.

med-g35.l10.q4.t: It is a common mild side effect, and the vaccine is still studied for safety
med-g35.l10.q4.p: A child gets a vaccine and has a sore arm for a day. What is the best way to understand it?
med-g35.l10.q4.e: A sore arm is a typical mild effect. It does not mean the person has the disease.

med-g35.l11.q1.t: Protein, found in foods like beans, eggs and fish
med-g35.l11.q1.p: Which nutrient is mainly used to build and repair muscles and other cells?
med-g35.l11.q1.e: Protein builds and repairs cells. Carbohydrates are the main quick fuel.

med-g35.l11.q2.t: Water, because the body is mostly water and loses some daily
med-g35.l11.q2.p: Which drink is the best everyday choice for your body?
med-g35.l11.q2.e: Water hydrates without added sugar. Sugary drinks give extra sugar that the body does not need in large amounts.

med-g35.l11.q3.t: No single food has every nutrient, so variety is needed
med-g35.l11.q3.p: A child eats only white bread every day. What is the main problem?
med-g35.l11.q3.e: A varied diet covers more nutrients. White bread provides carbohydrate but little else.

med-g35.l11.q4.t: Their immune system reacts strongly to peanuts, so they must avoid them
med-g35.l11.q4.p: A classmate has a peanut allergy. What does that mean?
med-g35.l11.q4.e: Food allergies are strong immune reactions. They can be serious, so the person avoids the food.

med-g35.l12.q1.t: About an hour of moderate to vigorous activity
med-g35.l12.q1.p: About how much activity do health groups suggest for children and teens each day?
med-g35.l12.q1.h: It adds up through the day.
med-g35.l12.q1.e: The suggestion is about an hour a day, and it can be spread out in several parts.

med-g35.l12.q2.t: Weight-bearing play such as running, jumping and dancing
med-g35.l12.q2.p: Which activity especially helps bones grow strong?
med-g35.l12.q2.e: Bones get stronger when they bear weight. Inactivity does not build bone.

med-g35.l12.q3.t: The heart is a muscle and gets stronger when it works harder
med-g35.l12.q3.p: Why does regular exercise make the heart stronger over time?
med-g35.l12.q3.e: Like other muscles, the heart adapts to work. It is not bone, and it keeps beating during exercise.

med-g35.l12.q4.t: Stop, rest, and tell an adult about it
med-g35.l12.q4.p: During a game, a child feels a sharp pain in the ankle. What is the best choice?
med-g35.l12.q4.e: Sharp pain can mean injury. Stopping and telling an adult prevents it getting worse.

med-g35.l13.q1.t: Repair work takes place and growth hormone is released in children
med-g35.l13.q1.p: What happens in the body during deep sleep?
med-g35.l13.q1.e: Deep sleep supports repair and growth. The heart and brain keep working, and the brain also sorts memories.

med-g35.l13.q2.p: About how much sleep do school-age children usually need each night?
med-g35.l13.q2.e: Health groups suggest around nine to twelve hours for school-age children.

med-g35.l13.q3.t: Too little sleep makes attention, learning and mood harder to manage
med-g35.l13.q3.p: A student who stays up late often finds it hard to pay attention in class. What is the best explanation?
med-g35.l13.q3.e: Lack of sleep affects attention and mood. Sleep matters for the brain, not just the muscles.

med-g35.l13.q4.t: A regular bedtime in a dark, quiet room with screens off
med-g35.l13.q4.p: Which habit best helps a child fall asleep more easily?
med-g35.l13.q4.e: Routine and a calm, dark room help sleep. Bright light and exciting content make it harder.

med-g35.l14.q1.t: Chemical messengers carried in the blood that tell the body what to do
med-g35.l14.q1.p: In the study of the body, what are hormones?
med-g35.l14.q1.e: Hormones are made by glands and signal other parts of the body. They drive puberty.

med-g35.l14.q2.t: Growing taller in spurts and developing stronger body odor
med-g35.l14.q2.p: Which of these is a normal change during puberty for most people?
med-g35.l14.q2.e: Growth spurts and stronger sweat odor are common. Washing daily helps with the odor.

med-g35.l14.q3.t: The timing varies from person to person, and both are normal
med-g35.l14.q3.p: One child starts puberty at 9 and a friend has not started at 13. What is the best way to see this?
med-g35.l14.q3.h: There is a wide normal range.
med-g35.l14.q3.e: Normal timing covers a wide range. A doctor can answer worries, but a later start is often normal too.

med-g35.l14.q4.t: Ask a parent, caregiver, school nurse or doctor for accurate answers
med-g35.l14.q4.p: A child has questions about changes in their body. What is the best thing to do?
med-g35.l14.q4.e: Trusted adults and health professionals give accurate information. Random sources can be wrong or unsafe.

med-g35.l15.q1.t: Taking slow deep breaths and talking to someone you trust
med-g35.l15.q1.p: Which of these is a healthy way to cope with a big feeling?
med-g35.l15.q1.e: Slow breathing calms the body's alarm response, and talking helps. Hiding feelings and skipping sleep usually make things worse.

med-g35.l15.q2.t: Tell a trusted adult right away, even if asked to keep it secret
med-g35.l15.q2.p: What should you do if a friend says they want to hurt themselves?
med-g35.l15.q2.e: This is a time to tell an adult at once. Keeping that kind of secret can leave a friend in danger.

med-g35.l15.q3.t: It is a sign to tell a trusted adult, since help is available
med-g35.l15.q3.p: A child has felt very sad for several weeks and no longer enjoys favorite games. What does this suggest?
med-g35.l15.q3.e: Weeks of sadness and loss of interest are signs that help could be useful. Many such problems are treatable.

med-g35.l15.q4.t: It is a sign of strength, and counselors and doctors can treat many problems
med-g35.l15.q4.p: Which statement about asking for help with mental health is accurate?
med-g35.l15.q4.e: Asking for help is wise, and treatments exist for many conditions such as anxiety. Children can and do need this help too.

med-g35.l16.q1.t: Press a clean cloth on it to stop the bleeding
med-g35.l16.q1.p: What is the first step for a small cut that is bleeding?
med-g35.l16.q1.e: Pressure with a clean cloth slows bleeding. Rubbing hard and using butter can cause more harm.

med-g35.l16.q2.t: Cool it under cool running water for several minutes
med-g35.l16.q2.p: What should you do first for a small burn?
med-g35.l16.q2.e: Cool running water is the standard first step. Ice, butter and oil can damage skin or trap heat.

med-g35.l16.q3.t: Someone will not wake up and you cannot get a response
med-g35.l16.q3.p: Which of these is a time to call 911 in the United States?
med-g35.l16.q3.e: A person who will not wake up is an emergency. Small scrapes and mild sunburn can be handled with an adult.

med-g35.l16.q4.t: Stay calm, say where you are, tell what happened, and stay on the line
med-g35.l16.q4.p: When you call for emergency help, which is the best way to act?
med-g35.l16.q4.e: The call taker needs the location and the problem. Hanging up early can stop help from reaching you.

med-g35.l17.q1.t: A parent, caregiver, doctor or nurse, who checks the label
med-g35.l17.q1.e: Medicine should come from a trusted adult who reads the label. Sharing medicine with friends can be harmful.

med-g35.l17.q2.t: What it is for, how much to take and any warnings
med-g35.l17.q2.p: What does the label on a medicine tell you?
med-g35.l17.q2.e: Labels give use, amount and warnings. They are there to keep people safe.

med-g35.l17.q3.t: Follow the doctor's directions about how long to take them
med-g35.l17.q3.p: A child feels better after two days of antibiotics and wants to stop. What is the safest choice?
med-g35.l17.q3.e: The doctor sets the length of treatment. Stopping early or sharing leftovers can be unsafe and unhelpful.

med-g35.l17.q4.t: Call Poison Control or 911 right away rather than waiting for symptoms
med-g35.l17.q4.p: A younger child finds a bottle of vitamins that look like candy and swallows several. What should an adult do?
med-g35.l17.q4.e: Vitamins count as medicines and can poison children in large amounts. Poison Control can advise quickly.

med-g35.l18.q1.t: Cares for the health of babies, children and teenagers
med-g35.l18.q1.e: A pediatrician is a doctor for children. Dentists care for teeth and pharmacists prepare medicines.

med-g35.l18.q2.t: A careful study that tests whether a treatment works and is safe
med-g35.l18.q2.e: Clinical trials test new treatments in people under careful rules before approval.

med-g35.l18.q3.t: They can check growth and find or prevent problems early
med-g35.l18.q3.p: Why do doctors suggest check-ups even when a child feels healthy?
med-g35.l18.q3.e: Check-ups track growth and catch concerns early. They do not replace healthy habits.

med-g35.l18.q4.t: A paramedic gives emergency care, and a physical therapist helps people move after injury
med-g35.l18.q4.p: Which pair of workers is matched correctly with its job?
med-g35.l18.q4.e: Paramedics give emergency care and physical therapists help recovery. The other pairs mix up the jobs.

med-g68.l01.q1.t: The nucleus, which stores the genetic instructions
med-g68.l01.q1.p: Which part of a cell contains the DNA that holds the instructions for building proteins?
med-g68.l01.q1.h: Think of the control center of the cell.
med-g68.l01.q1.e: DNA is kept in the nucleus. Mitochondria release energy and ribosomes build proteins from the instructions, but neither is the main storage site of DNA.

med-g68.l01.q2.t: Releasing usable energy from sugar and oxygen
med-g68.l01.q2.p: What is the main job of mitochondria in a cell?
med-g68.l01.q2.h: They are often called the power stations.
med-g68.l01.q2.e: Mitochondria release usable energy from nutrients. The membrane, not mitochondria, controls what enters and leaves, so that option describes the wrong part.

med-g68.l01.q3.t: Each cell type has a shape that suits its particular job
med-g68.l01.q3.p: A nerve cell is long and thin while a red blood cell is a small flat disc. What best explains this difference?
med-g68.l01.q3.h: Think about what each cell has to do.
med-g68.l01.q3.e: Cell shape fits function: nerve cells send signals over distance and red blood cells carry oxygen. Almost all cells share the same DNA, so different DNA does not explain it.

med-g68.l01.q4.t: Different cells use different parts of the same instruction set
med-g68.l01.q4.p: A scientist notes that skin cells and muscle cells in the same person have nearly identical DNA yet behave very differently. Which conclusion best fits this?
med-g68.l01.q4.e: Cells in one body share the same DNA but switch on different genes. The claim that DNA is lost or gained is wrong, since almost every cell keeps a full copy.

med-g68.l02.q1.t: Epithelial, connective, muscle and nervous tissue
med-g68.l02.q1.p: Which choice lists the four main types of tissue in the body?
med-g68.l02.q1.h: One covers surfaces, one supports, one moves, one signals.
med-g68.l02.q1.e: The four basic tissue types are epithelial, connective, muscle and nervous. Cardiac, skeletal and smooth are types of muscle, not tissue categories.

med-g68.l02.q2.t: A group of organs that work together to do a large job
med-g68.l02.q2.h: Think of the digestive system as an example.
med-g68.l02.q2.e: An organ system is organs cooperating, like the stomach, intestines and liver in digestion. Identical cells doing a shared job is a tissue.

med-g68.l02.q3.t: They coordinate to deliver more oxygen to working muscles
med-g68.l02.q3.p: While running, your breathing and heart rate both increase. What does this show about the body systems?
med-g68.l02.q3.h: Muscles need more oxygen when you exercise.
med-g68.l02.q3.e: The respiratory and circulatory systems work together to supply oxygen. Systems do not operate in isolation, so the claim that they work separately is wrong.

med-g68.l02.q4.t: Homeostasis, where the body adjusts to keep conditions steady
med-g68.l02.q4.p: On a hot day a person sweats and their skin flushes, and their core temperature stays near normal. Which idea explains this best?
med-g68.l02.q4.h: The body keeps its internal conditions in a narrow range.
med-g68.l02.q4.e: Sweating and widened skin blood vessels release heat, which is homeostasis. Metabolism does not stop, and heat is not a germ that immunity could attack.

med-g68.l03.q1.p: Which nutrient is broken into amino acids that the body uses to build muscle and enzymes?
med-g68.l03.q1.h: Amino acids are the building blocks of this nutrient.
med-g68.l03.q1.e: Proteins are digested into amino acids. Carbohydrates become sugars and fats become fatty acids, so they do not supply amino acids.

med-g68.l03.q2.t: All the chemical reactions that keep a living body going
med-g68.l03.q2.p: What does the term metabolism describe?
med-g68.l03.q2.h: It includes both breaking down and building up.
med-g68.l03.q2.e: Metabolism covers all the body's chemical reactions, including building molecules and releasing energy. Digestion is only one part of it.

med-g68.l03.q3.t: Talk to a trusted adult or doctor, since growing bodies need enough food to develop
med-g68.l03.q3.p: A teen skips most meals for weeks to lose weight and feels tired and dizzy. What is the most sensible advice?
med-g68.l03.q3.h: Think about what the growing body needs.
med-g68.l03.q3.e: Under-eating during growth can harm health, and a clinician can help. Vitamins do not replace the energy and protein found in food, so that option is wrong.

med-g68.l03.q4.t: Health depends on overall variety and balance, not one food
med-g68.l03.q4.p: A student says that a single food, such as one trendy "superfood," can cover all nutrition needs. Which response is best supported by what we know?
med-g68.l03.q4.h: Consider why varied diets are recommended.
med-g68.l03.q4.e: No single food supplies every nutrient the body needs, so variety matters. Eating huge amounts of one food does not fix the gaps and can cause other problems.

med-g68.l04.q1.t: Washing hands with soap for about twenty seconds
med-g68.l04.q1.p: Which action best blocks the route by which germs travel from hands to the mouth or eyes?
med-g68.l04.q1.h: The soap and the time both matter.
med-g68.l04.q1.e: Soap and about twenty seconds of scrubbing remove germs effectively. A quick rinse removes far fewer, and dirty gloves can spread germs.

med-g68.l04.q2.t: An animal such as a mosquito or tick that carries a germ between hosts
med-g68.l04.q2.p: What is a vector in the spread of disease?
med-g68.l04.q2.h: Think of malaria and Lyme disease.
med-g68.l04.q2.e: Vectors, like mosquitoes and ticks, carry germs from one host to another. A medicine that kills germs is not a vector.

med-g68.l04.q3.p: A stomach illness hits many people who ate at the same picnic. Which route of spread is most likely?
med-g68.l04.q3.h: What did all the sick people share?
med-g68.l04.q3.e: A shared meal pointing to stomach illness suggests contaminated food or water. Outdoor air spread is unlikely to affect only people who ate the food.

med-g68.l04.q4.t: Identify who was exposed and test or separate those who are sick
med-g68.l04.q4.p: A school nurse notices many cases of the same illness in a single classroom within two days. What is the best first public health step?
med-g68.l04.q4.h: Stopping the chain of spread begins with knowing who is involved.
med-g68.l04.q4.e: Tracing exposures and separating the sick breaks the chain of spread. Giving antibiotics to everyone is wrong because the cause may be a virus and antibiotics do not treat viruses.

med-g68.l05.q1.p: Which type of germ is a single living cell that can reproduce on its own?
med-g68.l05.q1.h: The other main germ needs a host cell to copy itself.
med-g68.l05.q1.e: Bacteria are single-celled organisms that divide on their own. Viruses cannot reproduce without a host cell, and antibodies are made by the immune system rather than being germs.

med-g68.l05.q2.t: Colds are caused by viruses, and antibiotics act on bacteria
med-g68.l05.q2.p: Why do antibiotics not help against a cold?
med-g68.l05.q2.h: Think about which type of germ antibiotics target.
med-g68.l05.q2.e: Antibiotics target bacterial processes, and the common cold is viral. Colds are not caused by bacteria, so that distractor is incorrect.

med-g68.l05.q3.t: Antibiotic resistance, where bacteria survive the drug
med-g68.l05.q3.p: A doctor tells a patient to finish a prescribed antibiotic course unless told otherwise, and also not to ask for antibiotics for viral illness. What problem do both pieces of advice help prevent?
med-g68.l05.q3.e: Misuse of antibiotics lets resistant bacteria survive and spread. Antibiotics do not shrink viruses or drain the immune system.

med-g68.l05.q4.t: The bacterial infection may be treated with an antibiotic, while the viral one is not
med-g68.l05.q4.p: A patient has a sore throat and a doctor runs a test that shows Streptococcus bacteria growing. Compared with a sore throat from a cold virus, what is the key difference in approach?
med-g68.l05.q4.h: Match the medicine to the type of germ.
med-g68.l05.q4.e: A confirmed bacterial infection can be treated with an antibiotic, and a viral cold is not. The reverse statement is wrong because antibiotics do not act on viruses.

med-g68.l06.q1.p: Which cells make antibodies that stick to a specific germ?
med-g68.l06.q1.h: They are a type of white blood cell.
med-g68.l06.q1.e: B cells produce antibodies. Red blood cells carry oxygen and platelets help blood clot, so neither makes antibodies.

med-g68.l06.q2.t: Gives it a safe preview of a germ so it builds memory
med-g68.l06.q2.p: What does a vaccine do for the immune system?
med-g68.l06.q2.e: Vaccines train the immune system and produce memory cells without causing the full disease. They do not replace the immune system or destroy all germs.

med-g68.l06.q3.t: Herd immunity makes it hard for the germ to find hosts
med-g68.l06.q3.p: A baby is too young for a certain vaccine, but most people around her are immune to the disease. Why is she somewhat protected?
med-g68.l06.q3.h: A germ needs new hosts to keep spreading.
med-g68.l06.q3.e: When most people are immune, the germ rarely reaches vulnerable people, which is herd immunity. Babies can catch many infections, so the last option is false.

med-g68.l06.q4.t: Memory cells that respond faster and stronger to a germ they have seen before
med-g68.l06.q4.p: After a first infection with a germ, a person gets only a mild illness the second time they meet it. Which part of the immune system best accounts for this?
med-g68.l06.q4.e: Memory B and T cells allow a quick, strong response on re-exposure. Skin and acid are general barriers that do not learn from past infection, and red blood cells have no role in recognition.

med-g68.l07.q1.t: Hormone signals from the brain that activate the reproductive organs
med-g68.l07.q1.p: What triggers the start of puberty?
med-g68.l07.q1.e: Puberty begins when the brain signals the reproductive organs to produce more sex hormones. Food and sleep influence health but do not start puberty on a set day.

med-g68.l07.q2.t: The shedding of the uterine lining when pregnancy has not occurred
med-g68.l07.q2.h: It happens roughly monthly after cycles settle.
med-g68.l07.q2.e: A period is the shedding of the uterus lining when no pregnancy has occurred. Release of an egg is ovulation, which is a different event.

med-g68.l07.q3.t: Timing varies widely among healthy teens, and a doctor can check if she is concerned
med-g68.l07.q3.p: A 12-year-old is worried because friends have started puberty and she has not. What is the most accurate thing to tell her?
med-g68.l07.q3.e: Puberty normally starts across a wide age range, and a clinician can reassure or investigate. Claiming it always begins at the same age is incorrect.

med-g68.l07.q4.t: Many infections cause no symptoms, so testing is how they are found early
med-g68.l07.q4.p: A teen says that if they feel fine, they cannot have a sexually transmitted infection, so testing is pointless. Which response is most accurate?
med-g68.l07.q4.e: Many STIs can be present without symptoms, so testing and talking to a clinician matters. The belief that all infections cause obvious symptoms is wrong.

med-g68.l08.q1.t: Strong feelings lasting weeks and interfering with daily life
med-g68.l08.q1.p: Which description fits a mental health condition rather than ordinary stress?
med-g68.l08.q1.h: Think about how long it lasts and how much it disrupts life.
med-g68.l08.q1.e: Conditions involve persistent, impairing symptoms. Brief worry or short sadness are normal, expected emotions.

med-g68.l08.q2.p: Which habit is known to help protect mental health?
med-g68.l08.q2.h: The brain handles emotions better when rested.
med-g68.l08.q2.e: Regular sleep supports emotional regulation. Withdrawing from friends and suppressing feelings usually make things worse.

med-g68.l08.q3.t: Take it seriously and tell a trusted adult, even if they asked you to keep it secret
med-g68.l08.q3.p: A friend tells you privately that they have been thinking of hurting themselves and asks you to promise to keep it secret. What is the best response?
med-g68.l08.q3.e: Self-harm thoughts need an adult's help, and a friend's safety matters more than a secret. Telling someone to cheer up dismisses a serious concern.

med-g68.l08.q4.t: These may be signs of depression, so a parent, doctor or counselor should be consulted
med-g68.l08.q4.p: A student who used to love soccer now stays in bed, has lost interest in friends, and feels low most days for over a month. Which interpretation is most reasonable?
med-g68.l08.q4.h: Persistent low mood plus lost interest is a pattern clinicians look for.
med-g68.l08.q4.e: Weeks of low mood and loss of interest fit the pattern of depression and merit professional evaluation. Calling it laziness ignores that it is a health condition.

med-g68.l09.q1.p: Which brain chemical is strongly linked to the reward system?
med-g68.l09.q1.e: Dopamine is a neurotransmitter central to reward. Insulin controls blood sugar, hemoglobin carries oxygen and collagen is a structural protein.

med-g68.l09.q2.t: Needing more of a drug to get the same effect
med-g68.l09.q2.p: What does tolerance mean in the context of drug use?
med-g68.l09.q2.h: The brain adapts to repeated exposure.
med-g68.l09.q2.e: Tolerance means the brain adapts so that a larger amount is needed for the same effect. It does not mean the drug is harmless.

med-g68.l09.q3.t: The brain areas for planning and impulse control are still developing
med-g68.l09.q3.p: Why are teens at higher risk of lasting harm from substance use than adults?
med-g68.l09.q3.e: The prefrontal region is still maturing during the teen years, which raises risk. The reward system exists in teens and is very active.

med-g68.l09.q4.t: Illegal pills may contain fentanyl, and an unknown dose can slow or stop breathing
med-g68.l09.q4.p: A person is told that a pill bought from an unknown seller looks identical to a prescription painkiller. Why is taking it especially dangerous?
med-g68.l09.q4.e: Counterfeit pills can contain fentanyl in unpredictable amounts, which can suppress breathing. The belief that look-alike pills are identical is the dangerous myth.

med-g68.l10.q1.t: By attaching to a specific target such as a receptor, enzyme or transporter
med-g68.l10.q1.p: How do most drugs produce their effect in the body?
med-g68.l10.q1.e: Most drugs bind to a target molecule. They do not rewrite DNA in every cell or replace blood.

med-g68.l10.q2.t: An effect of a drug other than the one intended
med-g68.l10.q2.h: Drugs rarely affect only one thing.
med-g68.l10.q2.e: A side effect is an additional effect beyond the intended one. It is not the therapeutic goal.

med-g68.l10.q3.t: Accidentally giving too much acetaminophen, which can damage the liver
med-g68.l10.q3.p: A parent gives a child a cold medicine and also a separate fever reducer, and both contain acetaminophen. What is the main concern?
med-g68.l10.q3.h: Check the active ingredients on every label.
med-g68.l10.q3.e: Duplicate ingredients can add up to an overdose, and acetaminophen overdose harms the liver. The medicines do not neutralize each other.

med-g68.l10.q4.t: Not share it, and suggest the friend talk to a doctor or pharmacist instead
med-g68.l10.q4.p: A teen has leftover prescription medicine from a past illness and a friend has similar symptoms. Which choice is the safest?
med-g68.l10.q4.h: Doses and conditions differ person to person.
med-g68.l10.q4.e: Prescriptions are chosen for a specific person, weight, condition and other medicines. Splitting a dose is not automatically safe.

med-g68.l11.q1.t: Checking safety in a small group of people
med-g68.l11.q1.p: What is the main goal of a Phase 1 clinical trial?
med-g68.l11.q1.h: It is the first stage in humans.
med-g68.l11.q1.e: Phase 1 mainly checks safety in a small group. Large effectiveness testing is Phase 3.

med-g68.l11.q2.t: To show what happens without the new treatment for comparison
med-g68.l11.q2.p: Why do trials often use a control group?
med-g68.l11.q2.h: Without a comparison, you cannot tell what caused a change.
med-g68.l11.q2.e: A control group reveals how people do without the treatment. If everyone received the new treatment there would be no comparison.

med-g68.l11.q3.p: In a trial, neither the patients nor the doctors know who gets the real drug and who gets the placebo. What does this blinding prevent?
med-g68.l11.q3.h: Expectations can change how people feel and report.
med-g68.l11.q3.e: Blinding keeps beliefs from influencing reports and judgments. It does not stop the drug entering the body or prevent side effects.

med-g68.l11.q4.t: There was no control group, and so few people cannot show cause
med-g68.l11.q4.p: A company reports that five patients felt better after trying a new tablet and says this proves it works. What is the strongest criticism?
med-g68.l11.q4.h: People often recover on their own or respond to expectation.
med-g68.l11.q4.e: Without a control group and with a tiny sample, improvement could be chance or natural recovery. Large randomized, controlled trials are needed.

med-g68.l12.q1.t: Promises of a miracle cure for many unrelated problems
med-g68.l12.q1.p: Which of these is a warning sign of a misleading health claim?
med-g68.l12.q1.e: Claims of a cure-all are a classic red flag. The other options are signs of careful evidence.

med-g68.l12.q2.t: Two things occurring together does not prove one causes the other
med-g68.l12.q2.p: What does the phrase "correlation is not causation" mean?
med-g68.l12.q2.e: A link between two things may be due to a third factor or chance. It does not follow that one causes the other.

med-g68.l12.q3.t: Colds go away on their own, so the tea may get credit for improvement it did not earn
med-g68.l12.q3.p: A video says, "My cousin drank this tea and her cold vanished, so it cures colds." What is the main flaw?
med-g68.l12.q3.h: What would have happened without the tea?
med-g68.l12.q3.e: Without a comparison, natural recovery looks like a cure. The claim is not necessarily false, but it is not evidence.

med-g68.l12.q4.t: The absolute risk may still be very small, so more detail is needed
med-g68.l12.q4.p: A headline says a food "raises your risk of a disease by 50 percent." The disease affects 2 in 10,000 people. What should a careful reader conclude?
med-g68.l12.q4.h: Compare relative change to the starting point.
med-g68.l12.q4.e: A 50 percent rise on a very small baseline is still a small absolute risk. The headline does not say that half the population will be affected.

med-g68.l13.q1.t: Check that the scene is safe for you
med-g68.l13.q1.p: What should be your first step when you come across an injured person?
med-g68.l13.q1.h: A second victim helps no one.
med-g68.l13.q1.e: Scene safety comes first. Moving an injured person or giving drinks can cause harm.

med-g68.l13.q2.p: Where on the body do you push during hands-only CPR?
med-g68.l13.q2.h: You are trying to squeeze the heart between the breastbone and spine.
med-g68.l13.q2.e: Compressions go on the center of the chest. Pushing elsewhere does not circulate blood effectively.

med-g68.l13.q3.t: Call or have someone call emergency services, start compressions and get an AED
med-g68.l13.q3.p: A classmate collapses, does not respond and is not breathing normally. What is the best sequence?
med-g68.l13.q3.h: Time matters when the heart has stopped.
med-g68.l13.q3.e: Early calls, compressions and an AED give the best chance. Waiting delays life-saving help.

med-g68.l13.q4.t: Cool the burn under cool running water for several minutes
med-g68.l13.q4.p: A person gets a minor burn on the hand from a hot pan. Which choice is the best immediate action?
med-g68.l13.q4.e: Cool running water removes heat and reduces damage. Ice can damage tissue further, and butter traps heat and raises infection risk.

med-g68.l14.q1.p: Which health professional is an expert in medicines and checks that they are safe together?
med-g68.l14.q1.h: You often see them at a counter filling prescriptions.
med-g68.l14.q1.e: Pharmacists specialize in medicines and interactions. Epidemiologists study patterns of disease in populations.

med-g68.l14.q2.t: How disease spreads and who is affected within a population or community
med-g68.l14.q2.e: Epidemiologists study disease patterns in populations. Bone repair belongs to surgeons.

med-g68.l14.q3.t: Many health careers need shorter programs than a medical degree
med-g68.l14.q3.p: A student likes science and helping people but dislikes the idea of long years of school. Which statement is most accurate?
med-g68.l14.q3.h: Think of the variety of roles.
med-g68.l14.q3.e: Roles such as EMT, medical assistant or lab technician have shorter training paths. Not all careers need medical school.

med-g68.l14.q4.t: A public health worker who plans water and sanitation programs
med-g68.l14.q4.p: A community has dirty drinking water causing repeated illness. Which professional is most likely to design a solution at the level of the whole community?
med-g68.l14.q4.h: The problem is about a population, not one patient.
med-g68.l14.q4.e: Public health workers address community-wide causes. The other professionals treat individual patients for different conditions.

med-g912.l01.q1.t: The control center, such as the hypothalamus
med-g912.l01.q1.p: In a homeostatic loop, which component compares the measured value with the set point?
med-g912.l01.q1.h: Think about which part makes the decision.
med-g912.l01.q1.e: The control center integrates sensor input and compares it with the set point. Sensors only detect the variable; effectors carry out the response.

med-g912.l01.q2.t: The response opposes the original change and so returns the variable toward its set point
med-g912.l01.q2.p: Which statement best describes negative feedback?
med-g912.l01.q2.h: Negative here means the response works against the change.
med-g912.l01.q2.e: Negative feedback reverses the stimulus, which stabilizes variables like temperature. The second option describes positive feedback.

med-g912.l01.q3.t: Beta cells release insulin, tissues take up glucose and the liver stores it, so glucose falls
med-g912.l01.q3.p: After a large meal, blood glucose rises. Which sequence correctly describes the usual response?
med-g912.l01.q3.e: Insulin from beta cells promotes uptake and storage. Glucagon does the opposite and acts between meals, so options pairing glucagon with a glucose fall are wrong.

med-g912.l01.q4.t: Immune signals have raised the hypothalamic set point, so the body is working to reach a higher temperature
med-g912.l01.q4.p: A patient with a fever reports feeling cold and begins shivering even though body temperature is already above 37 C. What best explains this?
med-g912.l01.q4.h: Compare the actual temperature with the new target.
med-g912.l01.q4.e: In fever the set point rises, so the actual temperature is below the new target and cold-defense responses fire. The set point has changed; the sensors are not broken.

med-g912.l02.q1.t: It must generate enough pressure to push blood through the whole systemic circuit
med-g912.l02.q1.p: Why is the wall of the left ventricle thicker than the right?
med-g912.l02.q1.h: Compare how far each ventricle sends blood.
med-g912.l02.q1.e: Systemic resistance is much higher than pulmonary resistance, so the left ventricle needs more muscle. The pulmonary circuit is the lower-pressure one.

med-g912.l02.q2.p: Which structure is the heart's natural pacemaker?
med-g912.l02.q2.h: It starts each normal beat in the right atrium.
med-g912.l02.q2.e: The sinoatrial node fires fastest and sets the rhythm. The atrioventricular node delays and relays the signal to the ventricles.

med-g912.l02.q3.p: A resting adult has a heart rate of 70 beats per minute and a stroke volume of 70 mL. Approximately what is the cardiac output?
med-g912.l02.q3.h: Cardiac output is rate times stroke volume; convert mL to liters.
med-g912.l02.q3.e: 70 x 70 mL = 4900 mL, or about 4.9 L/min. The other options come from slipping a decimal place.

med-g912.l02.q4.t: It falls, because lower vascular resistance reduces pressure at the same cardiac output
med-g912.l02.q4.p: A drug causes widening of small arteries without changing heart rate or stroke volume. What is the most likely effect on blood pressure, and why?
med-g912.l02.q4.h: Pressure depends on flow and resistance together.
med-g912.l02.q4.e: Pressure is roughly cardiac output times resistance, so lowering resistance lowers pressure when output is unchanged. The third option ignores resistance entirely.

med-g912.l03.q1.t: Across the thin walls of alveoli and surrounding capillaries
med-g912.l03.q1.p: Where does gas exchange between air and blood occur?
med-g912.l03.q1.h: Look for the thinnest barrier with blood vessels beside it.
med-g912.l03.q1.e: Alveoli provide a huge, thin surface next to capillaries. Bronchi and the trachea only conduct air.

med-g912.l03.q2.t: CO2 falls and blood becomes less acidic (higher pH)
med-g912.l03.q2.p: A person breathes rapidly and deeply during a panic attack. What happens to blood CO2 and pH?
med-g912.l03.q2.h: Faster breathing blows off more of the gas that forms acid.
med-g912.l03.q2.e: Hyperventilation removes CO2, lowering carbonic acid and raising pH. The kidneys act over hours, not instantly.

med-g912.l03.q3.p: Which hormone causes the kidney collecting duct to reabsorb more water?
med-g912.l03.q3.h: Its name says it opposes urine production.
med-g912.l03.q3.e: Antidiuretic hormone inserts water channels in the collecting duct. Aldosterone mainly drives sodium retention, with water following secondarily.

med-g912.l03.q4.t: Slower breathing that retains CO2 and so raises carbonic acid
med-g912.l03.q4.p: A man has had several days of severe vomiting and his blood has become alkaline. Which compensation is expected?
med-g912.l03.q4.h: Retaining the acid-forming gas would push pH back down.
med-g912.l03.q4.e: The lungs compensate for alkalosis by hypoventilating to retain CO2. Faster breathing would make the alkalosis worse.

med-g912.l04.q1.t: Nervous signals are fast and targeted, while hormonal signals are slower and last longer
med-g912.l04.q1.p: Which statement correctly contrasts the nervous and endocrine systems?
med-g912.l04.q1.e: Neurons conduct quickly along specific pathways, while hormones travel in blood and act over minutes to hours. Both systems influence heart rate.

med-g912.l04.q2.p: Which autonomic branch increases heart rate and widens the airways during stress?
med-g912.l04.q2.e: Sympathetic activity prepares for action. The parasympathetic branch slows the heart and favors digestion.

med-g912.l04.q3.t: High TSH with low thyroid hormone
med-g912.l04.q3.p: In a patient whose thyroid gland itself has failed, what pattern of TSH and thyroid hormone is expected?
med-g912.l04.q3.h: Low output removes the negative feedback on the pituitary.
med-g912.l04.q3.e: Low thyroid hormone removes feedback, so the pituitary raises TSH. Low TSH with low hormone would point to a pituitary problem instead.

med-g912.l04.q4.t: The pituitary is not producing enough TSH, so the thyroid is under-stimulated rather than failing on its own
med-g912.l04.q4.p: A patient has low thyroid hormone and a low TSH, and imaging shows a pituitary tumor. Why does this differ from primary thyroid failure?
med-g912.l04.q4.h: Locate the fault in the loop: which level is not sending the signal?
med-g912.l04.q4.e: In secondary hypothyroidism the pituitary fails to make enough TSH, so both TSH and thyroid hormone are low. The healthy-thyroid, high-TSH pattern would not match the lab findings.

med-g912.l05.q1.p: Which sign of inflammation is caused mainly by increased blood flow to the injured area?
med-g912.l05.q1.h: Think about what widened vessels deliver.
med-g912.l05.q1.e: Mediators like histamine widen vessels, increasing blood flow, which gives redness and heat. Swelling is due to leaky vessels, and pain to stimulation of nerve endings.

med-g912.l05.q2.p: Which cell type is typically the first to arrive in large numbers in acute bacterial inflammation?
med-g912.l05.q2.h: It is the main early responder, ahead of the cells that clear debris later.
med-g912.l05.q2.e: Neutrophils dominate early; macrophages arrive later to clear debris and organize repair. Plasma cells secrete antibodies later in the adaptive response.

med-g912.l05.q3.t: Cardiac muscle mainly heals by collagen scar, which does not contract like muscle
med-g912.l05.q3.p: Why does a heart attack that kills heart muscle often leave lasting weakness even after healing?
med-g912.l05.q3.h: Compare scar tissue with the tissue it replaces.
med-g912.l05.q3.e: Cardiac muscle has very limited regeneration, so a collagen scar fills the defect; it holds together but does not contract. Full regeneration would not leave weakness.

med-g912.l05.q4.t: It blocks enzymes that make prostaglandins, which are mediators of pain and inflammation
med-g912.l05.q4.p: A patient takes ibuprofen for a swollen, painful ankle after a sprain. Which statement best explains why it relieves pain and swelling?
med-g912.l05.q4.h: Consider which chemical mediators the drug class targets.
med-g912.l05.q4.e: NSAIDs inhibit cyclooxygenase enzymes and so reduce prostaglandins. They do not remove neutrophils or the injury; increasing histamine would worsen swelling.

med-g912.l06.q1.t: Colds are caused by viruses, and antibiotics target bacterial structures
med-g912.l06.q1.p: Why are antibiotics ineffective against the common cold?
med-g912.l06.q1.h: Identify the type of pathogen first.
med-g912.l06.q1.e: Antibiotics act on bacterial features such as cell wall synthesis or bacterial ribosomes. Common colds are viral.

med-g912.l06.q2.t: Plasma cells, the differentiated form of B cells
med-g912.l06.q2.p: Which cell is the direct source of the antibodies released into the blood?
med-g912.l06.q2.h: Antibodies are secreted proteins from the adaptive branch.
med-g912.l06.q2.e: Activated B cells differentiate into plasma cells, which are the cells that secrete antibodies. Cytotoxic T cells kill infected cells directly rather than secreting antibodies.

med-g912.l06.q3.t: It creates memory cells so a later exposure triggers a faster, stronger response
med-g912.l06.q3.p: How does a vaccine provide protection against a later infection?
med-g912.l06.q3.h: Ask what the immune system retains after the first exposure.
med-g912.l06.q3.e: Vaccines induce an adaptive response and memory. Supplying finished antibodies is passive immunity, which fades.

med-g912.l06.q4.t: Surviving bacteria carrying resistance traits were selected and then multiplied
med-g912.l06.q4.p: A patient stops a prescribed antibiotic early because they feel better, and weeks later the infection returns and no longer responds to the same drug. Which mechanism best explains the second result?
med-g912.l06.q4.h: Think of natural selection acting on a bacterial population.
med-g912.l06.q4.e: Incomplete or unnecessary use leaves the more resistant bacteria alive to multiply. Immune memory against the drug or an allergy does not make bacteria resistant.

med-g912.l07.q1.t: Spread of cancer cells to distant sites through blood or lymph
med-g912.l07.q1.p: In cancer biology, what does the term metastasis describe?
med-g912.l07.q1.h: The word relates to spread, not growth in place.
med-g912.l07.q1.e: Metastasis is dissemination to distant organs and is what chiefly makes cancer deadly. A benign tumor does not invade or spread.

med-g912.l07.q2.t: A brake or repair gene whose loss lets damaged cells keep dividing
med-g912.l07.q2.p: Which description fits a tumor suppressor gene such as TP53?
med-g912.l07.q2.h: The word suppressor tells you its normal job.
med-g912.l07.q2.e: Tumor suppressors restrain growth or repair DNA, and loss of function contributes to cancer. The accelerator description fits oncogenes.

med-g912.l07.q3.p: A cancer that arises from epithelial cells lining the colon is best classified as which type?
med-g912.l07.q3.h: Epithelial origin has its own name.
med-g912.l07.q3.e: Cancers of epithelial tissue are carcinomas. Sarcomas arise from connective tissue; lymphoma and leukemia come from lymphatic and blood-forming cells.

med-g912.l07.q4.t: Many chemotherapy drugs damage all rapidly dividing cells, including gut lining and hair follicle cells
med-g912.l07.q4.p: A patient receiving chemotherapy has nausea and hair loss. Which explanation best accounts for both effects?
med-g912.l07.q4.h: Ask what property of cancer cells chemotherapy exploits and who else shares it.
med-g912.l07.q4.e: Classic chemotherapy exploits rapid division, which gut epithelium and hair follicles share. It does not selectively target neurons or cause metastasis.

med-g912.l08.q1.p: In autosomal recessive disease, two carrier parents have what chance of an affected child in each pregnancy?
med-g912.l08.q1.h: Each parent passes one of two copies at random.
med-g912.l08.q1.e: Each parent passes the faulty copy with probability one half, so both do with probability one quarter. One half applies to a dominant condition with one affected parent.

med-g912.l08.q2.t: Type 1 diabetes, where T cells destroy insulin-producing beta cells
med-g912.l08.q2.p: Which condition is the best example of an autoimmune disease?
med-g912.l08.q2.h: Look for the immune attack on a normal tissue.
med-g912.l08.q2.e: Type 1 diabetes is immune-mediated destruction of beta cells. The others are genetic or chromosomal and not driven by a loss of immune tolerance.

med-g912.l08.q3.t: X-linked recessive, because males have only one X chromosome
med-g912.l08.q3.p: Which pattern of inheritance explains why males are more often affected by hemophilia A than females?
med-g912.l08.q3.h: Count the X chromosomes in each sex.
med-g912.l08.q3.e: A recessive variant on the X shows in males who have no second X to compensate. Autosomal inheritance affects both sexes equally.

med-g912.l08.q4.t: 1 in 4, because each pregnancy is an independent event
med-g912.l08.q4.p: A couple are both carriers of a CF variant and their first child is unaffected. What is the probability their second child is affected?
med-g912.l08.q4.h: Do earlier births change the odds of the next one?
med-g912.l08.q4.e: Each conception is independent, so risk stays 1 in 4. The one-in-three figure is a misapplication that treats births as depleting a pool.

med-g912.l09.q1.t: Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells, so little insulin is made
med-g912.l09.q1.p: What is the basic defect in type 1 diabetes?
med-g912.l09.q1.h: Think about which cell makes insulin and what happens to it.
med-g912.l09.q1.e: Type 1 is immune-mediated loss of beta cells. Insulin resistance is the central problem in type 2 diabetes.

med-g912.l09.q2.t: Average blood glucose over roughly the previous two to three months
med-g912.l09.q2.p: Hemoglobin A1c is useful because it reflects what?
med-g912.l09.q2.h: Red blood cells live for months.
med-g912.l09.q2.e: Glucose attaches to hemoglobin in red cells that live about 120 days, so A1c averages glucose over that period. A single glucose reading captures only one moment.

med-g912.l09.q3.t: Prolonged high glucose damages small blood vessels and nerves, causing neuropathy and retinopathy
med-g912.l09.q3.p: A man with long-standing type 2 diabetes develops numbness in his feet and reduced vision. What is the most likely general explanation?
med-g912.l09.q3.h: Think about chronic rather than acute effects of high glucose.
med-g912.l09.q3.e: Chronic hyperglycemia injures small vessels and nerves. Ketoacidosis is an acute event and is not the usual cause of these long-term complications.

med-g912.l09.q4.t: Respiratory compensation for metabolic acidosis from ketone accumulation
med-g912.l09.q4.p: A 15-year-old with known type 1 diabetes has two days of vomiting and abdominal pain, deep rapid breathing, a fruity breath odor and a glucose of 450 mg/dL. What process best explains the rapid deep breathing?
med-g912.l09.q4.h: Without insulin, fat is broken down into acids; how does the body respond to acid?
med-g912.l09.q4.e: Ketoacids lower blood pH and the lungs blow off CO2 to compensate (Kussmaul breathing). Vomiting alone would tend toward alkalosis, but the findings of high glucose and ketones indicate acidosis.

med-g912.l10.q1.t: The peak pressure in the arteries when the ventricle contracts
med-g912.l10.q1.p: Which of the following best describes systolic blood pressure?
med-g912.l10.q1.e: Systolic is the pressure during contraction. Diastolic is the lowest pressure between beats.

med-g912.l10.q2.t: They inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, an enzyme in cholesterol synthesis in the liver
med-g912.l10.q2.p: Why do statin drugs lower LDL cholesterol?
med-g912.l10.q2.h: The name of the enzyme appears in the drug mechanism.
med-g912.l10.q2.e: Statins reduce hepatic cholesterol synthesis, increasing LDL clearance from blood. Blocking dietary absorption is the mechanism of a different drug class.

med-g912.l10.q3.t: Rupture of a plaque followed by clot formation that blocks the artery
med-g912.l10.q3.p: What event most directly causes a sudden heart attack in a person with coronary atherosclerosis?
med-g912.l10.q3.h: The word sudden hints at a clot rather than slow narrowing.
med-g912.l10.q3.e: Plaque rupture triggers thrombosis and abrupt occlusion. Slow narrowing causes stable angina, not infarction by itself.

med-g912.l10.q4.t: Fixed narrowing of coronary arteries limits blood supply when oxygen demand rises with exertion
med-g912.l10.q4.p: A 58-year-old smoker with untreated hypertension and diabetes reports chest pressure on exertion that resolves with rest. Which mechanism best explains the symptom?
med-g912.l10.q4.h: Note the link to exertion and relief with rest.
med-g912.l10.q4.e: Exertional chest pressure relieved by rest is typical of stable angina from fixed coronary narrowing. A complete clot would cause pain at rest and tissue death, as in infarction.

med-g912.l11.q1.t: Airflow narrowing in asthma is variable and largely reversible
med-g912.l11.q1.p: Which feature best distinguishes asthma from COPD?
med-g912.l11.q1.h: Consider whether the obstruction comes and goes.
med-g912.l11.q1.e: Asthma is characterized by variable, reversible narrowing. COPD is mainly smoking-related and progressive.

med-g912.l11.q2.t: It stimulates beta-2 receptors, relaxing bronchial smooth muscle
med-g912.l11.q2.p: How does albuterol relieve acute wheezing?
med-g912.l11.q2.e: Agonist action at beta-2 receptors relaxes airway smooth muscle within minutes. Controller therapy such as inhaled corticosteroids reduces inflammation over days to weeks.

med-g912.l11.q3.t: Resistance to flow rises steeply as the radius of a tube shrinks
med-g912.l11.q3.p: Why does a small decrease in airway radius cause a large increase in resistance?
med-g912.l11.q3.h: Think of drinking through a thinner straw.
med-g912.l11.q3.e: Flow resistance is very sensitive to radius in a tube, so modest narrowing from muscle tightening and swelling markedly impairs airflow. Length is not the driver here.

med-g912.l11.q4.t: The airway inflammation is untreated, since relievers relax muscle but do not reduce inflammation
med-g912.l11.q4.p: A child with asthma uses a short-acting albuterol reliever several times a week and wakes at night with cough, but is not on any controller medicine. Which reasoning best explains why more frequent symptoms are expected?
med-g912.l11.q4.h: Compare what a reliever treats with what a controller treats.
med-g912.l11.q4.e: Relievers act on muscle spasm only; ongoing inflammation continues to drive symptoms, which is why asthma should not be managed with a short-acting reliever alone (GINA 2025) and needs anti-inflammatory treatment. Inhaler use does not scar the airway.

med-g912.l12.q1.p: Which pair correctly lists pharmacokinetic processes?
med-g912.l12.q1.h: Pharmacokinetics is what the body does to the drug.
med-g912.l12.q1.e: Absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion are the four pharmacokinetic processes. The other pairs describe pharmacodynamics.

med-g912.l12.q2.p: A drug that binds a receptor and blocks it without activating it is called what?
med-g912.l12.q2.h: It prevents the usual messenger from acting.
med-g912.l12.q2.e: Antagonists occupy the receptor without activating it. Agonists activate it.

med-g912.l12.q3.t: Reduced liver metabolism, including less first-pass clearance, leaves more active drug in circulation
med-g912.l12.q3.p: Why can liver disease increase the risk of toxicity from some oral drugs?
med-g912.l12.q3.h: Where do many drugs get broken down?
med-g912.l12.q3.e: The liver metabolizes many drugs, so impaired function raises levels. The liver does not control absorption from the gut in the way the second option suggests.

med-g912.l12.q4.t: Higher blood thinner levels with increased risk of bleeding
med-g912.l12.q4.p: A patient on a narrow-therapeutic-index blood thinner starts a new medicine that inhibits the liver enzyme that clears the blood thinner. What is the expected consequence?
med-g912.l12.q4.h: Slower clearance has what effect on drug level?
med-g912.l12.q4.e: Inhibiting the clearing enzyme slows metabolism so the drug accumulates, increasing bleeding risk. Lower levels would result from enzyme induction, the opposite situation.

med-g912.l13.q1.p: Which blood protein is a key marker of heart muscle cell death in suspected heart attack?
med-g912.l13.q1.h: It is released from damaged cardiac muscle.
med-g912.l13.q1.e: Troponin leaks from injured cardiac muscle cells. Creatinine reflects kidney filtration, and ALT reflects liver cell injury.

med-g912.l13.q2.p: A test that rarely misses people who have the disease is described as having high what?
med-g912.l13.q2.h: It is about the true positives among those who have the disease.
med-g912.l13.q2.e: Sensitivity is the fraction of diseased people who test positive. Specificity concerns healthy people testing negative.

med-g912.l13.q3.p: A rising serum creatinine on repeat blood tests most directly suggests which problem?
med-g912.l13.q3.h: Creatinine is cleared by the kidneys.
med-g912.l13.q3.e: Creatinine is a muscle waste product filtered by the kidneys, so a rise suggests reduced filtration. Platelets and red cells are measured on a blood count instead.

med-g912.l13.q4.t: Because healthy people vastly outnumber diseased people, so the small false positive rate yields many more false alarms than true cases
med-g912.l13.q4.p: A screening test has 95 percent sensitivity and 95 percent specificity and is applied to a population where the disease affects 1 in 1000. Why will most positive results be false?
med-g912.l13.q4.h: Estimate how many healthy people there are and how many fall into the 5 percent.
med-g912.l13.q4.e: With 99900 healthy people, 5 percent false positives is about 5000, much larger than about 95 true positives. Specificity is a property of the test and does not itself change with prevalence.

med-g912.l14.q1.p: Which imaging method uses no ionizing radiation and is commonly used first to examine a fetus?
med-g912.l14.q1.e: Ultrasound relies on reflected sound and is the standard first-line fetal imaging tool. CT, X-ray and PET all involve ionizing radiation.

med-g912.l14.q2.t: The MRI scanner uses a very strong magnetic field that can move or heat some metal devices
med-g912.l14.q2.p: Why must patients be screened for certain metal implants before MRI?
med-g912.l14.q2.e: MRI uses a powerful magnet and radio waves, so some implants are unsafe. It does not use ionizing radiation, and contrast dye is not used in every scan.

med-g912.l14.q3.t: A CT scan of the head
med-g912.l14.q3.p: A patient arrives after a head injury and the clinician needs the fastest test to look for bleeding inside the skull. Which is most appropriate?
med-g912.l14.q3.h: Choose speed and sensitivity for blood and bone.
med-g912.l14.q3.e: CT is quick and detects acute bleeding and fractures well, which is why it is used in head trauma. Ultrasound waves are blocked by bone.

med-g912.l14.q4.t: Ultrasound first, because it avoids radiation and can answer many abdominal questions
med-g912.l14.q4.p: A healthy pregnant woman has right-sided abdominal pain. Which approach best weighs risk and benefit for the first imaging step?
med-g912.l14.q4.h: Which tool is radiation-free and widely available?
med-g912.l14.q4.e: Ultrasound is the usual first choice. Absolutely refusing all imaging is wrong because other methods such as MRI can be used if needed.

med-g912.l15.q1.t: The number of existing cases at a point in time
med-g912.l15.q1.e: Prevalence counts existing cases at a point in time. New cases over a period define incidence.

med-g912.l15.q2.p: Which study design starts with people who already have a disease and compares them with similar people without it?
med-g912.l15.q2.h: It works backward from the outcome.
med-g912.l15.q2.e: Case-control studies identify cases and controls, then look back at exposures. A cohort study follows exposed and unexposed people forward.

med-g912.l15.q3.p: A pathogen has a basic reproduction number R0 of 4. Using the simple threshold formula, roughly what fraction of the population must be immune to stop sustained spread?
med-g912.l15.q3.h: The threshold is 1 minus 1 over R0.
med-g912.l15.q3.e: 1 - 1/4 = 0.75. The 25 percent value is just 1/R0, which is the susceptible fraction, not the immune fraction.

med-g912.l15.q4.t: Smoking is a confounder linked to both lighter carrying and lung cancer, so lighters are unlikely to be causal
med-g912.l15.q4.p: A study finds that people who carry lighters have higher rates of lung cancer. What is the best interpretation?
med-g912.l15.q4.h: Ask what third factor leads to both.
med-g912.l15.q4.e: Smoking explains both lighter carrying and lung cancer, so the association is confounded. Reverse causation is implausible because lighters are typically carried before disease appears.

med-g912.l16.q1.t: To balance known and unknown differences between groups by chance
med-g912.l16.q1.p: What is the main purpose of random assignment in a clinical trial?
med-g912.l16.q1.e: Randomization spreads participant characteristics by chance so outcome differences can be attributed to the treatment. It cannot guarantee improvement.

med-g912.l16.q2.t: The observed data would be fairly surprising if the treatment truly had no effect
med-g912.l16.q2.p: Which statement about a p-value below 0.05 is most accurate?
med-g912.l16.q2.h: A p-value is about the data under the no-effect assumption.
med-g912.l16.q2.e: The p-value gives how surprising the data are under no effect; it says nothing about importance or bias. A statistically significant result can still be clinically trivial.

med-g912.l16.q3.p: A drug reduces the risk of an event from 4 percent to 3 percent. What is the number needed to treat?
med-g912.l16.q3.h: Divide 1 by the absolute risk reduction.
med-g912.l16.q3.e: Absolute risk reduction is 1 percentage point, or 0.01, so NNT is 100. A 25 percent relative reduction could tempt the answer 25 or 4.

med-g912.l16.q4.t: It used a surrogate outcome, so benefit on patient-centered outcomes is not shown
med-g912.l16.q4.p: A trial of a new cholesterol drug reports that the drug lowers a blood lab value more than placebo but does not report whether heart attacks or deaths changed. What is the key limitation?
med-g912.l16.q4.h: Compare a lab number with what patients actually care about.
med-g912.l16.q4.e: Improving a lab value does not guarantee fewer heart attacks, so surrogate endpoints need caution. The trial did have a placebo group, so the second option contradicts the stem.

med-g912.l17.q1.p: Which ethical principle refers to respecting a patient right to make informed decisions about their own care?
med-g912.l17.q1.e: Autonomy is respect for the patient informed choice. Justice concerns fair distribution of resources, and beneficence concerns doing good.

med-g912.l17.q2.t: The patient has decision-making capacity and is told about the risks, benefits and alternatives
med-g912.l17.q2.p: Which element is required for valid informed consent?
med-g912.l17.q2.h: Consider both who decides and what they are told.
med-g912.l17.q2.e: Valid consent requires capacity, disclosure of relevant information including alternatives, understanding and voluntariness. Passive non-objection is not consent.

med-g912.l17.q3.t: By emergency exception, since delay would risk serious harm and a reasonable person would be presumed to consent
med-g912.l17.q3.p: An unconscious adult arrives at an emergency department with a life-threatening bleed and no surrogate can be reached. How is treatment generally justified?
med-g912.l17.q3.h: Think about what the law presumes when delay is dangerous.
med-g912.l17.q3.e: The emergency exception allows treatment without explicit consent when a patient cannot decide and delay risks serious harm. A court order is not needed.

med-g912.l17.q4.t: Respect the refusal, document the discussion, and continue to offer alternatives and support
med-g912.l17.q4.p: A 45-year-old with decision-making capacity declines a recommended operation after a thorough discussion of risks and benefits. Her surgeon believes the choice is mistaken. What is the ethically appropriate response?
med-g912.l17.q4.h: Capacity is not the same as agreeing with the clinician.
med-g912.l17.q4.e: A capable adult may refuse treatment, and disagreement alone does not show incapacity. Overriding the choice by involving family would violate autonomy.

med-g912.l18.q1.t: Check that the scene is safe, then check responsiveness and call for help
med-g912.l18.q1.p: What is the first thing a rescuer should do on finding a collapsed person?
med-g912.l18.q1.h: A rescuer must not become a second casualty.
med-g912.l18.q1.e: Scene safety comes first, followed by responsiveness and calling for help. Beginning breaths immediately is not the first step.

med-g912.l18.q2.t: About 100 to 120 per minute, about 5 to 6 cm deep
med-g912.l18.q2.p: For adult CPR, approximately what compression rate and depth are recommended?
med-g912.l18.q2.h: Fast and hard, but not extreme.
med-g912.l18.q2.e: Guidelines specify roughly 100 to 120 compressions per minute at about 5 to 6 cm. Shallow, slow compressions do not move enough blood.

med-g912.l18.q3.t: It delivers a shock only if it detects a shockable rhythm such as ventricular fibrillation
med-g912.l18.q3.p: What does an automated external defibrillator do when it analyzes a heart rhythm?
med-g912.l18.q3.h: The device decides whether a shock is appropriate.
med-g912.l18.q3.e: AEDs shock only shockable rhythms; compressions are still needed because the device does not circulate blood.

med-g912.l18.q4.t: Call emergency services, start hard fast chest compressions, and have the AED brought and used
med-g912.l18.q4.p: A bystander finds an adult who is unresponsive, not breathing normally and only occasionally gasping. A defibrillator is nearby, and the bystander is untrained in rescue breaths. What is the best action?
med-g912.l18.q4.e: Occasional gasping can occur in cardiac arrest, so CPR should start. Compression-only CPR is acceptable for untrained rescuers, and waiting wastes critical minutes.

med-g912.l19.q1.t: Paid, supervised specialty training taken after medical school
med-g912.l19.q1.p: What is residency in the United States physician pathway?
med-g912.l19.q1.h: It comes after the MD or DO degree.
med-g912.l19.q1.e: Residency is supervised, paid clinical training in a specialty after earning the degree. The admissions exam comes before medical school.

med-g912.l19.q2.p: Which professional typically holds a doctorate focused on medication expertise and drug interactions?
med-g912.l19.q2.h: Think about who dispenses and reviews medicines.
med-g912.l19.q2.e: Pharmacists complete a doctorate in pharmacy and specialize in drugs. Respiratory therapists focus on breathing support instead.

med-g912.l19.q3.t: Both can be licensed to practice medicine in all states and train in residencies
med-g912.l19.q3.p: Which statement about MD and DO physicians in the United States is most accurate?
med-g912.l19.q3.h: Look for the claim that treats both as full physicians.
med-g912.l19.q3.e: MD and DO graduates can be licensed with full practice rights and attend residency. The claim that DOs cannot prescribe or operate is incorrect.

med-g912.l19.q4.t: Becoming a registered nurse, with the option of graduate training to become a nurse practitioner
med-g912.l19.q4.p: A student wants a clinical career with direct patient care, hands-on bedside work and a shorter route than medical school, but is open to later advancing to prescribing roles. Which path best fits?
med-g912.l19.q4.h: Match each requirement of the student to a route.
med-g912.l19.q4.e: Nursing offers bedside care and a stepwise route to advanced practice. Pathology requires a medical degree, and the other options do not meet the stated needs.

med-g912.l20.q1.t: People often try remedies at their worst and improve by chance, crediting the remedy
med-g912.l20.q1.p: Why is a personal testimonial weak evidence that a remedy works?
med-g912.l20.q1.e: Many illnesses improve on their own, so an anecdote cannot separate treatment effect from natural course or placebo. It is not necessarily false, only uncontrolled.

med-g912.l20.q2.t: A single product claimed to cure many unrelated serious diseases
med-g912.l20.q2.p: A website sells a supplement that it says cures cancer, diabetes and arthritis, and claims doctors hide the truth. Which feature is the strongest warning sign?
med-g912.l20.q2.e: A cure for many unrelated diseases is a classic mark of fraud. Photos, addresses and Latin names do not signal deception.

med-g912.l20.q3.t: Natural does not mean safe, since some plant products harm the liver or interact with prescribed medicines
med-g912.l20.q3.p: Which statement about natural remedies is most accurate?
med-g912.l20.q3.h: Consider that many drugs originated in plants.
med-g912.l20.q3.e: Plants contain active compounds that can cause harm or interactions. In the United States, supplements do not require proof of effectiveness before sale.

med-g912.l20.q4.t: The absolute risk rises to about 2 in 10000, a small absolute change despite sounding large
med-g912.l20.q4.p: A headline says a new food doubles your risk of a rare disease. The underlying risk without the food is 1 in 10000. What is the most useful reading?
med-g912.l20.q4.e: Doubling 1 in 10000 gives 2 in 10000, so the absolute increase is tiny. Observational links can also be confounded, so causation is not shown.

med-global-health.l01.q1.t: Years of life lost to premature death plus years lived with disability
med-global-health.l01.q1.p: The DALY is calculated as the sum of which two components?
med-global-health.l01.q1.h: One component counts early death, the other counts illness that continues.
med-global-health.l01.q1.e: DALY = YLL + YLD. Healthy life expectancy is a different summary measure, not a component of the DALY.

med-global-health.l01.q2.t: It combines deaths prevented and disability avoided into a single comparable unit across diseases
med-global-health.l01.q2.p: A health ministry compares two programmes using cost per DALY averted. Why is this metric useful for priority-setting?
med-global-health.l01.q2.h: Think about comparing a fatal disease with a disabling one.
med-global-health.l01.q2.e: DALYs put fatal and non-fatal burdens on one scale. They do not capture community preference and rely on modelled estimates with uncertainty.

med-global-health.l01.q3.p: Which condition is most likely to rank higher by DALYs than by number of deaths?
med-global-health.l01.q3.h: Look for a condition that causes long disability but few deaths.
med-global-health.l01.q3.e: Depression causes many years of disability but few direct deaths. The other conditions are mostly fatal and so rank high by deaths too.

med-global-health.l01.q4.t: Country A has 15,000 DALYs and Country B has 5,000, so A has the larger burden
med-global-health.l01.q4.p: Country A has 500 deaths from a disease, each at an age with 30 years of remaining life expectancy. Country B has 4,000 people with a chronic condition of disability weight 0.25 lasting 5 years each. Which statement best compares total burden?
med-global-health.l01.q4.h: Multiply deaths by years lost; multiply people by weight by years.
med-global-health.l01.q4.e: A: 500 x 30 = 15,000 YLL. B: 4,000 x 0.25 x 5 = 5,000 YLD. The option claiming 20,000 forgets to multiply by the weight.

med-global-health.l01.q5.t: Improved death registration and cause-of-death certification may be revealing deaths previously unrecorded or miscoded
med-global-health.l01.q5.p: Between two years a low-income country reports a large rise in recorded noncommunicable-disease deaths, while infection deaths are unchanged. Which interpretation is most defensible before concluding the disease pattern has changed?
med-global-health.l01.q5.h: Ask whether measurement, not biology, changed.
med-global-health.l01.q5.e: Weak vital registration means real changes and artefacts are hard to separate. The other options misread DALY weights or assume a zero-sum relationship that does not exist.

med-global-health.l02.q1.t: Mortality rose stepwise as civil service grade fell, even among people with stable jobs
med-global-health.l02.q1.p: Which finding from the Whitehall studies best illustrates the social gradient in health?
med-global-health.l02.q1.h: The gradient affects everyone on the ladder, not only the poorest.
med-global-health.l02.q1.e: Whitehall found a graded relationship across the hierarchy. A threshold effect at the bottom alone would not be a gradient.

med-global-health.l02.q2.t: Upstream, because they change the conditions that shape exposure across a population
med-global-health.l02.q2.p: A city taxes sugar-sweetened drinks and subsidises school meals. In the downstream-upstream framework, these are best described as which kind of action?
med-global-health.l02.q2.h: Ask whether the action changes the environment or treats a patient.
med-global-health.l02.q2.e: Taxes and school meals alter the environment for whole populations, which is upstream. Downstream action means clinical treatment of established disease.

med-global-health.l02.q3.t: Tackle the inequitable distribution of power, money and resources
med-global-health.l02.q3.p: Which of the WHO Commission on Social Determinants of Health (2008) overarching recommendations is correctly stated?
med-global-health.l02.q3.h: The Commission looked beyond clinics to wider structures.
med-global-health.l02.q3.e: The Commission urged action on daily living conditions, on the distribution of power, money and resources, and on measurement. It did not call for a global provider or health-ministry-only policy.

med-global-health.l02.q4.t: Reverse causation: ill health may have caused the fall in income rather than the reverse
med-global-health.l02.q4.p: A study finds that people in poor health later earn less. A researcher claims low income therefore causes ill health. What is the most important weakness in that inference?
med-global-health.l02.q4.h: Which direction could the arrow point?
med-global-health.l02.q4.e: Sickness can lower earnings, so a cross-sectional link does not show direction. Large samples narrow, not widen, confidence intervals.

med-global-health.l02.q5.t: Assess housing, air quality, employment and food access and act on the largest modifiable gaps alongside clinical services
med-global-health.l02.q5.p: Two districts have equal clinic numbers but life expectancy differs by twelve years. Which proposed response is best aligned with the social determinants evidence?
med-global-health.l02.q5.h: Equal clinics but unequal outcomes suggests the cause lies elsewhere.
med-global-health.l02.q5.e: Where clinic supply is already equal, the remaining gap points to conditions of life. Staffing alone narrows it modestly, and lifestyle-only or genetic explanations ignore structural drivers.

med-global-health.l03.q1.t: Death rates fall, producing rapid population growth
med-global-health.l03.q1.p: In the demographic transition, which change typically comes first?
med-global-health.l03.q1.h: Sanitation and vaccines act before family size changes.
med-global-health.l03.q1.e: Mortality typically falls before fertility, so growth accelerates before it slows. Fertility decline follows later.

med-global-health.l03.q2.p: A household contains a stunted child and an overweight mother. This is a typical example of which concept?
med-global-health.l03.q2.h: Both under- and over-nutrition appear in one place.
med-global-health.l03.q2.e: Coexisting undernutrition and overweight is the double burden of malnutrition. It shows the transition is uneven rather than finished.

med-global-health.l03.q3.t: Equity may require unequal resources so that avoidable, unfair differences in health are reduced
med-global-health.l03.q3.p: Which statement correctly distinguishes equality from equity in health?
med-global-health.l03.q3.h: Fair does not always mean identical.
med-global-health.l03.q3.e: Equity is about reducing avoidable unfair gaps, which can mean giving more to those with greater need. Equality means giving each the same.

med-global-health.l03.q4.t: The absolute gap is unchanged at 80 while the ratio rose from 3 to 9
med-global-health.l03.q4.p: Under-five mortality in the poorest quintile falls from 120 to 90 per 1,000, and in the richest from 40 to 10. Which conclusion is correct?
med-global-health.l03.q4.h: Subtract for the gap, divide for the ratio, before and after.
