med-global-health.l03.q4.e: 120-40 = 80 and 90-10 = 80, so the absolute gap is unchanged, while the ratio went from 3 to 9. Reporting only absolute change would conceal widening relative inequality.

med-global-health.l03.q5.t: Stunting is concentrated among poorer children, so the inequality works against the poor
med-global-health.l03.q5.p: A concentration index for child stunting in a country is -0.15. What is the correct interpretation?
med-global-health.l03.q5.h: Sign tells you which end of the socioeconomic ranking carries the burden.
med-global-health.l03.q5.e: A negative concentration index means the variable is concentrated among the poor, so for an ill-health indicator the inequality is unfavourable to the poor. The value of -0.15 is moderate, not near zero, and the index is a distributional measure that says nothing about the trend.

med-global-health.l04.q1.p: Which is the correct definition of the maternal mortality ratio?
med-global-health.l04.q1.h: The denominator is births, not women.
med-global-health.l04.q1.e: The ratio uses live births as the denominator. The rate per women of reproductive age is a different indicator.

med-global-health.l04.q2.p: A woman with severe pre-eclampsia is at risk of eclamptic seizures. Which drug is the standard prophylaxis in this setting?
med-global-health.l04.q2.h: The treatment prevents seizures rather than bleeding.
med-global-health.l04.q2.e: Magnesium sulfate prevents and treats eclamptic seizures. Tranexamic acid and oxytocin address postpartum bleeding, not seizure prevention.

med-global-health.l04.q3.t: Delay in deciding to seek care
med-global-health.l04.q3.p: In the Three Delays model, a family that waits two days before seeking care because they do not recognise a danger sign illustrates which delay?
med-global-health.l04.q3.h: This delay happens before travel begins.
med-global-health.l04.q3.e: Not recognising danger signs is the first delay, the decision to seek care. The second concerns transport, and the third concerns quality at the facility.

med-global-health.l04.q4.t: Delays two and three are unaddressed, so training alone cannot prevent the deaths
med-global-health.l04.q4.p: A district trains many birth attendants, yet maternal deaths from haemorrhage persist. An audit finds roads are impassable during rains and the health centre lacks oxytocin and blood. Which analysis best fits?
med-global-health.l04.q4.h: Match each audit finding to a delay.
med-global-health.l04.q4.e: Impassable roads reflect the delay in reaching care, and missing oxytocin or blood reflects the delay in receiving care. Training addresses only part of the chain.

med-global-health.l04.q5.t: Assess for all danger signs and conditions together, then give an antibiotic for pneumonia plus oral rehydration salts and zinc
med-global-health.l04.q5.p: A 2-year-old has cough, fast breathing and diarrhoea with mild dehydration at a rural clinic. Which approach reflects Integrated Management of Childhood Illness reasoning?
med-global-health.l04.q5.h: The strategy is to treat the whole child, not a single complaint.
med-global-health.l04.q5.e: IMCI trains workers to assess and treat several conditions at once, here pneumonia and diarrhoea with ORS plus zinc. Treating one complaint misses concurrent illness, and automatic referral or antimalarial use ignores assessment.

med-global-health.l05.q1.t: Enough of the population is immune that sustained transmission cannot occur
med-global-health.l05.q1.p: Herd immunity for an infection is best described as which situation?
med-global-health.l05.q1.h: It is a property of a population, not of one person.
med-global-health.l05.q1.e: Herd immunity means transmission chains break because too few susceptible people remain. It does not require 100 percent vaccination or perfect individual protection.

med-global-health.l05.q2.p: An infection has R0 of 5. Using the simple threshold formula, what proportion of the population must be immune to stop sustained spread?
med-global-health.l05.q2.e: 1 - 1/5 = 0.8. The 20 percent figure is 1/R0 itself, which is the susceptible proportion allowed rather than the immune proportion required.

med-global-health.l05.q3.t: No animal reservoir, visible disease, lasting immunity and an effective vaccine
med-global-health.l05.q3.p: Which feature of smallpox made eradication feasible?
med-global-health.l05.q3.h: Think of features that make cases easy to find and the disease impossible to hide.
med-global-health.l05.q3.e: Smallpox lacked animal reservoirs and its cases were visible, so ring vaccination worked. A silent carrier state would have made eradication harder, not easier.

med-global-health.l05.q4.t: A circulating vaccine-derived poliovirus emerging from the oral vaccine in an under-immunised community
med-global-health.l05.q4.p: A district reports a case of paralytic polio caused by a virus genetically related to the Sabin strain after a period of low routine coverage. Which explanation is most consistent?
med-global-health.l05.q4.h: Which vaccine contains live attenuated virus that can mutate?
med-global-health.l05.q4.e: The oral vaccine uses live attenuated virus that can revert and circulate where immunity is low. The inactivated vaccine cannot revert, and wild types 2 and 3 have been certified eradicated.

med-global-health.l05.q5.t: Raise coverage with a second routine dose and targeted catch-up in the zero-dose pockets
med-global-health.l05.q5.p: A district with 82 percent first-dose measles coverage has recurrent outbreaks concentrated in a few remote villages. Which plan is best justified?
med-global-health.l05.q5.h: Outbreaks cluster where susceptible children gather.
med-global-health.l05.q5.e: Coverage is well below the roughly 95 percent needed and susceptible pockets sustain transmission. Outbreaks in under-covered groups do not show vaccine failure, and ring vaccination alone is too slow for measles.

med-global-health.l06.q1.p: Which malaria parasite species is responsible for most deaths and dominates in sub-Saharan Africa?
med-global-health.l06.q1.h: One species causes cerebral malaria through sequestration.
med-global-health.l06.q1.e: P. falciparum causes most severe disease and death. P. vivax is the most geographically widespread outside Africa but is less often fatal.

med-global-health.l06.q2.t: The drug can cause haemolysis in G6PD-deficient patients
med-global-health.l06.q2.p: Why must G6PD status be considered before giving primaquine for P. vivax?
med-global-health.l06.q2.h: Think about red blood cells under oxidative stress.
med-global-health.l06.q2.e: Primaquine produces oxidative stress and can cause haemolysis in G6PD deficiency. G6PD does not metabolise or inactivate the drug.

med-global-health.l06.q3.t: Young children in areas with strongly seasonal transmission such as the Sahel
med-global-health.l06.q3.p: Seasonal malaria chemoprevention is best targeted at which group and setting?
med-global-health.l06.q3.h: The strategy matches drug cover to the rainy season peak.
med-global-health.l06.q3.e: Seasonal chemoprevention gives antimalarial courses to children during the high-transmission season in the Sahel. Pregnant women are served by intermittent preventive treatment, a different strategy.

med-global-health.l06.q4.t: Partial artemisinin resistance should be considered, and the case reported for surveillance
med-global-health.l06.q4.p: A 4-year-old in East Africa is treated with an artemisinin-based combination for falciparum malaria; parasites clear slowly on day 3. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
med-global-health.l06.q4.h: Delayed parasite clearance is the clinical signature to watch.
med-global-health.l06.q4.e: Delayed clearance is the marker of partial artemisinin resistance, now documented in parts of East Africa. P. vivax hypnozoites cause relapses, not slow clearance, and the other options are unrelated mechanisms.

med-global-health.l06.q5.t: Intermittent preventive treatment with sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine plus an insecticide-treated net
med-global-health.l06.q5.p: A pregnant woman in a high-transmission area attends antenatal care with no symptoms. Which preventive measure is supported for her?
med-global-health.l06.q5.h: This group has a specific chemoprevention strategy tied to antenatal visits.
med-global-health.l06.q5.e: Intermittent preventive treatment in pregnancy with sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine, plus a net, is the established approach. Primaquine is avoided in pregnancy and artesunate is not used as daily prophylaxis.

med-global-health.l07.q1.t: Resistance to at least isoniazid and rifampicin
med-global-health.l07.q1.p: What is the standard definition of multidrug-resistant tuberculosis?
med-global-health.l07.q1.h: Two cornerstone drugs of the six-month regimen.
med-global-health.l07.q1.e: MDR-TB means resistance to at least isoniazid and rifampicin. Rifampicin plus fluoroquinolone resistance describes a more extensive category.

med-global-health.l07.q2.p: A patient on isoniazid reports tingling in the feet. Which supplement is given to reduce this adverse effect?
med-global-health.l07.q2.h: Isoniazid interferes with the activation of one B vitamin.
med-global-health.l07.q2.e: Isoniazid causes peripheral neuropathy by interfering with pyridoxine metabolism, so pyridoxine is given. Thiamine deficiency also causes neuropathy but is not the mechanism here.

med-global-health.l07.q3.t: It detects the bacterium and rifampicin resistance within hours
med-global-health.l07.q3.p: What is the main advantage of the Xpert MTB/RIF assay in programmes?
med-global-health.l07.q3.h: The name includes the drug it screens for.
med-global-health.l07.q3.e: Xpert detects M. tuberculosis and the rpoB mutation signalling rifampicin resistance rapidly. It does not distinguish latent from active infection or test all drugs.

med-global-health.l07.q4.t: Probable multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, requiring a resistant-disease regimen rather than standard first-line therapy
med-global-health.l07.q4.p: A 38-year-old man with HIV has cough, night sweats and weight loss. Sputum Xpert shows M. tuberculosis with rifampicin resistance. What is the most likely clinical conclusion?
med-global-health.l07.q4.h: Rifampicin resistance usually accompanies isoniazid resistance.
med-global-health.l07.q4.e: Rifampicin resistance is a proxy for MDR-TB, so first-line therapy would likely fail. A positive Xpert indicates active bacillary disease, not a latent infection.

med-global-health.l07.q5.t: Rifampicin induces liver enzymes and lowers levels of some antiretrovirals, so regimen or doses need adjusting
med-global-health.l07.q5.p: A patient with tuberculosis and HIV needs antiretroviral therapy while on rifampicin. Which issue most affects regimen design?
med-global-health.l07.q5.h: Think about which direction enzyme induction moves drug levels.
med-global-health.l07.q5.e: Rifampicin is a strong enzyme inducer and lowers levels of drugs cleared by those enzymes, so antiretroviral choice or dosing is adapted. It is an inducer, not an inhibitor.

med-global-health.l08.q1.t: 95 percent of people living with HIV diagnosed, 95 percent of those diagnosed on treatment, and 95 percent of those on treatment virally suppressed
med-global-health.l08.q1.p: What do the UNAIDS 95-95-95 targets, set for 2025, mean?
med-global-health.l08.q1.h: Each step builds on the previous group.
med-global-health.l08.q1.e: The targets are for knowing status, being on treatment, and having viral suppression, each a share of the previous group (diagnosed, then treated, then suppressed). The other options mix prevention measures or resources.

med-global-health.l08.q2.t: Sustained viral suppression on antiretroviral therapy prevents sexual transmission
med-global-health.l08.q2.p: The principle that undetectable equals untransmittable rests on which finding?
med-global-health.l08.q2.h: The prevention effect comes from the treated partner.
med-global-health.l08.q2.e: Suppression of viral load by treatment prevents sexual transmission, as supported by HPTN 052 and later studies. Treatment controls but does not cure HIV.

med-global-health.l08.q3.t: A high barrier to resistance, good tolerability and low-cost generic availability
med-global-health.l08.q3.p: Which feature explains why dolutegravir-based regimens are preferred first-line?
med-global-health.l08.q3.h: Think about clinical and programmatic advantages.
med-global-health.l08.q3.e: Dolutegravir combines potency, a high resistance barrier and affordable generics. It does not cure HIV and is not tied to isoniazid.

med-global-health.l08.q4.t: Continue therapy throughout pregnancy and delivery, as sustained suppression makes transmission very unlikely
med-global-health.l08.q4.p: A woman with HIV, virally suppressed on dolutegravir-based therapy for two years, is pregnant. What is the most appropriate counselling about mother-to-child transmission?
med-global-health.l08.q4.e: Continuing suppressive therapy lowers transmission to very low levels. Stopping therapy would raise viral load and risk. Recommendations on infant feeding depend on suppression and setting, so a universal ban is incorrect.

med-global-health.l08.q5.t: The third step, viral suppression among those on treatment, because it is furthest from its target
med-global-health.l08.q5.p: A health programme reaches 92 percent of people living with HIV diagnosed, 90 percent of those on treatment, and 78 percent of those treated suppressed. Which gap should the programme prioritise first against the 95-95-95 targets?
med-global-health.l08.q5.h: Compare each step to 95 and look for the largest shortfall.
med-global-health.l08.q5.e: Step three, at 78 percent, is 17 points short of 95, the largest gap (steps one and two are 3 and 5 points short). The targets are each 95, so no value below that meets them.

med-global-health.l09.q1.t: A common-source exposure affecting many people at about the same time
med-global-health.l09.q1.p: An epidemic curve showing a single sharp peak of cases within one incubation period usually suggests which pattern?
med-global-health.l09.q1.h: Think about one exposure event rather than chains of infection.
med-global-health.l09.q1.e: A single sharp peak points to a point-source exposure such as one contaminated meal. Person-to-person spread produces successive peaks separated by roughly one serial interval.

med-global-health.l09.q2.t: The proportion of confirmed cases who die from the disease
med-global-health.l09.q2.p: What does the case fatality ratio measure?
med-global-health.l09.q2.h: The denominator is people with the disease.
med-global-health.l09.q2.e: The case fatality ratio is deaths among cases divided by cases. The reproduction number describes spread and the incubation period describes timing.

med-global-health.l09.q3.t: Bodies of people who died of Ebola remain highly infectious and traditional funeral contact was a major route of spread
med-global-health.l09.q3.p: In Ebola response, why were safe and dignified burial teams a key control measure?
med-global-health.l09.q3.h: Consider what happens during washing and touching of the deceased.
med-global-health.l09.q3.e: The dead can transmit Ebola through direct contact with body fluids, and funerals involved close contact. Cause-of-death determination was not the purpose.

med-global-health.l09.q4.t: Trace and monitor funeral attendees and offer safe burial and isolation of symptomatic contacts
med-global-health.l09.q4.p: Cases in three villages show onsets spaced about 10 to 14 days apart and all affected people attended one funeral of a person who died of a febrile illness with bleeding. Which first control step is most appropriate?
med-global-health.l09.q4.h: Target the shared exposure and the people exposed to it.
med-global-health.l09.q4.e: The cluster pattern implies person-to-person spread seeded at a funeral, so contact tracing and safe burial are central. National vaccination without contact tracing is not targeted and a boil-water notice misses the exposure.

med-global-health.l09.q5.t: Vaccinating contacts of confirmed cases and contacts of those contacts, with immediate or delayed timing
med-global-health.l09.q5.p: Ring vaccination in the 2015 Guinea Ebola trial involved which approach?
med-global-health.l09.q5.h: The rings are social networks around each case.
med-global-health.l09.q5.e: Ring vaccination offers vaccine to the contacts and contacts of contacts around each case. Whole-city vaccination is not ring vaccination, and recovered workers already have immunity.

med-global-health.l10.q1.t: A binding instrument for states parties, in force since 2007
med-global-health.l10.q1.p: What is the legal status of the International Health Regulations (2005)?
med-global-health.l10.q1.h: They were adopted by the World Health Assembly and bind countries that accept them.
med-global-health.l10.q1.e: The IHR (2005) are legally binding on states parties. Advice such as temporary recommendations is non-binding, but the Regulations themselves bind.

med-global-health.l10.q2.t: The WHO Director-General, after consulting an Emergency Committee
med-global-health.l10.q2.p: Who determines that an event is a Public Health Emergency of International Concern?
med-global-health.l10.q2.h: An expert committee advises, but one official decides.
med-global-health.l10.q2.e: Under the IHR the Director-General makes the determination after considering the Emergency Committee. The affected state is consulted but does not declare it alone.

med-global-health.l10.q3.t: Most funding comes from voluntary, often earmarked contributions rather than assessed fees
med-global-health.l10.q3.p: Which statement about WHO funding is accurate?
med-global-health.l10.q3.h: Think about who decides how the money can be spent.
med-global-health.l10.q3.e: Voluntary, earmarked funds make up most of the budget and give donors influence. Assessed contributions are a minority share.

med-global-health.l10.q4.t: The IHR require measures that significantly interfere with traffic to be justified by public health rationale, and the state must report it
med-global-health.l10.q4.p: State X imposes a ban on all arrivals from a country with an outbreak, going beyond WHO temporary recommendations, and cites no evidence. Which statement best reflects the IHR framework?
med-global-health.l10.q4.h: The Regulations impose a justification and reporting duty, not a penalty.
med-global-health.l10.q4.e: The IHR require measures beyond WHO advice to be justified and reported, but WHO has no power to impose penalties. Neither an absolute ban on measures nor unlimited discretion matches the text.

med-global-health.l10.q5.t: WHO lacks enforcement tools, depends on voluntary funding, and states have exceeded advice on travel restrictions without penalty
med-global-health.l10.q5.p: Analysts disagree about WHO's effectiveness. Which observation best supports the argument that its binding rules have limited leverage?
med-global-health.l10.q5.h: Look for evidence about enforcement, not about structure or mandate.
med-global-health.l10.q5.e: Absence of enforcement, dependence on donors and unpenalised deviations show limited leverage. The other options describe governance, tools and definitions, not leverage.

med-global-health.l11.q1.t: Grants to strengthen surveillance, laboratories and workforce capacity in lower-income countries
med-global-health.l11.q1.p: The Pandemic Fund, launched in 2022 and hosted by the World Bank, provides what?
med-global-health.l11.q1.h: It funds the capacity that keeps detection working.
med-global-health.l11.q1.e: The Fund finances capacity building in lower-income countries. It does not pay for patents or border closures.

med-global-health.l11.q2.t: Outcomes also depended on trust, leadership, communication and adaptability that composite indexes capture poorly
med-global-health.l11.q2.p: Why did high scores on pre-pandemic preparedness indexes not reliably predict COVID-19 outcomes?
med-global-health.l11.q2.h: Capacity on paper is different from performance in a crisis.
med-global-health.l11.q2.e: Composite indices cover formal capacities but miss social and political factors that shaped outcomes. They were not simply wealth rankings or stockpile counts.

med-global-health.l11.q3.t: Researchers wanting prompt sample and sequence access and providing countries wanting a fair share of resulting benefits
med-global-health.l11.q3.p: The central tension in negotiating pathogen access and benefit sharing is between which interests?
med-global-health.l11.q3.h: The question is who benefits when samples are shared.
med-global-health.l11.q3.e: The core tension is prompt access to pathogen material versus fair benefit sharing. Others are real debates but are not the focus of this negotiation.

med-global-health.l11.q4.t: Formal capacity does not guarantee performance; communication, trust and operational surge capacity are core components of preparedness
med-global-health.l11.q4.p: A country scores highly on a preparedness index but has high early COVID-19 mortality. A review finds inconsistent public messaging, low testing early on and overwhelmed hospitals. Which conclusion is best supported?
med-global-health.l11.q4.h: The review identifies failures the index did not measure.
med-global-health.l11.q4.e: The findings point to gaps in operational and social capacity that indices miss. The other options overgeneralise or dismiss measures such as testing that the review flagged.

med-global-health.l11.q5.t: Pooled mechanisms need binding supply commitments and regional manufacturing capacity before the next emergency
med-global-health.l11.q5.p: Early in a pandemic, high-income countries secure most vaccine doses through bilateral contracts while a pooled facility struggles to deliver. What is the most important structural lesson commonly drawn?
med-global-health.l11.q5.h: The problem lay in supply and bargaining power, not in the concept alone.
med-global-health.l11.q5.e: Analyses emphasise commitments and distributed manufacturing so pooled facilities are not outbid. Abandoning pooling or banning contracts does not address the supply problem.

med-global-health.l12.q1.t: Tobacco use, harmful alcohol use, unhealthy diet and physical inactivity
med-global-health.l12.q1.p: Which set lists the four main behavioural risk factors shared by major noncommunicable diseases?
med-global-health.l12.q1.h: These are behaviours, not metabolic intermediates.
med-global-health.l12.q1.e: The four behavioural risk factors are tobacco, alcohol, diet and inactivity. The last option lists metabolic risk factors, which are intermediates between behaviour and disease.

med-global-health.l12.q2.t: Raising tobacco taxes and prices, which reduces consumption especially among young and low-income people
med-global-health.l12.q2.p: Which intervention has the strongest evidence as a population-level tobacco control measure?
med-global-health.l12.q2.e: Tax-driven price rises reduce smoking across groups and raise revenue. Voluntary labelling and awareness alone have weaker evidence.

med-global-health.l12.q3.t: 90 percent of girls fully vaccinated against HPV by age 15
med-global-health.l12.q3.p: According to the WHO cervical cancer elimination strategy, what is the 2030 vaccination target?
med-global-health.l12.q3.e: The first target is 90 percent of girls vaccinated by 15, followed by 70 percent screening and 90 percent treatment. The 70 figure applies to screening, not to vaccination.

med-global-health.l12.q4.t: A care-cascade failure in detection, drug supply, adherence and follow-up rather than lack of effective medicines
med-global-health.l12.q4.p: A primary care programme finds that most adults with hypertension are undiagnosed or untreated even though cheap drugs exist. Which diagnosis of the problem best fits the evidence?
med-global-health.l12.q4.h: Effective drugs exist, so look at delivery.
med-global-health.l12.q4.e: The care cascade identifies where patients are lost from detection to control, and cheap effective drugs exist. Claims of drug unavailability in principle or universal resistance are not supported.

med-global-health.l12.q5.t: Taxes change relative prices and shift consumption at population level, whereas education alone usually produces smaller and less durable effects, so equity impacts should still be assessed
med-global-health.l12.q5.p: A government considers a sugar-sweetened beverage tax versus an education campaign alone. Which statement best reflects the evidence-based reasoning?
med-global-health.l12.q5.h: Compare structural change with information change.
med-global-health.l12.q5.e: Pricing policies tend to produce measurable population shifts, and equity should be examined because taxes can be regressive in cost but progressive in health benefit. Information-only effects are typically smaller.

med-global-health.l13.q1.t: General taxation funds care that is often delivered by publicly employed providers and is free at the point of use
med-global-health.l13.q1.p: Which description matches the Beveridge model of health care?
med-global-health.l13.q1.h: Think of the British National Health Service.
med-global-health.l13.q1.e: Beveridge systems are tax-funded with public providers. The payroll fund model is Bismarck, the single insurer is national health insurance, and the last is the out-of-pocket model.

med-global-health.l13.q2.t: Providers are largely private while one public insurer pays the bills
med-global-health.l13.q2.p: Which feature distinguishes a single-payer national health insurance model from a Beveridge model?
med-global-health.l13.q2.h: The question is who delivers care, not only who pays.
med-global-health.l13.q2.e: In single-payer systems such as Canada, private providers are paid by one public insurer. In Beveridge systems the state often also owns and employs the providers.

med-global-health.l13.q3.p: A country finances care through compulsory employer and employee contributions to several regulated non-profit funds, and insurers must accept all applicants. This is best classed as which model?
med-global-health.l13.q3.h: Multiple regulated funds funded by payroll are the signature.
med-global-health.l13.q3.e: Multiple regulated sickness funds financed by payroll contributions define the Bismarck model. A single-payer model would have only one insurer.

med-global-health.l13.q4.t: Life expectancy reflects income, behaviour, education and social conditions as well as the health system, so the comparison does not isolate the system
med-global-health.l13.q4.p: Country P ranks higher than Country Q on life expectancy, and a commentator concludes that P's financing model is superior. Which objection is strongest?
med-global-health.l13.q4.h: Many factors affect the outcome besides the system.
med-global-health.l13.q4.e: Population outcomes depend on many determinants, so a simple comparison confounds the system with other factors. The idea that models cannot matter at all overstates the point.

med-global-health.l13.q5.t: A shift from a Bismarck-type model to a single-payer national health insurance model
med-global-health.l13.q5.p: A country replaces its many competing sickness funds with one public insurer that pays the same private clinics and hospitals as before. What is the most accurate description of the change?
med-global-health.l13.q5.h: Look at who pays, then at who provides.
med-global-health.l13.q5.e: Moving from several funds to one public payer, with providers unchanged, converts the model to single-payer. The unchanged providers do not stop the payer structure from changing.

med-global-health.l14.q1.t: All people can obtain needed quality health services without suffering financial hardship
med-global-health.l14.q1.p: Which definition best matches universal health coverage?
med-global-health.l14.q1.h: It has both a service dimension and a financial dimension.
med-global-health.l14.q1.e: UHC means access to needed, effective services plus financial protection. It does not require every service to be free or any particular budget share.

med-global-health.l14.q2.t: Capitation, which risks under-provision of services
med-global-health.l14.q2.p: A payment system gives providers a fixed amount per enrolled person regardless of how many services each uses. This is called what, and what incentive risk does it carry?
med-global-health.l14.q2.h: A fixed payment per person means more care costs the provider more.
med-global-health.l14.q2.e: Capitation pays per enrolled person, which encourages efficiency but can encourage skimping. Fee-for-service is the one that tends to encourage volume.

med-global-health.l14.q3.t: It exceeds both the 10 percent and 25 percent thresholds
med-global-health.l14.q3.p: A household spends 30 percent of its annual income on one hospital stay. Under a common threshold definition of catastrophic health expenditure, which statement is correct?
med-global-health.l14.q3.e: Thirty percent exceeds both 10 and 25 percent. Impoverishment is a separate measure involving the poverty line.

med-global-health.l14.q4.t: Removing fees improved access but must be paired with increased financing for supplies and staff to preserve quality
med-global-health.l14.q4.p: A government abolishes user fees at public clinics. Attendance rises sharply, but stock-outs and staff overload follow. Which analysis is most reasonable?
med-global-health.l14.q4.h: The fee was replaced by tax money, or it was not.
med-global-health.l14.q4.e: Experience shows that fees deter use and that abolition needs compensating financing. A rise in use after removing fees indicates a barrier was lifted, not that fees helped.

med-global-health.l14.q5.t: Use tax funding to subsidise or pool coverage for people outside formal employment, as Thailand did in 2002
med-global-health.l14.q5.p: A country wants to cover informal workers who cannot pay payroll contributions. Which approach is most consistent with the financing evidence?
med-global-health.l14.q5.e: Thailand's scheme used general taxation to cover people outside formal work. Direct payment at the time of illness and individual savings accounts do not pool risk.

med-global-health.l15.q1.p: The WHO Model List of Essential Medicines first appeared in which year?
med-global-health.l15.q1.h: It came before the 1978 Alma-Ata conference.
med-global-health.l15.q1.e: The first Model List was published in 1977. 1994 is the year the TRIPS Agreement was concluded, and 2001 is the Doha Declaration.

med-global-health.l15.q2.t: Government authorisation to produce or import a patented product without the patent holder's consent, under conditions
med-global-health.l15.q2.p: What is a compulsory licence under TRIPS flexibilities?
med-global-health.l15.q2.h: The compulsion is on the patent holder.
med-global-health.l15.q2.e: A compulsory licence lets a government permit generic use without consent. A voluntary licence, such as those negotiated by the Patent Pool, is a different mechanism.

med-global-health.l15.q3.t: TRIPS should be interpreted and implemented to support public health and access to medicines
med-global-health.l15.q3.p: What did the Doha Declaration of 2001 affirm?
med-global-health.l15.q3.h: It was a response to the AIDS medicines dispute.
med-global-health.l15.q3.e: Doha affirmed that TRIPS does not prevent members from protecting public health and confirmed the use of flexibilities. It did not invalidate patents.

med-global-health.l15.q4.t: Allowing generics made under compulsory licence in one country to be exported to countries without manufacturing capacity
med-global-health.l15.q4.p: A country has the legal right to issue compulsory licences but has no domestic pharmaceutical manufacturers. What was the 2003 WTO General Council decision designed to address?
med-global-health.l15.q4.h: The problem was lack of a place to make the drug.
med-global-health.l15.q4.e: The decision, later made a permanent amendment, enables export to countries lacking capacity. It does not cancel patents or ban exports.

med-global-health.l15.q5.t: It is a substandard or falsified product, and low price does not guarantee quality, so procurement should use quality-assured sources
med-global-health.l15.q5.p: A national tender finds that a cheap generic antimalarial is available but a laboratory test shows it contains a fraction of the stated active ingredient. What is the most accurate classification and implication?
med-global-health.l15.q5.h: Quality is a separate barrier from price, stock and prescribing.
med-global-health.l15.q5.e: A product that fails content specifications is substandard, or falsified if deliberately misrepresented, so quality assurance is needed. Retraining or subsidising does not fix content.

med-global-health.l16.q1.t: Health for All by the year 2000 through primary health care
med-global-health.l16.q1.p: The Declaration of Alma-Ata (1978) called for what goal?
med-global-health.l16.q1.e: Alma-Ata set the goal of Health for All by 2000 through primary health care. Smallpox eradication was declared in 1980 under a different programme.

med-global-health.l16.q2.t: Limited resources should go first to a few cost-effective interventions against leading causes of child death
med-global-health.l16.q2.p: What was the main argument of the selective primary health care proposal of 1979?
med-global-health.l16.q2.h: Selective means choosing a limited package.
med-global-health.l16.q2.e: Walsh and Warren proposed targeting cost-effective interventions such as immunisation and oral rehydration. Critics said this neglected social determinants.

med-global-health.l16.q3.t: It encourages ethical recruitment and discourages active recruitment from countries with critical shortages, on a voluntary basis
med-global-health.l16.q3.p: What does the WHO Global Code of Practice on the International Recruitment of Health Personnel (2010) do?
med-global-health.l16.q3.e: The Code is a voluntary instrument promoting ethical practice. It is not a ban on emigration or a binding quota system.

med-global-health.l16.q4.t: Expand midwifery and community-level cadres with training, supervision and a reliable referral pathway for complications
med-global-health.l16.q4.p: A country needs to expand skilled birth coverage quickly in rural districts with few doctors. Which strategy is best supported by the task-shifting evidence?
med-global-health.l16.q4.h: Trained cadres plus referral are the key.
med-global-health.l16.q4.e: Task shifting works when cadres are trained, supervised and backed by referral for complications. Waiting for specialists would delay coverage, and untrained volunteers cannot provide skilled care.

med-global-health.l16.q5.t: Programmes relying on unpaid labour without supervision and supplies are fragile, which supports formal recognition and fair pay
med-global-health.l16.q5.p: A community health worker programme collapses after workers, mostly women, go months unpaid with no supplies or supervision. What is the most likely lesson?
med-global-health.l16.q5.h: The failure is in design and support, not in the idea.
med-global-health.l16.q5.e: Evidence shows that supervision, supplies and remuneration sustain programmes. The collapse says nothing about the concept being inherently ineffective.

med-global-health.l17.q1.t: Respect for persons, beneficence and justice
med-global-health.l17.q1.p: Which three principles were named in the Belmont Report of 1979?
med-global-health.l17.q1.h: The report followed the Tuskegee study.
med-global-health.l17.q1.e: Belmont named respect for persons, beneficence and justice. The second option mixes Beauchamp and Childress terms with veracity, which is not a Belmont principle.

med-global-health.l17.q2.t: The voluntary consent of the human subject
med-global-health.l17.q2.p: What did the Nuremberg Code of 1947 place first among its requirements?
med-global-health.l17.q2.h: It came out of the trial of physicians who experimented on prisoners.
med-global-health.l17.q2.e: The Code opens by stating that voluntary consent is absolutely essential. Ethics committee review was introduced later, notably in Helsinki.

med-global-health.l17.q3.t: An effective regimen existed, so withholding it from the control group was said to be unethical
med-global-health.l17.q3.p: In the 1990s zidovudine controversy, what was the central objection to placebo-controlled trials?
med-global-health.l17.q3.h: The question is what the control arm should receive.
med-global-health.l17.q3.e: Critics argued that a proven regimen already existed, so placebo denied participants effective treatment. Defenders cited local standard of care and feasibility.

med-global-health.l17.q4.t: Require justification that placebo is warranted and that participants will not face added risk of serious harm, and plan for post-trial access
med-global-health.l17.q4.p: A sponsor proposes a vaccine trial in a low-income country with a placebo arm, although an effective vaccine exists but is unaffordable locally. Which committee response best reflects current Helsinki principles?
med-global-health.l17.q4.h: The standard is the best proven intervention, with narrow exceptions.
med-global-health.l17.q4.e: Helsinki permits placebo only if no proven intervention exists or for compelling reasons without added risk of serious harm. Automatic approval or blanket rejection ignores that structure, and waivers cannot replace protection.

med-global-health.l17.q5.t: Parachute research, criticised for lacking local leadership, benefit sharing and capacity building
med-global-health.l17.q5.p: Researchers from a wealthy university collect blood samples in a village, publish without local authors and leave no capacity. Which term and criticism apply?
med-global-health.l17.q5.h: Think about researchers who drop in and leave.
med-global-health.l17.q5.e: Parachute or helicopter research describes extractive collaboration. The other terms concern trial design and analysis, not partnership ethics.

med-global-health.l18.q1.p: Which list contains the four humanitarian principles?
med-global-health.l18.q1.h: One of them concerns taking sides.
med-global-health.l18.q1.e: The four principles are humanity, neutrality, impartiality and independence. Proportionality is a rule of humanitarian law, not one of these principles.

med-global-health.l18.q2.t: Returning a person to a place where they face persecution or serious harm
med-global-health.l18.q2.p: What does the principle of non-refoulement prohibit?
med-global-health.l18.q2.h: It concerns where a refugee can be sent.
med-global-health.l18.q2.e: Non-refoulement bars return to persecution. Treating wounded combatants is required by the Geneva Conventions, not forbidden.

med-global-health.l18.q3.t: One death per 10,000 people per day
med-global-health.l18.q3.p: A crude mortality rate above what level is conventionally used as an emergency threshold in humanitarian settings?
med-global-health.l18.q3.e: The standard emergency threshold is above one death per 10,000 people per day. The other figures express different time units and thresholds.

med-global-health.l18.q4.t: Safe water and sanitation, measles vaccination, oral rehydration and malnutrition treatment, with outbreak surveillance
med-global-health.l18.q4.p: A displaced camp reports a crude mortality rate of 2 per 10,000 per day, with most deaths from diarrhoea, measles and malnutrition in children. Which set of priorities is best?
med-global-health.l18.q4.h: Match the interventions to the leading killers.
med-global-health.l18.q4.e: The rate is above the emergency threshold, and the leading causes call for water, sanitation, vaccination and nutrition measures. Chronic disease and tertiary hospitals are lower priorities in the acute phase.

med-global-health.l18.q5.t: Two defensible strategies weighing access against advocacy, each with costs
med-global-health.l18.q5.p: One agency keeps its observations of abuses confidential to preserve access to detainees. Another publicly denounces abuses even if it risks expulsion. How should this difference be understood?
med-global-health.l18.q5.h: Neither choice is dictated by law.
med-global-health.l18.q5.e: The Red Cross movement and MSF represent different traditions, with trade-offs between access and testimony. International humanitarian law does not dictate either choice.

med-global-health.l19.q1.t: Selection: the drug kills susceptible bacteria and resistant ones survive and multiply
med-global-health.l19.q1.p: Which process best explains how antibiotic resistance becomes common in a bacterial population?
med-global-health.l19.q1.e: Resistance spreads because the drug selects pre-existing resistant organisms. It is the bacteria, not the patient, that resist, and bacteria do not adapt deliberately.

med-global-health.l19.q2.t: Last-resort antibiotics to be saved for infections caused by multidrug-resistant organisms
med-global-health.l19.q2.p: In WHO's AWaRe classification, what does the Reserve group contain?
med-global-health.l19.q2.h: The name describes how the drugs are kept.
med-global-health.l19.q2.e: Reserve drugs are last-resort options. Access means first-line options and Watch means higher resistance potential for specific indications.

med-global-health.l19.q3.t: It confers transferable resistance to colistin, a last-line antibiotic, and spreads between bacteria and across species
med-global-health.l19.q3.p: Why is the discovery of the plasmid-borne mcr-1 gene considered significant?
med-global-health.l19.q3.e: Plasmid-borne resistance can spread horizontally, and colistin is a last-line drug. The other options do not describe mcr-1.

med-global-health.l19.q4.t: Screening and isolating colonised patients, reinforcing hand hygiene and cleaning, and reviewing carbapenem prescribing
med-global-health.l19.q4.p: A hospital sees a rise in carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales infections. Which response is most likely to reduce spread?
med-global-health.l19.q4.h: Reduce both transmission and selection pressure.
med-global-health.l19.q4.e: Infection control plus stewardship targets spread and selection. Broader carbapenem use raises selection pressure, and ignoring surveillance hides the problem.

med-global-health.l19.q5.t: The measure may reduce misuse but could block access to life-saving treatment, so it should be paired with improved access to prescribers and diagnostics
med-global-health.l19.q5.p: A minister proposes banning antibiotic sales without prescription in a rural region where no clinic is within a day's travel. What is the most balanced analysis?
med-global-health.l19.q5.h: Both excess and access problems are real.
med-global-health.l19.q5.e: Policy must weigh misuse against unmet need, since many deaths are from lack of access. Neither a guarantee of elimination nor dismissal of access is supported.

med-global-health.l20.q1.t: Article 12 of the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights
med-global-health.l20.q1.p: Which treaty article sets out the right to the highest attainable standard of physical and mental health?
med-global-health.l20.q1.h: It sits in the Covenant on economic, social and cultural rights.
med-global-health.l20.q1.e: Article 12 of the ICESCR recognises this right. Alma-Ata is a declaration, not a treaty with numbered rights articles of that kind.

med-global-health.l20.q2.p: According to General Comment 14, which set lists the essential features of the right to health?
med-global-health.l20.q2.h: Four features that begin with A, A, A and Q.
med-global-health.l20.q2.e: General Comment 14 names availability, accessibility, acceptability and quality. The other lists are plausible but not the Committee's framework.

med-global-health.l20.q3.t: They can fragment health systems and draw staff away from general services while reflecting donor priorities
med-global-health.l20.q3.p: What is the main criticism of vertical disease programmes?
med-global-health.l20.q3.h: Single-disease focus can mean parallel structures.
med-global-health.l20.q3.e: Critics point to fragmentation and staff diversion. Defenders note that they often produce measurable results and capacity, so they do not never work.

med-global-health.l20.q4.t: The integrated programme is likelier to continue with domestic financing, while the parallel structure is likelier to collapse
med-global-health.l20.q4.p: A donor ends funding for an HIV programme run with its own parallel supply chain. In a neighbouring country, a similar programme was integrated into national systems. What outcome does the integration argument predict?
med-global-health.l20.q4.h: Integration with national systems is the sustainability argument.
med-global-health.l20.q4.e: Alignment with country systems supports continuity when aid shifts. The case does not show that parallel systems build stronger national capacity.

med-global-health.l20.q5.t: Advocates call for local leadership, equitable authorship and direct funding, while some caution that the practical measures need to be specified and tested
med-global-health.l20.q5.p: Which statement best captures the debate about decolonising global health?
med-global-health.l20.q5.h: There is both a call for change and a caution about vagueness.
med-global-health.l20.q5.e: The debate involves proposals for power-sharing and a caution about the loose use of the term. The other options misstate what advocates and critics say.

med-histo-embryo.l01.q1.t: Hematoxylin, a basic dye, binds the negatively charged ribosomal RNA in the cytoplasm
med-histo-embryo.l01.q1.p: Which feature gives a cell rich in rough endoplasmic reticulum and free ribosomes a blue-purple cytoplasm on an H&E slide?
med-histo-embryo.l01.q1.h: Think about which dye is basic and what charge RNA carries.
med-histo-embryo.l01.q1.e: Hematoxylin acts as a basic dye and binds acidic, negatively charged molecules such as RNA and DNA, producing basophilia. Eosin, being acidic, stains positively charged proteins pink.

med-histo-embryo.l01.q2.t: Smooth endoplasmic reticulum, which hypertrophies to metabolise lipids and detoxify drugs in these cells
med-histo-embryo.l01.q2.p: A biopsy shows hepatocytes with abundant foamy, pale cytoplasm after chronic drug exposure. Which organelle is most likely expanded to explain this?
med-histo-embryo.l01.q2.e: Smooth ER proliferates in hepatocytes exposed to drugs and is lipid-rich, so it looks pale. Rough ER would make the cytoplasm basophilic, not foamy.

med-histo-embryo.l01.q3.t: Keratin in epithelial cells and vimentin in mesenchymal-derived cells
med-histo-embryo.l01.q3.p: Which pairing of intermediate filament and cell lineage is correct?
med-histo-embryo.l01.q3.h: Match each protein to the tissue where it gives strength.
med-histo-embryo.l01.q3.e: Keratins mark epithelia and vimentin marks mesenchymal cells. The other pairings swap lineages, for example desmin belongs to muscle and glial fibrillary acidic protein to astrocytes.

med-histo-embryo.l01.q4.t: A tumour of epithelial origin, a carcinoma, because keratin intermediate filaments mark epithelial cells
med-histo-embryo.l01.q4.p: A 58-year-old man has a lung mass that on biopsy shows sheets of undifferentiated cells. Immunostaining is strongly positive for keratin and negative for vimentin. This result best supports which interpretation?
med-histo-embryo.l01.q4.e: Keratin positivity indicates epithelial differentiation, so carcinoma is most likely. A sarcoma would be expected to be vimentin positive, and muscle tumours express desmin.

med-histo-embryo.l01.q5.t: Failure of lysosomal acid hydrolase activity, causing a storage disease from impaired breakdown of material
med-histo-embryo.l01.q5.p: A child has progressive coarse features and cognitive decline. Biopsy shows cells swollen with undigested material inside membrane-bound acidic vesicles. Deficiency of which organelle function is most likely?
med-histo-embryo.l01.q5.e: Lysosomes digest material using acid hydrolases at low pH, and loss of one enzyme leads to accumulation of its substrate. Mitochondrial and Golgi defects do not produce this pattern of vesicular storage.

med-histo-embryo.l02.q1.p: Which epithelium lines the urinary bladder and changes its surface cell shape as the organ fills?
med-histo-embryo.l02.q1.h: Think of an epithelium built to stretch.
med-histo-embryo.l02.q1.e: Urothelium lines the renal pelvis, ureters and bladder and allows distension. The others are found in skin, kidney tubules and airways respectively.

med-histo-embryo.l02.q2.t: Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium, a single layer despite its layered appearance
med-histo-embryo.l02.q2.p: Sections of the trachea show one layer of cells whose nuclei lie at different heights, with cilia and goblet cells, all touching the basement membrane. This is best classified as which type?
med-histo-embryo.l02.q2.h: Count how many cell layers actually reach the basement membrane.
med-histo-embryo.l02.q2.e: Every cell touches the basement membrane, so it is a single layer, pseudostratified. Staggered nuclei only give the impression of layers.

med-histo-embryo.l02.q3.t: Holocrine, in which the whole cell disintegrates and becomes the secretion
med-histo-embryo.l02.q3.p: Sebaceous glands release their oily product by which mode of secretion?
med-histo-embryo.l02.q3.h: The product is the cell itself.
med-histo-embryo.l02.q3.e: Sebaceous glands are the classic holocrine example, as the lipid-filled cells die and form sebum. Merocrine glands use exocytosis and apocrine glands lose only the apical part.

med-histo-embryo.l02.q4.t: Faulty dynein arms in the axoneme, which impairs ciliary motion and the embryonic left-right determination
med-histo-embryo.l02.q4.p: A 9-year-old with recurrent sinusitis, bronchiectasis and a heart located on the right side has infertility concerns raised in the family history. Which cellular defect best explains the full picture?
med-histo-embryo.l02.q4.h: Immotile cilia affect mucus and also embryonic nodal flow.
med-histo-embryo.l02.q4.e: Primary ciliary dyskinesia from defective dynein causes poor mucociliary clearance and randomised laterality, as in Kartagener syndrome, plus sperm immotility. Desmosome or laminin defects do not randomise organ position.

med-histo-embryo.l02.q5.t: Metaplasia, a reversible replacement of one mature epithelium by another that tolerates the injury
med-histo-embryo.l02.q5.p: A long-term smoker has bronchoscopy showing a patch of stratified squamous epithelium where ciliated pseudostratified epithelium would normally be. What is the best description?
med-histo-embryo.l02.q5.h: One mature type replaces another under chronic stress.
med-histo-embryo.l02.q5.e: Squamous metaplasia is an adaptive change to chronic irritation. Dysplasia is disordered growth, and breaching the basement membrane defines invasion rather than metaplasia.

med-histo-embryo.l03.q1.p: Which collagen type forms the fine reticular meshwork supporting the spleen and lymph nodes?
med-histo-embryo.l03.q1.h: It is also called reticular collagen.
med-histo-embryo.l03.q1.e: Type III collagen makes reticular fibres. Type I is in tendon and bone, type II in cartilage, and type IV in basal laminae.

med-histo-embryo.l03.q2.t: The mast cell, with granules containing histamine and heparin
med-histo-embryo.l03.q2.p: Which cell found in connective tissue releases histamine upon cross-linking of surface-bound IgE?
med-histo-embryo.l03.q2.h: It carries IgE receptors and is central in allergic reactions.
med-histo-embryo.l03.q2.e: Mast cells carry IgE on their surface and degranulate on cross-linking. Plasma cells secrete antibody but do not degranulate in this way.

med-histo-embryo.l03.q3.t: Dense regular connective tissue of tendons
med-histo-embryo.l03.q3.p: Which tissue has parallel bundles of type I collagen with rows of compressed fibroblasts between them?
med-histo-embryo.l03.q3.h: Parallel arrangement implies force in one direction.
med-histo-embryo.l03.q3.e: Tendons and ligaments are dense regular tissue. The dermis is dense irregular, with interwoven fibres resisting force in multiple directions.

med-histo-embryo.l03.q4.t: Hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues, which requires ascorbic acid as a cofactor
med-histo-embryo.l03.q4.p: A sailor on a long voyage with little fresh food develops bleeding gums, perifollicular haemorrhages and poor wound healing. Which step of collagen synthesis is most directly impaired?
med-histo-embryo.l03.q4.h: Scurvy is a vitamin C deficiency.
med-histo-embryo.l03.q4.e: Vitamin C is needed for hydroxylation of proline and lysine, so unstable collagen results. Lysyl oxidase needs copper, which is relevant in a different deficiency, but scurvy acts earlier.

med-histo-embryo.l03.q5.t: Fibrillin-1, a scaffold on which elastic fibres are assembled in the matrix
med-histo-embryo.l03.q5.p: A tall, thin 22-year-old has lens subluxation and aortic root dilation. Which extracellular matrix component is most likely defective?
med-histo-embryo.l03.q5.e: Marfan syndrome results from fibrillin-1 mutation, which affects elastic fibres in the lens and aorta. Type V collagen defects are linked to a form of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

med-histo-embryo.l04.q1.p: Which cell type resorbs bone using a ruffled border?
med-histo-embryo.l04.q1.h: It is a multinucleated cell derived from the monocyte lineage.
med-histo-embryo.l04.q1.e: Osteoclasts resorb bone with acid and proteases at the ruffled border. Osteoblasts build bone and osteocytes maintain it.

med-histo-embryo.l04.q2.t: Fibrocartilage, containing thick type I collagen
med-histo-embryo.l04.q2.p: Which cartilage resists compression and shear in the intervertebral disc and has no perichondrium?
med-histo-embryo.l04.q2.e: Fibrocartilage, with thick type I collagen bundles, lacks a perichondrium and forms discs and menisci. Hyaline cartilage has type II collagen and is found on joint surfaces.

med-histo-embryo.l04.q3.t: Intramembranous ossification directly from condensed mesenchyme
med-histo-embryo.l04.q3.p: The flat bones of the skull form mainly by which process?
med-histo-embryo.l04.q3.e: Flat skull bones are intramembranous. Long bones form by endochondral ossification on a cartilage model.

med-histo-embryo.l04.q4.t: Proliferation of chondrocytes in the growth plate, because of a gain-of-function receptor mutation
med-histo-embryo.l04.q4.p: A 4-year-old has short limbs, a large head and normal trunk length with normal intelligence; both parents are of average height. Which process is primarily affected?
med-histo-embryo.l04.q4.e: Achondroplasia is caused by activating FGFR3 mutation, which restrains growth plate chondrocyte proliferation and so endochondral growth. Intramembranous bone is spared, which is why the skull vault is relatively large.

med-histo-embryo.l04.q5.t: Abundant unmineralised osteoid because calcium and phosphate are insufficient to mineralise matrix
med-histo-embryo.l04.q5.p: A 3-year-old with bowed legs has widened, cupped growth plates and a low serum phosphate. Biopsy would most likely show which finding in bone?
med-histo-embryo.l04.q5.h: The matrix is made but not hardened.
med-histo-embryo.l04.q5.e: Rickets features unmineralised osteoid and disorganised growth plate cartilage from vitamin D deficiency. Osteogenesis imperfecta, by contrast, features defective collagen.

med-histo-embryo.l05.q1.t: Scattered peripherally just beneath the sarcolemma, as the fibre is multinucleated
med-histo-embryo.l05.q1.p: Where are the nuclei of a skeletal muscle fibre found?
med-histo-embryo.l05.q1.h: Skeletal fibres form by fusion of many myoblasts.
med-histo-embryo.l05.q1.e: Skeletal muscle fibres are multinucleated with peripheral nuclei. Central nuclei are typical of cardiac and smooth muscle cells.

med-histo-embryo.l05.q2.t: The A band, which spans the full length of the thick filaments
med-histo-embryo.l05.q2.p: During contraction of a sarcomere, which band does NOT change in length?
med-histo-embryo.l05.q2.h: Filament length stays constant in the sliding theory.
med-histo-embryo.l05.q2.e: The A band equals thick filament length and is constant. The I band and H zone shorten and the sarcomere shortens between Z discs.

med-histo-embryo.l05.q3.t: Calcium binds calmodulin, which activates myosin light-chain kinase, and troponin is absent
med-histo-embryo.l05.q3.p: Which mechanism distinguishes smooth muscle activation from skeletal muscle activation?
med-histo-embryo.l05.q3.h: Troponin is missing in this tissue.
med-histo-embryo.l05.q3.e: Smooth muscle uses a calmodulin and myosin light-chain kinase pathway. Troponin C is the skeletal and cardiac mechanism.

med-histo-embryo.l05.q4.t: Satellite cells located beneath the basal lamina of each fibre
med-histo-embryo.l05.q4.p: A 6-year-old boy has progressive proximal weakness, calf enlargement and a Gowers sign. A biopsy would most likely show muscle fibres of variable size with necrosis and replacement by fat and fibrosis. Which regenerative cell population normally repairs injured fibres and becomes exhausted in this disease?
med-histo-embryo.l05.q4.h: Which stem cell sits between sarcolemma and basal lamina?
med-histo-embryo.l05.q4.e: Satellite cells are the muscle stem cells that fuse to repair fibres. In Duchenne dystrophy repeated damage and regeneration eventually fail and fibrofatty replacement follows.

med-histo-embryo.l05.q5.t: Mechanical coupling through desmosomes and rapid electrical spread through gap junctions
med-histo-embryo.l05.q5.p: A section of heart muscle shows branched cells, single central nuclei and dark-staining transverse lines crossing between adjacent cells. These lines contain structures that allow which two functions?
med-histo-embryo.l05.q5.e: Intercalated discs combine anchoring junctions with gap junctions so that the heart acts as a functional syncytium. Tight junctions and synapses are not features of these discs.

med-histo-embryo.l06.q1.p: Which glial cell myelinates axons of the central nervous system?
med-histo-embryo.l06.q1.e: Oligodendrocytes myelinate multiple central axons. Schwann cells do so in the periphery, one segment per cell.

med-histo-embryo.l06.q2.p: Which connective tissue layer surrounds a single fascicle of a peripheral nerve and contributes to the blood-nerve barrier?
med-histo-embryo.l06.q2.e: Perineurium wraps each fascicle. Endoneurium surrounds single axons and epineurium surrounds the whole nerve.

med-histo-embryo.l06.q3.t: Microglial cell, which acts as the resident macrophage of the brain
med-histo-embryo.l06.q3.p: Which cell derives from yolk sac precursors rather than neural ectoderm?
med-histo-embryo.l06.q3.e: Microglia come from the yolk sac, unlike the other glia and neurons, which arise from neuroectoderm.

med-histo-embryo.l06.q4.t: Schwann cells, because peripheral myelin is a distinct antigenic target from central myelin
med-histo-embryo.l06.q4.p: A 30-year-old develops ascending symmetric weakness and absent reflexes two weeks after a diarrhoeal illness. Nerve conduction shows slowed velocities. Which cell is the target of the autoimmune attack, and why is the central nervous system spared?
med-histo-embryo.l06.q4.e: Guillain-Barre syndrome attacks Schwann cell myelin, so the periphery is affected and the central nervous system is spared. Oligodendrocytes are targeted in multiple sclerosis.

med-histo-embryo.l06.q5.t: Retrograde axonal transport along microtubules powered by the motor protein dynein
med-histo-embryo.l06.q5.p: A farmer bitten by a rabid animal on the hand develops encephalitis weeks later, although the bite was far from the brain. Which cellular process best explains the delay?
med-histo-embryo.l06.q5.h: Which direction is toward the cell body, and which motor does it?
med-histo-embryo.l06.q5.e: Rabies travels retrograde in axons using dynein. Kinesin moves cargo outward towards the synapse, and saltatory conduction is an electrical not a transport phenomenon.

med-histo-embryo.l07.q1.p: Which white cell has a bilobed nucleus and large bright red granules?
med-histo-embryo.l07.q1.h: Bright red granules with major basic protein.
med-histo-embryo.l07.q1.e: Eosinophils have bilobed nuclei and eosinophilic granules. Basophil granules are dark blue.

med-histo-embryo.l07.q2.p: Which hormone, made mainly by peritubular interstitial cells of the kidney in response to hypoxia, drives red blood cell production?
med-histo-embryo.l07.q2.h: It is named after the red cell.
med-histo-embryo.l07.q2.e: Erythropoietin responds to low oxygen delivery. Thrombopoietin acts on megakaryocytes and G-CSF on neutrophils.

med-histo-embryo.l07.q3.t: Residual ribosomal RNA in the cytoplasm of the young red cell
med-histo-embryo.l07.q3.p: Reticulocytes appear bluish on a special stain because they retain which component?
med-histo-embryo.l07.q3.e: Reticulocytes have lost their nucleus but still hold ribosomal RNA, which stains blue. A raised count shows marrow response to anaemia or bleeding.

med-histo-embryo.l07.q4.t: Haemoglobin synthesis is limited while cell division continues, giving small hypochromic cells
med-histo-embryo.l07.q4.p: A 25-year-old woman with heavy periods has fatigue and pallor. A smear shows small red cells with wide central pallor, and the reticulocyte count is low for the degree of anaemia. Which interpretation of the cell appearance is most accurate?
med-histo-embryo.l07.q4.e: In iron deficiency, haemoglobin production lags so cells divide extra times and are small and pale. Delayed nuclear maturation describes megaloblastic anaemia, which gives macrocytes.

med-histo-embryo.l07.q5.t: A left shift, reflecting release of immature neutrophil forms from the marrow in response to infection
med-histo-embryo.l07.q5.p: A 62-year-old man has an elevated white cell count with many band neutrophils and a few metamyelocytes after pneumonia. Which description fits this finding?
med-histo-embryo.l07.q5.e: A left shift means more immature neutrophils such as bands. A right shift means hypersegmented neutrophils, typical of megaloblastic anaemia.

med-histo-embryo.l08.q1.p: Which capillary type has wide gaps and an incomplete basement membrane and is found in the liver and spleen?
med-histo-embryo.l08.q1.h: It allows passage of whole cells.
med-histo-embryo.l08.q1.e: Sinusoidal capillaries have large gaps. Continuous capillaries are found in muscle and brain, and fenestrated in endocrine glands and intestine.

med-histo-embryo.l08.q2.t: Hassall corpuscles within a paler region
med-histo-embryo.l08.q2.p: Which feature best identifies the thymic medulla on a slide?
med-histo-embryo.l08.q2.e: Hassall corpuscles are in the medulla. The cortex is dense with thymocytes, and follicles and periarteriolar sheaths are features of nodes and spleen.

med-histo-embryo.l08.q3.t: The paracortex, where high endothelial venules admit lymphocytes from blood
med-histo-embryo.l08.q3.p: In which region of a lymph node do T cells chiefly reside?
med-histo-embryo.l08.q3.e: The paracortex is the T cell zone. Follicles hold B cells, and medullary cords hold plasma cells.

med-histo-embryo.l08.q4.t: Absent or hypoplastic thymic tissue, so thymocytes cannot mature into functioning T cells
med-histo-embryo.l08.q4.p: A 5-year-old with a 22q11 deletion has tetany from hypocalcaemia and recurrent viral and fungal infections. Which histologic finding would be expected in the thymus?
med-histo-embryo.l08.q4.e: DiGeorge syndrome involves failed development of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches, giving thymic hypoplasia and low T cells, as well as parathyroid hypoplasia. B cell defects produce a different pattern.

med-histo-embryo.l08.q5.t: Overwhelming infection with encapsulated bacteria such as Streptococcus pneumoniae, because red pulp macrophages no longer clear opsonised organisms
med-histo-embryo.l08.q5.p: A 19-year-old has a splenectomy after a motorcycle crash. Which long-term risk is explained by loss of a specific splenic function?
med-histo-embryo.l08.q5.h: Think about filtering and opsonised bacteria.
med-histo-embryo.l08.q5.e: The spleen filters blood and removes opsonised encapsulated bacteria, so asplenic patients need vaccination. Adult erythropoiesis occurs in the marrow, not the spleen.

med-histo-embryo.l09.q1.p: Which cell of the alveolar wall secretes pulmonary surfactant?
med-histo-embryo.l09.q1.h: It is cuboidal and also repairs the lining.
med-histo-embryo.l09.q1.e: Type II pneumocytes make surfactant in lamellar bodies. Type I pneumocytes are thin squamous cells that form the gas exchange surface.

med-histo-embryo.l09.q2.t: Absence of cartilage and glands, with club cells in the epithelium
med-histo-embryo.l09.q2.p: Which feature identifies a bronchiole as opposed to a bronchus on a slide?
med-histo-embryo.l09.q2.e: Bronchioles lack cartilage and glands and have club cells. Cartilage plates and glands mark bronchi, and C-shaped rings mark the trachea.

med-histo-embryo.l09.q3.t: The fused basal laminae of type I pneumocytes and capillary endothelium
med-histo-embryo.l09.q3.p: Which structure forms part of the blood-air barrier?
med-histo-embryo.l09.q3.e: The barrier is type I cell cytoplasm, the fused basal laminae and the capillary endothelium. Macrophages are not a continuous layer.

med-histo-embryo.l09.q4.t: Collapsed alveoli lined by eosinophilic hyaline membranes from too little surfactant
med-histo-embryo.l09.q4.p: A baby born at 28 weeks develops grunting and cyanosis within hours, and chest radiography shows a ground-glass pattern. Which histologic picture would be expected?
med-histo-embryo.l09.q4.e: Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome shows atelectasis and hyaline membranes because type II cells are immature. Neutrophil-filled alveoli describe lobar pneumonia, not this setting.

med-histo-embryo.l09.q5.t: Neuroendocrine (Kulchitsky) cells of the respiratory epithelium of the airway
med-histo-embryo.l09.q5.p: A 65-year-old long-term smoker has a central lung mass with ectopic ACTH secretion. Biopsy shows small blue cells with scant cytoplasm and neuroendocrine granules. Which normal tracheobronchial cell is the likely origin?
med-histo-embryo.l09.q5.e: Small cell carcinoma is thought to arise from neuroendocrine cells. Type II pneumocytes are more closely linked to adenocarcinoma.

med-histo-embryo.l10.q1.p: Which gastric cell secretes hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor?
med-histo-embryo.l10.q1.e: Parietal cells make HCl and intrinsic factor. Chief cells make pepsinogen and G cells make gastrin.

med-histo-embryo.l10.q2.t: Paneth cell, with eosinophilic apical granules
med-histo-embryo.l10.q2.p: Which small intestinal cell, found at the base of the crypts, secretes lysozyme and defensins?
med-histo-embryo.l10.q2.e: Paneth cells have antimicrobial granules and sit at the crypt base. M cells sample antigen over Peyer patches.

med-histo-embryo.l10.q3.t: Between the circular and longitudinal muscle layers of the muscularis externa
med-histo-embryo.l10.q3.p: Which layer contains the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus?
med-histo-embryo.l10.q3.e: The myenteric plexus lies between the two muscle layers. The submucosal plexus lies in the submucosa.

med-histo-embryo.l10.q4.t: Absorption through the reduced surface area provided by villi and microvilli
med-histo-embryo.l10.q4.p: A 28-year-old has chronic diarrhoea, weight loss and iron deficiency. Duodenal biopsy shows blunted villi, elongated crypts and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes. Which function is primarily lost?
med-histo-embryo.l10.q4.e: Coeliac disease flattens villi and so reduces absorptive area, causing malabsorption. Brunner glands and parietal cells are not the primary lesion.

med-histo-embryo.l10.q5.t: Loss of intrinsic factor so vitamin B12 cannot be absorbed in the terminal ileum
med-histo-embryo.l10.q5.p: A 55-year-old woman has fatigue, glossitis and paraesthesias with a macrocytic anaemia. Gastric biopsy shows atrophy of body glands with loss of parietal cells. Which mechanism explains the anaemia?
med-histo-embryo.l10.q5.h: Which vitamin needs a gastric binding protein?
med-histo-embryo.l10.q5.e: Intrinsic factor from parietal cells is required for B12 uptake at the terminal ileum. Without it, megaloblastic anaemia and neurologic signs follow.

med-histo-embryo.l11.q1.p: Which cells of the liver sinusoid store vitamin A and become collagen-producing in cirrhosis?
med-histo-embryo.l11.q1.h: They live in the space of Disse.
med-histo-embryo.l11.q1.e: Stellate cells store vitamin A and become myofibroblasts in fibrosis. Kupffer cells are the sinusoidal macrophages.

med-histo-embryo.l11.q2.t: A hepatic artery branch, a portal vein branch and a bile duct
med-histo-embryo.l11.q2.p: What is contained in each portal triad of the liver?
med-histo-embryo.l11.q2.h: Three vessels that bring in blood and carry bile out.
med-histo-embryo.l11.q2.e: The triad has artery, portal vein and bile duct. The central vein is at the centre of the lobule, not in the triad.

med-histo-embryo.l11.q3.p: Which hormone from duodenal I cells causes gallbladder contraction and pancreatic enzyme secretion?
med-histo-embryo.l11.q3.e: Cholecystokinin contracts the gallbladder and stimulates acinar enzyme release. Secretin stimulates ductal bicarbonate.

med-histo-embryo.l11.q4.t: Centrilobular necrosis in zone 3, because that region has most cytochrome P450 and least oxygen
med-histo-embryo.l11.q4.p: A 30-year-old takes an overdose of acetaminophen and develops liver failure. Which pattern of necrosis is expected, and why?
med-histo-embryo.l11.q4.e: Zone 3 hepatocytes near the central vein have the highest cytochrome P450 activity, producing toxic metabolites, and the lowest oxygen. Periportal damage suggests other toxins such as phosphorus.

med-histo-embryo.l11.q5.t: Trypsinogen, which is activated within the gland and activates other zymogens and causes autodigestion
med-histo-embryo.l11.q5.p: A 60-year-old with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back has markedly elevated serum lipase after heavy alcohol use. Premature activation of which acinar product is central to the pathology?
med-histo-embryo.l11.q5.h: A zymogen turning on in the wrong place.
med-histo-embryo.l11.q5.e: Acute pancreatitis involves intra-acinar trypsinogen activation, causing autodigestion. Insulin and secretin do not digest tissue.

med-histo-embryo.l12.q1.p: Which cells of the glomerulus form the slit diaphragm with nephrin?
med-histo-embryo.l12.q1.e: Podocyte pedicels are bridged by slit diaphragms containing nephrin. Mesangial cells provide support and clear debris.

med-histo-embryo.l12.q2.p: Which nephron segment has a dense brush border and bright pink cytoplasm and reabsorbs about two thirds of filtrate?
med-histo-embryo.l12.q2.e: The proximal tubule has the brush border and high mitochondrial content. The distal tubule has no brush border.

med-histo-embryo.l12.q3.t: Modified smooth muscle cells in the afferent arteriole
med-histo-embryo.l12.q3.p: Which cells of the juxtaglomerular apparatus secrete renin?
med-histo-embryo.l12.q3.e: Juxtaglomerular cells in the afferent arteriole release renin. The macula densa senses sodium chloride and signals them.

med-histo-embryo.l12.q4.t: Diffuse effacement of podocyte foot processes, with usually good response to corticosteroids
med-histo-embryo.l12.q4.p: A 6-year-old has periorbital oedema and heavy proteinuria with a normal light microscopic biopsy. Which electron microscopic finding is expected, and what is the likely response to treatment?
med-histo-embryo.l12.q4.e: Minimal change disease shows effaced foot processes on electron microscopy and responds to steroids. Subepithelial humps describe post-infectious glomerulonephritis.

med-histo-embryo.l12.q5.t: Juxtaglomerular cells release renin, which leads to angiotensin II and aldosterone effects
med-histo-embryo.l12.q5.p: A 70-year-old has severe hypotension from haemorrhage. Which sequence best describes the juxtaglomerular response that protects glomerular filtration?
med-histo-embryo.l12.q5.h: Low perfusion triggers the renin cascade.
med-histo-embryo.l12.q5.e: Reduced afferent pressure and low distal chloride trigger renin release and the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. Erythropoietin comes from peritubular interstitial cells and acts over days.

med-histo-embryo.l13.q1.e: The zona glomerulosa secretes mineralocorticoids. The fasciculata makes cortisol and the reticularis makes androgens.

med-histo-embryo.l13.q2.t: Posterior lobe, derived from neuroectoderm of the forebrain
med-histo-embryo.l13.q2.p: Which pituitary lobe derives from a downgrowth of the diencephalon and stores oxytocin and ADH?
med-histo-embryo.l13.q2.e: The neurohypophysis is neural in origin and holds axon terminals of hypothalamic neurons. The anterior lobe derives from Rathke pouch.

med-histo-embryo.l13.q3.t: Parafollicular C cells between the follicles
med-histo-embryo.l13.q3.p: Which thyroid cell type secretes calcitonin?
med-histo-embryo.l13.q3.e: C cells secrete calcitonin and give rise to medullary carcinoma. Follicular cells make thyroid hormone.

med-histo-embryo.l13.q4.t: Chromaffin cells of the medulla, which are derived from the neural crest
med-histo-embryo.l13.q4.p: A 35-year-old has episodic headaches, palpitations and sweating with sustained hypertension. A 4-cm adrenal mass shows nests of cells with granular cytoplasm. Which normal cell is the mass derived from, and what is its embryonic origin?
med-histo-embryo.l13.q4.e: Pheochromocytoma arises from chromaffin cells, modified sympathetic neurons of neural crest origin. Cortical tumours would be mesodermal.

med-histo-embryo.l13.q5.t: Parafollicular cells, which are neuroendocrine cells of neural crest origin
med-histo-embryo.l13.q5.p: A 28-year-old woman with a neck mass has a thyroid biopsy that shows sheets of cells staining positive for calcitonin with amyloid deposits in the stroma. Which cell of origin is most likely?
med-histo-embryo.l13.q5.h: Which cell makes the stained hormone?
med-histo-embryo.l13.q5.e: Calcitonin-positive tumour with amyloid is medullary thyroid carcinoma, from C cells. Follicular tumours stain for thyroglobulin.

med-histo-embryo.l14.q1.p: Which testicular cell makes testosterone under LH stimulation?
med-histo-embryo.l14.q1.e: Leydig cells are the interstitial testosterone producers. Sertoli cells support germ cells and form the blood-testis barrier.

med-histo-embryo.l14.q2.t: Sertoli cells with tight junctions between them
med-histo-embryo.l14.q2.p: Which cells of the testis form the blood-testis barrier?
med-histo-embryo.l14.q2.e: Sertoli cell tight junctions separate basal and adluminal compartments. Leydig cells lie outside the tubules.

med-histo-embryo.l14.q3.t: A round spermatid transforms into a spermatozoon without further cell division
med-histo-embryo.l14.q3.h: It is a remodelling, not a division.
med-histo-embryo.l14.q3.e: Spermiogenesis is the differentiation of spermatids into sperm with acrosome formation and flagellar growth. The divisions occur earlier.

med-histo-embryo.l14.q4.t: Impaired spermatogenesis and an increased risk of germ cell tumour
med-histo-embryo.l14.q4.p: A 1-year-old boy has an empty right scrotum and a non-palpable testis on that side. If uncorrected, which long-term risks are most characteristic?
med-histo-embryo.l14.q4.e: Cryptorchidism causes impaired spermatogenesis because of the higher temperature and raises germ cell tumour risk. Orchiopexy is usually done in infancy.

med-histo-embryo.l14.q5.t: Transition zone, which surrounds the urethra, while carcinoma usually arises peripherally
med-histo-embryo.l14.q5.p: A 68-year-old man has urinary hesitancy and a smooth, symmetric, enlarged prostate on rectal examination. Which zone is primarily involved, and why is it different from where most carcinoma arises?
med-histo-embryo.l14.q5.e: Benign hyperplasia involves the transition zone around the urethra and so obstructs flow, whereas carcinoma usually arises in the peripheral zone palpable on rectal examination.

med-histo-embryo.l15.q1.p: Which ovarian cells make androgens under LH that granulosa cells convert to oestrogen?
med-histo-embryo.l15.q1.e: Theca interna cells produce androgens under LH, and granulosa cells aromatise them under FSH.

med-histo-embryo.l15.q2.p: At the time of ovulation, the oocyte is arrested in which stage?
med-histo-embryo.l15.q2.h: It finishes meiosis II only on fertilisation.
med-histo-embryo.l15.q2.e: The secondary oocyte arrests in metaphase of meiosis II at ovulation. The primary oocyte is arrested in prophase I until the LH surge.

med-histo-embryo.l15.q3.t: Tortuous sawtooth glands with secretions under the influence of progesterone
med-histo-embryo.l15.q3.p: Which endometrial feature marks the secretory phase of the cycle?
med-histo-embryo.l15.q3.e: Progesterone from the corpus luteum produces coiled, secretory glands. Straight glands are the proliferative phase.

med-histo-embryo.l15.q4.t: The ampulla is the usual site of fertilisation, and impaired ciliary transport leaves the embryo there
med-histo-embryo.l15.q4.p: A 27-year-old has sudden lower abdominal pain, a positive pregnancy test and a mass in the adnexa with no intrauterine gestational sac. Which feature explains the usual site of this problem?
med-histo-embryo.l15.q4.e: Fertilisation normally occurs in the ampulla, and scarring or impaired ciliary function can lead to implantation there. The infundibulum has no endometrium.

med-histo-embryo.l15.q5.t: The endocervical columnar epithelium meets ectocervical squamous epithelium, where metaplastic cells are exposed to human papillomavirus
med-histo-embryo.l15.q5.p: A 32-year-old has an abnormal Pap smear. Colposcopy shows an acetowhite lesion at the cervical transformation zone. Which histologic fact best explains why this region is vulnerable?
med-histo-embryo.l15.q5.e: The squamocolumnar junction undergoes squamous metaplasia, and high-risk HPV infects these cells. The ectocervix is stratified squamous, not columnar.

med-histo-embryo.l16.q1.p: Which epidermal layer contains keratohyalin granules?
med-histo-embryo.l16.q1.h: Its name hints at its appearance.
med-histo-embryo.l16.q1.e: The stratum granulosum has keratohyalin granules and lamellar bodies. The basale holds the stem cells.

med-histo-embryo.l16.q2.p: Which epidermal cell type presents antigen and contains Birbeck granules?
med-histo-embryo.l16.q2.e: Langerhans cells are dendritic antigen-presenting cells with Birbeck granules. Merkel cells are touch receptors.

med-histo-embryo.l16.q3.t: The amount and type of melanin produced by the melanocytes, not their number
med-histo-embryo.l16.q3.p: Which cell type determines most of the difference in skin colour between individuals?
med-histo-embryo.l16.q3.e: Melanocyte number is similar across people; melanin amount, type and melanosome packaging differ.

med-histo-embryo.l16.q4.t: Desmosomes in the stratum spinosum, which causes intraepidermal blisters
med-histo-embryo.l16.q4.p: A 55-year-old has flaccid, easily ruptured blisters in the mouth and skin. Immunofluorescence shows a net-like pattern of IgG between keratinocytes. Which structure is attacked?
med-histo-embryo.l16.q4.e: Pemphigus vulgaris targets desmoglein in desmosomes, causing intraepidermal acantholysis. Pemphigoid targets hemidesmosomes with subepidermal blisters.

med-histo-embryo.l16.q5.t: Retained hair follicles and sweat gland ducts supply epithelial cells that re-epithelialise the wound
med-histo-embryo.l16.q5.p: A child suffers a superficial partial-thickness scald that spares the deep dermis. Which statement best explains why it will likely heal without grafting?
med-histo-embryo.l16.q5.e: Epidermal appendages preserve keratinocyte stem cells so the wound resurfaces. Fibroblasts and fat cannot form epidermis.
