med-histo-embryo.l17.q1.p: At which stage is a primary oocyte arrested from foetal life until just before ovulation?
med-histo-embryo.l17.q1.e: Primary oocytes are arrested in prophase of meiosis I until the LH surge. The secondary oocyte arrests at metaphase II.

med-histo-embryo.l17.q2.t: The cortical reaction, which modifies the zona pellucida so it blocks further sperm
med-histo-embryo.l17.q2.p: Which event prevents polyspermy after the first sperm fuses with the oocyte?
med-histo-embryo.l17.q2.e: Cortical granule enzymes alter zona proteins so other sperm cannot bind. The acrosome reaction helps the first sperm enter.

med-histo-embryo.l17.q3.t: The inner cell mass, also called the embryoblast
med-histo-embryo.l17.q3.p: Which structure of the blastocyst gives rise to the embryo proper?
med-histo-embryo.l17.q3.e: The embryoblast makes the embryo. The trophoblast makes the placenta.

med-histo-embryo.l17.q4.t: Nondisjunction in maternal meiosis I after prolonged arrest of the oocyte in prophase
med-histo-embryo.l17.q4.p: A 41-year-old woman has a pregnancy with trisomy 21 confirmed by karyotype. Studies show the extra chromosome is of maternal origin. Which error is the most common cause?
med-histo-embryo.l17.q4.h: Think of how long oocytes wait.
med-histo-embryo.l17.q4.e: Most trisomy 21 arises from maternal meiosis I nondisjunction, and risk rises with age. Translocation is a minority cause and does not depend on maternal age.

med-histo-embryo.l17.q5.t: Transport to and penetration of the zona pellucida, because sperm cannot swim to the oocyte
med-histo-embryo.l17.q5.p: A couple has infertility. The man has sperm with absent dynein arms and immotile flagella, and normal sperm count. Which step of fertilisation is most directly prevented?
med-histo-embryo.l17.q5.e: Immotile sperm cannot reach or penetrate the oocyte; intracytoplasmic sperm injection bypasses this. The later events occur only after penetration.

med-histo-embryo.l18.q1.p: Which hormone from the syncytiotrophoblast maintains the corpus luteum in early pregnancy?
med-histo-embryo.l18.q1.h: The basis of urine pregnancy tests.
med-histo-embryo.l18.q1.e: hCG acts like LH to sustain the corpus luteum. FSH is a pituitary hormone.

med-histo-embryo.l18.q2.p: During gastrulation, which structure induces the overlying ectoderm to become neural plate?
med-histo-embryo.l18.q2.h: It persists later as the nucleus pulposus.
med-histo-embryo.l18.q2.e: The notochord induces neural plate formation. The streak is the site of ingression, not the inducer.

med-histo-embryo.l18.q3.t: The epiblast, whose cells move through the primitive streak
med-histo-embryo.l18.q3.p: Which layer is the source of the definitive germ layers in gastrulation?
med-histo-embryo.l18.q3.h: All three come from one layer.
med-histo-embryo.l18.q3.e: The epiblast gives rise to all three germ layers; hypoblast cells are displaced by definitive endoderm.

med-histo-embryo.l18.q4.t: Persistent remnants of the primitive streak whose pluripotent cells form all three germ layers
med-histo-embryo.l18.q4.p: A newborn has a large mass at the base of the spine containing hair, cartilage and glandular tissue. Which embryologic origin best explains this finding?
med-histo-embryo.l18.q4.e: Sacrococcygeal teratoma arises from primitive streak remnants and contains multiple germ layers. Failure of caudal neuropore closure causes spina bifida, with no such tissue.

med-histo-embryo.l18.q5.t: Closure of the neural tube at the caudal neuropore; folate supplementation before conception
med-histo-embryo.l18.q5.p: A pregnant woman has a mid-trimester screen with high maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein and a follow-up scan showing a lumbosacral defect. Which developmental event failed, and which measure reduces risk?
med-histo-embryo.l18.q5.e: Open neural tube defects raise alpha-fetoprotein, and periconceptional folic acid reduces risk. High-dose vitamin A is itself teratogenic.

med-histo-embryo.l19.q1.p: Which structure is derived from neural crest?
med-histo-embryo.l19.q1.e: Melanocytes derive from neural crest. The lens and anterior pituitary are surface ectoderm and the liver is endoderm.

med-histo-embryo.l19.q2.t: The lining of the thymus and parathyroids
med-histo-embryo.l19.q2.p: Which structure is of endodermal origin?
med-histo-embryo.l19.q2.e: The pharyngeal pouches give thymus and parathyroid epithelium from endoderm. The adrenal cortex is mesodermal and the medulla is neural crest.

med-histo-embryo.l19.q3.p: Which tissue arises from intermediate mesoderm?
med-histo-embryo.l19.q3.e: Intermediate mesoderm forms kidneys and gonads. Heart and vessels are lateral plate and the vertebrae paraxial.

med-histo-embryo.l19.q4.t: Failure of closure of the body wall by lateral folding, giving exposed bowel without a sac
med-histo-embryo.l19.q4.p: A newborn has abdominal contents herniated through a defect lateral to the umbilicus, with no covering membrane. Which developmental failure is most likely?
med-histo-embryo.l19.q4.h: No sac suggests a wall defect.
med-histo-embryo.l19.q4.e: Gastroschisis is a body wall defect from abnormal lateral folding with no sac. Omphalocele is covered by a membrane and occurs in the midline at the umbilicus.

med-histo-embryo.l19.q5.t: The enteric ganglia arise from neural crest cells that migrate caudally along the gut
med-histo-embryo.l19.q5.p: A newborn has not passed meconium for 48 hours, and has a distended abdomen. Rectal biopsy shows no ganglion cells in the submucosa and myenteric layer. Which statement about embryology is correct?
med-histo-embryo.l19.q5.e: Enteric ganglion cells derive from neural crest, and Hirschsprung disease is arrested caudal migration, often involving the RET gene. The smooth muscle is mesodermal, but the ganglia are not.

med-histo-embryo.l20.q1.p: Which foetal structure carries well-oxygenated blood from the placenta to the foetus?
med-histo-embryo.l20.q1.h: Venous in name but oxygenated here.
med-histo-embryo.l20.q1.e: The umbilical vein carries oxygenated blood to the foetus. The umbilical arteries carry deoxygenated blood back to the placenta.

med-histo-embryo.l20.q2.p: The aorticopulmonary septum is formed by which cells?
med-histo-embryo.l20.q2.h: The same population that forms many conotruncal structures.
med-histo-embryo.l20.q2.e: Neural crest cells form the spiral septum, and defects in their migration cause conotruncal anomalies.

med-histo-embryo.l20.q3.p: Which adult structure is the remnant of the foetal ductus arteriosus?
med-histo-embryo.l20.q3.h: It connects the pulmonary trunk and aortic arch.
med-histo-embryo.l20.q3.e: The ductus arteriosus becomes the ligamentum arteriosum. The umbilical vein becomes the ligamentum teres.

med-histo-embryo.l20.q4.t: Prostaglandin E1 to maintain ductal patency so mixing of the two circulations can occur
med-histo-embryo.l20.q4.p: A newborn has cyanosis not relieved by oxygen and a narrow mediastinum with an egg-shaped heart. Which intervention keeps the baby alive until definitive surgery?
med-histo-embryo.l20.q4.e: In transposition the circulations run in parallel, so survival depends on shunts such as the ductus, which prostaglandin E1 keeps open. Indomethacin would close it and worsen cyanosis.

med-histo-embryo.l20.q5.t: Abnormal neural crest migration that causes anterior displacement of the aorticopulmonary septum
med-histo-embryo.l20.q5.p: A 4-month-old with a 22q11 deletion has cyanotic spells. Echocardiography shows pulmonary stenosis, overriding aorta, a ventricular septal defect and right ventricular hypertrophy. Which developmental error is most likely?
med-histo-embryo.l20.q5.e: Tetralogy of Fallot results from anterior and cephalad displacement of the spiral septum, linked to neural crest abnormalities and 22q11 deletion. Atrial defects are a different problem.

med-histo-embryo.l21.q1.p: Which cranial nerve supplies derivatives of the first pharyngeal arch?
med-histo-embryo.l21.q1.e: Arch 1 is supplied by the trigeminal nerve. The facial nerve supplies arch 2.

med-histo-embryo.l21.q2.p: Which pouch gives rise to the inferior parathyroid glands and the thymus?
med-histo-embryo.l21.q2.h: Inferior comes from the more rostral pouch of the pair.
med-histo-embryo.l21.q2.e: Pouch 3 gives the inferior parathyroids and thymus; pouch 4 gives the superior parathyroids.

med-histo-embryo.l21.q3.p: Which signalling centre in the limb bud specifies the anterior-posterior axis with sonic hedgehog?
med-histo-embryo.l21.q3.e: The zone of polarising activity secretes sonic hedgehog. The apical ectodermal ridge secretes FGFs for proximal-distal outgrowth.

med-histo-embryo.l21.q4.t: Persistence of a pharyngeal cleft that was not obliterated by the overgrowth of the second arch
med-histo-embryo.l21.q4.p: A newborn has a lateral neck cyst along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid. Which developmental failure explains this?
med-histo-embryo.l21.q4.e: A branchial cleft cyst arises from persisting cervical sinus remnants of the clefts, along the anterior sternocleidomastoid. Thyroglossal cysts lie in the midline and move with swallowing.

med-histo-embryo.l21.q5.t: The palatine shelves of the maxillary prominences failed to rise and fuse in the midline
med-histo-embryo.l21.q5.p: A newborn has a cleft of the secondary palate only, and a normal lip and philtrum. Which statement correctly describes the underlying failure?
med-histo-embryo.l21.q5.h: The lip and the secondary palate are separate processes.
med-histo-embryo.l21.q5.e: The secondary palate forms by fusion of palatine shelves, which is distinct from fusion of the prominences that forms the lip and primary palate.

med-histo-embryo.l22.q1.p: Which period is the time of greatest susceptibility to structural malformation?
med-histo-embryo.l22.q1.e: The embryonic period of organogenesis is the most vulnerable for structural defects.

med-histo-embryo.l22.q2.p: Which drug exposure in the second and third trimesters is linked to foetal renal failure and oligohydramnios?
med-histo-embryo.l22.q2.e: ACE inhibitors and ARBs impair the foetal renin-angiotensin system and reduce renal perfusion. Tetracyclines stain teeth.

med-histo-embryo.l22.q3.p: A structural defect resulting from abnormal mechanical forces on an originally normal tissue, such as clubfoot with oligohydramnios, is called what?
med-histo-embryo.l22.q3.e: A deformation arises from mechanical forces on normal tissue. A malformation is a primary defect of morphogenesis.

med-histo-embryo.l22.q4.t: Alcohol consumed during pregnancy, causing a foetal alcohol spectrum disorder
med-histo-embryo.l22.q4.p: A newborn has microcephaly, a smooth philtrum, thin upper lip, short palpebral fissures and a small ventricular septal defect. Which maternal exposure is most likely?
med-histo-embryo.l22.q4.e: Smooth philtrum, thin upper lip and short palpebral fissures typify foetal alcohol syndrome. Retinoid embryopathy has ear and thymic anomalies.

med-histo-embryo.l22.q5.t: Rubella, which causes a classic triad of ocular, auditory and cardiac anomalies
med-histo-embryo.l22.q5.p: A newborn has cataracts, sensorineural deafness and a continuous machine-like murmur from a patent ductus arteriosus. Which maternal infection in early pregnancy is most likely?
med-histo-embryo.l22.q5.e: Congenital rubella causes cataracts, deafness and patent ductus arteriosus. Cytomegalovirus gives periventricular calcification, and toxoplasmosis gives diffuse calcification.

med-histo-embryo.l23.q1.p: How many arteries and veins are in a normal umbilical cord?
med-histo-embryo.l23.q1.h: The artery carries blood away from the foetus.
med-histo-embryo.l23.q1.e: The normal cord has two arteries and one vein in Wharton jelly.

med-histo-embryo.l23.q2.p: Which condition is associated with polyhydramnios?
med-histo-embryo.l23.q2.e: Oesophageal atresia prevents swallowing of fluid and causes polyhydramnios. Renal agenesis causes oligohydramnios.

med-histo-embryo.l23.q3.p: Which maternal immunoglobulin class crosses the placenta to give the newborn passive immunity?
med-histo-embryo.l23.q3.e: Maternal IgG is actively transported across the placenta. IgM is too large.

med-histo-embryo.l23.q4.t: Placenta accreta arises where the decidua basalis is deficient, as over a uterine scar, so villi invade the myometrium
med-histo-embryo.l23.q4.p: A 33-year-old at 34 weeks with a prior caesarean has painless vaginal bleeding. Ultrasound shows the placenta covering the internal os. Which statement best explains the risk of adherent placenta at delivery?
med-histo-embryo.l23.q4.h: Think about what normally limits trophoblast invasion.
med-histo-embryo.l23.q4.e: The decidua basalis normally restrains trophoblast invasion, and a deficient decidua over a scar permits accreta. The other options describe unrelated structures.

med-histo-embryo.l23.q5.t: Between days 4 and 8, with a risk of twin-to-twin transfusion owing to shared vessels
med-histo-embryo.l23.q5.p: Ultrasound of a twin pregnancy shows one placenta, a thin membrane between the twins and two amniotic sacs. At which time did the embryo most likely divide, and which complication is most characteristic?
med-histo-embryo.l23.q5.e: Division between days 4 and 8 gives monochorionic diamniotic twins who share placental vessels and risk transfusion syndrome. Monoamniotic twins divide later.

med-history.l01.q1.t: surgical cases, mainly injuries, with examination, diagnosis and prognosis
med-history.l01.q1.p: The Edwin Smith Papyrus is best known as an ancient Egyptian text on:
med-history.l01.q1.h: Think of cases in a consistent format.
med-history.l01.q1.e: The Smith Papyrus is a trauma and surgical text. The other topics belong to different kinds of document.

med-history.l01.q2.t: an exorcist who sought a supernatural cause of an illness and used ritual
med-history.l01.q2.p: In Mesopotamian medicine, the ashipu was most like which kind of healer?
med-history.l01.q2.e: The ashipu used ritual and sought supernatural causes, while the asu worked with drugs and bandages.

med-history.l01.q3.t: The texts show careful case classification and prognosis alongside ritual
med-history.l01.q3.p: Why do historians caution against calling ancient Egyptian and Mesopotamian medicine purely superstitious?
med-history.l01.q3.e: Surviving texts combine empirical observation with ritual. Microscopes and germ theory came much later.

med-history.l01.q4.t: an early practice of prognosis that distinguished curable from incurable cases
med-history.l01.q4.p: A papyrus case concludes that the physician should not treat a severe skull injury, even though it describes the wound carefully. A historian would most reasonably interpret this as evidence of:
med-history.l01.q4.h: The text sorts cases by outcome.
med-history.l01.q4.e: The verdict format shows prognostic reasoning, which later became central in Greek medicine. The other readings are not supported by the text.

med-history.l01.q5.t: Medical practice and its outcomes were already subject to law and social expectations
med-history.l01.q5.p: The Code of Hammurabi sets fees and penalties for surgeons. What does this most clearly show about medicine in ancient Mesopotamia?
med-history.l01.q5.h: Fees and penalties are legal matters.
med-history.l01.q5.e: Fee schedules and penalties show that medical outcomes had legal consequences. They do not show that surgery was forbidden.

med-history.l02.q1.t: Blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile
med-history.l02.q1.p: What were the four humors in humoral theory?
med-history.l02.q1.e: The humors were fluids. Heat, cold, dryness and moisture are the qualities associated with them, and the elements are separate.

med-history.l02.q2.t: He dissected mainly animals and applied the findings to humans
med-history.l02.q2.p: Why did Galen's anatomy contain errors about the human body?
med-history.l02.q2.h: Think about whose bodies he cut open.
med-history.l02.q2.e: Galen's dissections were largely of animals such as pigs and monkeys, so some descriptions did not match human anatomy.

med-history.l02.q3.t: has natural causes in the body and is no more divine than other diseases
med-history.l02.q3.p: The Hippocratic work on the sacred disease argues that epilepsy:
med-history.l02.q3.h: This text is a landmark in naturalistic explanation.
med-history.l02.q3.e: The treatise argues for natural causes. This is a key example of the Greek move from supernatural to natural explanation.

med-history.l02.q4.t: Galen described the rete mirabile seen in animals and assumed humans had it too
med-history.l02.q4.p: A medieval scholar finds that his Galenic textbook describes a structure in the human brain that he cannot locate in any human body. Which explanation best fits the history of Galen's sources?
med-history.l02.q4.h: Consider the source of Galen's observations.
med-history.l02.q4.e: The rete mirabile is found in some animals and not in humans, an example of animal anatomy applied to humans.

med-history.l02.q5.t: A powerful system can become an obstacle to progress when it is treated as final
med-history.l02.q5.p: What does the history of Galen's authority best illustrate?
med-history.l02.q5.h: Think of more than a thousand years.
med-history.l02.q5.e: Galen's system was brilliant but was held as unquestionable for centuries. It was not entirely wrong or useless.

med-history.l03.q1.t: a clinical treatise distinguishing smallpox from measles
med-history.l03.q1.e: Al-Razi's treatise on smallpox and measles is a landmark in clinical description. The other achievements belong to later periods.

med-history.l03.q2.t: A hospital in the medieval Islamic world, often supported by charitable endowment
med-history.l03.q2.h: The Persian word means place of the sick.
med-history.l03.q2.e: Bimaristans were hospitals with wards, physicians, pharmacies and teaching, funded in part by waqf endowments.

med-history.l03.q3.t: organized medical knowledge systematically and was used in European universities for centuries
med-history.l03.q3.p: The Canon of Medicine by Ibn Sina (Avicenna) is important because it:
med-history.l03.q3.h: Think of its long use as a textbook.
med-history.l03.q3.e: The Canon was a comprehensive and systematic work widely used in Europe. It did not prove Galen right on everything or introduce germ theory.

med-history.l03.q4.t: That blood passes through invisible pores in the septum between the ventricles
med-history.l03.q4.p: Ibn al-Nafis wrote in the thirteenth century that blood passes from the right heart to the lungs and then to the left heart. Which Galenic view did this contradict?
med-history.l03.q4.h: The route of blood through the heart.
med-history.l03.q4.e: Ibn al-Nafis rejected Galen's pores in the septum and described pulmonary transit. The other ideas were not what he addressed.

med-history.l03.q5.t: It was a creative stage in a long chain that combined Greek, Indian, Persian and Arabic ideas
med-history.l03.q5.p: A popular article claims the Islamic Golden Age invented modern science from nothing. Which response best reflects the historians' view in the lesson?
med-history.l03.q5.h: Neither pure invention nor mere copying.
med-history.l03.q5.e: Scholars preserved, criticized and extended earlier work. Claims of pure invention or of mere copying both distort the record.

med-history.l04.q1.t: The Italian for forty, from the forty days that ships were held in Venice
med-history.l04.q1.p: What does the word quarantine come from?
med-history.l04.q1.e: Quarantine comes from the Italian for forty. Ragusa used thirty days in 1377 and Venice later used forty.

med-history.l04.q2.t: was based on direct human dissection and corrected many of Galen's errors
med-history.l04.q2.p: Vesalius's De humani corporis fabrica (1543) was important because it:
med-history.l04.q2.e: Vesalius used human dissection and corrected Galen. The circulation was described later by Harvey.

med-history.l04.q3.t: ligatures to tie blood vessels instead of boiling oil or cautery
med-history.l04.q3.p: Ambroise Paré changed battlefield surgery by using:
med-history.l04.q3.h: Sixteenth century, and a way to stop bleeding.
med-history.l04.q3.e: Paré used ligatures. Chloroform, carbolic acid and gloves belong to the nineteenth century.

med-history.l04.q4.t: As an effective practical measure that worked without any knowledge of germs
med-history.l04.q4.p: A fourteenth-century city council, believing plague spreads from travelers, requires arrivals from infected ports to wait outside the walls for a fixed period. How should a historian assess this policy?
med-history.l04.q4.e: Isolation could slow spread even though the cause was unknown. Ragusa and Venice adopted such rules in the fourteenth century.

med-history.l04.q5.p: Modern studies of ancient DNA from plague victims have identified which cause of the Black Death?
med-history.l04.q5.h: A bacterium carried by fleas on rodents.
med-history.l04.q5.e: Ancient DNA evidence points to Yersinia pestis. Measles, cholera and ergot fungus are different diseases.

med-history.l05.q1.t: The heart pumps blood in a circuit around the body, since the volume pumped is too large to be newly made
med-history.l05.q1.p: What was Harvey's main argument in De Motu Cordis (1628)?
med-history.l05.q1.e: Harvey argued from the amount of blood pumped that blood must circulate. The other views are the Galenic ideas that he overturned.

med-history.l05.q2.t: pathological anatomy, linking symptoms in life to organ findings at autopsy
med-history.l05.q2.p: Morgagni's De Sedibus et Causis Morborum (1761) helped found:
med-history.l05.q2.e: Morgagni correlated clinical histories with autopsy findings. Germ theory and sanitation came later.

med-history.l05.q3.t: Capillaries connecting arteries and veins in the lung of a frog
med-history.l05.q3.p: What did Marcello Malpighi observe in 1661 that supported Harvey's theory?
med-history.l05.q3.h: Harvey could not see the link between small vessels.
med-history.l05.q3.e: Malpighi saw capillaries with a microscope. Leeuwenhoek described bacteria, and Harvey demonstrated venous valves.

med-history.l05.q4.t: It compared treatments in similar patients at the same time, an early form of controlled comparison
med-history.l05.q4.p: In Lind's 1747 comparison, sailors with scurvy were divided into pairs and each pair received a different remedy. Why is this considered an important step even though the Navy was slow to act on the result?
med-history.l05.q4.h: Think about the design, not the size.
med-history.l05.q4.e: Lind compared remedies in similar patients under the same conditions. The trial was small and unblinded, and vitamin C was identified later.

med-history.l05.q5.h: A French physician listening to the chest.
med-history.l05.q5.e: Laennec invented the stethoscope. The others made contributions in microscopy, bedside medicine and pathology.

med-history.l06.q1.t: cholera spread through contaminated water from the Broad Street pump
med-history.l06.q1.p: John Snow's 1854 investigation of cholera in Soho concluded that:
med-history.l06.q1.e: Snow traced cases to a water pump. Koch identified the cholera bacterium later, and the chlorinated lime was Semmelweis's method.

med-history.l06.q2.t: handwashing with a chlorinated lime solution before examining patients
med-history.l06.q2.p: Semmelweis reduced deaths from puerperal fever in Vienna in 1847 by requiring:
med-history.l06.q2.h: Doctors carried something from the autopsy room.
med-history.l06.q2.e: Semmelweis introduced handwashing with chlorinated lime. Carbolic acid was Lister's method, and penicillin had not yet been discovered.

med-history.l06.q3.t: Criteria for linking a specific microbe to a disease, with recognized limits such as carriers
med-history.l06.q3.p: Which is the best statement of Koch's postulates?
med-history.l06.q3.h: They were about proving a cause.
med-history.l06.q3.e: The postulates are criteria for establishing that a microbe causes a disease. They have limits because some microbes cannot be cultured and carriers exist.

med-history.l06.q4.t: He had strong data showing that handwashing cut deaths but offered no mechanism, and the idea implicated doctors
med-history.l06.q4.p: A historian argues that Semmelweis was rejected not simply because he was wrong. Which evidence best supports this view?
med-history.l06.q4.h: Data without explanation and a threat to professional identity.
med-history.l06.q4.e: Semmelweis had compelling data but no germ theory, and his proposal implied that physicians caused deaths. The other claims are not supported.

med-history.l06.q5.t: It moved from antisepsis, killing germs on contact, to asepsis, keeping germs out with sterilization
med-history.l06.q5.p: Lister used carbolic acid on wounds and instruments in 1867. How did surgery later change from his approach?
med-history.l06.q5.e: Surgeons moved from chemical antisepsis toward sterile technique. Penicillin came decades later and did not replace sterile technique.

med-history.l07.q1.t: Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston, in 1846
med-history.l07.q1.p: Where and when was the public demonstration of ether anesthesia that changed surgical practice?
med-history.l07.q1.h: William Morton and John Collins Warren.
med-history.l07.q1.e: The famous demonstration was at Massachusetts General in October 1846. Simpson's chloroform came in Edinburgh in 1847, and Long's earlier use was not published at the time.

med-history.l07.q2.t: studying doses and inhalers to make the giving of anesthetics safer
med-history.l07.q2.p: John Snow is also remembered in the history of anesthesia for:
med-history.l07.q2.h: He gave chloroform to Queen Victoria.
med-history.l07.q2.e: Snow studied anesthetic dosing and delivery. Ether was not his invention, and gloves and carbolic acid belong to others.

med-history.l07.q3.t: Longer operations exposed more patients to infection before antisepsis and asepsis
med-history.l07.q3.p: Why did anesthesia not at first reduce surgical death rates?
med-history.l07.q3.h: Think about what longer, deeper operations allowed.
med-history.l07.q3.e: More extensive operations meant more infection, and the benefit came when anesthesia was combined with antisepsis and asepsis.

med-history.l07.q4.t: The recipient's immune system did not reject genetically identical tissue, since effective immunosuppression was not yet available
med-history.l07.q4.p: A 1950s surgeon describes the first successful kidney transplant, performed in 1954 between identical twins. Why was identical twinship important to that success?
med-history.l07.q4.e: Genetically identical tissue avoids immune rejection, which was needed before immunosuppressive drugs existed. Vessels still had to be joined.

med-history.l07.q5.p: Who performed the first human heart transplant in 1967?
med-history.l07.q5.e: Barnard performed it in South Africa. Gibbon developed the heart-lung machine, and Murray performed the first kidney transplant.

med-history.l08.q1.t: Deliberate infection with material from smallpox to cause a milder illness and later immunity
med-history.l08.q1.e: Variolation used smallpox itself. Cowpox use was Jenner's vaccination, and isolation was a separate measure.

med-history.l08.q2.t: 1980, after the last natural case in 1977
med-history.l08.q2.p: When was smallpox declared eradicated worldwide?
med-history.l08.q2.e: The WHO declared smallpox eradicated in 1980. The other dates concern Jenner, the Salk trial and the Sabin vaccine.

med-history.l08.q3.t: Salk used inactivated virus by injection, and Sabin used weakened live virus by mouth
med-history.l08.q3.p: What is a main difference between the Salk and Sabin polio vaccines?
med-history.l08.q3.e: Salk's vaccine is inactivated and injected, while Sabin's is a live weakened oral vaccine. Polio is a viral disease, not bacterial.

med-history.l08.q4.t: manufacturing control and oversight are essential to vaccine safety
med-history.l08.q4.p: The 1955 Cutter incident, in which some polio vaccine contained live virus, is best interpreted as showing that:
med-history.l08.q4.e: The problem was inadequate inactivation in manufacturing. The vaccine concept was not disproved, and the incident led to stronger oversight.

med-history.l08.q5.t: Surveillance to find cases, followed by ring vaccination of the people around each case
med-history.l08.q5.p: A public health officer in 1970 wants to eliminate smallpox from a region with few health workers. Which strategy used in the global campaign was especially suited to this?
med-history.l08.q5.h: Find the cases and surround them.
med-history.l08.q5.e: Surveillance and containment with ring vaccination was efficient and effective. Universal same-day vaccination was not practical.

med-history.l09.q1.p: Who discovered in 1928 that a mold killed bacteria on a culture plate?
med-history.l09.q1.h: At St Mary's Hospital in London.
med-history.l09.q1.e: Fleming made the observation. Florey and Chain later purified penicillin, Domagk worked on Prontosil, and Waksman on streptomycin.

med-history.l09.q2.p: Streptomycin, discovered by the team of Selman Waksman in 1943, was important as the first effective drug for:
med-history.l09.q2.h: A lung disease caused by a mycobacterium.
med-history.l09.q2.e: Streptomycin was the first effective drug against tuberculosis. Salvarsan was for syphilis, and sulfonamides were used for streptococcal infections.

med-history.l09.q3.t: The sulfonamides, since the active part of the dye was sulfanilamide
med-history.l09.q3.p: The Prontosil work of Gerhard Domagk in 1935 led to which class of drugs?
med-history.l09.q3.h: A dye with a surprising active fragment.
med-history.l09.q3.e: Prontosil was converted in the body to sulfanilamide. Penicillin and arsenicals came from different sources.

med-history.l09.q4.t: Resistance genes can be transferred between bacteria, and surviving bacteria multiply when the drug removes competitors
med-history.l09.q4.p: A hospital finds that a once-reliable antibiotic now fails against a common bacterium, and that resistance is spreading to other species of bacteria. Which feature of bacteria best explains the rapid spread?
med-history.l09.q4.e: Selection favors resistant survivors, and genes can spread horizontally. Drugs do not create specific resistance mutations to order.

med-history.l09.q5.t: The Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act of 1938, which required safety review of new drugs
med-history.l09.q5.p: The 1937 sulfanilamide elixir disaster, in which a solvent poisoned more than a hundred people, led to which regulatory change in the United States?
med-history.l09.q5.h: The date of the disaster tells you which law followed.
med-history.l09.q5.e: The 1938 Act required premarket safety review. Kefauver-Harris followed thalidomide, and the 1906 Act came earlier.

med-history.l10.q1.t: Using statistics to show that most deaths came from disease and by improving sanitation
med-history.l10.q1.p: What was Florence Nightingale's most important contribution to the reform of army hospitals?
med-history.l10.q1.e: Nightingale used data to demonstrate that disease killed more than wounds and pushed for sanitary reform.

med-history.l10.q2.t: be linked to universities and require laboratory science and clinical training
med-history.l10.q2.p: The Flexner Report of 1910 recommended that medical schools:
med-history.l10.q2.e: Flexner called for university links and scientific training. Many weak schools closed as a result.

med-history.l10.q3.t: It showed the value of positive-pressure ventilation and led to dedicated intensive care units
med-history.l10.q3.p: What was the main significance of the 1952 Copenhagen polio epidemic for hospital care?
med-history.l10.q3.h: Think about patients who could not breathe.
med-history.l10.q3.e: Ventilation by tube and bag saved many lives and led to ICUs. The Salk vaccine came later, and the nursing school was founded in 1860.

med-history.l10.q4.t: Patients were allocated by random numbers concealed from the investigators
med-history.l10.q4.p: The 1948 MRC streptomycin trial is often called the first properly randomized clinical trial. Which feature best supports that description?
med-history.l10.q4.e: Random allocation concealed from those enrolling patients reduces bias. Patient choice or physician choice would not.

med-history.l10.q5.p: Which pair of programs was created in the United States in 1965 and changed who could pay for hospital care?
med-history.l10.q5.e: Medicare covers older adults and Medicaid covers some low-income people. The other pairs are older or serve different purposes.

med-history.l11.q1.p: Who is regarded as the first woman to receive a modern medical degree in the United States?
med-history.l11.q1.e: Blackwell graduated in 1849. Crumpler was the first Black woman, Garrett Anderson qualified in Britain, and Nightingale was a nurse.

med-history.l11.q2.p: After the Flexner Report era, which two historically Black medical schools in the United States remained?
med-history.l11.q2.h: One is in Washington, D.C., the other in Nashville.
med-history.l11.q2.e: Howard University and Meharry Medical College remained. The other names are not that pair of medical schools.

med-history.l11.q3.t: Dosing and side effects were studied mostly in men, which left gaps in evidence for women
med-history.l11.q3.p: The FDA's 1977 guideline recommending exclusion of women of childbearing potential from early drug trials had which consequence?
med-history.l11.q3.h: Think about who was left out of the data.
med-history.l11.q3.e: Women were underrepresented, so evidence on their dosing and effects was thin. The NIH Revitalization Act of 1993 later required inclusion.

med-history.l11.q4.t: Acknowledge the surgical advance while recognizing that the enslaved women could not give consent
med-history.l11.q4.p: A historian is asked to evaluate J. Marion Sims's fistula repair. Which approach is most consistent with the lesson?
med-history.l11.q4.h: Both facts are true and must be held together.
med-history.l11.q4.e: The ethical analysis weighs the benefit to later patients against the absence of consent. Neither pretending consent existed nor denying any value is accurate.

med-history.l11.q5.t: It shapes who practices, what questions are asked, and whom the evidence describes
med-history.l11.q5.p: Why does the history of who was excluded from medical schools and research matter to medical knowledge?
med-history.l11.q5.h: The lesson ends with this point.
med-history.l11.q5.e: Who is allowed to practice and who is studied affect what is known and whom care serves. The other claims are false.

med-history.l12.q1.t: Smoking causes lung cancer in men and is a health hazard
med-history.l12.q1.p: What did the 1964 US Surgeon General's report conclude?
med-history.l12.q1.e: The report found that smoking causes lung cancer in men and is a hazard. It did not recommend a ban.

med-history.l12.q2.t: A large sewer network for London after the Great Stink of 1858
med-history.l12.q2.p: Joseph Bazalgette is associated with which public health achievement?
med-history.l12.q2.e: Bazalgette was the engineer of London's sewers. Snow made the map, and Chadwick wrote the report.

med-history.l12.q3.t: treats dehydration from diarrhea with a simple solution of salts and sugar at low cost
med-history.l12.q3.p: Oral rehydration therapy is a public health milestone because it:
med-history.l12.q3.e: It treats the dehydration, not the cause, and works at low cost without a hospital. It does not replace vaccines or water treatment.

med-history.l12.q4.t: Many declines began earlier, so sanitation, nutrition and housing clearly mattered, though credit is debated
med-history.l12.q4.p: A student argues that vaccines and antibiotics alone explain the fall in deaths from infectious diseases in the early twentieth century. What is the best reply from the lesson?
med-history.l12.q4.e: Many infectious disease declines preceded specific drugs, which points to broader public health factors. Historians still debate the shares.

med-history.l12.q5.t: It was among the studies linking smoking to lung cancer that helped establish the causal connection
med-history.l12.q5.p: Why do historians point to the Doll and Hill study of 1950 in the history of tobacco?
med-history.l12.q5.e: The case-control evidence linked smoking and lung cancer. Random assignment to smoke would have been unethical and was not done.

med-history.l13.q1.t: Neutral Spain's press reported on it freely, although the disease did not necessarily begin there
med-history.l13.q1.p: Why is the 1918 influenza pandemic often called the Spanish flu?
med-history.l13.q1.e: The name came from press coverage in neutral Spain. The origin of the pandemic is uncertain.

med-history.l13.q2.p: Which treatment transformed HIV infection into a manageable chronic condition from the mid 1990s?
med-history.l13.q2.e: Combination antiretroviral therapy suppresses the virus. Penicillin, polio vaccine and streptomycin do not treat HIV.

med-history.l13.q3.t: Many deaths occurred among healthy young adults, often involving secondary bacterial pneumonia
med-history.l13.q3.p: What was unusual about the mortality pattern of the 1918 influenza?
med-history.l13.q3.e: Healthy young adults died in large numbers, many of pneumonia. In ordinary seasonal flu the elderly are most at risk.

med-history.l13.q4.t: Early, sustained non-pharmaceutical measures were associated with better outcomes, although many other factors differed
med-history.l13.q4.p: A city in 1918 closed schools and public gatherings early and maintained the measures for several weeks. A later analysis finds its death rate was lower than in a city that waited. Which conclusion is best supported, with appropriate caution?
med-history.l13.q4.h: No vaccine and no antibiotics existed.
med-history.l13.q4.e: Retrospective comparisons suggest early and sustained measures helped, but they are observational. Neither vaccines nor antibiotics existed in 1918.

med-history.l13.q5.t: Greater patient involvement in drug testing and faster access to promising treatments
med-history.l13.q5.p: During the early AIDS epidemic, activist groups pressed for changes in research. What was a lasting effect of this activism?
med-history.l13.q5.e: Activism increased patient involvement and speeded access to treatments. Randomized trials and consent remained.

med-history.l14.q1.t: A reference sequence of the human genome, declared complete in 2003
med-history.l14.q1.p: What did the Human Genome Project produce?
med-history.l14.q1.e: The project produced a reference sequence. It did not itself cure diseases or map the neurons.

med-history.l14.q2.t: targets the abnormal protein produced by the BCR-ABL gene fusion in chronic myeloid leukemia
med-history.l14.q2.p: Imatinib is a landmark example of precision medicine because it:
med-history.l14.q2.e: Imatinib inhibits the protein made by BCR-ABL. It is a targeted drug, not a general chemotherapy or a gene-editing method.

med-history.l14.q3.t: They add many small effects, and they perform less well in groups that were underrepresented in the studies
med-history.l14.q3.p: Why do polygenic risk scores remain imperfect predictors?
med-history.l14.q3.e: Polygenic scores combine many small effects and are trained on data that may not represent everyone. They are not perfect.

med-history.l14.q4.t: Tighter oversight, with more attention to conflicts of interest and to the risks of viral vectors
med-history.l14.q4.p: Jesse Gelsinger died in 1999 during a gene therapy trial. Which was the main consequence for the field?
med-history.l14.q4.e: The case prompted stricter oversight and greater attention to conflicts of interest. Gene therapy research continued and later succeeded.

med-history.l14.q5.t: The score may be less accurate for groups that were underrepresented in the data, widening inequities
med-history.l14.q5.p: A hospital plans to use a polygenic score developed mainly from data on people of European ancestry to counsel patients of other ancestries. Which concern is most consistent with the lesson?
med-history.l14.q5.h: Who is included in the data?
med-history.l14.q5.e: Scores trained on narrow data can perform worse for others. The lesson stresses that benefits depend on who is included.

med-history.l15.q1.t: withheld approval of thalidomide, so the United States was largely spared the birth defects
med-history.l15.q1.p: Frances Kelsey is remembered because, as an FDA reviewer, she:
med-history.l15.q1.h: She did not approve a drug.
med-history.l15.q1.e: Kelsey withheld approval of thalidomide, partly for lack of safety data. Others discovered the link to birth defects.

med-history.l15.q2.p: The Kefauver-Harris Amendments of 1962 required that new drugs be shown to be:
med-history.l15.q2.e: The 1962 amendments added proof of effectiveness to safety. Prescription status and animal testing were not the central change.

med-history.l15.q3.t: Women who chose the therapy differed in other ways that affected their health, which randomized trials avoid
med-history.l15.q3.p: Why did observational studies mislead physicians about hormone therapy after menopause?
med-history.l15.q3.h: Think about who chooses a treatment.
med-history.l15.q3.e: Self-selection and confounding can create false associations, which randomization addresses. The Women's Health Initiative changed the view.

med-history.l15.q4.t: Compare outcomes in similar patients who do and do not receive the treatment
med-history.l15.q4.p: A treatment is widely used because many clinicians report that patients improve afterward. Pierre Louis's work on bloodletting suggests which first step?
med-history.l15.q4.h: Improvement after a treatment is not proof.
med-history.l15.q4.e: Comparison with similar untreated patients tests whether the treatment caused improvement. Anecdote and authority can mislead.

med-history.l15.q5.t: a dismissed idea can turn out to be correct, so openness must be paired with strong evidence
med-history.l15.q5.p: The story of Marshall, Warren and Helicobacter pylori is included to show that:
med-history.l15.q5.h: The reversal ran the other way.
med-history.l15.q5.e: The case shows that a rejected idea can be right, which calls for openness together with evidence. Not every rejected idea is vindicated.

med-immuno.l01.q1.t: Antigen receptors built by somatic gene rearrangement in each clone
med-immuno.l01.q1.p: Which feature best distinguishes adaptive from innate immunity?
med-immuno.l01.q1.h: Think about how the receptors are generated.
med-immuno.l01.q1.e: Lymphocyte receptors are assembled by gene rearrangement, producing clonal specificity and memory. The other options describe innate features.

med-immuno.l01.q2.t: Dendritic cell that has matured and migrated to the node
med-immuno.l01.q2.p: Which cell is the main link that carries antigen from tissues to lymph nodes to start a T cell response?
med-immuno.l01.q2.h: Which innate cell upregulates costimulatory molecules?
med-immuno.l01.q2.e: Mature dendritic cells migrate to lymph nodes and present antigen with costimulation. Neutrophils are short-lived and do not prime naive T cells.

med-immuno.l01.q3.t: Persistence of memory B and T cells from the first infection
med-immuno.l01.q3.p: A 30-year-old man has a deep puncture wound. Within hours the wound is red and swollen, and neutrophils fill the tissue. Which finding most directly explains why a second exposure years later will yield a faster antibody response?
med-immuno.l01.q3.h: Which arm of immunity keeps a record?
med-immuno.l01.q3.e: Memory lymphocytes allow a faster, larger secondary response. Pattern receptors are germline-encoded and are not expanded by clonal selection.

med-immuno.l01.q4.t: Cytokine release from macrophages after sensing viral RNA
med-immuno.l01.q4.p: A research team infects mice lacking RAG1 with a virus. Compared with normal mice, which response would still occur normally in the first hours?
med-immuno.l01.q4.h: RAG enzymes are needed for receptor rearrangement.
med-immuno.l01.q4.e: RAG1 deficiency removes T and B cells, but macrophage sensing is germline-encoded and intact. Antibody and CD8 responses depend on rearranged receptors.

med-immuno.l01.q5.t: Lack of receptors made by somatic gene rearrangement
med-immuno.l01.q5.p: Which feature of natural killer cells and innate lymphoid cells separates them from T and B cells?
med-immuno.l01.q5.h: Think about the receptor, not the function.
med-immuno.l01.q5.e: These lymphoid cells use germline-encoded receptors, not rearranged ones. They do secrete cytokines and do not need prior exposure.

med-immuno.l02.q1.t: C3b produced by cleavage of C3 by a convertase enzyme
med-immuno.l02.q1.p: Which complement component is the major opsonin and the central convergence point of all three pathways?
med-immuno.l02.q1.h: All pathways converge on one cleavage event.
med-immuno.l02.q1.e: C3 cleavage yields C3b, which coats microbes for phagocytosis. C5a is a chemoattractant, not the main opsonin.

med-immuno.l02.q2.t: C5a is a potent neutrophil chemoattractant and anaphylatoxin
med-immuno.l02.q2.p: Which pair correctly matches a complement fragment with its main function?
med-immuno.l02.q2.h: The small cleavage fragments are called anaphylatoxins.
med-immuno.l02.q2.e: C5a attracts neutrophils and triggers mast cell degranulation. C3b opsonizes, and the MAC is the terminal effector, not an activator.

med-immuno.l02.q3.t: Deficiency of a late component such as C7 or C8
med-immuno.l02.q3.p: A 22-year-old has had two episodes of meningococcal meningitis. CH50 is nearly absent, while C3 and C4 levels are normal. Which deficiency is most likely?
med-immuno.l02.q3.h: Which step is most needed to lyse Neisseria?
med-immuno.l02.q3.e: Terminal component defects prevent MAC formation, causing recurrent Neisseria infection with normal C3 and C4. C3 deficiency would lower C3 and cause severe pyogenic infections.

med-immuno.l02.q4.t: Unchecked bradykinin from loss of C1 inhibitor activity
med-immuno.l02.q4.p: A 28-year-old has recurrent episodes of facial and laryngeal swelling without urticaria or itching. C4 is low between attacks, and antihistamines and steroids do not help. Which mechanism underlies the attacks?
med-immuno.l02.q4.h: Think about what C1 inhibitor also regulates.
med-immuno.l02.q4.e: C1 inhibitor also restrains kallikrein and factor XII, so deficiency raises bradykinin. IgE-mediated angioedema would have urticaria and respond to antihistamines.

med-immuno.l02.q5.t: Vaccination against Neisseria meningitidis before therapy begins
med-immuno.l02.q5.p: A 35-year-old has episodic dark morning urine, anemia and venous thrombosis. Flow cytometry shows red cells lacking CD55 and CD59. Treatment with a C5 inhibitor is started. Which risk must be addressed beforehand?
med-immuno.l02.q5.h: C5 blockade impairs the membrane attack complex.
med-immuno.l02.q5.e: Blocking C5 prevents MAC formation and increases susceptibility to Neisseria. TB and Pneumocystis risk relates to other immunosuppressants.

med-immuno.l03.q1.t: Integrins such as LFA-1 and Mac-1 on the neutrophil surface
med-immuno.l03.q1.p: Which molecule on neutrophils binds ICAM-1 on endothelium during firm adhesion?
med-immuno.l03.q1.h: Rolling uses selectins; firm adhesion uses another family.
med-immuno.l03.q1.e: Integrins bind ICAM-1 for tight adhesion. Selectin ligands mediate rolling, and chemokine receptors activate the integrins.

med-immuno.l03.q2.t: Interleukin 6 acting on hepatocytes via gp130 signaling
med-immuno.l03.q2.p: Which cytokine is the principal inducer of hepatic acute-phase proteins such as C-reactive protein?
med-immuno.l03.q2.e: IL-6 is the main driver of hepatic acute-phase synthesis. IFN-gamma activates macrophages, and IL-4 drives IgE switching.

med-immuno.l03.q3.t: Absence of the CD18 integrin subunit on leukocytes
med-immuno.l03.q3.p: A newborn has delayed umbilical cord separation, recurrent skin infections without pus and a neutrophil count of 40,000/µL. Which defect is most likely?
med-immuno.l03.q3.h: Neutrophils are made but cannot leave the vessels.
med-immuno.l03.q3.e: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1 lacks CD18, so cells cannot adhere and migrate, causing neutrophilia without pus. Oxidase defects have normal migration.

med-immuno.l03.q4.t: Streptococcus pneumoniae that produces no catalase of its own
med-immuno.l03.q4.p: A 5-year-old boy has recurrent lymphadenitis and a liver abscess from Staphylococcus aureus. Dihydrorhodamine oxidation is absent after stimulation. Which organism would be least likely to cause infection in this child?
med-immuno.l03.q4.h: Which organisms supply their own hydrogen peroxide?
med-immuno.l03.q4.e: In chronic granulomatous disease, catalase-negative organisms generate hydrogen peroxide that the phagocyte can use, so they are usually killed. Catalase-positive organisms destroy it.

med-immuno.l03.q5.t: Fibrinogen promotes stacking of red cells so they settle faster
med-immuno.l03.q5.p: Why is the erythrocyte sedimentation rate elevated in systemic inflammation?
med-immuno.l03.q5.h: Think about which acute-phase protein affects red cell aggregation.
med-immuno.l03.q5.e: Fibrinogen is a positive acute-phase protein that causes rouleaux. Albumin is a negative acute-phase reactant and falls.

med-immuno.l04.q1.t: TLR4 with MD-2 and CD14 at the cell surface
med-immuno.l04.q1.p: Which Toll-like receptor recognizes bacterial lipopolysaccharide?
med-immuno.l04.q1.h: It is a Gram-negative outer membrane component.
med-immuno.l04.q1.e: TLR4 senses lipopolysaccharide. TLR3 and TLR9 detect nucleic acids, and TLR5 senses flagellin.

med-immuno.l04.q2.t: Caspase-1 which cleaves pro-IL-1 beta and pro-IL-18
med-immuno.l04.q2.p: Which enzyme is activated by the NLRP3 inflammasome to process pro-IL-1 beta into its active form?
med-immuno.l04.q2.h: It is sometimes called interleukin-converting enzyme.
med-immuno.l04.q2.e: Caspase-1 is the inflammatory caspase of the inflammasome. Caspases 3, 8 and 9 mainly drive apoptosis.

med-immuno.l04.q3.t: NK cell activation due to loss of inhibitory self MHC class I signals
med-immuno.l04.q3.p: A virus infects hepatocytes and sharply reduces surface MHC class I. CD8 T cell recognition falls. Which innate mechanism is most likely to detect and kill these cells?
med-immuno.l04.q3.e: KIRs and NKG2A deliver inhibitory signals through self class I, so loss of it releases NK killing. IgE and mast cells are not the key route here.

med-immuno.l04.q4.t: Anakinra, an antagonist of the interleukin 1 receptor
med-immuno.l04.q4.p: A child has recurrent fever, rash and joint pain from infancy. Serum IL-1 beta is high, and genetic testing shows a gain-of-function variant in an inflammasome component. Which therapy targets the dysregulated pathway?
med-immuno.l04.q4.h: Which cytokine does the inflammasome release?
med-immuno.l04.q4.e: Autoinflammatory syndromes with inflammasome activation respond to IL-1 blockade. Eculizumab targets complement, not IL-1.

med-immuno.l04.q5.t: NF-kappa B activation downstream of most Toll-like receptors
med-immuno.l04.q5.p: A patient with a nonsense mutation in MyD88 has severe recurrent pyogenic infections in childhood. Which signaling step is impaired in this patient?
med-immuno.l04.q5.h: MyD88 is an adaptor for TLR and IL-1 receptor signaling.
med-immuno.l04.q5.e: MyD88 links most TLRs and IL-1R family receptors to NF-kappa B. The other pathways use different adaptors and kinases.

med-immuno.l05.q1.t: Dendritic cells, macrophages and B cells that present antigen
med-immuno.l05.q1.p: Which cells express MHC class II molecules under normal conditions?
med-immuno.l05.q1.h: They are the professional antigen-presenting cells.
med-immuno.l05.q1.e: Class II is restricted to professional antigen-presenting cells and thymic epithelium. Class I is on nearly all nucleated cells.

med-immuno.l05.q2.t: Exchange of the CLIP fragment for peptide by HLA-DM in the endosome
med-immuno.l05.q2.p: Which step is specific to loading peptides onto MHC class II molecules?
med-immuno.l05.q2.e: HLA-DM removes CLIP so antigenic peptide can bind. TAP, beta-2 microglobulin and proteasome processing belong to the class I pathway.

med-immuno.l05.q3.t: Loss of TAP so peptides cannot enter the endoplasmic reticulum
med-immuno.l05.q3.p: A virus-infected cell fails to express surface MHC class I, and peptide loading is defective. Cytosolic peptides are present at normal levels. Which defect best explains this?
med-immuno.l05.q3.h: Peptides must get from the cytosol into the ER.
med-immuno.l05.q3.e: TAP moves cytosolic peptides into the ER for class I loading. HLA-DM and the invariant chain are class II elements.

med-immuno.l05.q4.t: HLA-B27, which is a class I allele and a risk modifier
med-immuno.l05.q4.p: A 24-year-old man has low back pain and morning stiffness for 6 months, with sacroiliac joint inflammation on imaging. Which HLA allele is most strongly associated with his condition?
med-immuno.l05.q4.e: HLA-B27 is strongly associated with ankylosing spondylitis. The other alleles have associations with different diseases.

med-immuno.l05.q5.t: Toxin cross-linking class II with the TCR beta chain outside the groove
med-immuno.l05.q5.p: A 20-year-old woman has fever, diffuse erythroderma, hypotension and multiorgan dysfunction while using a tampon. Which mechanism explains the massive cytokine release?
med-immuno.l05.q5.h: Superantigens do not need normal antigen processing.
med-immuno.l05.q5.e: Superantigens link class II and the V-beta region of the TCR, activating many T cells nonspecifically. A TAP blockade would reduce class I presentation, not cause a cytokine storm.

med-immuno.l06.q1.t: RAG1 and RAG2 recombinases that cut gene segments for joining
med-immuno.l06.q1.p: Which enzymes carry out V(D)J recombination in developing lymphocytes?
med-immuno.l06.q1.h: The genes are named recombination-activating genes.
med-immuno.l06.q1.e: RAG1 and RAG2 initiate V(D)J recombination. AID acts later in germinal centers on mature B cells.

med-immuno.l06.q2.t: Death by neglect in the cortex because survival signals are absent
med-immuno.l06.q2.p: What is the outcome for a double-positive thymocyte whose TCR cannot bind self MHC at all?
med-immuno.l06.q2.h: This describes the failure of positive selection.
med-immuno.l06.q2.e: Cells that cannot recognize self MHC receive no survival signal and die by neglect. Clonal deletion is for cells with too high self affinity.

med-immuno.l06.q3.t: Failure of AIRE-driven tissue antigen display in thymic epithelium
med-immuno.l06.q3.p: A 3-year-old with chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis develops hypoparathyroidism and adrenal insufficiency. The child has autoantibodies to several endocrine tissues. Which defect best explains the disease?
med-immuno.l06.q3.h: Which gene controls display of self antigens in the medulla?
med-immuno.l06.q3.e: AIRE deficiency allows self-reactive T cells to escape deletion, causing APECED. FOXP3 loss causes IPEX, which has enteropathy and neonatal diabetes.

med-immuno.l06.q4.t: Deletion at 22q11.2 with low T cell counts and normal B cell counts
med-immuno.l06.q4.p: A newborn has a conotruncal heart defect, tetany with low calcium, and a very small thymic shadow. Which finding is most likely on further testing?
med-immuno.l06.q4.h: Third and fourth pharyngeal pouch derivatives are affected.
med-immuno.l06.q4.e: 22q11.2 deletion impairs thymus and parathyroid development with cardiac outflow anomalies. BTK and CD40L defects are B cell or switching disorders.

med-immuno.l06.q5.t: Very low or absent T and B cells with NK cells present
med-immuno.l06.q5.p: An infant has absent T cells and B cells, recurrent infections and failure to thrive. Genetic testing finds a null mutation in RAG1. Which feature would be expected on the immunologic work-up?
med-immuno.l06.q5.h: NK cells do not use RAG.
med-immuno.l06.q5.e: RAG null causes T-B-NK+ SCID since NK cells do not rearrange receptors. T-B+NK- SCID is seen with common gamma chain or JAK3 defects.

med-immuno.l07.q1.t: CD28 on the T cell binding B7 on the antigen-presenting cell
med-immuno.l07.q1.p: Which receptor-ligand pair provides the classic second signal for naive T cell activation?
med-immuno.l07.q1.h: Without it the cell becomes anergic.
med-immuno.l07.q1.e: CD28 and B7 deliver costimulation. PD-1 and PD-L1 deliver an inhibitory signal, and CD4 with class II is a coreceptor interaction.

med-immuno.l07.q2.t: Th2 cells, which depend on the transcription factor GATA3
med-immuno.l07.q2.p: Which Th subset and transcription factor drive IgE class switching and eosinophil recruitment?
med-immuno.l07.q2.h: IL-4, IL-5 and IL-13 are its cytokines.
med-immuno.l07.q2.e: Th2 cells produce IL-4, IL-5 and IL-13. Th1 cells target intracellular microbes through IFN-gamma.

med-immuno.l07.q3.t: Th1 differentiation and macrophage activation against mycobacteria
med-immuno.l07.q3.p: A 6-month-old develops disseminated infection with BCG after vaccination. IFN-gamma levels are low and a mutation in the IL-12 receptor beta-1 chain is found. Which process is most directly impaired?
med-immuno.l07.q3.e: IL-12 receptor defects impair Th1 cells and IFN-gamma-driven macrophage killing of mycobacteria. Th17 defects would affect extracellular bacteria and fungi.

med-immuno.l07.q4.t: Greater CD28 access to B7 so that T cell priming is enhanced
med-immuno.l07.q4.p: A patient with metastatic melanoma is given an antibody that blocks CTLA-4. Which immunologic effect most directly explains the antitumor action?
med-immuno.l07.q4.h: CTLA-4 competes with CD28 for the same ligands.
med-immuno.l07.q4.e: CTLA-4 blockade removes competition for B7, increasing priming. PD-1 and PD-L1 blockade acts mainly in peripheral tissues and tumors.

med-immuno.l07.q5.t: T-bet expression and IFN-gamma secretion by the differentiating cells
med-immuno.l07.q5.p: A culture of naive CD4 T cells is stimulated in the presence of IL-12 and IFN-gamma. Which result is expected?
med-immuno.l07.q5.h: This is the signature of the macrophage-activating subset.
med-immuno.l07.q5.e: IL-12 and IFN-gamma induce Th1 differentiation through T-bet. The other combinations correspond to Th2, Tfh and Th17 cells.

med-immuno.l08.q1.t: IgG, through the neonatal Fc receptor on the placenta
med-immuno.l08.q1.p: Which immunoglobulin isotype crosses the placenta?
med-immuno.l08.q1.h: It gives the newborn passive protection.
med-immuno.l08.q1.e: Only IgG crosses the placenta, using FcRn. IgM is too large, and secretory IgA is transported into secretions.

med-immuno.l08.q2.t: Activation-induced cytidine deaminase in germinal center B cells
med-immuno.l08.q2.p: Which enzyme is required for both somatic hypermutation and class switch recombination?
med-immuno.l08.q2.e: AID drives both processes in germinal centers. TdT and RAG act during primary V(D)J rearrangement.

med-immuno.l08.q3.t: A CD40 ligand mutation on helper T cells impairing class switching
med-immuno.l08.q3.p: A 4-year-old boy has recurrent pyogenic sinopulmonary infections. IgM is normal, IgG, IgA and IgE are very low, and lymph nodes lack germinal centers. Which defect is most likely?
med-immuno.l08.q3.h: IgM is preserved while other classes are low.
med-immuno.l08.q3.e: CD40L deficiency prevents class switching, giving hyper-IgM syndrome with normal or high IgM. BTK deficiency gives low IgM too, with absent B cells.

med-immuno.l08.q4.t: Conjugation recruits T helper cells so B cells class switch
med-immuno.l08.q4.p: A 1-year-old with a polysaccharide capsule infection has poor antibody responses to the plain polysaccharide vaccine but responds well to a protein-conjugated version. What explains the improved response?
med-immuno.l08.q4.h: Think about T-dependent versus T-independent antigens.
med-immuno.l08.q4.e: Linking a polysaccharide to a protein carrier makes the antigen T-dependent, so helper T cells enable switching and memory. Polysaccharides alone are T-independent.

med-immuno.l08.q5.t: It is a dimer carried across epithelium by the polymeric Ig receptor
med-immuno.l08.q5.p: Which feature explains why IgA is effective at mucosal surfaces?
med-immuno.l08.q5.e: Dimeric IgA is transported by pIgR and acquires secretory component. IgM is the pentamer, and IgE binds mast cells.

med-immuno.l09.q1.t: JAK3 phosphorylating STAT proteins that move to the nucleus
med-immuno.l09.q1.p: Which signaling pathway is used by the common gamma chain cytokine receptors?
med-immuno.l09.q1.h: The mutated kinase causes an autosomal recessive SCID.
med-immuno.l09.q1.e: Gamma chain receptors signal through JAK3 and STATs. Lck, ZAP-70 and BTK work in antigen receptor signaling.

med-immuno.l09.q2.t: TNF-alpha, produced by activated macrophages and T cells
med-immuno.l09.q2.p: Which cytokine is most responsible for maintaining granuloma integrity against intracellular infection?
med-immuno.l09.q2.h: Blocking it can reactivate latent tuberculosis.
med-immuno.l09.q2.e: TNF-alpha sustains granulomas, so its blockade risks reactivation of latent infection. IL-10 is suppressive.

med-immuno.l09.q3.t: Screening for latent tuberculosis infection before treatment began
med-immuno.l09.q3.p: A 45-year-old with rheumatoid arthritis begins a monoclonal antibody against TNF-alpha. Three months later she has fever, weight loss and an upper lobe cavity. Which preventive step would most likely have lowered this risk?
med-immuno.l09.q3.h: Think about what TNF blockade does to granulomas.
med-immuno.l09.q3.e: TNF blockade impairs granuloma containment, so screening for latent TB is standard. HLA-B typing is relevant to other drug reactions.

med-immuno.l09.q4.t: Receptors for IL-2, IL-7 and IL-15 cannot signal, impairing T and NK development
med-immuno.l09.q4.p: A 7-month-old has persistent thrush, chronic diarrhea and failure to thrive. Flow cytometry shows absent T and NK cells and normal B cell counts. Sequencing shows a mutation in JAK3. Which statement best explains the finding?
med-immuno.l09.q4.h: JAK3 serves the common gamma chain.
med-immuno.l09.q4.e: JAK3 is required for gamma chain cytokines, including IL-7 and IL-15, which are essential for T and NK cells. B cells are present but dysfunctional.

med-immuno.l09.q5.t: A fall in blood and tissue eosinophil counts that reduces exacerbations
med-immuno.l09.q5.p: A 38-year-old with severe eosinophilic asthma, with frequent exacerbations, is started on a biologic that blocks the IL-5 pathway. Which change would most likely follow?
med-immuno.l09.q5.h: IL-5 recruits and sustains one granulocyte type.
med-immuno.l09.q5.e: IL-5 supports eosinophil maturation and survival, so blocking it lowers eosinophils. Anti-IgE agents lower IgE, which is not the IL-5 effect.

med-immuno.l10.q1.t: It drives medullary expression of tissue-restricted self antigens
med-immuno.l10.q1.p: What is the role of AIRE in tolerance?
med-immuno.l10.q1.h: It allows T cells to meet self antigens in the thymus.
med-immuno.l10.q1.e: AIRE promotes expression of peripheral antigens in medullary epithelium so reactive T cells are deleted. FOXP3 and Fas have separate roles.

med-immuno.l10.q2.t: Receptor editing by new light chain rearrangement to change specificity
med-immuno.l10.q2.p: An immature B cell in bone marrow binds a multivalent self antigen strongly. Which first response is typical?
med-immuno.l10.q2.h: Central B cell tolerance involves changing the receptor.
med-immuno.l10.q2.e: Receptor editing is the first line of central B cell tolerance, with deletion or anergy if it fails. Germinal center events occur in mature cells after activation.

med-immuno.l10.q3.t: Mutation in FOXP3 causing absent regulatory T cell function
med-immuno.l10.q3.p: A male infant has intractable watery diarrhea, eczema and early insulin-dependent diabetes. Which abnormality is most likely?
med-immuno.l10.q3.h: The syndrome is X-linked and begins in infancy.
med-immuno.l10.q3.e: FOXP3 loss causes IPEX, with enteropathy, endocrinopathy and dermatitis. AIRE loss causes APECED, with candidiasis, which presents later.

med-immuno.l10.q4.t: Fas-mediated apoptosis that normally deletes activated lymphocytes
med-immuno.l10.q4.p: A 9-year-old has persistent lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly with autoimmune hemolytic anemia and thrombocytopenia. Lymphocyte counts are elevated with unusual double-negative T cells. Which pathway is most likely defective?
med-immuno.l10.q4.h: The syndrome is an autoimmune lymphoproliferative disorder.
med-immuno.l10.q4.e: Fas defects prevent activation-induced cell death and cause lymphoproliferation with cytopenias. CTLA-4 haploinsufficiency has a different presentation.

med-immuno.l10.q5.t: Antibodies to streptococcal M protein cross-reacting with the heart
med-immuno.l10.q5.p: A 12-year-old develops fever, migratory arthritis and a new heart murmur 3 weeks after untreated streptococcal pharyngitis. Which mechanism best explains the cardiac injury?
med-immuno.l10.q5.h: It is a form of molecular mimicry.
med-immuno.l10.q5.e: Rheumatic fever arises from cross-reactive antibodies and T cells after group A streptococcal infection. Direct invasion is not the mechanism.

med-immuno.l11.q1.t: Histamine released within minutes of IgE cross-linking
med-immuno.l11.q1.p: Which mediator is preformed in mast cell granules and responsible for early vasodilation in anaphylaxis?
med-immuno.l11.q1.h: Think about what is stored versus newly made.
med-immuno.l11.q1.e: Histamine and tryptase are preformed in granules. Leukotrienes are newly synthesized, and IL-5 acts later.

med-immuno.l11.q2.t: Indirect Coombs test used in prenatal and transfusion screening
med-immuno.l11.q2.p: Which test uses a patient's serum to detect free antibody that binds reagent red cells?
med-immuno.l11.q2.h: The antibody is free in the patient's plasma.
med-immuno.l11.q2.e: The indirect Coombs test detects circulating antibody in serum. The direct test detects antibody already coating the patient's own red cells.

med-immuno.l11.q3.t: Intramuscular epinephrine, with histamine from IgE-activated mast cells
med-immuno.l11.q3.p: A 19-year-old develops urticaria, wheeze and hypotension 10 minutes after eating a shrimp dish. Which immediate treatment is correct, and which mediator drives the event?
med-immuno.l11.q3.h: The first-line drug reverses airway and vascular collapse.
med-immuno.l11.q3.e: Anaphylaxis is IgE-mediated, and epinephrine is first-line. Antihistamines and steroids are adjuncts and do not treat airway or circulatory compromise.

med-immuno.l11.q4.t: The alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen in basement membranes
med-immuno.l11.q4.p: A 26-year-old has hemoptysis and hematuria. Biopsy of the kidney shows crescentic glomerulonephritis with linear IgG deposition along the basement membrane. Which target antigen is most likely involved?
med-immuno.l11.q4.h: Linear immunofluorescence implies binding to a continuous structure.
med-immuno.l11.q4.e: Anti-GBM disease targets the noncollagenous domain of the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen. The other antigens belong to other type II diseases.

med-immuno.l11.q5.t: Maternal IgG against fetal Rh D antigen crossing the placenta and coating cells
med-immuno.l11.q5.p: A newborn develops jaundice within 24 hours of birth, with anemia and a positive direct Coombs test. The mother is Rh D negative, and this is her second pregnancy. Which mechanism explains the neonatal hemolysis?
med-immuno.l11.q5.e: Maternal IgG anti-D from earlier sensitization crosses the placenta. IgM is too large to do so, and the reaction is a type II mechanism.

med-immuno.l12.q1.t: T cell mediated injury appearing 48 to 72 hours after exposure
med-immuno.l12.q1.p: Which feature characterizes a type IV hypersensitivity reaction?
med-immuno.l12.q1.e: Type IV is T cell mediated and delayed. Types I, II and III are antibody mediated.

med-immuno.l12.q2.t: Low serum C3 and C4 with granular immune deposits in glomeruli
med-immuno.l12.q2.p: Which finding best supports active type III hypersensitivity in lupus nephritis?
med-immuno.l12.q2.e: Immune complex disease consumes complement and shows granular deposits. Linear staining indicates an anti-basement-membrane antibody.

med-immuno.l12.q3.t: Circulating immune complexes that deposit and activate complement
med-immuno.l12.q3.p: A 35-year-old receives equine antithymocyte globulin. Ten days later she has fever, rash, joint pain and low serum C3. Which process explains these findings?
med-immuno.l12.q3.h: The timing of 1 to 2 weeks after a foreign protein is typical.
med-immuno.l12.q3.e: This is serum sickness, a type III reaction with low complement. IgE reactions occur in minutes, and T cell reactions need no complement consumption.

med-immuno.l12.q4.t: Sensitized T cells reacting to a hapten bound to skin proteins
med-immuno.l12.q4.p: A 28-year-old nurse develops a pruritic, vesicular eruption on her hands 2 days after beginning use of a new glove type. Patch testing is positive for a rubber additive. Which cell type mediates the reaction?
med-immuno.l12.q4.h: The timing and eczema point away from IgE.
med-immuno.l12.q4.e: Allergic contact dermatitis is a type IV reaction in which hapten-specific T cells respond. IgE-mediated contact urticaria would occur within minutes.

med-immuno.l12.q5.t: Interferon-gamma release assay, which is not affected by BCG vaccination
med-immuno.l12.q5.p: A 40-year-old immigrant from a country with routine BCG vaccination has a 12 mm tuberculin skin test induration, with no symptoms and a normal chest film. Which test best clarifies whether the result reflects infection rather than vaccination?
med-immuno.l12.q5.h: Look for an in vitro assay with specific antigens.
med-immuno.l12.q5.e: Release assays use antigens absent from BCG, so they are not affected by it. Repeating a skin test does not remove the BCG confounder.

med-immuno.l13.q1.t: Anti-double-stranded DNA, which also tracks with nephritis activity
med-immuno.l13.q1.p: Which autoantibody is most specific for systemic lupus erythematosus?
med-immuno.l13.q1.h: ANA is sensitive but not specific; look for a more specific one.
med-immuno.l13.q1.e: Anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith are specific for lupus. The other antibodies belong to different diseases.

med-immuno.l13.q2.t: c-ANCA against proteinase 3 in granulomatosis with polyangiitis
med-immuno.l13.q2.p: Which pairing of autoantibody and disease is correct?
med-immuno.l13.q2.h: The cytoplasmic pattern corresponds to proteinase 3.
med-immuno.l13.q2.e: c-ANCA with PR3 is characteristic of granulomatosis with polyangiitis. Anti-histone suggests drug-induced lupus, and anti-Scl-70 is linked to diffuse disease.

med-immuno.l13.q3.t: Anti-mitochondrial antibody directed against pyruvate dehydrogenase
med-immuno.l13.q3.p: A 52-year-old woman with fatigue and pruritus has elevated alkaline phosphatase and a normal bile duct on ultrasound. Which autoantibody is most likely positive?
med-immuno.l13.q3.h: Cholestatic pattern in a middle-aged woman.
med-immuno.l13.q3.e: Primary biliary cholangitis is characterized by anti-mitochondrial antibodies. Anti-smooth muscle antibodies suggest autoimmune hepatitis.

med-immuno.l13.q4.t: Anti-SSA (Ro) antibody crossing the placenta to the fetal heart
med-immuno.l13.q4.p: A 28-year-old woman with lupus is pregnant. Her baby is born with a heart rate of 55 beats per minute and complete heart block. Which maternal antibody is most likely responsible?
med-immuno.l13.q4.e: Maternal anti-Ro/SSA IgG crosses the placenta and injures the fetal conduction system. Anti-dsDNA is linked to nephritis, not heart block.

med-immuno.l13.q5.t: Antibodies that activate the TSH receptor on follicular cells
med-immuno.l13.q5.p: A 31-year-old woman has heat intolerance, weight loss, a diffuse goiter and exophthalmos. Which mechanism explains the hyperthyroidism?
med-immuno.l13.q5.h: This is a stimulatory type II reaction.
med-immuno.l13.q5.e: Graves disease results from stimulating anti-TSH receptor antibodies. Hashimoto disease involves anti-TPO antibodies and T cell destruction, causing hypothyroidism.

med-immuno.l14.q1.t: BTK, the gene for Bruton tyrosine kinase in pre-B cell signaling
med-immuno.l14.q1.p: Which gene is mutated in X-linked agammaglobulinemia?
med-immuno.l14.q1.h: It arrests B cell development at the pre-B stage.
med-immuno.l14.q1.e: BTK is required for pre-B receptor signaling. CD40LG causes hyper-IgM, and IL2RG causes X-linked SCID.

med-immuno.l14.q2.t: Anaphylaxis after transfusion of blood products that contain IgA
med-immuno.l14.q2.p: Which complication is a recognized risk of selective IgA deficiency?
med-immuno.l14.q2.h: Anti-IgA antibodies recognize donor protein as foreign.
med-immuno.l14.q2.e: Patients with anti-IgA antibodies can react to IgA in blood products. The others are not features of isolated IgA deficiency.

med-immuno.l14.q3.t: Lifelong immunoglobulin replacement is the mainstay of treatment
med-immuno.l14.q3.p: A 9-month-old boy has three episodes of pneumococcal otitis media and pneumonia. Tonsils are not visible, CD19 positive cells are absent, and all immunoglobulin classes are very low. Which statement is correct?
med-immuno.l14.q3.h: The defect is limited to the B cell lineage.
med-immuno.l14.q3.e: XLA is managed with immunoglobulin replacement. Transplant and enzyme replacement are used for SCID forms.

med-immuno.l14.q4.t: Common variable immunodeficiency, a diagnosis of exclusion
med-immuno.l14.q4.p: A 26-year-old has recurrent sinusitis and pneumonia, chronic diarrhea with Giardia, and immune thrombocytopenia. IgG and IgA are low, and vaccine responses are poor. B cell numbers are normal. Which diagnosis is most likely?
med-immuno.l14.q4.h: Adult onset, low IgG with autoimmunity, and normal B cells.
med-immuno.l14.q4.e: CVID presents in young adulthood with low IgG and IgA, poor vaccine response and autoimmunity. XLA has absent B cells.

med-immuno.l14.q5.t: T cell CD40 ligand deficiency impairing switching and macrophage help
med-immuno.l14.q5.p: A 3-year-old boy has pneumonia from Pneumocystis jirovecii, normal IgM and very low IgG, IgA and IgE. Which pathogenic mechanism is most likely?
med-immuno.l14.q5.h: Opportunistic infection suggests a T cell contribution.
med-immuno.l14.q5.e: CD40L deficiency causes hyper-IgM with impaired T cell help to macrophages, which allows Pneumocystis. BTK deficiency does not typically allow opportunistic infection.

med-immuno.l15.q1.t: T-negative, B-positive, NK-negative with nonfunctional B cells
med-immuno.l15.q1.p: What is the characteristic cell pattern in X-linked SCID due to common gamma chain deficiency?
med-immuno.l15.q1.h: IL-7 and IL-15 signaling are both lost.
med-immuno.l15.q1.e: IL2RG mutations remove signaling for IL-7 and IL-15, leaving T and NK cells absent but B cells present. RAG defects give T-B-NK+.

med-immuno.l15.q2.t: Eczema, small-platelet thrombocytopenia and recurrent infections
med-immuno.l15.q2.h: It is X-linked and affects the actin cytoskeleton.
med-immuno.l15.q2.e: The classic triad is eczema, microthrombocytopenia and infections. The other triads describe ataxia-telangiectasia, hyper-IgE and Chediak-Higashi.

med-immuno.l15.q3.t: Repair of DNA double-strand breaks owing to ATM kinase mutation
med-immuno.l15.q3.p: A 4-year-old has gait ataxia, small vascular malformations on the conjunctivae, recurrent sinopulmonary infections and a low IgA. Alpha-fetoprotein is elevated. Which process is defective?
med-immuno.l15.q3.h: The disease carries radiosensitivity and lymphoma risk.
med-immuno.l15.q3.e: Ataxia-telangiectasia results from ATM mutation and defective DNA repair. LYST defects cause Chediak-Higashi syndrome.

med-immuno.l15.q4.t: STAT3, causing impaired Th17 differentiation and IL-17 production
med-immuno.l15.q4.p: A 6-year-old has cold staphylococcal skin abscesses, eczema, coarse facial features, retained primary teeth and multiple fractures. IgE is markedly elevated. Which gene is most likely mutated?
med-immuno.l15.q4.e: Autosomal dominant STAT3 mutation impairs Th17 cells, leading to staphylococcal and candidal infection with high IgE. CYBB and ITGB2 cause phagocyte disease with normal IgE.

med-immuno.l15.q5.t: Avoid live vaccines, give irradiated blood and refer for transplant
med-immuno.l15.q5.p: A newborn screened with T cell receptor excision circle testing has very low values. The infant has persistent thrush and no thymic shadow on chest radiograph. Which management step is most appropriate?
med-immuno.l15.q5.h: Think of the SCID emergency measures.
med-immuno.l15.q5.e: SCID requires avoiding live vaccines, using irradiated products and early stem cell transplant. Live vaccines can cause disseminated disease.

med-immuno.l16.q1.t: CCR5, which allows entry into CD4 T cells and macrophages
med-immuno.l16.q1.p: Which coreceptor is used by HIV in early infection, and mutated in some resistant people?
med-immuno.l16.q1.h: A deletion in this gene confers relative resistance.
med-immuno.l16.q1.e: Early strains are mostly CCR5-tropic. CXCR4 usage tends to appear later.

med-immuno.l16.q2.t: Nucleic acid amplification for viral RNA in plasma
med-immuno.l16.q2.p: Which test best detects HIV in the window period soon after exposure?
med-immuno.l16.q2.e: Viral RNA appears before antibodies. Antibody and Western blot tests are insensitive in early infection, and CD4 count is not diagnostic.

med-immuno.l16.q3.t: Loss of CD4 T cell help impairs macrophage activation against fungi
med-immuno.l16.q3.p: A 38-year-old man with HIV has CD4 count 80 cells per microliter, fever, headache and a positive serum cryptococcal antigen. Which statement best reflects the reason for his susceptibility?
med-immuno.l16.q3.h: CD4 cells activate macrophages through IFN-gamma.
med-immuno.l16.q3.e: Defective CD4 T cell-driven macrophage activation allows intracellular and opportunistic fungal infection. B cell loss is not the main problem in HIV.

med-immuno.l16.q4.t: Immune reconstitution syndrome unmasking an existing infection
med-immuno.l16.q4.p: A 33-year-old man starts antiretroviral therapy for HIV with CD4 count of 30. Four weeks later he has new fever and enlarging cervical lymph nodes with caseating granulomas. Viral load has fallen. Which explanation is most likely?
med-immuno.l16.q4.h: Falling viral load and recovering CD4 suggest the therapy is working.
med-immuno.l16.q4.e: IRIS occurs when recovering immunity reacts to a subclinical infection after starting therapy. Treatment failure would show rising viral load.

med-immuno.l16.q5.t: Encapsulated bacteria such as pneumococcus and Haemophilus influenzae
med-immuno.l16.q5.p: A 6-year-old with sickle cell disease and autosplenectomy has fever of 39.8 C and appears toxic. Which organism group poses the greatest risk because of his immune defect?
med-immuno.l16.q5.h: The spleen clears opsonized encapsulated organisms.
med-immuno.l16.q5.e: Asplenia impairs clearance of encapsulated bacteria. Catalase-positive infection is characteristic of chronic granulomatous disease.

med-immuno.l17.q1.t: Preformed recipient antibodies to donor antigens fixing complement
med-immuno.l17.q1.p: What causes hyperacute rejection of a transplanted kidney?
med-immuno.l17.q1.h: It occurs within minutes to hours.
med-immuno.l17.q1.e: Hyperacute rejection results from preformed antibodies, such as ABO or HLA antibodies, with complement activation. T cell infiltration describes acute cellular rejection.

med-immuno.l17.q2.t: Tacrolimus, which binds FKBP12 and blocks calcineurin activity
med-immuno.l17.q2.p: Which drug inhibits calcineurin and so reduces IL-2 gene transcription in T cells?
med-immuno.l17.q2.h: The drug class also includes cyclosporine.
