med-immuno.l17.q2.e: Tacrolimus and cyclosporine inhibit calcineurin. Sirolimus acts on mTOR and mycophenolate on purine synthesis.

med-immuno.l17.q3.t: Acute antibody-mediated rejection, a complement-fixing type II process
med-immuno.l17.q3.p: A 45-year-old kidney recipient has a rising creatinine 8 months after transplant. Biopsy shows peritubular capillaritis with C4d deposition and circulating donor-specific antibodies. Which type of rejection is most likely?
med-immuno.l17.q3.h: C4d marks classical pathway activation by antibody.
med-immuno.l17.q3.e: C4d with donor-specific antibodies indicates antibody-mediated rejection. Acute cellular rejection shows lymphocytic tubulitis without C4d.

med-immuno.l17.q4.t: Donor T cells recognizing recipient HLA antigens in skin, liver and gut
med-immuno.l17.q4.p: A 30-year-old has a bone marrow transplant for leukemia. Three weeks later he has a maculopapular rash, cholestatic jaundice and watery diarrhea. Which mechanism best explains this?
med-immuno.l17.q4.h: The graft contains immunocompetent cells that see the host as foreign.
med-immuno.l17.q4.e: Acute GVHD results from donor T cells attacking recipient tissues. Rejection involves the recipient attacking the graft.

med-immuno.l17.q5.t: Reduced breakdown of the metabolite 6-mercaptopurine raising marrow toxicity
med-immuno.l17.q5.p: A kidney transplant recipient on azathioprine is started on allopurinol for gout. Within weeks, he develops marked leukopenia. Which mechanism is most likely?
med-immuno.l17.q5.e: Xanthine oxidase inhibition slows metabolism of 6-mercaptopurine, raising its toxic levels. Azathioprine is not a calcineurin or mTOR inhibitor.

med-immuno.l18.q1.t: Pembrolizumab, used in melanoma and lung cancer
med-immuno.l18.q1.p: Which monoclonal antibody blocks the PD-1 receptor on T cells?
med-immuno.l18.q1.h: The suffix and the name differ from the CTLA-4 antibody.
med-immuno.l18.q1.e: Pembrolizumab and nivolumab target PD-1. Ipilimumab targets CTLA-4, rituximab CD20 and trastuzumab HER2.

med-immuno.l18.q2.t: A high burden of mutation-derived neoantigens
med-immuno.l18.q2.p: Which feature would predict a good response of a tumor to checkpoint inhibitors?
med-immuno.l18.q2.h: The immune system needs foreign-looking targets.
med-immuno.l18.q2.e: High neoantigen load provides targets for released T cells. Loss of antigen processing is a mechanism of resistance.

med-immuno.l18.q3.t: Immune-related hypophysitis causing secondary adrenal insufficiency
med-immuno.l18.q3.p: A 62-year-old with metastatic melanoma on combination checkpoint therapy develops fatigue, hypotension, hyponatremia and low cortisol. ACTH is low. Which process is most likely?
med-immuno.l18.q3.h: Low ACTH points to the pituitary.
med-immuno.l18.q3.e: Checkpoint inhibitors can inflame the pituitary, causing central adrenal insufficiency. Colitis would present with diarrhea and normal ACTH axis.

med-immuno.l18.q4.t: Tocilizumab, an antibody that blocks the interleukin 6 receptor
med-immuno.l18.q4.p: A 28-year-old with refractory B cell lymphoma receives CD19-directed CAR T cells. Two days later he has fever of 39.5 C, hypotension and elevated IL-6 and ferritin. Which therapy targets the likely mechanism?
med-immuno.l18.q4.e: CAR T cell cytokine release syndrome is driven by IL-6, and tocilizumab is used. Eculizumab and omalizumab target other pathways.

med-immuno.l18.q5.t: CD8 cells cannot see the cells, but NK cells may be activated
med-immuno.l18.q5.p: A tumor biopsy shows markedly reduced surface MHC class I expression. Which statement about immune escape is correct?
med-immuno.l18.q5.e: Loss of class I hides tumors from CD8 cells but removes the inhibitory signal for NK cells. Class II is recognized by CD4 cells.

med-immuno.l19.q1.t: The carrier protein recruits T helper cells for switching and memory
med-immuno.l19.q1.p: Why are conjugate vaccines more immunogenic than plain polysaccharide vaccines in infants?
med-immuno.l19.q1.h: It converts a T-independent antigen to a T-dependent one.
med-immuno.l19.q1.e: Conjugation to a protein engages T helper cells. Conjugate vaccines do not replicate.

med-immuno.l19.q2.t: A live attenuated vaccine, such as measles, mumps and rubella
med-immuno.l19.q2.p: Which vaccine type is most likely to be contraindicated in a person with severe combined immunodeficiency?
med-immuno.l19.q2.h: Which type can replicate in the host?
med-immuno.l19.q2.e: Live attenuated vaccines can cause disseminated disease in people without T cell function. The other types cannot replicate.

med-immuno.l19.q3.t: Tetanus immune globulin together with tetanus toxoid at a separate site
med-immuno.l19.q3.p: A 26-year-old unvaccinated man has a deep puncture wound from a rusty nail. Which management provides both immediate and lasting protection against tetanus?
med-immuno.l19.q3.h: One component gives immediate antitoxin and one gives memory.
med-immuno.l19.q3.e: Immune globulin gives immediate passive antitoxin, and toxoid starts active immunity. Antibody alone would give no memory.

med-immuno.l19.q4.t: Rabies immune globulin and vaccine together, since vaccine antibody lags
med-immuno.l19.q4.p: A 2-year-old is bitten by a stray dog, and rabies is a concern. Which is correct about the preventive approach?
med-immuno.l19.q4.h: The vaccine takes days to weeks to produce antibody.
med-immuno.l19.q4.e: Post-exposure prophylaxis combines passive antibody for immediate cover with vaccine for lasting immunity. Immune globulin is infiltrated around the wound.

med-immuno.l19.q5.t: Maternal IgG transferred across the placenta that wanes in months
med-immuno.l19.q5.p: A 3-month-old infant is exposed to an adult with measles. Compared with an older child with no vaccine history, which feature best explains why the infant may have partial protection?
med-immuno.l19.q5.e: Maternal IgG crossing the placenta gives temporary protection that declines over months. A 3-month-old has not yet formed memory cells.

med-immuno.l20.q1.t: Western blot, in which proteins are transferred to a membrane and probed
med-immuno.l20.q1.p: Which laboratory method detects proteins using specific antibodies after size separation on a gel?
med-immuno.l20.q1.h: The directional blots are named for compass points.
med-immuno.l20.q1.e: Western blotting detects proteins. Southern detects DNA and northern detects RNA.

med-immuno.l20.q2.t: A narrow gamma-region spike that immunofixation assigns to one clone
med-immuno.l20.q2.p: Which finding on serum protein electrophoresis suggests a monoclonal gammopathy?
med-immuno.l20.q2.e: A sharp spike reflects a single clone, and immunofixation identifies its type. A broad band is polyclonal.

med-immuno.l20.q3.t: Classical pathway consumption by immune complexes, as in lupus nephritis
med-immuno.l20.q3.p: A 34-year-old has fever, malar rash and hematuria. CH50 is low, with low C3 and low C4. Which interpretation fits best?
med-immuno.l20.q3.h: Both C3 and C4 are consumed.
med-immuno.l20.q3.e: Low C3 and C4 with low CH50 indicate classical pathway consumption. Terminal defects show absent CH50 with normal C3 and C4.

med-immuno.l20.q4.t: Sequencing of the BTK gene on the X chromosome
med-immuno.l20.q4.p: A 20-year-old with recurrent infections has flow cytometry showing absent CD19 positive B cells with normal T cell counts. Which assay would best confirm the diagnosis at the genetic level?
med-immuno.l20.q4.h: Absent B cells in a male with recurrent infections.
med-immuno.l20.q4.e: Absent B cells suggest X-linked agammaglobulinemia, and BTK sequencing confirms it. The dihydrorhodamine assay tests phagocyte oxidative burst.

med-immuno.l20.q5.t: Maternal antibody bound to the infant red cells
med-immuno.l20.q5.p: A newborn of an O-positive mother has jaundice, and the infant is A-positive. The direct Coombs test is positive. What does this result indicate?
med-immuno.l20.q5.h: The direct test examines the patient's own cells.
med-immuno.l20.q5.e: A positive direct Coombs test shows antibody or complement on the patient's own red cells, as in ABO hemolytic disease. The indirect test detects free serum antibody.

med-micro.l01.q1.t: A thick peptidoglycan layer that traps the crystal violet-iodine complex
med-micro.l01.q1.p: Which structure accounts for the retention of crystal violet by Gram-positive bacteria after alcohol decolorisation?
med-micro.l01.q1.h: Think about which wall thickness holds the stain complex.
med-micro.l01.q1.e: The thick peptidoglycan wall retains the complex. A thin wall under an outer membrane describes Gram-negatives, which lose the stain when alcohol disrupts the outer membrane.

med-micro.l01.q2.t: Gram-negative rods with an outer membrane containing porins
med-micro.l01.q2.p: A drug is effective against Staphylococcus aureus but is too large to pass through porin channels. Which organism group will it most likely fail to treat?
med-micro.l01.q2.h: Porins are in a specific membrane.
med-micro.l01.q2.e: The outer membrane of Gram-negative rods limits entry of large molecules such as vancomycin. Gram-positive cocci lack that barrier, so such drugs reach their target.

med-micro.l01.q3.t: It is the toxic component that activates TLR4 and drives septic shock
med-micro.l01.q3.p: Which statement about lipid A of lipopolysaccharide is correct?
med-micro.l01.q3.h: Think about what part of LPS the immune system senses.
med-micro.l01.q3.e: Lipid A is the endotoxin and is sensed by TLR4. The O antigen is variable and defines serotype but is not the toxic moiety.

med-micro.l01.q4.t: Lipid A released from the outer membrane and sensed by macrophages
med-micro.l01.q4.p: A 64-year-old woman has fever, hypotension and a urinary catheter. Blood cultures grow pink rods. Her low blood pressure is most directly caused by which bacterial component?
med-micro.l01.q4.h: Pink rods in blood point to which wall type?
med-micro.l01.q4.e: Gram-negative rods release lipid A, which triggers cytokine-mediated vasodilation and shock. Capsule aids evasion but does not itself cause hypotension; teichoic acids belong to Gram-positives.

med-micro.l01.q5.t: Endospores containing dipicolinic acid and a dehydrated core
med-micro.l01.q5.p: A 28-year-old farm worker has a cut that forms a necrotic lesion. A smear shows large Gram-positive rods, and the culture regrows after being boiled. Which structure explains the regrowth?
med-micro.l01.q5.e: Spores are dehydrated, dipicolinic acid-rich and survive boiling, matching a Bacillus or Clostridium organism. Mycolic acid is characteristic of mycobacteria, which are not spore-formers.

med-micro.l02.q1.t: Transformation by a naturally competent organism such as pneumococcus
med-micro.l02.q1.p: Which mechanism of gene transfer involves uptake of naked DNA from the environment by a competent cell?
med-micro.l02.q1.h: The DNA is free in the surroundings.
med-micro.l02.q1.e: Transformation is uptake of free DNA. Conjugation requires direct cell contact via a pilus, and transduction needs a phage.

med-micro.l02.q2.t: Obligate anaerobes such as Bacteroides fragilis and Clostridium
med-micro.l02.q2.p: Which bacteria lack superoxide dismutase and catalase and so die in oxygen?
med-micro.l02.q2.h: Think about organisms found in abscesses and the gut lumen.
med-micro.l02.q2.e: Obligate anaerobes cannot detoxify reactive oxygen. Facultatives have those enzymes, and aerotolerant organisms tolerate oxygen.

med-micro.l02.q3.t: Lysogenic conversion by a prophage that encodes the toxin
med-micro.l02.q3.p: A harmless strain acquires the gene for a toxin after being infected by a temperate virus that integrates into its chromosome. This process is called what?
med-micro.l02.q3.h: A temperate phage inserted into the genome is a prophage.
med-micro.l02.q3.e: A prophage encoding a toxin converts the host, as with diphtheria and Shiga toxin. Transformation uses naked DNA, not phage.

med-micro.l02.q4.t: Conjugative plasmid transfer of the resistance gene between Enterobacterales
med-micro.l02.q4.p: A hospital ward sees Klebsiella, Escherichia coli and Enterobacter isolates in unrelated patients, all resistant to the same third-generation cephalosporin and carrying an identical resistance gene. What mechanism most likely explains this pattern?
med-micro.l02.q4.h: The same gene in different species suggests a mobile element.
med-micro.l02.q4.e: An identical gene across species points to a plasmid moved by conjugation. Independent mutations would produce different changes, and phages are usually species-restricted.

med-micro.l02.q5.t: The rough bacteria took up capsule genes released from dead bacteria by transformation
med-micro.l02.q5.p: Heat-killed smooth encapsulated pneumococci are mixed with living rough nonencapsulated pneumococci and injected into a mouse, which dies. Live smooth bacteria are recovered. What explains the finding?
med-micro.l02.q5.h: Dead cells cannot conjugate or revive.
med-micro.l02.q5.e: Naked DNA from the dead cells was taken up by competent living cells, which is transformation (Griffith). Conjugation needs a living donor.

med-micro.l03.q1.t: ADP-ribosylation of elongation factor 2, halting protein synthesis
med-micro.l03.q1.p: What is the mechanism of action of diphtheria toxin?
med-micro.l03.q1.e: Diphtheria toxin ADP-ribosylates EF-2. Cholera toxin acts on Gs, and Shiga toxin cleaves 28S rRNA.

med-micro.l03.q2.t: Exotoxins are secreted proteins that can be made into toxoids, unlike endotoxin
med-micro.l03.q2.p: Which statement correctly distinguishes exotoxins from endotoxin?
med-micro.l03.q2.h: Toxoid vaccines need a protein antigen.
med-micro.l03.q2.e: Exotoxins are generally proteins and strongly immunogenic, so toxoids work. Endotoxin is lipid A, and it acts via TLR4.

med-micro.l03.q3.t: Tetanus toxin blocks inhibitory interneuron release, and botulinum toxin blocks acetylcholine release
med-micro.l03.q3.p: Tetanus toxin and botulinum toxin both cleave SNARE proteins. Why do they produce spastic and flaccid paralysis respectively?
med-micro.l03.q3.h: Consider which synapses each toxin reaches.
med-micro.l03.q3.e: Tetanus toxin travels retrograde to inhibitory interneurons and blocks glycine and GABA, while botulinum acts at the neuromuscular junction on acetylcholine release.

med-micro.l03.q4.t: Cross-linking MHC class II to the T cell receptor, causing polyclonal T cell activation
med-micro.l03.q4.p: A 19-year-old woman using a tampon develops fever, hypotension, a diffuse erythematous rash and multi-organ dysfunction. The toxin responsible most likely acts by which mechanism?
med-micro.l03.q4.h: The syndrome is driven by cytokine release from T cells.
med-micro.l03.q4.e: TSST-1 is a superantigen binding outside the peptide groove, activating many T cells. A lecithinase (alpha toxin) causes gas gangrene instead.

med-micro.l03.q5.t: ADP-ribosylation of Gs, locking it active so adenylate cyclase stays on
med-micro.l03.q5.p: After travel, a 30-year-old has rice-water diarrhea and severe dehydration. The toxin raises intracellular cAMP in enterocytes. Which description of the underlying molecular event is correct?
med-micro.l03.q5.h: Compare with the pertussis toxin target.
med-micro.l03.q5.e: Cholera toxin modifies Gs. Pertussis toxin modifies Gi, and the heat-stable toxin of enterotoxigenic E. coli raises cGMP.

med-micro.l04.q1.t: Lactobacillus species that maintain a low vaginal pH
med-micro.l04.q1.p: Which organism is the predominant member of the normal vaginal flora in a healthy reproductive-age woman?
med-micro.l04.q1.e: Lactobacilli keep the pH acidic. E. coli and Candida can be present in small numbers but are not dominant.

med-micro.l04.q2.t: Loss of colonisation resistance allowing a resistant organism to overgrow the gut
med-micro.l04.q2.p: A patient on broad-spectrum antibiotics develops severe watery diarrhea. Which concept best explains the susceptibility?
med-micro.l04.q2.h: What do commensals normally do against invaders?
med-micro.l04.q2.e: Antibiotics suppress the flora and permit C. difficile overgrowth. The other options describe mechanisms that do not occur.

med-micro.l04.q3.t: Those with absent splenic function after trauma
med-micro.l04.q3.p: Which patient group is most predisposed to overwhelming sepsis with Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae because opsonised bacteria are poorly cleared from the blood?
med-micro.l04.q3.h: Which organ clears opsonised bacteria from blood?
med-micro.l04.q3.e: Without a spleen, opsonised encapsulated bacteria are poorly cleared. Terminal complement deficiency predisposes mainly to Neisseria rather than pneumococcus or Haemophilus, and neutropenia to Pseudomonas and fungi.

med-micro.l04.q4.t: Biofilm formation on the foreign material, which shields it from host defences
med-micro.l04.q4.p: A 58-year-old man had a prosthetic hip placed four months ago. He now has dull pain and a low-grade fever, and the joint culture grows coagulase-negative staphylococci on three samples. This organism is pathogenic here primarily because of which feature?
med-micro.l04.q4.h: Skin commensals cause trouble where something foreign sits.
med-micro.l04.q4.e: S. epidermidis forms biofilms on prosthetic material. It lacks the potent exotoxins of S. aureus.

med-micro.l04.q5.t: Many pathogens cannot be cultured in pure form, so the postulates cannot be satisfied
med-micro.l04.q5.p: A team wants to prove that a newly discovered bacterium causes a chronic disease but cannot grow it in culture. Which limitation of Koch postulates does this illustrate?
med-micro.l04.q5.h: Pure culture is a required step.
med-micro.l04.q5.e: Postulates need isolation in pure culture, which fails for unculturable organisms. Carriers and multi-causal disease are other limits, but not the one tested here.

med-micro.l05.q1.t: Coagulase reaction clotting rabbit plasma in the tube
med-micro.l05.q1.p: Which test best distinguishes Staphylococcus aureus from coagulase-negative staphylococci?
med-micro.l05.q1.e: S. aureus is coagulase-positive. Catalase separates staphylococci from streptococci, and bacitracin and optochin are tests for streptococci.

med-micro.l05.q2.t: An altered penicillin-binding protein with low drug affinity
med-micro.l05.q2.p: What explains methicillin resistance in MRSA?
med-micro.l05.q2.e: mecA encodes PBP2a. Beta-lactamase mediates penicillin resistance but is overcome by methicillin, and porin loss applies to Gram-negatives.

med-micro.l05.q3.t: Resistance to bacitracin and a positive hippurate test
med-micro.l05.q3.p: Which feature identifies a beta-hemolytic streptococcus as group B rather than group A?
med-micro.l05.q3.h: Group A is the one that is bacitracin-sensitive.
med-micro.l05.q3.e: Group B is bacitracin-resistant and hippurate-positive. Optochin sensitivity identifies pneumococcus.

med-micro.l05.q4.t: Antibodies to M protein cross-react with cardiac and joint antigens
med-micro.l05.q4.p: A 17-year-old has fever, a diffuse sandpaper-like rash and a red tongue after pharyngitis. A different child has joint pain, carditis and chorea weeks after pharyngitis. Which statement best explains why the second child has damage after the organism is gone?
med-micro.l05.q4.e: Rheumatic fever is due to cross-reactive immune responses. Immune complex deposition with low C3 characterises poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, a different sequela.

med-micro.l05.q5.t: Staphylococcus aureus with septic emboli to the lungs
med-micro.l05.q5.p: A 34-year-old man who injects drugs has fever, a new tricuspid regurgitation murmur and multiple round lung opacities. Blood cultures grow clusters of Gram-positive cocci, catalase-positive and coagulase-positive. Which organism is the most likely cause?
med-micro.l05.q5.h: Right-sided endocarditis and the coagulase result point to one species.
med-micro.l05.q5.e: S. aureus causes acute tricuspid endocarditis in people who inject drugs, with septic pulmonary emboli. S. epidermidis is coagulase-negative.

med-micro.l06.q1.t: Clostridioides difficile, which produces toxins A and B
med-micro.l06.q1.p: Which organism causes pseudomembranous colitis after antibiotic exposure?
med-micro.l06.q1.e: C. difficile toxins A and B cause colitis after disruption of flora. C. perfringens causes gangrene and a self-limited food poisoning.

med-micro.l06.q2.t: Polymerisation of host actin that propels the bacterium
med-micro.l06.q2.p: A pregnant woman develops fever and flu-like illness after eating unpasteurised soft cheese. Which feature of the likely organism explains its spread from cell to cell?
med-micro.l06.q2.e: Listeria forms actin tails to move between cells. Alpha toxin is the lecithinase of C. perfringens, and edema factor is the cyclase of anthrax.

med-micro.l06.q3.t: Nocardia: aerobic, weakly acid-fast, causes lung and brain abscesses
med-micro.l06.q3.p: Which pair correctly matches the filamentous organism with its features?
med-micro.l06.q3.e: Nocardia is aerobic and weakly acid-fast, and affects immunocompromised hosts. Actinomyces is anaerobic and non-acid-fast and causes sulfur granule lesions.

med-micro.l06.q4.t: Blocked release of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction
med-micro.l06.q4.p: A 4-month-old, previously healthy and fed honey-sweetened water, has poor feeding, a weak cry, drooping eyelids and generalised hypotonia. What is the underlying pathology?
med-micro.l06.q4.e: Infant botulism produces flaccid paralysis through blocked acetylcholine release. Blocked inhibitory release causes the spasticity of tetanus.

med-micro.l06.q5.t: An anaerobic spore-forming rod with a terminal round spore
med-micro.l06.q5.p: A 29-year-old man steps on a rusty nail and later has jaw stiffness, a fixed grin and painful spasms triggered by noise. The organism responsible is best described as which of the following?
med-micro.l06.q5.e: Clostridium tetani is an anaerobic spore-former with a terminal spore. The first option describes B. anthracis, the second C. diphtheriae, the last Listeria.

med-micro.l07.q1.t: Salmonella enterica serotype Typhi from human stool
med-micro.l07.q1.p: On MacConkey agar, which organism is a non-lactose fermenter?
med-micro.l07.q1.e: Salmonella and Shigella do not ferment lactose and give colourless colonies. E. coli, Klebsiella and Enterobacter ferment it.

med-micro.l07.q2.t: Struvite stones and recurrent urinary infection
med-micro.l07.q2.p: A urine culture grows a swarming organism that produces urease and raises urine pH. What complication is most associated with this organism?
med-micro.l07.q2.h: Alkaline urine precipitates magnesium ammonium phosphate.
med-micro.l07.q2.e: Proteus urease produces ammonia and alkaline urine, promoting struvite stones. The other stones are not related to infection.

med-micro.l07.q3.t: Enterohemorrhagic E. coli of serotype O157:H7
med-micro.l07.q3.p: Which organism produces Shiga toxin and ferments sorbitol poorly on selective media?
med-micro.l07.q3.e: O157:H7 produces Shiga toxin and is sorbitol-negative. ETEC causes watery diarrhea through heat-labile and heat-stable toxins.

med-micro.l07.q4.p: A 19-year-old college student has fever, headache and neck stiffness. A rapidly spreading petechial rash and hypotension develop, and the Gram stain of CSF shows kidney-shaped intracellular diplococci. Which finding is the patient most likely to have?
med-micro.l07.q4.e: Meningococcus can cause Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome with adrenal hemorrhage. Disseminated gonorrhea gives arthritis and pustules but rarely meningitis.

med-micro.l07.q5.t: A motile, non-lactose-fermenting rod that persists in the gallbladder
med-micro.l07.q5.p: A 26-year-old woman has a stepwise rising fever for one week, relative bradycardia, rose spots on the abdomen and constipation after returning from South Asia. Which description best fits the organism?
med-micro.l07.q5.e: Salmonella Typhi is a motile non-lactose fermenter with chronic gallbladder carriage. The first option describes Shigella.

med-micro.l08.q1.t: Pseudomonas aeruginosa, an oxidase-positive aerobic rod
med-micro.l08.q1.p: Which organism produces blue-green pigment and a grape-like odour and is a common cause of infection in burn wounds?
med-micro.l08.q1.e: Pseudomonas aeruginosa makes pyocyanin and is oxidase-positive. Acinetobacter is oxidase-negative and does not produce this pigment.

med-micro.l08.q2.t: It is a urease-positive curved rod whose enzyme buffers gastric acid
med-micro.l08.q2.p: Which statement about Helicobacter pylori is correct?
med-micro.l08.q2.h: The urea breath test relies on this enzyme.
med-micro.l08.q2.e: The urease releases ammonia and supports colonisation. The organism is not acid-fast and does not form pseudomembranes.

med-micro.l08.q3.t: Haemophilus influenzae type b causing epiglottitis
med-micro.l08.q3.p: A 4-year-old child is not vaccinated and has a sudden high fever, drooling, a muffled voice and a tripod posture. Which organism is the classic cause?
med-micro.l08.q3.e: Epiglottitis in unvaccinated children is classically due to Hib. Diphtheria causes a pseudomembrane but a different presentation.

med-micro.l08.q4.t: Urinary antigen test for Legionella pneumophila serogroup 1
med-micro.l08.q4.p: A 62-year-old man with fever, dry cough, watery diarrhea and confusion has a sodium of 127 mmol/L and a lobar infiltrate. Gram stain of sputum shows few organisms and many neutrophils. Which diagnostic approach is most appropriate?
med-micro.l08.q4.h: Few organisms on Gram stain plus hyponatremia suggests an atypical cause.
med-micro.l08.q4.e: This picture suggests Legionella, for which urinary antigen testing is rapid. Optochin identifies pneumococcus, and Legionella stains poorly.

med-micro.l08.q5.t: Inactivation of Gi by pertussis toxin, impairing lymphocyte homing
med-micro.l08.q5.p: A 3-month-old unvaccinated infant has bursts of coughing followed by apnea, and the white count is 35,000 per microliter with 70 percent lymphocytes. Which mechanism most directly explains the lymphocytosis?
med-micro.l08.q5.h: Think about the toxin that targets Gi.
med-micro.l08.q5.e: Pertussis toxin modifies Gi and blocks lymphocyte entry to tissues so they accumulate in blood. Cholera toxin acts on Gs.

med-micro.l09.q1.t: Mycolic acid, a long-chain fatty acid in the wall
med-micro.l09.q1.p: What cell wall component makes mycobacteria acid-fast?
med-micro.l09.q1.h: The stain uses carbol fuchsin and acid-alcohol.
med-micro.l09.q1.e: Mycolic acids make the wall waxy and acid-fast. Lipid A is part of Gram-negative LPS, and teichoic acids are Gram-positive.

med-micro.l09.q2.t: Peripheral neuropathy from impaired vitamin B6 activity
med-micro.l09.q2.p: Which adverse effect is classically associated with isoniazid and prevented by pyridoxine?
med-micro.l09.q2.e: Isoniazid causes B6-responsive neuropathy. Optic neuritis is ethambutol, orange fluids are rifampin, and hyperuricemia is pyrazinamide.

med-micro.l09.q3.t: A positive skin test can follow BCG vaccination or nontuberculous exposure
med-micro.l09.q3.p: Which statement about tuberculin skin testing and interferon gamma release assays is correct?
med-micro.l09.q3.h: The skin test uses a purified protein derivative with many shared antigens.
med-micro.l09.q3.e: Skin test cross-reactivity with BCG and environmental mycobacteria causes false positives. The release assays use antigens absent from BCG.

med-micro.l09.q4.t: Th1-driven macrophage activation with granuloma caseation
med-micro.l09.q4.p: A 52-year-old man with long-standing alcohol use has three months of cough, night sweats and weight loss. Chest radiograph shows an apical cavity. Which immune mechanism produces the tissue necrosis seen in this lesion?
med-micro.l09.q4.e: Caseating necrosis arises from Th1 and interferon gamma activated macrophages in granulomas. Immune complex deposition is not the mechanism in tuberculosis.

med-micro.l09.q5.t: Mycobacterium avium complex, because CD4 depletion permits dissemination
med-micro.l09.q5.p: A 41-year-old man with advanced HIV and a CD4 count of 30 cells per microliter has fever, night sweats, diarrhea and hepatosplenomegaly. Blood cultures grow acid-fast bacilli. Which organism is most likely, and what is the key host factor?
med-micro.l09.q5.h: Think about what level of CD4 count predisposes to this organism.
med-micro.l09.q5.e: MAC disseminates at very low CD4 counts. M. kansasii causes cavitary lung disease and M. leprae grows in cool tissues.

med-micro.l10.q1.p: Which test is nontreponemal and used to monitor treatment response in syphilis?
med-micro.l10.q1.h: The antibody it detects is against cardiolipin.
med-micro.l10.q1.e: RPR and VDRL are nontreponemal and track disease activity. The treponemal tests stay positive for life.

med-micro.l10.q2.t: Borrelia burgdorferi transmitted by Ixodes ticks
med-micro.l10.q2.p: A hiker has an expanding annular rash with central clearing 10 days after a tick bite in New England. Which organism and vector are responsible?
med-micro.l10.q2.e: Erythema migrans is typical for B. burgdorferi from Ixodes ticks. R. rickettsii causes a centripetal petechial rash.

med-micro.l10.q3.t: Aortitis of the ascending aorta with aneurysm formation
med-micro.l10.q3.p: Which finding is typical of tertiary syphilis?
med-micro.l10.q3.e: Cardiovascular syphilis, gummas and neurosyphilis are tertiary. Chancre is primary and the palms-and-soles rash with condylomata lata is secondary.

med-micro.l10.q4.t: Release of bacterial products as spirochetes are killed
med-micro.l10.q4.p: A 29-year-old man has a painless genital ulcer. After a single dose of penicillin, he develops fever, chills and myalgias within hours that resolve within a day. What best explains this reaction?
med-micro.l10.q4.e: Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction follows rapid killing of spirochetes. Anaphylaxis would present with hives, wheeze and hypotension, and it does not resolve in a day without therapy.

med-micro.l10.q5.t: Leptospira interrogans, a spirochete from animal urine
med-micro.l10.q5.p: A 24-year-old farm worker who swam in a flooded river has a week of fever, conjunctival suffusion and calf pain, and then jaundice, a rising creatinine and bleeding. Which organism is most likely?
med-micro.l10.q5.e: Leptospira from urine-contaminated water produces Weil disease. Borrelia recurrentis causes relapsing fever without renal failure.

med-micro.l11.q1.t: The elementary body, which is metabolically inactive
med-micro.l11.q1.p: Which form of Chlamydia is the infectious extracellular form?
med-micro.l11.q1.e: Elementary bodies infect. Reticulate bodies are the replicating intracellular form, and Chlamydia does not form spores.

med-micro.l11.q2.t: The organism has no cell wall, so it has no peptidoglycan target
med-micro.l11.q2.p: Why does a beta-lactam fail to treat Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection?
med-micro.l11.q2.h: Think about what the drug attacks.
med-micro.l11.q2.e: Mycoplasma lacks a cell wall. Chlamydia is intracellular, but Mycoplasma is not obligate intracellular.

med-micro.l11.q3.t: Coxiella burnetii, the cause of Q fever
med-micro.l11.q3.p: Which organism is acquired by inhaling aerosols from livestock birthing products rather than by a vector?
med-micro.l11.q3.e: Q fever is aerosol-acquired from livestock. The others are all arthropod-borne rickettsial diseases.

med-micro.l11.q4.t: Start doxycycline now, because delay increases mortality in this disease
med-micro.l11.q4.p: A 9-year-old in Georgia has fever, headache and a rash that began at the wrists and ankles and spread to the palms, soles and trunk after a tick exposure. The laboratory results are pending. What is the most appropriate approach to this patient?
med-micro.l11.q4.h: The organism infects endothelium and kills when untreated.
med-micro.l11.q4.e: Rocky Mountain spotted fever is treated empirically with doxycycline, as delay raises mortality. The organism is a rickettsia, and beta-lactams are ineffective.

med-micro.l11.q5.t: Pelvic inflammatory disease with tubal scarring and infertility
med-micro.l11.q5.p: A 22-year-old man has urethritis, and a nucleic acid amplification test is positive for an organism with a biphasic life cycle that cannot be grown on routine agar. Which complication is most associated with untreated infection in a woman?
med-micro.l11.q5.h: Consider the genital serovars D to K.
med-micro.l11.q5.e: Urogenital serovars cause PID and infertility. LGV (L1 to L3) causes buboes, and trachoma (A to C) causes conjunctival scarring.

med-micro.l12.q1.p: Which organism is associated with unpasteurised dairy products and undulant fever?
med-micro.l12.q1.h: Think of goat and sheep milk.
med-micro.l12.q1.e: Brucella causes undulant fever from raw milk. Francisella is linked to rabbits, Pasteurella to bites, and Yersinia pestis to fleas.

med-micro.l12.q2.p: A patient has a rapidly spreading cellulitis within 12 hours of a cat bite. Which organism is the most likely cause?
med-micro.l12.q2.e: Pasteurella multocida causes fast cellulitis after cat and dog bites. Bartonella causes a lymph node syndrome over weeks.

med-micro.l12.q3.t: Bipolar-staining rods with a safety pin appearance
med-micro.l12.q3.p: Which description fits Yersinia pestis on a stained smear?
med-micro.l12.q3.e: Y. pestis shows bipolar staining. Club-shaped palisades are C. diphtheriae, and branching filaments describe Nocardia.

med-micro.l12.q4.t: Progression to pneumonic disease with person-to-person droplet spread
med-micro.l12.q4.p: A 47-year-old rancher in New Mexico has fever and a painful, enlarged inguinal node with overlying erythema after being bitten by fleas while clearing a prairie dog burrow. Gram stain of a node aspirate shows bipolar-staining Gram-negative rods. If untreated, what is the greatest public health concern?
med-micro.l12.q4.h: Think about the three forms of this infection.
med-micro.l12.q4.e: Bubonic plague can seed the lungs, and pneumonic plague spreads by droplets. Gallbladder carriage describes Salmonella Typhi.

med-micro.l12.q5.t: Anaplasma phagocytophilum, transmitted by Ixodes ticks
med-micro.l12.q5.p: A 36-year-old woman living in the northeastern United States has fever, myalgia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia and raised transaminases, without rash. A blood smear shows intracytoplasmic clusters in neutrophils. Which organism is the most likely cause?
med-micro.l12.q5.h: Which cell type holds the morulae?
med-micro.l12.q5.e: Anaplasma infects neutrophils and is carried by Ixodes ticks. Ehrlichia chaffeensis infects monocytes and R. rickettsii infects endothelium.

med-micro.l13.q1.t: Poxviruses, which carry their own replication machinery
med-micro.l13.q1.p: Which viral family replicates its DNA genome in the cytoplasm using its own enzymes?
med-micro.l13.q1.h: Most DNA viruses use the nucleus.
med-micro.l13.q1.e: Poxviruses are the main exception and replicate in the cytoplasm. The other three replicate in the nucleus.

med-micro.l13.q2.t: E6 and E7 inactivate p53 and Rb, removing cell cycle control
med-micro.l13.q2.p: Which mechanism explains how high-risk HPV types promote cervical cancer?
med-micro.l13.q2.h: Two viral proteins, two host tumor suppressors.
med-micro.l13.q2.e: E6 degrades p53 and E7 inhibits Rb. The c-myc translocation mechanism relates to Burkitt lymphoma with EBV.

med-micro.l13.q3.t: Reassortment of genome segments between two strains in one cell
med-micro.l13.q3.p: Antigenic shift in influenza A results from which process?
med-micro.l13.q3.e: Reassortment produces new HA and NA combinations and pandemic risk. Point mutations produce drift.

med-micro.l13.q4.t: Infection of erythroid progenitors, halting red cell production temporarily
med-micro.l13.q4.p: A 22-year-old woman with sickle cell disease has fatigue, pallor and a sudden fall in hemoglobin, with reticulocytopenia, after her niece had a slapped-cheek rash. What is the mechanism of the sudden anemia?
med-micro.l13.q4.e: Parvovirus B19 targets erythroid precursors via the P antigen, causing aplastic crisis in chronic hemolysis. Cold agglutinins are linked to Mycoplasma.

med-micro.l13.q5.t: BK virus, which reactivates in immunosuppressed transplant recipients
med-micro.l13.q5.p: A 49-year-old kidney transplant recipient has painless hematuria and a rising creatinine. Biopsy shows nuclear inclusions in tubular epithelium with a polyomavirus-positive stain. Which virus is the most likely cause?
med-micro.l13.q5.e: BK virus reactivates in kidney transplant recipients causing nephropathy. JC virus causes PML.

med-micro.l14.q1.t: In dorsal root ganglia and cranial nerve ganglia
med-micro.l14.q1.p: Where does varicella-zoster virus remain latent?
med-micro.l14.q1.e: VZV is latent in sensory ganglia. B cells are the EBV reservoir, and monocytes are the CMV reservoir.

med-micro.l14.q2.t: It requires activation by viral thymidine kinase before inhibition of polymerase
med-micro.l14.q2.p: Why does acyclovir selectively target infected cells?
med-micro.l14.q2.e: Acyclovir is phosphorylated by viral thymidine kinase and then terminates DNA chains. Neuraminidase inhibition is for influenza.

med-micro.l14.q3.p: Which virus is associated with owl-eye intranuclear inclusions and congenital hearing loss?
med-micro.l14.q3.e: CMV inclusions are owl-eye and congenital CMV causes deafness. EBV causes mononucleosis.

med-micro.l14.q4.t: Activated cytotoxic CD8 T cells reacting to the infected B cells
med-micro.l14.q4.p: A 27-year-old has had two weeks of fever, a very sore throat and neck nodes, and the monospot test is positive. His blood smear shows large atypical lymphocytes. Which cell type accounts for most of these atypical lymphocytes?
med-micro.l14.q4.h: The infected cell is not the one on the smear.
med-micro.l14.q4.e: Most atypical lymphocytes are expanded, activated CD8 T cells that kill EBV-infected B cells. The infected B cells are a minority and are not the cells that dominate the smear.

med-micro.l14.q5.t: Begin intravenous acyclovir while sending CSF HSV PCR
med-micro.l14.q5.p: A 34-year-old with a new fever, headache and personality change has temporal lobe enhancement on MRI and a CSF showing red cells and lymphocytes. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
med-micro.l14.q5.e: HSV encephalitis needs empirical intravenous acyclovir pending PCR. Ganciclovir is used for CMV, and oral therapy is inadequate.

med-micro.l15.q1.t: Neuraminidase, used to release virions from the cell
med-micro.l15.q1.p: Which viral protein of influenza is blocked by oseltamivir?
med-micro.l15.q1.h: The drug is a neuraminidase inhibitor.
med-micro.l15.q1.e: Oseltamivir inhibits neuraminidase. M2 is the target of the older adamantanes, to which most strains are resistant.

med-micro.l15.q2.p: A 5-year-old has a barking cough, inspiratory stridor and a steeple sign on neck radiograph. Which virus is most likely responsible?
med-micro.l15.q2.e: Parainfluenza is the classic cause of croup. RSV causes bronchiolitis in infants.

med-micro.l15.q3.t: The virus spreads slowly along nerves, leaving time for immunity
med-micro.l15.q3.p: Why is rabies postexposure prophylaxis effective after a bite?
med-micro.l15.q3.h: Think about the route to the brain.
med-micro.l15.q3.e: Rabies moves through peripheral nerves slowly, so vaccine and immune globulin can act before CNS invasion.

med-micro.l15.q4.t: Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis with progressive cognitive decline
med-micro.l15.q4.p: A 6-year-old unvaccinated child has fever, cough, runny nose and red eyes, followed by white spots on the buccal mucosa and then a rash that began on the face and spread downward. Which complication is a late, rare consequence of this infection years later?
med-micro.l15.q4.e: Measles can cause SSPE years later. Reye syndrome follows aspirin use with influenza or varicella.

med-micro.l15.q5.t: It is a leading cause of severe childhood diarrhea and is vaccine-preventable
med-micro.l15.q5.p: A 4-year-old has fever, vomiting, profuse watery diarrhea and dehydration in winter. A stool antigen test is positive for a segmented double-stranded RNA virus. Which statement about this virus is correct?
med-micro.l15.q5.e: Rotavirus is a naked segmented dsRNA virus and vaccines reduce severe disease. Hantaviruses are rodent-borne.

med-micro.l16.q1.p: Which HIV protein binds CD4 on the host cell?
med-micro.l16.q1.h: It is on the envelope surface.
med-micro.l16.q1.e: gp120 binds CD4 and a coreceptor. gp41 then drives fusion.

med-micro.l16.q2.p: A patient has HBsAg positive for more than six months, anti-HBc IgG positive and anti-HBc IgM negative. What does this indicate?
med-micro.l16.q2.h: Duration of the surface antigen matters.
med-micro.l16.q2.e: Persistent HBsAg beyond six months defines chronic infection. Vaccination alone gives anti-HBs only.

med-micro.l16.q3.t: It is a defective RNA virus that requires HBsAg to be infectious
med-micro.l16.q3.p: Which statement about hepatitis D virus is correct?
med-micro.l16.q3.e: Hepatitis D needs hepatitis B surface antigen for its envelope. Fecal-oral spread describes hepatitis A and E.

med-micro.l16.q4.t: Cryptococcal antigen in CSF with a high opening pressure
med-micro.l16.q4.p: A 38-year-old man with untreated HIV and a CD4 count of 60 cells per microliter has headache, fever and a stiff neck. India ink shows encapsulated yeast. Which test and finding are most consistent with this diagnosis?
med-micro.l16.q4.e: Cryptococcal meningitis is diagnosed with CSF antigen and often has high opening pressure.

med-micro.l16.q5.t: HIV RNA nucleic acid test or antigen-antibody combination assay
med-micro.l16.q5.p: A 31-year-old with fever, sore throat and a rash after unprotected sex has a negative HIV antibody result. Which test is most useful to detect infection at this stage?
med-micro.l16.q5.e: Acute infection precedes antibody; RNA or p24 antigen detects it. CD4 count does not diagnose HIV.

med-micro.l17.q1.t: Ergosterol, which is the main sterol of the membrane
med-micro.l17.q1.p: Which fungal membrane component is targeted by amphotericin B?
med-micro.l17.q1.e: Amphotericin B binds ergosterol. Echinocandins target glucan, and terbinafine blocks squalene epoxidase.

med-micro.l17.q2.t: Histoplasma capsulatum, found in Ohio and Mississippi river valleys
med-micro.l17.q2.p: A dimorphic fungus is a mold at 25 C and a yeast at 37 C. Which organism fits, and where is it endemic?
med-micro.l17.q2.h: Cold is mold, hot is yeast.
med-micro.l17.q2.e: Histoplasma is dimorphic and endemic in those valleys. Aspergillus is a mold only, and Candida and Cryptococcus are yeasts.

med-micro.l17.q3.t: Broad nonseptate hyphae with right-angle branching in ketoacidosis
med-micro.l17.q3.p: Which hyphal description and risk setting match Mucorales?
med-micro.l17.q3.h: A black eschar in the sinuses.
med-micro.l17.q3.e: Mucorales are broad and nonseptate and typically affect people with ketoacidosis. Acute-angle septate hyphae describe Aspergillus.

med-micro.l17.q4.t: A polysaccharide capsule excluding the ink from around the yeast
med-micro.l17.q4.p: A 36-year-old man with HIV, CD4 count 40 cells per microliter, has a subacute headache. CSF analysis shows a high opening pressure and a positive India ink preparation. Which feature of the organism does the stain highlight?
med-micro.l17.q4.h: The ink marks the background, not the organism.
med-micro.l17.q4.e: Cryptococcus has a capsule that excludes ink. Intracellular yeast describes Histoplasma, and spherules are Coccidioides.

med-micro.l17.q5.t: A mold-active azole such as voriconazole
med-micro.l17.q5.p: A 52-year-old with leukemia has three weeks of neutropenia and persistent fever. CT shows nodules with a halo sign, and a biopsy shows septate hyphae with acute-angle branching. Which agent is the most appropriate class for this infection?
med-micro.l17.q5.e: Mold-active azoles are first-line for invasive aspergillosis. Terbinafine and griseofulvin are for superficial dermatophyte infection.

med-micro.l18.q1.t: Giardia lamblia, a pear-shaped binucleate flagellate
med-micro.l18.q1.p: Which protozoan causes foul, fatty, nonbloody diarrhea after drinking untreated stream water?
med-micro.l18.q1.h: The duodenum is involved and blood is absent.
med-micro.l18.q1.e: Giardia causes malabsorptive diarrhea. Entamoeba causes bloody dysentery.

med-micro.l18.q2.t: The drugs cause hemolysis in patients with the enzyme defect
med-micro.l18.q2.p: Why must G6PD status be checked before primaquine or tafenoquine?
med-micro.l18.q2.h: These drugs treat the dormant liver stage.
med-micro.l18.q2.e: Primaquine class drugs can cause hemolysis in G6PD deficiency. They are used to clear hypnozoites of vivax and ovale.

med-micro.l18.q3.t: Plasmodium falciparum, which infects red cells of all ages
med-micro.l18.q3.p: Which species of Plasmodium is dangerous because infected red cells adhere to endothelium and parasitemia is high?
med-micro.l18.q3.e: P. falciparum infects all ages of red cells and sequesters in vessels. Vivax and ovale form hypnozoites but cause lower parasitemia.

med-micro.l18.q4.t: Sandflies carrying the promastigote form of the parasite
med-micro.l18.q4.p: A 29-year-old man has had two weeks of fever and a sore on the leg after travel to South Asia. Now he has massive splenomegaly, pancytopenia and a high gamma globulin level. Bone marrow shows intracellular amastigotes in macrophages. Which vector transmits the organism?
med-micro.l18.q4.e: Leishmania is transmitted by sandflies. Reduviid bugs transmit T. cruzi, and tsetse flies transmit African trypanosomes.

med-micro.l18.q5.t: Empirical treatment for cerebral toxoplasmosis with repeat imaging
med-micro.l18.q5.p: A 33-year-old man with AIDS has headache, fever and focal weakness. MRI shows multiple ring-enhancing lesions, and serology is positive for IgG to a parasite acquired from cat feces. Which management approach is the most appropriate?
med-micro.l18.q5.h: Response to therapy is part of the diagnosis.
med-micro.l18.q5.e: Toxoplasma encephalitis is treated empirically and response is judged by imaging. Biopsy is reserved for non-response.

med-micro.l19.q1.t: Cellophane tape applied to the perianal skin in the morning
med-micro.l19.q1.p: Which test detects Enterobius vermicularis eggs?
med-micro.l19.q1.e: The tape test finds pinworm eggs. Urine microscopy is for S. haematobium.

med-micro.l19.q2.t: Praziquantel, which increases calcium permeability in the worm
med-micro.l19.q2.p: Which drug is first-line for schistosomiasis?
med-micro.l19.q2.h: It acts on trematodes and many cestodes.
med-micro.l19.q2.e: Praziquantel treats schistosomes. Albendazole and ivermectin treat nematodes mainly.

med-micro.l19.q3.t: Squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder from S. haematobium
med-micro.l19.q3.p: A patient with chronic hematuria from Egypt is at increased risk of which cancer?
med-micro.l19.q3.e: S. haematobium is associated with squamous bladder cancer. Clonorchis is linked to cholangiocarcinoma.

med-micro.l19.q4.t: Swallowing eggs passed in the stool of a person carrying the adult worm
med-micro.l19.q4.p: A 44-year-old man from Central America has new generalised seizures. CT shows multiple small cystic lesions, one with an eccentric dot. The brain lesions are cysticerci of Taenia solium. Which exposure most directly caused them?
med-micro.l19.q4.h: The larval stage affects tissue after egg ingestion.
med-micro.l19.q4.e: Neurocysticercosis arises from swallowing T. solium eggs passed in the stool of a tapeworm carrier. CDC states that eating pork cannot cause cysticercosis, and pork cysts cause only intestinal tapeworm.

med-micro.l19.q5.t: Hyperinfection with Strongyloides driven by corticosteroid immunosuppression
med-micro.l19.q5.p: A 62-year-old man born in Southeast Asia is started on high-dose prednisone for vasculitis and soon has fever, abdominal pain, and Gram-negative bacteremia with diffuse pulmonary infiltrates. Which mechanism best explains this course?
med-micro.l19.q5.e: Strongyloides autoinfection becomes hyperinfection with steroids and carries enteric bacteria into blood. Ivermectin is the treatment.

med-micro.l20.q1.t: Autoclaving with saturated steam under pressure
med-micro.l20.q1.p: Which method is the standard for sterilizing heat-stable surgical instruments?
med-micro.l20.q1.e: Steam autoclaving kills spores. Alcohol and quaternary compounds are disinfectants and are not sporicidal.

med-micro.l20.q2.t: Soap and water washing, because alcohol does not kill spores
med-micro.l20.q2.p: A hospital ward has an outbreak of Clostridioides difficile. Which hand hygiene measure is most appropriate?
med-micro.l20.q2.e: Alcohol does not remove or kill spores, so washing is preferred. Gloves do not replace hand hygiene.

med-micro.l20.q3.t: Alteration of the D-Ala-D-Ala terminus to D-Ala-D-Lac
med-micro.l20.q3.p: Which mechanism produces vancomycin resistance in enterococci?
med-micro.l20.q3.h: The cell wall precursor is changed.
med-micro.l20.q3.e: VanA and VanB replace the terminal D-Ala with D-Lac, lowering binding. Ribosomal methylation affects macrolides.

med-micro.l20.q4.t: Airborne precautions in a negative-pressure room
med-micro.l20.q4.p: A patient in a hospital has fever and a productive cough, and is found to have pulmonary tuberculosis with cavities. Which isolation setting is most appropriate?
med-micro.l20.q4.e: TB requires airborne precautions with a negative-pressure room and respirator. Droplet precautions do not contain small particles.

med-micro.l20.q5.t: Likely skin contamination during the collection of the sample
med-micro.l20.q5.p: Two sets of blood cultures taken from separate sites grow coagulase-negative staphylococci in only one of four bottles, and the patient has no device or fever. What is the most reasonable interpretation?
med-micro.l20.q5.h: One bottle, a skin commensal, no symptoms.
med-micro.l20.q5.e: A single positive of a skin commensal in a well patient most likely reflects contamination. True bacteremia is typically positive in several sets.

med-neuro.l01.q1.t: Broca area in the inferior frontal gyrus
med-neuro.l01.q1.p: Which area of the dominant hemisphere is needed for speech production?
med-neuro.l01.q1.e: Broca area produces speech, and lesions give non-fluent speech with relatively preserved comprehension.

med-neuro.l01.q2.t: Conduction aphasia, from a lesion of the arcuate fasciculus
med-neuro.l01.q2.p: Which aphasia has fluent speech, good comprehension and poor repetition?
med-neuro.l01.q2.h: The pathway between the two areas.
med-neuro.l01.q2.e: Disconnecting Wernicke from Broca area spares comprehension and fluency but impairs repetition.

med-neuro.l01.q3.t: Hemispatial neglect of the left side of space, sometimes with anosognosia
med-neuro.l01.q3.p: A lesion of the right (non-dominant) parietal lobe most typically produces which finding?
med-neuro.l01.q3.e: The right parietal lobe is dominant for spatial attention, so its lesion causes left neglect. Gerstmann syndrome is a dominant parietal lesion.

med-neuro.l01.q4.t: Right anterior cerebral artery, supplying the medial frontal lobe where the leg is represented
med-neuro.l01.q4.p: A 70-year-old right-handed woman has sudden weakness of the left leg more than the left arm, with sparing of the face and a flat affect and abulia. Which vascular territory is most likely infarcted?
med-neuro.l01.q4.e: Leg-predominant weakness with abulia indicates the anterior cerebral artery territory. Middle cerebral lesions favour face and arm.

med-neuro.l01.q5.t: The left posterior superior temporal gyrus, because its damage causes fluent comprehension failure
med-neuro.l01.q5.p: A 62-year-old right-handed man has fluent speech full of wrong words, cannot follow commands and cannot repeat a phrase, but has no weakness. He has a superior quadrantanopia. Which site is most likely affected?
med-neuro.l01.q5.h: Fluent but meaningless speech; temporal radiations produce a visual field defect.
med-neuro.l01.q5.e: This is Wernicke aphasia. The adjacent optic radiations in the temporal lobe (Meyer loop) explain the superior field cut.

med-neuro.l02.q1.p: Which cranial nerve nuclei are found in the medulla?
med-neuro.l02.q1.e: The medulla has the nuclei of IX, X, XI (cranial root) and XII; the pons has V to VIII; the midbrain has III and IV.

med-neuro.l02.q2.p: Which structure links the abducens nucleus to the contralateral oculomotor nucleus for conjugate horizontal gaze?
med-neuro.l02.q2.e: The medial longitudinal fasciculus links VI and III nuclei, and lesions cause internuclear ophthalmoplegia.

med-neuro.l02.q3.t: Ipsilateral face and contralateral body loss of pain and temperature, with hoarseness
med-neuro.l02.q3.p: Which finding is characteristic of lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome?
med-neuro.l02.q3.e: Spinal trigeminal nucleus gives ipsilateral face loss; the crossed spinothalamic tract gives contralateral body loss. Nucleus ambiguus involvement gives hoarseness.

med-neuro.l02.q4.t: A left medial longitudinal fasciculus lesion, due to demyelination from multiple sclerosis
med-neuro.l02.q4.p: A 24-year-old woman reports double vision. On looking to the right, the left eye fails to adduct while the right eye abducts with nystagmus, and convergence is intact. Which lesion is most likely, and which disease is likely given her age?
med-neuro.l02.q4.h: Left eye fails on right gaze, with preserved convergence.
med-neuro.l02.q4.e: Failure of left eye adduction on right gaze indicates a left MLF lesion, and bilateral internuclear ophthalmoplegia in a young adult suggests multiple sclerosis. Preserved convergence argues against a third nerve lesion.

med-neuro.l02.q5.t: The right ventral midbrain, involving the oculomotor fascicle and cerebral peduncle
med-neuro.l02.q5.p: A 55-year-old with hypertension has a right-sided ptosis, a dilated right pupil and the right eye looking down and out, with left arm and leg weakness. Where is the lesion?
med-neuro.l02.q5.h: Ipsilateral third nerve plus contralateral long tract signs.
med-neuro.l02.q5.e: This is Weber syndrome from a ventral midbrain lesion. The cranial nerve sign is ipsilateral while the corticospinal fibres have yet to cross, so weakness is contralateral.

med-neuro.l03.q1.p: Which cranial nerve supplies the superior oblique muscle?
med-neuro.l03.q1.e: The trochlear nerve supplies the superior oblique and is the only one to exit dorsally.

med-neuro.l03.q2.t: A left upper motor neurone lesion, because the lower face has mostly contralateral input
med-neuro.l03.q2.p: A patient with a right facial droop that spares the forehead most likely has which type of lesion?
med-neuro.l03.q2.h: The forehead has bilateral cortical input.
med-neuro.l03.q2.e: Forehead sparing indicates an upper motor neurone lesion contralateral to the droop; lower motor neurone lesions affect the whole half of the face.

med-neuro.l03.q3.p: Which nerve forms the efferent limb of the gag reflex?
med-neuro.l03.q3.e: The glossopharyngeal nerve is afferent and the vagus is efferent for the gag reflex.

med-neuro.l03.q4.t: Microvascular ischaemia of the central nerve fibres that spares the peripheral parasympathetic fibres
med-neuro.l03.q4.p: A 60-year-old with diabetes has acute double vision, right ptosis and the right eye deviated down and out. The right pupil reacts normally to light. Which cause is most likely?
med-neuro.l03.q4.e: Diabetic third nerve palsy is classically pupil-sparing because ischaemia hits the central fibres, whereas compression affects the superficial pupillomotor fibres early.

med-neuro.l03.q5.t: The facial nerve proximal to the origin of the nerve to stapedius in the facial canal
med-neuro.l03.q5.p: A 45-year-old woman wakes with a droop of the entire right face, a dry right eye, loss of taste in the anterior right tongue and sounds that seem too loud on the right. Where is the lesion?
med-neuro.l03.q5.e: Loss of lacrimation, taste and stapedius function means the lesion lies proximal to the stapedius branch, within the canal. A cortical lesion would spare the forehead.

med-neuro.l04.q1.p: Which tract carries pain and temperature sensation?
med-neuro.l04.q1.h: Crosses in the anterior white commissure.
med-neuro.l04.q1.e: The spinothalamic tract carries pain and temperature and crosses near the level of entry.

med-neuro.l04.q2.t: In the pyramidal decussation of the caudal medulla
med-neuro.l04.q2.p: Where do the majority of lateral corticospinal tract fibres cross?
med-neuro.l04.q2.h: Around 90 percent cross in the medulla.
med-neuro.l04.q2.e: The pyramidal decussation sits in the caudal medulla. Internal arcuate fibres belong to the dorsal column pathway.

med-neuro.l04.q3.t: Syringomyelia, from a central cavity damaging the crossing fibres
med-neuro.l04.q3.p: Which cord syndrome gives loss of pain and temperature in a cape distribution with preserved light touch?
med-neuro.l04.q3.e: A central syrinx interrupts decussating spinothalamic fibres and spares dorsal columns, giving dissociated sensory loss.

med-neuro.l04.q4.t: A right hemisection of the cord, which interrupts ipsilateral motor and dorsal column fibres
med-neuro.l04.q4.p: A 38-year-old has a stab wound to the thoracic cord. He has weakness and loss of vibration in the right leg and loss of pain and temperature in the left leg. What is the lesion?
med-neuro.l04.q4.h: Dorsal columns and corticospinal fibres are uncrossed at cord level.
med-neuro.l04.q4.e: This is Brown-Sequard syndrome on the right: ipsilateral motor and dorsal column loss, contralateral pain and temperature loss.

med-neuro.l04.q5.t: Dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts, in subacute combined degeneration
med-neuro.l04.q5.p: A 66-year-old vegetarian has paraesthesias, loss of vibration and position sense in the feet, spastic weakness and a positive Romberg test. Which pair of tracts is involved?
med-neuro.l04.q5.e: B12 deficiency damages the dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts. Pain and temperature are usually spared.

med-neuro.l05.q1.p: Which artery supplies the lateral convexity of the cerebral hemisphere, including the face and arm motor areas?
med-neuro.l05.q1.h: The largest branch of the internal carotid.
med-neuro.l05.q1.e: The middle cerebral artery supplies the lateral convexity. The anterior cerebral supplies the medial surface, where the leg lies.

med-neuro.l05.q2.t: The occipital pole has dual blood supply, partly from the middle cerebral artery
med-neuro.l05.q2.p: A posterior cerebral artery occlusion causes a homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing. Why is the macula spared?
med-neuro.l05.q2.e: The occipital pole receives collateral supply from middle cerebral branches, so central vision is spared.

med-neuro.l05.q3.t: Basilar artery occlusion destroying the ventral pons
med-neuro.l05.q3.h: Consciousness and vertical eye movements are preserved.
med-neuro.l05.q3.e: Ventral pontine infarction interrupts corticospinal and corticobulbar fibres but spares the reticular formation and vertical gaze.

med-neuro.l05.q4.t: Left middle cerebral artery superior division, which supplies the lateral frontal convexity
med-neuro.l05.q4.p: A 72-year-old man with atrial fibrillation has sudden right face and arm weakness, expressive speech difficulty with good comprehension, and gaze deviation to the left. Which vessel is occluded?
med-neuro.l05.q4.h: The lateral frontal convexity includes Broca area.
med-neuro.l05.q4.e: The superior division of the left middle cerebral artery supplies Broca area and the face and arm motor cortex. Gaze deviates toward the lesion.

med-neuro.l05.q5.t: Left posterior inferior cerebellar artery or vertebral artery, which supplies the lateral medulla
med-neuro.l05.q5.p: A 64-year-old woman has sudden vertigo, vomiting, left facial pain and temperature loss, right body pain and temperature loss, hoarseness and left Horner syndrome. Which artery is the most likely culprit?
med-neuro.l05.q5.e: This is Wallenberg syndrome from PICA or vertebral occlusion. AICA infarction would add facial paralysis and deafness.

med-neuro.l06.q1.e: The choroid plexus produces most CSF; arachnoid granulations absorb it.

med-neuro.l06.q2.p: Which haematoma is lens-shaped, does not cross suture lines and is classically associated with a lucid interval?
med-neuro.l06.q2.e: Epidural bleeding is arterial and confined by sutures, giving a biconvex shape.

med-neuro.l06.q3.t: Lateral ventricle, foramen of Monro, third ventricle, aqueduct, fourth ventricle, foramina of Luschka and Magendie
med-neuro.l06.q3.p: Which CSF circulation sequence is correct?
med-neuro.l06.q3.h: The foramen of Monro connects the lateral and third ventricles.
med-neuro.l06.q3.e: CSF flows from the lateral ventricles to the third through the foramen of Monro, then through the aqueduct to the fourth ventricle and out to the subarachnoid space.

med-neuro.l06.q4.t: Normal pressure hydrocephalus, a communicating hydrocephalus that may improve after CSF diversion
med-neuro.l06.q4.p: A 74-year-old has a shuffling, wide-based gait, new urinary urgency and memory decline over six months. CT shows enlarged ventricles without prominent sulcal atrophy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
med-neuro.l06.q4.h: Triad of gait, bladder, and cognition.
med-neuro.l06.q4.e: Gait apraxia, incontinence and dementia with ventriculomegaly indicate normal pressure hydrocephalus. Alzheimer atrophy would widen sulci.

med-neuro.l06.q5.t: Compression of the left cerebral peduncle against the tentorium, known as the Kernohan notch
med-neuro.l06.q5.p: A 35-year-old with a large right hemispheric mass becomes drowsy and develops a dilated right pupil with right-sided limb weakness on the same side as the mass. Which mechanism best explains the ipsilateral weakness?
med-neuro.l06.q5.h: A false localising sign from the opposite peduncle.
med-neuro.l06.q5.e: In uncal herniation the shifted brainstem presses the contralateral peduncle on the tentorial edge, producing ipsilateral hemiparesis (Kernohan phenomenon).

med-neuro.l07.q1.p: Which thalamic nucleus relays visual information to the occipital cortex?
med-neuro.l07.q1.h: Geniculate nucleus on the lateral side.
med-neuro.l07.q1.e: The lateral geniculate nucleus relays vision; the medial geniculate handles hearing.

med-neuro.l07.q2.p: A lesion of the left optic tract produces which visual field defect?
med-neuro.l07.q2.h: Posterior to the chiasm both eyes are affected.
med-neuro.l07.q2.e: The left tract carries the right visual field from both eyes, so the right field is lost in both.

med-neuro.l07.q3.t: Louder in the affected ear, because the bone conduction is not masked by ambient noise
med-neuro.l07.q3.p: In a patient with unilateral conductive hearing loss, the Weber test is expected to be which?
med-neuro.l07.q3.e: In conductive loss the tone is heard louder in the affected ear. In sensorineural loss it lateralises to the better ear.

med-neuro.l07.q4.t: Bitemporal hemianopia, because the chiasm compresses the crossing nasal retinal fibres from below
med-neuro.l07.q4.p: A 45-year-old woman has headaches, galactorrhoea and amenorrhoea and has been bumping into objects on both sides. Which visual field finding would be expected, and why?
med-neuro.l07.q4.e: A pituitary adenoma pushes up on the chiasm and damages the crossing nasal retinal fibres, which carry temporal fields.

med-neuro.l07.q5.t: Right superior quadrantanopia, because the Meyer loop fibres sweep through the temporal lobe
med-neuro.l07.q5.p: A 68-year-old has a left temporal lobe stroke. Which visual finding would be expected?
med-neuro.l07.q5.e: Meyer loop carries the lower retinal (upper visual field) fibres through the temporal lobe, giving a contralateral superior quadrantanopia.

med-neuro.l08.q1.p: Which finding is characteristic of a lower motor neurone lesion?
med-neuro.l08.q1.e: Fasciculations, wasting and flaccid weakness mark LMN lesions.

med-neuro.l08.q2.t: Spastic weakness, brisk reflexes and an extensor plantar response in the limbs
med-neuro.l08.q2.p: Which combination fits an upper motor neurone lesion?
med-neuro.l08.q2.e: UMN lesions cause spasticity, hyperreflexia and a Babinski sign. Fatigable weakness suggests a neuromuscular junction disorder.

med-neuro.l08.q3.p: Which reflex tests the S1 root?
med-neuro.l08.q3.e: The ankle jerk tests S1. The knee jerk tests L3-L4 and the biceps C5-C6.

med-neuro.l08.q4.t: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, which affects both upper and lower motor neurones
med-neuro.l08.q4.p: A 58-year-old man has tongue fasciculations, wasting of the hand muscles, brisk knee jerks, extensor plantar responses and no sensory loss. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
med-neuro.l08.q4.h: Both neurone populations, no sensory change.
med-neuro.l08.q4.e: Combined UMN and LMN signs without sensory loss indicate motor neurone disease. Myelopathy would give sensory signs and Guillain-Barre gives areflexia.

med-neuro.l08.q5.t: Cerebral shock followed by release of spinal reflexes from the loss of descending inhibition
med-neuro.l08.q5.p: A 70-year-old has an acute stroke with flaccid left arm weakness and absent reflexes on day one. Reflexes become brisk with spasticity by two weeks. Which explanation is best?
med-neuro.l08.q5.e: Acute UMN lesions initially cause shock with flaccidity. Later the loss of descending inhibition leaves spasticity and hyperreflexia.

med-neuro.l09.q1.p: Which cells are the sole output neurones of the cerebellar cortex?
med-neuro.l09.q1.h: They release GABA onto the deep nuclei.
med-neuro.l09.q1.e: Purkinje cells are the only cortical output and are inhibitory to the deep nuclei.

med-neuro.l09.q2.t: The right side, ipsilateral to the lesion
med-neuro.l09.q2.p: A lesion of the right cerebellar hemisphere would cause ataxia on which side?
med-neuro.l09.q2.e: Each cerebellar hemisphere controls the ipsilateral limbs because of double decussation.

med-neuro.l09.q3.t: Cerebellar ataxia is present with the eyes open and does not worsen much when they are closed
med-neuro.l09.q3.p: Which feature separates cerebellar ataxia from sensory ataxia?
med-neuro.l09.q3.h: Which ataxia depends on vision to compensate?
med-neuro.l09.q3.e: Sensory ataxia is vision-dependent and worsens when the eyes close, whereas cerebellar ataxia persists with the eyes open.

med-neuro.l09.q4.t: Medulloblastoma, a vermian tumour that obstructs the fourth ventricle
med-neuro.l09.q4.p: A 5-year-old has two weeks of morning headaches, vomiting and unsteady walking with a wide-based gait. MRI shows a midline mass in the fourth ventricle with dilated lateral ventricles. Which diagnosis is most likely?
med-neuro.l09.q4.h: A small round blue cell tumour of the vermis.
med-neuro.l09.q4.e: Medulloblastoma commonly arises in the vermis of children and causes obstructive hydrocephalus. Pilocytic astrocytomas are more often hemispheric and cystic.

med-neuro.l09.q5.t: Search for an underlying gynaecological or breast malignancy that drives the paraneoplastic syndrome
med-neuro.l09.q5.p: A 55-year-old woman develops subacute pancerebellar ataxia and her serum contains anti-Yo antibodies. Which further step is most appropriate?
med-neuro.l09.q5.e: Anti-Yo antibodies are associated with paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration, typically with ovarian or breast cancer.

med-neuro.l10.q1.p: Parkinson disease involves loss of neurones in which structure?
med-neuro.l10.q1.e: Dopaminergic neurones of the pars compacta degenerate in Parkinson disease; the caudate degenerates in Huntington disease.

med-neuro.l10.q2.t: It disinhibits the thalamus by inhibiting the internal globus pallidus and so facilitates movement
med-neuro.l10.q2.p: Which statement best describes the direct pathway of the basal ganglia?
med-neuro.l10.q2.h: Two inhibitory steps equal a net release.
med-neuro.l10.q2.e: Striatal inhibition of the internal pallidum releases the thalamus, so movement is facilitated.

med-neuro.l10.q3.t: A CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the huntingtin gene, inherited in an autosomal dominant manner
med-neuro.l10.q3.p: Huntington disease is caused by which genetic mechanism?
med-neuro.l10.q3.e: Huntington disease is an autosomal dominant CAG repeat disorder on chromosome 4. GAA repeats cause Friedreich ataxia.

med-neuro.l10.q4.t: Atrophy of the caudate nucleus with enlargement of the frontal horns of the lateral ventricles
med-neuro.l10.q4.p: A 38-year-old has irritability, clumsiness and irregular, dance-like movements of the limbs. His father died in an institution at 50. Which imaging finding is most expected?
med-neuro.l10.q4.e: Huntington disease causes caudate atrophy, so the frontal horns look boxed out. The hummingbird sign suggests progressive supranuclear palsy.

med-neuro.l10.q5.t: Progressive supranuclear palsy, an atypical parkinsonism with early falls and gaze palsy
med-neuro.l10.q5.p: A 70-year-old man has bradykinesia and rigidity but had falls and a vertical gaze limitation within the first year, and levodopa gave little benefit. Which diagnosis is most likely?
med-neuro.l10.q5.h: Atypical features include early falls and poor response.
med-neuro.l10.q5.e: Early postural instability and vertical gaze palsy with poor levodopa response point to progressive supranuclear palsy.

med-neuro.l11.q1.p: Which hypothalamic nucleus controls circadian rhythm?
med-neuro.l11.q1.h: It lies above the optic chiasm.
med-neuro.l11.q1.e: The suprachiasmatic nucleus receives retinal input and sets the body clock.

med-neuro.l11.q2.p: Which structure is in the Papez circuit between the fornix and the thalamus?
med-neuro.l11.q2.e: The circuit is hippocampus, fornix, mammillary bodies, anterior thalamus, cingulate gyrus.

med-neuro.l11.q3.t: Anterograde amnesia with impaired formation of new declarative memories
med-neuro.l11.q3.p: Bilateral removal of the medial temporal lobes primarily causes which deficit?
med-neuro.l11.q3.e: Hippocampal damage impairs the formation of new declarative memories while procedural learning is preserved.

med-neuro.l11.q4.t: Give parenteral thiamine, since glucose alone may precipitate or worsen Wernicke encephalopathy
med-neuro.l11.q4.p: A 52-year-old man with chronic alcohol use is brought in confused, with horizontal nystagmus and a broad-based gait. What is the most important immediate step?
med-neuro.l11.q4.e: Wernicke encephalopathy needs urgent thiamine, and a glucose load given first can worsen it by consuming thiamine-dependent metabolism.

med-neuro.l11.q5.t: Failure of antidiuretic hormone release from supraoptic and paraventricular neurones, so the kidney cannot concentrate urine
med-neuro.l11.q5.p: A 40-year-old develops excessive thirst and passes large volumes of dilute urine after a pituitary stalk injury. Urine osmolality rises after desmopressin. Which explanation is most accurate?
med-neuro.l11.q5.h: The response to desmopressin tells you the kidney works.
med-neuro.l11.q5.e: Central diabetes insipidus is lack of ADH, and the urine concentrates after desmopressin. Nephrogenic disease would not respond.

med-neuro.l12.q1.p: Crossed signs, with ipsilateral cranial nerve palsy and contralateral hemiparesis, localise a lesion to where?
med-neuro.l12.q1.e: Ipsilateral cranial nerve deficits with contralateral long tract signs localise to the brainstem.

med-neuro.l12.q2.p: A patient has dense weakness of the face, arm and leg on one side with no cortical signs. Where is the lesion most likely located?
med-neuro.l12.q2.e: A small lesion in the posterior limb of the internal capsule can affect all corticospinal fibres, giving pure motor hemiparesis.

med-neuro.l12.q3.p: Vertical gaze palsy with pupillary light-near dissociation localises to which structure?
med-neuro.l12.q3.e: The dorsal midbrain contains the pretectal area and vertical gaze centres; a pineal tumour can compress it.

med-neuro.l12.q4.t: The left ventral pons, affecting the facial and abducens fascicles and the corticospinal tract
med-neuro.l12.q4.p: A 60-year-old has left facial weakness including the forehead, inability to abduct the left eye and right hemiparesis. Where is the lesion?
med-neuro.l12.q4.h: Ipsilateral cranial nerves and contralateral limbs.
med-neuro.l12.q4.e: Forehead involvement shows a lower motor neurone facial lesion, and abducens plus the crossed hemiparesis place it in the left ventral pons.

med-neuro.l12.q5.t: The left spinal trigeminal tract and the left spinothalamic tract in the lateral medulla
med-neuro.l12.q5.p: A 45-year-old has sudden loss of pain and temperature on the left face and right body, with a left Horner syndrome, hoarseness and ataxia of the left limbs. Which structure explains the crossed sensory pattern?
med-neuro.l12.q5.h: Face fibres have not crossed; body fibres have.
med-neuro.l12.q5.e: Lateral medullary infarction damages the ipsilateral spinal trigeminal tract (face) and the already-crossed spinothalamic tract (contralateral body).

med-neuro.l13.q1.p: Which imaging test is performed first in a patient with a suspected acute stroke to exclude haemorrhage?
med-neuro.l13.q1.h: Fast, widely available, and sensitive to blood.
med-neuro.l13.q1.e: Non-contrast CT excludes haemorrhage quickly, which determines whether thrombolysis is possible.

med-neuro.l13.q2.p: Which drug is given to reduce the risk of ischaemia from vasospasm after aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage?
med-neuro.l13.q2.h: It acts on vascular smooth muscle calcium channels.
med-neuro.l13.q2.e: Nimodipine improves outcome after subarachnoid haemorrhage. Alteplase and anticoagulants increase bleeding risk.

med-neuro.l13.q3.t: Rupture of small penetrating arteries in chronic hypertension
med-neuro.l13.q3.p: Which cause of intracerebral haemorrhage most commonly affects the basal ganglia and thalamus?
med-neuro.l13.q3.e: Hypertensive microaneurysms of penetrating arteries cause deep bleeds, whereas amyloid angiopathy typically causes lobar haemorrhage.

med-neuro.l13.q4.t: To dissolve the fibrin clot with a plasminogen activator, to rescue the penumbra around the infarct core
med-neuro.l13.q4.p: A 70-year-old man with atrial fibrillation develops sudden right-sided weakness and aphasia 90 minutes ago. CT shows no haemorrhage. Which statement correctly explains the aim of urgent treatment?
med-neuro.l13.q4.h: Time is brain; the penumbra is salvageable.
med-neuro.l13.q4.e: Reperfusion by thrombolysis or thrombectomy aims to rescue the penumbra. Immediate anticoagulation does not lyse an established clot.

med-neuro.l13.q5.t: A saccular aneurysm of the circle of Willis, linked with polycystic kidney disease
med-neuro.l13.q5.p: A 38-year-old woman with polycystic kidney disease has a sudden, severe headache that she calls the worst of her life, with neck stiffness. CT shows blood in the basal cisterns. Which vascular lesion is the most likely source?
med-neuro.l13.q5.h: Thunderclap headache and a kidney disease association.
med-neuro.l13.q5.e: Subarachnoid haemorrhage commonly arises from a saccular aneurysm, and autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease raises the risk.

med-neuro.l14.q1.p: Which drug is first-line for childhood absence epilepsy and blocks T-type calcium channels?
med-neuro.l14.q1.e: Ethosuximide blocks thalamic T-type calcium channels. Sodium channel blockers can worsen absence seizures.

med-neuro.l14.q2.p: Which adverse effect is characteristic of phenytoin?
med-neuro.l14.q2.h: Think of the gums and hair.
med-neuro.l14.q2.e: Phenytoin causes gingival hyperplasia and hirsutism. Valproate causes pancreatitis and carbamazepine hyponatraemia.

med-neuro.l14.q3.p: Which antiseizure drug acts mainly by binding the synaptic vesicle protein SV2A?
med-neuro.l14.q3.h: A newer drug with a unique target.
med-neuro.l14.q3.e: Levetiracetam binds SV2A. Lamotrigine blocks sodium channels and phenobarbital enhances GABA-A action.

med-neuro.l14.q4.t: Carbamazepine, because sodium channel blockade may aggravate absence seizures
med-neuro.l14.q4.p: A 15-year-old has brief staring spells many times daily, with sudden onset and offset and no postictal confusion. A routine EEG with hyperventilation shows generalised 3-Hz spike and wave. Which treatment is inappropriate because it may worsen the disorder?
med-neuro.l14.q4.h: Match the syndrome with the mechanism.
med-neuro.l14.q4.e: Carbamazepine and phenytoin can worsen absence and myoclonic seizures. Ethosuximide and valproate are effective.

med-neuro.l14.q5.t: Carbamazepine, which induces hepatic enzymes and lowers the levels of oestrogen and progestin
med-neuro.l14.q5.p: A 20-year-old woman with epilepsy takes an antiseizure drug and an oral contraceptive. She becomes pregnant. Which drug is the most likely explanation, based on enzyme induction?
med-neuro.l14.q5.e: Carbamazepine induces cytochrome P450 enzymes and reduces contraceptive efficacy. Valproate is an inhibitor.

med-neuro.l15.q1.t: Amyloid plaques and tau neurofibrillary tangles
med-neuro.l15.q1.p: Which pair of pathological findings is characteristic of Alzheimer disease?
med-neuro.l15.q1.e: Alzheimer disease has amyloid-beta plaques and hyperphosphorylated tau tangles.

med-neuro.l15.q2.t: The amyloid precursor protein gene lies on chromosome 21, so they carry an extra copy
med-neuro.l15.q2.p: Why do many people with Down syndrome develop Alzheimer pathology early?
med-neuro.l15.q2.h: Think about which gene is on chromosome 21.
med-neuro.l15.q2.e: The APP gene is on chromosome 21, so extra copies increase amyloid production.

med-neuro.l15.q3.t: Fluctuating cognition with well-formed visual hallucinations and parkinsonism
med-neuro.l15.q3.p: Which feature best distinguishes dementia with Lewy bodies from Alzheimer disease?
med-neuro.l15.q3.e: Fluctuations, visual hallucinations and parkinsonism define dementia with Lewy bodies. Rapid decline with myoclonus suggests prion disease.

med-neuro.l15.q4.t: Behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia, a disorder with tau or TDP-43 pathology
med-neuro.l15.q4.p: A 58-year-old man has 18 months of increasingly inappropriate jokes, compulsive eating, apathy and loss of empathy. Memory testing is relatively normal. MRI shows frontal and anterior temporal atrophy. Which diagnosis is most likely?
med-neuro.l15.q4.e: Early personality change with frontal and anterior temporal atrophy indicates behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia.

med-neuro.l15.q5.t: Prion disease, a transmissible misfolded protein disorder that has no effective cure
med-neuro.l15.q5.p: A 60-year-old develops rapidly progressive dementia over 4 months with startle myoclonus and ataxia. EEG shows periodic sharp-wave complexes. What is the most likely cause?
med-neuro.l15.q5.e: Rapid decline, myoclonus and periodic sharp waves are typical of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, a prion disorder.

med-neuro.l16.q1.p: Which cell is the target of damage in multiple sclerosis?
med-neuro.l16.q1.e: MS damages central myelin made by oligodendrocytes, while the peripheral nervous system is spared.

med-neuro.l16.q2.t: Oligoclonal IgG bands that are absent in the paired serum sample
med-neuro.l16.q2.p: Which cerebrospinal fluid finding supports a diagnosis of multiple sclerosis?
med-neuro.l16.q2.e: Oligoclonal bands in CSF only reflect intrathecal IgG synthesis. Albuminocytologic dissociation suggests Guillain-Barre syndrome.

med-neuro.l16.q3.t: It blocks alpha-4 integrin, which reduces lymphocyte entry to the brain and allows JC virus to reactivate
med-neuro.l16.q3.p: Natalizumab carries a risk of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy because it does which?
med-neuro.l16.q3.h: It limits immune surveillance of the CNS.
med-neuro.l16.q3.e: Natalizumab blocks alpha-4 integrin and reduces CNS immune surveillance, allowing JC virus to cause progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy.

med-neuro.l16.q4.t: She has optic neuritis, and the MRI lesions put her at high risk of developing multiple sclerosis
