med-neuro.l16.q4.p: A 27-year-old woman has painful loss of vision in the left eye over 4 days, with a left relative afferent pupillary defect and a normal fundus. MRI of the brain shows two ovoid periventricular lesions. Which statement is most accurate?
med-neuro.l16.q4.h: Retrobulbar neuritis has a normal disc.
med-neuro.l16.q4.e: Painful monocular visual loss with a normal fundus is retrobulbar optic neuritis, and periventricular lesions point to multiple sclerosis.

med-neuro.l16.q5.t: Antibodies against aquaporin-4 on astrocyte foot processes, in neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder
med-neuro.l16.q5.p: A 35-year-old woman has severe bilateral visual loss and then a transverse myelitis extending over five vertebral segments on MRI. Which finding is expected?
med-neuro.l16.q5.e: Longitudinally extensive myelitis with severe optic neuritis suggests neuromyelitis optica with aquaporin-4 antibodies.

med-neuro.l17.q1.t: Raised protein with a normal white cell count
med-neuro.l17.q1.p: Which finding is characteristic of cerebrospinal fluid in Guillain-Barre syndrome?
med-neuro.l17.q1.e: Guillain-Barre shows raised protein without pleocytosis. Neutrophils and low glucose indicate bacterial infection.

med-neuro.l17.q2.p: Which autoantibody target is found in most cases of myasthenia gravis?
med-neuro.l17.q2.e: Most patients have antibodies to the postsynaptic acetylcholine receptor. Presynaptic calcium channel antibodies cause Lambert-Eaton syndrome.

med-neuro.l17.q3.p: Which nerve is compressed at the fibular head, giving foot drop and sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot?
med-neuro.l17.q3.h: Crossing legs is a classic cause.
med-neuro.l17.q3.e: The common peroneal nerve is superficial at the fibular head and is prone to compression.

med-neuro.l17.q4.t: Intravenous immunoglobulin or plasma exchange, with close monitoring of breathing
med-neuro.l17.q4.p: A 35-year-old has had 3 days of ascending leg weakness, absent knee and ankle jerks and mild tingling, two weeks after a diarrhoeal illness. His forced vital capacity has fallen. Which treatment is most appropriate?
med-neuro.l17.q4.e: Guillain-Barre syndrome is treated with immunoglobulin or plasma exchange, and corticosteroids do not help. Respiratory function is monitored.

med-neuro.l17.q5.t: Antibodies against presynaptic calcium channels, associated with small cell lung cancer
med-neuro.l17.q5.p: A 62-year-old smoker has proximal leg weakness, dry mouth and absent reflexes. Strength improves briefly after repeated contraction. Which underlying mechanism and association are most likely?
med-neuro.l17.q5.e: Lambert-Eaton syndrome results from presynaptic calcium channel antibodies, often with small cell lung cancer, and strength improves with sustained effort. Myasthenia worsens with effort.

med-neuro.l18.q1.p: Which drug class acts as serotonin 5-HT1B/1D agonists for acute migraine?
med-neuro.l18.q1.e: Triptans are 5-HT1B/1D agonists. Gepants block the CGRP receptor.

med-neuro.l18.q2.t: Unilateral periorbital pain with ipsilateral lacrimation and restlessness
med-neuro.l18.q2.p: Which feature best distinguishes cluster headache from migraine?
med-neuro.l18.q2.e: Cluster headache has severe unilateral periorbital pain with autonomic features and agitation. Migraine patients tend to lie still.

med-neuro.l18.q3.p: Which drug is used for prevention of cluster headache?
med-neuro.l18.q3.e: Verapamil is used for cluster prevention; oxygen and subcutaneous sumatriptan are acute treatments.

med-neuro.l18.q4.t: Start high-dose corticosteroids at once, before temporal artery biopsy confirms the diagnosis
med-neuro.l18.q4.p: A 70-year-old woman has a new headache for 2 weeks, jaw pain on chewing, scalp tenderness and an ESR of 90. She reports brief loss of vision in one eye. What is the most appropriate step?
med-neuro.l18.q4.e: Giant cell arteritis threatens vision, so corticosteroids are started immediately and biopsy follows because histology remains positive for some time.

med-neuro.l18.q5.t: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension, treated with weight loss and acetazolamide
med-neuro.l18.q5.p: An obese 26-year-old woman has daily headaches, transient visual obscurations and bilateral papilloedema. MRI is normal and lumbar puncture shows a high opening pressure with normal CSF. Which diagnosis and treatment are most appropriate?
med-neuro.l18.q5.e: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension features papilloedema, normal imaging and raised pressure; weight loss and acetazolamide are the mainstay.

med-neuro.l19.q1.t: Carbidopa blocks peripheral dopa decarboxylase so more levodopa reaches the brain
med-neuro.l19.q1.p: Why is levodopa combined with carbidopa?
med-neuro.l19.q1.h: It cannot cross the blood-brain barrier.
med-neuro.l19.q1.e: Carbidopa inhibits peripheral decarboxylation, raising brain levodopa and lowering peripheral side effects.

med-neuro.l19.q2.t: Memantine, an NMDA receptor channel blocker
med-neuro.l19.q2.p: Which drug mechanism is correctly paired?
med-neuro.l19.q2.e: Memantine blocks NMDA channels. Donepezil inhibits acetylcholinesterase and baclofen is a GABA-B agonist.

med-neuro.l19.q3.t: Barbiturates increase the duration of GABA-A chloride channel opening and can act without GABA at high doses
med-neuro.l19.q3.p: Why are barbiturates more dangerous than benzodiazepines in overdose?
med-neuro.l19.q3.e: Barbiturates prolong channel opening and at high doses open it directly, so there is no ceiling effect. Benzodiazepines only increase frequency in the presence of GABA.

med-neuro.l19.q4.t: Atropine to block muscarinic effects and pralidoxime to reactivate acetylcholinesterase
med-neuro.l19.q4.p: A farmer exposed to an insecticide has salivation, lacrimation, diarrhoea, bradycardia, miosis and muscle fasciculations. Which treatment pair is appropriate?
med-neuro.l19.q4.e: Organophosphates inhibit acetylcholinesterase; atropine blocks muscarinic effects and pralidoxime restores the enzyme.

med-neuro.l19.q5.t: Blockade of striatal D2 receptors in an already dopamine-depleted nigrostriatal system
med-neuro.l19.q5.p: A 72-year-old with Parkinson disease is given haloperidol for hospital delirium and develops severe rigidity and immobility within a day. Which mechanism best explains this?
med-neuro.l19.q5.e: Haloperidol blocks D2 receptors and worsens parkinsonism; antipsychotics with weak D2 blockade are preferred in these patients.

med-neuro.l20.q1.p: Which maximum Glasgow Coma Scale total score indicates a fully alert, normal patient?
med-neuro.l20.q1.e: The scale runs from 3 to 15, and 15 is fully normal.

med-neuro.l20.q2.t: Lymphocytes, mildly raised protein and normal glucose
med-neuro.l20.q2.p: Which cerebrospinal fluid pattern fits viral meningitis?
med-neuro.l20.q2.h: A milder picture than bacterial disease.
med-neuro.l20.q2.e: Viral meningitis has lymphocytic pleocytosis with normal glucose. Bacterial disease has neutrophils and low glucose.

med-neuro.l20.q3.p: Which tumour arises from arachnoid cap cells and contains psammoma bodies?
med-neuro.l20.q3.e: Meningiomas arise from arachnoid cap cells and may contain psammoma bodies.

med-neuro.l20.q4.t: Empirical aciclovir for presumed herpes simplex encephalitis without waiting for confirmation
med-neuro.l20.q4.p: A 40-year-old has 3 days of fever, confusion and a seizure. MRI shows temporal lobe hyperintensity and CSF shows lymphocytes with red cells. What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
med-neuro.l20.q4.h: Temporal lobe and lymphocytic CSF with blood.
med-neuro.l20.q4.e: Herpes simplex encephalitis has high mortality without prompt aciclovir, so treatment is started empirically.

med-neuro.l20.q5.t: Metastases from a primary tumour such as lung cancer, which are often multiple at that junction
med-neuro.l20.q5.p: A 62-year-old smoker has headaches and a seizure. MRI shows several ring-enhancing lesions at the grey-white junction with surrounding oedema. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
med-neuro.l20.q5.h: Multiple lesions at the grey-white junction.
med-neuro.l20.q5.e: Multiple ring-enhancing lesions at the grey-white junction in a smoker suggest brain metastases, often from the lung.

med-path.l01.q1.t: Metaplasia, a reversible replacement of one mature cell type by another
med-path.l01.q1.p: A person who has smoked for years has bronchial biopsy showing stratified squamous epithelium in place of ciliated columnar epithelium. What is this change?
med-path.l01.q1.h: The cell type changed, not the number or size.
med-path.l01.q1.e: Chronic irritation drives stem cells to produce squamous cells, which is metaplasia and can regress if smoking stops. Dysplasia involves disordered, atypical cells, not just a different mature type.

med-path.l01.q2.t: Hypertrophy, as cardiac myocytes enlarge in response to pressure overload
med-path.l01.q2.p: Which change best explains why the myocardium thickens in long-standing systemic hypertension?
med-path.l01.q2.h: Adult cardiac muscle cells do not divide appreciably.
med-path.l01.q2.e: Terminally differentiated myocytes respond by getting larger, not more numerous. Hyperplasia needs dividing cells, which adult myocytes mostly are not.

med-path.l01.q3.t: Reprogramming of stem cells in response to chronic acid exposure, which leaves a field at risk of dysplasia and adenocarcinoma
med-path.l01.q3.p: A 58-year-old man with 15 years of heartburn has an endoscopic biopsy showing intestinal-type columnar cells with goblet cells in the distal oesophagus. Which statement best describes the underlying process?
med-path.l01.q3.h: Think about what cell changes and what the persistent irritant does to cancer risk.
med-path.l01.q3.e: Barrett oesophagus is metaplasia from stem cell reprogramming, and it predisposes to dysplasia and adenocarcinoma. The distractor of direct transformation of mature cells is wrong because mature cells do not change type.

med-path.l01.q4.t: Profound membrane damage with irreversible mitochondrial dysfunction
med-path.l01.q4.p: A 62-year-old man presents 3 hours after chest pain begins. Cardiac myocytes are leaking intracellular proteins into the blood. Which finding best indicates that injury has become irreversible?
med-path.l01.q4.h: Reversible injury still has a recoverable energy supply.
med-path.l01.q4.e: Irreversible injury is defined by loss of mitochondrial function and membrane integrity. Swelling and chromatin clumping occur early and can be reversed if oxygen returns.

med-path.l01.q5.t: Less ATP slows the sodium pump, so sodium and water accumulate in the cell
med-path.l01.q5.p: Which sequence best explains why a hypoxic cell swells early?
med-path.l01.q5.h: Think about what the Na+/K+ ATPase needs.
med-path.l01.q5.e: Failing oxidative phosphorylation reduces ATP, impairing the pump and letting sodium and water in. Anaerobic glycolysis does produce lactate, but that lowers pH rather than causing swelling.

med-path.l02.q1.t: Coagulative necrosis, with the tissue outline preserved for days
med-path.l02.q1.p: Which pattern of necrosis is typical of an ischaemic infarct in the kidney?
med-path.l02.q1.h: Solid organs outside the brain share one pattern.
med-path.l02.q1.e: Ischaemia in solid organs gives coagulative necrosis. Liquefactive necrosis is characteristic of brain infarcts and abscesses.

med-path.l02.q2.t: Caspase 9, through formation of the apoptosome
med-path.l02.q2.p: A cell undergoing apoptosis releases cytochrome c from mitochondria. Which molecule is activated next in this pathway?
med-path.l02.q2.e: Cytochrome c with APAF1 forms the apoptosome that activates caspase 9. Caspase 8 is the initiator of the extrinsic death-receptor pathway.

med-path.l02.q3.t: Overexpression of BCL2 that prevents mitochondrial release of cytochrome c
med-path.l02.q3.p: A 40-year-old woman has a lymph node biopsy showing follicular lymphoma with t(14;18). Which mechanism most directly explains the survival of her tumor cells?
med-path.l02.q3.h: The 14;18 translocation places a gene under the immunoglobulin heavy chain promoter.
med-path.l02.q3.e: The translocation drives BCL2 overexpression, which blocks intrinsic apoptosis. Increased BAX would promote death, not survival.

med-path.l02.q4.t: Zone 3 hepatocytes have the highest cytochrome P450 activity and make the toxic metabolite
med-path.l02.q4.p: A 25-year-old woman is admitted after an intentional acetaminophen overdose. Transaminases are very high and biopsy shows necrosis around the central veins. Which is the best explanation for the distribution of injury?
med-path.l02.q4.h: Think about where drug metabolism is most active in the lobule.
med-path.l02.q4.e: NAPQI is made by P450 enzymes concentrated in centrilobular hepatocytes, which are also low in oxygen. High glutathione stores would protect cells, not injure them.

med-path.l02.q5.t: Returning oxygen generates a burst of free radicals and calcium overload
med-path.l02.q5.p: Why can an ischaemic tissue appear more damaged shortly after blood flow is restored?
med-path.l02.q5.h: Oxygen is needed, but it also fuels something harmful.
med-path.l02.q5.e: Reperfusion injury arises from reactive oxygen species, calcium influx and inflammation. The fibrinoid necrosis answer describes immune-mediated vessel injury, not reperfusion.

med-path.l03.q1.t: Selectins, such as P-selectin and E-selectin
med-path.l03.q1.p: Which adhesion molecule family mediates the initial rolling of leukocytes along activated endothelium?
med-path.l03.q1.e: Selectins give weak, transient binding that produces rolling. Integrins mediate the later firm adhesion, and PECAM-1 is involved in transmigration.

med-path.l03.q2.t: High protein content due to increased vascular permeability
med-path.l03.q2.p: Which feature distinguishes an exudate from a transudate?
med-path.l03.q2.h: Think about what passes through a leaky vessel.
med-path.l03.q2.e: Exudates form when permeability rises, letting protein leak. Transudates result from hydrostatic or oncotic imbalance with an intact barrier.

med-path.l03.q3.t: NADPH oxidase deficiency, so phagocytes cannot generate superoxide
med-path.l03.q3.p: A 6-year-old boy has recurrent abscesses of lymph nodes and lung due to Staphylococcus aureus and Aspergillus. A dihydrorhodamine flow cytometry test shows no oxidative burst. Which defect is most likely?
med-path.l03.q3.h: The test measures the burst itself, and catalase-positive organisms are the problem.
med-path.l03.q3.e: Chronic granulomatous disease is a defect of NADPH oxidase. In CD18 deficiency neutrophils would be raised in blood and the test would be normal.

med-path.l03.q4.t: Interferon gamma secreted by T-helper 1 lymphocytes
med-path.l03.q4.p: A 30-year-old woman has a chest radiograph with hilar lymphadenopathy. A lymph node biopsy shows non-caseating granulomas. Which cell product is most important for activating the macrophages that form them?
med-path.l03.q4.e: Th1 cells release interferon gamma, which activates macrophages into epithelioid cells. IL-4 favours the humoral and allergic responses, not granuloma formation.

med-path.l03.q5.t: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency from CD18 integrin mutations
med-path.l03.q5.p: A child born with delayed separation of the umbilical cord, recurrent infections without pus and very high blood neutrophil counts most likely has which defect?
med-path.l03.q5.h: Neutrophils are made but cannot leave the blood.
med-path.l03.q5.e: Adhesion failure keeps neutrophils in the circulation and explains the lack of pus. Chronic granulomatous disease causes abscesses and granulomas.

med-path.l04.q1.p: Which type of tissue can regenerate after injury but is normally quiescent?
med-path.l04.q1.h: Quiescent cells re-enter the cell cycle when needed.
med-path.l04.q1.e: Stable cells sit in G0 but can proliferate after injury. Labile cells divide continuously, and permanent cells cannot divide meaningfully.

med-path.l04.q2.p: Which cell is responsible for contraction of a healing skin wound?
med-path.l04.q2.h: This cell shares features of a fibroblast and a smooth muscle cell.
med-path.l04.q2.e: Myofibroblasts pull the wound edges together. Keratinocytes re-epithelialise the surface but do not contract the wound.

med-path.l04.q3.t: Impaired hydroxylation of proline and lysine in collagen, so it cannot cross-link
med-path.l04.q3.p: A 70-year-old malnourished man develops perifollicular haemorrhages, swollen bleeding gums and a surgical wound that has reopened. Which biochemical defect best explains the poor healing?
med-path.l04.q3.h: The vitamin is a cofactor for modifying collagen after translation.
med-path.l04.q3.e: Scurvy causes defective collagen hydroxylation, giving fragile vessels and poor wound strength. Vitamin K deficiency causes bleeding but not the gum and perifollicular findings with collagen weakness.

med-path.l04.q4.t: This is a keloid, and it extends beyond the original wound edges
med-path.l04.q4.p: A 28-year-old woman has a firm, raised scar that has grown well beyond the margins of her original ear-piercing site. Biopsy shows thick, glassy bundles of collagen. Which statement is most accurate?
med-path.l04.q4.h: Compare what happens at the wound boundary.
med-path.l04.q4.e: A keloid grows beyond the wound and recurs after excision, while a hypertrophic scar remains within it. Granulation tissue is the soft, vascular stage that precedes the scar.

med-path.l04.q5.t: Activation of hepatic stellate cells into collagen-producing myofibroblasts
med-path.l04.q5.p: Which change drives the progression from chronic liver injury to cirrhosis?
med-path.l04.q5.h: A cell that stores vitamin A changes its role.
med-path.l04.q5.e: Stellate cells become myofibroblasts and lay down collagen, producing fibrosis. Increased collagen degradation would limit scarring, not drive it.

med-path.l05.q1.t: Congestive hepatomegaly with a nutmeg appearance of the liver
med-path.l05.q1.p: Which finding is typical of chronic right-sided heart failure?
med-path.l05.q1.h: Right-sided failure backs blood up into the systemic veins.
med-path.l05.q1.e: Systemic venous congestion affects the liver, producing the nutmeg pattern. Hemosiderin-laden macrophages in the lung indicate left-sided failure.

med-path.l05.q2.t: Reduced plasma oncotic pressure from urinary albumin loss
med-path.l05.q2.p: A man with nephrotic syndrome develops periorbital and leg swelling. Which mechanism most directly explains the edema?
med-path.l05.q2.h: Think about which protein is lost in the urine.
med-path.l05.q2.e: Albumin loss lowers oncotic pressure, so fluid stays in the tissue. Increased hydrostatic pressure is the mechanism in heart failure, not nephrosis.

med-path.l05.q3.t: Widespread microthrombi consume platelets and clotting factors while fibrinolysis is activated
med-path.l05.q3.p: A 52-year-old woman with pneumonia and septic shock develops oozing from IV sites and bleeding gums. Labs show low platelets, prolonged PT and PTT, low fibrinogen and a markedly raised D-dimer. Which mechanism best explains the bleeding?
med-path.l05.q3.h: The same process causes both clotting and bleeding.
med-path.l05.q3.e: DIC is a consumptive coagulopathy triggered by sepsis. A vitamin K deficiency would not lower platelets or raise D-dimer.

med-path.l05.q4.t: A deficiency of an intrinsic pathway factor impairs generation of thrombin on the platelet plug
med-path.l05.q4.p: A 7-year-old boy has recurrent bleeding into the knee joints and a prolonged aPTT with a normal PT, platelet count and bleeding time. Which explains the pattern of bleeding?
med-path.l05.q4.h: Joint bleeds suggest a secondary hemostasis problem.
med-path.l05.q4.e: A prolonged aPTT with normal PT fits an intrinsic factor deficiency such as hemophilia A or B. A platelet adhesion defect would prolong bleeding time and cause mucosal bleeding.

med-path.l05.q5.p: Which test result most directly reflects plasmin degradation of cross-linked fibrin?
med-path.l05.q5.h: This marker shows a clot has formed and then broken down.
med-path.l05.q5.e: D-dimer is a fragment of cross-linked fibrin broken down by plasmin. PT tests the extrinsic and common pathways, not fibrinolysis.

med-path.l06.q1.p: Which element of Virchow triad is the main driver of thrombus formation in the left atrial appendage during atrial fibrillation?
med-path.l06.q1.h: The atrium fibrillates rather than contracting.
med-path.l06.q1.e: Atrial fibrillation produces stasis, which allows clots to form. Endothelial injury is the main driver of arterial thrombi over plaques.

med-path.l06.q2.t: Alternating pale and dark layers called lines of Zahn
med-path.l06.q2.p: Which feature of a thrombus indicates that it formed in flowing blood before death?
med-path.l06.q2.e: Lines of Zahn are layers of platelets and fibrin alternating with red cells, and they mark antemortem thrombi. Postmortem clots are gelatinous without layers.

med-path.l06.q3.t: Factor V Leiden mutation causing resistance to inactivation by activated protein C
med-path.l06.q3.p: A 34-year-old woman 3 weeks after a long-haul flight and on oral contraceptives has sudden dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain. CT shows a saddle embolus. Her father had a similar event at a young age. Which inherited abnormality is the most common cause of this family history?
med-path.l06.q3.h: This is the most common inherited thrombophilia.
med-path.l06.q3.e: Factor V Leiden is the most common inherited cause of venous thrombosis, and oestrogen adds risk. Antithrombin deficiency is rarer, and the others cause bleeding.

med-path.l06.q4.t: Fat embolus from marrow released at the fracture site
med-path.l06.q4.p: A 22-year-old man has a femur fracture. Two days after surgery he develops hypoxia, confusion and a petechial rash over the chest. Which type of embolus is most likely?
med-path.l06.q4.h: The triad has a respiratory, a neurologic and a skin component.
med-path.l06.q4.e: Fat embolism after long-bone fracture classically produces hypoxia, neurologic change and petechiae. A thromboembolus would not explain the petechial rash.

med-path.l06.q5.t: The lung has a dual blood supply from the pulmonary and bronchial arteries
med-path.l06.q5.p: Why do small pulmonary emboli rarely cause pulmonary infarction in a healthy person?
med-path.l06.q5.h: Think about the vascular supply of the lung.
med-path.l06.q5.e: Bronchial arteries maintain oxygenation, so infarction mostly occurs when the lung is already congested. The lung does not have end arteries.

med-path.l07.q1.t: Enzymes, because a heterozygote keeps enough activity to be healthy
med-path.l07.q1.p: Which category of protein is most often affected in autosomal recessive disorders?
med-path.l07.q1.e: Enzyme deficiency usually needs loss of both alleles before the metabolic block is significant. Structural and receptor defects are more often dominant.

med-path.l07.q2.t: All daughters are carriers and no sons are affected
med-path.l07.q2.p: A man with an X-linked recessive disease has children with a woman who is not a carrier. What is the outcome for their children?
med-path.l07.q2.h: A father passes his X to daughters only.
med-path.l07.q2.e: The father gives his X to every daughter and his Y to every son, so daughters are obligate carriers and sons receive the normal maternal X.

med-path.l07.q3.t: Aortic root dilation leading to dissection
med-path.l07.q3.p: A 17-year-old tall, thin boy has arachnodactyly, a high arched palate, and upward lens dislocation. He is at greatest risk of which life-threatening complication?
med-path.l07.q3.h: Fibrillin 1 forms part of the elastic fibre in the aortic media.
med-path.l07.q3.e: Marfan syndrome weakens the aortic media and causes root dilation and dissection. Mitral valve prolapse also occurs, but the dominant life-threat is dissection.

med-path.l07.q4.t: Defective chloride secretion produces dehydrated, thick mucus that impairs clearance
med-path.l07.q4.p: A 4-year-old boy has recurrent Pseudomonas pneumonia, greasy foul stools and poor weight gain. A sweat chloride test is high. Which mechanism most directly explains his lung disease?
med-path.l07.q4.h: The sweat test points to a chloride channel.
med-path.l07.q4.e: CFTR dysfunction reduces chloride and water secretion, so secretions become thick. Primary ciliary dyskinesia would not give a high sweat chloride.

med-path.l07.q5.p: Two unaffected parents have a child with autosomal recessive disease. What is the chance that their next child is affected?
med-path.l07.q5.h: Each parent is a heterozygous carrier.
med-path.l07.q5.e: Two carriers each transmit the mutant allele with probability one half, so one in four children are affected.

med-path.l08.q1.p: Which trinucleotide repeat expansion causes fragile X syndrome?
med-path.l08.q1.h: The expansion is in a CpG-rich region that becomes methylated.
med-path.l08.q1.e: Fragile X is a CGG expansion with gene silencing by methylation. CAG expansion causes Huntington disease.

med-path.l08.q2.t: Prader-Willi syndrome through loss of the paternal contribution
med-path.l08.q2.p: A child inherits both copies of chromosome 15 from the mother. What disorder results?
med-path.l08.q2.h: Imprinted genes in 15q11-q13 are expressed from the paternal copy in one disorder.
med-path.l08.q2.e: Maternal uniparental disomy leaves no active paternal copy of the imprinted region, giving Prader-Willi syndrome. Angelman syndrome results from loss of the maternal copy.

med-path.l08.q3.t: Bicuspid aortic valve or coarctation of the aorta
med-path.l08.q3.p: A 15-year-old girl has short stature, a webbed neck, widely spaced nipples and primary amenorrhea. Which cardiovascular lesion is most likely?
med-path.l08.q3.h: This is a monosomy of the X chromosome.
med-path.l08.q3.e: Turner syndrome is associated with left-sided obstructive lesions such as coarctation. AV septal defects are typical of Down syndrome.

med-path.l08.q4.p: A 9-month-old boy has developmental regression, an exaggerated startle response, a cherry-red macula and no hepatosplenomegaly. Which enzyme is most likely deficient?
med-path.l08.q4.h: The cherry-red spot is present in two storage diseases, but only one lacks organomegaly.
med-path.l08.q4.e: Tay-Sachs disease is hexosaminidase A deficiency with no organomegaly. Niemann-Pick disease also has a cherry-red macula but with hepatosplenomegaly.

med-path.l08.q5.t: Mitochondria in the zygote derive almost entirely from the oocyte
med-path.l08.q5.p: A man with a mitochondrial DNA mutation has a family in which all affected offspring are children of affected mothers only. Why do affected fathers not transmit the disease?
med-path.l08.q5.h: Think about which gamete contributes cytoplasm.
med-path.l08.q5.e: Sperm mitochondria are excluded from the zygote, so inheritance is maternal. Imprinting affects nuclear genes, not mitochondrial DNA.

med-path.l09.q1.t: Invasion through the basement membrane into underlying tissue
med-path.l09.q1.p: Which feature is the most reliable histologic indicator that an epithelial tumor is malignant?
med-path.l09.q1.h: This is what separates carcinoma in situ from invasive carcinoma.
med-path.l09.q1.e: Invasion through the basement membrane defines invasive carcinoma. A fibrous capsule and a well-differentiated pattern point toward benign behaviour.

med-path.l09.q2.t: Differentiation is the grade, while node and liver involvement define the stage
med-path.l09.q2.p: A pathologist reports a colon cancer as moderately differentiated, with tumor cells in 3 of 14 regional nodes and a single liver metastasis. Which statement correctly separates grade from stage?
med-path.l09.q2.h: One describes how the cells look, the other how far they have spread.
med-path.l09.q2.e: Grade is based on histologic differentiation, while stage reflects extent of spread (TNM). Stage is usually the stronger predictor of survival.

med-path.l09.q3.t: Hematogenous spread through venous invasion carries cells to the first capillary bed in the lung
med-path.l09.q3.p: A 62-year-old man has a large renal mass. CT shows tumor extending into the renal vein and inferior vena cava, and several small lung nodules. Which feature of this tumor best explains the pulmonary nodules?
med-path.l09.q3.h: Venous blood from the kidney goes to the right heart and then the lungs.
med-path.l09.q3.e: Renal cell carcinoma characteristically invades veins and spreads by the blood to the lung. Lymphatic spread would first involve nodes, not scattered lung nodules.

med-path.l09.q4.t: Carcinoma in situ, a full-thickness dysplasia without invasion
med-path.l09.q4.p: A cervical biopsy from a 29-year-old woman shows atypical cells with large hyperchromatic nuclei in all layers of the epithelium. The basement membrane is intact. Which diagnosis is most accurate?
med-path.l09.q4.h: Atypia is present, but check the basement membrane.
med-path.l09.q4.e: Full-thickness atypia without breaching the basement membrane is carcinoma in situ. Invasive carcinoma would need breach of the membrane.

med-path.l09.q5.t: Loss of E-cadherin-mediated adhesion between epithelial cells
med-path.l09.q5.p: Which change allows tumor cells to detach from their neighbours early in metastasis?
med-path.l09.q5.h: Think about the adhesion molecule that holds epithelial cells together.
med-path.l09.q5.e: Loss of E-cadherin weakens cell-cell contacts. Matrix metalloproteinases would be increased, not lost, to degrade the basement membrane.

med-path.l10.q1.p: Which oncogene is activated in most cases of chronic myeloid leukemia?
med-path.l10.q1.e: The Philadelphia chromosome fuses BCR to ABL and makes a constitutively active tyrosine kinase. MYC is activated in Burkitt lymphoma.

med-path.l10.q2.t: Loss of GTPase activity so the protein stays in the active GTP-bound state
med-path.l10.q2.p: Which mutation best explains a RAS-driven tumor?
med-path.l10.q2.h: RAS is turned off by hydrolysing GTP.
med-path.l10.q2.e: Oncogenic RAS mutations impair GTP hydrolysis, so signalling is continuous. A gain of function is the point, so losing GTP binding would not cause cancer.

med-path.l10.q3.t: Increased copies of a growth factor receptor gene cause excessive growth signalling
med-path.l10.q3.p: A 47-year-old woman has an invasive breast carcinoma that overexpresses HER2 due to gene amplification. Which is the best description of how this oncogene contributes to the tumor?
med-path.l10.q3.h: Amplification means more copies of the gene.
med-path.l10.q3.e: HER2 amplification raises receptor tyrosine kinase signalling, and trastuzumab targets it. A fusion kinase describes BCR-ABL, and a loss of G1 arrest describes RB or p53 loss.

med-path.l10.q4.t: A transcription factor gene placed beside an immunoglobulin gene promoter is overexpressed
med-path.l10.q4.p: A 20-year-old has a rapidly growing jaw mass. Biopsy shows a starry sky pattern of tumor cells with many mitoses interspersed with macrophages. Cytogenetics shows a translocation involving chromosome 8. Which mechanism most likely drives proliferation?
med-path.l10.q4.h: This is Burkitt lymphoma and the oncogene is a transcription factor.
med-path.l10.q4.e: The t(8;14) places MYC next to the immunoglobulin heavy chain promoter, and MYC is a transcription factor. BCL2 overexpression is the follicular lymphoma mechanism.

med-path.l10.q5.t: Melanoma, which is treated with a BRAF inhibitor
med-path.l10.q5.p: Which cancer is characteristically associated with the BRAF V600E mutation?
med-path.l10.q5.h: This is a kinase mutation commonly found in skin cancer.
med-path.l10.q5.e: BRAF V600E is common in melanoma and is targeted by specific inhibitors. N-MYC amplification occurs in neuroblastoma, but it is not typically treated with BRAF inhibitors.

med-path.l11.q1.t: Every retinal cell already carries the first hit, so one somatic mutation is enough
med-path.l11.q1.p: In Knudson two-hit hypothesis, why do inherited retinoblastoma cases occur earlier and bilaterally?
med-path.l11.q1.h: The first hit is in the germline.
med-path.l11.q1.e: Inherited cases start with one defective allele in all cells, so a single somatic hit suffices in many cells. Sporadic cases need two separate hits in one cell.

med-path.l11.q2.t: G1 arrest through p21, with apoptosis if the damage cannot be repaired
med-path.l11.q2.p: Which event normally follows DNA damage in a cell with functional p53?
med-path.l11.q2.e: p53 induces p21 and cell cycle arrest, and triggers apoptosis if repair fails. Phosphorylated RB would promote cell cycle entry.

med-path.l11.q3.p: A 28-year-old woman has a sarcoma. Her brother had adrenocortical carcinoma at age 5 and her mother had premenopausal breast cancer. Which gene is most likely mutated in this family?
med-path.l11.q3.h: Think of a syndrome with sarcomas, breast and adrenal cancers.
med-path.l11.q3.e: Li-Fraumeni syndrome from germline TP53 mutation causes multiple early cancers of these types. Lynch syndrome mainly causes colorectal and endometrial cancer.

med-path.l11.q4.t: Loss of APC function leads to accumulation of beta-catenin and activation of MYC
med-path.l11.q4.p: A 19-year-old has hundreds of colonic polyps, and his father had colon cancer at 40. Which molecular abnormality is the underlying defect?
med-path.l11.q4.h: Polyposis points to the Wnt pathway.
med-path.l11.q4.e: Familial adenomatous polyposis comes from APC mutation. Mismatch repair deficiency causes Lynch syndrome, which has few polyps.

med-path.l11.q5.t: E6 degrades p53 and E7 inactivates RB
med-path.l11.q5.p: Which viral protein pair explains how high-risk HPV promotes cervical cancer?
med-path.l11.q5.h: One targets the guardian of the genome and the other targets the G1 checkpoint.
med-path.l11.q5.e: E6 promotes p53 degradation and E7 binds RB, releasing E2F. The reversed pairing is a common distractor.

med-path.l12.q1.p: Which tumor marker is most useful for monitoring recurrence of colorectal cancer after resection?
med-path.l12.q1.h: This oncofetal antigen is raised in many gut cancers.
med-path.l12.q1.e: CEA is used to follow colorectal cancer. AFP is used for hepatocellular carcinoma and yolk sac tumors.

med-path.l12.q2.t: Hypercalcemia in squamous cell carcinoma of the lung
med-path.l12.q2.p: Which paraneoplastic syndrome is caused by tumor secretion of PTH-related peptide?
med-path.l12.q2.h: Think about which electrolyte PTH-like peptide raises.
med-path.l12.q2.e: PTHrP raises serum calcium and is typical of squamous cell carcinoma. Renal carcinoma makes erythropoietin, which causes polycythemia.

med-path.l12.q3.t: Antibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels reduce acetylcholine release
med-path.l12.q3.p: A 66-year-old smoker has weakness that improves with repeated muscle use, dry mouth and absent reflexes, with a central lung mass. Which mechanism explains the weakness?
med-path.l12.q3.h: Strength improves with use in this presynaptic disorder.
med-path.l12.q3.e: Lambert-Eaton syndrome with small cell lung cancer involves presynaptic calcium channel antibodies. Postsynaptic receptor antibodies describe myasthenia gravis, which worsens with use.

med-path.l12.q4.t: Loss of T cell inhibition allows autoimmune inflammation of normal tissue
med-path.l12.q4.p: A 70-year-old man receiving a PD-1 inhibitor for melanoma develops severe watery diarrhea and abdominal pain, and colonoscopy shows inflamed mucosa. Which mechanism most likely explains this?
med-path.l12.q4.h: The drug releases a brake on T cells.
med-path.l12.q4.e: Checkpoint inhibitors remove inhibitory signalling, which can cause immune-related colitis. These drugs do not usually cause profound neutropenia.

med-path.l12.q5.t: Aerobic glycolysis, known as the Warburg effect
med-path.l12.q5.p: Which feature best explains the high glucose uptake of tumors on FDG-PET imaging?
med-path.l12.q5.h: Tumors use glucose even when oxygen is available.
med-path.l12.q5.e: The Warburg effect describes increased glucose uptake and glycolysis in cancer cells. Telomerase relates to replicative immortality, not to glucose uptake.

med-path.l13.q1.t: Foam cells derived from macrophages that have taken up oxidised LDL
med-path.l13.q1.p: Which cell type forms the fatty streak in early atherosclerosis?
med-path.l13.q1.h: The cell is filled with lipid droplets.
med-path.l13.q1.e: Monocyte-derived macrophages ingest oxidised LDL to become foam cells. Smooth muscle cells and matrix form the later fibrous cap.

med-path.l13.q2.t: Macrophage removal of dead myocytes, with the wall at its weakest
med-path.l13.q2.p: Which feature of an infarct is typical at 5 days after onset?
med-path.l13.q2.h: Think about when risk of rupture is highest.
med-path.l13.q2.e: At 3 to 7 days macrophages digest necrotic muscle before scar forms, which is the highest risk period for rupture. Dense scar takes about two months.

med-path.l13.q3.t: Rupture of the ventricular free wall with hemopericardium
med-path.l13.q3.p: A 66-year-old man had an anterior infarct 5 days ago and now develops sudden hypotension, muffled heart sounds and jugular venous distention. Which complication is most likely?
med-path.l13.q3.e: Free wall rupture occurs when necrotic muscle is soft, causing tamponade. Dressler syndrome occurs weeks later and does not cause tamponade physiology this suddenly.

med-path.l13.q4.t: Partial or transient occlusion causing subendocardial necrosis in the zone farthest from the epicardial vessels
med-path.l13.q4.p: A 58-year-old man has 20 minutes of chest pain at rest. ECG shows ST depression and troponin is elevated. Which pathologic process best explains the pattern of necrosis?
med-path.l13.q4.h: ST depression with a positive troponin is not transmural.
med-path.l13.q4.e: Non-ST elevation infarction is subendocardial because that layer is most vulnerable to reduced flow. Stable angina does not raise troponin.

med-path.l13.q5.t: Posterior descending branch of the right coronary artery
med-path.l13.q5.p: Which vessel supplies the inferior wall of the left ventricle in a right-dominant circulation?
med-path.l13.q5.h: Dominance depends on which artery gives the posterior descending branch.
med-path.l13.q5.e: The RCA gives the posterior descending artery in about 80 percent. The LAD supplies the anterior wall and anterior septum.

med-path.l14.q1.t: Mitral stenosis with a fish-mouth orifice
med-path.l14.q1.p: Which is the typical valve lesion in chronic rheumatic heart disease?
med-path.l14.q1.h: This valve is most often affected.
med-path.l14.q1.e: Chronic rheumatic disease thickens and fuses the mitral commissures. Tricuspid and pulmonary involvement are uncommon.

med-path.l14.q2.t: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy from sarcomere gene mutations
med-path.l14.q2.p: Which cardiomyopathy is characterised by asymmetric septal hypertrophy and myocyte disarray?
med-path.l14.q2.h: Think about young athletes who die suddenly.
med-path.l14.q2.e: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is an autosomal dominant sarcomere disease with disarray. Dilated disease has thin walls and a large cavity.

med-path.l14.q3.t: Staphylococcus aureus infecting a previously normal valve
med-path.l14.q3.p: A 32-year-old man who injects drugs has fever, a new tricuspid regurgitant murmur and multiple septic pulmonary emboli. Which organism is the most likely cause?
med-path.l14.q3.h: Right-sided disease in an injection drug user.
med-path.l14.q3.e: S. aureus is the usual cause in injection drug users and attacks normal valves, especially the tricuspid. Viridans streptococci typically infect abnormal valves after dental procedures.

med-path.l14.q4.t: Granulomatous inflammation with giant cells disrupting the internal elastic lamina
med-path.l14.q4.p: A 72-year-old woman has new temporal headache, jaw pain on chewing and a raised ESR. Which histologic finding is most likely on biopsy of the temporal artery?
med-path.l14.q4.h: This is a large-vessel arteritis in older adults.
med-path.l14.q4.e: Giant cell arteritis shows granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells. Polyarteritis nodosa shows segmental fibrinoid necrosis in medium arteries.

med-path.l14.q5.p: A 9-year-old has fever for six days, conjunctivitis, a strawberry tongue and swollen hands. Which complication must be prevented?
med-path.l14.q5.h: This is a vasculitis of medium vessels in children.
med-path.l14.q5.e: Kawasaki disease is treated with immunoglobulin to prevent coronary aneurysm. Chorea is a feature of rheumatic fever.

med-path.l15.q1.t: Reduced FEV1/FVC ratio with raised residual volume
med-path.l15.q1.p: Which pulmonary function pattern is expected in emphysema?
med-path.l15.q1.h: Air is trapped behind obstructed airways.
med-path.l15.q1.e: Obstruction reduces the ratio and traps air, raising residual volume. Restriction reduces total lung capacity with a normal or high ratio.

med-path.l15.q2.t: An imbalance between protease activity and antiprotease protection in the lung
med-path.l15.q2.p: Which pathogenic mechanism best explains emphysema in smokers?
med-path.l15.q2.e: Smoking increases neutrophil elastase and inactivates alpha-1 antitrypsin by oxidation. Surfactant deficiency is the problem in neonatal respiratory distress.

med-path.l15.q3.p: A 38-year-old man who has never smoked has progressive dyspnea. Chest imaging shows lower lobe emphysema, and liver enzymes are mildly raised. Which finding is expected on liver biopsy?
med-path.l15.q3.h: This is a misfolded protein retained in the endoplasmic reticulum.
med-path.l15.q3.e: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency causes accumulation of misfolded protein, seen as PAS-positive globules. Mallory-Denk bodies point to alcoholic injury.

med-path.l15.q4.t: Golden-brown beaded ferruginous bodies in the fibrotic parenchyma
med-path.l15.q4.p: A 62-year-old retired shipyard worker has progressive dyspnea. CT shows bilateral lower-lobe fibrosis and calcified pleural plaques. Biopsy would most likely show which finding?
med-path.l15.q4.e: Asbestos fibres coated with iron and protein form ferruginous bodies, and pleural plaques are characteristic. Silica produces whorled nodules in the upper zones.

med-path.l15.q5.t: Macrophages in granulomas convert vitamin D to its active form
med-path.l15.q5.p: A 27-year-old Black woman has bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, cough and a raised serum calcium. Which mechanism explains the hypercalcemia?
med-path.l15.q5.e: Sarcoid granulomas make calcitriol independent of regulation. PTHrP secretion would be seen in squamous cell cancers.

med-path.l16.q1.t: Apical cavitation with caseation and hemoptysis
med-path.l16.q1.p: Which feature is typical of secondary (reactivation) pulmonary tuberculosis?
med-path.l16.q1.h: Reactivation prefers a high oxygen tension.
med-path.l16.q1.e: Reactivation disease localises to the apices and cavitates. The Ghon complex is a feature of primary infection.

med-path.l16.q2.t: Adenocarcinoma, which often has an EGFR or ALK alteration
med-path.l16.q2.p: Which lung cancer type is most characteristically peripheral and found in non-smokers?
med-path.l16.q2.h: This is the most common type overall.
med-path.l16.q2.e: Adenocarcinoma is peripheral and is the typical type in non-smokers, with targetable drivers. Small cell carcinoma is central and smoking-related.

med-path.l16.q3.p: A 64-year-old smoker has right ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis and shoulder pain radiating down the arm. Imaging shows an apical lung mass. Which structure is directly invaded to cause the eye findings?
med-path.l16.q3.e: Apical tumors invade the sympathetic chain, causing Horner syndrome. The superior vena cava produces facial plethora, not ptosis or miosis.

med-path.l16.q4.t: Chemotherapy is the mainstay because disease is usually disseminated at diagnosis
med-path.l16.q4.p: A 56-year-old man has a central lung mass, rapid progression and widespread metastases within months. Biopsy shows sheets of small blue cells with scant cytoplasm, nuclear moulding and neuroendocrine markers. Which management principle follows from this histology?
med-path.l16.q4.e: Small cell carcinoma is highly aggressive and chemosensitive, and surgery is rarely curative. Imatinib targets BCR-ABL and KIT, not this tumor.

med-path.l16.q5.t: Surfactant deficiency with hyaline membranes and a low L/S ratio
med-path.l16.q5.p: A premature infant born at 29 weeks has grunting and cyanosis soon after birth. Chest film shows a ground-glass pattern. Which finding is expected?
med-path.l16.q5.e: Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome is from surfactant deficiency and hyaline membranes. Transient tachypnea is typical of term infants after caesarean delivery.

med-path.l17.q1.p: Which organism is most associated with chronic antral gastritis and duodenal ulcers?
med-path.l17.q1.h: It survives in acid by producing urease.
med-path.l17.q1.e: H. pylori causes type B gastritis and most duodenal ulcers. The other organisms cause enteric infection rather than chronic gastritis.

med-path.l17.q2.t: Transmural inflammation with skip lesions and non-caseating granulomas
med-path.l17.q2.p: Which feature best distinguishes Crohn disease from ulcerative colitis?
med-path.l17.q2.h: One disease is transmural and patchy.
med-path.l17.q2.e: Crohn disease is transmural and patchy, and can form fistulas. Ulcerative colitis is continuous from the rectum and limited to the mucosa and submucosa.

med-path.l17.q3.t: Autoantibodies destroy parietal cells and block intrinsic factor, so vitamin B12 is not absorbed
med-path.l17.q3.p: A 45-year-old woman has fatigue, a macrocytic anemia and glossitis. Biopsy of the gastric body shows atrophic gastritis, and the serum gastrin is high. Which mechanism explains her anemia?
med-path.l17.q3.h: High gastrin reflects a lack of acid.
med-path.l17.q3.e: Autoimmune gastritis causes parietal cell loss, achlorhydria and loss of intrinsic factor, producing pernicious anemia. Iron deficiency would produce a microcytic anemia.

med-path.l17.q4.p: A 68-year-old man has weight loss and a gastric biopsy showing cells with intracellular mucin pushing the nucleus to the side, with a thickened, rigid stomach wall. Which protein is most likely lost?
med-path.l17.q4.h: This is the diffuse type of gastric cancer.
med-path.l17.q4.e: Diffuse gastric cancer with signet ring cells is associated with loss of E-cadherin and poor cell cohesion. Intestinal-type tumors more often show APC pathway changes.

med-path.l17.q5.t: The splenic flexure, a watershed zone between arterial territories
med-path.l17.q5.p: Which location is most vulnerable to ischemic colitis during hypotension?
med-path.l17.q5.h: Think about where two arterial territories meet.
med-path.l17.q5.e: The splenic flexure lies between the superior and inferior mesenteric territories. The rectum has dual supply and is rarely ischemic.

med-path.l18.q1.p: Which serologic marker indicates acute hepatitis B infection?
med-path.l18.q1.h: This marker appears during the window period.
med-path.l18.q1.e: Core IgM indicates recent infection. Surface antibody alone indicates immunity from vaccination or past infection.

med-path.l18.q2.t: AST higher than ALT, typically in a ratio of about two to one
med-path.l18.q2.p: Which laboratory pattern is typical of alcoholic hepatitis?
med-path.l18.q2.h: Alcohol depletes pyridoxal phosphate needed for ALT.
med-path.l18.q2.e: In alcoholic liver disease AST is raised more than ALT, often by two to one. Viral hepatitis generally gives ALT higher than AST.

med-path.l18.q3.t: Impaired biliary copper excretion from a mutation in ATP7B
med-path.l18.q3.p: A 24-year-old man has tremor, personality change and a greenish-brown ring at the corneal limbus. Ceruloplasmin is low. Which defect explains his liver disease?
med-path.l18.q3.e: Wilson disease results from ATP7B mutation and copper accumulation. HFE mutation causes iron overload in hemochromatosis.

med-path.l18.q4.t: Lymphocytic destruction of small interlobular bile ducts with granulomas
med-path.l18.q4.p: A 52-year-old woman with pruritus and fatigue has a raised alkaline phosphatase and positive antimitochondrial antibodies. Biopsy would show which pattern?
med-path.l18.q4.h: Antimitochondrial antibodies define one disease of small ducts.
med-path.l18.q4.e: Primary biliary cholangitis destroys small bile ducts. Primary sclerosing cholangitis affects large ducts and is associated with p-ANCA and ulcerative colitis.

med-path.l18.q5.t: Adenocarcinoma of the head of the pancreas
med-path.l18.q5.p: A 62-year-old has painless jaundice, weight loss and a palpable nontender gallbladder. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
med-path.l18.q5.e: A palpable nontender gallbladder with painless jaundice points to a malignant distal obstruction. Gallstone disease is usually painful and the gallbladder is not palpable.

med-path.l19.q1.t: Heavy proteinuria with hypoalbuminemia and hyperlipidemia
med-path.l19.q1.p: Which finding is typical of nephrotic syndrome?
med-path.l19.q1.h: This syndrome is defined by protein loss.
med-path.l19.q1.e: Nephrotic syndrome has proteinuria over 3.5 g per day with edema. Red cell casts indicate a nephritic process.

med-path.l19.q2.p: A 7-year-old girl has periorbital edema, heavy proteinuria and normal light microscopy. Which finding on electron microscopy is expected?
med-path.l19.q2.h: The glomeruli look normal with light microscopy.
med-path.l19.q2.e: Minimal change disease shows only foot process effacement. Subepithelial humps are seen in post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.

med-path.l19.q3.t: Granular deposits of IgG and C3 in a lumpy-bumpy pattern
med-path.l19.q3.p: A 9-year-old boy develops cola-colored urine, hypertension and periorbital edema 2 weeks after a sore throat. Complement C3 is low. Which immunofluorescence pattern is expected?
med-path.l19.q3.h: The preceding infection and low C3 suggest immune complexes.
med-path.l19.q3.e: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis shows granular immune complex deposits. Linear staining indicates anti-GBM disease.

med-path.l19.q4.t: The alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen
med-path.l19.q4.p: A 21-year-old smoker has hemoptysis and hematuria. Biopsy of the kidney shows crescents and linear IgG deposits along the glomerular basement membrane. What is the target of the antibody?
med-path.l19.q4.h: This is a type II hypersensitivity reaction.
med-path.l19.q4.e: Goodpasture syndrome results from antibodies to the noncollagenous domain of the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen. Anti-PLA2R antibodies are found in membranous nephropathy.

med-path.l19.q5.p: Which kidney finding is characteristic of long-standing diabetes?
med-path.l19.q5.h: This lesion is named for two physicians.
med-path.l19.q5.e: Diabetic nephropathy produces Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules and basement membrane thickening. Spike and dome indicates membranous nephropathy.

med-path.l20.q1.p: Which urinary finding is characteristic of acute tubular necrosis?
med-path.l20.q1.h: Epithelial cell debris forms the casts.
med-path.l20.q1.e: Muddy brown casts are from sloughed tubular epithelial cells. Red cell casts point to glomerulonephritis.

med-path.l20.q2.t: Low urine sodium, because intact tubules avidly retain sodium
med-path.l20.q2.p: Which urinary finding best distinguishes prerenal azotemia from acute tubular necrosis?
med-path.l20.q2.h: Think about what healthy tubules do when volume is low.
med-path.l20.q2.e: In prerenal states the tubules work and conserve sodium and water. In acute tubular necrosis, sodium wasting and poor concentration occur.

med-path.l20.q3.t: A hypersensitivity reaction in the tubulointerstitium to the drug
med-path.l20.q3.p: A 35-year-old has fever, a new rash and rising creatinine 10 days after starting a beta-lactam antibiotic. Urinalysis shows white cell casts and eosinophils. Which mechanism is most likely?
med-path.l20.q3.h: Fever, rash and eosinophils suggest allergy.
med-path.l20.q3.e: Acute interstitial nephritis is an immune-mediated drug reaction. Direct tubular toxicity does not usually cause rash and eosinophilia.

med-path.l20.q4.p: A 55-year-old man has flank pain, hematuria and a palpable mass. His hematocrit is high and a renal vein is occluded by tumor. Which gene is most likely inactivated?
med-path.l20.q4.h: This is the most common renal cancer in adults.
med-path.l20.q4.e: Clear cell renal carcinoma is associated with VHL loss. WT1 is mutated in Wilms tumor in children.

med-path.l20.q5.p: A woman with recurrent urinary infection by Proteus has a large branching stone. Which composition is expected?
med-path.l20.q5.e: Struvite stones form in alkaline urine from urease-producing bacteria. Uric acid stones form in acidic urine.

med-path.l21.q1.t: Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin directed against the TSH receptor
med-path.l21.q1.p: Which antibody mediates hyperthyroidism in Graves disease?
med-path.l21.q1.h: This is a type II hypersensitivity that mimics a hormone.
med-path.l21.q1.e: In Graves disease the antibody stimulates the TSH receptor. Anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies are a feature of Hashimoto thyroiditis.

med-path.l21.q2.t: Optically clear nuclei with grooves and psammoma bodies
med-path.l21.q2.p: Which feature best identifies papillary thyroid carcinoma on histology?
med-path.l21.q2.h: The diagnosis rests on nuclear features.
med-path.l21.q2.e: Papillary carcinoma is defined by its nuclear changes. Follicular carcinoma requires capsular or vascular invasion.

med-path.l21.q3.p: A 32-year-old woman has a thyroid mass with amyloid-containing stroma, elevated serum calcitonin and a family history of adrenal tumors. Which gene is most likely mutated?
med-path.l21.q3.h: Parafollicular C cells are affected in this syndrome.
med-path.l21.q3.e: Medullary carcinoma with a family history of pheochromocytoma suggests MEN 2 with activating RET mutations. MEN1 mutation causes a different tumor triad.

med-path.l21.q4.t: A single parathyroid adenoma with atrophy of the remaining glands
med-path.l21.q4.p: A 56-year-old woman has kidney stones, bone pain and constipation. Calcium is high, phosphate is low and PTH is elevated. Which finding is most likely?
med-path.l21.q4.h: PTH is not suppressed despite high calcium.
med-path.l21.q4.e: Primary hyperparathyroidism is usually from a single adenoma. In malignancy-associated hypercalcemia, PTH is suppressed, not elevated.

med-path.l21.q5.t: Lymphocytic infiltrate with germinal centres and Hurthle cells
med-path.l21.q5.p: Which finding is typical of Hashimoto thyroiditis on biopsy?
med-path.l21.q5.h: This is a destructive autoimmune thyroiditis.
med-path.l21.q5.e: Hashimoto disease shows lymphoid follicles and oncocytic change. Scalloped colloid is a feature of Graves disease.

med-path.l22.q1.p: Which is the most common cause of Cushing syndrome overall?
med-path.l22.q1.e: Medication use is the leading cause. Among endogenous causes, a pituitary adenoma is the most common.

med-path.l22.q2.t: Primary has high ACTH, hyperpigmentation and hyperkalemia
med-path.l22.q2.p: Which pattern distinguishes primary from secondary adrenal insufficiency?
med-path.l22.q2.h: ACTH shares a precursor with a pigment-stimulating peptide.
med-path.l22.q2.e: In primary disease loss of cortisol drives ACTH up, and loss of aldosterone causes hyperkalemia. In secondary disease ACTH is low.

med-path.l22.q3.t: Alpha-adrenergic blockade to prevent unopposed alpha stimulation
med-path.l22.q3.p: A 35-year-old has episodic pounding headaches, sweating and blood pressure of 210/120 mm Hg during attacks. A 24-hour urine shows markedly raised metanephrines. Which management step is appropriate before a beta blocker is started?
med-path.l22.q3.h: A beta blocker alone leaves one receptor type unopposed.
med-path.l22.q3.e: Alpha blockade comes first, since beta blockade alone can cause severe hypertension from unopposed vasoconstriction. The other options do not treat catecholamine excess.

med-path.l22.q4.p: A 45-year-old man has hypercalcemia, peptic ulcers and a pituitary prolactinoma. Which gene is most likely mutated?
med-path.l22.q4.e: MEN 1 involves the pituitary, parathyroids and pancreas, including gastrinoma. RET mutation causes MEN 2.

med-path.l22.q5.t: High C-peptide with an insulinoma and low C-peptide with injected insulin
med-path.l22.q5.p: Which finding distinguishes insulinoma from surreptitious insulin injection?
med-path.l22.q5.h: Endogenous insulin is released with a byproduct.
med-path.l22.q5.e: Endogenous insulin comes with C-peptide, so an insulinoma gives high levels while injected insulin suppresses C-peptide.

med-path.l23.q1.t: Low ferritin with high total iron-binding capacity
med-path.l23.q1.p: Which laboratory pattern is typical of iron deficiency anemia?
med-path.l23.q1.h: The body increases its capacity to grab iron.
med-path.l23.q1.e: In iron deficiency stores are low and transferrin is raised. In chronic disease, ferritin is high and TIBC low.

med-path.l23.q2.t: Raised methylmalonic acid disrupts myelin synthesis in the spinal cord
med-path.l23.q2.p: Which mechanism causes the neurologic findings of vitamin B12 deficiency but not folate deficiency?
med-path.l23.q2.h: B12 is needed for two enzymatic reactions, and folate for only one.
med-path.l23.q2.e: B12 is the cofactor for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, and its deficiency raises methylmalonic acid. Folate deficiency raises homocysteine only.

med-path.l23.q3.p: A 19-year-old Black man develops dark urine and back pain two days after taking an antimalarial drug. The smear shows bite cells and blue-purple inclusions with a supravital stain. Which enzyme is deficient?
med-path.l23.q3.e: G6PD deficiency leaves red cells unable to regenerate glutathione, causing Heinz bodies. Pyruvate kinase deficiency does not typically show Heinz bodies.

med-path.l23.q4.p: A 6-year-old with sickle cell disease has fever and bone pain, and bone culture grows an organism. Which organism is most characteristic in these patients?
med-path.l23.q4.h: Think about osteomyelitis specific to this hemoglobinopathy.
med-path.l23.q4.e: Salmonella is a characteristic cause of osteomyelitis in sickle cell disease. Pneumococcus causes sepsis from functional asplenia, not typically osteomyelitis.

med-path.l23.q5.p: A 60-year-old has pancytopenia and a hypocellular, fatty bone marrow. Which diagnosis fits?
med-path.l23.q5.e: Aplastic anemia shows pancytopenia and a hypocellular marrow. Megaloblastic anemia gives a hypercellular marrow.

med-path.l24.q1.t: Reed-Sternberg cell, which is CD15 and CD30 positive
med-path.l24.q1.p: Which cell is characteristic of classical Hodgkin lymphoma?
med-path.l24.q1.e: Reed-Sternberg cells are diagnostic. Smudge cells occur in chronic lymphocytic leukemia.

med-path.l24.q2.p: Which translocation defines acute promyelocytic leukemia?
med-path.l24.q2.h: The treatment is a vitamin A derivative.
med-path.l24.q2.e: APL involves the retinoic acid receptor, which is why ATRA induces differentiation. t(9;22) is chronic myeloid leukemia.

med-path.l24.q3.t: Light chains cast and injure the tubules
med-path.l24.q3.p: A 65-year-old has back pain, anemia, creatinine rise and hypercalcemia. Serum electrophoresis shows a monoclonal spike, and X-ray shows punched-out skull lesions. What explains the renal injury?
med-path.l24.q3.h: Bence Jones protein is a clue.
med-path.l24.q3.e: Myeloma kidney is from filtered light chains forming casts with Tamm-Horsfall protein. Amyloid can occur but is not the main cause of renal failure here.

med-path.l24.q4.t: Deficiency of ADAMTS13, causing unusually large von Willebrand multimers
med-path.l24.q4.p: A 5-year-old has fever, confusion and petechiae with anemia, thrombocytopenia and renal insufficiency. Smear shows schistocytes, and PT and PTT are normal. Which defect explains these findings?
med-path.l24.q4.e: TTP results from ADAMTS13 deficiency and platelet-rich microthrombi. DIC would prolong PT and PTT.

med-path.l24.q5.p: A 55-year-old has an elevated hematocrit, low erythropoietin and itching after hot showers. Which mutation is most likely?
med-path.l24.q5.e: Polycythemia vera is driven by JAK2 mutation in most cases. BCR-ABL1 causes chronic myeloid leukemia.

med-path.l25.q1.t: A lens-shaped collection after tearing of the middle meningeal artery
med-path.l25.q1.p: Which finding is typical of an epidural hematoma?
med-path.l25.q1.h: Temporal bone fracture is the classic cause.
med-path.l25.q1.e: Epidural hematomas are arterial and lens-shaped. The crescent-shaped collection is a subdural hematoma.

med-path.l25.q2.t: A cystic space from liquefactive necrosis with surrounding gliosis
med-path.l25.q2.p: Which change is expected in the brain several weeks after a cerebral infarct?
med-path.l25.q2.h: The brain repairs by a different route than other organs.
med-path.l25.q2.e: The brain forms cystic spaces and gliosis rather than a collagen scar. Coagulative necrosis is characteristic of infarcts elsewhere.

med-path.l25.q3.p: A 70-year-old woman has progressive memory loss and difficulty with daily tasks. Autopsy shows diffuse cortical atrophy, extracellular plaques and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles. Which molecule forms the tangles?
med-path.l25.q3.h: The tangles are inside the neurons.
med-path.l25.q3.e: Neurofibrillary tangles are aggregates of hyperphosphorylated tau. Beta-amyloid forms the extracellular plaques.

med-path.l25.q4.t: Oligodendrocytes, with relative sparing of axons
med-path.l25.q4.p: A 28-year-old woman has transient visual loss in one eye, then months later leg weakness and a sensory level. MRI shows periventricular white matter lesions, and the CSF has oligoclonal bands. Which cell is primarily lost in the lesions?
med-path.l25.q4.h: Think about which cell produces CNS myelin.
med-path.l25.q4.e: Multiple sclerosis targets oligodendrocytes and CNS myelin. Schwann cells make peripheral myelin, which is attacked in Guillain-Barre syndrome.

med-path.l25.q5.t: Rupture of a berry aneurysm at the circle of Willis
med-path.l25.q5.p: A 55-year-old man has a sudden worst headache of his life with neck stiffness. CT shows blood in the basal cisterns. Which is the most likely source?
med-path.l25.q5.e: The most common cause of non-traumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage is a ruptured berry aneurysm. Charcot-Bouchard aneurysms cause intracerebral hemorrhage.

med-path.l26.q1.p: Which feature is characteristic of glioblastoma?
med-path.l26.q1.h: This tumor has necrosis surrounded by tumor cells.
med-path.l26.q1.e: Glioblastoma shows pseudopalisading necrosis. Whorls and psammoma bodies indicate meningioma.

med-path.l26.q2.t: Normal mineralisation of the reduced bone mass in osteoporosis
med-path.l26.q2.p: Which feature distinguishes osteoporosis from osteomalacia?
med-path.l26.q2.h: One disease has too little bone and the other has soft bone.
med-path.l26.q2.e: In osteoporosis the bone is reduced but normally mineralised and labs are usually normal. Osteomalacia has unmineralised osteoid.

med-path.l26.q3.p: A 16-year-old has knee pain and swelling. Radiograph shows a metaphyseal mass of the distal femur with periosteal elevation and a sunburst pattern. Which finding is most expected on biopsy?
med-path.l26.q3.h: This is the most common primary malignant bone tumor in adolescents.
med-path.l26.q3.e: Osteosarcoma is defined by malignant osteoid production. Ewing sarcoma occurs in the diaphysis with an onion-skin reaction.

med-path.l26.q4.t: Negative, with yellow crystals when parallel to the compensator axis
med-path.l26.q4.p: A 60-year-old man has sudden pain and swelling of the first metatarsophalangeal joint. Joint fluid shows needle-shaped crystals. What is the expected birefringence under polarised light?
med-path.l26.q4.h: Gout and pseudogout differ in crystal shape and birefringence.
med-path.l26.q4.e: Monosodium urate crystals are needle-shaped and negatively birefringent. Calcium pyrophosphate crystals are rhomboid and positively birefringent.

med-path.l26.q5.p: Which tumor is the most common soft tissue sarcoma of children?
med-path.l26.q5.h: It shows skeletal muscle differentiation with desmin.
med-path.l26.q5.e: Rhabdomyosarcoma is the most common soft tissue sarcoma in children. Liposarcoma and leiomyosarcoma mostly occur in adults.

med-path.l27.q1.t: Parakeratosis with Munro microabscesses and a thinned granular layer
med-path.l27.q1.p: Which feature characterises psoriasis on histology?
med-path.l27.q1.h: Neutrophils collect in the stratum corneum.
med-path.l27.q1.e: Psoriasis shows parakeratosis, loss of the granular layer and Munro microabscesses. A band-like lymphocytic infiltrate indicates lichen planus.

med-path.l27.q2.t: Intercellular IgG deposits in a fishnet pattern in the epidermis
med-path.l27.q2.p: Which immunofluorescence pattern is typical of pemphigus vulgaris?
med-path.l27.q2.h: The antibody targets desmosomes between keratinocytes.
med-path.l27.q2.e: Pemphigus is against desmoglein 3 and gives intercellular staining. Linear basement membrane staining indicates bullous pemphigoid.

med-path.l27.q3.p: A 68-year-old has tense bullae on the flexor surfaces, with intact oral mucosa. Biopsy shows a subepidermal split and eosinophils. Which structure is the target of the autoantibodies?
med-path.l27.q3.h: The blisters are tense, so the split is deep.
med-path.l27.q3.e: Bullous pemphigoid is directed against BP180 and BP230 in hemidesmosomes. Pemphigus attacks desmosomes and causes flaccid blisters.

med-path.l27.q4.t: Breslow thickness, the depth of tumor invasion in millimetres
med-path.l27.q4.p: A 52-year-old man has a 7 mm irregular, variegated, dark lesion on his back that has enlarged over several months. Excision shows atypical melanocytes invading the dermis. Which factor is the most important predictor of survival?
med-path.l27.q4.h: Measured with an ocular micrometer from the granular layer.
med-path.l27.q4.e: Depth of invasion is the strongest prognostic factor in melanoma. A history of sunburn is a risk factor but not a prognostic measure.

med-path.l27.q5.p: Which skin cancer is the most common and almost never metastasises?
med-path.l27.q5.h: It forms a pearly papule with telangiectasias.
med-path.l27.q5.e: Basal cell carcinoma is locally invasive but rarely metastasises. Squamous cell carcinoma can metastasise, particularly when arising in scars or in immunosuppressed patients.

med-path.l28.q1.t: Fibroadenoma, a mobile and well-circumscribed mass
med-path.l28.q1.p: Which is the most common benign breast tumor in young women?
med-path.l28.q1.h: It grows under the influence of estrogen.
med-path.l28.q1.e: Fibroadenoma is a common mobile benign tumor in young women. Phyllodes tumors are rarer and have a cellular stroma.

med-path.l28.q2.t: Loss of E-cadherin with single-file infiltration
med-path.l28.q2.p: Which histologic feature characterises invasive lobular carcinoma?
med-path.l28.q2.h: The cells do not stick together.
med-path.l28.q2.e: Lobular carcinoma lacks E-cadherin and grows in single files. Comedo necrosis is a feature of high-grade ductal carcinoma in situ.

med-path.l28.q3.p: A 35-year-old woman has a firm breast mass. Biopsy shows invasive carcinoma that is negative for estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor and HER2. Her mother had ovarian cancer at 45. Which gene is most likely mutated?
med-path.l28.q3.h: Triple-negative tumors and ovarian cancer in the family point to the same gene.
med-path.l28.q3.e: BRCA1 mutation is associated with triple-negative breast cancer and ovarian cancer. HER2 would be amplified, and the tumor would be HER2 positive.

med-path.l28.q4.t: This is inflammatory carcinoma, which carries a poor prognosis and is not infectious
med-path.l28.q4.p: A 55-year-old woman has an erythematous swollen breast with skin thickening like an orange peel, and no discrete mass. Biopsy shows tumor cells within dermal lymphatics. Which statement is correct?
med-path.l28.q4.h: The tumor cells have invaded lymphatics in the dermis.
med-path.l28.q4.e: Inflammatory breast carcinoma is dermal lymphatic invasion presenting as erythema and peau d'orange. The redness is not due to infection.

med-path.l28.q5.t: Axillary lymph node status as part of the tumor stage
med-path.l28.q5.p: Which prognostic factor is generally the most important in breast cancer?
med-path.l28.q5.h: This reflects the extent of spread.
med-path.l28.q5.e: Nodal status is one of the strongest predictors of outcome. Calcifications are a detection feature rather than a prognostic factor.

med-path.l29.q1.p: Which virus types are responsible for most cervical cancers?
med-path.l29.q1.h: E6 and E7 are the viral oncoproteins.
med-path.l29.q1.e: HPV 16 and 18 are the main high-risk types. Types 6 and 11 cause genital warts.

med-path.l29.q2.t: Mature cystic teratoma, which contains tissues from all germ layers
med-path.l29.q2.p: Which tumor of the ovary is the most common benign germ cell tumor?
med-path.l29.q2.h: It is called a dermoid cyst.
med-path.l29.q2.e: The mature teratoma is a benign tumor with skin, hair and teeth. Yolk sac tumors and dysgerminomas are malignant.

med-path.l29.q3.t: The fallopian tube ampulla, where scarring impairs transport of the embryo
med-path.l29.q3.p: A 22-year-old woman has sudden lower abdominal pain, vaginal spotting and 7 weeks of amenorrhea. Her hCG is positive and the uterus is empty on ultrasound. She had pelvic inflammatory disease a year ago. Which is the most likely site of implantation?
med-path.l29.q3.h: Think about the effect of previous infection on tubal function.
med-path.l29.q3.e: Tubal scarring after PID predisposes to ectopic pregnancy, most often in the ampulla. A cornual site is less common and carries a different risk.

med-path.l29.q4.t: 46,XX with all chromosomes from the paternal side
med-path.l29.q4.p: A 27-year-old has first-trimester bleeding with uterine size larger than dates and a markedly raised hCG. Pathology shows diffuse swelling of villi with trophoblastic proliferation and no fetal tissue. Which genotype is expected?
med-path.l29.q4.h: A complete mole has no maternal genetic contribution.
med-path.l29.q4.e: Complete moles arise from an empty egg fertilised by sperm that duplicates, giving 46,XX paternal. Partial moles are triploid and contain fetal tissue.

med-path.l29.q5.t: Endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma from unopposed estrogen
med-path.l29.q5.p: A 62-year-old obese woman has postmenopausal bleeding. Which condition most likely underlies this?
med-path.l29.q5.h: Adipose tissue converts androgens to estrogen.
med-path.l29.q5.e: Postmenopausal bleeding should prompt exclusion of endometrial carcinoma, and obesity increases unopposed estrogen. Adenomyosis typically occurs in premenopausal women.

med-path.l30.q1.p: Which testicular tumor is the most common single type and is highly radiosensitive?
med-path.l30.q1.h: Fried-egg cells in a lymphocytic stroma.
med-path.l30.q1.e: Seminoma is the most common germ cell tumor and responds to radiation. Yolk sac tumors secrete alpha-fetoprotein.

med-path.l30.q2.t: The left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein at a right angle
med-path.l30.q2.p: Why is a varicocele more common on the left side?
med-path.l30.q2.h: Look at where each testicular vein ends.
med-path.l30.q2.e: The left vein enters the renal vein, so renal vein obstruction raises pressure. The right vein drains directly into the inferior vena cava.

med-path.l30.q3.t: Urgent surgical exploration with detorsion and fixation of the testes
med-path.l30.q3.p: A 17-year-old has sudden severe testicular pain with nausea, a high-riding testis and absent cremasteric reflex. Which management is correct?
med-path.l30.q3.h: Time to reperfusion determines whether the testis survives.
med-path.l30.q3.e: Testicular torsion is a surgical emergency, because the testis can be lost within hours. Epididymitis would preserve the cremasteric reflex.

med-path.l30.q4.t: The vertebral venous plexus connected to the prostatic venous plexus
med-path.l30.q4.p: A 68-year-old man has bone pain. Radiographs show sclerotic lesions in the lumbar vertebrae, and PSA is 95 ng/mL. Which route most likely explains the spread to the spine?
med-path.l30.q4.h: This valveless plexus allows retrograde flow.
med-path.l30.q4.e: Batson plexus links pelvic veins with the vertebral veins, which explains axial skeleton spread. The portal system would carry cells to the liver.

med-path.l30.q5.p: Which prostate zone is the usual site of carcinoma?
med-path.l30.q5.h: Think about what is palpable on rectal examination.
med-path.l30.q5.e: Most prostate cancers arise in the peripheral zone and may be palpable. BPH arises in the transition zone.

med-pharm-principles.l01.q1.p: Which term describes the fraction of an administered dose that reaches the systemic circulation unchanged?
med-pharm-principles.l01.q1.h: An intravenous dose defines the reference value of one.
med-pharm-principles.l01.q1.e: Bioavailability (F) is the fraction reaching the systemic circulation unchanged, and IV dosing has F of 1. Clearance and volume of distribution describe elimination and spread, not the fraction absorbed.

med-pharm-principles.l01.q2.t: Its drainage reaches the systemic circulation without passing through the portal vein and liver
med-pharm-principles.l01.q2.p: Why does sublingual nitroglycerin avoid most first-pass metabolism?
med-pharm-principles.l01.q2.h: Think about where the venous blood from the mouth goes.
med-pharm-principles.l01.q2.e: Sublingual veins drain to the superior vena cava, bypassing the portal vein and the liver. The slower-absorption explanation is wrong because sublingual absorption is rapid.

med-pharm-principles.l01.q3.t: A larger fraction is un-ionized and the drug crosses membranes more easily
med-pharm-principles.l01.q3.p: A weak acid with pKa 4 is in a compartment at pH 2. Compared with plasma at pH 7.4, which statement is correct?
med-pharm-principles.l01.q3.h: A weak acid is un-ionized when the pH is below its pKa.
med-pharm-principles.l01.q3.e: At pH below pKa, a weak acid is mostly protonated and un-ionized, which is membrane-permeant. The opposite pattern applies to a weak base.

med-pharm-principles.l01.q4.t: Extensive hepatic and gut-wall extraction before the drug reaches the systemic circulation
med-pharm-principles.l01.q4.p: A 58-year-old man starts a new oral drug. Its oral AUC is 15 percent of its intravenous AUC. A sublingual dose of the same size gives an exposure close to the intravenous value. Which mechanism most likely explains the oral shortfall?
med-pharm-principles.l01.q4.h: The route that bypasses the portal vein restores exposure.
med-pharm-principles.l01.q4.e: Restoration of exposure by a route that avoids the portal circulation points to first-pass extraction. Protein binding and Vd would not change with the route of administration.

med-pharm-principles.l01.q5.t: Chelation with calcium reduces the amount of drug available for absorption
med-pharm-principles.l01.q5.p: A 30-year-old woman takes a tetracycline antibiotic with a calcium-rich dairy meal and her blood levels are far lower than expected, although the drug is fully dissolved in the stomach. What best explains this?
med-pharm-principles.l01.q5.h: Divalent cations form complexes with tetracyclines in the gut.
med-pharm-principles.l01.q5.e: Tetracyclines chelate divalent cations in the lumen, preventing absorption. Albumin displacement would not lower the amount absorbed, and dairy is not a CYP inducer.

med-pharm-principles.l02.q1.t: It is extensively distributed or sequestered in tissues outside the plasma
med-pharm-principles.l02.q1.p: A drug has a volume of distribution much larger than total body water. What does that imply?
med-pharm-principles.l02.q1.h: Vd is an apparent volume, not an anatomical space.
med-pharm-principles.l02.q1.e: A Vd above body water means most of the body drug lies in tissues relative to plasma. Plasma confinement would give a Vd near 3 litres.

med-pharm-principles.l02.q2.p: Which fraction of a plasma-bound drug can cross membranes and bind receptors?
med-pharm-principles.l02.q2.h: Bound drug acts as a reservoir.
med-pharm-principles.l02.q2.e: Only free drug is pharmacologically active and can be filtered or distributed; protein-bound drug is a reservoir.

med-pharm-principles.l02.q3.t: Redistribution from the brain to muscle and fat lowers brain concentration
med-pharm-principles.l02.q3.p: After a rapid intravenous dose of a highly lipid-soluble anesthetic, the patient wakes in minutes although drug is still present in the blood. The best explanation is:
med-pharm-principles.l02.q3.e: The brain fills and empties first because it is highly perfused; the drug then redistributes to less perfused tissues. Metabolism and excretion are too slow to explain this.

med-pharm-principles.l02.q4.t: A raised free fraction increases the active concentration at the same total level
med-pharm-principles.l02.q4.p: A 62-year-old woman with cirrhosis and a low serum albumin takes an acidic, highly protein-bound drug. Her total drug level is within the usual range but she has signs of excess effect. Which explanation fits best?
med-pharm-principles.l02.q4.h: Total levels measure bound plus free drug.
med-pharm-principles.l02.q4.e: With hypoalbuminemia, the free fraction of an acidic drug rises, so a normal total concentration contains more active drug. The other options do not follow from low albumin.

med-pharm-principles.l02.q5.t: Inflammation has loosened the blood-brain barrier tight junctions
med-pharm-principles.l02.q5.p: A 45-year-old man has meningitis. A polar antibiotic that usually reaches the cerebrospinal fluid poorly produces adequate levels this time. What is the most likely reason?
med-pharm-principles.l02.q5.h: Think about what happens to endothelial junctions during inflammation.
med-pharm-principles.l02.q5.e: Meningeal inflammation increases barrier permeability, allowing polar drugs to enter. Higher binding or induced efflux would reduce rather than raise CSF levels.

med-pharm-principles.l03.q1.p: Which enzyme family metabolizes the largest share of marketed drugs?
med-pharm-principles.l03.q1.h: It is also abundant in the gut wall.
med-pharm-principles.l03.q1.e: CYP3A4 handles the largest share of clinically used drugs. The other enzymes handle a few specific substrates.

med-pharm-principles.l03.q2.t: Conjugate the drug with a polar group such as glucuronic acid, making it more water soluble
med-pharm-principles.l03.q2.e: Phase II is conjugation, usually yielding inactive, polar products. Oxidation is phase I.

med-pharm-principles.l03.q3.p: A drug with high hepatic extraction has its clearance primarily determined by:
med-pharm-principles.l03.q3.h: If the liver removes nearly all drug passing through it, supply sets the limit.
med-pharm-principles.l03.q3.e: For high-extraction drugs, clearance approaches hepatic blood flow, so flow, not enzyme activity, is limiting.

med-pharm-principles.l03.q4.t: Saturation of conjugation leading to NAPQI formation that depletes glutathione and binds hepatocyte proteins
med-pharm-principles.l03.q4.p: A 24-year-old man presents several hours after an intentional acetaminophen overdose. Which mechanism underlies the liver injury expected over the next days?
med-pharm-principles.l03.q4.h: The toxic species is a reactive oxidative metabolite.
med-pharm-principles.l03.q4.e: Conjugation pathways saturate, so more drug goes through oxidation to NAPQI, which overwhelms glutathione. Glucuronides and sulfates are non-toxic.

med-pharm-principles.l03.q5.t: Reduced formation of the active metabolite and diminished therapeutic effect
med-pharm-principles.l03.q5.p: A 35-year-old woman receives a prodrug that requires CYP2D6 for activation and is also started on a strong CYP2D6 inhibitor. Which outcome is most likely?
med-pharm-principles.l03.q5.h: Inhibiting the enzyme that activates the drug removes the active product.
