med-pharm-principles.l03.q5.e: A prodrug depends on the enzyme to form its active form, so inhibition reduces effect. Phase II does not generate the active metabolite.

med-pharm-principles.l04.q1.p: Which of these is NOT filtered at the glomerulus to a significant degree?
med-pharm-principles.l04.q1.h: Large proteins stay in the plasma.
med-pharm-principles.l04.q1.e: Albumin-bound drug is too large to be filtered. Unbound small molecules, whether ionized or not, pass freely.

med-pharm-principles.l04.q2.t: It prolongs the half-life and can produce secondary plasma peaks
med-pharm-principles.l04.q2.p: Enterohepatic circulation of a drug usually has what effect?
med-pharm-principles.l04.q2.h: The drug is recycled between gut and liver.
med-pharm-principles.l04.q2.e: Biliary drug or conjugate is hydrolyzed in the gut and reabsorbed, so exposure is prolonged.

med-pharm-principles.l04.q3.t: More of the acid is ionized in tubular fluid and cannot diffuse back into the blood
med-pharm-principles.l04.q3.p: Alkalinizing the urine increases the renal excretion of a weak acid because:
med-pharm-principles.l04.q3.h: Ionized drug is trapped in the tubule.
med-pharm-principles.l04.q3.e: Higher pH ionizes weak acids, which reduces passive reabsorption. Filtration rate is unaffected.

med-pharm-principles.l04.q4.t: Reduced renal clearance of digoxin raises its plasma concentration
med-pharm-principles.l04.q4.p: A 72-year-old woman with chronic kidney disease takes digoxin. After starting a new drug that competes for renal tubular secretion, she develops nausea and visual disturbances. Which mechanism best explains her symptoms?
med-pharm-principles.l04.q4.h: Digoxin is mainly excreted unchanged by the kidney.
med-pharm-principles.l04.q4.e: Digoxin depends on renal elimination, so competition and falling GFR raise levels. It is not appreciably metabolized by CYP3A4.

med-pharm-principles.l04.q5.t: Intravenous sodium bicarbonate to alkalinize the urine
med-pharm-principles.l04.q5.p: A 19-year-old college student is brought in after an aspirin (salicylate) overdose. Which intervention exploits ion trapping to increase elimination?
med-pharm-principles.l04.q5.e: Alkalinization ionizes salicylate in the tubule and traps it. Probenecid and acidification would reduce excretion.

med-pharm-principles.l05.q1.t: Half-life equals 0.693 times volume of distribution divided by clearance
med-pharm-principles.l05.q1.p: Which equation correctly links half-life to the other pharmacokinetic parameters?
med-pharm-principles.l05.q1.h: Volume lengthens it and clearance shortens it.
med-pharm-principles.l05.q1.e: Half-life rises with Vd and falls with CL: t1/2 = 0.693 x Vd / CL. The other expressions invert one of the terms.

med-pharm-principles.l05.q2.p: After how many half-lives is a first-order drug about 94 percent eliminated?
med-pharm-principles.l05.q2.h: Each half-life removes half of what is left.
med-pharm-principles.l05.q2.e: After four half-lives about 6.25 percent remains, so roughly 94 percent is gone. Two half-lives remove 75 percent and three remove 87.5 percent.

med-pharm-principles.l05.q3.p: A drug has a Vd of 100 L and a clearance of 10 L per hour. Which half-life is closest to the correct value?
med-pharm-principles.l05.q3.e: 0.693 x 100 / 10 is about 6.9 hours. Using 20 hours or 10 hours ignores the 0.693 factor or misplaces the terms.

med-pharm-principles.l05.q4.t: Lower clearance and longer half-life with no change in volume of distribution
med-pharm-principles.l05.q4.p: A 68-year-old man with advanced chronic kidney disease takes a drug that is eliminated mainly unchanged by the kidney. Compared with a healthy adult, which pair of changes is expected?
med-pharm-principles.l05.q4.h: Half-life is dependent on CL and Vd.
med-pharm-principles.l05.q4.e: Loss of nephron mass reduces renal clearance; with unchanged Vd the half-life lengthens. A shorter half-life would require higher clearance.

med-pharm-principles.l05.q5.t: A larger volume of distribution from relatively greater body fat prolongs the half-life
med-pharm-principles.l05.q5.p: A 75-year-old woman has a lipophilic benzodiazepine whose hepatic clearance is unchanged by age, yet her half-life is far longer than her 30-year-old daughter's on the same drug. Which explanation best fits?
med-pharm-principles.l05.q5.h: Half-life depends on both volume and clearance.
med-pharm-principles.l05.q5.e: With clearance unchanged, a larger Vd lengthens t1/2. Induction would raise clearance and shorten t1/2, and absorption rate does not set elimination half-life.

med-pharm-principles.l06.q1.p: What determines how long it takes a repeatedly dosed drug to reach steady state?
med-pharm-principles.l06.q1.h: Time to plateau does not depend on dose size.
med-pharm-principles.l06.q1.e: Time to steady state depends on half-life, about four to five half-lives. Dose size changes the plateau height, not the time to reach it.

med-pharm-principles.l06.q2.p: If the maintenance dose rate is doubled and clearance is unchanged, the average steady-state concentration will:
med-pharm-principles.l06.q2.h: Css is proportional to rate of input divided by CL.
med-pharm-principles.l06.q2.e: Average steady-state concentration is proportional to input rate for first-order drugs. The time to reach it stays the same.

med-pharm-principles.l06.q3.p: A drug is given at an interval equal to its half-life. Approximately what is the ratio of steady-state to first-dose concentration (accumulation factor)?
med-pharm-principles.l06.q3.h: The remaining fraction after one half-life is one half.
med-pharm-principles.l06.q3.e: Accumulation is 1 divided by the fraction lost per interval; with half lost, the factor is about 2.

med-pharm-principles.l06.q4.t: Steady state has not been reached after the dose change, so the level will keep rising
med-pharm-principles.l06.q4.p: A 55-year-old woman on a long-term renally cleared drug has her dose increased, and a trough drawn two days later is well below the range expected at the new dose. The half-life of the drug is 36 hours. What is the best interpretation?
med-pharm-principles.l06.q4.e: Two days is under two half-lives, so the plateau is not reached. Judging it now would misread normal accumulation as failure.

med-pharm-principles.l06.q5.t: Unchanged average concentration with a smaller peak-to-trough swing
med-pharm-principles.l06.q5.p: A 44-year-old man receives an extended-release formulation in place of an immediate-release product with the same daily dose and bioavailability. Which change would be expected at steady state?
med-pharm-principles.l06.q5.h: Average depends on dose rate and clearance, not formulation.
med-pharm-principles.l06.q5.e: Mean steady-state concentration depends on dose rate, bioavailability and clearance. Slower release reduces fluctuation but the half-life, and so the time to steady state, is unchanged.

med-pharm-principles.l07.q1.p: Which parameter mainly determines the size of a loading dose?
med-pharm-principles.l07.q1.h: The dose fills an apparent volume to a target concentration.
med-pharm-principles.l07.q1.e: Loading dose is roughly target concentration times Vd, divided by bioavailability. Clearance governs the maintenance rate.

med-pharm-principles.l07.q2.p: Which parameter mainly determines the maintenance dose rate?
med-pharm-principles.l07.q2.h: At steady state input balances elimination.
med-pharm-principles.l07.q2.e: Maintenance dose rate equals clearance times target concentration, corrected for bioavailability.

med-pharm-principles.l07.q3.t: Give the usual loading dose and lower the maintenance rate
med-pharm-principles.l07.q3.p: A patient has severe renal failure and needs a renally cleared drug that has a normal Vd. Which approach follows the principles?
med-pharm-principles.l07.q3.h: Volume is unchanged; clearance has fallen.
med-pharm-principles.l07.q3.e: Loading depends on Vd, which is unchanged, while maintenance depends on clearance, which is reduced. Lowering the load would delay the effect without reason.

med-pharm-principles.l07.q4.t: Usual loading dose given slowly, and a maintenance rate reduced in proportion to the fall in clearance
med-pharm-principles.l07.q4.p: A 70-year-old man has reduced renal perfusion from heart failure, so the clearance of a renally eliminated drug with a narrow safety margin is markedly reduced, while its volume of distribution is unchanged. Which pair of recommendations best applies the pharmacokinetic principles?
med-pharm-principles.l07.q4.h: Only one of the two parameters changed.
med-pharm-principles.l07.q4.e: Load follows Vd (unchanged), maintenance follows CL (reduced), and slow administration limits transient high levels in the central compartment.

med-pharm-principles.l07.q5.t: The loading dose requirement rises because more volume must be filled
med-pharm-principles.l07.q5.p: A 36-year-old woman with severe edema and a larger than normal volume of distribution needs rapid achievement of a target concentration of a hydrophilic drug. Compared with a person of normal fluid status, what would be expected to change?
med-pharm-principles.l07.q5.h: Volume of distribution appears in the load formula.
med-pharm-principles.l07.q5.e: Edema enlarges the apparent Vd of hydrophilic drugs, so a larger load is needed to reach the same concentration. Clearance is not what drives the load.

med-pharm-principles.l08.q1.t: A constant amount of drug is eliminated per unit time
med-pharm-principles.l08.q1.p: Which statement is characteristic of zero-order elimination?
med-pharm-principles.l08.q1.h: Enzymes are working at maximal capacity.
med-pharm-principles.l08.q1.e: Saturated elimination removes a fixed amount per hour. A constant fraction describes first-order elimination.

med-pharm-principles.l08.q2.p: For which of these drugs is saturable metabolism classically important in the therapeutic range?
med-pharm-principles.l08.q2.h: Small dose changes produce disproportionate level changes.
med-pharm-principles.l08.q2.e: Phenytoin's metabolizing enzymes saturate near the therapeutic range. The other drugs are cleared by first-order renal processes.

med-pharm-principles.l08.q3.t: Clearance falls and apparent half-life lengthens
med-pharm-principles.l08.q3.p: As the plasma concentration of a drug with saturable elimination increases, which change occurs?
med-pharm-principles.l08.q3.h: Maximal rate divided by a larger concentration.
med-pharm-principles.l08.q3.e: At saturation the fixed maximal rate removes a smaller fraction as concentration rises, so clearance falls and half-life lengthens.

med-pharm-principles.l08.q4.t: Saturation of the metabolizing enzyme, so a small dose rise exceeds the maximal elimination rate
med-pharm-principles.l08.q4.p: A 29-year-old man with epilepsy has a phenytoin level just below the target range. His dose is increased by a small amount, and two weeks later he has nystagmus, ataxia and a markedly high level. Which mechanism best explains the disproportionate rise?
med-pharm-principles.l08.q4.e: Near saturation of its enzyme, phenytoin clearance falls as concentration rises, so levels climb disproportionately. Induction would lower, not raise, levels.

med-pharm-principles.l08.q5.t: Elimination is saturated and proceeding at a constant rate regardless of concentration
med-pharm-principles.l08.q5.p: A 22-year-old man drinks several alcoholic drinks and a blood alcohol concentration is measured twice, two hours apart. The fall in concentration is the same each hour. What does this indicate?
med-pharm-principles.l08.q5.h: A constant amount, not a constant fraction, falls each hour.
med-pharm-principles.l08.q5.e: A linear fall means zero-order elimination because alcohol dehydrogenase is saturated. First-order elimination would give a curved fall on a linear scale.

med-pharm-principles.l09.q1.p: Which receptor family couples to Gq and raises intracellular calcium through IP3 and diacylglycerol?
med-pharm-principles.l09.q1.h: Think of smooth muscle contraction in blood vessels.
med-pharm-principles.l09.q1.e: Alpha-1 receptors signal through Gq and phospholipase C. Beta receptors use Gs and alpha-2 uses Gi, which act through cyclic AMP.

med-pharm-principles.l09.q2.p: Which type of receptor mediates the slowest effect, taking hours, by altering gene transcription?
med-pharm-principles.l09.q2.h: Time course follows the number of steps between binding and effect.
med-pharm-principles.l09.q2.e: Intracellular nuclear receptors change gene expression over hours. Ion channels act in milliseconds and GPCRs in seconds.

med-pharm-principles.l09.q3.t: A rightward shift with the maximum unchanged
med-pharm-principles.l09.q3.p: In a tissue with a large receptor reserve, a low dose of an irreversible antagonist first produces which change in the agonist dose-response curve?
med-pharm-principles.l09.q3.h: Spare receptors can still generate the full response.
med-pharm-principles.l09.q3.e: Spare receptors let the full maximum persist while more agonist is needed to occupy the remaining receptors, so the curve shifts right. Only after the reserve is exhausted does the maximum fall.

med-pharm-principles.l09.q4.t: Up-regulated beta receptors respond strongly to circulating catecholamines once the blockade is removed
med-pharm-principles.l09.q4.p: A 52-year-old man with hypertension has taken a beta-blocker for years and stops it abruptly. He develops palpitations, tachycardia and elevated blood pressure within days. Which mechanism best explains this?
med-pharm-principles.l09.q4.h: Chronic blockade changes the receptor number.
med-pharm-principles.l09.q4.e: Chronic antagonism up-regulates receptors, so stopping the drug leaves them hypersensitive to catecholamines. Down-regulation follows chronic agonist exposure, not antagonist exposure.

med-pharm-principles.l09.q5.t: Loss of beta-2 selectivity at high concentrations leads to stimulation of cardiac beta-1 receptors and skeletal muscle beta-2 receptors
med-pharm-principles.l09.q5.p: A 27-year-old asthmatic uses an inhaled beta-2 agonist and describes a rapid heartbeat and tremor when taking a high dose. What is the best explanation?
med-pharm-principles.l09.q5.e: Receptor selectivity is relative, so higher doses activate beta-1 receptors in the heart and beta-2 receptors in skeletal muscle (tremor). Gs, not Gi, increases heart rate.

med-pharm-principles.l10.q1.t: Affinity for the receptor without intrinsic activity
med-pharm-principles.l10.q1.p: Which property distinguishes an antagonist from an agonist?
med-pharm-principles.l10.q1.h: An antagonist binds but does not activate.
med-pharm-principles.l10.q1.e: An antagonist binds with affinity and has no intrinsic activity, so it blocks agonists. A full agonist has both affinity and maximal intrinsic activity.

med-pharm-principles.l10.q2.t: Shifting it to the right in parallel without changing the maximum
med-pharm-principles.l10.q2.p: A competitive antagonist changes an agonist dose-response curve by:
med-pharm-principles.l10.q2.h: More agonist can overcome the block.
med-pharm-principles.l10.q2.e: Competitive antagonism is surmountable, so the same maximum is reached at a higher agonist dose. A lowered maximum indicates non-competitive antagonism.

med-pharm-principles.l10.q3.p: Protamine neutralizes heparin by direct binding, with no action on a receptor. This is best classified as:
med-pharm-principles.l10.q3.h: The two drugs bind each other.
med-pharm-principles.l10.q3.e: Chemical antagonism is direct binding between drugs. Physiological antagonism requires separate receptors with opposite effects.

med-pharm-principles.l10.q4.t: Displacement of the full agonist with lower intrinsic activity produces a net fall in receptor stimulation
med-pharm-principles.l10.q4.p: A 34-year-old man dependent on a full opioid agonist is given a high-affinity partial agonist at the same receptor. Within an hour he develops sweating, agitation and abdominal cramps. Which mechanism best accounts for this?
med-pharm-principles.l10.q4.h: High affinity lets it take over the receptor.
med-pharm-principles.l10.q4.e: The partial agonist replaces the full agonist but produces a smaller effect, so withdrawal is precipitated. Receptor loss is not involved.

med-pharm-principles.l10.q5.t: The antagonist has a shorter duration of action than the agonist it was reversing
med-pharm-principles.l10.q5.p: A 41-year-old woman is given naloxone for opioid overdose and wakes. Forty minutes later she becomes sedated with slow breathing again. The long-acting opioid is still present. What principle explains this?
med-pharm-principles.l10.q5.h: Compare the duration of the two drugs.
med-pharm-principles.l10.q5.e: A competitive antagonist that wears off before the agonist lets the agonist effect return, so monitoring and sometimes repeat dosing are needed.

med-pharm-principles.l11.q1.t: The EC50, the concentration giving half the maximal effect
med-pharm-principles.l11.q1.p: On a graded dose-response curve, potency is best described by:
med-pharm-principles.l11.q1.h: Position of the curve along the dose axis.
med-pharm-principles.l11.q1.e: Potency is the location of the curve, measured by EC50 or ED50. Maximum effect is efficacy, and the last choice describes the therapeutic index.

med-pharm-principles.l11.q2.t: They are independent, so a more potent drug is not necessarily more efficacious
med-pharm-principles.l11.q2.p: Which statement about potency and efficacy is correct?
med-pharm-principles.l11.q2.h: Position and ceiling of the curve are separate.
med-pharm-principles.l11.q2.e: Potency and efficacy vary independently. A drug can act at lower doses but plateau at a lower maximal effect.

med-pharm-principles.l11.q3.t: P is more potent and Q is more efficacious
med-pharm-principles.l11.q3.p: Drug P has an EC50 of 2 mg and a maximal effect of 40 percent. Drug Q has an EC50 of 20 mg and a maximal effect of 90 percent. Which conclusion is correct?
med-pharm-principles.l11.q3.h: Compare the position of each curve and the plateau.
med-pharm-principles.l11.q3.e: P reaches half its effect at a lower dose (more potent), but Q has the greater maximum (more efficacious).

med-pharm-principles.l11.q4.t: The loop diuretic has greater maximal efficacy
med-pharm-principles.l11.q4.p: A 60-year-old man with pulmonary edema receives a diuretic at increasing doses. The thiazide-type agent at a very high dose still produces less urine output than a loop diuretic at its maximum. Which property does this describe?
med-pharm-principles.l11.q4.h: The ceiling of the curve is what differs.
med-pharm-principles.l11.q4.e: Higher maximal diuresis is efficacy. Comparing potency would require the dose that gives half-maximal effect, which this question does not describe.

med-pharm-principles.l11.q5.t: Responsiveness is relatively uniform, with little variation between individuals
med-pharm-principles.l11.q5.p: In a quantal dose-response experiment, 50 percent of animals show the intended effect at 5 mg, and the curve is very steep. What does a steep curve imply about the population?
med-pharm-principles.l11.q5.h: A steep curve means that most responders cluster close to the median.
med-pharm-principles.l11.q5.e: A steep quantal curve means most individuals respond across a narrow dose range. It does not by itself show a wide therapeutic index.

med-pharm-principles.l12.q1.p: The therapeutic index in animal studies is calculated as:
med-pharm-principles.l12.q1.e: A larger TD50/ED50 ratio means a wider safety margin. The inverted ratio would give a smaller number for safer drugs.

med-pharm-principles.l12.q2.p: Which of these drugs has a narrow therapeutic index?
med-pharm-principles.l12.q2.e: Lithium has a small margin between therapeutic and toxic levels. The other drugs have wide margins in usual use.

med-pharm-principles.l12.q3.t: Pharmacokinetic tolerance arises from increased drug clearance, for example enzyme induction
med-pharm-principles.l12.q3.p: Which feature distinguishes pharmacokinetic from pharmacodynamic tolerance?
med-pharm-principles.l12.q3.h: One changes drug concentration; the other changes response at a given concentration.
med-pharm-principles.l12.q3.e: Enzyme induction lowers the concentration achieved, which is pharmacokinetic. Receptor changes alter response at the same concentration, which is pharmacodynamic.

med-pharm-principles.l12.q4.t: Tolerance has developed unevenly, so the risk of respiratory depression rises with escalating doses while analgesic benefit wanes
med-pharm-principles.l12.q4.p: A 49-year-old man on chronic opioid therapy for cancer pain has escalated his dose because pain relief has waned. His pain is partly controlled, but his respiratory rate is low and his pupils are small. Which statement best describes the underlying problem?
med-pharm-principles.l12.q4.h: Tolerance is not equal for every effect.
med-pharm-principles.l12.q4.e: Tolerance to analgesia and euphoria develops faster than to respiratory depression and miosis, narrowing the safety margin. Complete uniform tolerance is not how opioids behave.

med-pharm-principles.l12.q5.t: An idiosyncratic reaction from a genetic difference in response
med-pharm-principles.l12.q5.p: A 31-year-old man develops hemolytic anemia after taking an antimalarial drug that most people tolerate. Testing shows G6PD deficiency. How should this reaction be classified?
med-pharm-principles.l12.q5.h: The reaction is unrelated to the main action and depends on genetics.
med-pharm-principles.l12.q5.e: Idiosyncratic reactions are abnormal responses with a genetic basis, here G6PD deficiency. They are not an exaggeration of the therapeutic effect.

med-pharm-principles.l13.q1.t: New enzyme protein must be synthesized after increased gene transcription
med-pharm-principles.l13.q1.p: Why does the effect of an enzyme inducer take days to develop?
med-pharm-principles.l13.q1.e: Inducers raise transcription through nuclear receptors, so new protein takes days to appear. Rapid activation is not the mechanism.

med-pharm-principles.l13.q2.p: Which of these is a recognized strong inducer of CYP3A4?
med-pharm-principles.l13.q2.h: It is an antituberculosis drug that lowers levels of many other drugs.
med-pharm-principles.l13.q2.e: Rifampin induces CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein. Ketoconazole inhibits CYP3A4, and the others are inhibitors of different enzymes.

med-pharm-principles.l13.q3.t: Little change in clearance after intravenous dosing, but a marked fall in oral bioavailability
med-pharm-principles.l13.q3.p: A drug with high hepatic extraction, cleared mainly according to blood flow, is taken by mouth with an enzyme inducer such as rifampin. What is the expected result?
med-pharm-principles.l13.q3.h: Separate systemic clearance from what survives first pass.
med-pharm-principles.l13.q3.e: Blood flow limits systemic clearance of a high-extraction drug, so induction changes it little, but induced gut-wall and liver enzymes remove more of an oral dose on first pass, so bioavailability falls. Low-extraction drugs show the clearance change directly.

med-pharm-principles.l13.q4.t: CYP3A4 induction lowered plasma concentrations of the contraceptive steroids
med-pharm-principles.l13.q4.p: A 38-year-old woman taking an oral contraceptive starts rifampin for tuberculosis and conceives 6 weeks later. Which mechanism best explains the contraceptive failure?
med-pharm-principles.l13.q4.h: The delay matches the time course of enzyme induction.
med-pharm-principles.l13.q4.e: Induction lowers steroid levels below the contraceptive threshold. Inhibition would raise levels, and gastric pH is not the cause.

med-pharm-principles.l13.q5.t: Inhibition of CYP3A4 raised simvastatin concentrations and the risk of myopathy
med-pharm-principles.l13.q5.p: A 66-year-old man on a stable simvastatin dose is started on clarithromycin and develops muscle pain and dark urine a week later. Which mechanism most likely explains the muscle toxicity?
med-pharm-principles.l13.q5.h: Clarithromycin is a mechanism-based CYP3A4 inhibitor.
med-pharm-principles.l13.q5.e: Strong CYP3A4 inhibition raises statin exposure, causing myopathy and possibly rhabdomyolysis. Induction would reduce rather than raise exposure.

med-pharm-principles.l14.q1.p: Which food or drink inhibits intestinal CYP3A4 and can increase the bioavailability of some drugs?
med-pharm-principles.l14.q1.h: Think of felodipine and some statins.
med-pharm-principles.l14.q1.e: Grapefruit juice irreversibly inhibits gut CYP3A4. Vitamin K affects warfarin, tyramine affects MAOIs and calcium chelates tetracyclines.

med-pharm-principles.l14.q2.t: An SSRI with a monoamine oxidase inhibitor
med-pharm-principles.l14.q2.p: Which combination is most likely to cause serotonin syndrome?
med-pharm-principles.l14.q2.h: Two drugs that raise synaptic serotonin.
med-pharm-principles.l14.q2.e: SSRIs and MAOIs both increase serotonin, and combined use is dangerous. The other pairs act on different systems.

med-pharm-principles.l14.q3.t: A lower INR because vitamin K opposes warfarin
med-pharm-principles.l14.q3.p: A person taking warfarin starts eating much more spinach than before. What effect is expected?
med-pharm-principles.l14.q3.h: Warfarin inhibits vitamin K-dependent clotting factor synthesis.
med-pharm-principles.l14.q3.e: More dietary vitamin K supplies the substrate warfarin blocks, so effect falls. The lesson is a consistent intake, not avoidance.

med-pharm-principles.l14.q4.t: Tyramine is not broken down by gut MAO and releases norepinephrine from sympathetic nerve terminals
med-pharm-principles.l14.q4.p: A 47-year-old man who takes phenelzine, a non-selective MAOI, eats aged cheese and cured meats at a party. An hour later he has a severe headache, flushing and a blood pressure of 220/120 mm Hg. Which mechanism best explains this?
med-pharm-principles.l14.q4.h: MAO normally breaks down dietary amines.
med-pharm-principles.l14.q4.e: Inhibited MAO lets tyramine reach the circulation and release stored norepinephrine, causing a hypertensive crisis. The other options do not describe a known mechanism.

med-pharm-principles.l14.q5.t: Additive pharmacodynamic effects on potassium and renal function from the three drugs
med-pharm-principles.l14.q5.p: A 73-year-old woman takes lisinopril, spironolactone and ibuprofen for chronic knee pain. She develops weakness and a serum potassium of 6.4 mEq/L. Which statement best describes the interaction?
med-pharm-principles.l14.q5.h: Consider how each drug alters potassium handling or renal perfusion.
med-pharm-principles.l14.q5.e: ACE inhibitors and potassium-sparing diuretics each cause retention, and NSAIDs impair renal prostaglandin-dependent perfusion. This is a combined pharmacodynamic risk.

med-pharm-principles.l15.q1.t: Predictable from the drug's pharmacology, dose-related and common
med-pharm-principles.l15.q1.p: Which description fits a type A adverse drug reaction?
med-pharm-principles.l15.q1.e: Type A reactions are exaggerations of the known pharmacology and are dose-related. Unpredictable reactions are type B.

med-pharm-principles.l15.q2.p: Which antidote works by replenishing glutathione stores in acetaminophen poisoning?
med-pharm-principles.l15.q2.h: It provides cysteine for glutathione synthesis.
med-pharm-principles.l15.q2.e: N-acetylcysteine supports glutathione and detoxification of NAPQI. Flumazenil is for benzodiazepines, fomepizole blocks alcohol dehydrogenase and pralidoxime reactivates cholinesterase.

med-pharm-principles.l15.q3.p: A rash appearing 10 days after starting an antibiotic, without wheeze or hypotension, most likely reflects which mechanism?
med-pharm-principles.l15.q3.e: A rash after days fits a delayed T-cell reaction. IgE reactions develop within minutes to an hour of exposure.

med-pharm-principles.l15.q4.t: Antibodies against heparin-platelet factor 4 complexes activate platelets and cause thrombosis
med-pharm-principles.l15.q4.p: A 56-year-old woman receiving heparin for 7 days has a platelet count fall from 250 to 90 x 10^9/L and a new deep venous thrombosis. Which mechanism best explains this?
med-pharm-principles.l15.q4.h: This reaction causes clotting as well as a low platelet count.
med-pharm-principles.l15.q4.e: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia is antibody-mediated activation of platelets by PF4-heparin complexes, which paradoxically promotes thrombosis. Bone marrow suppression would not cause clots.

med-pharm-principles.l15.q5.t: Support ventilation and give a competitive receptor antagonist, with monitoring for return of toxicity
med-pharm-principles.l15.q5.p: A 25-year-old man is found drowsy with pinpoint pupils and a respiratory rate of 6 per minute after a suspected opioid overdose. Which approach best follows the logic of antidotal therapy?
med-pharm-principles.l15.q5.h: Short-acting antagonist against a longer-lasting agonist.
med-pharm-principles.l15.q5.e: Naloxone competitively antagonizes opioid receptors but may wear off before a long-acting opioid, so monitoring continues. Urinary alkalinization is not used for opioids.

med-pharm-principles.l16.q1.p: Which genetic variant predicts hypersensitivity to abacavir?
med-pharm-principles.l16.q1.h: It is tested before starting the drug.
med-pharm-principles.l16.q1.e: HLA-B*57:01 is associated with abacavir hypersensitivity, and screening is standard. HLA-B*15:02 relates to carbamazepine.

med-pharm-principles.l16.q2.p: TPMT or NUDT15 deficiency increases the risk of which toxicity with mercaptopurine?
med-pharm-principles.l16.q2.h: Inactivation of the thiopurine is reduced.
med-pharm-principles.l16.q2.e: Reduced inactivation raises active thiopurine nucleotide levels and causes bone marrow suppression. Neuropathy relates to isoniazid and NAT2.

med-pharm-principles.l16.q3.t: Less active metabolite is formed and antiplatelet effect may be reduced
med-pharm-principles.l16.q3.p: A patient who is a CYP2C19 poor metabolizer takes the prodrug clopidogrel. What is the expected effect?
med-pharm-principles.l16.q3.h: Poor metabolizers cannot activate the prodrug well.
med-pharm-principles.l16.q3.e: Loss of CYP2C19 function reduces conversion to the active form. This differs from an active drug, where poor metabolism would raise levels.

med-pharm-principles.l16.q4.t: CYP2D6 ultrarapid metabolizer producing excess morphine
med-pharm-principles.l16.q4.p: A 5-year-old child recovering from tonsillectomy receives codeine and develops profound sedation and slow breathing. Which genotype most plausibly explains this?
med-pharm-principles.l16.q4.e: Ultrarapid CYP2D6 metabolizers convert codeine to morphine quickly, raising the risk of respiratory depression. A poor metabolizer would have little effect.

med-pharm-principles.l16.q5.p: A 62-year-old man of Han Chinese ancestry is about to start carbamazepine for neuralgia. Which pre-treatment test is most relevant to predicting a severe cutaneous reaction?
med-pharm-principles.l16.q5.h: The association is HLA-based and ancestry-dependent.
med-pharm-principles.l16.q5.e: HLA-B*15:02 predicts carbamazepine-induced SJS/TEN in people of certain Asian ancestries. DPYD relates to fluoropyrimidines and G6PD to oxidant drugs.

med-pharm-principles.l17.q1.p: Which neurotransmitter is released by sympathetic postganglionic fibers to sweat glands?
med-pharm-principles.l17.q1.h: Sweat glands are a classic exception.
med-pharm-principles.l17.q1.e: Sweat glands are supplied by sympathetic cholinergic fibers acting on muscarinic receptors. Norepinephrine is the usual sympathetic postganglionic transmitter.

med-pharm-principles.l17.q2.p: What is the rate-limiting enzyme in catecholamine synthesis?
med-pharm-principles.l17.q2.e: Tyrosine hydroxylase converts tyrosine to DOPA and limits the pathway. The later enzymes are not rate-limiting.

med-pharm-principles.l17.q3.t: A reflex fall in heart rate through the baroreceptor reflex
med-pharm-principles.l17.q3.p: Phenylephrine, a selective alpha-1 agonist, raises blood pressure. What is the expected heart rate response in a person with intact reflexes?
med-pharm-principles.l17.q3.h: The pressure rise triggers a reflex.
med-pharm-principles.l17.q3.e: Pure vasoconstriction raises pressure and activates baroreceptor-mediated vagal slowing. Phenylephrine lacks beta-1 effect, so direct stimulation is absent.

med-pharm-principles.l17.q4.t: Irreversible inhibition of acetylcholinesterase that causes acetylcholine accumulation
med-pharm-principles.l17.q4.p: A 44-year-old farm worker is brought in after exposure to an insecticide. He has drooling, tearing, wheezing, diarrhea, small pupils, slow heart rate and muscle fasciculations. Which mechanism best explains this?
med-pharm-principles.l17.q4.h: The picture is of excessive cholinergic stimulation.
med-pharm-principles.l17.q4.e: Organophosphates irreversibly inhibit acetylcholinesterase, raising ACh at muscarinic and nicotinic sites. Muscarinic blockade would produce dry mucosa and dilated pupils.

med-pharm-principles.l17.q5.p: A 70-year-old man receives a drug before surgery and develops dry mouth, flushed warm skin, dilated pupils, urinary retention and a heart rate of 120. Which drug class is most likely responsible?
med-pharm-principles.l17.q5.e: Muscarinic blockade produces dry mucosa, mydriasis, retention and tachycardia. A cholinesterase inhibitor causes the opposite picture, and a beta-blocker would slow the heart.

med-pharm-principles.l18.q1.p: Which phase of clinical development is mainly designed to assess safety, tolerability and pharmacokinetics in a small group, often healthy volunteers?
med-pharm-principles.l18.q1.h: It is the first time the drug is given to humans.
med-pharm-principles.l18.q1.e: Phase 1 studies assess safety and pharmacokinetics. Phase 2 assesses preliminary efficacy and dose, and phase 3 confirms efficacy.

med-pharm-principles.l18.q2.p: What application must a sponsor file before starting human trials in the United States?
med-pharm-principles.l18.q2.h: It comes before clinical trials rather than after.
med-pharm-principles.l18.q2.e: The IND permits human testing. The NDA or BLA requests marketing approval after trials, and the ANDA is for generics.

med-pharm-principles.l18.q3.p: A generic version of an approved tablet is submitted for approval. Which type of evidence is the central requirement?
med-pharm-principles.l18.q3.e: An ANDA relies on the reference product's efficacy and safety and requires bioequivalence. New phase 3 trials are not needed.

med-pharm-principles.l18.q4.t: Pre-approval trials lack the size to detect rare adverse events that post-marketing surveillance can find
med-pharm-principles.l18.q4.p: A 3,000-patient phase 3 program for a new antihypertensive shows no case of a serious liver reaction. After two years of marketing and one million exposures, spontaneous reports describe liver failure in about 1 in 20,000 users. What best explains the discovery?
med-pharm-principles.l18.q4.e: A 1 in 20,000 event is unlikely to appear in 3,000 subjects. Surveillance does not prove causation by itself, but flags signals for evaluation.

med-pharm-principles.l18.q5.t: Accelerated approval based on a surrogate endpoint
med-pharm-principles.l18.q5.p: A drug for a serious rare cancer receives approval based on tumor shrinkage in a small single-arm trial, with a requirement for a later randomized trial of survival. Which pathway is this?
med-pharm-principles.l18.q5.h: Surrogate endpoint with confirmatory trial required.
med-pharm-principles.l18.q5.e: Accelerated approval uses a surrogate reasonably likely to predict benefit and requires confirmatory trials. Advisory votes are not binding.

med-pharm-principles.l19.q1.t: Organogenesis, from about the third to the eighth week after conception
med-pharm-principles.l19.q1.p: During which period of pregnancy is exposure to a teratogen most likely to cause major structural malformations?
med-pharm-principles.l19.q1.e: Major structural defects arise mainly during organogenesis. Very early exposure tends to be all-or-none, and late exposure causes functional or neonatal effects.

med-pharm-principles.l19.q2.t: ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers
med-pharm-principles.l19.q2.p: Which drug class is associated with fetal renal injury and oligohydramnios when used in the second and third trimesters?
med-pharm-principles.l19.q2.h: Think of drugs that reduce glomerular filtration pressure.
med-pharm-principles.l19.q2.e: Inhibiting the renin-angiotensin system impairs fetal renal function. Heparin does not cross the placenta appreciably.

med-pharm-principles.l19.q3.t: Immature glucuronidation causes accumulation and toxicity such as gray baby syndrome
med-pharm-principles.l19.q3.p: Why is chloramphenicol hazardous in neonates?
med-pharm-principles.l19.q3.h: The drug is cleared by conjugation.
med-pharm-principles.l19.q3.e: Neonatal glucuronidation is immature, so chloramphenicol builds up. Albumin is lower, not higher, in neonates.

med-pharm-principles.l19.q4.t: Neural tube defects and later neurodevelopmental effects
med-pharm-principles.l19.q4.p: A 28-year-old woman with epilepsy takes valproate and asks about pregnancy. Which fetal risk is most firmly associated with first-trimester valproate exposure?
med-pharm-principles.l19.q4.h: This anticonvulsant interferes with folate-dependent development.
med-pharm-principles.l19.q4.e: Valproate is a recognized teratogen linked to neural tube defects and neurodevelopmental effects. Tooth staining is a tetracycline effect.

med-pharm-principles.l19.q5.t: Displacement of bilirubin from albumin raises free bilirubin that crosses the immature blood-brain barrier
med-pharm-principles.l19.q5.p: A 3-week-old infant is given a sulfonamide while jaundiced and develops signs of bilirubin encephalopathy. Which mechanism best explains this?
med-pharm-principles.l19.q5.h: Think of albumin binding sites in a neonate with high bilirubin.
med-pharm-principles.l19.q5.e: Sulfonamides compete with bilirubin for albumin, raising free bilirubin that enters the brain. UGT induction would lower bilirubin.

med-pharm-principles.l20.q1.t: Low muscle mass lowers creatinine production, so a normal value may hide reduced clearance
med-pharm-principles.l20.q1.p: Why can serum creatinine be misleading in a frail older adult?
med-pharm-principles.l20.q1.e: Reduced muscle mass produces less creatinine, so a normal value may overstate kidney function.

med-pharm-principles.l20.q2.t: An adverse effect misread as a new condition and treated with another drug
med-pharm-principles.l20.q2.p: A prescribing cascade is best described as:
med-pharm-principles.l20.q2.h: The new drug treats the side effect of the first.
med-pharm-principles.l20.q2.e: A cascade begins when a drug effect is mistaken for a disease. It is a prescribing pattern, not a pharmacokinetic process.

med-pharm-principles.l20.q3.t: The maintenance dose rate, through smaller doses or a longer interval
med-pharm-principles.l20.q3.p: In severe renal failure, a renally cleared drug that has a normal Vd and no active metabolite is started. Which element should be reduced?
med-pharm-principles.l20.q3.e: Maintenance depends on clearance, which fell. The loading dose follows Vd, which is unchanged.

med-pharm-principles.l20.q4.t: Reduced first-pass extraction raises the oral bioavailability of the drug
med-pharm-principles.l20.q4.p: A 78-year-old woman with cirrhosis and portal-systemic shunting takes an oral drug with a high first-pass extraction. She develops excess effect on a dose that was well tolerated before her liver disease. Which mechanism best explains this?
med-pharm-principles.l20.q4.e: Shunting and reduced hepatocyte function allow more drug to reach the systemic circulation. Albumin is typically lower in cirrhosis, not higher.

med-pharm-principles.l20.q5.t: Accumulation of the active metabolite morphine-6-glucuronide when renal clearance falls
med-pharm-principles.l20.q5.p: A 82-year-old man with advanced kidney disease receives repeated morphine for pain and becomes profoundly sedated, although his dose has not changed. Which mechanism best accounts for this?
med-pharm-principles.l20.q5.h: A metabolite is active and renally cleared.
med-pharm-principles.l20.q5.e: Morphine-6-glucuronide is active and cleared by the kidney, so it accumulates in renal failure and causes prolonged sedation.

med-pharm-systems.l01.q1.t: Accumulation of bradykinin because ACE also degrades it
med-pharm-systems.l01.q1.p: Which feature explains why ACE inhibitors, but not ARBs, commonly cause a dry cough?
med-pharm-systems.l01.q1.h: Think about the second name for ACE.
med-pharm-systems.l01.q1.e: ACE is kininase II, so inhibiting it raises bradykinin, which sensitizes airway sensory nerves. ARBs leave bradykinin metabolism untouched, and neprilysin inhibition is a separate mechanism.

med-pharm-systems.l01.q2.p: Which electrolyte profile is most characteristic of chronic thiazide diuretic therapy?
med-pharm-systems.l01.q2.h: Thiazides and loops differ in calcium handling.
med-pharm-systems.l01.q2.e: Thiazides reduce urinary calcium excretion, so calcium rises, while potassium and sodium fall. Loop diuretics produce the hypocalcemia and hypomagnesemia pattern.

med-pharm-systems.l01.q3.t: Second-trimester onward exposure risks fetal renal injury
med-pharm-systems.l01.q3.p: A pregnant woman at 14 weeks is taking lisinopril for hypertension. What is the main reason this needs to change?
med-pharm-systems.l01.q3.h: Consider what angiotensin II does for fetal glomerular filtration.
med-pharm-systems.l01.q3.e: RAAS inhibitors are fetotoxic through impaired fetal renal perfusion and function. Maternal angioedema is rare and not the reason, and aldosterone falls rather than rises.

med-pharm-systems.l01.q4.t: Efferent dilation lowers glomerular pressure; expected, so continue monitoring
med-pharm-systems.l01.q4.p: A 63-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and albuminuria starts an ACE inhibitor. Two weeks later creatinine has risen 20 percent from baseline and potassium is 5.3 mEq/L; he is euvolemic and normotensive. Which explanation and action are best?
med-pharm-systems.l01.q4.h: Which glomerular arteriole does angiotensin II constrict?
med-pharm-systems.l01.q4.e: Removing efferent constriction lowers intraglomerular pressure, giving a small creatinine rise that is acceptable and renoprotective. Switching to an ARB would not change this effect, and potassium supplements would worsen the hyperkalemia.

med-pharm-systems.l01.q5.p: A 58-year-old woman with heart failure takes furosemide and presents with ringing in the ears and hearing loss after a rapid intravenous dose, along with muscle cramps. Serum shows low calcium. Which drug change would NOT add to the hearing loss or the calcium loss?
med-pharm-systems.l01.q5.h: Think about which agents share the ototoxic or calcium-wasting profile.
med-pharm-systems.l01.q5.e: Thiazides reduce urinary calcium excretion and are not notably ototoxic. A second loop agent adds ototoxic and calcium-wasting effects, and cisplatin and aminoglycosides are both ototoxic. Ethacrynic acid, sometimes used in sulfonamide allergy, is still a loop diuretic and also ototoxic.

med-pharm-systems.l02.q1.p: Which calcium channel blocker subclass acts mainly on cardiac conduction rather than vascular smooth muscle?
med-pharm-systems.l02.q1.e: Verapamil and diltiazem slow SA and AV nodal conduction and reduce contractility. The others listed are dihydropyridines with vascular predominance.

med-pharm-systems.l02.q2.t: Metoprolol, because beta-1 selectivity limits bronchospasm and hypoglycemia masking
med-pharm-systems.l02.q2.p: A hypertensive patient with asthma and diabetes needs a beta blocker after a myocardial infarction. Which choice is most appropriate and why?
med-pharm-systems.l02.q2.e: Cardioselective agents spare beta-2 receptors. Nonselective agents can trigger bronchospasm and blunt hypoglycemia recovery, and ISA agents are not preferred after infarction.

med-pharm-systems.l02.q3.t: Venodilation lowers preload and wall tension, reducing myocardial oxygen demand
med-pharm-systems.l02.q3.p: Why do nitrates relieve exertional angina at low doses?
med-pharm-systems.l02.q3.h: Nitric oxide acts mostly on which vessels at low dose?
med-pharm-systems.l02.q3.e: Nitric oxide from nitrates raises cyclic GMP, relaxing veins most, which lowers preload. The other mechanisms describe different drug classes.

med-pharm-systems.l02.q4.t: Additive suppression of AV nodal conduction by both drugs
med-pharm-systems.l02.q4.p: A 66-year-old man with angina and a heart rate of 48 is given diltiazem on top of metoprolol. An hour later he is dizzy with a BP of 80/50 and complete heart block on ECG. What best explains this event?
med-pharm-systems.l02.q4.h: Both drugs act on the same node through different pathways.
med-pharm-systems.l02.q4.e: Diltiazem and a beta blocker together depress the SA and AV nodes and inotropy. Diltiazem is not a dihydropyridine, and the primary problem is pharmacodynamic rather than metabolic.

med-pharm-systems.l02.q5.t: Avoid it: PDE5 inhibition plus a nitrate may cause severe hypotension
med-pharm-systems.l02.q5.p: A 52-year-old man has taken isosorbide dinitrate for angina and now reports an erectile dysfunction pill from an online source. Which counseling point is best?
med-pharm-systems.l02.q5.h: Both drug classes converge on the same second messenger.
med-pharm-systems.l02.q5.e: Nitrates generate nitric oxide and PDE5 inhibitors block cyclic GMP degradation, so the effects synergize dangerously. The mechanisms are not independent, and the timing options do not remove the risk.

med-pharm-systems.l03.q1.p: Which drug class reduced mortality in HFrEF in the PARADIGM-HF trial compared with enalapril?
med-pharm-systems.l03.q1.e: PARADIGM-HF showed sacubitril-valsartan lowered cardiovascular death and heart failure hospitalization. Loop diuretics and digoxin do not reduce mortality, and ivabradine reduces hospitalization only.

med-pharm-systems.l03.q2.t: Allow a washout of ACE inhibitor before starting because of angioedema risk
med-pharm-systems.l03.q2.p: A patient with HFrEF is switched from lisinopril to sacubitril-valsartan. What is the key safety rule?
med-pharm-systems.l03.q2.h: Think bradykinin degradation by two enzymes.
med-pharm-systems.l03.q2.e: Both ACE and neprilysin degrade bradykinin; blocking both raises angioedema risk, so a washout is required. Diuretics do not need to be stopped and digoxin is not the issue.

med-pharm-systems.l03.q3.t: Na+/K+-ATPase inhibition raising intracellular calcium via the exchanger
med-pharm-systems.l03.q3.p: What is the principal mechanism by which digoxin increases myocardial contractility?
med-pharm-systems.l03.q3.e: Raised intracellular sodium reduces calcium extrusion via the exchanger, so calcium rises and contraction strengthens. The other mechanisms belong to dobutamine, milrinone and class III agents.

med-pharm-systems.l03.q4.t: Reduced digoxin clearance plus hypokalemia increasing pump binding
med-pharm-systems.l03.q4.p: A 72-year-old woman with HFrEF and atrial fibrillation on digoxin develops nausea, yellow-tinged vision and frequent premature ventricular beats. She recently started clarithromycin and her potassium is 3.1 mEq/L. Which contributing factors best explain the presentation?
med-pharm-systems.l03.q4.h: Potassium competes with digoxin at the pump.
med-pharm-systems.l03.q4.e: Clarithromycin inhibits P-glycoprotein, raising digoxin levels, and low potassium increases digoxin binding to the pump, favoring arrhythmias. Hyperkalemia is seen in acute overdose, not in this setting.

med-pharm-systems.l03.q5.t: An SGLT2 inhibitor such as dapagliflozin
med-pharm-systems.l03.q5.p: A 60-year-old man with HFrEF and an ejection fraction of 25 percent remains in sinus rhythm at 82 on maximal tolerated carvedilol, sacubitril-valsartan, spironolactone and a loop diuretic, without diabetes. Which addition is best supported for lowering cardiovascular death and hospitalization?
med-pharm-systems.l03.q5.h: This class helps even without diabetes.
med-pharm-systems.l03.q5.e: DAPA-HF and EMPEROR-Reduced showed benefit of SGLT2 inhibitors in HFrEF with or without diabetes. Thiazolidinediones cause fluid retention and non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers worsen HFrEF.

med-pharm-systems.l04.q1.p: Which antiarrhythmic class consists of potassium channel blockers that prolong repolarization?
med-pharm-systems.l04.q1.e: Class III drugs prolong the action potential by blocking potassium channels. Class IB shortens it, class II is beta blockade and class IV is calcium channel blockade.

med-pharm-systems.l04.q2.p: Which toxicity is most characteristic of chronic amiodarone therapy?
med-pharm-systems.l04.q2.e: Amiodarone causes pulmonary fibrosis, hepatotoxicity and thyroid disturbances. The lupus-like syndrome is a feature of procainamide.

med-pharm-systems.l04.q3.t: CAST showed higher mortality with class IC drugs after infarction
med-pharm-systems.l04.q3.p: Why is flecainide avoided after myocardial infarction?
med-pharm-systems.l04.q3.e: CAST found excess death with flecainide and encainide in post-infarction patients with ventricular ectopy. Flecainide has little effect on repolarization and is not a beta blocker.

med-pharm-systems.l04.q4.t: Intravenous magnesium sulfate with correction of potassium
med-pharm-systems.l04.q4.p: A 45-year-old woman taking sotalol for atrial fibrillation starts a diuretic for edema and develops palpitations and syncope. ECG shows a long QT interval and polymorphic ventricular tachycardia that twists around the baseline. Which is the best immediate treatment?
med-pharm-systems.l04.q4.h: Name the rhythm first, then the electrolyte that stabilizes it.
med-pharm-systems.l04.q4.e: This is torsades de pointes; magnesium suppresses early afterdepolarizations. Procainamide and amiodarone also prolong QT, and adenosine acts on the AV node and does not treat this.

med-pharm-systems.l04.q5.t: Methylxanthines such as caffeine competing at adenosine receptors
med-pharm-systems.l04.q5.p: A 30-year-old man with a regular narrow-complex tachycardia of 190 is given a rapid intravenous drug that produces a few seconds of asystole followed by sinus rhythm and brief chest tightness. He had taken a large amount of caffeine earlier. If the same drug is repeated later, what would most likely reduce its efficacy?
med-pharm-systems.l04.q5.h: Adenosine acts at receptors blocked by xanthines.
med-pharm-systems.l04.q5.e: Caffeine and theophylline antagonize adenosine receptors and blunt response, whereas dipyridamole prolongs adenosine action. Adenosine lasts seconds, so hepatic induction is irrelevant.

med-pharm-systems.l05.q1.p: Which enzyme is the target of statins?
med-pharm-systems.l05.q1.h: The rate-limiting step of cholesterol synthesis.
med-pharm-systems.l05.q1.e: Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase and thereby upregulate LDL receptors. ATP-citrate lyase is the bempedoic acid target and lipoprotein lipase is activated by fibrates.

med-pharm-systems.l05.q2.t: A monoclonal antibody against PCSK9 such as evolocumab
med-pharm-systems.l05.q2.p: A patient well controlled on a statin and ezetimibe still has a very high LDL. Which add-on prevents LDL receptors from being degraded and so increases receptor recycling?
med-pharm-systems.l05.q2.h: Think about the protein that tags LDL receptors for degradation.
med-pharm-systems.l05.q2.e: PCSK9 inhibitors raise surface LDL receptor numbers. Sequestrants, fibrates and niacin lower lipids through different mechanisms and none acts on receptor degradation.

med-pharm-systems.l05.q3.t: CYP3A4 inhibition raises simvastatin exposure and the risk of rhabdomyolysis
med-pharm-systems.l05.q3.p: Why is the combination of simvastatin and clarithromycin hazardous?
med-pharm-systems.l05.q3.e: Macrolides like clarithromycin inhibit CYP3A4, so statin levels climb and myopathy can follow. Clarithromycin is an inhibitor rather than an inducer, and neither drug acts on NPC1L1 in this way.

med-pharm-systems.l05.q4.t: Gemfibrozil inhibits statin glucuronidation, raising statin levels
med-pharm-systems.l05.q4.p: A 58-year-old man on high-intensity atorvastatin has a triglyceride level of 700 mg/dL and a history of pancreatitis. A fibrate is chosen. Several weeks after adding gemfibrozil he has diffuse muscle pain and tea-colored urine, and creatine kinase is markedly elevated. What best explains the event?
med-pharm-systems.l05.q4.h: This fibrate is the one most associated with statin level elevation.
med-pharm-systems.l05.q4.e: Gemfibrozil impairs statin glucuronidation and OATP uptake, raising statin exposure. It does not induce CYP3A4, and fenofibrate is the safer fibrate partner.

med-pharm-systems.l05.q5.t: Bempedoic acid, with hyperuricemia and tendon rupture risk
med-pharm-systems.l05.q5.p: A 45-year-old woman with familial hypercholesterolemia has a persistently high LDL on the statin dose she can tolerate, because higher doses cause myalgias. She wants an add-on that lowers hepatic cholesterol synthesis upstream of HMG-CoA reductase. Which drug and key adverse effect pair is correct?
med-pharm-systems.l05.q5.e: Bempedoic acid is activated mainly in the liver, sparing muscle, and raises uric acid with tendon risk. Ezetimibe blocks absorption rather than synthesis, and flushing belongs to niacin.

med-pharm-systems.l06.q1.t: It irreversibly acetylates COX-1, blocking thromboxane A2
med-pharm-systems.l06.q1.p: How does aspirin inhibit platelet aggregation?
med-pharm-systems.l06.q1.e: Aspirin acetylates COX-1 irreversibly for the life of the platelet. P2Y12 blockade is clopidogrel, antithrombin activation is heparin, and VKORC1 inhibition is warfarin.

med-pharm-systems.l06.q2.t: Omeprazole inhibits CYP2C19, which is needed to activate clopidogrel
med-pharm-systems.l06.q2.p: A patient on clopidogrel after stent placement starts omeprazole for reflux. Why might this reduce antiplatelet efficacy?
med-pharm-systems.l06.q2.e: Clopidogrel needs CYP2C19 for bioactivation, and omeprazole is an inhibitor of that enzyme. The other mechanisms do not reflect how this interaction occurs.

med-pharm-systems.l06.q3.p: Which agent is used to reverse the anticoagulant effect of dabigatran?
med-pharm-systems.l06.q3.h: A specific antibody fragment against a direct thrombin inhibitor.
med-pharm-systems.l06.q3.e: Idarucizumab binds dabigatran. Protamine reverses heparin, vitamin K reverses warfarin more slowly, and andexanet alfa targets factor Xa inhibitors.

med-pharm-systems.l06.q4.t: Stop heparin, start argatroban; antibodies bind PF4-heparin complexes
med-pharm-systems.l06.q4.p: A 62-year-old woman is on heparin after a knee replacement. On day 7 her platelet count falls from 250 to 90 thousand per microliter, and she develops a new deep vein thrombosis. Which is the best management and underlying mechanism?
med-pharm-systems.l06.q4.h: The paradox is clotting, not bleeding, with a falling platelet count.
med-pharm-systems.l06.q4.e: This is heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, an immune reaction against PF4-heparin that activates platelets. Low molecular weight heparin carries a lower but real HIT risk and cross-reacts, so it is not a safe switch.

med-pharm-systems.l06.q5.t: Warfarin remains preferred; dabigatran did worse in mechanical valves
med-pharm-systems.l06.q5.p: A 55-year-old man with a mechanical aortic valve and atrial fibrillation is on warfarin. The clinician considers switching to a direct oral anticoagulant for convenience. Which statement best guides the decision?
med-pharm-systems.l06.q5.e: In RE-ALIGN, dabigatran was harmful versus warfarin in patients with mechanical valves. DOAC data apply to nonvalvular atrial fibrillation, and aspirin alone is inadequate for valve thrombosis prevention.

med-pharm-systems.l07.q1.p: Which antidiabetic drug class acts by closing the beta-cell ATP-sensitive potassium channel?
med-pharm-systems.l07.q1.e: Sulfonylureas bind SUR1, causing depolarization and insulin release. Biguanides, thiazolidinediones and alpha-glucosidase inhibitors act elsewhere.

med-pharm-systems.l07.q2.p: A patient with type 2 diabetes and recurrent genital yeast infections is most likely taking which drug?
med-pharm-systems.l07.q2.h: Glucose in the urine feeds fungi.
med-pharm-systems.l07.q2.e: SGLT2 inhibitors cause glucosuria and increase genital mycotic infections. The others do not cause glucosuria.

med-pharm-systems.l07.q3.t: Contraindicated with personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or MEN2
med-pharm-systems.l07.q3.p: Which warning applies to GLP-1 receptor agonists such as semaglutide?
med-pharm-systems.l07.q3.e: GLP-1 agonists have a boxed warning from rodent thyroid C-cell tumors. Lactic acidosis relates to metformin, and sulfa cross-reactivity is not a recognized issue.

med-pharm-systems.l07.q4.t: Add an SGLT2 inhibitor or GLP-1 receptor agonist with proven outcomes
med-pharm-systems.l07.q4.p: A 67-year-old man with type 2 diabetes, coronary artery disease and an eGFR of 42 has an A1c of 8.5 percent on metformin. He has no history of pancreatitis or thyroid cancer. Which next step has the strongest evidence of cardiovascular benefit independent of glucose lowering?
med-pharm-systems.l07.q4.h: Think of the outcome trials, not just glycemia.
med-pharm-systems.l07.q4.e: SGLT2 inhibitors and select GLP-1 agonists reduced major cardiovascular events in outcome trials. Glyburide risks hypoglycemia in renal impairment, and pioglitazone causes fluid retention.

med-pharm-systems.l07.q5.t: Euglycemic ketoacidosis from SGLT2 inhibition and insulin lack
med-pharm-systems.l07.q5.p: A 28-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes taking an SGLT2 inhibitor off-label presents with nausea, vomiting and rapid deep breathing after a prolonged fast. Glucose is 190 mg/dL, anion gap is high and ketones are positive. Which is the best explanation?
med-pharm-systems.l07.q5.h: Glucose is only modestly raised but there is acidosis.
med-pharm-systems.l07.q5.e: SGLT2 inhibitors promote ketogenesis and can cause DKA at near-normal glucose, especially in insulin-deficient states. HHS has markedly high glucose without ketosis and metformin is the lactic acid risk.

med-pharm-systems.l08.q1.p: Which enzyme do methimazole and propylthiouracil inhibit?
med-pharm-systems.l08.q1.e: Thionamides block thyroid peroxidase. Propylthiouracil additionally inhibits peripheral deiodination, but that is not the shared target, and the symporter is blocked by perchlorate.

med-pharm-systems.l08.q2.t: Calcium binds levothyroxine in the gut and reduces its absorption
med-pharm-systems.l08.q2.p: A hypothyroid patient on stable levothyroxine begins taking calcium carbonate tablets with breakfast, and TSH rises. What is the best explanation?
med-pharm-systems.l08.q2.e: Divalent and trivalent cations bind levothyroxine and impair absorption, so dose timing is separated. Estrogen raises binding globulin and enzyme inducers raise metabolism, but calcium does neither.

med-pharm-systems.l08.q3.t: Propylthiouracil, since methimazole is teratogenic early
med-pharm-systems.l08.q3.p: Which antithyroid drug is preferred in the first trimester of pregnancy, and why?
med-pharm-systems.l08.q3.h: Recall the malformations linked to one thionamide in early pregnancy.
med-pharm-systems.l08.q3.e: Methimazole is associated with aplasia cutis and choanal atresia in early gestation, so propylthiouracil is used briefly, then often changed because of hepatotoxicity. Radioactive iodine is contraindicated in pregnancy.

med-pharm-systems.l08.q4.t: Agranulocytosis; stop the drug and check the neutrophil count urgently
med-pharm-systems.l08.q4.p: A 35-year-old woman taking an antithyroid drug for Graves disease develops fever and sore throat over two days. Which toxicity should be suspected and what is the best next step?
med-pharm-systems.l08.q4.h: Febrile illness with a drug that suppresses marrow lineage.
med-pharm-systems.l08.q4.e: Thionamide-induced agranulocytosis presents with fever and pharyngitis and requires stopping the drug and checking counts. Continuing the drug or giving iodide first would worsen the situation.

med-pharm-systems.l08.q5.t: Its iodine load can cause hyper- or hypothyroidism
med-pharm-systems.l08.q5.p: A 70-year-old man on long-term amiodarone for atrial fibrillation presents with weight loss, tremor, palpitations and a suppressed TSH. Which statement best describes the drug effect?
med-pharm-systems.l08.q5.h: Amiodarone is about 37 percent iodine by weight.
med-pharm-systems.l08.q5.e: Amiodarone can cause both thyrotoxicosis and hypothyroidism through iodine excess and direct toxicity. It does not induce thyroid peroxidase or act at the TSH receptor.

med-pharm-systems.l09.q1.p: Which laboratory pattern is typical shortly after a patient starts systemic glucocorticoids?
med-pharm-systems.l09.q1.h: Think demargination of one cell line.
med-pharm-systems.l09.q1.e: Glucocorticoids demarginate neutrophils and reduce lymphocytes and eosinophils. The other patterns reverse one or more of those cell-line effects.

med-pharm-systems.l09.q2.t: HPA axis suppression may leave the adrenal glands unable to respond to stress
med-pharm-systems.l09.q2.p: A man has taken prednisone daily for four months and now needs to stop. What is the main reason for tapering rather than stopping abruptly?
med-pharm-systems.l09.q2.h: Negative feedback shuts down CRH and ACTH.
med-pharm-systems.l09.q2.e: Chronic steroids suppress ACTH and atrophy the adrenal cortex, so tapering allows recovery. Relapse can occur but is not the main reason, and mineralocorticoid excess does not follow withdrawal.

med-pharm-systems.l09.q3.p: Which glucocorticoid has minimal mineralocorticoid activity and the longest duration of action?
med-pharm-systems.l09.q3.h: Used for cerebral edema and antenatal lung maturation.
med-pharm-systems.l09.q3.e: Dexamethasone is potent and long-acting with almost no salt retention. Hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone have significant mineralocorticoid effect, and prednisolone has an intermediate duration.

med-pharm-systems.l09.q4.t: Chronic glucocorticoid excess: myopathy, insulin resistance, fat redistribution, bone loss
med-pharm-systems.l09.q4.p: A 54-year-old woman has taken prednisone 20 mg daily for polymyalgia rheumatica for six months. She now has difficulty rising from a chair, a fasting glucose of 148 mg/dL, new central weight gain and a bone density T-score of -2.8. Which statement best explains these findings?
med-pharm-systems.l09.q4.h: Match each finding to a catabolic steroid effect.
med-pharm-systems.l09.q4.e: These are classic iatrogenic Cushing features. Prednisone has weak mineralocorticoid action, and adrenal insufficiency would give hypoglycemia rather than hyperglycemia.

med-pharm-systems.l09.q5.t: Secondary adrenal suppression; give intravenous hydrocortisone
med-pharm-systems.l09.q5.p: A 60-year-old man who has taken dexamethasone for months for a brain tumor undergoes emergency abdominal surgery and becomes hypotensive and hypoglycemic after induction, with sodium 128 and potassium 4.6 mEq/L. Which is the most likely mechanism and best treatment?
med-pharm-systems.l09.q5.h: Think about why potassium is not very elevated.
med-pharm-systems.l09.q5.e: Long-term exogenous steroid causes secondary adrenal insufficiency, where the renin-angiotensin axis stays intact, so potassium is usually normal. Treatment is stress-dose hydrocortisone; fludrocortisone alone would not replace glucocorticoid.

med-pharm-systems.l10.q1.t: Beta-2 adrenergic receptor on airway smooth muscle
med-pharm-systems.l10.q1.p: Which receptor activation produces bronchodilation and is the target of albuterol?
med-pharm-systems.l10.q1.h: Cyclic AMP rises in the muscle.
med-pharm-systems.l10.q1.e: Albuterol stimulates beta-2 receptors, raising cyclic AMP and relaxing smooth muscle. M3 stimulation constricts, so M3 blockade is therapeutic instead.

med-pharm-systems.l10.q2.t: Muscarinic receptor blockade reducing secretions and bladder contraction
med-pharm-systems.l10.q2.p: A COPD patient on tiotropium develops difficulty urinating and dry mouth. Which mechanism explains this?
med-pharm-systems.l10.q2.e: Tiotropium blocks muscarinic receptors, so dry mouth and urinary retention are expected. Beta-2 agonists cause tremor and tachycardia rather than anticholinergic effects.

med-pharm-systems.l10.q3.e: Inhibition of CYP1A2 slows clearance and increases toxicity risk. Smoking, rifampin and phenytoin induce metabolism and lower levels.

med-pharm-systems.l10.q4.t: An inhaled corticosteroid, considering a leukotriene antagonist
med-pharm-systems.l10.q4.p: A 34-year-old woman with moderate asthma, using albuterol five times weekly and waking at night twice a month, also has nasal polyps and develops wheezing after taking ibuprofen. Which add-on is best matched to this pathophysiology as well as to her uncontrolled symptoms?
med-pharm-systems.l10.q4.h: This pattern involves overproduction of cysteinyl leukotrienes after COX blockade.
med-pharm-systems.l10.q4.e: Aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease shifts arachidonic acid toward leukotrienes, and inhaled steroids are the core therapy with leukotriene modifiers as adjuncts. LABA alone is unsafe in asthma, and theophylline or a muscarinic antagonist alone neither treats the underlying inflammation nor the leukotriene pathway.

med-pharm-systems.l10.q5.t: Mepolizumab, a monoclonal antibody against interleukin-5
med-pharm-systems.l10.q5.p: A 40-year-old man has severe asthma with frequent exacerbations on high-dose inhaled corticosteroid plus long-acting beta agonist. Blood eosinophils are 600 per microliter and total IgE is normal. Which biologic best matches the phenotype?
med-pharm-systems.l10.q5.h: Eosinophil biology depends on one cytokine.
med-pharm-systems.l10.q5.e: Eosinophilic asthma responds to anti-IL-5 therapy. Omalizumab suits allergic asthma with elevated IgE, and montelukast and roflumilast are small molecules rather than antibodies.

med-pharm-systems.l11.q1.p: Which drug class irreversibly inhibits the gastric H+/K+ ATPase?
med-pharm-systems.l11.q1.e: PPIs bind the pump covalently after acid activation. H2 blockers act at histamine receptors, and misoprostol is the prostaglandin analog.

med-pharm-systems.l11.q2.t: It is a prostaglandin E1 analog that causes uterine contractions
med-pharm-systems.l11.q2.p: Why is misoprostol contraindicated in pregnancy?
med-pharm-systems.l11.q2.h: It is also used for labor induction.
med-pharm-systems.l11.q2.e: Prostaglandin analogs stimulate uterine contraction and can cause miscarriage. The other mechanisms describe different GI drug classes.

med-pharm-systems.l11.q3.p: Which adverse effect carries a boxed warning for metoclopramide?
med-pharm-systems.l11.q3.e: Prolonged D2 blockade can cause irreversible tardive dyskinesia. Ondansetron is the antiemetic more associated with QT prolongation.

med-pharm-systems.l11.q4.t: Lactulose, which acidifies colonic contents so ammonia becomes trapped as ammonium
med-pharm-systems.l11.q4.p: A 70-year-old man with cirrhosis presents with confusion, asterixis and a flapping tremor after a gastrointestinal bleed. Ammonia is elevated. Which treatment best explains its mechanism of lowering blood ammonia?
med-pharm-systems.l11.q4.h: Acidification of the colon traps a diffusible base.
med-pharm-systems.l11.q4.e: Lactulose is metabolized to acids, converting NH3 to NH4+, which is not absorbed, and speeds transit. Rifaximin is often added, and the other options do not lower ammonia this way.

med-pharm-systems.l11.q5.t: Omeprazole inhibits CYP2C19, so a weaker inhibitor such as pantoprazole is preferred
med-pharm-systems.l11.q5.p: A 62-year-old woman with a coronary stent on clopidogrel has reflux and needs a PPI. Her cardiologist worries about reduced antiplatelet effect. Which statement best explains the concern and the response?
med-pharm-systems.l11.q5.h: A prodrug needs a particular enzyme.
med-pharm-systems.l11.q5.e: The interaction is mostly through CYP2C19 inhibition by omeprazole and esomeprazole. Pantoprazole has less effect, and the other statements describe mechanisms that do not occur.

med-pharm-systems.l12.q1.p: What is the antidote for acetaminophen overdose?
med-pharm-systems.l12.q1.e: N-acetylcysteine restores glutathione and detoxifies NAPQI. Fomepizole treats toxic alcohols, flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines and hydroxocobalamin treats cyanide.

med-pharm-systems.l12.q2.t: Loss of prostaglandin-mediated afferent arteriolar dilation reduces glomerular filtration
med-pharm-systems.l12.q2.p: Why can NSAIDs precipitate acute kidney injury in a patient with heart failure on a diuretic?
med-pharm-systems.l12.q2.e: NSAIDs remove prostaglandin-mediated afferent dilation, so GFR falls in volume-dependent states. NSAIDs lower, not raise, prostaglandins.

med-pharm-systems.l12.q3.t: Blocked thiopurine breakdown raises levels and marrow toxicity
med-pharm-systems.l12.q3.p: A patient who is stable on allopurinol is started on azathioprine. What is the key concern?
med-pharm-systems.l12.q3.e: Blocking xanthine oxidase leaves more active thiopurine, so dose reduction is needed. Allopurinol does not induce TPMT.

med-pharm-systems.l12.q4.p: A 48-year-old man with gout starts allopurinol and, three weeks later, has fever, a diffuse blistering rash with mucosal involvement and eosinophilia; he is of Han Chinese descent. Which genetic factor is most associated with this reaction?
med-pharm-systems.l12.q4.h: This pharmacogenomic association is tested before allopurinol in some populations.
med-pharm-systems.l12.q4.e: HLA-B*58:01 predisposes to allopurinol severe cutaneous reactions. HLA-B*57:01 relates to abacavir and HLA-B*15:02 to carbamazepine.

med-pharm-systems.l12.q5.t: CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein inhibition raised colchicine exposure
med-pharm-systems.l12.q5.p: A 75-year-old man with gout and chronic kidney disease takes colchicine and is prescribed clarithromycin for pneumonia. Several days later he develops vomiting, diarrhea, muscle weakness and neutropenia. What best explains the toxicity?
med-pharm-systems.l12.q5.h: Both transporter and enzyme are involved.
med-pharm-systems.l12.q5.e: Clarithromycin is a strong CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein inhibitor, and renal impairment reduces clearance, so colchicine toxicity follows. Induction would lower, not raise, exposure.

med-pharm-systems.l13.q1.p: Which enzyme is inhibited by the cyclosporine-cyclophilin and tacrolimus-FKBP12 complexes?
med-pharm-systems.l13.q1.e: Calcineurin inhibition blocks NFAT activation and IL-2 transcription. mTOR is the sirolimus target, and the other enzymes are antimetabolite targets.

med-pharm-systems.l13.q2.p: Which adverse effect is classically associated with cyclosporine but less with tacrolimus?
med-pharm-systems.l13.q2.e: Gingival hyperplasia and hirsutism are cyclosporine features, while tacrolimus more often causes diabetes. Sirolimus causes poor wound healing and mycophenolate causes marrow suppression.

med-pharm-systems.l13.q3.p: Before starting a TNF-alpha inhibitor, which screening test is most important?
med-pharm-systems.l13.q3.h: TNF is needed to maintain granulomas.
med-pharm-systems.l13.q3.e: TNF blockade can reactivate latent tuberculosis, and hepatitis B screening is also standard. TPMT testing relates to thiopurines and HLA-B*58:01 to allopurinol.

med-pharm-systems.l13.q4.t: Azole CYP3A4 inhibition raising tacrolimus levels and nephrotoxicity
med-pharm-systems.l13.q4.p: A 41-year-old kidney transplant recipient on tacrolimus presents with a creatinine rise, tremor, potassium 5.6 mEq/L and hypertension after starting an antifungal for oral candidiasis. Which pair best explains the picture?
med-pharm-systems.l13.q4.h: This transplant drug is a CYP3A4 substrate with a narrow window.
med-pharm-systems.l13.q4.e: Azoles raise tacrolimus exposure, causing nephrotoxicity, tremor, hyperkalemia and hypertension. Induction would increase rejection risk, not toxicity.

med-pharm-systems.l13.q5.t: Leucovorin, which bypasses the blocked reductase step
med-pharm-systems.l13.q5.p: A 36-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis on weekly methotrexate develops mouth ulcers, cough and a low white count after mistakenly taking it daily for a week. Which agent most directly counters high-dose methotrexate toxicity?
med-pharm-systems.l13.q5.h: Reduced folate is delivered downstream of the enzyme block.
med-pharm-systems.l13.q5.e: Leucovorin supplies reduced folate downstream of dihydrofolate reductase. Mesna is for cyclophosphamide, and the others do not address folate depletion.

med-pharm-systems.l14.q1.p: What is the molecular target of beta-lactam antibiotics?
med-pharm-systems.l14.q1.e: Beta-lactams acylate PBPs and block cell-wall cross-linking. The other targets belong to aminoglycosides, quinolones and sulfonamides respectively.

med-pharm-systems.l14.q2.t: Cilastatin inhibits renal dehydropeptidase that inactivates imipenem
med-pharm-systems.l14.q2.p: Why is imipenem administered together with cilastatin?
med-pharm-systems.l14.q2.e: Cilastatin prevents hydrolysis by dehydropeptidase I and preserves the drug. It does not inhibit carbapenemases, and imipenem itself can lower the seizure threshold.

med-pharm-systems.l14.q3.t: Replacement of D-Ala-D-Ala with D-Ala-D-lactate lowers drug binding affinity
med-pharm-systems.l14.q3.p: Which mechanism explains vancomycin resistance in vancomycin-resistant enterococci?
med-pharm-systems.l14.q3.e: VRE alter the peptidoglycan precursor target so vancomycin binds poorly. PBP2a causes MRSA resistance and ribosomal methylation causes macrolide resistance.

med-pharm-systems.l14.q4.t: It displaces bilirubin and can precipitate with calcium, so avoid it
med-pharm-systems.l14.q4.p: A 6-day-old preterm neonate with hyperbilirubinemia is treated for suspected meningitis with ceftriaxone while also receiving intravenous calcium-containing nutrition. Which concern is most important?
med-pharm-systems.l14.q4.h: Two separate neonatal hazards are combined.
med-pharm-systems.l14.q4.e: Ceftriaxone competes for bilirubin binding and can precipitate with calcium, so it is avoided in hyperbilirubinemic neonates and with calcium infusions. Gray baby syndrome is a chloramphenicol effect.

med-pharm-systems.l14.q5.t: Rate-related histamine release; slow the infusion
med-pharm-systems.l14.q5.p: A 52-year-old man with MRSA bacteremia receives vancomycin by rapid infusion and develops flushing and pruritus over the face and upper trunk with mild hypotension, without wheeze or urticaria elsewhere. Which is the best explanation and response?
med-pharm-systems.l14.q5.h: The rate, not the drug identity, matters.
med-pharm-systems.l14.q5.e: Vancomycin infusion reaction is non-IgE histamine release related to infusion speed, and slowing the infusion usually resolves it. True anaphylaxis is rare, and nephrotoxicity does not cause flushing.

med-pharm-systems.l15.q1.p: Which antibiotic class binds the 30S ribosomal subunit and is bactericidal?
med-pharm-systems.l15.q1.e: Aminoglycosides are unusual in being bactericidal ribosomal inhibitors. Tetracyclines also bind 30S but are bacteriostatic, and macrolides and oxazolidinones bind 50S.

med-pharm-systems.l15.q2.t: Peripheral neuropathy from pyridoxine depletion, prevented by vitamin B6
med-pharm-systems.l15.q2.p: Which toxicity is characteristic of isoniazid, and what prevents it?
med-pharm-systems.l15.q2.e: Isoniazid depletes pyridoxine, causing neuropathy that B6 prevents. Optic neuritis is ethambutol, hyperuricemia pyrazinamide and orange secretions rifampin.

med-pharm-systems.l15.q3.p: Which adverse effect is a boxed warning for fluoroquinolones?
med-pharm-systems.l15.q3.h: Risk is higher with concurrent corticosteroids.
med-pharm-systems.l15.q3.e: Fluoroquinolone boxed warnings include tendinopathy and rupture, neuropathy, CNS effects and myasthenia exacerbation. The other effects belong to chloramphenicol, aminoglycosides and metronidazole.

med-pharm-systems.l15.q4.t: Trimethoprim blocks collecting-duct ENaC and tubular creatinine secretion
med-pharm-systems.l15.q4.p: A 30-year-old woman with HIV on a trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole regimen for Pneumocystis prophylaxis develops a serum potassium of 5.9 mEq/L and a rise in creatinine of modest degree, without a change in true glomerular filtration. Which mechanism best explains this?
med-pharm-systems.l15.q4.e: Trimethoprim resembles amiloride and blocks ENaC, causing hyperkalemia, and it competes for creatinine secretion, raising creatinine without lower GFR. Sulfonamide crystalluria is real but does not explain the hyperkalemia.

med-pharm-systems.l15.q5.t: Ciprofloxacin inhibits CYP1A2, raising theophylline concentrations to toxic levels
med-pharm-systems.l15.q5.p: A 45-year-old man on theophylline for COPD starts ciprofloxacin for a urinary infection and develops palpitations, tremor and a generalized seizure. Which interaction is the best explanation?
med-pharm-systems.l15.q5.h: Recall the enzyme that clears theophylline.
med-pharm-systems.l15.q5.e: CYP1A2 inhibition by ciprofloxacin slows theophylline clearance and causes toxicity including seizures. The drug is an inhibitor, not an inducer, and additive seizure threshold lowering is secondary.

med-pharm-systems.l16.q1.t: It is first phosphorylated by viral thymidine kinase
med-pharm-systems.l16.q1.p: Why is acyclovir selectively active in herpes-infected cells?
med-pharm-systems.l16.q1.h: The first activation step uses a viral enzyme.
med-pharm-systems.l16.q1.e: Viral thymidine kinase concentrates the active drug in infected cells. Neuraminidase inhibitors are used for influenza instead.

med-pharm-systems.l16.q2.p: Which test should be performed before prescribing abacavir?
med-pharm-systems.l16.q2.e: HLA-B*57:01 predicts abacavir hypersensitivity. HLA-B*58:01 relates to allopurinol, TPMT to thiopurines and tropism testing to maraviroc.

med-pharm-systems.l16.q3.p: Which antiviral is activated by the cytomegalovirus UL97 kinase and has marrow suppression as a main toxicity?
med-pharm-systems.l16.q3.e: Ganciclovir is phosphorylated by UL97 and causes cytopenias. Foscarnet needs no activation and causes nephrotoxicity and electrolyte disturbances.

med-pharm-systems.l16.q4.t: Stopping drugs active against hepatitis B allowed a viral flare
med-pharm-systems.l16.q4.p: A 38-year-old man with HIV and chronic hepatitis B stops his tenofovir-emtricitabine-containing regimen on his own. Two months later he has fatigue, jaundice and markedly raised aminotransferases. What is the most likely explanation?
med-pharm-systems.l16.q4.h: Some of these drugs have a second target virus.
med-pharm-systems.l16.q4.e: Tenofovir, emtricitabine and lamivudine suppress hepatitis B, so stopping can cause a severe flare. The patient was not on abacavir, and tenofovir toxicity affects the kidney.

med-pharm-systems.l16.q5.t: Ritonavir inhibits CYP3A4, raising statin levels; switch to pravastatin
med-pharm-systems.l16.q5.p: A 55-year-old man on a ritonavir-boosted HIV regimen is also taking simvastatin and begins to have severe muscle pain with dark urine. What mechanism explains the toxicity, and which change is best?
med-pharm-systems.l16.q5.h: Boosters are named for what they do to CYP3A4.
med-pharm-systems.l16.q5.e: Ritonavir inhibits CYP3A4, which markedly raises simvastatin exposure; a statin with less CYP3A4 dependence is safer. Ritonavir is an inhibitor, not an inducer, and is not an integrase inhibitor.

med-pharm-systems.l17.q1.t: Ergosterol in the fungal cell membrane
med-pharm-systems.l17.q1.p: Which cell component is the target of amphotericin B?
