med-pharm-systems.l17.q1.e: Amphotericin binds ergosterol and creates membrane pores. The other options are targets of echinocandins, terbinafine and azoles.

med-pharm-systems.l17.q2.t: Afferent vasoconstriction and tubular injury cause renal potassium and magnesium wasting
med-pharm-systems.l17.q2.p: A patient receiving amphotericin B develops hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia and rising creatinine. Which statement best explains this?
med-pharm-systems.l17.q2.e: Amphotericin damages tubular cells and constricts the afferent arteriole, producing wasting of potassium and magnesium and renal tubular acidosis. Liposomal forms reduce this.

med-pharm-systems.l17.q3.p: Which antifungal class inhibits beta-1,3-glucan synthase and is first-line for invasive candidiasis?
med-pharm-systems.l17.q3.e: Echinocandins weaken the fungal wall by blocking glucan synthesis. Azoles inhibit ergosterol synthesis, polyenes bind ergosterol and allylamines inhibit squalene epoxidase.

med-pharm-systems.l17.q4.t: Negative inotropy plus CYP3A4 inhibition, so avoided here
med-pharm-systems.l17.q4.p: A 60-year-old man with advanced heart failure and onychomycosis is prescribed oral itraconazole. Which concern is most important?
med-pharm-systems.l17.q4.h: Think of the heart and the cytochrome.
med-pharm-systems.l17.q4.e: Itraconazole has negative inotropic effects and is a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor, so it is avoided in heart failure. Squalene accumulation is terbinafine and flucytosine is the 5-fluorouracil prodrug.

med-pharm-systems.l17.q5.p: A 48-year-old man with HIV has headache, fever and a positive cerebrospinal fluid cryptococcal antigen. During induction with liposomal amphotericin plus a second agent, his neutrophil count falls. Which second agent is most likely responsible?
med-pharm-systems.l17.q5.h: This drug is a pyrimidine antimetabolite.
med-pharm-systems.l17.q5.e: Flucytosine is converted to 5-fluorouracil and suppresses marrow, and it is paired with amphotericin for cryptococcal meningitis. Echinocandins are not active against Cryptococcus.

med-pharm-systems.l18.q1.p: Which gene encodes the altered penicillin-binding protein of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus?
med-pharm-systems.l18.q1.e: mecA encodes PBP2a, which has low affinity for most beta-lactams. vanA relates to vancomycin resistance, gyrA to quinolone resistance and erm to macrolide resistance.

med-pharm-systems.l18.q2.t: More frequent or extended dosing keeps concentrations above the MIC for longer
med-pharm-systems.l18.q2.p: Which dosing pattern follows from the time-dependent killing of beta-lactams?
med-pharm-systems.l18.q2.h: Time above MIC is the driver.
med-pharm-systems.l18.q2.e: Beta-lactam efficacy tracks the fraction of the interval above the MIC. Peak-driven once-daily dosing is characteristic of aminoglycosides.

med-pharm-systems.l18.q3.p: Which antibiotic class is generally preferred for serious infections caused by extended-spectrum beta-lactamase producing Enterobacterales?
med-pharm-systems.l18.q3.e: Carbapenems are stable to ESBL hydrolysis. ESBLs hydrolyze cephalosporins, penicillins and aztreonam.

med-pharm-systems.l18.q4.t: Selection of mutants overproducing chromosomal AmpC beta-lactamase
med-pharm-systems.l18.q4.p: A 70-year-old man has an Enterobacter cloacae bloodstream infection that initially responded to ceftriaxone, then relapsed with cephalosporin resistance during therapy. Which mechanism best explains this course?
med-pharm-systems.l18.q4.h: Inducible chromosomal enzyme under cephalosporin pressure.
med-pharm-systems.l18.q4.e: Third-generation cephalosporins select derepressed AmpC mutants in organisms like Enterobacter. mecA is staphylococcal and the other mechanisms involve different drug classes.

med-pharm-systems.l18.q5.t: Stop the inciting antibiotic if possible and use oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin
med-pharm-systems.l18.q5.p: A 66-year-old woman hospitalized for pneumonia develops profuse watery diarrhea on day 6 of broad antibiotics; stool testing is positive for toxin-producing Clostridioides difficile. Which next step best reflects current principles?
med-pharm-systems.l18.q5.h: Oral vancomycin works precisely because it stays in the gut.
med-pharm-systems.l18.q5.e: Oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin are preferred, and the precipitating antibiotic should be stopped if possible. Intravenous vancomycin does not reach the colon lumen and antimotility drugs are risky.

med-pharm-systems.l19.q1.t: QRS widening with arrhythmias and seizures from sodium channel blockade
med-pharm-systems.l19.q1.p: Which adverse effect is most closely linked to tricyclic antidepressant overdose?
med-pharm-systems.l19.q1.h: These drugs block more than reuptake pumps.
med-pharm-systems.l19.q1.e: Cardiac sodium channel blockade widens the QRS and causes arrhythmia, treated with sodium bicarbonate. Tyramine crises are MAOI toxicity.

med-pharm-systems.l19.q2.t: Tyramine escapes gut MAO-A breakdown and displaces norepinephrine from nerve terminals
med-pharm-systems.l19.q2.p: A patient taking phenelzine eats aged cheese and cured meat at a party and develops a severe headache with a blood pressure of 220/120. What mechanism explains this?
med-pharm-systems.l19.q2.h: MAO normally destroys a dietary amine.
med-pharm-systems.l19.q2.e: MAOIs prevent tyramine metabolism in the gut, so absorbed tyramine releases large amounts of norepinephrine. SSRIs, not MAOIs, would be linked with reuptake blockade.

med-pharm-systems.l19.q3.p: Which antidepressant lowers the seizure threshold and is contraindicated in patients with a seizure disorder or bulimia?
med-pharm-systems.l19.q3.h: It is also used for smoking cessation.
med-pharm-systems.l19.q3.e: Bupropion carries a dose-related seizure risk. Mirtazapine and the SSRIs listed do not have this dominant effect.

med-pharm-systems.l19.q4.t: Stop both drugs, give a benzodiazepine, cyproheptadine if needed
med-pharm-systems.l19.q4.p: A 35-year-old woman on sertraline is given tramadol after a dental procedure. Within hours she has agitation, diaphoresis, diarrhea, a temperature of 39.2 degrees Celsius, tremor and inducible ankle clonus with hyperreflexia. Which is the best next step and why?
med-pharm-systems.l19.q4.h: Rapid onset with clonus and hyperreflexia.
med-pharm-systems.l19.q4.e: This is serotonin syndrome from additive serotonergic effects, with clonus and hyperreflexia distinguishing it from NMS. Dantrolene and bromocriptine are for other syndromes.

med-pharm-systems.l19.q5.t: A washout of about five weeks because of the long-lived metabolite
med-pharm-systems.l19.q5.p: A 60-year-old man on fluoxetine for 6 months must switch to an MAOI for refractory depression. What is the most important consideration?
med-pharm-systems.l19.q5.h: Long half-life of an active metabolite.
med-pharm-systems.l19.q5.e: Fluoxetine and norfluoxetine persist, so combining with an MAOI risks serotonin syndrome and a long washout is needed. Classic MAOIs inhibit irreversibly.

med-pharm-systems.l20.q1.p: Blockade of which dopamine pathway explains antipsychotic-induced hyperprolactinemia?
med-pharm-systems.l20.q1.h: Dopamine normally inhibits prolactin from the pituitary.
med-pharm-systems.l20.q1.e: Blocking tuberoinfundibular D2 receptors removes inhibition of prolactin release. Mesolimbic blockade explains antipsychotic effect and nigrostriatal blockade explains extrapyramidal effects.

med-pharm-systems.l20.q2.t: An anticholinergic such as benztropine or diphenhydramine
med-pharm-systems.l20.q2.p: A young man given haloperidol develops sustained eye deviation and neck spasm within hours. What is the best treatment?
med-pharm-systems.l20.q2.e: Acute dystonia responds quickly to anticholinergics. VMAT2 inhibitors treat tardive dyskinesia and propranolol treats akathisia.

med-pharm-systems.l20.q3.t: Regular absolute neutrophil counts to detect agranulocytosis
med-pharm-systems.l20.q3.p: Which monitoring is required for patients receiving clozapine?
med-pharm-systems.l20.q3.h: This drug is reserved for treatment resistance because of a hematologic risk.
med-pharm-systems.l20.q3.e: Clozapine causes severe neutropenia and requires ANC monitoring. The other tests relate to lithium, phenytoin and vigabatrin or thioridazine.

med-pharm-systems.l20.q4.t: Stop the antipsychotic; cool, benzodiazepines, dantrolene if severe
med-pharm-systems.l20.q4.p: A 28-year-old man starts haloperidol and 3 days later has fever of 40 degrees, lead-pipe rigidity, confusion, labile blood pressure and a creatine kinase of 12,000 U/L. His reflexes are normal and there is no clonus. Which management is most appropriate?
med-pharm-systems.l20.q4.h: Rigidity and normal reflexes distinguish this from a serotonergic syndrome.
med-pharm-systems.l20.q4.e: This is neuroleptic malignant syndrome, treated by stopping the agent and supportive care. Cyproheptadine is for serotonin syndrome, and continuing the antipsychotic would worsen NMS.

med-pharm-systems.l20.q5.t: Reduced renal lithium clearance from the ACE inhibitor and NSAID raised serum lithium
med-pharm-systems.l20.q5.p: A 40-year-old man with bipolar disorder stable on lithium starts lisinopril and ibuprofen for hypertension and knee pain. Two weeks later he has coarse tremor, vomiting, ataxia and confusion. Which mechanism best explains this?
med-pharm-systems.l20.q5.h: Lithium is handled by the kidney like sodium.
med-pharm-systems.l20.q5.e: ACE inhibitors and NSAIDs reduce lithium clearance, raising levels and causing toxicity. Lithium is not hepatically metabolized, and the findings are not those of serotonin syndrome.

med-pharm-systems.l21.q1.t: They increase the frequency of chloride channel opening in the presence of GABA
med-pharm-systems.l21.q1.p: How do benzodiazepines enhance GABA-A receptor function?
med-pharm-systems.l21.q1.e: Benzodiazepines raise opening frequency and need GABA, which limits their effect. Barbiturates increase duration and can open the channel directly.

med-pharm-systems.l21.q2.p: Which benzodiazepines are preferred in elderly patients and in liver disease because they are cleared by direct glucuronidation?
med-pharm-systems.l21.q2.h: The mnemonic uses the first letters LOT.
med-pharm-systems.l21.q2.e: Lorazepam, oxazepam and temazepam avoid phase I oxidation and active metabolites. Diazepam and chlordiazepoxide produce long-acting active metabolites.

med-pharm-systems.l21.q3.t: It is a 5-HT1A partial agonist with minimal sedation and no dependence liability
med-pharm-systems.l21.q3.p: Which feature distinguishes buspirone from benzodiazepines?
med-pharm-systems.l21.q3.e: Buspirone is a serotonergic anxiolytic that is only minimally sedating and has no abuse potential. It does not act on GABA-A receptors.

med-pharm-systems.l21.q4.t: Additive respiratory depression, hence the boxed warning on co-prescribing
med-pharm-systems.l21.q4.p: A 62-year-old man taking an opioid for chronic pain is also prescribed alprazolam. One evening he is found with slow shallow breathing and unrousable. Which statement best explains the risk?
med-pharm-systems.l21.q4.e: Opioids and benzodiazepines additively depress respiration, hence the FDA boxed warning. Benzodiazepines do not antagonize mu receptors.

med-pharm-systems.l21.q5.t: Downregulated GABA-A and upregulated NMDA signaling; benzodiazepines restore inhibition
med-pharm-systems.l21.q5.p: A 45-year-old woman with a long history of heavy daily drinking stops abruptly and, 36 hours later, has a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. Which pharmacologic mechanism best explains alcohol withdrawal seizures and the first-line treatment?
med-pharm-systems.l21.q5.e: Chronic ethanol shifts the balance toward excitation, so withdrawal causes seizures and benzodiazepines are first-line. Flumazenil can worsen withdrawal.

med-pharm-systems.l22.q1.p: Which antiepileptic is first-line for absence seizures alone and blocks T-type calcium channels?
med-pharm-systems.l22.q1.e: Ethosuximide blocks thalamic T-type calcium channels. Carbamazepine and phenytoin are sodium channel blockers that can worsen absence seizures.

med-pharm-systems.l22.q2.p: Which HLA allele predicts carbamazepine-induced Stevens-Johnson syndrome in people of Asian ancestry?
med-pharm-systems.l22.q2.h: Screening is recommended in at-risk populations.
med-pharm-systems.l22.q2.e: HLA-B*15:02 is associated with carbamazepine SJS. HLA-B*57:01 is abacavir and HLA-B*58:01 is allopurinol.

med-pharm-systems.l22.q3.t: Hepatic metabolism becomes saturated, producing zero-order kinetics
med-pharm-systems.l22.q3.p: Why can small dose increases of phenytoin cause disproportionate rises in drug level and toxicity?
med-pharm-systems.l22.q3.e: Phenytoin metabolism saturates at therapeutic levels, so concentration rises steeply with dose. The other options do not describe its nonlinear kinetics.

med-pharm-systems.l22.q4.t: High teratogenic risk, so alternatives are considered
med-pharm-systems.l22.q4.p: A 24-year-old woman with generalized epilepsy is well controlled on valproate and plans pregnancy. Which counseling statement is best?
med-pharm-systems.l22.q4.e: Valproate is a major teratogen, so alternatives such as lamotrigine or levetiracetam are considered where possible. Enzyme inducers do not reduce risk and have their own hazards.

med-pharm-systems.l22.q5.t: Valproate inhibits lamotrigine metabolism, raising levels and the risk of severe rash
med-pharm-systems.l22.q5.p: A 32-year-old woman on lamotrigine is started on valproate for added control. Two weeks later she has fever and a spreading rash with oral mucosal erosions. What best explains this event?
med-pharm-systems.l22.q5.h: Dose adjustment is required when combining them.
med-pharm-systems.l22.q5.e: Valproate inhibits glucuronidation of lamotrigine, roughly doubling its half-life, and rapid titration raises Stevens-Johnson risk. Valproate does not induce lamotrigine metabolism.

med-pharm-systems.l23.q1.e: Dantrolene reduces calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Sugammadex and neostigmine reverse neuromuscular blockers, and flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines.

med-pharm-systems.l23.q2.p: A volatile anesthetic with a low blood:gas partition coefficient will produce which effect?
med-pharm-systems.l23.q2.e: Poorly soluble agents like desflurane and nitrous oxide equilibrate quickly, so brain levels follow alveolar levels. Solubility affects both onset and offset together.

med-pharm-systems.l23.q3.t: The acidic environment increases the ionized fraction, which reduces tissue penetration
med-pharm-systems.l23.q3.p: Which local anesthetic feature explains why infected tissue is hard to anesthetize?
med-pharm-systems.l23.q3.h: Weak bases cross membranes in the neutral form.
med-pharm-systems.l23.q3.e: Local anesthetics are weak bases, so in acidic tissue more drug is ionized and fails to penetrate. Infected tissue is acidic, not alkaline.

med-pharm-systems.l23.q4.t: A ryanodine receptor variant causing uncontrolled calcium release
med-pharm-systems.l23.q4.p: A 9-year-old boy is induced with sevoflurane and succinylcholine. Within 15 minutes he has masseter rigidity, tachycardia, a temperature of 39.5 degrees Celsius, rising end-tidal carbon dioxide and potassium of 6.2 mEq/L. Which underlying defect is most likely?
med-pharm-systems.l23.q4.h: Triggered by volatile agents plus a depolarizing blocker.
med-pharm-systems.l23.q4.e: The picture is malignant hyperthermia from RYR1 abnormality, treated with dantrolene. Cholinesterase deficiency prolongs paralysis but does not cause hyperthermia and hypercarbia.

med-pharm-systems.l23.q5.t: Ketamine, because catecholamine release supports blood pressure
med-pharm-systems.l23.q5.p: A hypotensive 50-year-old trauma patient needs emergency intubation. Which induction agent, with the cited reason, is most appropriate?
med-pharm-systems.l23.q5.e: Ketamine tends to preserve or raise blood pressure by sympathetic stimulation. Propofol lowers blood pressure, and dexmedetomidine causes hypotension and bradycardia.

med-pharm-systems.l24.q1.p: Which sign is part of the classic opioid overdose triad?
med-pharm-systems.l24.q1.e: The triad is depressed consciousness, respiratory depression and miosis. Mydriasis occurs in withdrawal or with many other toxidromes.

med-pharm-systems.l24.q2.p: Why is codeine unsafe in a child who is an ultrarapid CYP2D6 metabolizer?
med-pharm-systems.l24.q2.e: CYP2D6 converts codeine to morphine, so ultrarapid metabolizers get excessive exposure. Normeperidine is a meperidine metabolite.

med-pharm-systems.l24.q3.t: It displaces the full agonist but activates the receptor less
med-pharm-systems.l24.q3.p: A person on full-agonist opioids is given buprenorphine and develops sudden withdrawal symptoms. What is the mechanism?
med-pharm-systems.l24.q3.e: A partial agonist with high affinity displaces a full agonist and lowers net receptor stimulation. Buprenorphine does not induce metabolism.

med-pharm-systems.l24.q4.t: Naloxone wore off before the long-acting opioid; observe and repeat dosing
med-pharm-systems.l24.q4.p: A 36-year-old man is found unresponsive with a respiratory rate of 5 and pinpoint pupils. He becomes alert after intranasal naloxone, then 45 minutes later becomes drowsy with shallow breathing again. Which explanation and plan are best?
med-pharm-systems.l24.q4.e: Naloxone has a shorter duration than many opioids, so renarcotization can occur and monitoring or repeat dosing is required. The initial response confirms opioid toxicity.

med-pharm-systems.l24.q5.t: Methadone prolongs QT and CYP inhibitors raise its levels
med-pharm-systems.l24.q5.p: A 41-year-old man with opioid use disorder is on methadone and starts an antibiotic and an antifungal; an ECG shows a QTc of 520 ms. Which statement best explains the hazard?
med-pharm-systems.l24.q5.h: Think of multiple QT effects plus metabolism.
med-pharm-systems.l24.q5.e: Methadone is QT-prolonging and is cleared by CYP3A4 and other enzymes, so inhibitors raise exposure. It is a full agonist and does not shorten QT.

med-pharm-systems.l25.q1.t: Mesna, which binds the toxic metabolite acrolein
med-pharm-systems.l25.q1.p: Which agent protects the bladder from cyclophosphamide-induced hemorrhagic cystitis?
med-pharm-systems.l25.q1.h: A thiol compound given with hydration.
med-pharm-systems.l25.q1.e: Mesna conjugates acrolein in the urine. Leucovorin rescues methotrexate, dexrazoxane protects against anthracycline cardiotoxicity and amifostine is used with cisplatin.

med-pharm-systems.l25.q2.p: Which chemotherapy agent is most associated with cumulative dose-dependent cardiomyopathy?
med-pharm-systems.l25.q2.h: Anthracyclines generate free radicals in the heart.
med-pharm-systems.l25.q2.e: Anthracyclines cause cumulative cardiomyopathy. Vincristine causes neuropathy, bleomycin pulmonary fibrosis and cisplatin renal and ear toxicity.

med-pharm-systems.l25.q3.p: Which treatment prevents or treats tumor lysis syndrome by converting uric acid to allantoin?
med-pharm-systems.l25.q3.e: Rasburicase is a urate oxidase that breaks down existing uric acid, while allopurinol only prevents new formation. It is contraindicated in G6PD deficiency.

med-pharm-systems.l25.q4.t: Bleomycin causes pulmonary fibrosis and cisplatin causes ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity
med-pharm-systems.l25.q4.p: A 32-year-old man with a germ cell tumor is treated with bleomycin, etoposide and cisplatin. After three cycles he has a dry cough, exertional dyspnea and bibasilar crackles with reduced diffusing capacity; he also reports ringing in the ears. Which statement best links the drugs to the toxicities?
med-pharm-systems.l25.q4.h: Match each drug to its signature organ.
med-pharm-systems.l25.q4.e: Bleomycin has dose-related lung toxicity and little marrow suppression, and cisplatin is toxic to the cochlea and kidney. The other pairings misassign toxicities.

med-pharm-systems.l25.q5.t: Tumor lysis syndrome; hydration plus rasburicase
med-pharm-systems.l25.q5.p: A 6-year-old receiving induction chemotherapy for acute lymphoblastic leukemia has a markedly elevated white count. After the first dose, she has potassium 6.4 mEq/L, phosphate 8.1 mg/dL, calcium 6.8 mg/dL, uric acid 14 mg/dL and creatinine rising. What is the best explanation and prevention approach?
med-pharm-systems.l25.q5.h: Rapid cell death releases intracellular contents.
med-pharm-systems.l25.q5.e: The pattern of hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia and hyperuricemia is tumor lysis syndrome. Hydration and rasburicase or allopurinol are standard prevention, and mesna addresses bladder toxicity only.

med-pharm-systems.l26.q1.p: Which tyrosine kinase is inhibited by imatinib in chronic myeloid leukemia?
med-pharm-systems.l26.q1.e: Imatinib blocks the BCR-ABL fusion kinase. EGFR, BRAF and HER2 are targets of other agents.

med-pharm-systems.l26.q2.t: It is a partial agonist in the endometrium and an antagonist in breast tissue
med-pharm-systems.l26.q2.p: Why does tamoxifen increase the risk of endometrial cancer while protecting against breast cancer recurrence?
med-pharm-systems.l26.q2.e: Tamoxifen has tissue-specific effects: antagonism in breast and agonism in endometrium and bone. It does not inhibit aromatase.

med-pharm-systems.l26.q3.p: Which adverse effect is the main reason for cardiac monitoring with trastuzumab?
med-pharm-systems.l26.q3.e: Trastuzumab can cause a usually reversible decline in left ventricular function. QT effects and tyramine crises belong to other drug groups.

med-pharm-systems.l26.q4.t: Immune-mediated colitis; hold the drug and give glucocorticoids
med-pharm-systems.l26.q4.p: A 64-year-old man with metastatic melanoma on pembrolizumab develops profuse watery diarrhea, abdominal pain and weight loss; stool studies are negative for infection. Which diagnosis and treatment are best?
med-pharm-systems.l26.q4.h: Checkpoint blockade releases T cells against normal tissue.
med-pharm-systems.l26.q4.e: Colitis is a common immune-related adverse event, and treatment is holding the drug with steroids. Infection should be excluded, and mesna and rasburicase are unrelated.

med-pharm-systems.l26.q5.t: Initial rise in LH and testosterone causes a tumor flare; an antiandrogen is given first
med-pharm-systems.l26.q5.p: A 70-year-old man with prostate cancer is started on leuprolide. Two weeks later he has worsening bone pain and urinary retention from spinal metastasis. Which mechanism and prevention are best?
med-pharm-systems.l26.q5.h: Agonists first stimulate the receptor before downregulating it.
med-pharm-systems.l26.q5.e: GnRH agonists briefly increase LH and testosterone before suppression, and an antiandrogen blunts the flare. Aromatase and CYP17 inhibitors are different drug classes.

med-pharm-systems.l27.q1.p: Which antidote is used for methanol or ethylene glycol poisoning to block formation of toxic metabolites?
med-pharm-systems.l27.q1.e: Fomepizole blocks alcohol dehydrogenase. Hydroxocobalamin treats cyanide, deferoxamine treats iron and pralidoxime reactivates cholinesterase.

med-pharm-systems.l27.q2.p: A patient has a normal pulse oximetry reading but is dizzy and confused after sitting near a faulty heater; carboxyhemoglobin is elevated. What is the principal initial treatment?
med-pharm-systems.l27.q2.h: Competes for the hemoglobin binding site.
med-pharm-systems.l27.q2.e: Carbon monoxide has high affinity for hemoglobin, and high-concentration oxygen speeds dissociation. Methylene blue treats methemoglobinemia.

med-pharm-systems.l27.q3.p: Which pair correctly links an overdose to its antidote?
med-pharm-systems.l27.q3.e: Digoxin Fab fragments bind and neutralize the glycoside. Protamine reverses heparin, vitamin K reverses warfarin and deferoxamine treats iron.

med-pharm-systems.l27.q4.t: Atropine for muscarinic effects and pralidoxime to reactivate cholinesterase
med-pharm-systems.l27.q4.p: A 45-year-old farm worker arrives with drooling, wheezing, bradycardia, small pupils and muscle twitching after spraying a pesticide. Which treatment pair best addresses this condition?
med-pharm-systems.l27.q4.h: Excess acetylcholine at muscarinic and nicotinic receptors.
med-pharm-systems.l27.q4.e: Organophosphate poisoning causes cholinergic crisis, so atropine blocks muscarinic effects and pralidoxime restores the enzyme. Physostigmine and neostigmine would worsen it.

med-pharm-systems.l27.q5.t: IV sodium bicarbonate to alkalinize urine, dialysis if severe
med-pharm-systems.l27.q5.p: A 25-year-old woman presents with tinnitus, vomiting, deep rapid breathing and fever after an overdose of aspirin. Arterial blood gas shows pH 7.35, low bicarbonate and low PCO2. Which approach is best?
med-pharm-systems.l27.q5.e: Alkalinization traps salicylate and speeds excretion, and severe cases need hemodialysis. N-acetylcysteine is for acetaminophen.

med-pharm-systems.l28.q1.p: Which drug is a strong inducer of cytochrome P450 enzymes?
med-pharm-systems.l28.q1.e: Rifampin induces many CYP enzymes. The others are inhibitors.

med-pharm-systems.l28.q2.t: Induction of hepatic CYP3A4 accelerates hormone metabolism
med-pharm-systems.l28.q2.p: Which interaction explains reduced oral contraceptive efficacy in a woman taking carbamazepine?
med-pharm-systems.l28.q2.h: Think about enzyme induction over weeks.
med-pharm-systems.l28.q2.e: Carbamazepine induces CYP3A4, lowering estrogen and progestin exposure. CYP2D6 inhibition is not the mechanism.

med-pharm-systems.l28.q3.p: Which genetic deficiency predisposes to hemolysis with primaquine, dapsone and rasburicase?
med-pharm-systems.l28.q3.h: Red cells depend on NADPH to withstand oxidant stress.
med-pharm-systems.l28.q3.e: G6PD deficiency leaves red cells vulnerable to oxidant drugs. The other deficiencies affect thiopurines, fluoropyrimidines and succinylcholine.

med-pharm-systems.l28.q4.t: The INR falls because of enzyme induction, requiring higher warfarin doses
med-pharm-systems.l28.q4.p: A 58-year-old woman on stable warfarin starts rifampin for tuberculosis. Which INR trend and mechanism are expected over the next weeks?
med-pharm-systems.l28.q4.e: Rifampin induces CYP enzymes, lowering warfarin effect, and adjustment is needed on both starting and stopping. Displacement effects are transient.

med-pharm-systems.l28.q5.t: The drug causes craniofacial, cardiac and central nervous system malformations
med-pharm-systems.l28.q5.p: A 29-year-old woman with severe cystic acne is prescribed isotretinoin; her physician requires two forms of contraception and monthly pregnancy tests. What best explains this requirement?
med-pharm-systems.l28.q5.h: A retinoid with a strict risk-management program.
med-pharm-systems.l28.q5.e: Isotretinoin is a potent teratogen with craniofacial, cardiac and CNS defects. Neural tube defects relate to valproate, limb defects to thalidomide and renal injury to ACE inhibitors.

med-physiology.l01.q1.p: In a young adult man, which fluid compartment contains the largest share of total body water?
med-physiology.l01.q1.h: About two thirds of body water is inside cells.
med-physiology.l01.q1.e: Intracellular fluid is roughly two thirds of total body water. Interstitial fluid is the largest part of the ECF but still much smaller than the ICF.

med-physiology.l01.q2.t: Deuterium oxide space minus the inulin space
med-physiology.l01.q2.p: Which indicator combination allows calculation of intracellular fluid volume in a research subject?
med-physiology.l01.q2.h: ICF is not measured directly; it is a difference between two spaces.
med-physiology.l01.q2.e: ICF equals total body water (deuterium oxide) minus ECF (inulin). Inulin minus albumin gives interstitial volume, not ICF.

med-physiology.l01.q3.t: Secondary active cotransport driven by the sodium gradient
med-physiology.l01.q3.p: Which transporter mechanism best describes SGLT1 in the small intestine?
med-physiology.l01.q3.h: The pump that sets the sodium gradient is a different protein.
med-physiology.l01.q3.e: SGLT1 couples glucose uptake to sodium moving down its gradient, which the Na+/K+-ATPase maintains. It does not hydrolyze ATP itself, and facilitated diffusion (GLUT) needs no sodium.

med-physiology.l01.q4.t: ECF volume decreases, ICF volume unchanged, and plasma osmolarity unchanged
med-physiology.l01.q4.p: A 68-year-old man with a prolonged diarrheal illness has lost 3 L of fluid that is isotonic to plasma and has replaced none of it. Assuming no compensatory change yet, which pattern of volume change is expected?
med-physiology.l01.q4.h: Isotonic loss leaves osmolarity alone, so there is no osmotic driving force across cell membranes.
med-physiology.l01.q4.e: With isotonic loss, osmolarity is unchanged, so water does not shift across cell membranes; only the ECF shrinks. A rise in osmolarity with ICF loss would describe pure water loss.

med-physiology.l01.q5.t: Inhibited Na+/K+-ATPase, then raised intracellular Na+, then reduced Ca2+ extrusion by Na+/Ca2+ exchange
med-physiology.l01.q5.p: A 55-year-old woman with heart failure takes digoxin and develops increased cardiac contractility. The effect on contractility is best explained by which sequence?
med-physiology.l01.q5.h: Think of what a sodium gradient normally drives in the cardiac myocyte.
med-physiology.l01.q5.e: Digoxin inhibits the pump, intracellular sodium rises, the exchanger extrudes less calcium, and the extra calcium strengthens contraction. Pump stimulation would do the opposite.

med-physiology.l02.q1.p: The resting membrane potential of most neurons lies close to the equilibrium potential of which ion?
med-physiology.l02.q1.h: Resting membrane permeability is dominated by open leak channels for one ion.
med-physiology.l02.q1.e: Resting permeability to potassium is highest, so the membrane potential approaches E(K). Sodium has a small leak that keeps the potential somewhat less negative than E(K).

med-physiology.l02.q2.p: A cell has intracellular K+ of 150 mM and extracellular K+ of 5 mM. Using 61.5 mV times log10 of the concentration ratio, the equilibrium potential for potassium is closest to which value?
med-physiology.l02.q2.e: 61.5 times log(5/150) is about -91 mV. A value of -61 mV would result from a tenfold ratio, and a positive sign would require more K+ outside than inside.

med-physiology.l02.q3.t: Hyperpolarization toward -80 mV and reduced likelihood of reaching threshold
med-physiology.l02.q3.p: If a drug increases a neuron's membrane permeability to chloride and the chloride equilibrium potential is -80 mV with resting potential -70 mV, what is the expected effect on the cell?
med-physiology.l02.q3.h: An opened channel pulls the potential toward that ion's equilibrium potential.
med-physiology.l02.q3.e: Greater chloride conductance moves the potential toward E(Cl) of -80 mV, making threshold harder to reach. Chloride does not follow sodium toward its equilibrium.

med-physiology.l02.q4.t: E(K) becomes less negative, depolarizing the cell and inactivating sodium channels
med-physiology.l02.q4.p: A 62-year-old man with chronic kidney disease misses dialysis and presents with weakness and ECG changes including peaked T waves. His serum potassium is 7.4 mmol/L. Which statement best explains the effect of this change on myocytes?
med-physiology.l02.q4.h: Think about the ratio of inside to outside potassium and what depolarization does to Na+ channel gates.
med-physiology.l02.q4.e: Raising extracellular K+ makes E(K) less negative, depolarizing the cell; prolonged depolarization inactivates sodium channels and slows conduction. Hyperpolarization is typical of hypokalemia.

med-physiology.l02.q5.t: It falls only slightly at first, because the gradients run down slowly
med-physiology.l02.q5.p: Investigators inhibit the Na+/K+-ATPase in an isolated nerve with ouabain. In the first few minutes, what happens to the resting potential, and why?
med-physiology.l02.q5.h: The pump sets the gradients slowly; the voltage comes mostly from K+ leak.
med-physiology.l02.q5.e: Direct electrogenic contribution is a few millivolts, so the potential falls modestly at first and then declines as gradients dissipate. Collapse to zero would require the gradients to finish dissipating.

med-physiology.l03.q1.t: Na+ channel inactivation plus delayed-rectifier K+ channel opening
med-physiology.l03.q1.p: Which event is responsible for the repolarization phase of a typical neuronal action potential?
med-physiology.l03.q1.h: Two things end the upstroke, one removing sodium influx and one adding potassium efflux.
med-physiology.l03.q1.e: Na+ inactivation plus delayed K+ channel opening repolarizes the membrane. The pump is too slow to account for a millisecond event.

med-physiology.l03.q2.p: Which change would be expected to increase conduction velocity in an unmyelinated axon?
med-physiology.l03.q2.h: A wider cable has lower internal resistance.
med-physiology.l03.q2.e: Larger diameter lowers axial resistance and lengthens the length constant, increasing speed. Higher capacitance slows depolarization of the next segment.

med-physiology.l03.q3.t: SNARE proteins needed for acetylcholine vesicle fusion
med-physiology.l03.q3.p: Which molecule is the direct target of botulinum toxin at the neuromuscular junction?
med-physiology.l03.q3.h: The toxin acts before any ACh reaches the cleft.
med-physiology.l03.q3.e: Botulinum toxin cleaves SNARE proteins and blocks release. Receptor blockade describes curare, and esterase effects describe cholinesterase inhibitors.

med-physiology.l03.q4.t: Antibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels
med-physiology.l03.q4.p: A 58-year-old man who smokes has proximal leg weakness, dry mouth and absent reflexes. Strength improves briefly after repeated voluntary contraction. Which pathology is most likely?
med-physiology.l03.q4.h: Improvement with repetitive use points to accumulating presynaptic calcium.
med-physiology.l03.q4.e: The picture is Lambert-Eaton syndrome, in which antibodies reduce presynaptic calcium entry; calcium builds with repeated firing. Myasthenia gravis worsens with use and typically spares reflexes and autonomic function.

med-physiology.l03.q5.t: Fewer functional postsynaptic nicotinic receptors, lowering end-plate potentials
med-physiology.l03.q5.p: A 27-year-old woman has ptosis and diplopia that worsen late in the day, with improvement after an edrophonium test. Which change at the junction explains her weakness?
med-physiology.l03.q5.h: Edrophonium prolongs acetylcholine action, which helps if receptors, not release, are limiting.
med-physiology.l03.q5.e: Myasthenia gravis reduces functional receptors, so some end-plate potentials fail to reach threshold; esterase inhibition improves it. Presynaptic calcium failure would describe Lambert-Eaton.

med-physiology.l04.q1.p: Which protein binds calcium to initiate contraction in skeletal muscle?
med-physiology.l04.q1.h: The thin filament carries the calcium sensor.
med-physiology.l04.q1.e: Troponin C binds calcium and moves tropomyosin off actin. Calmodulin and MLCK serve that role in smooth muscle.

med-physiology.l04.q2.t: Cardiac muscle depends on calcium entry that triggers calcium-induced release, while skeletal muscle does not
med-physiology.l04.q2.p: Which statement correctly compares cardiac and skeletal muscle excitation-contraction coupling?
med-physiology.l04.q2.h: Only one of these muscles needs outside calcium to contract.
med-physiology.l04.q2.e: Cardiac RyR2 is triggered by calcium entering through L-type channels. In skeletal muscle RyR1 is mechanically coupled to the voltage sensor and does not require extracellular calcium.

med-physiology.l04.q3.t: The refractory period lasts as long as the twitch, preventing summation
med-physiology.l04.q3.p: Why does the cardiac action potential plateau make tetanus impossible?
med-physiology.l04.q3.h: Consider how long the cell is unexcitable.
med-physiology.l04.q3.e: The long plateau keeps sodium channels inactivated until contraction is mostly over. Cardiac muscle has troponin, unlike smooth muscle.

med-physiology.l04.q4.t: Blockade of the sarcoplasmic reticulum ryanodine receptor
med-physiology.l04.q4.p: A 24-year-old man develops rigidity, temperature of 40.5 C, tachycardia and dark urine within minutes of receiving succinylcholine and a volatile anesthetic. Which drug target explains the specific treatment?
med-physiology.l04.q4.h: The abnormal calcium release is inside the muscle fibre.
med-physiology.l04.q4.e: The picture is malignant hyperthermia from uncontrolled RyR1 calcium release, treated with dantrolene, which blocks the channel. Esterase inhibition would worsen cholinergic stimulation.

med-physiology.l04.q5.t: Raised cAMP inhibits myosin light-chain kinase, reducing myosin phosphorylation
med-physiology.l04.q5.p: A 40-year-old woman with asthma is given inhaled albuterol and her airway smooth muscle relaxes. Which mechanism best explains the effect?
med-physiology.l04.q5.e: Beta-2 stimulation raises cAMP, which reduces MLCK activity and so myosin phosphorylation. Smooth muscle has no troponin or T tubule system as in skeletal muscle.

med-physiology.l05.q1.t: Inward calcium current through L-type channels
med-physiology.l05.q1.p: Which ionic current mainly produces the upstroke (phase 0) of the sinoatrial node action potential?
med-physiology.l05.q1.h: Nodal cells differ from ventricular cells in what drives phase 0.
med-physiology.l05.q1.e: SA node phase 0 depends on L-type calcium channels. Fast sodium channels drive the ventricular upstroke, and the funny current is a nonselective cation current active in phase 4.

med-physiology.l05.q2.t: Small, calcium-dependent nodal cells conduct slowly, giving filling time
med-physiology.l05.q2.p: Why is conduction through the AV node deliberately slow?
med-physiology.l05.q2.h: Slow conduction gives ventricles time to fill.
med-physiology.l05.q2.e: AV nodal cells are small and depend on slow calcium channels, producing the delay that lets the ventricles fill. Cardiac tissue is not myelinated, and fibre size is small, not large.

med-physiology.l05.q3.t: Adenosine activation of A1 receptors that open potassium channels in nodal tissue
med-physiology.l05.q3.p: A 34-year-old woman has a regular supraventricular tachycardia at 190 beats per minute. A drug given by rapid injection briefly slows AV node conduction and terminates the rhythm. What is its mechanism?
med-physiology.l05.q3.h: The drug acts for seconds and hyperpolarizes nodal cells.
med-physiology.l05.q3.e: Adenosine opens potassium channels through A1 receptors, hyperpolarizing the AV node and interrupting re-entry. Beta stimulation would speed conduction, and sodium channel block would not target the node.

med-physiology.l05.q4.t: Progressive fatigue of AV nodal conduction, with a block at the node
med-physiology.l05.q4.p: A 71-year-old man has a rhythm strip on which the PR interval lengthens with each successive beat until a P wave is not followed by a QRS, after which the pattern restarts. The most likely site and mechanism of the delay is which of the following?
med-physiology.l05.q4.h: Progressive lengthening before a dropped beat is a recognizable pattern.
med-physiology.l05.q4.e: This describes Mobitz type I (Wenckebach) block, a decremental conduction failure at the AV node. Type II has constant PR intervals, and third-degree block shows independent atrial and ventricular rates.

med-physiology.l05.q5.t: The intrinsic SA node rate lies near 100, normally held lower by vagal tone that is now absent
med-physiology.l05.q5.p: A heart transplant recipient, with the donor heart denervated, has a resting rate near 100 beats per minute. Which explanation is most accurate?
med-physiology.l05.q5.h: Consider what the vagus does to a resting heart.
med-physiology.l05.q5.e: At rest the vagus holds the SA node below its intrinsic rate, so a denervated heart beats faster. The AV node has a slower intrinsic rate and would not be faster than the SA node.

med-physiology.l06.q1.t: Closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves at the start of systole
med-physiology.l06.q1.p: Which event produces the first heart sound (S1)?
med-physiology.l06.q1.h: The first sound is the start of systole.
med-physiology.l06.q1.e: S1 is produced by AV valve closure when ventricular pressure exceeds atrial pressure. S2 is semilunar closure.

med-physiology.l06.q2.p: A patient has an end-diastolic volume of 150 mL and an end-systolic volume of 60 mL. What is the ejection fraction?
med-physiology.l06.q2.h: Stroke volume divided by end-diastolic volume.
med-physiology.l06.q2.e: SV is 90 mL and EF is 90/150, or 60 percent. 90 percent confuses the stroke volume in mL with the percentage.

med-physiology.l06.q3.p: During which phase of the cardiac cycle is ventricular volume constant while ventricular pressure is rising?
med-physiology.l06.q3.h: All valves are closed while pressure builds.
med-physiology.l06.q3.e: During isovolumetric contraction both valves are closed and volume is fixed. In isovolumetric relaxation volume is also constant but pressure falls.

med-physiology.l06.q4.t: A taller loop with a markedly higher peak ventricular pressure than aortic pressure
med-physiology.l06.q4.p: A 72-year-old man has syncope on exertion and a harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border. Compared with normal, which finding would a left ventricular pressure-volume loop show?
med-physiology.l06.q4.h: The valve is the obstruction ahead of the ventricle.
med-physiology.l06.q4.e: Aortic stenosis forces the ventricle to generate pressure far above aortic pressure, so the loop is taller. Mitral regurgitation, not stenosis, abolishes true isovolumetric phases.

med-physiology.l06.q5.t: No true isovolumetric contraction, since the ventricle empties backward into the atrium
med-physiology.l06.q5.p: A 45-year-old woman has a holosystolic apical murmur radiating to the axilla. Which feature of her pressure-volume loop best reflects the underlying lesion?
med-physiology.l06.q5.h: The low-pressure atrium is an escape route from the first moment of contraction.
med-physiology.l06.q5.e: Mitral regurgitation lets the ventricle eject into the atrium as soon as pressure rises, so isovolumetric phases are lost. Mitral stenosis would reduce filling, a different lesion.

med-physiology.l07.q1.p: Which term describes the force the ventricle generates at a given preload and afterload?
med-physiology.l07.q1.e: Contractility is the intrinsic force generation independent of loading. Compliance describes volume change per unit pressure.

med-physiology.l07.q2.p: A patient has oxygen consumption of 300 mL/min, arterial oxygen content of 190 mL per litre and mixed venous oxygen content of 150 mL per litre. What is the cardiac output by the Fick principle?
med-physiology.l07.q2.h: Divide consumption by the arteriovenous difference.
med-physiology.l07.q2.e: CO is 300 divided by 40, or 7.5 L/min. Using the wrong difference (50 mL/L) would give 6 L/min.

med-physiology.l07.q3.t: Stroke volume falls and end-systolic volume rises
med-physiology.l07.q3.p: On a pressure-volume loop, which change accompanies an increase in afterload with unchanged contractility and preload?
med-physiology.l07.q3.h: A harder ejection leaves more blood behind.
med-physiology.l07.q3.e: Greater afterload reduces ejection and leaves more blood in the ventricle. The ESPVR slope reflects contractility and does not change with afterload.

med-physiology.l07.q4.t: A flatter end-systolic pressure-volume line and a larger end-systolic volume
med-physiology.l07.q4.p: A 63-year-old man with a prior myocardial infarction has dyspnea. Echocardiography shows a dilated left ventricle and an ejection fraction of 30 percent. Which finding on a pressure-volume loop best matches his condition?
med-physiology.l07.q4.h: Reduced contractility lowers the end-systolic slope.
med-physiology.l07.q4.e: Systolic failure reduces contractility, flattening the ESPVR and leaving a larger ESV with a rightward-shifted loop. A steeper line would indicate increased contractility.

med-physiology.l07.q5.t: The venous return curve shifts left because mean systemic filling pressure falls
med-physiology.l07.q5.p: During hemorrhage with a 20 percent loss of blood volume, which change on Guyton curves best explains the initial fall in cardiac output?
med-physiology.l07.q5.h: Think about the x intercept of the venous return curve.
med-physiology.l07.q5.e: Blood loss lowers mean systemic filling pressure, shifting the venous return curve left and lowering output. The cardiac curve is initially unchanged.

med-physiology.l08.q1.p: If a vessel radius is halved and all else remains constant, resistance to flow changes by what factor?
med-physiology.l08.q1.h: Resistance depends on radius to the fourth power.
med-physiology.l08.q1.e: Poiseuille's law makes resistance inversely proportional to r^4, so halving the radius multiplies resistance by 16.

med-physiology.l08.q2.p: A blood pressure is 126/76 mmHg. What is the approximate mean arterial pressure?
med-physiology.l08.q2.h: Add one third of the pulse pressure to the diastolic pressure.
med-physiology.l08.q2.e: Pulse pressure is 50, one third is about 17, so MAP is about 93. The value 101 is the simple average of the two pressures, which overestimates MAP.

med-physiology.l08.q3.p: At the arteriolar end of a capillary, capillary hydrostatic pressure is 32 mmHg, interstitial hydrostatic pressure 2 mmHg, capillary oncotic pressure 24 mmHg and interstitial oncotic pressure 4 mmHg. Assuming a reflection coefficient of 1, what is the net filtration pressure?
med-physiology.l08.q3.h: Subtract the net oncotic pull from the net hydrostatic push.
med-physiology.l08.q3.e: Net hydrostatic push is 32 - 2 = 30, net oncotic pull is 24 - 4 = 20, so net is +10 outward. +14 results from ignoring interstitial pressures.

med-physiology.l08.q4.t: Decreased capillary oncotic pressure favouring net filtration
med-physiology.l08.q4.p: A 52-year-old man with cirrhosis has bilateral leg swelling and ascites. Serum albumin is low. Which change in Starling forces best explains the swelling?
med-physiology.l08.q4.h: Albumin is the main source of plasma oncotic pressure.
med-physiology.l08.q4.e: Low albumin lowers capillary oncotic pressure and so favours filtration, causing edema. Venous obstruction would raise hydrostatic pressure, but it is not the main problem here.

med-physiology.l08.q5.t: Laplace's law, in which wall tension rises as radius increases at a given pressure
med-physiology.l08.q5.p: A 65-year-old man has an abdominal aortic aneurysm whose diameter has doubled over several years. Which principle best explains why the larger aneurysm is at higher risk of rupture?
med-physiology.l08.q5.h: Think about tension in a thin-walled cylinder.
med-physiology.l08.q5.e: By Laplace's law, wall tension is pressure times radius, so enlargement raises tension and further stretching. Poiseuille's law describes resistance, not wall stress.

med-physiology.l09.q1.p: Which nerve carries baroreceptor information from the carotid sinus to the brainstem?
med-physiology.l09.q1.h: The aortic arch uses the vagus; the carotid sinus uses another cranial nerve.
med-physiology.l09.q1.e: The carotid sinus afferent travels in the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX). The aortic arch afferent uses the vagus.

med-physiology.l09.q2.t: Reduced baroreceptor firing, increased sympathetic outflow and reduced vagal tone
med-physiology.l09.q2.p: A 30-year-old man stands up abruptly. Which reflex response restores blood pressure within seconds?
med-physiology.l09.q2.h: Standing lowers the pressure the carotid sinus sees.
med-physiology.l09.q2.e: Standing reduces pressure at the baroreceptors, so firing falls, sympathetic tone rises and vagal tone falls. Hormonal changes act over longer times.

med-physiology.l09.q3.p: Which tissue most strongly shows vasoconstriction in response to local hypoxia?
med-physiology.l09.q3.h: The lung diverts blood from poorly ventilated alveoli.
med-physiology.l09.q3.e: Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction matches perfusion to ventilation. In other beds hypoxia causes vasodilation.

med-physiology.l09.q4.t: ACE inhibition, lowering angiotensin II and increasing bradykinin
med-physiology.l09.q4.p: A 58-year-old man with hypertension starts a new medication and develops a persistent dry cough. Which mechanism most directly accounts for the cough and the drug's antihypertensive effect?
med-physiology.l09.q4.h: The cough comes from a peptide that the enzyme normally degrades.
med-physiology.l09.q4.e: ACE inhibitors lower angiotensin II and raise bradykinin, which causes cough. ARBs block the AT1 receptor and do not raise bradykinin.

med-physiology.l09.q5.t: Low renal perfusion, then increased renin, then more angiotensin II and aldosterone
med-physiology.l09.q5.p: A 66-year-old woman with a narrowed right renal artery has hypertension. Which sequence best explains the hypertension?
med-physiology.l09.q5.h: The kidney senses reduced pressure as a sign of low volume.
med-physiology.l09.q5.e: Reduced renal perfusion triggers renin release and so angiotensin II and aldosterone, raising systemic pressure. ANP is released by atrial stretch, not by renal ischemia.

med-physiology.l10.q1.p: Which lung capacity equals expiratory reserve volume plus residual volume?
med-physiology.l10.q1.h: It is the volume left at the end of a quiet exhalation.
med-physiology.l10.q1.e: FRC is ERV plus RV. Vital capacity excludes residual volume, and total lung capacity includes the inspiratory volumes.

med-physiology.l10.q2.p: A patient breathes with a tidal volume of 400 mL at 20 breaths per minute, with an anatomic dead space of 150 mL. What is the alveolar ventilation?
med-physiology.l10.q2.h: Subtract dead space from each breath before multiplying.
med-physiology.l10.q2.e: Alveolar ventilation is (400 - 150) x 20 = 5 L/min. Minute ventilation, 8 L/min, ignores dead space.

med-physiology.l10.q3.t: Increased compliance, raised FRC and a reduced FEV1/FVC ratio
med-physiology.l10.q3.p: Which change is expected in a patient with emphysema compared with a healthy adult?
med-physiology.l10.q3.h: Loss of elastic tissue changes how far the lung recoils.
med-physiology.l10.q3.e: Emphysema destroys elastic tissue, so compliance rises, FRC and RV rise, and airflow is obstructed. A normal ratio with low TLC fits restriction.

med-physiology.l10.q4.t: Deficient surfactant, raising surface tension and promoting alveolar collapse
med-physiology.l10.q4.p: A premature infant born at 29 weeks develops tachypnea, grunting and hypoxemia within hours of birth. A chest radiograph shows diffuse ground-glass opacities. Which mechanism best explains the lung findings?
med-physiology.l10.q4.h: Think about type II pneumocyte maturity and the Law of Laplace.
med-physiology.l10.q4.e: Premature type II cells make too little surfactant, so surface tension is high and alveoli collapse. Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency causes emphysema in adults, not neonatal collapse.

med-physiology.l10.q5.p: A 60-year-old man with progressive dyspnea has an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.85, a reduced FVC and a reduced total lung capacity. His lung compliance is low. Which condition best fits these findings?
med-physiology.l10.q5.h: Both capacities fall in proportion, and the lung is stiff.
med-physiology.l10.q5.e: A normal or high ratio with reduced TLC and low compliance indicates restrictive disease such as pulmonary fibrosis. Obstructive disorders reduce the ratio.

med-physiology.l11.q1.p: Which factor shifts the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve to the right?
med-physiology.l11.q1.h: A right shift lowers hemoglobin affinity for oxygen.
med-physiology.l11.q1.e: Raised 2,3-BPG, CO2, H+ and temperature all shift the curve right. The other three shift it left.

med-physiology.l11.q2.p: A subject at sea level breathes room air with PaCO2 of 48 mmHg. Using a respiratory quotient of 0.8 and water vapour pressure of 47 mmHg, what is the approximate PAO2?
med-physiology.l11.q2.h: Compute 0.21 x 713, then subtract PaCO2 divided by 0.8.
med-physiology.l11.q2.e: PAO2 = 150 - 48/0.8 = 150 - 60 = 90 mmHg. A value of 100 would correspond to a PaCO2 of 40.

med-physiology.l11.q3.p: A man breathing 100 percent oxygen has a persistently low arterial PO2. Which cause of hypoxemia is most strongly suggested?
med-physiology.l11.q3.h: One cause is not corrected by raising inspired oxygen.
med-physiology.l11.q3.e: Shunted blood bypasses ventilated alveoli, so extra oxygen barely helps. Hypoventilation, altitude and mild mismatch respond.

med-physiology.l11.q4.t: Oxygen content is reduced and the dissociation curve is shifted to the left
med-physiology.l11.q4.p: A 35-year-old woman found in a closed garage with a running car engine has headache and confusion. Pulse oximetry shows 98 percent and arterial PO2 is normal. Which statement best describes her blood?
med-physiology.l11.q4.h: Normal PO2 and a normal-looking oximeter do not guarantee normal content.
med-physiology.l11.q4.e: Carbon monoxide occupies binding sites, lowering content, and increases affinity of remaining sites, shifting the curve left. Standard oximetry reads carboxyhemoglobin as oxygenated.

med-physiology.l11.q5.t: Reduced diffusion capacity leaves too little time for equilibration when transit time shortens
med-physiology.l11.q5.p: A 58-year-old man with pulmonary fibrosis has normal resting oxygen saturation but becomes hypoxemic during exercise. His DLCO is reduced. Which explanation is best?
med-physiology.l11.q5.h: At rest, oxygen has a reserve of capillary transit time.
med-physiology.l11.q5.e: Thickened membranes slow equilibration; at rest there is spare time, but exercise shortens transit time and unmasks diffusion limitation. Anemia would not lower DLCO relative to normal membranes.

med-physiology.l12.q1.p: Which region of the upright lung has the highest ventilation-perfusion ratio?
med-physiology.l12.q1.h: Perfusion rises more steeply than ventilation toward the bottom.
med-physiology.l12.q1.e: Perfusion falls off more than ventilation toward the apex, so V/Q is highest there and lowest at the base.

med-physiology.l12.q2.p: A pulmonary vascular resistance calculation uses a mean pulmonary artery pressure of 25 mmHg, a wedge pressure of 10 mmHg and a cardiac output of 5 L/min. What is the resistance?
med-physiology.l12.q2.h: Divide the transpulmonary gradient by the flow.
med-physiology.l12.q2.e: Resistance is (25 - 10) / 5 = 3 Wood units. Dividing by the wedge pressure alone would give a wrong answer.

med-physiology.l12.q3.t: Pulmonary embolism that blocks perfusion to ventilated alveoli
med-physiology.l12.q3.p: Which condition increases alveolar dead space?
med-physiology.l12.q3.h: Dead space means ventilation without perfusion.
med-physiology.l12.q3.e: An embolus removes perfusion from ventilated alveoli, increasing dead space. Consolidation and collapse reduce ventilation, behaving like shunt.

med-physiology.l12.q4.t: Ventilated alveoli that receive no blood flow add CO2-free gas to the exhaled sample
med-physiology.l12.q4.p: A 48-year-old woman has sudden pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea after a long flight. Her oxygen saturation is 90 percent, and her end-tidal CO2 is lower than her arterial CO2 by a wide margin. Which mechanism best explains the low end-tidal CO2?
med-physiology.l12.q4.h: Think about what an unperfused alveolus contributes to exhaled gas.
med-physiology.l12.q4.e: Embolic obstruction makes dead-space alveoli whose gas contains no CO2, diluting the expired sample. The reverse describes shunt, which does not add dead-space gas.

med-physiology.l12.q5.t: Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction diverting blood to better-ventilated regions
med-physiology.l12.q5.p: A 24-year-old man develops a localized pneumonia in the right lower lobe with alveoli filled with exudate. His oxygen saturation drops, and does not rise much with 100 percent oxygen. Which compensatory mechanism limits the severity of hypoxemia in the affected lobe?
med-physiology.l12.q5.h: The pulmonary vessels respond to alveolar oxygen, unlike systemic vessels.
med-physiology.l12.q5.e: Alveolar hypoxia constricts local arterioles, diverting blood from the consolidated lobe. Vasodilation would increase shunt and worsen hypoxemia.

med-physiology.l13.q1.t: Peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies
med-physiology.l13.q1.p: Which receptors are the only ones that respond to a fall in arterial PO2?
med-physiology.l13.q1.h: Central receptors sense hydrogen ion in cerebrospinal fluid.
med-physiology.l13.q1.e: Only peripheral chemoreceptors detect low arterial PO2; central chemoreceptors respond to CSF H+ derived from CO2.

med-physiology.l13.q2.p: A patient has arterial pH 7.25, PCO2 28 mmHg and bicarbonate 12 mmol/L, with sodium 140 and chloride 100 mmol/L. What is the anion gap?
med-physiology.l13.q2.h: Subtract chloride and bicarbonate from sodium.
med-physiology.l13.q2.e: 140 - 100 - 12 = 28 mmol/L, markedly raised. A value of 12 would be bicarbonate alone.

med-physiology.l13.q3.p: A patient has pH 7.55, PCO2 30 mmHg and bicarbonate 25 mmol/L shortly after a panic attack. Which disorder is present?
med-physiology.l13.q3.h: The primary change is in PCO2, in the direction that raises pH.
med-physiology.l13.q3.e: Low PCO2 with raised pH and near-normal bicarbonate indicates acute respiratory alkalosis. In metabolic alkalosis, bicarbonate would be raised.

med-physiology.l13.q4.t: Appropriate respiratory compensation for a metabolic acidosis
med-physiology.l13.q4.p: A 24-year-old man with type 1 diabetes has vomiting and abdominal pain. Arterial pH is 7.20 and bicarbonate 8 mmol/L with deep rapid breathing; PCO2 is 21 mmHg. Using Winter's formula, which interpretation is correct?
med-physiology.l13.q4.h: Compute 1.5 x bicarbonate + 8 and compare with the measured value.
med-physiology.l13.q4.e: Expected PCO2 is 1.5 x 8 + 8 = 20 (18 to 22), so 21 is appropriate compensation. Values above the range would suggest a coexisting respiratory acidosis.

med-physiology.l13.q5.t: Reversal of the Haldane effect and worsened ventilation-perfusion matching
med-physiology.l13.q5.p: A 68-year-old woman with long-standing COPD has chronic hypercapnia. After receiving high-flow oxygen in an emergency room she becomes drowsy and her PCO2 rises. Which mechanism most likely contributes?
med-physiology.l13.q5.h: More than one process explains why oxygen can raise PCO2 in these patients.
med-physiology.l13.q5.e: Excess oxygen can release hypoxic vasoconstriction, worsening V/Q matching, and oxygenated hemoglobin binds less CO2 (Haldane), raising PaCO2; reduced hypoxic drive also contributes. Oxygen does not stimulate central receptors.

med-physiology.l14.q1.p: Which substance, freely filtered and neither reabsorbed nor secreted, has a clearance equal to the glomerular filtration rate?
med-physiology.l14.q1.h: It is an inert polysaccharide that is not handled by tubules.
med-physiology.l14.q1.e: Inulin is freely filtered and neither reabsorbed nor secreted, so its clearance equals GFR. PAH is secreted and estimates plasma flow.

med-physiology.l14.q2.p: A patient has urine creatinine 60 mg/dL, urine flow 2 mL/min and plasma creatinine 1.0 mg/dL. What is the creatinine clearance?
med-physiology.l14.q2.h: Clearance equals U x V divided by P.
med-physiology.l14.q2.e: Clearance = 60 x 2 / 1 = 120 mL/min. Omitting the urine flow would give 60.

med-physiology.l14.q3.p: Which change would be expected to increase filtration fraction?
med-physiology.l14.q3.h: Filtration fraction is GFR divided by plasma flow.
med-physiology.l14.q3.e: Efferent constriction raises glomerular pressure, increasing GFR while lowering plasma flow, so the fraction rises. Afferent constriction lowers both.

med-physiology.l14.q4.t: Loss of prostaglandin afferent dilation and angiotensin II efferent constriction
med-physiology.l14.q4.p: A 72-year-old woman with heart failure takes an ACE inhibitor and a loop diuretic and starts an NSAID for knee pain. Within days her creatinine doubles. Which mechanism most directly explains the fall in GFR?
med-physiology.l14.q4.h: Each drug removes a mechanism that kept glomerular pressure up.
med-physiology.l14.q4.e: NSAIDs reduce afferent dilating prostaglandins and ACE inhibitors reduce efferent constriction, so glomerular pressure falls in a volume-depleted patient. Tubuloglomerular feedback is not the main target.

med-physiology.l14.q5.t: Increased hydrostatic pressure in Bowman space opposing filtration
med-physiology.l14.q5.p: A 30-year-old man has a kidney stone obstructing the ureter. Which change in glomerular Starling forces on the affected side explains the fall in GFR?
med-physiology.l14.q5.h: Back pressure acts on the urinary side of the filter.
med-physiology.l14.q5.e: Obstruction raises Bowman space hydrostatic pressure, opposing filtration. Bowman space oncotic pressure is essentially zero, so it is not the answer.

med-physiology.l15.q1.p: Which nephron segment reabsorbs most of the filtered sodium and water?
med-physiology.l15.q1.h: About two thirds of the filtrate is reclaimed here, isosmotically.
med-physiology.l15.q1.e: The proximal tubule reabsorbs roughly two thirds of filtered sodium and water. The thick ascending limb takes about a quarter.

med-physiology.l15.q2.t: Na+-K+-2Cl- cotransporter in the thick ascending limb
med-physiology.l15.q2.p: Which transporter is the target of furosemide?
med-physiology.l15.q2.h: The loop diuretic acts in the loop.
med-physiology.l15.q2.e: Furosemide inhibits NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb. NCC is the thiazide target and ENaC is blocked by amiloride.

med-physiology.l15.q3.t: Decrease, because distal tubular calcium reabsorption is enhanced
med-physiology.l15.q3.p: A 45-year-old man with recurrent calcium kidney stones is given a thiazide diuretic. What is the expected change in urinary calcium and why?
med-physiology.l15.q3.h: Thiazides have the opposite calcium effect of loop diuretics.
med-physiology.l15.q3.e: Blocking NCC lowers cell sodium, favouring calcium reabsorption through the basolateral Na+/Ca2+ exchanger and so reducing urinary calcium. Loop diuretics have the opposite effect.

med-physiology.l15.q4.t: Inhibition of SGLT2 in the early proximal tubule
med-physiology.l15.q4.p: A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes starts a new agent and develops glucose in the urine with a plasma glucose of 120 mg/dL and a genital yeast infection. Which target best explains the drug effect?
med-physiology.l15.q4.h: Glucose in the urine at a low plasma level means reabsorption was blocked.
med-physiology.l15.q4.e: SGLT2 inhibitors block most proximal glucose reabsorption, causing glucosuria at normal plasma glucose and predisposing to genitourinary infection. NKCC2 inhibition would not cause glucosuria.

med-physiology.l15.q5.t: Increased distal flow and aldosterone enhancing potassium and hydrogen secretion
med-physiology.l15.q5.p: A 66-year-old woman with heart failure takes a loop diuretic and has a serum potassium of 3.0 mmol/L with a bicarbonate of 32 mmol/L. Which mechanism best accounts for these findings?
med-physiology.l15.q5.h: More fluid reaches a segment that exchanges sodium for potassium and hydrogen.
med-physiology.l15.q5.e: Loop diuretics raise distal flow and activate aldosterone through volume contraction, promoting K+ and H+ secretion, hence hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis. Reduced delivery would cause the opposite.

med-physiology.l16.q1.p: Which receptor and second messenger mediate the effect of ADH on the collecting duct?
med-physiology.l16.q1.h: The aquaporin insertion pathway uses a Gs-coupled receptor.
med-physiology.l16.q1.e: V2 receptors raise cAMP and insert aquaporin 2. V1 receptors act on vascular smooth muscle through IP3.

med-physiology.l16.q2.p: A patient has urine osmolality 450 mOsm/kg, plasma osmolality 300 mOsm/kg and urine flow 2 mL/min. What is the free water clearance?
med-physiology.l16.q2.h: Compute osmolar clearance first, then subtract it from the urine flow.
med-physiology.l16.q2.e: Osmolar clearance is 450 x 2 / 300 = 3 mL/min, so free water clearance is 2 - 3 = -1 mL/min. A positive sign would mean dilute urine.

med-physiology.l16.q3.p: Which structure maintains the corticomedullary osmotic gradient by acting as a countercurrent exchanger?
med-physiology.l16.q3.h: It is the capillary system that parallels the loop.
med-physiology.l16.q3.e: The vasa recta remove water and solute without washing out the medullary gradient. The thick ascending limb generates the gradient.

med-physiology.l16.q4.p: A 38-year-old woman treated with lithium has polyuria and thirst. After water deprivation her urine osmolality stays at 160 mOsm/kg, and it does not change after desmopressin. Which diagnosis best fits?
med-physiology.l16.q4.h: Failure to respond to exogenous ADH points to the kidney.
med-physiology.l16.q4.e: Lack of a response to desmopressin indicates collecting duct resistance, as with lithium. Central DI would concentrate urine after desmopressin.

med-physiology.l16.q5.t: Water retention from nonosmotic ADH release, with sodium excreted normally
med-physiology.l16.q5.p: A 64-year-old man who smokes has a serum sodium of 123 mmol/L, appears euvolemic, and has urine osmolality of 420 mOsm/kg and urine sodium of 52 mmol/L. Which mechanism best explains his hyponatremia?
med-physiology.l16.q5.h: Concentrated urine in a hyponatremic patient means the kidney is retaining water.
med-physiology.l16.q5.e: This is SIADH, as can occur with small-cell lung cancer. Water is retained under ADH, and sodium excretion follows intake. Primary polydipsia would give dilute urine.

med-physiology.l17.q1.p: Which hormone, released from stretched atria, promotes sodium excretion?
med-physiology.l17.q1.e: ANP promotes natriuresis by dilating the afferent arteriole and inhibiting collecting-duct sodium reabsorption. Aldosterone retains sodium.

med-physiology.l17.q2.p: Which of the following would shift potassium from the extracellular fluid into cells?
med-physiology.l17.q2.h: One of these drives the Na+/K+-ATPase.
med-physiology.l17.q2.e: Insulin stimulates the Na+/K+-ATPase and uptake of potassium. Mineral acid acidosis, cell breakdown and digoxin toxicity raise extracellular potassium.

med-physiology.l17.q3.t: It increases distal calcium reabsorption and decreases proximal phosphate reabsorption
med-physiology.l17.q3.p: Which statement correctly describes the action of parathyroid hormone on the nephron?
med-physiology.l17.q3.h: PTH raises serum calcium and lowers serum phosphate.
med-physiology.l17.q3.e: PTH increases calcium reabsorption in the distal tubule and decreases proximal phosphate reabsorption (phosphaturia). The reverse pattern would lower calcium.

med-physiology.l17.q4.t: Escape through pressure natriuresis and natriuretic peptides
med-physiology.l17.q4.p: A 44-year-old woman has hypertension, serum potassium of 2.9 mmol/L, bicarbonate 31 mmol/L and no edema. Plasma renin activity is low and aldosterone is high. Which mechanism best explains the lack of edema?
med-physiology.l17.q4.h: Sustained retention is limited by the kidney's own response to volume.
med-physiology.l17.q4.e: Volume expansion raises pressure, which promotes natriuresis, with ANP contributing, so sodium balance returns after a modest gain. Aldosterone does not cause sodium loss.

med-physiology.l17.q5.p: A 29-year-old man with a crush injury has potassium of 7.0 mmol/L and ECG changes. Which intervention protects the heart without lowering serum potassium?
med-physiology.l17.q5.h: This works by counteracting membrane depolarization, not by moving potassium.
med-physiology.l17.q5.e: Calcium raises the threshold potential, restoring the gap to the resting potential, without changing potassium. Insulin and albuterol shift potassium into cells, and loop diuretics remove it.

med-physiology.l18.q1.p: Which enzyme on the proximal tubule brush border converts luminal carbonic acid to carbon dioxide and water?
med-physiology.l18.q1.e: Luminal carbonic anhydrase converts H2CO3 to CO2 and water, allowing bicarbonate reclamation. Acetazolamide inhibits it.

med-physiology.l18.q2.p: A patient has urine sodium 30, potassium 20 and chloride 90 mmol/L. What is the urine anion gap and what does it suggest?
med-physiology.l18.q2.h: Compute Na + K - Cl, then recall what ammonium pairs with.
med-physiology.l18.q2.e: The gap is 30 + 20 - 90 = -40, a negative gap reflecting ammonium excreted with chloride, as in diarrheal acidosis.

med-physiology.l18.q3.p: Which renal tubular acidosis is associated with hyperkalemia?
med-physiology.l18.q3.h: Low aldosterone prevents potassium and hydrogen secretion.
med-physiology.l18.q3.e: Type 4 RTA results from aldosterone deficiency or resistance, giving hyperkalemia. Types 1 and 2 typically show hypokalemia.

med-physiology.l18.q4.t: Failure of hydrogen secretion by distal intercalated cells
med-physiology.l18.q4.p: A 33-year-old woman has recurrent kidney stones, a serum bicarbonate of 16 mmol/L, a normal anion gap and a serum potassium of 3.1 mmol/L. Her urine pH is 6.4. Which defect is most likely?
med-physiology.l18.q4.h: A urine that cannot be acidified despite systemic acidosis suggests the final acidification step is impaired.
med-physiology.l18.q4.e: Type 1 RTA features inability to acidify urine below about 5.5, hypokalemia and stones. Proximal RTA acidifies urine once the filtered bicarbonate load is reduced.

med-physiology.l18.q5.t: Volume depletion and hypochloremia promote bicarbonate reabsorption
med-physiology.l18.q5.p: A 25-year-old man with several days of vomiting has a bicarbonate of 36 mmol/L, a potassium of 2.9 mmol/L, and a urine chloride below 10 mmol/L. Which statement best explains why the alkalosis persists?
med-physiology.l18.q5.h: The low urine chloride shows the kidney is retaining it.
med-physiology.l18.q5.e: Volume contraction, hypochloremia and secondary hyperaldosteronism maintain the alkalosis, which responds to saline. A primary aldosterone excess would show high urine chloride.

med-physiology.l19.q1.h: They sit in the distal stomach.
med-physiology.l19.q1.e: Gastrin comes from antral G cells. S cells secrete secretin, and D cells secrete somatostatin.

med-physiology.l19.q2.p: Which GI hormone is released in response to acid in the duodenum and stimulates pancreatic bicarbonate secretion?
med-physiology.l19.q2.h: Think of what neutralizes duodenal acid.
med-physiology.l19.q2.e: Secretin responds to acid and drives ductal bicarbonate secretion. CCK responds to fat and protein and stimulates enzyme secretion and gallbladder contraction.

med-physiology.l19.q3.p: Which transporter is responsible for the absorption of fructose across the brush border?
med-physiology.l19.q3.h: It is facilitated, not coupled to sodium.
med-physiology.l19.q3.e: GLUT5 carries fructose across the apical membrane. SGLT1 carries glucose and galactose with sodium, and GLUT2 is basolateral.

med-physiology.l19.q4.t: Autonomous gastrin driving excess acid secretion
med-physiology.l19.q4.p: A 41-year-old man has recurrent duodenal and jejunal ulcers, diarrhea and a fasting serum gastrin markedly elevated, with gastric pH of 1.5. Which mechanism best explains his ulcers?
med-physiology.l19.q4.h: A high gastrin level with very acidic stomach contents shows feedback is bypassed.
med-physiology.l19.q4.e: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome is a gastrinoma causing unregulated acid secretion and ulcers. Atrophic gastritis also raises gastrin, but gastric pH would be high.

med-physiology.l19.q5.t: Loss of bile salt reabsorption and loss of intrinsic factor-bound B12 uptake
med-physiology.l19.q5.p: A 52-year-old woman who had the terminal ileum resected for Crohn disease has watery diarrhea, steatorrhea and later macrocytic anemia. Which pairing of absorptive defects best explains her findings?
med-physiology.l19.q5.h: The terminal ileum has two special jobs unrelated to sugar.
med-physiology.l19.q5.e: Terminal ileum reabsorbs bile salts and the B12-intrinsic factor complex, so resection causes bile-acid diarrhea, fat malabsorption and B12 deficiency. Iron is absorbed in the duodenum.

med-physiology.l20.q1.p: Which hypothalamic factor tonically inhibits prolactin secretion?
med-physiology.l20.q1.h: Pituitary stalk damage causes prolactin to rise.
med-physiology.l20.q1.e: Dopamine inhibits lactotrophs, so dopamine antagonists or stalk lesions raise prolactin. TRH can stimulate prolactin.

med-physiology.l20.q2.p: A patient has low free T4 and a high TSH. Which diagnosis fits?
med-physiology.l20.q2.h: The pituitary is responding appropriately to low hormone.
med-physiology.l20.q2.e: Low T4 with a high TSH shows an intact pituitary and a failing thyroid. Central hypothyroidism has low or inappropriately normal TSH.

med-physiology.l20.q3.p: Which enzyme attaches iodine to tyrosine residues on thyroglobulin?
med-physiology.l20.q3.e: Thyroid peroxidase oxidizes iodide and incorporates it into thyroglobulin. Deiodinases convert T4 to T3 in tissues.

med-physiology.l20.q4.t: Antibodies that stimulate the TSH receptor
med-physiology.l20.q4.p: A 36-year-old woman has weight loss, tremor, heat intolerance, a diffusely enlarged thyroid and exophthalmos. Her TSH is suppressed and free T4 is elevated. Which pathology best explains her hyperthyroidism?
med-physiology.l20.q4.h: TSH is low, so the stimulus is not coming from the pituitary.
med-physiology.l20.q4.e: Graves disease involves stimulating TSH receptor antibodies, which raise T4 and suppress TSH by feedback. A TSH-secreting adenoma would give high TSH.

med-physiology.l20.q5.t: Prolonged steroids suppressed ACTH, causing adrenal atrophy and cortisol deficiency
med-physiology.l20.q5.p: A 57-year-old man has taken high-dose prednisone daily for a year for vasculitis and abruptly stops it. He later develops hypotension, vomiting and weakness. Which sequence best explains the presentation?
med-physiology.l20.q5.h: Negative feedback acts on both the hypothalamus and the pituitary.
med-physiology.l20.q5.e: Exogenous glucocorticoid suppresses the axis, so the cortex atrophies and cannot respond when the drug is stopped. Aldosterone is mostly regulated by angiotensin II and potassium.

med-physiology.l21.q1.p: Which glucose transporter is insulin-dependent in skeletal muscle and adipose tissue?
med-physiology.l21.q1.h: It translocates to the membrane when insulin binds.
med-physiology.l21.q1.e: GLUT4 is inserted into the membrane in response to insulin. GLUT1 is a basal transporter, and GLUT2 is in liver, beta cells and kidney.

med-physiology.l21.q2.p: Which event directly links glucose metabolism to insulin release in beta cells?
med-physiology.l21.q2.h: Depolarization is needed for calcium entry.
med-physiology.l21.q2.e: Rising ATP closes K-ATP channels, depolarizing the cell, opening calcium channels and triggering exocytosis. Sulfonylureas mimic this closure.

med-physiology.l21.q3.t: High calcium, high PTH, low phosphate
med-physiology.l21.q3.p: Which pattern of laboratory results best fits primary hyperparathyroidism?
med-physiology.l21.q3.h: PTH raises calcium and promotes phosphaturia.
med-physiology.l21.q3.e: Autonomous PTH raises calcium and lowers phosphate. Low calcium with high PTH and high phosphate is typical of chronic kidney disease.

med-physiology.l21.q4.t: Tumour production of PTH-related peptide acting on PTH receptors
med-physiology.l21.q4.p: A 62-year-old man with lung cancer has calcium 14 mg/dL, low phosphate and a suppressed PTH. Which mechanism most likely explains the hypercalcemia?
med-physiology.l21.q4.h: PTH is suppressed by the high calcium.
med-physiology.l21.q4.e: PTH-related peptide mimics PTH at its receptor, causing hypercalcemia while the gland is suppressed. A parathyroid adenoma would have high PTH.

med-physiology.l21.q5.t: It is likely depleted, since potassium shifts out of cells and is lost in urine
med-physiology.l21.q5.p: A 19-year-old with type 1 diabetes presents with vomiting and deep breathing. Glucose is 520 mg/dL, bicarbonate 8 mmol/L and potassium 5.6 mmol/L. Which statement about his total body potassium is correct?
med-physiology.l21.q5.h: Serum potassium and total body potassium can differ greatly.
med-physiology.l21.q5.e: Without insulin, potassium moves out of cells and is lost in the osmotic diuresis; potassium falls sharply once insulin is given. Insulin lowers, not raises, extracellular potassium.

med-physiology.l22.q1.p: Which cells in the testis produce testosterone in response to LH?
med-physiology.l22.q1.h: They lie between the seminiferous tubules.
med-physiology.l22.q1.e: Leydig cells respond to LH. Sertoli cells respond to FSH and support spermatogenesis.

med-physiology.l22.q2.t: A surge of LH caused by sustained high estradiol exerting positive feedback
med-physiology.l22.q2.p: What triggers ovulation in the normal menstrual cycle?
med-physiology.l22.q2.h: The feedback of estradiol changes sign at mid-cycle.
med-physiology.l22.q2.e: Sustained high estradiol exerts positive feedback and causes the LH surge. Progesterone is made after ovulation.

med-physiology.l22.q3.p: Which hormone maintains the corpus luteum in early pregnancy?
med-physiology.l22.q3.h: It resembles LH and appears in urine pregnancy tests.
med-physiology.l22.q3.e: hCG acts on the LH receptor to sustain the corpus luteum until the placenta makes enough progesterone. Estriol is a late placental estrogen.

med-physiology.l22.q4.p: A 24-year-old man has a 46,XY karyotype, normal testes, and a blind-ending vagina with absent uterus and tubes. Testosterone is normal for a man, and he has female external genitalia with scant body hair. Which defect best explains his presentation?
med-physiology.l22.q4.h: Testes formed, and the paramesonephric ducts regressed, but the target tissues did not respond to androgen.
med-physiology.l22.q4.e: Androgen insensitivity leaves testes producing AMH (so no uterus) and testosterone that cannot act, giving female external genitalia. 5-alpha-reductase deficiency causes ambiguous genitalia that virilize at puberty.

med-physiology.l22.q5.t: Continuous stimulation desensitizes gonadotrophs, lowering LH and FSH
med-physiology.l22.q5.p: A 29-year-old woman has been using a long-acting GnRH agonist for endometriosis and reports hot flashes and amenorrhea. Which mechanism best explains these effects?
med-physiology.l22.q5.h: Pulsatility is the key to GnRH action.
med-physiology.l22.q5.e: Sustained GnRH receptor stimulation downregulates the receptor, so gonadotropins and estradiol fall, producing menopausal symptoms. Pulsatile stimulation is the physiologic pattern.

med-physiology.l23.q1.p: Which change is typical of moderate dynamic exercise?
med-physiology.l23.q1.h: Active muscle beds dilate in large numbers.
med-physiology.l23.q1.e: Metabolic vasodilation in muscle lowers total peripheral resistance. Cardiac output and the arteriovenous oxygen difference rise.

med-physiology.l23.q2.p: At maximal exercise, oxygen consumption is 3.6 L/min and the arteriovenous oxygen difference is 150 mL/L. What is the cardiac output?
med-physiology.l23.q2.h: Use the Fick relationship and convert units.
med-physiology.l23.q2.e: 3,600 mL/min divided by 150 mL/L is 24 L/min. Using 200 for the difference would give 18.

med-physiology.l23.q3.t: Renal bicarbonate excretion that corrects the respiratory alkalosis
med-physiology.l23.q3.p: Which change is part of acclimatization to high altitude over several days?
med-physiology.l23.q3.h: The alkalosis from hyperventilation is eventually reversed by an organ other than the lung.
med-physiology.l23.q3.e: The kidneys excrete bicarbonate, restoring pH and allowing greater ventilation. Erythropoietin and 2,3-BPG rise, and pulmonary pressures rise.
