med-physiology.l23.q4.p: A 30-year-old woman climbs rapidly to 4,000 m and develops headache, nausea and insomnia. Which prophylactic drug acts by creating a metabolic acidosis that stimulates ventilation?
med-physiology.l23.q4.h: The enzyme inhibited is carbonic anhydrase.
med-physiology.l23.q4.e: Acetazolamide causes bicarbonate loss and metabolic acidosis, which stimulates breathing and speeds acclimatization. Loop and thiazide diuretics cause alkalosis.

med-physiology.l23.q5.t: Buffering of lactic acid generates CO2, and acidosis stimulates chemoreceptors
med-physiology.l23.q5.p: A 26-year-old cyclist exercising above the lactate threshold has rapid, deep breathing, with arterial PCO2 lower than at rest and a falling pH. Which explanation best accounts for the ventilation?
med-physiology.l23.q5.h: Ventilation outpaces CO2 production once acid accumulates.
med-physiology.l23.q5.e: Lactate is buffered by bicarbonate, raising CO2, and the fall in pH stimulates peripheral chemoreceptors; ventilation then outruns CO2, lowering PCO2. Arterial PO2 is typically maintained.

med-physiology.l24.q1.p: Which finding is a late sign of hemorrhage in a young healthy adult?
med-physiology.l24.q1.h: Compensation holds pressure until reserves are exhausted.
med-physiology.l24.q1.e: Systolic pressure is maintained by compensation until a large loss, so hypotension is late. Tachycardia and a narrow pulse pressure appear early.

med-physiology.l24.q2.t: Transcapillary refill of interstitial fluid into the vasculature
med-physiology.l24.q2.p: Several hours after a moderate hemorrhage, a patient's hematocrit falls without further bleeding. Which mechanism explains this?
med-physiology.l24.q2.h: Starling forces change when arterial pressure falls.
med-physiology.l24.q2.e: Lower capillary hydrostatic pressure favours reabsorption, shifting fluid into plasma and diluting red cells. Erythropoiesis takes days.

med-physiology.l24.q3.t: Low cardiac output, low wedge pressure, high systemic vascular resistance
med-physiology.l24.q3.p: Which hemodynamic profile is expected in hypovolemic shock?
med-physiology.l24.q3.h: There is not enough volume to fill the heart.
med-physiology.l24.q3.e: Loss of volume lowers filling pressures and output, with reflex vasoconstriction. High wedge pressure would indicate cardiogenic shock.

med-physiology.l24.q4.t: Low cardiac output with high central venous pressure
med-physiology.l24.q4.p: A 55-year-old man is hypotensive with distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds and clear lung fields after a stab wound to the chest. Which hemodynamic profile best fits his condition?
med-physiology.l24.q4.h: Something external is stopping the heart from filling.
med-physiology.l24.q4.e: Cardiac tamponade restricts filling, causing low output with raised venous pressure (obstructive shock). Hypovolemic shock would show flat neck veins.

med-physiology.l24.q5.t: Widespread vasodilation with low systemic resistance
med-physiology.l24.q5.p: A 70-year-old woman has fever, warm flushed skin and a blood pressure of 78/40 mmHg after a urinary infection. Cardiac output is high and systemic vascular resistance is low. Which mechanism best explains her hypotension?
med-physiology.l24.q5.h: Warm skin and high output suggest low resistance, not low volume.
med-physiology.l24.q5.e: In septic (distributive) shock, vasodilation lowers resistance so pressure falls despite high output. Cardiogenic shock would have low output and cool skin.

med-prek2.l01.q1.t: It helps you think and tells your body what to do
med-prek2.l01.q1.p: What is the job of your brain?
med-prek2.l01.q1.h: Think of the boss of your body.
med-prek2.l01.q1.e: The brain helps you think, remember, and tell your body what to do. The heart pumps blood, which is a different job.

med-prek2.l01.q2.p: Which body part helps you walk, run, and jump?
med-prek2.l01.q2.h: Think about what you use at the playground.
med-prek2.l01.q2.e: Legs and feet help us move around. Hands and arms help with holding and waving.

med-prek2.l01.q3.p: What do your lungs help you do?
med-prek2.l01.q3.e: Lungs fill with air when you breathe in. Taste, hearing, and bending use other body parts.

med-prek2.l01.q4.t: All bodies are special and different, and deserve care
med-prek2.l01.q4.p: A friend uses a wheelchair to get around. What is true about bodies?
med-prek2.l01.q4.e: Every body is a little different, and each one is special. Having a different body does not make anyone less able to belong.

med-prek2.l02.q1.p: Which sense do you use with your ears?
med-prek2.l02.q1.e: Ears are for hearing. Eyes are for seeing.

med-prek2.l02.q2.p: How many senses do you have?
med-prek2.l02.q2.h: Count see, hear, smell, taste, touch.
med-prek2.l02.q2.e: We usually learn five senses: seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, and touching.

med-prek2.l02.q3.p: You touch a very hot cup and quickly pull your hand back. Which sense helped keep you safe?
med-prek2.l02.q3.e: Your skin feels hot and cold and sends a message to your brain. Taste and smell do not help with a hot cup you touch.

med-prek2.l02.q4.p: You smell smoke in your home. What should you do?
med-prek2.l02.q4.e: Smells can warn us of danger. Telling a grown-up quickly keeps everyone safe, and waiting or searching alone is not safe.

med-prek2.l03.q1.h: You can feel it beat in your chest.
med-prek2.l03.q1.e: The heart squeezes to push blood all around your body. Bones, not the heart, hold you up.

med-prek2.l03.q2.p: What keeps your brain safe, like a helmet?
med-prek2.l03.q2.h: It is a hard bone in your head.
med-prek2.l03.q2.e: The skull is the bony case around the brain. Lungs and stomach are in the chest and belly.

med-prek2.l03.q3.t: Your body wants more blood and air to keep going
med-prek2.l03.q3.p: After you run fast, your heart beats faster. Why might that be?
med-prek2.l03.q3.h: Think of what hard-working muscles need.
med-prek2.l03.q3.e: When you move hard, your muscles need more oxygen, so the heart pumps faster. A fast heartbeat after running is normal.

med-prek2.l03.q4.t: Wear a helmet when you ride a bike
med-prek2.l03.q4.p: Which is a good way to protect your head?
med-prek2.l03.q4.e: A helmet helps protect your head and brain in a fall every time you ride, not just sometimes.

med-prek2.l04.q1.p: What do you need to wash your hands well?
med-prek2.l04.q1.e: Soap and water together help wash germs off. Wiping on clothes does not clean your hands.

med-prek2.l04.q2.t: About as long as singing Happy Birthday twice
med-prek2.l04.q2.p: How long should you rub your hands with soap?
med-prek2.l04.q2.e: Rubbing for about twenty seconds, like singing Happy Birthday two times, gives soap time to work.

med-prek2.l04.q3.t: Before you eat and after you use the bathroom
med-prek2.l04.q3.p: When is it a good time to wash your hands?
med-prek2.l04.q3.e: Germs are too small to see, so wash at key times such as before eating and after the bathroom, even when hands look clean.

med-prek2.l04.q4.p: You need to sneeze and have no tissue. What is a good thing to do?
med-prek2.l04.q4.h: Catch the germs where they will not spread.
med-prek2.l04.q4.e: Sneezing into your elbow keeps germs off your hands and away from other people. Sneezing into bare hands spreads germs to what you touch.

med-prek2.l05.q1.t: Helps it grow and fix itself
med-prek2.l05.q1.p: What does sleep do for your body?
med-prek2.l05.q1.h: Your body is busy at night.
med-prek2.l05.q1.e: During sleep the body grows and repairs itself, and the brain sorts what you learned.

med-prek2.l05.q2.t: Brushing teeth and reading a story
med-prek2.l05.q2.p: Which is part of a good bedtime routine?
med-prek2.l05.q2.e: Calm steps like brushing teeth and reading help the body get ready for sleep. Loud screens and candy make sleeping harder.

med-prek2.l05.q3.t: Your body and brain did not get enough rest
med-prek2.l05.q3.p: You feel grumpy and cannot listen well after a night of very little sleep. Why?
med-prek2.l05.q3.e: Not enough sleep can make a person grumpy and make it hard to listen and learn.

med-prek2.l05.q4.t: Tell a grown-up so they can help you feel safe
med-prek2.l05.q4.p: You feel scared in the dark at bedtime. What can you do?
med-prek2.l05.q4.e: Telling a grown-up helps you feel safe. Hiding feelings or wandering alone does not help.

med-prek2.l06.q1.p: What is the best drink for your body?
med-prek2.l06.q1.h: It has no sugar in it.
med-prek2.l06.q1.e: Water helps your body stay cool, move, and think well without added sugar.

med-prek2.l06.q2.p: Which food helps build strong bones and teeth?
med-prek2.l06.q2.e: Dairy foods have calcium that helps bones and teeth grow strong. Candy does not.

med-prek2.l06.q3.p: It is a hot day and you have been running. What should you do?
med-prek2.l06.q3.h: Your body loses water when it sweats.
med-prek2.l06.q3.e: You sweat when it is hot, so you need to drink water to replace it.

med-prek2.l06.q4.t: Only share food that a trusted grown-up says is safe
med-prek2.l06.q4.p: A friend has a food allergy. What is the right thing to do?
med-prek2.l06.q4.e: For people with allergies, even a small amount of a food can make them very sick, so a grown-up should check what is safe.

med-prek2.l07.q1.t: Make your heart and muscles stronger
med-prek2.l07.q1.p: What can moving and playing do for your body?
med-prek2.l07.q1.e: Exercise strengthens the heart, lungs, muscles, and bones. It does not remove your need for sleep.

med-prek2.l07.q2.p: What should you wear when riding a bike or scooter?
med-prek2.l07.q2.h: It protects the top of your body.
med-prek2.l07.q2.e: A helmet protects your head. The other items do not protect you in a fall.

med-prek2.l07.q3.t: Stop, rest, drink water, and tell a grown-up
med-prek2.l07.q3.p: You feel dizzy while running at recess. What is the best choice?
med-prek2.l07.q3.e: Dizziness is a sign to stop and rest. Telling a grown-up is a good idea.

med-prek2.l07.q4.p: Which of these counts as moving your body?
med-prek2.l07.q4.h: You use your muscles to do it.
med-prek2.l07.q4.e: Dancing uses your muscles and gets your heart pumping. The other choices are mostly sitting or lying still.

med-prek2.l08.q1.p: Which of these is a feeling?
med-prek2.l08.q1.e: Sad is a feeling. Shoes, tables, and windows are things.

med-prek2.l08.q2.p: What can happen in your body when you are scared?
med-prek2.l08.q2.h: Feelings show up in the body.
med-prek2.l08.q2.e: When you are scared, your heart can beat faster. This is a normal body reaction.

med-prek2.l08.q3.t: Use words to say how you feel
med-prek2.l08.q3.p: You feel mad because a friend took your toy. What is a good choice?
med-prek2.l08.q3.h: All feelings are okay, but not all actions are.
med-prek2.l08.q3.e: It is okay to feel mad. Using words is a safe way to show it, while hitting hurts people.

med-prek2.l08.q4.t: It helps the feeling seem smaller and easier to share
med-prek2.l08.q4.p: Why does it help to name a feeling, like saying "I feel nervous"?
med-prek2.l08.q4.e: Naming a feeling helps you understand it and tell others. It does not make the feeling last longer.

med-prek2.l09.q1.p: What is one way to calm down when a feeling is big?
med-prek2.l09.q1.h: Smell the flower, blow the candle.
med-prek2.l09.q1.e: Slow deep breaths help the body calm down. Holding your breath or yelling does not.

med-prek2.l09.q2.t: A trusted grown-up, like a parent or teacher
med-prek2.l09.q2.p: Who can you talk to about your feelings?
med-prek2.l09.q2.e: A trusted grown-up who listens is a good person to talk to. Hiding feelings can make them heavier.

med-prek2.l09.q3.t: Tell a trusted grown-up so they can help
med-prek2.l09.q3.p: You have felt sad and worried for many days. What is the best next step?
med-prek2.l09.q3.e: When a feeling lasts many days, a grown-up can help. Keeping it secret makes it harder to get help.

med-prek2.l09.q4.t: "Something is bothering me and I need help."
med-prek2.l09.q4.p: You do not know the right words for how you feel. What can you say?
med-prek2.l09.q4.h: You do not need perfect words.
med-prek2.l09.q4.e: You can say that something is bothering you and ask for help. Good listeners will understand.

med-prek2.l10.q1.p: What does a dentist take care of?
med-prek2.l10.q1.e: A dentist takes care of teeth and gums.

med-prek2.l10.q2.t: Twice a day, morning and before bed
med-prek2.l10.q2.p: How often should you brush your teeth?
med-prek2.l10.q2.e: Brushing in the morning and before bed helps keep teeth healthy.

med-prek2.l10.q3.p: Which helper checks how your body is growing and can help you feel better when you are sick?
med-prek2.l10.q3.h: They work in a clinic or hospital.
med-prek2.l10.q3.e: Doctors check how children grow and help them get better. The other workers help the community in other ways.

med-prek2.l10.q4.t: Their jobs are to help keep people healthy
med-prek2.l10.q4.p: Why are doctors, nurses, and dentists called helpers?
med-prek2.l10.q4.h: Think about why they do the job.
med-prek2.l10.q4.e: Health workers help people stay healthy and get well. They are on your side.

med-prek2.l11.q1.t: A visit to the doctor when you are well, to make sure you are growing
med-prek2.l11.q1.p: What do we call a check-up visit to the doctor?
med-prek2.l11.q1.h: You do not have to be sick.
med-prek2.l11.q1.e: A check-up is a visit to see how your body is growing, even when you feel fine.

med-prek2.l11.q2.t: Listening to your heart and lungs
med-prek2.l11.q2.p: What is a stethoscope used for?
med-prek2.l11.q2.h: Doctors put it on your chest.
med-prek2.l11.q2.e: A stethoscope helps a doctor hear your heart and lungs.

med-prek2.l11.q3.t: Take slow breaths and look away at something fun
med-prek2.l11.q3.p: You feel nervous about getting a shot. What might help?
med-prek2.l11.q3.e: Breathing slowly and focusing on something else can make a shot easier. It is okay to feel nervous.

med-prek2.l11.q4.t: It helps you understand what is happening and not feel scared
med-prek2.l11.q4.p: Why is it good to ask the doctor questions?
med-prek2.l11.q4.e: Asking questions helps you know what to expect, which makes visits less scary.

med-prek2.l12.q1.p: Who decides who can touch your body?
med-prek2.l12.q1.e: You have the right to say who touches you. You can say no.

med-prek2.l12.q2.t: Say stop, go away, and tell a trusted grown-up
med-prek2.l12.q2.p: If something makes you feel uncomfortable, what should you do?
med-prek2.l12.q2.e: You can say stop, move away, and tell a trusted grown-up. It is never your fault.

med-prek2.l12.q3.t: Tell a trusted grown-up, even if the person said not to
med-prek2.l12.q3.p: A person asks you to keep a secret about touching your private parts. What is right?
med-prek2.l12.q3.h: Some secrets should always be told.
med-prek2.l12.q3.e: Secrets about touching are not okay. Tell a trusted grown-up. You will not be in trouble for telling.

med-prek2.l12.q4.t: Tell another trusted grown-up until someone helps
med-prek2.l12.q4.p: You told a grown-up about something scary, but they did not listen. What next?
med-prek2.l12.q4.e: If one person does not help, keep telling other trusted grown-ups. You deserve help.

med-prek2.l13.q1.e: Only a trusted grown-up, such as a parent or school nurse, should give medicine to a child.

med-prek2.l13.q2.t: No, even if it looks or tastes like candy
med-prek2.l13.q2.p: Is medicine the same thing as candy?
med-prek2.l13.q2.e: Medicine is not candy. Too much can make you very sick, even if it looks yummy.

med-prek2.l13.q3.t: Do not touch it, and tell a grown-up right away
med-prek2.l13.q3.p: You find a pill on the floor at a friend's house. What should you do?
med-prek2.l13.q3.e: Never touch or taste unknown pills. A grown-up can handle it safely.

med-prek2.l13.q4.t: Tell a grown-up and do not give the medicine yourself
med-prek2.l13.q4.p: Your sibling feels sick and you have your grandma's medicine. What is the best choice?
med-prek2.l13.q4.h: Medicine for one person can harm another.
med-prek2.l13.q4.e: Medicine that helps one person may hurt someone else. Only a grown-up should decide about medicine.

med-prek2.l14.q1.t: Wear sunscreen, a hat, and play in the shade
med-prek2.l14.q1.p: How can you protect your skin from the sun?
med-prek2.l14.q1.e: Sunscreen, hats, sunglasses, and shade all help protect skin and eyes from the sun.

med-prek2.l14.q2.t: A person you do not know well
med-prek2.l14.q2.p: What do we mean when we say stranger?
med-prek2.l14.q2.h: You have not met them before.
med-prek2.l14.q2.e: A stranger is someone you do not know well. Most are kind, but you should still be careful.

med-prek2.l14.q3.t: Say no, go away, and tell a trusted grown-up
med-prek2.l14.q3.p: A stranger offers you candy and asks you to come to their car. What do you do?
med-prek2.l14.q3.e: Never go with a stranger. Say no, move away quickly, and tell a trusted grown-up.

med-prek2.l14.q4.t: A worker with a name tag or a police officer
med-prek2.l14.q4.p: You get lost in a store. Who is a good person to ask for help?
med-prek2.l14.q4.h: Look for someone whose job is to help.
med-prek2.l14.q4.e: Store workers with name tags and police officers are safe helpers. Never go outside with someone you do not know.

med-premed-behavioral.l01.q1.t: Gamma-aminobutyric acid, which opens chloride channels to hyperpolarize cells
med-premed-behavioral.l01.q1.p: Which neurotransmitter is the primary inhibitory transmitter of the brain?
med-premed-behavioral.l01.q1.h: Think about the molecule that calms neural firing.
med-premed-behavioral.l01.q1.e: GABA is the main inhibitory transmitter. Glutamate is its excitatory counterpart, so it is the opposite of the right answer.

med-premed-behavioral.l01.q2.t: Broca area in the left inferior frontal lobe, which supports speech production
med-premed-behavioral.l01.q2.p: A patient has halting, effortful speech with short phrases but understands questions well. Which area is most likely damaged?
med-premed-behavioral.l01.q2.h: Production is impaired while comprehension is preserved.
med-premed-behavioral.l01.q2.e: Broca area damage causes nonfluent speech with preserved comprehension. Wernicke damage causes fluent but meaningless speech with poor comprehension.

med-premed-behavioral.l01.q3.t: The thalamus, which acts as a relay station for most sensory pathways
med-premed-behavioral.l01.q3.p: Which structure relays most sensory information to the cerebral cortex?
med-premed-behavioral.l01.q3.h: Smell is the exception to this rule.
med-premed-behavioral.l01.q3.e: The thalamus relays nearly all sensory input to the cortex. The hypothalamus is homeostatic and endocrine, not a general relay.

med-premed-behavioral.l01.q4.t: Left posterior superior temporal gyrus, the region needed for understanding speech
med-premed-behavioral.l01.q4.p: A 58-year-old man has a stroke. Afterward he is fluent and speaks quickly, but his sentences are meaningless and he cannot follow commands, although he seems unaware of a problem. Which lesion best explains this?
med-premed-behavioral.l01.q4.h: Fluent nonsense with poor comprehension points to a specific language region.
med-premed-behavioral.l01.q4.e: This is Wernicke aphasia from left posterior temporal damage. Left frontal damage would instead give halting speech with preserved comprehension.

med-premed-behavioral.l01.q5.t: Hippocampus, because it is needed to consolidate new declarative memories
med-premed-behavioral.l01.q5.p: A 30-year-old woman after bilateral medial temporal lobe damage can recite her childhood address and ride a bicycle but cannot recall what she ate an hour ago. Which structure is most critical to this deficit?
med-premed-behavioral.l01.q5.h: Old memories and skills are intact; new event memory is not.
med-premed-behavioral.l01.q5.e: Hippocampal damage impairs formation of new declarative memories. The amygdala shapes emotional memory but does not account for a complete failure to encode events.

med-premed-behavioral.l02.q1.t: Transduction, the conversion of energy into an electrical neural signal
med-premed-behavioral.l02.q1.p: What is the term for converting physical energy into neural signals at a receptor?
med-premed-behavioral.l02.q1.h: It describes what photoreceptors and hair cells do.
med-premed-behavioral.l02.q1.e: Transduction is receptor conversion of energy to neural signals. Adaptation is a decline in response over time and is a different process.

med-premed-behavioral.l02.q2.t: It is a constant proportion of the starting stimulus intensity
med-premed-behavioral.l02.q2.p: According to Weber law, which is true of the just noticeable difference?
med-premed-behavioral.l02.q2.h: Adding one candle matters in a dark room but not a bright one.
med-premed-behavioral.l02.q2.e: The difference threshold scales with the baseline stimulus. A fixed absolute amount would ignore that baseline.

med-premed-behavioral.l02.q3.t: Sensitive in dim light, absent from the fovea, and not color-selective
med-premed-behavioral.l02.q3.p: Rods differ from cones in that rods are:
med-premed-behavioral.l02.q3.e: Rods support low-light vision and give no color. Cones occupy the fovea and give color and acuity.

med-premed-behavioral.l02.q4.t: Her response criterion, because she now requires less evidence to say yes
med-premed-behavioral.l02.q4.p: A radiologist is told that missing a cancer will carry severe consequences, and over the next month she reports many more suspicious nodules, most of which prove benign. Her ability to tell cancers from normal tissue is unchanged. According to signal detection theory, what changed?
med-premed-behavioral.l02.q4.h: Sensitivity stayed constant while hits and false alarms both rose.
med-premed-behavioral.l02.q4.e: A more liberal criterion raises hits and false alarms together without changing sensitivity. A real gain in sensitivity would raise hits without raising false alarms.

med-premed-behavioral.l02.q5.t: Loss of the left visual field in both eyes, a left homonymous hemianopia
med-premed-behavioral.l02.q5.p: A 45-year-old man has a tumor pressing on the right optic tract after the chiasm. Which visual field defect is expected?
med-premed-behavioral.l02.q5.h: Fibers from both eyes carrying one side of space travel together after the chiasm.
med-premed-behavioral.l02.q5.e: A post-chiasm lesion produces a contralateral homonymous hemianopia. Bitemporal loss arises from a lesion at the chiasm itself.

med-premed-behavioral.l03.q1.t: Bottom-up processing driven by the features of the stimulus itself
med-premed-behavioral.l03.q1.p: Processing that begins with raw sensory features and builds toward a whole percept is called:
med-premed-behavioral.l03.q1.h: The direction of flow is from stimulus to brain.
med-premed-behavioral.l03.q1.e: Bottom-up processing is stimulus driven. Top-down is the opposite and uses expectations to interpret input.

med-premed-behavioral.l03.q2.t: Closure, the tendency to fill in missing parts of a familiar shape
med-premed-behavioral.l03.q2.p: Seeing a circle with a small gap as a complete circle illustrates which Gestalt principle?
med-premed-behavioral.l03.q2.h: The mind supplies what the image leaves out.
med-premed-behavioral.l03.q2.e: Closure completes incomplete shapes. Figure-ground is about separating an object from its background, not completing it.

med-premed-behavioral.l03.q3.t: A binocular depth cue based on slightly different images in each eye
med-premed-behavioral.l03.q3.p: Retinal disparity is an example of which kind of cue?
med-premed-behavioral.l03.q3.h: The prefix refers to using both eyes.
med-premed-behavioral.l03.q3.e: Disparity requires two eyes. Monocular cues such as interposition and linear perspective work with one eye.

med-premed-behavioral.l03.q4.t: Inattentional blindness, in which an unexpected object goes unnoticed while attention is elsewhere
med-premed-behavioral.l03.q4.p: A 34-year-old driver following GPS looks directly at a stopped motorcycle ahead but does not register it until braking is too late. He has normal vision. Which concept best explains this?
med-premed-behavioral.l03.q4.h: Visual input reached the eye, but attention was committed elsewhere.
med-premed-behavioral.l03.q4.e: Failing to see an unexpected salient object when attention is directed elsewhere is inattentional blindness. Adaptation involves a constant stimulus, which is not the case here.

med-premed-behavioral.l03.q5.t: The ventral stream to the temporal lobe, which supports object recognition
med-premed-behavioral.l03.q5.p: A 62-year-old woman after a stroke cannot name or describe a key shown to her, but can accurately reach out and grasp it when asked. Which pathway is most likely damaged?
med-premed-behavioral.l03.q5.h: Knowing what an object is differs from knowing how to act on it.
med-premed-behavioral.l03.q5.e: Preserved grasping with impaired recognition suggests ventral stream damage. Dorsal damage would give the opposite pattern, with poor reaching but intact recognition.

med-premed-behavioral.l04.q1.t: Conditioned stimulus that produces a learned response of salivation
med-premed-behavioral.l04.q1.p: In Pavlov experiments, the bell after training is best described as a:
med-premed-behavioral.l04.q1.h: The bell acquired its power through pairing.
med-premed-behavioral.l04.q1.e: After pairing the bell is a conditioned stimulus. It would be neutral only before training.

med-premed-behavioral.l04.q2.t: Negative reinforcement, because an unpleasant stimulus is removed
med-premed-behavioral.l04.q2.p: A child cleans her room to stop her parent from nagging. Her cleaning increases. This is:
med-premed-behavioral.l04.q2.h: The behavior rose; ask what was taken away.
med-premed-behavioral.l04.q2.e: Behavior increased by removing an aversive stimulus, which is negative reinforcement. Punishment would decrease the behavior.

med-premed-behavioral.l04.q3.t: Variable-ratio, rewarding after an unpredictable number of responses
med-premed-behavioral.l04.q3.p: Which reinforcement schedule produces the high steady response rate that is most resistant to extinction?
med-premed-behavioral.l04.q3.e: Variable-ratio schedules give steady, extinction-resistant responding. Fixed-ratio gives a pause after each reward and extinguishes faster.

med-premed-behavioral.l04.q4.t: Stimulus generalization of a conditioned fear to similar white-coated people
med-premed-behavioral.l04.q4.p: A 6-year-old receives a shot from a nurse in a white coat. Weeks later he cries when he sees any white coat, including a pharmacist at a store. Which process explains the crying at the pharmacist?
med-premed-behavioral.l04.q4.h: The response spread to stimuli resembling the original one.
med-premed-behavioral.l04.q4.e: Responding to stimuli similar to the conditioned stimulus is generalization. Discrimination would mean he reacts only to the nurse who gave the shot.

med-premed-behavioral.l04.q5.t: Observational learning in which behavior is acquired by watching a rewarded model
med-premed-behavioral.l04.q5.p: A 9-year-old watches a classmate receive praise for sharing and begins to share more often, though no one has praised him. Which concept best accounts for this change?
med-premed-behavioral.l04.q5.e: He imitated a model whose behavior was rewarded, which is observational learning. Operant shaping would require that he himself be reinforced.

med-premed-behavioral.l05.q1.t: Procedural memory, which holds learned skills expressed through performance
med-premed-behavioral.l05.q1.p: Which type of long-term memory is responsible for knowing how to ride a bicycle?
med-premed-behavioral.l05.q1.h: You use it without consciously recalling a lesson.
med-premed-behavioral.l05.q1.e: Procedural memory is implicit and skill-based. Episodic memory concerns events, so a bicycle skill does not depend on it.

med-premed-behavioral.l05.q2.t: Retroactive interference, in which newer learning disrupts older learning
med-premed-behavioral.l05.q2.p: Learning a new phone number makes it harder to recall your old number. This is:
med-premed-behavioral.l05.q2.h: Which direction does the disruption run?
med-premed-behavioral.l05.q2.e: New learning impairing old memory is retroactive interference. Proactive interference would be the old number making the new one hard to learn.

med-premed-behavioral.l05.q3.t: Items from the end of the list still being active in working memory
med-premed-behavioral.l05.q3.p: A student recalls the first and last items in a long list best. The recency effect is attributed to:
med-premed-behavioral.l05.q3.h: Think about what is still active just after the list ends.
med-premed-behavioral.l05.q3.e: Recency reflects the last items remaining in working memory. Primacy, not recency, is explained by transfer to long-term storage.

med-premed-behavioral.l05.q4.t: Anterograde amnesia with confabulation, with immediate repetition preserved
med-premed-behavioral.l05.q4.p: A 56-year-old man with long-standing heavy alcohol use is confused, ataxic and cannot form new memories. He fills gaps with fluent but false stories about his day. A thiamine deficiency is suspected. Which memory finding is the hallmark of the chronic phase?
med-premed-behavioral.l05.q4.h: The patient invents details to fill what he cannot form or recall.
med-premed-behavioral.l05.q4.e: Korsakoff syndrome features prominent anterograde amnesia with confabulation. Procedural skills are typically spared, which rules out a loss of them.

med-premed-behavioral.l05.q5.t: Reconstructive memory altered by the wording of a leading question
med-premed-behavioral.l05.q5.p: A witness to a car crash is asked how fast the cars were going when they smashed into each other. A week later she reports seeing broken glass that was not at the scene. Which idea best explains this error?
med-premed-behavioral.l05.q5.h: Think about how the question was phrased and what it implied.
med-premed-behavioral.l05.q5.e: Wording can alter and add to what is remembered, since memory is reconstructed. Primacy concerns list position and does not explain added details.

med-premed-behavioral.l06.q1.t: Availability heuristic, which relies on ease of recalling instances
med-premed-behavioral.l06.q1.p: Which heuristic estimates likelihood by how easily examples come to mind?
med-premed-behavioral.l06.q1.e: Availability uses ease of recall. Representativeness uses similarity to a prototype and can neglect base rates.

med-premed-behavioral.l06.q2.t: Accommodation, the revision of a schema to fit new information
med-premed-behavioral.l06.q2.p: A child has a schema for dog and calls a cat a dog, then learns it is a different animal and creates a new category. This change is:
med-premed-behavioral.l06.q2.e: Changing or adding a schema is accommodation. Assimilation would be calling the cat a dog and leaving the schema unchanged.

med-premed-behavioral.l06.q3.t: Functional fixedness, in which an object is seen only in its usual use
med-premed-behavioral.l06.q3.p: Using a screwdriver only to turn screws and never thinking to use it as a lever is an example of:
med-premed-behavioral.l06.q3.h: Focus on the way the object is viewed.
med-premed-behavioral.l06.q3.e: Functional fixedness is limiting an object to its customary function. Mental set concerns persisting with a strategy rather than an object use.

med-premed-behavioral.l06.q4.t: Availability, because recent similar cases make one diagnosis feel most likely
med-premed-behavioral.l06.q4.p: A 27-year-old woman with sharp pleuritic chest pain after a long flight is told by a resident that it is probably musculoskeletal, since the previous five similar patients had that diagnosis. The resident does not consider pulmonary embolism. Which bias is most clearly shown?
med-premed-behavioral.l06.q4.h: Recent vivid cases are shaping the estimate.
med-premed-behavioral.l06.q4.e: Basing probability on recently encountered cases is the availability heuristic. Hindsight bias applies after an outcome is known, not at the time of the judgment.

med-premed-behavioral.l06.q5.t: Fluid intelligence declining while crystallized intelligence is maintained
med-premed-behavioral.l06.q5.p: A 70-year-old retired engineer scores lower than he did at 30 on a timed test of novel puzzles but higher on a vocabulary and general knowledge test. Which pattern does this reflect?
med-premed-behavioral.l06.q5.h: Novel problem solving and stored knowledge age differently.
med-premed-behavioral.l06.q5.e: Fluid abilities such as novel puzzles decline with age while accumulated knowledge holds up. The reverse pattern would not match these results.

med-premed-behavioral.l07.q1.t: Phoneme, the smallest unit of sound that distinguishes meaning
med-premed-behavioral.l07.q1.p: The smallest unit of sound that can change the meaning of a word is a:
med-premed-behavioral.l07.q1.h: The difference between bat and pat.
med-premed-behavioral.l07.q1.e: A phoneme is the smallest sound unit that distinguishes words. A morpheme is a unit of meaning and not of sound.

med-premed-behavioral.l07.q2.t: Overregularization, which shows application of a learned rule too widely
med-premed-behavioral.l07.q2.p: A two-year-old says that she goed to the park. This best illustrates:
med-premed-behavioral.l07.q2.h: She applied the regular past-tense rule to an irregular verb.
med-premed-behavioral.l07.q2.e: Applying the regular rule to an irregular verb is overregularization. Telegraphic speech drops function words and is not about misapplied rules.

med-premed-behavioral.l07.q3.t: Chomsky, who argued that humans are biologically prepared for grammar
med-premed-behavioral.l07.q3.p: Which theorist proposed that humans have an innate capacity for language acquisition, often called universal grammar?
med-premed-behavioral.l07.q3.e: Chomsky proposed innate grammatical capacity. Skinner favored learning through reinforcement, the opposite emphasis.

med-premed-behavioral.l07.q4.t: Arcuate fasciculus, which links the receptive and expressive regions
med-premed-behavioral.l07.q4.p: A 64-year-old woman after a stroke speaks fluently with normal grammar and comprehends instructions, but cannot repeat the phrase no ifs, ands or buts and substitutes wrong sounds. Which structure is most likely damaged?
med-premed-behavioral.l07.q4.h: Comprehension and fluency are intact; repetition fails.
med-premed-behavioral.l07.q4.e: Conduction aphasia from arcuate fasciculus damage disconnects the language areas. Damage to Broca or Wernicke areas would impair fluency or comprehension respectively.

med-premed-behavioral.l07.q5.t: Language may influence perception modestly, a weak form of linguistic relativity
med-premed-behavioral.l07.q5.p: A researcher finds that speakers of a language with two separate words for light blue and dark blue sort blue shades into groups slightly faster than speakers of a language with one word. Which interpretation fits best?
med-premed-behavioral.l07.q5.h: The result is a small speed difference, not an inability.
med-premed-behavioral.l07.q5.e: A modest speed advantage supports weak linguistic relativity. The strong deterministic version predicts an inability to see the difference, which was not found.

med-premed-behavioral.l08.q1.t: Resistance phase, with continued coping and persistent hormonal elevation
med-premed-behavioral.l08.q1.p: Which phase of Selye general adaptation syndrome involves sustained resistance with elevated cortisol?
med-premed-behavioral.l08.q1.h: It comes between the initial shock and the breakdown.
med-premed-behavioral.l08.q1.e: The resistance phase involves ongoing coping with elevated stress hormones. Exhaustion follows when resources run out.

med-premed-behavioral.l08.q2.t: The body responds first and the feeling follows from perceiving it
med-premed-behavioral.l08.q2.p: According to the James-Lange theory, a person who sees a bear and then runs feels fear because:
med-premed-behavioral.l08.q2.h: Which comes first, the feeling or the body response?
med-premed-behavioral.l08.q2.e: James-Lange holds that perceived bodily change produces the emotion. Cannon-Bard says they occur simultaneously.

med-premed-behavioral.l08.q3.t: Emotion-focused coping, which manages the feelings the stressor causes
med-premed-behavioral.l08.q3.p: A person facing a layoff cannot change the decision and chooses to talk with friends and exercise to manage distress. This is:
med-premed-behavioral.l08.q3.e: Managing feelings about an unchangeable stressor is emotion-focused coping. Problem-focused coping would target the layoff directly.

med-premed-behavioral.l08.q4.t: Sustained cortisol and allostatic load that impair immunity and hippocampal function
med-premed-behavioral.l08.q4.p: A 44-year-old man with years of caregiving strain has hypertension, frequent infections and trouble recalling recent conversations. Which mechanism best links his chronic stress to these findings?
med-premed-behavioral.l08.q4.h: Think of long-term exposure to stress hormones.
med-premed-behavioral.l08.q4.e: Chronic HPA activation raises blood pressure and suppresses immunity and impairs hippocampal memory function. Brief surges are adaptive, not the cause of chronic harm.

med-premed-behavioral.l08.q5.t: Schachter-Singer, which says arousal is labeled by cognitive appraisal of context
med-premed-behavioral.l08.q5.p: A volunteer given an injection of epinephrine is placed with a confederate acting cheerful and reports feeling euphoric, while another volunteer with a hostile confederate reports anger. Which theory does this support?
med-premed-behavioral.l08.q5.h: The same arousal was labeled differently depending on the setting.
med-premed-behavioral.l08.q5.e: Identical arousal labeled differently by context supports the two-factor theory. James-Lange would predict distinct arousal patterns for different emotions.

med-premed-behavioral.l09.q1.t: Drive-reduction theory, which stresses restoring physiological balance
med-premed-behavioral.l09.q1.p: Which theory says behavior is motivated by a need to reduce internal tension created by unmet physiological needs?
med-premed-behavioral.l09.q1.h: Think of hunger as an uncomfortable drive.
med-premed-behavioral.l09.q1.e: Drive-reduction theory links behavior to reducing a need-based drive. Incentive theory emphasizes external rewards instead.

med-premed-behavioral.l09.q2.t: Belonging and love, which includes friendship, intimacy and community
med-premed-behavioral.l09.q2.p: In Maslow hierarchy, which need is addressed immediately after physiological and safety needs?
med-premed-behavioral.l09.q2.e: Belonging and love is the third level. Esteem is the fourth, and self-actualization is last.

med-premed-behavioral.l09.q3.t: Leptin, released by adipose tissue to signal that energy is adequate
med-premed-behavioral.l09.q3.p: Which hormone, released by fat cells, signals long-term energy stores and suppresses appetite?
med-premed-behavioral.l09.q3.h: The hunger hormone has the opposite effect.
med-premed-behavioral.l09.q3.e: Leptin from fat cells signals energy sufficiency and suppresses appetite. Ghrelin stimulates hunger.

med-premed-behavioral.l09.q4.t: The overjustification effect, in which a reward lowers intrinsic interest
med-premed-behavioral.l09.q4.p: A teacher gives stickers for reading to children who already read for pleasure. After the program ends, those children read less in free time than before. Which concept best explains this outcome?
med-premed-behavioral.l09.q4.h: An external reward was added to an already enjoyed activity.
med-premed-behavioral.l09.q4.e: Extrinsic rewards for an inherently enjoyed activity can reduce later intrinsic interest. Drive reduction concerns physiological needs and does not apply.

med-premed-behavioral.l09.q5.t: Ventromedial hypothalamus, which promotes satiety when it is active
med-premed-behavioral.l09.q5.p: A 22-year-old woman with a gradual onset of rapid weight gain and constant hunger is found to have a lesion near the base of the brain. Damage to which hypothalamic region best explains the overeating?
med-premed-behavioral.l09.q5.h: Which center normally signals that you have had enough?
med-premed-behavioral.l09.q5.e: Ventromedial lesions remove the satiety signal and cause overeating. The lateral hypothalamus promotes eating, so a lesion there would reduce intake.

med-premed-behavioral.l10.q1.t: The id, which seeks immediate gratification of instinctual impulses
med-premed-behavioral.l10.q1.p: In Freud model, which part of personality operates by the pleasure principle?
med-premed-behavioral.l10.q1.h: It is the most primitive part.
med-premed-behavioral.l10.q1.e: The id seeks immediate gratification. The ego follows the reality principle.

med-premed-behavioral.l10.q2.t: Displacement, which redirects feeling from a threatening to a safer target
med-premed-behavioral.l10.q2.p: A man furious at his boss comes home and snaps at his wife instead. This defense mechanism is:
med-premed-behavioral.l10.q2.h: The target of the anger changed.
med-premed-behavioral.l10.q2.e: Redirecting feelings to a safer target is displacement. Projection would be believing the boss is angry at him.

med-premed-behavioral.l10.q3.t: Conscientiousness, a tendency toward organization, diligence and self-discipline
med-premed-behavioral.l10.q3.p: Which Big Five trait best predicts longevity and academic and job performance?
med-premed-behavioral.l10.q3.h: Think of the trait of reliability and self-control.
med-premed-behavioral.l10.q3.e: Conscientiousness is the strongest predictor of these outcomes. Extraversion relates more to sociability and positive affect.

med-premed-behavioral.l10.q4.t: An internal locus of control, with outcomes attributed to her own actions
med-premed-behavioral.l10.q4.p: A 35-year-old woman believes that her promotions result from effort and planning, and that a failed project was due to her own mistakes that she can correct. This pattern most closely reflects:
med-premed-behavioral.l10.q4.h: She sees her own actions as determining results.
med-premed-behavioral.l10.q4.e: Attributing outcomes to one own actions is internal locus of control. Reciprocal determinism is a Bandura concept about mutual influence and does not imply fixed traits.

med-premed-behavioral.l10.q5.t: The Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory, a validity-scaled self-report
med-premed-behavioral.l10.q5.p: A clinician wants an objective personality test whose items were selected because they separated diagnostic groups, with scales to detect inconsistent or defensive responding. Which instrument fits?
med-premed-behavioral.l10.q5.h: Look for the self-report with built-in validity scales.
med-premed-behavioral.l10.q5.e: The MMPI is an empirically derived self-report with validity scales. The Rorschach is projective and subjectively interpreted.

med-premed-behavioral.l11.q1.t: Object permanence, knowing that hidden things still continue to exist
med-premed-behavioral.l11.q1.p: In Piaget theory, understanding that an object continues to exist when out of sight is called:
med-premed-behavioral.l11.q1.h: It develops during the sensorimotor stage.
med-premed-behavioral.l11.q1.e: Object permanence is the awareness that hidden objects persist. Conservation is a later, concrete operational achievement.

med-premed-behavioral.l11.q2.t: Secure attachment, with the caregiver used as a base and easy comfort
med-premed-behavioral.l11.q2.p: A toddler explores a playroom, checks back with her mother, is upset when she leaves and is quickly comforted when she returns. This pattern indicates which attachment style?
med-premed-behavioral.l11.q2.h: Distress at separation and easy comfort at reunion is the healthy pattern.
med-premed-behavioral.l11.q2.e: Secure infants show distress at separation and are readily comforted. Avoidant infants show little distress and ignore the caregiver.

med-premed-behavioral.l11.q3.t: Identity versus role confusion, centered on forming a coherent sense of self
med-premed-behavioral.l11.q3.p: Which of Erikson psychosocial crises characterizes adolescence?
med-premed-behavioral.l11.q3.e: Adolescence is identity versus role confusion. Intimacy versus isolation follows in young adulthood.

med-premed-behavioral.l11.q4.t: The older child reached the concrete operational stage and grasps conservation
med-premed-behavioral.l11.q4.p: A 5-year-old watches water poured from a short wide glass into a tall narrow one and insists the tall glass holds more. A 9-year-old shown the same task says it is the same amount because nothing was added or removed. Which explanation fits the difference?
med-premed-behavioral.l11.q4.h: Compare the stages that surround ages five and nine.
med-premed-behavioral.l11.q4.e: Conservation emerges in the concrete operational stage. The younger child is preoperational, not sensorimotor, and has already developed object permanence.

med-premed-behavioral.l11.q5.t: Ongoing prefrontal maturation and heightened reward sensitivity in social settings
med-premed-behavioral.l11.q5.p: A 16-year-old with normal intelligence repeatedly takes dangerous risks in groups but reasons well about risk in a quiet interview. Which developmental factor best explains the gap?
med-premed-behavioral.l11.q5.h: Think about which brain region matures into the mid-twenties.
med-premed-behavioral.l11.q5.e: The prefrontal cortex is still maturing and reward systems are especially active with peers. A fully mature prefrontal cortex would not explain the pattern.

med-premed-behavioral.l12.q1.t: Positive symptoms, which reflect an excess or distortion of normal function
med-premed-behavioral.l12.q1.p: Hallucinations and delusions in schizophrenia are classified as:
med-premed-behavioral.l12.q1.h: They add something that is not normally present.
med-premed-behavioral.l12.q1.e: Hallucinations and delusions are positive symptoms. Negative symptoms such as flat affect reflect diminished function.

med-premed-behavioral.l12.q2.t: A history of at least one manic episode of elevated or irritable mood
med-premed-behavioral.l12.q2.p: Which feature distinguishes bipolar disorder from major depressive disorder?
med-premed-behavioral.l12.q2.e: A past manic episode defines bipolar disorder. The other features can all occur in major depression.

med-premed-behavioral.l12.q3.t: A vulnerability, often genetic, combined with an environmental stressor
med-premed-behavioral.l12.q3.p: The diathesis-stress model proposes that disorders arise from:
med-premed-behavioral.l12.q3.e: The model combines predisposition with stress. A single deterministic gene would ignore the stress component.

med-premed-behavioral.l12.q4.t: Posttraumatic stress disorder, with intrusion, avoidance and hyperarousal
med-premed-behavioral.l12.q4.p: A 24-year-old graduate student after a car accident has nightmares, avoids driving, is startled by loud sounds, and feels detached from friends. The symptoms have lasted three months. Which diagnosis best fits?
med-premed-behavioral.l12.q4.h: A trauma preceded intrusion, avoidance and arousal symptoms.
med-premed-behavioral.l12.q4.e: The pattern after a traumatic event with intrusion, avoidance, negative mood and arousal is PTSD. A specific phobia would not include nightmares and detachment.

med-premed-behavioral.l12.q5.t: Schizophrenia, with both positive and negative symptoms for over six months
med-premed-behavioral.l12.q5.p: A 20-year-old man over eight months has become withdrawn, speaks little, shows a flat face, and says that neighbors broadcast his thoughts. He has no mood episodes. Which diagnosis fits best?
med-premed-behavioral.l12.q5.h: Note the duration and the absence of mood episodes.
med-premed-behavioral.l12.q5.e: Delusions with negative symptoms for over six months without mood episodes fit schizophrenia. The mood disorders would require a mood episode.

med-premed-behavioral.l13.q1.t: Fundamental attribution error, favoring dispositions over situations
med-premed-behavioral.l13.q1.p: Overestimating personality and underestimating the situation when explaining others behavior is called the:
med-premed-behavioral.l13.q1.h: It concerns how we explain other people.
med-premed-behavioral.l13.q1.e: The fundamental attribution error favors dispositional explanations of others. The actor-observer difference is a related but distinct contrast between self and others.

med-premed-behavioral.l13.q2.t: Cognitive dissonance, with an attitude changed to match the behavior
med-premed-behavioral.l13.q2.p: A man who smokes but believes smoking is harmful feels uncomfortable and decides that the health risks are exaggerated. This is best explained by:
med-premed-behavioral.l13.q2.h: Inconsistency produces discomfort that is reduced.
med-premed-behavioral.l13.q2.e: Changing a belief to reduce inconsistency with behavior is dissonance reduction. The peripheral route concerns persuasion, not self-justification.

med-premed-behavioral.l13.q3.t: One confederate disagreed with the rest of the group and gave a different answer
med-premed-behavioral.l13.q3.p: In Asch studies, conformity dropped sharply when:
med-premed-behavioral.l13.q3.h: A single ally had a large effect.
med-premed-behavioral.l13.q3.e: Even one dissenter greatly reduces conformity. Larger unanimous groups raise it, so a bigger agreeing group would not reduce it.

med-premed-behavioral.l13.q4.t: The peripheral route, with persuasion by cues such as speaker status
med-premed-behavioral.l13.q4.p: A hospital wants staff to adopt a new hand hygiene protocol. A busy resident who skims a poster is more persuaded by a famous surgeon smiling in the image than by the data table beside it. Which route to persuasion is operating?
med-premed-behavioral.l13.q4.h: Attention is low and surface cues dominate.
med-premed-behavioral.l13.q4.e: Low attention with attractiveness and status cues is the peripheral route. The central route would involve careful scrutiny of the data.

med-premed-behavioral.l13.q5.t: The $1 group had insufficient external justification and shifted their attitude
med-premed-behavioral.l13.q5.p: A study asks volunteers to do a dull task and then tell the next person it was enjoyable. One group is paid $1 and another $20. Later, the $1 group rates the task as more enjoyable. Which explanation fits?
med-premed-behavioral.l13.q5.h: Which group lacked a good reason for the lie?
med-premed-behavioral.l13.q5.e: With little external justification, the $1 group reduced dissonance by changing their attitude. The $20 group had a reason for their behavior, so no attitude change was needed.

med-premed-behavioral.l14.q1.t: Bystander effect, tied to diffusion of responsibility among observers
med-premed-behavioral.l14.q1.p: The reduced likelihood that any one person helps when others are present is the:
med-premed-behavioral.l14.q1.e: The bystander effect results from diffusion of responsibility. Social loafing concerns effort in group tasks, not helping.

med-premed-behavioral.l14.q2.t: A landlord refuses to rent to a family because of its ethnic background
med-premed-behavioral.l14.q2.p: Which is an example of discrimination rather than prejudice?
med-premed-behavioral.l14.q2.h: Discrimination is an action, not an attitude.
med-premed-behavioral.l14.q2.e: Refusing to rent is behavior, which is discrimination. Private belief or unease is an attitude or stereotype.

med-premed-behavioral.l14.q3.t: Competition between the groups for scarce resources and rewards
med-premed-behavioral.l14.q3.p: Which condition is NOT part of Allport contact hypothesis for reducing prejudice?
med-premed-behavioral.l14.q3.e: Competition for scarce resources increases hostility. The other conditions promote reduced prejudice.

med-premed-behavioral.l14.q4.t: Group polarization and groupthink, with strengthened views and suppressed dissent
med-premed-behavioral.l14.q4.p: After a team reviews a case, each member leaves more extreme in the initial cautious view than before the meeting, and a junior member who disagreed said nothing. Which pairing of concepts best explains this?
med-premed-behavioral.l14.q4.h: Views grew more extreme, and dissent was silenced.
med-premed-behavioral.l14.q4.e: Strengthening of initial leanings is group polarization, and silenced dissent is groupthink. Deindividuation concerns anonymity in a crowd, which is not described.

med-premed-behavioral.l14.q5.t: Structural discrimination, unequal treatment built into policy and practice
med-premed-behavioral.l14.q5.p: A hospital sets a policy under which patients without a permanent address are never scheduled for follow-up, though no staff member holds any ill will toward them. Which concept does this best illustrate?
med-premed-behavioral.l14.q5.h: The harm flows from a rule, regardless of anyone intent.
med-premed-behavioral.l14.q5.e: A policy producing unequal treatment regardless of intent is structural discrimination. Implicit bias concerns individual automatic associations rather than formal rules.

med-premed-behavioral.l15.q1.t: Functionalism, as developed by Durkheim and later by Parsons
med-premed-behavioral.l15.q1.p: Which sociological theory views society as a system of interdependent parts that each serve a function?
med-premed-behavioral.l15.q1.h: Think of society as a body with organs.
med-premed-behavioral.l15.q1.e: Functionalism stresses interdependent parts serving social stability. Conflict theory stresses competition and power.

med-premed-behavioral.l15.q2.t: Intergenerational upward mobility, a higher position than that of parents
med-premed-behavioral.l15.q2.p: A person who grew up in a poor family and becomes a physician has experienced:
med-premed-behavioral.l15.q2.h: Compare the person with the parents.
med-premed-behavioral.l15.q2.e: Moving above the parental position is intergenerational upward mobility. Social reproduction would mean remaining at the parental position.

med-premed-behavioral.l15.q3.t: Knowledge, skills and habits that confer advantage in social settings
med-premed-behavioral.l15.q3.h: It is not financial or relational capital.
med-premed-behavioral.l15.q3.e: Cultural capital is knowledge and tastes valued by society. Social capital refers to networks of relationships.

med-premed-behavioral.l15.q4.t: Symbolic interactionism, which asks how shared meaning arises in interaction
med-premed-behavioral.l15.q4.p: A sociologist studies how a hospital ward constructs the meaning of a good patient through everyday talk between nurses and patients, and how labels shape the way people are treated. Which perspective is she using?
med-premed-behavioral.l15.q4.h: Focus on meaning built through face-to-face interaction.
med-premed-behavioral.l15.q4.e: Studying meanings built in daily interaction is symbolic interactionism. Conflict theory would focus on power imbalances between groups.

med-premed-behavioral.l15.q5.t: Institutional racism, with policies that shaped neighborhood resources
med-premed-behavioral.l15.q5.p: A 54-year-old man with diabetes lives in a neighborhood shaped decades earlier by lending practices that denied mortgages to residents based on race. The area has few grocery stores and clinics. Which concept most directly links history to his current health risk?
med-premed-behavioral.l15.q5.h: Policies from the past shaped where resources are now.
med-premed-behavioral.l15.q5.e: Historical lending practices that shaped neighborhood resources illustrate institutional racism. The sick role is about patient obligations and does not explain neighborhood conditions.

med-premed-behavioral.l16.q1.t: Unfair and avoidable, linked to social or economic disadvantage
med-premed-behavioral.l16.q1.p: A health inequity is best defined as a difference in health that is:
med-premed-behavioral.l16.q1.h: It involves both fairness and avoidability.
med-premed-behavioral.l16.q1.e: An inequity is a disparity judged unfair and avoidable. Not every difference between groups is an inequity.

med-premed-behavioral.l16.q2.t: Rose with each step down in employment grade, a social gradient
med-premed-behavioral.l16.q2.p: The Whitehall studies of British civil servants found that mortality:
med-premed-behavioral.l16.q2.h: Even people with stable jobs and care access showed a pattern.
med-premed-behavioral.l16.q2.e: Mortality showed a graded relationship with grade. The data did not show the highest rates among the top grades.

med-premed-behavioral.l16.q3.t: Intersectionality, a framework for overlapping identities and systems
med-premed-behavioral.l16.q3.p: Which term describes overlapping social identities that together produce experiences not captured by each identity alone?
med-premed-behavioral.l16.q3.h: The term is associated with Crenshaw.
med-premed-behavioral.l16.q3.e: Intersectionality addresses overlapping identities and systems. Acculturation concerns cultural change through contact.

med-premed-behavioral.l16.q4.t: Disagree, since racial gaps are tied to chronic stress, care quality and exposure
med-premed-behavioral.l16.q4.p: A clinic notes that Black women in its catchment area have higher rates of severe pregnancy complications than white women of the same insurance status. A trainee proposes that genetic differences explain the gap. Which response is most consistent with current evidence?
med-premed-behavioral.l16.q4.h: Race is a social category, and exposures differ.
med-premed-behavioral.l16.q4.e: Racial gaps are strongly linked to social and care-related factors such as stress and quality of care. Insurance status alone does not remove those differences.

med-premed-behavioral.l16.q5.t: An effort to address social needs, a step toward upstream causes
med-premed-behavioral.l16.q5.p: A hospital adds screening for housing and food insecurity to its visits and connects patients to resources. In public health terms, this is best described as:
med-premed-behavioral.l16.q5.h: It targets conditions that cause illness, not only the illness.
med-premed-behavioral.l16.q5.e: Screening for social needs addresses determinants that produce risk. Health literacy testing measures understanding of information, which is not what the screening does.

med-premed-behavioral.l17.q1.t: Precontemplation, with no current intention to change the behavior
med-premed-behavioral.l17.q1.p: In the transtheoretical model, a patient who is not planning to change in the next six months is in:
med-premed-behavioral.l17.q1.h: The stage before any consideration of change.
med-premed-behavioral.l17.q1.e: Not intending to change is precontemplation. Contemplation involves weighing change seriously.

med-premed-behavioral.l17.q2.t: Teach-back, which confirms that information was understood correctly
med-premed-behavioral.l17.q2.p: Which technique asks a patient to restate the treatment plan in his own words to check understanding?
med-premed-behavioral.l17.q2.e: Teach-back checks understanding by having the patient explain. Reflective listening mirrors what the patient said rather than testing comprehension.

med-premed-behavioral.l17.q3.t: Treat resistance as information and explore ambivalence with empathy
med-premed-behavioral.l17.q3.p: A core stance of motivational interviewing toward patient resistance is to:
med-premed-behavioral.l17.q3.h: The style is collaborative, not confrontational.
med-premed-behavioral.l17.q3.e: MI explores ambivalence with empathy and treats resistance as information. Confrontation tends to strengthen resistance.

med-premed-behavioral.l17.q4.t: Low perceived severity and perceived barriers, since symptoms are absent and side effects exist
med-premed-behavioral.l17.q4.p: A 52-year-old man with hypertension says that he skips his pill because he feels fine and the pills make him tired, and he does not think his blood pressure is a serious problem. Which health belief model constructs are most directly involved?
med-premed-behavioral.l17.q4.h: He does not see the condition as serious and sees costs of treatment.
med-premed-behavioral.l17.q4.e: He underestimates severity and perceives side effects as barriers. The statement about tiredness and feeling fine points to those two constructs, not to self-efficacy.

med-premed-behavioral.l17.q5.t: Placebo effect for the relief and nocebo effect for the side effects
med-premed-behavioral.l17.q5.p: In a trial of a pain drug, participants given an inert tablet that they believe is an analgesic report meaningful pain relief, and some in the inert group report side effects. Which pair of effects is illustrated?
med-premed-behavioral.l17.q5.h: Positive expectation helps; negative expectation harms.
med-premed-behavioral.l17.q5.e: Relief from expectation is the placebo effect and harm from expectation is the nocebo effect. The reverse pairing assigns them incorrectly.

med-premed-behavioral.l18.q1.t: Random assignment of participants to the conditions of the study
med-premed-behavioral.l18.q1.p: Which feature of an experiment most directly supports causal inference?
med-premed-behavioral.l18.q1.h: It makes the groups comparable at the start.
med-premed-behavioral.l18.q1.e: Random assignment balances groups and supports causal claims. A correlation alone cannot show causation.

med-premed-behavioral.l18.q2.t: Reliable but not valid, because it is consistent but wrong
med-premed-behavioral.l18.q2.p: A scale always reads 2 kilograms too heavy, giving the same value each time. This scale is:
med-premed-behavioral.l18.q2.e: Consistent but systematically wrong readings are reliable but not valid. A consistent error does not make a measure valid.

med-premed-behavioral.l18.q3.t: The median, which is the middle value and resists outliers
med-premed-behavioral.l18.q3.p: Which measure of central tendency is least affected by a few extremely high incomes in a sample?
med-premed-behavioral.l18.q3.h: Think of what happens to the middle value when one value grows.
med-premed-behavioral.l18.q3.e: The median resists outliers. The mean is pulled toward extreme values.

med-premed-behavioral.l18.q4.t: The design cannot show direction or exclude confounds, so cause is not established
med-premed-behavioral.l18.q4.p: A study of 400 adults finds that those who sleep less than six hours also report more depressive symptoms (r = 0.35). A journalist writes that short sleep causes depression. Which critique is most valid?
med-premed-behavioral.l18.q4.h: Consider reverse causation and a third variable.
med-premed-behavioral.l18.q4.e: A correlation cannot establish direction or exclude confounds, since depression may disturb sleep. With 400 participants, r of 0.35 would be significant, so the first option is wrong.

med-premed-behavioral.l18.q5.t: The result is statistically significant but may lack practical importance
med-premed-behavioral.l18.q5.p: A trial reports p = 0.03 for a drug that lowers a symptom score by an amount too small for patients to notice. Which interpretation is most accurate?
med-premed-behavioral.l18.q5.h: Distinguish statistical significance from effect size.
med-premed-behavioral.l18.q5.e: A small p-value shows the data are unlikely under the null but says nothing about size. The p-value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true.

med-premed-biochem.l01.q1.t: The pH at which it carries no net charge
med-premed-biochem.l01.q1.p: What is the isoelectric point of a molecule?
med-premed-biochem.l01.q1.e: At the pI the positive and negative charges balance. Half-protonation is the pKa of a single group, and solubility is usually lowest, not highest, at the pI.

med-premed-biochem.l01.q2.p: What is the approximate pI of glycine, with pKa values of 2.3 and 9.6?
med-premed-biochem.l01.q2.h: Average the two pKa values flanking the neutral form.
med-premed-biochem.l01.q2.e: (2.3 + 9.6) / 2 = 5.95. Adding them instead of averaging would give 11.9.

med-premed-biochem.l01.q3.p: Which amino acid side chain has a pKa near physiological pH and often acts as a catalytic acid and base in enzymes?
med-premed-biochem.l01.q3.h: Look for a pKa within one unit of 7.
med-premed-biochem.l01.q3.e: Histidine is the only side chain with a pKa close to neutral. Lysine and arginine remain protonated at physiological pH.

med-premed-biochem.l01.q4.t: Toward the cathode because it is positively charged
med-premed-biochem.l01.q4.p: At pH 7.4 a peptide has a pI of 9.0. In which direction does it move in an electric field?
med-premed-biochem.l01.q4.h: Compare the pH to the pI.
med-premed-biochem.l01.q4.e: The pH is below the pI, so the peptide is net positive and moves toward the cathode. Net negative charge would need pH above pI.

med-premed-biochem.l01.q5.t: It migrates more slowly because glutamate, which is negatively charged, is replaced by neutral valine
med-premed-biochem.l01.q5.p: A 7-month-old with sickle cell trait has haemoglobin electrophoresis at pH 8.6, where proteins are net negative and migrate toward the anode. How does HbS differ from HbA?
med-premed-biochem.l01.q5.h: Count the change in charge per beta chain.
med-premed-biochem.l01.q5.e: Losing one negative charge per beta chain reduces net negative charge, so HbS travels less far toward the anode. Valine is neutral, and this is not a charge-conserving substitution.

med-premed-biochem.l02.q1.t: The hydrophobic effect that buries nonpolar side chains
med-premed-biochem.l02.q1.p: Which force is the main driver of protein folding in water?
med-premed-biochem.l02.q1.h: Think about the core of a globular protein.
med-premed-biochem.l02.q1.e: Burying nonpolar groups frees ordered water and drives folding. Disulfides stabilise but are not the main driver.

med-premed-biochem.l02.q2.t: Vitamin C is needed to hydroxylate proline and lysine residues
med-premed-biochem.l02.q2.p: Why does scurvy affect collagen stability?
med-premed-biochem.l02.q2.h: Think about an enzyme cofactor needed for post-translational modification.
med-premed-biochem.l02.q2.e: Hydroxylation by prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases requires ascorbate and stabilises the triple helix. Collagen contains glycine at every third position by its sequence, not through a vitamin-dependent step.

med-premed-biochem.l02.q3.t: Non-covalent structure is lost while peptide bonds remain intact
med-premed-biochem.l02.q3.p: What happens to a protein when it is denatured by urea?
med-premed-biochem.l02.q3.h: Anfinsen unfolded ribonuclease and let it refold.
med-premed-biochem.l02.q3.e: Urea disrupts hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic packing, not covalent peptide bonds. Hydrolysis requires proteases or strong acid.

med-premed-biochem.l02.q4.t: A shift from alpha-helix-rich to beta-sheet-rich structure
med-premed-biochem.l02.q4.p: Which change characterises the conversion of the normal cellular prion protein to the disease form?
med-premed-biochem.l02.q4.e: The pathological isoform has the same sequence but a beta-sheet-rich conformation. It contains no nucleic acid.

med-premed-biochem.l02.q5.t: The bulkier residue disrupts tight packing in the triple helix and weakens the collagen
med-premed-biochem.l02.q5.p: A 4-year-old boy has recurrent fractures, blue sclerae and a family history of similar problems, and sequencing finds a glycine-to-serine substitution in a collagen chain at a Gly-X-Y position. Which mechanism best explains the bone fragility?
med-premed-biochem.l02.q5.h: Why is every third residue glycine?
med-premed-biochem.l02.q5.e: Glycine is the only residue small enough to fit at the centre of the helix, so a larger side chain disturbs packing. Collagen defects do not cause amyloid, and serine has no thiol to form disulfides.

med-premed-biochem.l03.q1.t: The substrate concentration at which the rate is half of Vmax
med-premed-biochem.l03.q1.p: What does Km represent in the Michaelis-Menten equation?
med-premed-biochem.l03.q1.e: Km is the substrate level giving v = Vmax / 2. Vmax is the maximum velocity, and enzymes do not alter the equilibrium constant.

med-premed-biochem.l03.q2.p: With Vmax = 100 umol/min and Km = 2 mM, what is the velocity at [S] = 6 mM?
med-premed-biochem.l03.q2.e: 100 x 6 / 8 = 75. A velocity of 60 would apply if Km were 4 mM.

med-premed-biochem.l03.q3.t: Apparent Km increases and Vmax is unchanged
med-premed-biochem.l03.q3.p: What effect does a competitive inhibitor have on the kinetic parameters?
med-premed-biochem.l03.q3.e: Competitive inhibition raises the substrate level needed to reach half-maximal rate, but sufficient substrate still reaches Vmax. A lowered Vmax belongs to noncompetitive inhibition.

med-premed-biochem.l03.q4.t: Competitive inhibition with the same Vmax
med-premed-biochem.l03.q4.p: On a Lineweaver-Burk plot, two lines (with and without inhibitor) cross on the y-axis. What does this indicate?
med-premed-biochem.l03.q4.e: A shared y-intercept means the same Vmax, which is the signature of competitive inhibition. Uncompetitive inhibition gives parallel lines.

med-premed-biochem.l03.q5.t: They compete with ethylene glycol at alcohol dehydrogenase, slowing production of toxic metabolites
med-premed-biochem.l03.q5.p: A 31-year-old is brought in after drinking antifreeze containing ethylene glycol. Why might intravenous ethanol or fomepizole reduce toxicity?
med-premed-biochem.l03.q5.e: Competition for alcohol dehydrogenase slows formation of the toxic acids, allowing renal excretion of the parent compound. A competitive inhibitor does not raise Vmax.

med-premed-biochem.l04.q1.p: Which factor shifts the haemoglobin oxygen-dissociation curve to the right?
med-premed-biochem.l04.q1.e: High 2,3-BPG stabilises the T state and lowers affinity. Carbon monoxide shifts the curve to the left.

med-premed-biochem.l04.q2.p: Why does fetal haemoglobin have a higher oxygen affinity than adult haemoglobin?
med-premed-biochem.l04.q2.h: Think about the gamma chain and the effector.
med-premed-biochem.l04.q2.e: HbF has gamma chains that interact weakly with 2,3-BPG, so the molecule favours oxygen. It is still a cooperative tetramer.

med-premed-biochem.l04.q3.t: It loads nearly fully in lungs and unloads over a small drop in PO2 in tissues
med-premed-biochem.l04.q3.p: Why does a sigmoidal curve suit haemoglobin better than a hyperbolic curve for oxygen delivery?
med-premed-biochem.l04.q3.e: Cooperativity gives a steep region over the tissue range, so large amounts are released. A hyperbolic carrier of high affinity would hold on to oxygen.

med-premed-biochem.l04.q4.t: Lower pH and higher CO2 reduce haemoglobin affinity for oxygen
med-premed-biochem.l04.q4.e: Acid and CO2 from active tissue favour the T state and unloading. A higher pH has the opposite effect.

med-premed-biochem.l04.q5.t: Carboxyhaemoglobin is read as oxyhaemoglobin, and the left-shifted curve impairs release of the remaining oxygen
med-premed-biochem.l04.q5.p: A 40-year-old man is found confused in a garage with a running car. His pulse oximeter reads 98%, arterial PO2 is normal and he has headache and tachycardia. Which explanation fits?
med-premed-biochem.l04.q5.h: Think about what two-wavelength oximetry cannot tell apart.
med-premed-biochem.l04.q5.e: Carbon monoxide occupies haem sites and left-shifts the curve, while the oximeter misreads the complex. Cyanide would be a different toxin, and a T-state shift would lower, not raise, the reading.

med-premed-biochem.l05.q1.t: Three sodium ions out and two potassium ions in, for one ATP
med-premed-biochem.l05.q1.p: What is the stoichiometry of the Na+/K+-ATPase per cycle?
med-premed-biochem.l05.q1.h: The pump is electrogenic and removes net positive charge.
med-premed-biochem.l05.q1.e: The pump removes three Na+ and brings in two K+, creating a net outward current. The reversed ratio would make the cell less negative, not more.

med-premed-biochem.l05.q2.t: GLUT4, which is moved to the plasma membrane after insulin signalling
med-premed-biochem.l05.q2.p: Which GLUT transporter is insulin-dependent and found in skeletal muscle and adipose tissue?
med-premed-biochem.l05.q2.e: GLUT4 is stored in vesicles and inserted into the membrane in response to insulin. GLUT1 is constitutive and not insulin-dependent.

med-premed-biochem.l05.q3.p: About how much free energy is needed to concentrate an uncharged solute tenfold at 310 K?
med-premed-biochem.l05.q3.h: Use RT ln of the concentration ratio.
med-premed-biochem.l05.q3.e: RT ln 10 = 2.577 x 2.303 = 5.9 kJ/mol. The ATP hydrolysis figure is the value for a different quantity, not for this concentration change.

med-premed-biochem.l05.q4.t: It stiffens fluid membranes at body temperature and prevents tight packing in the cold
med-premed-biochem.l05.q4.p: Why does cholesterol help the membrane remain functional across temperature changes?
med-premed-biochem.l05.q4.e: Cholesterol restricts the movement of fatty acid tails when warm and disrupts packing when cold. It forms no covalent bonds and does not carry ions.

med-premed-biochem.l05.q5.t: Low extracellular potassium leaves more pump sites free for digoxin, which increases pump inhibition
med-premed-biochem.l05.q5.p: A 72-year-old woman with heart failure takes digoxin and furosemide and presents with nausea, visual changes and arrhythmia. Serum potassium is 2.9 mmol/L. Which mechanism links her potassium level to digoxin toxicity?
med-premed-biochem.l05.q5.h: Digoxin and K+ compete at the same site.
med-premed-biochem.l05.q5.e: With less potassium to compete, more pumps bind digoxin, raising intracellular sodium and calcium. The proposed higher clearance would reduce, not raise, toxicity.

med-premed-biochem.l06.q1.p: Which compound has the highest phosphoryl transfer potential among these?
med-premed-biochem.l06.q1.h: It drives the last step of glycolysis.
med-premed-biochem.l06.q1.e: PEP releases about -62 kJ/mol on hydrolysis, more than ATP or creatine phosphate. Glucose 6-phosphate has a much lower value.

med-premed-biochem.l06.q2.t: -16.7 kJ/mol, so the coupled reaction is favourable
med-premed-biochem.l06.q2.p: Glucose + Pi to glucose 6-phosphate has delta G degrees prime of +13.8 kJ/mol. What is the delta G degrees prime when it is coupled to ATP hydrolysis (-30.5 kJ/mol)?
med-premed-biochem.l06.q2.h: Add the two free energy changes.
med-premed-biochem.l06.q2.e: The sum is 13.8 minus 30.5, giving -16.7 kJ/mol. Adding the magnitudes would wrongly treat the ATP term as positive.

med-premed-biochem.l06.q3.p: Which tissue lacks glucose 6-phosphatase and so cannot release free glucose into the blood?
med-premed-biochem.l06.q3.h: Think of who exports glucose in fasting.
med-premed-biochem.l06.q3.e: Muscle traps glucose 6-phosphate and uses it locally. Liver and kidney can release glucose.

med-premed-biochem.l06.q4.t: NADPH provides reducing power for biosynthesis and antioxidant defence
med-premed-biochem.l06.q4.p: What is the principal role of NADPH compared with NADH?
med-premed-biochem.l06.q4.e: NADPH, made in the pentose phosphate pathway, supports fatty acid synthesis and glutathione reduction. NADH is the one feeding the respiratory chain.

med-premed-biochem.l06.q5.t: Red blood cells, because they have no mitochondria to oxidise other fuels
med-premed-biochem.l06.q5.p: A 55-year-old man has fasted for three days. Which tissue would still be dependent on glucose rather than on ketone bodies or fatty acids, and why?
med-premed-biochem.l06.q5.h: Which cell lacks the organelle that oxidises other fuels?
med-premed-biochem.l06.q5.e: Red cells have no mitochondria, so they rely on anaerobic glycolysis. The heart readily oxidises fatty acids and ketones.

med-premed-biochem.l07.q1.p: Which enzyme is the main rate-limiting step of glycolysis?
med-premed-biochem.l07.q1.h: It is activated by AMP and fructose 2,6-bisphosphate.
med-premed-biochem.l07.q1.e: PFK-1 is the committed step and the principal control point. Aldolase and enolase catalyse near-equilibrium reactions.

med-premed-biochem.l07.q2.t: Two ATP, four made and two used
med-premed-biochem.l07.q2.p: What is the net ATP yield from glycolysis of one glucose to two pyruvate?
med-premed-biochem.l07.q2.e: Two ATP are spent and four are made, so the net is two. The figure four forgets the investment phase.

med-premed-biochem.l07.q3.p: Which enzyme is NOT used to bypass an irreversible step in gluconeogenesis?
med-premed-biochem.l07.q3.e: Phosphoglycerate kinase catalyses a reversible step shared by both pathways. The others bypass the irreversible kinase steps.

med-premed-biochem.l07.q4.t: It regenerates NAD+ from NADH so glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate oxidation can continue
med-premed-biochem.l07.q4.p: Why does lactate dehydrogenase activity let glycolysis continue without oxygen?
med-premed-biochem.l07.q4.e: Without NAD+ regeneration, glycolysis would stall at GAPDH. LDH does not itself produce ATP.

med-premed-biochem.l07.q5.t: Reduced glycolytic ATP impairs membrane pumps, so cells swell and become rigid and are cleared by the spleen
med-premed-biochem.l07.q5.p: A 6-month-old infant has pallor, jaundice and splenomegaly. Blood film shows haemolysis, and enzyme assay shows deficient pyruvate kinase. Why do the red cells fail?
med-premed-biochem.l07.q5.h: Red cells only have glycolysis for ATP.
med-premed-biochem.l07.q5.e: ATP depletion causes membrane damage and splenic clearance. Heinz bodies are typical of G6PD deficiency, a different problem.

med-premed-biochem.l08.q1.p: Which vitamin-derived cofactor is needed by E1 of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex?
med-premed-biochem.l08.q1.e: E1 decarboxylates pyruvate using thiamine pyrophosphate. Biotin is used by carboxylases such as pyruvate carboxylase.

med-premed-biochem.l08.q2.p: What is the yield of reduced coenzymes and GTP per acetyl-CoA entering the TCA cycle?
med-premed-biochem.l08.q2.e: There are three NAD+-linked dehydrogenases, one FAD-linked step and one substrate-level phosphorylation. Two NADH with two FADH2 miscounts the NAD+ steps.

med-premed-biochem.l08.q3.p: Which TCA cycle enzyme is also complex II of the respiratory chain?
med-premed-biochem.l08.q3.h: It uses FAD and is membrane bound.
med-premed-biochem.l08.q3.e: Succinate dehydrogenase is embedded in the inner membrane and passes electrons to ubiquinone. The other enzymes are in the matrix.

med-premed-biochem.l08.q4.t: It supplies acetyl-CoA and ketones that bypass the defective enzyme
med-premed-biochem.l08.q4.p: Why can a high-fat, low-carbohydrate diet help a child with PDH deficiency?
med-premed-biochem.l08.q4.h: Think about alternative sources of acetyl-CoA.
med-premed-biochem.l08.q4.e: Fatty acids and ketones give acetyl-CoA without PDH, and less carbohydrate means less lactate. Raising pyruvate would worsen lactic acidosis.

med-premed-biochem.l08.q5.t: Give thiamine first, since glucose metabolism needs thiamine-dependent enzymes that are already impaired
med-premed-biochem.l08.q5.p: A 52-year-old man with chronic alcohol use is brought in confused with nystagmus, ataxia and lactic acidosis. A nurse is about to start dextrose infusion. What is the best reasoning?
med-premed-biochem.l08.q5.e: Thiamine-dependent PDH and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase are deficient, and a glucose load can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy. Human liver does not ferment glucose to ethanol.

med-premed-biochem.l09.q1.p: Which respiratory chain complex does NOT pump protons?
med-premed-biochem.l09.q1.h: It is also a TCA cycle enzyme.
med-premed-biochem.l09.q1.e: Complex II passes electrons from FADH2 to ubiquinone without a proton-pumping step. This is why FADH2 yields less ATP than NADH.

med-premed-biochem.l09.q2.p: About 10 protons are pumped per NADH, and about 4 protons are needed per ATP. What is the ATP yield per NADH?
med-premed-biochem.l09.q2.h: Divide protons pumped by protons per ATP.
med-premed-biochem.l09.q2.e: 10 / 4 = 2.5 ATP. The figure of 3 is the older estimate that ignored the cost of moving phosphate and ATP across the membrane.

med-premed-biochem.l09.q3.p: Which agent blocks the flow of protons through the ATP synthase and so stops electron transport?
