med-premed-biochem.l09.q3.h: Respiratory control: no ATP synthesis, no flow.
med-premed-biochem.l09.q3.e: Oligomycin blocks F0, the gradient builds and electron transport stops. Dinitrophenol instead carries protons across and uncouples.

med-premed-biochem.l09.q4.t: Salicylate uncouples oxidative phosphorylation, releasing energy as heat
med-premed-biochem.l09.q4.p: Why does a large aspirin overdose cause fever?
med-premed-biochem.l09.q4.h: Think about what uncouplers do with the proton gradient.
med-premed-biochem.l09.q4.e: Uncoupling raises oxygen use while ATP is not made, so the energy appears as heat. Complex IV inhibition would lower oxygen use, which is not what happens.

med-premed-biochem.l09.q5.t: Cytochrome c oxidase is inhibited, so tissues cannot use oxygen and anaerobic glycolysis produces lactate
med-premed-biochem.l09.q5.p: A 28-year-old chemist is found unresponsive after a laboratory accident, with a pulse of 130, lactate of 14 mmol/L and bright-red venous blood. Which mechanism explains the picture?
med-premed-biochem.l09.q5.e: Cyanide blocks complex IV, so oxygen stays in the blood and lactate rises. Uncoupling would raise, not lower, oxygen consumption.

med-premed-biochem.l10.q1.p: Which enzyme is the rate-limiting step of the pentose phosphate pathway?
med-premed-biochem.l10.q1.e: G6PD controls the oxidative phase and is regulated by NADPH levels. Transketolase is part of the reversible non-oxidative phase.

med-premed-biochem.l10.q2.t: McArdle disease, due to muscle phosphorylase deficiency
med-premed-biochem.l10.q2.p: In which glycogen storage disease is there no rise in lactate during ischaemic forearm exercise, along with cramps and myoglobinuria?
med-premed-biochem.l10.q2.h: Muscle cannot start glycolysis from glycogen.
med-premed-biochem.l10.q2.e: Without muscle phosphorylase the glycogen is unavailable, so lactate does not rise. Pompe disease causes cardiomegaly and hypotonia instead.

med-premed-biochem.l10.q3.t: Fructose 1-phosphate, which traps phosphate and inhibits glycogen breakdown and gluconeogenesis
med-premed-biochem.l10.q3.p: Which accumulates in hereditary fructose intolerance and causes hypoglycaemia?
med-premed-biochem.l10.q3.e: Deficiency of aldolase B causes fructose 1-phosphate to accumulate. Galactose 1-phosphate is the intermediate in galactosaemia.

med-premed-biochem.l10.q4.t: Too little NADPH leaves glutathione unable to protect red cells from oxidants
med-premed-biochem.l10.q4.p: How does G6PD deficiency lead to haemolysis?
med-premed-biochem.l10.q4.e: Without NADPH, oxidant damage precipitates haemoglobin as Heinz bodies. Mature red cells have no DNA to synthesise.

med-premed-biochem.l10.q5.p: A 2-week-old breast-fed infant has jaundice, vomiting and hepatomegaly, with cataracts and an Escherichia coli sepsis. Reducing substances are present in the urine and glucose oxidase testing is negative. Which enzyme is deficient?
med-premed-biochem.l10.q5.h: Lactose in milk is the trigger.
med-premed-biochem.l10.q5.e: Classic galactosaemia presents after lactose feeding with sepsis risk. Galactokinase deficiency causes cataracts alone, without liver injury.

med-premed-biochem.l11.q1.p: What is the rate-limiting step of fatty acid oxidation?
med-premed-biochem.l11.q1.e: CPT-I controls entry of long-chain acyl groups into mitochondria and is inhibited by malonyl-CoA. This links synthesis to oxidation.

med-premed-biochem.l11.q2.p: What is the approximate net ATP yield from complete oxidation of palmitate?
med-premed-biochem.l11.q2.h: Seven cycles, eight acetyl-CoA, minus activation.
med-premed-biochem.l11.q2.e: Seven cycles give 28 ATP and eight acetyl-CoA give 80, minus 2 for activation. The figure 129 is the older value using 3 and 2 ATP.

med-premed-biochem.l11.q3.t: It lacks the transferase that activates acetoacetate to acetoacetyl-CoA
med-premed-biochem.l11.q3.p: Why can the liver make ketone bodies but not use them?
med-premed-biochem.l11.q3.e: Liver does not express the thiophorase enzyme, so ketones pass to peripheral tissues. Hepatic mitochondria do oxidise acetyl-CoA normally.

med-premed-biochem.l11.q4.t: They inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, which upregulates hepatic LDL receptors
med-premed-biochem.l11.q4.p: What is the mechanism by which statins lower plasma LDL?
med-premed-biochem.l11.q4.h: The committed step of cholesterol synthesis.
med-premed-biochem.l11.q4.e: Lower hepatic cholesterol raises LDL receptor expression and plasma clearance. Bile-acid binding describes resins.

med-premed-biochem.l11.q5.t: Medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency, which impairs fasting fatty acid oxidation
med-premed-biochem.l11.q5.p: A 9-month-old becomes lethargic and hypoglycaemic after a viral illness with poor feeding. Ketones are low, and urine organic acids show dicarboxylic acids. Which defect fits best?
med-premed-biochem.l11.q5.h: Low ketones during fasting means fat is not being oxidised.
med-premed-biochem.l11.q5.e: Hypoketotic hypoglycaemia with dicarboxylic aciduria is the signature of MCAD deficiency. Glucose 6-phosphatase deficiency would give lactic acidosis and hepatomegaly.

med-premed-biochem.l12.q1.p: Which cofactor is needed by aminotransferases such as ALT and AST?
med-premed-biochem.l12.q1.e: Aminotransferases use PLP to carry the amino group as pyridoxamine. TPP is used by decarboxylases such as PDH.

med-premed-biochem.l12.q2.p: Which enzyme is the regulated, rate-limiting step of the urea cycle and is activated by N-acetylglutamate?
med-premed-biochem.l12.q2.h: It is in the mitochondrial matrix.
med-premed-biochem.l12.q2.e: CPS I combines ammonia and bicarbonate and needs N-acetylglutamate. Arginase is the last step and releases urea.

med-premed-biochem.l12.q3.t: Carbamoyl phosphate accumulates and enters pyrimidine synthesis
med-premed-biochem.l12.q3.p: Why does ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency raise urinary orotic acid?
med-premed-biochem.l12.q3.h: Where does excess carbamoyl phosphate go?
med-premed-biochem.l12.q3.e: Mitochondrial carbamoyl phosphate leaves the matrix and enters the cytosolic pyrimidine pathway. In CPS I deficiency there is none to spill.

med-premed-biochem.l12.q4.t: It acidifies the colon so NH3 is converted to NH4+ and trapped
med-premed-biochem.l12.q4.p: How does lactulose lower blood ammonia in hepatic encephalopathy?
med-premed-biochem.l12.q4.h: Think about the charge of ammonium.
med-premed-biochem.l12.q4.e: Lactulose is metabolised by colonic bacteria to acids, favouring the charged ammonium, which cannot be absorbed. It is not absorbed itself.

med-premed-biochem.l12.q5.t: Branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase, with accumulation of leucine, isoleucine and valine
med-premed-biochem.l12.q5.p: A 3-day-old term infant, previously well, has poor feeding, a sweet maple-syrup odour of the urine and progressive lethargy with seizures. Which enzyme is deficient and which amino acids accumulate?
med-premed-biochem.l12.q5.h: The enzyme complex shares cofactors with PDH.
med-premed-biochem.l12.q5.e: Maple syrup urine disease is a defect of branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase. Phenylketonuria causes a mousy odour and presents later.

med-premed-biochem.l13.q1.p: Which G protein activates phospholipase C?
med-premed-biochem.l13.q1.e: Gq couples to phospholipase C. Gs raises cyclic AMP through adenylyl cyclase.

med-premed-biochem.l13.q2.t: It locks Gs in its active state, raising cyclic AMP and chloride secretion
med-premed-biochem.l13.q2.p: How does cholera toxin cause watery diarrhoea?
med-premed-biochem.l13.q2.h: ADP-ribosylation of a stimulatory G protein.
med-premed-biochem.l13.q2.e: Constitutive Gs activity raises cAMP and opens CFTR, so chloride and water flow into the lumen. Pertussis toxin is the one acting on Gi.

med-premed-biochem.l13.q3.t: It inhibits PDE5, so cyclic GMP rises in smooth muscle
med-premed-biochem.l13.q3.h: Think about which cyclic nucleotide is broken down by PDE5.
med-premed-biochem.l13.q3.e: PDE5 degrades cGMP, so blocking it prolongs nitric oxide signalling. Blocking guanylyl cyclase would have the opposite effect.

med-premed-biochem.l13.q4.t: Ras stays active and the growth signal is persistent
med-premed-biochem.l13.q4.p: What is a typical outcome of a Ras mutation that removes its GTPase activity?
med-premed-biochem.l13.q4.h: The GTPase turns the signal off.
med-premed-biochem.l13.q4.e: Without GTP hydrolysis Ras remains GTP-bound and active, promoting proliferation. An inactive form would not be oncogenic.

med-premed-biochem.l13.q5.t: Inhibiting the constitutively active BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase to switch off proliferative signalling
med-premed-biochem.l13.q5.p: A 48-year-old man has fatigue, splenomegaly and a white count of 120,000 per microlitre with immature granulocytes. Cytogenetics shows t(9;22). Which treatment mechanism is the best fit?
med-premed-biochem.l13.q5.h: The translocation creates a fusion kinase.
med-premed-biochem.l13.q5.e: Imatinib targets the BCR-ABL fusion in chronic myeloid leukaemia. Methotrexate is non-specific and is not the targeted therapy for this lesion.

med-premed-biochem.l14.q1.p: How many hydrogen bonds join a G-C base pair?
med-premed-biochem.l14.q1.h: G-C pairs are stronger than A-T.
med-premed-biochem.l14.q1.e: G-C has three bonds and A-T has two, so G-C rich DNA melts at a higher temperature.

med-premed-biochem.l14.q2.p: In a double-stranded DNA sample 30% of the bases are adenine. What percentage is guanine?
med-premed-biochem.l14.q2.h: A equals T, and G equals C.
med-premed-biochem.l14.q2.e: A + T = 60%, leaving 40% for G + C, so G is 20%. Thirty percent would be the thymine value.

med-premed-biochem.l14.q3.p: Which enzyme removes RNA primers and fills the gap in bacterial replication?
med-premed-biochem.l14.q3.e: Polymerase I removes primers and fills gaps. Ligase then seals the final nick but cannot fill a gap.

med-premed-biochem.l14.q4.p: Which repair pathway is defective in xeroderma pigmentosum?
med-premed-biochem.l14.q4.e: Nucleotide excision repair removes bulky lesions such as UV dimers. Mismatch repair is the pathway lost in Lynch syndrome.

med-premed-biochem.l14.q5.t: Loss of DNA mismatch repair, which allows replication errors in repeated sequences to persist
med-premed-biochem.l14.q5.p: A 39-year-old woman has a strong family history of colorectal and endometrial cancer, and her tumour shows microsatellite instability. Which defect most likely underlies this?
med-premed-biochem.l14.q5.h: Microsatellites slip when mismatches are not corrected.
med-premed-biochem.l14.q5.e: Lynch syndrome results from mismatch repair gene mutations. Defective homologous recombination is the BRCA mechanism and does not give microsatellite instability.

med-premed-biochem.l15.q1.p: Which of these is the start codon in mRNA?
med-premed-biochem.l15.q1.e: AUG initiates translation and codes methionine. UAA and UGA are stop codons.

med-premed-biochem.l15.q2.p: A template strand 3-prime TACGGATTT 5-prime is transcribed and translated. What peptide results?
med-premed-biochem.l15.q2.h: Write the complementary mRNA, then read codons.
med-premed-biochem.l15.q2.e: The mRNA is 5-prime AUGCCUAAA, which reads Met-Pro-Lys. The third codon is AAA, which codes lysine, so no stop codon is read in frame.

med-premed-biochem.l15.q3.p: Which antibiotic class blocks entry of aminoacyl-tRNA into the A site of the bacterial 30S subunit?
med-premed-biochem.l15.q3.e: Tetracyclines bind the 30S subunit and block tRNA entry. Macrolides and chloramphenicol act on the 50S subunit.

med-premed-biochem.l15.q4.t: A premature stop codon truncates the protein
med-premed-biochem.l15.q4.p: What is the effect of a nonsense mutation?
med-premed-biochem.l15.q4.e: A nonsense mutation creates UAA, UAG or UGA early. Replacement of one residue is a missense mutation.

med-premed-biochem.l15.q5.t: Eukaryotic RNA polymerase II, inhibited by alpha-amanitin
med-premed-biochem.l15.q5.p: A 61-year-old forager develops vomiting and diarrhoea 12 hours after eating wild mushrooms, apparently improves, then develops jaundice and rising transaminases. Which molecular target explains the toxin?
med-premed-biochem.l15.q5.h: A death cap mushroom toxin blocks mRNA synthesis.
med-premed-biochem.l15.q5.e: Alpha-amanitin inhibits RNA polymerase II, causing hepatocyte death. Diphtheria toxin is the one that modifies elongation factor 2.

med-premed-biochem.l16.q1.p: In the lac operon, which condition gives maximal expression?
med-premed-biochem.l16.q1.h: Needs both the inducer and cyclic AMP.
med-premed-biochem.l16.q1.e: Allolactose releases the repressor and low glucose raises cAMP, activating CAP. With glucose present, expression is low even with lactose.

med-premed-biochem.l16.q2.p: If cystic fibrosis affects 1 in 2500 people, what is the approximate carrier frequency by Hardy-Weinberg?
med-premed-biochem.l16.q2.e: q = 0.02, so 2pq is about 0.039, close to 1 in 25. One in 50 is q, the allele frequency.

med-premed-biochem.l16.q3.t: An in-frame three-base deletion that removes one phenylalanine
med-premed-biochem.l16.q3.p: Which change describes the usual cystic fibrosis mutation, F508del?
med-premed-biochem.l16.q3.h: Three bases are a whole codon.
med-premed-biochem.l16.q3.e: Deleting three bases removes one amino acid without shifting the frame, but the protein misfolds. A repeat expansion is the mechanism of Huntington disease.

med-premed-biochem.l16.q4.t: It loosens chromatin and increases transcription
med-premed-biochem.l16.q4.p: What is the usual effect of histone acetylation on transcription?
med-premed-biochem.l16.q4.h: Acetylation neutralises positive charge on histones.
med-premed-biochem.l16.q4.e: Reduced histone-DNA attraction opens chromatin. Deacetylation has the opposite effect.

med-premed-biochem.l16.q5.t: Genomic imprinting, in which only one parental copy of the region is normally expressed
med-premed-biochem.l16.q5.p: A newborn has hypotonia and poor feeding, later developing hyperphagia and obesity. Testing shows a deletion on the paternally inherited chromosome 15q11-q13. Which concept best explains why the same deletion on the maternal chromosome causes a different syndrome?
med-premed-biochem.l16.q5.e: Imprinting makes the region functionally haploid, so the missing parental allele determines the syndrome (Prader-Willi from paternal loss, Angelman from maternal). Mitochondrial inheritance is maternal but does not explain a chromosome 15 deletion.

med-premed-chem.l01.q1.p: Which quantum number determines the shape of an orbital (s, p, d or f)?
med-premed-chem.l01.q1.h: Shape letters s, p, d, f correspond to l = 0, 1, 2, 3.
med-premed-chem.l01.q1.e: The azimuthal number l sets the subshell shape. The principal number n sets the shell and mainly the size and energy, not the shape.

med-premed-chem.l01.q2.t: Atomic radius decreases as effective nuclear charge increases
med-premed-chem.l01.q2.p: Moving from left to right across a period, which change is expected for main-group elements?
med-premed-chem.l01.q2.h: Think about protons added without a new shell.
med-premed-chem.l01.q2.e: Adding protons across a period raises Z_eff while the shell stays the same, pulling electrons in. New shells are added only down a group, which is why the radius-increase option is wrong.

med-premed-chem.l01.q3.t: [Ar] 3d6, because the 4s electrons are lost first
med-premed-chem.l01.q3.p: What is the ground-state electron configuration of the Fe2+ ion (Z = 26)?
med-premed-chem.l01.q3.h: Neutral iron is [Ar] 4s2 3d6; which electrons leave first?
med-premed-chem.l01.q3.e: Transition metals lose their outermost 4s electrons before 3d electrons, giving 3d6. Removing 3d electrons first would incorrectly give 4s2 3d4.

med-premed-chem.l01.q4.t: One eighth, since three half-lives have elapsed
med-premed-chem.l01.q4.p: A PET isotope has a half-life of 110 minutes. What fraction of its activity remains after 330 minutes?
med-premed-chem.l01.q4.h: Count how many half-lives fit into the elapsed time.
med-premed-chem.l01.q4.e: 330 / 110 = 3 half-lives, so the fraction is (1/2)^3 = 1/8. Decay is exponential, not linear, so dividing by 3 is wrong.

med-premed-chem.l01.q5.t: About 100 MBq remains because two half-lives elapsed, so a nearby cyclotron site reduces wasted activity
med-premed-chem.l01.q5.p: A 58-year-old man is to have a PET-CT. The 18F-labelled tracer (half-life about 110 min) is delivered with 400 MBq of activity at the calibration time and injected 220 minutes later. Which statement is correct?
med-premed-chem.l01.q5.h: Two half-lives; apply exponential decay twice.
med-premed-chem.l01.q5.e: 220 min is two half-lives, so 400 to 200 to 100 MBq; short half-lives favour nearby production. The linear-decay option is wrong because decay is exponential.

med-premed-chem.l02.q1.t: Trigonal pyramidal, with one lone pair on nitrogen
med-premed-chem.l02.q1.p: Which molecular geometry does ammonia (NH3) have, according to VSEPR theory?
med-premed-chem.l02.q1.h: Count both bonds and lone pairs: four domains.
med-premed-chem.l02.q1.e: Nitrogen has three bonds and one lone pair, giving a pyramidal shape. A true tetrahedral shape requires four bonded atoms, as in methane.

med-premed-chem.l02.q2.t: Its linear shape makes the two bond dipoles cancel each other
med-premed-chem.l02.q2.p: Why is carbon dioxide a nonpolar molecule even though each C=O bond is polar?
med-premed-chem.l02.q2.h: Think about vector sums of dipoles.
med-premed-chem.l02.q2.e: In a linear molecule equal dipoles point opposite ways and cancel. The bent shape is water, where dipoles add up.

med-premed-chem.l02.q3.t: Resonance gives the C-N bond partial double-bond character
med-premed-chem.l02.q3.p: What explains the planar, rigid character of the peptide bond between two amino acids?
med-premed-chem.l02.q3.h: Consider delocalisation of the nitrogen lone pair into the carbonyl.
med-premed-chem.l02.q3.e: Delocalisation shortens and stiffens the C-N bond, so the six atoms lie in one plane. The bond is not a full double bond, and an sp3 nitrogen would allow free rotation.

med-premed-chem.l02.q4.t: sp2, with trigonal planar geometry around the carbon
med-premed-chem.l02.q4.p: What is the hybridisation of a carbonyl carbon in a ketone?
med-premed-chem.l02.q4.h: Count the electron domains: C=O plus two single bonds.
med-premed-chem.l02.q4.e: Three domains give sp2 and 120 degree angles. sp3 would apply only if the carbon had four single bonds.

med-premed-chem.l02.q5.t: X dissolves better in water through hydrogen bonding, while Y crosses lipid membranes more easily
med-premed-chem.l02.q5.p: Two drug candidates have similar molar mass. Candidate X carries three hydroxyl groups and a primary amine, while candidate Y is a mostly hydrocarbon with one ether oxygen. Which prediction is most reasonable?
med-premed-chem.l02.q5.h: Match like-dissolves-like to the functional groups.
med-premed-chem.l02.q5.e: Hydroxyl and amine groups hydrogen bond with water, while a hydrocarbon prefers lipid. Hydroxyl groups are polar, so the statement that they are nonpolar is wrong.

med-premed-chem.l03.q1.t: The number of moles of solute is unchanged by dilution
med-premed-chem.l03.q1.p: Which principle is used in the dilution equation C1 x V1 = C2 x V2?
med-premed-chem.l03.q1.h: Adding solvent changes concentration, not the amount of solute.
med-premed-chem.l03.q1.e: Only solvent is added, so moles of solute stay constant. Total volume rises, so volume is not conserved.

med-premed-chem.l03.q2.t: 25 mL of the stock, diluted up to 250 mL
med-premed-chem.l03.q2.p: What volume of 2.0 M stock is needed to prepare 250 mL of 0.20 M solution?
med-premed-chem.l03.q2.e: V1 = 0.20 x 250 / 2.0 = 25 mL. Using 50 mL would give 0.40 M, which would result from a dilution factor of 5, not 10.

med-premed-chem.l03.q3.p: Normal saline contains 9.0 g of NaCl (58.44 g/mol) per litre. About how many mmol of Na+ are present per litre?
med-premed-chem.l03.q3.h: Convert grams to moles; one Na+ per formula unit.
med-premed-chem.l03.q3.e: One formula unit yields one Na+, so 154 mmol/L. The figure 308 is the osmolarity, counting both Na+ and Cl-.

med-premed-chem.l03.q4.t: 2.61 g, from 0.0145 mol at a 1:1 ratio
med-premed-chem.l03.q4.p: Using 2.00 g of salicylic acid (138.12 g/mol) with excess acetic anhydride, the theoretical yield of aspirin (180.16 g/mol) is closest to which value?
med-premed-chem.l03.q4.h: Mass to moles, apply 1:1, then moles to mass.
med-premed-chem.l03.q4.e: 0.01448 mol x 180.16 = 2.61 g. Mass of one reactant alone does not equal product mass, because the product incorporates an acetyl group.

med-premed-chem.l03.q5.t: The glucose is metabolised, leaving free water that dilutes plasma sodium despite an isotonic bag
med-premed-chem.l03.q5.p: A 70-year-old woman recovering from surgery receives several litres of 5% dextrose in water and develops a serum sodium of 124 mmol/L. Which chemical explanation fits best?
med-premed-chem.l03.q5.h: Think about what remains after the solute is consumed.
med-premed-chem.l03.q5.e: Once glucose is metabolised only water remains, which dilutes sodium. Glucose is not ionic, and the bag is roughly isotonic, not hypertonic.

med-premed-chem.l04.q1.p: Under which condition is a reaction spontaneous at constant temperature and pressure?
med-premed-chem.l04.q1.h: Gibbs free energy combines enthalpy and entropy.
med-premed-chem.l04.q1.e: A negative delta G means the process is favourable. A negative delta H alone is not enough because the T delta S term may outweigh it.

med-premed-chem.l04.q2.t: Above 250 K, where T delta S exceeds delta H
med-premed-chem.l04.q2.p: A process has delta H = +20 kJ/mol and delta S = +80 J/mol K. At what temperature does it become spontaneous?
med-premed-chem.l04.q2.h: Set delta G = 0 and solve, keeping units consistent.
med-premed-chem.l04.q2.e: T = 20 / 0.080 = 250 K; above that the entropy term outweighs the enthalpy. A positive delta H means low temperatures stay nonspontaneous.

med-premed-chem.l04.q3.p: A reaction has delta G degrees = -5.7 kJ/mol at 298 K. What is its equilibrium constant, approximately?
med-premed-chem.l04.q3.h: Use delta G degrees = -RT ln K.
med-premed-chem.l04.q3.e: ln K = 5700 / (8.314 x 298) = 2.3 so K is about 10. A negative delta G degrees means K is greater than 1, so 0.1 cannot be right.

med-premed-chem.l04.q4.t: The net delta G of the coupled pair is negative
med-premed-chem.l04.q4.p: Why can an endergonic reaction proceed in a cell when coupled to ATP hydrolysis?
med-premed-chem.l04.q4.h: Free energy changes of coupled reactions add.
med-premed-chem.l04.q4.e: The sum of the two delta G values is what decides the direction. Coupling does not alter the equilibrium constant of the individual step.

med-premed-chem.l04.q5.t: It stays folded, with delta G (unfolding) near +28 kJ/mol and melting near 333 K
med-premed-chem.l04.q5.p: A small protein unfolds with delta H = +400 kJ/mol and delta S = +1.2 kJ/mol K. At body temperature (310 K), which outcome is predicted, and what is the melting temperature?
med-premed-chem.l04.q5.h: Compute delta G = delta H - T delta S, then find T where it is zero.
med-premed-chem.l04.q5.e: delta G = 400 - 310 x 1.2 = +28 kJ/mol, so unfolding is unfavourable at 310 K; Tm = 400 / 1.2 = 333 K. A negative value would apply only above that temperature.

med-premed-chem.l05.q1.t: By experiment, for example from initial-rate data
med-premed-chem.l05.q1.p: How is the order of a reaction with respect to a reactant determined?
med-premed-chem.l05.q1.e: Reaction orders must be measured. Coefficients match orders only for a true elementary step, so they cannot be read directly for the overall reaction.

med-premed-chem.l05.q2.p: A drug follows first-order elimination with a half-life of 6 hours. What percentage of the dose remains after 24 hours?
med-premed-chem.l05.q2.h: Count half-lives, then halve each time.
med-premed-chem.l05.q2.e: 24 / 6 = 4 half-lives, so (1/2)^4 = 6.25%. Twenty-five percent would apply after only two half-lives.

med-premed-chem.l05.q3.p: Doubling [A] doubles the rate and doubling [B] quadruples the rate. Which rate law fits?
med-premed-chem.l05.q3.h: Exponent = log2 of the rate change.
med-premed-chem.l05.q3.e: A factor of 2 gives order 1, and a factor of 4 gives order 2. The option with squared A reverses the two reactants.

med-premed-chem.l05.q4.t: It lowers the activation energy and leaves K and delta G unchanged
med-premed-chem.l05.q4.p: What is the effect of adding a catalyst to a reaction?
med-premed-chem.l05.q4.h: A catalyst alters the path, not the endpoints.
med-premed-chem.l05.q4.e: Catalysts speed forward and reverse steps equally, so equilibrium is reached sooner but not shifted. They do not change delta G.

med-premed-chem.l05.q5.t: About 18 hours, as three half-lives are required
med-premed-chem.l05.q5.p: A 45-year-old man is admitted after an overdose of a drug cleared by first-order kinetics with a half-life of 6 hours. The plasma level is 80 mg/L and will be treated when it falls to 10 mg/L. About how long will this take without intervention?
med-premed-chem.l05.q5.h: From 80 to 10 is how many halvings?
med-premed-chem.l05.q5.e: 80 to 40 to 20 to 10 is three halvings, so 18 hours. Zero-order elimination would give a linear fall instead, which is not what this drug does.

med-premed-chem.l06.q1.t: The reaction proceeds toward products until Q equals K
med-premed-chem.l06.q1.p: If the reaction quotient Q is smaller than K, what happens?
med-premed-chem.l06.q1.h: Compare current ratio with the equilibrium ratio.
med-premed-chem.l06.q1.e: A small Q means too little product, so the net change is forward. K itself is fixed unless temperature changes.

med-premed-chem.l06.q2.p: H2 + I2 giving 2 HI has K = 50. Starting with 1.0 M H2 and 1.0 M I2 only, what is the equilibrium [HI]?
med-premed-chem.l06.q2.h: Set up an ICE table; HI equals 2x.
med-premed-chem.l06.q2.e: x = 0.78, so [HI] = 2x = 1.56 M. The value 0.78 is x itself, not the HI concentration, and 0.22 M is the leftover H2.

med-premed-chem.l06.q3.p: Which change alters the numerical value of an equilibrium constant?
med-premed-chem.l06.q3.h: K is fixed for a given reaction at a given condition.
med-premed-chem.l06.q3.e: Only temperature changes K. Concentration and pressure shifts move the position, and a catalyst leaves K unchanged.

med-premed-chem.l06.q4.t: The common ion Cl- shifts the dissolution equilibrium toward solid AgCl
med-premed-chem.l06.q4.p: Why does adding NaCl to a saturated silver chloride solution lower the dissolved silver?
med-premed-chem.l06.q4.h: Apply Le Chatelier to the dissolution equilibrium.
med-premed-chem.l06.q4.e: Extra Cl- raises Q above Ksp, so AgCl precipitates. Ksp itself stays constant at fixed temperature.

med-premed-chem.l06.q5.t: Exhaled CO2 lowers dissolved CO2, so H+ is consumed as the equilibrium shifts toward CO2 and water
med-premed-chem.l06.q5.p: A 22-year-old woman has a panic attack, breathing rapidly, with tingling in her lips and hands and an arterial pH of 7.52. Which equilibrium reasoning best explains the pH change?
med-premed-chem.l06.q5.h: Removing CO2 pulls the carbonic acid equilibrium in one direction.
med-premed-chem.l06.q5.e: Loss of CO2 pulls H2CO3 and H+ down, producing respiratory alkalosis. The bicarbonate is not raised by CO2 loss, so options relying on that are wrong.

med-premed-chem.l07.q1.p: What is the pH of a 0.010 M solution of the strong acid HCl?
med-premed-chem.l07.q1.e: [H+] = 0.010 M, so pH = 2. The value 12 would be pOH.

med-premed-chem.l07.q2.p: What is the approximate pH of 0.10 M acetic acid (Ka = 1.8 x 10^-5)?
med-premed-chem.l07.q2.h: Solve x squared = Ka x concentration.
med-premed-chem.l07.q2.e: x = sqrt(1.8 x 10^-6) = 1.3 x 10^-3 M. Taking [H+] as the full 0.10 M would treat it as a strong acid.

med-premed-chem.l07.q3.t: Protonated and uncharged, with about 3% ionised
med-premed-chem.l07.q3.p: At a pH 1.5 units below its pKa, a weak acid is mostly in which form?
med-premed-chem.l07.q3.e: 10^-1.5 is about 0.03, so the uncharged form dominates. A half and half split occurs only at pH equal to pKa.

med-premed-chem.l07.q4.t: It equals Kw, which is 1.0 x 10^-14 at 25 degrees C
med-premed-chem.l07.q4.p: Why does the Ka times Kb product for a conjugate pair equal a fixed number?
med-premed-chem.l07.q4.e: Summing the acid and base reactions gives the autoionisation of water, so Ka x Kb = Kw. The number 7 is the neutral pH, not a constant.

med-premed-chem.l07.q5.t: It increases the ionised fraction of salicylate in the tubule, which reduces reabsorption and speeds excretion
med-premed-chem.l07.q5.p: A 19-year-old presents with tinnitus, rapid breathing and vomiting after taking an unknown number of aspirin tablets. Why is intravenous sodium bicarbonate given to raise urine pH?
med-premed-chem.l07.q5.h: Charged species cannot easily diffuse back across membranes.
med-premed-chem.l07.q5.e: Salicylate is a weak acid, and a higher urine pH favours the charged form that is trapped in the urine. A pKa is a fixed property of a molecule and is not changed by pH.

med-premed-chem.l08.q1.t: Within about one unit of its pKa
med-premed-chem.l08.q1.p: Over what pH range is a buffer most effective?
med-premed-chem.l08.q1.h: The ratio of base to acid should be near one.
med-premed-chem.l08.q1.e: Effectiveness is best when the ratio lies between roughly 1:10 and 10:1, which is about plus or minus one pH unit from pKa.

med-premed-chem.l08.q2.p: An acetate buffer has 0.20 M acetate and 0.10 M acetic acid (pKa 4.76). What is its pH?
med-premed-chem.l08.q2.e: log(2) = 0.30, so 4.76 + 0.30 = 5.06. A pH of 4.46 would result if the ratio were inverted.

med-premed-chem.l08.q3.t: The pH equals the pKa of the acid
med-premed-chem.l08.q3.p: At the half-equivalence point of a weak acid titration with strong base, which statement is true?
med-premed-chem.l08.q3.h: Half of the acid has been converted to conjugate base.
med-premed-chem.l08.q3.e: [A-] equals [HA], so the log term is zero and pH = pKa. The pH is 7 at equivalence only for a strong acid with a strong base.

med-premed-chem.l08.q4.p: Plasma has HCO3- of 24 mmol/L and PCO2 of 40 mmHg. Using pKa 6.1 and a solubility factor of 0.03, what is the pH?
med-premed-chem.l08.q4.h: 0.03 x 40 gives dissolved CO2; the ratio is 20.
med-premed-chem.l08.q4.e: 24 / 1.2 = 20 and log 20 = 1.30, so pH = 7.40. The value 6.10 would result if the ratio were 1.

med-premed-chem.l08.q5.t: Metabolic acidosis, since the low bicarbonate gives a ratio of 10 and a pH of about 7.10
med-premed-chem.l08.q5.p: A 30-year-old woman with poorly controlled type 1 diabetes has deep rapid breathing, glucose 480 mg/dL, arterial pH 7.10 and HCO3- 12 mmol/L with PCO2 initially at 40 mmHg. Which interpretation fits the buffer equation?
med-premed-chem.l08.q5.h: Compute HCO3- over 0.03 x PCO2, then take the log.
med-premed-chem.l08.q5.e: 12 / 1.2 = 10, so pH = 6.1 + 1 = 7.10, indicating a primary metabolic acidosis. The rapid breathing is compensation, not the cause, so respiratory alkalosis is wrong.

med-premed-chem.l09.q1.t: At the anode, with electrons flowing toward the cathode
med-premed-chem.l09.q1.p: In a galvanic cell, where does oxidation occur and which way do electrons flow in the external wire?
med-premed-chem.l09.q1.h: An ox and a red cat.
med-premed-chem.l09.q1.e: Oxidation happens at the anode and the electrons travel through the wire to the cathode where reduction occurs. The reverse assignment describes an electrolytic cell mislabelled.

med-premed-chem.l09.q2.p: A Zn-Cu cell has E degrees = +1.10 V and n = 2. What is delta G degrees (F = 96,485 C/mol)?
med-premed-chem.l09.q2.e: -2 x 96,485 x 1.10 = -212 kJ/mol. A positive sign would mean a non-spontaneous cell, which is incompatible with a positive potential.

med-premed-chem.l09.q3.p: Which expression gives the equilibrium potential of potassium with 4 mM outside and 140 mM inside at 37 degrees C?
med-premed-chem.l09.q3.h: Outside over inside for a cation, with log10.
med-premed-chem.l09.q3.e: Using outside over inside for K+ gives a negative potential, near -95 mV. Inverting the ratio gives the wrong sign.

med-premed-chem.l09.q4.t: A strongly exergonic transfer that releases energy used for proton pumping
med-premed-chem.l09.q4.p: In the mitochondrial chain electrons flow from NADH (about -0.32 V) to oxygen (about +0.82 V). What does this large positive difference indicate?
med-premed-chem.l09.q4.h: Positive potential difference means negative delta G.
med-premed-chem.l09.q4.e: delta E of 1.14 V gives about -220 kJ/mol, which is spontaneous. Oxygen is the reduced species, so the oxidation statement is reversed.

med-premed-chem.l09.q5.t: E_K rises from about -95 mV to about -80 mV, depolarising the membrane
med-premed-chem.l09.q5.p: A 68-year-old man with kidney failure has serum potassium of 7.0 mmol/L and peaked T waves on ECG. Assuming 140 mM intracellular potassium, what does the Nernst equation predict about E_K (37 degrees C)?
med-premed-chem.l09.q5.h: Raising the outside concentration changes the ratio inside to outside.
med-premed-chem.l09.q5.e: log(7/140) = -1.30, giving about -80 mV, so the cell is less negative. Hyperpolarisation would need a lower extracellular potassium.

med-premed-chem.l10.q1.t: Six, from the ring and its pi bonds plus two carbonyls
med-premed-chem.l10.q1.p: How many degrees of unsaturation does aspirin (C9H8O4) have?
med-premed-chem.l10.q1.e: (18 + 2 - 8) / 2 = 6. Four comes from the ring alone and ignores the carbonyls, while oxygen atoms do not count.

med-premed-chem.l10.q2.p: Which compound is the strongest acid?
med-premed-chem.l10.q2.e: Carboxylate resonance makes acetic acid by far the most acidic of the four. Phenol is less acidic because its conjugate base spreads charge less efficiently.

med-premed-chem.l10.q3.p: What is the IUPAC name of CH3CH2CH(OH)CH3?
med-premed-chem.l10.q3.h: Number from the end that gives OH the lowest locant.
med-premed-chem.l10.q3.e: The hydroxyl is on carbon 2 when numbered from the nearer end. Butan-3-ol breaks the lowest-locant rule.

med-premed-chem.l10.q4.p: At physiological pH 7.4 an alkylamine drug with a conjugate-acid pKa of 10 will be predominantly which form?
med-premed-chem.l10.q4.h: Compare pH with pKa of the ammonium form.
med-premed-chem.l10.q4.e: pH is far below the pKa, so protonation dominates, about 400-fold. Equal amounts would need pH equal to pKa.

med-premed-chem.l10.q5.t: Convert the acid to an ester prodrug that is hydrolysed in the body to the active acid
med-premed-chem.l10.q5.p: A formulation team wants better oral absorption for a carboxylic acid drug that is poorly absorbed because it is ionised in the gut. Which strategy follows from the organic chemistry?
med-premed-chem.l10.q5.h: Mask the charge, then unmask it later.
med-premed-chem.l10.q5.e: The neutral ester crosses membranes and esterases regenerate the acid. Salts and quaternary ammoniums are permanently charged and cross membranes poorly.

med-premed-chem.l11.q1.p: What is the relationship between two non-superimposable mirror-image molecules?
med-premed-chem.l11.q1.h: Think of left and right hands.
med-premed-chem.l11.q1.e: Enantiomers are mirror images that cannot be superimposed. Diastereomers are stereoisomers that are not mirror images.

med-premed-chem.l11.q2.p: Open-chain glucose has four stereocentres. How many stereoisomers does this give?
med-premed-chem.l11.q2.e: 2^4 = 16 stereoisomers. The value 8 would apply to three stereocentres.

med-premed-chem.l11.q3.t: It has stereocentres but is achiral because of an internal mirror plane
med-premed-chem.l11.q3.p: Which statement about meso-tartaric acid is correct?
med-premed-chem.l11.q3.e: An internal plane of symmetry cancels the chirality. A racemic mixture is a physical mix of two compounds, which is different.

med-premed-chem.l11.q4.p: In the CIP ranking of lactic acid, which order of priorities is correct from highest to lowest?
med-premed-chem.l11.q4.h: Rank by atomic number at the first point of difference.
med-premed-chem.l11.q4.e: Oxygen outranks carbon, and the COOH carbon (O, O, O) outranks the methyl carbon (H, H, H). Hydrogen is always lowest.

med-premed-chem.l11.q5.t: The chiral binding site forms diastereomeric complexes with the two enantiomers, with different energies
med-premed-chem.l11.q5.p: A racemic drug is found to have one enantiomer that binds a receptor with high affinity and a mirror-image enantiomer that binds only weakly. Which explanation is most accurate?
med-premed-chem.l11.q5.h: Receptors are made of chiral amino acids.
med-premed-chem.l11.q5.e: A chiral site discriminates by 3-D fit, so each enantiomer forms a complex of different energy. Enantiomers have identical connectivity and mass, which rules out the other options.

med-premed-chem.l12.q1.t: A single concerted step with inversion of configuration
med-premed-chem.l12.q1.p: Which feature describes an SN2 reaction?
med-premed-chem.l12.q1.e: SN2 is concerted with Walden inversion. The other options describe SN1 behaviour.

med-premed-chem.l12.q2.p: What is the major product stereochemistry when (R)-2-bromobutane reacts with hydroxide by SN2?
med-premed-chem.l12.q2.h: Backside attack inverts, and the priority order stays the same.
med-premed-chem.l12.q2.e: Inversion converts R into S since OH replaces Br at the top priority. A racemate would suggest SN1.

med-premed-chem.l12.q3.t: A strong bulky base with a secondary or tertiary alkyl halide
med-premed-chem.l12.q3.e: Strong bases remove beta protons in a concerted step, especially from hindered substrates. Weak nucleophile conditions favour SN1 and E1 instead.

med-premed-chem.l12.q4.t: Steric hindrance blocks backside attack at the carbon
med-premed-chem.l12.q4.p: Why does a tertiary alkyl halide not undergo SN2 readily?
med-premed-chem.l12.q4.h: Count the groups around the carbon.
med-premed-chem.l12.q4.e: Three alkyl groups shield the back of the carbon. A carbocation is stable at a tertiary carbon, which is why SN1 works.

med-premed-chem.l12.q5.t: Intramolecular displacement of chloride by nitrogen gives a strained aziridinium ion that guanine N7 attacks
med-premed-chem.l12.q5.p: A bis(2-chloroethyl)amine chemotherapy agent is found to react with DNA far faster than 1-chlorobutane does under the same conditions. Which mechanism best explains this?
med-premed-chem.l12.q5.h: Think of neighbouring-group participation by the lone pair on nitrogen.
med-premed-chem.l12.q5.e: The nitrogen lone pair makes an aziridinium ion, a strained and highly electrophilic species attacked at guanine N7. A primary carbocation would be too unstable to form.

med-premed-chem.l13.q1.p: Which carbonyl derivative is the least reactive toward nucleophilic acyl substitution?
med-premed-chem.l13.q1.h: Think about nitrogen lone pair resonance.
med-premed-chem.l13.q1.e: The nitrogen lone pair donates strongly into the carbonyl, making amides the least reactive. Acyl chlorides are the most reactive of the derivatives.

med-premed-chem.l13.q2.p: What type of functional group forms when the C1 aldehyde of glucose reacts with its own C5 hydroxyl group?
med-premed-chem.l13.q2.h: One alcohol added to an aldehyde.
med-premed-chem.l13.q2.e: One alcohol adding to the aldehyde gives a hemiacetal, and a second alcohol later makes the acetal as in a glycosidic bond. Imines require an amine.

med-premed-chem.l13.q3.t: The conjugate enolate is stabilised by resonance onto oxygen
med-premed-chem.l13.q3.p: Why is the proton alpha to a ketone carbonyl relatively acidic (pKa about 19)?
med-premed-chem.l13.q3.e: Delocalisation of the negative charge onto oxygen stabilises the enolate. Donation of electrons would make the hydrogen less, not more, acidic.

med-premed-chem.l13.q4.t: The strained amide acylates an active-site serine and blocks the enzyme
med-premed-chem.l13.q4.p: What is the mechanism of the beta-lactam ring in penicillin against bacterial transpeptidases?
med-premed-chem.l13.q4.h: Acyl substitution with a strained ring.
med-premed-chem.l13.q4.e: Ring strain makes the beta-lactam a reactive acylating agent that forms a covalent acyl-enzyme. Ribosome binding describes other antibiotic classes.

med-premed-chem.l13.q5.t: It hydrolyses the beta-lactam amide bond, opening the ring and removing the acylating ability
med-premed-chem.l13.q5.p: A 6-year-old with a bacterial infection fails to respond to amoxicillin, and the isolate carries a plasmid for a beta-lactamase. Which chemical change does the enzyme perform on the drug?
med-premed-chem.l13.q5.h: The enzyme destroys the reactive bond.
med-premed-chem.l13.q5.e: Beta-lactamases hydrolyse the strained amide so the drug cannot acylate the target. A methylated carboxylate would not account for loss of the reactive ring.

med-premed-chem.l14.q1.t: A strong band between 1650 and 1750 cm^-1
med-premed-chem.l14.q1.p: Which IR absorption is the most characteristic sign of a carbonyl group?
med-premed-chem.l14.q1.h: C=O stretches sit in the double-bond region.
med-premed-chem.l14.q1.e: C=O gives a strong stretch in the 1650 to 1750 region. The broad 3200 to 3600 band is O-H and the 2200 band is C triple bond N or an alkyne.

med-premed-chem.l14.q2.p: In proton NMR, a signal for a CH2 group next to a CH3 group is split into how many lines?
med-premed-chem.l14.q2.h: The CH2 sees three neighbouring hydrogens.
med-premed-chem.l14.q2.e: The CH2 has three equivalent neighbours, giving n + 1 = 4 lines. The methyl group, with two neighbours, would be the triplet.

med-premed-chem.l14.q3.p: A solution has absorbance 0.60 at the chosen wavelength, with epsilon = 6000 M^-1 cm^-1 and a 1 cm cuvette. What is the concentration?
med-premed-chem.l14.q3.e: 0.60 / 6000 = 1.0 x 10^-4 M. A value of 3.6 x 10^3 results from multiplying instead of dividing.

med-premed-chem.l14.q4.p: A mass spectrum shows molecular ion peaks of nearly equal height at M and M+2. Which element is most likely present?
med-premed-chem.l14.q4.h: Natural isotopes of this element are roughly 50 to 50.
med-premed-chem.l14.q4.e: Bromine isotopes 79 and 81 occur in about a 1:1 ratio. Chlorine gives roughly a 3:1 pattern.

med-premed-chem.l14.q5.p: An unknown compound C4H8O2 has a strong IR band at 1740 cm^-1 and no broad O-H band. Its proton NMR shows a 3H triplet at 1.2 ppm, a 3H singlet at 2.0 ppm and a 2H quartet at 4.1 ppm. Which is the structure?
med-premed-chem.l14.q5.h: The quartet near 4.1 ppm means CH2 attached to oxygen.
med-premed-chem.l14.q5.e: The ethyl pattern with an OCH2 shift and a methyl singlet at 2.0 ppm fits ethyl acetate. Methyl propanoate would give a 3H singlet near 3.7 ppm.

med-premed-chem.l15.q1.t: It accepts a hydride ion from the carbon bearing oxygen
med-premed-chem.l15.q1.p: Which reaction type does NAD+ perform when it oxidises an alcohol dehydrogenase substrate?
med-premed-chem.l15.q1.e: NAD+ takes H- from the carbinol carbon and becomes NADH. Phosphate transfer is the job of kinases using ATP.

med-premed-chem.l15.q2.t: Poor sulfur-carbonyl resonance makes the thioester more electrophilic
med-premed-chem.l15.q2.p: Why is acetyl-CoA a better acyl donor than an ordinary alkyl acetate?
med-premed-chem.l15.q2.h: Compare orbital overlap of S with C.
med-premed-chem.l15.q2.e: Sulfur overlaps poorly with the carbonyl carbon, leaving it more electrophilic. Oxygen, not sulfur, is the more electronegative atom.

med-premed-chem.l15.q3.t: A beta-keto acid such as acetoacetate
med-premed-chem.l15.q3.p: Which compound undergoes facile decarboxylation by forming an enol intermediate?
med-premed-chem.l15.q3.e: A ketone beta to the carboxyl accepts the electrons as CO2 leaves. Simple acids lack such an electron sink.

med-premed-chem.l15.q4.t: It stabilises the negatively charged tetrahedral intermediate by hydrogen bonding
med-premed-chem.l15.q4.p: What is the role of the oxyanion hole in a serine protease?
med-premed-chem.l15.q4.h: It lowers the energy of the transition state.
med-premed-chem.l15.q4.e: Backbone NH groups hydrogen-bond the oxyanion. The histidine, not the hole, activates serine.

med-premed-chem.l15.q5.t: It inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase, blocking conversion of methanol to formaldehyde and formic acid
med-premed-chem.l15.q5.p: A 35-year-old man presents with visual blurring, anion gap metabolic acidosis and a history of drinking windshield washer fluid containing methanol. Why is fomepizole given?
med-premed-chem.l15.q5.h: The toxic products come from an oxidation.
med-premed-chem.l15.q5.e: Blocking alcohol dehydrogenase prevents formation of the toxic metabolites. Fomepizole is not a buffer, although bicarbonate is used separately for acidosis.

med-premed-chem.l16.q1.p: How many pi electrons does benzene have, and which rule makes it aromatic?
med-premed-chem.l16.q1.e: Benzene has six pi electrons, which equals 4n + 2 for n = 1. Four pi electrons would be antiaromatic if planar and cyclic.

med-premed-chem.l16.q2.p: Nitration of nitrobenzene gives mainly which product?
med-premed-chem.l16.q2.h: Nitro is a deactivating, meta-directing group.
med-premed-chem.l16.q2.e: The nitro group withdraws electrons and directs meta. Activating groups are the ones that direct ortho and para.

med-premed-chem.l16.q3.t: The pyridine lone pair is outside the pi system, while pyrrole uses its lone pair in aromaticity
med-premed-chem.l16.q3.p: Why is pyridine basic while pyrrole is essentially not basic at nitrogen?
med-premed-chem.l16.q3.h: Count pi electrons and ask where the lone pair sits.
med-premed-chem.l16.q3.e: Protonating pyrrole would destroy its aromatic sextet, whereas the pyridine lone pair is free in an sp2 orbital. Both rings are planar and aromatic.

med-premed-chem.l16.q4.t: A molecular mass of 500 or less
med-premed-chem.l16.q4.p: Which feature does Lipinski rule of five set as an approximate limit for oral drug-likeness?
med-premed-chem.l16.q4.h: The five rules relate to size, lipophilicity and hydrogen bonding.
med-premed-chem.l16.q4.e: Mass under about 500 is one of the thresholds, with log P under about 5. The other options exceed the limits.

med-premed-chem.l16.q5.t: Saturated conjugation pathways shunt drug to cytochrome P450 oxidation, forming NAPQI that depletes glutathione, which acetylcysteine replenishes
med-premed-chem.l16.q5.p: A 26-year-old woman presents 12 hours after ingesting a large quantity of acetaminophen, with nausea but a normal examination. Which mechanism explains how delayed liver injury occurs and why acetylcysteine helps?
med-premed-chem.l16.q5.h: Think of a reactive electrophile and a thiol-based scavenger.
med-premed-chem.l16.q5.e: Overdose saturates conjugation, so oxidation yields the electrophile NAPQI that glutathione normally detoxifies. Acetylcysteine restores glutathione rather than chelating the drug.

med-skills.l01.q1.t: Use an open-ended question and let the patient speak without interruption
med-skills.l01.q1.p: Which approach best begins a medical interview after greetings?
med-skills.l01.q1.h: The patient story comes before the checklist.
med-skills.l01.q1.e: Open-ended invitations elicit the patient narrative and the most important concerns. Closed questions at the start tend to narrow the story prematurely.

med-skills.l01.q2.t: Radiation, which describes whether the symptom travels to other areas
med-skills.l01.q2.p: Which element of OLDCARTS describes whether chest pain spreads to the jaw or arm?
med-skills.l01.q2.h: Think of where else the pain is felt.
med-skills.l01.q2.e: Spread to another site is radiation. Character is the quality of the pain, such as pressure or sharpness.

med-skills.l01.q3.t: Do you feel the room spinning, nearly faint, or unsteady on your feet?
med-skills.l01.q3.p: A patient says that he has been dizzy. Which follow-up question best clarifies the symptom?
med-skills.l01.q3.h: Dizzy can mean three very different things.
med-skills.l01.q3.e: Asking the patient to distinguish spinning, near-fainting and unsteadiness separates different mechanisms. The other options suggest a cause and lead the history.

med-skills.l01.q4.t: Setting an agenda early by asking what else she wanted to discuss
med-skills.l01.q4.p: A 45-year-old woman comes for fatigue. As the visit ends, with her hand on the door, she says she has been having thoughts of hurting herself. Which earlier step would most likely have surfaced this concern sooner?
med-skills.l01.q4.h: The major concern appeared at the end of the visit.
med-skills.l01.q4.e: Early agenda setting with repeated asking of anything else lets major concerns emerge up front. A longer review of systems does not guarantee her to raise a sensitive concern.

med-skills.l01.q5.t: Relief at rest with onset on exertion, a pattern typical of angina
med-skills.l01.q5.p: A 62-year-old man reports chest discomfort. He says it comes on when climbing stairs, feels like a heavy pressure, and goes away within five minutes of resting. He also says it does not change when he presses on his chest or takes a deep breath. Which feature of the history most strongly favors a cardiac cause?
med-skills.l01.q5.h: Think about the supply and demand relationship the history reveals.
med-skills.l01.q5.e: A predictable exertional trigger with relief at rest is the classic angina pattern. Lack of tenderness lowers the odds of a musculoskeletal cause but does not itself prove a cardiac one.

med-skills.l02.q1.t: To compare what the patient actually takes against the recorded list and resolve differences
med-skills.l02.q1.p: What is the purpose of medication reconciliation at transitions of care?
med-skills.l02.q1.h: It is a safety check on lists.
med-skills.l02.q1.e: Reconciliation resolves discrepancies between the actual and recorded regimens. Replacing the list without comparison would lose drugs the patient still takes.

med-skills.l02.q2.t: 30 pack-years, found by multiplying packs per day by years
med-skills.l02.q2.p: A patient smoked one and a half packs per day for 20 years. How many pack-years is this?
med-skills.l02.q2.h: Multiply packs per day by years.
med-skills.l02.q2.e: One and a half packs times 20 years equals 30 pack-years. Adding the two numbers has no meaning.

med-skills.l02.q3.t: To screen for symptoms the patient may not have mentioned across organ systems
med-skills.l02.q3.p: Which is the best use of the review of systems?
med-skills.l02.q3.h: It looks beyond the chief complaint.
med-skills.l02.q3.e: The ROS screens for unreported symptoms by system. Details of the main complaint belong in the HPI.

med-skills.l02.q4.t: Medication history including over-the-counter products, asked specifically
med-skills.l02.q4.p: A 70-year-old woman presents with confusion and constipation. Her chart lists amlodipine and metformin only. A careful history reveals that she began an over-the-counter sleep aid containing an anticholinergic antihistamine two weeks ago. Which step in the history was most important for identifying this?
med-skills.l02.q4.h: The chart did not list everything she takes.
med-skills.l02.q4.e: Asking specifically about non-prescription drugs revealed the offending agent. The chart list alone would have missed it.

med-skills.l02.q5.t: Explain confidentiality and its limits, then ask part of the history with the patient alone
med-skills.l02.q5.p: A 16-year-old girl comes with her mother for abdominal pain. The clinician wants to ask about sexual activity and safety at home. What is the most appropriate approach?
med-skills.l02.q5.h: Adolescents often disclose more when alone.
med-skills.l02.q5.e: Time alone with a clear explanation of confidentiality and its limits supports honest disclosure. Asking in front of the parent may suppress answers.

med-skills.l03.q1.t: A qualified medical interpreter, in person, by video or by phone
med-skills.l03.q1.p: Who is generally preferred as an interpreter in clinical encounters?
med-skills.l03.q1.h: Training matters for accuracy and confidentiality.
med-skills.l03.q1.e: Qualified interpreters reduce errors and protect confidentiality. Family members, especially children, are discouraged for those reasons.

med-skills.l03.q2.t: This sounds frightening. Can you tell me more about what worries you most?
med-skills.l03.q2.p: Which response best shows empathy to a patient who says she is terrified about her test result?
med-skills.l03.q2.h: Name the emotion and invite more.
med-skills.l03.q2.e: Naming the emotion and inviting elaboration is empathic. Immediate reassurance ignores what she is feeling.

med-skills.l03.q3.t: Check understanding by having the patient restate the plan in their own words
med-skills.l03.q3.p: The teach-back method is used to:
med-skills.l03.q3.h: It assesses how well the clinician explained.
med-skills.l03.q3.e: Teach-back tests whether the explanation worked by having the patient restate it. Providing a handout does not test understanding.

med-skills.l03.q4.t: List the options, explain benefits, harms and uncertainty, and explore his values
med-skills.l03.q4.p: A 55-year-old man with a small, slow-growing prostate abnormality is weighing options that each have different harms and benefits, and he says he is unsure what matters most. Which approach is best?
med-skills.l03.q4.h: The decision depends on his preferences as well as on facts.
med-skills.l03.q4.e: A preference-sensitive decision calls for shared decision making with options, harms, uncertainty and his values. Choosing for him would be paternalistic.

med-skills.l03.q5.t: Speak directly to the patient in short sentences and let the interpreter relay them
med-skills.l03.q5.p: During a visit using a telephone interpreter, a clinician keeps looking at the phone and asks the interpreter, "Does she take her medicine?" Which correction is most appropriate?
med-skills.l03.q5.h: The conversation is between clinician and patient.
med-skills.l03.q5.e: Addressing the patient directly in short sentences preserves the relationship and accuracy. Idioms and long compound questions raise the risk of error.

med-skills.l04.q1.t: Perception, in which the patient understanding of the situation is assessed
med-skills.l04.q1.p: In the SPIKES protocol, what does the P stand for?
med-skills.l04.q1.e: P is perception, assessing what the patient already understands. Setting covers the privacy arrangements.

med-skills.l04.q2.t: Cardiopulmonary resuscitation only, in the event of cardiac arrest
med-skills.l04.q2.p: A do-not-resuscitate order applies to which intervention?
med-skills.l04.q2.h: It is a narrow, specific order.
med-skills.l04.q2.e: A DNR order covers CPR only. It does not mean withholding other treatment, which is a common misunderstanding.

med-skills.l04.q3.t: It is a clinical judgment that is specific to a decision and a time
med-skills.l04.q3.p: Which statement about decision-making capacity is correct?
med-skills.l04.q3.e: Capacity is assessed clinically for each decision and can change. A court decides legal competence, and neither dementia nor refusal alone removes capacity.

med-skills.l04.q4.t: Ask what he understands about the scan and how much he wants to know
med-skills.l04.q4.p: A 38-year-old man in the clinic is told that his scan shows a mass. He looks stunned and asks, "Is it cancer?" The clinician has not yet learned what he understands. What is the most appropriate next step?
med-skills.l04.q4.h: Check perception and invitation before delivering news.
med-skills.l04.q4.e: SPIKES calls for assessing perception and invitation before sharing knowledge. Premature reassurance and withholding both fail to respect his need for honest, paced information.

med-skills.l04.q5.t: Respect her refusal, since she shows understanding, appreciation and reasoning
med-skills.l04.q5.p: A 76-year-old woman with mild dementia is offered a feeding tube after a stroke. She tells the team she understands that the tube would help her get nutrition, that without it she may weaken, and that she does not want it because she wants natural death. She repeats this consistently. Her daughter wants the tube placed. What is the best action?
med-skills.l04.q5.h: Dementia is not the same as lack of capacity.
med-skills.l04.q5.e: She meets the elements of capacity for this decision, so her informed refusal governs. A diagnosis of dementia alone does not transfer decisions to a relative.

med-skills.l05.q1.t: A falsely high reading, because more pressure is needed to occlude the artery
med-skills.l05.q1.p: A blood pressure cuff that is too small for the patient arm will most likely produce which result?
med-skills.l05.q1.h: Think about how much pressure it takes to compress the artery with a narrow bladder.
med-skills.l05.q1.e: An undersized cuff overestimates pressure. An oversized cuff underestimates it.

med-skills.l05.q2.t: Respiratory rate, which rises in many serious illnesses before others
med-skills.l05.q2.p: Which vital sign is often the earliest and most sensitive sign of acute deterioration?
med-skills.l05.q2.h: It is the one most often left uncounted.
med-skills.l05.q2.e: Tachypnea often precedes other changes in serious illness. Blood pressure usually falls late because of compensation.

med-skills.l05.q3.t: Carbon monoxide poisoning, in which carboxyhemoglobin is read as oxygenated
med-skills.l05.q3.p: Which condition can give a falsely normal pulse oximetry reading despite severe tissue hypoxia?
med-skills.l05.q3.h: The device cannot tell two hemoglobin forms apart.
med-skills.l05.q3.e: Carboxyhemoglobin is read as oxyhemoglobin, so saturation appears normal. Methemoglobinemia pushes readings toward about 85 percent instead.

med-skills.l05.q4.t: Orthostatic hypotension, with a minimal rise in heart rate that suggests a blunted reflex
med-skills.l05.q4.p: A 68-year-old man on a beta-blocker and an alpha-blocker for prostate symptoms feels faint on standing. Supine BP is 138/82 with HR 66. After three minutes standing, BP is 108/70 with HR 70. Which interpretation is best?
med-skills.l05.q4.h: Look at the size of the drop and at the heart rate response.
med-skills.l05.q4.e: The systolic drop exceeds 20 mm Hg and the heart rate barely changes, consistent with blunting by the beta-blocker. A normal compensatory response would raise the heart rate.

med-skills.l05.q5.t: White-coat hypertension, with elevated office readings and normal home readings
med-skills.l05.q5.p: A 45-year-old woman has a clinic reading of 148/94 on two visits, but home averages of 122/76 over a week. Which term describes this?
med-skills.l05.q5.h: The elevated readings appear only in the clinic.
med-skills.l05.q5.e: Elevated office but normal home values define white-coat hypertension. Masked hypertension is the reverse.

med-skills.l06.q1.t: Bilirubin, the pigment released from heme breakdown
med-skills.l06.q1.p: Scleral icterus indicates elevation of which substance?
med-skills.l06.q1.e: Icterus is bilirubin deposition. Carotenemia tints the skin but spares the sclera.

med-skills.l06.q2.t: A hard, painless, fixed node that has persisted for many weeks
med-skills.l06.q2.p: Which lymph node finding is most concerning for malignancy?
med-skills.l06.q2.h: Consistency, mobility and tenderness all matter.
med-skills.l06.q2.e: Hard, painless, fixed and persistent nodes raise concern for malignancy. Soft, tender, mobile nodes are usually reactive.

med-skills.l06.q3.t: Lung cancer and other chronic hypoxic conditions of the lungs
med-skills.l06.q3.p: Clubbing of the fingernails is associated with which condition?
med-skills.l06.q3.h: Think of chronic thoracic or hypoxic disease.
med-skills.l06.q3.e: Clubbing accompanies lung cancer, bronchiectasis and cyanotic heart disease. Spoon nails, or koilonychia, belong with iron deficiency.

med-skills.l06.q4.t: Raised intracranial pressure, which produces bilateral papilledema
med-skills.l06.q4.p: A 58-year-old man reports severe headache and blurred vision. Fundoscopy shows swollen optic discs with blurred margins in both eyes. Which condition does this most strongly suggest?
med-skills.l06.q4.h: Bilateral disc swelling is a sign of pressure.
med-skills.l06.q4.e: Bilateral disc swelling signals papilledema from raised intracranial pressure. Diabetic retinopathy would show hemorrhages and exudates rather than disc swelling.

med-skills.l06.q5.t: Thyroid ultrasound and measurement of thyrotropin, then further tests as findings dictate
med-skills.l06.q5.p: A 34-year-old woman has a 1.5 cm firm thyroid nodule that moves with swallowing. She is clinically euthyroid. Which next step best fits standard evaluation?
med-skills.l06.q5.h: A palpable nodule needs characterization before action.
med-skills.l06.q5.e: Ultrasound with a thyrotropin level is the standard first evaluation of a nodule. Most nodules are benign but a small share are malignant, so reassurance alone would be unsafe.

med-skills.l07.q1.t: S3, a low-pitched sound of rapid ventricular filling
med-skills.l07.q1.p: Which heart sound is heard in early diastole and often suggests volume overload in an older adult?
med-skills.l07.q1.h: It sounds like the word Kentucky in a gallop.
med-skills.l07.q1.e: S3 is early diastolic and signals volume overload or systolic dysfunction in adults. S4 is late diastolic, occurring just before S1.

med-skills.l07.q2.t: Mitral regurgitation, with backflow of blood into the left atrium
med-skills.l07.q2.p: A holosystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla is most characteristic of:
med-skills.l07.q2.h: Systolic timing and axillary radiation point to one valve.
med-skills.l07.q2.e: An apical holosystolic murmur radiating to the axilla indicates mitral regurgitation. Mitral stenosis is diastolic.

med-skills.l07.q3.t: Valsalva strain, which reduces venous return to the heart
med-skills.l07.q3.p: Which maneuver decreases the murmur of aortic stenosis but increases the murmur of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
med-skills.l07.q3.h: Reduced preload narrows the outflow tract in one condition.
med-skills.l07.q3.e: Valsalva reduces preload, which worsens dynamic outflow obstruction in HCM and lowers flow across a fixed stenosis. Squatting does the opposite.

med-skills.l07.q4.t: Heart failure with ventricular dilation, with elevated filling pressure
med-skills.l07.q4.p: A 70-year-old woman has exertional dyspnea and orthopnea. Examination shows jugular venous distension, bibasilar crackles, an S3, and a laterally displaced apex impulse. Which diagnosis best explains these findings?
med-skills.l07.q4.h: Combine neck veins, S3 and apex displacement.
med-skills.l07.q4.e: Elevated JVP, crackles, S3 and a displaced apex indicate heart failure with ventricular enlargement. Pulmonary fibrosis would not displace the apex or cause an S3.

med-skills.l07.q5.t: Pericarditis, with a friction rub from inflamed pericardial layers
med-skills.l07.q5.p: A 25-year-old man has fever, sharp chest pain that eases when he sits forward, and a scratchy three-component sound over the left sternal border. Blood pressure is normal and jugular veins are not distended. Which diagnosis fits?
med-skills.l07.q5.h: The sound is scratchy and positional pain eases when leaning forward.
med-skills.l07.q5.e: A pericardial friction rub with positional pain indicates pericarditis. Tamponade would show muffled sounds, hypotension and raised venous pressure, which are absent.

med-skills.l08.q1.t: Stony dull, as over fluid filling the pleural space
med-skills.l08.q1.p: Percussion over a large pleural effusion typically gives which note?
med-skills.l08.q1.e: Pleural fluid produces a stony dull percussion note. Hyperresonance suggests air, as in pneumothorax.

med-skills.l08.q2.t: Consolidated lung, which conducts vibrations better than air
med-skills.l08.q2.p: Tactile fremitus is most increased over:
med-skills.l08.q2.e: Consolidated lung transmits vibration well, so fremitus increases. Fluid or air in the pleural space reduces it.

med-skills.l08.q3.t: Wheezing from narrowed airways, as in asthma or COPD
med-skills.l08.q3.p: Diffuse high-pitched continuous expiratory sounds with a prolonged expiratory phase are typical of:
med-skills.l08.q3.h: Think of airway narrowing that is worse on exhalation.
med-skills.l08.q3.e: Expiratory wheeze with prolonged expiration indicates lower airway obstruction. Stridor is an inspiratory sound from the upper airway.

med-skills.l08.q4.t: Spontaneous pneumothorax, with hyperresonance and diminished breath sounds
med-skills.l08.q4.p: A 22-year-old tall thin man develops sudden left chest pain and breathlessness. The left chest is hyperresonant with decreased breath sounds and the trachea is central. His blood pressure and neck veins are normal. Which diagnosis is most likely?
med-skills.l08.q4.h: Tall, thin, young, sudden onset, hyperresonance.
med-skills.l08.q4.e: The habitus, abrupt onset and hyperresonant chest with decreased breath sounds indicate pneumothorax. An effusion would be dull to percussion.

med-skills.l08.q5.t: Perform needle decompression or finger thoracostomy without waiting for imaging
med-skills.l08.q5.p: A 60-year-old man after a fall has severe respiratory distress, absent breath sounds on the right, hyperresonance, distended neck veins, hypotension and a trachea deviated to the left. What is the best immediate action?
med-skills.l08.q5.h: This is a clinical diagnosis requiring immediate treatment.
med-skills.l08.q5.e: Tension pneumothorax is diagnosed clinically and treated at once by decompression. Waiting for imaging risks cardiovascular collapse.

med-skills.l09.q1.t: Palpation can alter bowel sounds and give a misleading impression
med-skills.l09.q1.p: Why is auscultation performed before palpation in the abdominal examination?
med-skills.l09.q1.h: Touching the abdomen can stimulate the bowel.
med-skills.l09.q1.e: Palpation can change bowel activity, so listening comes first. The other statements are not true.

med-skills.l09.q2.t: Rovsing sign, which suggests inflammation of the appendix
med-skills.l09.q2.p: Pain provoked by pressing the left lower quadrant and felt in the right lower quadrant is called:
med-skills.l09.q2.h: Pain at a site remote from the pressure.
med-skills.l09.q2.e: Rovsing sign refers pain to the right lower quadrant in appendicitis. Murphy sign relates to the gallbladder.

med-skills.l09.q3.t: Ascites, with free fluid moving to the dependent side
med-skills.l09.q3.p: Shifting dullness on abdominal percussion suggests which finding?
med-skills.l09.q3.h: The dull border moves when the patient rolls.
med-skills.l09.q3.e: Fluid shifts with position, changing the border of dullness. Gas in obstruction would give tympany.

med-skills.l09.q4.t: Malignant obstruction of the common bile duct, as in pancreatic cancer
med-skills.l09.q4.p: A 68-year-old woman has jaundice, weight loss and a palpable, nontender gallbladder. Which diagnosis is most strongly suggested?
med-skills.l09.q4.h: A distended gallbladder that does not hurt is a clue.
med-skills.l09.q4.e: Courvoisier sign points to malignant bile duct obstruction. With stones, chronic inflammation usually leaves a shrunken, scarred gallbladder that cannot distend.

med-skills.l09.q5.t: A positive obturator sign, supporting an inflamed appendix near the pelvic wall
med-skills.l09.q5.p: A 24-year-old man has fever and right lower quadrant pain. He has pain on passively rotating the flexed right hip inward, and rebound tenderness at McBurney point. Which interpretation fits best?
med-skills.l09.q5.e: Pain on internal rotation of the flexed hip is the obturator sign, supporting a pelvic appendix. No single negative sign rules out appendicitis.

med-skills.l10.q1.t: Flaccid weakness with atrophy, fasciculations and reduced reflexes
med-skills.l10.q1.p: A lower motor neuron lesion typically produces which finding?
med-skills.l10.q1.h: The final common pathway is damaged.
med-skills.l10.q1.e: Lower motor neuron lesions give flaccid weakness, atrophy, fasciculations and hyporeflexia. Spasticity and Babinski sign are upper motor neuron features.

med-skills.l10.q2.t: A left upper motor neuron lesion, such as a stroke affecting the cortex
med-skills.l10.q2.p: A patient with a right facial droop that spares the forehead most likely has:
med-skills.l10.q2.h: The forehead receives bilateral cortical input.
med-skills.l10.q2.e: Forehead sparing indicates an upper motor neuron lesion, and a left cortical lesion drops the right lower face. Bell palsy affects the forehead as well.

med-skills.l10.q3.t: Loss of proprioceptive input, a sensory ataxia from dorsal column disease
med-skills.l10.q3.p: A positive Romberg test, in which the patient is steady with eyes open but falls with eyes closed, indicates:
med-skills.l10.q3.h: Visual input compensates until it is removed.
med-skills.l10.q3.e: Romberg tests proprioception and visual compensation. A cerebellar lesion causes instability with eyes open as well.

med-skills.l10.q4.t: A lesion in the right internal capsule affecting corticospinal fibers
med-skills.l10.q4.p: A 65-year-old man has sudden left-sided weakness of the face, arm and leg with hyperreflexia and an upgoing left plantar response. Which lesion best explains this?
med-skills.l10.q4.h: The corticospinal tract crosses below the lesion site.
med-skills.l10.q4.e: The left body is controlled by the right hemisphere, and the compact capsule explains face, arm and leg weakness together. A left hemisphere lesion would cause right-sided signs.

med-skills.l10.q5.t: Right hemisection of the cord at about T10, a Brown-Sequard pattern
med-skills.l10.q5.p: A 30-year-old man has loss of vibration sense and weakness in the right leg, and loss of pain and temperature sensation in the left leg, both starting below the level of T10. Which lesion is most consistent?
med-skills.l10.q5.h: Dorsal column and corticospinal signs are ipsilateral; spinothalamic loss is contralateral.
med-skills.l10.q5.e: Ipsilateral weakness and vibration loss with contralateral pain and temperature loss indicate a right-sided hemisection. A left-sided lesion would reverse the sides.

med-skills.l11.q1.t: Morning stiffness lasting more than an hour that improves with use
med-skills.l11.q1.p: Which feature best favors inflammatory arthritis over osteoarthritis?
med-skills.l11.q1.h: Consider the duration of morning stiffness.
med-skills.l11.q1.e: Prolonged morning stiffness that eases with activity is typical of inflammatory arthritis. Use-related pain and bony enlargement favor osteoarthritis.

med-skills.l11.q2.t: The anterior cruciate ligament, which restrains forward tibial shift
med-skills.l11.q2.p: The Lachman test is used to assess the integrity of which structure?
med-skills.l11.q2.h: It is a more sensitive version of the anterior drawer.
med-skills.l11.q2.e: The Lachman test examines the ACL. The McMurray test is used for meniscal tears.

med-skills.l11.q3.t: Arthrocentesis to exclude septic arthritis and to look for crystals
med-skills.l11.q3.p: A single acutely hot, swollen, painful knee should first prompt:
med-skills.l11.q3.h: The danger lies in what cannot be missed.
med-skills.l11.q3.e: Aspiration is needed to exclude infection and identify crystals. Septic arthritis can destroy a joint rapidly, so waiting is unsafe.

med-skills.l11.q4.t: Arrange urgent MRI of the spine for suspected cauda equina syndrome
med-skills.l11.q4.p: A 45-year-old man with back pain has new urinary retention, numbness over the perineum and bilateral leg weakness. Which is the most appropriate next step?
med-skills.l11.q4.h: Saddle anesthesia and bladder dysfunction are red flags.
med-skills.l11.q4.e: These features suggest cauda equina syndrome, a surgical emergency needing urgent MRI. Delay risks permanent deficit.

med-skills.l11.q5.t: Carpal tunnel syndrome, with median nerve compression at the wrist
med-skills.l11.q5.p: A 50-year-old woman has nocturnal numbness of the thumb, index and middle fingers, relieved by shaking her hand. Tapping over the wrist reproduces the tingling. Which diagnosis is most likely?
med-skills.l11.q5.h: The distribution is the median nerve and Tinel sign is positive.
med-skills.l11.q5.e: Median-distribution numbness and a positive Tinel sign indicate carpal tunnel syndrome. Ulnar involvement would affect the little finger.

med-skills.l12.q1.t: A one-sentence abstract summary of the case using semantic qualifiers
med-skills.l12.q1.p: What is a problem representation in clinical reasoning?
med-skills.l12.q1.h: It condenses the case into abstract terms.
med-skills.l12.q1.e: A problem representation is a concise abstract summary that retrieves illness scripts. A full list of causes is the differential, not the summary.

med-skills.l12.q2.t: Aortic dissection, pulmonary embolism and acute coronary syndrome in the emergency setting
med-skills.l12.q2.p: Which list contains only diagnoses that must not be missed in acute chest pain?
med-skills.l12.q2.e: The cannot-miss list includes dissection, pulmonary embolism and acute coronary syndrome. The others are common but generally benign.

med-skills.l12.q3.t: Patients may have several unrelated diseases at the same time
med-skills.l12.q3.p: Hickam dictum, in contrast with Occam razor, reminds clinicians that:
med-skills.l12.q3.h: It counsels against forcing one unifying diagnosis.
med-skills.l12.q3.e: Hickam dictum says patients can have multiple diseases. Occam razor favors a single unifying diagnosis.

med-skills.l12.q4.t: Disagree, since bacterial meningitis is a cannot-miss diagnosis needing urgent evaluation
med-skills.l12.q4.p: A 22-year-old woman has acute fever, headache, neck stiffness and photophobia. A resident says that viral meningitis is far more common than bacterial meningitis and proposes discharge with fluids. Which reasoning is most appropriate?
med-skills.l12.q4.h: Likelihood is not the only criterion.
med-skills.l12.q4.e: Likelihood matters but the dangerous, treatable diagnosis must be excluded promptly. Young adults can and do develop bacterial meningitis.

med-skills.l12.q5.t: Microcytosis suggests iron deficiency, so a source of blood loss should be sought
med-skills.l12.q5.p: A 67-year-old man has new anemia with MCV of 72 fL, fatigue and weight loss. A trainee lists vitamin B12 deficiency first. Which comment best improves the reasoning?
med-skills.l12.q5.h: Use the semantic qualifier from the lab result.
med-skills.l12.q5.e: A low MCV points toward iron deficiency and a search for occult blood loss in an older man. B12 deficiency causes macrocytosis, so it does not fit.

med-skills.l13.q1.t: Sensitivity divided by one minus specificity
med-skills.l13.q1.p: Which expression gives the positive likelihood ratio?
med-skills.l13.q1.h: It compares true positive and false positive rates.
med-skills.l13.q1.e: LR+ equals sensitivity divided by one minus specificity. The second option is the negative likelihood ratio.

med-skills.l13.q2.t: Positive predictive value falls and negative predictive value rises
med-skills.l13.q2.p: When the prevalence of a disease in the tested population falls, with sensitivity and specificity held constant, what happens?
med-skills.l13.q2.h: False positives dominate when disease is rare.
med-skills.l13.q2.e: Lower prevalence lowers PPV and raises NPV. Sensitivity and specificity are test properties that do not change with prevalence in principle.

med-skills.l13.q3.t: 0.08, since one minus sensitivity divided by specificity is small
med-skills.l13.q3.p: A test with sensitivity 95 percent and specificity 60 percent has a negative likelihood ratio closest to:
med-skills.l13.q3.h: LR- is (1 - sens) divided by spec.
med-skills.l13.q3.e: LR- is 0.05 divided by 0.60, about 0.08. The value 2.4 is the positive likelihood ratio.

med-skills.l13.q4.t: The posttest probability is still low, about 1 percent, so most positives are false
med-skills.l13.q4.p: A 35-year-old woman with a very low pretest probability of a rare disease (about 1 in 1000) tests positive on a test with positive likelihood ratio 10. Which statement is most accurate?
med-skills.l13.q4.e: Pretest odds of about 0.001 times 10 gives about 0.01, roughly 1 percent. A test cannot rescue a very low pretest probability.

med-skills.l13.q5.t: Pulmonary embolism is essentially excluded, and imaging is not needed
med-skills.l13.q5.p: A 40-year-old man with chest pain after a flight has a low Wells score for pulmonary embolism. A high-sensitivity D-dimer is negative. What is the best interpretation?
med-skills.l13.q5.h: High sensitivity with low pretest probability allows exclusion.
med-skills.l13.q5.e: A sensitive test with a negative result in a low-probability patient can rule out disease. D-dimer is useful for exclusion but not confirmation.

med-skills.l14.q1.t: Anchoring, which leaves the first impression unrevised despite evidence
med-skills.l14.q1.p: Locking onto the first diagnosis and failing to adjust to new data is called:
med-skills.l14.q1.h: The first impression acts like a ship anchor.
med-skills.l14.q1.e: Anchoring is excess weight on the initial impression. Availability concerns ease of recall.

med-skills.l14.q2.t: Psych-out error, in which a physical complaint is attributed to mental illness
med-skills.l14.q2.p: A patient with schizophrenia presents with abdominal pain and the pain is attributed to his psychiatric illness without examination. This error is best described as:
med-skills.l14.q2.h: The label explains away a new symptom.
med-skills.l14.q2.e: Attributing a physical complaint to the psychiatric history is a psych-out error. Satisficing involves stopping after finding one abnormality.

med-skills.l14.q3.t: A diagnostic time-out asking what else it could be and what is not fitting
med-skills.l14.q3.p: Which strategy is most directly aimed at reducing premature closure?
med-skills.l14.q3.h: Slow down at the moment of decision.
med-skills.l14.q3.e: A time-out prompts alternatives and findings that do not fit. Broad unfocused testing does not address the thinking error.

med-skills.l14.q4.t: Availability and anchoring, with a recent case and a first impression driving the plan
med-skills.l14.q4.p: A 60-year-old man with a recent leg fracture develops shortness of breath. The resident, who saw three pneumonia cases that week, diagnoses pneumonia and orders antibiotics. A chest radiograph is clear and the patient is hypoxic and tachycardic. Which two biases are most evident?
med-skills.l14.q4.h: Recent cases and a first impression shaped the thinking.
med-skills.l14.q4.e: Recent pneumonia cases make the diagnosis available, and the early impression anchored the plan. Nothing here shows a label inherited from handoff.

med-skills.l14.q5.t: Framing and diagnostic momentum, with a label carried forward without questioning
med-skills.l14.q5.p: A handoff describes a 28-year-old as the drug seeker in bed 4 who has abdominal pain. The night physician does not examine him. He is later found to have appendicitis. Which pair of contributors is most appropriate?
med-skills.l14.q5.h: A label shaped the encounter before the patient was seen.
med-skills.l14.q5.e: A stigmatizing label passed forward frames the case and carries momentum. The other options do not explain the label being transferred.

med-skills.l15.q1.t: The central 95 percent of values in a healthy reference population
med-skills.l15.q1.p: Reference ranges for laboratory tests are typically defined to include:
med-skills.l15.q1.h: By design, a small share of healthy people fall outside.
med-skills.l15.q1.e: Ranges usually cover the central 95 percent of healthy individuals, so about 5 percent of healthy people are outside it for a single test.

med-skills.l15.q2.t: Troponin indicates myocardial injury, which has several non-infarction causes
med-skills.l15.q2.p: Why can a rise in troponin not be equated with myocardial infarction on its own?
med-skills.l15.q2.h: Injury and infarction are not synonyms.
