publishing-business.l17.q3.t: It can chill other publishers' interest and hold you to one house
publishing-business.l17.q3.p: A contract has an option clause giving the publisher the right to match any offer for your next book. What is the author's main concern?
publishing-business.l17.q3.e: Matching rights can deter other buyers; first-look options with short windows are less restrictive.

publishing-business.l17.q4.t: The right to have the publisher's royalty records inspected by an accountant
publishing-business.l17.q4.p: What practical power does an audit clause give an author?
publishing-business.l17.q4.h: Statements are only claims until checked.
publishing-business.l17.q4.e: Audit rights allow verification of statements, which otherwise rely on trust.

publishing-business.l17.q5.t: Territories not granted can be licensed elsewhere, such as to a UK or translation publisher
publishing-business.l17.q5.p: Why does an author care about territory in a contract?
publishing-business.l17.q5.h: Think about selling in other regions.
publishing-business.l17.q5.e: Retaining territories lets the author or agent license them separately.

publishing-business.l18.q1.t: You own the list and are not at the mercy of a platform's algorithm
publishing-business.l18.q1.p: Why is an email newsletter valued by many authors?
publishing-business.l18.q1.e: A list you own lets you reach readers directly even if social platforms change.

publishing-business.l18.q2.p: An author has 400 subscribers and assumes a 5 percent purchase rate. How many sales?

publishing-business.l18.q3.p: If the author grows the list to 1,000 and the same 5 percent applies, how many additional sales are expected compared with 400?

publishing-business.l18.q4.t: It violates retailer rules, can get reviews removed and damages trust
publishing-business.l18.q4.p: Why is paying a service for batches of five-star reviews a bad idea?
publishing-business.l18.q4.h: Think about platform enforcement and honesty.
publishing-business.l18.q4.e: Fake or paid reviews breach policies and can lead to removals or penalties and reader distrust.

publishing-business.l18.q5.t: A backlist or series plus steady audience-building
publishing-business.l18.q5.p: Which plan best supports long-term sales after launch day?
publishing-business.l18.q5.e: Sustained work and more titles keep readers returning long after the spike.

publishing-business.l19.q1.p: Records of income and expenses should be kept from the start, ideally in a separate account.
publishing-business.l19.q1.h: Consider what you need at tax time.
publishing-business.l19.q1.e: Good records prove income and deductions and make filing and any audits far easier.

publishing-business.l19.q2.p: An author earns 5,000 dollars in royalties with expenses of 1,200 dollars. What is the net profit?

publishing-business.l19.q3.p: Expenses were cover 600 dollars, editing 500 dollars and ads 100 dollars. What is the total?

publishing-business.l19.q4.t: No employer withholds tax from royalties
publishing-business.l19.q4.p: Why do many self-employed authors make estimated tax payments during the year?
publishing-business.l19.q4.e: Without payroll withholding, taxpayers often pay quarterly estimates to avoid a large bill and penalties.

publishing-business.l19.q5.t: A separate tax funding Social Security and Medicare, on top of income tax
publishing-business.l19.q5.h: It is separate from income tax.
publishing-business.l19.q5.e: Self-employed people pay both halves of Social Security and Medicare contributions, commonly figured at 15.3 percent with adjustments.

publishing-business.l20.q1.t: Plain text, Markdown, Fountain, Word (.docx) and PDF
publishing-business.l20.q1.p: Which file types can the Lorea authoring studio import for a manuscript?
publishing-business.l20.q1.e: The import tool reads txt, md, fountain, docx and pdf files.

publishing-business.l20.q2.t: A purchase screen, unless they are the author or hold a licence
publishing-business.l20.q2.p: A reader opens a paid Lorea book they have not purchased and do not own. What do they see?
publishing-business.l20.q2.e: Paid books gate access behind purchase, with exceptions for the author and licence holders.

publishing-business.l20.q3.t: Connect payments so earnings can be paid out
publishing-business.l20.q3.p: An author wants to sell a priced book on Lorea. What should she do first?
publishing-business.l20.q3.h: A priced book needs a way to pay you.
publishing-business.l20.q3.e: Priced books only pay out when payouts are connected, so set that up before publishing.

publishing-business.l20.q4.t: A useful platform record, not a replacement for government copyright registration
publishing-business.l20.q4.p: What is the right understanding of Lorea's creation certificate or content fingerprint?
publishing-business.l20.q4.h: Separate platform records from legal registration.
publishing-business.l20.q4.e: Registration with a copyright office has specific legal effects that a platform record does not.

publishing-business.l20.q5.t: Editing quality, contracts and rights decisions, taxes, and any print ISBN or copyright registration
publishing-business.l20.q5.p: Which task still remains the author's responsibility even when publishing on Lorea?
publishing-business.l20.q5.h: Tools help but do not do the business for you.
publishing-business.l20.q5.e: Platform tools handle writing, publishing and reading; legal, tax and print-distribution matters stay with the author.

sports-history.l01.q1.p: Who won the first World Cup in 1930?
sports-history.l01.q1.e: Uruguay hosted and won, beating Argentina 4-2 in Montevideo.

sports-history.l01.q2.p: How many teams played in the 1930 World Cup?
sports-history.l01.q2.e: The museum records 13 teams at the first World Cup.

sports-history.l01.q3.p: Which trophy was awarded from 1930 to 1970?
sports-history.l01.q3.e: The Jules Rimet Trophy was used from 1930 until 1970, when Brazil kept it.

sports-history.l01.q4.p: What does the 1930 final show about early World Cups?
sports-history.l01.q4.e: Uruguay won on home soil, a pattern later repeated by Italy, England, Argentina and France.

sports-history.l02.q1.p: Which country was the first back-to-back champion?

sports-history.l02.q2.p: Why were the 1942 and 1946 tournaments not played?
sports-history.l02.q2.e: Both were cancelled because of World War II.

sports-history.l02.q3.p: Which team lost the 1938 final to Italy?
sports-history.l02.q3.e: Italy beat Hungary 4-2 in the 1938 final in Paris.

sports-history.l02.q4.p: If the World Cup was held in 1938 and resumed in 1950, about how many years was the gap?
sports-history.l02.q4.e: 1950 minus 1938 is twelve years, with 1942 and 1946 cancelled.

sports-history.l03.q1.e: It is the name for Uruguay's 2-1 win over Brazil in the 1950 decider.

sports-history.l03.q2.p: The United States beat England 1-0 at the 1950 World Cup.
sports-history.l03.q2.e: The museum records the United States beating England 1-0.

sports-history.l03.q3.e: The 1950 final was played at the Estadio do Maracana in Rio.

sports-history.l03.q4.t: The hosts lost a final they were expected to win
sports-history.l03.q4.p: Why did 1950 matter for Brazilian football memory?
sports-history.l03.q4.e: Hosts Brazil were favourites but lost to Uruguay, a defeat that became a national memory.

sports-history.l04.q1.p: Who won the 1954 World Cup, in Bern?
sports-history.l04.q1.e: West Germany beat Hungary 3-2 in the Miracle of Bern.

sports-history.l04.q2.p: How old was Pele when he scored twice in the 1958 final?
sports-history.l04.q2.e: He was 17 and is the youngest World Cup winner.

sports-history.l04.q3.p: Who scored a record 13 goals in a single World Cup in 1958?
sports-history.l04.q3.e: Just Fontaine of France scored 13 in 1958, still unbeaten.

sports-history.l04.q4.t: No single region owned the sport
sports-history.l04.q4.p: What does Brazil's 1958 and 1962 success show?
sports-history.l04.q4.e: After a European win in 1954, Brazil's back-to-back titles showed the sport was global.

sports-history.l05.q1.p: How many World Cups has Brazil won?
sports-history.l05.q1.e: The museum lists five titles: 1958, 1962, 1970, 1994 and 2002.

sports-history.l05.q2.p: What happened to the Jules Rimet Trophy after 1970?
sports-history.l05.q2.e: It was retired with Brazil's third title and kept by Brazil.

sports-history.l05.q3.p: Which defender played three consecutive World Cup finals?
sports-history.l05.q3.e: Cafu holds the record for final appearances with three.

sports-history.l05.q4.p: Which moment from 1970 is called the save of the century?
sports-history.l05.q4.e: Gordon Banks clawed away Pele's downward header.

sports-history.l06.q1.p: Who scored a hat-trick in the 1966 final?
sports-history.l06.q1.e: Geoff Hurst scored three as England beat West Germany 4-2 aet.

sports-history.l06.q2.p: Which trophy did Beckenbauer lift in 1974?
sports-history.l06.q2.e: The FIFA World Cup Trophy replaced the Rimet Trophy in 1974.

sports-history.l06.q3.e: West Germany beat the Netherlands 2-1 in Munich.

sports-history.l06.q4.t: Admired style did not guarantee the trophy
sports-history.l06.q4.p: What does the 1974 final show about style versus results?
sports-history.l06.q4.e: The Netherlands influenced the game but lost to the German side.

sports-history.l07.q1.p: Who won the Golden Boot while leading Argentina to the 1978 title?
sports-history.l07.q1.e: Mario Kempes won the Golden Boot in 1978.

sports-history.l07.q2.e: Italy beat West Germany 3-1 in Madrid.

sports-history.l07.q3.e: The final was played at the Estadio Monumental in Buenos Aires.

sports-history.l07.q4.p: What did Paolo Rossi achieve in 1982?
sports-history.l07.q4.e: He won both the Golden Boot and Golden Ball, then the Ballon d'Or.

sports-history.l08.q1.t: The Hand of God and the Goal of the Century
sports-history.l08.q1.p: Which two goals did Maradona score in the 1986 quarter-final?
sports-history.l08.q1.e: He scored with his fist and then slalomed past half of England's team.

sports-history.l08.q3.p: Which stadium hosted both the 1970 and 1986 finals?
sports-history.l08.q3.e: Estadio Azteca hosted both and will host a third World Cup in 2026.

sports-history.l08.q4.t: He dominated the tournament as its best player
sports-history.l08.q4.e: Maradona won the Golden Ball and carried Argentina to the title.

sports-history.l09.q1.p: Who scored the late penalty that won the 1990 final?
sports-history.l09.q1.e: Brehme scored the penalty in the 1-0 win over Argentina.

sports-history.l09.q2.p: What was historic about the 1994 final?
sports-history.l09.q2.e: It ended 0-0 and Brazil won 3-2 on penalties.

sports-history.l09.q3.p: Which player skied the final penalty in 1994?
sports-history.l09.q3.e: Baggio's miss gave Brazil the title.

sports-history.l09.q4.p: Which player lit up Italia 90 at age 38 with a corner-flag dance?
sports-history.l09.q4.e: Roger Milla's celebration is one of the most remembered moments.

sports-history.l10.q1.p: Who scored twice with headers in the 1998 final?
sports-history.l10.q1.e: Zidane scored two headers against Brazil.

sports-history.l10.q2.p: Which two countries co-hosted the 2002 World Cup?
sports-history.l10.q2.e: The 2002 tournament was co-hosted by South Korea and Japan.

sports-history.l10.q3.p: Who scored both goals in the 2002 final?
sports-history.l10.q3.e: Ronaldo scored both as Brazil beat Germany 2-0.

sports-history.l10.q4.t: Fastest World Cup goal at 11 seconds
sports-history.l10.q4.p: Which record did Hakan Sukur set in 2002?
sports-history.l10.q4.e: The museum lists his 11-second goal as the fastest in World Cup history.

sports-history.l11.q1.e: It finished 1-1 and Italy won 5-3 on penalties.

sports-history.l11.q2.p: Who scored Spain's winner in the 2010 final?
sports-history.l11.q2.e: Iniesta scored the only goal in extra time.

sports-history.l11.q3.e: Spain beat the Netherlands at Soccer City in Johannesburg.

sports-history.l11.q4.t: It was the first held in Africa
sports-history.l11.q4.p: Which was a first in World Cup history in 2010?
sports-history.l11.q4.e: It was the first World Cup hosted in Africa and Spain's first title.

sports-history.l12.q1.p: What was the semi-final score when Germany played Brazil in 2014?

sports-history.l12.q2.p: Who scored the winner in the 2014 final?
sports-history.l12.q2.e: Gotze scored in extra time against Argentina.

sports-history.l12.q3.p: Who won the 2018 Golden Boot with 6 goals?
sports-history.l12.q3.e: Kane won the Golden Boot in 2018 with 6 goals.

sports-history.l13.q1.p: Which country hosted the 2022 World Cup?

sports-history.l13.q2.e: Argentina won 4-2 on penalties after a 3-3 draw.

sports-history.l13.q3.p: Who won the 2022 Golden Boot with 8 goals?
sports-history.l13.q3.e: Mbappe scored 8, one more than Messi.

sports-history.l13.q4.p: Which team became the first African side in a World Cup semi-final in 2022?
sports-history.l13.q4.e: Morocco beat Spain and Portugal and finished fourth.

sports-history.l14.q1.p: How many teams played in the 2026 World Cup?
sports-history.l14.q1.e: The 2026 event has 48 teams and 104 matches.

sports-history.l14.q2.e: The final was scheduled for 19 July 2026 at MetLife Stadium.

sports-history.l14.q3.p: Which stadium has hosted three World Cups (1970, 1986 and 2026)?
sports-history.l14.q3.e: Estadio Azteca is the only stadium to host three World Cups.

sports-history.l14.q4.p: How many World Cup stadiums are in Canada?
sports-history.l14.q4.e: Canada has BMO Field and BC Place; the USA has 11 and Mexico 3.

theatre-scripts.l01.q1.t: The writer's notes about movement, setting, sound and mood
theatre-scripts.l01.q1.p: In a play script, what are stage directions?
theatre-scripts.l01.q1.h: They are not spoken by the characters.
theatre-scripts.l01.q1.e: Stage directions are the writer's instructions for how the scene looks and moves, separate from the dialogue.

theatre-scripts.l01.q2.p: Which part of a play carries most of the storytelling, since there is no narrator?
theatre-scripts.l01.q2.h: Think about what the characters do to each other with words.
theatre-scripts.l01.q2.e: In a script, characters mostly reveal the story through what they say to one another.

theatre-scripts.l01.q3.p: Which Shaw play is noted in the library for stage directions that read like essays?
theatre-scripts.l01.q3.h: It is the one about a phonetics professor.
theatre-scripts.l01.q3.e: The library note on Pygmalion (1913) says Shaw's stage directions are essays and worth reading for how to write character.

theatre-scripts.l01.q4.t: A scene is a smaller unit within the larger movement of an act
theatre-scripts.l01.q4.p: How is a scene usually different from an act?
theatre-scripts.l01.q4.h: Think of one as a section and the other as a sub-section.
theatre-scripts.l01.q4.e: Acts are the big movements of a story, and scenes are smaller units marked by a change of place or time.

theatre-scripts.l02.q1.t: The central character whose wants and choices drive the story
theatre-scripts.l02.q1.h: Think about who the story follows.
theatre-scripts.l02.q1.e: The protagonist is the main character whose desires and decisions push the plot forward.

theatre-scripts.l02.q2.p: In Hamlet, the prince's father is described by a ghost as having been what?
theatre-scripts.l02.q2.h: The ghost has a grievance about the king's death.
theatre-scripts.l02.q2.e: The library blurb says Hamlet is told by his father's ghost that his uncle murdered him.

theatre-scripts.l02.q3.p: Which play is described in the library as the purest dilemma, with two irreconcilable obligations?
theatre-scripts.l02.q3.e: The Cid forces its hero to avenge his father by killing the father of the woman he loves.

theatre-scripts.l02.q4.t: It forces a choice that costs something whichever way the character goes
theatre-scripts.l02.q4.p: Why is a dilemma stronger than a simple obstacle in drama?
theatre-scripts.l02.q4.e: A bind between two obligations means every option has a price, which keeps tension high.

theatre-scripts.l03.q1.p: Which of these is a comedy in the library?
theatre-scripts.l03.q1.e: Lysistrata (411 BCE) is listed as Comedy / Satire; the others are tragedies.

theatre-scripts.l03.q2.t: Going to the underworld to bring a great playwright back to Athens
theatre-scripts.l03.q2.p: What does The Frogs show Dionysus doing?
theatre-scripts.l03.q2.h: It involves a descent and a contest between playwrights.
theatre-scripts.l03.q2.e: In The Frogs, Dionysus descends to the underworld and stages a contest between Aeschylus and Euripides.

theatre-scripts.l03.q3.p: Which pairing of play and label matches the library?
theatre-scripts.l03.q3.h: One label means a blend of two modes.
theatre-scripts.l03.q3.e: The Cid is labelled a tragicomedy in the library data.

theatre-scripts.l03.q4.t: Comedy used to criticise people or society
theatre-scripts.l03.q4.h: Think about Tartuffe and the hypocrite.
theatre-scripts.l03.q4.e: Satire uses humour to expose greed, hypocrisy or folly, as in Volpone and Tartuffe.

theatre-scripts.l04.q1.t: A speech by a character alone that reveals their thoughts to the audience
theatre-scripts.l04.q1.e: A soliloquy lets the audience hear a character's private reasoning.

theatre-scripts.l04.q2.t: The audience but not the other characters on stage
theatre-scripts.l04.q2.p: An aside is usually heard by whom?
theatre-scripts.l04.q2.h: It is a quick whisper outside the scene.
theatre-scripts.l04.q2.e: An aside is a brief remark meant for the audience while the others on stage are not supposed to hear it.

theatre-scripts.l04.q3.p: According to the library, how should one study the Hamlet soliloquies?
theatre-scripts.l04.q3.e: The library says to study Hamlet's soliloquies as structure, not poetry.

theatre-scripts.l04.q4.t: They give the audience knowledge that other characters lack
theatre-scripts.l04.q4.p: Why do soliloquies and asides create suspense?
theatre-scripts.l04.q4.e: When the audience hears private thoughts the other characters do not, tension and intimacy grow together.

theatre-scripts.l05.q1.p: Which Greek work is the only surviving complete trilogy, according to the library?
theatre-scripts.l05.q1.e: The Oresteia is described as the only surviving complete Greek trilogy.

theatre-scripts.l05.q2.h: The library dates it to 431 BCE.

theatre-scripts.l05.q3.p: In Oedipus the King, who is the murderer the king is hunting?
theatre-scripts.l05.q3.h: This is the reversal and recognition.
theatre-scripts.l05.q3.e: The library says the king hunts a murderer who turns out to be himself.

theatre-scripts.l05.q4.t: A court of law is invented
theatre-scripts.l05.q4.p: What ends the cycle of blood-vengeance in the Oresteia?
theatre-scripts.l05.q4.e: The trilogy resolves the chain of vengeance when a court of law replaces revenge.

theatre-scripts.l06.q2.t: Sex, until the men negotiate peace
theatre-scripts.l06.q2.p: In Lysistrata, what do the women of the Greek city-states withhold?
theatre-scripts.l06.q2.h: It is a protest aimed at ending a war.
theatre-scripts.l06.q2.e: The women agree to withhold sex until the men make peace.

theatre-scripts.l06.q3.p: In The Frogs, whom does Dionysus want to bring back to Athens?
theatre-scripts.l06.q3.h: He holds a contest in the underworld.
theatre-scripts.l06.q3.e: He goes to the underworld to bring back a great playwright, choosing between Aeschylus and Euripides.

theatre-scripts.l06.q4.t: Every character must take it completely seriously
theatre-scripts.l06.q4.p: What does the library say about how a comic premise like Lysistrata works?
theatre-scripts.l06.q4.e: The library says a comic engine only works if every character takes it completely seriously.

theatre-scripts.l07.q1.t: The emotional flavour an audience is meant to taste
theatre-scripts.l07.q1.p: What does rasa mean in Sanskrit drama?
theatre-scripts.l07.q1.e: Rasa is the emotional flavour that Sanskrit drama is built around.

theatre-scripts.l07.q2.p: Who wrote Sakoontala; or, The Lost Ring?
theatre-scripts.l07.q2.e: The library credits Kalidasa, in Monier Williams' translation.

theatre-scripts.l07.q3.t: A ring recovered from a fish
theatre-scripts.l07.q3.p: What object brings the king's memory back in Sakoontala?
theatre-scripts.l07.q3.e: A ring found in a fish ends the effect of the curse.

theatre-scripts.l07.q4.t: It builds around emotional flavour, rasa, rather than conflict
theatre-scripts.l07.q4.p: How does the library say Sanskrit drama differs from conflict-driven drama?
theatre-scripts.l07.q4.h: Reading it changes what a scene can be built around.
theatre-scripts.l07.q4.e: The library says it recalibrates what a scene can be organised around: rasa instead of conflict.

theatre-scripts.l08.q1.p: Which play is by Christopher Marlowe?
theatre-scripts.l08.q1.e: The Tragical History of Doctor Faustus is Marlowe's.

theatre-scripts.l08.q2.p: Which of these Shakespeare plays does the library date to c. 1611?
theatre-scripts.l08.q2.h: It is a romance set on an island.
theatre-scripts.l08.q2.e: The library dates The Tempest to c. 1611, the latest of the group.

theatre-scripts.l08.q3.p: Who wrote Volpone, dated 1606 in the library?
theatre-scripts.l08.q3.h: A rich Venetian fakes an illness.
theatre-scripts.l08.q3.e: Volpone; or, The Fox is by Ben Jonson.

theatre-scripts.l08.q4.t: It observes them almost exactly: one place, one day
theatre-scripts.l08.q4.p: What does the library say about The Tempest and the classical unities?
theatre-scripts.l08.q4.e: The library says the play keeps one place and one day, showing constraints can concentrate a story.

theatre-scripts.l09.q1.e: Tartuffe; or, The Hypocrite is by Moliere.

theatre-scripts.l09.q2.e: The School for Scandal is by Richard Brinsley Sheridan.

theatre-scripts.l09.q3.p: In Tartuffe, when does the title character first appear, according to the library?
theatre-scripts.l09.q3.h: The first two acts are all about him.
theatre-scripts.l09.q3.e: The library says Tartuffe does not appear until Act III.

theatre-scripts.l09.q4.t: Its songs use popular tunes rather than arias
theatre-scripts.l09.q4.p: What does the library say about the form of The Beggar's Opera?
theatre-scripts.l09.q4.e: The Beggar's Opera is a ballad opera: highwaymen and thief-takers staged with popular tunes.

theatre-scripts.l10.q1.p: Which play ends with the famous sound of a door closing?
theatre-scripts.l10.q1.e: The library notes the door closing at the end of A Doll's House.

theatre-scripts.l10.q2.p: Which Ibsen play is the template for every whistleblower story?
theatre-scripts.l10.q2.e: In An Enemy of the People a doctor reveals the spa baths are contaminated.

theatre-scripts.l10.q3.t: Retrospective: the play begins after the catastrophe
theatre-scripts.l10.q3.p: What does the library call Ibsen's method in Ghosts?
theatre-scripts.l10.q3.e: The plot of Ghosts is the digging up of something that already happened.

theatre-scripts.l10.q4.p: Which year is A Doll's House dated to in the library?
theatre-scripts.l10.q4.e: The library lists A Doll's House as 1879.

theatre-scripts.l11.q1.t: The meaning beneath the words characters say
theatre-scripts.l11.q1.e: Subtext is what characters really mean or want beneath their spoken words.

theatre-scripts.l11.q2.p: Which play features a town that mistakes a clerk for a government inspector?
theatre-scripts.l11.q2.e: In The Inspector-General a provincial town bribes a penniless clerk it takes for an inspector.

theatre-scripts.l11.q3.p: Which play does the library call the founding text of subtext?
theatre-scripts.l11.q3.e: The library says The Sea-Gull is the founding text of subtext.

theatre-scripts.l11.q4.t: It is an ensemble play with no protagonist that never loses focus
theatre-scripts.l11.q4.p: What is notable about Gorky's The Lower Depths, according to the library?
theatre-scripts.l11.q4.h: It takes place in a flophouse cellar.
theatre-scripts.l11.q4.e: The library calls it an ensemble with no protagonist that holds focus, a model for many voices in one place.

theatre-scripts.l12.q1.p: Which play has two men each inventing a fictitious relative?
theatre-scripts.l12.q1.e: The Importance of Being Earnest is built on those invented relatives.

theatre-scripts.l12.q2.p: Which Shaw play is the origin of the makeover story?
theatre-scripts.l12.q2.h: A flower girl is passed off as a duchess.
theatre-scripts.l12.q2.e: Pygmalion (1913) is described as the origin of the makeover story.

theatre-scripts.l12.q3.p: What object is the spine of Lady Windermere's Fan?
theatre-scripts.l12.q3.e: The library says everything turns on where the fan is and who saw it there.

theatre-scripts.l12.q4.t: It has the wit removed and relies on rhythm and repetition
theatre-scripts.l12.q4.p: What does the library say about Salome compared with Wilde's comedies?
theatre-scripts.l12.q4.e: Salome is called Wilde with the wit removed, hypnotic and repetitive.

theatre-scripts.l13.q1.p: Which play is described as arguably the most perfect one-act in English?
theatre-scripts.l13.q1.h: Synge, set on the Aran Islands.
theatre-scripts.l13.q1.e: The library calls Riders to the Sea arguably the most perfect one-act in English.

theatre-scripts.l13.q2.h: A murder is solved with props in a kitchen.

theatre-scripts.l13.q3.p: In Pirandello's Six Characters in Search of an Author, what do the characters demand?
theatre-scripts.l13.q3.e: The six unfinished characters demand that their story be completed.

theatre-scripts.l13.q4.t: It is noted as one of the first plays by a Black American woman to be professionally staged
theatre-scripts.l13.q4.p: Which statement about Rachel matches the library?
theatre-scripts.l13.q4.e: The library says Rachel is one of the first plays by a Black American woman to be professionally staged.

thinking-methods.l01.q1.t: Does a plant given 10 mL of water a day grow taller than one given 5 mL a day?
thinking-methods.l01.q1.p: Which of these is the most testable question?
thinking-methods.l01.q1.h: Look for something you could measure with a tool.
thinking-methods.l01.q1.e: It names something to change (water amount) and something to measure (height), so an experiment can answer it.

thinking-methods.l01.q2.p: A question about what people ought to do can be settled just by measuring something in a lab.
thinking-methods.l01.q2.e: Measurements can inform value questions but cannot settle them alone; they need different kinds of reasoning.

thinking-methods.l01.q3.t: Which sports drink has the highest sugar content per 100 mL, measured by the same method?
thinking-methods.l01.q3.p: A student asks, "Which sports drink is best?" Which rewrite makes it testable?
thinking-methods.l01.q3.h: Pick the one with a measurable quantity and a clear method.
thinking-methods.l01.q3.e: It specifies a measurable quantity and a consistent method, so the comparison can be repeated by anyone.

thinking-methods.l01.q4.t: Because the second defines how mood is measured and what is compared, while the first leaves both vague
thinking-methods.l01.q4.p: Why is "Does cold weather make people feel unhappy?" harder to test than "Do people report lower scores on a mood survey on days below 0 C?"
thinking-methods.l01.q4.h: Think about which wording tells you what to record.
thinking-methods.l01.q4.e: The second wording defines how happiness is measured (a survey score) and what is compared (cold vs other days); the first leaves both undefined.

thinking-methods.l02.q1.t: The window has a hole about 5 cm wide with cracks spreading from it.
thinking-methods.l02.q1.p: Which statement is an observation rather than an inference?
thinking-methods.l02.q1.h: An observation is what you can directly see or measure.
thinking-methods.l02.q1.e: The size of the hole and cracks can be directly seen; the other statements explain how or why it happened.

thinking-methods.l02.q2.t: A proposed explanation that makes a testable prediction
thinking-methods.l02.q2.h: It is a proposal, not a result.
thinking-methods.l02.q2.e: A hypothesis proposes an explanation and leads to predictions that tests can check.

thinking-methods.l02.q3.t: An animal dug there, and a camera placed nearby will show it
thinking-methods.l02.q3.p: You see a bare patch of soil near a tree and fresh paw prints in it. Which is the best inference to test next?
thinking-methods.l02.q3.h: Choose the one that gives you a way to check.
thinking-methods.l02.q3.e: It is a reasonable explanation of what was seen and it suggests a test (a camera), unlike the other options.

thinking-methods.l02.q4.t: Swap in a new battery and see whether the brightness changes
thinking-methods.l02.q4.p: Two students observe the same dim light bulb. One infers a weak battery, the other a faulty bulb. What is the best next step?
thinking-methods.l02.q4.h: Design a test that distinguishes the two explanations.
thinking-methods.l02.q4.e: Changing only the battery gives a result that favours one inference over the other.

thinking-methods.l03.q1.t: Some possible observation could show it to be wrong
thinking-methods.l03.q1.p: What does it mean for a hypothesis to be falsifiable?
thinking-methods.l03.q1.h: Think about whether evidence could count against it.
thinking-methods.l03.q1.e: A falsifiable hypothesis makes predictions that could fail, so evidence could count against it.

thinking-methods.l03.q2.t: This metal expands when heated from 20 C to 100 C.
thinking-methods.l03.q2.h: Which one forbids some measurable outcome?
thinking-methods.l03.q2.e: The metal claim predicts a measurable change, and failing to see expansion would count against it.

thinking-methods.l03.q3.t: Fertilised plants average 22 cm and unfertilised ones 22 cm
thinking-methods.l03.q3.p: A hypothesis says "Plants given fertiliser X grow taller than unfertilised plants." Which result would count against it?
thinking-methods.l03.q3.h: Look for the result that does not show the predicted difference.
thinking-methods.l03.q3.e: No difference in height is what the hypothesis forbids, so that result would count against it.

thinking-methods.l03.q4.t: It no longer forbids any outcome, so evidence cannot test it
thinking-methods.l03.q4.p: A theory is changed after each failed prediction so that it can never be wrong. What is the main problem?
thinking-methods.l03.q4.h: Think about what a claim must rule out.
thinking-methods.l03.q4.e: If every result can be accommodated, the claim rules out nothing and so says nothing testable.

thinking-methods.l04.q1.p: In a test of how water temperature affects how fast sugar dissolves, what is the dependent variable?
thinking-methods.l04.q1.h: It is the thing you measure as the outcome.
thinking-methods.l04.q1.e: The dissolving time is the measured outcome; temperature is the independent variable.

thinking-methods.l04.q2.p: In a fair test, you change several variables at once so the results are richer.
thinking-methods.l04.q2.h: Think about which change caused the result.
thinking-methods.l04.q2.e: Changing several things at once makes it impossible to tell which one caused the effect.

thinking-methods.l04.q3.t: The amount of light each plant gets
thinking-methods.l04.q3.p: A student tests whether fertiliser affects bean height. Which is a controlled variable?
thinking-methods.l04.q3.h: A controlled variable is deliberately kept the same.
thinking-methods.l04.q3.e: Light must be kept equal for all plants so it cannot explain a height difference.

thinking-methods.l04.q4.t: Grain size is a confounding variable that also changes dissolving time
thinking-methods.l04.q4.p: Hot-water sugar used fine grains and cold-water sugar used coarse grains. What is the main flaw?
thinking-methods.l04.q4.h: Ask what else differed between the two cups.
thinking-methods.l04.q4.e: Grain size changed along with temperature, so the effect of temperature cannot be separated.

thinking-methods.l05.q1.t: To see how much results vary and reduce the effect of chance
thinking-methods.l05.q1.h: Think about random variation between measurements.
thinking-methods.l05.q1.e: Repeating shows the spread of results and lets averaging reduce random error.

thinking-methods.l05.q2.t: The number of individuals or observations included
thinking-methods.l05.q2.p: What does sample size mean in a study?
thinking-methods.l05.q2.h: It is about how many were studied.
thinking-methods.l05.q2.e: Sample size is the count of individuals or observations in the study.

thinking-methods.l05.q3.p: Five timings of a cart are 12, 14, 13, 15 and 11 seconds. What is the mean?
thinking-methods.l05.q3.h: Add all the values and divide by how many there are.

thinking-methods.l05.q4.t: It shows the results are precise but does not remove the systematic error
thinking-methods.l05.q4.p: Five trials with a badly calibrated scale all read 2 g too high. What does repeating achieve?
thinking-methods.l05.q4.h: Consider whether agreement among trials proves they are right.
thinking-methods.l05.q4.e: Repeat measurements agree with each other (precision) but the systematic offset remains, so the answers are all off in the same way.

thinking-methods.l06.q1.t: Accuracy is closeness to the true value; precision is closeness of repeated measurements to each other
thinking-methods.l06.q1.p: What is the difference between accuracy and precision?
thinking-methods.l06.q1.h: One compares to the truth, the other compares trials to each other.
thinking-methods.l06.q1.e: Accuracy compares a measurement to the true value; precision describes how tightly repeated measurements cluster.

thinking-methods.l06.q2.p: What kind of error is a scale that always reads 2 g too high?
thinking-methods.l06.q2.h: It pushes every reading the same way.
thinking-methods.l06.q2.e: A consistent offset in every reading is a systematic error, which averaging does not remove.

thinking-methods.l06.q3.p: You measure g as 9.5 m/s2 and the accepted value is 10.0 m/s2. What is the percent error?
thinking-methods.l06.q3.h: Divide the difference by the accepted value, then multiply by 100.
thinking-methods.l06.q3.e: The difference is 0.5 and 0.5 / 10.0 x 100 = 5 percent.

thinking-methods.l06.q4.t: The ranges overlap, so the difference may not be meaningful
thinking-methods.l06.q4.p: Two groups report 12.4 cm plus or minus 0.3 cm and 12.6 cm plus or minus 0.3 cm for a length. What can you conclude?
thinking-methods.l06.q4.h: Compare the ranges, not just the central values.
thinking-methods.l06.q4.e: The ranges 12.1 to 12.7 cm and 12.3 to 12.9 cm overlap, so the difference between the values could be due to uncertainty.

thinking-methods.l07.q1.p: Which graph is best for comparing the number of students who chose each of five lunch options?
thinking-methods.l07.q1.e: A bar chart compares counts across separate categories.

thinking-methods.l07.q2.p: By convention, which variable goes on the horizontal axis?
thinking-methods.l07.q2.h: It is the one you chose to change.
thinking-methods.l07.q2.e: The independent variable normally goes on the x-axis and the dependent variable on the y-axis.

thinking-methods.l07.q3.p: A straight line passes through (0 s, 0 m) and (4 s, 10 m). What is its slope?
thinking-methods.l07.q3.h: Slope is rise divided by run.
thinking-methods.l07.q3.e: The slope is 10 m / 4 s = 2.5 m/s.

thinking-methods.l07.q4.t: The truncated axis makes a small difference look large
thinking-methods.l07.q4.p: A bar chart of two values (50 and 52) has a vertical axis starting at 49. What is the problem?
thinking-methods.l07.q4.h: Think about how bar heights are compared by eye.
thinking-methods.l07.q4.e: Starting the axis at 49 makes one bar look many times taller than the other even though they differ by about 4 percent.

thinking-methods.l08.q1.t: The middle value when the numbers are ordered
thinking-methods.l08.q1.p: What is the median of a set of numbers?
thinking-methods.l08.q1.h: Think of lining the numbers up in order.
thinking-methods.l08.q1.e: The median is the middle value of the ordered list.

thinking-methods.l08.q2.t: A value far away from the others
thinking-methods.l08.q2.h: It stands apart from the rest.
thinking-methods.l08.q2.e: An outlier is a data point that lies unusually far from the other values.

thinking-methods.l08.q3.p: For the scores 3, 4, 5, 6 and 22, what are the mean and median?
thinking-methods.l08.q3.h: Add and divide for the mean; take the middle value for the median.
thinking-methods.l08.q3.e: The sum is 40, so the mean is 8, and the middle ordered value is 5.

thinking-methods.l08.q4.t: Check whether it came from a mistake, and report what you do with it
thinking-methods.l08.q4.p: One reading in your data set is far from the rest. What should you do first?
thinking-methods.l08.q4.h: Investigate before acting, and be open about it.
thinking-methods.l08.q4.e: An outlier may be an error or a real result, so check the cause and state how you handled it.

thinking-methods.l09.q1.p: Ice cream sales and sunburn cases rise together in summer. What best explains this?
thinking-methods.l09.q1.e: Sunny hot weather is a confounder that increases both ice cream sales and sunburn.

thinking-methods.l09.q2.p: A strong correlation between two quantities proves that one causes the other.
thinking-methods.l09.q2.h: Think about third factors and coincidence.
thinking-methods.l09.q2.e: Correlation alone does not show cause; confounders, reverse causation or chance can produce it.

thinking-methods.l09.q3.t: Randomly assigning students to use the app or not, then comparing scores
thinking-methods.l09.q3.p: Which design gives the strongest evidence that a new study app improves test scores?
thinking-methods.l09.q3.h: Think about spreading unknown differences evenly.
thinking-methods.l09.q3.e: Random assignment balances unknown factors across groups, so a difference is more likely due to the app.

thinking-methods.l09.q4.t: Age affects both shoe size and reading ability
thinking-methods.l09.q4.p: Children with larger shoe sizes score higher on a reading test. Which explanation is most likely?
thinking-methods.l09.q4.h: Ask what changes in children as they get older.
thinking-methods.l09.q4.e: Older children have larger feet and have also had more reading practice, so age is the confounder.

thinking-methods.l10.q1.p: For a simple pendulum, which plot gives a straight line?
thinking-methods.l10.q1.e: Because T^2 = (4 pi^2 / g) L, T squared against L is a straight line through the origin.

thinking-methods.l10.q2.t: Because straight lines are easy to judge by eye and fit
thinking-methods.l10.q2.p: Why do scientists often linearise data?
thinking-methods.l10.q2.h: Consider how easy it is to spot a bend in a line.
thinking-methods.l10.q2.e: Straight lines make deviations obvious and let you read quantities from the slope.

thinking-methods.l10.q3.p: A graph of T squared against L has slope 4.0 s^2/m. Using g = 4 pi^2 / slope with pi^2 about 9.87, what is g?

thinking-methods.l10.q4.t: Consider that the model or method may fail there, for example a large swing angle, and investigate
thinking-methods.l10.q4.p: Your T squared against L points curve away from a straight line at large lengths. What is the most sensible response?
thinking-methods.l10.q4.h: A bend is information about the model.
thinking-methods.l10.q4.e: Systematic departure from a line suggests the model has limits or the method has a problem, which is worth investigating.

thinking-methods.l11.q1.t: The answer to the question, stated plainly
thinking-methods.l11.q1.p: In claim, evidence, reasoning, what is the claim?
thinking-methods.l11.q1.e: The claim is the answer to the question; the evidence and reasoning back it up.

thinking-methods.l11.q2.t: Explains why the evidence supports the claim using a scientific idea
thinking-methods.l11.q2.p: What does the reasoning part of a CER argument do?
thinking-methods.l11.q2.h: It connects the evidence to the claim.
thinking-methods.l11.q2.e: Reasoning links evidence to claim by invoking a principle or mechanism.

thinking-methods.l11.q3.p: Water in a foam cup cooled from 80 C to 62 C in 20 minutes; in a metal cup it cooled from 80 C to 48 C. How much more did the metal-cup water cool?
thinking-methods.l11.q3.e: The foam cup dropped 18 C and the metal cup 32 C, so the metal water cooled 14 C more.

thinking-methods.l11.q4.t: Temperatures recorded each 5 minutes in three repeated trials
thinking-methods.l11.q4.p: Which is the strongest piece of evidence for the claim "The foam cup keeps water warm longer"?
thinking-methods.l11.q4.e: Repeated, quantitative measurements are specific evidence that bears directly on the claim.

thinking-methods.l12.q1.t: The limits you must work within, such as cost or time
thinking-methods.l12.q1.p: In engineering design, what are constraints?
thinking-methods.l12.q1.h: Think of the limits, not the goals.
thinking-methods.l12.q1.e: Constraints are limits on the design; criteria describe what success looks like.

thinking-methods.l12.q2.t: A first working model used for testing
thinking-methods.l12.q2.h: It is built to be tested and improved.
thinking-methods.l12.q2.e: A prototype is an early working model that is tested and revised.

thinking-methods.l12.q3.p: A craft-stick bridge must hold at least 5 kg and use no more than 100 sticks. Which is a criterion rather than a constraint?
thinking-methods.l12.q3.h: Which one describes what counts as success?
thinking-methods.l12.q3.e: Holding at least 5 kg is what success looks like; the others are limits on resources.

thinking-methods.l12.q4.t: Defining the problem and researching users
thinking-methods.l12.q4.p: Testing a prototype shows it works but nobody wants to use it because of a need the team never asked about. What step was skipped or rushed?
thinking-methods.l12.q4.h: The mismatch is about the need, not the build.
thinking-methods.l12.q4.e: A design can pass tests and still fail if the problem and users were not properly understood at the start.

thinking-methods.l13.q1.t: Improving one goal at the cost of another
thinking-methods.l13.q1.p: What is a trade-off in design?
thinking-methods.l13.q1.h: Gains in one area usually cost something in another.
thinking-methods.l13.q1.e: A trade-off means gaining on one criterion usually costs something on another, such as strength versus weight.

thinking-methods.l13.q2.p: A prototype that fails a test is a wasted effort.
thinking-methods.l13.q2.h: Think about what the failure reveals.
thinking-methods.l13.q2.e: A failed test shows where the design is weak, so it provides useful information for improving it.

thinking-methods.l13.q3.p: Cost has weight 3 and strength weight 2. Option A scores cost 4, strength 3. Option B scores cost 2, strength 5. Which has the higher weighted total?
thinking-methods.l13.q3.h: Multiply each score by its weight and add.
thinking-methods.l13.q3.e: A: 3 x 4 + 2 x 3 = 18. B: 3 x 2 + 2 x 5 = 16. A is higher.

thinking-methods.l13.q4.t: Because early failures are cheap to find and fix compared with later ones
thinking-methods.l13.q4.p: Why do engineers build cheap, rough early prototypes?
thinking-methods.l13.q4.h: Think about the cost of discovering problems late.
thinking-methods.l13.q4.e: Problems found early cost far less to fix than problems found after manufacturing.

thinking-methods.l14.q1.t: A simplified representation used to explain or predict
thinking-methods.l14.q1.p: What is a model in science and engineering?
thinking-methods.l14.q1.h: It leaves out details on purpose.
thinking-methods.l14.q1.e: Models simplify reality for a purpose, and may be equations, graphs, physical scales or programs.

thinking-methods.l14.q2.t: Comparing its predictions with real measurements
thinking-methods.l14.q2.p: What does validating a model mean?
thinking-methods.l14.q2.h: Consider checking it against the real world.
thinking-methods.l14.q2.e: Validation tests the model by comparing what it predicts with what is actually measured.

thinking-methods.l14.q3.p: A spring model says extension = 2 cm per newton. What extension does it predict for 5 N?
thinking-methods.l14.q3.h: Multiply the rate by the force.
thinking-methods.l14.q3.e: 2 cm per newton x 5 N = 10 cm, valid while the spring behaves linearly.

thinking-methods.l14.q4.t: The prediction goes beyond the range where the model was tested
thinking-methods.l14.q4.p: Your spring model works up to 5 N but is then used for a 50 N load. What is the main concern?
thinking-methods.l14.q4.h: Think about where the model has actually been checked.
thinking-methods.l14.q4.e: Models are only trusted within tested ranges; real springs can stop behaving linearly or break at large loads.

thinking-methods.l15.q1.t: The ratio of failure load to expected working load
thinking-methods.l15.q1.p: What is a factor of safety?
thinking-methods.l15.q1.h: It compares what breaks it with what it normally carries.
thinking-methods.l15.q1.e: Factor of safety is failure load divided by working load.

thinking-methods.l15.q2.t: It helps designers understand the needs of the people who will use the product
thinking-methods.l15.q2.p: What does empathy contribute to design thinking?
thinking-methods.l15.q2.e: Empathy means observing and listening to users so that the design meets their real needs.

thinking-methods.l15.q3.p: A cable fails at 6000 N and is expected to carry 1500 N. What is its factor of safety?
thinking-methods.l15.q3.h: Divide failure load by working load.

thinking-methods.l15.q4.t: Who benefits, who bears the risk, and did users understand it?
thinking-methods.l15.q4.p: A phone app is legal but quietly shares users' location with third parties. Which question best captures the ethical issue?
thinking-methods.l15.q4.h: Ethics asks about people affected, not just rules.
thinking-methods.l15.q4.e: Ethical analysis considers who gains, who is exposed to risk and whether people were informed, beyond legality.

thinking-methods.l16.q1.t: Real science uses varied methods, with shared habits of checking claims against evidence
thinking-methods.l16.q1.p: Which statement about the scientific method is most accurate?
thinking-methods.l16.q1.h: Astronomers cannot run experiments on stars.
thinking-methods.l16.q1.e: Fields differ in method, but all check claims against evidence and stay open to revision.

thinking-methods.l16.q2.p: Which thinker argued that a claim is scientific if evidence could show it false?
thinking-methods.l16.q2.e: Karl Popper proposed falsifiability as a mark of scientific claims.

thinking-methods.l16.q3.t: Ibn al-Haytham: Book of Optics, which stressed testing ideas about light by experiment
thinking-methods.l16.q3.h: Match each person to their approximate time and work.
thinking-methods.l16.q3.e: Ibn al-Haytham wrote the Book of Optics around the early eleventh century; Bacon wrote Novum Organum in 1620.

thinking-methods.l16.q4.t: Gather observations, make predictions from models, and test them against new observations
thinking-methods.l16.q4.p: Astronomers study stars they cannot manipulate. Which approach fits science best here?
thinking-methods.l16.q4.h: Science can test claims without controlling the object.
thinking-methods.l16.q4.e: Observational sciences test models by checking predictions against new observations, without controlling the system.

thinking-methods.l17.q1.p: All metals conduct electricity, and copper is a metal, so copper conducts electricity. What kind of reasoning is this?
thinking-methods.l17.q1.h: It moves from a general rule to a specific case.
thinking-methods.l17.q1.e: Deduction applies a general statement to a specific case; with true premises and valid logic the conclusion must hold.

thinking-methods.l17.q2.p: Inferring that all swans are white from seeing only white swans is which kind of reasoning?
thinking-methods.l17.q2.e: Induction generalises from specific cases; its conclusion is probable, not certain.

thinking-methods.l17.q3.t: Abduction; test it, for example by checking for a sprinkler or other signs of rain
thinking-methods.l17.q3.p: You find the lawn wet and conclude it probably rained. Which reasoning is this, and what should follow?
thinking-methods.l17.q3.h: It picks the best explanation of an observation.
thinking-methods.l17.q3.e: Abduction proposes the best explanation, which then needs testing because other explanations remain possible.

thinking-methods.l17.q4.t: What evidence supports that, and what would count against it?
thinking-methods.l17.q4.p: A friend states a claim with confidence. Which Socratic question best tests it?
thinking-methods.l17.q4.h: Look for questions that probe evidence and assumptions respectfully.
thinking-methods.l17.q4.e: It asks for evidence and for conditions under which the claim would fail, which exposes assumptions without attacking the person.

thinking-methods.l18.q1.t: Either we buy this bike or we never cycle again.
thinking-methods.l18.q1.p: Which is an example of a false dilemma?
thinking-methods.l18.q1.h: It offers only two options when more exist.
thinking-methods.l18.q1.e: A false dilemma presents two choices as if they were the only ones.

thinking-methods.l18.q2.t: Breaking a problem into smaller parts
thinking-methods.l18.q2.p: What does decomposition mean in computational thinking?
thinking-methods.l18.q2.h: Think of splitting something big into pieces.
thinking-methods.l18.q2.e: Decomposition splits a large problem into smaller, easier parts.

thinking-methods.l18.q3.p: You must find a number from 1 to 100 by guessing, and each answer tells you "higher" or "lower". By always guessing the middle, what is the most guesses you need?
thinking-methods.l18.q3.h: Each guess halves the remaining range.
thinking-methods.l18.q3.e: Each guess halves the options, and 2^7 = 128 is at least 100 while 2^6 = 64 is not, so at most 7 guesses.

thinking-methods.l18.q4.t: Negative feedback that pushes the system back toward a set point
thinking-methods.l18.q4.p: A thermostat switches heating off when the room is too warm. What does this illustrate?
thinking-methods.l18.q4.e: The response counteracts the change and stabilises the temperature, which is negative feedback.

world-mythology.l01.q1.t: A traditional story that carries meaning for a community
world-mythology.l01.q1.p: When scholars of religion call a story a myth, what are they mainly describing?
world-mythology.l01.q1.h: Think about the scholarly meaning, not the everyday one.
world-mythology.l01.q1.e: In scholarship, myth names a kind of traditional, meaning-bearing story and does not judge whether it is true.

world-mythology.l01.q2.p: Calling a story a myth, in the scholarly sense, automatically means the story is false.
world-mythology.l01.q2.h: Consider what job the word does.
world-mythology.l01.q2.e: The scholarly term describes the role of a story in a community and makes no claim about its truth.

world-mythology.l01.q3.t: They were retold aloud by different people and communities
world-mythology.l01.q3.p: Why do myths usually exist in many versions?
world-mythology.l01.q3.h: Think about how stories travel before printing.
world-mythology.l01.q3.e: Oral retelling by different villages, priests and poets produces variants, which are part of the evidence.

world-mythology.l01.q4.t: Many troubles escape into the human world
world-mythology.l01.q4.p: In Hesiod's Works and Days, what happens when the jar in the Pandora story is opened?
world-mythology.l01.q4.h: The jar is a container of misfortunes.
world-mythology.l01.q4.e: In Hesiod's poem, troubles escape from the jar and spread among humans.

world-mythology.l01.q5.p: The lesson recommends describing myths with attribution, such as "according to the Poetic Edda," instead of stating them as plain fact.
world-mythology.l01.q5.h: Consider how to be accurate and respectful together.
world-mythology.l01.q5.e: Attribution names the source and respects the tradition without asserting or mocking the story.

world-mythology.l02.q1.p: Which approach sets myths from different cultures side by side?
world-mythology.l02.q1.e: The comparative approach looks for resemblances and patterns across cultures.

world-mythology.l02.q2.t: A charter that justifies customs and social arrangements
world-mythology.l02.q2.p: Malinowski argued that myths often act as what for a society?
world-mythology.l02.q2.h: Think of a document that gives a group its authority.
world-mythology.l02.q2.e: In Malinowski's functional view, myths support customs, rituals and social arrangements.

world-mythology.l02.q3.p: Which scholar is associated with the structural approach and pairs of opposites?
world-mythology.l02.q3.h: He looked for underlying patterns such as nature and culture.
world-mythology.l02.q3.e: Levi-Strauss analyzed myths as patterns of oppositions, such as raw and cooked, and how they are mediated.

world-mythology.l02.q4.p: Euhemerus argued that gods were originally deified humans.
world-mythology.l02.q4.h: The word euhemerism comes from his name.
world-mythology.l02.q4.e: Euhemerus proposed that the gods began as human rulers or heroes who were later worshiped.

world-mythology.l02.q5.t: Comparison may flatten real differences or suggest links that are coincidence
world-mythology.l02.q5.p: Which is a fair criticism of comparative studies?
world-mythology.l02.q5.h: Think about what could go wrong when you line things up.
world-mythology.l02.q5.e: Similar-looking motifs may arise independently, and differences between cultures can be lost.

world-mythology.l03.q1.t: The writer's time, purpose and beliefs may have shaped the version we have
world-mythology.l03.q1.p: Why does it matter who wrote a myth down?
world-mythology.l03.q1.h: Consider what a recorder might add or leave out.
world-mythology.l03.q1.e: Written texts are snapshots shaped by their authors, so recorders must be considered as evidence.

world-mythology.l03.q2.p: The Norse myths we know come mostly from Icelandic writers of about the thirteenth century.
world-mythology.l03.q2.e: The Poetic Edda manuscript and Snorri's Prose Edda both date to the thirteenth century.

world-mythology.l03.q3.p: Who wrote the Prose Edda, around 1220?
world-mythology.l03.q3.h: He was an Icelandic chieftain and scholar.
world-mythology.l03.q3.e: Snorri Sturluson wrote the Prose Edda as a handbook for poets.

world-mythology.l03.q4.t: According to Snorri, Thor traveled to the land of giants
world-mythology.l03.q4.p: Which phrase best shows careful source-aware writing?
world-mythology.l03.q4.h: Pick the wording that names a source.
world-mythology.l03.q4.e: Naming the source avoids claiming more than the evidence shows.

world-mythology.l03.q5.p: Where no early text survives for a tradition, claims about its myths should be treated as reconstruction.
world-mythology.l03.q5.e: Without early written evidence, accounts rely on later or indirect sources and are reconstructions.

world-mythology.l04.q1.p: Which tradition listed in the lesson is described as continuing today?
world-mythology.l04.q1.h: Look for a religion with present-day followers.
world-mythology.l04.q1.e: Shinto is among the living traditions named; Egyptian state religion is the extinct example.

world-mythology.l04.q2.p: All stories from Indigenous nations are meant to be freely shared with anyone.
world-mythology.l04.q2.h: Remember the example of initiated people.
world-mythology.l04.q2.e: Some stories are restricted or belong to particular families or nations.

world-mythology.l04.q3.t: Name the nation and prefer sources the community has shared
world-mythology.l04.q3.p: What is a respectful way to write about a story from a specific nation?
world-mythology.l04.q3.e: Accuracy and respect both require naming the nation and using material the community has chosen to share.

world-mythology.l04.q4.t: It dismisses what is sacred to believers and misuses the scholarly term
world-mythology.l04.q4.p: Why is it a problem to call a living tradition's sacred story a myth in the sense of falsehood?
world-mythology.l04.q4.e: The scholarly meaning of myth does not mean falsehood, and using the everyday sense disrespects believers.

world-mythology.l04.q5.p: Insider and outsider descriptions of the same story can both count as evidence.
world-mythology.l04.q5.e: Insiders and outsiders notice different things, and a careful student weighs both.

world-mythology.l05.q1.p: What does the name Enuma Elish come from?
world-mythology.l05.q1.h: Many ancient works were named this way.
world-mythology.l05.q1.e: The title comes from the first words, usually translated "When on high."

world-mythology.l05.q2.p: In the Enuma Elish, who defeats Tiamat?
world-mythology.l05.q2.h: He becomes supreme among the gods.
world-mythology.l05.q2.e: Marduk defeats Tiamat and forms heaven and earth from her body.

world-mythology.l05.q3.p: In the poem, humans are made from the blood of the defeated god Kingu.
world-mythology.l05.q3.h: Humans exist to do the gods' work.
world-mythology.l05.q3.e: The poem says humans were formed from Kingu's blood to serve the gods.

world-mythology.l05.q4.t: Marduk, its hero, was Babylon's patron god, so the poem raises him to the top
world-mythology.l05.q4.p: Why do many scholars link the epic with the city of Babylon?
world-mythology.l05.q4.e: Marduk was Babylon's patron, so many read the epic as exalting him and his city.

world-mythology.l05.q5.t: It is one voice among several Mesopotamian creation ideas
world-mythology.l05.q5.p: Which statement about Enuma Elish is most accurate?
world-mythology.l05.q5.h: The lesson says other texts differ.
world-mythology.l05.q5.e: Other Mesopotamian texts present different ideas, so the poem is not the whole tradition.

world-mythology.l06.q1.p: Who is Gilgamesh in the epic?
world-mythology.l06.q1.e: Gilgamesh is the king of Uruk, probably based on a real early ruler.

world-mythology.l06.q2.p: Enkidu and Gilgamesh begin as enemies and become friends.
world-mythology.l06.q2.e: They fight, then form a close friendship.

world-mythology.l06.q3.t: Utnapishtim tells him about a great flood and eternal life
world-mythology.l06.q3.p: What do Gilgamesh and Utnapishtim have in common in the story?
world-mythology.l06.q3.e: Utnapishtim survived a flood and was granted eternal life, and he tells Gilgamesh his story.

world-mythology.l06.q4.t: A snake takes it while he bathes
world-mythology.l06.q4.p: How does Gilgamesh lose the plant that renews youth?
world-mythology.l06.q4.h: A creature of the water's edge appears.
world-mythology.l06.q4.e: In the epic, a snake eats the plant while Gilgamesh is bathing.

world-mythology.l06.q5.t: The tablets are damaged, so some lines are reconstructed
world-mythology.l06.q5.p: Why might translations of the epic differ?
world-mythology.l06.q5.h: Consider the condition of clay tablets.
world-mythology.l06.q5.e: Gaps in the damaged tablets mean modern editions restore some lines in different ways.

world-mythology.l07.q1.p: In the Osiris myth, who kills Osiris?
world-mythology.l07.q1.h: Set is the god of disorder.
world-mythology.l07.q1.e: Set kills Osiris out of jealousy.

world-mythology.l07.q2.p: The most continuous ancient telling of the Osiris story is by a Greek writer, Plutarch, writing around 100 CE.
world-mythology.l07.q2.h: Remember it was an outsider's account.
world-mythology.l07.q2.e: Plutarch's On Isis and Osiris is the fullest continuous version, though it is much later than Egyptian sources.

world-mythology.l07.q3.t: Religious writings carved inside royal pyramids around 2400 BCE
world-mythology.l07.q3.h: They appear at the end of the Old Kingdom.
world-mythology.l07.q3.e: They are the earliest large collection of Egyptian religious writing, carved in pyramids.

world-mythology.l07.q4.t: The living king was identified with Horus and the dead king with Osiris
world-mythology.l07.q4.p: How did the myth support Egyptian kingship?
world-mythology.l07.q4.h: Think about the father and son.
world-mythology.l07.q4.e: The king was linked with Horus in life and with Osiris after death.

world-mythology.l07.q5.p: Egyptian sources agree on every detail of the Osiris story.
world-mythology.l07.q5.e: Details vary from source to source.

world-mythology.l08.q1.p: In the tradition of Heliopolis, what existed before creation?
world-mythology.l08.q1.e: Creation began with Nun, from which a mound and the god Atum arose.

world-mythology.l08.q2.p: According to the Memphis tradition on the Shabaka Stone, how did Ptah create?
world-mythology.l08.q2.e: Ptah conceived in the heart and created by speaking.

world-mythology.l08.q3.p: Egyptians told several different creation accounts from different religious centers.
world-mythology.l08.q3.e: Different temples preserved different, coexisting accounts.

world-mythology.l08.q4.t: Through the underworld, called the Duat
world-mythology.l08.q4.p: Where does the sun god Ra travel at night in the standard picture?
world-mythology.l08.q4.h: He faces dangers like the serpent Apep.
world-mythology.l08.q4.e: Ra passes through the Duat and is reborn at dawn.

world-mythology.l08.q5.t: Renewal from the waters of chaos
world-mythology.l08.q5.p: What common thread links the Egyptian creation accounts?
world-mythology.l08.q5.h: Think about Nun and the dawn.
world-mythology.l08.q5.e: Order emerges from primeval waters, and the sun's daily rebirth expresses the same renewal.

world-mythology.l09.q1.p: What does the title Theogony mean?
world-mythology.l09.q1.e: Theogony means the birth or genealogy of the gods.

world-mythology.l09.q2.h: A Titan, urged on by his mother.
world-mythology.l09.q2.e: Cronus overthrows Ouranos at his mother Gaia's urging.

world-mythology.l09.q3.p: In the poem, Rhea saves Zeus from being swallowed by Cronus.
world-mythology.l09.q3.e: Rhea hides the infant Zeus, and he later frees his siblings.

world-mythology.l09.q4.p: Roughly when do the earliest major written Greek sources, such as Hesiod and Homer, date?
world-mythology.l09.q4.e: The Theogony and Homeric epics are dated to about 700 BCE or the eighth century BCE.

world-mythology.l09.q5.t: Local cults and later authors told different versions of the same stories
world-mythology.l09.q5.p: Why is it misleading to speak of one fixed Greek canon?
world-mythology.l09.q5.e: Different regions and writers varied details, so Greek myth is a patchwork over many centuries.

world-mythology.l10.q1.p: Which poem tells of Odysseus's difficult journey home?
world-mythology.l10.q1.h: Odysseus's name is in the title.
world-mythology.l10.q1.e: The Odyssey follows Odysseus's return to Ithaca.

world-mythology.l10.q2.p: The Iliad focuses on the anger of Achilles during the Trojan War.
world-mythology.l10.q2.h: It covers a few weeks, not the whole war.
world-mythology.l10.q2.e: The Iliad centers on Achilles' anger.

world-mythology.l10.q3.t: They reshaped familiar stories to explore justice, fate and choice
world-mythology.l10.q3.p: What did the Athenian tragedians such as Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides do with myths?
world-mythology.l10.q3.e: Tragedians changed emphasis to raise questions that mattered to their audience.

world-mythology.l10.q4.t: Different authors tell the same myth differently
world-mythology.l10.q4.p: What does the example of Medea in Euripides and Ovid show?
world-mythology.l10.q4.e: Writers varied, so one should name the author when discussing a myth.

world-mythology.l10.q5.p: The identity of Homer and the way the epics took shape are still debated.
world-mythology.l10.q5.h: Scholars call this the Homeric question.
world-mythology.l10.q5.e: The date and process of composition and Homer's identity remain debated.

world-mythology.l11.q1.p: Which Greek god did Romans match with Jupiter?

world-mythology.l11.q2.p: The story that Rome was founded in 753 BCE by Romulus is a traditional founding legend, not a documented event.
world-mythology.l11.q2.e: The date and the story are traditional, not independently documented.

world-mythology.l11.q3.t: Virgil's epic about Aeneas, a Trojan refugee who settles in Italy
world-mythology.l11.q3.e: Virgil's Aeneid follows Aeneas from Troy to Italy.

world-mythology.l11.q4.t: Stories of transformation from Greek and Roman tradition
world-mythology.l11.q4.p: Ovid's Metamorphoses is mainly about what?
world-mythology.l11.q4.e: The Metamorphoses retells stories in which characters change form.

world-mythology.l11.q5.t: Poets under Augustus shaped it with artistic and political aims
world-mythology.l11.q5.p: Why do many scholars call Roman myth literary and political?
world-mythology.l11.q5.e: Roman myth reached us mainly through poets whose work served artistic and political purposes.

world-mythology.l12.q1.t: A manuscript of about the 1270s preserving the Poetic Edda
world-mythology.l12.q1.e: It is the main manuscript of the Poetic Edda poems.

world-mythology.l12.q2.t: As a handbook for poets who needed the old myths used in verse
world-mythology.l12.q2.p: Why was the Prose Edda written, according to the lesson?
world-mythology.l12.q2.e: Snorri wrote it so poets could understand the mythic references in traditional verse.

world-mythology.l12.q3.p: Iceland accepted Christianity around the year 1000.
world-mythology.l12.q3.h: This is a key date for the Norse sources.
world-mythology.l12.q3.e: The conversion happened around 1000, two centuries before these texts were written.

world-mythology.l12.q4.t: Christians wrote them down about two centuries after conversion and may have shaped them
world-mythology.l12.q4.p: What is the main caution about the Norse sources?
world-mythology.l12.q4.h: Look at who wrote and when.
world-mythology.l12.q4.e: The writers were Christians working long after the old religion ended.

world-mythology.l12.q5.p: Which poem in the Poetic Edda has a seeress describing creation and the end of the world?
world-mythology.l12.q5.h: Its name means the seeress's prophecy.
world-mythology.l12.q5.e: Voluspa presents a seeress describing the gods' origin, destruction and rebirth.

world-mythology.l13.q1.p: Where do the main sources for Celtic mythology come from?
world-mythology.l13.q1.h: Antiquity left almost nothing in Celtic writing.
world-mythology.l13.q1.e: Most sources are medieval texts from Ireland and Wales.

world-mythology.l13.q2.p: Ancient Celtic peoples left extensive written myths in their own languages.
world-mythology.l13.q2.h: The lesson says they left almost none.
world-mythology.l13.q2.e: We rely on outsiders' descriptions and later medieval manuscripts.

world-mythology.l13.q3.p: Which figure is central to the Ulster Cycle?
world-mythology.l13.q3.h: Think of the Cattle Raid of Cooley.
world-mythology.l13.q3.e: Cu Chulainn is the hero of the Ulster Cycle and the Tain Bo Cuailnge.

world-mythology.l13.q4.t: The core tales of the Welsh Mabinogion
world-mythology.l13.q4.p: What are the Four Branches of the Mabinogi?
world-mythology.l13.q4.h: They feature Pwyll, Rhiannon and Bran.
world-mythology.l13.q4.e: They are the central group of medieval Welsh tales.

world-mythology.l13.q5.t: In medieval Irish tradition, the Tuatha De Danann were a supernatural people
world-mythology.l13.q5.h: Match the claim to the source.
world-mythology.l13.q5.e: Attributing to medieval Irish tradition stays within the evidence.

world-mythology.l14.q1.t: Prince Vladimir set up an idol of him in Kiev
world-mythology.l14.q1.p: What does the Primary Chronicle report about Perun?
world-mythology.l14.q1.h: A pagan idol and a ruler.
world-mythology.l14.q1.e: The chronicle says Vladimir set up idols including Perun's.

world-mythology.l14.q2.p: Tales of Baba Yaga were collected mainly in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.
world-mythology.l14.q2.e: Such folklore was gathered much later than pre-Christian times, so it may not preserve ancient belief.

world-mythology.l14.q3.t: Few early written records survive, and chroniclers were Christians
world-mythology.l14.q3.p: Why is Slavic mythology hard to reconstruct?
world-mythology.l14.q3.h: The lesson lists kinds of evidence.
world-mythology.l14.q3.e: The evidence is late, indirect or written by Christians with their own aims.

world-mythology.l14.q4.t: Ask what evidence supports each name
world-mythology.l14.q4.p: A chart shows a complete Slavic pantheon. What is the best response?
world-mythology.l14.q4.e: Many names rest on reconstruction, so the evidence for each should be checked.

world-mythology.l14.q5.p: The conversion of Rus' is traditionally dated to 988.
world-mythology.l14.q5.h: This is a traditional date tied to Vladimir.
world-mythology.l14.q5.e: 988 is the traditional date for the conversion of Rus'.

world-mythology.l15.q1.t: A collection of early Sanskrit hymns
world-mythology.l15.q1.h: It is the oldest layer of Hindu texts.
world-mythology.l15.q1.e: The Rig Veda is a collection of over a thousand hymns, composed orally in early Sanskrit.

world-mythology.l15.q2.p: The Bhagavad Gita is a dialogue between which two figures?
world-mythology.l15.q2.h: It is part of the Mahabharata.
world-mythology.l15.q2.e: The Gita is the conversation between the warrior Arjuna and Krishna.

world-mythology.l15.q3.p: The Ramayana tells of Rama's loss of Sita to the demon-king Ravana and of Rama's eventual victory.
world-mythology.l15.q3.e: Sita is abducted by Ravana, whom Rama defeats.

world-mythology.l15.q4.t: It questions who truly knows how creation began
world-mythology.l15.q4.p: What does the Nasadiya hymn do?
world-mythology.l15.q4.e: The hymn asks who really knows about creation and suggests that even the highest overseer may not.

world-mythology.l15.q5.t: Many retellings differ and none is the single authoritative telling
world-mythology.l15.q5.p: Why does the lesson say "a version of the Ramayana"?
world-mythology.l15.q5.h: Think about retellings in many languages.
world-mythology.l15.q5.e: Different versions change plots and meanings, so no single telling can stand for all.

world-mythology.l16.q1.t: Stories of the Buddha's previous lives
world-mythology.l16.q1.e: They recount previous lives of the Buddha-to-be as a bodhisattva.

world-mythology.l16.q2.p: In the Jatakas, the bodhisattva can be born as an animal.
world-mythology.l16.q2.e: He appears as animals such as a hare, a monkey or a deer, as well as humans.

world-mythology.l16.q3.p: Roughly how many tales does the Pali collection traditionally count?
world-mythology.l16.q3.h: The number is in the hundreds.
world-mythology.l16.q3.e: The traditional count is about 547, though it varies by source.

world-mythology.l16.q4.t: The king of the gods honors the hare by marking its likeness on the moon
world-mythology.l16.q4.p: What happens at the end of the hare's story?
world-mythology.l16.q4.e: The guest, who is the king of the gods, honors the hare on the moon.

world-mythology.l16.q5.t: To teach virtues cultivated across lifetimes and the working of karma
world-mythology.l16.q5.p: What is the usual purpose of a Jataka?
world-mythology.l16.q5.e: The tales show generosity, patience and compassion built across many lives.

world-mythology.l17.q1.p: According to the usual story, what does Pangu do?
world-mythology.l17.q1.e: Pangu separates heaven from earth, and his body becomes features of the world.

world-mythology.l17.q2.p: When is the Pangu story first recorded, roughly?
world-mythology.l17.q2.h: It is later than many people expect.
world-mythology.l17.q2.e: Earlier Chinese texts do not contain him, so the story is relatively late.

world-mythology.l17.q3.p: Journey to the West was published in the sixteenth century and draws on the real pilgrimage of the monk Xuanzang.
world-mythology.l17.q3.e: The Ming-dynasty novel was inspired by Xuanzang's seventh-century journey for Buddhist texts.

world-mythology.l17.q4.t: The Monkey King in Journey to the West
world-mythology.l17.q4.e: Sun Wukong is the mischievous Monkey King who accompanies Xuanzang in the novel.

world-mythology.l17.q5.t: By dredging channels to guide the waters
world-mythology.l17.q5.p: How did Yu the Great deal with the flood, in the stories?
world-mythology.l17.q5.h: He is remembered for engineering, not escape.
world-mythology.l17.q5.e: Yu tamed floods by channeling rather than simply blocking the water.

world-mythology.l18.q1.p: In what year was the Kojiki completed?
world-mythology.l18.q1.e: The Kojiki was completed in 712 CE and the Nihon Shoki in 720 CE.

world-mythology.l18.q2.p: Who hides in a cave so that the world goes dark?
world-mythology.l18.q2.e: Amaterasu hides in a cave after Susanoo's destructive behavior.

world-mythology.l18.q3.p: The Nihon Shoki is written in Classical Chinese and often gives alternative variants of a story.
world-mythology.l18.q3.h: It was compiled at the court.
world-mythology.l18.q3.e: The Nihon Shoki uses Classical Chinese and records variant versions.

world-mythology.l18.q4.t: Partly to show the legitimacy of the imperial line
world-mythology.l18.q4.p: Why did the court compile these books?
world-mythology.l18.q4.h: Think about the sun goddess's descendants.
world-mythology.l18.q4.e: The myths link the ruling family to the sun goddess.

world-mythology.l18.q5.t: Twentieth-century governments used them to support nationalist ideology
world-mythology.l18.q5.p: Why is interpreting these myths politically sensitive?
world-mythology.l18.q5.h: Think about the modern history of use.
world-mythology.l18.q5.e: State ideology in the twentieth century used these myths, so interpretation requires care.

world-mythology.l19.q1.p: Which work records the Dangun story?
world-mythology.l19.q1.e: The Samguk Yusa, a thirteenth-century collection, records the Dangun story.

world-mythology.l19.q2.t: It becomes a woman and bears Dangun
world-mythology.l19.q2.p: In the Dangun story, what happens to the bear?
world-mythology.l19.q2.e: The bear endures in the cave, becomes human, and gives birth to Dangun.

world-mythology.l19.q3.p: The traditional date of 2333 BCE for Gojoseon's founding is established by archaeology.
world-mythology.l19.q3.e: The date is traditional and not independently established.

world-mythology.l19.q4.p: Who wrote the Samguk Sagi, completed in 1145?
world-mythology.l19.q4.e: Kim Busik compiled the history of the Three Kingdoms.

world-mythology.l19.q5.t: A national origin story is central today but is recorded in a medieval source
world-mythology.l19.q5.p: Why does the Dangun tale illustrate source awareness?
world-mythology.l19.q5.h: Think about the date of the record.
world-mythology.l19.q5.e: It shows how culturally central stories may be known through particular later records.

world-mythology.l20.q1.t: The sky father and the earth mother
world-mythology.l20.q1.p: In Maori tradition, who are Ranginui and Papatuanuku?
world-mythology.l20.q1.e: They are the sky father and earth mother whose children separate them.

world-mythology.l20.q2.p: Which child pushes his parents apart to let in light?
world-mythology.l20.q2.h: The god of forests and birds.
world-mythology.l20.q2.e: Tane, god of forests, pushes sky and earth apart.

world-mythology.l20.q3.p: Maui is known in many Polynesian traditions for slowing the sun or fishing up islands.
world-mythology.l20.q3.h: He is a hero with a hook.
world-mythology.l20.q3.e: These feats are widely told, with island-specific details.

world-mythology.l20.q4.t: They often reflect the choices of outsiders who compiled them
world-mythology.l20.q4.p: Why should we be careful with printed nineteenth-century collections of Maori tradition?
world-mythology.l20.q4.h: Think about who held the pen.
world-mythology.l20.q4.e: Collections by missionaries and officials may reflect their selection and view.

world-mythology.l20.q5.t: Say which iwi it belongs to
world-mythology.l20.q5.p: What is a respectful way to present a version of a Maori story?
world-mythology.l20.q5.e: Versions differ by iwi and family, so attribution is important.

world-mythology.l21.q1.t: They include many distinct nations, each with its own stories
world-mythology.l21.q1.p: Which statement about Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples is accurate?
world-mythology.l21.q1.e: There are many nations with their own languages, laws and stories.

world-mythology.l21.q2.p: The English word Dreaming refers only to old stories and not to law and responsibility.
world-mythology.l21.q2.h: The lesson says it includes ongoing laws.
world-mythology.l21.q2.e: It includes creative-era events and the continuing laws and relationships arising from them.

world-mythology.l21.q3.t: Remembered journeys of ancestral beings, held in song, painting and dance
world-mythology.l21.q3.p: What are songlines, in the lesson's account?
world-mythology.l21.q3.e: Ancestral journeys are remembered in song and serve as maps, law and knowledge.

world-mythology.l21.q4.t: Not seek or retell it, and rely on what communities have chosen to share
world-mythology.l21.q4.p: What should outsiders do with restricted knowledge?
world-mythology.l21.q4.e: Restricted knowledge belongs to initiated people and is not for outsiders to retell.

world-mythology.l21.q5.p: Treating the Rainbow Serpent as one single myth erases differences between regions.
world-mythology.l21.q5.e: Stories that share a figure differ across regions and nations.

world-mythology.l22.q1.p: Which people tell of the orisha and of Ife as a place of creation?
world-mythology.l22.q1.e: The Yoruba tradition speaks of the orisha, with Ife as a place of beginnings.

world-mythology.l22.q2.t: A Yoruba tradition of divination using a large body of oral verses
world-mythology.l22.q2.h: It is a system, not a person.
world-mythology.l22.q2.e: Ifa divination relies on a large corpus of oral verses.

world-mythology.l22.q3.p: Yoruba beliefs are part of religions in the Americas, such as Santeria (Lucumi) in Cuba and Candomble in Brazil.
world-mythology.l22.q3.e: Through the transatlantic slave trade Yoruba traditions entered these living religions.

world-mythology.l22.q4.p: In the Akan tale, how does Ananse win the sky god's stories?
world-mythology.l22.q4.e: Ananse completes hard tasks set by the sky god Nyame.

world-mythology.l22.q5.t: Africa has thousands of cultures, so a generic label would be inaccurate
world-mythology.l22.q5.p: Why does the lesson name particular peoples instead of discussing African myth in general?
world-mythology.l22.q5.e: A continent of thousands of cultures cannot be summarized as one tradition.

world-mythology.l23.q1.p: Who published Conversations with Ogotemmeli in 1948?
world-mythology.l23.q1.e: Griaule published conversations held in 1946 with the elder Ogotemmeli.

world-mythology.l23.q2.t: Many Dogon he met did not recognize parts of the system Griaule described
world-mythology.l23.q2.p: What did Walter van Beek report?
world-mythology.l23.q2.h: He worked among the Dogon in the 1980s.
world-mythology.l23.q2.e: Van Beek reported that parts of the described system were unfamiliar to many Dogon.

world-mythology.l23.q3.p: Most scholars accept the claim that the Dogon had secret knowledge of Sirius's companion star.
world-mythology.l23.q3.e: Most scholars reject it, noting possible outside influence or misunderstanding.

world-mythology.l23.q4.t: Test sources by asking how an account was gathered and what later researchers found
world-mythology.l23.q4.p: What is the main lesson of the Dogon case?
world-mythology.l23.q4.e: A famous account can be contested, so one should examine its method and later evidence.

world-mythology.l23.q5.p: The lesson says Griaule's work is important but contested.
world-mythology.l23.q5.e: It remains influential while its reliability is debated.

world-mythology.l24.q1.p: Which people produced the Popol Vuh?
world-mythology.l24.q1.h: They live in the highlands of Guatemala.
world-mythology.l24.q1.e: The Popol Vuh is a K'iche' Maya text.

world-mythology.l24.q2.p: In the Popol Vuh, from what are the successful humans made?
world-mythology.l24.q2.e: After mud and wood failed, humans were made from maize.
